3.label: White sacrifices the c4-bishop on f7 with check on move 3, before any supporting pieces are developed, losing a full piece for one pawn.
3.description: All 10/10 positions feature White playing Bxf7+ on move 3 from a bishop stationed on c4, sacrificing a full minor piece for a single pawn with check. In every case, White has only developed the light-squared bishop (and has e4 played), with no knights, no queen access, and no other pieces positioned to follow up on the king's displacement. 8/10 positions arise from the Italian Game setup (1.e4 e5 2.Bc4 Nc6/d6), while 2/10 come from a Modern Defense setup (1.e4 g6 2.Bc4 Bg7). The refutation is identical in all cases: Black simply captures with Kxf7, pockets the extra piece, and the king retreats or remains safe because White has zero attacking infrastructure. The average cp_loss is 354, consistently representing exactly the value of the sacrificed bishop minus one pawn. This is a classic beginner error inspired by the Fried Liver Attack or Scholar's Mate concepts, applied when the prerequisite conditions (Ng5, Qf3/Qh5 support) are completely absent.

16.label: Repositioning the queen to a 'multi-purpose' square instead of immediately capturing or eliminating a critical enemy piece (usually a knight).
16.description: In 9/9 positions, the player chose a non-forcing queen repositioning move when a concrete, urgent action was required. In 7/9 positions, the best move was specifically capturing an enemy knight (Nxb6, Rxf7, Nxe2, Bxd5, Nxe5, Bxh5) or delivering a forcing knight move (Ne6+). The remaining 2/9 required specific queen placements that directly challenged the opponent (Qd8 to confront an attacking queen, Qh3 to avoid a fork). In all cases, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.1), meaning these were sharp positions demanding precision, yet the player defaulted to a 'positional' queen relocation. The queen moves chosen were universally non-capturing, non-checking repositioning moves to central or active-looking squares (c5, f6, e3, d7, d3, d6, g4, b4) that appear multi-purpose but fatally surrender tempo at the critical moment.

4.label: King moves forward/actively in endgames when retreat to safety was necessary, walking into checks, checkmates, or leaving material undefended.
4.description: All 10 positions feature king moves that advance toward the center, toward the opponent, or toward the board edge, when the correct moves were almost universally king retreats toward the back rank. In 3/10 positions (1, 3, 7), the advancing king walked into immediate checkmate. In 2/10 positions (2, 4), the king stepped onto a square vulnerable to a pawn check that created a deflection/combination winning material. In 2/10 positions (5, 10), the king advanced away from a pawn it was defending, leaving it hanging for the opponent's rook. In 3/10 positions (6, 8, 9), the king moved toward the wrong side of the board, allowing tempo-gaining pawn advances or rook checks that created permanent positional damage. The correct moves were retreats like Kf2/Kg2/Ke2/Kd2 for White or Kg6/Kh7/Kg7/Ke8 for Black in 9/10 cases. The average cp_loss of 3105 reflects the catastrophic nature of these over-aggressive king marches, with 9/10 occurring in endgames where king centralization instincts are strongest but where specific tactical vulnerabilities punish forward movement.

1.label: White plays en passant captures that remove their own strategically dominant advanced pawn, trading positional dominance for a temporary pawn easily recaptured by the opponent.
1.description: All 10/10 positions feature White making an en passant capture (exf6 in 5 cases, dxc6, gxf6, fxg6, and exd6 twice). In every case, the capturing pawn was a powerful advanced pawn (e5 in 7/10, d5/g5/f5 in the others) that served as the backbone of White's spatial advantage—restricting enemy pieces, keeping the center closed, or shielding the king. In 7/10 positions, White's king was still in the center or exposed, meaning the closed structure provided critical protection. After the en passant capture, the opponent recaptures easily (often with a knight gaining development tempo in 6/10 cases, e.g., Nxf6 attacking the queen), opening files or releasing positional pressure that immediately benefits the better-developed/castled side. The average cp_loss of 240 reflects that these captures consistently squander large advantages (from +87 to +465 before the move) while better alternatives—maintaining the advanced pawn and exploiting its constraining power—were available in all cases (avg 2.2 good moves).
1.old_chip: Reflexive en passant surrenders key pawn

9.label: Playing a quiet king repositioning move when the position urgently demands active piece play or an immediate tactical shot.
9.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player choosing a quiet king move (no check, no capture) when the correct approach involved active piece play with a non-king piece. In 10/10 cases, the best available move used a rook, bishop, queen, or pawn rather than the king. In 3/10 positions (Positions 2, 7, 8), the missed move was a forced checkmate or decisive tactical blow (Ra6+ mating in 3, Qxa1+ mating in 3, Rd7+ skewer winning a full rook). In 4/10 positions (1, 5, 6, 9), the best move involved activating or repositioning a piece to contest a critical file or square. In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 10), the king move directly worsened the king's safety by walking into tactical vulnerabilities (checks, mating nets, or loss of blockading duty). The average cp_loss of 3139 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, and the average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these were narrow, critical moments requiring precision rather than general improvement moves.

15.label: Capturing a seemingly vulnerable or misplaced knight with a major piece while ignoring a far more important tactical or strategic need in the position.
15.description: All 10/10 positions involve capturing a knight that appears tempting — described as 'misplaced,' 'trapped,' 'stray,' 'stranded,' or 'on the edge' — while a much stronger move exists. In 8/10 cases a rook does the capturing, and in 2/10 a queen. The knights targeted are consistently peripheral or infiltrated pieces: on squares like b1 (3 positions), e1 (3 positions), h8, f1, f6, b5, a5. In every case the knight appears to be 'free' or a nuisance that should be removed, yet capturing it either relocates the major piece to a passive square (7/10), abandons a critical defensive duty like back-rank coverage (3/10), misses a more valuable capture such as a rook or bishop (4/10), or squanders a forcing attacking sequence (4/10). The analyses consistently use language like 'wrong capture,' 'captured wrong piece,' and 'material greed.' Only 1.2 good moves existed on average, meaning the correct alternative was narrow and required resisting the instinct to grab apparently free material.

11.label: An already-exposed king makes a seemingly natural retreating or consolidating move that walks onto a square with worse tactical vulnerabilities—open files, dangerous diagonals, or away from critical defensive duties.
11.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move in the middlegame where the king is already exposed and lacking pawn shelter. In 9/10 cases the move is a significant blunder (avg cp_loss 3065), while position 8 is the rare correct version. The kings attempt to consolidate or escape pressure, but 8/10 walk onto open files or diagonals that allow immediate tactical exploitation (checks, pins, skewers). In 6/10 positions the king abandons defense of a critical pawn (c7 in positions 2, 9, 10; f7 in position 4; g6 in position 6; g5 in position 1), allowing captures with check or tempo. The average number of good moves available was only 1.1, indicating these are razor-sharp positions requiring extreme precision. In 7/10 cases the refutation begins with a check or capture-with-check exploiting the new king square. The pattern consistently appears when the king is uncastled or has left its castled position and the player makes an intuitive 'escape' move rather than finding the one precise defensive resource (often a counterattacking piece move like Ne4, Qxf4, or Ne3).

0.label: Playing a non-urgent a/b-pawn push (or equivalent flank move) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
0.description: 8/10 moves are literal a-pawn or b-pawn advances (a4, a5, b3, b4), with the remaining two being Qa5 (queen to the a-file rim) and f6 (a different flank pawn push). 10/10 positions had concrete tactical opportunities or urgent threats being ignored: missed winning combinations (Bxf7+ in Position 8, Ncb4+ in Position 6), missed pawn captures (Qxf3 in Position 9), undefended pieces left hanging (knight on c6 in Position 10, g6 pawn in Position 7), or invasion squares left unguarded (d7 in Position 5, d-file pin in Position 2). The 'tempo_loss' motif appears explicitly in 7/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' appears in 10/10. The average cp_loss of 265 reflects that these positions uniformly punish passivity—the opponents had one clear best punishment available in 8/10 cases, indicating the tactical exploitation was straightforward once the tempo was gifted.

8.label: Aggressive flank pawn advances (g or b file) that ignore critical tactical vulnerabilities or more urgent positional needs.
8.description: 10/10 positions feature pawn advances, and 9/10 are specifically wing pawn pushes on the g-file (7 times: g4 or g5) or b-file (3 times: b4 or b5), with only 1 central pawn push (e3). All 10 moves are attacking in intent — trying to chase enemy pieces off strong squares or gain flank space — but every single one ignores a more critical demand in the position. In 4/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 9), the pawn advance leaves a piece undefended or removes a pawn's control of a critical square, directly enabling a tactical refutation. In 3/10 positions (6, 10, and partially 1), a forcing move (check, capture, or piece exchange) was available that was far superior. In 3/10 positions (2, 3, 7), the advance ignores an urgent developmental or defensive need on the opposite side of the board. The average cp_loss of 2955 is extreme, with 3/10 positions involving missed forced mates. The positions span both colors (Black 7, White 3) and feature diverse tactical motifs, but the unifying thread is always the same: a slow, non-forcing pawn push chosen over the position's actual critical requirement.

12.label: Moving the bishop to a passive or edge square when the position demands immediate concrete action (king moves, captures, or tactical shots).
12.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being repositioned to a less active square — typically a back-rank, corner, or rim square — when the position urgently required a different type of move entirely. In 8/10 cases, the bishop destination was on rank 1, 7, or 8 (b8, g8, f8, h8, e7, g7, g7, c1), placing the piece in a passive or trapped location. In 6/10 positions, the correct move was a king move (Kxc4, Kxf4, Ke1, Ke7, Kb3/Kc3) or a pawn capture, not a bishop move at all. In 2/10 cases (Bh8, Bg8), the bishop was directly punished tactically — trapped or forked. In the remaining positions, the tempo loss allowed the opponent to execute their plan (advancing passed pawns, capturing undefended pawns, or consolidating). The average cp_loss of 430 reflects how catastrophic these quiet repositioning moves are when concrete play is required. Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow positions demanding precision rather than general maneuvering.

18.label: King moves in pawn endgames that aggressively pursue opponent's pawns while abandoning defense of critical own pawns or missing tempo-essential alternatives.
18.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring king moves, with 9/10 being pure king-and-pawn endgames. In at least 5/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 6, 9), the king moved toward the opponent's pawns to attack them while leaving its own critical pawn undefended (g3 in pos 1, g-pawn blockade in pos 2, f5 attack in pos 6, d5 in pos 9). In 2/10 positions (4, 7), the king moved when a preparatory pawn push was required first to fix the structure. In 1/10 (position 10), the king took a direct path instead of triangulating. Only 2/10 positions (3, 8) had essentially zero centipawn loss, suggesting the feature sometimes fires on forced king moves in losing positions. The average cp_loss among genuine mistakes is very high (~1300cp), reflecting how catastrophic tempo errors are in pawn endgames where single tempi decide promotion races.

17.label: King moves to an apparently safer square that actually walks into a checkmate or devastating tactical sequence, often when a sacrifice or different king square was required.
17.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet king relocation (never a capture) where the player instinctively tries to escape pressure but moves to a square with worse tactical vulnerabilities. In 7/10 positions, the move results in checkmate within 1-4 moves or forced mate (positions 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10 walk into mate; position 9 loses a won endgame). In 5/10 positions (1, 4, 7, 8, 10), the correct move was a piece sacrifice or queen trade rather than any king move at all. In 4/10 positions (3, 5, 6, 9), the correct move was a king move to a DIFFERENT square — typically the 'other' adjacent square (Kh8 instead of Kf8 in positions 3, 9; Kg8 instead of Ke8 in position 6; Ka1 instead of Kc1 in position 5). The average cp_loss of 5683 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirms these are razor-thin positions where the 'natural' escape is the one fatal choice. 10/10 king destinations are on the back rank (1st or 8th), and in 8/10 cases the refutation involves a check or mate exploiting the king's new position on an open file, diagonal, or rank it just entered.

19.label: Rook repositioned to a positionally natural square (7th rank, open file, attacking a pawn) instead of playing the available forcing continuation (check, mate, or critical capture).
19.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to an 'active-looking' destination that follows general positional principles—7th rank penetration (Rh7, Rd7, Rb7), open file occupation (Rg8, Rc1, Rc5), or pawn attack (Re6, Rb3)—while a more forcing rook move or alternative piece move delivers check, checkmate, or addresses the most urgent tactical demand. In 4/10 positions, the best move was a rook check on an adjacent square (Re5+ instead of Re6, Rg7+ instead of Rh7, Rg5+ instead of Rc5, Rb8+ instead of Rb7). In 3/10 positions, an immediate checkmate was available (Rh3#, Rd4→Rf4#, Rb8+→Rxd8#). In 8/10 positions, the game was in the endgame phase where tempo is critical. The average cp_loss of 4890 is astronomical, reflecting that these 'natural' rook moves frequently squander forced mates or massive tactical advantages. The consistent thread is choosing a non-forcing rook destination that 'looks right' based on general principles over the specific tactical requirement of the position.

2.label: Bishop moves to an aggressively-placed but undefended square where it is immediately captured or won tactically.
2.description: 7/10 positions involve a bishop being moved to a square where it is immediately lost — either captured outright (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6) or won via a tactical sequence like a fork (position 9). 4/10 of these bishop moves deliver check (Bg5+, Ba3+, Bb4+, Bb4+), exemplifying the classic 'patzer sees a check, patzer plays a check' error where the forcing nature of the move blinds the player to the piece being en prise. In position 1 (Ba4), the bishop lands on an unprotected square where the queen captures it. In position 9 (Bb4), the bishop is won by a queen fork on a4. The remaining 3/10 positions (c3, Qd7, fxg4) share the broader theme of making an 'active-looking' move that creates a tactical vulnerability — advancing past a capturable piece, self-obstructing a defensive square, or removing a geometrically critical pawn. The avg cp_loss of 312 reflects that these moves typically lose a full minor piece worth of value.

14.label: Playing a passive consolidating move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent's knight to jump to a devastating square with fork or invasion threats.
14.description: 10/10 positions feature a slow, non-forcing move (9/10 are pawn pushes like e6, g5, f5, a5, d3, g3; 1/10 is passive piece development Be6) played when the position demands urgent action. In 8/10 cases, the direct punishment is a knight jumping to a powerful square: Ng5 fork (position 1), Nf6+ fork (position 2), Nc3 fork (position 4), Nc7 fork (position 6), Ndb5-Nd6 invasion (positions 7-9), and Nd6+ sacrifice (position 10). The remaining cases involve similar tempo exploitation via piece invasions. 8/10 positions feature an exposed or uncastled king that makes the knight strike especially lethal. The common intent behind the blundered moves is 'building' — solidifying structure, grabbing space, or preparing long-term plans — while ignoring that the opponent's knight is one move away from executing a devastating tactical blow. The best moves in all 10 positions either develop quickly (Nf6, castling), neutralize the knight threat prophylactically (h6, Be6 blocking), or address the tactical urgency directly.

10.label: Moving a minor piece (usually a bishop) to an undefended square where it immediately hangs to a simple capture by a pawn or piece already controlling that square.
10.description: 8/10 positions involve a bishop moving to a square where it is immediately capturable for free or near-free, and 9/10 are minor piece moves (8 bishops, 1 knight) to undefended squares. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 7, 10), the bishop lands on a square directly attacked by an adjacent pawn (hxg4, fxe5). In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 5), the piece lands on a square attacked along an open line by a rook, knight, or queen. In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 8), the piece move creates a tactical vulnerability where either the moved piece or a newly undefended piece hangs. Position 2 (Bd5) and position 9 (d2) are slight variants — one ignores an immediate checkmate while placing the piece en prise, the other overextends a pawn into blockade. The consistent thread across all 10 is the player choosing an 'active-looking' or aggressive square for a piece without verifying that the destination is safe from immediate capture. The average cp_loss of 2183 reflects that several of these blunders lose a full piece outright.

6.label: Playing a natural-looking rook deployment or activation move while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis that demands a concrete response.
6.description: 8/9 positions feature a rook being moved (the exception, Kxb7, leaves a rook hanging). In every case, the move follows a 'sensible' positional principle—placing rooks on open files (Rd1, Rad1, Rhe1, Rab8, Rhb1), defending a pawn (Rb1), capturing material (Rxf5), or repositioning for activity (Re3)—but fatally ignores an immediate concrete tactical vulnerability. 9/9 positions had a critical tactical issue unaddressed: hanging pieces (4/9), forks (2/9), king safety/mate threats (2/9), or overloaded defenders (1/9). The average good moves available was only 1.2, meaning these positions demanded precise calculation rather than general principles. The average centipawn loss of 1458 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—several involve losing material outright or allowing forced mate. The consistent thread is a player on 'autopilot' making the move that looks most natural for rook placement while missing that the position contains a specific tactical demand that overrides all positional considerations.

20.label: The queen voluntarily relocates to a seemingly active or aggressive square while abandoning an essential defensive duty, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the unguarded element.
20.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move that prioritizes apparent activity or aggression over concrete defensive requirements. In 6/10 cases the queen moves toward the kingside (Qh6, Qh4, Qg4, Qh5, Qe5, Qh4) seeking attack that never materializes; in 4/10 it moves elsewhere (Qc7, Qd7, Qf2, Qa2+) to seemingly logical squares. The critical commonality is that every move abandons a specific defensive function: guarding a key square (d5 in position 1, g6 in position 7), protecting a piece (a8-rook in position 2, c7-pawn in position 8), maintaining back-rank coverage (positions 4 and 5), contesting a critical file (positions 3 and 9), or preventing a tactical mechanism like discovered check (position 10). In 8/10 positions, the opponent's refutation directly exploits the newly undefended element within 1-2 moves. The average cp_loss of 2101 reflects that these voluntary queen displacements frequently allow forced mates (3/10) or decisive material gain (5/10). Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions demanding precise defensive judgment rather than creative aggression.

5.label: Critical positions with exactly one acceptable move where passed pawn promotion timing determines the outcome.
5.description: All 10/10 positions share exactly 1 good move available, creating razor-thin decision points. 9/10 positions feature passed pawns or imminent promotion threats as the dominant strategic factor. 7/10 are endgames, and the remaining 3 middlegame positions all involve simplification decisions that transition into pawn-race dynamics. The mistakes (where cp_loss is significant) consistently involve tempo loss in the context of pawn races: Position 2 retreats the king instead of advancing a pawn, Position 4 trades the active rook entering a lost pawn endgame, Position 5 trades queens before neutralizing a counterattacking pawn, Position 7 abandons a critical file allowing mate before promotion, Position 8 captures in the wrong order, and Position 9 gives a purposeless check. Notably, 3/10 positions (1, 6, 10) have very low cp_loss where the player actually found the only good move, suggesting the feature detects the positional pattern (single-path pawn race criticality) rather than exclusively the mistake itself.

7.label: Moving the knight to a seemingly attractive square in an endgame when king activation or a different priority was required.
7.description: 10/10 positions involve knight moves that appear natural or aggressive but misaddress the position's critical need. In at least 6/10 positions, the best move was king activation (Kf3, Ke6, Kf1, Ke3, Kd5), yet the player chose a knight relocation instead. 8/10 positions are endgames where tempo is precious and piece coordination with the king is paramount. The played knight moves fall into several subtypes: going to unstable central squares easily challenged by pawns (Ne4 in positions 5, 7, 8), retreating to passive/irrelevant squares far from the action (Ng2, Nf8, Na4), or arriving at 'active' squares without proper preparation (Ng6 without h4 first). In all cases, the knight move burns a critical tempo while failing to address the position's most urgent demand—typically blockading/creating passed pawns or activating the king to contest the opponent's advancing pawns. The average cp_loss of 217 reflects that these moves consistently transform holdable or winning positions into losing ones.

13.label: Playing natural-looking or passive moves in critical positions where a concrete single-move tactic (checkmate, winning capture, or fork prevention) was available.
13.description: All 10 positions share a remarkably low average of only 1.6 good moves available, indicating razor-thin margins where only one or two continuations maintain the evaluation. In 6/10 positions, there was exactly ONE good move. The missed tactics include: mate in 1 (2/10 positions: Re1# and Qh1#), simple winning captures of undefended/hanging pieces (3/10: Bxa6, Nxd5, Bxe3), preventing/avoiding forks (2/10: Ke6 walked into Nxc7+, Kh1 walked into Nf2+), and avoiding creating tactical vulnerabilities (3/10: Bg5 enabled Greek gift, Qe2 walked onto attacked square, Nxf3+ resolved opponent's problems). In every case, the player chose a move that LOOKS reasonable—a king safety move, a natural development, a flashy capture with check—but missed the concrete tactical reality of the position. The average cp_loss of 2176 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights. 5/10 moves are king moves, suggesting a tendency to default to king repositioning when the position demands immediate tactical action.

22.label: Non-forcing pawn advance to the 3rd rank when the position demands immediate tactical action or urgent development.
22.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking pawn move (9/10 specifically to the 3rd rank from the mover's perspective: b3, g3, f3, b6, f6, g6). In every case, the position demanded immediate forcing action — 9/10 had missed tactics available (checks, captures, or forks), 8/10 involved king safety crises (either the opponent's exposed king needed to be attacked or one's own king needed protection via development rather than pawn moves). The average cp_loss of 3053 is catastrophic, with 4/10 positions converting forced checkmates into merely large advantages. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical-decision moments where precision was required. The b3 move specifically appears 4/10 times for White, suggesting a habitual 'comfort move' pattern. All 10 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag — the pawn move accomplishes nothing concrete while allowing the opponent to solve their problems (castling to safety, contesting open files, activating pieces, or defusing mating attacks).

25.label: Playing a slow, non-urgent pawn advance on the a/b/g/h files when the position demands immediate piece activity or central action.
25.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing flank pawn advance (a-file or h-file in 7/10 cases; b-file or g-file in 3/10) in positions that demanded urgent concrete action. 10/10 analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. The best moves available were overwhelmingly piece-activity moves: king centralization (Ke7, Kd6, Ke4, Kd3, Ke6 in 6/10), rook activation to key files (Rd7, Rf4 in 2/10), or central pawn breaks (d5, f5 in 2/10). The average number of good moves was only 1.2, meaning these were extremely narrow positions where precision was mandatory — yet the player chose a move addressing a long-term, non-urgent concern (queenside expansion, kingside space, pawn structure prophylaxis) while ignoring the immediate tactical crisis. The refutations consistently show the opponent exploiting the free tempo to achieve a decisive positional milestone: reaching a blockade square, creating an unstoppable passed pawn, or activating a rook to a dominant file/rank.

31.label: An unsound bishop sacrifice capturing on f7 (or f2) with check in the opening, when insufficient pieces are developed to generate a follow-up attack.
31.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing the opponent's f-pawn with check in the opening phase, with both kings still in the center. 9/10 are White playing Bxf7+ from c4, and 1/10 is the mirror image (Black playing Bxf2+ from c5). In all 10 cases, the sacrificing side has woefully insufficient piece development to sustain an attack after the king captures — typically only 1-2 pieces are developed while the remaining army sits on starting squares. In all cases, the opponent's king simply captures the bishop and retreats to safety within 1-2 moves (Kxf7-g8, Kxf7-e8, or Kxf2 with adequate shelter), leaving the sacrificing side down a full minor piece for just one pawn. 10/10 positions had at least 3 good alternative moves available, all involving natural development (Nf3, Nc3, d3, d4, etc.) that maintained the position's balance. The average cp_loss is 342, representing approximately a full piece's worth of deterioration in every case.

21.label: Playing a non-forcing, preparatory or repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action on the critical threat.
21.description: 5/6 positions show the player making a quiet, 'natural-looking' move (pawn push, king move, or piece repositioning) that ignores an urgent tactical or strategic demand. In 5/6 cases the move is tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the player had a forcing or precise move available but chose something preparatory instead, giving the opponent time to execute their plan. In Position 9 (Kb3), the player moved the king when b7 was an immediate promotion threat; in Position 6 (a6), the pawn was pushed before the necessary prophylactic Kb2; in Position 4 (e3), a structural pawn move ignored a hanging bishop; in Position 7 (Qb7), the queen abandoned its active file for a passive target. Position 10 (Kf2) represents a subtler variant where the king goes to the wrong square by one, blocking a key piece. The common thread is that all moves look reasonable in isolation but fail to address the position's most urgent concrete requirement, costing between 91-244 centipawns (avg 165) as the opponent exploits the gifted tempo.

30.label: A slow rook-pawn advance (h3/h6/a6) intended as prophylaxis that actually creates a target or hook enabling the opponent's attack.
30.description: 9/10 positions feature h-pawn advances (h3 for White, h6 for Black) and 1/10 features a6, all played as prophylactic measures to prevent opponent activity (stopping g5, Bg4, b5, etc.). In every case, the pawn move backfires catastrophically: 7/10 positions see the opponent advance the very pawn the move was meant to stop (g4 after h3, g5 after h6, b5 after a6), now with greater force because the rook-pawn provides a 'hook' to exchange against. In 3/10 positions (Positions 2, 6, 10), the pawn enables a direct piece sacrifice on the weakened square (Bxh6, Bxh3, Bxf7+/Nxg5+). 8/10 positions feature one king still in the center or opposite-side castling, meaning tempo is critical and the prophylactic move wastes irreplaceable time. The average cp_loss of 246 reflects how devastating these seemingly quiet moves are. In all 10 positions, active alternatives existed—central breaks (e4/e5/d4), piece improvements (Nc4, Ne5, Rfc1), or tactical shots—that would have exploited the opponent's vulnerabilities rather than passively addressing phantom threats.

26.label: Capturing a piece on a square where the opponent's queen can recapture with check, exposing the king to a mating attack.
26.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a capture on square X, and the devastating refutation is the opponent's queen recapturing on that exact square with check (Qx_+). Specifically: Bxd7 allows Qxd7# (Position 1), exd5 allows Qxd5+ (Position 2), Bxf3 allows Qxf3+ (Position 3), cxd5 allows Qxd5+ (Position 4), Nxg6 allows Qxg6+ (Position 5), cxb3 allows Qxb3+ (Positions 6 and 9), hxg6 allows Qxg6+ (Position 7), fxg6 allows Qxg6+ (Position 8), and Rxh4 allows Qxh4+ (Position 10). In 8/10 cases, the queen recapture with check leads to forced checkmate within 1-5 moves. In 10/10 cases, the player's king is already exposed or on the back rank. The captured piece was typically either an attacking piece the player wanted to eliminate (a bishop on g6 pressuring the king, a knight on d5, etc.) or material that appeared free — but it was actually serving as a shield blocking the queen's access to a lethal checking square. The intent behind the captures was logical (removing dangerous pieces or winning material), but the players uniformly failed to calculate the immediate queen recapture with check and its consequences.

24.label: Quiet, non-forcing pawn advances played in positions that demand immediate tactical action—either seizing a critical opportunity or addressing an urgent defensive need.
24.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance in a middlegame position where the tactical demands are acute. In 7/10 cases the pawn push is on the queenside (b3, b5, c4) while the critical action is elsewhere (king safety, back-rank threats, piece activation). The average centipawn loss is an extraordinary 3141, with 3/10 positions resulting in forced mate after the move. In 8/10 positions, the best moves involved piece activity (rook activation, knight jumps like Nd6+, queen centralization) rather than pawn moves. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were high-precision positions where the slow pawn push was uniquely catastrophic. The refutations consistently exploit the tempo gift: 4/10 involve immediate mating attacks, 3/10 involve piece infiltrations enabled by the wasted move, and 3/10 exploit structural weaknesses created by the pawn advance itself (opened files, abandoned squares, broken chains).

23.label: Playing f3/f6 to chase an active enemy bishop when a concrete tactical blow would win material immediately.
23.description: 8/10 positions feature pushing the f-pawn (f3 for White or f6 for Black) to expel an annoying enemy bishop, while 1/10 uses c6 to chase a bishop on b5, and 1/10 develops a knight into the bishop's target square instead of chasing it. In all 10 cases, a much stronger tactical move was available — typically a direct capture or combination winning material (Nxg4 capturing a hanging bishop in 3 positions, Bxf6 removing a defender in 2 positions, Nxf6+ with a forcing sequence, Nxc2+ as a fork, and Bxd3 capturing a hanging queen). The average cp_loss of 315 reflects that these positions universally demanded concrete tactical execution rather than prophylactic pawn moves. 9/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, confirming the tactical precision required. The enemy bishop being chased sat on g4 (5 positions), e5/g5 (3 positions), or b5 (2 positions) — always on an active diagonal creating tension that the player resolved passively instead of exploiting tactically.

28.label: King moves forward or toward the center into exposed squares when it should retreat to safety or a non-king tactical move should be played instead.
28.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves as the blunder, and in 8/10 cases the king advances toward the center or toward the opponent's attacking pieces (Ke6 forward from d7, Kg3 forward from f2, Kd5 central from c6, Kf5 forward from g4, Kd5 central from e6, Kg5 forward from h4, Ke4 forward from f3, Kc5 forward from b6, Kg6 forward from h7, Kb3 forward from c2). In 8/10 positions, the correct move was to retreat the king toward the back rank or corner (Ke8, Ke3, Kc7, Kh4, Kf5, Kg2, Ka6, Kh6). In 2/10 positions (6 and 10), the correct move was not a king move at all but a tactical capture (Bxh1 capturing a queen, Nxd3 capturing a queen). The average centipawn loss of 5738 reflects catastrophic consequences, with 7/10 resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating razor-thin survival margins where any forward king step was immediately fatal.

33.label: A rook is advanced to an intermediate rank (3rd-6th) for vague attacking purposes while ignoring concrete tactical vulnerabilities, leaving pieces hanging or abandoning critical defensive duties.
33.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving from its home rank to a middle rank (3rd, 4th, 5th, or 6th) without a capture or check — a classic 'rook lift' intended to create attacking potential. In 7/10 positions, the rook lift directly abandoned back-rank or second-rank defensive duties, leaving another piece undefended (Positions 1, 2, 6, 8) or the king exposed (Positions 5, 10, 4). In 8/10 positions, a concrete tactical strike or essential preparatory move was available instead (Nf5, Be4, Qg3, f5, etc.). The moved rook frequently became a target itself — in Positions 10 and 7, it was immediately attacked with tempo by a knight or pawn, forcing a humiliating retreat. In Positions 9 and 4, the rook landed on an undefended square vulnerable to forks or self-blocks. Only 2/10 positions had more than 2 good alternatives, confirming these were critical moments requiring precision rather than speculative play. The average cp_loss of 299 reflects that these aren't subtle positional inaccuracies but concrete tactical oversights disguised as active moves.

34.label: A piece captures a pawn but lands on a square where it is immediately recaptured (usually by the opponent's queen), losing the piece for just one pawn.
34.description: All 10/10 positions involve a piece (bishop in 6, rook in 3, knight in 1) capturing a pawn and landing on a square where it is immediately captured by the opponent. In 9/10 positions, the refutation is the opponent's queen recapturing the piece on the capture square (Qxd6, Qxb6, Qxa4, Qxc5, Qxc7, Qxc4, Qxe5, etc.), while 1/10 involves a rook recapture. The average cp_loss of 364 reflects that in every case the player traded a piece worth ~300-500cp for a pawn worth ~100cp, with no compensation. In all 10 positions, the player had 2-3 good alternatives that involved patient maneuvering, development, or piece improvement rather than material grabbing. The captures targeted pawns that appeared weak or undefended (b6, d6, e4, a4, c5, c7, c4, e5) but the capture square was covered by an opponent's piece that could immediately recapture.

32.label: Advancing a non-central pawn (a, b, c, f, g, or h file) in endgame positions involving passed pawn races and exposed kings.
32.description: 10/10 positions feature a pawn push on a non-central file (a-file: 2, b-file: 2, c-file: 2, f-file: 1, g-file: 1, h-file: 2). 9/10 are endgame positions and 10/10 involve passed pawn themes where the pushed pawn is either already passed or aims to become one. 10/10 positions feature exposed or weakly-shielded kings on both sides with open central files. In 6/10 cases the pawn advance is actually the correct or near-correct move (cp_loss ≤ 13), while in 4/10 cases it's a significant error (cp_loss 174-301). The positions where the advance is wrong (positions 3, 4, 6, 9) all share a common thread: a more forcing piece move (queen checks, knight captures, rook captures) was available but the player defaulted to the mechanical pawn push instead.

36.label: Playing an 'active-looking' queen or bishop move (often a check) instead of a simple capture or tactic that wins material outright.
36.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen or bishop move (6 queen moves, 4 bishop moves) chosen for its apparent activity or aggression while a straightforward material-winning opportunity goes unexploited. 6/10 of the played moves are checks (Bc5+, Qb3+, Qc6+, Bh3+, Qe4+, Qa5+), reflecting the classic 'patzer sees a check' instinct. In 9/10 positions, the best move was a simple capture of a hanging or inadequately defended piece: Qd4+ forks a bishop (Pos 1), Qxf8 captures an undefended queen (Pos 3), Qxg4 takes a hanging knight (Pos 6), Qxd4 takes a hanging bishop (Pos 9), Qxh3 wins a loose rook (Pos 8), Ng6# delivers immediate checkmate (Pos 10), Ng4 enables winning a bishop (Pos 5), and Qxe4 captures a free pawn with tempo (Pos 4). The average cp_loss is 1441, reflecting how costly it is to choose appearance over substance. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than general improvement.

35.label: King moves forward to an active-looking central or near-central square in a pawn endgame, often committing to the wrong flank or ignoring a tempo subtlety.
35.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames with king moves to central or near-central squares (ranks 3-6, files b-e). 9/10 are pure king-and-pawn endgames (one includes a bishop). The specific destination squares cluster heavily on the c-file (Kc5 ×3, Kc4 ×2, Kc6 ×1) and e-file (Ke4 ×2, Ke3 ×1), plus one Kb4. When these moves ARE mistakes (6/10 positions have cp_loss > 5), the common error is the king advancing aggressively toward one flank's pawn targets while the critical breakthrough or defensive need exists on the opposite wing (positions 1, 2), or committing the king before a necessary triangulation/tempo maneuver (position 4), or choosing direct blockade over urgent counterplay (position 7). However, 4/10 positions have cp_loss ≤ 6, and 2 are actually the engine's top choice, suggesting the feature detects the general pattern of forward king moves in simplified endgames rather than exclusively flagging errors.

27.label: Non-forcing moves (pawn pushes or slow piece maneuvers) played when the position demanded a concrete tactical solution — a check, capture, or forcing sacrifice.
27.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing move (no check, no capture) played in a position that required an immediate concrete tactical response. 7/10 moves are single-step pawn advances (d6, g3, f3, f6, e4, d5, c6) aimed at generic positional goals like challenging the center, gaining space, or chasing pieces. The remaining 3/10 are piece moves (Ng3, Ne3, Ra7) that similarly avoid forcing continuations. In contrast, the best moves in these positions frequently involved captures (Qxc1, Rxh3+), checks (Nb7+, Qxc6+), or precise defensive forcing moves (f5 closing the kingside). The average number of good moves was only 1.9, confirming these were narrow positions demanding precision. The average cp_loss of 3184 (with 4/10 exceeding 1000cp, including two forced mates missed) reflects the catastrophic cost of playing 'routine' in tactically critical moments. The consistent thread is a player who sees a general strategic idea (challenge the center, push toward the opponent, place a piece on a natural square) while missing the one forcing continuation that solves the position.

41.label: Developing or repositioning a bishop to a natural-looking square when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
41.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop move to a 'logical' development square (Bd3 x3, Be3 x2, Bb7 x2, Be4, Bg2), with the remaining position (c6) being a similarly slow positional move. In all 10 cases, the position contained a critical tactical demand—a forcing capture, a king safety emergency, or a concrete threat to address—that required immediate attention. The best moves in these positions were overwhelmingly concrete: captures (fxe4, cxd5, Qxd5+, Nxc4), king moves (Kb1), or forcing advances (f4, Nd5). The average cp_loss of 1216 and the fact that only 1.5 good moves were available on average confirms these are sharp positions with narrow tactical solutions, where the slow bishop deployment catastrophically misses the window for action. 7/10 positions involved king safety concerns (exposed kings, uncastled monarchs, weak pawn shields), and in every case the bishop move failed to address the most pressing vulnerability.

38.label: Slow positional or developmental moves played in positions demanding immediate tactical attention to a concrete threat.
38.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a natural-looking 'improving' move (piece development, repositioning, or a positional pawn break) while ignoring the position's most critical tactical demand. In 6/10 positions, the blunder is specifically a bishop move to a seemingly active square (Bb7, Bc3, Bd6, Bc1, Bd3, Bb7). The remaining 4 are similarly 'quiet' moves (c4 pawn break, g5 pawn advance, Nec6 knight repositioning, Qd6 queen centralization). In 7/10 positions, there was an immediate tactical threat that required defensive action—such as a mating attack on the h-file (positions 1, 9), a fork opportunity (position 2), or an undefended piece about to be captured (positions 7, 10). In 5/10 positions, the move actively worsened the position by abandoning a key defensive duty: removing a piece that guarded a critical square (positions 2, 6), blocking a friendly piece's defensive line (positions 5, 7), or abandoning protection of a key piece (position 10). The average cp_loss of 1397 and average of only 2.2 good moves confirms these are critical positions where the 'calm' move is catastrophically wrong. The consistent thread is a player operating in 'positional mode' when the position screams for concrete calculation.

39.label: Rook moves to seemingly aggressive squares while ignoring that the player's own major piece (queen or the rook itself) is immediately capturable.
39.description: All 9/9 positions feature rook moves that prioritize activity—seizing files, attacking enemy pieces, or invading ranks—while overlooking an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 4/9 positions (Rf6, Re2, Rg5, Rab8), the rook itself moves to a square where it is directly capturable or becomes hanging after a short forcing sequence. In 4/9 positions (Rd2, Rb1, Rg3, Rg8 position 8), the rook move removes critical defense from the player's own queen, leaving it unguarded and immediately capturable. In 1/9 positions (Rg8 position 7), the rook ignores a lethal tactical threat (Rxc4+ leading to forced mate) to make an irrelevant attacking gesture. The common thread is that each rook move appears purposeful—challenging a file, attacking a queen, invading the 7th rank, or pressuring the opponent—but the player failed to verify whether their own pieces remained safe after the move. The average cp_loss of 2379 reflects that these oversights typically result in loss of a full major piece or worse.

37.label: King moves to a vulnerable square instead of the one correct centralizing or capturing move, walking into checks, forks, skewers, or mating patterns.
37.description: All 10 positions feature king moves that go to the wrong square when very few good options exist (avg 1.7 good moves). In 9/10 positions, the best move was king centralization (typically toward e/d files: Ke6 in 4 cases, Kxd6/Kxe5 captures in 2 cases, Kd3/Kc3/Kc4 in 3 cases). The played moves instead drift laterally or toward the wing/edge. In 6/10 positions, the king walked directly into an immediate tactical catastrophe: mating nets (positions 3, 5), forks (position 8), skewers (position 10), or forcing check sequences (positions 7, 9). In the remaining 4/10, the king moved to a passive or peripheral square that allowed the opponent's pieces to dominate strategically (positions 1, 2, 4, 6). The average cp_loss of 4014 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in catastrophic blunders (>750cp) while 5/10 were moderate errors (134-293cp). Endgame phase dominates (8/10), and Black commits this error far more often (7/10).

48.label: An unsupported pawn advance is pushed hoping to create activity, but the opponent simply captures it with advantage.
48.description: All 10/10 positions feature a speculative single-step pawn advance (f4, c5, g5, d5, h4, e4, b5, e5, f4, d5) that is immediately capturable by the opponent. In 10/10 cases, the primary refutation involves directly capturing the advanced pawn, after which the side that pushed either loses material outright or suffers decisive structural/positional damage. The intent behind each push was aggressive—creating counterplay, challenging the opponent's center, opening lines, or chasing pieces—but in every case the pawn was insufficiently supported. Critically, in 10/10 positions the better alternatives were piece moves (rook repositioning, knight activation, king safety improvements) or more restrained pawn advances, not aggressive breaks. The average cp_loss of 226 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but genuine miscalculations about whether the resulting position after the pawn exchange justifies the advance.

46.label: Non-forcing knight or bishop repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo when an immediate forcing continuation (check, capture, or pawn break) was available.
46.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet minor piece move (5 knights, 5 bishops) that is neither a check nor a capture — purely a repositioning move. In 9/10 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as a primary tag, and in all 10/10, a more forcing alternative existed (checks in positions 2, 6, 7, 8, 9; pawn breaks in positions 1, 5; immediate tactical threats in the rest). In at least 7/10 cases, the piece being moved was already on an optimal or critical square (e.g., knight on c7 covering promotion in pos 1, bishop on e5 restricting the king in pos 2, knight on f3 paralyzing the king in pos 4, knight on e6 assisting a mating attack in pos 6, bishop on b5 blocking a critical rank in pos 10). The average cp_loss of ~2906 reflects that these 'improving' moves catastrophically squander positions where decisive action was required immediately, often converting forced mates into merely large advantages.

47.label: Playing a quiet developing or repositioning move while ignoring an immediate tactical obligation involving a hanging or undefended piece.
47.description: 10/10 positions share the same fundamental error: the player makes a non-forcing, quiet piece move (development, repositioning, or retreat) while a critical piece is tactically vulnerable — either their own piece is en prise, they remove a key defender from a piece, or they miss capturing an opponent's hanging piece. 8/10 positions have 'hanging_piece' as the primary tactical motif. In every case, the move played is a natural-looking developing move (knight repositioning, bishop development, queen retreat) that would be perfectly reasonable in a calm position, but catastrophically ignores an immediate one-move tactical emergency. The resulting punishment is always material loss: a full exchange (positions 2, 5, 6), a full piece (positions 4, 7, 10), a pawn with lasting damage (positions 1, 3, 8), or a squandered winning capture (position 9). 7/10 occur in the opening phase where development is psychologically prioritized, making the trap of 'just developing' particularly seductive. All 10 moves are non-forcing (0 checks, 0 captures, 0 direct threats), and all ignore threats that require exactly one move to resolve.

29.label: Forward/attacking moves toward the opponent's exposed king in simplified endgame positions, prioritizing aggression over defensive precision.
29.description: 9/10 positions are endgames with both kings exposed and weak pawn shields. In 8/10 positions, the two kings are within 2 diagonal squares of each other. All 10 moves are forward/aggressive — advancing toward the opponent's king via checks (3/10: Nd5+, Rb5+, Nd4+), attacking pawns near the opponent's king (Kc4, Ke4, Kh4, Ka4, Nf6), or placing pieces aggressively toward the opponent's side (Qc5, Rf8). None are retreating or defensive moves. When these moves are mistakes (6/10 with cp_loss >100), the correct alternative was typically a defensive/retreating move: Kf2 instead of Kh4, Ka2 instead of Ka4, Ke2 instead of Rf8, Rd1 instead of Rb5+. However, 4/10 positions show this same aggressive impulse actually being correct (Nd5+, Nd4+, Ke4, Kc4 with 0-77cp loss), suggesting the feature detects the aggressive-approach pattern itself rather than just the error.

44.label: Quiet one-square king repositioning moves played when the position demands concrete tactical action or urgent piece play.
44.description: 9/10 positions feature a one-square king move (Kb7, Kg2, Kg7, Kf2, Kb2, Kf8) with no capture, no escape from check, and no direct threat created. The remaining position (h5) is a similarly slow, non-forcing move. In 7/10 positions, these moves are genuine mistakes (avg ~220cp loss among the errors), where forcing tactical sequences were available: position 1 missed Bd4-Bxf2-Rxg2+, position 3 left a bishop hanging, position 5 allowed a Ng4+ fork, position 7 missed Rd4+/Bg6+ winning a rook, position 9 allowed c4 neutralizing a passed pawn. In 3/10 positions (2, 4, 10), the king move was actually fine (0 cp loss) because the advantage was so overwhelming that tempo didn't matter. The feature consistently fires on the decision to play a quiet king improvement move—a 'general positional improvement' instinct—rather than calculating concrete variations.

53.label: Advancing a passed pawn one square closer to promotion before addressing a more urgent need (king activation, piece coordination, or immediate tactical threats).
53.description: All 10/10 positions feature the exact same move type: a passed pawn being pushed one square closer to its promotion square. The pawns advanced include c4→c3 (2x), b3→b2 (3x), g4→g3, a3→a2, g3→g2, d6→d7, and a5→a6. In every case, the advance was premature because a preparatory move was required first. In 4/10 positions (1, 4, 7, 10), the correct move was king activation before pawn advance. In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 8), the advance ignored an immediate checkmate or piece-trapping threat. In 3/10 positions (2, 6, 9), the advance allowed a tactical counterblow that neutralized or captured the pawn. The average centipawn loss was an extraordinary 4057, with 4/10 positions resulting in immediate mate or forced mate. Only 1.7 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical decision points demanding precision rather than 'obvious' pawn pushes.

49.label: A rook already on its optimal square is moved to a seemingly active but inferior square, surrendering the critical control or pressure that was the foundation of the position.
49.description: In 10/10 positions, a rook that was already perfectly placed on a dominant square (controlling a critical file, restraining a passed pawn, pinning pieces, or enabling a tactical sequence) was relocated to what appeared to be a more aggressive or purposeful square. In 8/10 cases the rook moved to attack a specific target (a pawn, piece, or rank), while in 1 case it retreated defensively (Ree1) and 1 case it moved in front of a passer instead of behind it (Rd6). The rook's original square was the linchpin of the position in every case: 4/10 involved abandoning 8th-rank domination that paralyzed the opponent's pieces or enabled mating patterns (Re7, Rf8, Ree1, Rh7), 2/10 involved leaving a file that prevented pawn promotion (Rb2, Rd6), 2/10 involved abandoning first-rank penetration that created pins or restricted enemy pieces (Rc6, Rf4-from-f1), and 2/10 involved vacating an open file that the opponent immediately seized (Rf4-from-d4, Rh2). The average cp_loss was 3195, with 5/10 positions losing a forced mate or near-mate, confirming that these are catastrophic rather than marginal errors.

51.label: A powerfully-placed knight captures a nearby piece for material, when a much stronger tactical continuation leveraging the knight's position was available.
51.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight occupying a dominant square (centralized outpost like e4, d5, e5, c4, f4, or e3) makes a capture of a nearby minor piece — typically a passive bishop on d2, e3, c2, e2, d3, e7, or d7. The capture appears to gain material or force a favorable trade, but in every case the knight was the single most powerful piece in the position, generating threats far exceeding the value of the captured target. 9/10 positions had a clearly superior tactical move available: forks (Nxf2+, Nxg3, Nce5 in positions 3, 5, 10), sacrifices (Nxh3+ in position 2), move-order improvements (Bxf5 in position 1), devastating retreats (Nd5 in position 6), or pawn breaks leveraging the knight's presence (e5 in positions 8, 9). The average cp_loss was 280, with only 1.2 good moves available on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments. In every case, the refutation was a simple recapture (Qxd2, Nxe3, Qxe2, fxe3, Qxe7, etc.) that eliminated all attacking potential, showing the capture was trivially refuted by normal play.

52.label: A rook retreats or slides to the player's own second rank as a slow preparatory move, missing an immediate concrete tactical opportunity.
52.description: All 9/9 positions feature a rook moving to the player's own second rank (2nd rank for White, 7th rank for Black): Rh2, Re2, Rh2, Re2, Rc7, Re2, Rb2, Ra7, Rd2. In every case, the rook move is a non-forcing, non-capturing 'building' move — typically intended to double rooks, support a file, or prepare future pressure — played when the position demanded immediate tactical action. 8/9 positions had a concrete tactical blow available (usually a knight fork or material-winning capture), and the slow rook move gifted the opponent a critical tempo to neutralize the threat. The average cp_loss of 250 reflects how costly this single wasted tempo is. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were sharp positions with narrow paths to maintain the advantage. 7/9 were played by White; both Black instances (Rc7, Ra7) additionally created piece vulnerabilities — self-obstruction blocking the queen's retreat, or placing the rook on an undefended square subject to a knight fork.

50.label: A non-forcing pawn advance played when a superior piece move would exploit concrete tactical or positional opportunities.
50.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the blunder, and in 9/10 cases the best available move was a piece move (typically a knight jump: Nb7, Ne3, Ne2, Nc4, Ne5 in 5 positions; or bishop/rook activation: Ra8, Bg6, Bf4 in 3 positions). In 6/10 positions, the pushed pawn was immediately capturable by the opponent (Nxf6, Nxf5, Bxg4, fxg6, Qxa6, Rxb6), meaning the pawn advance simply dropped material. In the remaining 4/10 cases, the pawn move wasted a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape (positions 4, 9, 10 where the opponent's king escaped to safety, and position 3 where a hanging piece was ignored). The average cp_loss of 259 reflects that these slow pawn moves squandered positions with an average +247cp advantage. All positions had 1-3 good moves available, almost all involving piece activation rather than pawn structure play.

45.label: Making a tempting capture (usually with the Queen) that removes the capturing piece from a critical defensive post, leaving another piece or square fatally unguarded.
45.description: 7/9 positions involve a capture that removes the moving piece from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function — typically guarding another piece or blocking a dangerous line. In 6/9 cases, it is specifically the Queen that makes the erroneous capture (Qxe7 x2, Qxe3, Qxd3 x2, Qxe7), and in nearly all of these, an alternative recapture with a lesser piece (King, pawn) would have maintained the defense. Position 1: Qxe7 abandons defense of g8 rook (should be Qxd5 or Kxe7). Position 2: Qxe3 abandons defense of c4 bishop (should be fxe3). Position 3: Qxd3 abandons defense of a1 rook (should be cxd3). Position 4: Qxd3 misses Ne6+ fork while the queen moves off d2 (should be Ne6+ or cxd3). Position 5: Qxe7 unblocks the b5-e8 diagonal allowing Bxc6+ (should be Kxe7). Position 6: dxc6 leaves the b5 bishop undefended (should be Ba4 first). Position 7: gxh4 opens the g5 square for the opponent's bishop attack. The remaining 2 positions (Qf8, Bb3) share the broader theme of making a passive/materialistic move while ignoring a far more urgent tactical priority (forced mate). The average cp_loss of 2408 and average of only 1.1 good moves available confirms these are extremely narrow positions where precise awareness of defensive responsibilities was critical.

54.label: A slow pawn advance challenging the opponent's strong advanced pawn when urgent tactical or developmental needs demand immediate attention.
54.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance that creates diagonal contact with an opponent's strong advanced pawn (c6 vs d5 in 4 positions, f6 vs e5 in 2, b3 vs c4 in 2, a6 vs b5 in 1, e6 vs d5 in 1). In every case, the pawn break is a reasonable positional idea in the abstract—aimed at liberating blocked bishops, dissolving the opponent's space advantage, or creating counterplay—but is played at precisely the wrong moment. In 4/10 positions (3, 5, 6, 8), a piece was hanging or trappable and needed immediate rescue. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 10), the king remained uncastled and opening the position proved catastrophic. In 2/10 positions (4, 7), the break created permanent structural damage in an endgame. In 1/10 (position 9), an urgent winning tactic needed immediate execution. The best moves across all positions consistently prioritized piece activity, piece safety, or king safety over structural concerns. The average cp_loss of 291 reflects how severely these tempo-losing pawn moves are punished when concrete threats exist.

43.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move when the position demands an immediate forcing response (capture, check, or pawn break).
43.description: All 10/10 positions share the same fundamental error: choosing a quiet, non-forcing move (no capture, no check, no pawn break) in a tactically critical position where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation. 6/10 are king moves that walk into tactical danger (Kf2 into a fork, Kg2 into diagonal/h-file attacks, Kc2 into rook invasion, Kd7 onto an open file, Ka6 into a mating net, and one king retreat that missed Kc6). 3/10 are passive rook repositioning that miss critical captures or exchanges (Re8 instead of Qxa6, Rf1 instead of Ra8+ mate-in-3, Re8 instead of Rxc1). 2/10 are quiet queen development moves that miss central pawn strikes (Qe2 instead of d4, Qe7 instead of fxe5). The average good moves available was only 1.4, confirming these were razor-thin decision points. The average cp_loss of 2122 reflects that quiet moves in such positions are catastrophic—the forcing alternative was typically the ONLY way to maintain the position.

56.label: Instead of capturing an enemy bishop that is en prise or directly capturable, the player makes an indirect move (developing a piece or pushing a pawn) that merely threatens or challenges it.
56.description: In 10/10 positions, an enemy bishop was immediately capturable (hanging or directly takeable), yet the player chose an indirect response instead of the simple capture. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 6, 10), White had a Black bishop intruding deep in their territory (usually on c3 or f3) that could be taken by a pawn (bxc3, gxf3) or piece (Nxc3, Qxf3), but instead developed a piece to d2 or e2. In the other 5/10 positions (3, 4, 7, 8, 9), Black faced a strong White bishop (on d5, b5, c6, or f5) capturable by a piece or pawn, but pushed a pawn (c6 or g6) or moved a bishop (Bd7) to challenge it indirectly. All 10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.3), and the correct move was always the direct capture. The average cp_loss was 491, reflecting that the indirect moves either gave the opponent's piece time to retreat to an equally strong square, allowed the opponent to exchange it favorably on their own terms, or left undefended material hanging.
56.old_chip: Chasing capturable pieces instead of taking

61.label: A check (usually with a rook) that allows the opponent's king to escape by capturing an undefended piece belonging to the checking side.
61.description: In 10/10 positions, the player delivers a check and the opponent's king escapes by moving to a square that simultaneously captures one of the checking player's undefended pieces. The refutation is always Kx[piece]: Position 1 (Kxe2 takes knight), Position 2 (Kxf2 takes knight), Position 3 (Kxe4 takes knight), Position 4 (Kxg3 takes rook), Position 5 (Kxg5 takes knight), Position 6 (Kxb1 takes rook), Position 7 (Kxc2 takes rook), Position 8 (Kxg7 takes rook), Position 9 (Kxe6 takes knight), Position 10 (Kxh3 takes bishop). In every case, the hanging piece was either the player's most active attacking piece or a critical asset maintaining counterplay. 8/10 moves were rook checks, 2/10 were queen checks. The exposed enemy king (present in all 10 positions) tempted the player into giving a 'free' check without noticing that the king's escape square was occupied by their own undefended piece.

60.label: Playing Qh4/Qh5 as the first move of a kingside attack when a preparatory sacrifice or forcing move was needed first to make the queen arrival decisive.
60.description: All 10 positions feature the queen being deployed to an aggressive kingside square (h4 in 8/10, h5 in 1/10, g4 in 1/10) as part of a mating attack. In at least 7/10 positions, the correct plan actually involved Qh4/Qh5 as the SECOND move of a combination, but the player skipped the essential preparatory move. Specifically, 6/10 positions required a preliminary sacrifice before the queen arrived: Bxh2+ (positions 5, 9, 10), Rh1+ (position 3), Rxh2 (position 2), and Bxg4 (position 6). By playing the queen move first without the preparatory deflection/destruction of the pawn shield, White gains a critical tempo to defend (g3, f3, Ne4, Ng3, Re2, or Qxg4+ forcing trades). The average cp_loss of 1185 reflects that several positions squandered forced checkmates (position 10: mate-in-3 missed, costing 9448cp). Only 1/10 positions (Position 1) correctly played the queen to h5 where it WAS the best move, serving as the model showing what happens when the preparation is already complete.

59.label: Queen captures material on a square directly accessible to the opponent's queen, allowing an immediate devastating queen trade or queen loss.
59.description: In 9/10 positions, the player's queen captures a pawn or piece on a square that is directly in the line of attack of the opponent's queen, allowing the opponent to immediately recapture (Qxc2→Qxc2, Qxe5→Qxe5, Qxg5→Qxg5, Qxb2→Qxb2, Qxd4→Qxd4, Qxa5→Qxa5, Qc4→Qxc4, Qxg4→Qxg4, Qxc2→Qxc2). The 10th position (Qxc6) follows the same greedy capture impulse but results in allowing immediate checkmate rather than queen recapture. In every case, the opponent's queen has a clear diagonal or file path to the target square that the player either missed or underestimated. The resulting queen trade is catastrophic because the player's queen was essential—either providing critical defensive coverage for an exposed king (5/10), maintaining sole source of counterplay in a worse position (4/10), or preventing immediate threats (1/10). The average cp_loss of 3150 reflects that many of these are effectively queen-for-pawn exchanges. Typically 2-3 good alternatives existed that kept the queen active and safe.

63.label: A knight captures a rook on a corner square (a1/a8/h8), prioritizing material gain over king safety and piece coordination, resulting in the knight becoming trapped and the opponent launching a devastating counterattack.
63.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight capture (Nx_) that prioritizes raw material gain over urgent positional needs. 9/10 are knight captures on corner squares (a1, a8, or h8), specifically taking rooks that appear 'free.' In every case, the knight was previously on a powerful, active square (f7 in 4/10, c7 in 3/10, c2 in 2/10) where it created multiple simultaneous threats; by capturing the rook, it trades dynamic dominance for static material while becoming trapped or irrelevant in the corner. 8/10 positions involve an exposed king (either the player's own uncastled king on e1/f2, or the opponent's exposed king that could be exploited tactically). In 7/10 positions, the best move was either castling (O-O) or a central tactical strike (Nxd5, dxe5, Bxe5, d4) that maintained pressure on the opponent's vulnerable king. The average cp_loss of 2180 is extreme, with 2/10 positions resulting in immediate forced checkmate after the capture. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points where the one correct priority—king safety and piece coordination over material—was consistently missed.

42.label: Piece (usually king) advances to a seemingly active square that directly enables an immediate tactical blow by the opponent.
42.description: 7/10 positions feature king moves that step onto tactically vulnerable squares where checks, forks, or mates become possible. In Position 9, Ke8 walks into Qh8#; in Position 10, Kb6 enables Nxc4+ fork; in Position 6, Kf7 allows Qf4+ winning bishop and pawn with checks; in Position 7, Kc4 allows Qg4+ followed by Qxf3+ winning the rook; in Position 1, Kf2 allows Rxg2+ with check (versus Kf1 where the capture has no check). The 3 non-king moves share the same structural error: Qe2 (Position 2) blocks the rook's retreat enabling Bf6 winning the exchange; Rhe8 (Position 8) develops passively allowing the same Bf6 tactic; R5e7 (Position 5) retreats when Rxf5 was the only correct forcing move. Position 4 (Kg4, 0cp loss) appears to be an outlier where the feature fires on the winning side's best move. 9/10 positions feature at least one exposed king, and the common thread is that the played move looks natural (escorting a pawn, centralizing, developing) but creates or worsens a specific tactical vulnerability that didn't exist before.

40.label: Superficially attractive aggressive moves (checks, piece excursions, advances) that waste critical tempo and dissipate a winning position.
40.description: All 10/10 positions involve moves that LOOK active or aggressive but concretely lose tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterattack. 3/10 are pointless checks (Rh4+, Bb4+, Rc1+) where the checking piece gets traded off or must retreat. 4/10 are bishop moves to squares where they become targets or abandon crucial duties (Bg4 hangs to Nxe5+, Bg5 abandons key diagonal, Bb4+ wastes tempo to c3, Bb5 retreats from a winning f1 square). The remaining 3 are aggressive-looking moves that create weaknesses (g5 leaves f5 hanging, b6 invites Bxe6, Nf3 to 'natural' square misses blocking the e-file). In every case, the BEST move was either a quiet consolidating move (Kd8, Bd2, Ne2), a concrete material capture (Nxe5, Bxg2), or a pressure-maintaining piece placement (Nc5, Nf4). The average cp_loss of 2064 is catastrophic, and only 2.1 good moves were available on average, meaning these are critical moments where precision was essential but players defaulted to cosmetically attractive moves.

57.label: A slow, non-forcing move (usually a pawn push) played in a position that demands immediate tactical or forcing action, resulting in a critical tempo loss.
57.description: 9/10 positions involve non-forcing, non-checking, non-capturing moves, and 8/10 are specifically quiet pawn pushes (a3, a6, f6, f5, g5, h6, c6, h4). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, confirming the core pattern. In every case, the position demanded immediate action: in positions 7, 8, and 9, the best move was a check (e4+ or c5+) that would gain decisive tempo; in positions 1 and 2, piece activity was urgently needed to address an imminent threat (g5 fork, Rd7 invasion); in positions 6 and 10, the pawn push created structural weaknesses the opponent immediately exploited. The average cp_loss of 303 reflects severe punishment, and the average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are critical moments with narrow margins. Only 1/10 positions (the Rf7 move) wasn't a pawn push, but it shared the same passive character. The positions span all phases (opening through endgame) but consistently feature exposed kings and concrete tactical opportunities that the quiet move ignores.

66.label: A rook is moved to an open file where the opponent's queen already sits, allowing the queen to capture it (often with devastating follow-up tactics).
66.description: In 10/10 positions, a rook is developed to an open file where the opponent's queen is already positioned on that same file, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability. The opponent's queen can simply capture the rook, and the player either cannot recapture due to back-rank mate threats (5/10 positions: 1, 2, 4, 5, 8), loses the rook outright because it's undefended or the capture leads to further material gains (4/10 positions: 3, 6, 7, 9), or loses tempo that allows exploitation of another hanging piece (1/10: position 10). In 8/10 cases, the move specifically brings the previously inactive rook (from a1, h1, a8, b8, or f1) to what appears to be the most natural active file, making it a seductive 'developing' move. The position features consistently show the opponent's queen listed on the target file (e.g., 'White Queen on open d-file' or 'Black Queen on open e-file'). The average centipawn loss of 1293 reflects the catastrophic nature of essentially offering a rook to the opponent's queen.

65.label: Repositioning an already-developed minor piece to a worse or more exposed square, wasting a critical tempo when the position demands urgent action.
65.description: All 9/9 positions involve moving an already-developed minor piece (7/9 bishops, 2/9 knights) to a new square that is either passive, immediately challengeable, or inferior to its starting post. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/9 analyses, confirming the central issue. In 7/9 cases, the piece ends up on a square where the opponent gains time attacking it (Bf4 challenged by ...Ng6, Bc3 kicked by ...b4, Bg4 punished by Qd4, Ng4 left without targets, Ng6 targeted by Qf5+h5, Bc4 allowing ...Bg4 pin, Be2 blocking Ne2). In 6/9 positions, the player's king remained uncastled or exposed, and the repositioning move ignored this urgent need. The average cp_loss of 220 reflects that these aren't tactical oversights but strategic misjudgments—choosing piece shuffling over pawn breaks (f4 in position 2), castling (position 7), or maintaining active pressure (Bc5/Qd3 in position 6). Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise action rather than passive maneuvering.

70.label: Playing a quiet piece repositioning move when an enemy piece was hanging and could be captured for free.
70.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a quiet developing or repositioning move (placing a piece on a seemingly active square) while completely ignoring a free capture of an enemy piece. The missed captures included queens (3/10: positions 5, 7, 10), rooks (3/10: positions 1, 2, 4), bishops (2/10: positions 8, 9), and other material (2/10: positions 3, 6). In every case, the correct move was a simple capture (Rxa8, hxg6, Nxd8, exf6, hxg6, Bxd5, Bxf5, Nxd6, cxb6, dxe5) that required no deep calculation—the target piece was undefended or insufficiently defended. Instead, players chose moves that looked purposeful (centralizing knights, developing bishops to active diagonals, repositioning queens) but were catastrophic because they left free material on the board. The average cp_loss of 541 reflects that these were not subtle positional errors but massive tactical oversights. Only 1.2 good moves existed on average, meaning the capture was essentially the only reasonable option.

62.label: Queen captures the opponent's queen as the sole move maintaining a large existing advantage, typically in endgame or late middlegame positions.
62.description: All 10 positions feature a queen capturing the opponent's queen (Qx opponent's Q), with 10/10 positions already heavily winning for the capturing side (700+ centipawns or forced mate). In all 10 cases, exactly 1 good move was available — the queen capture itself — with alternatives losing 300-750+ centipawns of advantage. 9/10 moves were the engine's top choice with 0 cp loss, while 1/10 (Position 10, Qxb7) was a 209cp mistake where an intermediate move (zwischenzug Bxc5+) should have preceded the queen capture. The opponent's queen was consistently undefended or directly capturable: hanging on an open file (6/10), capturable along a diagonal (2/10), or capturable with check (2/10). The phase was endgame in 6/10 and middlegame in 4/10, reflecting that these queen-trade situations arise most commonly in simplified positions where one side dominates.
62.old_chip: Queen takes queen in won positions

55.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a position with exposed kings that demands immediate concrete tactical action.
55.description: 10/10 positions feature at least one king that is exposed, uncastled, or has a critically weak pawn shield. In 8/10 positions, the player chose a non-forcing move (pawn advance, passive retreat, or wrong capture order) when the position demanded an immediate forcing solution—a check, a capture of an undefended piece, or a direct attack on the vulnerable king. The tactical tags 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' appear in 9/10 and 10/10 positions respectively, confirming the core pattern: squandering a critical tempo in positions where urgency is maximal. In 5/10 cases the wasted move was specifically a pawn advance (a4, h4, h5, b3, gxf4) that created no immediate threat. The 2 positions with near-zero cp_loss (both Rxd7) represent cases where the player correctly addressed the most urgent threat (a passed pawn one square from promotion), showing the feature activates on the positional pattern itself—extreme tactical urgency around king safety—rather than exclusively on mistakes. The best moves across all positions share the trait of being the most forcing option available: checks (a3+), captures of hanging pieces (Nxb4, Nxe4), direct king attacks (Ng7, Ne5, Qh5), or urgent defensive moves (Qg7, castling).

71.label: A passive king retreat when the position demands urgent active piece play (captures, blocks, or counterattacks) to address concrete tactical threats.
71.description: 10/10 positions feature a king move played in the middlegame when the position demanded concrete piece action. In 8/10 cases, the correct move involved active piece play: capturing an attacking piece (Qxg5, hxg5), blocking a critical file or diagonal (Qf5, Ne7, Be6, Rf7, f5, Qf2), or launching a counterattack (Ne5, Bd5, g5). The average cp_loss of 3914 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in immediate or near-immediate checkmate after the king move. In 7/10 cases, the king moved to a square that was actively MORE dangerous—walking onto open files (Kd7 twice), back-rank squares allowing checks with tempo (Kg8, Kh8), or lethal diagonals (Kf6, Kf1). Only 2/10 positions (positions 3 and 7) had minimal cp_loss, both being already-hopeless positions where the distinction was academic. The average number of good moves available was just 1.5, showing these were critical-moment positions requiring calculation rather than instinct.

72.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) onto a diagonal where an enemy bishop is aimed, blocked only by a rook that can move away to deliver a devastating discovered attack.
72.description: 8/10 positions show the identical geometric error: the blundering move places a piece directly onto a diagonal controlled by the opponent's bishop, where only a single rook currently blocks that diagonal. In 7/10 cases the piece is specifically the king (Kg3, Kg7, Kg3, Ka1, Kg8, Ke8, Kf1), walking into the firing line of a bishop blocked by a rook screen piece. Position 9 (Bb7) places a bishop onto an opponent's controlled diagonal with a removable blocker. The punishing discovered attacks in 9/10 positions involve a rook moving off the blocking square—simultaneously delivering a discovered check from the bishop while the rook captures material, delivers its own attack, or relocates with tempo. Positions 7 and 8 are partial outliers involving hanging pieces rather than pure discovered checks, but the overall pattern is overwhelmingly consistent. The average cp_loss of 2192 reflects how catastrophic these errors are—4/10 result in immediate checkmate or mate-in-2.

64.label: Queen moves to active-looking squares instead of addressing concrete tactical requirements in the position.
64.description: 10/10 positions feature queen moves to seemingly active or aggressive squares. In 8/10 positions, these moves are genuine mistakes (avg cp_loss ~3943 for the blunders), while 2/10 (positions 7 and 8) are actually correct moves where the queen reposition is justified.
