The consistent pattern in the mistakes is that a concrete tactical requirement existed — a hanging piece to capture (2/8: positions 1, 6), a critical square or pawn to defend (4/8: positions 2, 3, 4, 10), a forced mating sequence to execute correctly (1/8: position 9), or the queen landing on a vulnerable square where it gets trapped (1/8: position 5). In all 8 blunder cases, the player chose a 'general improvement' queen move that looks active (centralizing, attacking pawns, creating threats, or giving check) over the position's specific tactical demand. The queen moves are universally non-captures (10/10), and 8/10 are non-checks, suggesting the pattern involves repositioning rather than forcing moves.

69.label: A piece performing a vital defensive or blocking role retreats passively, immediately exposing the target it was protecting to tactical exploitation.
69.description: 10/10 positions involve retreating a knight or rook from a square where it performed an essential defensive function — guarding a vulnerable pawn, blocking a dangerous diagonal, or controlling a critical square — to a passive back-rank square (e8, e1, d1, d2, or e3). In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 5), a rook leaves the f-file, directly abandoning defense of the f7 or f2 pawn, which is immediately captured with devastating effect (including a forced mate in position 3). In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 6, 7, 10), a knight retreats to e8, removing its guard of a critical square (h7, the g7-h8 diagonal, or simply ceding tempo). In 2/10 cases (positions 8, 9), a knight retreats from a central blockading/protecting post (e4 or g2), allowing an advancing pawn to trap a piece or promote. The average cp_loss of 1275 reflects how catastrophic these retreats are — they appear safe and developmental but immediately expose a tactical vulnerability that was being held together by that single piece.

67.label: Rook moves to the back rank (1st or 8th) in positions with an advanced passed pawn one square from queening, typically to force an exchange enabling promotion.
67.description: 9/10 positions feature an advanced passed pawn on the 2nd or 7th rank (one square from promotion). 9/10 moves are rook moves, with 5/10 being literally 'Rb1' and 7/10 placing the rook on the promotion rank (1st rank for Black, 8th for White). The mechanism is remarkably consistent: the rook goes to the same rank as the promotion square, either forcing a rook exchange after which the pawn promotes (positions 2, 8, 9, 10), supporting promotion from behind (position 3), or attacking defenders of the promotion square (position 1). In 6/10 cases this is the correct move (0 cp loss), but in position 6 it's a catastrophic blunder because immediate promotion c1=Q+ was available with a discovered check—the player defaulted to the 'rook behind passed pawn' pattern when direct promotion was superior. Position 7 (Rg6) and position 5 (Rd4) are partial outliers where the rook moves in promotion-related positions but not directly to the queening rank.

74.label: Playing a pawn to the square where a knight should naturally develop (c3/f3 or c6/f6), permanently obstructing piece development in the opening.
74.description: 9/10 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to the knight's ideal development square: f3 blocks Ng1-f3 (positions 1, 3, 7), c3 blocks Nb1-c3 (positions 2, 5, 8), f6 blocks Ng8-f6 (positions 4, 9), and c6 blocks Nb8-c6 (position 6). The remaining position (10, Kd2) shares the broader theme of blocking piece development with a non-developing move. All 10 positions occur in the opening phase with kings still in or near the center. The average cp_loss of 240 reflects how devastating these moves are — they waste a critical tempo while simultaneously creating a permanent bottleneck in piece coordination. In 7/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify the blocked knight as the primary reason the move fails. The moves are consistently played with positional intent (preparing e4, supporting d4, controlling e5) but are catastrophically mistimed because the development cost far outweighs the structural benefit.

68.label: Playing a non-forcing piece move to a seemingly attractive square when the position demanded immediate concrete action (captures, pawn pushes, or checks).
68.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing piece move (no checks, no captures) that repositions a piece to a superficially appealing square while missing critical tactical opportunities. The best moves were overwhelmingly concrete and forcing: captures (Nxe3, cxb5), pawn advances to promotion (c2, a7), checkmates (Qb8+), or tempo-gaining moves that attacked specific targets (Nf3 hitting a bishop). In 10/10 cases the played move was tagged as 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic'. The average cp_loss of 2086 is enormous, and the average good moves available was only 1.8, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision. 8/10 positions had the player choosing piece 'improvement' over immediate tactical execution, while 2/10 (Qd2, Bc6) chose an aggressive-looking piece move that addressed the wrong target entirely. The positions span queens (4), knights (4), bishops (2), and rooks (1), confirming this is piece-type-agnostic.

73.label: Capturing an enemy rook (appearing free or advantageous) while overlooking a devastating king safety threat created or enabled by the capture.
73.description: All 10/10 positions involve capturing an enemy rook — this is perfectly consistent across the dataset. In 8/10 cases the capture is a significant blunder (avg cp_loss 4752), while 2/10 are actually the best move in already-lost positions. The core error pattern: the player sees a rook that can be taken and grabs it, but the capture either exposes their own king to a mating attack (positions 1, 3, 7, 8), walks the king into a deadly square (positions 4, 6, 8, 9), removes a critical defensive pawn (position 7), or misses a stronger intermediate move that would safely win even more (positions 2, 9). In 3/10 positions, the rook was captured with the WRONG piece (dxe4 instead of Qxe4; Kxe7 instead of Nxe7; Rxg7 instead of Kxg7), where the correct recapture would have maintained king safety. The refutations consistently involve immediate checks, discovered attacks, or mating sequences exploiting the newly-exposed king — 7/10 positions result in forced checkmate after the capture.
73.old_chip: Greedy rook captures ignore king danger

75.label: Passive queen retreat to a back-rank square when a concrete tactical opportunity (capture, fork, or mating attack) demands immediate action.
75.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen retreating to a passive back-rank or second-rank square (d1, e2, c2, d2 for White; d8, e8 for Black) from an actively-placed position. In every case, a concrete tactical opportunity was available: 3/10 positions had hanging pieces or free captures (positions 3, 7, 10), 2/10 had forced mates requiring immediate action (positions 4, 5), and 5/10 had tactical combinations winning material through forks, pins, or piece coordination (positions 1, 2, 6, 8, 9). The average cp_loss of 1251 confirms these are catastrophic errors. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions demanding precise tactical execution rather than passive consolidation. 8/10 moves were played by White, and all 10 occurred in the middlegame when attacking momentum was at its peak.

79.label: Playing a non-essential flank pawn move (usually a- or h-file) instead of urgently needed king centralization or active piece play in the endgame.
79.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves as the mistake, and 8/10 are specifically on the a-file or h-file (the rim). The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (8/10). In every case, the position demanded immediate king activation or forcing play: positions 1, 2, and 3 all needed king centralization (Kc3, Kd3, Ke3 respectively); positions 4, 5, and 6 needed either a forcing move (c3, Nc7) or addressing an immediate kingside crisis; positions 7, 8, and 10 needed active piece maneuvering rather than pawn commitments. The average cp_loss of 1072 is inflated by one catastrophic case (position 2 where f4 physically blocked the king's destination square), but 7/10 positions lost substantial value (50+ cp). Only 2.3 good moves were available on average, showing these were critical moments demanding precision. The unifying error is that these pawn pushes feel prophylactic or space-gaining but waste the one tempo needed for the position's primary demand—typically king centralization or a forcing tactical sequence.
79.old_chip: Rim pawn push over king activation

78.label: Playing a quiet bishop development or pawn push when the position demanded an urgent queen move to address tactical or defensive needs.
78.description: In 10/10 positions, the best available move was a queen move (Qa5, Qb5, Qe3, Qb3, Qxg5, Qxd5, etc.), yet the player chose a bishop development (7/10: Bd6×3, Bc5, Be7, Bc4, Bb5) or pawn push (3/10: c5, c4, c6) instead. The queen moves were needed for diverse reasons — exploiting a hanging piece (1/10), preventing knight forks (2/10), addressing king safety via counterplay (3/10), defending vulnerable pawns (2/10), or simplifying a dangerous position (2/10) — but in every case, the player defaulted to a 'natural-looking' quiet move that ignored the position's tactical urgency. The played moves appeared logical on the surface (developing a piece, gaining space) but uniformly wasted the critical tempo needed for the queen to fulfill its unique role as the most versatile piece. 8/10 positions featured an uncastled king, further amplifying the cost of the wasted tempo.

76.label: A piece (usually a bishop) is repositioned to a seemingly active square while a critical central pawn break or capture goes unplayed, allowing the opponent to seize the center with tempo.
76.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a piece redeployment move (8/10 were bishop moves) instead of executing an available central action — typically a pawn break (e5, d5, f5) or a central capture (Nxd4, Nxe4). In 9/10 cases the best move directly engaged the opponent's center. The piece moves looked superficially purposeful — attacking something (Nb4 targeting Bc2, Bg4 eyeing e2), retreating prophylactically (Bf7, Bd7, Be7), or seeming aggressive (Bf4, Bh3) — but in every case they wasted a critical tempo. The punishment in 9/10 positions involved the opponent advancing a central pawn (d5, e5, or f5) with tempo against the now-misplaced piece, seizing space and initiative simultaneously. The average cp_loss of 244 reflects that these positions were at critical tension points where one tempo determined who controlled the center. 9/10 were Black moves, suggesting this pattern particularly afflicts the second player who faces a white center demanding immediate challenge.

80.label: Moving the undeveloped h-rook to a central file as a generic 'developing' move when the position demands an urgent concrete action.
80.description: In 8/10 positions, the move specifically involves the h-rook (Rh prefix in notation) being transferred to a central or semi-central file (e8 in 5 cases, g8 in 2, f8/f1/e1 in others). All 10 moves are rook activations to seemingly natural squares — open or semi-open files where a rook 'belongs.' However, in every case the position demanded something far more urgent: 4/10 positions required addressing king safety (positions 3, 4, 9, 10 where king evacuation or avoiding self-blocking was critical), 3/10 required executing an immediate tactical shot (positions 1, 2, 7 with missed combinations), and 3/10 needed specific defensive tasks like protecting a key pawn or contesting the correct file (positions 5, 6, 8). The average cp_loss of 1067 is extreme, and 7/10 positions had only 1 good move available, confirming these are critical moments where generic development is catastrophic. The self-blocking sub-pattern (positions 9, 10) where the rook occupies the king's escape square is particularly devastating.

82.label: Non-forcing 'improving' moves (pawn pushes and quiet rook/king moves) played in positions where immediate forcing tactical solutions were required.
82.description: All 10/10 positions feature a slow, non-forcing move played in a position with acute tactical tension demanding immediate action. 5/10 are pawn advances (g4, c5, g4, h4, c5), 4/10 are quiet rook moves to 'active' squares (Re2, Rd8, Re8, Rd8), and 1/10 is a king move (Ke6). In every case, the best available move was a forcing tactical solution: checks (Qh1+, Qh2#, Qf8+), captures (Bxh6, Bxh6), or active piece moves creating immediate threats (Nc3, Nd4, Qg5, Qb7, Nd4). The played moves all look 'reasonable' in a vacuum—advancing pawns for space, activating rooks on open files, centralizing a king—but catastrophically waste a tempo in positions where the opponent has lethal tactical resources ready to execute. 7/10 positions featured exposed kings (either the player's or opponent's), making tempo especially critical. The average cp_loss of 3128 reflects that these quiet moves frequently convert winning positions into losing ones or miss forced checkmates.

81.label: Moving a powerfully-placed bishop away from its critical square, surrendering positional or tactical advantages it was providing.
81.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop voluntarily relocated from a dominant, functionally critical square to a passive or peripheral one. In 8/10 cases, the bishop occupied a central or advanced outpost (d5, e6, d4, c3, c2, f5, e2, g6) where it was performing an irreplaceable role—blocking an open file (3/10: d4 blocking d-file, e2 blocking e-file), supporting a mating net or tactical combination (3/10: d4 in position 5, f5 in position 10, e6 in position 2), anchoring central control (2/10: d5 in positions 4 and 7), or restricting enemy pieces deep in their camp (2/10: c3 in position 9, c2 in position 6). The destination squares are consistently less effective: rim squares like h5, g2, g7, g6, b2, a4 (7/10) or retreats to diagonals where the bishop performs no concrete function. The average cp_loss of 1179 reflects that these moves consistently squander decisive advantages, with 6/10 positions losing 200+ centipawns and one converting forced mate into a mere advantage.

77.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move (bishop retreat, pawn push, or piece shuffle) when the position demands immediate concrete action such as a capture, check, or forcing advance.
77.description: All 10 positions feature a player choosing a quiet, non-forcing move—typically a piece repositioning or pawn push—when the position demanded urgent concrete action. 7/10 moves involved tactical motifs tagged as 'tempo_loss', and 9/10 were tagged 'missed_tactic'. The best moves in each case were forcing: captures (Bxh2, Qxg7 threat), checks (Qf6+, Bf4+), forcing pawn advances (e5), or castling (O-O). Instead, players chose slow alternatives: bishop retreats to seemingly reasonable squares (5/10: Bg6×2, Bg3, Bb3, Bg4), quiet pawn pushes (4/10: c6, g3, b3, f6), or a knight retreat from a dominant post (1/10: Nc4). The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are positions with narrow critical paths where the specific forcing move was essential. In 8/10 cases, the quiet move either created a new structural weakness (g3 leaving h3 hanging, f6 allowing Qxg7#, Bg4 weakening f7) or simply surrendered the initiative by allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterattack (b3 letting Black play ...Bf7, Bb3 letting Black play ...Bd6, c6 blocking the bishop from c6).

58.label: Playing a natural-looking move that ignores the single most urgent tactical requirement in a position demanding precision.
58.description: All 10 positions share the characteristic of having very few good moves (avg 1.8), meaning they demand precise tactical identification of the one critical action required. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 6, 8, 9), the best move was a simple capture of undefended or poorly-defended material that the player overlooked in favor of a plausible alternative. In 4/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 8, 10), the blunder placed a piece on a square where it became immediately vulnerable to a concrete tactic (fork, skewer, or capture). In 6/10 cases, the blunder was a rook move, with 4 of those being rook pawn-grabs that created tactical liabilities (back-rank weakness, premature simplification, walking into traps). The remaining moves (Bg8, b4, g3, Qf6) were quiet repositioning or consolidation moves played when forcing tactics demanded immediate attention. Across all positions, the player chose a move that appeared active or constructive on the surface but either created a new vulnerability or failed to exploit an existing one, in positions where only 1-2 moves maintained the evaluation.

87.label: The king marches forward or toward the center when it should retreat, stay put, or yield the tempo to non-king moves, walking into tactical vulnerabilities.
87.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that advances the king forward (toward the opponent's side or deeper into the center) from an already somewhat exposed square. In 10/10 cases, the king was already vulnerable and the advancing move increased its exposure to checks, mating nets, or coordinated piece attacks. In 7/10 positions, the player was already losing, and the forward king march catastrophically accelerated defeat—5/10 positions converted from a losing-but-survivable evaluation into forced checkmate (positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 9). The best alternatives consistently involved either retreating the king (8/10), making non-king moves like pawn pushes (positions 4, 7, 8), or at minimum advancing in a different direction toward opponent weaknesses rather than into opponent strength (position 10). The common tactical punishment was checks exploiting the king's new exposed square (Rf6+, Re7+, Qd2+, Bc3+, Qc2+), often leading to mating patterns where the king became trapped by its own pawns or opponent piece coordination. The average cp_loss of 3679 reflects that 5 of these moves were immediately game-ending blunders while the other 5 were meaningful inaccuracies.

83.label: A bishop (or piece) is passively retreated or relocated when the position demanded a forcing resolution — typically capturing/exchanging the piece or executing a concrete tactical strike.
83.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop move (the exception being Ned7, which follows the same logic). In all 10 cases, the played move is a non-forcing, non-capturing relocation of a piece that was under tension or at a critical decision point. In 6/10 positions, the clearly best move was an exchange/capture (Bxc3 in positions 2 and 10, Bxf3 in positions 5 and 7, dxe4 in position 4, Nd3+ in position 8). In the remaining 4 positions, the best moves were either retreats to specifically safe squares (positions 1, 3, 6) or a completely different tactical blow (position 9). The common thread is that every blunder moves a piece to a square where it becomes passive, vulnerable, trapped, or tempo-losing, while a concrete forcing continuation was available. 8/10 positions involved Black's bishop; the average cp_loss was 252, indicating these are severe mistakes. In 8/10 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed, confirming these were critical decision points requiring precise calculation rather than quiet consolidation.

85.label: Moving the bishop to a seemingly active square when the position demands a more urgent action (usually king activity or a very specific bishop placement).
85.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being repositioned to a square that appears constructive but wastes a critical tempo. In 8/10 positions (endgames), king activity was the paramount concern — positions 1, 4, 8, and 9 explicitly required king moves as the best alternative, while the bishop move squandered the one tempo needed. In 6/10 cases, the bishop had ONE specific correct square (c2 instead of e2, g5 instead of d2, staying near the king instead of going to d7) that addressed the actual positional requirement, but the player chose a different 'active-looking' square. The average cp_loss of 2895 is catastrophic, with 4/10 positions converting to forced mate. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where every tempo matters. The bishop moves typically look like 'improvement' moves — centralizing, attacking a pawn, or seeking activity — but they uniformly fail to address the true tactical or strategic priority.

88.label: In rook endgames, the rook moves to directly attack an enemy pawn but becomes passively placed, abandoning critical active functions like checking distance, file control, or restraining passed pawns.
88.description: 10/10 positions are rook endgames where the played move is a rook relocation that targets a specific enemy pawn. In every case, the attacked pawn is either easily advanced past the rook (positions 1, 5, 8, 10), adequately defended by the king's approach (positions 3, 4), or irrelevant to the position's critical needs (positions 2, 6, 7, 9). The correct moves consistently prioritized rook activity over material threats: 7/10 positions required maintaining checking distance or lateral mobility (positions 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10), while 6/10 featured the rook needing to be placed behind a passed pawn rather than in front of or beside it (positions 1, 2, 3, 9, 10, and implicitly 7). The average cp_loss of 1156 reflects catastrophic positional damage from what appears superficially logical. Only 2.1 good moves existed on average, indicating these are critical moments where pawn-chasing impulses clash with narrow defensive requirements.

92.label: A non-forcing advance of the a-pawn or h-pawn that wastes a critical tempo when concrete tactical action (captures, castling, piece maneuvers) was urgently required.
92.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-square advance of a rook pawn (a-file or h-file): 7/10 are h-pawn pushes (six to h6, one to h3), and 3/10 are a-pawn pushes (a3, a6, a4). All 10 moves are non-capturing, non-checking, and create no immediate forcing threat. In every case, the best moves available were concrete actions: castling (3/10 positions demanded O-O-O), captures or exchanges (axb3, hxg6, Nxf3, Nxe6 in 6/10), or forcing piece maneuvers (Ng5, e6 breakthrough in 2/10). The average cp loss of 301 reflects that these positions all had narrow margins where only 1-3 good moves existed, making the tempo waste catastrophic. 9/10 positions were tagged 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The opponent's refutation typically involves exploiting the free tempo for central action (e5 pushes, Nxf3+ checks), piece invasions (Nd3), or simply retreating the 'threatened' piece to safety (Ba8, Bh8) leaving the advanced pawn stranded and useless.

84.label: Repositioning a minor piece to an apparently useful square when the position urgently demands addressing a critical king safety issue, usually via a king move.
84.description: In 8/8 positions, the blunder was a minor piece (bishop or knight) repositioning move that ignored a critical king safety crisis. In 6/8 positions, the correct move was specifically a KING move (Kh2, Kf1/Kh1, Kd2, Kd7, Kc8, Kh8) or direct king-safety action (Qg4 attacking exposed king, queen retreats for defense). The played moves (Be6, Bd6, Bc4, Ne2+, Nf1, Ng3, Bg6, Nc4) all look 'reasonable' in isolation—improving a piece, blocking a file, giving check, challenging an enemy piece—but catastrophically misjudge the positional priority. In 7/8 positions, a king was critically exposed (either the player's own on d3, c3, e7, g1, d7, or the opponent's on f6/g8), and the position demanded immediate crisis management rather than piece improvement. The average cp_loss of 1425 reflects how severely these positions punish the failure to recognize king safety as the #1 priority.

89.label: Moving a piece to an apparently active square while one's own exposed king desperately needed that piece for defense or required an immediate simplifying trade.
89.description: All 10/10 positions feature the moving side's king critically exposed (tagged king_safety in every case), and in every instance the played move sends a piece (queen 5/10, rook 4/10, knight 1/10) to a square that appears active or aggressive while completely ignoring the urgent defensive crisis around the player's own king. In 8/10 positions, the result is immediate forced checkmate (within 1-26 moves). The best available moves in these positions consistently involved either trading down material to eliminate mating threats (positions 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 10 — where captures/exchanges were the top choice) or placing the piece in a specifically defensive/blocking role near the king (positions 4, 5, 6, 7). The average cp_loss of 5619 reflects that most of these moves convert survivable-but-losing positions into immediate forced mates. 8/10 positions are endgames where material is already reduced, making the king's exposure even more lethal since fewer pieces remain to provide shelter.

94.label: An aggressive-looking pawn advance is played instead of addressing an urgent concrete tactical need in the position.
94.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance that appears purposeful or aggressive but critically ignores the tactical demands of the position. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), the player pushes a pawn while an immediate tactical threat exists that requires piece play to address or exploit. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 6), Black pushes a passed d-pawn to d3 specifically while f7 is under double attack from Ng5+Bc4, ignoring the crisis entirely. In 2/10 cases (positions 7, 8), the pushed pawn was actively serving as a critical shield on a diagonal—removing it allowed immediate tactics including one instant checkmate. In 2/10 cases (positions 9, 10), the pawn advance was a premature structural break that handed the opponent an outpost or breakthrough tempo. The average cp_loss of 2164 is extremely high because these moves often allow forced checkmates (positions 5, 8) or decisive material gains. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than general play.

93.label: Playing a quiet g-pawn advance (g3 or g6) as a defensive/prophylactic measure when the position demands an immediate forcing move.
93.description: 8/10 positions involve the exact same geometric move: a one-square g-pawn advance (g6 for Black in 4 positions, g3 for White in 4 positions). The remaining 2 outliers (e6, a5) are analogous slow pawn pushes. In all 10 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of the best evaluation, and that move was always a forcing piece action — typically a check (Qe3+, Qxf3+, Qxc3+, Qxd5+), a capture (Rxd6, Nxf6), or an active piece redeployment (Ra2, Qf3, Nc4, Ng6). The g-pawn push is consistently motivated by perceived kingside defensive needs: preventing infiltration on the g-file, creating king luft, or challenging an attacking piece. In 7/10 positions, the pawn move actively creates new weaknesses (dark-square holes on f6/f3, fixed pawn targets, blocked knight squares), compounding the tempo loss with structural damage.

90.label: A rook voluntarily leaves an actively-placed square, abandoning a vital defensive or tactical function it was performing.
90.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving away from a square where it was performing a critical function — whether supporting a tactical threat, defending the king, controlling a key file, or protecting a piece. In 6/10 cases the rook retreated backward (Rff1, Rdd1, Rf2, Rff1, Rd8 overextension, Rd2), while in 4/10 it shifted sideways along a rank to attack something less important (Rc6 ×2, Rc5, Rb3). The consequences varied but always stemmed from the same cause: 3/10 left pieces hanging (Positions 3, 9, 10 — undefended knight on e6, g4 pawn), 3/10 exposed the king to mating attacks (Positions 5, 7, 8), 2/10 cleared critical files/ranks for the opponent (Positions 2, 6), and 2/10 allowed devastating tactical shots like forks (Positions 1, 6). The average centipawn loss was extremely high (2201), and in 7/10 positions there were only 1-2 good alternatives, indicating these were positions requiring precise rook placement. In every case, the better moves involved either keeping the rook on its active square and moving something else, or moving a DIFFERENT rook to the desired file.

98.label: A rook lift intended to swing toward the enemy king is too slow, allowing the defender to consolidate or counterattack.
98.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to an intermediate rank (3rd, 4th, or 6th) with the intent of swinging laterally toward the opponent's king — a classic 'rook lift' maneuver. In every case, the attacker has a strong queen already targeting the enemy king and a clearly winning or advantageous position. The critical error is that the rook lift is one tempo too slow: 9/10 positions had an immediate forcing move available (a queen check, a bishop sacrifice, a pawn push with tempo, or a direct capture) that would have maintained the attack's momentum. After the slow rook lift, the defender gains the crucial tempo needed to consolidate — via moves like ...g6 (shoring up the pawn shield), ...Qe7/Qh7 (offering a neutralizing queen trade), ...f5 (blocking diagonals), ...Nh7-Nf6 (rerouting defenders), or ...Qa1+ (exploiting the vacated back rank). The average cp_loss of 364 reflects positions collapsing from winning to equal. 8/10 moves were played by White, and all 10 occurred in the middlegame during active kingside attacks.

91.label: Playing slow, non-forcing pawn advances or piece repositionings in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action.
91.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn advances (d3, e6, f4, f4, d6, h4, e3, d6) and 2/10 feature knight moves (Nd4+, Nd5), but all 10 share the critical trait of being non-forcing moves played in positions demanding immediate tactical resolution. In 10/10 cases, the position had a concrete opportunity — either a winning tactic to execute (positions 1, 7) or an opponent's tactic to prevent (positions 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10) or a key defensive piece to maintain (position 8) or a check to avoid giving (position 5). The average number of good moves available was only 2.1, confirming these were positions requiring precise, concrete play rather than flexibility. Instead, players chose moves that appeared constructive on the surface — supporting pawns, building center, preparing development, centralizing pieces — but that fundamentally ignored the tactical demands of the moment. The refutations frequently involved forks (6/10 positions), exploiting exactly the tempo the slow move gifted. Critically, 9/10 positions were in the opening or early middlegame with kings still in or near the center, amplifying the cost of wasted tempi.

95.label: A pawn capture that opens a file or diagonal pointing directly at the player's own king or undefended pieces, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the newly opened line.
95.description: All 8 positions feature pawn captures that resolve tension by moving the pawn away from its file, thereby opening that file (or a diagonal) which the opponent immediately exploits. In 6/8 positions, the opened line points directly at the capturer's own king: Position 2 (cxd5 opens c-file toward king on c8), Position 3 (dxe6 opens a4-e8 diagonal toward king on e8), Position 4 (cxb4 opens c-file toward king on c8), Position 7 (hxg5 opens h-file toward king on g4), Position 8 (exf5 opens e-file toward king on e8), and Position 5 (dxe5 opens lines enabling f5 kingside assault). In the remaining 2/8 cases, the capture leaves pieces vulnerable on the newly opened lines (Position 1: rook exposed on c5 after dxe5; Position 6: knight on a6 left hanging after bxc5). All captures appear superficially attractive—winning material or relieving pressure—but the structural cost of removing the shielding pawn is catastrophic. The average cp_loss of 1430 reflects how devastating these self-inflicted structural wounds are. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points requiring the player to resist the natural-looking capture.
95.old_chip: Pawn capture opens line against own king

101.label: Playing a non-urgent single-square rook pawn advance (a6/h3/h6) in positions demanding immediate tactical action or development.
101.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square advance of a rook pawn (a-pawn or h-pawn) — specifically 7/10 are ...a6 and 3/10 are h3 or h6. In every case, the position required immediate concrete action: capturing an attacked piece (Position 7: Nxd2 wins White's queen), executing a winning tactic (Position 8: Bg5 wins the exchange), urgent development (Positions 9-10: Nf6 or Nf5 to contest critical squares), or active piece repositioning to address threats (Positions 1, 5, 6: Nd4, Ne5, Bb7). The average cp_loss of 300 reflects that these aren't just slightly suboptimal — they're catastrophic tempo losses at critical moments. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, confirming these were razor-sharp positions with narrow paths to survival. In 4/10 cases the pawn itself became an immediate target (Positions 2, 3 where Bxa6 captures it; Position 1 where the h3 pawn becomes a tactical hook). In 6/10 cases, the tempo gifted to the opponent allowed a decisive tactical blow (d5 fork, queen invasion, Kg2 escape, Bc4/Ng5 attacks on f7).

99.label: King captures a pawn in a pawn endgame where both sides have advanced/promoting passed pawns, often losing a critical tempo or committing the king to a poor square.
99.description: All 10/10 positions are pawn endgames featuring active promotion races with at least one highly advanced passed pawn (typically 1-2 squares from queening). In every case, the king captures an enemy pawn (Kx__) while the opponent has an unstoppable or nearly-unstoppable passed pawn. The kings are universally exposed and separated from each other (often on opposite wings). In the positions where the capture is genuinely costly (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 9 — averaging ~2040 cp_loss), the error stems from the king committing to a poor square (corner/edge) or spending a tempo on material gain when advancing own pawns was more urgent. However, 5/10 positions show the capture as the best or near-best move (cp_loss ≤ 60), indicating the feature fires on the structural situation (king taking a pawn amid a promotion race) rather than exclusively on blunders. The average of 1.9 good moves available confirms these are extremely narrow, concrete positions where pawn-race tempo calculations are decisive.

96.label: Moving the queen to a seemingly active square when the correct move was to exchange queens or keep the queen on its critical defensive post.
96.description: All 10 positions feature non-capture, non-check queen repositioning moves to squares that appear active but are actually dysfunctional. In 8/10 cases, the best move was explicitly a queen exchange (Qxf5, Qxg4, Qxf3+, Qxc5, Qxe4, Qxf2) or a move that forced a favorable queen trade (Nxd5 forcing Qxc5, Nf8+ leading to Qxf3+). Instead, players slid their queen to a different square—often one that looks aggressive (Qh5 'attacking the king', Qg5 'creating threats', Qb3 'targeting pawns')—but in reality abandoned a critical function. In 6/10 positions the queen was actively defending something vital (a rook on f2, the e-file, an X-ray on d1, the f3 square preventing mate), and moving it away immediately left material or squares hanging. The average cp_loss of 2157 reflects that these weren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments, with 3/10 resulting in immediate forced mate or piece loss. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions demanded precision—yet the queen trade was typically the most natural simplifying move available.

100.label: Bishop captures a pawn near the opponent's king shelter, prioritizing material or superficial king exposure over a more forcing or constructive continuation.
100.description: All 10 positions feature a bishop capturing a pawn (Bx_), and 9/10 target pawns forming or adjacent to the opponent's king shelter (g6 three times, h2 twice, h3 twice, f7 once, g3 once, with c7 as the lone outlier). In 9/10 cases this is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 338 excluding the one correct instance). The common thread is that the bishop capture appears to weaken the opposing king's pawn cover or win 'free' material, but actually squanders tempo, displaces the bishop from a more powerful post, or misses a far stronger forcing sequence. In 4/10 positions (1, 4, 9, 10), a more forcing preparatory move was needed before the capture could work. In 4/10 positions (5, 6, 7, 8), the bishop left a dominant central or active square to grab a peripheral pawn, losing coordination. In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 9), the same capture would have been correct one move later after proper preparation. Position 2 (cp_loss 0) represents the pattern executed correctly—where the capture IS the prepared blow after coordination is already optimal.

102.label: Moving the queen to an apparently aggressive kingside square (mostly f3-f6/g4-g6) when a more forcing tactical or positional move was required.
102.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move to a central-kingside square that appears active but fails to address the position's concrete demands. 7/10 moves land on the f-file (Qf3, Qf4×4, Qf5, Qf6), while the remaining 3 go to adjacent squares (Qg4, Qg6, Qd4). In 6/10 positions, there was a specific tactic available that the queen move either missed entirely (positions 2, 3, 6) or actively interfered with (positions 1, 6, 9). In 4/10 positions, the queen move primarily loses tempo, allowing the opponent to execute a key pawn break or force the queen to retreat (positions 5, 8, 10, 4). The average cp_loss of 283 and average of only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are narrow positions demanding precise calculation rather than general piece improvement. In 8/10 cases, the queen immediately becomes a target—vulnerable to knight attacks (positions 1, 4, 9), pawn advances (positions 5, 8, 10), or queen exchanges that defuse the attacking side's initiative (position 7).

104.label: King captures an adjacent enemy queen as the only move avoiding immediate checkmate, entering a still-decided pawn endgame.
104.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical move structure: the king captures an enemy queen that is on an adjacent square, transitioning from a piece-imbalanced endgame into a pure pawn endgame. In 10/10 cases, only 1 good move was available, and in 9/10 positions the alternative king moves led to forced checkmate (ranging from #-4 to #-16). The captures were essentially compulsory despite the resulting pawn endgame remaining decisively lost for the capturing side in 9/10 cases (avg eval magnitude ~620cp after capture). Position 10 is a slight variant where the winning side captured the queen reflexively, missing a faster forced mate. The feature consistently identifies positions where a queen has wandered adjacent to the enemy king in an endgame, creating a forced capture that merely converts a mating attack into a technically won pawn endgame for the opponent.

103.label: Moving a queen or rook to a seemingly active square while ignoring an immediate tactical obligation, wasting a critical tempo.
103.description: All 10/10 positions feature a major piece (queen or rook) being repositioned to an apparently purposeful square — often aiming for a file battery, flank attack, or material target — while the position demands immediate concrete action. The moves are uniformly non-forcing (0/10 involve checks or captures) and prioritize a speculative plan over urgent tactical needs. In 5/10 positions the move leaves the player's own piece hanging or undefended (Positions 1, 4, 5, 7, 8). In 3/10 the player fails to capture an opponent's hanging piece (Positions 2, 6, 7). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 analyses and 'missed_tactic' in 9/10, confirming the core pattern: the moved piece looks like it's doing something constructive but actually accomplishes nothing concrete while granting the opponent a free move to either capture hanging material, consolidate defensively, or neutralize attacking chances. The average cp_loss of 1225 reflects how catastrophic wasting tempo is in sharp positions.

106.label: Developing a bishop to a long diagonal (b2/b7/g7) as a routine positional move while ignoring an urgent tactical demand in the position.
106.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to a fianchetto-style long diagonal (Bb7 in 6 positions, Bb2 in 3, Bg7 in 1) — a 'natural-looking' quiet developing move that completely ignores a concrete tactical emergency. In 5/10 positions, the move ignores a direct king safety threat (sacrifice on g6, Bxh6, Qxh2#, enemy piece on g3). In 3/10 positions, it misses a winning tactical opportunity the player could have seized (Ng5 fork, winning a stranded knight, exploiting a pin). In 2/10 positions, it allows a crushing pawn advance (e5) that wins material or severely cramps the position. The average cp_loss of 1284 reflects the catastrophic nature of prioritizing slow development over concrete tactics. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, meaning these were typically critical moments with narrow defensive or offensive windows — exactly when routine development is most dangerous.

86.label: Playing 'improving' or 'active-looking' moves that ignore immediately available decisive tactics or create fatal vulnerabilities.
86.description: 9/10 positions share the pattern of a player choosing an intuitively appealing 'improving' move—centralizing a piece, advancing a pawn, or repositioning—while missing a concrete, forcing tactical reality. In 2/10 positions (1, 10), the player centralized a knight (Nfd5, Ne4) while a simple winning capture was available (Rd1# mate, Qxe5 free piece). In 5/10 positions (2, 4, 7, 9, and arguably 5), the player advanced a pawn (f4, f5, d4, c5+) that either removed a critical defensive barrier (positions 2, 7) or was immediately capturable with check/tempo gain (position 9). In 2/10 positions (3, 8), the player repositioned a rook to an 'improved' square that actually created tactical vulnerabilities (undefended pawns, skewer geometry). The average cp_loss of 2205 is extreme, driven by two positions where immediate checkmate was missed. The average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are critical positions demanding precise calculation, yet the played moves consistently reflect 'general principle' thinking rather than concrete analysis.

109.label: King moves to a seemingly safe adjacent square that creates a critical tactical vulnerability, when only one specific neighboring square survives.
109.description: All 10/10 positions feature an exposed king under heavy pressure choosing between adjacent squares, with an average of only 1.2 good moves available. In every case, the king retreats to what appears to be a natural shelter square but actually creates a devastating tactical vulnerability. The correct square was always immediately adjacent to the chosen one: 3/10 needed Kg8, 3/10 needed Kh7, 2/10 needed Kd2, 1/10 needed Kh6, 1/10 needed Ka3. The wrong square typically differs from the correct one by stepping onto a dangerous line (diagonal in positions 1, 8), abandoning defense of a critical pawn (positions 2, 6, 10), walking into a mating pattern (positions 3, 9), or allowing a check that gains constructive tempo (positions 4, 5, 7). The average cp_loss of 4145 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the wrong choice, demonstrating how catastrophic a one-square difference can be under attack.

105.label: Routine piece placement to d2/d3/d7 that ignores concrete tactical demands or creates self-interference.
105.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece moving to the d-file on the player's own side — d2 or d3 for White (6 positions), d7 for Black (4 positions). These are uniformly quiet, non-forcing 'developing' moves: 5/10 are knights to d2, 2/10 are bishops to d3, 2/10 are knights to d7, and 1/10 is a queen to d7. In 7/10 positions, the move occurs in the opening phase. The common flaw is that these passive placements either create self-interference (5/10: the piece on d2/d7 blocks another piece from defending a critical square — e.g., Nd2 blocking Qd1's defense of d4 in position 3, Nd7 blocking Bc8's access to e6 in position 9) or simply waste tempo while ignoring urgent tactical needs (8/10 ignore a concrete threat like a hanging piece, fork opportunity, or critical pawn breakthrough). In 3/10 positions, d5 was the correct pawn thrust that would have exploited central tension, but the player chose passive piece placement instead. The average cp_loss of 302 reflects that these 'natural' moves are catastrophically punished by tactics the move either enables or fails to prevent.

108.label: Moving the corner rook one file over to the b-file (or g-file) as a passive 'activation' move when the position demands immediate tactical or defensive action.
108.description: All 9/9 positions feature a rook being moved from its corner file (a or h) to the adjacent file (b or g) on the back rank — 7/9 are specifically the a-rook to the b-file (Rab8 or Rab1), while 2/9 are rook-to-g8 moves. In every case, the position contained an urgent concrete demand: 4/9 had a winning tactic available (fork, pawn capture winning a piece, queen capture via open file), 3/9 required immediate defensive attention to king safety threats or hanging pieces, and 2/9 needed central tension resolved before slow moves were permissible. The average cp_loss of 1375 is catastrophic, with multiple positions swinging from winning to losing or even to forced mate. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical-precision positions masquerading as quiet developmental moments. The rook move looks natural and constructive — activating a dormant piece — but in every case it addresses zero concrete threats or opportunities in the position.

115.label: A knight jumps to a forcing square (check or fork) but is immediately captured because it has no support on its landing square.
115.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight aggressively leaps to a central attacking square (f3, f6, e3, or e5) delivering check or creating a fork, but the knight is completely undefended on that square and is simply captured. 9/10 moves were checks or discovered checks, and 1/10 was a fork (Ne3 attacking queen and rook). The refutation in all 10 cases is a straightforward capture of the hanging knight: by pawn (4/10: gxf6, exf6, fxe5, dxe5), by rook (2/10: Rxf3, Rxf6), by bishop (2/10: Bxf6, Bxe3), by queen (1/10: Qxf3), or by knight (1/10: Nxf3). The player was seduced by the forcing nature of the move—assuming the opponent must respond to the check by moving the king or to the fork by saving the attacked piece—but completely overlooked that a defender already covers the landing square. In several cases (Positions 2, 7, 10), the player's idea would have worked if the opponent played the cooperative response (moving the king), but the simple capture was always available and devastating.

111.label: The losing side plays a king approach move in a decided pawn endgame where the king is too far from the opponent's passed pawn to change the outcome.
111.description: 10/10 positions feature the LOSING side making a king move in a deeply decided endgame (all evaluations exceed 500cp against the moving side). 10/10 positions involve at least one unstoppable passed pawn that the opponent's king is trying to approach or intercept. The defending king is typically 4-6 files away from the critical pawn, making the race geometrically impossible. 6/10 positions show 0 centipawn loss, confirming these aren't true errors but rather forced defensive moves in hopeless positions where all options are equivalent. The average of 2.8 good moves reflects that multiple king paths lead to the same lost outcome. 9/10 are pure pawn endgames (one includes a bishop), and the common thread is a distant king futilely marching toward an unstoppable promotion.
111.old_chip: Futile king chase in lost endgame

110.label: Playing slow positional or developmental moves while an immediate tactical crisis demands urgent attention.
110.description: All 10/10 positions feature an immediate critical threat (mate, hanging piece, unstoppable promotion, or devastating check sequence) that the player completely ignores in favor of a 'quiet' move — typically a pawn advance (5/10: c5, h4, c5, a5, e5) or piece repositioning (5/10: Bc5, Bd3, Qc1, Ba5, Bd6). In 10/10 cases, the position demanded emergency action: addressing a mating threat (positions 2, 4), defending a hanging/attacked piece (positions 1, 3, 6), blocking a promotion (position 9), or neutralizing an attack on an exposed king (positions 5, 7, 8, 10). The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were razor-sharp positions with essentially one correct defensive resource. In 7/10 cases, the played move not only fails to address the threat but actively creates a NEW weakness (opening squares for enemy pieces, removing defenders, hanging material). The average cp_loss of 3193 reflects the catastrophic nature of ignoring emergencies.

112.label: King moves from a safe edge/rim square onto a back rank or open diagonal where opponent's pieces immediately exploit the geometric vulnerability.
112.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves that voluntarily walk onto a critical line — either the back rank or an open diagonal — where the opponent's pieces can immediately deliver checks, win material, or deliver checkmate. In 8/10 cases, the king moves to the back rank (g8, f8, c1, g1) enabling back-rank mates or forcing checks (Rd8+, Qh8#, Rf1#). In 7/10 cases, the destination square also sits on a dangerous diagonal (a2-g8, a7-g1, a8-g2) where queens or bishops deliver tempo-gaining checks. The correct alternative was almost always a king retreat to the corner or rim — Kh8 instead of Kg8 (positions 1, 10), g6 instead of Kg8 (positions 2, 6), Ka1 instead of Kc1 (position 9), Kh1 instead of Kg1/Kg2 (positions 5, 7). The average cp_loss of 3989 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in immediate or near-immediate checkmate. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, confirming these were razor-thin decision points where only one king square was safe.

97.label: Making a natural-looking move that pursues a secondary goal while leaving a critical piece or square undefended, allowing the opponent to exploit the new vulnerability with a forcing move.
97.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a move with a clear purpose (attacking an opponent's piece, developing, centralizing, or advancing the king) but which fatally left a critical piece or square undefended. In 7/10 cases, the blunder specifically attacks or threatens an opponent's piece, but the target can evade or the threat can be ignored because the opponent has a stronger counter-forcing move (check, fork, or tempo-gaining capture) that wins the newly-undefended material. In 8/10 positions, the refutation involves a forcing move that gains tempo (check in positions 3,6,7,8,10; fork/capture with threat in positions 1,2,4,5,9), directly exploiting the piece left en prise. The average number of good moves available was only 1.9, indicating these are critical-moment positions where the player needed to find a specific tactical solution rather than play a 'normal' move. In all cases, the blunder prioritizes a secondary strategic aim over the position's actual tactical priority—whether that's maintaining a blocking piece (positions 3,10), protecting a hanging piece (positions 1,2,5,6,8), addressing a vulnerability (positions 4,9), or respecting king safety (positions 3,7).

117.label: Playing a slow, non-urgent pawn advance (typically on a flank) while an immediate tactical threat demands concrete action.
117.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn push that wastes a critical tempo in a position requiring urgent concrete play. 9/10 are flank pawn advances (a-file: 6 positions, c-file: 3 positions, g-file: 1 position), with only 1 central push (e4). In 8/10 cases, the opponent has an active or imminent kingside attack that the pawn move completely ignores. The tag 'tempo_loss' applies to all 10 positions, and 'king_safety' appears in 8/10. The average number of good moves available was only 1.8, meaning these positions demanded precise, concrete responses — yet the player chose a slow positional pawn advance instead. The average cp_loss of 1198 reflects how catastrophic these tempo wastes are: the opponent immediately escalates their tactical threats with the gifted free move. In 6/10 cases, the refutation involves a piece sacrifice, fork, or mating attack that was already threatened but becomes unstoppable after the wasted tempo.

118.label: A knight moves to an apparently active square but removes itself from a critical defensive role, leaving a piece, pawn, or square fatally unguarded.
118.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving to a 'natural' or seemingly active square while unknowingly abandoning a crucial defensive function from its origin square. In 4/10 positions (Positions 1, 3, 8, and partially 5), the knight on b8 was the sole defender of the c6 pawn and moved away (to d7 or a6), allowing immediate captures on c6. In 2/10 positions (4 and 7), a knight defended another knight (d4), and its departure to a 'better' square left the partner piece hanging to a simple capture. In Position 6, a knight on d1 guarded b2 and moved to e3; in Position 9, a knight on e7 guarded c8 and moved to d5 allowing back-rank mate. In Position 10, a knight on h2 served as a latent recapture resource for g4 and moved to f3 where both it and g4 became targets. In Position 5, the knight on c1 could block checks on d3 but moved to b3, enabling a mating attack. The average cp_loss of 2141 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights. 9/10 were middlegame positions where the defensive role was non-obvious, and all involved the knight appearing to improve its activity while fatally compromising the position's structural integrity.

107.label: King or queen moves to a central/active square as a generic improvement while ignoring a concrete tactical requirement in the position.
107.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet (non-capturing, non-checking) King or Queen moves toward central or 'active' squares. 7/10 are King moves and 3/10 are Queen moves. 8/10 occur in endgames where 'centralize your king' is a dominant heuristic. In 8/10 positions (excluding the 2 with 0cp loss), the player chose a general positional improvement over a specific concrete action: Position 1 centralizes the king into a fork; Position 4 plays Qd4 instead of Qh2#; Position 7 plays Qg5 instead of Qxe7 winning the exchange; Position 8 plays Ke6 instead of g7+ forcing mate; Position 10 plays Ke3 instead of repositioning the rook on the a-file. Even in positions 2 and 5 (where the move happens to be correct), the move still fits the pattern of a quiet royal piece step toward the center. The feature detects the behavioral pattern of 'improve my most important piece's position' regardless of whether a forcing tactical action exists.

123.label: A quiet pawn push to harass the opponent's queen when a concrete tactical opportunity (fork, capture, check, or combination) demanded immediate execution.
123.description: All 10/10 positions feature an identical pattern: a pawn advance (h3, b6, a3, a5, h5, h4, g3, a6) played specifically to attack or chase the opponent's queen from an active square. In every case, the queen was perceived as annoying or threatening, but a far stronger concrete move existed — winning material (5/10: fork winning the queen, capturing a hanging piece, taking an undefended pawn, capturing a bishop, winning the b-pawn), delivering a forcing check (2/10), or executing a decisive combination (3/10: Bxg7 ripping open the king, Qb3+ exploiting a diagonal, g4 driving a bishop off a critical pawn). The average centipawn loss was 283, with 8/10 positions having only 1 good move available, demonstrating these were critical-precision moments. In 7/10 cases the queen simply relocated to an equal or superior square after the pawn push, and in 4/10 the pawn advance actively weakened the pusher's own king shelter or pawn structure.

119.label: Capturing an active or threatening enemy knight when a superior tactical or strategic resource exists elsewhere.
119.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player capturing an enemy knight that appears dangerous, menacing, or annoying — yet in every case a significantly better move was available. The captured knights were typically centralized intruders (d3, d4, e3, e5 in 7/10 positions), near-king attackers (g4, h6 in 2/10), or seemingly free material (a3 in 1/10). The better moves varied: in 3/10 positions the player missed winning bigger material outright (capturing a queen in positions 2, 7; winning a free bishop in position 5); in 3/10 the knight capture fatally compromised king safety by opening lines (positions 4, 8) or allowing tempo-gaining recaptures (position 5); in 2/10 a move-order finesse was needed before the capture (positions 6, 9); and in 2/10 the knight could have been won more efficiently without the trade's concessions (positions 1, 10 — where Qf2 trapped the knight entirely). The average cp_loss of 2063 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights, with 3/10 resulting in forced checkmate.

114.label: Capturing an enemy piece near your own king that allows the opponent's queen to recapture on that square with devastating king attacks.
114.description: In 10/10 positions, the player captures an enemy piece that appears threatening or free, and in 10/10 cases the refutation is the opponent's queen recapturing on the exact same square (Qxh6 in 4 positions, Qxh3 in 3 positions, Qxa6+, Qxf3+, and Qxd7# in the others). The captured piece was positioned near the player's own king in 9/10 cases, and the act of capturing it either removed a critical defensive piece (the fianchettoed g2 bishop in 3/10), opened a file toward the player's own king (g-file opened via gxh6 in 3/10, h-file via gxh3 in 1/10), or placed a piece on a square aligned with a mating diagonal/file (2/10). The queen's arrival on the capture square is lethal because 7/10 involve immediate checkmate threats (Qh7#, Qg7#, Qh2#, Qxd7#), and 8/10 refutations involve check or unstoppable mate. Only 1.6 good alternatives existed on average, indicating these are critical moments demanding precise calculation rather than instinctive piece removal.

120.label: A bishop captures a central pawn when it should be maintaining its defensive/positional role or addressing a more urgent threat.
120.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a pawn on a central or near-central square (c4, d4, d5×2, d6, e4, e5×3, f5). In every case, the bishop was serving a more important purpose before the capture — either defending the king (positions 7, 10), maintaining positional pressure (positions 5, 8), or simply sitting on a safe square (positions 1, 4). In 4/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 6, 10), the bishop lands on the capture square completely undefended and is immediately recaptured or exploited through tempo-gaining moves. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 7, 8), the bishop successfully captures but trades itself for inadequate material, removing a piece doing critical work. In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 9), the capture ignores a more urgent tactical threat that the opponent immediately exploits. The average centipawn loss of 1174 reflects the severity — these aren't subtle inaccuracies but position-wrecking material greed decisions. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, suggesting these arose in tense positions requiring discipline.

121.label: Routine castling played on autopilot when the position demands concrete calculation of immediate tactical threats or opportunities.
121.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling moves (8 O-O, 2 O-O-O) played as 'natural' developing moves that ignore urgent tactical demands. In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 6, 7), castling misses a concrete tactic the player should execute first (capturing a hanging piece, winning the exchange via Nf3+, or preventing a forced combination). In 4/10 positions (4, 5, 8, 9), castling moves the king INTO a specific structural weakness that becomes immediately exploitable (g6 pawn captured, d6 advance enabled, b-file ripped open, e7 bishop left hanging). In 2/10 positions (1, 10), castling removes the king from a square where it was defending a critical piece or guarding against pawn breaks. The average cp_loss of 291 confirms these are serious errors, not marginal inaccuracies. Notably, 8/10 positions featured a rook on the open e-file creating the ILLUSION that the king urgently needed to move, when in fact the king on the e-file was often serving a useful function (making Rxe7 check rather than a free capture, or defending pieces on adjacent squares). The best alternatives across all positions involved either manual king walks (Kf2, Kd8), queen moves to relieve pressure, or immediate tactical strikes.

124.label: Promoting a pawn to a queen when the opponent's rook immediately captures it, instead of first deflecting the rook, improving piece placement, or maintaining the pawn as a threat.
124.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn promoting to a queen that is immediately captured by the opponent's rook on the next move. In every single case, the opponent's rook was already positioned on the promotion file (or could reach the promotion square in one move), making the capture trivial and obvious. The better alternatives fell into consistent sub-patterns: in 5/10 positions the correct move was a king maneuver to improve placement before the inevitable exchange (positions 1, 2, 7, 8, 9); in 2/10 positions the correct move was a piece sacrifice to deflect or exchange the rook off the critical file before promoting (positions 6, 10); in 2/10 positions the correct move was to advance another pawn first to improve the resulting position after the exchange (positions 4, 5); and in 1/10 position an underpromotion was optimal due to subtle tablebase differences (position 3). The cp_loss ranged widely from 0 to 464, but the structural error was identical: releasing the tension of a promotion threat by committing to it prematurely, allowing a clean rook-captures-queen exchange that left the promoting side worse than if the pawn had remained as a persistent positional asset.

122.label: Moving a bishop to a seemingly active central square where it becomes tactically exposed or wastes a critical tempo.
122.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being repositioned (non-capture, non-check) to a central or semi-central square (f5, g4, e6, f4, d5, f6, c5, e4) that appears active but is tactically flawed. In 4/10 positions (5, 8, 10, and partially 6), the bishop lands on a square where it can be immediately captured by an opponent's piece (knight, rook, or pawn with tempo). In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 4), the bishop abandons a dominant outpost (h7, h3, f7) where it was performing a crucial strategic function — imprisoning enemy pieces or fueling a diagonal battery attack. In 9/10 positions, the move wastes a tempo when immediate tactical action or counterplay was available (Ra6, Nxe5, b5, Qa8, exd6, a5, d3, Nf6). The average cp_loss of 309 reflects how these 'improving' bishop moves consistently transform winning/equal positions into significantly worse ones. Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical decision points demanding precision rather than aesthetics.

116.label: Knight repositions to a seemingly reasonable square, abandoning a dominant outpost, blocking a critical pawn break, or landing on a tactically vulnerable square.
116.description: All 10 positions feature knight moves that appear natural or developing but catastrophically miss the position's concrete demands. 3/10 involve retreating a knight from a dominant outpost (Ne4→c3, Nf5→g3, Nd2→f3 abandoning Nc4), surrendering the positional backbone of the advantage. 4/10 place the knight on a square where it can be captured with devastating structural or tactical consequences (Nf3 captured by bishop destroying pawn shield in positions 2, 7, 10; Ng6 captured allowing mating attack in position 8). 2/10 block a critical pawn advance by occupying the pawn's target square (Nc6 blocking ...c6, Nc4 blocking c4 break). 8/10 moves land on the third rank (f3, g3, c3) or its equivalent (g6 for Black), suggesting these are 'routine' repositioning moves to squares that look standard but are concretely wrong. The average cp_loss of 1203 reflects that these moves squander enormous advantages because they prioritize piece placement aesthetics over the position's concrete tactical and strategic requirements.

126.label: A rook moves to a seemingly active square but abandons its essential defensive duty, typically back-rank coverage or protection of a key piece/pawn, enabling an immediate tactical punishment.
126.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook move (the 10th is a king move with the same thematic error) that leaves a critical defensive station for an illusory aggressive square. 5/10 positions directly result in back-rank checkmate or mating nets after the rook vacates the 8th rank (Positions 1, 4, 5, 7, 8). 3/10 involve the rook abandoning defense of a key pawn or square, enabling captures or forks (Positions 2, 6, 10). The remaining cases involve the rook landing on an exposed square where it becomes trapped or exchanged unfavorably (Position 9) or missing a superior tactical option entirely (Position 3). The average cp_loss is extremely high (3764), reflecting that these 'active' rook moves frequently convert survivable losing positions into immediate forced checkmates. 7/10 positions had only 1-3 good moves available, indicating extremely narrow defensive requirements that the players failed to recognize.

113.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning (usually rooks to defensive squares) when the position demands an immediate active or forcing move.
113.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves as the blunder (the remaining two are a queen retreat and a pawn push). In all 10 cases, the played move is a slow, non-forcing repositioning to a 'natural-looking' square — defending a pawn, doubling on a file, or improving placement — while the position demanded immediate concrete action. The best moves across these positions required urgent measures: king escape (2/10), contesting a critical file with the correct piece (3/10), active counterplay/attack (3/10), or a simple capture (2/10). The common error is prioritizing a logical-seeming but slow improvement when the opponent has a forcing plan that executes in one tempo. In 7/10 positions, the blunder specifically gives the opponent a free tempo to execute a decisive invasion, sacrifice, or forcing sequence. The average cp_loss of 3026 reflects that these 'reasonable-looking' passive moves frequently cross a critical threshold from defensible to lost.

128.label: Advancing the knight-file pawn (b or g) to challenge an enemy bishop deeply embedded on the adjacent rook file near one's own king, fatally weakening the king's shelter or losing critical tempo.
128.description: In 10/10 positions, an enemy bishop sits intrusively on the rook file adjacent to the player's king (h2 in positions 1 and 6, h7 in positions 4, 5, and 8, a2 in positions 3 and 7, a7 in positions 2, 9, and 10). In every case, the player advances the neighboring knight-file pawn one square (g3, g6, b3, or b6) attempting to chase, trap, or restrict this bishop. In 7/10 positions the pawn advance catastrophically weakens the king's pawn shield, enabling immediate tactical exploitation (discovered attacks, captures of the weakened pawn, or checkmate via newly opened diagonals). In 3/10 positions (2, 9, 10) the pawn advance primarily loses decisive tempo when forcing moves were available. The best moves instead involved piece development (6/10), forcing checks or captures (3/10), or tactical piece exchanges that addressed the bishop without structural damage (4/10). The average cp_loss of 2185 reflects multiple positions where this pattern led to immediate checkmate.

135.label: Playing a non-urgent wing pawn advance (a, b, or h file) when the position demands immediate tactical action such as piece activation, king flight, or threat defense.
135.description: All 10/10 positions feature single-step pawn advances on flank files (a-file: 6 positions, b-file: 2 positions, h-file: 2 positions) played when the position urgently required a different type of move. In 7/10 positions, the critical need was king safety—either creating flight squares, fleeing with the king, or maintaining a pawn shield. In 6/10 cases, the pawn push directly allowed forced checkmate where none existed before (positions 4, 6, 7, 9, 10 went from large advantage to forced mate; position 1 was already mate). In 4/10 positions, the correct move involved piece activation (rook repositioning or knight moves). The average cp_loss of 4738 is catastrophically high because these flank pawn moves are maximally irrelevant to the critical sector of the board. 8/10 moves were played by Black. The positions span middlegame (5) and endgame (5) equally, showing this pattern occurs regardless of phase whenever the player defaults to a 'quiet' wing pawn push instead of addressing an emergency.

133.label: Player makes a piece/pawn move to 'improve' their position while their exposed king urgently needed to move to safety.
133.description: 9/10 positions feature an exposed king on an open file or vulnerable square where the engine's best move was a king retreat/evacuation (Kd8, Kf8, Kc8, Kd7, Kb6, Kh7, Kh3, Kc1). Instead, the player chose a 'developing' or 'shielding' move with another piece—typically a bishop to e6/e7/d6 (7/10 positions), but also a pawn push or knight/rook move. In 8/10 cases the king was centralized or exposed with open files aimed directly at it. The played moves look natural (blocking files, developing pieces, bolstering pawn shields), but they fatally ignore the one-move window to evacuate the king, allowing the opponent to exploit the king's continued exposure via sacrifices, pawn advances with tempo, or forced tactical sequences. Position 10 (cp_loss=0) is the exception where Be6 was actually correct because the king's exposure was irrelevant given Black's overwhelming attack.

132.label: Developing a bishop to a long diagonal (especially b2/b7) as a 'natural' move while ignoring concrete tactical threats, vulnerabilities, or superior alternatives.
132.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to a seemingly natural long-diagonal square, with 7/10 specifically going to b2 or b7 (classic fianchetto squares). In every case, the position demanded concrete action rather than routine development. In 5/10 positions, the bishop lands on a diagonal blocked by a fixed pawn (e5 blocking b2 in positions 1,7; d5 blocking b7 in positions 3,9; e5 blocking the diagonal utility in position 5), rendering it strategically useless. In 4/10 positions, the bishop lands on an undefended or tactically vulnerable square that is immediately exploitable (Be3 attacked by Re2, Bf4 attacked via Rd4, Bb2 forkable by Qb6+, Bb7 targetable by Rb1). In 2/10 positions, the move specifically misses a winning tactic (Ng3 fork in position 10, Ba3+ winning sequence in position 2). The average cp_loss of 294 reflects catastrophic consequences, and only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where the 'natural-looking' bishop move was a seductive trap.

139.label: In a King's Gambit structure, White moves the f-pawn forward (fxe5 or f5) before developing Nf3, catastrophically opening the h4-e1 diagonal to Qh4+.
139.description: All 10/10 positions arise from King's Gambit structures (1.e4 e5 2.f4) where White's f-pawn has already advanced from f2 to f4, partially weakening the kingside. In every case, White then moves the f-pawn again—8/10 via fxe5 capture and 2/10 via f4-f5 advance—before developing any pieces, particularly without a knight on f3 to guard h4. All 10/10 positions feature the White king still on e1 with a weak pawn shield, and in all 10/10 the primary refutation is Qh4+ exploiting the now completely unguarded h4-e1 diagonal. The resulting tactical sequence typically continues with g3 Qxe4+ forking king and h1 rook (8/10) or Ke2 Qxe4+ with perpetual checks winning material (2/10). In every case, the best moves were developing moves (Nf3, d3, Bc4, Nc3) that either guard h4 directly or maintain the f-pawn as a diagonal shield. Average cp_loss was 369, representing roughly a full rook's worth of material.

134.label: King voluntarily moves to a square where it becomes entombed or cornered, enabling immediate checkmate or inescapable perpetual check.
134.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that reduces the king's available escape squares, walking into a mating net or perpetual check cage. In 7/10 positions the result is immediate forced checkmate (within 1-2 moves), while in 3/10 the result is perpetual check drawing a won position. 7/10 moves go toward the board edge (h-file: Kh1, Kh1, Kh6, Kh5, Kh6; a-file: Ka6, Ka6), while 3/10 move to central squares equally fatal due to surrounding pieces (Ke6, Kd7, Kd6). In nearly every case (9/10), the king's own pawns or pieces block critical escape squares on the destination, creating a self-entombment effect. The average cp_loss of 6046 reflects the catastrophic nature — these moves overwhelmingly convert playable or winning positions into checkmates or forced draws. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these arise in positions demanding precise king placement where the margin for error is essentially zero.

131.label: Playing aggressive-looking queen moves (usually checks) that allow the opponent to favorably trade queens, eliminating the player's dynamic compensation.
131.description: 8/10 positions feature queen moves that directly invite or allow a queen exchange, and 6/10 of those are queen checks specifically. In every case, the refutation involves the opponent simply capturing the queen (Qxb6, Qxd5, Qxd4, Qxe3, Qxe4, Qxe6, Qxc3, Qxb4), transforming a dynamic position into a statically lost endgame. The critical shared context is that in 9/10 positions, the blundering side relied on queen activity for compensation—whether it was pressure against an exposed king (positions 4, 5, 9, 10), piece coordination threats (positions 1, 3, 7), or perpetual check potential (position 6). Once queens are traded, these dynamic factors vanish while structural deficiencies (passed pawns, pawn majorities, extra material) become decisive. The 2/10 bishop moves are variants: Bf3 (position 2) attacks the queen hoping for tempo but loses time when the queen sidesteps, and Bf7 (position 8) ignores the urgent need to trade queens, representing the inverse error. The average cp_loss of 1184 reflects how catastrophic these simplifications are—the player essentially trades away their only active piece for a hopelessly lost technical position.
131.old_chip: Checks that invite fatal queen trades

137.label: A king move that appears to improve safety or centralize but actually walks into a square where the king becomes tactically exploitable through checks, mating nets, or open-file attacks.
137.description: 10/10 positions feature a king move (including one castling move) that worsens the king's tactical situation. In 8/10 cases, the king moves to a square where it immediately becomes vulnerable to forcing checks or mating attacks along newly-created lines (open files, diagonals, or adjacency to capturable pieces). In 7/10 positions, the position demanded a non-king move—typically an aggressive tactical shot (Rxg2+, Bh3+, Bc3, Rxd6, Be5, Rhe8, Kg2-staying-put). The average cp_loss of 4078 reflects that these are catastrophic blunders. In 6/10 cases, the refutation involves an immediate check or forced mate exploiting the king's new square. The moves share an 'instinctive safety-seeking' quality: the player perceives their king as threatened and moves it to what appears safer or more central, but the destination square is actually more exposed to the opponent's attacking resources.

140.label: Moving a piece onto a square where an enemy pawn advance simultaneously attacks it and another piece, creating an unavoidable double attack.
140.description: 10/10 positions share the same devastating pattern: the played move places a piece on a square that creates a dual vulnerability with another friendly piece, both sitting on adjacent diagonals of an advancing enemy pawn. In 7/10 cases, a central pawn advance (e5 in positions 1,2,5,7; f4 in position 3; e4 in position 9; d4 in position 4) creates the fork. In 2/10 cases (positions 6 and 9), a c-pawn or e-pawn advance forks two minor pieces on the b3/d3 or d3/f3 squares. In 2/10 positions (8 and 10), the pawn advance delivers check against the king, gaining tempo to capture an adjacent piece on the next move. The piece types vary widely (Queen: 2, Bishop: 3, Knight: 2, King: 2, Pawn: 1), confirming the pattern is about the geometric relationship to the advancing pawn rather than the piece type. All 10 moves had superior alternatives (avg 2.6 good moves available) that specifically avoided the vulnerable square.

138.label: The queen repositions to an apparently active square but abandons its critical role protecting a key piece, leaving that piece hanging or tactically exploitable.
138.description: In 8/8 positions, the player makes a quiet queen repositioning move (no checks, no captures) that looks purposeful but severs a critical defensive connection. In 5/8 cases, the queen specifically abandons protection of a knight (d7 knight in positions 1, 5, 6; a5 knight in position 7; e5 knight in position 8), leaving it immediately capturable. In 2/8 cases (positions 3 and 4), the queen abandons coordination defending an embedded bishop on f2. In position 10, the queen moves to a square that enables a forced exchange sequence. The average cp_loss of 394 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors—they leave full pieces hanging. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions demanding precise defensive awareness rather than creative queen maneuvers. The refutations consistently involve simply capturing the now-undefended piece (Nxd7, Qxd7, Bxe5, Bxa5, Rgxf2, Qxf2, Rxg5).

129.label: Rook moves to the first/back rank in positions with advanced passed pawns near promotion, often as a stereotyped response rather than calculating the sharpest continuation.
129.description: 10/10 positions feature rook moves in positions with advanced passed pawns (typically 1-2 squares from promotion). 6/10 moves specifically go to the first rank (Re1 or Rb1), and 7/10 are played by Black with a pawn on a2, c2, or f2.
