The feature captures a recognizable endgame pattern—placing the rook behind a passed pawn on its promotion square—but critically, this template move is not always optimal. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 6) the move is indeed best (0 cp loss), but in the remaining cases the player applies this 'rook behind passed pawn' heuristic when a sharper move exists: immediate promotion (position 7, 9511 cp loss), a queen check sequence (position 8, 275 cp loss), capturing an enemy pawn (position 9, 523 cp loss), or king activation (position 10, 154 cp loss). The average good moves available is only 1.8, confirming these are narrow positions where the 'obvious' rook maneuver may not be correct.

127.label: Moving a rook that is performing a critical positional function (guarding key squares, controlling files, blockading) to create redundant/doubled pressure, when the other rook should move or immediate tactical action is required.
127.description: 9/10 positions feature disambiguated rook moves (Rff2, Rgf4, Ree3, Rfg5, Red2, Rde5, Rdh7, Rhg6, Ree7), meaning two rooks could reach the destination and the player chose the WRONG one. In every case, the moved rook was performing a vital function on its original square: guarding the king's escape route (Position 1, Rff2 blocked d2), controlling a critical central square (Position 8, Rdh7 abandoned d5 control), blockading a dangerous pawn (Position 10, Ree7 left e8 blockade), maintaining multi-purpose pressure (Position 4, Rfg5 abandoned f5's versatile role), or occupying an open file that shouldn't be vacated (Position 3, Ree3 left the e-file). 8/10 positions had the player attempting to double rooks or create file/rank batteries, but the 'preparation' move was punished because the abandoned function was immediately exploited. The average cp_loss of 4042 reflects catastrophic consequences—including 4 positions leading to forced mate. Position 6 (Qg5) follows the same spirit: a non-forcing 'threatening' piece move when immediate decisive action was required.

143.label: Advancing a passed (or advanced) pawn when the position demands addressing an urgent tactical need such as king safety, piece vulnerability, or a forcing sequence.
143.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the blunder move — specifically an advanced or passed pawn being pushed one square further toward promotion. In 9/10 cases, the pawn pushed is explicitly a passed pawn or creates one. The common error is prioritizing the 'slow' threat of pawn promotion over an immediate tactical crisis: in 7/10 positions the urgent issue was king safety (exposed king on f5, h7, e5, h8, h2, g7, or back-rank vulnerability), in 3/10 the issue was a piece left hanging or a deflection tactic exploiting undefended material, and in 2/10 a forced mating sequence was available instead. The best moves in all 10 positions involved either prophylactic king moves (Kg8, Kg3, Kg4), piece coordination/defense (Rdc1, Nd4, Rab8, Rf7), or forcing tactical sequences (Re8+, Qd4+). The average cp_loss of 4032 reflects that many of these pawn pushes converted winning positions into losses or equal positions into disasters, because they wasted a critical tempo on a non-forcing move while the opponent had immediate tactical resources available.

130.label: Playing an ambitious or attacking move while overlooking that a piece is undefended and can be captured.
130.description: 9/10 positions feature the player making an aggressive move (check, pawn advance, tactical shot) while a piece is hanging or becomes hanging as a direct consequence. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 8), the moved piece lands on a square directly controlled by an opponent's bishop, allowing immediate capture. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 7, 9), the move ignores that an existing friendly piece is en prise and will be captured with tempo (check or fork). In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 10), a pawn advance removes or fails to address the defense of a hanging piece. In position 3, the move creates a mating threat but ignores an intermediate capture with check. Position 2 is the weakest fit, involving tempo loss in a mating attack rather than a strict hanging piece, though it shares the pattern of choosing an ambitious move over the concrete forcing continuation. The average cp_loss of 1237 reflects catastrophic material loss. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical tactical moments requiring precision rather than ambition.

142.label: The queen captures a piece (usually a rook) on a remote back-rank square, displacing itself from critical king-safety duties or missing a stronger intermediate move.
142.description: 10/10 positions feature a queen capturing a piece on the first or eighth rank, with 7/10 specifically targeting corner squares (a1, h1, a8, h8) and the remaining 3 on near-corner or edge back-rank squares (b8, g1, g8, e8). In 8/10 positions, the core punishment is a devastating attack against the player's own king that the displaced queen cannot return to defend — the opponent launches mating attacks (positions 1, 4, 7, 8, 9), perpetual checks (position 4), or forces unfavorable queen trades (position 2). In 3/10 positions (3, 6, 10), a stronger intermediate move (check or zwischenzug) should have been inserted before the capture to gain tempo or displace the opponent's king first. The average cp_loss of 5867 reflects that 7/10 positions involved evaluation swings exceeding 9000cp (often from winning/equal to forced mate against). Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, meaning these were critical decision points demanding precision over greed.

146.label: Playing a preparatory fianchetto pawn move (b3/b6/g3/g6) when the position demands immediate tactical or developmental action.
146.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance to prepare a bishop fianchetto (b3, b6, g3, or g6) that is confirmed in every analysis as intending to place a bishop on the long diagonal. In 10/10 cases, the move ignores an urgent concrete demand — whether a tactical threat (fork in positions 2 and 7, sacrifice in position 10, check in position 8), a critical central tension requiring resolution (positions 1, 5, 8), or king safety concerns with the king still in the center (positions 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). 8/10 positions occur in the opening phase where development tempo is at a premium. The average cp_loss of 277 reflects how severely a single slow preparatory pawn move can be punished when tactical dynamics are ripe. In 6/10 cases, the b-pawn moves (b3 or b6) preparing a queenside fianchetto, while 4/10 feature g-pawn moves (g3 or g6) preparing a kingside fianchetto. The positions vary in the specific punishment (forks, pins, sacrifices, positional domination), but the root cause is identical: prioritizing a multi-move positional plan over the position's immediate tactical requirements.

125.label: Choosing a materialistic capture or aggressive pawn advance instead of the correct forcing move (check, sacrifice, or piece coordination).
125.description: 8/10 positions show the player choosing a move motivated by material gain (capturing a piece/pawn) or aggressive advancement when a stronger forcing continuation existed. In 5/10 cases the move is a pawn advance (e6, f5, d5, c6, d6), and in 3/10 it's a piece capture (Qxd3, Rxb7, Bxg6). The correct moves missed were forcing checks or sacrifices in 5/10 positions (Qe1+ for mate, Rg7+ for fork, Nd3+ for counterplay, Nxe4 for free piece, Ka4 for survival), and preparatory piece-activation moves in 4/10 positions (Rhg1, Bd3/Be2, Re5, Qb6). The average cp_loss of 2181 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical moments demanding precision where the player defaulted to the superficially obvious option. In 3/10 positions specifically (positions 1, 3, 7), a pawn advance removed protection from the player's own bishop, leaving it hanging. In 3/10 positions (4, 5, 10), a capture grabbed material but missed a far stronger forcing sequence involving checks.

147.label: A speculative wing pawn advance (a/b/g/h file) that is either immediately capturable or wastes critical tempo when piece activity or central play was required.
147.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance on the a, b, g, or h file — never a central pawn move. In 6/10 positions (positions 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9), the advanced pawn was directly capturable for free, typically by a bishop with a clear diagonal (Bxg5 in three cases, Bxb5, Qxb4, Bxg4). In the remaining 4/10 (positions 1, 6, 8, 10), the pawn was not immediately hanging but constituted a pure tempo loss when decisive piece moves (Rhe1, Nb5, fxe4, f5) were available. The best moves across all positions were universally piece-developing, centralizing, or tactical in nature — never flank pawn advances. The average cp_loss of 297 reflects the severity: these positions demanded precision and urgency, yet the players chose slow, non-forcing pawn lunges that either gifted material or surrendered the initiative. In 8/10 cases, the pawn advanced into territory controlled by an opponent's piece (especially dark-squared bishops on the c1-h6 diagonal for g5 pushes).

144.label: King moves toward an advanced passed pawn to support promotion when a more forcing or tactically precise alternative exists.
144.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves in endgames with advanced passed pawns (typically 1-2 squares from promotion). In 9/10 cases, the king moves directly toward the passed pawn with the intent of escorting it to promotion. The common error is that this 'natural' approach is suboptimal: in 4/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 10) the king ends up misplaced or stranded after the pawn resolves (e.g., Kg7 leads to king stuck on h8, Kf7 strands king on g8). In 3/10 positions (3, 6, 9) a forcing tactical move (check, capture, or deflection) was available that would have converted more efficiently. In 2/10 (8, 9) the king move directly allowed the opponent to neutralize the pawn. Only 3/10 positions had more than one good move available, confirming these are narrow positions demanding precision over natural play. Average cp_loss of 233 is inflated by several catastrophic blunders (positions 4, 6, 9) where the escort approach completely threw away the game.

149.label: A central pawn advance (d/e/f file) that relinquishes control of a critical adjacent square, gifting the opponent's knight a dominant outpost.
149.description: All 10 positions feature a one-square central pawn advance (d, e, or f file) that permanently surrenders pawn control over a diagonally adjacent square. In 8/10 positions, the opponent's knight immediately occupies the newly unguarded square as a powerful outpost (Position 1: e4 gives up d4; Position 2: e5 gives up d5; Position 3: d4 gives up e4; Position 4: d4 gives up c4; Position 5: d4 gives up e4; Position 6: d5 gives up c5; Position 9: e4 gives up d4; Position 10: d5 gives up e5). In the remaining 2/10, the pawn advance still creates critical structural weaknesses — Position 7's f5 blocks its own knight from the f5 outpost while surrendering e4, and Position 8's f5 weakens dark squares allowing tactical exploitation. The intent behind these moves typically appears aggressive — chasing a piece, gaining space, or restricting the opponent — but in every case the cure is worse than the disease. The average centipawn loss is 239, and the refutations are consistently clear (one best punishment in 10/10 cases), indicating these are sharply punishable errors rather than gradual inaccuracies.

151.label: Bishop moves to a peripheral square (a/b/g/h-file), abandoning a critical function and losing tempo to an immediate counter-attack.
151.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop relocating from a useful post to a peripheral square (a-file, b-file, g-file, or h-file), where it is immediately punished. In 7/10 cases the bishop lands on the actual rim (a- or h-file: Ba4, Ba4, Ba6, Ba5, Ba7, Bh4, Bg4), with the remaining 3 landing on near-rim squares (Bb6, Bc7, Bb5). The common punishment mechanism is tempo loss: in 6/10 positions the bishop is directly attacked with a pawn or piece advance (b3, b4, Rdc1, Re1), forcing retreat or loss. In 4/10 cases, the bishop's departure from its original square leaves critical defensive functions unattended (king safety in positions 2, 4, 7; square control in position 5). The average cp_loss of 227 reflects that these are not minor inaccuracies but significant blunders, typically swinging evaluations by 1.5-3 pawns. Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these errors occurred in demanding positions where central/defensive moves were required rather than peripheral 'activation.'

157.label: The player makes a routine or greedy move while their own queen is en prise to a simple one-move capture.
157.description: All 9/9 positions share the exact same critical error: the player's queen is undefended and immediately capturable, yet they play some other move—often a capture or seemingly useful developing move—instead of saving their queen. In 9/9 cases, the primary refutation is a direct one-move capture of the player's queen (Nxe4, exf4, Bxd1, Bxa5, Bxe2, Nxd3, Rxb2, Bxg6, cxb5). The moves played are diverse in type—captures (fxe4, cxb5, Bxe5, fxe6, Bxc3, bxc4), a development move (Nc3), a pawn push (d3), and a flank advance (a4)—but all share the defining characteristic of ignoring the queen's immediate peril. In 6/9 positions, the blundering move is itself a capture, suggesting the player was focused on winning material rather than noticing their queen was attacked. The average cp_loss of 397 reflects that losing a queen (or allowing an overwhelmingly favorable queen capture) is typically game-ending.

150.label: Capturing seemingly free material on an open file where the piece becomes pinned, trapped, or attacked along that same line.
150.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures of apparently undefended material (9/10 are pawn captures) where the capturing piece lands on an open file or line that the opponent immediately exploits. In 7/10 positions, the refutation involves a rook seizing the same open file to create a pin against the player's own king or queen (positions 1, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 use rook-on-file pins; position 2 features recapture with check along the same file). In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 6), the piece becomes trapped or displaced after landing on the capture square. A striking sub-pattern: 6/10 positions involve the player's king sitting on the same file as the capturing piece, creating a direct pin motif. The uncastled king on the e-file appears in 5/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 7, 8), while g-file king alignment appears in 2/10 (9, 10). In every case, 2-3 safe alternatives existed that prioritized development, consolidation, or piece safety over material gain.

152.label: A bishop relocates to a seemingly active or logical square but unknowingly abandons a critical defensive or tactical function, typically leaving a knight hanging or exposing a devastating tactical blow.
152.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop move that looks natural or active but fatally breaks a hidden tactical connection. In 7/10 cases, the bishop was directly or indirectly protecting a knight from capture (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 9 leave knights immediately hanging; positions 3, 10 remove threats that prevent knight/piece captures). In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 6, 10), the bishop's departure from a specific diagonal removes coordination that allowed a devastating tactical blow (fork, sacrifice, or pawn capture of a defended piece). The average cp_loss of 350 reflects that these are catastrophic errors, not small inaccuracies. 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available, confirming these are narrow decision points. The bishops typically move from squares where they served non-obvious guardian roles (c4 protecting f7, e3 supporting c3, f4 blocking g-file, d6 covering f6) to squares that appear aggressive or safe (b5, g3, b3, g5, c5, b6) but are tactically irrelevant to the position's critical tension.

148.label: A powerfully-placed piece (usually a knight) is moved away from its dominant position to grab material or pursue a seemingly attractive tactical idea, when maintaining position or finding a more forcing continuation was superior.
148.description: 8/10 positions involve knight moves specifically, and in 7/10 the piece starts on a strong central or attacking outpost (e4 twice, d5, d3, g4, f6, b6) before relocating to an inferior square. In 5/10 positions the move involves a capture (Nxh1, Nxg4, Nxh2, Bxf6, plus Nd2 attacking material), revealing that material greed often motivates the error. The common thread is that the piece was exerting maximum influence from its current square — controlling key squares, supporting attacks, or defending critical points — and the player moved it for a short-term tactical lure. In positions 1 and 2, a knight on e4 moves to d2 where it becomes tactically vulnerable. In positions 3 and 7, pieces self-block their own rooks on critical files. In positions 5, 8, and 9, pieces capture pawns/material but sacrifice attacking momentum or defensive duties. In position 10, a key attacking bishop is traded away, releasing all pressure. The average cp_loss of 1210 reflects that several positions involved missing forced mates, underscoring how costly it is to abandon a dominant piece configuration.

145.label: Moving a piece (usually a bishop) to a seemingly improved square in an endgame when the position demands concrete pawn advances or tactical execution.
145.description: 7/10 positions involve bishop moves, with the remaining 3 being queen moves (2) and a king/knight move each. 7/10 occur in endgame positions. The defining characteristic is a quiet, non-capturing piece repositioning move to what appears to be a more 'active' square. In the 7/10 positions where this constitutes a mistake (avg cp_loss ~160 excluding the 0-loss positions), the correct alternatives were concrete forcing actions: pawn advances (h4 in position 1, b4 in positions 3/6), tactical combinations (Rxf6+ in position 9), or more functional placements addressing the actual critical factor (king centralization in position 7, bishop to c6 via f3 in positions 2/4). The 3/10 positions with 0 cp_loss (positions 5, 8, 10) represent cases where piece repositioning genuinely WAS the correct plan, suggesting the feature detects this move pattern universally rather than strictly errors.

136.label: Impulsive material-grabbing moves (usually pawn captures) that sacrifice a superior position by giving the opponent critical tempo or activating dormant pieces.
136.description: 8/10 positions involve captures (mostly pawn captures), and in 9/10 positions the moving side held a clear advantage before the blunder. The consistent pattern is: the player sees available material (usually a pawn) and grabs it immediately, when the position instead demanded a quieter preparatory or consolidating move. In Position 1, Nxe4 grabs a pawn but removes the key f6-defender; in Position 2, Bxa4 captures an isolated pawn but exposes the bishop and back rank; in Position 3, Nxf5 wins the f5-pawn but trades the well-placed knight and gives the bishop tempo; in Position 7, Bxe6 captures a pawn but trades away White's dominant attacking piece; in Position 8, bxc5 takes the c5-pawn but dramatically activates White's bishop; in Position 10, hxg2 captures the pawn without the crucial Bb6+ intermezzo, losing a decisive tempo. Even the non-capture blunders (Ne3 in Position 9, Nf4 in Position 4) share the theme of making an aggressive-looking move that removes a piece from its defensively critical post. The better alternatives in all cases were either piece-improving moves (Ne4, Ba2, Nh5), preparatory moves (Bb6+, Rg8, b5), or moves maintaining tension (Bxf3, Nf6). Only 1/10 positions (Position 6, gxf5) was actually correct, appearing as noise.

153.label: Pawn captures pawn on the wing files (a/b or g/h) to resolve direct pawn tension in simplified endgame positions.
153.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring a pawn-takes-pawn capture on the flank files. Specifically, 7/10 involve the a- or b-file (axb or bxa or cxb), and 6/10 involve the g- or h-file (hxg, gxh, gxf). Every single move resolves direct pawn tension where two pawns are in contact on adjacent wing files. While 5/10 positions show the capture as the best or near-best move (≤11cp loss), the remaining positions reveal significant errors: Position 8 lost 1113cp by releasing queenside tension that maintained a winning zugzwang, Position 9 lost 154cp through poor timing allowing king infiltration, Position 2 lost 74cp via move-order error (should have repositioned king first), and Position 10 lost 65cp by capturing with the wrong pawn. The feature detects this structural move pattern — the mechanical act of exchanging wing pawns — which in endgames frequently represents a critical decision point where maintaining tension, changing move order, or choosing which pawn captures can be the difference between winning and drawing.

159.label: King (or piece affecting king safety) moves to a square that creates immediate tactical vulnerability — checks, forks, or mates — when safer retreats were available.
159.description: 9/10 positions feature direct king moves to squares that prove immediately exploitable (the exception, Nd7, self-blocks the king's escape square enabling mate). In 7/10 cases, the king moves forward or toward the center (Kh4, Kf3, Ke7, Kf7, Ke3, Kd6, Kd8) rather than retreating to safety; the remaining king moves (Kh8, Ke8) retreat but to the WRONG square that creates new tactical vulnerabilities (diagonal/file exposure). In all 10 positions, the best alternatives involved retreating the king to back-rank or corner squares (Kg1/Kf1, Ke1/Kf1/Kd1, Kc8/Ke8, Kf8, Kb7) or eliminating the threatening piece. The average cp_loss of 4884 reflects that 6/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the move. Only 1.8 good moves existed on average, showing these arise in already-critical positions where precise king placement is the sole survival requirement.

141.label: Playing a natural-looking or principled move in a critical position that demands one specific concrete solution, resulting in severe evaluation loss.
141.description: All 10 positions share a critical characteristic: they are extremely narrow decision points (average 1.5 good moves available) where the player chose a 'textbook' or 'obvious-looking' move instead of the one precise move the position demanded. In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 7), a pawn move specifically removed a critical defensive guard of a square or line, allowing opponent exploitation via check or capture. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 9), a piece move that appears active (knight development, knight check) ignored an urgent tactical need or squandered a positional asset. In 3/10 positions (2, 8, 10), the player chose the wrong pawn advance or a passive move when a concrete tactical shot or precise intermezzo was required. The consistent thread is that the correct moves were often non-obvious (quiet pawn moves like c3/b3, queen exchanges like Qa5, defensive intermezzos like Rc4+, tactical shots like Bd5) while the blunders followed general principles (develop pieces, advance pawns, make captures, give checks) without calculating the position's specific demands. The average cp_loss of 354 reflects that these positions punish generic play severely.

154.label: Pawn captures that resolve pawn tension in positions with exposed kings, often when more forcing moves (checks, piece attacks) were available.
154.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (notation: [file]x[file][rank]), and all 10/10 positions have at least one severely exposed or weakly-shielded king mentioned in the position features. In 7/10 cases with significant centipawn loss (positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10), the pawn capture was suboptimal because a more forcing continuation existed—typically an immediate check or piece move exploiting the exposed king. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 7), the pawn capture was actually correct (0-16 cp loss), suggesting the feature fires on the move TYPE + position TYPE rather than exclusively on errors. The captures frequently occur on the kingside (hxg5 appears 3 times, hxg4 and fxg4 once each—5/10 on the g-file). The mistakes share a common theme of choosing a 'natural' material-gaining or tension-resolving pawn capture over a more dynamic continuation that directly exploits king vulnerability.

163.label: Capturing a central pawn with a pawn when a piece (usually a knight) should have taken instead, removing critical structural protection.
163.description: In 9/10 positions, the player captured a central pawn with another pawn when a piece capture (typically a knight) was clearly superior: positions 1, 7, 8, and 10 all had Nxd5/Nxe4/Nxf5 as the best move versus the played exd5/dxe4/exf5; positions 6 and 9 had multiple knight captures available (Nexc5/Ndxc5/Ncxe5/Ndxe5); position 5 had Ne4 as the best alternative. In all cases, the pawn capture removed a structurally vital defender, opening lines, diagonals, or squares that enabled devastating tactical punishment. The refutations consistently exploited newly-cleared diagonals (positions 7, 9), exposed hanging pieces (positions 1, 2, 3, 6), knight forks on vacated squares (positions 1, 5, 6, 7), or accelerated pawn storms against exposed kings (positions 8, 10). The average cp_loss of 278 reflects that these are severe errors with clear alternatives available (avg 2.3 good moves).

155.label: A piece relocates to a seemingly constructive square while leaving a critical defensive obligation unmet, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
155.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a piece (knights in 6/10, bishops in 2/10, rooks in 2/10) to a 'constructive-looking' square — centralizing, developing, attacking, or repositioning — while that piece (or its previous position) was performing a critical defensive function. In 4/10 cases (Nf7, Ne5, Rh6, Ne3), the moved piece itself became immediately capturable on its new square. In 3/10 cases (Nxe4, Nd4, Rf1), the departure left another piece or pawn fatally undefended. In 2/10 cases (Nfd2, Bd7), the piece self-blocked the king's escape square enabling immediate checkmate. In 1/10 cases (Bb6), a tempo was wasted on repositioning while mate-in-2 threats went unaddressed. The average cp_loss of 3940 reflects catastrophic consequences, and the average of only 1.6 good moves available shows these were razor-sharp positions requiring defensive precision rather than 'improving' moves. The connecting thread is that each move prioritized piece placement aesthetics over concrete calculation of what becomes undefended.

165.label: King moves that leave a previously-defended piece or pawn unguarded, allowing immediate capture.
165.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a king move (including one castling move) that abandons a critical defensive responsibility. In 9/10 cases, the king was directly guarding a specific piece or pawn, and by moving away, that asset becomes immediately capturable: Position 1 (Kc8 leaves a7 pawn), Position 2 (Kf5 leaves d5 pawn), Position 3 (Ke3 leaves c2 pawn), Position 4 (Kc6 leaves bishop on e6), Position 5 (Ke4 leaves c5 pawn), Position 7 (Kg5 leaves e6 pawn inadequately covered), Position 8 (Kc6 leaves knight on e7), Position 9 (O-O places rook on f8 as a tactical target), and Position 10 (Kd6 leaves f6 pawn). In 1/10 (Position 6), the king move creates a fork vulnerability rather than directly unguarding a piece. The best moves in all positions either maintain the king's defensive post, first secure the defended asset with another piece, or address the threat before relocating the king. The average cp_loss of 345 reflects that these undefended assets are typically captured cleanly and immediately.

156.label: Moving a knight to a natural-looking square when the position urgently demands a king move, pawn advance, or different piece entirely.
156.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves (plus 1 bishop move with identical logic) that look like normal piece development or repositioning but catastrophically ignore an urgent positional demand. In 5/10 positions, the correct move was a king escape (Kf8, Kb8, Kg1, Ke2, or similar). In 3/10 positions, the correct move was a pawn advance (c6 or c3) that the knight physically blocked by occupying its destination square (positions 4, 7, 10). In 1/10, the correct move was using the OTHER knight to the same square (position 6: Ndf6 vs Ngf6). In 1/10, the correct move was a queen move to the same square the knight went to (position 9: Qg3 vs Ng3). The average number of good moves was only 1.2, meaning these were narrow critical moments where only one idea worked. The knight moves all appeared superficially reasonable—centralizing, developing, saving material, or creating activity—but each one either landed on a tactically vulnerable square (captured immediately in 4/10), blocked a critical pawn (3/10), or abandoned a dominant post (3/10).

164.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn move in a position that demands an immediate tactical response to a critical threat or opportunity.
164.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (g6, f6, d5, h6, b3, a6, f5, c4, e5) and 1/10 is a non-forcing bishop move (Bb5), all sharing the characteristic of being slow, non-forcing moves in positions requiring urgent action. 8/10 positions had only 1-3 good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating razor-sharp tactical moments with no margin for passive play. 10/10 positions had the played move miss a critical tactic (capture, check, or forcing sequence). In 5/10 cases, the correct move was a capture of a dangerous enemy piece (Qxc8, Rxf2, Kxf2, Bxf7-related, Bd5). In 3/10 cases, the correct move was a forcing check or attack (Bd4+, Nd5, Nc6). The blunders consistently represent 'autopilot' moves — prophylactic pawn pushes (h6 for luft, a6 preventing Nb5, b3 for fianchetto, g6 for fianchetto) or aggressive-looking but strategically misguided advances (e5, f5, d5) — played in positions where the tactical situation demanded immediate concrete action.

161.label: Premature space-gaining pawn advances (predominantly b-pawn pushes) that remove the pawn from a critical defensive duty, creating immediate tactical or structural vulnerabilities.
161.description: 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance intended to gain space or expand on the flank, but which immediately weakens the position by removing that pawn from a defensive role. 6/10 are specifically b-pawn advances (b4 appears 4 times for White, b5 and b6 once each for Black), while the remaining 4 are analogous advances on other files (e5 twice, h4 once, f5 once). In every case, the player had 2-3 good alternatives focused on development, piece activity, or concrete central action. The common intent was always spatial expansion or piece restriction, but the actual consequence was always the creation of a specific weakness: 4/10 removed defense of an adjacent pawn or piece (b4 undefending c3 or leaving itself hanging), 3/10 abandoned control of a critical central square (e5 creating holes on d5, b6 weakening c6), 2/10 opened a dangerous diagonal or file toward the player's own king/queen, and 1/10 blocked a crucial pawn break. The average cp_loss of 335 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but severe miscalculations of priorities—slow expansion in positions demanding concrete action.

171.label: Playing a slow, prophylactic pawn move to the 3rd rank when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
171.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance to the 3rd rank from the player's perspective (White: f3, h3, a3, c3, b3; Black: a6, f6, b6, a6, b6). In every case, the position contained a forcing tactical resource — a capture (6/10), a check (3/10), or an aggressive pawn break (3/10) — that the player ignored in favor of a passive prophylactic pawn push. 10/10 analyses identify tempo_loss as the primary error. The average number of good moves available was only 1.5, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision rather than consolidation. The moves typically aimed to support another pawn, prevent a future threat, or stabilize structure, but the wasted tempo allowed opponents to seize initiative, develop pieces, neutralize key attackers, or execute counterattacks. The positions span all phases (7 middlegame, 2 opening, 1 endgame) and both sides equally (5 White, 5 Black), confirming the pattern is about the move type rather than positional context.

169.label: Voluntarily relocating the king (usually via castling) into a zone where the opponent's pieces are already positioned to exploit it tactically.
169.description: 10/10 positions feature the player voluntarily moving their king to a new square — 7/10 via O-O-O, 1/10 via O-O, and 2/10 via manual king moves (Ke2, Kc7, Kh7). In every single case, the king lands on a square or in a zone where the opponent's already-active pieces can immediately generate tactical threats: open files exploited by rooks (8/10 had rooks aimed at the castled king's file — c-file in positions 7,8; b-file in positions 4,10; g-file in position 5; a-file in position 3), diagonal attacks by queens (positions 1,9), or tempo-gaining pawn advances (position 7's g4-f5). The average cp_loss of 319 reflects the severity — these aren't subtle positional errors but catastrophic misjudgments about king safety. 10/10 positions had the opponent's pieces already oriented toward the destination zone BEFORE the king arrived. In 8/10 cases, better alternatives existed that either kept the king in place or addressed the position's real needs (piece development, counterplay, prophylaxis). The blunders share the common thread of prioritizing the general principle of 'get the king to safety' over the concrete assessment of which squares are actually safe given the opponent's piece configuration.

168.label: Moving a rook passively to the player's own back rank (f1/g1/e1 or f8/g8) when the position demands aggressive or tactically precise action.
168.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the player's own back rank, with 9/10 specifically going to kingside back-rank squares (f1, g1, f8, g8). In every case, the move is passive or defensive in nature—either retreating from an active position or repositioning without purpose—while the position demanded concrete tactical action. In 3/10 positions, the player missed a forced checkmate (positions 3, 4, 7). In 4/10, the rook abandoned a critical open file (c-file or similar) that was providing essential attacking or defensive pressure. In 2/10, the move created a new tactical vulnerability (hanging piece on b3, or enabling Rexg2). The average cp_loss of 4034 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors: passive rook shuffling in sharp positions is almost always wrong. The positions span both sides equally (5 White, 5 Black) and are overwhelmingly middlegame (8/10), suggesting this pattern emerges in complex tactical positions where defensive instincts override calculation.
168.old_chip: Passive rook retreats to back rank

167.label: Queen captures or checks that appear forcing but misplace the queen or trade it prematurely, missing a stronger tactical resource.
167.description: All 10 positions feature queen moves (7/10 captures, 3/10 checks) that look natural and aggressive but are tactically misguided. In 7/10 cases, the queen captures material (pawns in positions 6, 10; pieces/queens in positions 2, 3, 5, 7, 9), while 3/10 deliver purposeless checks (positions 1, 4, 8). In 8/10 positions, the best move was a non-queen move or a different queen move entirely (c3, fxg6, Rxd1, Nd5, Nc4+, Nxd1, Kxf2, Qxf3, Qxc3+, Qxc6+). The average cp_loss of 405 reflects how severely these 'obvious' queen moves miss the mark. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, meaning these were critical moments demanding precise calculation rather than instinctive forcing moves. The common failure mode is the queen being attracted to an immediately visible gain (free pawn, queen trade, check) while ignoring that a quieter move preserves a decisive tactical advantage — whether that's trapping a piece, maintaining attacking pressure, saving an endangered piece, or exploiting a zwischenzug.

172.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing pawn advance to the player's 3rd rank when the position demands immediate tactical action.
172.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance to the player's own 3rd rank (f3, h3, a3, g3 for White; c6, h6, f6 for Black). Every move is non-capturing, non-checking, and prophylactic/structural in nature — solidifying pawn chains, preventing piece incursions, or 'preparing' future advances. In 9/10 positions, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as the core error, and 9/10 feature a clear missed tactic that required immediate forcing play (checks, captures, or active piece moves). The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, indicating these were narrow tactical moments where precision was mandatory. In 7/10 positions, the opponent's refutation directly exploited the wasted tempo by consolidating, escaping a mating net, or seizing the initiative. The positions span middlegame (7/10) and endgame (3/10), with both colors (5 White, 5 Black), but the unifying thread is always the same: a player chose a slow prophylactic pawn nudge in a position screaming for immediate dynamic action.

162.label: Playing a quiet pawn advance or non-forcing move when an immediate tactical forcing move (check, capture, or decisive threat) was available.
162.description: 8/10 moves played are single-square pawn advances (b3, e7, a5, c5, d4, f3, h5, h4), while the remaining 2 are quiet piece moves (Na5, Bb4). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions. In 8/10 cases, the best available move was a forcing continuation: a check (Qh4+, g3+, Qxf7+, e6+), a capture (Nxb4, Qxe4/Qg4 winning a hanging piece), or an immediate tactical strike (Ng6 forking). The 2 positions with 0cp loss (e7 creating dual promotion threats, c5 advancing connected passers) are notably the cases where the pawn push ITSELF was the forcing move—creating unstoppable promotion threats. The common mistake pattern is selecting a slow, non-forcing advance that appears to improve the position incrementally while overlooking a concrete tactical shot that would have been immediately decisive. Average cp_loss among the actual blunders is ~1434, reflecting how catastrophic the tempo waste is in sharp positions.

170.label: King moves to a more exposed square, stepping onto lines or squares where enemy pieces can immediately exploit its new position with checks, pins, forks, or mating patterns.
170.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a king move that worsens the king's safety by stepping onto a tactically compromised square. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9), the best move was NOT a king move at all — the player reflexively moved the king when a piece move would solve the problem. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 6, 7, 10), a king move was reasonable but the player chose the WRONG direction. The king consistently moves onto dangerous open lines: onto open files allowing rook exploitation (positions 7, 8, 9), onto diagonals enabling pins or checks (positions 2, 10), toward enemy attacking pieces (positions 1, 6), onto central squares allowing forks (position 3), or to the back rank enabling mating patterns (position 4). The average cp_loss of 3246 and only 1.2 good moves available confirm these are razor-sharp positions where the instinctive 'escape' king move is catastrophically wrong.

166.label: Capturing undefended material on the rim of the board (h-file pawns, corner rooks) instead of pursuing more forcing or positionally sound continuations.
166.description: 9/9 positions feature captures on peripheral squares: 5/9 are queen captures on the h-file (Qxh8, Qxh6×3, Qxh1+), 2/9 are bishop captures on a1 (Bxa1×2), and the remaining captures target b4 and b5. In 8/9 cases these are clear mistakes where the player grabs apparently 'free' material on the board's edge while a superior forcing move exists. The correct alternatives consistently involve either checks/forcing pawn advances first (Positions 1, 2), maintaining attacking piece coordination (Positions 7, 10), or keeping defensive pieces on critical posts (Positions 8, 9). In 7/9 positions, the capture displaces the player's piece to a passive peripheral square far from the critical theater of action. The average cp_loss of ~2531 reflects that these greedy captures often miss forced checkmates or allow devastating counterattacks exploiting newly created weaknesses (back-rank threats, exposed kings, discovered attacks).

158.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move in a critical position where only one specific forcing or defensive action works.
158.description: All 10 positions share the characteristic of having extremely few good options (avg 1.4 good moves), demanding one precise action. In 7/10 cases, king safety was the critical ignored priority (positions 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10). In 2/10 cases, a hanging piece or decisive tactic was missed (positions 4, 7). In 1/10, active counterplay was the sole saving resource (position 1). The played moves consistently address a secondary concern—material gain via captures (gxf3, Bxd3, gxf5 = 3/10), slow pawn advances (b5, b4 = 2/10), or quiet piece repositioning (Rb7, Rf1, Rb1, Ree1, Bf6 = 5/10)—while the correct moves were overwhelmingly forcing or urgent: checks (Re4+, Qxb8+), major captures (Nxd8, Nxc8, Qxd6), or emergency king escapes (Kh1, Kg2). The enormous average cp_loss of 3135 reflects that these are 'cliff-edge' positions where only one move holds.

175.label: Castling as a default 'safe' move when a time-sensitive tactical opportunity demands immediate action.
175.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose to castle (O-O or O-O-O) when a specific forcing tactical shot was available that was far stronger. The average cp_loss was 258, indicating these were severe mistakes. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions were razor-sharp with a single critical path. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 6, 8), castling actively created a NEW tactical vulnerability by placing the king or rook on a square exploitable by forks, skewers, or overloaded defenders. In 6/10 positions (3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10), castling simply wasted a crucial tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or neutralize a time-sensitive combination. Notably, 2/10 positions (5, 10) featured textbook Greek Gift sacrifices (Bxh7+) that were missed in favor of castling. In 3/10 positions (4, 7, 9), knight or queen tactics winning material were available. The consistent thread is a player defaulting to the general principle of 'get the king safe' rather than calculating the concrete position-specific opportunity.

160.label: Playing a defensive piece move near the king when the only saving move was a king escape, king capture, or counter-intuitive sacrifice.
160.description: In 8/10 meaningful positions (excluding positions 3 and 7 where the move was essentially best in a resignable position), the player placed a piece adjacent to their own king as a 'bodyguard' (Rg2 near Kh2, Qg1 near Kh1, Qf1 near Kg1, Nf3 near Kh1, Rg8 near Kh8, Re8 near Kg8) instead of finding the only saving resource. In 5/10 positions, the correct move was specifically a KING move (Kh1, Kxh7, Kf7, Kg1, or the king capture variant). The average number of good moves was just 1.1, meaning these are razor-sharp critical moments where only one precise move works. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3937 reflects that the 'natural' defensive clustering of pieces near the king fails to address the root vulnerability—the king itself needs to escape, capture a restricting piece, or the player needs a counter-sacrifice (like Qxd1 for perpetual in position 5). 7/10 moves place the moved piece within one square of the player's own king, creating the illusion of defense.
160.old_chip: Shielding King Instead Of Moving It

177.label: A non-forcing pawn advance played in a critical position that demands immediate tactical action with pieces.
177.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn push (h4, f4, f5, d5, g5, f4, f4, c5, b4, g4) played in lieu of an immediately necessary piece move. In every case, the position contained urgent tactical demands: 6/10 had winning combinations available (Rh3, Qe4, Qf6+, Rg6, Re4, Be5+), 2/10 required addressing an immediate threat to a piece (hanging queen on d1, lethal Bd4+ check), and 2/10 needed precise piece maneuvers to maintain an advantage (Kd7 forcing a winning trade, h4/Kg3 maintaining structure). The average cp_loss of 2055 is catastrophic, with 2/10 resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points demanding precision. 7/10 of the pawn pushes were on the kingside (f/g/h files), often weakening the king's shelter or second rank, but the defining commonality is that ALL are slow, non-forcing moves in positions where tempo was paramount.

181.label: Placing a minor piece on the player's own second rank as a routine developing move while a concrete tactical demand goes unaddressed.
181.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (bishop or knight) being developed to the player's second rank (e7/d7 for Black, e2/d2 for White) during the opening phase. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical requirement—unresolved central tension (2/10), hanging pieces or pawns (3/10), available tactical shots being missed (3/10), or vulnerability to forks/combinations (4/10)—that demanded a concrete, forcing response. Instead, the player chose a generic, safe-looking developing move to the most conservative available square. The average centipawn loss was 323, indicating these aren't minor inaccuracies but severe blunders. The moves split evenly between Black (5/10) and White (5/10). In 7/10 cases, only 1-3 good alternatives existed, meaning the positions were tactically sharp and required specific responses rather than routine development. The piece types varied (6 bishop moves, 4 knight moves) but all shared the second-rank destination and the 'autopilot development' character.

180.label: Bishop develops to b4 or b5 undefended while the king remains on the e-file, allowing a queen fork check on a4 or a5.
180.description: In 10/10 positions, a bishop moves to the b-file (Bb4 for Black or Bb5 for White) during the opening while the player's king remains uncastled on the e-file. In 9/10 positions, the bishop lands completely undefended. The critical punishment in 8/10 positions is a queen check on the a-file (Qa4+ against Bb4, or Qa5+ against Bb5) that simultaneously attacks the undefended bishop, winning it outright — a textbook fork exploiting the geometric alignment of the king on e1/e8 and the bishop on b4/b5 along the a4-e8 or a5-e1 diagonal. Position 1 features the mirror version (Qb5+ wins Bb4), and position 10 requires a preliminary exchange (Bxd4) to open the diagonal before Qa4+. Only 2/10 positions (positions 2 and 6) feature slightly different refutation mechanisms, though even those punish the same fundamental error of placing the bishop on an exposed, undefended b-file square. The average cp_loss of 382 reflects that this typically loses a full minor piece.

176.label: A space-gaining pawn advance is chosen over urgent concrete piece play or available tactical shots, wasting a critical tempo.
176.description: All 10/10 positions feature non-capturing, non-forcing pawn advances (b5, e5, e4, g4, g4, e5, f4, g5, d4, e4) pushed aggressively toward the opponent's territory when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 8/10 cases, the best move involved active piece play (rook invasions, captures, discovered checks, or developing moves like castling). In 7/10 positions, the pawn advance either weakened the player's own structure or removed a pawn from a critical defensive duty (e.g., e3 protecting a bishop in positions 3 and 10, f5 maintaining pawn chain integrity in position 7, g-file pawns weakening king shelter in positions 4 and 5). The average cp_loss of 297 reflects that these moves look natural and aggressive—gaining space or attacking enemy pieces—but are fundamentally the wrong TYPE of move for positions requiring forcing continuations. Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, indicating these positions demanded precision rather than general play.

178.label: A routine pawn-takes-pawn capture that ignores an urgent tactical threat, often opening critical lines against the player's own king.
178.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing a pawn (pxp) as the blunder move, making this pattern perfectly consistent geometrically. In every case, the capture appears natural — winning material, resolving tension, or damaging the opponent's structure — but catastrophically ignores a more urgent tactical reality. In 7/10 positions, the primary consequence involves king safety: the capture either removes a defensive pawn that shields the king (positions 1, 10), opens a diagonal or file toward the player's own monarch (positions 1, 2, 10), or is played while an immediate checkmate threat exists (positions 3, 7 — both allowing mate-in-1). In 3/10 positions (5, 6, 9), the capture wastes a critical tempo when a forcing move (check, development to cover a weakness, or addressing a hanging piece) was required. The average cp_loss of 3086 is extreme, with 3/10 resulting in immediate or near-immediate checkmate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these were positions demanding precise, non-obvious play where the 'autopilot' pawn capture was the trap.

185.label: Moving the queen to an active-looking but exposed square in the opening before completing minor piece development and castling, allowing the opponent to gain tempi by attacking it.
185.description: All 10/10 positions involve a queen move during the opening phase while at least one king (usually both) remains in the center uncastled. In 10/10 cases, the best alternatives were simple developing moves (castling, developing minor pieces, or supportive pawn moves). The queen lands on squares that appear aggressive but create immediate tactical vulnerabilities: in 7/10 positions, the opponent punishes by attacking the queen with a knight jump (Nb5, Nd5, Nb4, Nd4) that simultaneously threatens the queen and a devastating fork (typically Nc7+ or Nd3+). In the remaining cases, the queen is driven back by simple pawn pushes (g3, f5) or discovered attacks, gaining the opponent multiple tempi. The average cp_loss of 252 reflects how devastating these tempo losses are in undeveloped positions where every move counts toward king safety and piece coordination.

174.label: Automatic pawn captures that resolve tension when a piece capture or more dynamic move was needed to maintain the position's energy.
174.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn captures (dxe4, fxg3, exd5, bxc4, exd4, cxd4, cxd4, bxc3), while the remaining 2 are similarly reflexive piece captures (Nxd6, Bxe3). In at least 5/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 6, 7), the correct move was to capture on the SAME square with a piece instead of a pawn — Rxg3# instead of fxg3, Rxc4 instead of bxc4, Qxd4 instead of exd4/cxd4, Rxd4 instead of cxd4. In the remaining positions, the best move was either not to capture at all (positions 1, 3, 8 where Rb7, Kb1, and Rxd5 were best) or to capture a different target first as a move-order finesse (positions 9, 10 where Bxf1 and Bxh7+ were critical predecessors). All 10 moves share the quality of being the most 'obvious' or 'automatic' capture in the position — the kind of move made quickly without deeper calculation — when the position demanded either more active piece engagement or precise tactical sequencing.

173.label: Capturing or pursuing material (usually a pawn) that leaves the aggressive piece on a tactically exposed square where it becomes vulnerable to pins, forks, or tempo-gaining attacks.
173.description: 7/10 positions involve directly capturing a pawn (Nxe4, Rxe4, Rxe5, Rxd5, Rxd3, Rxd5, and Rhf7 doubling on a pawn), with 5/10 specifically being rook captures on the d- or e-file. In each case, the capturing piece lands on a square where it immediately becomes a tactical target: pinned on a file (Position 1: Re1 pins knight), pinned on a diagonal (Position 8: Ba6 pins rook), forked (Position 7: Nf6+ forks rook and king), attacked with tempo by a bishop (Positions 6 and 9: Bd4/Bc4 hit the rook), or exposed to a queen infiltration (Position 2: Qf3+). The remaining 3/10 positions (two b5 pawn pushes and g4) share the same underlying greed — pushing a pawn aggressively that either hangs immediately or weakens the position tactically. In all 10 cases, superior alternatives existed (avg 2.6 good moves) that prioritized development, king safety, or prophylactic play over material gain. The refutations consistently exploit the newly-created target with a one-move tactical blow.

182.label: A knight performing an essential defensive function (blocking a file, shielding the king, or holding a key square) is relocated to a seemingly active square, catastrophically exposing the king.
182.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight moving away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive role, directly enabling a king-safety catastrophe. In at least 7/10 cases, the knight was specifically blocking an open or semi-open file (c-file in Position 2, g-file in Positions 5, 6, and 9, e-file in Positions 7 and 10, d-file pressure in Position 3), and its removal allowed immediate rook or queen penetration along that file with check or checkmate. In 4/10 positions the punishment was immediate mate or mate-in-4 or fewer (Positions 2, 6, 8, 9). The knight destinations are diverse (e6, d5, b4, e5, e4, f5, f3, e3, f8, g3) but share the characteristic of appearing 'active' — attacking material, centralizing, or threatening forks — while actually being tactically irrelevant compared to the defensive function abandoned. 10/10 positions have exposed or vulnerable kings as a precondition, and in every case the player prioritized knight activity over defensive necessity.

186.label: A bishop captures a seemingly free pawn on the a2/c2/a7/c7 square and becomes trapped or critically displaced, losing tempo or material.
186.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing an apparently undefended pawn on the opponent's back rank along the a- or c-file (8/10 are Bxa2, 1/10 Bxc2, 1/10 Bxa7, 1/10 Bxc7). In 7/10 cases, the bishop is literally trapped after the capture—most commonly by a b-pawn advance (b3 traps the bishop on a2 in positions 2, 3, 8, and 9; b6 traps it on a7 in position 5; Ba4+c4 seals it on a2 in position 7; rooks attack it on c2 in position 4). In the remaining 3/10 cases, the bishop suffers catastrophic tempo loss by abandoning a critical central post for a peripheral pawn, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative. All 10 positions are middlegames where the player had 2-3 good alternatives (avg 2.5) that maintained or improved their position through piece development, attacks, or prophylaxis rather than material greed. The average centipawn loss of 290 reflects that these pawn grabs consistently transform winning or equal positions into losing ones.

183.label: Aggressive forward pawn pushes chosen over superior piece development, castling, or tactical piece moves that the position demanded.
183.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance that looks aggressive or space-gaining but is premature given the position's true needs. In 10/10 cases, the best moves involved piece play rather than pawn play (development like Nc3/Nf4, castling like O-O-O, piece repositioning like Bb2/Ra3, or captures/exchanges like Bxe6/dxc5). In 7/10 positions, the player's king remained uncastled in the center while making the pawn push. In 8/10 positions, the pawn advance either opened lines benefiting the opponent's better-developed pieces, removed a pawn from a critical defensive role, or dissolved the player's own advantageous structure. The average centipawn loss of 287 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but major strategic errors — the positions consistently demanded piece coordination and king safety over territorial pawn expansion. The common psychological thread is that the forward pawn push appears proactive and threatening, masking the fact that the position requires attending to fundamental positional duties first.
183.old_chip: Premature pawn advance over piece play

187.label: A quiet bishop development or repositioning move played in a position that demands immediate concrete action (tactical strike, active counterplay, or forcing continuation).
187.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking bishop move to a 'natural-looking' square (Be6, Bc3, Bd2, Be7, Bb3, Bd7, Be2, Bg3) when the position urgently required forceful play. In 7/10 cases, a specific tactical shot was available (knight forks in positions 1/4/8, piece captures in 3/5, knight invasions in 2/10). In 4/10 cases, the player squandered a winning initiative by failing to create immediate threats (positions 6, 7, 9, 10). The bishop moves share a tempo-wasting quality — 9/10 analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif. In 4/10 positions, the bishop itself became a target on its new square (captured by knight in positions 1, 5, 7; captured directly in position 9). The average cp_loss of 347 reflects that these positions sit at critical inflection points where one quiet move allows the opponent to consolidate, counterattack, or execute their own tactics. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow positions demanding precision rather than routine development.

193.label: Retreating a knight or bishop to a passive starting/edge square instead of executing an available tactical blow.
193.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (knight or bishop) retreating to a passive square on the edge or corner of the board: Nb1 appears 4 times, Ba2 twice, Ba7 twice, plus Nb8, Ba1, and Bh2. Every single move goes to the first/second rank or the a/h-file rim. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded immediate tactical action — winning combinations (Nxg6, Rd8#, Nxf7, Nd5 forks, Re8+ checks) were available but ignored in favor of a prophylactic or 'safe' retreat. The average centipawn loss is an astronomical 2319, with 2/10 positions missing forced checkmate. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments requiring precision. In 8/10 positions, the retreat gave the opponent a free tempo to neutralize threats (capture hanging pieces, create escape squares, block diagonals). The retreated pieces uniformly land on squares where they contribute nothing — b1/b8 (starting squares), a1/a2/a7 (corners and rim), h2 (buried behind pawns).

179.label: Moving a rook (or piece) to a natural-looking square while ignoring the position's immediate tactical demands, either missing a forcing opportunity or abandoning a critical function.
179.description: 9/10 positions involve rook moves and 10/10 involve a piece being repositioned to a seemingly improved or active square that ignores the position's tactical urgency. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10), the player missed a superior forcing continuation — a sacrifice, pawn push, or tactical combination — in favor of a 'natural' repositioning. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8), the repositioning move created a new tactical vulnerability by placing the piece on a capturable/trappable square or abandoning a critical defensive function. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 8/10 positions and 'piece_activity' in all 10, confirming that these moves look active but accomplish nothing concrete while gifting the opponent decisive time. The average cp_loss of 1338 is extreme, reflecting that these seemingly reasonable moves occur in tactically critical positions where one precise move was required. In 6/10 cases only 1-2 good moves existed, making these high-stakes moments where 'improving' moves are catastrophic.

188.label: Premature pawn advance in king-and-pawn endgames where the king should be repositioned first.
188.description: 10/10 positions are pure pawn endgames (king+pawns only, with one queen-vs-pawns exception). 10/10 moves played are pawn advances toward promotion. In the 6 positions with meaningful cp_loss (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6), the best move was consistently a king move (Kb3, Kd6, Ke6, a5-fixing-then-king, Kb1, Kh3) rather than the pawn push actually played. The critical principle violated is 'king leads the pawn' — advancing the pawn prematurely either surrenders opposition (position 1: -551→-2), burns tempo reserves needed for zugzwang (position 6: -564→-19), or allows the defending king to reach a drawing zone (position 4: 0→+597). The remaining 4 positions (7, 8, 9, 10) have negligible cp_loss (0-11cp) where the pawn push was acceptable or even optimal, but share the identical structural signature: a passed pawn being pushed in a minimal-material endgame.

191.label: A bishop delivers check but is simply captured by the opponent, losing a critical piece for no compensation.
191.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop delivering check that is immediately captured by the opponent, resulting in significant material or strategic loss. In 8/10 cases, the bishop is directly recaptured on its checking square (by rook, knight, bishop, or queen). In 5/10 positions, the captured bishop was a critical attacking piece whose removal collapsed a mating net (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 9). In 5/10 positions, a forced checkmate was available via a different move but the player was seduced by the 'forcing' nature of the check. The average cp_loss of 4023 reflects that these positions often had spectacular tactical resources that the premature bishop check squandered. In 3/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 8), the opponent's recapture itself created additional tactical problems like forks or cascading hanging pieces. The consistent error is prioritizing the tempo of 'check' over the permanent cost of losing the bishop.

184.label: Queen moves to a seemingly active square that is actually tactically vulnerable — hanging, pinnable, or fatally abandoning a defensive duty.
184.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that appear purposeful (giving check, creating threats, centralizing) but place the queen on a square where it becomes a tactical liability. In 5/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 6, 9), the queen lands on a square where it directly hangs to an enemy piece (rook on the same rank/file or knight attacking the square). In 1/10 (position 1), the queen lands on a square creating an absolute pin. In 4/10 (positions 3, 7, 8, 10), the queen abandons a critical defensive post — guarding e7 against mate, covering the back rank, or defending a hanging piece — to make a 'threatening' move. The average centipawn loss is enormous (5118), with 6/10 positions involving missed forced mates or immediately winning captures. 4/10 moves give check (Qc4+, Qb6+, Qa4+, and arguably Qd2 in position 5 invites check), and 4/10 specifically go to b6, suggesting the pattern particularly fires when the queen makes long-range lateral/diagonal jumps to 'active-looking' squares without calculating the opponent's one-move tactical reply.

192.label: Capturing a weak pawn (usually f7/f2) with a piece expecting to win material via fork, but the capture is premature, uses the wrong piece, or ignores a more urgent priority, resulting in the attacking piece being stranded or devastating counterplay.
192.description: 8/9 positions involve captures on f7 or f2 (the classically weak f-pawn squares), with the remaining position (Nxb2) targeting an analogous weak pawn near the opponent's king. 7/9 moves use a knight for the capture, typically hoping to create a fork on queen and rook. In 5/9 positions, the capturing knight becomes trapped or stranded (usually on h8 or h1) after the opponent ignores the fork and launches a counterattack. In 3/9 positions (Positions 3, 7, 9), the player captured with the WRONG piece—using the knight instead of the bishop (or vice versa)—forfeiting the critical tempo that a check would provide. In 4/9 positions (Positions 2, 4, 6, 10), the opponent punishes by ignoring the apparent material loss and instead launching a queen invasion (Qxg2 in three cases, Qh5 in one) that devastates the attacker's exposed king. All 9 positions feature at least one uncastled king, and 6/9 occur in the opening phase, suggesting these are pattern-recognition failures where players apply standard tactical templates (Fried Liver forks, Bxf2+ sacrifices) without verifying the prerequisites are met.

194.label: Pawn captures that remove a structurally critical pawn, opening files or diagonals the opponent immediately exploits for devastating attacks.
194.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (pxp) as the blunder. In 9/10 cases, the captured pawn was serving as a critical defensive barrier—blocking a file from rook invasion (positions 1, 6, 8), shielding the king from diagonal attacks (positions 2, 4, 10), or maintaining structural tension that kept opponent pieces passive (positions 3, 5, 7). The immediate punishment in 8/10 positions involves the opponent exploiting the newly opened line: rook invasions to the 7th rank (positions 1, 6, 10), checkmate via open file/diagonal (positions 2, 4, 8), or piece captures along cleared diagonals (positions 3, 5). The average cp_loss of ~3000 reflects the catastrophic nature of these structural concessions, with 3/10 resulting in forced checkmate. Position 9 (bxa6) is the slight outlier—a wrong-move-order pawn capture that enables a knight fork rather than opening a line—but still shares the core theme of a greedy pawn capture that ignores tactical consequences.

189.label: An aggressive forward pawn advance chosen instead of the concrete piece activity (captures, centralization, or development) the position demanded.
189.description: All 10/10 positions feature a forward pawn advance (d5, f5, f4, c4, c5, a4, h4) as the blunder, while the best moves were overwhelmingly piece actions: 7/10 had a capture or piece development as the top recommendation (exf4, exf5, Bxc4, Bb4, Nd5, etc.), and the remaining positions called for prophylactic piece-supporting moves (a6, c3, a3). In 8/10 cases the pawn advance either lost material directly or created an irreparable structural weakness. The average cp_loss of 264 confirms these are severe errors, and the average of only 1.7 good alternatives shows these were demanding positions requiring precise piece-based solutions, not speculative pawn play. The pawn pushes span all sectors of the board (center: d5×2, c4, c5; kingside: f5×2, f4, h4; queenside: a4×2), confirming the pattern is about the TYPE of move rather than any specific direction.

198.label: Aggressive rook moves to the 7th/2nd rank (often doubling) that prioritize a 'classically strong' formation over immediate tactical necessities.
198.description: 8/10 positions feature a rook moving specifically to the 7th rank (or 2nd rank for Black), and 5/10 involve doubling rooks on that rank (Rgg7, Rgg2, Ree7, Rdd7, Rgg2 — all disambiguated notation indicating a second rook joining the first). The remaining moves (Rg6, Re5, Rd2) are similarly aggressive rook deployments prioritizing 'dominant' placement. In every case, the player chose a move that looks textbook-powerful — rooks on the 7th is a foundational positional principle — but ignored a more urgent concrete need: 4/10 abandoned back-rank defense allowing devastating checks, 3/10 ignored critical passed pawn threats, 2/10 missed immediate forced mates, and 1/10 left the rook literally en prise. The average cp_loss of 3186 is extreme, with 3/10 involving mate-related swings. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow positions demanding calculation, not general principles.

202.label: Retreating a piece to the player's own back rank (1st/8th) when active play was required, surrendering initiative or creating self-blocking problems.
202.description: 9/10 positions involve a piece literally moving to the player's own back rank (1st rank for White, 8th rank for Black), with the remaining position (Qg2) being a deep retreat toward the back. All 10 moves are defensive/passive in nature, chosen to consolidate or protect rather than to attack. In 6/10 cases the best move was an active capture, check, or king march (Qxb5, Qe6+, Be5+, Rxe7, exd4, Kd1). In 3/10 positions the retreat physically blocked the king's escape square, enabling perpetual check (Re1 blocking Ke1), checkmate (Rc8 blocking Kc8), or rook infiltration (Nf1 blocking Kf1). The average cp_loss of 2048 reflects that several positions involved missed forced mates. All positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.7), indicating critical moments where the only correct approach was active, not passive.

204.label: The King captures a Queen or Rook on an adjacent square, typically transitioning into a simplified pawn endgame.
204.description: All 9/9 positions feature the King capturing a major piece (Queen in 7/9 cases, Rook in 2/9 cases) on an immediately adjacent square. In 8/9 positions this occurs in the endgame phase. In 6/9 positions the capture is actually the best or only viable move (cp_loss 0-3), while in the remaining positions it is a significant blunder (Position 8: Kxf7 walks into an f-file pin losing the Queen; Position 9: Kxf8 walks into back-rank mate Rd8#; Position 10: marginal 40cp loss). The consistent thread is that only 1 good move was available in every position, and the 'obvious' instinct is always to capture the hanging major piece with the King. The feature detects this specific geometric pattern of a King moving one square to capture a high-value piece, which simplifies into a pawn endgame. When the move IS wrong, it's because the King's new square creates a tactical vulnerability (pin, back-rank mate) or because a different capturer preserves greater advantage.

203.label: A non-forcing b-pawn advance (b4 or b5) played when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a tactical emergency elsewhere on the board.
203.description: 10/10 positions feature a slow, non-forcing flank pawn advance (9/10 specifically the b-pawn to b4 or b5, 1/10 the g-pawn to g5) played instead of addressing an urgent tactical demand. In 7/10 positions the center was closed or semi-closed, likely tempting the player into believing flank expansion was strategically appropriate. However, every single position had a concrete tactical issue requiring immediate attention: 4/10 involved an overloaded or sole defender that could be removed (positions 5, 6, 9, and indirectly 1), 3/10 involved king safety emergencies requiring defensive measures (positions 1, 7, 8), 3/10 involved missed winning tactics or critical central strikes (positions 4, 10, and 3). The average cp_loss of 1216 is enormous, and the average number of good moves was only 2.3, confirming these were critical positions demanding precision. In 5/10 positions, the b-pawn advance directly created or worsened a tactical vulnerability (removing defense of c3 in position 5, overextending in positions 2/3, enabling central simplification in position 10). The remaining positions simply wasted a critical tempo while threats were already in motion.

199.label: King captures an enemy piece (usually a rook) that has invaded or is adjacent to the king's position, typically simplifying into a won endgame.
199.description: All 9/9 positions feature king moves, with 8/9 being king captures of an enemy piece directly adjacent to the king. Specifically, 7/9 captures target a rook that has invaded the king's vicinity (Kxe2, Kxf7, Kxf8, Kxc2, Kxf2, Kxf7, Kxc2), 1/9 captures a knight (Kxg4), and 1/9 is a non-capturing king advance (Kf4). Remarkably, 7/9 positions show 0-1 cp_loss, meaning the king capture is the engine's top choice. Only 2/9 (Kf4 at 231cp loss, Kxf2 at 118cp loss) are actual mistakes where the king walked into a check sequence. The positions consistently feature the capturing side already having a large winning advantage (avg eval ~+700-800cp equivalent), with the opponent's piece being en prise or sacrificed. The average number of good alternatives is only 1.1, confirming these are nearly forced captures. The pattern represents positions where the 'obvious' recapture of an invading piece is typically correct but occasionally walks into discovered/sequential checks.

195.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing king or pawn move that wastes a critical tempo in a time-sensitive endgame position where exact move order determines the outcome.
195.description: 10/10 positions feature tempo_loss as a tagged motif, and 10/10 involve passed pawns where timing is paramount. The moves are all quiet single-square advances (king steps or pawn pushes) with no checks, captures, or immediate threats. 8/10 are endgames, typically pawn races or queen-vs-pawn/rook-vs-pawn scenarios. In 4/10 positions (positions 2, 4, 5, 9), the error is a specific move-order mistake between king and pawn—pushing the pawn when the king should reposition first (positions 2, 4, 5) or moving the king when the pawn should push immediately (position 9). In 3/10 positions (6, 7, 8), the quiet move allows the opponent to seize the initiative with checks or forcing moves. In position 10, a slow pawn push squanders an immediate tactical win via forced rook exchange. 6/10 moves specifically involve h-file pawns or king moves to the h-file (Kh5, h3, h2, h3, Kh4, h4), suggesting a sub-pattern of kingside rim maneuvers that appear natural but waste time.
195.old_chip: Quiet tempo waste in pawn races

196.label: Greedy or forcing captures (pawns, pieces, or checks) that initiate exchanges before necessary preparation, trading away the player's active pieces and dynamic advantage.
196.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player initiating a capture or forcing move (check) that directly leads to a piece exchange, but doing so prematurely. In 7/10 cases the move involves a rook (Rd1+, Rxe4, Rxd6, Rb1+, Re8+, Re8, Rxb3), while 3/10 involve bishop captures (Bxf2, Bxh4, Bxa5). In every case, the correct alternative was either a preparatory/intermediate move that would have made the same capture stronger later (positions 3, 8, 10 — explicit move-order errors where axb5, dxc4, or dxc4 should precede the capture), maintaining piece tension rather than forcing trades (positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 9 — where the player's rook was their most active piece and should have been preserved), or avoiding a pawn grab that broke critical piece coordination (positions 4, 7 — where bishops left defensive posts to grab material). The average cp_loss of 267 and average of only 1.6 good moves shows these are positions where the 'obvious' aggressive capture is a trap. In 8/10 positions, the refutation involves the opponent simply recapturing and then exploiting what the premature exchange exposed (undefended pieces, lost coordination, or structural weaknesses).

208.label: Castling as a routine developing move when the position demands immediate tactical action to resolve critical piece tensions.
208.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling moves (9 O-O, 1 O-O-O) played when urgent tactical opportunities or necessities existed that required priority. In 10/10 cases, both kings were still in or near the center, creating a false sense of urgency about king safety. In 10/10 positions, there were active piece tensions (pins, forks, hanging pieces, overloaded defenders) demanding immediate resolution. The average cp_loss of 296 is extremely high, and only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow tactical positions requiring precise calculation rather than general principles. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a concrete tactical strike (Nxc6, Qd4, Qa4, Nxb4, Qf3, axb4, or a6 neutralizing pressure). After castling, 8/10 positions were punished by the opponent exploiting either the wasted tempo (capturing now-undefended pieces) or the new king position itself (fork targets on f1, open files toward the castled king, diagonal attacks). The pattern consistently shows players choosing 'textbook development' over position-specific tactical demands.

207.label: King moves to a square where it can immediately be checked or mated, losing a critical tempo that transforms the position from survivable to lost.
207.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves (the exception being b5, a pawn move-order error in a king-pawn endgame). In at least 8/10 cases, the king specifically steps onto a rank, file, or diagonal where an opponent's piece or promoting pawn can deliver check or checkmate immediately. The consistent pattern is that an adjacent or alternative king square existed that would have avoided the check: Position 3 (Kd3 vs Kd2 avoids Rc3+), Position 4 (Ke2 vs Kd2 avoids f1=Q+), Position 5 (Kg7 vs Kg8 avoids Rc7+), Position 6 (Kg2 walks into Qxh2#), Position 9 (Kd7 vs Kxe8 avoids c8=Q+), and Position 10 (Ke2 vs Kd2 moves away from queenside). In 6/10 positions the cp_loss exceeded 450, and 4/10 resulted in immediate forced checkmate. The average good moves available was only 1.5, indicating these were already narrow defensive positions where precise king placement was the sole path to survival.

197.label: Prematurely resolving pawn tension or structure that was constraining the opponent, when patience and piece improvement was required.
197.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn moves (5 pawn captures + 3 pawn advances) that dissolve structural constraints the player's pawns were imposing on the opponent. In positions 1, 2, 3, 7, and 9 (gxh5, exf5, fxg5, dxe5, exd6), the player captures an enemy pawn that releases a blockade, restraint, or cramping effect—freeing the opponent's pieces or creating a mobile enemy majority. In positions 4, 6, and 10 (g4, b4, h6), pawn advances destroy defensive structure or hand the opponent a useful lever. The remaining 2 positions (Bc4 and Bxf3) involve bishop moves that immediately alter pawn structure to the opponent's benefit (Bc4 hangs to bxc4; Bxf3 removes a key defender). In 9/10 positions, the best moves involved improving piece placement (king centralization, knight maneuvers, rook activation) while explicitly maintaining the existing pawn tension. The average cp_loss of 217 reflects that these structural concessions are deeply damaging, often converting winning positions into drawn or lost ones.

200.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing positional move when the position demands immediate tactical action (capture, check, or combination).
200.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push, knight maneuver, or passive rook move) when a concrete tactical opportunity existed. 6/10 moves were slow pawn advances (d3, f3, f6, e3, c5, cxb5), 3/10 were knight repositioning moves to the rim or a vulnerable square (Na4, Na5, Ne7), and 1/10 was a preparatory rook move (Re3).
