The best moves in these positions were almost always forcing: captures of hanging pieces (Rxf4, Qxf6, Qxb2 in positions 6, 10, 8), tactical combinations (Nxd5 in position 1), checks exploiting king exposure (Qh4+ in position 4), or urgent piece activation (Qh2, f4 in positions 5, 2). The average number of good moves available was only 2.0, with 6/10 positions having just 1 good move, confirming these were critical-accuracy moments that demanded precise tactical play. The average cp_loss of 1216 reflects the catastrophic cost of 'playing positionally in a tactical position.'

209.label: Moving a bishop one diagonal square in a quiet repositioning when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
209.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop moving exactly one square diagonally in a non-capturing, non-checking repositioning move. In every case, the position contained a concrete tactical opportunity (a hanging piece, a forcing combination, a critical pawn break, or a checking sequence) that was missed in favor of a quiet bishop nudge. The moves went from active squares to passive ones: Bc4→d3, Bf4→g3, Bc5→d6, Be4→f3, Bf5→e6 (twice), Bf5→g6, Bc5→b4, Bf4→g5. In 7/9 positions, the best move was a capture or forcing move. The average cp_loss of 255 reflects how these innocuous-looking one-square retreats squander decisive advantages. 8/9 positions had only 1-3 good moves available, meaning these were sharp positions requiring precision rather than quiet maneuvering. The blunders occurred equally in openings (4) and middlegames (5), suggesting this is a general pattern of choosing prophylaxis over tactics.

213.label: Playing a prophylactic king move to a corner square (usually Kh1) in a dynamic middlegame position that demands immediate concrete action.
213.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves to corner or near-corner squares (8/10 specifically Kh1, plus Ka1, Kg1, Kh8, Kh2) during the middlegame. In 9/10 cases these moves are significant mistakes (avg cp_loss 266 excluding the one correct instance). 9/10 analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The positions uniformly demanded immediate concrete action: capturing hanging material (Positions 4, 9, 10), resolving critical pawn tension (Positions 2, 3, 7, 8), or maintaining an attack (Position 6). Instead, the player reflexively tucked the king into the corner as a prophylactic/safety measure. The average number of good moves was only 1.6, showing these are critical positions with narrow best paths. Position 1 (cp_loss 0) is the exception that proves the rule — there Kh1 was correct because it had a concrete tactical purpose (clearing g1 for Rg1 with a devastating file attack), distinguishing purposeful king preparation from aimless prophylaxis.

214.label: The queen captures a piece but the opponent's recapture comes with check, gaining a decisive tempo advantage.
214.description: In 9/9 positions, the player captures a piece with their queen (Qx...), and the critical refutation is that the opponent recaptures on that same square with check. In 7/9 cases, the recapture is specifically the opponent's queen taking back with check (Qxf5+, Qxe4+, Qxe3+, Qxe3+, Qxf3+, Qxd3+, Qxg5+). In 1/9 the queen recapture is immediate checkmate (Qxd6#). In 1/9 a rook recaptures with discovered/direct check (Rxg8+). The exposed king position is critical context — 9/9 positions feature a king on an open diagonal or file that enables the check after recapture. The tempo gained from the check then allows the opponent to win additional material (capturing an undefended piece, as in positions 1, 2, 4, 7), launch an unstoppable mating attack (positions 3, 5, 8), or deliver immediate checkmate (position 6). The average cp_loss of 2148 reflects that these seemingly attractive captures are catastrophic.

211.label: A quiet rook repositioning move to a seemingly natural square when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
211.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing rook move to a 'logical' square (open file, semi-open file, or b-file for queenside play) that completely ignores the position's urgent tactical requirements. In 10/10 cases, the rook move is a quiet developing/improving move with zero immediate threats. The positions split into several failure modes: in 3/10 positions (4, 8, 9), a winning tactical blow existed (Qe6 fork, Qxa1+ capture, or preventing Ba3 pin); in 3/10 positions (5, 7, 10), the rook move abandoned defense of a piece or pawn (b2 pawn twice, c4 bishop once); in 3/10 positions (2, 3, 6), the rook move wasted tempo when a more urgent action was needed (f5 attacking a bishop, castling, or seizing the e-file); and in 1/10 (position 1), the rook moved directly into a tactical combination. The average cp_loss of 375 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical moments misread as routine. The common thread is treating a tactically sharp position as a quiet maneuvering phase.

215.label: Developing a knight passively to a rim square (h6, h3, a6, a3) instead of using the queen to capture a hanging piece or deliver a winning check.
215.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight being moved to a rim square (Nh6 in 5 positions, Nh3 in 1, Na6 in 1, Na3 in 2). In 8/10 positions, the best move was a queen move — specifically Qxg5 capturing a hanging knight (5 positions), Qxg4 capturing a hanging knight (1 position), or Qa4+/Qa5+ delivering check that wins material (3 positions). The common thread is overwhelming: the player chose a slow, passive knight development to the board's edge when a powerful queen action was available that would have won material immediately. The average cp_loss of 351 reflects that these were almost always positions where a full piece could be won outright. Only 1/10 positions (the c5 middlegame) deviates from the knight-to-rim pattern, though it shares the theme of a passive move ignoring a concrete tactical opportunity.

201.label: Playing a natural-looking improving move in a position where one specific forcing tactical shot was required.
201.description: 10/10 positions featured a player choosing a 'reasonable-looking' move (pawn advance, quiet development, routine capture) when the position demanded one specific forcing move. The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were critical junctures with extremely narrow winning paths. In 6/10 cases the blunder was a pawn move (d4, d4, e5, cxb6, g4, fxe5) motivated by generic positional goals like gaining space or making exchanges. In 4/10 cases it was a quiet piece repositioning (Bb5×2, Bg5, Qh3). The missed moves were consistently more forcing: captures of hanging pieces (positions 2, 8, 10), intermediate checks (position 5), exchange sacrifices (position 4), tactical pawn strikes exploiting specific piece placement (positions 3, 7), discovered attacks (position 9), or maintaining existing tactical pressure (position 1). The average cp_loss of 1260 reflects that these positions had massive tactical energy that the played moves completely ignored.

190.label: The player moves a piece to a square where it can be immediately captured by a forcing reply (often with check or an intermediate move).
190.description: In 6/10 positions (2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10), the piece that moved is directly captured on the exact square it landed on — Qa1 taken by Rxa1, Bxh6 by Kxh6, Re3 by Nxe3, Rxh6 by gxh6 (after intermediate check), Rg1 by Bxg1+, and Bf4 by Bxf4+. In 4 of those 6, the capture comes WITH CHECK, making it impossible to save the piece. In 2 additional positions (6, 9), the piece captures a pawn but creates an immediately exploitable tactical vulnerability (opening a file or removing a defender that enables a check). The remaining 2 positions (1, 7) fit more loosely — creating tactical vulnerabilities rather than direct piece loss. The average cp_loss of 1973 reflects the catastrophic nature of placing pieces on tactically indefensible squares. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating positions where precise defensive play was required but the player chose an aggressive or greedy-looking move instead.
190.old_chip: Piece moved to en prise square

206.label: A rook delivers check (usually discovered) but lands on the wrong square, missing a far stronger continuation using the same check mechanism with a different destination.
206.description: All 10/10 positions involve a rook move that delivers check, and 9/10 involve a discovered check where the rook vacates a line to uncover an attack from a bishop or queen behind it. The critical shared error in 9/10 positions is that multiple rook destinations deliver the same discovered check, but the player chose the wrong landing square. In 4/10 cases the correct square delivered immediate checkmate (Positions 3, 7, 8, 9), while in 5/10 others the correct square won decisive material or maintained a drawing mechanism. The wrong-square choices consistently prioritized material gain (capturing a pawn on g3, attacking a queen on e5, grabbing f7) or superficially aggressive placement over the square that constructed a mating net or preserved critical attacking geometry. Position 6 (0 cp_loss) represents the correctly-executed version of this same pattern, confirming the feature detects the discovered-check-via-rook mechanism itself.

205.label: Moving a bishop (or minor piece) to reposition, develop, or capture material when the position demands an immediate, more forcing tactical continuation.
205.description: 9/10 positions feature bishop moves and 1/10 a knight move, all sharing the characteristic of being 'natural-looking' piece improvements that catastrophically misjudge the tactical demands of the position. In 5/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7), the minor piece move specifically enables the opponent to force a queen exchange that was previously impossible—the piece was blocking a critical line or its removal disrupted coordination that prevented simplification. In 2/10 cases (positions 8, 9), the player made a quiet developing/retreating bishop move while missing a forced checkmate (mate in 1 and mate in 5). In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 10), the bishop move either placed the piece on a tactically vulnerable square, grabbed material when sharper play was required, or threatened something that should have been executed immediately. The average cp_loss of 2332 reflects the extreme tactical sensitivity of these positions. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments demanding precision rather than generic improvement. The unifying thread is a player in 'positional mode'—repositioning, developing, or capturing pawns—when the position screams for immediate tactical resolution.

210.label: Playing a non-forcing 'improving' move (especially castling) when the position demands the single concrete tactical continuation.
210.description: All 10 positions share a critical feature: only ~1 good move existed (avg 1.1 good moves available), yet the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move instead. 6/10 moves were castling (5 O-O-O, 1 O-O), and 7/10 were king moves (adding Kh3). The remaining 3 were quiet piece developments (Bh4, Bb5, Ba6, Ne5). None of the played moves were checks, captures, or direct threats requiring an immediate response. In contrast, the best moves in every case were concrete and specific: a pawn advance to block perpetual (d5), a queen centralization threatening a pin (Qe4), a rook attack on a trapped queen (Rb3), a bishop development creating a tactical battery (Bc4), a queen trade offer (Qh5), a king retreat from tactical danger (Kd8), a rook attack on a loose piece (Rh4), a knight fork winning material (Nc5), castling with check gaining tempo (O-O+), and a rook invasion winning a piece (Re7). The average cp_loss was 314, reflecting positions where general principles catastrophically failed and only calculation could find the answer.

223.label: Voluntarily exchanging the last pair of rooks (or queens) transitions into a losing pawn endgame that was holdable or winning with pieces on the board.
223.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook capturing the opponent's rook (1/10 is a queen trade), voluntarily liquidating into a pure pawn or minor-piece endgame that is dramatically worse than keeping major pieces on the board. In 9/10 cases the resulting endgame is lost due to the opponent's superior king centralization (8/10), dangerous passed pawns (7/10), or pawn majorities (4/10). The average cp_loss of 374 reflects the catastrophic misjudgment of the simplified position. In all 10 positions, at least one good alternative existed that maintained the major piece's activity—typically using the rook for harassment, checking, or restraining passed pawns from a distance. 7/10 moves were captures with check, suggesting the players were drawn in by the forcing nature of the exchange. 9/10 occurred in endgames where the rook was the sole remaining defensive/attacking resource. The consistent error is overestimating one's chances in the resulting pawn endgame while underestimating the dynamic compensation provided by an active rook.

212.label: Bishop captures a pawn (or moves to a square) where it is immediately recaptured, trading a full bishop for insufficient compensation.
212.description: 10/10 positions involve a bishop moving to a square where it is immediately captured or recaptured by the opponent. In 8/10 cases, the bishop specifically captures a pawn and is then recaptured, resulting in a catastrophic bishop-for-pawn trade (losing ~2 pawns of material). The remaining cases involve the bishop capturing a knight when a better target existed (Position 10) or moving to a square where it is taken for free (Position 7). The recaptures frequently come with additional tactical consequences: in 4/10 positions the recapture creates a tempo/threat (discovered attack on the queen in Pos 1, check in Pos 4, fork setup in Pos 7, queen invasion in Pos 10). The consistent error is that the player sees an apparently 'free' pawn and reflexively captures it with the bishop without verifying whether the landing square is safe from recapture. Average cp_loss of 1222 confirms these are devastating mistakes, not marginal inaccuracies.

225.label: A rook is brought from a corner file to a central file as a 'developing' move, when the position demands immediate concrete action (tactics, prophylaxis, or piece safety).
225.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving from the a-file (or h-file in one case) to a central file (d or e), specified with the prefix 'Ra' or 'Rh' indicating it's the previously-inactive rook being brought into play. These are textbook 'developing' moves that would be reasonable in quiet positions, but in every case the position demanded urgent concrete action instead. In 6/10 positions, the player needed to address immediate king safety concerns (either their own exposed king or a prophylactic move to prevent an incoming attack). In 3/10 positions, a piece was tactically vulnerable and needed relocation before centralizing the rook (hanging bishop, trapped rook, or piece subject to a fork). In 2/10 positions, a powerful tactical strike was available that the slow rook move squandered. The average centipawn loss was 259 with only 1.5 good moves available on average, confirming these are critical moments where the generic move is catastrophically wrong. The common thread is that the player defaults to a 'safe-looking' positional move — activating the last rook — rather than reading the specific tactical demands of the position.

220.label: Advancing a passed pawn with check in a pure king-and-pawn endgame, a tempting but often premature forcing move.
220.description: All 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with both kings exposed and in close proximity (often near-opposition on the same file or adjacent files). 9/10 moves are single-step pawn advances that deliver check to the opposing king, while the remaining move (b4) is a pawn advance in an identical structural context. The pawns advanced are central or semi-central (b, c, e, f files) moving to the 4th, 5th, or 6th rank. In 5/10 positions the pawn check was correct (0-2 cp loss), gaining critical tempo to drive the opponent's king from a blockading square. In the other 5/10 positions it was a serious error (220-744 cp loss), where the pawn advance was premature — either self-blocking the player's own king's infiltration path (positions 6, 10), allowing the opponent's king to step to a superior blockading square (positions 4, 8), or advancing before necessary preparatory moves (position 9). The feature consistently activates on this specific decision point: the moment a player can push a passed pawn with check in a pawn endgame.

222.label: Knight moves to seemingly strong squares where the piece is tactically vulnerable due to inadequate support, leading to material loss.
222.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves to aggressive-looking squares that turn out to be tactically flawed. 4/10 specifically play Ne4 where the knight appears centralized but is inadequately supported—after exchanges the recaptured pawn on e4 hangs (positions 1, 5) or a double attack wins the piece back with interest (positions 4, 8). 2/10 play Ng4 where the knight attacks something but hangs to a queen capture or gets chased to a horrible square (positions 2, 10). The remaining knight moves go to the rim or corner (Na2 gets trapped, Na5 wastes tempo, Nd4 leads to exchanges losing a pawn). The single outlier (Rxg7+) shares the thematic thread of a speculative aggressive piece move without sufficient tactical justification. In all cases, better alternatives involved simple development (castling, central pawn breaks like ...d5 or ...e5) rather than premature piece lunges. The average cp_loss of 359 reflects that these moves often squander significant advantages or create losing positions from equality.

224.label: Premature forward pawn advances that destroy the player's own structural support, removing critical pawn defenders from pieces, chains, or king shelter.
224.description: All 10/10 positions feature an aggressive-looking forward pawn advance that actually undermines the player's own position. In 7/10 cases the pawn was an e- or f-pawn (f5 appeared 5 times, e4/e5 appeared 3 times), and in 9/10 cases the best alternative was a piece move, development, or castling rather than any pawn advance. The critical commonality is that the advanced pawn was performing an essential structural role before being pushed: in positions 1, 5, and 7, the f4-pawn supported a dominant e5 knight or pawn chain; in position 4, the f5-pawn guarded the centralized Ne4; in position 9, the a5-pawn maintained mutual protection with b4; in positions 8 and 10, the e-pawn maintained a powerful central pawn duo; in positions 2 and 3, the pawn protected king safety or dark squares. After advancing, 8/10 positions allowed the opponent to simply capture the pawn or exploit the newly unguarded piece/square. The average cp_loss of 276 reflects that these moves convert advantages into equality or worse. Only 2.5 good moves existed on average, yet in 8/10 positions at least 3 safe alternatives maintained the evaluation.

217.label: Rook moves to a peripheral square (typically a-file or h-file edge), abandoning its critical defensive or blockading duty near advancing passed pawns or an exposed king.
217.description: 10/10 positions are rook endgames where the blundering move sends the rook to a distant, passive square far from the position's critical tension. 8/10 moves land on the a-file or h-file (the absolute board edges: Rh1×3, Ra8×2, Ra6, Rh8, Ra2), while the remaining two (Rc3, Re7+) similarly move the rook away from where it's needed. In every case, the position features dangerous passed pawns (10/10) or immediate mating threats (3/10 result in mate-in-1 or forced mate). The correct moves consistently required keeping the rook near the critical pawn (e.g., Rf1 to blockade, Rh3 to pressure, Rg1 for proximity) or prioritizing king activation first (2/10 positions where the king should have moved before the rook). The average cp_loss of 3842 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in immediate forced checkmate, showing these passive rook placements can be instantly fatal when threats are concrete.

221.label: A knight moves from a central or functional square to the rim/periphery, abandoning critical tactical or defensive duties when immediate action was required.
221.description: 8/9 positions feature a knight moving from a central or actively-placed square to a peripheral square (a-file, h-file, b-file, or g-file), while the position demanded immediate tactical engagement. The most common specific move is Na4 (appearing in 5/9 positions), where the c3-knight leaves its central post for the a4 rim square, typically aiming for a slow Nc5 or Nb6 outpost plan. The remaining cases (Ng5, Nb6, Nh5, Nc5) follow the same principle: abandoning a square where the knight performed critical work. In 6/9 positions, an immediate tactic was available (fork, material win, or forced sequence) that went unplayed. In 5/9 positions, the decentralized knight became tactically vulnerable (trapped, undefended, or targetable by pawn thrusts). The one move with 0 cp_loss (Ne5) actually centralizes the knight, confirming the inverse pattern. The average cp_loss of 234 reflects how severely these slow maneuvering moves are punished when concrete tactics exist.

216.label: King advances aggressively in simplified endgame positions where both kings are exposed and pawn targets exist, often choosing the wrong destination square.
216.description: This feature fires on positions featuring aggressive king movement in simplified endgames with exposed kings on both sides. 8/10 positions are endgames, and 8/10 moves are king moves advancing toward enemy pawns. All 10 positions share the characteristic of both kings being exposed with weak or absent pawn shields, creating mutual vulnerability. Critically, 4/10 positions show 0 cp loss (the king move IS correct), indicating the feature captures the general PATTERN of king marching in exposed endgames rather than purely mistakes. Among the 6 actual errors, the common thread is selecting the wrong destination square: the king goes to a passive edge square instead of an active central one (Kh7 instead of Kg5), retreats when a capture is available (Kf8 instead of Kxe6), moves onto an open file enabling perpetual checks (Kg7), or walks into a checkmate net (Kh5). 7/10 positions feature pawn endgames or rook endgames with passed pawns as the dominant strategic element. The feature appears most sensitive to positions with 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.5), indicating razor-thin precision requirements where a single tempo or square choice determines the outcome.

219.label: Playing an aggressive or improving move while failing to address an immediate lethal threat to one's own king.
219.description: 8/10 positions feature king_safety as the primary tactical motif, and in all 10 cases the player chose a 'proactive' move (attacking an opponent's piece, advancing a pawn, centralizing) while their position demanded immediate defensive or tactical action. In 5/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 9, 10), the opponent had a forced checkmate that the move either created or failed to prevent. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 7, 9), the blunder specifically removed a piece or pawn that was guarding a critical square near the player's own king. The average cp_loss of 4128 is extraordinarily high because these moves typically convert survivable positions into immediate mates or crushing material losses. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise defensive calculation. 6/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves, confirming the positions demanded finding the one urgent response rather than choosing among several reasonable plans.

227.label: Playing a proactive positional/strategic move while ignoring a critical immediate tactical requirement such as a hanging piece, mating threat, or defensive necessity.
227.description: In 5/6 positions, the player chose an 'improving' move—centralizing a piece, advancing a pawn, or repositioning for attack—while a concrete tactical demand went unaddressed. In 2/6 positions (Kc6, f4), the move directly ignored a hanging piece that could be captured or that became undefended. In 1/6 positions (Nc5), the move ignored an immediate checkmate threat. In 1/6 positions (Rg6), the move walked into a forced tactical sequence by neglecting the defensive priority. In 1/6 (g5), a pawn was advanced into vulnerability when active piece play was required. The one exception (Be4, 0cp loss) was not a genuine error. The consistent thread is that players had a 'plan' in mind—king centralization, pawn storms, knight forks, attacking moves—and executed it without checking for the most urgent tactical obligation in the position. The average cp_loss of 3288 reflects that these 'plan-based' moves often had catastrophic consequences, with 3/6 positions showing losses exceeding 400cp.

230.label: A bishop makes a greedy capture (usually of a pawn) and either hangs on the destination square or is voluntarily traded away despite being the position's most critical piece.
230.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capture (Bx__) that constitutes a materialistic grab gone wrong. In 8/10 cases, the bishop captures a pawn; in 2/10 it captures a knight. The punishment falls into two sub-categories: in 4/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 10), the bishop is immediately hanging on its destination square and gets captured by an opponent's piece (queen, knight, or rook) — a simple tactical oversight. In the other 6/10 positions (2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9), the bishop is recaptured or traded, but the catastrophe is strategic — the bishop was performing an irreplaceable positional function (blockading passed pawns, defending key squares, maintaining dual-flank pressure, or providing the only piece activity) that far outweighed the material gained. The average cp_loss of 363 reflects that these are severe errors. The captures frequently land on rim/edge squares (a3, a5, a6, h6×2, g4) where bishops are most vulnerable, and 6/10 occur in endgames where the bishop's long-range versatility is at its peak strategic value.

231.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing piece repositioning move (usually the queen) in a position that demands immediate tactical exploitation.
231.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing repositioning move played when a concrete tactical blow was available. 7/10 are queen moves to seemingly natural squares (Qe2 x3, Qc7 x3, Qe7 x1), with the remaining 3 being other quiet piece placements (Ke2, Bg7, Bb7). In every case, the position demanded an immediate forcing move — a central pawn break (d4 in 3/10), a piece capture/fork (Nxd4/Nxd5 in 3/10), or a concrete piece activation (Re8, Rab8, Nb5 in 4/10). The average cp_loss is 277 with only 1.5 good moves available on average, confirming these are critical moments requiring precision. 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic'. The common thread is that the played moves look strategically reasonable — connecting rooks, developing pieces, improving queen placement — but fatally misjudge the tactical urgency, giving the opponent time to consolidate a vulnerability that could have been exploited immediately.

228.label: Quiet rook repositioning to natural-looking squares when the position demands an immediate forcing or safety-critical move.
228.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking rook move to a seemingly logical square (open file, attacking an enemy piece, developing). In every case, only 1 good move existed (avg good moves: 1.0), and the average centipawn loss was a catastrophic 3010cp. The best moves were overwhelmingly non-rook moves or fundamentally different rook moves: 5/10 required a piece move (Kd2, Bh5+, Ng5, Qxg3+, O-O), 3/10 required the rook to go to a specific different square (Re1 not Rb1, Re8 not Rg8, Rg1 not Rh2), and 2/10 required a different rook entirely. In 7/10 positions, the rook move was reacting to or targeting an enemy bishop (on b2, g2, e7, b7) — a secondary concern that distracted from the primary tactical demand. In 6/10 cases, the missed opportunity involved king safety (either exploiting an exposed enemy king or protecting one's own). The positions universally had narrow tactical solutions where one tempo was the difference between winning/surviving and losing.

234.label: Advancing a passed pawn (or aggressive pawn) when the position demands addressing an immediate tactical threat or maintaining piece activity.
234.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn advances (e6, e4, c6, c6, b4, c4, d3, e6, e3), with only 1/10 being a piece move (Ne4) that shares the same 'aggressive but non-forcing' quality. At least 7/10 specifically involve advancing a passed pawn or a pawn intended to become dangerous. In every case, the best moves required piece activity (queen checks in 5/10, queen repositioning in 3/10, prophylactic piece moves in 2/10) rather than pawn advances. The positions uniformly punished the pawn push because it was non-forcing—creating no check or capture—while the opponent had immediate tactical resources (back-rank mates in 4/10, king-hunting attacks in 3/10, material wins via the weakened pawn in 3/10). The avg cp_loss of 3178 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' pawn pushes were, often allowing forced mates or decisive material loss.

232.label: A knight moves to an undefended square that lies on an enemy bishop's diagonal, allowing immediate capture and material loss.
232.description: 9/10 positions show the identical tactical pattern: a knight relocates to a square directly attacked by an enemy bishop along its diagonal, where it can be captured for free. In Position 1, Ne3 lands on the g1 bishop's diagonal; in Position 2, Na4+ lands on the c2 bishop's diagonal; in Positions 3 and 4, Nf4 lands on diagonals controlled by bishops on c1 and d6 respectively; in Position 5, Nb5 lands on the e2 bishop's diagonal; in Position 6, Ne5 lands on the b2 bishop's long diagonal; in Position 7, Nd6 lands on the g3 bishop's diagonal; in Position 9, Nf6+ lands on the d8 bishop's diagonal; and in Position 10, Nd6 lands on the e5 bishop's diagonal. Position 8 is the slight outlier where the knight moves to e4 (on the g2 bishop's diagonal) but the primary punishment is positional rather than a direct capture. In all cases, the knight was previously on a safe square and better alternatives existed that kept the knight protected or actively engaged without entering the danger zone.

238.label: A piece moves to an undefended square directly accessible to an enemy rook along an open rank or file, allowing immediate capture.
238.description: In 10/10 positions, the blundering side moved a piece (queen, knight, bishop, or rook) to a square that was undefended and sat directly on the same rank or file as an enemy rook with no intervening pieces. The refutation in every case was the rook simply sliding along that open line to capture the piece. The capturing rook moved along a rank in 7/10 cases (Rxg4 along 4th rank, Rxc4 along 4th rank, Rxe6 along 6th rank, Rxd6 along 6th rank, Rxc2 along 2nd rank, Rxb2 along 2nd rank, Rxb4 along a rank) and along a file in 3/10 cases (Rxg6+ along g-file, Rxd3 along d-file, Rxf5 along f-file). The blundered piece was a queen in 3/10 cases, a knight in 3/10, a bishop in 2/10, and a rook in 2/10. The average cp_loss was 2278, reflecting that these are typically full-piece or full-queen losses. In all 10 positions, the player had multiple good alternatives (avg 2.1) that avoided placing a piece on the vulnerable square.

236.label: Advancing a pawn prematurely in a pawn endgame when king activity or a different pawn advance was critical for maintaining the tempo balance.
236.description: 10/10 positions are pawn endgames (or near-pawn endgames) where the player advances a pawn that either wastes a critical tempo or creates a fixed structural weakness. In 7/10 cases, the correct move involved either king activity first (Positions 1, 4, 9, 10) or advancing a DIFFERENT pawn (Positions 1, 5, 6, 10). In 6/10 positions, the advanced pawn becomes a fixed target that the opponent's king can attack (Positions 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, and the g3 in Position 10). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'pawn_structure' in 10/10. Critically, the average number of good moves was only 1.8, indicating these are razor-thin positions where choosing the wrong pawn is immediately punishing. The moves are predominantly flank pawns (8/10 on a, b, g, or h files), advanced when the decisive action needed to happen elsewhere — typically king penetration toward a vulnerability or a passed pawn race on the opposite wing.

237.label: Playing quiet non-capturing moves when an enemy piece is hanging and simply capturable.
237.description: 8/10 positions feature an undefended enemy piece (often deeply infiltrated into the player's position) that could be captured immediately, yet the player chose a quiet repositioning or pawn move instead. In positions 1 (axb3 captures queen), 2 (Rxa1 captures rook), 3 (fxg3 captures queen), 4 (Qxf3 captures bishop), 5 (Bxf2/Kxf2 captures rook), 6 (Kxg7 captures queen), 8 (Qxe2 captures bishop), and 9 (Nxe7 captures queen), the sole or primary good move was a simple capture of a hanging piece. The remaining 2/10 positions (7 and 10) involve pushing g4 which creates a newly hanging pawn capturable by the opponent's queen. In 9/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, and the average cp_loss was nearly 4000, indicating catastrophic consequences. The played moves were universally quiet (pawn pushes, piece repositioning, king walks) rather than forcing moves.

218.label: Major piece (Queen/Rook) makes an impressive infiltrating move deep into enemy territory when a more forcing, concrete tactical blow was available.
218.description: 10/10 positions feature a Queen or Rook making an aggressive move, typically infiltrating to the 7th rank or deep into the opponent's position. 8/10 moves land on the 7th rank (or its equivalent 2nd rank for Black): Qf7, Qe7, Ra7, Qd7+, Qxc7 for White, and Qd2, Rd2 for Black. 7/10 are Queen moves and 3/10 are Rook moves. Among the 7 actual mistakes, the superior alternative was consistently a more concrete/forcing action: capturing an undefended piece (Nxf4 in pos 2, Rxf2 in pos 10), a decisive fork (Nxf3+ in pos 4), pushing a passed pawn (d6 in pos 5), delivering a precise check (Qd3+ in pos 8), or simplifying via queen trade (Qxg6+ in pos 6, Qxd5 in pos 9). In 5/7 mistakes, the best move used a DIFFERENT piece than the one moved. The 3 non-mistakes (positions 1, 3, 7) show that the infiltration IS sometimes correct—specifically when no simpler forcing move exists and the infiltration itself leads to forced mate. The common thread is positions where the player is already winning (8/10 positions have the moving side with a significant advantage), making this primarily a conversion-stage error of choosing impressive-looking activity over immediately decisive action.

226.label: Natural-looking defensive piece moves in sharp positions that miss the single forcing continuation, surrendering a critical tempo to the opponent.
226.description: All 10 positions share a remarkably consistent pattern: a sharp position with only ~1 good move available (avg 1.2), where the player chose a passive or defensive-looking piece move instead of the one forcing/active continuation that was required. 9/10 positions feature tempo_loss as the primary consequence, and 10/10 involve a reduction in piece_activity. The played moves overwhelmingly address a perceived threat (6/10 are queen moves defending squares like f7, e5, or f2; 3/10 are rook moves shoring up files), but the correct moves were forcing plays: attacking the opponent's exposed queen (positions 1, 7, 9), executing a tactical blow (positions 5, 8), occupying a dominant outpost (position 4), or challenging an attacking piece with tempo (positions 2, 3, 6, 10). In 7/10 cases the position required exploiting the opponent's king in the center or exposed pieces, but the player chose consolidation over confrontation. The avg cp_loss of 297 reflects that in 'only-move' positions, passive play is catastrophically punished.

239.label: Playing a prophylactic h-pawn advance (h3/h6) to create king escape space while an urgent tactical crisis — typically a hanging piece — demands immediate forcing action.
239.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same move type: a single-square h-pawn advance (h3 for White in 7/10, h6 for Black in 3/10) intended as 'luft' to give the king an escape square. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand that made this quiet move catastrophic. In 8/10 positions, a major piece was hanging (undefended rook in positions 1, 3, 7, 8; undefended queen in position 4; undefended bishop in position 10; piece capturable with check/deflection in positions 2, 8). In the remaining 2/10, a critical passed pawn needed immediate capture (position 5) or the only available counterplay required a forcing capture with check (position 6). The average centipawn loss was 1412, with only 1.6 good moves available on average, confirming these were high-precision moments where the slow prophylactic move was uniquely punishing. The king was on the back rank in 9/10 positions (h1 or h8), explaining the psychological impulse toward creating luft, but in every case the correct approach was to solve the tactical crisis through active forcing play rather than passive prevention.

233.label: A knight is moved from a critical defensive square (usually on the f-file) to a passive or rim square, fatally weakening king protection.
233.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight being voluntarily moved from an active defensive post to a passive square, with devastating consequences for king safety. In 8/10 cases, the knight departed from the f-file (f6 in 4 positions, f3 in 3 positions, f2 in 1 position), where it was performing essential defensive duties guarding key kingside squares. The destinations are uniformly passive: h2/h7 in 4/10 (rim squares), d7 in 3/10 (blocked/passive), and a4/d3/c5 in the remaining 3 (decentralized or misplaced). The consistent consequence is that the opponent immediately exploits the unguarded squares: Qh6+ infiltration after Nf6 leaves (positions 5, 8), mating attacks down the h-file after Nf3 leaves (positions 4, 7), rook invasions through h1 after Nf2 leaves (position 3), and pawn breakthroughs after structural defenders depart (positions 1, 2, 9, 10). Average cp_loss of 3135 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 3/10 resulting in forced checkmate.

244.label: Castling moves the king away from a piece it was solely defending, leaving that piece hanging to an opponent's major piece already targeting it.
244.description: 10/10 positions feature the identical tactical error: the king (on e1 or e8) is the sole defender of an adjacent piece, and castling removes that defense, leaving the piece freely capturable. In 7/10 positions, Black's king on e8 defends a piece on e7 (6 cases) or d7 (1 case), and castling kingside or queenside abandons it. In 3/10 positions, White's king on e1 defends a piece on e2, and O-O leaves it hanging. The opponent already has a major piece (queen in 8/10 cases, rook in 2/10) directly targeting the now-undefended square along the open e-file or a clear diagonal. The refutation is always a simple capture of the hanging piece (Qxe7, Rxe7, Qxe2, Qxd7), requiring no deep calculation. The best alternatives consistently involve either moving the king to a non-castling square (Kf8, Kf7, Kf2) that preserves the defensive relationship, blocking the attacking line first, or driving the attacker away before castling.

242.label: Playing a wing pawn advance (typically h- or a-file) that wastes a critical tempo when piece activation, king centralization, or a concrete tactical idea is urgently needed.
242.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances as the mistake, with 8/10 being wing pawn pushes (h-file: 6 positions, a-file: 2 positions). In 7/10 positions the phase is endgame, where tempi are especially precious. The correct alternatives in 8/10 cases involved piece or king moves (bishop activation, rook repositioning, king centralization, or exploiting a tactical pin), while only 2/10 required a different pawn advance. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'piece_activity' in 9/10. The average cp_loss is extremely high (1082), reflecting how catastrophic wasting a tempo on a committal pawn move can be in simplified positions. In every case, the pawn advance either weakened the player's own structure, opened lines that favored the opponent, or simply ceded initiative at a critical moment when the position demanded immediate action.

247.label: Queen captures a peripheral b/g pawn (on the 2nd or 7th rank), abandoning a superior central role for greedy material gain that allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
247.description: 10/10 positions feature the queen capturing a wing pawn on one of four specific squares: g2 (4 positions), b2 (2 positions), b7 (3 positions), or g7 (2 positions). In every case, the queen leaves an active central post (typically e4, d4, d5, g4, or g5) to grab a peripheral pawn on the knight-file's 2nd/7th rank. 10/10 positions had the queen moving AWAY from the center toward the board's edge. 9/10 positions featured at least one uncastled king, making tempo and initiative critically important. 10/10 had superior alternatives that involved capturing a central piece, developing, or maintaining queen centralization. The average cp_loss was 1267, reflecting how catastrophic these pawn grabs are. Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, meaning these were critical decision points. The refutations consistently exploit the queen's displacement through tempo-gaining attacks (Bf3, Rg1, O-O-O, Qh5+), development with initiative, or mating attacks against exposed kings that the distant queen cannot help defend.

240.label: Rook (or queen) moved to an aggressive-looking square, often with check, when a concrete capture or sacrifice was the correct action.
240.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves and 5/10 deliver check, but in nearly every case the 'aggressive' move abandons a strong position or gives a pointless check that the opponent easily sidesteps. The correct move in 6/10 positions was a concrete capture or sacrifice (Rxg7+, Rxe6, Rxc1, Qxe7, Qxf5, Ng4 blocking), while the played move chose superficial activity instead. 9/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' — the opponent gains time because the aggressive-looking piece ends up misplaced or the check drives the king to safety. In Position 1, Rh4+ drives the king to g8 where Rxg7+ no longer works; in Position 4, Re8+ abandons the dominant e5 post for a meaningless check; in Position 9, Qb8+ allows the king to reach g7 enabling the lethal f6+ advance; in Position 10, Rg5 leaves e6 unattacked. Position 8 (Rb5+, cp_loss=0) confirms the pattern by showing what a well-calculated check looks like — one that maintains a forced mating net rather than giving the opponent an escape route.
240.old_chip: Flashy rook moves miss concrete tactics

229.label: A piece (usually a rook) moves to a superficially attractive square, abandoning the position from which a concrete winning tactic was available.
229.description: In 7/9 positions, the blunder is specifically a rook move that looks active (going to an open file, capturing a pawn, threatening a piece, moving to the 7th rank) but actually leaves the critical square where the tactic existed. In Position 1, the rook leaves d4 (where Rxc4 won material) for d3. In Position 2, the rook grabs h2 instead of addressing the promotion via Rc8. In Position 3, the rook goes to h4 instead of executing Rxf2 which opened a decisive diagonal. In Position 8, the rook leaves the e-file for c7 instead of playing R7e5 with a double attack. In Position 10, the rook moves to e6 instead of playing Rxb2+ which won an exchange. Positions 4 and 6 show the same pattern with a knight and rook respectively abandoning optimal squares. The average cp_loss of 1410 and average good moves of 1.8 confirm these are critical tactical moments with narrow paths to success, where the player chose the 'natural-looking active move' over the one concrete winning shot.

241.label: Advancing the b-pawn to deal with an infiltrated enemy bishop, fatally weakening the king's pawn shelter and opening critical lines/squares for attack.
241.description: In 7/10 positions, there is a deeply infiltrated enemy bishop (on a2 in positions 2, 3, 9, 10; on c2 in position 1; on a7 in positions 5 and 6) and the player advances a b-pawn (b3 or b6) specifically to chase, trap, or block this bishop. In all cases the king is castled queenside or nearby (king on c1 in 5 positions, c8 in 2 positions). The b-pawn advance then catastrophically weakens the king's shelter — opening the a3 square for queen checks/mates (positions 2, 3, 10), opening the a6-c8 diagonal (position 5), creating pawn lever targets (position 9), or simply wasting a critical defensive tempo (positions 1, 6). The remaining 3 positions (b5, d5, g5) follow the broader pattern of a slow pawn push to address a positional nuisance while ignoring urgent tactical needs, with the advance weakening king safety. 9/10 positions feature a king that is queenside-castled or centrally placed. The average cp_loss of 3118 reflects that many of these allow immediate forced mates or massive material loss.

243.label: Moving a rook to double or coordinate with the other rook when the position demands immediate forcing action.
243.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking rook repositioning move, and 8/10 use algebraic disambiguation (Rcd3, Rdc7, Rdf7, etc.) indicating two rooks were available and the player chose to move one toward the other for 'coordination.' In every case, the analyses identify tempo_loss as the core issue (10/10 tagged). The positions consistently demanded urgent concrete action: missed forced mates (position 2), missed en passant checks (position 10), missed tactical strikes like Qxa6+ (position 8), failure to resolve critical pawn tension (positions 4, 5), or failure to address a trapped/vulnerable piece (position 7). Instead, the player opted for what appeared to be a logical preparatory rook maneuver — doubling on a file, lifting to a rank, or aligning rooks — that accomplished nothing concrete while gifting the opponent a critical tempo. The average cp_loss of 1142 and average of only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are narrow critical moments where the slow rook move is uniquely catastrophic.

249.label: A bishop is moved to a seemingly active or natural developing square where it becomes a tactical target or the tempo is critically wasted.
249.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being repositioned to what appears to be an active, developing, or pressuring square — but the square is tactically compromised. In 7/10 cases, the bishop lands on a square where it can be directly captured or trapped with structural/material consequences: Be6 appears 3 times and is punished by Nxe6 fxe6 (opening the f-file and creating weak pawns exploitable by forks or queen invasions), Bg4 appears twice with the bishop exposed to rook attacks or pawn advances, Bg5 twice where capture wrecks pawn structure or the move ignores queen safety, and Bh5 once where Rh4 attacks it fatally. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 7, 8), the bishop development is not directly punished by capturing it, but rather the non-forcing nature of the move wastes a critical tempo when a concrete tactic (Nc3 fork, Qxf6, Bh5+) was available. The average cp_loss of 1156 reflects that these are severe errors. The positions are split between Black (6/10) and White (4/10), all in the middlegame, with an average of 2.4 good alternatives available — showing these mistakes are avoidable with proper tactical awareness.

245.label: King moves that waste a critical tempo in time-sensitive positions where immediate concrete action or a different king direction was required.
245.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves that lose a decisive tempo. In 6/10 cases, a non-king move was urgently needed first (pawn breaks like b3, a4, exd4; captures like Rxg5; checks like g5+; or piece repositioning like Bf6). In 4/10 cases, the king needed to move but to a different square/direction (e.g., Kf3 instead of Kg4, Kf4 instead of Kg3, Ke7 instead of Kd5). The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (8/10) where tempo is critical due to pawn races, king penetration races, or narrow defensive windows. The average cp_loss of 248 is high, and the average of only 1.7 good moves indicates razor-sharp positions with minimal margin for error. 9/10 analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The common thread is that the player makes a 'natural-looking' king improvement move—often toward a pawn they want to capture or defend—without recognizing that the position demands immediate concrete action elsewhere.

254.label: A knight gives check on a square where it can simply be captured, losing material for no compensation.
254.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight delivering check on a square where it is immediately capturable by the opponent, resulting in a net loss of material. In 8/10 cases, the primary tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' — the knight lands on a square unprotected by any friendly piece and is simply taken. The average centipawn loss of 407 confirms these are severe blunders. In 9/10 positions, the strongest refutation begins with capturing the knight (Qxg4, Bxd3, Rxe2, Qxh6, hxg3, etc.), while only in 1/10 does the best refutation involve sidestepping rather than capturing. The best moves available were typically quiet developing or consolidating moves (Qd1, Qxa3, Qe5+, cxb4, Nxd3+, Rg3, Bd3, Nxb3, Qc1+) that maintained piece coordination rather than throwing material away. In 6/10 cases, the player had a well-placed knight already and the check actually worsened its position by moving it to an undefended square. The pattern is consistent across both sides (White 4/10, Black 6/10) and phases (opening 2/10, middlegame 8/10).

250.label: Moving a bishop (or minor piece) to a seemingly strong central square where it is immediately captured, attacked with tempo, or creates a fatal tactical vulnerability.
250.description: 9/10 positions involve bishop moves (Be4, Bf4+, Bd3, Bd4, Bd6, Bd7, Bc5, Bd4, Bd4) and 1/10 a knight move (Nc3), all placing the piece on an apparently active or dominant square. In 8/10 positions, the piece is immediately captured or driven back with tempo on the very next move (Rxd4 in positions 4, 9; Rxf4 in position 2; Rxd6 in position 5; e4 kicking in position 3; b4+ in position 8; Qa8+ in position 7; b4 in position 10). In 6/10 positions, the piece lands on or adjacent to an open file controlled by an enemy rook, making it directly capturable. The average cp_loss of 279 confirms these are severe errors, not marginal inaccuracies. All positions share the trait that 2-3 good alternatives existed that addressed concrete positional needs (activating rooks, creating luft, pawn breaks) rather than pursuing aesthetic piece placement. The consistent error is prioritizing a piece's apparent activity on a 'strong square' over its tactical safety in the concrete position.

246.label: Non-capturing rook moves to seemingly active squares in open endgame positions, missing more concrete or purposeful continuations.
246.description: 10/10 positions feature non-capturing rook moves in endgame or late middlegame positions with exposed kings and open files. In the positions where these are actual mistakes (6/10 with cp_loss ≥13), the rook relocates to a square that appears active or centralized but lacks a concrete purpose — missing immediate captures (Rxf3+ in Position 9, Rxf8 in Position 10), critical defensive posts (Rf7 in Position 1), or optimal restrictive placements (cutting off the king in Position 5). Even the 4/10 positions with 0-1 cp_loss share the same geometric signature: a rook sliding to a new rank/file in an open position with weak king positions on both sides. The common board state includes exposed kings (10/10), open files (10/10), and rook endgame or rook-dominant material (10/10). The consistent error pattern is prioritizing general rook activity over specific concrete actions.

235.label: The player voluntarily moves a piece (usually the king) to an exposed or non-functional square, ignoring a forcing tactical punishment that exploits the displacement.
235.description: 8/10 positions feature a move that voluntarily displaces the player's own piece to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable, structurally disconnected from its duties, or exposed to forcing replies. 5/10 moves are king moves (Kg3, Kg5, Kxc5, Kxc1, Kd7) where the king walks to an exposed or incorrect square, while 3/10 are bishop moves (Bh3, Bxb4, and the correct Bxf3) that remove a piece from a functional defensive role. The common punishment pattern involves the opponent exploiting the displaced piece with tempo-gaining tactics: knight forks after Kxc5, pawn kicks (h6+) after Kg5, clearance sacrifices (Bxh2+) after Bxb4, captures of undefended pawns (Nxb2) after Bh3, and rook invasions against abandoned passed pawns after Kg3/Kd7. In 7/10 positions with actual errors, the better alternatives involved either staying put, retreating to safety, or prioritizing pawn advancement/defensive preparation rather than making the 'active-looking' displacement. The feature consistently fires when the moved piece ends up on a square that is worse than where it started, enabling a specific opponent reply that wasn't possible before.

255.label: Capturing a piece on a square where an advanced pawn (or piece) recaptures with promotion-check or checkmate.
255.description: In 8/10 positions, the player captures a piece on a square that is the promotion square of an advanced enemy pawn (on the 7th rank), allowing that pawn to recapture with immediate promotion to queen/rook WITH CHECK or CHECKMATE. The two remaining positions (4 and 6) follow the same structural logic: a capture lands on a square where the opponent's recapture delivers an immediate lethal blow (Rxh3# and Rxg8+ leading to forced mate). In all 10 cases, the capture appears to win material (taking a queen or rook), but the recapture is more devastating than the initial capture. In 9/10 positions the recapture comes with check or checkmate. The average cp_loss is enormous (6584) because 7/10 positions result in forced mate after the recapture. Only 1 good move was available in every single position, indicating these are critical junctures where any deviation from the single correct continuation is catastrophic.

251.label: A pawn captures an enemy piece (knight or bishop) for apparent material gain, but the pawn was serving a critical structural or defensive role whose removal creates a devastating tactical vulnerability.
251.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing a minor piece (bishop or knight), appearing to win material cheaply. In every case, the moved pawn was serving a more important purpose on its original square than the material it gained. In 5/10 positions (2, 8, 9, 10, and partially 7), the pawn was blocking a critical file or supporting another piece — its removal opened lines for devastating checks, forks, or discovered attacks against the player's own king or pieces. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 6), the pawn capture wasted a crucial tempo on material collection while an urgent tactical threat (undefended piece, uncastled king, or forcing sequence) demanded immediate attention. In 3/10 positions (5, 6, 7), the capture specifically left the player's own piece hanging because the capturing pawn had been part of that piece's defensive coordination. The average cp_loss of 380 reflects that these are catastrophic errors — converting winning positions to losing ones (6/10 cases) or squandering large advantages — because the 'free piece' was actually a tactical trap exploiting the pawn's removal from its post.

256.label: A passive or prophylactic pawn advance played in a critical position where an active piece move (usually a rook activation or tactical capture) was required.
256.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing pawn push as the blunder. In 9/10 cases, the best move was an active piece move — typically a rook move (Rc8, Rb7+, Rc1, Rb5, Rxe3) or a capture/piece activation (Qxb6, Nxe4, Ng5). The average cp_loss of 1202 and only 1.4 good moves available confirm these are critical moments requiring precise, active responses. The pawn moves share a common intent: they attempt to prophylactically restrain, block, or shore up a weakness slowly, when the position's tension demands immediate tactical engagement. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 7, 9, and indirectly 6), the pawn advance catastrophically releases restraint on the opponent's passed pawn or removes a critical blockade function. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 8, 10), the pawn move ignores an urgent piece-based threat or tactical necessity. Notably, in 2/10 positions (8 and 9), the player pushed a pawn to the exact square where the correct piece needed to go (g5 instead of Ng5; b5 instead of Rb5).

253.label: Bishop moves to a passive edge square (back rank, corner, or rim file) in endgames, wasting critical tempo and abandoning active diagonals.
253.description: 10/10 positions feature bishop moves in endgames, and 9/10 involve the bishop relocating to a square on the rim of the board (rank 1/2, rank 7/8, or the a/h files). Specific destinations include corners (h1, a1), back-rank squares (e1, e1, f1, c1), near-corner squares (h2), edge-file squares (h6), and near-back-rank squares (c7). The two positions with 0 cp_loss (Positions 1 and 8) still feature the same geometric pattern but occur in completely won positions where the move order doesn't matter. In the remaining 8 positions with actual cp_loss (avg ~1200cp excluding the 0-loss cases), the bishop abandons a centralized or functionally critical square (g3, f3, c4, f6, e3) for a passive rim square. 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these are precisely the moments where the passive retreat is most punishing.

263.label: Moving a rook to the back rank on the b-file to attack an enemy queen deeply placed on b7/b2, when this is tactically unsound or strategically counterproductive.
263.description: All 10/10 positions feature an enemy queen infiltrated deep into the player's position on b7 (6 positions, Black plays Rb8) or b2 (4 positions, White plays Rb1), and the blunder is always the reflexive rook-to-back-rank move to 'attack' the queen. This natural-looking response fails for varied but related reasons: in 3/10 positions (1, 6, 9) the queen captures an undefended piece (typically a knight on c6) instead of retreating, often with check; in 3/10 positions (5, 7, 8) the rook on b8/b1 is itself captured or won tactically due to diagonal control or X-ray attacks; in 2/10 positions (3, 4) the rook move neglects a critical positional need (like castling) allowing devastating tactical blows; and in 2/10 positions (2, 10) the queen happily retreats to a far superior square, gaining rather than losing from being 'chased.' The average cp_loss of 324 reflects that these are severe blunders. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points requiring precise play rather than reflexive piece moves.

259.label: A reflexive pawn capture that grabs immediate material while ignoring a more important tactical or strategic priority.
259.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture (xNotation) as the mistake, where the player takes seemingly free or natural material but misses something far more important. In 4/10 positions (3, 7, 8, 9), the pawn capture catastrophically opens a line (diagonal or file) against the player's own king, inviting devastating checks or attacks. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 6, 10), the capture grabs a low-value pawn while a forced mate or hanging piece worth far more was available. In 2/10 positions (1, 5), the capture prematurely releases pawn tension that was serving a critical structural or strategic purpose. The average cp_loss of 2061 reflects that many of these are catastrophic (two missed forced mates), while the average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these were positions demanding precision. The common thread is a player defaulting to the most obvious material-gaining pawn capture without evaluating whether maintaining tension, developing, attacking the king, or capturing a higher-value target was superior.

262.label: A reflexive, non-capturing king move to perceived safety when an active capture or forcing move was required.
262.description: All 10/10 positions feature a passive king retreat (always a non-capturing move, always toward an edge or corner) played instead of an active tactical solution. In 7/10 cases, the correct move was a simple capture of a hanging or undefended piece (Rxd8, Qxg5, hxg5, Rxc8, Bxb7, Kxf7, and Rxc4 available). In the remaining 3/10, the correct move was an active piece deployment addressing concrete threats (Qe8, Re7, Rg2). The king moves predominantly gravitate toward the h-file (7/10: Kh7×3, Kh2, Kh8, Kh3, Kh1), with the remainder going to back-rank corners (Kc8, Kf8, Kg8). The average cp_loss of 3144 and average of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these are narrow, critical positions where the one correct active move was replaced by a fear-driven retreat. In 6/10 cases the king move actually worsened king safety by walking into checks, diagonals, or mating nets.

248.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning moves that ignore the position's most urgent tactical requirement (exposed king, hanging piece, or must-capture threat).
248.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet piece development or repositioning move when the position demanded an immediate, often forcing response to a critical tactical problem. In 7/10 cases, the blunder was a rook or bishop moving to a 'natural-looking' square (Rg8, Rb8, Bg5, Rb1, Rb8, Bg7, Be7) that appeared purposeful — chasing an enemy piece, developing, or saving material — but failed to address the actual emergency. In 5/10 positions, the king was stuck in the center or gravely exposed, and the best move required active counterplay (Qh4) or neutralizing a check-giving retreat (Qd7 blocking Bc6+). In 3/10 positions (Pos 2, 5, 9), the queen itself was hanging or about to be captured, yet the player developed another piece instead. The average cp_loss of 1142 and average of only 2.0 good moves confirm these are demanding positions with narrow solutions where the 'obvious-looking' natural move is catastrophically wrong.

258.label: Playing a secondary-purpose move in a position with only one correct idea, wasting the critical tempo needed to address an immediate tactical or strategic emergency.
258.description: All 10 positions share a remarkably narrow decision point (average 1.3 good moves available) where the position demanded addressing ONE urgent requirement — yet the player chose a move pursuing a peripheral or secondary goal instead. In 9/10 positions, the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The urgent requirements varied: addressing hanging pieces (positions 1, 4, 6), neutralizing a passed pawn (positions 2, 10), executing a time-sensitive tactic (position 3), defusing an attack on an exposed king (positions 5, 9), or activating a critical piece (positions 7, 8). In every case, the played move looks purposeful — repositioning a rook (4/10), advancing the king toward material (2/10), retreating a piece to a natural-looking square (2/10) — but completely ignores what the position actually demands. 8/10 positions involved pursuing wing/peripheral activity while the critical action was in the center or on the opposite side. The average cp_loss of 1220 reflects how catastrophic it is to waste even one tempo in these razor-sharp positions.

261.label: Moving a rook one square sideways to an adjacent file as quiet 'development' when the position demands immediate tactical action or critical defensive duty.
261.description: 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to an adjacent file (typically b-file or c-file) as a non-forcing 'improvement' move in positions requiring immediate concrete action. 7/10 specifically move a rook to b1/b8 from a neighboring file, while 2/10 go to c1 and 1/10 slides to g8 from h8. In 6/10 cases, a forcing tactical sequence was available (sacrifices, discovered checks, captures with tempo) that the rook move completely ignored. In 4/10 cases, the rook was abandoning a critical defensive post (guarding a pawn, blocking a file, or covering a key square). The average cp_loss of 1265 reflects how catastrophic these tempo losses are—8/10 positions had the opponent's king exposed or vulnerable, meaning the wasted tempo allowed consolidation or counterattack. Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments where precise play was essential.

268.label: A slow, non-forcing one-square pawn advance on the a, b, or h file in a position that urgently required immediate tactical action or forcing moves.
268.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step flank pawn advance (h3 in 4 positions, h6 in 2, b3 in 2, a3 in 1, a6 in 1) — exclusively on the a, b, or h files. In every case, the move is described as 'prophylactic' or 'preparatory' (creating king luft, preventing hypothetical piece intrusions, preparing fianchetto or pawn chains). Critically, 10/10 positions had concrete tactical opportunities available: capturing a hanging queen (exf6), sacrificial attacks (Rxe6+, Bxe6+), forcing captures (Rxg2+), penetrating moves (Rc8), or centralizing strikes (Nd4, e5, Nc4). The average number of good moves was only 1.5, meaning these were narrow tactical positions demanding precision. 9/10 positions list 'tempo_loss' as a primary tag, and 9/10 are in the middlegame phase where tempi are critical. The average centipawn loss of 282 reflects how devastating it is to waste a move on prophylaxis when the position has a short tactical shelf-life.
268.old_chip: Quiet flank pawn when tactics demand

264.label: Advancing a pawn past the point where it could capture an enemy pawn, sealing the file instead of opening it and wasting a critical tempo.
264.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances (never captures or piece moves), with 7/10 being h-pawn pushes (h5-h6 or h4-h3). In at least 7/10 positions, a pawn capture was available or among the best alternatives: hxg6 was best or second-best in positions 1, 2, 3, 4, and 8; hxg3 was the winning move in position 7; axb7+ was the second-best move in position 9. The remaining positions (5, 6, 10) feature similar speculative pawn advances that ignore immediate tactical crises. The consistent error is choosing the 'aggressive-looking' advance over the concrete capture that would open files, create real threats, or gain tempo. In 8/10 positions, the move was explicitly tagged as a tempo loss. The average cp_loss of 1301 reflects how catastrophic these decisions are — the pawn push looks threatening but creates no concrete problems while gifting the opponent time to execute their own plans.

266.label: Playing a knight check to a tempting but inferior destination square when a different knight check (or move) to a better square was available.
266.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight delivering check to the wrong square. In 9/10 cases, a discovered check mechanism exists (knight moves to unmask a bishop/queen), and the player chose a suboptimal landing square for the knight. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 8, 9), the correct move was a different discovered check square that maintained a forced mating attack (all had #+3 to #+6 available). In 2/10 positions (3, 7), the knight check led to a rook fork on a8, but the knight became permanently trapped there. In 3/10 positions (5, 6, 10), the discovered check removed the knight from a square where it was needed for a superior tactical combination. In position 1, the knight check neglected urgent defensive needs. The consistent error is prioritizing the superficially attractive property of the destination square (fork, capture, centralization) over calculating what follow-up threats the knight actually enables from that square.

252.label: Pawn captures or advances that resolve structural tension while leaving own pieces, pawns, or king fatally undefended.
252.description: 9/10 positions involve pawn moves (7/10 are pawn captures specifically), with the remaining position (O-O-O) functionally equivalent in removing a defender from a key square. In all 10 cases, the player resolves pawn tension or changes the structure in a way that seems natural—capturing an enemy pawn, gaining space, creating a passed pawn—but ignores that the move leaves their own material critically undefended or opens lines against their own king. Specifically: 5/10 positions directly leave a piece hanging (Bf5 in position 1, Bc4 in position 3, Ra8 in position 4, the a7 pawn in position 5, the d4 pawn in position 8), 2/10 fatally weaken the king by advancing its pawn shield (positions 6 and 10), and 3/10 create positional/tactical holes by releasing tension prematurely (positions 2, 7, 9). The good alternatives consistently prioritize piece safety, development, or maintaining the protective tension before resolving structure—with an average of 2.2 good moves available, these were avoidable errors where the player chose an impulsive structural change over defensive awareness.

269.label: Bishop makes a capture that removes it from a critical defensive or positional role, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
269.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capture (Bx...) where the bishop was performing an essential defensive function prior to the move. In 8/10 cases, the bishop was guarding a critical square (f8 in positions 2 and 6, the a5-e1 diagonal in position 3, h7 in position 6), protecting a piece (c3 knight in positions 1 and 3, e5 pawn in position 5), shielding the king from a discovered attack (position 8), or blockading a passed pawn (position 7). In 2/10 cases (positions 1 and 5), the error is specifically a wrong-piece recapture where the pawn should have taken instead of the bishop. The captures always appear attractive—eliminating a strong enemy piece, winning material, or simplifying—but the bishop's departure instantly exposes a lethal tactical flaw. The resulting punishments range from back-rank mates (positions 2, 6), hanging pieces (positions 1, 3, 5), discovered checks (position 8), pawn promotions (position 7), to insufficient compensation for sacrificed material (position 10). Average cp_loss of 3065 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in immediate checkmate or forced mate.

265.label: Pawn captures pawn to resolve tension in endgame positions involving passed pawns and promotion races.
265.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture, and 8/10 occur in endgame positions centered on passed pawns and pawn promotion races. The captures universally resolve tension between adjacent file pawns (a×b, h×g, b×c, g×f, e×d). Crucially, when these moves ARE mistakes (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 8), the error is that the exchange either creates a more dangerous passed pawn for the opponent via recapture (4/10), clears a promotion path for another enemy pawn (2/10), or wastes a critical tempo on an irrelevant capture (1/10). However, 5/10 positions show the move as essentially the best available option (cp_loss ≤ 35), indicating the feature fires on the structural pattern itself—pawn exchanges in passed-pawn contexts—rather than exclusively on blunders. The average cp_loss of 1833 is heavily skewed by two catastrophic blunders (8913, 8938) where the pawn capture enabled immediate forced mate.

257.label: Moving a rook or bishop to a seemingly natural square (open file, active diagonal) while ignoring an immediate tactical emergency, often making the moved piece itself a target.
257.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move (8/10 rook moves, 2/10 bishop moves) played in a sharp tactical position where only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.6). In 6/10 cases, the piece moved TO a square where it became directly vulnerable to a tactical blow: forks (Rf1, Rc8×2, Re1), profitable capture (Bg3), or forced retreat with tempo loss (Bg2). In 4/10 cases, the move failed to address an existing hanging piece or critical threat (Rg8 failed to actually defend the bishop, Rg1 ignored a hanging knight, Rb8×2 ignored urgent development/tactical needs). The moves all LOOK natural — placing rooks on open files (f, g, c, e, b-files) or bishops on active diagonals — but were catastrophically wrong because the positions demanded immediate tactical resolution. Average cp_loss of 332 confirms these are severe blunders, and the consistent presence of knight forks (5/10), hanging pieces (3/10), or back-rank themes (1/10) as refutations shows these quiet moves consistently walked into concrete tactical punishments.

271.label: Non-forcing bishop repositioning to an apparently active square when the position demands concrete tactical action or the bishop was performing a critical defensive function.
271.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a quiet (non-checking, non-capturing) bishop move to a square that appears attractive—attacking a piece, controlling a key diagonal, or centralizing. However, in every case this 'improvement' is punished because it either abandons a critical defensive duty the bishop was fulfilling on its original square (4/10: positions 2, 3, 8, 9 where the bishop guarded g7, controlled f5, protected d7, or needed to block the e-file), places the bishop on a tactically vulnerable square where it's immediately exploited (3/10: positions 1, 4, 5 where Nh3+, Nf5, or Nf7 refute), or is simply too slow when forcing moves like checks, pawn breaks, or knight forks were available (5/10: positions 5, 6, 7, 8, 10). The average cp_loss of 269 reflects that these moves consistently squander significant advantages or convert advantages into losses. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating critical moments demanding precision rather than general piece improvement.

267.label: A bishop or queen is quietly repositioned to a seemingly useful square while the position demands an urgent tactical response.
267.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing piece repositioning move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played in a critical position where only 1-3 good moves exist. 6/10 are bishop moves (Bd4, Bf6, Bc6, Ba2, Bd4, Ba4) and 4/10 are queen moves (Qe8, Qb2, Qb4, Qa6), all moving to squares that appear strategically useful (controlling diagonals, covering promotion squares, centralizing). The critical shared error is that each move ignores an immediate tactical emergency: in 5/10 cases the position demanded addressing king safety (castling, evacuating the back rank, or not removing a key defender); in 2/10 cases a piece was left hanging; in 2/10 cases a forcing move with check was required to gain essential tempo; and in 1/10 case the only saving move was a queen sacrifice with check. The average cp_loss of 2115 and average good moves of only 1.6 confirm these are narrow positions where the player chose a 'nice-looking' quiet move over the one critical tactical response.

275.label: Moving a pawn or knight that was the sole piece blocking an enemy bishop's diagonal attack on the player's own queen, resulting in immediate queen capture.
275.description: 9/10 positions show the exact same tactical catastrophe: the player moves a piece (pawn or knight) that was the ONLY blocker on a diagonal between an enemy bishop and their own queen, allowing the bishop to capture the queen outright. In 7/10 cases, it's a pawn advance or capture (e5, e4, e6, exf5, cxb6, exf5, e6) that clears the diagonal. In 3/10 cases, it's a knight relocating (Ng3, Nf5, Nd5) off the blocking square. The enemy bishop was already pre-aimed at the queen in every case — sitting on g5, h4, g3, or similar — patiently waiting for the blocker to move. Position 6 is the one slight outlier, where exf5 ignores a hanging knight on an open file rather than specifically unblocking a diagonal to the queen. The refutation in 9/10 positions is simply Bxd8, Bxc7, Bxd1, or Bxf3 — a direct bishop capture of the undefended queen. The average cp_loss of 473 reflects that these are essentially queen-losing blunders.

270.label: King moves played in heavily winning endgame positions with advanced passed pawns, sometimes missing stronger forcing tactical alternatives.
270.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves in endgame positions where the moving side holds a massive advantage (evaluations ranging from +582 to forced mate). 8/10 positions feature advanced passed pawns near promotion as a central theme. The average number of good moves is only 1.6, indicating narrow positions requiring precision. In 5/10 positions the king move was actually optimal (0 cp_loss), but in the remaining positions the king move was a catastrophic error: 2/10 positions (positions 4 and 5) featured the player making a centralizing king move while missing a simple bishop capture of an undefended rook along an open diagonal (cp_loss ~9500 each). 1/10 (position 8) missed a forcing rook move that created an unstoppable dual promotion threat. The feature consistently fires on positions where a king is being repositioned in a dominant endgame with promotion threats, regardless of whether that repositioning is correct or a devastating oversight.

277.label: Reflexive captures exchanging major pieces on open files when maintaining tension preserves tactical or positional advantages.
277.description: 10/10 positions feature captures of major pieces on open or semi-open files (8/10 are rook captures, 2/10 queen captures). In 9/10 cases, the move is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss ~2964 excluding the correct move). The consistent error is initiating an exchange when pieces confront each other on an open file, prioritizing simplification over dynamic advantages. In 3/10 positions (1, 3, 9), the exchange destroys an existing forced tactical/mating pattern (fork, discovered check, or preparatory attack). In 3/10 positions (2, 5, 6), the exchange removes a piece from a critical role—either defensive shielding of the king or attacking firepower needed for counterplay. In 2/10 positions (4, 7), the capture enables the opponent's beneficial recapture that activates their pieces or attacks key squares. In 1/10 (position 8), the capture removes a defender from its post, allowing a mating attack. Position 10 (0cp loss) was actually correct, suggesting the feature identifies the *pattern* of open-file major piece captures rather than guaranteeing error.

278.label: A quiet bishop repositioning move played in a critical position where an immediate tactical or forcing response was required, surrendering a crucial tempo.
