278.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking bishop move that repositions the bishop to a seemingly reasonable square while ignoring the position's urgent demands. In 8/10 cases, the bishop moves backward or sideways to a more passive square (Bd3, Bc2, Bc3, Bf7, Bg3, Bd8, Bg1, Bf6). In 9/10 positions the move occurs in the middlegame where tactical precision is paramount. The average centipawn loss is an enormous 2193, and only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical decision points where the position demanded one specific forcing idea. In 7/10 cases, the retreated bishop either lands on an undefended/tactically vulnerable square (Bc2 allowing Re2+, Bg3 allowing Qxg3+, Bd6 allowing Nc4, Be6 allowing Rd8#) or abandons a critical defensive function (Be6 unblocks the d-file, Bf7 abandons e6 control, Bg1 abandons central defense). In 9/10 positions, a forcing alternative existed (check, capture, or active centralization) that was clearly superior.

274.label: Playing an impulsive check to a corner or edge square instead of the more decisive move (usually checkmate) to a nearby central square.
274.description: 9/10 positions feature a check (the lone exception, Bh1, is still a move to the h1 corner). 8/10 moves land on a corner square (h1 three times, b1 twice, h8 twice, c1 once). In 8/10 positions, a forced checkmate was available (positions 1,2,3,4,7,8,10 had mate-in-1 through mate-in-8; position 6 had a winning attack). Critically, in 7/10 cases the correct move was just ONE SQUARE AWAY from the played move along the same line: Qg2# instead of Qh1+ (positions 1,5), Qc2# instead of Qb1+ (positions 2,3), Qe5# instead of Qf7+ (position 8), Qf3+ instead of Qc1+ (position 10). The average cp_loss of 5862 reflects that these are catastrophic blunders, typically converting forced checkmates into merely large advantages. The player is consistently drawn to the dramatic-looking check on the board's edge while missing the quiet but lethal move to a more functional central square.

281.label: Playing a quiet piece-improving move when a critical capture (taking a hanging, trapped, or dominant enemy piece) was the only acceptable option.
281.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet repositioning or developing move instead of making a critical capture that was available. The best move in every case was a capture: Rxh1 (pos 1), Qxe6+ (pos 2), Rxa1 (pos 3), dxe5 (pos 4), fxe4/Nxc6 (pos 5), Rxd3 (pos 6), axb4 (pos 7), Qxa1 (pos 8), exd4 (pos 9), Nxd5 (pos 10). Instead, the player made developing or maneuvering moves (knight hops, bishop developments, queen repositions, rook doublings). In 8/10 cases the missed capture targeted a piece that was either undefended/hanging (positions 1, 3, 7, 8) or a dominant enemy piece requiring immediate exchange (positions 4, 6, 9, 10). Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions with an extremely narrow correct path — always a capture. The blunders averaged 333cp loss, reflecting how catastrophic the failure to capture was.

276.label: Playing a natural-looking piece centralization or development move when the position demands an immediate forcing or emergency response.
276.description: In 9/10 positions, the player chose a non-forcing piece improvement move (typically a minor piece moving to a 'nice' central or active square) while ignoring an urgent tactical necessity. 8/10 moves were minor piece moves (5 knight moves: Nc5, Nf5, Ne3, Nf3, Nd4; 3 bishop moves: Bd6, Bb5, Bd5) to squares that looked attractive but addressed nothing critical. 9/10 positions featured severe king safety crises — either the player's own king was fatally exposed (positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 10) or the opponent's king was ripe for exploitation (positions 1, 5, 9). The correct moves in these positions were overwhelmingly forcing or concrete: immediate checks (Qg4+, Qe7), emergency defensive pawn moves creating king shelter (b6, a6, Rf8), file-blocking moves (Ne2), or critical captures (Nxa7). The average good moves available was only 1.8, confirming these were razor-sharp positions with essentially one correct response. The common failure is evaluating moves by positional aesthetics (centralization, activity) rather than recognizing the position's concrete tactical demands.

283.label: A pawn advance to chase an enemy knight that wastes a critical tempo and either weakens squares, opens lines for the opponent, or ignores a superior tactical option.
283.description: All 9/9 positions feature the exact same pattern: the player advances a pawn (c6, c3, f6, or a3) specifically to attack/chase an enemy knight occupying an aggressive outpost (Nb5 in 3 positions, Nd5 in 3 positions, Nd4 in 2 positions, Nb4 in 2 positions, Ng5 in 1 position). In every case, a better move existed—typically a developing move, a capture, or castling. The refutations reveal that the pawn advance either: weakens a critical square the knight can now exploit (5/9: allowing Nd6+, Nd3+, Ndf3+, Bg6+ through opened diagonal, or Nf4 relocation), wastes tempo allowing opponent coordination (3/9: delaying castling against e-file battery, letting opponent consolidate), or ignores that the knight was simply capturable for free (1/9: Nxd4). The average cp_loss of 314 reflects how severely these 'natural-looking' pawn kicks backfire. In 8/9 positions, the king was still in the center or otherwise vulnerable, making tempo especially critical.

272.label: A non-forcing rook move on a contested open file when the position demands either exchanging rooks or playing a concrete tactical alternative.
272.description: All 10/10 positions feature rooks from both sides contesting the same open file, and in every case the player makes a passive or misguided rook move instead of resolving the file tension through exchange or finding a concrete non-rook tactic. In 6/10 positions (1, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10), the best move involved exchanging rooks on the contested file (Rxe1, Rxd1, Rxa1, Rxc1, Rfd8→Rxc8, Rxe6). In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 9, 10), the rook moved OFF the contested file entirely (e→d, e→g, c→d, e→f), immediately surrendering file control. In 4/10 positions (1, 5, 6, 8), the rook advanced to an exposed square on the same file where it could be captured under unfavorable structural or tactical terms. In 2/10 positions (2, 7), the rook made a slow repositioning move ignoring urgent tactical demands elsewhere. The punishment consistently involved the opponent either capturing the exposed rook to devastating effect (positions 4, 5, 6, 8) or seizing the now-uncontested file to penetrate the 7th rank (positions 9, 10). Average cp_loss was 303 with only 1.4 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical moments demanding precision.

286.label: Moving the queen to g4 or g5 seeking illusory kingside attacks while abandoning critical duties elsewhere on the board.
286.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen moving to g4 or g5 (7 to g5, 3 to g4) during the middlegame with same-side kingside castling. In every case, the queen arrives on a seemingly aggressive kingside square but has no concrete threats—no checks, no captures, and no forcing follow-ups. The punishment varies but shares a common theme: 6/10 positions involved the queen abandoning defense of pieces or pawns (hanging knight in pos 1, undefended rook exposed to forks in pos 2-3, unguarded b5 pawn in pos 10, loss of support for central knight in pos 4, abandoning queenside in pos 5/7/8). In 3/10 positions, the queen was immediately punished by a tempo-gaining pawn push (h4, f5, or f4) forcing an embarrassing retreat. In 8/10 positions, the best move involved addressing concrete positional priorities—developing pieces, exchanging queens, challenging key enemy pieces, or defending critical pawns—rather than pursuing kingside adventures. The average cp_loss of 332 reflects how severely these speculative queen sorties are punished.

284.label: Moving the queen to an aggressive-looking square instead of executing an immediately available concrete capture or tactical combination.
284.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing queen relocation to a square that appears threatening but accomplishes nothing forcing. In 9/10 cases, the best move was an immediate capture (Qxg3, Nxc5, Nxf2, Qxe4, Nxg3, Ngxe5, Nxe6, dxe5, or a forcing queen trade with Qe6+). The queen moves predominantly target the kingside (7/10 go to g5/g6/h3/h4/h6), suggesting the player is drawn to 'attacking' placements over concrete execution. In 10/10 cases the played move is non-capturing and repositional, while the correct move was a decisive tactical action — usually a capture by a different piece entirely (6/10 best moves use a knight or pawn, not the queen). The average cp_loss of 290 reflects that these positions had narrow windows where only 1-2 moves preserved the advantage, and the speculative queen move squandered the opportunity.

273.label: The queen is moved to a seemingly active or aggressive square that is actually tactically or strategically inferior to an available alternative queen move.
273.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved their queen to a square that appeared strong (centralized, attacking, material-grabbing) but was actually a mistake—and in all 10 cases, the best move was also a queen move (or queen trade) to a different square. The player correctly identified that the queen should be active but chose the wrong destination. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 5), the queen moved to a square where it became trapped or hangable (Bf8 attacking Qd6, Re1 trapping Qe3, Qxa4 capturing the queen, Rec1 trapping Qxc2). In 4/10 positions (6, 8, 9, 10), the queen abandoned a dominant attacking post (e5, f7, g3, e6) for a peripheral square, missing forced mates or devastating forcing continuations. In 2/10 positions (3, 7), the queen went to a peripheral square losing critical defensive coverage of key pieces or squares. The average cp_loss was 3095, with 4 positions involving missed forced mates. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating high-precision moments where the queen destination choice was critical.

260.label: Playing a routine pawn capture or advance when the position critically demanded a piece move to address the dominant tactical issue.
260.description: 9/10 moves played were pawn moves (captures or advances), and in 8/10 positions the correct move was a piece move (king retreat, knight fork, rook exchange, bishop capture, or queen capture). The players consistently chose a 'small' pawn action — capturing a piece (positions 1, 4, 8, 10), threatening a piece (positions 5, 6, 7), or advancing for space/passed pawns (positions 2, 3) — while the position demanded a specific piece move to address a critical tactical priority. In 4/10 positions the pawn move fatally opened a line to the player's own king (positions 1, 4, 10) or removed a key defender (position 2). In 3/10 positions a hanging piece could simply be captured by a piece but was merely threatened by a pawn (positions 5, 6, 7). In 2/10 positions a winning piece maneuver was available but the player grabbed lesser material with a pawn (positions 3, 8). The one outlier (position 9, Bxc3+) reversed the pattern — a piece capture was played when a pawn capture was the correct move-order prerequisite — but still reflects the same underlying error of choosing the wrong capture type.

279.label: Single-step pawn pushes delivering check to the opponent's king, often prioritizing tempo over structural integrity.
279.description: 6/9 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to deliver check (c4+, g5+, f4+, c4+, g4+, d3+). An additional position (g6) is a pawn advance without check, making 7/9 pawn pushes total. The remaining 2 outliers (Nd3, Rxf7) relate tangentially—Rxf7 was a capture on the same square where Bxf7+ WITH check was correct, and Nd3 ignored a tempo-gaining capture. Among the 6 pawn checks, 2/6 were actually the best move (cp_loss 0), 1/6 was a minor inaccuracy (17cp), and 3/6 were significant to catastrophic blunders (91-9234cp). The feature captures the structural pattern of a pawn delivering check regardless of quality, but when these moves ARE mistakes, they share a consistent mechanism: the irreversible pawn advance weakens the player's own structure or grants the opponent's king access to better squares that the pawn formerly controlled.

287.label: A pawn push that attacks an enemy bishop when the position demands something far more urgent.
287.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to attack a diagonally-adjacent enemy bishop — the classic 'put the question to the bishop' move. Three positions play ...a6 against a bishop on b5, two play ...h6 against a bishop on g5, and the remainder target bishops on c5 (b4), c4 (b5), g4 (h3), f4 (g5), and b4 (a3). In every case, the position demanded something far more urgent: 7/10 had critical king safety issues (uncastled kings, back-rank threats, or forced mates), 6/10 had immediately available tactical shots that were missed, and the average cp_loss of 2950 reflects that several positions (3/10) threw away forced checkmates. The bishop-chasing pawn push was consistently the wrong priority — in some cases the bishop actually improved when 'chased' (positions 1, 3), in others the tempo loss allowed the opponent to escape lethal threats (position 5), and in others it enabled devastating counterblows (positions 6, 9, 10).

280.label: A piece (usually a rook) makes a natural-looking repositioning move while the king faces a critical threat, and the move either self-blocks escape squares, places the piece on a vulnerable square, or fails to address the mating attack.
280.description: All 10/10 positions feature a critically exposed king under immediate tactical pressure, where the player makes a piece repositioning move that appears constructive but fatally ignores the king's peril. 8/10 moves are rook moves (Rc8, Rf1, Rc1, Rf1, Rg1, Rd7, Rb8, Rd7), with the remaining 2 being minor piece moves to similar squares (Bf1, Nd6). In 7/10 positions, the piece moves to a back-rank square (1st or 8th rank), and in 9/10 it moves to ranks 1-2 or 7-8. The devastating consequences vary: in 2/10 cases the piece directly blocks the king's escape square enabling immediate checkmate (positions 1, 2); in 4/10 cases the piece lands on a tactically exploitable square (capturable with check, pinnable, or on a vulnerable diagonal — positions 5, 6, 8, 9); and in the remaining cases the piece move wastes critical tempo when the king needed immediate defense (positions 3, 7, 10). The average cp_loss of 5817 is extreme, with 6/10 positions resulting in forced mate. In every case, better alternatives existed that prioritized king safety — either king escape moves, file-blocking moves, or forcing simplifications.

288.label: Capturing material (usually with the king) that lands the piece on a fatally exposed square where it faces immediate tactical punishment.
288.description: 7/10 positions feature king captures (Kxe7, Kxe2, Kxd3, Kxf5, Kxg4, Kxf3, and position 7), while 8/10 moves overall are captures. In all 10 positions, the moved piece ends up on a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to tactical exploitation — the king walks into mating nets (positions 1, 2, 7, 9), checks and forks (positions 6, 10), or another piece lands where it directly hangs (positions 4, 5). Positions 3 and 8 represent a related sub-pattern where the player captures with the wrong piece (Qxe5 instead of Nxe5, Bxf5 instead of Nxf5), choosing a capture that needlessly exposes higher-value material. The average cp_loss of 5621 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 6/10 positions converting to forced checkmate. In 8/10 cases only 1-2 good alternatives existed, indicating these are narrow decision points where materialistic instinct overrode safety assessment.

285.label: Playing an active-looking piece move (usually rook to 7th rank or infiltration square) targeting secondary pawns while ignoring a critical tactical obligation in the position.
285.description: 7/10 positions involved a rook move to an aggressive-looking square, with 6/10 specifically being rook-to-seventh-rank moves (Rd7, Rd7, Rb7, Ra7, Rf7, Rd2-as-infiltration). In every case, the position demanded a more urgent action: capturing a hanging/critical piece (positions 2, 3, 10), addressing an immediate mating threat (positions 1, 5, 9), or supporting a passed pawn promotion (positions 6, 7). The played moves all share the characteristic of looking 'active' or 'aggressive'—placing pieces on traditionally desirable squares or targeting enemy pawns—while completely ignoring the primary tactical or strategic imperative. The correct moves were consistently more concrete: simple captures (Rxa8, gxf5, Rxe2), defensive blocks (Qe4, Qb3), or promotion support (Rd8). The average cp_loss of 3122 reflects that these 'active-looking' moves often walked into devastating refutations because the player was operating on general principles rather than calculating the position's specific demands.

293.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn move (typically on the flank) when the position demands immediate tactical or strategic action.
293.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-capturing pawn advances played in positions that demanded immediate forcing action. 7/10 moves were specifically queenside flank pawn pushes (b3 ×3, b6 ×2, c3, c4), with the remaining 3 being kingside pawn moves (g3, g4, f5). The average number of good moves available was only 1.9, indicating these were high-tension positions requiring precision rather than prophylaxis. In 8/10 positions, the best move was either a piece move (Bg7, Ne4, Bd3, Qb6, Kb2, Nc3) or a forcing pawn capture/advance resolving critical tension (dxe5, exf6, g4 locking structure, d6 attacking a piece). The tagged tactical motif was 'tempo_loss' in 7/10 cases. The core problem in every case was spending a tempo on a non-urgent structural adjustment while an immediate threat demanded attention—whether a hanging piece (positions 1, 8, 9), critical pawn tension needing resolution (positions 5, 7), an exposed king needing exploitation (position 2), or a defensive weakness needing protection (positions 4, 6).

290.label: Playing an aggressive-looking or centralizing piece move that fatally neglects the position's most critical tactical vulnerability.
290.description: 10/10 positions show the same fundamental error: the player makes a move that appears to improve piece activity or centralization (Be5, Ng5, Be6, Qe4, Bf4, etc.) while a critical tactical vulnerability goes unaddressed. In 8/10 cases, the ignored threat directly involves king safety—either the player's own king (positions 1, 2, 3, 7, 9) or abandoning defense of the opponent's mating pattern (positions 4, 7, 10). In 3/10 positions, the neglected issue is a back-rank or mating pattern (positions 4, 7, 10), and in 2/10 the move allows immediate checkmate (positions 3, 10). The best moves in all 10 positions prioritize addressing the concrete tactical demand—defensive moves, forcing simplifications, or covering critical squares—rather than cosmetic piece improvement. The average cp_loss of 3089 reflects how catastrophic these 'looks good but misses the point' moves are, with 4/10 resulting in immediate mate or mate-in-few.

302.label: Quiet bishop relocation moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action like pawn breaks or king activation.
302.description: All 10 positions feature quiet bishop moves (no captures, no checks) that reposition the piece to a seemingly improved square but squander a decisive tempo. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'piece_activity' in 10/10. In 7/10 positions, the correct move was either a pawn break (g5 in positions 3, 8; g4+ in position 7; h5/h3+ in positions 5, 10) or king activation (positions 2, 10), not a bishop move at all. In positions 1, 6, and 10, the bishop was already optimally placed and the repositioning actually degraded its function (leaving critical squares uncontrolled). In 8/10 endgame positions, the tempo loss allowed the opponent to either activate their king, advance a passed pawn, or seize a critical pawn break themselves. The average cp_loss of 195 reflects positions where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic due to the razor-thin margins of endgame play.

295.label: A bishop makes a greedy-looking capture that trades away its superior positional value, often activating the opponent's recapturing piece.
295.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop making a capture (Bx__) that appears to gain material or simplify favorably, but is actually a strategic mistake because the capturing bishop was performing a more important role than the piece/pawn taken. In 8/10 positions, the opponent's recapture directly activates a previously passive piece (often another bishop moving to the vacated square with improved diagonal scope). In 7/10 positions, the captured target was an awkwardly-placed or less valuable piece (misplaced knights in positions 1, 3, 6, 8; a pawn in positions 7, 9, 10). In 6/10 positions, the blunder specifically relieved the opponent's coordination problems or development difficulties. The average cp_loss of 270 reflects that these aren't tactical oversights but fundamental misjudgments about piece value — the player correctly identified a target but failed to recognize their bishop was worth more alive than the material gained.
295.old_chip: Bishop captures away its own value

294.label: Capturing an available enemy major piece (usually a rook) when a more forcing continuation exists or a different capture method was superior.
294.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures of enemy major pieces — 9/10 specifically capture rooks, while 1/10 captures a queen. The captures target pieces that are undefended or readily available for taking. In 4/10 positions, the capture was actually the best or near-best move (0 cp loss), but in the remaining 6/10, the materialistic grab missed something critical: 2/10 missed immediate checkmate (positions 5 and 6, losing ~9300cp each), 2/10 captured with the wrong piece (positions 2 and 8, where the bishop/rook should have been preserved), and 2/10 missed a more forcing move order involving an intermediate check before the capture (positions 1 and 9). The feature consistently fires on the instinctive 'grab the big piece' move regardless of whether it's optimal, suggesting it detects the materialistic impulse to capture a major piece rather than the quality of the decision.

298.label: Bishop captures (or moves to) a low-priority pawn while a critical tactical threat—often checkmate—goes unaddressed.
298.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves as the blunder, and 6/10 are specifically bishop captures of pawns (Bxb3, Bxb7, Bxb4, Bxc4, Bxh3, plus Bf7 overextending toward material). In nearly every case, the bishop prioritizes a small material gain or repositioning while a devastating tactical threat exists—5/10 positions result in immediate checkmate or forced mate after the move. The common defensive failure is king safety: 9/10 positions feature an exposed or back-rank-vulnerable king that demanded urgent attention. The 2-3 non-bishop moves (h5, d5, Rd2) share the broader pattern of choosing a 'greedy' or aggressive action while ignoring a more urgent tactical necessity, but the bishop-captures-pawn motif is overwhelmingly dominant. Average cp_loss of 5149 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights, not marginal inaccuracies.
298.old_chip: Greedy bishop grabs pawn, ignores threat

304.label: A slow, non-forcing pawn push (almost always on the queenside) played when the position demands immediate tactical action or urgent defense.
304.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance (no captures, no checks) played in a position with a critical tactical emergency. 9/10 moves are on the a, b, or c files (queenside flank pawn pushes), with the lone exception being g4. In every case, the position demanded concrete, forcing action: defending against an immediate tactic (positions 1, 6, 9, 10), maintaining a mating attack (position 5), securing perpetual check before it disappears (position 8), pushing a time-critical passed pawn (positions 3, 4), completing development/castling (position 2), or maintaining active piece pressure (position 7). Instead, the player chose a positionally-motivated but non-urgent pawn push that addresses none of the immediate tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 2270 reflects how catastrophic these tempo losses are — including two cases where forced mates were missed (positions 5 and 9). Every single analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as a core tag, confirming that the shared mechanism is squandering the one critical move needed to address an urgent tactical situation.

299.label: A prophylactic one-square flank pawn advance (b3/b6/g3/g6) played when the position demands immediate tactical or developmental action.
299.description: 10/10 positions feature a one-square flank pawn advance on the b-file or g-file (b6×3, b3×3, g6×2, g3×1, b4×1) played as a perceived prophylactic or preparatory move. In every case, the position contains an urgent tactical crisis that the pawn move completely ignores. 9/10 positions involved at least one king still in the center (either the player's own uncastled king needing safety, or the opponent's exposed king that could be exploited). The best moves in 8/10 positions involved piece development or immediate castling. The average cp_loss of 350 reflects how these tempo-wasting moves allow opponents to either resolve their own weaknesses (positions 2, 4, 6) or exploit undefended pieces/pawns (positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10). In 6/10 cases, the pawn move defended a secondary target (b7, b2, g2) while a primary target (d5, e3, f2, e5 knight, e6) was left catastrophically unguarded.

289.label: Aggressive-looking moves (typically pawn advances) that waste a critical tempo by ignoring an urgent defensive or positional requirement, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created weakness.
289.description: 7/10 positions feature pawn advances (f4 in 4/10, plus d5, c4, b4), while the remaining 3/10 are piece moves/captures (Rg4, Bxe4, Nxe5) that similarly prioritize offense over defense. In all 10 positions, the move appears active — gaining space, material, or piece activity — but fatally ignores a critical positional need. In 5/10 positions, the move specifically removes a key defensive element (f2-pawn guarding the second rank or diagonal in positions 5 and 7; bishop guarding a diagonal in position 9; knight guarding the back rank in position 10; b5-pawn guarding the a4 square in position 6). In 5/10 positions, the move wastes a critical tempo when an urgent task demanded attention (eliminating a passed pawn in positions 1 and 3; centralizing the king in position 4; exploiting an uncastled king in position 8; avoiding giving an outpost in position 2). The average good moves available was only 1.5, confirming these are razor-sharp positions where one tempo determines the outcome. All 10 refutations immediately exploit the specific weakness created by the move.

303.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn advance in a sharp position where a concrete tactical resource (check, capture, or forced sequence) demanded immediate execution.
303.description: 9/10 positions feature a non-forcing pawn push (b4, b5, f3, e5, c3, d3, f3, d6, d6) and 1/10 a passive king move (Kf8), all sharing the critical flaw of being quiet moves in positions requiring forcing play. In 10/10 cases, the best move was a concrete tactical resource: captures (Bxd5, Qxe3+, cxd4), checks (Qd8+, Qa5+), or moves creating immediate threats (Qe7, d4 with tempo). The average cp_loss of 331 reflects the severity, and the average of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these were tactically narrow positions demanding precision. In 7/10 cases the missed best move was a check or capture. The blundered moves are universally 'natural-looking' positional ideas—gaining space (b4, b5, e5), strengthening structure (c3, f3), attacking pieces non-forcibly (d3, d6)—that catastrophically waste the tempo needed for a concrete solution. 8/10 positions had only 1 good move within 50cp of best, confirming the razor-sharp nature of these moments.

292.label: Advancing a pawn or piece with a slow strategic plan while ignoring an immediate tactical requirement that demands precise action.
292.description: 8/9 positions show the player making a forward-advancing move (6/9 are pawn pushes: h5, a5, a4, d6, h2, c3; plus Kxc5 capturing a pawn, Na5 advancing a knight, and Rf8 repositioning a rook) when the position contains a critical, time-sensitive tactical demand that must be addressed first. In 7/9 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of the best, indicating razor-sharp positions requiring concrete calculation rather than planful play. The correct moves were typically non-obvious or 'quiet' actions: resolving central tension (fxe4), prophylactic pawn moves (g3), king repositioning (Kf7), or seizing central space (e4) — moves that address the position's immediate concrete requirement. The blunders instead pursue a secondary goal (creating a passed pawn, winning material, attacking on a flank, advancing a piece) that looks purposeful but catastrophically ignores the position's #1 demand. The average cp_loss of 1429 reflects how punishing these critical moments are when the player defaults to 'auto-pilot' advancing moves.

291.label: Non-forcing moves (especially edge pawn pushes) that waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical action.
291.description: 7/10 positions feature moves directed to the a-file or h-file (a5, h4×3, a4, Kh5, Kh2), while the remaining 3 (Nf3, Nf6, Ke7) are similarly quiet, 'natural-looking' moves. All 10 moves share the property of being non-forcing—no checks, captures, or immediate threats—in positions where the average number of good moves was only 1.6, indicating extreme tactical urgency. In 6/10 positions, there was exactly one good move available. The average centipawn loss was 2124, reflecting catastrophic consequences. The best moves in these positions were typically forcing tactical shots (Rxg3+, Nxd5, Rxe6) or urgent defensive evacuations (Qf7, Be5, Nd7). 8/10 positions featured a concrete one-move tactic being missed or an immediate threat being ignored. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, confirming the unifying theme of squandering a critical tempo on a slow move.

296.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing piece relocation in a position that demanded immediate tactical resolution through checks, captures, or concrete threats.
296.description: All 10/10 positions share the critical feature that the player chose a quiet piece repositioning move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) when the position was tactically critical with only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.5). In 10/10 cases, the position demanded a forcing continuation — whether a capture (positions 7, 9: taking a hanging piece/bishop), a check-first sequence (positions 1, 6, 9: exploiting exposed kings), a trade-first move order (positions 2, 5: eliminating a piece before retreating), or an escape (position 3: king fleeing). Instead, the player made a consolidating/repositioning move that appeared positionally sensible — defending a square, improving piece placement, or connecting pieces — but catastrophically ignored the concrete tactical demands. In 4/10 positions the quiet move directly left a piece hanging (positions 4, 5, 7, 10), in 3/10 it gave the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate or activate (positions 2, 6, 9), in 2/10 it fatally blocked escape routes or eliminated drawing resources (positions 3, 8), and in 1/10 it addressed a secondary threat while ignoring the primary one (position 1).

282.label: Non-forcing piece moves to passive or vulnerable squares in positions demanding immediate tactical action.
282.description: 9/10 positions feature non-forcing moves (no checks, no meaningful captures) made in positions where only 1-2 good moves exist (avg 1.8). 7/10 are minor piece moves (4 knight, 3 bishop), and 4/10 specifically land on b2 or c2 squares—classic 'tucking away' destinations. In at least 5/10 cases, the moved piece itself becomes immediately capturable (Bc2 won by Rc1/Rd2+, Ne7 hanging to Qxe7, Bb2 allows bxc4 winning the other bishop, Na4 ignoring Rxe1#). In the remaining cases, the slow tempo allows opponent's tactical threats to become unstoppable (Bxh2+ sacrifice, Qd4+ checks, e-pawn promotion). The positions are all tactically critical (avg cp_loss 3260) where a forcing response—capture, check, or prophylaxis—was required. The consistent error is choosing a 'positional improvement' move in a position that demands concrete calculation.

305.label: Playing a passive king move to the h1/h8 corner as false prophylaxis when the position demands immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo and often worsening king safety.
305.description: 8/10 positions feature the literal move Kh1 (White) or Kh8 (Black), tucking the king into the absolute corner square. The remaining 2 positions involve the king already sitting on h1/h8 while the player makes another passive move (h6, Rxb6) that ignores threats to that cornered king. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded urgent concrete action—a tactical strike (Nxh5, Bxd5, Qxe6+), a critical defensive break (f5, Ng6), or addressing an immediate mating threat (Nc6, h4). Instead, the player chose a 'prophylactic' king move that accomplished nothing constructive. The average centipawn loss was 2177, reflecting positions where one wasted tempo proved catastrophic. In 7/10 positions, the corner placement specifically enabled tactical refutations exploiting the trapped king: Bxh6 sacrifices on the exposed h-pawn (positions 1, 4, 6), removal of f2-defense enabling Rxf2 or Nxf2# (positions 5, 8), or opening g-file attacks toward the cornered monarch (position 3). Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, confirming these were sharp positions where the one wasted tempo was decisive.

307.label: Moving a knight to an active central square while ignoring an immediate tactical emergency (mate threat, hanging piece, or king vulnerability).
307.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving from a peripheral or less-active square to a classically strong central outpost (c4, c5, c6, d3, d5, e3, e4, e5), yet in every case there is an urgent tactical crisis left unaddressed. In 5/10 positions, the blunder allows immediate checkmate or a forced mating sequence (Positions 1, 4, 6 allow mate-in-1 or mate-in-2; Position 2 allows a queen-winning rook lift; Position 7 allows a queen-winning d-file check). In 3/10 positions, a piece is left hanging (Positions 8, 10 leave rook/bishop undefended; Position 3 misses a free rook capture). In 2/10 positions, the move order error allows defensive resources the opponent wouldn't otherwise have (Positions 5, 9). The origin squares are overwhelmingly peripheral: 7/10 moves originate from rim or edge squares (a4, a5, a6, b2, c2, d2, d7). The average cp_loss of ~3196 is catastrophic, reflecting that these 'improving' moves routinely walk into forced mates or decisive material loss. All 10 positions offered between 1-3 reasonable alternatives that addressed the immediate threat first.

297.label: Playing a superficially attractive or natural-looking move that removes a piece from a critical tactical function, ignoring the concrete demands of the position.
297.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a move that appeared active, aggressive, or positionally natural (centralization, capture, pawn advance, open-file occupation) while ignoring that the moved piece — or the resulting position — had a critical tactical requirement that was violated. In 7/10 cases (f4, Bxh2, b5, Nh5, Ne4, Rd4, and Rd8), the moved piece was directly performing a vital defensive or combinational function: blocking a diagonal (Ne4 blocked Bg5-d8, costing the queen), guarding a mating square (Nh5 left e2 unguarded, allowing Qe2#), shielding the king (Bxh2 removed the d6 bishop), participating in a winning combination (Rd4 removed the g4 rook from the Ng3+ fork), or maintaining piece coordination (f4 blocked own knight's access to f4). In 3/10 cases (Nd4, Ng5, Qxc4), the piece was placed on a vulnerable or tactically inferior square when a concrete opportunity demanded something else entirely. The average cp_loss of 1249 and average of only 1.7 good moves available shows these are critical moments where precision was required but the player defaulted to generic-principle moves instead of calculating the position's specific tactical truth.

306.label: Playing routine knight development to f3/f6 (or similarly 'natural' moves) instead of calculating concrete forcing moves that win material or address immediate crises.
306.description: 7/10 positions feature a knight being developed to f3 or f6 as the blunder move, with the remaining 3 being similarly 'natural-looking' active moves (Bg5+, g4, Nce7). In every case, the position demanded a specific concrete forcing move: 5/10 positions had an available queen check on an open diagonal (usually Qh5+) that won material by force, 3/10 had an undefended piece that could be captured outright (Bxb5, Bxg4, Bxg4), and 2/10 required addressing an immediate tactical threat rather than developing. The average cp_loss of 1246 reflects catastrophic missed opportunities. 9/10 positions were in the opening or early middlegame where both kings remained in the center, creating the tactical conditions (open diagonals, hanging pieces) that rewarded forcing moves over development. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these were sharp positions with narrow best-move windows that autopilot development completely missed.

310.label: Playing a king-safety move (usually castling) when a simple capture of hanging or vulnerable material was available.
310.description: All 10/10 positions share the same fundamental error: the player chose to relocate their king (8/10 via castling, 2/10 via king walks) when the correct move was an immediate capture of material. In Position 1, Nxg8 won a queen; Position 3, Qxa1 won a rook; Positions 4, 6, 7 needed capturing hanging knights with Qxe5/dxe5; Position 5 required gxf3 to take a bishop; Position 8 needed Bxf3 winning a piece with no recapture; Position 9 demanded exf6 capturing a knight; Position 10 called for Rxe5 taking a bishop. In every case, the material was either completely undefended (7/10) or could be taken without adequate recapture (3/10). The average cp_loss of 468 and average of only 1.1 good moves confirm these were critical moments where the single correct answer was always a capture, never a king move.

301.label: Playing active-looking 'improving' moves (developing pieces, centralizing knights, advancing pawns) while ignoring an immediate tactical emergency that demands defensive action.
301.description: All 10/10 positions share a critical feature: the player chose an active, ambitious, or 'improving' move while a concrete tactical emergency existed in the position. In 5/10 cases the blunder was a knight move to a seemingly strong square (Nf3×2, Ne4, Nc4, Na6); in 4/10 it was an aggressive pawn advance (c5, c3, g5, f5); in 1/10 it was a bishop development (Bf4). The correct moves were almost always defensive or prophylactic in nature: 6/10 positions required addressing king safety (moving the king, defending a mating square, or not removing a defensive piece from a critical diagonal); 3/10 required capturing an undefended piece or not placing one's own piece where it could be captured profitably; 1/10 required addressing a piece under immediate double attack. The average number of good moves available was only 1.8, confirming these are critical positions where one narrow defensive resource exists but the player instead 'does their own thing.' In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 6, 8, and to some extent 5), the specific mechanism was moving a piece that was serving a crucial defensive function — blocking a dangerous diagonal or file — to an 'active' square, thereby allowing a devastating check or mate.

309.label: Advancing a pawn (usually a passed pawn) forward impatiently when preparation, piece coordination, or a more urgent tactical priority should come first.
309.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances as the blundering move. In at least 8/10 cases, the pawn being advanced is specifically a passed pawn (d6, e2, f4, g6, b3, g2, b7, d3 are all passed pawn pushes; g4 and b5 are aggressive non-passed pushes ignoring tactical issues). The common thread is that the player sees an advanced pawn and instinctively pushes it further toward promotion, when the position actually demands something else first: addressing an opponent's immediate threat (positions 1, 10), eliminating a key defender before advancing (position 2), maintaining king mobility (position 3), keeping proper pawn coordination/move order (positions 5, 9), not opening lines for the opponent (position 8), or executing an immediate tactic like checkmate (position 7). In 7/10 positions there was only 1 good move available, indicating these are critical moments where the 'obvious' pawn push is a trap. The average cp_loss of 2168 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors.

317.label: A losing side captures with their only remaining rook, eliminating their sole source of counterplay and defensive resources.
317.description: In 10/10 positions, the move is a rook capture (Rx__) that trades away the moving side's last significant piece. In 9/10 positions, the side making the move was already losing (avg eval heavily against them), and the rook was their only remaining active piece providing counterplay or defense. In 8/10 cases, the better alternatives involved relocating the rook to a different file or rank to KEEP it alive (e.g., Rd1, Rf1, Ra1, Rc2, Rh2, Rf7). The captures occurred on contested files where both rooks faced each other: the e-file (5/10), f-file (3/10), a-file (1/10), and c-file (1/10). After the trade, the position consistently collapsed because the naked king and pawns had zero defensive resources against the opponent's remaining army. The cp_loss ranged from trivial (5-13cp in already-mated positions) to catastrophic (9000+ when converting from 'losing' to 'forced mate').

312.label: Repositioning a piece (usually a knight) to a seemingly useful square while ignoring an immediate checkmate or devastating tactical threat that only one specific move could address.
312.description: 9/9 positions had exactly 1 good move available, creating a razor-thin defensive requirement. In 6/9 positions, the refutation after the blunder was forced checkmate (positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 9 allowed mate in 1-3 moves; position 5 allowed a crushing attack). 7/9 moves were knight repositioning moves (Nf5, Ng3, Nc3, Nf6, Ng6, Nf3, plus Qd1/Rc8/Bf1 as non-knight variants), all sharing the characteristic of being quiet, non-forcing piece placements to apparently useful squares. None of the blundering moves were captures or checks — they were all developmental or repositioning moves that appeared 'natural' but were completely irrelevant to the critical threat. The average cp_loss of 5548 reflects that most blunders allowed immediate or near-immediate checkmate. In every case, the one saving move directly addressed the mating threat (blocking, interposing, eliminating the attacker, or fleeing), while the played move improved a piece's position as if no emergency existed.

300.label: Playing a superficially attractive aggressive move (check, capture, advance) that is tactically unsound or premature, when a more precise preparatory or forcing move was required.
300.description: All 10 positions share a critical pattern: the player chooses a tempting-looking aggressive move over a less obvious but far stronger continuation. In 8/10 cases, the played move is a capture, check, or aggressive piece advance (Ne6, hxg6, Nxe5, Nxd6+, fxg6, Nb6+, gxh6, c7), while only 2/10 are other move types (c4 pawn break, Nd8 retreat). The best moves in each position demanded either preparation before the aggressive action (positions 2,3,6,9 where a preliminary exchange, capture, or breakthrough was needed FIRST), restraint/quiet consolidation (positions 4,7,8 where maintaining piece placement was superior), or a different forcing move entirely (positions 1,5,10 where a more lethal tactic existed). The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were narrow positions requiring precision, yet players consistently chose the 'exciting' option. In 4/10 cases (positions 2,5,6,8), the move directly left a piece or pawn hanging or allowed an unfavorable trade. In 3/10 cases (positions 3,9,10), the move was a move-order error where the right idea was executed in the wrong sequence. The average cp_loss of 1195 confirms these are catastrophic errors arising from choosing flash over substance.

319.label: Black develops or repositions a bishop to a square where an enemy piece immediately captures it with check or checkmate, exploiting the king's proximity.
319.description: In 10/10 positions, Black moves a bishop to a seemingly natural or defensive square that is directly attacked by an enemy piece. In 9/10 cases, the capturing piece delivers check or checkmate upon taking the bishop (8/10 result in immediate checkmate or forced mate within 1-3 moves). The queen is the capturing piece in 8/10 positions, with a rook (position 6) and knight (position 9) in the other two. The exposed/uncastled king is adjacent to or aligned with the bishop's destination square in every case, turning what appears to be a developing/blocking/defensive move into self-destruction. The destination squares cluster around the king: e7 (3x), e6 (2x), g7 (2x), d7, d8, c6. In all 10 positions, only 1 good move was available within 50cp of best, indicating these arise in already critical positions where the player desperately seeks natural-looking defensive moves but overlooks that the destination square is fatally compromised.

313.label: Passive, non-forcing moves played in critical positions where a specific forcing continuation (check, capture, or concrete threat) was required to maintain the position's evaluation.
313.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no immediate threats) played in positions that demanded precise tactical responses. 6/10 moves are queen relocations to seemingly natural squares (Qe1, Qd2, Qe5, Qb2, Qd2), 2/10 are passive bishop developments (Bd7 twice), and 1/10 each are a rook repositioning and pawn advance. In every case, the position contained a specific forcing resource — a capture of an undefended piece (2/10: positions 2 and 10), a check-first sequence enabling a tactical combination (3/10: positions 6, 7, 8), a king move addressing an immediate mating threat (1/10: position 3), or active piece play preventing the opponent's tactical strike (4/10: positions 1, 4, 5, 9). The average good moves available was only 1.8, confirming these were narrow positions demanding precision. The average cp_loss of 1331 reflects the catastrophic consequences of ceding tempo at critical moments. The unifying thread is that 10/10 played moves gave the opponent a free tempo to execute a tactic that the correct forcing move would have prevented or preempted.

308.label: Playing a slow, repositioning piece move in a position that demands an immediate forcing action (capture, recapture, or mating blow).
308.description: 10/10 positions share the pattern of a player choosing a quiet piece improvement move when an immediate concrete action was required. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 5, 7), a forced checkmate was available but the player chose a repositioning move instead. In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 9), an immediate capture/recapture was necessary to maintain material balance but the player developed a piece instead. In the remaining 4/10 positions, critical forcing sequences existed that the player bypassed in favor of 'improving' moves. The average centipawn loss of 3068 is astronomically high, and the average number of good moves was only 1.9, confirming these are razor-sharp positions with narrow correct paths. 8/10 positions were in the middlegame where tactical alertness is paramount. The moves themselves are exclusively non-forcing: no captures (except one check, Nf7+, which was the *wrong* forcing move), consisting of 5 knight repositions, 3 bishop developments, 1 queen relocation, and 1 pawn push—all 'quiet' by nature.

316.label: Passive bishop or queen repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical or dynamic action.
316.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-forcing piece relocations (7/10 bishop moves, 3/10 queen-to-c2 moves) to seemingly 'useful' squares when the position critically demanded immediate action. The average number of good moves was only 1.6, meaning these were all high-precision moments where only concrete play maintained the evaluation. In 6/10 positions, the piece moved away from a square where it performed a critical function (defending a pawn, controlling a key square, or maintaining tactical pressure). In 8/10 cases, the position required either an immediate central break (d4, e4, cxd5), a forcing tactical sequence (Qa4+, Nc4, dxc4), or maintaining a piece on its active post. The common thread is that the player chose a 'positional improvement' move—relocating a piece to a square that looks reasonable in isolation—while completely missing that the position's concrete demands made such quiet maneuvering a catastrophic tempo loss.

311.label: Playing routine bishop development or repositioning moves in positions that demand immediate tactical or defensive action for king safety.
311.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop move (the 10th, Rxf5, is a capture on the square where the bishop should have captured instead). In all 10 positions, king safety is the dominant concern — either the player's own king is under attack or the opponent's king creates a tactical opportunity. The average cp_loss is an enormous 2242, and on average only 1.4 good moves existed, showing these are razor-sharp positions with extremely narrow solutions. In every case, the correct move was NOT the bishop move played — it was either a defensive resource (Rf2, Bh5, Re1), an active counter-tactic (Qxf3, Nc6, Bxf5+), or a necessary preparation before the bishop move could be played safely (gxf4, dxe4). The blundering bishop moves variously: abandon critical defensive squares (2/10 — Bg4 leaving h1, Bd2 leaving g5), place the bishop where it's immediately captured or tactically exploited (4/10 — Bg3, Bg5, Bg4 allowing zwischenzug, Bxf5 opening lines), or simply waste the crucial tempo needed for survival (4/10 — Bc4, Bxg3, Bf4, Rxf5). 9/10 are middlegame positions where the tactical complexity is highest.

320.label: A quiet, non-forcing pawn advance squanders a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate action.
320.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn push played when the position urgently required something else. The 'something else' varies: in 3/10 positions a decisive tactic was available (skewer, mate-in-2, piece capture with check), in 4/10 positions a piece needed to be activated or repositioned first (rook to d3, king toward center, queen maintaining attack), and in 3/10 positions a more precise pawn move was needed (a4 instead of a3, gxf4 instead of g4, f5 instead of h6). The average cp_loss of 1161 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical junctures where the slow pawn push is uniquely punished. 9/10 positions are endgames where single tempi are decisive. The tagged motif 'tempo_loss' appears explicitly in 9/10 analyses. The moves span all areas of the board (a-h files, both sides) confirming the pattern is about the *nature* of the move rather than its geometric direction.

318.label: A knight moves to an apparently active or aggressive square, but its departure removes critical defensive coverage or leaves it tactically vulnerable, enabling immediate punishment.
318.description: All 10/10 positions feature knight moves to seemingly strong squares (d4, d5, e5, d7, a5, h5, g4) that appear aggressive or purposeful — attacking pieces, occupying outposts, or challenging opponent's pieces. However, in 7/10 cases the knight was performing a vital defensive function on its original square (guarding e7, h7/h5, e4, g6, d5, or providing general central coverage), and its departure immediately creates a tactical vulnerability. In 3/10 cases (Na5, Ne5×2), the knight arrives on a square where it simply hangs or can be captured with devastating structural consequences. The king is uncastled for the blundering side in 7/10 positions, amplifying the cost of removing defensive pieces. In every case, 2-3 quiet alternatives (development, castling, prophylaxis) maintained equality, but the player chose the 'active' knight move instead. The average cp_loss of 324 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors — they're one-move tactical catastrophes disguised as strong centralizing ideas.
318.old_chip: Knight leaves post for fool's errand

323.label: Playing a quiet rook move to the b-file when the position demands immediate tactical action elsewhere.
323.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the b-file (Rb1 or Rb8) as a seemingly natural developing/activating move, while a critical tactical obligation goes unaddressed. In 9/10 positions, there was a specific one-move tactic available (winning material, defending a hanging piece, or executing a combination) that the rook move simply ignores. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow positions demanding precision rather than quiet development. In 7/10 cases, the rook move left a specific piece or pawn undefended (d5 knight, e5 pawn, d5 pawn, a7 pawn, or placed the rook itself en prise). In 4/10 cases, the player missed an offensive tactic (Qxf6 fork, Nb4 queen trap, Bxb3 deflection, Nd5 preventing Ng5). The b-file rook move appears to be a 'default' developing move that players reach for when they perceive the position as strategic rather than tactical — it addresses secondary concerns (b-file pressure, pawn protection) while catastrophically ignoring the true demands of the position.

321.label: Moving the only piece defending against checkmate to play an 'active' or greedy move, allowing immediate mate.
321.description: 9/10 positions resulted in checkmate-in-one after the blunder, with an average cp_loss of 8632. In every case, the player moved a major piece (queen in 7/10, rook in 3/10) away from a critical defensive duty to pursue an offensive or materialistic goal. In 6/10 positions, the moved piece was explicitly the sole defender of the mating square (Rg5 abandoned h-file coverage of h1; Qxh6 and Qxc7 removed queen defense of g2; Qg4 left f8 unguarded; Rb7 removed the back-rank rook; Qc7 ignored g2 defense). In 3/10 positions (Qe5, Qd2, Rc8), the player ignored an already-existing mate threat by playing an irrelevant 'active' move rather than specifically removing a defender. The mating patterns exploited include back-rank mates (5/10), queen-delivers-mate-on-g2 (3/10), diagonal-supported queen mates on g7/b7 (2/10), and bishop-delivered mates (1/10). Only 1/10 positions (Qe6) showed a milder version with 110cp loss rather than immediate mate.

325.label: Developing the b-knight to a passive square (d2/d7/c3) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
325.description: All 10 positions feature developing the queenside knight (b1 for White, b8 for Black) to a 'natural' square, with 9/10 going to the most passive option (d2 or d7) and 1/10 to c3. In every case, the player chose automatic-looking development over a critical tactical opportunity: 10/10 positions had a forcing move available (captures, pawn breaks, discovered checks) that the knight move completely ignored. The tactical opportunities missed varied widely — Position 2 missed Nxe4 (pawn grab justified by a fork), Position 3 missed Bxe2 (exploiting an overloaded defender), Position 5 missed b4 (time-critical pawn attack), Position 7 missed exf6+ (discovered check) — but the error type is identical: playing a quiet, routine knight development in a position screaming for concrete calculation. In 7/10 positions, the knight development actively created new vulnerabilities: blocking retreat squares (Position 4, creating a trapped piece), leaving the knight itself undefended (Positions 1, 6, 8), or adding a secondary target for forks (Position 9). The average cp_loss of 295 reflects that these are critical moments where only 1-3 good moves existed (avg 1.7), making the routine choice especially costly.

326.label: A non-forcing pawn exchange resolves tension when a much more dynamic tactical or strategic move demands immediate execution.
326.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn-takes-pawn moves that resolve existing structural tension in a routine, 'housekeeping' manner while missing a far stronger forcing continuation. In 7/10 cases, the missed best move was a concrete tactic (sacrifice, check, or piece capture: Bxf7+, Qh5+, Rxf6, Nf5, g4, Nd2, Re4). In 10/10 positions, only 1-3 good moves existed (avg 1.3), meaning the position demanded precision rather than autopilot. The pawn captures all look natural and 'safe'—resolving an enemy pawn that was creating tension against the player's structure—but in every case, the tension was either non-urgent or actually serving a useful purpose. By spending the move on a structural simplification, the player gifted the opponent a critical tempo: 6/10 positions saw the opponent use that tempo to consolidate defenses or neutralize a crushing threat (e.g., ...Rf8 blocking doubled rooks, ...Bxd4 saving a piece, ...Bxf3 removing a key defender). The average cp_loss of 281 confirms these are severe mistakes born from pattern-matching ('capture back') rather than concrete calculation.

329.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn advance in a position that demands immediate tactical action (checks, captures, or defensive piece moves) to address an urgent king safety or material threat.
329.description: All 9/9 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance played in a critically sharp position where immediate forcing moves were required. In 9/9 cases, the best moves were piece moves (queen checks, rook repositions, bishop captures, or defensive blocks) rather than pawn pushes. In 7/9 positions, king safety was the primary concern being ignored—either the player's own king was about to be mated (positions 1, 7) or the opponent's exposed king could be exploited (positions 4, 6, 8), or perpetual check needed to be prevented (position 2). The average cp_loss of 2573 reflects that these positions had extreme tactical urgency. In 6/9 cases, the pawn push was on the queenside or center (c4×3, c5, b5, d3) while the critical action was on the kingside or along central files. In 5/9 positions, only 1 good move existed, confirming these were narrow tactical positions requiring precision. The common thread across all analyses is the 'tempo_loss' tag—every pawn push effectively hands a free move to the opponent in a position where a single tempo decides the game.

315.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that pursues a secondary plan while ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
315.description: All 10 positions share a critical structural feature: extremely narrow good-move counts (avg 1.9 good moves available), meaning the position demands one specific action NOW. In 10/10 cases, the player chose a move that addresses a secondary concern—development (Ne7), space (g5, h5, a5), repositioning (Nb8, Qb6, Kd7), routine play (O-O), or a flashy but flawed tactic (Nxf7 x2)—while the position's true priority was completely different. In 4/10 positions, the best move was a concrete capture that resolved a critical tension (Bxb2, Bxe5, Bxd3, Nc5 attacking). In 3/10, it was an urgent king safety move (Ke7, O-O-O, c4 enabling castling). In 2/10, it was calm consolidation (d3). In 1/10, it was activating the most passive piece immediately (Rc4). The blunders typically created or ignored a concrete vulnerability: leaving pieces undefended (5/10: b7 bishop, h5 pawn, b5 pawn, c4 pawn, d7 bishop pinned), trapping own pieces (2/10: knight on h8), or exposing the king (3/10: Kd7, Ne7 blocking escape, O-O walking into attack). The average centipawn loss of 290 reflects that these positions severely punish inaccuracy.

333.label: Capturing with the queen when a pawn or minor piece should take on the same (or nearby) square, exposing the queen to tempo attacks or abandoning a critical defensive role.
333.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a queen capture (Qx__) when a less valuable piece should have taken the material instead. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a pawn capture on the same square (exd5, cxd4, hxg3, fxe6, cxd5, fxe3, fxe5). In 2/10, a bishop capture was optimal (Bxe5, Bxd5). The consistent punishment mechanism is that the queen becomes exposed on its new square and is attacked with tempo (7/10 positions), the queen abandons a critical defensive assignment (positions 4 and 6), or the queen trade leads to a structurally lost endgame (position 10). The average cp_loss of 281 reflects how severely these 'wrong piece captures' are punished. In every case, only 1-2 good moves existed, meaning these were high-precision decision points where the instinct to use the most powerful piece for the capture proved catastrophic.

332.label: A pawn advance attacks a well-placed enemy knight, but the knight relocates to a superior square or the pawn move creates fatal weaknesses.
332.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn move that directly attacks an enemy knight: b3 attacks Nc4 (positions 1, 9), c4 attacks Nd5 (position 2), a3 attacks Nb4 (position 3), f3 attacks Ne4 (position 4), f6 attacks Ne5 (position 5), f4 attacks Ne5 (position 6), c5 attacks Nd4 (position 7), b4 attacks Nc5 (position 8), and g5 attacks Nf6 (position 10). In at least 7/10 cases, the knight relocates to a demonstrably superior square: Na3+ with check (pos 1), Nf4 enabling Nh3+/Nf2+ (pos 2), Nc3 delivering a fork (pos 4), Nc6 with fork threats (pos 5), Ne6 winning the f4 pawn (pos 8), Nb6 attacking the d5 knight (pos 9), and Nxe4 winning a central pawn (pos 10). In 3/10 cases the pawn move primarily creates structural weaknesses rather than directly improving the knight's square: a3 wastes tempo when Nd6/Nf6+ wins (pos 3), f4 leaves the c5-knight unprotected (pos 6), c5 removes c6-pawn control of b5 (pos 7). The average cp_loss of 288 reflects these being severe errors, and only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating positions where concrete calculation was demanded rather than general principles.
332.old_chip: Pawn chases knight to better square

336.label: A knight captures a pawn that is protected by an adjacent pawn, expecting tactical compensation that doesn't exist after the simple pawn recapture.
336.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight capturing a pawn (Nx_) that is defended by an adjacent pawn, where the straightforward pawn recapture cleanly wins the knight. In every case, the refutation is a simple pawn take-back: fxe5, dxe5, exd5, fxe4, exd4, dxe5, axb4, axb5, and axb3. The player consistently overestimates the tactical threats generated by the knight landing (apparent forks, attacks on pieces, opened lines, checks) and assumes the defending pawn 'cannot' recapture due to these phantom threats. In reality, the pawn recapture is always safe and leaves the opponent up a full piece for merely one pawn. The average cp_loss of 329 reflects losing approximately a full minor piece. Central pawn captures dominate (6/9 on e4/e5/d4/d5), with 3/9 on the b-file (b3/b4/b5). The pattern appears in both openings (2/9) and middlegames (7/9), affecting both White (5/9) and Black (4/9) equally.

314.label: Playing a non-forcing, non-developing move (typically a pawn push) when the position urgently demands piece activation, development, or addressing king safety.
314.description: 10/10 positions share the pattern of ignoring an immediate tactical or developmental need in favor of a slow, non-forcing move. 7/10 of the actual moves played are pawn pushes (b4, f3, a5, d6, d4, f6, b5), while the remaining 3 are piece moves that abandon critical defensive duties (Qc6, Qd7) or dissipate attacking force prematurely (Rg5+). In 8/10 positions, the blundering side has an uncastled or exposed king, making tempo especially critical. In 9/10 positions, the best alternative involved piece development or activation (Nc6, Nd2, Nc4, Bf5, Bh6, etc.) rather than pawn moves. The refutations in 8/10 cases directly exploit king safety vulnerabilities that the slow move failed to address. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses and 'piece_activity' in 9/10, confirming that the core error is wasting a critical tempo on a non-urgent action while the opponent gains time to exploit structural or king-safety weaknesses.

327.label: Playing routine piece development moves to natural back-rank squares in positions demanding immediate concrete tactical action.
327.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing, non-capturing piece development move to a 'natural' square on the 2nd/3rd rank (from the player's perspective): e7 appears 5 times (Black), d2 twice (White), plus Qe2, Qd7, and Be3. In every case, the position demanded sharp concrete action — either exploiting a tactic (4/10: positions 4, 5, 8, 10 where winning moves like Qxe6, Rxf7, f5 were available) or addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability (6/10: positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 where the 'developing' move created or exposed a tactical flaw). The average cp_loss of 298 confirms these are severe errors. Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, meaning these were critical positions requiring precision rather than routine play. 8/10 positions involved unresolved king safety issues (uncastled kings or weak pawn shields), adding urgency the players ignored.

324.label: Playing a non-forcing move (typically a pawn advance) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a tactical or structural emergency.
324.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move when the position demanded immediate concrete action. 7/10 of the played moves were pawn advances (gxh7, h4, a5, g6, c4, g5, d5), and the remaining 3 were quiet piece/king moves (Bf6, Bf4, Kb7). In contrast, the best moves in 10/10 positions involved active piece operations: piece development (Nd2, Ne2), king centralization (Kd4, Ke3), tactical captures/exchanges (Bxe5, Rxe5, Bb5), or defensive piece repositioning (Be1, Rd8). The average number of good moves was only 1.7, meaning these were critical decision points where precision was essential. In 8/10 positions, the played move not only wasted time but actively created new weaknesses or enabled opponent tactics: g6 allowed Nxg6, d5 drove the knight to the devastating b4 square, g5 exposed f2, c4 locked the structure creating a king invasion highway, and h4 left the king on a fork square. The positions spanned all phases (7 middlegame, 2 endgame, 1 opening) and both sides (6 White, 4 Black), confirming this is a universal decision-making error rather than a phase-specific or side-specific pattern.

337.label: A knight captures a pawn that is attacking a bishop, when the correct move was to simply retreat the bishop to safety.
337.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight capturing a pawn that is threatening/attacking a bishop, with the best move in every case being a simple bishop retreat (Bg3 in 7/10, Bb3 in 2/10). Specifically, 7/10 positions involve Nxg5 where White's bishop on h4 is being challenged by Black's g5 pawn, and the correct response was Bg3. 2/10 involve Nxb5 where White's bishop on a4 is attacked by Black's b5 pawn, with Bb3 being correct. In all these cases, the opponent simply recaptures the knight with an adjacent pawn (hxg5 or cxb5), winning a full piece for only 1-2 pawns. The average cp_loss of 253 reflects the consistent material miscalculation of trading a knight (~300cp) for insufficient pawn compensation. 6/10 occurred in the opening phase, suggesting players are tempted by 'active' captures rather than quiet retreats when still developing. Only 1/10 (the Bf4 endgame position) breaks the knight-capture pattern but shares the theme of an incorrect piece move when a retreat/reposition was essential.

322.label: Moving a bishop to an apparently active or aggressive square while it was performing a critical defensive function, leaving key squares, pawns, or pieces fatally unguarded.
322.description: 9/10 positions feature bishop moves (Be5, Be3, Bd3, Bd6, Be6, Bd3, Bf2, Bc3, Bc5), with one queen move (Qb2) sharing the same underlying error pattern. In at least 6/10 cases, the moved piece was directly defending a critical square or pawn from its original position: Bd3 (pos 3) removed the f1 bishop defending g2 allowing instant checkmate; Bf2 (pos 7) removed the e3 bishop defending the f4 pawn; Bc5 (pos 10) removed the f8 bishop defending g7. In 3/10 cases (Be5, Bd6, Bd3 pos 6), the bishop 'attacked' the opponent's queen expecting it to retreat, but the queen had a stronger tactical response (capturing a hanging piece or enabling a fork). In 8/10 positions, the move was a quiet, non-capturing bishop repositioning that looked natural or aggressive but ignored an immediate tactical or defensive necessity. The average cp_loss of 2173 reflects that many of these abandonments are catastrophic (3 allow checkmate). Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions demanded precise defensive awareness.

339.label: Moving the king to the h-file corner (Kh1/Kh8) as a misapplied prophylactic when the position demands immediate concrete action.
339.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical move pattern: the king shuffles one square from g1 to h1 (8 positions) or g8 to h8 (2 positions) as a pseudo-prophylactic move, typically intended to escape a diagonal or avoid vague future threats. In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete action — defending an attacked piece (3/10), capturing a hanging/advanced pawn (2/10), developing pieces (3/10), or creating active threats (2/10). The average cp_loss of 329 reflects catastrophic consequences. In 6/10 positions, the Kh1/Kh8 move specifically CREATED a new tactical vulnerability that didn't exist before: in 4/10, it placed the king on a square reachable by a knight fork from f2 (Nxf2+); in 1/10, it made Nxf7+ a check; in 1/10, it abandoned the sole defense of the f2 pawn. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical positions requiring precision, making the tempo waste especially devastating.

334.label: Defensive king moves to the back rank that walk into immediate tactical refutations, played instead of required forcing moves (checks, captures, or perpetuals).
334.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move played with prophylactic/defensive intent in the middlegame, where the player perceived king danger and tried to sidestep threats by relocating the king. In every case, the position demanded an aggressive forcing move instead (perpetual checks in 3/10, captures with check in 3/10, piece development/activity in 4/10). Critically, 8/10 positions saw the king walk directly into a back-rank or first-rank tactical vulnerability—the very thing the player was trying to avoid. The refutations exploit the king's new square: 6/10 feature immediate Rh1+/Qh1+ checks along the first rank after Kf1, 2/10 feature Qh8+ exploiting the king on f8, 1/10 creates a fatal c-file pin after Kc8, and 1/10 allows immediate Rg8# on the back rank after Ke8. The average cp_loss of 5153 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in immediate checkmate or mate-in-2, while the remaining featured material losses of 300-600cp. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than intuitive king retreats.

335.label: A knight voluntarily leaves a strong or functionally essential square for a weaker, less relevant one, abandoning its defensive or tactical role in the position.
335.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight is moved from a square where it performed a critical function (defending key weaknesses, controlling invasion squares, or enabling concrete tactics) to a less effective square that fails to address the position's primary demands. In 8/10 cases, the knight moved FROM a central or near-central square (d5, e4, e2, c4, c8, e7) TO a rim or peripheral square (b4×2, c3, f1, b2, a7, b6, c6). In 9/10 positions, the knight's departure directly enabled the opponent's primary threat: allowing pawn captures (Positions 1, 4), passed pawn advances (Positions 3, 6, 10), rook invasions (Positions 8, 9), or tactical combinations (Positions 7, 5). The average centipawn loss was 1232, with 3/10 positions resulting in immediate tactical catastrophe (trapped piece, back-rank mate, forced checkmate). In 7/10 positions, the best move instead involved maintaining the knight's current post while using other pieces or pawns to improve the position.

341.label: King moves in won elementary pawn endgames (K+P vs K or K+PP vs K) where the winning side maneuvers their king to escort a passed pawn to promotion.
341.description: 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with minimal material (1-2 pawns maximum on the board). 10/10 moves are king moves made by the side with a decisive advantage (evaluations ranging from ±530 to ±1110). 10/10 positions involve a passed pawn that needs king support to promote. The winning technique in all cases revolves around classic K+P endgame principles: shouldering, outflanking, opposition, and king-ahead-of-pawn positioning. 7/10 moves are optimal or near-optimal (≤9 cp loss), indicating this feature primarily detects the POSITION TYPE rather than errors. When mistakes do occur (positions 6 and 7, with 126 and 18 cp loss respectively), they involve moving the king when immediately advancing the pawn was more efficient—a tempo loss that allows the defending king to improve its position. The average of only 2.3 good moves available confirms these are narrow, forcing positions where precision matters.

342.label: King moves toward an inactive sector of the board while the decisive battle requires its presence elsewhere, losing critical tempi.
342.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves that travel in the wrong direction relative to the critical theater of operations. In 5/10 positions (Positions 1, 2, 5, 4, 7), the king advances toward the kingside where the pawn structure is completely locked, while the winning/drawing plan requires the king to march toward the queenside or center. In 2/10 positions (9, 10), the king prematurely advances to c6, either losing the opposition or abandoning the critical d6 blockade square. Position 3 shows the king retreating toward the corner (Kg8) when escape required moving toward the open center (Ke8). Position 8 shows premature king relocation (Kd2) before a necessary preparatory move. The average cp_loss of 1080 reflects that these directional errors are catastrophic in endgame positions where king activity is the decisive factor. 8/10 positions required the king to head toward a specific zone (usually queenside or center), and the played move sent it to the opposite flank or wrong square, giving the opponent 1-2 critical tempi to either invade, establish opposition, or neutralize the position.

330.label: Developing a bishop to g4 or g5 when an opposing bishop already pressures the f3/f6 knight, creating exploitable tactical vulnerabilities.
330.description: In 10/10 positions, a bishop is developed to g4 (Black) or g5 (White) in a position where the opposing side already has a bishop on the corresponding diagonal (g5/h4 for White or g4/h5 for Black) that pressures the f3 or f6 knight. This creates a 'mirrored bishop' tension where the f-knight becomes a critical tactical weak point. In 8/10 cases, the primary refutation involves capturing or removing the f3/f6 knight (via Bxf6, Bxf3, or forcing Nxg4), which then exposes a hanging piece, undefended queen, or overloaded defender. In 7/10 positions, the blundering side apparently intended to attack the opponent's queen with the bishop development, treating it as a natural tempo-gaining move. In 6/10 positions, the knight on f3/f6 was already pinned to the queen by the opposing bishop, making Bg5/Bg4 leave the newly-developed bishop tactically undefended. The average cp_loss of 321 reflects that these mistakes typically cost a full piece.

338.label: Quiet queen moves to seemingly natural squares that abandon critical functions or create tactical vulnerabilities, missing that the position required a more forcing or precise response.
338.description: All 10/10 positions feature non-capturing, non-checking queen moves that appear reasonable on general principles but fail concretely. In 6/10 cases (Qd1, Qb7, Qc7, Qg4, Qg3, Qb6), the queen abandons defense of a critical square or piece, allowing the opponent to seize control of files, execute knight forks, or win undefended material. In 3/10 cases (Qf7, Qe3, Qe4), the queen lands on a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable to discovered attacks, traps, or double threats. In 1/10 cases (Qe6), the queen centralizes passively when a forcing double-attack existed. The best moves were often also queen moves but to different, more precise squares (7/10 positions), showing the error is square selection rather than piece selection. The average cp_loss of 337 reflects critical-moment positions disguised as quiet ones, where players defaulted to 'natural-looking' repositioning rather than calculating concrete tactical consequences. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were high-precision moments that punish general-principle thinking.

340.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move (castling, pawn push, or piece repositioning) in a narrow critical position that demanded immediate concrete action — typically a check or capture.
340.description: All 10/10 positions share a striking commonality: the played move is always non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), while the correct move was a concrete forcing blow in 8/10 cases (checks or captures: Qa5+, Qxd6, Qxf6, Qe2, Rxh6, Bxc5, Bxh7+, Qd4+). The positions were extremely narrow with an average of only 1.2 good moves available, meaning one specific tactical answer existed and the player instead chose a 'general principles' move. 3/10 played O-O (routine castling), 3/10 played quiet pawn moves (d3, a3, h6), 3/10 played non-capturing queen repositioning (Qd7, Qc7, Qb3), and 1/10 played a king move (Kd1). The average cp_loss of 443 reflects catastrophic cost. The best moves missed include 3 queen forks/checks, 3 simple captures of material, 1 Greek gift sacrifice, and 1 forced queen trade — all concrete, calculable actions that were passed over in favor of autopilot development or prophylaxis.
