344.label: Playing a quiet one-square pawn advance near your own king (g3/c3/g6/c6) as a prophylactic 'housekeeping' move when the position demands immediate concrete action.
344.description: All 10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance to the third rank on the same wing as the player's castled king (g3 in 6/10, c3 in 2/10, g6 in 2/10, c6 in 1/10). In every case, the king is nearby (10/10 moves are on the same flank as the player's king). These moves mimic 'luft' or structural consolidation but waste a critical tempo: 5/10 positions had clear hanging pieces or back-rank tactics available (Rxb5+, Bxd8, Qd8+, Qxa7, Qd3), while the remaining 5/10 either self-destructively weakened the pawn shield (opening the a8-h1 diagonal in Position 8, creating dark-square holes in Position 4) or allowed the opponent to lock in a permanent structural advantage. The average cp_loss of 1256 reflects catastrophic consequences. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow critical moments demanding precision—yet the players chose the most generic, low-effort pawn push possible.

328.label: Non-forcing minor piece maneuvers that place the piece on a tactically vulnerable square or abandon a critical defensive post, when the position demands concrete tactical action.
328.description: All 10/10 positions feature minor piece moves (7 bishop moves, 3 knight moves) that look superficially reasonable — repositioning, capturing a pawn, or 'improving' piece placement — but catastrophically ignore the position's tactical demands. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 10, and partially 3), the minor piece moves to an undefended square where it is simply captured or immediately exploited. In 3/10 positions (5, 6, 8), a minor piece retreats from a critical defensive/active post, allowing the opponent to execute devastating forks or tactical combinations (Nf3+ in pos 5, consolidation in pos 6, Bxf2+/Ne3+ in pos 8). In 2/10 positions (7, 9), the minor piece makes a slow positional move while a far stronger concrete continuation exists. The 'missed_tactic' tag appears in 9/10 positions, 'tempo_loss' in 8/10, and 'piece_activity' in 9/10. Average cp_loss of 1289 and only 1.5 good moves available on average confirm these are critical moments where precise calculation was mandatory but the player defaulted to a quiet piece move instead.
328.old_chip: Slow Minor Piece Moves Ignore Tactics

343.label: A bishop is passively repositioned to a 'safe' diagonal square when a concrete tactical opportunity (usually a capture) demands immediate execution.
343.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved without capturing to a quiet repositioning square (g6 in 5 cases, g3 in 2, f5/f4/e6 in the remaining 3). In every case, the bishop moves to what appears to be a stable, defensible square along a diagonal rather than engaging in a concrete tactical action. 8/10 positions had the best move being a capture (Bxe2 in 3 positions, plus Bxe7, Nxd4, gxf4, Nxd5, Rxd6), and in 3/10 cases (positions 4, 7, 9) the very bishop that retreated should itself have captured on e2. The average cp_loss of 251 reflects that these passive retreats consistently miss winning or near-winning tactical opportunities. 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating critical moments demanding calculation rather than prophylaxis. The tactical motif is overwhelmingly tempo loss (8/10 explicitly tagged), as the retreat grants the opponent a free move to seize the initiative—whether through pawn advances (f5, g4, c4), knight invasions (Ncb5, Na5), or piece captures (Nxd6, Rxd6).

348.label: King moves in endgames where a single tempo in the king's path determines the game outcome (win vs. draw, or draw vs. loss).
348.description: 10/10 positions are endgames featuring king moves in positions where king races and passed pawn dynamics are decisive. 10/10 have both kings exposed with weak or absent pawn shields. 9/10 are pure pawn endgames (one has a bishop/knight, one a rook). The average number of good moves is only 1.5, indicating razor-thin margins where only 1-2 king directions maintain the evaluation. 5/10 positions show 0 cp_loss (the feature fires on correct moves too), while the blunders (120, 116, 215, 153 cp_loss) all involve choosing the wrong direction or wrong priority for the king, often turning wins into draws or draws into losses by a single tempo. The consistent thread is that the position demands choosing the ONE correct king path in a pawn race, and alternatives fail because the king arrives one move too late to the critical sector.

345.label: In rook endgames, the rook repositions to an apparently active square while abandoning a critical defensive function, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated control.
345.description: All 10/10 positions are rook endgames where the player makes a rook repositioning move that looks active or purposeful but fatally abandons a crucial defensive responsibility. In 10/10 cases, the move is a non-capturing, non-checking rook move to a 'natural-looking' square (7th rank, toward a target pawn, onto an open file). The consistent error is that the rook was performing an essential defensive function on or near its current post — guarding a key square (positions 1, 5, 10 where it controlled g3/f2/f2), maintaining back-rank defense (positions 3, 8, 9), cutting off an enemy king or preserving checking distance (positions 4, 7), or maintaining pressure from the correct file (positions 2, 6). The correct moves in 8/10 positions involve either keeping the rook near its current post, moving it to a less flashy but more functional square, or using a non-rook move entirely (king move or pawn push). The average cp_loss of 1217 reflects catastrophic consequences, as abandoning the defensive function typically allows immediate tactical exploitation — promotions, back-rank mates, or decisive pawn captures.

347.label: Playing a flashy, aggressive bishop move (usually a check or capture) that loses the bishop for insufficient compensation when quieter moves were far superior.
347.description: All 10/10 positions feature bishop moves that look aggressive or forcing. 7/10 are bishop checks (Bxf2+, Bh2+, Bh2+, Bh2+, Bd2+, Bh7+, Bxh7+), while the remaining 3/10 are bishop captures or moves to attacked squares (Bxc7, Bxf3, Ba4). In every case, the bishop is either sacrificed outright or moved to a square where it is immediately captured, without generating sufficient compensation. 5/10 specifically involve bishop sacrifices on the h-file near the enemy king (three Bh2+ and two Bh7+/Bxh7+ Greek Gift attempts). The correct alternatives were consistently quieter moves: retreats (Bf8 in position 4), captures of other pieces (Nxe4 in positions 7 and 3), simple development (Bd7 in position 5), or consolidating moves (Bd3, Kg2 in position 8). The average cp_loss of 1263 reflects that these aggressive bishop deployments consistently squandered large advantages or converted balanced positions into losing ones.

346.label: Moving a rook to a seemingly active but strategically irrelevant square when the position urgently demands a different action (defense, pawn push, or piece development).
346.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that appear purposeful on the surface—checking (2/10: Rf2+, Rh7+), capturing (1/10: Rxa7), or repositioning to open files/ranks (7/10: Rb1, Rh7, Ra3, Rg8, Rb8, Ra7, Re1)—but critically waste tempo in positions demanding urgent action elsewhere. In 7/10 cases, the best move was NOT a rook move at all (Nf6, f5, Bd4, Kd7, Be5+, h5, d6), indicating the player defaulted to 'improve the rook' when the position's true priority lay with a different piece or a pawn advance. In 8/10 positions, the rook move either abandoned a critical defensive duty (guarding back rank, controlling 2nd rank, defending a pawn) or moved to a tactically vulnerable square. The average cp_loss of 1191 is extreme, with 3/10 positions featuring the rook moving into direct capture (Rf2+ into bishop, Rxa7 into bishop, Rb1 into back-rank deflection). The consistent thread is a player who sees 'active rook placement' as a default good idea without checking whether the position's concrete demands require something entirely different.

353.label: Moving a bishop to a quiet square instead of making the necessary bishop exchange (Bx capture) that the position demands for concrete tactical or structural gains.
353.description: In 9/10 positions, the best move was a bishop capture (Bxe3, Bxe6, Bxa6, or Bxd2) that would have either damaged the opponent's pawn structure, won material through a tactical sequence, or eliminated a key defensive piece. Instead, the player passively repositioned their bishop to a quiet square (d3, d6, e7, e5, b5, c2) — avoiding the exchange in favor of 'keeping the bishop.' In 4/10 cases the correct move was specifically Bxe3 (fxe3 doubling pawns + tactical follow-up), in 3/10 it was Bxe6 (fxe6 damaging kingside structure), and the remaining cases involved Bxa6 (winning material) and Bxd2 (eliminating a passed pawn supporter). The played moves universally resulted in tempo loss, as the repositioned bishop ended up on inferior squares (often blocking own pawns or losing coordination). 7/10 positions were in the opening phase, suggesting a systematic reluctance to trade bishops early.
353.old_chip: Passive bishop retreat dodges critical exchange

351.label: A major piece is sent to the opponent's back rank in a seemingly aggressive move that is actually counterproductive — the piece gets captured, stranded, or the invasion abandons a more critical function.
351.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen or rook being sent directly to the opponent's back rank (1st or 8th rank), creating the appearance of an aggressive invasion or back-rank attack. In 6/10 cases a rook makes the move (Rb8, Re8, Re1, Rd8+, Rd1, Rc8) and in 4/10 a queen does (Qe1, Qd1, Qf8+, Qe8). The moves look threatening — targeting enemy rooks, delivering checks, forking pieces, or pressing the back rank — but in every case the invasion is premature or fundamentally flawed. In 3/10 positions (Re8, Re1, Rc8) the piece abandons a critical defensive or active post. In 3/10 (Qd1, Qf8+, Qe8) the piece walks onto an undefended square where it gets captured or the attack is easily parried. In 2/10 (Rd8+, Rd1) the move invites simplification that eliminates the player's advantage. In 2/10 (Rb8, Qe1) the piece reaches the back rank but creates no real threat while leaving something else hanging or unaddressed. Back-rank tactical themes appear in 8/10 positions, confirming that players are drawn to back-rank geometry but execute it with incorrect timing or move order.

349.label: Playing non-forcing moves (especially rim pawn pushes) in positions demanding immediate tactical action, wasting a critical tempo.
349.description: 6/9 positions feature rim pawn pushes (5 h-pawn moves: h6, h5, h4, h5, h3; plus one a-pawn: a3), while the remaining 3 are passive piece moves (Rg2, Qg8, Bd1). All 9/9 moves are non-forcing—no checks, no captures, no direct threats—played in positions where the evaluation demanded immediate concrete action. In 9/9 positions the correct move involved either addressing an urgent tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, back-rank threat, mating attack) or seizing a decisive tactical opportunity (fork, material capture). The average cp_loss is extreme (4540), with 4/9 positions resulting in forced checkmate after the error. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating razor-sharp positions where precision was critical. The moves all share the characteristic of looking 'normal' or 'prophylactic' while completely ignoring the burning tactical reality of the position.

357.label: A queen check with no follow-up that displaces the queen from critical duties while the opponent's king safely sidesteps to a better square.
357.description: All 9/9 positions feature a queen delivering check (+) that the opponent's king easily sidesteps, after which the queen is fatally misplaced. In 7/9 cases, the refutation is simply the king walking to a square where it's actually SAFER than before (Kh2, Kg6, Kf1, Kh1, Kb2, etc.), while the queen is left stranded far from its essential duties. In 6/9 positions, the correct move was either a quiet defensive move (Rg8, Kg8, g5, Qh6) or a different tactical resource entirely (Nxh3+, Qxe1, Qe2+), meaning the player chose an aggressive-looking but purposeless check over a harder-to-find solution. The average cp_loss of 4687 reflects how catastrophic these checks are—5/9 positions swing directly into forced mate. In every single case, exactly 1 good move existed, indicating these are critical moments where the instinct to give check is maximally punished.

350.label: A piece moves to an apparently threatening or active square, but the threat is shallow and easily refuted by a simple pawn kick, exchange, or one-move response, leaving the aggressor worse off.
350.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player moves a piece forward to an ostensibly aggressive square — creating a visible threat (fork, attack on queen, pressure on a diagonal) — but the threat is too slow or easily parried, and the move is immediately punished. In 3/10 positions (6, 7, 10), a knight jumps to b5 threatening Nc7+ fork, but is simply kicked by ...a6 to a horrible square. In 4/10 positions (2, 8, 9, plus 1), a queen moves to an exposed square where it can be profitably exchanged or its departure abandons critical defensive duties. In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 5), a bishop moves to an active-looking diagonal but is immediately challenged by a pawn (d5, f4) or its removal from a key square enables a devastating tactic. The refutations are consistently embarrassingly simple — often single-move pawn pushes (a6, d5, f4) or immediate captures — yet the blunderer's position collapses catastrophically (average cp_loss: 1239). Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were demanding positions where the 'obvious' aggressive option was precisely wrong.

331.label: Playing superficially active or forcing moves that ignore the position's concrete critical demands, wasting crucial tempo.
331.description: 9/10 positions show a player choosing a move that appears purposeful (aggressive placement, check, counterplay attempt) but fundamentally misreads the position's priorities, wasting decisive tempo. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/10 positions, and 'piece_activity' in 8/10, confirming the core pattern: pieces move to squares that serve a secondary or imaginary objective while the real battle rages elsewhere. In 3/10 cases the move is a pointless/counterproductive check (h6+, Re1+, Rd8+—though Rd8+ is actually correct with 0 cp_loss, making it an outlier). In 3/10 cases rooks move to files for apparent pressure that accomplishes nothing (Rb8, Rb7, Rg1). In 2/10 cases knights abandon active central squares for passive/rim squares (Na5, Ncd2). The average cp_loss of 1055 is enormous, and only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where playing a 'cosmetically active' move instead of the concrete requirement is catastrophic. 9/10 positions featured exposed kings (either side), meaning tactical precision—not vague activity—was demanded.

359.label: A non-urgent flank pawn advance wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate tactical action with pieces.
359.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet pawn advance (overwhelmingly on flank files: 6/10 on a/b-files, 2/10 on g/h-files) played in positions that demand urgent piece activity or threat-addressing moves. In 9/10 positions, the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. In 9/10, 'missed_tactic' appears—the player had a concrete tactical resource available (back-rank defense, queen invasion, piece repositioning, capturing an attacker) but chose a slow positional pawn push instead. The tactical emergencies varied: 2/10 involved immediate checkmate threats ignored (positions 5 and 7), 2/10 left pieces hanging (positions 1 and 8), 2/10 missed fork/combination opportunities (positions 4 and 10), and 4/10 squandered a narrow window for active counterplay or piece exploitation (positions 2, 3, 6, 9). The average centipawn loss of 2965 reflects the catastrophic nature of wasting tempo in critical moments. Only 2.0 good moves existed on average, indicating these were tactically demanding positions with narrow paths to survival.

358.label: Developing a bishop to a natural square when the position demands an immediate concrete action (capture, pawn thrust, or forcing move).
358.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a 'natural' developing square (c4, c5, d2, e3, e6, f4, f5) when the position critically demands something more forcing. In 10/10 cases the move is a non-capturing, non-checking bishop development that looks reasonable but misses the tactical pulse of the position. The missed best moves are diverse — pawn captures (Qxd5, Nxf4), central pawn thrusts (d5 in 3 positions), piece attacks (g4 trapping a knight, Be7 attacking a queen), and file contests (Rd8) — but they all share being concrete and forcing. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these are razor-sharp positions where one specific action was demanded. The blunder consistently stems from prioritizing 'completing development' or 'putting a piece on an active diagonal' over calculating the specific tactical requirements of the moment. In 7/10 positions, the bishop being developed was the last inactive minor piece, suggesting the player was motivated by a general principle (develop all pieces) rather than reading the position's concrete demands.

360.label: Playing a quiet repositioning move (usually a king walk or queen shift) while completely overlooking a simple capture of an undefended enemy major piece.
360.description: 10/10 positions featured an enemy major piece (8 rooks, 2 queens) that was hanging and could be captured with a simple one-move take. In every single case, the player instead made a non-tactical repositioning move—6/10 were king moves (Kf7, Kg5, Kxd6, Kb5, Kh2, Kh6), 3/10 were queen relocations (Qd4, Qh4, Qc2), and 1/10 was a rook slide (Re2). The best move in each position was a straightforward capture: Bxd6, gxf3, Qxe7/Bxe7, Nxf3/Rxf3, Nxe7, Qxe5, cxd6, Qxg5, exd5, Bxe7—none requiring more than one move of calculation. 9/10 positions had only 1 good move available (the capture itself), with average cp_loss of 2541. The players appeared focused on king safety concerns, positional plans, or attack ideas while the free material sat in plain sight, suggesting a pattern of 'looking past' the obvious tactical gift.

363.label: Playing a superficially forcing queen check that drives the opponent's king to a better square or misses a superior non-checking (or differently-checking) move.
363.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen delivering check that turns out to be counterproductive. In 6/10 cases, the best move was either a non-queen move or a non-checking move entirely (Bb4+ in Position 1, Qa6 capturing the pawn in Position 2, Qxc3 in Position 6, Re1+ in Position 9, c5+ in Position 10, Qf4+ forcing interposition in Position 5). In the remaining 4/10, the correct move was a queen check but from a critically different square (Qb7+ not Qa7+, Qe1+ not Qf4+, Qc4+ not Qd2+, Qd5# not Qc5+). The consistent error is choosing the most obvious-looking queen check without verifying whether it actually restricts the opponent's king or achieves a concrete goal. Tags of 'tempo_loss' appeared in 10/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 9/10. The average centipawn loss was 2195, with 4/10 positions having only one good move available, demonstrating these are high-precision moments where the reflexive check is catastrophic.

362.label: A knight is moved to a visually dominant central square, but the position demanded a more concrete action (capture, pawn break, or preparatory move), and the knight can be immediately neutralized.
362.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight being played to a 'strong-looking' central square (e5 in 5 positions, f4 in 2, c5 in 2, e4 in 1, c3 in 1), prioritizing piece placement aesthetics over the concrete tactical demands of the position. In 6/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, and partially 5), the opponent can immediately and favorably exchange the newly-placed knight, simplifying their problems or deflecting a key defender. In 2/10 cases (positions 4, 8), the knight physically blocks a crucial pawn advance (c-pawn or e-pawn) that was the source of the player's advantage. In 2/10 cases (positions 1, 5), the knight move misses a concrete hanging-piece capture that would have won material outright. In 1/10 (position 9), the knight becomes an immediate target for a pawn storm. The average cp_loss of 273 confirms these are severe errors. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical positions demanding precision rather than general positional improvement.

356.label: Playing an aggressive-looking piece move (usually a knight) to an active square while ignoring a more critical immediate tactical threat such as mate, a hanging piece, or the removal of a key defender.
356.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a move that appeared active or aggressive — attacking the opponent's queen, centralizing a piece, or grabbing material — while completely overlooking a more urgent tactical reality. 6/10 moves were knight moves to seemingly strong squares (Ng4, Nc5, Nxe5, Nd4, Nd4, Nf3), with the remainder being similarly 'active' piece moves or captures. In 4/10 positions (Kd2, Nc5, Nd4-opening, Nf3), the ignored threat was immediate checkmate or a mating attack. In 3/10 positions (Ng4, Nc5, dxe5), the move removed a piece from a critical defensive function, allowing a devastating tactical blow. In 2/10 positions (Bxb5, Nxe5), the player grabbed lesser material while ignoring a more valuable hanging piece. In 1/10 (Bg3), the move fell one tempo short of executing the correct combination. The average centipawn loss of ~3971 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights — these aren't subtle positional errors but fundamental failures to check the opponent's most forcing replies before executing one's own plan.

364.label: Non-forcing wing pawn advances (typically h4/h5/g4) in positions demanding immediate tactical forcing moves like checks or passed pawn advances.
364.description: 9/10 positions feature a wing pawn advance (h4 in 4 cases, h5 in 3 cases, g4 in 1, b5 in 1) and the remaining position features Qh5 with the same thematic intent. In every case, the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation: 4/10 required perpetual checks to hold a draw (positions 1, 5, 6, 10), 3/10 required delivering forcing checks to maintain a winning attack (positions 2, 8, 9), and 3/10 required addressing critical tactical threats like back-rank weakness or mating nets (positions 3, 4, 7). The average centipawn loss of 3043 reflects the catastrophic nature of these tempo losses. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, confirming these were narrow positions where only forcing play survived. All 10 moves share the trait of being non-forcing (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) in positions where the opponent gains a decisive tempo to either escape a mating net, break a perpetual check pattern, or launch a counterattack.

355.label: King moves in the wrong direction during losing (or critical) pawn endgames, abandoning the key defensive square or task.
355.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves, and 8/10 are pure king-and-pawn endgames. In 9/10 cases, the moving side is already significantly losing (evaluations typically -550 to -750 from their perspective). The critical blunders (positions 1, 4, 8, 10) all share the pattern of the king moving in an intuitive but wrong direction: toward the center instead of toward an enemy pawn (pos 1), toward queenside counterplay instead of blockading a passed pawn (pos 4), centralizing suboptimally (pos 8), or abandoning the sole drawing square (pos 10). Many positions with negligible cp_loss (positions 2, 3, 5, 6, 9) represent hopeless king shuffles in already-resigned positions. The one non-king-move outlier (Re3, pos 7) shares the thematic connection of moving a piece in an 'active' direction while abandoning a critical defensive responsibility. The average of 2.0 good moves available confirms these are constrained positions where the correct defensive idea is narrow.
355.old_chip: King drifts in lost pawn endgames

352.label: Voluntarily repositioning a knight or bishop to a seemingly improved square that actually creates or allows a tactical disaster.
352.description: In 10/10 positions, the player voluntarily relocated a minor piece (8/10 knights, 2/10 bishops) to what appeared to be a better square — an outpost, a more central square, or a more active diagonal — but the move catastrophically backfired. In 6/10 cases (Nc4, Nge7, Nf5, Nh7, Nh2, Ng4), the primary problem was abandoning a critical defensive function on the departure square: the piece had been guarding a key pawn (e4 in pos. 3), controlling an invasion square (g4 in pos. 5), defending a vulnerable point (f7 in pos. 9), or maintaining essential central tension. In 4/10 cases (Bd4, Nxh5, Bf5, Nc6), the primary problem was that the destination square was tactically compromised — the piece hung outright, walked onto an undefended diagonal, or became trapped with no escape. The average cp_loss of 348 confirms these are severe errors, not marginal inaccuracies. Critically, in 9/10 positions there were 1-3 concrete alternatives (captures, pawn breaks, castling, or central strikes) that addressed the position's actual demands rather than 'improving' piece placement.

366.label: Moving the queen to a square directly controlled by an enemy knight, which simply captures it.
366.description: 8/10 positions show the identical tactical pattern: the queen is moved to a square where an enemy knight can immediately capture it (Nxh5, Nxd5, Nxd6, Nxf3, Nxd4, Nxd7, Nxb4, Nxg3). In 7/10 cases the queen move is a check, suggesting 'check blindness' — the player is so focused on delivering check that they overlook the knight's control of the destination square. The remaining 2 positions involve related knight-geometry errors: Position 3 features a knight overextending to f7 where it becomes permanently trapped, and Position 6 features a knight abandoning its dominant post. The average cp_loss is extremely high (4199) because the queen is worth approximately 9 pawns, and in most cases nothing is gained in return. The knight origins vary (f6, h2, e4, f5, c6, h5, etc.), confirming that players systematically underestimate knight control of non-adjacent squares due to its non-linear movement pattern.

368.label: Giving check with a queen or rook in the endgame that wastes tempo and fails to address the position's critical requirement (usually passed pawns or king activity).
368.description: 8/10 positions feature checks (Qf3+, Ra5+, Rf2+, Re2+, Rg1+, Rb5+, Qg7+, Qb6+) that accomplish nothing constructive—the opponent's king simply moves to an equal or superior square. The remaining 2/10 (Rc5, Rf8) are rook moves to the wrong rank that similarly waste a critical tempo. All 10/10 are endgame positions where the analyses unanimously identify 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. In every case, the correct move was either a quiet king advance (Positions 2, 5, 10), a precise rook placement addressing passed pawns (Positions 6, 8), or a concrete tactical operation (Position 7's Rxf7+). The checks typically allow the opponent's king to improve—e.g., Position 4 lets Black centralize on d5, Position 10 lets White escape to c2, Position 2 lets White reach e4 supporting passed pawns. In Position 9, the check is even blocked by the very pawn Black needed to restrain (c7 interposition). The average cp_loss of 2042 is inflated by two positions where checks hung material (Position 3: rook captured by bishop) or threw away forced mate (Position 10: mate-in-11 to -595).

369.label: Pawn captures that remove the player's own structurally critical pawn — one serving as a barricade against the opponent's pieces or pawns — enabling an immediate tactical exploitation of the opened position.
369.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture where the capturing pawn was performing a vital blocking or restraining function. In 10/10 cases, removing this pawn unleashes an immediate tactical response through the now-unguarded square, file, or diagonal. Specifically: in 3/10 positions (1, 2, 3) the e-pawn was removed, allowing the opponent's e-pawn to advance with a fork or discovered attack; in 3/10 positions (4, 8, 9) the d-pawn was removed, enabling piece captures with tempo against now-undefended squares; in 2/10 positions (5, 6) the f-pawn was removed, liberating the opponent's f-pawn advance to fork pieces; in 1/10 (position 10) the g-pawn was removed, opening a mating corridor to the king; and in 1/10 (position 7) the f-pawn captured in the wrong move order, allowing the opponent's king to centralize advantageously. The average cp_loss of 1196 reflects the catastrophic nature of these structural self-inflictions. In 8/10 positions only 1 good alternative existed, confirming these were narrow positions where the temptation to resolve tension was especially dangerous.

361.label: Non-forcing queen (or piece) repositioning to a seemingly active square when the position demands immediate checks, captures, or tactical strikes.
361.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move (8/10 queen moves, 1 knight move, 1 rook move) during a tactically critical middlegame moment. In 5/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 6, 8, and partially 2), the piece moved directly to a square controlled by an opponent's piece—resulting in it being immediately captured, forked, or exposed to a decisive tactical shot. In the remaining 5/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 7, 9, 10), the move abandoned a critical offensive or defensive function (guarding a diagonal check, restraining a pawn break, maintaining tempo in an attack, protecting a key pawn), gifting the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, simplify, or launch a counter-attack. All 10 positions had forcing alternatives available (checks, captures, threats) with only 1.7 good moves on average, indicating narrow tactical positions where precision was essential. The average centipawn loss of 2290 reflects catastrophic consequences—these are not subtle inaccuracies but game-deciding blunders caused by choosing 'looks reasonable' over 'concretely necessary.'

367.label: A minor piece is voluntarily repositioned from a square where it performed a critical function to a seemingly active but tactically vulnerable or irrelevant square, ignoring the position's urgent demands.
367.description: 10/10 positions involve quiet minor piece repositioning moves (7 bishop moves, 3 knight moves) that abandon a critical defensive or restraining function. In 9/10 cases the move is non-forcing (no check, no real threat), squandering tempo when concrete action was required. The piece typically leaves a square where it was either paralyzing the opponent (Bc2 preventing castling in pos 1, Nb4 threatening forks in pos 5), blockading a pawn (Ne1 blocking e2 in pos 9), or maintaining pressure on a key diagonal/file (Bg4 pressuring the king in pos 4, 8, 10). After the move, the piece frequently lands on a square where it becomes a tactical target — captured with check (pos 2: Nxc4+), captured outright (pos 4: Nxe6), or attacked with tempo-gaining pawns (pos 10: ...h5). In 8/10 positions, king safety was the critical factor being ignored. The average cp_loss of 1239 reflects how catastrophic these 'quiet improvements' are when the position demands forcing play.

374.label: A slow, prophylactic a-pawn or h-pawn advance played in a position that demands immediate tactical action, development, or urgent defense.
374.description: All 10 positions feature a single-step flank pawn advance (8/10 are rook-pawn moves: 6x a6, 2x a3, 2x h3, plus 1x f6) played in positions where the clock is ticking on a concrete tactical or developmental need. In 6/10 positions, the move was ...a6 by Black, typically intending to prevent Nb5 or prepare ...b5, while ignoring an immediate kingside attack or tactical opportunity. In 10/10 cases, the move constituted a critical tempo loss — the opponent used the gifted tempo to either launch a decisive attack (positions 1, 2, 6, 7), consolidate a defensive setup (positions 4, 9, 10), or seize the initiative through central action (positions 3, 5, 8). Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, meaning these were narrow positions demanding precision. The best moves in each case were concrete: captures (positions 4, 10), central pawn breaks (positions 3, 8), piece development (positions 5, 8), or direct defensive moves addressing king safety (positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 9). The blunders averaged 244cp loss, reflecting how devastating a single wasted tempo is when the position is tactically critical.

373.label: Moving the king quietly when the position demands immediate active play with pieces, pawns, or a different king direction.
373.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet king repositioning move chosen in a position that demanded urgent tactical action. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a non-king move addressing the critical threat (Rd1 blockade in positions 1&3, Rxc3+ sacrifice in position 6, Nf1 defense in position 9, Ra1/Qd4/Qd3+ active counterplay in positions 8/5/10). In 2/10 cases, a different king direction was needed (Ke1 forcing promotion with check in position 2, Kc4 centralization in position 7). The king moves share a defensive/retreating character — 5/10 are retreats toward a corner or back rank (Kb8, Ke8, Kh8, Kf8, Kh2), while others are sidesteps or small advances that fail to address the position's central crisis. The average cp_loss of 3018 is extreme, with 4/10 positions involving missed forced mates or promotions. Only 1.7 good moves existed on average, confirming these are narrow critical moments where the passive king move squanders the one opportunity to maintain the position.

365.label: In rook endgames with urgent threats (passed pawns, exposed kings), the player makes a non-forcing rook repositioning move instead of the required tempo-gaining action (king activation, check, or pin).
365.description: All 10/10 positions are rook endgames featuring passed pawns and exposed kings where tempo is critical. In every case, the player moves the rook to a seemingly reasonable square (b5, d7, a7, d8, etc.) that creates no immediate threat and addresses no urgent problem. The correct moves were frequently NOT rook moves at all: 4/10 required king activation (Kg2, Kg7), 2/10 needed a forcing check (Ra6+, g3+), and 2/10 demanded a rook move to a specific tactically motivated square (Ra4 to pin, Rh5 as a decoy sacrifice). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, confirming that the common sin is squandering a critical tempo. The average cp_loss of 1139 is heavily skewed by catastrophic cases (positions 1, 7, 10 where the tempo loss allowed unstoppable pawn promotion or forced mate), but even modest losses (positions 3, 4, 5 at 31-38cp) stem from the same root cause: the rook move looks active but accomplishes nothing forcing, giving the opponent a free move to execute their plan.

381.label: A rook (or blockading piece) moves off the file where it was restraining a dangerous passed pawn, allowing immediate advancement or promotion.
381.description: 10/10 positions feature a dangerous passed pawn (within 1-2 squares of promotion) that was being blockaded or restrained by the moving piece. In 9/10 cases, a rook that was sitting on the critical file controlling the pawn's advance moves laterally to a different file (Ra2 off c-file, Rg1 off c-file, Ra8 off f-file, Rc2 off e-file, Rd2 off a-file, Ra1 from h-file, Rf1 off d-file, Rf1 off b-file), instantly enabling the pawn to push or promote. In 1/10 (b3), a pawn attacks the blockading knight but gives it time to relocate to a superior square. The best moves in all positions either maintained the blockade (Rc1, Rxc2+, Bc5, Rxe3, Ra1-behind-pawn, Rc2, a6, Qh5, Rxb2, a3) or eliminated the passed pawn directly. The average cp_loss of 1108 reflects the catastrophic nature of releasing a near-promotion pawn.

354.label: In critically narrow positions with typically only one good move, the player chooses an active-looking or superficially logical alternative that catastrophically self-weakens.
354.description: 10/10 positions featured extremely limited good options (avg 1.4 good moves available), creating razor-thin defensive situations. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a quiet, defensive, or prophylactic resource (Bf8, g6, Be5, Bd6, Qc2, Kf6, Kf7, Rb1), while the chosen move was something 'active' — a capture (4/10: gxh5, Nxe4, Bxh5, Bxc7), piece 'activation' (3/10: Rd1, Bc6, Bd6), a check (Re1+), or castling (O-O-O). 8/10 positions centrally involved king safety as the critical concern, with open files or diagonals aimed at a vulnerable king. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2161 reflects that these moves specifically enabled the opponent to exploit newly-created weaknesses — often by removing a pawn/piece from a critical defensive post (positions 1, 5, 6, 9) or placing the king/pieces on exposed squares (positions 7, 8, 10). The common thread is that each move addresses an obvious concern (capture the threatening piece, develop naturally, give check, escape the center) while fatally undermining the deeper positional requirement.

375.label: Playing a non-forcing g or c pawn advance to the 3rd rank to chase or block a piece, instead of addressing an urgent tactical demand in the position.
375.description: 10/10 positions feature a flank pawn (g or c file) advancing one square to the 3rd rank from the player's perspective (g6/c6 for Black, g3/c3 for White) as a slow, non-forcing move in a position requiring immediate concrete action. In 7/10 positions, the move specifically pushes the g-pawn to chase an enemy queen posted aggressively on the h-file (h5 or h4). In the remaining 3/10, the c-pawn advances to 'solidify' or prepare a future move. In every case, the position contained a critical tactical element being ignored: hanging pieces in 4/10 (positions 2, 4, 5, 9), exposed king vulnerabilities exploited after the pawn move in 5/10 (positions 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 10), and forced mating patterns in 1/10. The average cp_loss of 1370 reflects that these 'natural-looking' pawn moves are catastrophic tempo losses in positions that demanded forcing moves (captures, checks, or immediate threats). Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points with essentially one correct path.

372.label: In rook endgames, making a rook repositioning move that looks active but wastes the critical tempo needed for the position's true priority (usually king activation or a more direct threat).
372.description: All 10/10 positions are rook endgames where the player made a rook move that appeared purposeful but was actually a tempo-wasting misdirection. In 6/10 positions, the best move was a KING move (Kg5, Kb4, Kd6, Kxh2, Kg5, Kd2), yet the player chose a rook repositioning instead. In 3/10 positions, the best move was a more immediately threatening rook move (Rc2 attacking a pawn base, Re7 targeting a passed pawn, Rd4 reaching h4 one tempo faster). 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The played rook moves share a common character: they go to squares that look active (occupying open files, attacking distant pawns, giving checks, blockading) but create no immediate concrete threat, allowing the opponent to improve their position or consolidate. The average cp_loss of 198 reflects that these tempo losses are often decisive in endgames where a single tempo determines whether a passed pawn promotes, a king reaches a critical square, or a fortress holds.

377.label: Playing a slow, repositioning major piece move (usually a rook) when the position demands immediate concrete/forcing action.
377.description: 9/10 positions feature rook moves and 1/10 a queen move — all are non-forcing major piece repositions (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) that appear 'useful' on the surface: doubling rooks (Rhg6, Rce7, Rac8), defending a pawn (Ra2, Rf7), placing a rook on an open file (Re1, Re2, Rc3), or repositioning to a 'better' square (Ra6, Qc5). In every case, the best move was concrete and forcing: a capture (Rxe4, Nxf3+, Bxd4 in 3/10), a check (Rh4+ in 1/10), an aggressive piece jump (Nh5, Qc3 in 3/10), or a pawn advance (d4, c4 in 3/10). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 8/10. The average cp_loss of 283 reflects how severely these quiet moves are punished in positions with expiring tactical opportunities or urgent defensive needs.

379.label: A bishop is moved away from a square where it was critically shielding the player's own king or guarding a key piece, immediately exposing a tactical vulnerability on the vacated line.
379.description: All 10 positions feature bishop moves where the bishop departs from a critical defensive station. In 8/10 positions, the bishop was blocking an open file or diagonal that led directly to the player's own king (e.g., blocking the e-file in positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 10; guarding the fianchetto king shelter in positions 1 and 5; preventing back-rank/promotion threats in position 4). In 9/10 positions this constitutes a genuine mistake (cp_loss > 0, averaging ~2218cp). The moves are motivated by aggressive intentions — 6/10 are captures seeking material, 3/10 are checks, and 1/10 is a development move — but all prioritize attack over a unique defensive function the bishop was performing. The refutations consistently exploit the newly opened line: checks or captures along the vacated diagonal/file appear in the primary refutation of 8/10 positions (Qxe4+, Qe3+, Qe4+, Qf2+, Qxh1+, Qh5+, Ra8, Ng4). Position 8 (cp_loss 0) is a borderline case where the move transposes to the same result, but still fits the geometric pattern of a bishop leaving a defensive diagonal to give check.

378.label: Queen relocations that leave the queen's ideal multi-purpose square for a seemingly active but functionally inferior one.
378.description: In 9/10 positions, the queen occupied a dominant square performing multiple critical functions simultaneously (attacking the enemy king, controlling key squares, defending pieces, or paralyzing opponent's army), and was moved to a square that appeared active—often via a check (4/10), capture (1/10), or centralization (4/10)—but actually abandoned its crucial role. In 5/10 cases the queen started on the f-file (f2, f6, f7) near the opponent's king. The common consequence was releasing pressure: allowing simplification via queen trade (positions 1, 3), exposing the queen to tempo attacks (position 2), driving the opponent's king to safety (position 5), freeing paralyzed opponent pieces (positions 6, 7), breaking perpetual check mechanisms (position 8), or leaving pieces undefended (positions 4, 10). Position 9 (0cp loss) was actually the best move—the queen check was genuinely forcing with mate threats—serving as the exception that highlights how the other 9 moves merely imitated forcing play without the tactical justification.

380.label: Player makes a tempting capture (usually eliminating an active enemy piece) while their own queen is left undefended, allowing the opponent to win it.
380.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture that appears attractive — typically removing a well-placed or threatening enemy piece. In 8/10 positions (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10), the capture directly leaves the player's own queen undefended, allowing the opponent to simply take it on the next move. Position 1 leaves both rooks hanging to a combination, and Position 9 involves a queen exchange that walks into a devastating fork. The average cp_loss of 1424 reflects that most of these blunders lose approximately a queen's worth of material. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise attention to the queen's safety before executing the tempting capture. The captures target knights (6/10), bishops (2/10), pawns (1/10), and a rook (1/10) — in every case an enemy piece that appeared dangerous or centralized, creating tunnel vision that obscured the vulnerability of the player's own most valuable piece.

383.label: A central move (usually Nxe5 with the knight) that enables the opponent's d-pawn to recapture on e5, creating a devastating pawn fork on the d6-bishop and f6-knight.
383.description: In 7/10 positions, Black plays Nxe5 capturing White's centralized knight with their own knight (rather than the bishop), which allows the crushing dxe5 pawn recapture that forks Black's bishop on d6 and knight on f6 simultaneously. In 6/7 of these Nxe5 cases, the best move was instead Bxe5 (capturing with the bishop), which removes the d6-bishop from the danger square before the pawn advances. The remaining 3/10 positions feature premature central pawn breaks (d5, d4, e5) that similarly enable the opponent's d-pawn to advance to e5, winning material through the same geometric fork or leaving pieces undefended. All 10 positions share a closed or semi-closed center where the d-pawn's advance to e5 was the critical tactical threat. The refutation in 9/10 positions involves specifically dxe5, and the evaluation swings average 361cp, typically representing loss of a full minor piece. The positions cluster in the opening (6/10) and early middlegame (4/10), almost always from Black's perspective (9/10).

382.label: A passive king repositioning move is played in an endgame (or quiet middlegame) when the position urgently demands an immediate concrete action — a capture, check, invasion, or forcing sequence.
382.description: 9/10 positions feature a king move as the mistake (the lone exception, Qd1, is a queen retreat that functions identically as a passive repositioning). 8/10 are endgame positions. In every case, the player treated the position as requiring slow maneuvering and chose to 'improve' the king's placement, when instead the position demanded urgent, concrete action: a rook invasion (Rd7 in pos. 1), an immediate capture (Rxe3 in pos. 9, exf3 in pos. 7), a forcing check (Rb1+ in pos. 3, Rb8+ in pos. 6, Qd8+ in pos. 10), or placement on the one correct square to prevent a specific threat (Kh6 preventing h4 in pos. 2, Kf2 avoiding diagonal in pos. 5, Bg3 freeing e1 in pos. 8). 10/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as a core theme. The average cp_loss is enormous (1097), reflecting that in 6/10 cases the position had only 1 good move available, making the tempo expenditure catastrophic. The king walks either toward the wrong flank (Kc6 in pos. 4 going queenside when kingside action matters), onto a tactically vulnerable square (Ke3 allowing Nd5+ fork, Kf1 allowing Bd3+ check), or simply wastes time when material hangs or forced sequences exist.

376.label: A piece (usually a knight) is moved to a seemingly-improving square while abandoning a vital defensive function or ignoring an urgent tactical necessity.
376.description: 7/10 positions involve knight moves specifically, with the remaining 3 being one pawn push and two rook moves. In 9/10 positions, the analysis tags 'tempo_loss' as a factor, and 8/10 tag 'missed_tactic' — the player chooses a repositioning/improving move when an immediate crisis demands attention. In 6/10 positions, the moved piece was actively performing a critical defensive function (blockading a passed pawn, guarding a back-rank square, covering a promotion path, or preserving an escape route for the king) and its departure allowed an immediate tactical blow. In the other 4/10, the piece wasn't defending per se, but the move ignored a more urgent tactical priority (a hanging piece, an immediate mating threat, a critical capture). The average cp_loss of 3875 is extreme, reflecting how catastrophic these 'reasonable-looking' repositioning moves are when they address the wrong priority. Only 2.0 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points with narrow correct paths.

384.label: Passive queen or bishop move to the d2/e2/e7 square that blocks a critical retreat path for another piece, allowing tactical exploitation.
384.description: All 10 positions occur in the opening phase with at least one king uncastled. The moves are uniformly passive queen or bishop placements to the d-file or e-file on the 2nd/7th rank (Qd2 in 5/10, Qe2 in 2/10, Qe7/Qd7/Be7/Bd2 in 3/10). In at least 7/10 positions, the moved piece physically blocks a critical retreat or transit square needed by another piece: Position 2 (Qd2 blocks Be3's retreat from d5-d4), Position 4 (Qd2 blocks the d3-d4 pawn advance), Position 7 (Qe7 blocks Bc5's retreat to e7), Position 8 (Be7 blocks Qf6's retreat to d8), Position 9 (Qe2 blocks both Nd4 and Bd3 retreats to e2). In all 10 positions, the slow tempo loss allows the opponent to execute a crushing central pawn break (d5, e5, f4, or d4 appearing in 9/10 refutations) or a concrete tactical shot that was missed. The average cp_loss of 261 confirms these are severe blunders, not marginal inaccuracies. Only 2.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions requiring precise action rather than quiet maneuvering.

386.label: Playing a 'natural' rook move to an open file (usually the e-file targeting the enemy king) when the position demands a more forcing, concrete, or urgent action.
386.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook move to an open or semi-open file aimed at the opponent's king, with 8/10 specifically being rook-to-e-file moves (Re1 or Re8). In 8/10 cases the opponent's king was still in the center, making the rook move appear logical under the principle 'put rooks on open files to target the king.' However, in every case the position demanded something more concrete: 3/10 positions had hanging or capturable pieces being ignored (positions 1, 8, 9), 2/10 had forced checkmate or perpetual check being either missed or allowed (positions 3, 4), 2/10 needed a tempo-gaining attacking move instead (positions 6, 7), 1/10 removed a rook from a critical defensive square (position 2), and 1/10 abandoned a dominant 7th-rank position (position 10). The average cp_loss of 1262 reflects that these 'natural-looking' moves often catastrophically miss forced wins or allow devastating tactics.

370.label: Superficially purposeful moves in tactically narrow positions that catastrophically overlook a concrete refutation.
370.description: All 10 positions share an extremely narrow set of acceptable continuations (average 1.4 good moves), creating critical decision points where the player must find the ONE specific tactical solution. Instead, the player consistently chose moves that appear logical and purposeful — advancing passed pawns (3/10: c7, e5, g4), gaining central space (2/10: both d4 moves), delivering checks (2/10: Ne5+, Qf5+), or repositioning pieces to apparently active squares (3/10: Ng6, Bc3, Rf7) — but each fatally ignores the most forcing tactical element in the position. In 6/10 cases, the move directly places material on a square where it is immediately captured (e5/Bxe5, Ne5+/Qxe5, Bc3/Rxc3, Qf5+/exf5, Rf7/exf7+, g4/Bxg4). In the remaining 4/10, the move creates an exploitable tactical weakness or squanders a critical tempo. The average centipawn loss of 5056 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — 4/10 result in immediate forced mate or queen loss. The consistent thread is a player executing a 'plan' without verifying it against the opponent's most forcing response.

371.label: Playing a tempting but non-forcing move (typically a pawn capture or quiet piece move) when exactly one decisive tactical blow exists that wins immediately.
371.description: 9/9 positions featured a single clearly best move (avg 1.2 good moves available) that was dramatically more powerful than all alternatives, yet the player chose a 'natural-looking' continuation instead. 5/9 moves played were pawn captures (bxc5, dxe5, fxg3, hxg5, Bxg5 taking a pawn), while 3/9 were quiet piece retreats/repositions (Rc7, Nd8, Ng8), and 1/9 was a knight centralization (Ne6). The missed winning moves included forced checkmates in 1-6 moves (positions 1, 3, 5), captures of completely hanging pieces (positions 2, 7), immediate pawn promotion (position 5), queen sacrifices (position 8), and forcing moves maintaining decisive attacks (positions 4, 10). The average centipawn loss of 3440 reflects that most of these blunders converted forced wins or checkmates into merely good positions. The consistent pattern is a player who sees something 'productive' (winning a pawn, centralizing a piece, chasing a queen) but fails to recognize the one move that ends the game immediately.

397.label: An actively placed rook diverts to capture an undefended edge pawn, abandoning critical central/attacking duties.
397.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing an undefended pawn on the edge of the board (a-file: 5, g-file: 3, h-file: 2, b-file: 1). In every case, the rook was powerfully placed before the capture — on the 7th rank threatening the opponent's position (6/10), on the 2nd rank creating invasion threats (3/10), or on a central file (1/10). The pawn grabbed was always peripheral and strategically insignificant compared to what the rook was doing in its active position. The punishments varied but all exploited the rook's absence: 4/10 allowed opponent's passed pawn to advance decisively (positions 2, 3, 9, 10), 3/10 missed devastating king attacks or forced mates that the active rook enabled (positions 5, 7, 8), and 3/10 simply lost coordination and tempo allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterattack (positions 1, 4, 6). The average cp_loss of 1210 reflects how catastrophic these diversions are — in 7/10 positions only 1 good move existed, showing these were critical moments requiring the rook to stay active.

395.label: Castling played as a routine safety move when the position demanded immediate concrete tactical action, either missing a winning combination or creating new vulnerabilities.
395.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling (7 O-O-O, 3 O-O) played when a specific tactical opportunity existed that the player overlooked. In 8/10 positions, only 1 good move was available within 50cp of optimal, meaning these were critical decision points requiring precision rather than routine development. The missed tactics varied: 2/10 missed capturing undefended pieces (Positions 1, 4), 1/10 missed a forced mate in 3 (Position 3), 2/10 missed winning attacking combinations (Positions 7, 9), 2/10 gave the opponent crucial tempo to save endangered pieces (Positions 6, 10), and 3/10 castled into the opponent's prepared attack or created new diagonal/file vulnerabilities (Positions 5, 8, 9). In 5/10 cases, castling directly created a new tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploited (hanging piece on f8, exposed diagonal to c8, Greek Gift on h7, pawn storm target, bishop capture on d1). The average cp_loss of 1226 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' moves were.

391.label: Moving a rook from a vital central/semi-central file to a wing file for a slow attacking plan, abandoning a critical defensive or operational function.
391.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being redeployed laterally from a central or semi-central file (d, e, or f) to a wing file (g or b, occasionally c). The notation consistently uses disambiguation (Reg8, Rfb1, Rdg1, etc.), confirming the player had two rooks and chose to redeploy one from its critical post. In 8/10 positions, the rook was specifically guarding a key pawn or enabling a crucial pawn break (e.g., defending e6 in positions 1/4/7, enabling the f3 break in positions 2/8/9, supporting d4 in position 10). In 4/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 7), the error is explicitly a 'wrong rook' choice where the other rook should have gone to the target square. In 6/10 positions (2, 3, 8, 9, 10, and 5), the issue is pursuing a slow flank operation while a time-critical tactical or positional need existed on the original file. The average cp_loss of 1196 (inflated by the missed mate in position 5) reflects how devastating these redeployments are—they consistently allow opponents to exploit the newly unguarded file, pawn, or square within 1-2 moves.

387.label: In endgames with passed pawns, the player repositions the bishop to a 'better' diagonal instead of making the critical king march or pawn advance.
387.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop being repositioned to a new diagonal (no captures, no checks) in positions dominated by passed pawn races. 9/10 are endgames and all 10 involve passed pawns as the central strategic element. Among the high-cp-loss positions (5/10 lost >300cp), the consistent pattern is choosing a bishop 'improvement' move when the position urgently demands a king march (positions 2, 3, 6: Kd5/Ke5, Ke3, f6 pawn break) or a concrete pawn advance (positions 5, 10: h6+, preventing g5). The low-cp-loss positions (1, 4, 7, 8) represent cases where the bishop repositioning happened to be optimal or near-optimal because the king lacked an urgent destination. The common thread is the player's instinct to place the bishop on an 'active' or 'centralized' square (Bg4, Bf6, Bd5, Be5, Ba6) when the endgame's critical requirement is tempo—racing to blockade, promote, or capture pawns before the opponent.

393.label: Advancing a pawn forward past a point of tension where capturing was clearly superior.
393.description: In 8/10 positions, the player's best move was a pawn capture resolving tension (exd4, dxe4, bxa4, dxe5, dxc4, cxb4, bxc5/dxc5), but instead they pushed the same pawn forward one square past the opposing pawn. The remaining 2/10 positions (g4 and d5 in position 4) still feature unnecessary pawn advances when holding or capturing was correct. In every case, the pawn advance either left the player's own pieces undefended (3/10 left a piece hanging), created an unstoppable passed pawn for the opponent (3/10), opened the center against their own exposed king (3/10), or eliminated a critical defensive pawn from its post (2/10). The consistent error is choosing the 'ambitious' forward push over the 'simple' lateral capture, reflecting a preference for space-gaining moves over tension-resolving ones. All 10 moves are single-square pawn advances, with 8/10 being central pawns (d or e file) or adjacent semi-central pawns (b or c file).

390.label: Non-forcing forward pawn pushes or knight jumps that look attacking but ignore an immediate tactical necessity — typically a hanging piece to capture, an attacked piece to save, or a winning combination to execute.
390.description: All 10 positions feature a forward-advancing, non-forcing move (8/10 pawn advances: g5×3, b4×2, e5, f5, h4; 2/10 knight jumps: Nd5, Nb5) chosen over a concrete tactical necessity. In 6/10 cases, a piece was hanging or undefended that needed to be captured or saved (positions 3, 4, 7, 8, 10 had hanging pieces to exploit; position 7 had a piece to evacuate). In 3/10 cases, the advance was a pure tempo loss when an immediate tactical sequence or defensive consolidation was required (positions 5, 6, 9). In 9/10 positions, the best move involved either a capture (Qxb7, Bxh6, exd5, Bxc5, Rxd2+) or a piece repositioning to address a concrete threat (Rhe1, Qf4, Rc2, Rf8, Rc4). Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions demanding precision, yet the chosen moves uniformly prioritized aggressive appearance over tactical reality. The average cp_loss of 1161 reflects how costly it is to ignore concrete demands in favor of 'looking active.'

396.label: A bishop captures a well-placed (usually centralized) knight, but the exchange backfires by activating the opponent's recapturing piece or removing the bishop from a critical defensive role.
396.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capture, with 9/10 specifically capturing a centralized knight. The most striking sub-pattern appears in 4/10 positions where Bxd4 allows Qxd4 with devastating queen centralization (positions 1, 2, 6, 9). In these cases, the queen lands on the powerful d4 square controlling multiple diagonals and files, often winning material (b2 pawn) or creating irresistible pressure. Beyond the queen-recapture cases, the remaining positions share the theme of the bishop being more valuable alive than the piece it captures: in position 5, the bishop on e7 was defending f8; in position 8, capturing on e4 activated Black's dormant b7-bishop; in position 7, capturing on d6 placed the bishop on a square where it became a target in a mating sequence; in position 10, the bishop was needed for long-term defense rather than being traded for a pawn. In 10/10 cases, a better move existed that either dealt with the centralized piece indirectly (with tempo via Ne4, Qa4+, or Qg4) or prioritized development/king safety over the exchange. The average cp_loss of 1176 reflects several catastrophic blunders where removing the 'annoying' piece triggered tactical disasters.

400.label: A queen repositioning move that ignores another piece left undefended, allowing its immediate capture.
400.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move (Qe4, Qc6, Qd2, Qf6, Qh4, Qf6, Qe7, Qb2, Qc2, Qe7) that leaves another friendly piece completely undefended and capturable on the very next move. In 10/10 cases the tactical motif is 'hanging_piece.' The abandoned piece is a knight in 6/10 positions (g3, c4, e5, f3, c5 twice) and a rook in 4/10 positions (c7, f8, d5, c3). The capturing move is a simple pawn capture in 7/10 cases (fxg3, bxc4, fxe5, exd5, bxc3, exf3, bxc5), making the refutation elementary. The queen moves themselves typically look active or purposeful—centralizing (Qe4, Qc6), attacking (Qh4, Qf6), developing (Qd2, Qc2, Qe7), or offering trades (Qb2)—but all share the fatal flaw of ignoring the most urgent tactical demand in the position. The best moves in each position (available in 1-3 options) all prioritize saving or relocating the threatened piece first.

392.label: Playing an irrelevant or premature pawn move (usually a wing advance) when the position demands immediate action with pieces to address the most urgent tactical or strategic need.
392.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (h5, e4, h5, f5, a5, a3, h6, axb4, dxe4) and 1/10 a bishop move to a wing square (Bh6) — all are non-forcing moves that fail to address the critical issue. In 10/10 cases, the best move involved either an active piece deployment (Ne6, Rd1, Qf3+, Bxg5, Nxe5) or a precise king move (Kg1/Ke1/Kg2, Kb5). The average good moves available was only 1.8, indicating razor-sharp positions where the one right move was essential. 10/10 positions tagged 'tempo_loss' — the wasted tempo allowed opponents to execute pawn breakthroughs (positions 2, 3, 5), piece infiltrations (position 6), mating attacks (positions 7, 8), or material wins (positions 9, 10). 6/10 involved wing pawn advances (h-file or a-file) that weakened the player's own pawn structure, while 2/10 involved materialistic pawn captures of the wrong target.

403.label: King moves forward or toward the center instead of retreating to the back rank or corner, walking into tactical vulnerabilities on open files, diagonals, or pawn breaks.
403.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved their king to a more exposed square when a safer retreat existed. In 8/10 cases, the best move was retreating the king toward the back rank or corner (Kg8, Kh8, Kb2, Kf1), while the blunder moved the king forward or centrally (Kf7, Kd7, Kc3, Ke2). Specifically, 4/10 involved the king stepping from g7/g8 to f7 instead of retreating to g8/h8; 2/10 involved the king advancing from c2 to c3 instead of retreating to b2/d2; and 1/10 moved the king forward from e1 to e2 instead of backward to f1. The average cp_loss was 1253 (inflated by one mate-in-1), with 7/10 positions having only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these were critical junctures demanding precise king safety calculation. In 9/10 cases, the refutation exploited the forward king placement through pawn breaks (g5 in 4 positions), open file invasions (Rc1+, Rc7), diagonal checks (Bf6+, Bh5#, Bh6), or captures of newly undefended pawns (Qxf7+).

401.label: Delivering a check (usually with the queen) that wastes tempo or allows the opponent's king to improve its position, when a more constructive move was available.
401.description: 10/10 positions feature a check being delivered, with 9/10 being queen checks and 1/10 a rook check. In 9/10 cases the check is a mistake (avg cp_loss ~3430 for the 9 errors). The key pattern: the player gives a check against an exposed or advanced king without a concrete follow-up plan, and the check either allows the opponent's king to reach a better square (Positions 2, 5, 7 where the king advances toward activity/safety) or wastes a critical tempo when an immediate tactical action was needed (Positions 1, 2, 10 where a capture was urgent). In 5/9 mistakes, a DIFFERENT check on a more precise square was the correct move (Positions 3, 4, 5, 6, 8), while in 4/9 a non-checking move like a capture was needed (Positions 1, 2, 7, 10). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/10 analyses. Position 9 (0 cp_loss) is the lone exception where the check was actually the only correct move, suggesting the feature broadly detects 'queen/piece check against exposed king' positions rather than exclusively bad ones.

404.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (7th/2nd) when it was more powerful one square back as a restraining force.
404.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical move type: pushing a passed pawn to the 7th rank (for White: a7, d7, h7, c7) or 2nd rank (for Black: b2, d2). In 8/10 cases this was a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 280 for the 8 errors), while 2/10 (positions 1 and 4) were actually correct with 0 cp loss. The consistent error in the 8 blundering cases is that the pawn was serving as a powerful restraining force on the 6th rank, tying down opponent pieces to blockade duty, and advancing it to the 7th rank either (a) made it a concrete capturable target (positions 2, 7, 9, 10), (b) freed opponent pieces from defensive obligations (positions 2, 9), (c) allowed a clean blockade that neutralized the threat (positions 3, 8), or (d) missed immediately decisive tactical alternatives like captures or piece improvements (positions 5, 6, 10). In 8/10 positions, the best moves instead involved improving piece coordination while maintaining the pawn as a static restraint. The feature activates on the specific geometric pattern regardless of whether it's correct, but overwhelmingly catches the classic 'premature advance' error.

394.label: Active-looking moves (checks, attacks, centralizations) that ignore a critical tactical requirement in the position.
394.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player chose a superficially aggressive or active move while missing a specific, concrete tactical priority. 6/10 moves are rook relocations to 'active' squares (Rc1, Rb6+, Rb8+, Ra5, Rd5, Rc3+), with 3 of those being checks. The remaining moves include knight 'improvements' (Ng6, Nf2), a pawn push to attack (e5), and a pawn capture for material (bxa4). In every case, the position demanded a precise tactical solution: a quiet defensive move (positions 1, 10), maintaining a critical blockade (position 3), executing an available capture/combination (positions 5, 8, 9), saving a hanging piece (position 7), centralizing for tactical reasons (positions 2, 6), or avoiding an exchange that enables promotion (position 4). The average cp_loss of 2128 and average of only 1.5 good moves confirms these are razor-sharp positions where only precise calculation works—yet the player defaults to general principles of activity. 8/10 positions involve passed pawn dynamics where the 'active' move fatally enables or ignores a promotion threat.

406.label: The queen captures a lower-value piece (usually a rook) on a square that is defended by an opponent's piece, resulting in an immediate recapture that wins the queen.
406.description: In 10/10 positions, the player used their queen to capture a less valuable piece — a rook in 7/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10) and a bishop in 3/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 8). In every case, the capture square was defended or reachable by an opponent's piece that immediately recaptured the queen, resulting in a catastrophic queen-for-lesser-piece exchange. The recapturing piece was the opponent's queen in 6/10 positions (via diagonal or open file), a knight in 3/10 positions (positions 1, 2, 8 — where the knight's non-obvious L-shaped coverage was overlooked), and a rook in 1/10 cases (position 6). The common thread is material greed: the player saw an apparently loose or valuable target and grabbed it without verifying whether the landing square was defended. The average centipawn loss of 324 closely matches the typical queen-minus-rook material deficit (~4 pawns).

398.label: Rook slides to a seemingly reasonable but suboptimal square, abandoning the file or rank where it served an essential defensive or offensive function.
398.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that reposition the rook away from its optimal placement. In 7/10 cases, the rook moves laterally along a rank to a different file (Re5, Rb3, Rb7×2, Rh1, Rd6, Re1), while 2/10 involve vertical file moves (Rd7, Ra8) and 1/10 is a near-lateral shift (Rc4). The critical shared error: in each position, the rook was on or near a key file/rank (the e-file in positions 2,3,6,7,8,9; the 7th rank in position 10; a deep infiltration square in position 4) and moved away, vacating the critical zone. In 6/10 cases, the rook specifically leaves the e-file or a file it needs to control. The consequences vary but consistently involve the opponent exploiting the vacated zone: back-rank invasions (positions 5,7), king infiltration to dominant squares (positions 3,8,10), forced simplifying exchanges (positions 4,6), or the rook becoming a tactical target (position 2). The average cp_loss is very high (2022), with 4/10 positions having catastrophic losses (>1000cp including two forced mates), confirming that rook placement on the correct file/rank is often the single most critical decision in these positions.

388.label: Forward pawn advances (typically to 5th/6th rank) in positions with mutually exposed kings where timing and move order are critical.
388.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn advances (c6, g4, d5, f5, f5, b6, h6, plus fxg5 as a pawn capture), with 7 of these pushing to the 5th or 6th rank. 9/10 positions feature at least one exposed king with a weak or nonexistent pawn shield. The average number of good moves is only 2.0, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where precision is paramount. When the pawn advance is correct (3/10 positions with 0 cp loss: c6, b6, h6), it creates an unstoppable passed pawn promotion threat that the opponent's exposed king cannot address. When incorrect (7/10 with significant cp loss), the pawn advance is premature—either removing a critical defender (g4 left the queen unguarded, fxg5 opened the e-file to the king), ignoring superior king activity (d5 and f5 in the endgames where Kf5 or Kh5 was correct), or weakening pawn structure that the opponent's pieces immediately exploit (f5 in position 8). The 2 non-pawn moves (Qb4, Rb1) share the same DNA: forward-looking aggressive moves that catastrophically overlook a tactical vulnerability created by their own king's exposure.

389.label: Playing an aggressive-looking or seemingly natural move while ignoring the position's single critical tactical obligation.
389.description: All 10 positions share a situation where the player had very few good options (avg 1.9 good moves) demanding precise play, yet chose a move that appeared active or logical but catastrophically ignored the position's most pressing concrete need. In 4/10 positions, the correct move was simply capturing a hanging or vulnerable piece (bxc4, Kxg6, Bxh3, Kxh2). In 3/10 positions, the correct move was addressing king safety or a critical defensive weakness (Be6, e5-first, Kd7). The blunders themselves often targeted the kingside/h-file area (8/10 moves land on the f or h files: h4, Ng5, Nxh5, Nxh4, Rh1, h6, Rf2+, exf5, Nf3), giving them a superficial appearance of aggression. The average cp_loss of 2293 reflects catastrophic consequences: in 4/10 cases the move hung a piece or allowed a devastating capture, in 3/10 it fatally weakened king safety, and in 3/10 it allowed a forced tactical sequence the player overlooked. Critically, 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, meaning these are narrow moments where choosing 'activity' over 'necessity' is immediately punished.

408.label: Bishop (or piece) deployed to an aggressive-looking attacking square while ignoring a more pressing tactical obligation in the position.
408.description: 9/10 positions involve bishop moves to attacking squares (Bg5 x4, Bg4 x2, Bh6, Bf5, Bb4+), with 1/10 being a queen move (Qh4) that follows the same logic. In all 10 positions, the player places a piece on a superficially active or threatening square—targeting an opponent's queen, aiming at the kingside, or giving check—while a concrete tactical problem goes unaddressed. 7/10 positions had the piece moved to a kingside attacking square (g4, g5, h4, h6, f5). The punishments vary: in 4/10 cases the aggressive piece itself becomes hanging or trapped (positions 5, 8, 9, and effectively 3 where f6 was left hanging), in 4/10 the opponent gains decisive tempo kicking or ignoring the piece (positions 1, 2, 4, 7), and in 2/10 the move exposes another piece to tactics (positions 6, 10). The average cp_loss of 263 reflects that these 'active' moves consistently squander significant advantages or create serious disadvantages. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions demanded specific solutions rather than general development—yet the players chose superficial aggression over addressing the critical issue.

399.label: Reflexive piece captures (mostly bishop takes) that break coordination when a pawn capture or non-capture was far superior.
399.description: All 10 positions feature a piece capture (8/10 with bishops, 2/10 with knights) that looks natural or obvious but severely damages the player's position. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 7, 10, and partially 6), the correct move was to capture on the SAME square with a PAWN instead, preserving the piece's influence while gaining structural benefits (opening files, attacking enemy pieces with tempo). In 5/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 5, 8, 9), the correct move was to NOT capture at all — instead retreating, developing, or maintaining tension. In 1/10 cases (position 3), a different capture target was needed. The consistent thread is that the player sees an opponent's active piece and instinctively exchanges it off, without recognizing that their OWN capturing piece was providing crucial coordination, defensive coverage, or enabling tactical motifs (Nc2+ forks, Rc3 invasions, Qxd3 tactics). 7/10 positions are in the opening phase where both kings are often still in the center, making the tempo/coordination loss especially punishing. The average cp_loss of 298 reflects positions where only 1.3 good moves existed on average — these are narrow decision points where the 'obvious' capture is a trap.

412.label: A passive, non-forcing king move played in a tactically critical position where urgent action with another piece or pawn was required.
412.description: All 10/10 positions feature a one-square king move played as a quiet 'repositioning' when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 10/10 cases, the king move was non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), while the best alternatives were forcing moves with other pieces or pawns: knight forks (positions 1, 2, 4), passed pawn advances (positions 3, 7), piece development (positions 6, 9, 10), or defensive piece placement to avoid back-rank mates (positions 5, 8). The average centipawn loss was ~3971, with 4/10 resulting in immediate or near-immediate checkmate for the opponent. In 6/10 positions, the king move directly exposed the king to tactical punishment (back-rank mates, discovered checks, or rook invasions). In the remaining 4/10, the king move simply wasted a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute threats that could have been preempted. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow tactical moments where precision was essential — yet the player chose the least committal, most passive option.

413.label: A pawn captures a rook for massive material gain, but the pawn was serving a critical defensive function whose removal causes tactical catastrophe.
413.description: All 10/10 positions feature exactly the same move type: a pawn captures an enemy rook, winning a full exchange or more in material. In every case, the capturing pawn was performing a vital structural or defensive role that far exceeded its material value. In 9/10 positions, the pawn removal fatally compromised king safety — opening files/diagonals to the king (positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 9), removing shelter pawns (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7), enabling back-rank mates (position 8), or allowing mating nets (position 3). Position 1 is the sole variant where the pawn was a blockader of a passed pawn rather than a king-shield pawn. Position 10 is unique in that the capture itself wasn't structurally catastrophic, but it missed a superior tactical sequence (Qxc8+ first). The average cp_loss of 3047 reflects that these 'free rook' captures consistently transform winning or defensible positions into lost or mated ones. In 7/10 cases, the refutation involves an immediate check or forcing sequence that exploits the newly opened line.

409.label: King centralizes or activates in the endgame but steps onto a square where the opponent gains a decisive tempo through a fork, check, or tactical blow.
409.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves that appear to be natural endgame centralization or activation but land the king on a tactically vulnerable square. In 7/10 cases, the king walks directly into a fork or check that wins material or critical tempo (Positions 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 involve knight forks or bishop/pawn checks on the new king square; Position 5 exposes a trapped piece). In the remaining 3/10 positions (1, 7, 9), the king move is a pure tempo loss that allows the opponent to advance a passed pawn or seize space unchallenged. The average centipawn loss is 294, indicating these are severe errors. 8/10 are endgames and 2/10 are late middlegames. The positions span both sides equally (5 White, 5 Black). In most cases, 2-3 good alternatives existed that either addressed the concrete tactical threat first (prophylaxis like b4, or active piece moves) or kept the king off the vulnerable square.
