The consistent error is prioritizing abstract king activity over calculating the opponent's concrete tactical responses to the king's new placement.

414.label: A rook delivers a pointless check on a square where it can be simply captured by the king (or adjacent pawn), sacrificing the player's critical defensive piece for nothing.
414.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check that hangs the rook to immediate capture. In 8/10 positions, the king directly captures the rook as the strongest refutation (Kxg7, Kxh7, Kxa2, Kxf7, Kxc6, Kxe7 etc.). In 1/10, a pawn captures (gxh4), and in 1/10, the king sidesteps to an improved square. In 9/10 cases, the blundering side was already losing, making these desperate last-gasp checks with no tactical follow-up. In 8/10 positions, the rook was the player's only remaining piece, meaning its loss left the king completely defenseless. 8/10 occurred in endgames where material preservation is paramount. The average cp_loss of 4810 reflects that 6/10 positions converted directly into forced checkmate after the rook was captured, typically via back-rank mates (positions 1, 2, 6, 8) enabled by removing the sole defensive piece.

385.label: Playing quiet, non-forcing moves in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action, either missing a winning shot or walking into a refutation.
385.description: All 10 positions share a critical feature: the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move (no checks, no forcing threats) in a position where only 1.9 good moves existed on average, meaning concrete calculation was essential. In 7/10 positions, there was a hanging or tactically vulnerable piece that the player either failed to capture or failed to protect (positions 3, 4, 8 missed winning captures; positions 1, 5, 9, 10 left pieces/squares undefended). The played moves are all non-forcing: routine pawn captures (dxc4, exf5, fxe5 — 3 positions), quiet pawn advances (d3, f3, g4 — 3 positions), or piece repositioning to 'natural' squares (Be6, Qh6, Bc5, Nc6 — 4 positions). Meanwhile, the best moves were typically forcing or concrete: tactical captures (Nxd4, Kxd5, Nxe5, Bxc6+), checks (Qa1+), or moves addressing the single most urgent threat. The avg cp_loss of 385 confirms these are catastrophic oversights in critical moments.

416.label: Advancing a passed pawn one square in a won King+Pawn vs King endgame instead of first improving the king's position.
416.description: All 10/10 positions are pure King+Pawn vs King endgames with a single passed pawn and a decisive advantage (avg eval ~±555cp). In every case, the move played is a one-square pawn advance toward promotion. In 7/10 positions, a king move was strictly better or equally good (Kf5, Kh5, Kc3, Kd2, Kb4, Ke4, Ke2), embodying the fundamental principle that 'the king should lead the pawn.' In the remaining 3/10, the pawn push was tied for best (0cp loss). The average cp_loss is only 7, making these nearly imperceptible inaccuracies — the positions remain completely won — but the feature consistently fires on the specific moment where a player chooses the direct pawn push over king optimization. All positions feature exposed kings on both sides, open centers, and an endgame phase where tempo and move order are the only factors determining evaluation differences.
416.old_chip: Pawn before king in K+P endgame

407.label: Knight moved to an aesthetically appealing square that is actually functionally inferior, ignoring the position's concrete demands.
407.description: All 10 positions feature a knight being relocated to a square that looks attractive on general principles (centralization, pawn attacks, outposts) but is concretely wrong. In 4/10 cases (Nd4, Nd6, Nd5, Nc6), the knight moves to a seemingly powerful central outpost that is actually vulnerable—easily attacked, driven away, or tactically exploitable. In 4/10 cases (Nb2, Ng5, Nc2, Nb1), the knight repositions to attack an enemy pawn but ends up hanging, passive, or too far from the critical sector. In 2/10 cases (Nb6, Nb8), the knight is 'activated' or rerouted but wastes critical tempo in positions requiring immediate action elsewhere. The best alternatives in 7/10 positions were NON-knight moves (king centralization, pawn advances, checks), revealing that the player fixated on 'improving' the knight when the position demanded something entirely different. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'piece_activity' in 9/10—the knight invariably ends up less functional after the move than before it. Average cp_loss of 308 confirms these are severe errors.

405.label: Queen moved to a seemingly active or natural square that ignores an immediate tactical refutation by the opponent.
405.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen repositioning moves (no checks, no captures) to squares that appear logical on general principles—centralization, file control, or attacking ambitions—but are immediately punishable through concrete tactics. In 4/10 positions (1, 6, 8, 9), the queen lands on a square directly vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks or forks (Be5 gaining tempo, Ba5 winning the queen, e3+ discovered check, d5 pawn fork). In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 7, 8), the queen abandons defense of a critical square or piece, enabling tactical exploitation (Nxd4 fork, Nd4-Nc6+ fork, Nxb6 winning material, e3+ discovered check). In 2/10 positions (5, 10), the queen move enables favorable simplification or misses a concrete winning tactic that was available. The average cp_loss of 310 reflects catastrophic consequences. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these arose at critical decision points where precise play was essential. The best moves were typically less flashy queen placements (retreats, queen trades, or defensive posts) that addressed the position's actual tactical demands rather than pursuing general improvement.

410.label: Non-urgent wing pawn advances in simplified positions with exposed kings, wasting critical tempo.
410.description: All 10 positions feature non-capturing pawn advances on the flanks (h-pawn in 5/10, b-pawn in 2/10, a/c/f-pawns in 3/10) in simplified positions where both kings are exposed and centralized. 7/10 are endgames and 3/10 are simplified middlegames; every single position features at least one exposed king. When these moves are mistakes (7/10 with cp_loss > 0, avg 1248cp for those), the error is consistently a tempo loss: the position demanded immediate concrete action (tactical strikes like Bxe6+ in Position 8, urgent king moves like Kc2 in Position 6, or precise pawn breaks like c5+ or g5 in Position 1) but instead the player chose a slow, preparatory flank pawn push. The 3/10 positions with 0 cp_loss (Positions 2, 5, 7) represent cases where the flank advance happened to be the most concrete continuation available. The feature consistently fires on one-square or two-square pawn advances on non-central files in positions with open geometry and active kings.

415.label: Advancing or promoting a passed pawn immediately in the endgame instead of first deflecting/displacing the piece that controls the promotion path.
415.description: All 10/10 positions involve advancing or promoting a passed pawn in the endgame — the moves are f7, c8=Q, h2, e3, c2, c3, g1=Q, g7, c1=Q, and d8=Q. Of these, 6/10 involve promotions (4 to queen on the move itself, 2 pushing to the 7th/2nd rank one step from promotion). When these are mistakes (8/10 had cp_loss > 0, avg 151cp), the consistent error is a move-order failure: the player advances the pawn directly into the control of an opposing piece without first deflecting that defender. In Position 2, c8=Q promoted into a rook's control (should have played Ke7 first). In Position 8, g7 pushed onto a bishop's diagonal. In Position 5, c2 pushed into a knight's capture range. In Position 4, e3 advanced without first repositioning the bishop to restrain the opponent's counter-pawn. In Position 9, c1=Q invited a clean exchange instead of maintaining the pawn as a restraining decoy. Only 2/10 positions (g1=Q and d8=Q) were actually correct, where the promotion was properly timed because no useful preparation existed.

418.label: Moving an already-active piece (usually the queen) to a seemingly better square instead of executing a concrete tactical opportunity or maintaining a critical defensive function.
418.description: 8/10 positions involve queen moves to 'natural-looking' squares (Qb6, Qc7, Qf6, Qb3, Qd8), while the remaining 2 involve knight repositioning (Nc6, Nf3) — all share the fundamental error of slow piece reshuffling when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 10/10 cases, the moved piece was already actively placed and contributing something important (defending a pawn, maintaining pressure on a diagonal, threatening a fork). The correct moves were always concrete: captures (Nxe4 in Position 5, Nxg6 in Position 7), forcing threats (Bd4+ in Position 8, Ng4 in Position 9, Bd3 in Position 4), or seizing open files (Rd8 in Position 3). 10/10 positions had the 'tempo_loss' tag, confirming the universal pattern of wasting critical time. The average cp_loss of 240 reflects how punishing these quiet reshuffling moves are when tactical opportunities exist. 6/10 occurred in the opening phase where development tempo is most precious, and 8/10 were played by Black, often in positions where the king remained uncastled and concrete action was urgent.

417.label: Black advances a pawn (typically non-forcing) while their king is critically exposed, ignoring immediate mating threats or tactical vulnerabilities.
417.description: 10/10 positions feature Black playing with a dangerously exposed king (on squares like b4, c6, d5, h8, h7 with weak or absent pawn shields). 9/10 moves are single-square pawn advances (f5, h5, c5, h5, e4, c5, a5, c3, g5), with only one king move (Kh7) as the exception. In 6/10 cases, the pawn push directly enables a forced checkmate or near-mate that didn't exist before the move. The pawns advance on various wings (kingside: 4, queenside: 4, center: 1), but the unifying factor is that they are non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures) played when the king requires immediate emergency attention. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 7), the pawn push specifically either removes a critical defensive pawn from its post (opening a lethal line), or blocks the king's own escape square. The correct moves were typically king retreats/escapes (Kc5, Kh7, Kg7), piece sacrifices to deflect attackers (Rb5, Rxe4+), or defensive piece repositioning (Qf8, Nf8).

421.label: Quiet rook repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding forcing or urgent action.
421.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking rook move to a new file — a seemingly natural 'developing' or 'improving' move that looks reasonable on the surface but catastrophically ignores the position's tactical demands. In 10/10 cases the rook move addresses a secondary concern (activating a passive rook, doubling on a quiet file, repositioning to an 'open' file) while the position screamed for either a forcing blow (Rxf3 in position 7, Re3+ in position 3, Qxf7+ in position 5, Rad1 in position 1) or an urgent defensive measure (g4 in position 2, Bxd5 in position 4, keeping the rook on its current file in positions 6 and 9). 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating razor-sharp situations where tempo was paramount. The average centipawn loss of 2120 — including two immediate forced mates — reflects how catastrophically these slow moves fail. In 6/10 cases the rook specifically abandons the critical file (d-file or b-file) where it was performing a vital function, and in 4/10 the rook moves toward an irrelevant sector while the main battle rages elsewhere.

411.label: Quiet rook (or king) repositioning moves that miss an immediate capture or forcing exchange, allowing the opponent to dictate exchange terms favorably.
411.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-capturing moves (8/10 rook moves, 2/10 king moves) played when an immediate capture or forcing exchange was available. In 8/10 positions, the single best move involved initiating a capture or exchange on the player's own terms (Rxc2, Nxd1, Rxb6, Rxe1+, Rxb2, Rxa4, etc.), but instead the player 'prepared' or 'repositioned.' The punishment in 8/10 cases involves the opponent seizing the exchange initiative — often trading rooks with check (positions 1, 2, 3, 7) or capturing an undefended piece (positions 4, 8). Positions 1, 2, and 9 specifically show doubling rooks on a file instead of immediately exchanging on that file. The average cp_loss of 341 reflects that these passive moves consistently surrender critical tempo, allowing opponents to either simplify into winning endgames, deflect key pieces via forced exchanges, or capture material outright.

426.label: Capturing with a valuable piece (Queen or Bishop) when a pawn or less active piece should recapture instead, exposing the capturer to tempo-gaining attacks.
426.description: 9/10 positions feature a player choosing the wrong piece to make a capture, with 7/10 specifically using a Queen or Bishop to recapture when a pawn capture was optimal (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9). In 4/10 cases a Bishop captured instead of a pawn (Bxe5/Bxd5/Bxe4/Bxd5), in 2/10 a Queen captured instead of a pawn (Qxe5/Qxf3), and in 1/10 a Queen captured instead of a Knight (Qxd2). Position 3 shows the reverse error (pawn instead of knight), position 7 shows a routine pawn recapture missing a tactic, and position 10 shows a wrong move-order for captures. The consistent consequence across all positions is that the wrong capturer either lands on an exposed square vulnerable to tempo-gaining pawn advances (f4 attacking Qe5, f3 attacking Be4, e5 enabling ...Bb4 pin on Qd2) or trades away the player's most active piece unnecessarily (Bc4 in positions 4 and 8). All 10 positions had exactly 1 good move available, confirming these are narrow decision points where the choice of capturing piece is the entire game.

420.label: King moves in simplified endgame positions where the king is actively repositioning as a primary piece.
420.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves in endgames with exposed, actively maneuvering kings. The positions are highly simplified: 4/10 are pure king-and-pawn endgames, 4/10 are rook endgames with few or no pawns, and 2/10 are minor piece endgames. In every case, both kings lack pawn shields and are noted as 'exposed.' The feature fires regardless of move quality—3/10 positions have cp_loss of 0 (the king move was optimal), while 4/10 have cp_loss over 387 (catastrophic errors). When the moves are mistakes, the common failing is prioritizing intuitive king activation over concrete tactical needs: in 2/10 cases a capture was available (Rxe2, Rxe5), in 2/10 the king walked into a tactical vulnerability (back-rank mate, rank skewer), and in 3/10 the king abandoned critical corresponding squares or committed prematurely. The feature appears to detect the general pattern of 'king repositioning as the main operation in a stripped-down endgame' rather than a specific error type.

425.label: Pushing a pawn (or piece) to attack a well-placed enemy knight, ignoring a far more critical tactical need while the knight finds an equal or better square.
425.description: 9/10 positions involve the player pushing a pawn to attack an enemy knight (the exception, position 5, uses a bishop to attack a knight, and position 7 chases a rook). In every case, the 'chasing' move is a tempo-wasting gesture: the targeted piece has an adequate or superior relocation square, while the pawn advance creates critical weaknesses or squanders a decisive tactical opportunity. Specifically: positions 1, 2, 9 play c4/b3 against a knight on d5/c4; positions 3, 6, 8 play f4/g5 against knights on g5/f4/h4; position 4 plays f5 against a knight on e4; position 10 plays b5 against a knight on a4. In 8/10 cases, the knight finds a stronger square after being 'chased' (d5, c5, f3+, c7, etc.). The average cp_loss is enormous (2086cp), and 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, meaning the tactical demands were acute and the chasing move represented a catastrophic misallocation of tempo.

430.label: Moving the castled f-rook to the e-file as a slow 'improving' move when concrete tactical action or f-file defense is required.
430.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player moving their f-rook (the rook remaining on f1/f8 after kingside castling) to a central file — 9/10 to the e-file and 1/10 to the d-file. In every case, this is a non-forcing, 'natural-looking' development move that contests an open or semi-open central file. The reason it fails falls into two overlapping categories: in 7/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10), a concrete tactical strike was available (capturing an undefended piece, delivering a check, winning material) and the slow rook move wastes the critical tempo needed to execute it. In 4/10 positions (5, 8, 9, 10), the f-rook was performing a vital defensive function on the f-file — guarding f7/f2, defending a piece on f5, or supporting a future f-pawn advance — and its departure enables tactical refutations exploiting the weakened f-file. The average cp_loss of 304 reflects that these positions punish passivity severely. In 8/10 positions, the opponent's primary refutation involves either exploiting the abandoned f-file weakness or simply consolidating during the gifted tempo.

433.label: A pawn capture that looks like winning material actually removes a critical defensive pawn that was blocking a mating line, file, or diagonal toward the player's own king.
433.description: 10/10 positions feature captures (9/10 are pawn captures, 1/10 is a king capture). In 8/10 positions with significant cp_loss (>100), the captured piece/pawn appeared to be free or dangerous material worth taking, but the pawn performing the capture was serving as a crucial shield blocking an attack corridor to the player's own king. Specifically: in Position 1, the e6 pawn blocked the e7 smothered mate square; in Position 2, the f5 pawn blocked diagonals to the exposed e8 king; in Position 5, the b7 pawn blocked the a6 diagonal and b-file; in Position 6, the g2 pawn sealed the g-file in front of the castled king; in Position 7, the h3 pawn sealed the h-file; in Position 8, the h5 pawn obstructed White's queen pathway; in Position 10, the d5 pawn blocked the a7-g1 diagonal. The 2/10 lower-loss positions (4 and 9) show the same structural pattern but with less lethal consequences. The average cp_loss of 4538 reflects that 6/10 positions resulted in immediate forced mate after the capture.

427.label: A pawn capture that removes a structurally critical defender-pawn from its post, catastrophically opening a diagonal or file that the opponent immediately exploits with a tactical blow.
427.description: All 10 positions feature a pawn capture where the chosen pawn was performing a critical defensive function—typically guarding a diagonal toward the king or blocking an open file. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 10), there was an alternative pawn or piece that could recapture on the same square without opening the fatal line (e.g., hxg3 instead of fxg3, cxb6 instead of axb6, Rxd3 instead of cxd3). In 4/10 positions (3, 6, 8, 9), the pawn capture was premature—a forcing move (check, queen trade, or fork) should have been played first to neutralize the opponent's tactical resources before the structurally weakening recapture. The consequence in 8/10 positions was opening a diagonal (usually the a7-g1 or a2-g8 diagonal when the f-pawn moved), while 2/10 opened a file (a-file in position 7, or removed king shelter in position 10). The punishment was consistently an immediate tactical shot along the newly opened line: queen checks (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9), bishop checks (position 5), pins (position 4), or decisive infiltration (positions 3, 8, 10).

419.label: Playing slow, positional-looking moves in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action, wasting critical tempi.
419.description: All 10 positions share a remarkably consistent pattern: the player chose a calm, non-forcing move (piece repositioning, pawn structure consolidation, or piece 'improvement') when the position had an extremely narrow tactical window requiring immediate concrete action (avg only 1.6 good moves available). In 8/10 positions, the move played was entirely quiet (no check, no capture, no direct threat). The resulting cp_loss averaged 1309—catastrophic—because these positions were precisely the ones where a single wasted tempo proved fatal. In 7/10 cases, the opponent's refutation involved exploiting a hanging piece, an undefended square, or a mating threat that existed BEFORE the blunder move but required immediate attention. The moves look superficially reasonable: Bd2 'develops,' b6 'supports structure,' Rc5 'centralizes,' Nd5 'occupies an outpost,' Ra3 'lifts the rook'—but all ignore an urgent concrete demand (save a piece, capture hanging material, block a mating diagonal, execute a double attack). In 6/10 positions, the correct move was a forcing tactical operation (a4 attacking a knight, Ne4 double attack, Qxa1+ capturing with check, Qxf2 winning material, Rxb7 removing a mating piece, bxc4 resolving tension).

428.label: Player makes a capture (usually winning a pawn) while missing a more valuable capture or more critical removal that was available in the same position.
428.description: 9/10 positions involve the player executing a capture that wins less material than the optimal capture available. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 7), a pawn captures another pawn when it could instead capture a full piece (knight, bishop, or rook) — often the same pawn could take in two directions, and the player chose the pawn-value target over the piece-value target. In 5/10 positions (2, 4, 6, 8, 9), a bishop or other piece captures the wrong enemy unit — typically a peripheral or passive target — while a more dangerous, actively threatening piece goes uncaptured (e.g., taking a rim knight instead of a centralized attacking piece, or grabbing a flank pawn instead of removing a tactical threat). Position 10 is a slight variant where a pawn push leaves a central pawn undefended, effectively creating a hanging piece. The consistent thread is that multiple captures exist, and the player selects the one that either wins less material or addresses a less urgent threat, often because the inferior target appears 'free' while the superior target requires recognizing a less obvious tactical geometry.

422.label: Rook moves to the first or eighth rank (especially h1) that appear to attack or defend but actually create or ignore tactical vulnerabilities caused by an exposed king.
422.description: 7/10 positions feature rook moves to the back rank (Rh1 appears in 5/10, plus Rb1, Rd1+, and Rh8+). The remaining moves go to penultimate ranks (a7, a2, Bf7). Among the 7 positions that are actual mistakes (cp_loss > 0), all involve a piece moving to the 1st or 8th rank while the moving side's king is dangerously exposed (king on e2 in positions 1 and 3, king on h2 in positions 4 and 7, king on d2 in position 2). In 4/7 mistake positions, the specific move Rh1 appears to attack an enemy queen on h3/h4 or defend the h3 pawn, but actually leaves g2 undefended or the rook itself as a hanging target after forced checks. The 3 positions with 0 cp_loss (a7, Rh8+, a2) represent cases where advancing to the back rank IS correct—typically forcing promotions or delivering checks in already-won positions—suggesting the feature detects the geometric pattern of back-rank piece placement rather than purely the mistake.

434.label: Premature wing pawn advances (a/b/g/h file) that ignore urgent central tactical or structural demands.
434.description: All 10/10 positions feature a flank pawn advance (5 queenside: b5, a4, b4, b5, a4; 5 kingside: g4, g5, g5, h5, g5) played when the center demanded immediate attention. In 10/10 cases, the best move involved central action: capturing a central pawn (positions 4, 5, 10), supporting a central pawn (positions 5, 6), developing a piece toward the center (positions 6, 7, 8), or addressing king safety through castling or a centrally-motivated break (positions 1, 2, 3, 9). The average cp_loss was 305 with only 1.4 good moves available on average, indicating these were critical positions demanding precision that the flank pawn completely ignored. In 4/10 positions, the flank advance directly left a central pawn or piece hanging (positions 5, 6, 7, 10). In 3/10 positions, it ignored an imminent king-safety crisis like the Greek Gift pattern (position 3) or an uncastled king on an open file (positions 2, 4). The refutations consistently exploited the wasted tempo by striking in the center with tactics (forks in positions 7 and 10, piece captures in positions 5 and 6, sacrificial attacks in position 3).

435.label: A knight jumps to an attractive-looking central or attacking square, but in doing so abandons a critical defensive responsibility, allowing an immediate tactical punishment.
435.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving to a seemingly strong square (d4, d5, e4, f5, c5, g5, d7 — classic 'outpost' or 'attacking' destinations) while leaving a critical defensive task unfulfilled. In 6/10 positions, the knight was guarding a specific pawn or square whose abandonment allowed a fork (positions 1, 3, 6, 9, 10) or removal-of-defender combination (positions 2, 7). In 2/10 positions (4, 5), the knight abandoned a square where it was needed for a specific defensive tactical solution (Nxh4, Rg3 support). In 1/10 (position 8), the knight left a dominant outpost for an inferior one, missing a concrete tactical win. In 1/10 (position 9), removing the knight allowed forced checkmate. The average cp_loss of 1261 and the fact that only 1.3 good moves were available on average confirm these were critical moments where the 'positionally attractive' knight move was catastrophically wrong. The pattern is remarkably consistent: the intent is always positional improvement or aggressive centralization, but the consequence is always a concrete tactical refutation exploiting the vacated defensive role.

424.label: Quiet, retreating king moves in endgame positions when either active king centralization or forcing piece moves were required.
424.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet king moves (no checks, no captures) that are passive or retreating in character. 9/10 occur in the endgame where king activity is paramount. In 6/10 positions, the best move was a forcing piece move (Re6+, Rd8+, Rb5, Bg2, etc.) rather than any king move at all, showing these players defaulted to 'safe' king shuffling instead of calculating concrete tactics. In the remaining 4/10 positions where a king move was best, the correct direction was consistently forward/active (Kf4 not Kh2, Ke4 not Kc6, Ke7 not Kg7, Ke6 not Kd7). The average cp_loss of 2160 is catastrophic, and only 1.5 good moves existed on average, indicating these are critical moments where passive instincts are maximally punished. Common consequences include: abandoning pawn defense (3/10), allowing tactical strikes like forks or back-rank mates (3/10), losing critical tempo in passed-pawn races (3/10), and self-blocking pieces (1/10).

436.label: Queen retreats to a passive square (often its starting square) instead of capitalizing on aggressive placement through captures, checks, or maintaining active pressure.
436.description: All 10 positions feature a queen that has already been developed to an active or infiltrated square, and the player retreats it passively rather than exploiting concrete tactical opportunities. 6/10 positions involve retreating the queen all the way back to d8 (its starting square), 3/10 retreat from b2 to b6, and the remaining positions feature similarly purposeless queen retreats (Qa4, Qg6). In 5/10 positions, the queen was missing a direct material-winning capture (Qxa1+, Qxg2, Qxd4, Qe5+ winning a rook). In the other 5/10, the queen needed to stay active or find a specific square to maintain pressure rather than retreat passively. 9/10 positions occur in the opening phase where tempo is paramount, and the average cp_loss of 265 reflects the severity of gifting multiple tempi. The common punishment pattern is that after the passive retreat, the opponent gains free development, central space (often d5 push), or launches an attack against the now-undefended king.

432.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing piece development or repositioning move when the position demands an immediate tactical or forcing continuation.
432.description: In 9/10 positions, the player chose a quiet piece-improving move (developing, repositioning, or blockading) when a concrete forcing move was available and required. 5/10 moves were specifically bishop repositioning moves (Bb1, Bb3, Bh3, Bd7, Bd3), all placing the bishop on a 'natural-looking' square while missing urgent tactics. The remaining errors followed the same logic: Nc3 (development before queen safety), Qb3 (quiet queen move missing a rank-clearing tactic), Raf8 (rook to wrong file abandoning critical pressure). In 8/10 cases, the best move was a forcing continuation—a check (Qb8+), a pawn thrust (f4, dxc5), a king march (Kc3, Ka3), or a direct threat (Qf6 threatening mate). The average cp_loss of 1218 reflects that these quiet moves often squandered forced mates or winning tactics. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points demanding precision rather than routine development.

437.label: A quiet, non-forcing bishop repositioning move played in a position that demanded an immediate tactical blow (often a forced mate or decisive combination).
437.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet bishop move (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) that retreats or repositions the bishop to a passive square, while the position contained a far stronger forcing continuation. In 5/10 cases, a forced checkmate in 2-4 moves was missed (positions 3, 5, 6, 9, 10). In the remaining 5 cases, a decisive tactical combination (queen invasion, deflection, or piece-trapping mechanism) was available. The correct moves were overwhelmingly non-bishop moves: queen checks/invasions (7/10), a pawn advance delivering check (1/10), a knight capture (1/10), and one active bishop move (Bg5 trapping a piece). Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than quiet maneuvering. The bishop moves were motivated by piece safety (saving from attack in 4/10), vague repositioning (4/10), or clearing diagonals (2/10)—all fundamentally misreading positions that demanded immediate tactical resolution.

438.label: Non-developing pawn advances in the opening that waste critical tempo when piece development is urgently needed, allowing the opponent to exploit with tactical strikes or space-gaining breaks.
438.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves (no piece moves) played in the opening phase when development is severely incomplete. 7/10 are specifically kingside wing pawn advances (g or h file: h5, h4, h5, g5, g4, h4, h6), while 3/10 are e-pawn pushes (e5, e6, e6) that create structural weaknesses. In every case, the side playing the move had multiple developing alternatives available (avg 2.3 good moves), and the pawn push neither develops a piece nor productively fights for the center. The average cp_loss of 213 reflects how severely these tempo-wasting moves are punished. In 9/10 positions, at least one king remains in the center, making the tempo loss especially costly. The refutations consistently involve the opponent exploiting the wasted move through piece invasions into weakened squares (Ng5, Ndb5, Nd4), central pawn breaks (c5, d5, dxe5), or direct attacks against the exposed king (Qh5+). The wing pawn pushes (7/10) specifically weaken the king's pawn shield or open diagonals, while the e-pawn pushes (3/10) create permanent dark-square holes (d5, d6) that enable devastating knight outposts.

431.label: Superficially aggressive moves (checks, pawn advances, rook improvements) that waste a critical tempo in winning positions, allowing the opponent to defend or neutralize the threat.
431.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player choosing an aggressive-looking move that superficially resembles the correct winning plan but loses a decisive tempo. In 4/10 positions, the player delivered a check with the wrong piece or the wrong pawn (f4+, Rfg4 preparing check, Bf7+, Nf2+), when an immediate different check or forcing move delivered mate. In 5/10 positions, a pawn was advanced prematurely (f3, a3, e6, d3, plus f4+) when piece activity or captures were required. In 2/10 positions, rooks were doubled/repositioned (Rfg4, Rgf3) when the immediate tactical blow or king improvement was needed. The unifying thread is that 10/10 played moves tagged as 'tempo_loss' — they look like they're building toward the winning plan but give the opponent exactly one move to organize a defense. The average cp_loss of 3065 reflects that 4/10 positions had forced mates available (avg ~9700 cp loss), while 6/10 were positional blunders (~250 cp average). Only 1.6 good moves existed on average, meaning these are critical positions requiring precision.

441.label: Moving a second rook to double on an open file when the position demands an immediate tactical action (capture, mate, or forcing sequence).
441.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player bringing their second rook to join the first on an open file — a textbook positional idea of doubling heavy pieces. However, in every case, a concrete tactical opportunity existed that demanded immediate action: 5/10 positions had a hanging or capturable piece (Positions 1, 3, 6, 9, 10), 3/10 had the opponent able to favorably exchange or exploit the alignment after doubling (Positions 2, 5, 7), 1/10 left a pawn undefended when the rook moved away from its guard duty (Position 4), and 1/10 missed a winning non-rook move (Position 8). The average cp_loss of 1217 (inflated by Position 6's missed checkmate-in-one) confirms these are severe errors. Only 1.6 good moves existed on average, meaning these were critical tactical moments disguised as routine positional decisions. The files targeted were: e-file (5/10), d-file (4/10), and a-file (1/10).

423.label: Playing a seemingly improving or activating move to a square where the piece is immediately captured or exploited, missing the one precise move the position demanded.
423.description: All 10 positions share a critical characteristic: only ~1.2 good moves existed on average (8/10 had exactly 1 good move), yet the player chose a 'natural-looking' improving move instead of the one required concrete response. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 7, 9), a piece was placed on a central or active-looking square where an enemy knight immediately captured or challenged it (Nxg6, Nxe5, Nxd5, Nxg6, plus d4/b4 harassing Nc5). In 2/10 positions (4, 6), an f-pawn was pushed to create apparent space/activity but allowed the opponent to lock the structure, neutralizing the player's advantage. In 3/10 positions (2, 8, 10), a rook was placed on a seemingly active square but either lost material or walked into a tactical disaster. The correct moves were consistently more concrete: captures (Nxe5, Bxf3 in positions 5, 9), quiet retreats (Bh7, Rd1, Re2 in positions 1, 2, 8), or specific pawn breaks (d5, g5 in positions 6, 7). The pattern reveals players choosing positional 'improvement' over tactical necessity at critical junctures.

443.label: A pawn capture removes the sole defender of a friendly piece (or critical passed pawn), leaving it immediately hanging.
443.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical mechanism: a pawn makes a diagonal capture, but that pawn was the sole protector of a friendly piece or key pawn on an adjacent square. In 6/10 cases the abandoned piece is a knight (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9), in 2/10 it's a bishop (positions 8, 10), and in 2/10 it's a critical passed pawn (positions 5, 7). The refutation in every case is trivially capturing the now-undefended piece/pawn. The captures always move the pawn diagonally away from the piece it was guarding — e.g., g-pawn captures on f-file leaving a piece on h-file undefended, e-pawn captures on f-file leaving a piece on d-file undefended, b-pawn captures on a-file leaving a piece on c-file undefended. The player's intent is always to win material or eliminate an enemy pawn/piece, but they fail to recognize their capturing pawn's critical defensive role. The average cp_loss of 376 reflects that this typically costs a full piece.

444.label: A knight captures a central pawn but lands on an undefended square where it is immediately recaptured, losing a piece for a pawn.
444.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight capturing a central or semi-central pawn (e5, e4, d5, d4, or c5) and landing on a square where it lacks adequate defense. In 8/10 cases, the knight is directly recaptured by a piece already targeting that square (rook on the file in positions 3 and 4, queen in positions 7 and 8, knight in positions 1 and 5, bishop in positions 2 and 9). In 2/10 cases (positions 6 and 10), an intermediate move (queen trade with check or a discovered diagonal attack) precedes the recapture, but the fundamental error is identical: the knight is won back immediately. The average cp_loss of 389 corresponds closely to the value of losing a minor piece for a pawn (~300cp plus positional damage). In every case, 2-3 safe alternatives existed that prioritized development, king safety, or piece coordination over the tempting pawn grab. The captured pawns are always central (c5/d4/d5/e4/e5), making them particularly tempting targets that appear to offer both material gain and centralization.

450.label: King moves away from the critical sector of the board where its presence is most urgently needed, allowing the opponent's primary threat to become unstoppable.
450.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves that retreat or sidestep in the wrong direction relative to the board's most important threat. In 7/10 cases, the king moves away from a dangerous passed pawn that needs blockading or contesting (positions 3, 5, 7, 8, 10 involve fleeing from the opponent's passer; positions 1, 2 involve abandoning central pawn control). In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 9), the king walks toward the back rank into a mating net instead of fleeing laterally to safety. In every case, the correct move was a king move in the opposite direction — toward the threat rather than away from it. The average cp_loss of 2063 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 3/10 resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these are positions where king direction is binary — one way survives, the other collapses. The phase split (7 endgame, 3 middlegame) confirms these predominantly occur in endgames where king activity and proximity to passed pawns is paramount.

429.label: Playing routine pawn captures or pushes (especially on wing files) in tactically critical positions that demand more forcing or active alternatives.
429.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (the 10th is Nh3, a knight move to the rim), with 6/10 being pawn captures specifically. 8/10 moves involve the a, b, g, or h files — peripheral wing actions. All 10 positions have at least one exposed or weakly-shielded king, creating tactical urgency. When these moves are mistakes (7/10 positions), the correct alternatives typically involve piece activity (Bc2, Qc1, Rc1, Ne2), forcing moves (h4+ check), or central breaks (d5). The 3 positions with 0cp loss (positions 4, 7, 9) happen to be endgames where the pawn capture IS the most forcing option, confirming the feature detects the move type/context rather than exclusively errors. The consistent pattern is positions of tactical tension where a 'mechanical' pawn move on the edge is played — it's usually wrong because it ignores urgency, but occasionally correct when no deeper tactic exists.

440.label: A minor piece (usually a bishop) is relocated from a square where it performs a critical defensive function to a seemingly active square, immediately allowing tactical exploitation of the abandoned responsibility.
440.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves and 2/10 feature knight moves — all minor piece relocations that look like natural improvements but fatally abandon a defensive duty. In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 7, and 1), the piece was blocking or supporting the e-file, and its departure enabled rook infiltration or a winning exchange sequence (Rxe8+ or Re2). In 3/10 positions (6, 9, 10), the piece was shielding the king along a diagonal, and its departure allowed devastating checks (Bf4+, Nf5+, Bxa3+). In 3/10 positions (4, 5, 8), the piece moved to a passive or peripheral square while missing a concrete tactical opportunity the original piece placement enabled. The average cp_loss is 1291, indicating these are catastrophic errors. All 10 moves appeared 'active' or 'improving' — centralizing, challenging an opponent's piece, or developing — but each removed a piece from a square performing an irreplaceable defensive coordination role. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, suggesting these occur at critical defensive moments where precision is required.

446.label: A passive, non-forcing bishop move (repositioning to a 'better' square) is played when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action such as a capture, check, or forcing sequence.
446.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop move as the mistake, and 10/10 are non-capturing, non-checking repositioning moves — simply shifting the bishop to a seemingly improved square. In 9/10 cases, a dramatically stronger forcing move was available: direct captures (Rxe7 winning a piece, exf5 capturing a hanging bishop, Rxd4 taking a hanging piece), mating sequences (Rh8 giving mate in 2, Na4+ forcing mate in 6), 7th-rank invasions (Rc7), or necessary preliminary exchanges (Bxf6 before repositioning). The average cp_loss is extremely high (2096), driven by 3/10 positions where forced checkmates were missed. Only 1/10 positions (Position 8, 12cp loss) was the bishop move actually correct — notably this was the only position where no superior forcing alternative existed. The consistent error is choosing slow piece improvement over concrete calculation: the players see a 'good square' for their bishop and play toward it without first checking captures, checks, and threats.

452.label: A passive king move to h7/h2 (the 'comfort square') squanders a critical tempo when an immediate tactical action — capturing a hanging piece, delivering perpetual check, or challenging an active enemy piece — was urgently required.
452.description: All 10 positions feature a king move to a rook-pawn file square (9/10 specifically to h7 or h2, with 1 Ka2 variant). In every case, the player's intent was prophylactic king safety — stepping off the back rank or creating 'luft' — but the position demanded exactly one forcing action. In 3/10 positions, the correct move was capturing a completely undefended major piece (Bxd8, Nxd8, Bxc1). In 4/10 positions, the king actually walked into a mating pattern (Qf5+/Qxf7#, Qf4+/Qxf2#, Bc2+ diagonal). In 3/10 positions, the tempo loss allowed the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative (missing perpetual check, failing to challenge a dominant rook). The average cp_loss was 3091 with an average of only 1.1 good moves available, confirming these are razor-sharp positions requiring the one precise tactical response. The consistent error is prioritizing a generic 'king safety' instinct over reading the specific tactical demands of the position.

442.label: Moving a piece or pawn to a passive peripheral square (predominantly the a-file) while ignoring an urgent tactical threat or critical defensive responsibility in the center.
442.description: 9/10 positions feature moves to rim or near-rim squares: specifically, 7/10 involve moves to the a-file (Na3 twice, Qa3, Qa5, Qa6, a6, axb6), while Qb6 and Nh6 are also edge-directed moves. Only Bf5 (1/10) is not a clear rim move, though it shares the pattern of placing a piece on an exposed, non-urgent square. In every case, the played move ignores the most critical tactical demand: 4/10 leave a piece hanging or the queen capturable (Qa3 hangs to a bishop, Qa5 hangs to a rook, Na3 leaves c1 undefended, Qa6 leaves d5 undefended), 3/10 waste a tempo allowing a crushing opponent breakthrough (a6 allows f5, axb6 opens a diagonal for Bc4+, Bf5 allows tempo-gaining b3+Re1+), and 3/10 fail to address an immediate fork or mating threat (Na3 ignores Ne2+ fork, Qb6 abandons kingside allowing Bh6 mate-in-5, Nh6 ignores winning Ne5). The 'missed_tactic' tag appears in all 10 analyses, and 'tempo_loss' in 9/10.

454.label: A central or semi-central pawn is advanced aggressively in a closed/semi-closed position, destroying the player's own pawn chain and creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
454.description: All 9/9 positions feature a pawn advancing from e3/e4/e6/d3/d4/f4 to the 4th or 5th rank (e4, e5, d4, d5, or f5) in positions with closed or semi-closed centers. In every case, the pawn was performing a critical structural role—supporting an adjacent pawn, guarding a key square, or blocking an enemy piece's access to important lines. 9/9 positions had at least 3 good quiet alternatives (developing moves, piece improvements, or prophylactic ideas) that maintained the existing advantage or equality. The advances uniformly create immediate tactical punishments: in 4/9 cases the advance leaves a piece or pawn hanging (Positions 2, 3, 8, 9), in 2/9 it opens critical lines exposing a piece (Positions 1, 6), in 2/9 it abandons control of a crucial square allowing a devastating piece invasion (Positions 4, 5), and in 1/9 it dissolves the player's own dominant pawn chain (Position 10). The average cp_loss of 251 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic structural collapses.

455.label: A piece (rook or queen) moves to the king's only flight square, enabling immediate checkmate.
455.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical tactical catastrophe: the player moves their own piece to the single square their king needs as an escape route, enabling an immediate or near-immediate checkmate. In 7/10 cases the self-blocking piece is a rook (Rd8, Rg8, Rg1, Rb8, Rg1, Rf8, Rg8), and in 3/10 it's a queen (Qd2, Qf8, Qd7). In 9/10 positions the result is checkmate-in-one; the remaining case (Position 9) results in forced mate-in-7 due to escape routes being cut off. The king is always on a corner or edge square (c8, h8, h2, a8, c1, g8, h1) with exactly one adjacent flight square that the blundering piece occupies. The checkmates delivered are queen mates along ranks or files (Qb7#, Qh6#, Qa6#, Qb2#, Qh7#, Qh3#, Qa8#) or discovered check mates (Bf1#). The average centipawn loss is 9585, with 8/10 positions shifting from a playable game directly to mate-in-1.

453.label: A routine king centralization move in an endgame that ignores a more concrete and urgent tactical priority (capture, check, pawn break, or prophylaxis).
453.description: All 10 positions feature a king move to a central or semi-central square in an endgame (8/10) or late middlegame (2/10), following the general principle of 'activate the king.' However, in 9/10 cases the position demanded a more concrete action: a piece delivering check with material gain (positions 1, 8), an immediate pawn capture (position 6 - Bxg2), a critical prophylactic pawn move (position 2 - h5), resolving pawn tension (position 5 - bxc6), or active piece play over passive king wandering (position 4 - Nd3). The 'tempo_loss' motif appears in 9/10 analyses because the king moves typically place the king on squares where the opponent gains tempo via checks, pawn advances with tempo (c5+ in position 6, f4+ in position 1, Ne2+ in position 8), or kingside breaks the misplaced king cannot contest (position 10). The average cp_loss of 136 reflects that these positions punish generic positional thinking when concrete calculation was required. Only 1/10 positions (position 9, cp_loss=0) was the king move actually correct, and notably that was the one case where capturing a specific pawn WAS the concrete priority.

447.label: Bishop delivers a check that backfires by helping the opponent's king find safety, allowing interpositions, or abandoning critical coordination duties.
447.description: 9/10 positions involve bishop moves (the exception being position 2's d7 pawn push), and 8/10 are specifically bishop checks that prove counterproductive. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 5, 7, 9), the bishop check drives the opponent's king to a demonstrably safer or more active square. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 5), forced checkmates were available but the player chose the inferior bishop check instead. In 2/10 cases (positions 8, 10), the bishop check allows a tactical refutation that wins the bishop or an undefended piece left behind. The average cp_loss of 3106 reflects that many of these are catastrophic blunders—4/10 positions had forced mates available that were missed. All 10 moves share the quality of looking aggressive and forcing while actually worsening the mover's position, with the consistent tag 'tempo_loss' appearing in all 10 analyses.

451.label: Moving the king (including castling) to a square that creates immediate tactical vulnerability, prioritizing general safety over concrete calculation.
451.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move (including castling) as the blunder, making this the clearest unifying pattern. In 8/10 cases, the king's destination square is directly exploitable by the opponent's pieces—specifically through knight forks (positions 4, 5, 7), diagonal checks/attacks (positions 2, 3, 8), discovered attacks (position 6), or open-file exposure (position 9). In 2/10 cases (positions 1 and 10), the king move itself isn't immediately punished by a geometric exploit on the destination square, but rather wastes tempo while a hanging piece goes uncaptured. The average cp_loss of 1302 reflects catastrophic consequences—3/10 positions swing from winning to losing, and 1/10 results in forced mate. In 9/10 positions, the best move was NOT a king move, indicating the player defaulted to king relocation when tactical action was required. Knights are the primary exploiting piece in 5/10 positions (forks on e7, f2, e5), while diagonal attacks account for 3/10.

457.label: Moving the rook from f8 to e8 (or away from a critical defensive post) abandons the defense of f7/f2, enabling immediate mating attacks.
457.description: 8/10 positions feature Black playing Re8, moving the rook from f8 where it defended the critical f7 pawn. In all 8 of these cases, the opponent had a queen and knight (typically Qh4/Qh5/Qh6 + Ng5) battery aimed at f7/h7, and the rook on f8 was the sole defender preventing a Qh7+/Qxf7# mating pattern. The remaining 2/10 positions show White making analogous errors: Re1 abandoning f2 defense (Position 3) and Rc1 vacating the e1 square needed to prevent back-rank mate (Position 10). In 7/10 positions, the immediate refutation involved Qh7+ followed by Qxf7# or Qh8#. The average cp_loss of 6796 reflects that 7/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these were extremely narrow defensive positions where the rook's placement on f8 was the single thread holding the position together.

458.label: King moves backward in endgames instead of advancing toward the critical zone, losing a decisive tempo.
458.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves that retreat toward the player's own back rank rather than advancing or taking the most direct path toward the critical area of play. 9/10 are explicitly identified as 'tempo_loss' errors. The kings retreat from active squares (c6→c7, d6→e7, f6→f5, e6→e7, g6→h7, g5→g4, c3→b2, h4→h3, b2→a2, g3→g2) when the best move either advances the king (Ka3, Kh4, Kg3) or maintains central presence (Kd7, Kc7, Kg7). In 8/10 cases, the better alternative was a king move to a more active square, and in the remaining 2, a pawn advance (g7, d4) was needed instead. The average cp_loss is high (1101) due to Position 3 where retreating from the winning king+pawn configuration threw away a forced mate, converting #+5 to a draw. All positions are pure endgames where single tempi are decisive.

445.label: Voluntary queen repositioning that abandons control of a key square, immediately exploited by the opponent (usually via a knight jump).
445.description: All 10/10 positions feature a voluntary queen move in the middlegame where the queen leaves a functional post for a seemingly reasonable but tactically flawed square. In 6-7/10 cases, the direct punishment involves an opponent's knight jumping to or through the square the queen no longer controls (Ng4, Nh4, Nd2, Ng6, Ng5, Ne5). The queen was previously the sole piece controlling that critical square, and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability. In the remaining 3-4 positions, the queen similarly abandons a crucial function (defensive diagonal in Position 8, active pressure in Position 3, basic safety in Position 10, initiative in Position 6) but is punished through other mechanisms. The moves appear plausible—centralizing, repositioning for attack, or avoiding perceived threats—but all share the fatal flaw of prioritizing the queen's destination over its current responsibilities. Average cp_loss of 241 confirms these are severe mistakes, and only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were often critical decision points.

456.label: A non-forcing, single-step pawn advance played in a critical position that demands immediate active piece play or tactical exploitation.
456.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, single-step pawn advance (e6, a4, g6, g4, f6, e6, c5, f5, a4, f6) played instead of an available active piece move or tactical strike. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a piece move (Bxc3+, Rc1, Ba4, exd4, Bb5, Re8, Nd5, Ng8) that either exploited a concrete tactical vulnerability or addressed an urgent positional need. The average number of good moves was only 2.3, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than general play. In 6/10 cases, the pawn push directly weakened the player's own king position (f6×2, g6, f5, e6×2 opening dark-square diagonals), while in 4/10 cases it simply wasted the tempo needed to address an immediate threat (trapped piece, hanging pawn, tactical fork). The consistent thread is choosing a slow, seemingly constructive but non-forcing pawn move in a position where the tactical clock is ticking—either the opponent has a vulnerability that can only be exploited NOW, or the player's own position has a problem that worsens with each wasted move.

449.label: Active-looking moves (pawn advances, piece centralizations, captures) that remove a critical defensive support, immediately creating an exploitable tactical vulnerability.
449.description: In 9/10 positions (excluding the 0cp-loss position 5), the played move appears purposeful and aggressive—gaining space, centralizing a piece, or winning material—but fatally removes protection from something the opponent immediately exploits. Specifically: 4/10 positions feature pawn advances that abandon control of a key square (d5 in positions 4 and 8 both abandon e5, enabling knight forks; f5 in position 9 leaves e5 hanging; h5 in position 2 leaves g5 unguarded). 3/10 feature knight moves to 'active' squares that create tactical vulnerabilities (Ng6 in position 3 unguards the a3-f8 diagonal; both Nf4 moves in positions 6-7 enable double attacks or forks). 1/10 features a pawn capture that removes the king's shield (gxf6 in position 10 enables mate-in-3). 1/10 features a premature exchange that lets a target piece escape (Rxc1+ in position 1). The common thread is that every move LOOKS like it accomplishes something positive while ACTUALLY self-inflicting an immediate concrete tactical refutation—never a slow positional concession but always an exploitable hole within 1-2 moves.

464.label: A one-square pawn advance to the player's third rank on a non-central file, squandering a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate action.
464.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance to the player's own third rank (3rd for White: b3, h3, a3, c3; 6th for Black: b6, b6, h6, g6, a6, a6), all on non-central files (a, b, c, g, or h — never d or e). 10/10 positions had urgent tactical or strategic demands that the pawn push completely ignored: mating threats requiring defensive queen repositioning (positions 1, 3), king centralization in endgames (positions 2, 7, 9), capturing to prevent a devastating passed pawn (position 5), active rook deployment to delay forced mate (position 6), or immediate pawn breaks that were available in one move but were instead 'prepared' by the slower two-step approach (positions 4, 10). The average cp_loss was 2892, with 5/10 resulting in forced checkmate or near-mate. Only 2.2 good moves existed on average, indicating these were narrow positions where the correct action was clear but the player defaulted to a quiet 'useful-looking' pawn push instead.

459.label: Playing seemingly purposeful piece moves, captures, or checks that ignore the position's single most urgent demand, wasting decisive tempo.
459.description: All 10/10 positions share the defining characteristic of tempo loss: the player chose a move that appears active, aggressive, or improving—repositioning a piece (Ne2, Nd5, Ng2, Bd7, Bh3, Rgb7, Qf6), giving check (Qe7+, b6+), or making a capture (gxh3)—but each failed to address the ONE critical action the position demanded. In 7/10 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of optimal (avg good moves: 1.7), meaning these were high-precision moments where the specific correct action was narrow. The correct moves were often unglamorous: king improvements (Kf2, Kf3, Kh7, Kg5 in 4/10), concrete pawn breaks (cxb6, g4 in 2/10), or piece-safety moves (Ba3, Bf5 in 2/10). The played moves averaged 1199cp loss—catastrophic blunders—because looking 'active' without addressing the position's core vulnerability (a hanging piece, a forced mate, a pawn structure collapse, or a simplification opportunity for the opponent) gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to consolidate or strike back.

439.label: Natural-looking moves (usually captures) played in positions where extreme king vulnerability demands single-move precision, catastrophically failing to address immediate mating or king-safety threats.
439.description: 10/10 positions feature critically exposed or vulnerable kings (kings on f7, f8, c8, d8, h4, h2, e1, or with shattered pawn shields). 6/10 positions have only 1 good move available, and the average is just 1.8 good moves—indicating razor-thin margins for error. 7/10 of the moves played are captures (Rxf4, Nxd4, Qxg7, Qxf6, Rxf2, Bxf7, Qb8), reflecting a materialistic instinct that overrides the critical defensive need. In 6/8 actual mistakes, the player captured material or placed a piece on a 'natural' square while a mating threat or devastating king-hunt existed. The refutations consistently exploit the unaddressed king weakness: 5/10 positions feature checkmate as the punishment (positions 3, 4, 5 immediately; positions 4 and 10 as threats). The 2 positions with 0 cp_loss (positions 4 and 10) represent the same position TYPE—critical king crises with only one legal/good response—where the player happened to find the forced move. Average cp_loss among the 8 actual mistakes is 2612cp, reflecting the catastrophic nature of errors in these positions.

461.label: Piece captures (mostly knight exchanges) that squander advantages because a preparatory move would have made the position far more favorable first.
461.description: All 10 positions feature a piece capture (7/10 knight captures, 3/10 bishop captures) where the player initiates or completes an exchange prematurely, missing a stronger preparatory move. In 9/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify a move-order error where the same capture (or a better one) would have been far more effective after preparation. In 8/10 positions, the premature capture either removes the player's own strongly-posted piece from an active square (e.g., a dominant centralized knight) or allows the opponent to recapture with improved piece coordination (e.g., a knight reaching a superior outpost). The correct alternatives consistently involved either a preparatory developing move (Re1 in position 3, Qe5 in position 10, Nce5 in position 5, Nf7 in position 4), a pawn advance that would accomplish more (f3 in positions 7 and 9, b5 in position 2), or a different tactical target entirely (Nxg2+ in position 6, Nac5 in position 1). The average cp_loss of 243 reflects the severity: these aren't minor inaccuracies but fundamental failures to sequence moves correctly, with only 1.1 good moves available on average, indicating sharp positions demanding precise calculation.

460.label: A piece (usually a knight) captures a pawn, abandoning its critical defensive or structural role, creating tactical vulnerabilities worth far more than the material gained.
460.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece capture that wins material (typically a pawn) but fatally disrupts the captor's defensive contribution. In 8/10 cases, it's specifically a knight making the greedy capture. The piece being moved was serving a crucial function: blocking a diagonal (Position 2 - pawn on d4 blocked Qc6-f3), defending key squares (Position 10 - Nf3 guarded against Re2 invasions), maintaining pawn integrity (Position 9 - Nc3 protected e4), or preventing opponent's piece jumps (Position 5 - Nc6 prevented Nf3-e5 attacking the queen). In at least 4/10 positions (1, 4, 8, 9), a pawn capture was the correct alternative to the piece capture, suggesting players instinctively prefer 'active' piece moves over 'passive' pawn recaptures. The average cp_loss of 1179 reflects how catastrophic these errors are — the immediate material gain of ~100cp (one pawn) is dwarfed by the resulting tactical explosions averaging nearly 12x that cost.

465.label: Playing a natural-looking or seemingly active knight move instead of a more forcing tactical continuation that wins decisive material or delivers checkmate.
465.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight move that appears active, centralizing, or aggressive but squanders a much stronger tactical opportunity. In 7/10 positions, the correct move was NOT a knight move at all — it was a queen check (positions 8, 9), a rook sacrifice/capture (positions 6, 10), a queen capture (position 3), or a piece capture with a different knight (position 4). In the remaining 3/10, the correct move was the SAME knight moving to a different, more forcing square (Nxc7+ instead of Nc3, Nf7+ instead of Ne4+, Nxc2+ instead of Nc6). The played knight moves range from quiet centralizations (Nc3, Nd5, Nf3, Nc6) to checks/forks (Ne4+, Ne6+, Nc7) that appear aggressive but extract far less than what was available. The average cp_loss of 3176 reflects that 4/10 positions involved missed forced mates. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow tactical positions demanding precision rather than general piece play.

468.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn move when an immediate piece capture (or piece-saving move) is available.
468.description: 9/10 positions feature a quiet pawn move (c3, d6, d6, c4, b4, b4, d5, d3, h6) and 1/10 a passive rook retreat (Ra8), all ignoring a critical tactical demand involving an undefended piece. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 6, 8), the player missed capturing an opponent's hanging or undefended piece outright (Bxf5, Bxe1, Bxe6, exf4). In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 7, 9), the player's own piece was en prise and needed saving or the tension needed resolving (bishop on c5 threatened by dxc5, rook on a8 x-rayed by Bd5, bishop on c4 capturable by dxc4). In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 10), the move left the player's own piece hanging by failing to include a forcing intermediate move (check or capture) first. The average cp_loss of 358 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirm these are high-stakes positions with nearly no margin for error, where the player consistently chose positional preparation over the single critical tactical action.
468.old_chip: Quiet pawn push ignores hanging piece

466.label: Advancing a pawn to create structural changes or passed pawns before completing necessary preparatory piece/king moves.
466.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance as the move played. In 7/10 cases this is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss ~450 for the errors), while 3/10 are correct or nearly correct. The critical distinguishing factor is TIMING: in the 7 erroneous positions, the correct alternatives involved piece repositioning first — king centralization (positions 1, 3, 9), rook relocation (positions 2, 10), king safety moves (position 7), or pawn chain consolidation (position 6). The pawn advance was often thematically correct as a LATER move but catastrophically premature when played immediately. In 8/10 positions the phase is endgame where tempo and move order are paramount. The pawn advances typically create irreversible structural commitments — exchanges that produce doubled pawns (position 1), isolated targets (position 2), dissolved pawn chains (positions 3, 6), or expose tactical vulnerabilities (positions 7, 10).

472.label: Playing a slow a-pawn or h-pawn advance (a3/a6/h3) in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical or developmental action.
472.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square rook pawn advance (a3 in 4 positions, a6 in 5 positions, h3 in 1 position) played as a 'prophylactic' or preparatory move in situations where the position urgently demanded concrete action. In 9/10 cases the stated intent was preventing a knight jump (Nb4/Nb5) or preparing queenside expansion (b4/b5), yet in every case these threats were either non-existent or far less important than the tactical opportunity being squandered. The positions featured time-sensitive elements: 4/10 had an exposed or uncastled king, 4/10 had hanging or trappable pieces, 7/10 had critical central tension requiring immediate resolution, and 8/10 had concrete tactical shots available (piece captures, pawn breakthroughs, or forcing sequences). The average centipawn loss was 268, with losses ranging from 188 to 692, confirming these are severe blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. Only 2.0 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions demanded precision rather than offering multiple acceptable options.

463.label: Moving the queen to e2 (White) or e7 (Black) in positions where an enemy knight can immediately exploit d4/d5 with tempo, creating forks or tactical combinations.
463.description: 7/10 positions involve a piece moving to the e2 or e7 square, with 6/10 being specifically queen moves (Qe2 three times, Qe7 three times) and one being Ne7 that blocks the queen from reaching its best square. In all queen-to-e2 cases (Positions 2, 3, 4), the punishment involves an enemy knight leaping to d4 with devastating effect—either forking the queen and f3-knight, or exploiting the queen's position on a vulnerable diagonal. In all queen-to-e7 cases (Positions 1, 5, 10), the punishment is Nd5 attacking the queen with tempo while creating secondary threats (Nxf6+ destroying kingside structure, Bxe7 winning material, or Nxc7+ forking). The remaining 3 positions (6, 8 with 0cp loss; 9 with 142cp loss) are outliers that don't follow this core pattern. The average cp_loss for the 7 matching positions exceeds 300cp, indicating catastrophic consequences. In 5/7 matching positions, the tactical motif is explicitly labeled 'fork,' while the other two involve pins/overloaded defenders enabled by the queen's vulnerable placement.

467.label: Playing a natural-looking bishop move (retreat, reposition, or premature capture) instead of the one precise forcing move the position demands.
467.description: 7/10 positions feature bishop moves specifically (Bf8, Be7, Bxg6, Bxe5, Bxd5+, Bxe4+, Be6), while the remaining 3 (h5, Rf1, Re3) share the same structural error of choosing a non-forcing move when immediate tactical action was required. The average number of good moves available was only 1.5, meaning these are narrow positions with one critical path. In 4/10 cases the bishop captured prematurely (Bxg6, Bxe5, Bxd5+, Bxe4+), giving the opponent a beneficial recapture or squandering an attacking piece before executing the correct forcing sequence first. In 3/10 cases the bishop retreated or repositioned passively (Bf8, Be7, Be6) when an aggressive pawn capture or piece activation was needed. The analyses tagged 'tempo_loss' in 8/10 positions and 'move_order' in 3/10. In every case, the correct move involved a DIFFERENT piece or a fundamentally different action (Rxg3, f4, Kb6, Qa7, Re1, Nc3, Nb4+, Rcb1, Bxh3, Qh4) that was more forcing or better-timed.

462.label: Playing a visually appealing or seemingly aggressive move in a sharp position that demanded a specific concrete forcing continuation.
462.description: All 9 positions share a critical characteristic: they are razor-sharp situations (avg 2.0 good moves available) where only one or two precise forcing moves maintain the evaluation, yet the player chose a 'seductive' alternative that looks natural or aggressive but is non-forcing. In 6/9 positions, the played move appears actively attacking or improving (Nxg6 sacrificing on the kingside, Ne3+ delivering check+fork, Rh7 occupying the 7th rank, Rhg4 doubling rooks, hxg6 opening lines, Kg2 centralizing). In 3/9, the move is plausible but passive when urgency was required (Ne2 retreating, a6 pushing prematurely, Rd1 repositioning). The best moves were consistently concrete and forcing: perpetual checks (2/9), pawn advances creating immediate promotion threats (2/9), captures resolving tension favorably (2/9), or castling/king safety moves (3/9). The enormous average cp_loss of 1346 reflects that these positions had no margin for imprecision—the 'attractive' alternative completely squanders a winning advantage, a saving perpetual, or a forced mate.

473.label: Moving a bishop to a seemingly active square that either abandons a critical function or creates a tactical vulnerability.
473.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to what appears to be a more active or centralized square, but the move is actually a significant mistake. In 4/10 cases (positions 3, 6, 7, 9), the bishop abandons a critical defensive or blocking function—guarding a file, shielding the king, or preventing an invasion. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 8, 10), the bishop lands on a square where it becomes immediately tactically exploitable via forks, skewers, or dual threats. In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 4), the bishop is 'improved' when a concrete tactical opportunity with a different move was available. The average cp_loss is extremely high (2141), with 3/10 positions resulting in forced mate or near-mate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, meaning these are critical-precision positions where the 'natural-looking' bishop move is uniquely punished. 8/10 moves were made by Black, suggesting this pattern often occurs under defensive pressure where players seek activity rather than addressing concrete threats.

469.label: Capturing a piece with a rook (or minor piece) that simplifies the position when a stronger forcing move or pressure-maintaining continuation was available first.
469.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook making a capture of an enemy piece (the exception is Position 4's Bxc6, still a piece exchange). In 8/10 positions, the capture was a clear mistake because it simplified tension prematurely. The better moves fell into two categories: in 4/10 positions (1, 3, 8, 10), a knight fork or forcing check was available that would have won significantly more material (Nf3+, Qxe5 enabling Nf3+, Nd6+ forking king and queen, Qxh6 enabling Nf6+). In 4/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 7), maintaining positional pressure or attacking the opponent's defensive structure first was correct (capturing the real threat instead, keeping a rook tied to blockade duty, using Nd4 to threaten a fork before exchanging, playing f5 to undermine defenders). Position 9 (0 cp loss) represents the pattern executed correctly—where removing the blockading piece IS the strongest continuation. The average cp_loss of 226 reflects that these premature captures consistently squander significant advantages by trading active positions for simplified ones.

448.label: Playing a seemingly active or natural piece placement move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical response.
448.description: 9/10 positions are tactically charged middlegames where the played move is a quiet piece relocation to an 'ambitious' square (7th rank, central outpost, infiltration square, or attacking diagonal). 9/10 moves are non-captures — quiet moves that look like positional improvements. Yet in 3/10 positions a forced mate was available (positions 4, 8, 9), in 3/10 a tactical capture/shot was the correct move (positions 2, 6, 7), and in the remaining cases precise defensive moves were required. The average cp_loss is 3061, reflecting the extreme cost of choosing appearance of activity over concrete calculation. Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, confirming these are critical moments requiring precision. The common thread is pieces going to plausible-looking squares (Rb7 on 7th rank, Be5 on central outpost, Qg2 infiltrating, Bh6 attacking fianchetto, Re7 'defending') while the actual position demanded forcing moves: discovered checks, captures of hanging pieces, file-opening for mating nets, or vacating escape squares.

478.label: Playing Qa5 (or Qa4) targeting the opponent's uncastled king on e1 instead of exploiting concrete tactical opportunities in the center.
478.description: 10/10 positions involve moving to the a5 square (9/10 are Queen moves to a5 or a4, 1/10 is a pawn move to a5). In all 10 positions, the opponent's king remains on e1, and the move targets (or prepares to target) the a5-e1 diagonal. 6/10 moves deliver check. 8/10 are played by Black. The critical shared error is that in every case, a far superior concrete option exists: 4/10 positions had a hanging piece available for capture (positions 1, 3, 7, 9), while the remaining 6 had critical central tension or tactical resources that demanded immediate attention. In all cases, the Qa5/Qa4 move is trivially refuted—most commonly by Bd2 blocking (appearing as the top refutation in 5/10 positions), which simultaneously develops a piece and attacks the misplaced queen. The average cp_loss of 315 reflects that these moves squander significant advantages, often converting winning positions into equal or losing ones.

474.label: A knight or bishop captures a pawn that is defended by an adjacent pawn, and the simple pawn recapture either wins the piece outright or creates a losing imbalance.
474.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (knight in 7/10, bishop in 3/10) capturing a pawn that is defended by a neighboring pawn. In every single case, the primary refutation is the straightforward pawn recapture (cxd4, dxe4, cxb5, hxg5, fxg4, exd5, cxb4). In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 8), the piece is simply lost outright after the pawn recapture with no meaningful compensation. In the remaining 7/10, the capturing side trades a piece for 1-2 pawns but the pawn recapture catastrophically transforms the position: it opens lines/diagonals favoring the opponent (9/10), displaces a key defensive piece from its post (positions 1, 5, 6, 10 all feature a bishop lured away from king defense), or frees previously locked enemy pieces (positions 7, 9). In 6/10 positions involving Nxd4/Nxd5, the pattern specifically involves cxd4 followed by Bxd4, where the recapturing bishop ends up misplaced or has abandoned critical defensive duties. The average cp_loss of 301 reflects losing roughly a full minor piece worth of value.

471.label: Non-forcing piece moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action (captures, pawn breaks, or checks).
471.description: All 10 positions share a striking pattern: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move when the position urgently demands concrete action. In every case, the best moves available were forcing — captures (positions 3, 9), pawn breaks (positions 4, 5, 10), checks (position 8), or tactically purposeful piece placements (positions 1, 2, 6, 7). Instead, the player chose a 'normal-looking' development or repositioning move. 7/10 moves place pieces on the back rank (Qc8×2, Ra1, Re1, Rf8, Ra8, Bb7), and the remaining 3 (Qd2, Qc2, Rf3) go to the second or third rank — all moving pieces backward or laterally to passive squares. 9/10 involve major pieces (5 rook moves, 4 queen moves). The average cp_loss of 319 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic tempo losses. In 6/10 cases, the position had only 1-2 good moves available, meaning the positions demanded precision rather than general development. The moved piece typically arrives at a square that is either tactically vulnerable (Ra1 to bishop-controlled square, Qd2/Qc2 to knight-fork squares) or simply irrelevant to the position's critical demands.

475.label: The queen makes an apparently aggressive move (check, capture, or centralization) that misses a precise tactical opportunity and fatally breaks piece coordination.
475.description: 9/10 positions involve queen moves (the exception being Re1 which shares the same conceptual error). In all 10 cases, the player chose a move that APPEARED active or aggressive — 4/10 were checks (Qh8+, Qh1+, Qg3+, Qg6 walking into check), 1/10 was a pawn capture (Qxh3), and the rest were centralizing or 'attacking' relocations — but each fundamentally misplaced the queen away from the position's critical tactical requirement. The average cp_loss of 2227 and average of only 1.2 good moves confirms these are extremely narrow positions demanding concrete calculation rather than instinctive aggression. In 7/10 cases the best move was a specific tactical strike (Nxe7, Qxd4, Qe5+, Qf7+, Nf6 tempo, Bxa4, Rg1 defense) that the 'aggressive' queen move bypassed entirely. The queen consistently lands on a square where it either becomes vulnerable to tactics (positions 2, 6), loses coordination with allied pieces (positions 3, 5, 8, 10), gives a premature/purposeless check (positions 4, 8), or allows the opponent time to consolidate (positions 1, 5, 7).

477.label: Quietly retreating a bishop along its diagonal to a 'better' square when the position demands immediate forcing action.
477.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved along its own diagonal in a non-forcing, repositioning manner — no captures, no checks, just quiet relocation.
