In 9/10 cases, the bishop retreats backward from an advanced/aggressive post toward the player's own side (Bg3 from c7 three times, Be3 from h6, Bb2 from g7, Bd5 from f7, Bc3 from h8, Bb6 from f2, Bb7 from g2). The remaining case (Be6) places the bishop on a vulnerable central square. In every instance, the bishop was serving a critical tactical function in its current position — controlling escape squares for checkmate (3/10), defending key squares around the king (2/10), maintaining tactical tension that protected other pieces (3/10), or creating immediate forcing threats (2/10). The retreats all look 'natural' or 'improving' but catastrophically ignore the concrete tactical demands of the position. The average cp_loss of 3111 reflects that these quiet moves occur in positions screaming for forcing play (captures, checks, queen trades, pawn pushes).

479.label: King moves to a square where the opponent can immediately deliver a devastating check (or check sequence) that was not possible on the previous square.
479.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that places the monarch on a square directly within the checking range of an enemy piece, enabling an immediate forcing sequence. In 10/10 cases, the opponent's first punishing move is a check or capture-with-check: Qf7# (pos 1), Qg2+ (pos 2), Qh7+ (pos 3), Qd8+ (pos 4), Bc5+ (pos 5), Bg4+ (pos 6), Qe2+ (pos 7), Nxg4+ or Qxg4 enabling Nxg4+ (pos 8), Nc5+/Nb6+ (pos 9), Qxe6+ (pos 10). In every case, a different king square was available that avoided the check entirely — 8/10 had an alternative king move as the best option (e.g., Kf8 instead of Kh7, Kd1 instead of Ke2, Kd8 instead of Kd7, Kf2 instead of Kg2), while 2/10 required a non-king move (Qd2, Rg2). The average cp_loss of 4105 and average of only 1.2 good moves confirms these are razor-sharp positions where the king's landing square is the critical decision, and the wrong square triggers catastrophic tactical consequences.

470.label: Capturing with the wrong pawn when two pawns can take on the same square, removing a pawn from a critical defensive duty.
470.description: In 8/10 positions, two pawns could capture on the same square and the player chose the wrong one (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10). In the remaining 2/10 (positions 4 and 9), a pawn capture was played when a non-pawn move was far superior. The consistent error across all 10 positions is that the pawn moved was performing a critical defensive function—guarding a key square against piece invasion (c6 guarding b5 in positions 2, 5, 7), blocking a file from rook/queen penetration (f-pawn blocking f-file in positions 6, 8), denying outpost squares (position 1), or shielding the king (position 9). In every case, the alternative capture (usually the e-pawn taking toward center, or the h-pawn on the kingside) preserved the defensive pawn while achieving the same material gain. The resulting punishment typically involved immediate piece invasion through the newly unguarded square or file: Nb5 (positions 2, 5), Bb4 pin (position 7), Rf7 penetration (position 6), Qe6+ (position 8), or Nxe4 (position 9).

476.label: Queen captures the opponent's queen (Qx queen trade) when a stronger non-simplifying move exists.
476.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player's queen capturing the opponent's queen directly (Qx on the square occupied by the enemy queen), resulting in a queen trade. In 9/10 cases this was a mistake (avg cp_loss 1259, heavily skewed by one missed mate-in-one). The errors share a common strategic thread: the player had an attacking advantage or a stronger tactical continuation that required keeping queens on the board, but chose the psychologically tempting 'biggest capture available' instead. In 4/10 positions (1, 7, 9, 10), a non-queen tactical shot existed (capturing a hanging piece, deflection first). In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 8), the queen trade removed attacking pressure against an exposed king, entering an endgame where the opponent's weaknesses vanished. In 1/10 (position 5), mate-in-one was missed entirely. Only 1/10 (position 2) was actually the best move, where the queen trade itself created a mating net. Across all mistake cases, only 1.3 good moves existed on average, showing these were critical-decision moments with narrow paths to maintain advantage.

481.label: Moving a rook to a seemingly active square while the other rook is left hanging or undefended, usually to a knight attack.
481.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moves a rook to an 'active' square (7th rank, open file, attacking position) while completely ignoring an immediate tactical threat to their OTHER rook. In 8/10 positions, the hanging rook is directly attacked by an enemy knight (positions 1-3: knight on e3/f2 attacks rook; positions 5, 7, 10: knight forks both rooks; position 4: knight captures rook on a2). In 9/10 positions, the refutation involves simply capturing the undefended rook for free or winning decisive material. The tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' in 8/10 positions. The player consistently prioritizes rook activation (seizing the 7th rank, centralizing, doubling on a file) over the elementary requirement to save a piece that is en prise. All 10 positions are middlegame, and the average cp_loss of 1197 reflects that leaving a whole rook hanging is catastrophic. Only 1.8 good moves existed on average, showing these were narrow tactical moments demanding precise defense rather than ambitious play.

480.label: Knight leaps forward to an aggressive-looking square while ignoring that it leaves pieces undefended or abandons critical defensive duties.
480.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight jumping to an apparently strong attacking or central square (Ne4 in 6/10, plus Ne5, Ng5, Ng4, Na5, Nxd5). In 7/10 cases, the knight move directly leaves another piece or pawn hanging — e.g., a bishop left undefended on b4 (positions 3, 9), another knight left capturable on e4 (position 4) or c6 (position 10), or a rook left en prise (position 2). In the remaining 3/10, the knight sortie is a premature attack that loses critical tempo while the king remains uncastled (positions 6, 8) or fails to address urgent positional needs (position 5). 8/10 occur in the opening phase where development and king safety should take priority. The average cp_loss is 378, reflecting how severely these speculative knight moves are punished. In every case, quiet developing moves, retreats, or immediate tactical exploitation of existing advantages were available — the player chose visual aggression over concrete evaluation.

486.label: Reflexive king retreats to corners or back-rank squares that either waste a critical tempo or walk into new tactical vulnerabilities.
486.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king moving to a corner square (a8, b8, h8, g8, g1, b1) or back-rank square (d1, e1) as a perceived prophylactic safety measure. In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete action — a tactic, a forced trade, or a critical pawn move — rather than a slow repositioning move. Approximately 6/10 positions (Kd1, Ka8, Kh8, Kg1×2, Ke1) saw the king walk directly INTO a new tactical vulnerability on the destination square (knight forks, discovered attacks, diagonal exploits, mating patterns). The remaining 4/10 (Kb8, Kb1, Kg1-tempo, Kg8) were pure tempo losses that left pieces hanging or allowed the opponent to consolidate/counterattack. The average cp_loss was an enormous 469, and only 1.2 good moves existed on average, indicating these were narrow positions requiring precise calculation that the player substituted with a generic safety instinct.

484.label: A pawn advances to attack a well-placed enemy knight, but the pawn move vacates the exact square the knight then exploits for a devastating fork.
484.description: In 9/10 positions, the player pushes a pawn to challenge or chase an enemy knight from a strong outpost, but the pawn advance directly vacates the critical square that enables a knight fork winning material. Specifically, in 8/10 positions the pawn literally moves OFF the square the knight then jumps to: c3 vacates c2 for Nc2+ (positions 2, 3, 9), f6 vacates f7 for Nf7 (positions 1, 4), c5 vacates c6 for Nc6+ (position 6), f4 vacates f3 for Nf3+ (position 7), c6 vacates c7 for Nc7+ (position 8), and d4 vacates d3 for Nd3 (position 10). Only 1/10 (position 5) has a different refutation mechanism, though even there a pawn chases a knight while ignoring a more urgent threat. The fork targets are remarkably consistent: king+rook (6 positions), king+queen (2 positions), or queen+rook (1 position). The average cp_loss of 316 reflects the catastrophic nature of losing a full exchange or queen to a single knight jump.

493.label: Developing a bishop to g4/g5 to 'pin' a knight, but the pin is illusory because the knight can move with decisive tactical effect, leaving the bishop undefended.
493.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop developed to the g-file (g4 or g5) attempting to pin a knight against the queen in the opening. In 5/10 positions (White playing Bg5), the 'pinned' Nf6 simply captures the undefended e4 pawn, simultaneously breaking the pin and leaving the Bg5 hanging with no recapture—netting a full piece. In the other 5/10 positions (Black playing Bg4), the bishop's departure from c8 leaves f7 fatally unguarded, enabling the classic Bxf7+/Ng5+ combination where the supposedly 'pinned' knight delivers check, after which Qxg4 captures the hanging bishop. In every case, both kings are still in the center (10/10), the bishop lands on an undefended square, and the critical tactical resource is that the 'pinned' piece can move profitably—either capturing material or delivering check—because the pin is not absolute. The average cp_loss of 374 reflects catastrophic material loss in all cases.

490.label: Developing a knight to a rim square (a- or h-file) in the opening where it becomes passive, tactically vulnerable, or fails to contest critical central squares.
490.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight moving to a rim square on the a-file or h-file (Nh6 x4, Nh3 x2, Na6 x2, Na3 x1), with only 1/10 (Nc6) deviating from the strict rim pattern. All 10 moves place a knight on the 3rd or 6th rank. 8/10 occur in the opening phase, representing premature or misguided development. In every case, the knight becomes an immediate tactical liability: in 4/10 positions the knight is directly captured (Bxh6, Bxa6, Bxa3); in 3/10 it fails to contest a critical central square (d4), enabling devastating Nd4 forks; in 2/10 it becomes a target for dark-square bishop maneuvers (Bg5-f6); and in 1/10 it enables a tempo-gaining retreat by the opponent. The average cp_loss of 293 reflects that these aren't just positional inaccuracies but often outright tactical blunders. In every position, natural central knight development (Nf6, Nc6, Ne2, Nd7) was available within 50cp of the best move.

485.label: Moving an already well-placed rook to a seemingly active but non-forcing square when an immediate check or forcing capture was available.
485.description: 9/10 positions involve rook moves (the exception being Qd5 in position 8, which follows the same logic). In 8/10 cases, the best move was an immediate check (R7b4+, Rgf7+, Rhg7+, Rh8+, Rxh2+, Rbe7+, Rxc6+, Re1+). The played moves are lateral slides along the 7th rank (Rgc7, Rhe7, Rgf7, Rxh7 — 4/10), retreats from active squares (R7h5, R6d3, Rh4 — 3/10), or shifts to seemingly natural but non-forcing squares (R3b6, Rgf2). In 7/10 positions, the player had doubled rooks on active files/ranks, and the disambiguation notation (R3, R7, Rg, Rh, R6) confirms two coordinated rooks were available. The common error is choosing to 'improve' the rook's position when the position demanded an immediate forcing blow. Position 7 (0 cp loss) appears to be a near-miss where all reasonable moves were equivalent.

482.label: Player resolves tension with an obvious capture instead of finding a stronger forcing move (usually a check or mate) that exploits specific tactical vulnerabilities.
482.description: 8/10 positions involve the player making a capture (6/10 are specifically pawn captures resolving central tension like exd3, fxe5, exd6, gxf6, dxe5). In at least 5/10 positions, the missed best move was a check or checkmate (Qa5+ in positions 1 and 9, Qd5+ in position 3, Qxb2# in position 5, and Qxd5 exploiting a hanging pawn in position 8). All 10 positions had only ~1 good move available (avg 1.1), indicating critical moments where precision was essential. The consistent error is defaulting to 'take what's offered' — the capture looks productive (winning a pawn, simplifying, gaining tempo) but actually squanders a much larger advantage. The 2 non-capture moves (Ne2 in position 4, Rc2 in position 10) still fit the broader pattern of choosing a 'logical-looking' quiet move over a specific tactical counter-blow (Nd3 blockading, Nd4 attacking). The average cp_loss of 1292 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — the reflex to capture blinds the player to geometric tactical patterns in the position.

499.label: A pawn attacks an aggressively-posted knight expecting retreat, but the knight leaps forward to deliver a devastating fork instead.
499.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical pattern: a pawn move attacks a knight on an advanced square (b5, g5, d5, or b4), assuming the knight must retreat, but the knight instead jumps one square further forward to deliver a crushing fork. Specifically, 5/10 positions feature ...a6 attacking a Nb5 which responds Nc7+ forking king on e8 and rook on a8. 3/10 feature ...h6 attacking a Ng5 which responds Nxf7 or Nf7 forking queen and rook. 2/10 feature a3 attacking a Nb4 which responds ...Nc2+ forking king on e1 and rook on a1. 1/10 features ...e6 attacking Nd5 which responds Nc7+. In every case the knight's forward destination is a fork square that was already tactically available before the pawn push—the pawn move wastes a critical tempo without addressing the real threat. 8/10 positions occur in the opening phase with uncastled kings, and the average centipawn loss is 364, indicating these are catastrophic blunders.

497.label: A rook is moved onto an open file where the opponent's queen can immediately capture it, initiating a favorable exchange sequence.
497.description: All 9/9 positions share an identical tactical pattern: a rook is moved to an open file (d-file in 6 cases, c-file in 2, a-file in 1) where the opponent's queen already controls that same file, allowing the queen to simply capture the rook. In 9/9 cases, the primary refutation is Qx(rook). The resulting exchange sequences are unfavorable because: in 5/9 positions, after the rook recaptures, a back-rank check or recapture wins additional material; in 3/9 positions, the queen capture leaves another piece (often the player's own queen) undefended on an open file; in 1/9, the exchange voluntarily trades away a dominant piece configuration for an inferior one. The opponent consistently had a Queen+Rook battery (or Queen alone) already established on the contested file. The player's intent in every case was the natural-looking idea of 'contesting the open file,' but they overlooked that their rook was stepping directly into the opponent's queen's capture square without adequate support or favorable recapture possibilities.

492.label: Pawn captures that remove a structurally critical defender for trivial material gain, catastrophically exposing the position to immediate tactical exploitation.
492.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (pxp) where the moving pawn was performing a vital defensive function — blocking a dangerous diagonal, shielding the king along an open file, or defending a key square. In 8/10 cases, the removed pawn was specifically blocking an opponent's piece from accessing a critical line: Position 1 and 10 (d-pawn blocking a bishop diagonal to b7/protecting c6), Position 3 (h-pawn keeping the h-file closed against a rook), Position 5 (d4-pawn blocking the a1-h8 diagonal), Position 7 (b-pawn providing a barrier against a-file invasion), Position 8 (g-pawn keeping opponent's bishop passive on f7), Position 9 (f-pawn restraining a passed d-pawn). In 2/10 cases (Positions 2 and 6), the capture was a tempo-wasting wing pawn grab while urgent tactical threats (queen infiltration, g-file exploitation) demanded immediate attention. The average cp_loss of 2043 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 4/10 resulting in forced mate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these occurred at critical decision points where accuracy was paramount.

483.label: Playing an ambitious attacking move (especially a flank pawn advance) in a critical position that demands defensive precision, ignoring the opponent's stronger immediate threats.
483.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player makes an aggressive-looking move when the position demands something else entirely. 6/10 moves are flank pawn advances (g4 appears 3 times, h4 once, g5 once, b5 once), while the remaining 4 are greedy/speculative piece moves (Nxb7 material grab, Nc4 piece repositioning, Rb1 rook activation attempt, Rg7+ speculative sacrifice). In every case, the position offered very few good alternatives (average 1.8 good moves), meaning these were knife-edge situations requiring precision. The correct moves in 8/10 positions were quiet, defensive, or restrictive (Kf1, Re1, Kg3, Re8, Qd3+, g3), but instead the player chose loud, forward-looking actions. 7/10 positions involved the player ignoring their own king safety vulnerability, and 8/10 resulted in the opponent immediately exploiting a weakness that the move either created (weakened pawn shield) or left unaddressed (back-rank threats, hanging pieces, diagonal attacks). The psychological thread is consistent: the player 'does something active' rather than addressing the real positional demand.

487.label: Playing an aggressive-looking piece penetration (usually rook to the 7th rank) instead of the position's actual critical requirement.
487.description: 7/10 positions feature rook moves, with 6 of those specifically placing the rook on the 7th rank (Re7, Rf7+, Rh7, Rf7+, Re7, Rb7). The remaining moves (Bc5+, Qb2, Qa3) share the same structural error: choosing a superficially aggressive or 'impressive' move over the objectively critical action. In 3/10 positions, the correct move was an immediate checkmate or forced mating sequence that was missed in favor of a penetrating rook move (positions 3, 4, 8). In 3/10 positions, the aggressive move abandoned a critical defensive function—protecting a piece (Rb7 left knight hanging), restraining a passed pawn (Rf7+ instead of Rc8), or maintaining a defensive mechanism (Rf7+ disrupted recapture on a8). In 2/10 positions, a pointless check was given that either drove the opponent's king to a better square or squandered a decisive tactical resource (Bc5+, Rf7+). The average cp_loss of 4041 reflects that these 'strong-looking' moves often miss something catastrophic. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these were positions requiring precision where the seductive aggressive option was uniquely punishing.

498.label: Queen (or key piece) captures tempting material but abandons a critical defensive or controlling function, allowing devastating tactical punishment.
498.description: 10/10 positions feature a capture of hanging or undefended material (pawns in 6/10, knights in 3/10, bishop in 1/10), with 9/10 being queen captures specifically. In every case, the capturing piece was performing a vital role before the capture: controlling key squares (Positions 5, 8), blocking diagonal/file attacks (Position 7), defending the king zone (Positions 1, 2, 4, 6), or staying out of tactical lines (Position 9). After the greedy capture, 8/10 positions are punished through king safety exploitation (perpetual checks, mating attacks, or decisive invasions), while 1/10 involves a discovered attack and 1/10 a hanging piece. The average cp_loss of 4118 is catastrophic, with 5/10 positions resulting in forced mate or near-mate evaluations. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions requiring discipline over greed.

501.label: A knight is jumped to a visually impressive central outpost (d5/e5/e4/d6) while abandoning a critical defensive duty on its original square.
501.description: All 10 positions feature a knight moving to a classically attractive central outpost square — 4/10 play Nd5, 3/10 play Ne5, 2/10 play Ne4, and 1/10 plays Nd6. In 9/10 cases, the knight departs from c3 or f3 (standard defensive knight posts) to reach these advanced squares. The universal error is that the knight was performing a vital but non-obvious defensive function: in 4/10 positions (Nc3→d5), the knight was guarding the e4 square, and its departure allows ...e4 or a piece capture exploiting the unguarded square. In 3/10 positions (Nf3→e5), the knight was preventing queen checks (Qh4+) or protecting the king/other pieces. In 2/10 positions (Nf6→e4), the knight's move leaves another piece undefended or invites a structurally damaging exchange. 8/10 positions involve White making the error. The average cp_loss is 259, indicating severe punishment. Only 2.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points requiring precision rather than attractive-looking aggression.

491.label: Bishop passively retreats to the player's own back rank (or board edge), often to blockade a passed pawn, sacrificing activity and tempo for static defense.
491.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to a square on rank 1, rank 8, or the a-file edge — all destination squares (a7, h8, b7, a1, a1, b1, a8, c1, e8, d1) lie on the absolute perimeter of the board. In 8/10 positions, the move involves the bishop retreating to the player's own back rank specifically. At least 6/10 positions involve a passed pawn where the bishop is being deployed as a passive blockader on or near the promotion square (positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 1126 is inflated by one extreme case, but 6/10 positions show losses of 130-592cp. Notably, 2/10 positions (1 and 6) show the move as actually best — indicating the feature detects the *pattern* of back-rank bishop deployment regardless of correctness, though it overwhelmingly correlates with error. The phase is predominantly endgame (8/10), consistent with passed-pawn scenarios where blockade decisions arise.

496.label: Knight relocates to a superficially attractive square while abandoning its essential positional or tactical function, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated role.
496.description: 8/10 positions feature knight moves (Nd2, Ne5, Nc7, Nd3, Nd7, Nf2, Nd7+, Nd3), making this overwhelmingly a knight-specific pattern. In at least 7/10 cases, the knight moves AWAY from its optimal square or fails to occupy it: Position 7 and 9 both abandon the c5 outpost for Nd7; Position 8 abandons the e4 outpost for Nf2; Position 10 goes to d3 instead of the blockading d5; Position 5 leaves a6 (supporting b-pawn promotion) for Nc7; Position 6 plays Nd3 prematurely before the critical pawn push. The moved-to squares consistently LOOK active—they attack pieces, give checks, or appear centralized—but the knight's departure from its critical post enables opponent counterplay: passed pawns promote (Positions 5, 6, 10), mating combinations dissolve (Position 9), outposts are seized by the opponent (Position 8), or pieces are left hanging (Positions 1, 4). The average cp_loss of 2089 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments about what the knight's most important job is.

494.label: Playing a non-forcing 'improving' move (piece repositioning or pawn push) when an immediate forcing tactical blow—typically a capture or check—was required.
494.description: In 10/10 positions, the played move was a quiet, non-forcing attempt to improve piece placement or gain space (6/10 piece repositionings: Bf5, Qg5, Qe2, Bg5, Rg3, Bb5; 4/10 positional pawn pushes: d6, c4, g4, b4). In 7/10 cases, the correct move was an immediate capture or check (Qxc5, Nxc3, Qxb2+, Nxg5, Nxe5, Rxf7+, plus Qxc5-style captures), while the remaining 3/10 required urgent consolidation (O-O, Kg1, h3/g6). The average number of good moves was only 1.8, confirming these were narrow critical moments demanding specific concrete action. The played moves all share the quality of 'looking active'—placing pieces on aggressive-seeming squares or pushing pawns for space—while completely ignoring the tactical demands of the position. The astronomical average cp_loss of 1249 reflects how catastrophic it is to play slowly in razor-sharp positions.

506.label: A pawn capture removes the file-blocker, exposing an undefended piece (rook or queen) to immediate capture on the newly opened file.
506.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing sideways (always the format [file]x[file]), which removes that pawn from its original file and opens it completely. In every case, the player's own piece (rook or queen) sits undefended on that newly opened file, and the opponent already has a major piece (rook or queen) aligned on the same file ready to capture it immediately. Specifically: 3/10 are hxg4 opening the h-file to a rook capture (positions 1, 4, 5), 2/10 are a-pawn captures opening the a-file to Rxa1 (positions 2, 6), 2/10 are c-pawn captures opening the c-file to queen/rook capture (positions 9, 10), 2/10 are d-pawn captures opening the d-file (positions 3, 7), and 1/10 is fxe4 opening the f-file (position 8). The punished piece is a rook in 8/10 cases and a queen in 2/10 cases. The opponent's capturing piece is already pre-aimed on the file before the pawn moves, making the refutation a simple one-move tactic in every instance.

507.label: A quiet one-square advance of a flank pawn (a, b, g, or h file) when the position urgently demands immediate tactical or active play.
507.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square advance of a rim or near-rim pawn (h6 in 4 cases, a6 in 2, b3 in 2, a3 in 1, g6 in 1, h3 in 1) played with vague 'prophylactic' or 'consolidating' intent. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand: 8/10 involved a dangerous passed pawn that needed immediate attention (either blocking, capturing, or racing against), 5/10 had a hanging piece or pawn that could be captured immediately, and 9/10 required immediate king activation or piece mobilization. The average number of good moves was only 1.8, meaning these were critical decision points with very narrow margins. The tactical motif in 9/10 positions was explicitly 'tempo_loss' — the flank pawn move accomplished nothing concrete while granting the opponent a free move to execute their plan (advance a passed pawn, activate their king, deliver a check, or seize a critical file). The punishments typically involved the opponent gaining one decisive tempo for king centralization (6/10) or advancing a passed pawn to an unstoppable position (7/10).

489.label: Player makes an intuitive or natural-looking move in a position where only one specific (often non-obvious) move avoids catastrophe.
489.description: All 10 positions share the critical characteristic of having essentially only one acceptable move (avg 1.2 good moves available) combined with catastrophic punishment for alternatives (avg 2136 cp_loss). In 5/10 positions the blunder was a capture that seemed natural (Qxd7, Rxd6, Rxc1, cxd6, Qxe7), while 3/10 involved quiet/prophylactic moves when forcing play was required (g3, g3, Bg5), and 2/10 were active moves to wrong squares (Rc8+, Rd1). Notably, 3/10 positions feature 'wrong piece to the right square' (Rxc1 vs Bxc1, Qxe7 vs Ndxe7, g3 vs Rg3), where the player identified the correct target square but used the wrong unit. In 8/10 positions, the played move either abandoned a critical defensive duty (rook leaving f1/d5, pawn blocking g3 retreat) or created a fatal vulnerability (opening files toward own king, placing pieces on hanging squares, creating pins). The best moves were consistently non-obvious: defensive king moves (Kd8), quiet repositioning (Ra1), non-greedy recaptures (Bxc1), or forcing queen maneuvers (Qb8+, Qh5+).

495.label: Playing non-forcing pawn pushes or greedy captures in positions that demand immediate tactical precision, missing checks, forks, or forced mates.
495.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn advances (d5, d6, h5, e4, b5, b5, c6, c7) that look aggressive or progressive but ignore the tactical demands of the position. The remaining 2/10 (Qxd2, Rc8) similarly chose 'natural-looking' moves over critical forcing continuations. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 6, and the analysis of position 9), the best move involved immediate checks or forced mating sequences. In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 6, 7), the pawn advance directly exposed the player's own king or opened lines to it. In 3/10 cases (positions 8, 10, and partially 2), the pawn advance was premature because it lacked piece support and could be immediately captured or blockaded. The average good moves available was only 2.0, confirming these were sharp positions with narrow paths to success. The average cp_loss of 3175 reflects that these 'natural' moves were catastrophic, often converting forced mates or decisive advantages into losing or equal positions.

505.label: A non-forcing rook repositioning move is played in a position demanding immediate tactical or forcing action from other pieces.
505.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking rook move to a seemingly natural square (open file, central file, or active rank) in positions that urgently demanded concrete forcing action. In 10/10 cases, the best move involved a DIFFERENT piece (bishop, queen, knight, or pawn) executing an immediate tactical strike or addressing a critical threat. The average cp_loss of 1179 is enormous, and only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were razor-sharp positions requiring precise calculation rather than general development. In 8/10 positions, the primary tag was 'tempo_loss' — the rook move gave the opponent a free tempo to either consolidate (5/10 positions where the player had the initiative) or intensify their attack (5/10 positions where the player was under pressure). In 7/10 positions, king safety was a critical factor that the rook move failed to address. The positions span both attacking scenarios (where Qe5, Bg5, f4 were needed to maintain initiative) and defensive emergencies (where Qd6, Bb3, Nd2 were needed to defuse threats).

488.label: A pawn advance that removes the pawn's critical role of protecting an adjacent piece, pawn, or key square, leaving something tactically vulnerable.
488.description: In 7/10 positions, the blundered pawn move directly removed the sole pawn defender of a neighboring piece or pawn: Position 1 (d4 unguards e4 pawn), Position 3 (g4 unguards h4 bishop), Position 4 (f4 unguards g4 bishop), Position 5 (h5 unguards g5 bishop), Position 6 (d5 unguards e5 pawn), Position 9 (e5 unguards d3 bishop/d5 square), and Position 10 (c5 unguards d5 pawn). In 2/10 positions (Positions 2 and 7), the pawn advance indirectly weakened the defensive structure enabling enemy pieces to reach protected targets (b5 opened the c-file allowing Nc3 to hit e4; g3 removed g2's support of the f3 knight). Only 1/10 (Position 8, h6) fits less cleanly as a tempo loss rather than direct guard removal. All 10 moves are single-step pawn advances, all are non-captures, and all leave material immediately or near-immediately hanging. The average cp_loss of 2085 reflects that removing a guard often triggers catastrophic tactical consequences including forced mate (2/10 positions).

503.label: King moves toward or near critical passed pawns (1-2 squares from promotion) when a piece should handle the blockade/support, creating fatal tactical vulnerabilities or losing tempo in the pawn race.
503.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves (the exception being c4, which still mishandles a passed pawn situation). All 10 positions contain at least one passed pawn within 1-2 squares of promotion. In 7/10 cases, the correct approach was to use a piece (bishop in 5 cases, rook in 2) rather than the king to blockade or support the critical pawn. The king moves create geometric catastrophes: in 3/10 the king walks onto a square allowing promotion with check or a fork (positions 5, 6, 10); in 3/10 the king blocks its own piece's critical line (positions 1, 4, 10); in 4/10 the king abandons a defensive post the pawn needed guarded (positions 3, 7, 8, 9). The average cp_loss of 1384 reflects that near-promotion positions are maximally punishing of tempo errors. The moves all appear 'logical' as king centralizations or king approaches toward the action, but they fatally misunderstand that pieces, not the king, should manage promotion-stage passed pawns.

502.label: A minor piece (usually a bishop) is moved to a seemingly active square instead of addressing an urgent tactical demand — typically a winning capture, critical defense, or forcing counterplay.
502.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves and all 10 involve quiet, non-forcing minor piece repositioning to squares that appear strategically appealing (centralized, aimed at the opponent's king, or on 'better' diagonals). In 4/10 cases, the player missed a straightforward winning capture (Nxb5 winning a rook, Nxd7 capturing a queen, Bxa1 taking a hanging rook, Nxc3 eliminating an intruder). In 3/10 cases specifically, a fianchettoed bishop on b7 was slid forward one square to c6, looking like a natural improvement but missing the critical resource (Bf3 tactical shot, queen evacuation, or capturing the opponent's queen). In the remaining cases, the missed best moves were defensive necessities (Na6 blocking a mating check, Qf1 protecting the king, Re6 challenging a dominant queen). The consistent thread is that the player sees a 'nice' square for their bishop/knight and prioritizes aesthetic piece placement over the actual tactical demands of the position. Average cp_loss of 1255 reflects that these seemingly innocuous moves often squander decisive advantages or allow forced wins.

508.label: A bishop is aggressively sent to the h-file or corner squares (h1, h2, h7, g2, f2) where it becomes stranded, trapped, or disconnected from the position.
508.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to the kingside edge of the board — specifically the h-file or immediately adjacent corner squares. 8/10 land directly on the h-file (h1, h2, or h7), with the remaining two on g2 and f2. 4/10 are failed Greek Gift sacrifices (Bh7+) where the king simply sidesteps with Kh8 or Kf8, leaving the bishop stranded with no follow-up. 2/10 feature Bh1 where the bishop is immediately sealed in by f2-f3 or becomes disconnected from the defense. 2/10 feature Bh2/Bh2+ where the bishop is trapped by g2-g3 or lacks escape squares. The refutations are consistently simple: in 6/10 positions the king merely sidesteps a check (Kh8, Kf8, Kh1), and in 3/10 a single pawn advance (f3 or g3) permanently entombs the bishop. The average cp_loss of 339 reflects that these moves typically cost between a large positional concession and a full piece. 7/10 positions had 2-3 good alternatives available, meaning the aggressive bishop lunge was chosen despite safe, solid options being readily accessible.

509.label: Queen moves to aggressive kingside squares (often with check) that look threatening but miss stronger concrete continuations, typically non-queen tactics.
509.description: 10/10 positions feature queen moves to attacking squares aimed at the opponent's king (g4, g5, h4, h5, f6, e4, a4). 6/10 deliver check, and nearly all target kingside squares on ranks 4-6. The core error in 8/10 positions (the ones with cp_loss > 0) is choosing the 'flashy' queen move over a more concrete tactical blow: in Position 4, Qh4 before the preparatory Bxh2+ sacrifice; in Position 8, Qe4+ instead of the devastating Nf4+ fork; in Position 10, Qg4+ instead of the deflection f3+; in Position 5, Qg4 instead of the precise Qh5; in Position 1, Qf6+ allowing Nf3 interposition versus the forcing Qh4+. In 7/10 cases, the superior alternative was either a non-queen move (Nf4+, f3+, Bxh2+, Rxe5, dxe5, Kxf8) or the queen to a different, more precise square. The moves share a common psychological pull: they appear to maintain or create attacking momentum but actually surrender tempo, allow productive blocks/trades, or abandon coverage of critical squares.

500.label: Playing a natural-looking positional move (pawn advance, quiet development, prophylaxis) while missing an immediate tactical obligation such as capturing a hanging piece, saving a threatened piece, or executing a critical intermezzo.
500.description: In 8/10 positions, the player chose a move that looks 'normal' or positionally reasonable—fianchettoing a bishop, advancing a pawn, capturing a threatening pawn—but completely missed that the position demanded an immediate concrete action. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 10), a piece was hanging (either the opponent's to capture or their own to save), yet the player made a routine developing or prophylactic move instead. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 8), a pawn was advanced rather than capturing with it, where the capture was decisively superior (gxf6 instead of g6, hxg3 instead of h3). In 2/10 positions (3, 4), Black played Bg7 instead of capturing White's undefended bishop on h6 with Nxh6/Bxh6. Position 6 shows a wrong move order—capturing material without the critical intermezzo check first. Position 9 shows an unsound sacrifice that looks aggressive but has no follow-up. The average cp_loss of 1395 and average good moves of only 1.8 confirm these are critical moments where only 1-2 concrete moves work, yet the player defaulted to a 'textbook' looking move.

504.label: Aggressive-looking knight moves to active squares (often with check or attacking a piece) that miss a stronger continuation or allow a counter-tactic.
504.description: 10/10 positions feature knight moves to seemingly powerful central or aggressive squares (e4 appears 3 times, plus f5, c3, f3, d5, c4, f4, e5). 5/10 deliver check and 4/10 directly attack the opponent's queen, making them appear forcing and strong. However, 8/10 are genuine mistakes (cp_loss >100). The errors break into consistent sub-types: in 3/10 positions (4, 5, 9) the knight goes to the WRONG aggressive square when a different destination was winning (Nf3+ instead of Nc4+, Nd5 instead of Nb5, Ne5 instead of Ng5+). In 3/10 positions (3, 7, 8) the knight move is premature — checking or capturing before executing a stronger preparatory move first (promoting before checking, pushing a pawn before checking). In 2/10 positions (1, 10) the knight lands on an active square but becomes tactically vulnerable or opens a counter-tactic. The common psychological trap is that knights on central squares delivering checks or attacks FEEL decisive, seducing players into insufficient calculation.

511.label: Advancing a pawn aggressively before repositioning pieces to support or benefit from the break, releasing tension or abandoning key defensive duties.
511.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances (d5, c5, e5, b4, f4, g5, e4, g6, c5, f3) played without the necessary piece preparation. In 9/10 cases, the best move was a piece repositioning (Ne5, Rc1, Rfe1, Qd6, Rg8, Nf6, Bxe6+, Rh8, Ra3/Nf6) that either prepared the same break for later or maintained the existing pawn tension that favored the player. In 8/10 positions, the premature advance released central or flank tension that the opponent exploited by opening lines for their own pieces. In 7/10 positions, the advanced pawn was actively performing a defensive duty—guarding a critical square (c6 guarding b5/d5, e5 controlling d4, f4 shielding king)—that was abandoned by the push. The tactical motif was 'positional_mistake' in 7/10 cases, confirming these are strategic rather than calculational errors. The average cp_loss of 255 reflects how severely premature breaks damage positions that were otherwise sound or even advantageous.

512.label: Playing a quiet, developing, or repositioning bishop move when the position demands an immediate forcing strike — typically a knight leap or sacrifice.
512.description: All 10 positions feature bishop moves that prioritize natural-looking development, repositioning, or non-critical captures/checks over urgent tactical demands. In 10/10 cases, the played move is a bishop move; in 9/10 cases, the best move was with a different piece entirely (6/10 demanded a knight move to an aggressive square: Nf4, Nxa6+, Nf6, Nb4, Nf5 twice; 2/10 demanded a bishop sacrifice with check: Bxh7+, Bxf5+; 1/10 a queen check). The bishop moves appear positionally logical — developing to active diagonals (Be6, Bb7, Bf5, Be3), centralizing (Bd4, Bf3), or giving check (Bh2+, Bxe3+) — but all share the fatal flaw of being non-forcing or insufficiently forcing, granting the opponent a critical tempo to execute counterplay, resolve tension, or consolidate. Average cp_loss is 231, with only 1.3 good moves available on average, indicating these are precision-demanding positions where the 'natural' bishop move is almost always the wrong choice.

515.label: A knight makes a tempting aggressive move (capture, centralization, or attack) but fatally vacates a square or role that was essential for defensive integrity.
515.description: All 10/10 positions involve knight moves that appear active or tactical but catastrophically abandon the knight's critical positional or defensive function. In 6/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10), the knight was specifically guarding the king—either covering invasion squares (e5, g3, h3) or blocking dangerous diagonals/files aimed at the monarch—and its departure enabled immediate tactical exploitation of king vulnerability. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 6, 9), the knight captured a pawn or piece that looked attractive but gave up a dominant centralization (d5 in positions 3 and 5) or attempted an unsound sacrifice. In 4/10 cases (4, 7, 8, 10), the knight moved to a square that looked aggressive but was tactically refutable—either hanging to a capture-with-check, enabling a queen invasion, or simply misplacing the piece on the rim. The refutations consistently exploit the exact square or function the knight vacated: Qe5+ after f6 is abandoned (positions 5, 7), Qg3+ after g3 is abandoned (position 2), Qb5+ after c6 is abandoned (position 10), and Qh8+/diagonal exploitation after f6 is vacated (positions 5, 9). Average cp_loss of 302 confirms these are severe errors, not marginal inaccuracies.

510.label: Advancing a pawn one square forward in an endgame position, often without proper preparation through king activation, captures, or correct move order.
510.description: All 10/10 positions involve a single-square pawn advance, and 8/10 occur in endgame positions (the remaining 2 are late middlegame/endgame transitions). The moves target central and kingside files: e-file (3x), d-file (2x), g-file (2x), f-file (2x), c-file (1x), advancing predominantly to the 5th or 6th rank. Notably, 4/10 positions show 0 cp loss — these are cases where advancing a clearly passed pawn toward promotion IS correct (positions 2, 4, 6, 9 all involve unstoppable passed pawns). However, the remaining 6/10 are genuine mistakes averaging ~233 cp loss, where the pawn push was premature. The feature appears to detect the broad pattern of 'pawn advances in simplified positions' — a move type that is highly tempting but requires precise timing. Kings are exposed in all positions (no castled positions), and pawn structure decisions are irreversible.

516.label: Moving a bishop to an aesthetically pleasing square while neglecting urgent tactical or positional demands in the position.
516.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop repositioning move that appears to centralize, activate, or improve the bishop's placement, but catastrophically ignores a more pressing need. The average cp_loss of 2106 reflects the severity of these errors. In 3/10 positions (3, 6, 8), the bishop move ignores direct king safety threats including immediate checkmate. In 3/10 positions (1, 7, 9), the move places the bishop where it can be challenged or where a piece becomes trapped/lost. In 2/10 positions (4, 5), the bishop abandons a critical restraining role, allowing the opponent a tempo-gaining pawn push that transforms the position. In 2/10 positions (2, 10), the bishop move leaves material hanging or invites a tactical invasion. The consistent thread is prioritizing 'where does the bishop look best?' over 'what does the position actually require?' — every position had at least 1 good move (avg 1.6) that addressed the real issue, yet the player chose bishop aesthetics over concrete necessity.

518.label: A routine rook-to-open-file move played when the position demands a specific concrete action (tactic, defense, or precise file choice).
518.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing rook move to a central or semi-open file (e, d, c, or f), appearing to 'improve' the rook's placement in a standard positional manner. However, in every case the position demanded something far more concrete: 7/10 positions had a specific tactic available (Nb5 fork, Nf5-Ne7+ fork, Nxg3+ mating sacrifice, Rf7+ king attack, Rxb4 winning a piece, etc.), while the remaining positions required urgent defensive measures or precise move-order considerations. The average cp_loss of 2152 is extraordinarily high, and 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating razor-sharp moments where generic improvement was catastrophic. In 4/10 cases the rook went to the wrong file specifically (e1 instead of f1, c1 instead of b1, d1 instead of e1), blocked by the player's own pieces. The connecting thread is a 'developing instinct' overriding concrete calculation—the player defaults to the heuristic of 'put rook on open file' when the position screams for a forcing continuation.

517.label: Advancing a flank pawn in the endgame when king centralization or activation was the priority.
517.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances, and every single move is on a wing file (a, b, f, g, or h — never a central d/e pawn). 9/10 positions are endgames. In the positions with meaningful cp_loss (positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10), the best move was almost always a KING move: Position 3's best was Kf5 (king to the exact square the pawn advanced to!), Position 5's best was Kd5/Kd4, Position 8's best was Kf4, Position 9's best was Kc5. The pawn advances create static targets (3/10 created fixed weaknesses that were captured), self-block the king (position 1 where g5 sealed the king's escape), or simply waste critical tempo (7/10 tagged as tempo_loss). The feature captures the specific error of choosing a passive/premature flank pawn push over dynamic king play in endgame positions where both kings are exposed and king activity is paramount.

514.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active but unprotected square where it becomes a tactical target, typically lost through checks or discovered attacks.
514.description: In 7/10 positions, the blundering move places a rook or knight on an undefended square that appears active but is immediately exploitable through forcing tactics. In 6/10 cases, the piece is directly won or captured via check sequences (Positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 7) or discovered attacks (Position 7). The moves share a common psychological pattern: they look purposeful—centralizing (Nd5), attacking (Rxa6, Ra6), activating (Rh5, Rh7, Rbg5)—but fatally overlook that the destination square lacks protection, enabling the opponent to win material with tempo. In 3/10 positions (3, 9, 10), the piece abandons a critical defensive/offensive post, enabling tactical exploitation of the vacated square or file rather than direct capture of the moved piece itself. Only 1/10 (Position 5) showed no actual error. The average cp_loss of 2086 reflects that these 'active' moves frequently collapse positions from winning/equal to lost in a single move.

520.label: An aggressive but non-forcing pawn advance played when a concrete piece tactic (check, capture, or fork) was available.
520.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance (f-pawn: 4, g-pawn: 3, d-pawn: 2, e-pawn: 1) chosen instead of a far superior move. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a forcing piece move involving a check or capture (Nxf2+ fork, Qh5+ mate, Nc6 winning queen, Rxf8+ favorable trade, Nh4+ checking sequence, Rf2 double attack). The pawn pushes all look aggressive—gaining space or attacking opponent pieces—but are fundamentally slow and non-forcing, giving the opponent time to consolidate or counterattack. In 5/10 positions, the pawn advance actively weakened the player's own position (exposing squares, allowing en passant, or surrendering critical pawn-capture resources). The average cp_loss of 1249 and average of only 1.3 good moves available confirm these were critical moments requiring tactical precision, where the player defaulted to a positional instinct instead of calculating forcing sequences.

524.label: A slow central pawn advance (d/e file) played as a positional move while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis requiring urgent attention.
524.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing central pawn push (7x e6, 1x e5, 1x e3, 2x d3, 1x d6) played as if the position were calm and developmental, when in fact an immediate tactical emergency existed. In 4/10 positions, the move left a piece directly hanging (bishop on h5, queen on d1, rook on a8, knight on c6). In 3/10 positions, the pawn move exposed another piece to a winning attack (queen vulnerable to fork, knight vulnerable to g5, f7 exposed to sacrifice). In 1/10 the pawn move literally enabled immediate checkmate by opening a rank. In 2/10 the move wasted a critical tempo when forced defensive moves were required. The average cp_loss of 1254 reflects that these aren't minor inaccuracies but catastrophic failures to address concrete threats. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise responses—yet the players chose generic structural moves instead.

513.label: Pawn advances or captures that prematurely release critical tension, block own pieces, or waste tempo when concrete piece action was required.
513.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves as the blunder. In 9/10 cases, the best alternative was a piece move or purposeful piece capture (Qf6, Nh4, Bh5, Bxf3, Nxf3, exd5, hxg2, Bxg5). The pawn moves consistently make an irreversible commitment at the exact moment the position demands maintaining flexibility or forcing piece action. In 3/10 positions, the pawn advance directly blocked the player's own piece (g6 trapping a bishop, e5 blocking a fianchettoed bishop, h2+ blocking the h-file for an attacking rook). In 3/10 positions (all h5), the pawn advance left a bishop on g4 tactically vulnerable to capture. In 2/10 positions, a pawn capture released tension that was serving a critical defensive function (dxc3 removing a queen-blocking barrier, hxg6 removing the threat that protected a knight). In 1/10, a slow flank pawn push (a4) wasted tempo while an active knight needed to strike immediately. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.8 good moves), meaning these pawn commitments occur at moments where one wrong move is catastrophic.

521.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn move (typically h6/h3/d3/d6) when the position demands immediate tactical exploitation of a concrete vulnerability.
521.description: 8/10 positions feature one-square pawn pushes (h6×3, h3×1, d3×2, d6×2), with the remaining 2 being similarly non-forcing moves (Bd6, Qg5). In all 10 positions, a concrete tactical opportunity existed — winning material via fork (4/10), exploiting a hanging/undefended piece (3/10), or seizing a decisive initiative through forcing moves (3/10). The average cp_loss of 259 reflects that these aren't minor inaccuracies but critical-moment failures. 8/10 positions occurred in the opening phase where tempo is paramount. In 9/10 cases, at least one king remained uncastled, creating the tactical vulnerabilities that demanded immediate exploitation. The moves share a 'prophylactic' or 'solidifying' intent — preventing Bg5 pins (h6), supporting the center (d3/d6), or securing pawns (h3) — but all catastrophically waste the one tempo needed to execute a winning combination before the opponent consolidates.

529.label: Capturing a piece on the exact square where an enemy passed pawn can recapture with promotion.
529.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical geometric pattern: the player captures a piece sitting on the promotion square (8th/1st rank) of an enemy passed pawn that is one square from queening. In every case, the enemy pawn recaptures on that square and promotes simultaneously (e.g., gxh8=Q, axb8=Q, cxd1=Q, bxa1=Q, dxc1=Q, dxe8=Q, cxb1=Q). The captures are overwhelmingly rook captures (9/10) with one queen capture. The promoted piece is devastating in all cases: in 3/10 positions the promotion delivers immediate checkmate, in 3/10 it comes with check gaining tempo, and in the remaining 4/10 it simply creates overwhelming material advantage. The best moves instead either capture the pawn itself (3/10), move the king off the back rank first (3/10), or retreat/reposition to avoid the promotion square entirely (4/10). Average cp_loss is enormous (~4753) because these moves typically convert survivable positions into forced mates or crushing material deficits.

527.label: A slow pawn push attempts to drive away an active enemy knight that has a superior tactical destination available, wasting a critical tempo.
527.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn move (a3 in 6 cases, g6 in 2, plus b3, c4, g4) played specifically to attack an enemy knight that appears dangerously active. In every single case, the knight does NOT need to retreat — instead it has a superior forward square available, typically delivering a fork (6/10: positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10), a check (3/10: positions 7, 8, 9), or enabling a central breakthrough (positions 1, 3). The attacked knights sat on b4 (6/10), f5 (2/10), h5 (1/10), and c4 (1/10), and their devastating destinations included d3 (fork in positions 6, 8), e5 (fork in position 10), d5 (outpost in position 2), d4 (outpost in positions 4, 5), f4 (outpost in position 5), and g7+ (check in positions 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 299 reflects how catastrophic this pattern is — the pawn move not only wastes tempo but often weakens the very squares the knight exploits.

522.label: Playing a slow, prophylactic rook-pawn push (a-pawn or h-pawn) when the position demands an immediate tactical blow.
522.description: 8/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing move played when a concrete winning or critical tactic was available. 6/10 moves are specifically single-step advances of the a-pawn (a6 x3) or h-pawn (h3, h6 x2) — the most peripheral, tempo-wasting pawn moves in chess. In 7/10 positions, the best available move was a piece capture or forcing tactical shot (Ng5, Nxd3, Rxe4, Bxf2+, Nxd5, Nxd4, Bxc7). The 'missed_tactic' tag appears in all 10 positions, and 'tempo_loss' appears in 8/10. The prophylactic intent is consistent: h3 to stop pawn advances, h6 to chase a knight, a6 to prevent pawn breaks or address queenside concerns. In each case, the player addressed a hypothetical future threat while ignoring a present tactical opportunity, gifting the opponent a free tempo to consolidate or execute their own plans. The average cp_loss of 2187 reflects that these positions were often at critical tactical crossroads where one tempo made the difference between winning and losing.

523.label: King decentralizes toward the board edge to approach and capture an enemy pawn in a pawn endgame.
523.description: 10/10 positions are pawn endgames (or near-pawn endgames) where the played move is a king step away from the center toward the edge of the board, targeting an enemy pawn for capture. In every case the king moves from a semi-central file (c, d, e, f, g) one square toward the rim (to b, f, g, or h files). 7/10 positions involve the king heading toward a specific enemy pawn on the wing (h7, g6, a6, b7, a2, a3, g5). When this is catastrophically wrong (3/10 positions with cp_loss >200: positions 3, 7, 9), the king abandons the center while the opponent's pawns on the opposite wing advance unchecked. When it's correct or near-correct (5/10 with cp_loss <30), the king is winning the pawn race because the opponent's king is too far away to create counterplay. The feature captures the specific decision point of 'should I walk my king toward this pawn or stay central/play a preparatory move first?'
523.old_chip: King marches to capture wing pawn

531.label: A knight captures a central pawn (d4/d5/e5) but lands on a square where it is immediately recaptured or creates no threats, resulting in material or tempo loss.
531.description: All 10/10 positions involve a knight capturing a central pawn on d4, d5, or e5 during the opening. In 7/10 cases (positions 1-5, 8, 9), the knight lands on the central square completely undefended, where it is immediately recaptured by an opponent's piece—typically a bishop on a diagonal (Bc4×d5, Bc5×d4, Bg7×d4) or another knight (Nf3×e5)—resulting in a clean piece loss for a pawn (avg ~280cp loss). In 3/10 cases (positions 6, 7, 10—identical positions), the knight recapture on d5 is technically legal but creates zero threats, squandering a development lead by giving the opponent a free tempo to castle (209cp loss each). The unifying thread is a 'natural-looking' knight capture of a central pawn that ignores a basic safety check: is the knight defended on its destination square, and does it create sufficient threats to justify landing there?

536.label: In King's Gambit positions, White prematurely captures fxe5 on move 3, removing the f4 pawn that shields the king on the h4-e1 diagonal, allowing Qh4+ winning the h1 rook.
536.description: All 10/10 positions are King's Gambit openings (1.e4 e5 2.f4) where White plays 3.fxe5 before developing any pieces. In every case, the f-pawn on f4 was the sole remaining barrier on the h4-e1 diagonal after f2 was vacated on move 2. By capturing on e5, White completely strips the diagonal of protection, enabling the devastating Qh4+ check. The refutation sequence Qh4+ → g3 → Qxe4+ → Qe2 → Qxh1 appears as the primary punishment in 10/10 positions, winning White's h1 rook via a queen fork on e4 that simultaneously checks the king and attacks the corner rook. The correct alternatives (Nf3, d3, Nc3, Bc4) all prioritize development or specifically guard h4 before resolving central tension. The average cp_loss is 353, equivalent to roughly a full rook — matching the material lost in the refutation line. 8/10 positions show the identical position after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 Nc6 3.fxe5, while 2/10 feature slight variations (2...d6 or 2...f5) but the same fatal mechanism.

533.label: A major piece (usually a rook) moves to a square where it is immediately captured for free by an opponent's bishop along a diagonal.
533.description: 10/10 positions show the exact same tactical oversight: a major piece moves to a square directly controlled by an enemy bishop's diagonal, and the bishop simply captures it. In 9/10 cases the blundering piece is a rook; 1/10 is a queen. The capturing bishop sits on a long diagonal (typically the a1-h8 or a8-h1 diagonal) and the player fails to notice its line of fire reaches the destination square. 7/10 of the moves are checks or attacks, suggesting the player is focused on the aggressive intent (harassing the king, attacking a pawn) rather than verifying the safety of the landing square. The refutation in all 10 cases is trivially simple: the bishop captures the piece outright, winning a full rook (or queen) for nothing. The average cp_loss of 2241 reflects these catastrophic material losses.

528.label: Playing a quiet king repositioning move when the position demands an immediate forcing capture or exchange with another piece.
528.description: All 10 positions feature king moves as the error. In 7/10 cases, the correct move was a concrete capture with a non-king piece (Rxf5, Rxd4, Nxe5, Qxf5, Nxf3, Nxe5, dxe4), while the player instead chose a passive king relocation. In the remaining 3/10, the king moved to the wrong square (Kb4 instead of Kb6, Kd6 instead of Kc4, and Kc3 which was actually near-optimal at only 4cp loss). The average cp_loss of 2291 reflects catastrophic consequences: positions with only 1.3 good moves on average meant these were 'only move' situations where a single forced tactical action was required. The king moves consistently represent a 'safety-first' or 'improve positioning' instinct that overrides the concrete tactical demand of the position—the player sees threats to their king and reflexively moves it, or seeks vague centralization, while the board screams for an immediate material exchange or capture.

526.label: Moving a bishop or knight to a seemingly active square where it is immediately capturable by an enemy piece, usually a rook controlling that file or rank.
526.description: 8/10 positions feature a minor piece (almost always a bishop) being placed on a square where it is directly hanging to an enemy piece, with the 'hanging_piece' tactical motif tagged explicitly in 8/10 cases. In 5/10 positions specifically, the bishop is placed on a square directly controlled by an enemy rook on the same file or rank (Bf7 hangs to Rf8, Bg3 hangs to Rf3, Bb2 hangs to Ra2, Be2 hangs to Re1, Bd3 hangs to Rd4). Position 1's Bf8 hangs to three pieces simultaneously. Position 3's Ne3 hangs to the king (Kxe3). Position 7's Nxc3 moves a defender away, leaving the queen hanging. The remaining 2/10 (positions 9-10) involve minor piece moves that ignore lethal back-rank mates, though even here the piece accomplishes nothing on its destination square. In all 10 cases, the player's intent was aggressive — attacking an enemy piece, penetrating enemy territory, or creating threats — but the piece lands on a square that is undefended and directly attacked. The average cp_loss of 2237 is extremely high, reflecting that these moves typically lose a full piece or worse.

519.label: Aggressive-looking moves (predominantly knight checks/attacks) that place pieces on squares where they are trivially captured by opponent pawns.
519.description: 7/10 positions involve knight moves played as aggressive attacks (checks, queen attacks, or forks). In 6/10 positions, the moved piece lands on a square directly capturable by an opponent's pawn (Ne6+ by fxe6, Nb5 by cxb5, Nf3+ by gxf3, Nxg3+ by hxg3, Qg6 by fxg6, Ne3 by fxe3). In the remaining positions, the aggressive move either leaves another piece hanging (Nh5 abandons queen defense, Rf4 leaves queen undefended) or ignores capturing an opponent's hanging piece (d5 instead of dxe5). The average good moves available was only 1.5, meaning these were critical positions demanding precision, yet players consistently chose the most visually aggressive option. 8/10 moves are checks, captures, or direct attacks on high-value pieces — the 'forcing' appearance seduced the player into overlooking that the move fundamentally loses material.

539.label: Playing a routine central pawn advance when the position demands an immediate tactical response to an urgent threat.
539.description: All 10/10 positions feature a one-square pawn advance (d5×3, e5×2, e4, d6, f3, f5, d3) played in lieu of addressing an immediate tactical emergency. In 10/10 cases, the best move was a piece move—king retreats (positions 1, 2, 3), knight retreats/captures (positions 5, 10), bishop captures (positions 4, 6), queen captures/trades (positions 7, 9), or a defensive pawn move addressing the specific threat (position 8). The pawn pushes all look structurally motivated—gaining space, challenging pawns, opening diagonals, supporting the center—but in every case they waste a critical tempo while an existential threat (checkmate in 2/10, king exposure in 5/10, hanging pieces in 2/10, weakening a critical defensive structure in 1/10) demands concrete action. The average cp_loss of 2274 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' moves are, with 2/10 allowing immediate forced mate.

535.label: Playing a routine king-safety move (usually castling) when the position demands immediate attention to hanging material or a forcing continuation.
535.description: 9/10 positions feature a king relocation move (7 castling O-O/O-O-O, plus Kb1 and Kc7), while 1/10 (Rb8) is a similarly quiet preparatory move. In all 10 cases, the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move that ignores an urgent tactical requirement. In 6/10 positions (1, 3, 7, 8, 10, and partially 2), the blunder leaves a piece or central pawn completely undefended, allowing the opponent to simply capture it. In 2/10 positions (5, 9), the player missed a devastating forcing continuation (e6+ check, Rxh2 sacrifice) that the quiet move gives the opponent time to neutralize. In 1/10 (position 6), castling queenside places the king directly into a tactical vulnerability (Bxc3 exploiting the open b-file). The average cp_loss of 1164 reflects that several of these squander winning or mating advantages. The consistent thread is treating the position as if it's still in 'development mode' when concrete calculation is demanded.

540.label: Passive knight (or minor piece) repositioning moves played in positions demanding immediate concrete tactical action or urgent defensive measures.
540.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves and 1/10 a bishop move — all are quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning maneuvers to seemingly 'better' squares. In every case, the position demanded something concrete and immediate: 5/10 missed a winning tactical shot (Bxc3, Nxd5, Nxe5, Qxe3, or a5 maintaining initiative), 4/10 missed urgent king safety measures (Kf1, Nf1/Kf2, g5 driving away an attacker, or Kh1/Bg2), and 1/10 missed a critical prophylactic move. The average cp_loss of 1182 reflects catastrophic consequences. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise calculation rather than general improvement. Tags like 'tempo_loss' appear in 9/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 8/10. The moves all share the character of treating a critical tactical moment as if it were a quiet positional one.

525.label: A natural-looking quiet repositioning move that wastes a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent tactical or strategic requirement.
525.description: All 10 positions share the pattern of a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, no captures, no pawn breaks) that appears reasonable on the surface but fundamentally misjudges the position's urgency. In 8/10 positions, 'tempo_loss' was explicitly identified as a core issue. The moves are all repositioning/developing moves played when concrete action was demanded: king retreating to the wrong corner or direction (4/10: Kc7, Ka8, Kc8, Ke2), queen moving to a passive or vulnerable square (3/10: Qg2×2, Qd7), routine development ignoring a critical tactical issue (3/10: Re8×2, Bd7). In 8/10 cases, the best alternative involved immediate active counterplay (pawn breaks like c5, exchanges like Bxc3, or precise placement like Be6/Ke1). The average cp_loss of 1133 with only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are positions of high urgency where the slow move is catastrophically wrong. In 7/10 positions, the refutation exploits the tempo directly — executing a plan (f5 break, Nd5 jump, Bxe5-Bf6 maneuver, Nb5+ check) that the correct move would have prevented or contested.

534.label: Rook moves to the 1st or 8th rank (or remote edge square), abandoning a critical active post where it was restraining the opponent's threats.
534.description: All 10 positions feature a rook move to a passive or remote square. 8/10 moves specifically send the rook to the back rank (1st or 8th rank: Ra8, Rh1, Rc8, Ra8, Rh8, Re1, Rd1, Rh1), while the remaining 2 (Rc4, Ra6) still relocate the rook away from its critical active post. In every case, the rook was performing a vital function before the move—blockading a passed pawn (positions 6, 8), defending the king (positions 1, 7, 9), preventing enemy rook invasion (position 5), controlling a key file (positions 4, 8), or enabling a tactical combination (position 10). The average cp_loss of 1996 is extremely high, with 2/10 resulting in forced mate, demonstrating how catastrophic passive rook misplacement can be. 7/10 positions were endgames where rook activity is paramount. The common error is prioritizing a seemingly safe or 'reorganizing' square over maintaining the rook's active functional role.
534.old_chip: Rook retreats to passive back rank

530.label: Advancing a wing pawn when the king urgently needs to move to escape mating threats or blockade passed pawns.
530.description: All 10 positions feature pawn advances (on the a, b, f, g, or h files) in endgame positions where the king faces an existential crisis. In 8/10 positions, the best alternative was a king move (Ke2, Kd2, Kc3, Kf4, Kh3, Kh5, Kd6, Kf5). In 10/10 positions, the tag 'tempo_loss' was identified as a core issue. 9/10 positions are endgames with exposed kings — exactly the phase where king activity is paramount. The pawn pushes are strategically motivated (creating passed pawns, attacking opponent's pawns, gaining space) but catastrophically mistime the priority: the king needs immediate attention. The highest cp_loss positions (1, 2, 4, 7, 10 — all >9000cp) share the specific pattern of a pawn advance allowing an immediate mating net to close around the exposed king. Only 2/10 positions had cp_loss under 100, confirming this feature reliably detects severe blunders rather than minor inaccuracies.

532.label: Passive rook repositioning to natural-looking squares that ignores urgent tactical demands, often placing the rook directly into a knight fork vulnerability.
532.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves to seemingly logical squares (open files, defending pieces, escaping attacks) that miss more urgent tactical requirements. In 6/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 6, 10, and partially 3), the rook specifically lands on a square exploitable by a knight fork — either the rook itself gets forked with another piece (king, queen, or second rook), or the move enables a fork on a different target by failing to prevent it. In the remaining 4/10 positions (2, 7, 8, 9), the rook move is a generic positional idea (doubling rooks, contesting files, consolidating) that misses a concrete forcing sequence (checks, captures, or piece sacrifices). The average cp_loss of 302 confirms these are severe blunders despite looking 'natural.' Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating critical positions where concrete calculation was required rather than general principles. The consistent error is prioritizing rook placement logic (open files, material safety, passive defense) over immediate tactical calculation.

537.label: Playing a natural-looking bishop or queen developing/repositioning move that ignores immediate concrete tactical demands of the position.
537.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing bishop (6/10) or queen (4/10) move to a seemingly useful square that completely ignores the position's urgent tactical requirements. In 10/10 cases the move was neither a check nor a capture — purely a 'developing' or 'repositioning' move. The tactical demands being ignored vary: in 3/10 positions the move allowed a knight fork (positions 3, 8, 9), in 3/10 it removed a defender from a critical piece or pawn (positions 1, 4, 10), in 3/10 it missed the player's own forcing tactical opportunity like a check or combination (positions 2, 6, 7), and in 1/10 it ignored immediate mating threats (position 5). The average cp_loss of 1244 reflects how severely these 'looks fine' moves are punished. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions demanding precision rather than general development.

543.label: Queen moves away from the critical zone where it was performing (or needed to perform) an essential defensive or attacking function, typically related to king safety.
543.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that relocate the queen away from the critical sector of the board. In 8/10 cases, king safety is the primary tactical motif being violated—the queen leaves a square where it defends key squares around an exposed king (Positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10) or abandons its role in a forcing attacking sequence (Position 6). In 9/10 positions, the move is non-capturing and non-forcing (only Position 9 gives check, but it's a tempo-losing check that allows defensive interposition). The average cp_loss of 4026 is extreme, with 4/10 positions resulting in immediate mate or missing forced mate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these are tactically critical moments demanding precision. The queen consistently moves to squares that appear superficially reasonable (centralized, pressuring pawns, checking) but are strategically irrelevant to the position's primary demand. In 6/10 positions, the queen retreats or moves to a more passive square (Qf8, Qd8, Qh8, Qd1, Qf2, Qc6); in the remaining cases, the queen moves to an active-looking but wrong square (Qa5, Qh6, Qe3, Qc7+).

550.label: Voluntarily moving the king to h7/h2 (or g2) as a false prophylactic, wasting a critical tempo and creating new tactical vulnerabilities in positions demanding concrete action.
550.description: All 10/10 positions feature a voluntary king move one step toward the rook-pawn file (7x Kh7, 2x Kh2, 1x Kg2) during the middlegame with no immediate threat forcing the move. In every case, the player intended the move as a 'safe' prophylactic tuck — stepping off a file, diagonal, or back rank — but the position demanded concrete tactical or strategic action instead. 10/10 positions had the king already reasonably safe before the move. The average cp_loss of 363 reflects that these positions were at critical junctures: only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning precision was required. In 8/10 positions, the king move directly created a new tactical vulnerability: enabling knight checks (Ng5+/Ng4+ in positions 1, 4, 7), opening discovered attack diagonals (position 8's fxe6+), enabling sacrifices (position 10's Rxg7+), making pawn recaptures illegal (position 5's hxg5 opening the h-file), or placing the king on a vulnerable diagonal for queen/bishop batteries (positions 6, 9). In the remaining 2/10, the pure tempo loss allowed the opponent to equalize or seize the initiative with central breaks.

547.label: Playing a check that is objectively worse than an alternative move (often another check to a different square or a non-check capture), because the forcing nature of check is seductive.
547.description: All 10/10 positions feature a move that delivers check but is significantly inferior to the best available option. In 7/10 cases, the move involves a discovered check mechanism where the piece lands on the wrong destination square (positions 1, 2, 7, 8, 9) or the discovered check itself is the wrong idea (positions 6, 10). In 5/10 positions, the best move was ALSO a check but to a superior square (Nxe5+ instead of Nb4+, Nf2+ instead of Nf4+, Bg6+ instead of Be4+, Bf7+ instead of Bxd5+, Nd4+ instead of Ng5+), revealing that the player recognized the check mechanism but chose the wrong execution. In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 6), the best move was NOT a check at all—a quiet move or simple capture was objectively superior. The average cp_loss of 2091 is extreme, with 3/10 positions converting forced checkmate into merely winning. Only 1.3 good moves existed on average, meaning these were precision-critical moments where the instinct to give check led to the wrong decision.

546.label: A piece captures a pawn on a peripheral square, becoming trapped or creating a tactical vulnerability that costs more than the pawn was worth.
546.description: 9/9 positions involve capturing a pawn with a significant piece. 7/9 captures occur on the a-file or h-file (a2, a7, h2, h7, h7, h7, h3), with the remaining two on central squares (d5, d6). 6/9 involve rooks doing the capturing. The critical shared consequence is that the capturing piece becomes misplaced: in 4/9 positions the piece is explicitly trapped after the capture (bishop on a2, bishop on h7, knight on h7, knight on h7), in 2/9 the capture leaves another piece hanging to a fork or direct attack (Nxd3+ fork, Rg1 winning the bishop), and in 2/9 the capture leads to an unfavorable simplification that surrenders coordination advantages. All 9 positions feature tempo_loss and piece_activity degradation as core consequences. 7/9 positions had the player's king in a vulnerable state (exposed or uncastled), meaning development and safety should have been prioritized over material. The average cp_loss of 369 reflects these being severe mistakes, not marginal inaccuracies.

541.label: Moving the queen (or piece) to an active-looking but undefended square where it is captured or its departure creates a fatal tactical vulnerability.
541.description: 9/10 positions involve queen moves (the outlier Nd7 follows the same logic). In 7/10 cases, the moved piece is directly captured or won through a short tactical sequence: Positions 1 (Qe7 taken by Qxe7), 2 (Qe3 won after deflection checks), 5 (Qc4 taken by Qxc4+), 6 (Qg5 lost to Rg4/Bxg7/Rxg7+), 7 (Qg6 taken by Qxg6), 10 (Nd7 taken by Bxd7), and to some extent 8 (Qxb7 leads to forced mate via queen exchange). In the remaining cases (3, 4, 9), the queen relocation abandons critical defensive duties, leaving the king fatally exposed to mating attacks or unstoppable checks. The common thread is that the player selects an 'active' or 'aggressive' destination square—centralization, attacking a pawn, pressuring the opponent—without verifying that the piece is safe on that square or that its departure doesn't collapse the position. The average cp_loss of 4362 reflects that many of these are game-ending blunders rather than minor inaccuracies.

544.label: Moving the rook to the opponent's back rank in an endgame, appearing active but abandoning the critical defensive or offensive task at hand.
544.description: 9/10 positions show the rook moving to the opponent's back rank (rank 8 for White, rank 1 for Black), while 1/10 (Rg2) shows a similar drift toward the opponent's side of the board. All 10 positions are endgames where the rook had an urgent local duty — defending a critical pawn (6/10), maintaining control of a key file (3/10), or capturing an undefended piece (1/10). In every case, the correct move kept the rook engaged with the immediate crisis on an intermediate rank (e.g., Rb2 not Rb8, Rh1 not Rh8, Rc7 not Rc8), used the rook for an aggressive check, or involved a different piece entirely. The blunder consistently creates a fatal tempo loss: the rook arrives at a distant square with no concrete threat, and the opponent exploits the abandonment of duties within 1-2 moves.
