Average cp_loss of 1157 reflects the severity — these aren't subtle inaccuracies but position-losing misdirections of the most powerful endgame piece.

551.label: Moving the queen to an apparently strong central square (c3-d5 range) when the position demands an immediate concrete action like a sacrifice, rook invasion, or tactical blow.
551.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen moving to a central square on the c or d file (ranks 3-7): four Qd3, two Qc3, one each of Qc6, Qc7, Qd4, Qd5. In every case, the queen centralization looks natural and 'improving' but misses a more forcing alternative. In 7/10 positions, a concrete tactic was available (Bxh7+ sacrifice in positions 1 and 3, Rxc6 exchange sacrifice in position 2, Qb1 battery in position 4, Rc2 invasion in position 5, Rad1 exploiting the d-file in position 6, Nd5 centralization in position 10). The tempo_loss tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and missed_tactic in 9/10. The queen on its new central square frequently creates fresh vulnerabilities: exposed to knight attacks with tempo (positions 1, 7, 10), blocks own bishop's diagonal (positions 3, 4), or abandons a critical defensive duty (positions 7, 9). Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where only concrete play maintained the evaluation.

545.label: A well-placed piece voluntarily relocates away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive or positional function, typically to a rim or passive square.
545.description: 8/10 positions involve minor piece moves (5 knights, 3 bishops) that relocate a piece from an important functional square to a worse one. In 6/10 cases, the destination is a rim square (Nh5, Na7, Bh2, Na4, Bb5, Bc3 on the edge of action). In 9/10 positions, the piece was performing a critical duty on its original square: blocking a mating path (Nc5 left d7 which blocked Qc7#), defending another piece (Na4 left c3 which defended Bb5), controlling a central break (Nh5 left f6 which prevented e5), maintaining queen mobility (d5 blocked the queen's diagonal), or simply occupying a dominant post (Nc3 retreated from the powerhouse e4 square). The common consequence is an immediate tactical vulnerability: 3/10 result in hanging/trappable pieces, 2/10 enable checkmate, 3/10 enable devastating positional breaks, and 2/10 create pure passivity. The average cp_loss of 1180 reflects how catastrophic abandoning a critical function can be.

552.label: Capturing a piece where the pawn recapture rips open a file directly toward the player's own king.
552.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundering side captures a piece (usually on the g-file) and the opponent's pawn recapture opens a devastating file (h-file, f-file, or g-file) aimed directly at the capturer's king, with a rook already positioned to exploit it. 8/10 moves are captures specifically on g3/g4/g5/h5, where the h-pawn or f-pawn recapture tears open the adjacent file. In 5/10 positions the refutation is specifically hxg5 (or hxg4) opening the h-file, while 3/10 feature fxg5/fxg3/fxe6 opening the f-file. The capturing piece is typically a bishop (8/10) that was itself serving a defensive shielding role for the player's king. In 7/10 positions the king was already exposed or castled on the side of the newly-opened file. The average cp_loss of 3190 reflects that many of these (3/10) result in forced mate, while others produce crushing attacks. All 10 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), indicating the player was often already under pressure and chose the most natural-looking but structurally fatal response.

554.label: Moving a piece or pawn to a square where it is immediately capturable by an opponent's piece already controlling that square.
554.description: 9/10 positions show the player moving a piece or pawn directly to a square that is already attacked by an enemy piece, resulting in immediate material loss. In 4/10 cases it was a queen placed en prise (Qc4 hung to a d3-pawn, Qc8 hung to multiple pieces, Qf5 hung to a bishop on the diagonal, Qb4 left a defensive square enabling its capture via discovered attack). In 2/10 cases a rook was placed on a square attacked by a bishop (Rd6 on a bishop diagonal) or capturable by queen/pawn (Rd5). In 2/10 cases a bishop was placed on an undefended square visible to a capturing piece (Ba6 to Bxa6, Bg4 to Qxg4 on an open diagonal). In 2/10 cases a pawn was pushed to an undefended square (c4 capturable by Bxc4, g5 capturable by Bxg5 or undermined by cxd6). The average cp_loss of 1262 reflects that these are typically full-piece or full-queen losses. The captures were all simple one-move threats, not complex tactics — the player simply failed to verify the destination square was safe.

548.label: Reactive king moves attempting to escape pressure that place the king on a tactically worse square, when a concrete pawn advance or piece action would have addressed the actual threat.
548.description: 10/10 positions feature a king moving one square as a 'defensive' escape from perceived pressure, but landing on a square with greater tactical vulnerability. In 6/10 positions (1,2,3,6,9 and partially 7), the correct move was a pawn advance (g3 or g6) to block the file or diagonal, rather than moving the king. In 7/10 positions (1,2,3,5,6,8,9), the king move specifically placed the king on a diagonal where a pawn capture or piece capture becomes check — most commonly the f1 square where hxg2+ or Qxg2+ gains tempo (positions 2,3,9), or f8 where Bxg7+ becomes check (positions 1,5). In 3/10 positions (3,5,10), the blunder resulted in immediate forced checkmate. The average cp_loss of 3968 is extreme, and only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these are narrow defensive positions that demanded concrete solutions rather than general king-flight instincts. All moves share the common intent of 'getting the king out of the firing line' but paradoxically move into a geometrically worse position.

557.label: A bishop attacked by a knight reflexively retreats one diagonal square to b3/g3/b6/g6, a square the attacking knight still controls or can immediately capture on.
557.description: In 10/10 positions, a bishop on the 4th or 5th rank (f4, c4, f5, or c5) is attacked by a knight on the adjacent h-file or a-file (h5, h4, a5, a4), and the player retreats the bishop exactly one diagonal square toward their own back rank to g3/b3/g6/b6. In 8/10 positions, the knight can immediately capture the bishop on its new square (Nxg3 or Nxb3), meaning the retreat accomplishes nothing defensively. In at least 6/10 positions, the attacking knight was itself completely undefended and could have been captured by the queen (Qxh5 or Qxe7), representing a missed free piece. The average centipawn loss is 364, reflecting that these reflexive retreats squander enormous tactical opportunities. The positions span both opening (5/10) and middlegame (5/10), predominantly from White's perspective (8/10), and typically feature closed centers where the knight-bishop tension is a critical tactical moment demanding calculation rather than autopilot retreat.

555.label: Giving a check with no concrete follow-up that displaces the attacker's piece to a worse square while the opponent's king comfortably sidesteps or the check is blocked constructively.
555.description: All 10/10 positions feature a check ('+') that accomplishes nothing forced or beneficial. In 9/10 cases the opponent's king simply sidesteps to a safe (often improved) square, and in 1/10 the check is blocked by a useful pawn advance. 6/10 are queen checks (often to corner/edge squares like a8, b8, b1), 3/10 are rook checks along open files, and 1/10 is a bishop check. The consistent consequence is that the checking piece ends up displaced from its optimal post: queens land on passive corner squares far from the action (a8, b8, b1), rooks leave active files for dead-end back ranks, and defenders abandon critical defensive duties. In 7/10 positions the opponent's king actually improves by moving (centralizing in endgames or reaching safer shelter). The average cp_loss of 254 confirms these are substantial errors, and the average of only 1.6 good moves available shows these were critical moments demanding constructive play rather than reflexive aggression.

553.label: A bishop is developed or repositioned to a square where it immediately becomes tactically exploitable—hanging, capturable with check, or winnable through a short forcing sequence.
553.description: 8/9 positions involve bishop moves (Bg7, Be5, Bb5, Bf6, Bd2, Be3, Bb7, Bc6), with only one knight move (Ng3) as an outlier. In 7/9 cases, the moved piece lands on a square where it is directly capturable or winnable through a short tactical sequence (hanging piece tagged in 7/9 analyses). The key pattern is a quiet repositioning/development move that places the bishop on an inadequately defended square, when the position demanded either a more forcing continuation or addressing an urgent tactical need. In 6/9 positions, the bishop is captured outright or won within 2-3 moves of the refutation. In 4/9 cases (Be3, Bd2, Be5, Bg7), the piece is captured with check or through a check-based sequence, compounding the error. The average cp_loss of 303 reflects that these moves typically lose a full piece worth of material or forfeit a decisive tactical resource.

549.label: Bishop captures material (usually pawns) while ignoring a more critical tactical necessity in the position.
549.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop captures grabbing material (Bxh3, Bxc4, Bxh6, Bxf5, Bxd4, Bxh6, Bxc2, Bxg6), with the remaining two being analogous greedy/misguided moves (Nxf2 grabbing a pawn, Kg8 ignoring a free piece). In every case, the capture prioritizes immediate material gain over the position's most pressing requirement. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 6, 8), a much stronger forcing move with checks or forks was available that would have won significantly more material. In 4/10 positions (4, 5, 7, 10), the capture ignored critical king safety concerns—either the player's own uncastled king or the premature removal of a defensive piece. In 2/10 positions (2, 9), the move left a major piece completely hanging on an open line. The average cp_loss of 1447 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions demanded precise play, yet the players consistently chose the most obvious-looking material gain over the deeper tactical truth.

556.label: Non-forcing pawn advances played in positions demanding immediate tactical action, wasting a critical tempo while urgent threats or opportunities go unaddressed.
556.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance played when the position contains an urgent tactical obligation. In 5/10 cases (Positions 2, 4, 8, 9, 10), the player completely ignores an existing threat or misses a forced winning/saving sequence. In 4/10 cases (Positions 1, 3, 5, 6), the pawn advance actively weakens the player's own structure by removing a pawn from a critical defensive role (guarding a piece, shielding the king, or controlling a key square). In 1/10 (Position 7), the player passes up a concrete material-winning move (Qxd6) for a prophylactic pawn push. The average cp_loss of 2076 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—3/10 resulted in forced checkmate. The moves span all wings (h-file: 3, b-file: 3, g/f/c/e: 4), confirming that the specific direction is irrelevant; what matters is the shared characteristic of choosing a slow, non-forcing pawn move in a position that screams for immediate piece action.

560.label: Retreating an actively placed bishop along its diagonal toward the board edge instead of playing a forcing tactical move.
560.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to a less active square along its current diagonal, retreating toward the edge of the board. In 8/10 cases the bishop retreats toward the g/h-file rim (Bg6, Bh6, Bg3, Bh4, Bh3, Bh5), while the remaining 2 retreat toward the a/b-file or back rank (Be1, Bb3). In 9/10 positions, a clearly superior forcing move existed — captures (Bxg4, Bxd4, Bxf6, Rxe4), checks (Qh5+, Rf3+), or tactical strikes (Nb5, exf6, Rae1) — that the player rejected in favor of conserving or repositioning the bishop. The average cp_loss of 1236 (excluding the 0-loss endgame) reflects how devastating these tempo losses are in positions demanding immediate action. 7/10 positions featured an exposed enemy king or open files that required exploitation before the opponent could consolidate. Only 1/10 (Position 9) was not actually a mistake, serving as a baseline showing that passive bishop retreats are acceptable only when the advantage is already overwhelming and no urgent tactics exist.

538.label: Piece moves to a seemingly active square while abandoning defense of tactically vulnerable material.
538.description: 7/10 positions clearly show a quiet, non-forcing piece redeployment that leaves a piece or pawn undefended or opens a tactical vulnerability. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 8, 9, 10), the moved piece directly abandoned defense of hanging material (a knight on h5, a rook on d2, the e5 pawn, the bishop itself on g6). In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 4), the piece moved to a square that abandoned critical king-safety coverage, enabling devastating attacks. In 1/10 cases (position 3), the move allowed a knight fork. The best alternatives in nearly all cases (8/10) either defended the vulnerable piece/pawn directly or created forcing counterplay that prevented the opponent from exploiting the weakness. Positions 6 and 7 (0 cp_loss each) appear to be noise/false positives where the quiet king advance happened to be correct in won pawn endgames. Position 5 (24 cp_loss) was a minor redundancy error. The average cp_loss of 248 reflects that ignoring immediate tactical obligations in favor of 'improving' moves is typically catastrophic.

563.label: Giving a reflexive queen check that accomplishes nothing constructive, when a superior non-check move or a more precise check was available.
563.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player giving a queen check (+) that turns out to be a serious blunder. The average centipawn loss is 4017, with 4/10 positions squandering a forced checkmate. In 6/10 cases, the check drives the opponent's king to a safer square (positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 10) or allows it to sidestep without consequence. In 4/10 positions, a different queen check on a more precise square was the winning move (positions 4, 6, 8, 9 — e.g., Qb5+ instead of Qh5+, Qh4+ instead of Qd4+). In 3/10 positions, a non-check move like capturing material (Qxe7, Qxf2) or a quiet simplification (Rc3) was clearly best. In 2/10 positions (2, 5), the check pulled the queen away from a critical square needed for a tactical combination. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were high-precision moments where the reflexive check was the worst instinct.

565.label: King voluntarily moves to a square adjacent to f7 (or f2), allowing the opposing queen to deliver checkmate or a devastating invasion on that square.
565.description: 9/10 positions involve a king move that places the monarch adjacent to the critical f7 square (or f2 for White), enabling the opponent's queen to deliver immediate checkmate or initiate a lethal forcing sequence. In 7/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10 with Ke7/Kf8), the queen delivers Qf7# as an immediate mate-in-one supported by a knight on e5. Position 4 mirrors this exactly with Kf1 allowing Qf2# supported by a knight on e4. Position 2 allows Qf7+ initiating a king hunt. Position 8 (Kd7) allows Qc7+ with a similar exposed-king pattern. Only position 6 (Ra2) is an outlier involving a missed hanging piece rather than a king safety blunder. In 5/10 positions, the correct defense was specifically g6, chasing the queen from h5 before it could access f7. All 10 positions had exactly 1 good move available, creating razor-thin margins where the natural-looking king development was fatally wrong.

571.label: A knight leaps aggressively from its developed square (f3/f6) to an unprotected forward square where it hangs to immediate capture, typically by the queen.
571.description: All 10/10 positions involve a knight jumping forward from its standard development square (f3 in 8/10 White positions, f6 in 2/10 Black positions) to an aggressive but completely undefended destination square (g5 in 7/10, h5 in 2/10, h4 in 1/10, e5 in 1/10). In every case, the knight has zero protection on its landing square. In 9/10 positions, the primary refutation is a simple queen capture (Qxg5, Qxh5, or Qxh4) along an unobstructed diagonal; in 1/10, a knight recapture (Nxe5). The intent behind the move is always aggressive — attacking a bishop (3/10 positions target Bf4/Bf5), targeting f7 in Italian-style positions (4/10), or attempting premature centralization (3/10). All 10/10 are opening-phase blunders with both kings still in center, and the average cp_loss of 452 confirms each loses approximately a full piece. The pattern represents players applying known aggressive knight motifs (Fried Liver Ng5, anti-London Nh5) in positions where the necessary preconditions are absent — specifically, the opponent's queen diagonal to the landing square is unobstructed.

558.label: Voluntarily eliminating one's own critical defensive resource (piece or pawn structure) in endgames through captures or committal pawn advances, when patient maneuvering was required.
558.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where the player makes a committal move that permanently destroys their own defensive infrastructure. In 6/10 cases, the move is a capture that trades away the player's last or most critical piece (Nxd5, Nxe4, Bxc5, Bxd1, Bxa5, hxg5), while in 4/10 cases it's a pawn advance that weakens the player's own structure (g4 twice, h4, b4). In nearly every case, the recommended alternatives are quiet maneuvering moves — king activation (Kf1, Kd1, Kf5, Kg7), piece repositioning (Na4, Be6), or maintaining the status quo. 8/10 positions feature the mistake being made by the already-losing side, suggesting these are impatient attempts to 'do something' that backfire by removing the very asset holding the position together. The consistent consequence is entering a position with zero counterplay: either a lost pawn endgame (positions 2, 5, 7, 8) or a locked structure where the opponent's passed pawns become unstoppable (positions 3, 9, 10).

564.label: Non-developing pawn advances or rim knight moves played while the position demands immediate concrete action against a tactical or developmental emergency.
564.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a slow, non-forcing move (8/10 are pawn advances like a4, g4, b5, e3, e6; 2/10 are Nh5 knight-to-rim maneuvers) while the position urgently demands addressing a concrete tactical vulnerability or developmental priority. In 10/10 positions, the played move ignores an immediate threat or necessity that the opponent exploits on the very next move. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/10 analyses, 'piece_activity' in 9/10, and 'development' in 7/10. The average cp_loss of 272 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but severe punishments for wasted time. In 7/10 positions, the refutation involves a direct tactical blow (fork, piece capture, knight invasion, pawn breakthrough) that was only possible because the slow move either created a new weakness (a4 opening b3 or b4 squares in positions 5, 8) or failed to address an existing one (hanging pieces in positions 1, 6, 7). The average of 2.5 good moves available confirms that better alternatives clearly existed but were ignored in favor of a strategically-motivated but tactically oblivious plan.

566.label: Playing a passive piece redeployment to the 7th/2nd rank when a prophylactic king move was the critical defensive requirement.
566.description: In 9/10 positions, the correct move was a quiet king retreat to safety (Kf8, Kh1, Kh8, Kf7, Kh2, Kh7, Kh8, Kh1), and in the remaining position (Position 8), the best move was c5 blocking a dangerous diagonal toward the king. Instead, all 10 players moved a non-king piece — rooks (7/10: Rf2×3, Rf7×2, Re7×1), queens (2/10: Qd7, Qf8, Qf6), or a bishop (1/10: Bd7) — typically to the 7th/2nd rank or back rank in what appeared to be a 'useful' defensive or consolidating gesture. The average cp_loss was enormous (3008), with 4/10 positions resulting in forced mate or near-mate after the mistake. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, confirming these were positions demanding precision where only the king move solved the core vulnerability.
566.old_chip: Piece move instead of king tuck

562.label: Playing a forcing move (usually a knight check) that closely resembles the winning combination but gets one critical detail wrong — wrong piece, wrong square, or wrong move order.
562.description: 8/9 positions show the player identifying the correct tactical theme but executing with a near-miss error. In 6/9 positions, a knight check is played to the wrong square (Ne2+ instead of Nf3#, Ng4+ instead of Nxe4+, Nf3+ instead of Ne2#) or prematurely (Nf7+ before Rxf6, Nf6+ abandoning a perpetual). In 2/9 positions, the player moves a bishop to d6 when a knight to d6+ would deliver check with a devastating fork — the wrong piece to the correct square. In 1/9, the wrong knight is chosen (Ngf7 instead of Nef7), leaving the other piece hanging. All moves share the quality of being superficially similar to the winning continuation — same target square, same piece type, or same tactical theme — but differ in one fatal geometric detail. The average cp_loss of 3471 reflects that these near-misses often squander checkmates or decisive material wins. Only 1/9 positions (Position 1) was actually correct, suggesting the feature detects the 'shape' of these almost-right forcing moves regardless of whether they happen to work.

559.label: A rook move (or king-shelter capture) that fatally obstructs the player's own king by blocking escape squares or abandoning a critical defensive post, enabling immediate mating threats.
559.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves, and in at least 6/10 the rook physically blocks its own king's escape square (Rh2 blocking h2 with king on h1 in positions 1, 5, 6; Rg2 blocking g1 with king on h2 in position 4; Rg8 blocking g8 with king on h8 in position 7; Rd7 blocking d7 with king on d6 in position 8). In 2/10 the rook abandons a critical defensive post near the king (Rg7 leaving g8 back-rank defense in position 10; Rc7 leaving b7 guard duty in position 3). The remaining 2/10 involve pawn captures (fxg3, gxh5) that destroy the king's pawn shield, serving the same functional role of fatally compromising king safety. 9/10 positions resulted in checkmate or forced mating sequences as punishment. The average number of good moves was only 1.3, indicating these are razor-edge positions where the self-obstructing move is the one catastrophic choice among very few alternatives. Back-rank mate is the explicit punishment in 6/10 cases.

542.label: Making the most immediately obvious or natural-looking move (usually capturing a pawn or occupying a prominent square) when more precise alternatives exist.
542.description: 7/10 positions involve king moves (6 of which are king captures of enemy pawns on the wing/edge: Kxh4, Kxa6, Kxh7, Kxa6, Kxa7, plus Ka5 approach), while the remaining 3 involve pieces jumping to visually active squares (Ne4 twice, Qg3, Qd6). The critical observation is that 5/10 positions have essentially 0 cp_loss (the 'obvious' move was actually correct), while 5/10 are genuine mistakes averaging ~200cp loss. In every case, the move represents the most immediately natural action in the position: take the hanging pawn, occupy the prominent central square, or move the queen to what looks active. When these moves ARE mistakes, the errors share consistent sub-patterns: 2/10 involve knights jumping to e4 where an exchange sequence leaves a pawn hanging, 2/10 involve queens abandoning critical e-file pressure for seemingly active but actually inferior squares, and 1/10 involves capturing a pawn with the king when a piece was hanging elsewhere. 8/10 positions feature open central files and exposed kings, and 6/10 are pure pawn endgames where tempo precision determines the outcome.

573.label: Moving a knight to g4 or g5 to attack f7/f2, but leaving it completely undefended and capturable.
573.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight jumping to g5 (6 cases) or g4 (3 cases) targeting the opponent's f-pawn, with 1/10 being a bishop to g4 instead. In all 10 positions, the piece lands on an undefended square in the opening phase with both kings still in the center. 8/10 are immediately punished by a simple queen capture of the hanging piece (Qxg5 or Qxg4), winning a full minor piece for nothing. The players are attempting a Fried Liver-style attack on f7 (White) or an f2-attack (Black), but the tactical prerequisites are absent — typically because the opponent's queen has an unobstructed path to capture the piece. In positions 2, 3, and 9 (identical Italian Game positions), the player confuses the Two Knights Defense (where Ng5 is theory) with a position where Black's bishop on c5 leaves the d8-g5 diagonal completely open. The average cp_loss of 394 confirms these consistently cost approximately a full piece.

569.label: The queen passively retreats to e8 (Black) or e1 (White), abandoning a critical defensive or tactical function from its previous square.
569.description: 9/10 positions involve moving the queen to e8 or e1 — the back rank on the e-file. 7/10 are Black playing Qe8 and 2/10 are White playing Qe1 (the remaining position, Ng1, is a thematically similar passive back-rank retreat). The common thread is that the queen leaves a square where it was performing an essential function — defending a pawn (c7 in Position 3, f7 in Position 8, c2 in Position 4), maintaining a tactical threat (Qh4+ in Position 5, recapturing on f6 in Position 1), or staying off a dangerous file (e-file alignment with opponent's rook in Position 9). In every case, the move appears to offer 'safety' or 'flexibility' on the back rank but actually surrenders something concrete. The average cp_loss of 301 reflects that these aren't subtle positional inaccuracies — they create immediate tactical exploitation. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating already-tense positions where the passive retreat was catastrophically wrong.

568.label: Knight repositioned to a seemingly active or central square that is immediately tactically vulnerable in an endgame.
568.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight is moved to what appears to be an active, centralized, or purposeful square but is immediately punishable. In 7/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, and partially 3), the knight can be captured within 1-2 moves of landing — either directly hanging (Positions 1, 7, 9), capturable via a forcing sequence like a check+capture (Positions 4, 10), or functionally lost by allowing the opponent to advance past it (Position 6). In the remaining 3/10 positions (2, 5, 8), the knight lands on a square where it loses critical tempo — being immediately kicked by a pawn (Position 2), missing a tempo-gaining check (Position 5), or losing access to a vital defensive resource (Position 8). All 10 moves share the surface appearance of logical knight development — centralization (Ne4, Nd3, Nf5), pawn attacks (Nh4, Ng7), or rerouting (Nd6, Nd2) — but all ignore concrete tactical vulnerabilities at the destination. 9/10 are endgames where such tactical oversights are decisive due to minimal remaining material.
568.old_chip: Knight to attractive but unsafe square

561.label: Playing a superficially active or natural move that wastes the crucial tempo needed to address the position's most urgent demand.
561.description: 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary error pattern. The moves consistently appear logical on the surface—checks (3/10: h2+, Bh2+, Bc5+), pawn advances that seem attacking (5/10: f3, c5, h2, b3, h4), captures/development that look natural (2/10: Nxf7, Nc6)—yet all fail to address what the position critically requires. The average good moves available is only 2.1, meaning these are high-stakes positions where only 1-3 moves work. In 6/10 positions, the correct move involved forcing sequences (Rb1+, Qxc4, Kf6 march, fxg4, Kb7) that directly tackled the urgent issue. The played moves instead addressed secondary concerns: shoring up pawn structure (f3, b3), premature promotion attempts (h2+, h2), pointless checks (Bh2+, Bc5+), irrelevant flank play (h4), or abandoned key positional assets (Nxf7 leaving d6). 6/10 positions were endgames where one tempo proved decisive.
561.old_chip: Critical tempo wasted on wrong priority

572.label: Advancing a pawn into an opponent's capture in the endgame, when patient king or piece play was required to maintain the advantage.
572.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance that is immediately punished by the opponent capturing the advanced pawn. In 9/10 cases, the phase is an endgame where patient play was essential. In at least 4/10 positions (h6, e6, f3, e6), the capture comes with check, gaining a devastating tempo. In 5-6/10 positions (b6, h6, e6, e6, d6, and arguably h4), the advanced pawn was a passed pawn or the player's primary strategic asset—pushing it into capture range eliminated the winning advantage entirely. The best alternatives consistently involved king centralization (Kf1, Kd6, Kd7, Kd4, Kf6), bishop maneuvering (Bg4, Bf5), or queenside pawn advances on the OTHER flank (b5, c5). The average cp_loss of 1289 reflects how catastrophic these captures are in simplified positions where one pawn's elimination often means the difference between winning and drawing. In 7/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, showing these are critical junctures where the temptation to 'do something' with the pawn leads to disaster.

578.label: Capturing a piece on the g-file with the h-pawn, allowing the opponent's h-pawn to recapture and rip open the h-file against the player's own castled king.
578.description: All 10/10 positions feature an h-pawn capturing a piece (bishop or knight) on g4 or g5, believing the material gain or piece elimination is favorable. In every case, the devastating refutation is the opponent's h-pawn recapturing (hxg5 or hxg4), which simultaneously opens the h-file as a direct attacking highway toward the capturer's castled king and often also attacks a key defensive piece (the knight on f6 or f3) with the newly advanced g-pawn. 9/10 positions involve the h-file opening directly against a castled king, while 1/10 (position 9) involves the h-file opening to win a hanging piece on h4. In 6/10 cases Black captures ...hxg5 with the king castled kingside; in 4/10 cases White captures hxg4. The captured piece typically appears annoying or free (a bishop pressuring f6/f3, or a knight on g5/g4), but eliminating it with the h-pawn is catastrophic because the opponent's rook on h1/h8 is already perfectly positioned to exploit the newly opened file. The average centipawn loss of 295 reflects positions swinging from advantage to disadvantage or from equality to a crushing attack.

567.label: A non-forcing piece repositioning move to a 'natural' square when the position demands immediate tactical action (check, capture, king evacuation, or covering a specific threat).
567.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-checking, non-capturing piece move to a conventionally desirable square in a position with extreme tactical urgency. 6/10 moves are bishop developments (Be7, Bf6, Bg5, Be3, Bd3, Be3), 3/10 are rook moves to open files (Re1, Re8, Rd7), and 1/10 is a knight centralization (Ne6). In 6/10 cases, the piece is placed on a square where it immediately hangs to a capture (often with check or devastating follow-up). In 3/10 cases (Bf6, Re8, Ne6), the player misses an immediately winning forcing sequence — including one missed checkmate in 2 (Ne6 instead of Qh3+). In 1/10 cases (Rd7), a free piece capture was available. The average cp_loss of 3915 and average good moves of only 1.7 confirm these are narrow, critical positions where the player defaulted to 'general improvement' thinking instead of calculating the specific tactical demands. The best moves in these positions were consistently forcing: checks (Qe2+, Qh3+), king evacuations (Kh7, Kf7, Kd2), tempo-gaining attacks (f3), or simple captures of hanging material (axb6).

576.label: Aggressive-looking rook moves (especially checks) that prioritize apparent activity over the objectively strongest continuation.
576.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that appear active or forcing but are mistakes. 5/10 are rook checks (Re6+, Rg1+, Rxf2+, Rf5+, Re2+) where the check looks forcing but either allows the king to escape a mating net (positions 1, 10), hangs the rook to a simple capture (position 3), or misses a much stronger quiet move (position 4, 5). The remaining 5/10 are non-checking rook moves to seemingly active squares (Rd8, Rd6, Rc4, Rb8, Ra5) that either place the rook en prise to the enemy queen (positions 6, 9), abandon critical defensive duties (positions 2, 8), or miss devastating tactical combinations (position 7). The average cp_loss of 2970 reflects catastrophic consequences, with 4/10 positions converting winning/mating positions into equality or loss. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than intuitive piece activation.

575.label: Hasty captures (usually pawn takes) that remove the capturing piece from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function, leaving another piece or the king fatally exposed.
575.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn captures and all 10 are captures that look natural or productive on the surface but critically remove the player's own piece from a square where it was performing an essential guarding role. In 4/10 positions (Positions 1, 5, 6, 7), the capturing piece was directly shielding another piece or blocking an attacking diagonal — the d-pawn guarding the rook on e4, the f-pawn guarding h7 or blocking the b1-h7 diagonal, the bishop providing tactical justification for leaving the queen en prise. In 5/10 positions (Positions 2, 3, 4, 8, 9), the core error was a move-order mistake: the capture should have been preceded by an intermediate preparatory move (relocating a queen, giving check, making an intermezzo capture) that would have secured the position first, but the player jumped directly to the obvious material-winning capture. In Position 10, the capture ignored an immediate existential threat to pursue speculative counterplay. The common refutation across all positions is that the opponent exploits the newly undefended piece or exposed line that the capture created — in 6/10 positions the refutation involves capturing a piece left hanging, and in 4/10 it involves exploiting a newly opened attacking line to the king.

580.label: Voluntarily exchanging a powerfully centralized knight for a passive or inferior opponent's piece, squandering accumulated positional advantage.
580.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight capture (Nx__) that surrenders the player's most dominant piece. In 8/10 cases, the player had a knight on a commanding outpost (d4, d5, e4, e5, or f4) and traded it for a clearly inferior or passive opponent's knight. 7/10 moves included check, suggesting the forcing/tempo-gaining nature of check lured players into premature exchanges. The analyses consistently describe the traded knight as 'dominant,' 'powerfully centralized,' or 'magnificently posted,' while the captured piece is labeled 'passive,' 'cramped,' or 'merely a defender.' In every case, stronger alternatives existed that maintained the knight's presence (e.g., Bg5 pins exploiting the knight, Rf7 penetrations, Nh3+ king attacks, or simply developing other pieces). The average cp_loss of 243 reflects the massive positional value being discarded — these knights were the linchpins of entire attacking formations.

581.label: A knight captures a rook trapped in the corner, burying itself out of play while ignoring critical king safety threats or superior tactical opportunities.
581.description: 8/10 positions feature a knight capturing a rook on a corner square (a1, h1, or h8), with 6/10 specifically being Nxa1. In the positions where this is a mistake (7/8 captures), the knight becomes completely trapped or irrelevant after landing in the corner. 7/10 positions feature an exposed or vulnerable king (either the capturing side's own king or the opponent's), and in every mistake case, the opponent exploits the tempo gained to launch devastating attacks against the exposed king. 6/10 positions explicitly involve a knight already on c2 that had been actively threatening the opponent's position before being removed to the dead corner. The 2-3 positions with 0-1 cp_loss (positions 6, 7, 10) represent edge cases where the corner capture was actually correct or the position was already lost regardless. The average cp_loss of 2930 is heavily driven by positions 2, 4, and 9 where the knight capture allowed immediate checkmate or mating attacks, demonstrating the catastrophic cost of this materialistic instinct.

570.label: Moving a piece to a natural-looking square that has a specific geometric vulnerability, in positions where only one correct move exists.
570.description: All 10 positions share a critical structural feature: extremely few good moves available (average 1.4), meaning the player faced a do-or-die decision. In every case, the player chose a destination square that appeared safe or active but had a concrete tactical flaw exploitable by the opponent. 4/10 positions involved moving the king to a corner square with a hidden vulnerability (Ka8 x3 walking into Nc7+ perpetual check patterns, Kh1 walking onto a mating diagonal). 4/10 involved bishop moves to squares that were tactically exposed (Bg2 to a square targetable by Qd5, Bc2 to a rook-attackable file, Be5 onto the same diagonal as the king, Bxc4 opening a fork square). The remaining 2 moves (Ng5 removing a critical guard, c6 choosing prophylaxis over immediate tactics) share the same failure mode: ignoring the ONE geometric detail that makes the chosen move catastrophic. The average cp_loss of 3055 reflects that these are game-deciding moments where the 'obvious' move is fatally wrong.

579.label: Aggressive single-step pawn advances to the 4th/5th rank that pursue a slow strategic plan while ignoring an immediate concrete need elsewhere on the board.
579.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking single-step pawn advance, with 8/10 pushing to the 5th rank and 2/10 to the 4th rank. In every case, the player chose a committal, irreversible pawn push pursuing a speculative strategic plan (creating a passer, opening a file, attacking a chain) when the position demanded concrete piece action: 4/10 required piece repositioning (rook or king moves), 2/10 missed a direct tactical capture (hanging piece, undefended rook), 2/10 needed a forcing exchange to neutralize threats, and 2/10 required playing on the opposite wing entirely. The avg cp_loss of 219 confirms these are serious errors. In 7/10 cases the pawn advance weakened the player's own structure or created targets for the opponent. Crucially, 6/10 positions had only 1 good move available, meaning these speculative pushes occurred at critical junctures where precision was essential. The flanks were favored (a/b-file: 5/10, g/h-file: 4/10, center: 1/10), suggesting the error involves seeking activity on a wing when the real action is centralized or tactical.

589.label: Moving the queen to an aggressive-looking square that achieves nothing concrete, wasting critical tempo while the opponent develops or exploits tactical vulnerabilities.
589.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves to seemingly active squares (Qa5, Qc5, Qf3, Qb6, Qg5, Qa4+) that look threatening but accomplish nothing concrete. 9/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. In 6/10 cases, the position was in the opening where development tempo is paramount. The best alternatives were consistently quiet structural moves (e6, a6, c4, f4, d5) or direct tactical captures (dxc3) — concrete actions that addressed the position's real demands. The queen moves all share the illusion of activity: 3/10 delivered checks (Qa5+, Qa4+) that were easily blocked with developing moves, 2/10 abandoned critical defensive duties (Qb6 leaving e7 unguarded, Qg5 opening the c5-f8 diagonal), and 5/10 simply placed the queen on an exposed square before supporting pieces were ready. In every case, the opponent punished the exposed queen through developing with tempo, tactical forks/discoveries against the wandering queen, or capturing material the queen left undefended.

588.label: Moving a rook from the f-file to the e-file (Rf1-e1 or Rf8-e8) that abandons critical kingside defense and allows immediate tactical punishment.
588.description: All 9/9 positions feature the identical geometric move: a rook sliding from the f-file to the e-file (Rfe1 for White or Rfe8 for Black). In every case, the rook on the f-file was serving a crucial defensive function near the castled king, and its departure to the e-file — a routine 'centralizing' move — exposed a lethal tactical vulnerability. In 7/9 positions, the punishment was checkmate or forced mate (ranging from #-1 to #+6). In 8/9 positions, the primary tactical motif was king safety, with queen-bishop mating batteries exploiting the now-unguarded kingside in 5/9 positions (Qg2#, Qg7#, or similar patterns). The f-file rook was needed either to support a defensive f-pawn push (f3 blocking a diagonal in positions 3, 4, 7), to physically guard the f8/f1 square against piece invasions (positions 5, 6, 9), or to protect pieces on the f-file (position 10, where it defended Nf3). The average cp_loss of 6616 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights of immediate threats disguised as natural development.

590.label: A prophylactic one-square pawn advance adjacent to the castled king that creates critical square weaknesses when an active piece move was required.
590.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance on a file adjacent to (or on) the castled king's position, intended as a passive defensive measure: 7/10 are g2-g3 by White, 2/10 are b7-b6 by Black (king castled queenside on b8), and 1/10 is h2-h3. In all cases, the pawn was part of the king's protective shield and the advance was motivated by prophylaxis (creating luft, chasing a piece, restricting enemy queen access). However, 10/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, and in every case the correct move was an ACTIVE piece move (f3 attacking a bishop in positions 1-2, Nxg5 capturing a queen in position 3, Nh4 displacing a queen in position 6, Nf3 defending actively in position 9, g3 challenging the queen in position 10, etc.). The pawn advance consistently created exploitable weaknesses: weakened adjacent squares (f3 in positions 6-7, c6 in positions 4/8, g3 in position 10), enabled back-rank tactics (positions 5, 9), or simply wasted a critical tempo (positions 1, 3). The average cp_loss of 347 reflects how these seemingly safe moves catastrophically undermine the king's safety.

574.label: Playing a non-forcing, seemingly reasonable move in a position that demands one specific concrete action—missing checkmates, free captures, or critical defensive resources.
574.description: All 10 positions share an extremely low number of good alternatives (avg 1.6) indicating critical moments requiring tactical precision, yet the played moves are universally non-forcing: 0/10 are checks, 0/10 capture defended pieces (only 2/10 are reactive pawn captures). In contrast, the best moves were typically forcing—Qxf1# (checkmate), Rh1 (threatening unstoppable Qxg2#), Rxd3 (capturing a hanging piece), Ne6+ (a desperate saving check), Rc6 (attacking an undefended knight), Bxf4 (eliminating a critical threat), Bd8 (blocking a lethal check). 6/10 blunders are pawn moves—including 3 instances of g6 weakening the king's dark squares, 2 pawn captures (gxh5, hxg4) that destroy the player's own pawn shelter, and 1 premature advance (d4). The remaining 4/10 are slow piece repositioning moves (Ra7, Ra2, Bf4, Nfe5) that ignore urgent tactical demands. The enormous average cp_loss of 2995 confirms these are catastrophic errors where the position's critical nature was completely misread.

586.label: Queen captures apparently free material, but the opponent's recapture delivers check to the capturing side's exposed king, leading to catastrophic loss.
586.description: 8/10 positions show the same core mechanism: the player's queen captures a piece that appears undefended or advantageous to take (usually a rook on an open file), but the recapture comes with check against the player's own exposed king. In Position 1, Qxe5 is met by Qxe5+ with forced mate. In Position 2, Qxe2 allows Rxe2+ with check devastating the b2 king. In Position 3, Qxh2 allows Qxh2+ checking the c2 king. In Position 4, Qxf5+ is met by Qxf5+ checking back. In Position 5, Qxf8+ allows Rxf8+ checking the f2 king. In Position 6, Qxf3 allows Qxf3+ leading to immediate mate. In Positions 7 and 9, Qxe8+ is met by Qxe8+ or Rxe8+ checking the uncastled king. In all these cases, the player's king was exposed (center, weak shield, or open file) making the check after recapture devastating. 2/10 positions (8 and 10) are partial outliers—one is a rook move ignoring king safety, the other a speculative queen sally—but both share the theme of prioritizing material/attack while ignoring the vulnerability of one's own king.
586.old_chip: Queen grabs piece, recaptured with check

585.label: Premature bishop sacrifice on f7 or f2 (or analogous forcing capture) that looks aggressive but is refuted by a simple recapture leaving the opponent up material.
585.description: 7/10 positions feature the specific pattern of Bxf2+ or Bxf7+ — a bishop sacrifice targeting the opponent's weakest pawn near the king — that lacks sufficient follow-up to justify the material investment. The remaining 3/10 positions (Qxb5+, Qxf8, Qxe6, Qxe5+) share the identical structural error: making a capture that appears forcing but allows a devastating simple recapture. 8/10 moves give check, which creates the illusion of sustained initiative, but in every case the opponent can calmly accept the material and consolidate. 7/10 positions occur in the opening phase with both kings still in/near the center. The average cp_loss of 1167 reflects that these are severe blunders — the attacker typically ends up a full piece down with no compensation. In all Bxf7/Bxf2 cases, the refutation is identical: Kxf2 or Kxf7 followed by the king walking back to safety (Kg1 or Ke8), leaving the sacrificer down a bishop for a pawn with a completely dissipated attack.

584.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful/active move in a position where only ONE precise move maintains the evaluation, squandering the critical tempo needed for the position's single winning or holding plan.
584.description: All 10 positions share a striking structural similarity: there were on average only 1.2 good moves available, meaning the position demanded extreme precision with essentially one correct path. In every case, the player chose a move that appears active, aggressive, or strategically motivated — checks (1/10), piece jumps to seemingly strong squares (4/10), captures (1/10), pawn advances (2/10), or rook placements on 'active' squares (2/10) — but this superficially attractive choice wasted the ONE critical tempo that the position offered. The 'tempo_loss' tactical motif was identified in 9/10 positions. In 8/10 cases, the best move addressed a more urgent priority that the played move ignored: an immediate pawn breakthrough (positions 1, 10), king centralization (2), winning material with check (3, 10), piece development (4, 5), addressing an immediate tactical threat (7), or eliminating a dangerous pawn (8). The average cp_loss of 287 reflects the severity — these aren't marginal inaccuracies but critical-moment failures where the narrow path was missed for a plausible-looking alternative.

593.label: King moves to a square that appears safer but actually exposes it to new checking sequences, open files, or mating patterns that didn't exist on the previous square.
593.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder, and in 9/10 cases the king walks to a square where it becomes MORE vulnerable to tactical exploitation than on its original square. In 8/10 positions the move converts a losing-but-survivable position into forced checkmate (avg cp_loss 6501). The pattern is remarkably consistent: the king move opens new lines of attack — Position 3 (Kh3) walks onto a pawn-check diagonal, Position 4 (Kc6) walks into d5+ pawn check, Position 5 (Kd2) enables Nxf3+, Positions 6-8 (Kg1/Kd1/Ke1) walk into back-rank or first-rank mating patterns, and Position 10 (Kb6) walks onto an open file for a rook check. The average number of good moves available was only 1.8, indicating these were already critical positions requiring precise defense, and the instinct to 'move the king to safety' was exactly wrong. In most cases the correct move was either an active piece move (capturing an attacker, trading material) or staying put, rather than the seemingly natural king retreat.

583.label: Playing a non-forcing piece development or repositioning move in a position that demands immediate concrete action (capture, pawn break, or prophylaxis).
583.description: 8/10 positions feature a significant blunder (avg 3041cp loss) where the player chose a quiet piece repositioning move instead of addressing an immediate tactical demand. All 10 moves share the same geometric character: they are non-forcing piece moves (no checks, no captures, no pawn moves) that place a piece on a 'natural-looking' square. In 8/10 cases, the correct move was a fundamentally different type of action—a capture (positions 1, 7, 9), a pawn break (positions 3, 5, 10), or an active confrontation/king march (positions 2, 6). The avg number of good moves available was only 1.4, meaning these were extremely narrow positions where only concrete responses worked. 8/10 were played by Black, and the phases span middlegame and endgame roughly equally. Positions 4 and 8 (0cp loss) still fit the move pattern—quiet piece repositioning—but happened to occur in already-decided positions where the opponent couldn't exploit the tempo loss.

577.label: Quiet approach moves toward obvious targets that look natural but miss the position's true tactical or structural demands.
577.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet (non-capture, non-check) moves directing a king or rook toward an opponent's piece or pawn — either a king marching toward a target (7/10) or a rook shifting to a contested file (3/10). In 8/10 cases, the move appears purposeful and 'correct by instinct' — contesting an open file, attacking a weak pawn, or approaching a target — but fails because the position demanded something more nuanced. The correct moves were typically either pawn breaks (positions 3, 9 needed c6 and f4), preparatory king safety moves (positions 7 needed Kh3), maintaining centralization rather than approaching (positions 2, 5 needed Kd4/Ke3), or avoiding self-obstruction (position 10). Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, showing these are razor-thin positions where the 'natural' approach fails. 2/10 positions (4, 8) were actually correct approaches, suggesting the feature detects the move pattern itself regardless of whether it succeeds.

592.label: Rook moves to an apparently active square (targeting pawns, entering open ranks, giving checks) while abandoning a critical defensive responsibility, allowing immediate tactical punishment.
592.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook relocating to what appears to be an 'active' square — the 7th rank (positions 1, 6), the 4th rank (positions 2, 5, 7, 10), the 2nd rank (positions 3, 9), the 5th rank (position 8), or delivering a check (position 4). In every case, the rook was needed for a specific defensive duty: preventing back-rank mates (positions 5, 10 — both resulting in immediate checkmate), guarding the king's vicinity (positions 7, 8 — both allowing forced mates), maintaining piece coordination for a key tactic (position 2), blockading a passed pawn (position 4), controlling a critical square (position 3 — f7), or protecting a hanging piece (position 6). The punishment was catastrophic: 4/10 positions resulted in immediate or near-immediate checkmate, and the average cp_loss was ~3966. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were precisely the moments demanding defensive discipline rather than ambitious rook redeployment. 8/10 positions were endgames where the rook's defensive role was paramount.

595.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move when an immediate tactical shot (usually a check) was available to maintain or convert a decisive advantage.
595.description: All 10 positions share one critical pattern: the player chose a quiet 'improving' move (repositioning a piece or pushing a pawn) in a position that demanded an immediate forcing continuation. In 6/10 positions, the best move was a check (Bc5+, c3+, Bh5+, Qh4+, Ra1+, Nxd3+); in 2/10 it was a capture of a vulnerable pawn (Nxg4, Bxd5); and in 2/10 it was an immediate aggressive threat (Qh2, g4). The played moves were universally non-capturing, non-checking, and created no immediate threat — they were developmental or positional in character (rook repositioning in 3/10, knight repositioning in 3/10, pawn advances in 4/10). The tempo_loss tag appears in 9/10 positions and missed_tactic in 10/10. The average cp_loss of 2173 is catastrophically high, with only 1.6 good moves available on average, confirming these are narrow tactical moments requiring precision. King safety was a factor in 9/10 positions — typically the opponent's king was exposed, making the forcing check especially devastating. The common punishment mechanism is that the free tempo allows the opponent to consolidate (castle, reposition a passive piece, or escape the king from danger) before the tactical opportunity can be exploited on the next move.

587.label: Superficially active or natural-looking moves (predominantly bishop moves/captures) that fundamentally misjudge the position's tactical demands, overlooking either a decisive threat, a key defensive requirement, or leaving pieces unprotected.
587.description: 7/10 positions involve bishop moves or captures (Bf6, Bg5, Bxg4, Bf6, Bxc5, Bxh3, Bf3), with the remaining 3 being other piece/pawn moves that share the same error pattern. In all 10 cases, the player chose a move that appeared purposeful—attacking a piece (3/10), capturing material (4/10), or repositioning defensively (3/10)—but critically overlooked the position's primary tactical requirement. The average number of good alternatives was only 1.4, meaning these were razor-sharp positions demanding one specific response. 6/10 positions featured the moved piece either becoming undefended or removing a critical defensive function: Bg5 broke coordination protecting Ng4, Bf6 abandoned back-rank coverage, fxg3 exposed the queen on g4, Bxh3 removed a piece that was paradoxically blocking mate, Rg7 vacated back-rank defense, and Bf3 placed the bishop en prise. 3/10 positions involved missing a much stronger tactical continuation (Bxg4 missed the intermezzo Qg3+, Bxc5 missed Qxf8#, Bf6 confused bishop placement for queen placement). The consistent thread is that all moves prioritize a secondary tactical idea while ignoring the position's critical demand.

596.label: The queen is quietly repositioned away from a critical square where it was enabling a winning tactic or performing an essential defensive/offensive function.
596.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing queen move (no captures, no checks) that repositions the queen away from a square where it was performing a vital tactical function. In 8/10 cases, the queen was actively contesting or dominating an open file (e-file, f-file, c-file, a-file, or b-file) and moved off it. In 6/10 positions, the player missed a concrete winning tactical shot available on the queen's original file (Qxa8, Qxf7+, Qxe1+, Qxc1, Bxh7+/Qxf8). In the remaining cases, the queen's departure allowed the opponent to seize control of the abandoned file or execute a tactical blow exploiting the queen's absence. The average cp_loss was 314, with only 1.3 good moves available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision rather than quiet consolidation. The moves typically shifted the queen just one file away (e→d, f→e, c→b, b→a) — subtle repositions that look like natural improving moves but catastrophically abandon the position's tactical core.

598.label: Moving the king forward off the back rank when a piece move or trade was needed, exposing it to immediate tactical exploitation.
598.description: All 10/10 positions feature a voluntary (not forced by check) king move stepping forward from the back rank or a sheltered square into the center of the board. In 10/10 cases, the king moved to an adjacent forward square (e1→d2, e8→f7, c1→b2, e8→d7 (×4), d1→c2, d1→e2, e8→e7), and in 10/10 cases the refutation exploited the king's new position with tactical blows—checks along newly-opened diagonals (6/10), file-based attacks (4/10), or knight forks (2/10). The correct moves were universally non-king moves: piece development (Rg1, Rd1, Nc3, h6), captures/trades (Rxc5, Bxf6, Qxd4), castling (O-O-O), or rook activation (Rc8, Rg8). Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, yet the king move was never among the best options. The positions span both colors (White 4/10, Black 6/10) and the king consistently walked toward open files or diagonals where the opponent's pieces could immediately punish it.

607.label: A rook is developed to a square on an unobstructed diagonal controlled by an enemy bishop, allowing it to be captured for the exchange.
607.description: 10/10 positions show the identical pattern: a rook is moved to a 'natural-looking' development square (an open or semi-open file) that happens to lie at the end of a long, completely unobstructed diagonal controlled by an enemy bishop. In every case, the bishop can simply capture the rook, winning the exchange. The diagonals involved are long (3-6 empty intervening squares), making them easy to overlook: positions 1 and 9 feature a bishop on f5/g6 reaching b1, positions 3, 4, and 10 feature a bishop on g3/f4 reaching b8, position 5 features a bishop on a6 reaching f1, position 6 features a bishop on d5 reaching g8, position 7 features a bishop on g5 reaching c1, position 8 features a bishop on a4 reaching e8, and position 2 features a bishop on b4 reaching e1. All 10 moves are rook relocations (not captures or checks), and all 10 refutations involve the bishop simply taking the rook. The average cp_loss of 336 closely matches the exchange value (~300cp) plus collateral positional damage.

582.label: Tempting captures or active-looking moves that grab material or occupy strong squares but immediately allow a devastating counter-tactic the player failed to foresee.
582.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a move that appeared to achieve something concrete — winning material, centralizing a piece, or challenging an opponent's piece — but overlooked an immediate one-move tactical response that refuted it. 6/10 moves were direct captures (5 with rooks: Rxc7, Rxd3+, Rxb2, Rxe5, Rxc3, plus Bxd5), and the remaining 4 were 'active-looking' placements (Nd4×2, Bd7, Rg1). In 9/10 cases, the refutation involved an immediate counter-capture or recapture that either won the moved piece outright (positions 1, 4, 5, 6), forced an unfavorable simplification into a drawn/worse endgame (positions 2, 3, 7), exploited a newly-undefended piece (position 9), or delivered forced mate (position 10). The best moves in all positions shared a common character: patient, restrained alternatives — quiet king moves (positions 1, 2, 8), piece retreats (positions 3, 4, 5), maintaining pieces rather than exchanging (positions 2, 7), or addressing the opponent's threat before capturing (positions 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 316 and only 2.2 good alternatives confirm these were critical moments where restraint was essential but greed prevailed.

591.label: Player makes a natural-looking developing move or reflexive capture instead of taking a hanging/undefended enemy piece.
591.description: 7/10 positions feature an undefended enemy piece (bishop on h6, bishop on a6, bishop on f2, knight on c2, bishop on g6) that should be captured immediately, but the player instead makes a 'natural' move — typically a fianchetto (Bg7 in 3/10, Bb7 in 1/10), a routine pawn capture (cxd4, a3), or a pawn push that threatens rather than takes (f5). In these 7 positions, the best move was simply Bxh6, Nxh6, Bxa6, Nxa6, Kxf2, Kxc2, or Nxg6+ — winning a full piece for free. The remaining 3/10 positions (fxg6, fxe3, gxh6) show the mirror error: making a reflexive pawn capture that opens a file catastrophically toward the player's own king, when the best move was to NOT capture. In all 10 cases, the player defaulted to an autopilot move rather than calculating the critical tactical feature of the position. Average cp_loss of 2520 reflects that these are massive blunders, with 4/10 leading to immediate forced mate or piece loss equivalent to a rook or more.

599.label: Passive queen moves to the 2nd rank (d2/e2/d7/e7) when an urgent tactical or concrete action is required, wasting critical tempo with the king still in the center.
599.description: All 10 positions feature a queen move to a 'natural developing square' on the player's second rank (d2/e2 for White, d7/e7 for Black) — the most stereotypical 'textbook' queen placement. In 10/10 cases, the moving side's king remains uncastled in the center. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded an urgent concrete action instead: an immediate capture (positions 2, 5), a critical pawn break (positions 4, 8), castling (position 3), a tactical strike like a knight fork (positions 6, 10), or a specific defensive square choice (positions 1, 7, 9). The queen moves all share a 'generic development' character — connecting rooks, preparing castling, or adding a defender — but accomplish nothing forcing while the opponent gains a tempo to exploit the uncastled king, execute a central break, or launch a tactical combination. 6/10 positions are in the opening phase, confirming these are premature or misguided developmental moves. The average cp_loss of 262 shows that these 'autopilot' moves consistently squander significant advantages or create serious disadvantages.

597.label: The queen moves away from a critical open file where it was the sole piece blocking an enemy attack against the player's own king, allowing devastating discovered attacks or direct invasions.
597.description: In 9/10 positions, the queen was positioned on an open file directly between an enemy heavy piece (rook or queen) and the player's own king, serving as the sole shield/blocker on that line. The blundering move relocates the queen off this critical file, immediately enabling discovered attacks or direct invasions. Specifically: 5/10 involved the e-file (positions 1-4 and 10), while the others involved the b-file (position 5), g-file (position 6), d-file (position 7), and c-file (position 8). In 8/10 cases, the refutation involved an explicit discovered check or discovered attack along the newly-opened file. The average cp_loss of 5024 reflects that these are catastrophic errors—4/10 resulted in immediate checkmate or forced mate. The motivations for the queen move varied: material greed (Qxh4, Qxf2, Bxa2-adjacent reasoning), repositioning for attack (Qf7, Qe7, Qf6, Qa4), or defensive confusion (Qd3, Qb3, Qg2). Position 9 is the slight outlier where the queen moved to a knight-forkable square rather than purely unblocking a file, though the king's exposure on an open file was still the underlying vulnerability.

600.label: King moves (including castling) that remove the king from a square where it was critically defending a piece or blocking a tactical sequence, allowing immediate exploitation.
600.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves (including castling as a king move) where the player relocates the king to a seemingly safer square, but the move removes a vital defensive connection. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 6, 10), the king was directly or indirectly defending an adjacent piece (e7 knight/bishop, h3 bishop, b8 rook), and moving it left that piece hanging to a simple capture. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 7, 9), the king moved to a square that enabled a check or mating sequence that was previously impossible (Qf4+ on h2, Rxh6 without check on g8, hxg6+ on h7, Qh2+ on g1). In 1/10 positions (8), the king move wasted a critical tempo when an immediate tactical capture (gxf3) was required. The average cp_loss of 1236 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors. The best moves in all positions either kept the king in place, moved it to the correct safe square (e.g., Kf8 instead of O-O, Kh1 instead of Kg1/Kh2), or prioritized concrete tactical action over king relocation.

604.label: Premature rook moves to active files while the king remains dangerously uncastled in the center.
604.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move played when the moving side's king is still in the center (e1 or e8). In 5/10 positions, the single best move was literally castling (O-O or O-O-O). The rook moves target seemingly logical squares — open files (d, f, g, c) — but ignore the critical king safety crisis. In 5/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 8, 10, and arguably 3), the rook move permanently surrenders castling rights by displacing the rook from its castling square. In 2/10 cases (positions 2 and 7), the rook specifically blocks the king's escape square, enabling immediate checkmate patterns. In the remaining cases (1, 6, 9), the rook move wastes a critical tempo when urgent central/developmental action was needed. The punishment in all 10 positions exploits the exposed central king — through open-file attacks, checks, forks, or outright checkmate. The average cp_loss of 2245 reflects that several of these are game-ending catastrophes.

594.label: Advancing a passed pawn one square closer to promotion when it accomplishes nothing because the opponent can easily blockade, wasting a critical tempo needed for piece/king preparation.
594.description: 8/10 positions involve pushing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (7th for White, 2nd for Black) or promoting it suboptimally. In all 8 pawn-advance cases, an opponent's bishop already controls or can trivially reach the promotion square, making the advance futile: Position 2 (a7 blockaded via ...Bb7+...c6), Position 3 (e7 blockaded by ...Be8), Position 4 (h2 with bishop controlling h1), Position 5 (c7 with bishop on e6 covering c8), Position 8 (a2 with bishop on e5 covering a1), Position 9 (a7 with bishop reaching a8 diagonal). In all cases, the tempo spent pushing the pawn was desperately needed for king activation (Positions 1, 3, 4, 8), piece coordination (Positions 2, 5), or maintaining flexibility (Position 9). The remaining 2/10 positions (Qxf2+ and Qxf7+) share the broader pattern of 'cashing in' prematurely—capturing with check appears forcing but simplifies away the attacker's advantage, analogous to the pawn pushes appearing threatening but achieving nothing. Average cp_loss of 1096 reflects that several of these tempo losses proved catastrophic in finely-balanced races.

606.label: A rook prematurely captures a pawn, abandoning a critical defensive post or failing to address a more urgent positional need first.
606.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing a pawn (Rx_) that appears free or tempting, but the rook's departure from its prior square creates a concrete tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 6, 10), the best move sequence shows the same pawn capture would be correct AFTER preparatory moves (advancing a pawn, moving the king, contesting a file), confirming these are move-order errors rather than the capture being inherently wrong. The consequences vary: 3/10 leave a piece hanging (positions 1, 2, 7), 5/10 fatally expose the king or back rank (positions 4, 5, 8, 9, 10), 1/10 allows a piece to be trapped (position 6), and 1/10 allows 7th-rank invasion (position 3). The average cp_loss of 3022 reflects that 4/10 positions result in checkmate or near-mate. In 7/10 cases only 1 good move existed within 50cp of optimal, indicating these positions were already demanding precise play before the pawn-grab error compounded the situation.

603.label: Ambitious rook repositioning to 'active' squares (especially 7th/2nd rank or attacking pawns) when the position demands a concrete tactical blow or simplifying exchange.
603.description: All 10 positions feature a rook move to a seemingly aggressive or active square that turns out to be a significant error. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 8), the best move was a rook exchange or simplification that the player avoided in favor of maintaining/increasing rook 'activity.' In 4/10 positions (2, 6, 7, 9), the best move was a concrete tactical strike with a different piece (pawn check, knight fork, pawn capture) that the player missed while pursuing rook penetration. In 3/10 positions, the rook moved to the 7th rank (Rc7, Rh7, Rd7); in 3/10 it penetrated to the 2nd rank (Rd2×2, Ra2); in 2/10 it moved to the back rank (Rd8×2); and 2/10 targeted specific pawns on intermediate ranks (Rh4, Rc6). The consistent error is prioritizing rook repositioning for long-term activity over the immediate tactical demands of the position. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision rather than general 'improvement' moves.

602.label: Bishop moves to a square where it is immediately captured or trapped, losing the piece for insufficient compensation.
602.description: All 10/10 positions involve a bishop moving to a square where it is immediately lost — either captured outright or trapped with no escape. In 5/10 cases (Bxe3, Bxb5, Bxd5, Bxg5, Bxf3), the bishop captures a pawn only to be recaptured by a piece that was already defending that square. In the other 5/10 cases (Bc3, Bg4, Bb3, Bd2, Bh5), the bishop moves to a square directly controlled by an opponent's piece — a bishop (Bc3), a pawn (Bg4→fxg4), a pawn advance (Bb3→...a4 traps it), a rook (Bd2→Rxd2), or a knight (Bh5→Nxh5). In 8/10 positions, the bishop was the player's most active or defensively critical piece before the blunder, meaning its loss was particularly devastating. The average cp_loss of 286 reflects that these aren't just pawn losses — they represent the surrender of a key piece. In 7/10 cases, the opponent had one clear best punishment (the recapture), making exploitation straightforward.

608.label: Speculative wing pawn advances in endgames when king activity or piece play should be prioritized instead.
608.description: 10/10 positions involve single-step pawn advances, and 9/10 occur in endgames. 8/10 moves are on the wing files (a-file: 3, g-file: 2, h-file: 3), with only 2 on semi-central files (c6, d6). In 7/10 positions, the best move was either a king move (positions 1, 5, 7, 9, 10) or a piece activation move (positions 2, 4), not a pawn push. The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where the pawn advance wastes a critical tempo. Positions 3 and 8 (with 0 and 30 cp loss respectively) show the feature also fires on structurally similar pawn advances that happen to be correct, suggesting the geometric pattern (flank pawn advance in endgame) is the trigger rather than the error itself. The devastating average cp_loss of 2094 is driven by cases where the pawn push ignores immediate threats (position 10: allows Bc1#) or abandons critical defensive duties like blockading (position 5: ignores c6 pawn) or promoting (position 6: misses d2 winning).

612.label: A rook delivers check (usually capturing a pawn) but is easily recaptured, leaving the attacker down decisive material with no compensation.
612.description: 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check as the blunder move, and 8/10 specifically involve the rook capturing a pawn with check near the opponent's king. In every case, the opponent has a straightforward recapture (by knight, queen, bishop, rook, or pawn) that leaves the checking side down significant material—typically a full rook for just a pawn—without generating sufficient attacking compensation. The player is seduced by the forcing nature of check combined with a capture, creating an illusion of initiative. In at least 4/10 positions (1, 5, 6, 7), there exists a specific mating trap if the opponent responds incorrectly (e.g., Kg8 allowing Qg7#, or Kh1 allowing Qxh3#), but the correct defense is always the obvious natural recapture. 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, indicating these were critical-precision moments where the temptation of a forcing check proved irresistible. The average cp_loss of 2187 reflects how catastrophically these speculative rook sacrifices backfire.

601.label: Aggressive-looking moves motivated by general principles (development, activity, checks, space) that overlook an immediate one-move tactical refutation by the opponent.
601.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: the player makes a move that appears to accomplish something positive — developing a piece (Bg5, Bf5), giving a check (Qh3+, Bh6+), seizing space or files (d4, b5, g5, Rd7), preparing something (a6), or winning material (Bxg4) — but each has a simple, immediate tactical refutation the player failed to calculate. In 4/10 positions (Bg5, Qh3+, d4, Bxg4), the moved piece or target square is directly capturable by the opponent. In 3/10 positions (Bf5, g5, b5), the move creates or exposes a structural/positional weakness the opponent exploits on the very next move. In 2/10 positions (Bh6+, Rd7), the 'aggressive' move actually blocks or strands the player's own attacking resources while enabling a devastating counter. In 1/10 (a6), a preparatory move fatally wastes tempo in a critical race. The average cp_loss of 1284 and average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding specific calculation rather than principled play — the blunder is consistently the 'natural-looking' choice that happens to have a concrete one-move refutation.

615.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing king move when the position urgently demands an active tactical move with another piece.
615.description: 9/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder (Kc5, Kf1×3, Kg1, Kd8, Kg8, Kc2, Kh8), with the remaining position (Qd2) being a similarly passive piece retreat. In all 10 cases, only 1-3 good moves existed (avg 1.4), meaning the positions demanded precise calculation rather than general improvement. The correct moves were overwhelmingly forcing or tactical: capturing a hanging piece (positions 3, 4), executing an exchange combination (position 5), advancing a critical passed pawn (position 9), creating a counter-threat (position 10), or maintaining active piece pressure (positions 2, 6, 8). Instead, players defaulted to a quiet king shuffle that accomplished nothing urgent. 7/10 positions saw the king move worsen king safety (walking into mating nets, open files, or back-rank threats), while 3/10 simply wasted a decisive tempo. The average cp_loss of 3912 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—several converted survivable positions into forced mates.

611.label: Playing slow, non-forcing repositioning moves (especially rook moves to files or prophylactic pawn pushes) in positions that demand immediate captures, checks, or concrete tactical strikes.
611.description: All 10/10 positions share the same fundamental error: the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) when the position screamed for immediate concrete action. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 positions, confirming this is the unifying thread. In 4/10 cases, the correct move was an immediate capture (Qxg3, Rxh8, Nxf4, Qxg7). In 3/10, it was a forcing tactical strike (g4 sacrifice, Nd5 blocking a fork, c7 push). In the remaining 3/10, it was an active piece move addressing the concrete demands of the position. Instead, 5/10 blunders were rook repositioning moves to files (Rc8, Rf8, Rb7, Re8, Rd1), 2/10 were prophylactic kingside pawn pushes (h3, g3), 2/10 were queen moves (Qb6, Qd1), and 1/10 was a routine center pawn push (d4). The common consequence was either walking a piece into a tactical shot (fork, back-rank capture) in 4/10 positions, or squandering a time-critical advantage by allowing the opponent to consolidate or simplify in 6/10 positions. The average cp_loss of 2223 reflects how catastrophically expensive these quiet moves are in sharp positions.

614.label: A routine pawn capture that misses a much stronger forcing piece move, often opening dangerous lines in the process.
614.description: All 9/9 positions feature a pawn capture (always notation like exf5, dxe4, cxd6, etc.) that looks natural or materialistic but is significantly inferior to a piece move. In 7/9 positions, the best move was a piece move delivering check, winning material, or creating forcing threats (Nxa2+, Rxf7, Nxc5, Rxe5+, Bxd4+, Bxd8, Rf4). In 6/9 cases, the pawn capture catastrophically opened a file or diagonal that was immediately exploited against the capturer's own king (positions 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 2401 is enormous because these captures typically transform defensible positions into lost ones or throw away winning advantages. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where precision was essential but the player defaulted to the most obvious materialistic option.
614.old_chip: Greedy pawn capture over piece move

610.label: Major piece (usually rook) directly captures a passed pawn or exchanges pieces to simplify a winning endgame position.
610.description: 10/10 positions feature major piece captures or forcing moves in positions with large advantages (avg eval ~600+ cp). 9/10 are endgame positions. 9/10 involve rook moves specifically (1 queen). 7/10 involve capturing an enemy pawn—usually a dangerous passed pawn near promotion (positions 2, 4, 5, 6 capture pawns on h3, a2, e2, d2 respectively, all within 1-2 squares of queening). 2/10 involve exchanging rooks to reach a won pawn endgame (positions 8, 10). The outlier (position 9, the catastrophic blunder) shows the pattern's failure mode: the player gave a hollow check (Rg1+) instead of making the correct major-piece capture (Rxe3+), moving the rook away from its optimal capturing square. 8/10 moves had 0 cp_loss, confirming this is primarily a pattern of correct endgame conversion technique rather than consistent errors.
