610.old_chip: Rook captures to simplify won endgames

605.label: Non-forcing piece moves played in positions demanding immediate concrete tactical action, where the 'improving' move fails to address a critical vulnerability.
605.description: All 10 positions share a defining characteristic: the player chose a quiet, repositioning or developing move in a position that demanded immediate tactical resolution. 7/10 moves are minor piece repositions (5 knight moves to seemingly active squares like Ng6, Nf6, Ng3, Nd7, Nf3, plus 2 bishop retreats Bb3, Bd2), while the remaining 3 (f5, Qxc2, and one Ng6) are similarly non-forcing moves that ignore the position's most urgent concrete demand. The average number of good moves available was only 1.9, confirming these are critical decision points with very narrow correct paths. In 10/10 cases, a specific immediate tactical issue existed—a hanging piece to capture (positions 1, 2, 9), a threat to defend (positions 3, 10), an attack to continue with checks (positions 4, 6), or a forcing central break to execute before the opponent consolidates (positions 5, 7, 8)—and in every case the player instead chose a 'natural-looking' piece improvement that gave the opponent a critical tempo to either execute their threat or escape danger.

621.label: The queen is moved to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured by an enemy piece, most often a knight.
621.description: 9/10 positions feature a queen move to a square where the queen immediately hangs (can be captured for free or in a catastrophically unfavorable exchange). In 6/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), the queen is captured by an enemy knight that already occupied a square controlling the queen's destination — the player failed to recognize the knight's attack pattern. In 3/10 positions (2, 8, 10), the queen hangs to capture along a diagonal by the opposing queen or bishop. The one outlier (position 9) is a pawn move rather than a queen move, but still involves a piece-safety oversight enabling the opponent to capture a key piece. The average cp_loss of 404 reflects that these moves typically lose the queen outright or force a devastating exchange. In many cases (positions 3, 7), the queen move was even a check, suggesting players were drawn to forcing moves without verifying the destination square's safety. All positions had 2-3 good alternatives available that kept the queen safe.

625.label: Playing a non-forcing king move to the corner square when the position demands the single available urgent tactical response.
625.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move to the nearest corner square (Kh1, Kh8, or Ka1) played as a prophylactic 'safety' move when the position had exactly one good move requiring immediate, forceful action. In 10/10 cases, the average number of good moves available was 1.0, meaning these were razor-sharp positions with zero margin for passivity. In 4/10 positions (2, 7, 8, 10), the correct move was capturing an undefended or hanging piece. In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 5), the correct move was an active piece centralization or development with tempo. In 2/10 positions (6, 9), the correct move was a critical defensive resource to avoid mate. The average centipawn loss of 3092 reflects that 3/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the king move. The prophylactic intent is consistent across all positions—players perceived vague future threats (diagonal checks, back-rank issues, discovered attacks) that either didn't exist or were irrelevant compared to the urgent tactical demand.
625.old_chip: Passive king tuck wastes critical tempo

609.label: Making a strategically-motivated move while overlooking that a piece (own or opponent's) is immediately capturable for free.
609.description: 7/10 positions have 'hanging_piece' as their primary tactical motif. In 5/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 6, 8, 10), the player directly moved their own piece to a square where it could be captured by an enemy piece they overlooked (Bf5 hung to Nxf5, Ng5 hung to Bxg5, Bf4 hung to Nxf4, Bxg7 hung to Bxg7 recapture, Nc4 became winnable via Qa4+ checks). In 1/10 (position 4), the player moved a pawn that was shielding a piece on a diagonal, leaving the rook on a8 capturable by Bxa8. In 1/10 (position 1), the player made a different move instead of capturing the opponent's completely undefended rook with Nxg2. The remaining 3/10 positions (5, 7, 9) share the broader pattern of making a 'nice-looking' move that ignores concrete tactical reality—passive queen retreat enabling a rook check, centralizing instead of capturing hanging pawns, or supporting a passer instead of advancing it. All 10 moves looked thematically reasonable (development, attack, structure, defense) but ignored basic one-move piece safety.

620.label: A piece moves to a seemingly aggressive or tempting square, failing to recognize it was the sole protector of another piece that immediately becomes capturable.
620.description: 8/10 positions show the same core pattern: the moved piece was performing a critical defensive function (sole defender of another piece or maintaining a pin/geometric relationship that protected a piece), and by moving it to a greedy or aggressive-looking square, the player left another piece completely undefended and immediately capturable. In positions 1, 4, 7, and 10, a queen or rook moves to an 'active' attacking square while it was the sole defender of another piece along a diagonal or file. In positions 5 and 8, the player captures the wrong target first (move-order errors) allowing the opponent to recapture the attacker. In positions 2 and 9, the move breaks a geometric relationship (a pin or file-blocking pawn) that was indirectly protecting a piece. Only 2/10 positions (d4 strategic closing and Kb1 king retreat) deviate from this precise tactical pattern, though even these share the broader theme of a self-damaging move that surrenders a critical positional function. The average cp_loss of 1324 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights—the player sees an attractive destination square but is blind to the defensive role the piece was fulfilling.

622.label: Non-forcing pawn advance aimed at an enemy bishop when the position demands immediate tactical action.
622.description: 8/10 positions feature a slow pawn advance specifically targeting an enemy bishop (h5 attacking Bg6/Bg4, a4 attacking Bb5, b5 attacking Bc4, a3 challenging Bb4, c5 challenging Bb4, b3 challenging Ba4, g4 attacking Bf3), while the remaining 2/10 are flank pawn advances in endgames that similarly waste critical tempo. In all 10 positions, the move is non-forcing (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) and ignores an urgent positional or tactical demand — whether that's a back-rank mating pattern (positions 1, 4, 5), a winning tactical strike available (position 2), dangerous passed pawns requiring immediate neutralization (positions 6, 9), or an exposed king needing protection (positions 7, 10). The average cp_loss of 2931 reflects that these tempo losses are catastrophic precisely because the positions are sharp. 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, confirming these are narrow tactical moments where the slow bishop-chasing pawn push is uniquely punished.

624.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (or toward promotion) in a pawn endgame, creating an immediate and typically unstoppable queening threat.
624.description: All 10/10 positions are pawn endgames (or near-pawn endgames) where the move played advances a passed pawn closer to promotion. Specifically, 6/10 push the pawn to the 7th rank (from the moving side's perspective: d7, h7, c7, b2, h2, a7), while the remaining 4 push to the 5th or 6th rank equivalent (e6, c3, a4, g3). In 9/10 positions the move is the engine's top recommendation with 0 cp_loss, and in 9/10 only 1-2 moves were within 50cp of best, indicating these are critical moments where ONLY the immediate pawn advance maintains the full advantage. The single blunder (h2, position 7, 543 cp_loss) represents pushing to the 7th rank prematurely when a blockade was available — the same geometric action but with a fatal timing error. All positions feature exposed kings with weak or absent pawn shields, both sides having passed pawns, and the core tension being a promotion race.

623.label: Rook moves that look forceful (infiltrating ranks, giving checks, capturing) but are played one tempo too early, before necessary preparation neutralizes tactical vulnerabilities.
623.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook making an aggressive-looking move — invading the 2nd/7th rank, advancing to the 6th/8th rank, giving check, or capturing — that is tactically premature. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 7), the rook invades an advanced rank without first neutralizing a tactical threat, allowing the opponent to exploit the rook's absence or the newly-created vulnerability. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 8, 10), the rook delivers a check that is counterproductive — either an unsound sacrifice, a check that improves the opponent's king, or a check that trades away the very piece generating mating threats. In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 9), the rook enters a premature exchange sequence that loses material or misses a stronger tactic. Critically, in at least 5/10 positions (1, 6, 7, 9, and partially 10), the same rook move to the same square becomes correct after one preparatory move — the error is purely one of move order. The best moves across all positions consistently involve either quiet preparation (prophylactic pawns, piece repositioning, neutralizing defenders) or a completely different tactical shot, before the rook activation becomes sound.

618.label: A major piece (rook or queen) moves to a square where it becomes vulnerable to a knight fork with the king.
618.description: 7/10 positions feature the identical tactical pattern: a rook or queen moves to a new square that creates a geometric vulnerability where an opponent's knight can deliver check to the king while simultaneously attacking the just-moved piece. In 6/10 positions (1,2,3,4,5,6), the moved rook is cleanly forked alongside the king by a knight check (Ne7+ forking Kg8/Rc8 in positions 1 and 5; Ne2+ forking Kg1/Rc1 or Rc3 in positions 2 and 6; Nd3+ forking Kf2/Rb2 in position 3; Nf6+ forking Kg8/Rd5 in position 4). Position 9 shows a closely related pattern where a queen moves to h5 and becomes hanging after an intermediate Nxf6+ check forces recapture. The remaining 3/10 positions (7,8,10) share the broader theme of moving a major piece to an inferior square that loses tempo or activity, but lack the specific knight-fork geometry. The average cp_loss of 277 reflects the catastrophic nature of walking a piece into a fork, typically losing a full exchange.

619.label: Advancing a pawn in the endgame when king activity, piece activation, or a different pawn's advance was the critical priority.
619.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances in the endgame that waste tempo or create weaknesses. In at least 5/10 positions (2, 7, 10, 1, 3), the best move was a king move or piece move rather than a pawn push — the player chose to push material forward instead of activating their most important endgame piece (the king) or using a rook. In 3/10 positions (4, 6, 9), the correct move was advancing a DIFFERENT pawn (the already-advanced one, or promoting immediately, or a more modest advance). The common thread is that the player instinctively pushes pawns forward — often aggressively by two squares (g4, f4, e4) — when the endgame demanded patience, king centralization, or precise move-order. 8/10 moves are flank or semi-central pawn advances (b4, g4, b3, g4, f4, h4, f4, f4), suggesting a pattern of trying to create passed pawns or gain space on the wings rather than addressing the position's core requirement. Average cp_loss of 1059 confirms these are highly consequential mistakes.

617.label: The player makes a tempting capture or active-looking move while leaving one of their own pieces critically undefended, allowing the opponent to win material or deliver checkmate.
617.description: In 9/10 positions, the player either captured material (7 captures) or made a seemingly active queen/rook move (3 cases), while critically ignoring that one of their own pieces was left unprotected. In 7/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10), the refutation was simply capturing the hanging piece — sometimes with check or leading to mate. The 'hanging piece' tactical motif was explicitly identified in 5/10 positions, with 'back_rank' exploitation in 2/10 and 'promotion_error' in 2/10, but all share the same root cause: tunnel vision on the offensive aspect of the move while ignoring a defensive obligation. The average cp_loss of 5018 reflects how catastrophic these oversights are — 5/10 led to forced checkmate. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow positions where the one correct move specifically addressed the defensive vulnerability that was ignored.

626.label: Capturing a dangerous passed pawn with a major piece (Queen/Rook), allowing the enemy king to recapture and enter a simplified endgame that squanders the advantage.
626.description: 10/10 positions are endgames where the player captures material with a major piece (5 Queen captures, 5 Rook captures). In at least 8/10 positions, the target is a passed pawn near promotion. In 9/10 cases, the capture comes with check. The critical shared error: in at least 7/10 positions (3,4,5,6,7,10 clearly, plus 1), the enemy king directly recaptures the major piece, trading a Queen or Rook for a mere pawn and entering a drastically simplified endgame. The correct approach in nearly all cases was to maintain the major piece by: bringing the king closer first (positions 1,4,7,10), using checking sequences to keep the piece active while neutralizing the pawn (positions 3,5), or advancing their own passed pawns to create dual threats (positions 9,10). Position 8 (0cp loss) and Position 2 (2cp loss) are mild outliers where the capture was nearly optimal, but still fit the geometric pattern of the move.

613.label: A quiet bishop move (usually one diagonal square) that looks like an improvement but removes the bishop from a square where it performed a critical defensive or controlling function.
613.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a seemingly natural or 'improved' square, with 9/10 being single-step diagonal relocations. In every case, the bishop was already performing a vital function on its original square that the player failed to recognize: controlling a key invasion square (positions 2, 3, 9 — bishop left e5 allowing king/queen access to c4 or d5), providing defensive coverage against back-rank or mating threats (positions 7, 4), or maintaining tactical tension that prevented the opponent from executing a combination (positions 1, 5, 6, 10). The average cp_loss of 4026 is extreme because in 4/10 cases the move converted a survivable position into forced mate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, showing these positions demanded precision. The moves were overwhelmingly played by Black (7/10) in middlegame positions (7/10), suggesting a pattern of active-looking bishop repositioning under pressure that actually collapses the defense.

631.label: Voluntarily exchanging one's own powerfully centralized knight — the linchpin of the position — for a less important enemy piece, dissipating a large positional or tactical advantage.
631.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight capture (Nx__) that removes the player's own most dominant, best-placed knight from the board. In 8/10 cases, the traded knight occupied a commanding central outpost (e4 in positions 1, 2, 6, 8; e5 in position 3; c4 in position 9; d5 in positions 7, 10) that was the cornerstone of the entire position's advantage. In 7/10 positions, the knight was exchanged for a clearly inferior enemy piece (passive knight on d2 in 4 cases, or a piece that could have been captured by a less valuable friendly piece). In 3/10 positions (5, 7, 10), the dominant knight was traded at the wrong moment — when a stronger forcing move should have preceded the capture. The average cp_loss of 356 reflects that these trades consistently squander large advantages (often converting winning positions into equal ones), because the centralized knight generated far more value alive than the material gained by its trade.

633.label: Moving a knight to an aggressive-looking square instead of executing the position's concrete tactical or defensive demand.
633.description: All 10/10 positions involve a knight jumping to an advanced, aggressive-looking square (g4, g5, h4, f4, c5, a5) that appears to create attacking threats, typically toward the opponent's king. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded a fundamentally different type of move: an immediate capture (Qxf4 in pos 8, Bxh6 in pos 9, Qxe6+ in pos 2), a forcing tactic (Nxf3+ in pos 5, c6 in pos 6, Bxg2 in pos 1), or maintaining the knight on its current dominant/defensive post (e4 in pos 3, f5 in pos 7, d5 in pos 10). In 7/10 positions, the knight abandoned a square where it served a critical defensive or tactical function. The average centipawn loss of 1296 reflects how severely these positions punish the tempo wasted on a speculative piece redeployment. Only 1.3 good moves existed on average, indicating these were razor-sharp positions requiring concrete solutions rather than slow piece maneuvering.

616.label: Moving a rook (or making an exchange) to directly contest the opponent's most dominant piece, when the position demanded a different, more creative continuation.
616.description: 7/10 positions involve rook moves attempting to challenge or contest an opponent's active piece (typically on the 7th rank or an open file), while the remaining 3/10 involve captures/exchanges of the opponent's strong centralized piece. In all 10 cases, the player chose the 'natural' reactive response to the opponent's most visually dominant piece rather than finding the one precise move the position required (avg only 1.4 good moves available). 4/10 positions involved back-rank exposure as the direct consequence (positions 1, 4, 5, 7), 3/10 involved using the wrong rook or abandoning a critical file (positions 1, 6, 9), and 5/10 involved missing a significantly stronger forcing continuation (positions 2, 3, 7, 8, 10). The rook moves specifically targeted the 7th/2nd rank (R8f7, Rc7, Rc7, Rf7, Rd2) or open files (Rfc1, Rfc1), while the captures (Bxd5, exf6, Bxd5+) exchanged on central squares. The correct moves were typically non-obvious: quiet king moves (Kh8), pawn thrusts (g4, axb4), piece activations (Bh4), or using the other rook (R5f7, Rac1).
616.old_chip: Reactive rook challenge misses stronger move

634.label: Unnecessary wing pawn advances in endgames that prematurely fix the pawn structure, allowing the opponent to lock or exploit the resulting weakness.
634.description: 10/10 positions feature pawn advances on the outermost files (a-file: 4 positions, h-file: 3 positions, g-file: 3 positions) during pure or near-pure pawn endgames. In every case, the advance commits the pawn structure on one flank before the timing is right, either locking pawns in a way that benefits the opponent (positions 1, 2, 5, 8), wasting a critical tempo that should be used for king activation (positions 6, 9, 10), creating structural weaknesses like unprotected neighboring pawns (positions 7, 8, 10), or releasing critical pawn tension that the opponent exploits with an immediate counter-lock (positions 2, 5). The better moves consistently involve either king activation first (6/10 positions list a king move as best), a different pawn advance order on the same flank (positions 1, 4), or challenging the opponent's pawns on the opposite flank (position 3). The average cp_loss of 333 reflects that endgame pawn structure decisions are often irreversible.

628.label: King moves to a more tactically vulnerable square when already exposed, typically walking toward enemy piece coordination rather than retreating to safer shelter.
628.description: All 10/10 positions involve king moves in situations where the king is already exposed and has extremely limited safe squares (avg 1.9 good moves available). In 8/10 cases, the king moves forward or toward enemy pieces rather than retreating to relative safety — Ke3 into the center, Kg3 into knight-fork range, Kd5 into a rook mating net, Kh3 into a queen-mate square, Kf4 into pawn-mate territory, Kg7 blocking its own bishop's defensive square. In 6/10 positions, the correct move was retreating the king toward the back rank or corner (Ke1, Ke2, Kg1, Kc7, Ke6, Kh7). The average cp_loss of 4561 is catastrophic, with 5/10 positions resulting in immediate or near-immediate forced mate after the king move. In 8/10 positions, the side making the move was already significantly losing, meaning these are king moves in desperate defensive positions where one wrong step is fatal. The positions consistently feature enemy pieces (queens, rooks, knights) coordinating around the king's destination square to create mating nets, discovered checks, or inescapable tactical patterns.

627.label: Playing a tempting aggressive move (usually a check) when a more precise forcing move on a different square or with a different piece/order was devastatingly stronger.
627.description: 7/10 positions feature the player delivering a check that is inferior to another available check — typically the piece lands on the wrong square (positions 2, 5, 6, 7, 9) or the checks are played in the wrong order (positions 3, 4). The remaining 3/10 positions (1, 8, 10) involve playing a non-forcing move when an immediate check was available that won material or forced a draw. In 9/10 positions, the best move was itself a check or forcing sacrifice. The critical commonality is that the player correctly identified the tactical theme (discovered checks in 6/10, back-rank pressure, king exposure) but executed it imprecisely — often the difference between the played move and the best move is literally one square (Re6 vs Re8, Rc7 vs Rb6, Nd4 vs Ne5, Rd2 vs Re2). The average cp_loss of 2050 reflects that these 'almost-right' moves frequently squander forced mates or decisive material wins.

629.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn move (push or capture) when a much stronger immediate tactical piece move was available.
629.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves — either pushes or captures — played in sharp tactical positions where a far superior forcing move with a piece existed. In 8/10 cases, the best available move was a piece action: a capture (Qxg5, Bxf6, Qxe6+, Rxd4), a check (Ba3+, Qg6 leading to fxe7+), or a defensive piece move (Rd1, Nb8). The blunders include 4/10 passed pawn advances (d6, f7, d6, h2) where the player prioritized promotion ambitions over urgent tactical needs, 3/10 routine pawn captures (fxg6, axb5, fxe5) where the player exchanged pawns instead of exploiting hanging pieces or delivering checks, and 3/10 aggressive-looking pawn pushes (f3, e3, g6) that appeared attacking but ignored immediate tactical realities. The average cp_loss of 1212 and average of only 1.1 good moves available confirm these are critical moments demanding precision, where the seductive simplicity of a pawn move led to catastrophic errors.

632.label: A rook is placed on the 1st/8th rank in a routine file-occupation move when the position demands immediate tactical action, leaving pieces hanging or missing critical shots.
632.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the player's back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black) on an open or semi-open file, giving the appearance of a natural developing/file-occupying move. In 7/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10), the move directly left a piece undefended or created a new tactical vulnerability that the opponent could exploit with a forcing sequence. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8), the player already had one rook actively placed (on the 2nd/7th rank or an aggressive square like g3/h6) and chose to 'develop' the second rook passively rather than exploit the first rook's activity. The average cp_loss of 346 reflects that these positions universally demanded immediate tactical engagement—captures, sacrifices, or knight maneuvers—rather than slow positional improvements. Only 2.0 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision that the back-rank rook move completely ignores.

635.label: Playing a non-urgent flank pawn advance while the player's own king faces an immediate tactical crisis requiring piece-based defense.
635.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances (no piece moves) played when the moving side's king is critically exposed to immediate tactical threats. 7/10 moves are b-file pawn pushes (b3, b4, b5×3, b6), with the remainder being a4, g4, g5, and d4 — all slow, non-defensive pawn moves. In 10/10 positions, the player's king is vulnerable: either on the back rank (6/10), exposed in the center (3/10), or on a weakened square (1/10). The refutations consistently exploit the wasted tempo with checks, discovered attacks, or mating sequences (5/10 result in forced mate or mate-in-one). The average cp_loss of 3000 reflects the catastrophic nature of spending a tempo on a positional pawn move when the position demands immediate tactical defense. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions required precise defensive play that was completely ignored in favor of general pawn expansion.

641.label: A minor piece captures on f2 or f7 without sufficient supporting pieces, and the simple recapture (usually by the king) leaves the attacker down a full piece for just a pawn.
641.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (knight in 9/10, bishop in 1/10) capturing the f-pawn directly in front of the opponent's king (f7 in 4/10 positions played by White, f2 in 6/10 positions played by Black). In every case, the sacrifice occurs in the opening (9/10) or early middlegame (1/10) when supporting pieces are insufficiently developed to generate compensation. The primary refutation in 9/10 cases is the simple king recapture (Kxf7 or Kxf2), with 1 case using Rxf2. After recapture, the sacrificing side is down a full minor piece for merely one pawn with no follow-up threats—no mating nets, no working forks, no discovered attacks. The average cp_loss of 327 corresponds closely to the value of a minor piece minus a pawn (~200-300cp net loss). In 10/10 positions, the attacker's remaining pieces were too undeveloped or poorly coordinated to exploit the slightly displaced king, and in 10/10 cases at least one simple developing or retreating move existed that maintained or improved the position.

636.label: Aggressive king advance onto an open file where the opponent's rook (or pawn) delivers a devastating tempo-gaining check.
636.description: 10/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder, and 9/10 occur in rook endgames. In every case, the king advances to what appears to be an active or centralizing square, but lands on an open file or rank where the opponent delivers an immediate check. Specifically: Position 1 (Kc5 → Rc2+ on c-file), Position 2 (Kd6 → Rd1+ on d-file), Position 3 (Ke3 → f4+ pawn check), Position 5 (Kh5 → Rh7# on h-file), Position 6 (Kf2 → Rxc2+ on c-file), Position 7 (Ke7 → Re2+ on e-file), Position 8 (Kg5 → Rh1/Rb5+ activity), Position 9 (Kg5 → Rg8+ on g-file), Position 10 (Kf6 → Rf4+ on f-file). In 8/10 positions, the correct move was a piece move (rook repositioning, capture, or queen check) rather than a king move. The average cp_loss of 1299 reflects the severity of walking into tactical shots. The king's intent was consistently described as 'centralizing' or 'supporting passed pawns' — natural endgame objectives that blind the player to immediate tactical vulnerabilities on open lines.

637.label: A knight makes a tempting capture but leaves a critical defensive post unguarded, allowing tactical exploitation.
637.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight making a materially-motivated capture (Nx__) that removes it from a square where it was performing an essential defensive function. In 8/10 cases, the knight was guarding key squares around its own king or blocking dangerous lines (f3 guarding e5/h4 diagonal in positions 3,4,7,10; f6 guarding kingside in positions 1,8; h6 guarding h7 in position 6; d4 as last defensive piece in position 2). The captures target central pawns (d4, d5, e4) or seemingly valuable pieces (d6, f7, f3) that appear 'free' or strategically desirable. In 7/10 positions the refutation involves an immediate tactical blow exploiting the vacated square — whether a queen check on an opened diagonal (positions 3,6), capture of a now-undefended pawn/piece (positions 4,7,10), or exploitation of the removed kingside defender (positions 1,8,9). The average cp_loss of 3057 reflects that these 'obvious' captures consistently transform competitive or winning positions into losing or mated ones.

642.label: A prophylactic king move one step toward the nearest corner wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate concrete action.
642.description: All 10/10 positions feature the exact same type of mistake: the king moves one square from its castled position toward the nearest corner (g8→h8, g1→h1, c1→b1, c8→b8) as a perceived prophylactic or 'improving' move. In every case, the position urgently required concrete action — capturing a hanging piece (3/10), launching an immediate attack (2/10), making a critical pawn break (3/10), or resolving file tension (2/10). The average centipawn loss was 254, and only 1.4 good moves existed on average, meaning these were narrow positions demanding precision. In 10/10 cases the opponent punished the wasted tempo by executing the very plan the player should have preempted: advancing pawns (b5, a4, f4, d5), capturing undefended pieces (Rxf6, Rxd5, Bxd4), or doubling on open files. The positions span both sides (5 White, 5 Black) and both castling directions (kingside and queenside), confirming the pattern is purely about the king-tuck geometry rather than a specific positional setup.

639.label: A reflexive pawn-takes-pawn capture resolves tension passively when a more forcing move (check, fork, or piece capture) should come first or instead.
639.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing an enemy pawn (pxp), making this the defining geometric signature. In 8/10 cases this is a genuine mistake (avg cp_loss 219 across those 8), while 2/10 happen to be the best move (0 cp loss), suggesting the feature detects the mechanical pattern of routine pawn captures. Among the 8 mistakes, the common error breaks into clear sub-types: in 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 7) the player captures with the pawn when a piece or king should capture the same target (Nxd5 not exd5, Kxg5 not hxg5, Nxg5 not hxg5); in 4/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 9, 10) the player makes the pawn capture when a different forcing move — typically a check or fork — should be played first or instead (Qxe4+, Ne3+, e4+, exd5+); and in 1/10 (position 6) the pawn capture is an unnecessary detour from an immediate promotion. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these are narrow positions demanding precision where the 'obvious' pawn capture is a trap.

638.label: Advancing a pawn to open or expand in a closed position when the move is either insufficiently prepared or ignores an immediate tactical opportunity.
638.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance in a closed or semi-closed center, and all 10/10 are characterized as either premature (lacking preparation) or mistimed (missing something more urgent). The positions split into two related sub-patterns: in 6/10 cases (e4, f5, f4, f4, e4, e5) the pawn break opens lines that immediately expose a vulnerability in the player's own position (undefended pieces, exposed king, or removed defensive resources); in 4/10 cases (b5, h4, b5, c4) the pawn advance is a slow strategic expansion that squanders a concrete tactical opportunity available that turn. The closed center is explicitly present in 8/10 positions and implied in the remaining 2. The average cp_loss of 266 reflects that these positions typically demanded one precise move (avg 1.8 good moves available), making the ill-timed pawn push especially costly. Tags 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic' appear in 8/10 analyses each, while 'pawn_structure' appears in all 10.
638.old_chip: Premature pawn break in closed position

645.label: Bishop captures a knight before a preparatory move, allowing the opponent's queen to recapture actively with intact pawn structure.
645.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a knight (Bx__), and in 9/10 cases the key refutation is the opponent's queen recapturing on the same square (Qxf6, Qxc6, Qxc3, Qxb5, Qxc4), which simultaneously maintains pawn structure integrity and activates the queen. In 9/10 positions, there existed a specific preparatory move (e5, Nd5, Ne5, Nfd5, c6, Bc5, e5, Bxe5) that should have preceded or replaced the capture—these preparation moves either denied the favorable queen recapture, created devastating follow-up tactics, or made the exchange unnecessary. The average cp_loss of 1196 reflects that these premature exchanges consistently dissipate winning attacks or large advantages into near-equality. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions demanding precise move-order calculation rather than general understanding.

640.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing flank pawn move when a concrete piece move would exploit the opponent's vulnerability.
640.description: All 10/10 positions feature a one-square pawn advance on a non-central file (a, b, c, f, g, or h) played when the position demanded immediate tactical piece action. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a piece move—most often a knight jump to a dominant square (Nd7, Nf5, Nd4, Ng5 in 5/10 positions). The blundered pawn moves share a common intent: they address a superficial positional concern (chasing a piece in 3/10, prophylaxis against a future threat in 3/10, challenging an enemy pawn in 3/10, or expanding on a flank in 1/10). In 8/10 positions, a clear tactical opportunity was missed. The average cp_loss of 244 reflects that these tempi are squandered at critical moments—7/10 positions featured an opponent with an exposed or uncastled king, incomplete development, or a hanging piece that required immediate concrete exploitation. The pawn moves frequently created new weaknesses (king safety compromised in 5/10, piece deflected from key diagonal in 2/10, pawn structure damaged in 4/10).

646.label: A rook greedily captures a pawn but lands on an undefended square where it is won back through a check or fork exploiting king vulnerability.
646.description: 8/10 positions feature a rook capturing a pawn (Rxa4, Rxd4, Rxh7, Rxe5, Rxa4, Rxb7, Rxd5, Rxh5), and in all 8 cases the rook moves to an undefended square where it is immediately won through a tactical reply exploiting the king's position. The mechanism is remarkably consistent: 6/8 rook captures are punished by a check or fork (Qd1+, Qe3+, Qb1+, Qd7+, Nd4+, Rxg6+) that gains tempo against the king while simultaneously attacking the now-hanging rook. The remaining 2/8 rook captures are punished by a direct attack on the undefended rook (Qd6) or by the rook's absence from a critical defensive post allowing a mating attack. The 2 non-rook positions (f6, hxg6) follow the same broader logic: a greedy capture/pawn move that leaves a major piece hanging to an intermediate tactic. In all 10 positions, better alternatives existed (avg 2.4 good moves available) that maintained piece safety or improved coordination without exposing material to tactical exploitation.

643.label: Advancing a pawn that shields the player's own king, catastrophically weakening king safety.
643.description: 9/10 positions involve pushing a pawn on the f-file or g-file directly in front of or adjacent to the player's own king (g3, g5, g6, g6, g6, f6, f6, g3), with 1/10 pushing a c-pawn near an exposed king on d3, and 1/10 moving the king itself to an exposed g2 square. In all 10 cases, the move removes or advances a pawn that was serving as critical shelter for the king, and the dominant tactical motif tagged in the analyses is 'king_safety' (9/10 primary motif). The average centipawn loss is enormous (3853), with 5/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate after the move. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where precise play was demanded. The g-pawn is the most common culprit (7/10 positions involve g-pawn advances), followed by f-pawn pushes (2/10). The refutations consistently exploit the opened lines, weakened squares, or exposed ranks created by the pawn advance — rook checks on newly opened ranks (positions 9, 10), piece invasions through weakened light/dark square complexes (positions 4, 5, 8), or mating nets against the denuded king (positions 3, 6, 9, 10).

648.label: A bishop is retreated to a passive square when the position demands an immediate urgent action (king march, pawn break, or critical defensive post).
648.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a passive or back-rank square (Bc1 x3, Bd8, Bf1, Bd1, Bg3, Bc7, Bd2), with the remaining position showing a similarly passive king retreat (Ke7). In all 10 cases, the move is a slow piece repositioning that squanders a critical tempo when the position demanded immediate action. 8/10 are endgame positions where the wasted tempo allows the opponent to execute a decisive king invasion (typically via e4-d3-c2 in positions 1-4 and 10), a structure-fixing pawn advance (positions 7-8), or an unstoppable attack (position 6). The average cp_loss of 199 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but serious mistakes. 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, indicating critical decision points with narrow margins where the slow bishop maneuver was particularly costly. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in all 10 analyses, confirming this as the unifying thread.

644.label: A rook passively shifts laterally to a different file, breaking the coordination of doubled/paired rooks and leaving the remaining piece undefended or the position tactically exploitable.
644.description: 9/10 positions involve a rook moving laterally along a rank to a different file (1/10 is a queen making a similar passive lateral shift). In at least 7/10 positions, the player had doubled rooks on an open file (usually the d-file) and moved one rook sideways to another file (c, e, g, or b), breaking the mutual protection between the paired rooks. In positions 1, 4, 6, 9, and 10, this directly left the partner rook undefended, enabling immediate tactical exploitation (forks, captures, pins). In positions 3, 5, and 7, the lateral rook shift abandoned a critical offensive role (7th-rank invasion, back-rank defense, or active file). All 10 moves share the characteristic of being quiet 'repositioning' moves—never captures, checks, or direct attacks—that appear to improve piece placement but actually destroy existing coordination. The average cp_loss of 332 reflects that these positions typically had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.5), making the lateral shift a critical error at a moment demanding precision.

651.label: Capturing a centrally-placed piece where the opponent's pawn recapture forks or attacks additional pieces that were adjacent to the capture square.
651.description: In 10/10 positions, the player captures an enemy piece on a central square (d4, e5, e4, d5, or b1), and the opponent recaptures with a pawn that immediately creates a devastating follow-up threat. In 8/10 cases, the recapturing pawn forks two pieces simultaneously (typically a piece on the file to the left and right of the capture square). Specifically, 6/10 involve Nxe5 where dxe5 forks pieces on d6 (bishop or queen) and f6 (knight). 2/10 involve Nxd4 where exd4 attacks pieces on the e-file (rook or queen on e3) and c-file (knight on c3). Position 9 shows Nxd5 where exd5 forks pieces on e6 and c6. Position 4 shows Nxe4 where dxe4 attacks the f3 knight. Even the outlier (Position 3, Rxb1) follows the same logic: cxb1 is a pawn recapture that promotes. In all cases, the player focused on eliminating the opponent's strong centralized piece without recognizing that the pawn recapture would weaponize the adjacent geometry.

649.label: Ambitious pawn advances (usually on the flank) that ignore urgent tactical threats, development needs, or king safety requirements.
649.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances played with aggressive intent when the position demands patience, consolidation, or addressing immediate threats. 8/10 are specifically flank pawn pushes (g5×4, g4×2, b5, b4), while 2/10 are semi-central advances (c4, d2). In every case, the best moves involved piece development, coordination, or consolidation (e.g., Nbd2, Rd1, O-O, Na6, Nc3) rather than pawn thrusts. The common punishment is that the pawn advance either weakens critical squares around the player's own king (6/10 positions), leaves pieces unprotected by removing pawn support (3/10), or wastes a critical tempo while ignoring immediate tactical threats (8/10). King safety was compromised or ignored in 7/10 positions, and development was incomplete in at least 6/10 cases. The average cp_loss of 312 reflects that these moves frequently transform winning or equal positions into losing ones by creating tactical vulnerabilities that did not previously exist.

630.label: Choosing an inferior target, capture direction, or attacking move when a clearly superior tactical opportunity was available, often with the same piece or pawn.
630.description: The defining pattern across these positions is selecting a superficially attractive option while missing a dramatically superior one at a narrow decision point (avg 1.8 good moves available). In 4/10 positions (3, 7, 8, 9), the SAME pawn had two legal captures or could capture vs. push, and the player chose the wrong direction—capturing a pawn instead of a bishop (dxe4 instead of dxc4 in positions 7/9, dxc3 instead of dxe3 in position 3) or pushing forward instead of capturing with check (b6 instead of bxa6+ in position 8). In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 6), a knight moved to an aggressive-looking but inferior square, abandoning coordination for a slow/phantom threat. In 2/10 positions (4, 5), the player chose a premature action over a patient/decisive one (e4 eliminating the opponent's weakness; Rf2+ missing forced mate via Qxg6+). Position 10 featured a tempo-wasting pawn push over immediate development. All 10 share the critical trait of tunnel vision on a lesser objective while the position's true key resource went unnoticed.

650.label: A rook delivers check to an exposed king, often impulsively, when quieter moves would maintain or increase the advantage.
650.description: 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check to an opposing king that is exposed (lacking pawn shelter or on an open file/rank). 7/10 occur in endgames where king activity is critical. While 5/10 moves are actually the best or near-best move (0cp loss), the remaining 5 lose significant value (38-9403cp) because the check allows the opponent's king to improve its position or misses a stronger non-checking alternative. The common thread across both good and bad instances is the geometric pattern: a rook sliding along a rank or file to deliver check to a king on an open square. When these checks ARE mistakes (positions 2, 5, 7, 8, 10), the consistent error is that a quiet prophylactic move (h6, Ra5, Rd1) or a different piece's check (Qc5+, Ne4+) was vastly superior. In 4/5 mistake cases, the check drives the opposing king to a better square than it occupied before.

653.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning moves (predominantly rook moves) that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical or developmental action.
653.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves to seemingly active squares (Rd1, Rb1, Rh7, Rc2, Rf5, Rb1, Re4, Rg5), with the remaining 2 being a quiet queen move (Qe5) and a knight retreat (Nb7). All 10 moves share a defining characteristic: they are non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no immediate threats) piece repositioning moves played in positions that demanded urgent action. 7/10 positions are explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. In every case, the best moves available were either forcing (checks, captures, development completing castling) or created immediate concrete threats. The blunders uniformly gave the opponent a free tempo to execute devastating plans: back-rank mates (positions 1, 9), development-exploiting attacks (positions 2, 3, 6), tactical strikes against now-undefended pieces (positions 4, 7), or consolidation that neutralizes counterplay (positions 8, 10). The average cp_loss of 2177 is extraordinarily high, with 3/10 positions resulting in immediate forced checkmate, indicating these 'quiet improving moves' are played at the most critical possible moments.

656.label: Voluntarily advancing the king toward the center or a target in positions where queens/active pieces remain, exposing it to immediate tactical exploitation.
656.description: All 10 positions feature a king move that advances the king forward from a relatively sheltered square toward the center or a tactical target. In 8/10 positions this occurs in the middlegame with queens still on the board. The most common motivation is approaching a passed pawn to capture it (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6) or attempting premature king centralization (positions 7, 9, 10). In 9/10 cases the king lands on a square vulnerable to immediate tactical punishment: diagonal queen checks (positions 1, 6, 9), knight forks (positions 3, 10), rook penetration (position 2), or outright checkmate (position 4). The average cp_loss of 2136 reflects several catastrophic results including two walk-into-mate positions. In every case, the better alternatives involved piece moves or pawn advances that addressed the same strategic concerns without exposing the king — 8/10 positions had the king starting on a back-rank or near-back-rank square where it was adequately safe.

647.label: Premature pawn advances in endgames where king moves were needed to maintain flexibility and control.
647.description: 10/10 positions are endgames where the mistake is a pawn advance rather than a king move (or preparatory piece move). In 8/10 positions, the best move was a king move (Kf3, Kf6, Kf7, Kc6, Bg6/Kf6, Kf3, Kh7, etc.), while the player instead committed a pawn forward. 8/10 moves are flank pawn pushes (f3, h5, h5, a5, g4, g3, h6, g6) with only 2/10 being central (d4, d4). The consistent error is resolving pawn tension or creating structural commitments prematurely—giving the opponent passed pawns (6/10), weakening critical squares (4/10), or enabling move-order exploitation (3/10). The average cp_loss of 129 reflects how these irreversible pawn commitments hand the opponent concrete targets or remove defensive flexibility that king moves would have preserved.

654.label: A quiet bishop developing/repositioning move to a square where an enemy knight can immediately capture it (or it wastes a critical tempo), when the position demanded concrete forcing play.
654.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop move (Bd7, Bd2, Be6, Bd3, Bd6, Bc1, Bc7) played as a natural-looking developing or defensive move in a position where aggressive counterplay was essential. In 7/10 cases, the bishop lands on a square where an enemy knight immediately captures it with advantage (Nxd7, Nxe6 fxe6, Nxd6, Nxc7+). In 8/10 positions, at least one king was uncastled, making tempo critical. The best moves in 8/10 positions were forcing moves (checks, captures, queen attacks like Qg5, Qd4, Bxf2+, Nxf6+) rather than quiet development. 6/10 moves went to the d-file specifically (Bd7×3, Bd2, Bd3, Bd6). The average cp_loss was 227 with only 1.5 good moves available on average, indicating these were critical positions requiring precision. The common thread is that players chose the 'natural' bishop move to address a perceived defensive need (break a pin, block an attack, protect a pawn) while missing that the bishop becomes a tactical target and the position's true demands were for concrete counterattacking moves.

652.label: Quiet bishop repositioning moves that abandon the bishop's critical current function or ignore more urgent tactical requirements.
652.description: 9/10 positions feature quiet (non-capturing) bishop moves to new squares, with an average cp_loss of 2884 indicating catastrophic errors. In 6/10 cases, the bishop was already performing a vital function (controlling a promotion square in Position 2, preventing a knight fork in Position 3, enabling a tactical combination from b7 in Position 9, maintaining a lethal pin in Position 10, defending e6 in Position 4, controlling d6 in Position 6). In 3/10 cases, the bishop move was a tempo-wasting 'improvement' when a completely different piece needed to act (capturing a hanging piece in Position 5, activating the king in Position 8, choosing the wrong discovered-check destination in Position 7). The destinations vary widely across the board (a6, a7, b6, c2, c7, e1, e6, g4) with no consistent geometric target, confirming the pattern is about the decision to reposition rather than the specific destination. 5/10 positions had only 1 good move available, showing these errors occurred at critical decision points where the position demanded concrete action rather than positional maneuvering.

657.label: A knight (or minor piece) voluntarily leaves a powerful or defensively critical square, either exposing a tactical vulnerability or squandering a concrete opportunity that existed from the original square.
657.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundering move is a knight relocation, and in 10/10 it is a minor piece voluntarily leaving a strong square for an inferior one. The critical function abandoned falls into two sub-types: in 5/10 positions (3, 4, 5, 10, and partially 2), the piece was defending a key square—most often c2—and its departure allowed an immediate tactical blow (fork or capture with check). In 4/10 positions (1, 7, 9, and partially 6), the knight was on a dominant central post (d5 or f5) where a concrete winning tactic existed (Ne3+, Nxe3, Nf4), and the move to an inferior square squandered that opportunity. The remaining positions (2, 8) feature knights leaving dominant outposts (d6, b4) for vulnerable rim/edge squares where they become hanging or useless. The average cp_loss of 423 reflects how catastrophic it is to remove a piece from its ideal station. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision.

659.label: Trading a bishop for an opponent's active/centralized piece (usually a knight) when maintaining tension or finding a more dynamic move was far superior.
659.description: In 9/10 positions, a bishop captures a knight (the 10th is a rook capturing a knight with identical logic). The target piece always appears to be the opponent's 'best piece' — a centralized knight on d4 (3 positions), a pressured knight on c6 (3 positions), a structurally important knight on c3 (2 positions), or a strong knight on e5 (1 position). In every case, the exchange backfires catastrophically. In 5/10 positions, the opponent's recapturing piece becomes MORE dominant than the piece that was eliminated (e.g., a bishop landing on the long diagonal after Bxc3, or a bishop centralizing on d4 after the knight is removed). In 4/10 positions, the exchange releases critical dynamic tension when a concrete tactical blow (Nd5, Rxe2, Nxg4) was available. In 8/10 positions, the better alternatives involved maintaining pressure, developing, or finding forcing moves rather than simplifying. The average cp_loss of 231 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but fundamental strategic/tactical errors disguised as 'removing the opponent's best piece.'

660.label: Moving the queen to f3 (White) or f6 (Black) as a superficially active centralization that abandons critical defensive responsibilities, leaving pieces or pawns hanging.
660.description: 9/10 positions feature a queen moving to the f3 square (White, 6 positions) or its mirror f6 (Black, 3 positions), with the remaining position (Kd8) sharing the identical conceptual error of abandoning a critical defensive post. In 6/10 cases, the move directly leaves a piece or pawn undefended (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10), resulting in immediate material loss. In the other positions, the queen move fails to address the most urgent need: developing pieces (position 5), exploiting a forcing tactical sequence (position 8), addressing king safety (position 7), or maintaining initiative with a forcing move (position 4). The average cp_loss of 351 reflects that these are catastrophic errors. The queen on f3/f6 appears active — eyeing the f-file, targeting f7/f2, or centralizing pressure — but in every case it either removes the queen from a square where it was performing an essential defensive function (back-rank coverage, piece protection, pawn blockade) or commits it to a square that fails to create threats urgent enough to compensate for what was abandoned.

662.label: Using a rook to capture a stranded or peripheral minor piece instead of pursuing a more dynamic continuation that maintains initiative or exploits the opponent's king weakness.
662.description: In 10/10 positions, the player used a rook to capture a minor piece (bishop or knight) that was stranded, offside, or relatively harmless — on squares like a1, a8, h8, b1, d8, c3, c6. In every case, the captured piece was described as 'offside,' 'out of play,' 'trapped,' or 'not contributing' to the opponent's active plans. The better moves consistently involved more dynamic actions: 4/10 required attacking the exposed king directly (Re5+, Qh5, Bxh3, gxf3), 3/10 required capturing a MORE DANGEROUS centralized or active piece instead (Bxe5, bxc5, Nxe6), 1/10 required capturing a higher-value piece entirely (Bxe2 winning the queen), and 2/10 required tactical strikes that generated initiative (Nxf3+, bxc5 creating a passed pawn). In 8/10 positions, the rook moved to a passive or disconnected square after the capture, removing it from active participation. The average cp_loss was 1323, with 3/10 positions involving exposed kings that could have been attacked directly. Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical-precision moments where the 'obvious' material grab was the one trap to avoid.

664.label: Moving a rook or queen aggressively to an undefended square where it is immediately captured for free.
664.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moves a major piece to a square where it is immediately captured by the opponent. 8/10 involve rooks specifically, while 2/10 involve queens. In 6/10 cases, the piece attempts a classic '7th rank infiltration' (Rc7, Re7, Re7, Rb2+, Re2+, Rc2) — moving to the opponent's second rank — but arrives undefended and is simply taken. 4/10 moves give check (Rb2+, Re2+, Rb8+, Qxg3+), suggesting the player was seduced by the forcing nature of the check without verifying the piece's safety after the check is dealt with. The average cp_loss of 2434 is extremely high because in most cases the player loses a full rook or queen for nothing. Only 2.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points where precision mattered most.

670.label: Playing a generic 'rook to the e-file' developing move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical or strategic action.
670.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same move pattern: placing a rook on the e-file (Re1 for White, Re8 for Black) as a natural-looking developing move in positions that demand urgency. In 10/10 cases, specific concrete alternatives existed—tactical shots (b4 fork in position 1, Bxf3/Qxd3 in position 8, cxb4 winning a pawn in position 10), centralizing moves (Nd5 in positions 2 and 9), or forcing pawn breaks (axb5 in position 6). Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical-moment positions. In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 9), moving the rook off the f-file specifically removed a key defender of f2/f7, enabling sacrificial attacks (Greek Gift, Bxe6+, Nxf6+ shattering pawns). In 7/10 positions, the move granted the opponent a crucial tempo to execute their plan—castling to safety (positions 1, 2), resolving pawn tension favorably (positions 6, 10), or launching a pawn storm (positions 7, 8). The average centipawn loss of 236 reflects how consistently devastating this 'reasonable-looking' move is in these sharp positions.

668.label: Capturing with a pawn instead of a piece, where the pawn recapture fatally weakens the player's own pawn structure, king safety, or positional restraint.
668.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a pawn capture (always in the format [pawn]x[target]) when a piece capture or piece move was superior. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a piece capture on the exact same square (Qxd6 vs cxd6, Bxc6 vs bxc6, Nxe5 vs dxe5, Bxf5 vs gxf5, Nxe4 vs dxe4, Nxf6 vs gxf6). In 1/10 the best piece capture was on a different square (Nxd5 vs gxf5), and in 1/10 the best move was a piece invasion (Rb7 vs dxe4). The pawn captures consistently caused structural damage: 6/10 specifically weakened the king's pawn shield (opening files toward the castled king or removing shelter pawns), 4/10 released a restraining pawn that allowed the opponent's central pawn to advance devastatingly (d5 advancing after dxe4 removed the blockader, d4 advance after dxe5), and 2/10 entombed the player's own bishop behind the captured pawn. Average cp_loss was 287, indicating these are serious mistakes. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, showing these were critical decision points demanding precision.

661.label: Rook moves to an aggressive-looking square that appears to gain activity but actually abandons critical duties, uses the wrong piece, or walks into a tactical refutation.
661.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to a square that appears active or purposeful — penetrating to the 7th rank, occupying an open file, attacking a piece, or delivering check — but the move is actually a significant mistake. In 3/10 positions (positions 2, 3, and partially 1), the rook goes to the exact square where the QUEEN should go instead, lacking the multi-directional power needed. In 3/10 positions (7, 9, 10), the rook abandons control of a critical file or rank that was restraining the opponent. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 6), the 'aggressive' rook move walks directly into a tactical refutation (fork, discovered check, or capture). In 1/10 (position 8), the rook chooses passive blockading over superior active counterplay. The average cp_loss of 1167 reflects these being high-stakes positions where the superficially attractive rook move dramatically worsens the evaluation. The consistent thread is that the player sees an 'active' destination for the rook and plays it without checking whether that activity actually accomplishes something concrete or whether it creates exploitable weaknesses.

655.label: Choosing a visually attractive or greedy move (capture, centralization, threat) over the one critical continuation demanded by the position.
655.description: 7/10 positions involve Queen moves to squares that appear strong (captures, central squares, threatening squares) but abandon a critical function or miss a stronger forcing sequence. In 6/10 cases, the best move was a forcing continuation (check, fork, or capture) that the player bypassed in favor of something 'tempting' — Position 1 missed Nf8+ for Qxf7, Position 5 missed Qd6+ for Qf6, Position 6 missed Rxc3 for Rg3+, Position 8 missed Nxf7 for Qxd6, Position 9 missed Qh5+ for Qe3. In 4/10 positions, the move specifically abandoned a critical defensive or offensive function the piece was performing — Position 4's Qd6 left the kingside unguarded, Position 8's Qxd6 abandoned g7 allowing mate, Position 9's Qe3 abandoned the f3-h1 diagonal. The average good moves available was only 1.9, confirming these are positions where precision was essential and the 'second-best looking' move was catastrophically wrong. Position 10 (Kg6, 0cp loss) appears to be an outlier where the position was already hopeless.

666.label: Moving a rook to the player's back rank (1st/8th) in a seemingly useful but actually passive manner, abandoning active duties or ignoring urgent positional/tactical needs.
666.description: 9/10 positions feature rook moves to the player's own back rank (1st or 8th rank), with the one outlier (Bxd5) sharing the thematic error of ignoring king safety for material concerns. The rook destinations cluster on the f-file (4/10: Rf1, Rf1, Rf8, Rf8) and g-file (3/10: Rcg1, Rg1, Rg8), with remaining moves to c8 and d8. In 5/10 positions, the move specifically abandons control of a critical open file (e-file or d-file) that was the player's primary structural asset. In 4/10 positions, the rook move either self-blocks the king's escape route or places the rook where it obstructs defensive coordination. The average cp_loss of 3790 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the move. In nearly every case (8/10), the position demanded urgent action addressing king safety or gaining tempo against the opponent's threats, but the player chose a seemingly logical but ultimately passive rook redeployment that appeared to serve a purpose (defending a pawn, preparing a break, doubling on a file) while missing the position's critical need.

658.label: Capturing a pawn or making a slow piece move while ignoring an urgent forcing continuation (usually a check) demanded by exposed king positions.
658.description: 9/10 positions feature at least one critically exposed king, and in all 10 cases the player chose a non-forcing move (typically a pawn capture or quiet piece reposition) over an urgent forcing alternative. 6/10 moves are captures targeting pawns (fxg3, Rxa5, Rxg2, Rxh4, Rxb3, Bxe3), while the remaining 4 are quiet piece/pawn moves (Bf3, Bb6, Bd4, b4). The correct moves in 5/10 positions involved giving check (h6+, Rc4+, Rc6+, Qxf3+, and implicitly Rb2+), while the others required capturing a key undefended piece (Qxd5, Qxc6) or addressing immediate defensive needs (Bf2, Kd2, Ra4). The blundered moves share the property of being 'natural-looking' in isolation—winning material or improving piece placement—but catastrophically ignore the position's forcing nature. 7/10 are endgame positions where kings are naturally exposed, amplifying the cost of tempo loss. The average cp_loss of 2211 reflects that ignoring king-related forcing moves in these open positions leads to mate or decisive material loss.

673.label: King moves toward the edge or corner of the board in endgames, when centralization or active play is required.
673.description: 10/10 positions are endgames where the played move is a king retreat toward the board's edge or corner. The destination squares are all within one step of a corner or on the outermost rank/file (a8, g1, b1, a1, h1, a2, c8, g1, a7, h7). In the most severe cases (4/10 positions with 8700-9400 cp loss), this retreat converts a 'merely lost' position into forced checkmate by allowing the opponent to construct an inescapable mating net against the board edge. In moderate cases (2/10 with 125-225 cp loss), the retreat wastes critical tempi needed for king activity. In the remaining 4/10 positions, the move incurs 0-3 cp loss because the position is already completely decided regardless of play. The consistent best alternatives across all positions direct the king toward the center (Ke3, Kd3, Kb5, Kf7, Ka6, etc.), maintaining maximum mobility and escape routes.

669.label: Premature queen checks (especially on h-file) that drive the opponent's king to safety and dissipate a winning attacking position.
669.description: 7/9 positions involve queen moves that are forcing but counterproductive, and 5/9 are specifically premature queen checks (Qh8+, Qh1+, Qh1+, Qxf6+, Qh8+). In 4/9 cases, the check lands specifically on h1 or h8 along the h-file. In virtually all positions, the player held a significant attacking advantage (average starting eval ~+300cp for the attacking side) and chose an immediately forcing move over a quieter but far stronger continuation. The correct alternatives were typically non-checking moves that maintained or intensified pressure: quiet pawn breaks (g4, f6, f5), piece centralization (Nd5, Ne4, Bxf3), or positional consolidation. The checks universally allowed the opponent's king to escape to a safe square (Kf7→e7, Kf2→e2/f3, Kd7) where the closed center or piece coordination provided shelter, completely neutralizing the attack. Positions 3 (f6) and 5 (d4) extend the pattern to aggressive pawn pushes that squander positional assets. Only position 6 (Qg3 hanging the queen) diverges as a pure tactical oversight rather than strategic impatience.

671.label: A rook is moved to a natural-looking but passive or irrelevant square, abandoning the critical sector of the board and losing decisive tempo.
671.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook repositioning move (never a capture or check) that sends the rook to a square that appears logical — doubling on an open file, contesting a file, or centralizing — but actually misidentifies where the battle's critical demands lie. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9), the rook moves to a file that is either blocked, already covered, or irrelevant to the main fight. In 4/10 positions (4, 5, 7, 10), the rook abandons a critical file or active post. Crucially, in 7/10 positions the best move was NOT a rook move at all — it was a pawn break (b4, c4, h4, b2, b5), piece activation (Bd5, Ng5, Qe3), or capturing an enemy pawn (Rxa4), meaning the player defaulted to a 'natural' rook improvement when the position demanded an entirely different type of action. The average cp_loss of 1166 reflects that these tempo-wasting moves allow the opponent to seize the initiative or execute a decisive plan unopposed.

675.label: A knight captures a high-value piece (queen or rook) when a stronger king attack — often an immediate checkmate — was available.
675.description: All 10 positions feature a knight capturing a major piece (queen or rook) on squares like d1, a1, h8, f8, a8, d8. In 9/10 cases this was a mistake because a more forcing continuation existed: 3/10 positions missed checkmate in one move (Qg2#, Qa2#, Qh5#), 2/10 missed forced mate sequences within 10 moves, and 4/10 missed significantly stronger attacking continuations involving checks or king exploitation. Only 1/10 (Position 1) was actually the best move. The average cp_loss of 4702 is heavily driven by the mate-missing cases. In nearly every case, the captured piece was on a back-rank or corner square (d1, a1, h8, f8, a8, d8), and the knight often ended up passive or misplaced after the capture (especially a1, h8, a8). The critical error in all cases was identical: the player's attention was captured by an available material gain — often the opponent's queen or rook hanging to the knight — while a more decisive tactical blow against the enemy king went unseen.

667.label: A queen or knight is voluntarily relocated to a seemingly active but functionally inferior square (typically b3, b6, or g3), abandoning a critical defensive or positional duty in an underdeveloped position.
667.description: 10/10 positions feature a queen or knight being moved to a new square that appears to create threats (targeting b-pawns, g-pawns, or repositioning) but actually abandons a critical responsibility. 7/10 are queen moves specifically (to b3, b6, or g3), while 3/10 are knight moves (Nb6 retreating from a dominant outpost, Nf3 retreating from a powerful centralized post). 8/10 occur in the opening phase where development is incomplete. 9/10 positions have at least one king still in the center, meaning tempo and piece function are especially critical. The target squares (b3, b6, g3, f3) all look purposeful—b3/b6 appear to pressure b-pawns or the d4 pawn, g3 appears to target g7 or the kingside—but in every case the piece was either needed where it was (defending a key square, maintaining pressure on a critical point) or the tempo spent relocating allowed the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation. The punishments are diverse but stem from the same root: the abandoned duty creates a concrete vulnerability (hanging piece, undefended pawn, open file, exposed king, vacated outpost).

663.label: A piece performing a critical defensive, attacking, or positional function is moved to capture material or attack a target, allowing immediate tactical punishment that far outweighs the gain.
663.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder is a direct capture or an attack on an enemy piece aimed at winning material. 5/10 moves are specifically bishop captures (Bxd3, Bxd5, Bxa2, Bxf2, Bxg4), while 3/10 are knight relocations (Nd6, Nh2, Nd4) and 2/10 are pawn advances attacking the enemy queen (h5, f5). In every case, the moved piece was performing an irreplaceable function: blockading a passed pawn (Bxf2), supporting a mating attack (Nd6), protecting a key square near the king (f5), coordinating piece activity (Bxg4, Nh2), or simply being needed for defense against an immediate threat (Bxd3, Bxd5 ignoring back-rank/mating threats). The average cp_loss of ~4000 is extreme, and only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these are positions where restraint/prophylaxis was mandatory but the player chose material greed instead. In 6/10 cases, the refutation involves a mating attack or forced checkmate that was enabled specifically by the piece leaving its post. The pattern consistently involves undervaluing the positional/defensive role of one's own piece relative to a concrete but insufficient material gain.

676.label: King moves forward or centrally to an exposed square where it becomes vulnerable to checks, deflections, or captures, when safer king retreats or non-king moves were available.
676.description: All 7/7 positions feature king moves to more central or forward squares that appear active but create tactical vulnerabilities. In 5/7 positions, the king walks into an open file or rank where it immediately faces checks (Positions 1, 4, 5, 6) or allows the opponent's king/pieces to exploit the exposure (Positions 3, 4). In 6/7 positions, the best move was either retreating the king to a safer square (Positions 1→R6e5, 3→Kb4, 4→Kd2, 6→Re1+) or moving a completely different piece (Position 5→Rf2). The punishments consistently involve the exposed king being harassed by checks along files/ranks (5/7), the king blocking its own pieces through self-interference (2/7), or the king abandoning defensive duties it held on its previous square (3/7). The cp_loss ranges from 0 to 9412, with 4/7 positions losing over 200cp, indicating these are mostly serious blunders rather than marginal inaccuracies.

674.label: A prophylactic or positional pawn advance played when the position demands immediate concrete action — development, castling, or a forcing tactical continuation.
674.description: All 10 positions feature a non-forcing pawn advance chosen over an urgent concrete need. 10/10 moves are pawn pushes; 7/10 involve f-pawn or g-pawn moves (g4, f3×3, f6×2, g5) that directly weaken the king's shelter, while the remaining 3 (c3, c6×2) are slow queenside pawns that waste a critical tempo. In 8/10 positions, the king (of the side playing the pawn move) was either uncastled, exposed, or facing immediate tactical threats that required attention. The average good-move count of only 1.7 indicates these were critical decision points demanding precision, not positions tolerating quiet play. In every case, the best move involved either piece development (Nf3, Ne2, d4), king safety (O-O), or an immediate tactical strike (Re7), while the pawn move either opened fatal diagonals (5/10 — positions 1,3,5,6,8), gave the opponent a tempo to launch decisive counterplay (3/10 — positions 2,4,10), or created tactical targets that didn't previously exist (2/10 — positions 7,9).

678.label: A knight is moved to a square where it has no protection and can be captured or exploited by the opponent.
678.description: All 10 positions feature a knight being relocated to a tactically vulnerable square. In 8/10 cases, the knight lands on a completely undefended square where it is immediately captured for free (Nd4 taken by bishop, Na6 taken by bishop, Ne2 taken after deflection, Nh6 taken by bishop along open diagonal, Ne4 taken by bishop, Nc7 taken by queen, and both Nb3 moves taken by an enemy piece). In the remaining 2/10 (Ne1, Nb1), the knight retreats to a passive square where it becomes a direct target for enemy pieces (Rc1 attacks Ne1; Qc2 exploits Nb1's abandonment of defensive duties). The average centipawn loss is 386, indicating these are severe blunders. In every case, the player had superior alternatives available (avg 2.1 good moves), typically involving active piece play, tactical strikes, or addressing immediate positional needs rather than slow knight repositioning. The knight moves are uniformly non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no threats) in positions that demanded tactical precision.

665.label: Piece repositioning that looks logical/active but overlooks a concrete tactical consequence, either by abandoning a critical defensive function or walking into the opponent's combination.
665.description: All 10 positions feature a piece move with clear logical intent (development, capture, defense, repositioning) that creates or enables a devastating tactical vulnerability. In 6/10 positions (Nf5, Nxe5, Nb5, Ne2, Bg7, Bg4), the moved piece was performing a critical defensive duty that the player failed to recognize — its relocation directly enabled the opponent's tactical blow (discovered attacks, forks, captures of undefended pieces). In 3/10 positions (Rf7, Qxd3, Bxf5), the piece moved TO a tactically vulnerable square where it became a target or walked into a combination. In 1/10 (Rg1), the player chose a defensive move when an immediate winning attack existed. The average cp_loss of 1198 confirms these are severe tactical oversights, not subtle positional errors. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, showing these were critical decision points requiring concrete calculation rather than general principles. The common thread across all 10 is prioritizing a 'natural-looking' purpose over checking for concrete tactical consequences.

679.label: King moves backward to the back rank, corner, or board edge, self-restricting its escape routes and enabling tactical exploitation.
679.description: 10/10 positions feature a king move toward the nearest board edge—8/10 retreat directly backward to the back rank (g2→g1, e7→e8, e2→e1, g7→g8, d2→d1, etc.) while 2/10 move sideways into a corner (b7→a7, g8→h8). In every case, the better alternative was a lateral move (Kc1, Kf1, Kg3, Kh6, Kh7) or staying more centrally placed, preserving 5-8 adjacent squares rather than the 3 available on an edge/corner. The tactical consequences vary but all stem from reduced mobility: 3/10 allow back-rank checkmate patterns, 2/10 enable perpetual checks in confined king corridors, 2/10 create file/diagonal alignments permitting captures with check, 2/10 cost a critical tempo allowing passed pawn promotion, and 1/10 walks into a direct mating net. The average cp_loss of 2964 reflects how catastrophic this self-restriction is—5/10 positions result in forced mate. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, meaning these were narrow decision points where choosing the wrong retreat direction was fatal.

680.label: A rook greedily captures a pawn and lands on a square where an enemy bishop exploits the diagonal to fork, pin, or win it.
680.description: In 10/10 positions, a rook captures an apparently free or tempting pawn. In 9/10 cases, the opponent's bishop then exploits the rook's new square along a diagonal—either forking the rook and king with check (positions 1, 4, 5, 6), pinning the rook to the king along a diagonal (positions 8, 9), or simply attacking the rook on an undefended square with a developing bishop move (positions 2, 7, 10). Position 3 uses a queen instead of a bishop but follows the same logic of the rook landing unprotected on an exploitable line. The key geometric commonality is that the rook moves to a square that shares a diagonal with either the player's own king or with the bishop's natural development path, and the opponent's bishop (already on the board or needing just one move) capitalizes immediately. Better alternatives in all positions involved piece development, king safety improvements, or maintaining active piece coordination rather than grabbing material.

672.label: Playing seemingly improving or natural-looking moves instead of the one concrete action the critical position demands.
672.description: All 10 positions share a defining characteristic: the position required immediate, specific concrete action (promoting a pawn, winning material, defending a rank, maintaining a key piece), but the player chose a move that 'looks good' — repositioning a piece, gaining space, or making a developing move — that wastes the critical tempo. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.6), indicating these are razor-sharp moments where only precise play works. The played moves appear reasonable on the surface: centralizing knights (Nd5, Nc6), activating rooks (Ra3, Rd7, Rg1, Re8, Rb1+), developing bishops (Bf4), or pushing pawns (c5, d4). But in each case, the move fails to address the ONE thing the position demands: an immediate passed pawn push (positions 1, 7), challenging a dominant enemy piece (positions 2, 9), maintaining critical file/rank control (positions 3, 4, 10), or winning material that's available right now (position 6). The average cp_loss of 2102 reflects how catastrophically wrong 'reasonable' moves can be when the position is concrete.

683.label: Advancing a peripheral pawn in an endgame when the position urgently demands piece repositioning or direct action against a passed pawn threat.
683.description: 10/10 positions are endgames featuring dangerous passed pawns (usually the opponent's, within 1-3 moves of promotion). 10/10 blundered moves are non-capturing flank pawn advances (a, b, f, g, or h file — never a central pawn). In every case, the correct move involved piece activity: rook repositioning to blockade or contest a promotion square (positions 1, 2, 9, 10), king centralization to support one's own pawns (positions 3, 7, 8), capturing the dangerous passed pawn directly (positions 4, 6), or a tactical piece sacrifice enabling immediate promotion (position 5). The pushed pawns are universally too slow — they require 3-6 more moves to promote while the opponent's passed pawn needs only 1-2 moves. 10/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 'passed_pawn', and the average cp_loss of 2107 reflects how catastrophically a single wasted tempo compounds in promotion races.
