681.label: A bishop is repositioned to an apparently active central square, ignoring urgent tactical demands and creating or allowing concrete exploitation.
681.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a 'nice-looking' square (d4 appears 4 times, e4 twice, plus c4, d3, e3, f4, g5) without any immediate threat, capture, or check. In every case, the position demanded concrete tactical action instead. In 4/10 positions (5, 6, 7, 10), the bishop lands on an undefended or forkable square and is immediately won or exploited. In 3/10 positions (4, 8, 9), the bishop move removes critical defensive coverage, allowing checkmate or a mating attack. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 3), the bishop creates a geometric vulnerability or ignores an urgent pawn/material threat. The average centipawn loss is an enormous 3183, with 3/10 positions involving mate or near-mate swings. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions demanding precision where 'improving' a bishop was a fatal luxury. The moves share the character of positional aesthetics overriding tactical reality — the player sees a strong diagonal or central square and repositions the bishop there, blind to the concrete refutation.

686.label: Advancing the f-pawn (f2-f3/f4 or f7-f6) fatally opens the diagonal to the castled king, allowing tactical exploitation through checks, pins, or material gain.
686.description: All 10/10 positions involve advancing the f-pawn forward from in front of a castled king (9 White playing f2-f3 or f2-f4, 1 Black playing f7-f6). In at least 8/10 positions, the core punishment directly exploits the newly opened long diagonal to the king (a7-g1 for White or a2-g8 for Black): positions 1,2,3,4,7,9 feature queen checks or attacks along that diagonal; position 6 allows Qd5+/Bd5+ on the opened a2-g8 diagonal; position 7 enables a devastating pin (Bc5) along the diagonal that prevents recapture on d4. Position 5 is a variant where f4 creates a tactically vulnerable pawn exploited by deflection, and position 10 is an extreme case where f4 misses checkmate in one. The average centipawn loss is enormous (1203cp), reflecting how the f-pawn serves as a critical shield. In 7/10 positions, the immediate refutation involves a queen check or attack on the newly opened diagonal. Same-side kingside castling appears in 9/10 positions, confirming the king is always directly behind the advancing pawn.

677.label: King advances or moves laterally in open positions when retreating, staying put, or pushing a passed pawn was more urgent.
677.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves in situations where the king is already exposed and away from pawn shelter. In 9/10 cases, the king advances or moves laterally rather than retreating to safety. In 8/10 positions, the side making the move is already losing significantly (eval >600cp against them or facing forced mate). The most devastating errors (positions 5 and 7, losing 516cp and 9341cp respectively) occurred when the king moved instead of pushing an immediately promoting passed pawn. In positions 2, 3, and 9 (losing 277, 14cp but #-16→#-2, and 194cp), the king advanced into tactical vulnerability — exposed to checks, mating nets, or piece coordination. In positions 1, 4, and 6, the king drifted toward secondary objectives (capturing pawns, approaching pieces) while abandoning its critical defensive or passed-pawn-supporting role. Only 2/10 positions (8 and 10) were actually the engine's top choice, suggesting the feature primarily detects the pattern of exposed-king-moves-in-desperate-positions rather than purely bad decisions.

693.label: Non-forcing flank pawn advances in critical positions where the king is exposed and immediate tactical or defensive action is urgently required.
693.description: All 9/9 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing pawn advance on a wing file (a, b, c, or h) played while the moving side's king is dangerously exposed. In 9/9 cases, the position demanded immediate forcing play — either a tactical shot (Be3+ in position 5, Qe3+ in position 2, Qg7 in position 6), urgent development (Bd7 in position 1, Nf6 in position 8), king evacuation (Kd7 in position 9), or defensive queen repositioning (Qf8 in position 7, Qa3 in position 10). The average number of good moves available was only 1.2, meaning these were razor-edge positions with almost no margin for error. The pawn moves all had superficially logical intent — attacking a bishop (b5 in positions 2, 10), challenging a piece (h6 in position 9), gaining space (a5, c5, h5) — but catastrophically wasted the one tempo needed to address an existential threat. 7/9 positions resulted in losses exceeding 600cp, with 4/9 allowing forced checkmate.

682.label: Moving the queen or king to an apparently attractive square that abandons a critical defensive responsibility, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
682.description: 10/10 positions involve moving the queen (7/10) or king (3/10) — the two highest-value pieces — to squares that appear active, aggressive, or centralizing but actually leave critical vulnerabilities exposed. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 8, 10, 6, 9), the queen specifically abandons defense of a particular square or piece (f2 twice, c2, g7, back rank), allowing the opponent to immediately capture or exploit the undefended target. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 7), the king moves to what seems like a more active/central square but walks directly into a tactical shot (mating net, skewer, open-file check). In position 2, the queen gives a 'tempting' check that accomplishes nothing while surrendering a winning advantage. The average cp_loss of 1322 reflects how catastrophic these errors are — the moves look plausible or even strong on the surface but create instant tactical collapses. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise defensive awareness rather than superficial activity.

690.label: The queen is moved to a peripheral or exposed square that looks active but abandons critical tasks, becoming vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks.
690.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a queen move to a square that appears aggressive or active but is fundamentally misguided. In 8/10 cases, the refutation involves an immediate tempo-gaining attack against the misplaced queen (pawn advance, rook attack, or knight fork). In 8/10 positions, a simpler concrete move was available — typically a capture (Qxg3, Qxb2, Qxg4, Qxe5, Qxf6, Qxd4) or a critical defensive/prophylactic move (Bxc5, Qe8, Rxb4). The queen destinations span the entire board (g4, h5, g5, a5, b1, c4, a5, h4, a7, b4) but share the common trait of being tactically vulnerable squares where the queen accomplishes nothing concrete while abandoning essential duties — whether defending a key pawn (4/10: b7, a5, d4, f5), maintaining counterplay potential (2/10), or simply capturing hanging material (4/10). The average cp_loss of 377 reflects how catastrophic queen misplacement is — one tempo lost with the strongest piece cascades into positional or material collapse.

689.label: When multiple pieces can capture a hanging queen, choosing the wrong capturing piece squanders significant advantage.
689.description: All 10/10 positions involve capturing an enemy queen (or equivalent high-value piece) that is en prise to multiple attackers simultaneously. In 7/10 positions, the player chose the wrong capturing piece, costing an average of ~1500cp among the errors. The critical decision is always WHICH piece makes the capture. In positions 1 and 5, the wrong pawn captured (hxg6+ instead of fxg6+), failing to open the f-file. In position 3, the knight captured instead of the rook (Nxc6 vs Rxc6), abandoning a dominant outpost. In position 7, the knight captured instead of the bishop (Nxg4 vs Bxg4), leaving the bishop hanging. In position 8, a pawn captured instead of a knight (exf5 vs Nxf5+), missing a tempo-gaining check. In position 9, the wrong knight captured (Ngxe4 vs Ndxe4), stripping kingside defense. In position 10, the queen was captured prematurely instead of exploiting a tactical sequence first. The 3/10 positions with near-zero cp_loss (positions 2, 4, 6) represent cases where the correct capturing piece was chosen, confirming the feature activates on the decision point itself.

691.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) to a square on an unobstructed diagonal where an enemy bishop or queen can immediately capture it.
691.description: 7/10 positions show the identical core error: a piece is moved to a square that lies directly on an unobstructed diagonal controlled by an enemy bishop or queen, allowing immediate capture. Specifically, positions 2 and 8 feature Qh3 captured by a bishop along the e6/d7-h3 diagonal; positions 1 and 10 feature a Rook moving to b8 captured by a bishop on the a1-h8 diagonal; position 3 features Qe2 captured by a queen along the a6-e2 diagonal; position 4 features Qd2 captured by a queen along the h6-d2 diagonal; position 6 features Qe3 captured by a bishop along the h6-e3 diagonal. The remaining 3/10 involve related patterns: position 5 is a piece moving to a square captured by a knight, position 9 allows a zwischenzug after a queen trade, and position 7 is a premature queen exchange. The attacking piece is typically 3-5 squares away along the diagonal, making it easy to overlook. 8/10 moves involve the queen, and 9/10 result in the moved piece being immediately lost or traded disadvantageously.

697.label: Moving a rook to the b-file as a slow preparatory move when the position demands immediate tactical action or urgent piece development.
697.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the b-file (Rb8 for Black in 8/10, Rb1 for White in 2/10), typically shifting one square laterally from the a-file. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand — whether defending against a mating threat (1/10 allowed Qxf7#), protecting a hanging piece or pawn (3/10), addressing a pin or fork vulnerability (2/10), or exploiting an opponent's exposed king (4/10). Instead of meeting these concrete demands, the player chose a quiet rook repositioning that accomplished nothing immediate. The average cp_loss of 1200 reflects that these positions were consistently sharp with narrow paths to survival: 7/10 had only 1-2 good moves available. In 8/10 positions, the primary refutation directly exploited the tempo gifted by the rook move — either seizing an open file, delivering a check/fork, or launching a combination that the extra tempo now enabled. The rook on b8/b1 frequently became a tactical liability itself, either as a fork target (Nc6 in position 10), a piece attacked with tempo (Bf5 in position 2), or simply a poorly placed piece on an irrelevant file.

692.label: Pawn captures that prematurely resolve critical pawn tension, surrendering a strategic or tactical asset that was more valuable maintained.
692.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (lowercase-x-lowercase notation) that release pawn tension which was serving as a positional anchor or enabling a stronger tactical sequence. In 10/10 cases, the better move involved either maintaining the tension, preparing first before capturing (move-order improvement), or finding an entirely different tactical path. 5/10 of the captures gave check, making them especially tempting but equally erroneous — the check gained a tempo but surrendered a far more valuable structural asset. The analyses repeatedly identify the same core error: 'premature capture' (Position 1), 'releasing critical pawn tension prematurely' (Position 3), 'voluntarily surrenders the structural asset' (Position 5), 'surrendering the powerful e5 pawn' (Position 6), 'releasing central pawn tension' (Position 10). In 8/10 positions, only 1 good move existed (within 50cp of best), indicating these are narrow critical moments where the natural-looking pawn capture is a trap. The average cp_loss of 350 reflects that these captures transform winning/equal positions into losing/drawn ones by releasing the constraint that was generating the advantage.

685.label: Queen (or piece) moves to a plausible-looking square while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical requirement—whether a hanging piece, a mating threat, a critical defensive duty, or a winning combination.
685.description: 9/10 positions feature queen moves (the exception being Bd6 in position 6, which follows the identical logic). In every case, the player deploys their queen to a square that appears reasonable or active—centralizing (Qd6, Qd7), attacking (Qg4, Qh5, Qh6), developing (Qe2, Qe7, Qb6), or retreating (Qe1)—while completely ignoring the position's concrete tactical demand. 10/10 positions involve an immediate threat or opportunity that required urgent attention: hanging pieces needing rescue (positions 4, 5, 10), back-rank mates (position 8), critical squares needing coverage (positions 2, 9), self-blocking of own pieces (position 3), winning tactics being missed (position 6), central breaks requiring defensive preparation (position 7), or diagonal vulnerabilities (position 1). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions and 'missed_tactic' in 9/10, confirming the pattern of wasted time. Exposed kings feature in 8/10 positions, heightening the cost of the wasted tempo. The average cp_loss of 2161 reflects how devastating these 'looks reasonable' moves become when the position actually required something concrete and specific.

684.label: Defensive moves that try to block an attacking diagonal or line but create new or worse vulnerabilities that the opponent exploits.
684.description: 7/10 positions involve a pawn or piece move explicitly attempting to block an attacking diagonal (e6 to block a bishop targeting f7 in positions 1, 2, 5, 6; g6 to block a queen's diagonal to h7 in position 10; g3 and Bg3 to block kingside attacking lines in positions 3 and 8). The remaining 3/10 (d3, cxd3, Rh3) are also passive defensive moves that create new structural weaknesses rather than actively addressing threats. In all 10 cases, the move fails because: the blocking square itself becomes a tactical target (e6 enabling Nxe6+ forks in positions 5-6, g3 enabling bishop sacrifices in positions 3 and 8), the move removes defense from other critical squares (d3 unguarding the c3 knight, Be6 unguarding b7), or the attacker simply reroutes around the block (g6 allowing Qh4-Qh7+ mate in position 10). The best moves in these positions universally involve active measures—counterattacks (Bxe5, Nxe5), forcing moves (d5, f4), or piece trades—rather than passive interposition.

695.label: A speculative flank pawn advance wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate piece action to address a tactical emergency.
695.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing pawn advance played in a position with an urgent tactical need. 9/10 moves are specifically kingside pawn pushes (g4, g5, g6, h4, h5, or f6), with only 1 queenside pawn push (c5). In every case, the best moves were piece moves or captures addressing an immediate tactical problem: relocating a hanging piece (2/10), castling to safety (2/10), moving the king to cover weak squares (3/10), contesting a critical file or rank (2/10), or delivering a forced checkmate (1/10). The pawn advances universally share the trait of being slow, speculative, non-forcing moves that neither defend a concrete threat nor create one the opponent must answer. In 7/10 cases the pawn push also actively created a new weakness — vacating a critical square (g5 in position 3, f5 in position 9, e6 in position 6), removing pawn protection from a square (f3 in position 5), or exposing the king. The average cp_loss of 1254 reflects that these tempo losses occur in razor-sharp positions where one wasted move is catastrophic.

687.label: Knight is moved to a less active square (rim, back rank, or away from a strong outpost) when the position demands immediate tactical action.
687.description: 9/10 positions involve knight moves that relocate the piece to a worse square, while 10/10 positions feature a missed concrete tactic as the best alternative. In 7/10 cases, the knight leaves a strong central or semi-central post (c4, c5, c6, e2, c3, f4, d7) for a peripheral or passive square (a5, a4, b4, g1, d1, f8, d5, d2). In 6/10 cases the knight specifically retreats toward the player's own back rank or the rim (a/h files). The positions share extremely high cp_loss (avg 321) and very few good moves available (avg 1.5), indicating sharp positions where the passive repositioning squanders decisive advantages or concrete winning tactics. The one non-knight move (h4) still fits the broader pattern of choosing a slow repositioning move over an immediate tactical strike (Nxg6).

694.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing bishop repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action (tactical strike, prophylaxis, or tempo-critical maneuver).
694.description: 9/10 positions feature bishop moves (Bd6, Bd7, Bb2, Be6, Bd6, Bb4, Bg2, Bb7, Bc6) and 1/10 a knight move (Nc5) — all are quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning moves with no check, capture, or direct threat. In every case, the position demanded concrete tactical action: 3/10 positions had forcing tactical shots available (Nc3+ sacrifice, Qxa8 capture, Bh4 attack on rook); 3/10 required prophylactic measures against an imminent threat (preventing Bf4+ skewer, avoiding Na4 fork, removing queen from danger); 2/10 were tempo-critical races where any non-essential move was fatal; and 2/10 self-blocked friendly pieces. The average cp_loss of 1201 is extreme, with 4/10 positions having only 1 good move available, confirming these are positions demanding precision where 'natural development' is catastrophic. 8/10 were played by Black, suggesting the pattern particularly afflicts the defending side seeking to 'improve' rather than solve concrete problems.

700.label: Queen delivers a check to a back-rank square (rank 1 or 8) that achieves nothing concrete, wasting tempo and misplacing the queen.
700.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen delivering check to a back-rank square (rank 1 or rank 8: a1, a8, b1, b8, c1, c8, f8). In every case, the opponent easily deals with the check—either by stepping the king to a safe square (7/10) or blocking with a useful interposition (3/10)—leaving the queen stranded far from the critical action. The analyses consistently identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif (9/10 positions), with 'pointless_check' and 'queen_misplacement' as recurring tags (6/10 and 5/10 respectively). Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions required precise play, yet players chose the superficially forcing but strategically empty check. The average centipawn loss of 1152 reflects that the queen's displacement from its powerful central/active post to a peripheral back-rank square often proved catastrophic for the position's dynamic balance.

701.label: An aggressive-looking knight move to a seemingly active square when the position demanded a simple pawn capture to resolve critical central tension.
701.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a knight move to a superficially attractive square (centralizing, attacking a piece, or threatening a fork) instead of making a concrete pawn capture that was urgently required. In 9/10 positions, the best move was a straightforward pawn capture resolving central/critical tension (axb5, Qxd4, dxe5, exd4, dxe5, Nxe5, Rxf4, dxe5, exd5, exd5). The knight moves all abandoned critical defensive responsibilities — in 7/10 cases the knight left a square where it guarded a key pawn (a6, d6, e6, f7) or controlled a vital diagonal/square. The refutations in 8/10 positions exploited the newly undefended pawn or square within one move. Average cp_loss was 227, and only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than ambition. 8/10 were played by Black, suggesting this is particularly common when defending a slightly worse position where the urge to 'do something active' overrides the need for concrete resolution.

688.label: Playing passive, non-forcing moves (piece relocations, pawn pushes) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
688.description: 10/10 positions share the pattern of choosing a non-forcing move when only immediate forcing action (captures, checks, or direct threats) could maintain the position. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a forcing capture or check (Nxd4, Nh6+, Qxg7+, Bxf8, Bxb5, Qxd5, d4 attacking a piece, Qf6 forcing trade). The played moves were consistently passive: piece relocations to non-threatening squares (Bh4, Bh5, Nh3, Bf5, Qf8 — 5/10), slow pawn pushes (h4, h4, a5 — 3/10), or suboptimal exchanges (Bxe5, Bxc6 — 2/10). The positions were extremely critical with an average of only 1.7 good moves available, meaning precision was required. 7/10 moves were made by White. 5/10 involved bishop moves specifically. The average centipawn loss of 1180 reflects catastrophic consequences — including one forced mate — demonstrating how punishing passivity is in these sharp positions.

699.label: Premature bishop sacrifices on h7 or h2 that lack the piece coordination needed for a successful kingside attack.
699.description: 6/10 positions feature a bishop capturing the h-pawn (h2 or h7) with check in a classic Greek Gift pattern that is tactically unsound. Specifically, 3/10 are Bxh2+ by Black and 2/10 are Bxh7+ by White, all in the middlegame with same-side castling. In every case, the attacker lacks critical supporting pieces (undeveloped knight, queen unable to reach h5/h4 quickly, no rook on the h-file) and after the king accepts the sacrifice and retreats to safety, the attack completely dissipates, leaving the sacrificer down a full bishop for one pawn. The remaining 4 positions show related h-file themes: Position 4 features a premature Rh2+ check, Position 10 involves Kxh2 (not actually a blunder), while Positions 5 and 8 are endgame errors that appear to be noise. The 7 middlegame positions averaged 279cp loss, and the common thread among the clear cases is attacking the h-pawn prematurely when the prerequisites for a successful Greek Gift (Ng5 access, queen path to h5/h4, supporting pieces) are absent.

698.label: Playing a quiet piece repositioning move to a seemingly active square when the position demanded an immediate capture, exchange, or forcing move.
698.description: In 9/10 positions, the best move was a direct capture or forcing exchange (Qxe7, Bb5+, Qxh8, Rxg8, Qxe6, Qxf6+, Qxd4, Qxe4, Qxe8+), yet the player chose a quiet piece development or repositioning move instead. All 10 blunder moves are non-capturing, non-checking piece placements to squares that appear active (Be3, Bc4, Bh5, Ng3, Ne5, Nf3, Qd2, Be6, Bd3, Ne4). In 8/10 cases the repositioned piece immediately becomes a tactical target—vulnerable to pawn attacks (f5 vs Ne4/Ne5, e4 vs Bd3, g6 vs Bh5), removal of the guard (Bxf3 vs Qd2), or the piece simply blocks a critical function (Bd3 blocking the d-file, Be6 blocking Qxe4). The average cp_loss of 1276 reflects the severity: these aren't positional inaccuracies but cases where a concrete, often elementary tactical opportunity (frequently a hanging piece or forced exchange) was ignored in favor of 'improving' piece placement.

696.label: A bishop is moved to a seemingly active or aggressive square, but this superficially appealing placement misses a stronger concrete forcing line in the position.
696.description: All 10/10 positions feature bishop moves to apparently active squares—attacking pieces, centralizing, pinning, or capturing pawns—that miss much stronger tactical resources. In 8/10 cases, a devastating concrete continuation existed (forced mate, discovered attack, queen sacrifice, decisive fork) that required either a different piece to move first or the same bishop to go to a different square. In at least 4/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 7, 10), the CORRECT move also involved the same bishop but deployed more precisely (e.g., Bg5+ for immediate mate vs. Bf4 preparing Bg5+; Qxf7+ THEN Bg5+ vs. premature Bg5). The bishop moves universally prioritize general activity principles (attack a piece, occupy a central diagonal, create a pin) over specific tactical demands. The average centipawn loss is extremely high (1333cp), with position 10 missing a mate-in-2 and position 6 converting +585 into -512. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, confirming these are sharp positions demanding calculation over intuition.

702.label: A pawn advance attempting to dislodge a well-placed enemy knight that fatally weakens the surrounding square complex or wastes a critical tempo.
702.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn move that directly attacks an enemy knight on an aggressive or central outpost: b3 kicks Nc4, h6 kicks Ng5, g5 kicks Nh4, c3 kicks Nd4, h3 kicks Ng4, f6 kicks Ne5, c6 kicks Nd5, c4 kicks Nb5, f3 kicks Ne4, and g3 kicks Nf4. In every case, the pawn advance creates a worse problem than the knight's presence—either weakening a critical square that the knight (or other pieces) immediately exploits (8/10), or wasting a decisive tempo when a more urgent action was required (10/10). In 7/10 positions, the knight actually ends up on a SUPERIOR square after the pawn push (Nf5, Nxe7+, Nd4, Ng3, Nh3+, Nxf7, Nxg6). In 8/10 positions, the weakened square is immediately adjacent to the player's own king. The correct moves instead addressed king safety (castling/king moves), developed pieces, made central counter-strikes, or executed concrete tactical combinations—none involved kicking the knight with a pawn.

714.label: The queen captures a peripheral pawn, removing itself from the critical sector of the board and allowing the opponent to exploit its absence with decisive attacks or tactics.
714.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen capturing a pawn (Qxa2, Qxh3, Qxb7, Qxf2, Qxh2, Qxb2) on a peripheral or semi-peripheral square while urgent tactical or defensive needs exist elsewhere. In 8/10 cases, the opponent's king is under active attack or the player's own king faces immediate threats that the queen should be addressing. In 9/10 positions, the queen moves further AWAY from the critical sector (usually the kingside where kings are under pressure). The average cp_loss of 3102 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in immediate checkmate or forced mate sequences after the pawn grab. In 10/10 cases, the best moves involved either defending the king, eliminating a dangerous enemy piece, or maintaining the queen's influence over the critical zone — never the greedy capture. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were already tense positions demanding precision rather than material acquisition.

712.label: A quiet, non-forcing queen repositioning move played when the position urgently demanded concrete tactical action with another piece or pawn.
712.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet queen moves (no captures, no checks) that reposition the queen to seemingly logical squares for coordination or regrouping purposes. In every case, the best move was a non-queen action: 6/10 positions demanded immediate pawn breaks or captures (fxe5, gxf4, d4, h6, f3-prevention), 3/10 required knight moves (Nc5, Ne4, Ne1), and 1/10 needed a rook move (Rhf8). The average cp_loss of 1221 reflects catastrophic tempo waste in time-critical positions. In 8/10 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating positions with narrow correct paths that specifically excluded slow queen maneuvers. The queen destinations were spread across the board (e8, e2, f6, e6, d2, d7, b6, d7, e1, g3) but all share the quality of being non-urgent, non-forcing squares. In 7/10 positions, the opponent's refutation directly exploited the wasted tempo by seizing initiative, consolidating, or punishing the queen's new placement as a tactical target.

707.label: A knight that was blocking a lethal queen-bishop diagonal toward g2/g7 is moved to a centralizing square, allowing immediate checkmate or decisive material gain along the opened diagonal.
707.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight stationed on f3, f6, or c3 that is the sole piece blocking a long diagonal (typically a1-h8 or a8-h1) aimed at the g-pawn sheltering the castled king. In all 10 cases, the knight is moved to an aggressive-looking central square (d4, d5, e4, e5, f5, g5). In 8/10 positions, the immediate refutation is Qxg7# or Qxg2# — checkmate in exactly one move — where a queen captures the g-pawn along the newly opened diagonal, supported by a fianchettoed or long-diagonal bishop (b2 supporting g7, or b7 supporting g2). Positions 1, 2, 4, and 5 show the knight leaving f6 to allow Qxg7#; positions 3, 6, 8, and 10 show the knight leaving f3 to allow Qxg2# (or Qxh1+). Position 9 shows the knight leaving c3 to allow a devastating Ne2+ invasion. Position 7 is a mild outlier where the knight jumps to a square where it's simply captured. The average cp_loss is enormous (7099), with 7/10 resulting in immediate forced checkmate. In all cases, multiple safe alternatives existed (avg 2.4 good moves), making these purely tactical oversights rather than forced errors.

706.label: Advancing a pawn in a pure king-and-pawn endgame when the king should move first or a different plan is needed.
706.description: All 9/9 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames where the move played is a pawn advance. 5/9 moves give check (c4+, e6+, g5+, g3+, g6+), making the pawn push feel like it gains tempo. In the positions with significant cp_loss (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 10), the correct move was invariably a king move instead: Kf7 instead of g6+ (position 10), Kc5 instead of e6+ (position 5), Ke5/Ke6/Kf7 instead of g5 (position 2), Ke7/Ke8 instead of g6 (position 9). The principle violated is 'king before pawn' — advancing the king to support or lead the pawn rather than pushing the pawn prematurely. 3/9 positions (4, 6, 7) show 0 cp_loss, indicating the feature fires on the move type (pawn push in K+P ending) regardless of whether it's actually a mistake, though it activates most strongly when it IS premature.
706.old_chip: Premature pawn push in K+P ending

715.label: A rook delivers a check with no constructive follow-up, wasting tempo and often improving the opponent's king position.
715.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check along an open file or rank, and in every case the check is easily parried while the opponent's position actually improves. In 8/10 positions, the opponent's king moves to a demonstrably better square after the check (centralizing, supporting pawns, or escaping danger). In 9/10 cases, the checking rook ends up on a worse square than it started or loses coordination with the player's overall plan. The average cp_loss of 1985 reflects that these are often game-changing mistakes in critical positions. In 7/10 positions, a quiet consolidating move (improving pawn structure, addressing passed pawns, or securing the king) was clearly superior. In 4/10 cases, the error is specifically a move-order mistake where the check needed a preparatory move first (g4, g3+, g6) to deny the opponent's king access to the improved square. Only 1/10 positions (Position 9) showed a negligible cost, confirming this pattern primarily captures consequential tempo-wasting checks rather than harmless transpositions.

719.label: Moving a minor piece to a square directly attacked by an adjacent enemy pawn, where it is immediately captured for free.
719.description: All 10/10 positions share the exact same tactical error: a minor piece (bishop or knight) is moved to a square that is within the capture range of an enemy pawn, and the piece is simply taken by that pawn with no compensation. Specifically, 6/10 positions involve bishops (Bh3×3, Bg5, Bf4, Bg4) and 4/10 involve knights (Ne3, Ne4, Nf6, Nb4). In every case, the refutation is a simple one-move pawn capture: gxh3 (3 positions), hxg5, exf4, hxg4, fxe3, dxe4, exf6+, and cxb4. The moves all appear to be purposeful—pinning (Bg4, Bg5), attacking (Bf4, Ne4), centralizing (Nf6, Ne3), or infiltrating (Nb4)—but the player completely overlooks that the destination square is controlled by a pawn sitting right next to it. The average cp_loss is 440, consistently representing a full piece lost for nothing.

708.label: Bishop gives check (usually discovered) but lands on the wrong square, failing to control a critical escape or interposition square that an alternative bishop move would cover.
708.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop move that delivers check — 8/10 are discovered checks where the bishop vacates a line to unleash another piece, while 2/10 are direct bishop checks. In 8/10 cases, there exists an alternative bishop move (often also giving check) to a DIFFERENT square that would be vastly superior because it controls the enemy king's escape square or prevents a key interposition. For example: Bg4+ instead of Bh3+ to control d1 (Position 6), Bg2+ instead of Bg4+ to control f1 (Position 7), Bg4+ instead of Bb3+ to control e2 (Position 8), Bh5+ instead of Be6+ to control g6 (Position 3), Bc4+ instead of Bd5+ to maintain perpetual (Position 5), and Bc2+ instead of Bg6+ for king defense (Position 10). The remaining 2/10 involve bishops leaving powerful posts to give pointless checks (Bh2+ abandoning g3, Bxa3+ allowing a hanging piece). The average cp_loss of 1340 reflects how catastrophic wrong-square checks are — including one position where forced mate becomes a draw.

705.label: Playing a natural-looking piece development or repositioning move in a critical position that demands an immediate concrete tactical response.
705.description: All 10 positions share a strikingly consistent pattern: the player chose a quiet, non-forcing piece move (no checks, no captures, no threats) when the position demanded specific concrete action. 8/10 moves are minor piece developments or repositionings (6 bishop moves: Be7×2, Bd7×3, Bb5; 3 knight moves: Nc3, Nd5, Nfd4), all to 'natural-looking' squares. In 8/10 positions, only 1 good move was available (avg 1.3), indicating razor-thin margins where autopilot development is fatal. The missed requirements varied: 4/10 needed to address an immediate material-winning pawn capture threat (dxc6 or exf6), 3/10 missed a concrete tactical opportunity (b4! fork, Qxd5+ winning pawns, Ng4 counter), 2/10 needed to address a direct mating/piece-loss threat, and 1/10 required an urgent king move in an endgame. In every case, the move played would be perfectly reasonable in a less critical moment but catastrophically ignores the position's tactical demands.

711.label: Playing a quiet rook move (or rook capture) in a position where the king faces immediate lethal threats, when only a forcing or desperate measure would survive.
711.description: In 8/9 positions, the blunder was a rook move or rook capture (Rc7, Rf7, Rf2, Re3, Re2, Ra2, Re2, Rxc3) with one pawn push (d6). All 9 positions featured critically exposed kings where only 1-2 moves survived (avg good moves: 1.1). The correct moves were consistently forcing or dramatic: queen sacrifices (Qf1+, Qf2), king marches (Kf2), captures with check (Bxd5+), decisive captures of the key attacking piece (Rxf5), pawn thrusts creating immediate threats (e6), or delivering checkmate (Qg7#). Instead, the player chose quiet rook repositioning to seemingly natural squares (second rank, seventh rank, open files) or captured a non-critical piece, all of which appeared 'improving' but fatally ignored the one-move timing constraint. The average cp_loss of 5479 reflects that 5/9 positions resulted in immediate forced checkmate after the blunder, showing these moves are catastrophically too slow.

717.label: Pushing a central pawn (d or e) forward in a closed position without adequate piece support, allowing the opponent to simply capture it for material gain.
717.description: All 10/10 positions feature a central pawn advance (d5, e5, d4, or e4) in a closed or semi-closed center where patient development was required. In every case, the pawn was insufficiently defended: the opponent could capture it and the player could not recapture satisfactorily, resulting in net material loss. 10/10 positions had a closed center before the push. 7/10 occurred in the opening phase where development was incomplete. In all 10 cases, the top recommended alternatives were quiet moves (piece development, prophylaxis, castling, or modest consolidation like d3 instead of d4). The average cp_loss was 254, indicating these are serious blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. The refutation in all 10 positions was simply capturing the advanced pawn — no complex tactics required — after which the opponent emerged with extra material and/or a dominant center.

703.label: Capturing or moving a piece to a square where a simple pawn or knight recapture creates a devastating material or structural consequence.
703.description: In 8/8 positions, the player moved a piece to a square controlled by an enemy pawn or knight, overlooking that the forced recapture would be catastrophic. In 6/8 cases, the devastating recapture was specifically a pawn recapture (dxe4 twice, cxd4, dxc2, axb5, dxe6) that either won material outright, created a lethal passed pawn, opened a critical file, or forced a losing simplification. In 2/8 cases (Ra2, Qd7+), a knight recapture won the piece cleanly. The consequences varied: 4/8 resulted in direct material loss (exchange or queen), 3/8 resulted in catastrophic simplification into a lost pawn endgame, and 1/8 resulted in opening the d-file for a decisive queen invasion. The average cp_loss of 386 reflects that these are severe miscalculations rather than subtle inaccuracies. The player consistently focused on removing a threatening enemy piece or invading an attractive square while failing to evaluate the elementary forced response.

710.label: Moving a rook (or queen) to an aggressive-looking square to target enemy pawns, while abandoning a critical defensive duty or landing on a tactically vulnerable square.
710.description: All 10 positions feature a rook (9/10) or queen (1/10) moving to an open rank or file to attack an enemy pawn — typically to the 2nd/7th rank (positions 2, 5, 7, 8, 10), the 3rd/6th rank (positions 1, 3, 6, 9), or the a-file (position 4). In every case, the 'active' pawn-targeting move is misguided because it either abandons a critical function or lands on a vulnerable square. Specifically: 3/10 positions placed the piece on an undefended or trappable square (positions 3, 5, 10 — Rf6 trapped by Kg7, Ra7 trapped by Kb8, Ra7 hanging to check+capture); 2/10 moved the rook away from defending another piece, leaving it hanging (positions 6 and 9 — both left a bishop on c2 undefended); 2/10 released crucial pressure on the enemy king (positions 1 and 4 — abandoning threats against h2 and g2 respectively); and 3/10 prioritized counterplay/pawn-grabbing over urgent king safety or consolidation needs (positions 2, 7, 8). The average cp_loss of 1185 is enormous, with 6/10 positions losing over 200cp and 2/10 leading to forced mate. Only 2.4 good moves were available on average, indicating narrow positions where the 'obvious active move' was a critical trap.

709.label: King moves in pure pawn endgames at critical junctures where only one move maintains the evaluation.
709.description: All 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with an average of only 1.2 good moves available, making them razor-sharp precision moments. Every move played is a one-square king move (no captures or checks). In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 8), the king move was a serious blunder (avg 401cp loss) because the correct move was an urgent pawn break (g5, g4, h4, g5 respectively) — the player defaulted to 'improve the king' when pawn timing was critical. In the remaining 6/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10), the king move WAS the correct choice (0-22cp loss), typically to escort or protect a passed pawn while alternatives would have abandoned it. The unifying thread is that all positions feature a single correct move in a pawn endgame where passed pawns or pawn breakthroughs are the decisive strategic element, and the king's exact placement determines the outcome.

716.label: Rook repositioning moves that leave a critical defensive post, exposing hanging material or the king to tactical exploitation.
716.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook sliding to a seemingly more active square while abandoning a critical defensive function. In 6/10 cases, the rook leaves a rank it was guarding (the 6th rank in positions 1, 5, 8; the 7th rank in positions 6, 7; the f-file/f6 square in position 10), directly allowing tactical blows. In 5/10 positions, the abandoned square results in a piece or pawn becoming immediately hanging (f6 bishop in pos 2, f1 rook in pos 3, b5 pawn in pos 8, f7 pawn in pos 10, d1 rook in pos 9). In 4/10 positions, the rook's departure enables a mating attack or devastating king hunt (positions 1, 5, 6, 7). The moves share the geometric property of being non-capturing, non-checking rook slides—pure repositioning moves—that prioritize apparent activity over actual defensive necessity. The average cp_loss of 3110 reflects how these seemingly reasonable improving moves catastrophically misread the position's tactical demands.

704.label: Capturing an undefended or en prise major piece (queen or rook) in an already-winning position where the opponent's king is exposed.
704.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture of a major piece (6/10 capture rooks, 4/10 capture queens), and in every case the capturing side already holds a large advantage with the opponent's king exposed or weakly shielded. 10/10 positions have at least one king flagged as exposed or with a weak pawn shield. The move played is always the 'obvious' material-winning capture. In 6/10 cases (Positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9), this capture IS the correct move — the only way to convert the advantage. In 4/10 cases (Positions 2, 5, 8, 10), a forced checkmate (mate in 2-4) was available but the player chose the material capture instead, resulting in catastrophic cp_losses averaging ~9500. The feature consistently activates on the moment of decision where a free major piece tempts the player in a position where the enemy king's weakness could also be exploited tactically. 7/10 moves use a rook as the capturing piece, and the average number of good moves available is just 1.2, indicating these are critical-decision positions with very narrow correct paths.

713.label: Non-forcing pawn advances that vacate critical squares or waste tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
713.description: All 10/10 positions feature single-step pawn advances that appear natural (gaining space, attacking pieces, or creating threats) but are catastrophically ill-timed. In 6/10 cases, the pawn advance directly vacates or removes the defense of a critical square (e5 vacates e6, e4 breaks g3's support, c5 vacates b5/c6, h4 vacates h5, d4 leaves c4 unguarded, b6 removes c6's defense), allowing immediate opponent exploitation of that square. In 4/10 cases (g4, a3, a4, f5), the pawn advance is primarily a tempo waste in positions requiring immediate tactical execution—forced mates, decisive knight forks, or kingside breakthroughs were available. The average good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are razor-sharp critical moments where only precise moves maintain the evaluation. The average cp_loss of 1136 reflects positions where the gap between 'natural-looking' and 'correct' is enormous. In 9/10 cases, the best move was a piece move or a different pawn entirely, while the player defaulted to a seemingly logical but non-forcing pawn push.
713.old_chip: Slow pawn pushes in sharp positions

718.label: A rook moves to a file occupied by the enemy queen, appearing to challenge it, but the queen is not actually vulnerable and the rook abandons a critical defensive responsibility.
718.description: In 10/10 positions, a rook is moved to a file or rank where it 'targets' an enemy queen that doesn't need to move. The queen either has a stronger forward square available (positions 1, 4), can simply ignore the attack while exploiting what the rook abandoned (positions 3, 5, 6, 7, 9), or the 'challenge' is too slow compared to concrete tactics that existed (positions 2, 8, 10). In every case, the rook move abandons a critical function: back-rank defense (positions 2, 4), control of a key file (positions 3, 7, 9), blocking a diagonal for the king (position 5), defending a piece (position 10), or simply wastes a tempo when forcing tactics were available (positions 1, 6, 8). The average cp_loss of 3020 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' moves are — 5/10 resulted in forced mate or near-mate. The positions span both sides (White 6, Black 4) and target every file (c, d, e, f, g, h), confirming the pattern is about the conceptual error rather than any specific geometry.

720.label: A passive, non-forcing bishop repositioning move played in a position that demanded an immediate concrete tactical continuation.
720.description: 9/10 positions feature a quiet bishop move (the exception being b6, also a non-forcing move), and all 10 share the same fundamental error: wasting a critical tempo on a 'developing' or 'improving' piece move when the position demanded an immediate forcing blow. In 10/10 positions the best move was a concrete tactical action — capturing a key piece (Bxe5, Nxg7, Nxd5), delivering a forcing check (Rd2+), launching a pawn break (c4, e5), or infiltrating with the queen (Qa6→Qd3). The tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' in 9/10 positions. The average cp_loss of 319 reflects that these positions had fleeting, dynamic advantages that evaporated the moment the opponent gained one free move to consolidate, counterattack, or capture the hanging tactical opportunity. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, confirming these were narrow critical moments. In 7/10 cases the opponent's refutation directly exploited the wasted tempo — either capturing a piece that was supposed to be sacrificed/used (Nxh5 in pos 5), launching a counterattack against an exposed king (Nxd5+ in pos 6, Qg5 in pos 2), or winning undefended material (Bc5+ winning rook in pos 8).

722.label: Playing quiet, non-forcing moves (development, pawn pushes, repositioning) when the position demands immediate tactical action through checks, captures, or urgent defense.
722.description: 9/10 positions feature moves tagged as 'tempo_loss' where the player chose a quiet structural or developmental move while a forcing tactical opportunity or critical defensive need was available. 10/10 positions had 'piece_activity' as a key factor, meaning the best moves all involved immediate active engagement (checks, captures, or direct threats). 5/10 moves were knight developments to passive or vulnerable squares (Na6 x2, Nd4 x2, Nh3), while 4/10 were one-square pawn advances (c6, a3, h4, b5) addressing long-term concerns. In every case, the best move involved a forcing operation: Position 1 needed Bf4 attacking the queen; Position 3 needed Rg8 contesting the g-file against mate; Position 5 needed Re3 with discovered attack ideas; Position 10 needed bxc5 capturing a hanging rook. The average cp_loss of 1210 reflects how catastrophic tempo waste is in sharp positions. 6/10 positions involved hanging pieces that either resulted from the move (placing a piece en prise) or were missed captures available as the best move.

727.label: A queen or rook moves to an undefended square that is already directly attacked by an opponent's piece, allowing immediate capture.
727.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical pattern: the player moves a major piece (queen in 6/10, rook in 4/10) to a square where it is immediately captured by an enemy piece with no recapture available. In 9/10 cases the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece.' The capturing piece exploits a pre-existing line of attack to the destination square — most commonly a diagonal (7/10 involve diagonal captures by queens or bishops: Qxc2+, Qxe2, Bxc6, Qxb3, Bxd3, Qxd6, Qxe7), while others involve file-based queen captures (Qxd1+, Qxe1#) or knight captures (Nxd4). In every case, the attacking line was open BEFORE the blunder — the player moved their piece INTO an already-existing threat rather than creating a new vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 5008 reflects that half these blunders result in immediate mate or queen loss. All positions had 3 good alternatives available on average, indicating these were avoidable one-move oversights rather than forced errors.

725.label: A slow h-pawn push (or similar non-developing pawn move) played to prevent a secondary future threat while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis requiring concrete action.
725.description: 8/10 positions feature an h-pawn push (h3, h4, h5, or h6), and all 10 are non-developing pawn moves played during the opening phase (8/10) or early middlegame (2/10). In every single case, the position demanded urgent concrete action — either capturing hanging material (positions 2, 5, 8), exploiting a devastating tactical shot (positions 1, 3), or developing pieces to defend a critical weakness like f7/f2 (positions 4, 7, 9, 10). Instead, the player chose a prophylactic pawn move addressing a secondary concern (preventing Ng5, Bg5, or Bg4 in most cases). 10/10 positions tagged as 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic'. The punishment typically involves exploiting the very weakness the player failed to address: f7/f2 sacrifices (4/10), capturing undefended central pawns (3/10), or piece invasions into squares the pawn push abandoned (3/10). The average cp_loss of 259 reflects that these are not subtle positional inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments of priority.

729.label: Playing g6/g3 to prepare a bishop fianchetto while the player's own king remains in the center, wasting a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate development, tactical action, or castling.
729.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical geometric move — advancing the g-pawn one square (g6 for Black, g3 for White) — with the explicit intent of fianchettoing the bishop. In every single case (10/10), the moving side's king is still uncastled and sitting in the center. The positions universally demanded something more urgent: in 4/10 cases a concrete tactic was available (capturing a hanging piece, delivering check, or executing a central break with tempo), in 4/10 cases the priority was straightforward piece development preparing castling (Be7, Be2), and in 2/10 cases a prophylactic move was needed to address an immediate threat. The fianchetto preparation was too slow in all cases because the uncastled king created exploitable vulnerabilities — the g-pawn advance itself often worsened matters by weakening critical squares (f3/f6, h3/h6) or opening diagonals toward the king. The average centipawn loss of 278 reflects that opponents could exploit the tempo loss with pins, forks, discovered attacks, piece invasions, or central breaks before the fianchetto could be completed.

724.label: A bishop captures a seemingly attractive knight target (often on a peripheral square), abandoning the bishop's critical tactical or defensive role in the position.
724.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a knight, with the target knights predominantly located on rim or semi-peripheral squares (a3, a4, b4, b5, c4, c5, g4, h4). In 8/10 cases, the captured knight appeared loose, offside, or poorly placed, making the capture look natural or even 'free.' However, in every case the bishop was performing a far more important function: in 4/10 positions the bishop was the linchpin of a winning tactical combination (Bxa2+/Nb4+ fork, f4/Nd4/Nc2 fork, Bb4+ check); in 3/10 it was defending a critical square against immediate tactical threats (d3 against knight forks, preventing intermediate checks); in 3/10 it was maintaining positional dominance or dark-square control. The refutations consistently exploit the bishop's absence: intermediate checks with recapture (3/10), knight forks on newly undefended squares (2/10), recaptures that activate the opponent's pieces (3/10), or elimination of attacking potential through simplification (2/10). The average cp_loss of 323 reflects how devastating these 'natural-looking' captures are.

721.label: Playing a developing or repositioning move while leaving a piece, pawn, or critical square undefended, when the position demanded addressing an immediate tactical obligation first.
721.description: In 9/10 positions, the player made a 'purposeful-looking' move (typically piece development or king repositioning) while ignoring a more urgent concrete demand in the position. In 5/10 cases, the move directly left a piece or pawn en prise (positions 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 — rook on a8, rook on a1, c4 pawn, f2 pawn, c4 bishop). In 3/10 cases, the move abandoned defensive duties allowing a tactical blow (positions 5, 7, 8 — Ne3 fork, square abandonment on e4/h5, Bxf2+ deflection). In 2/10 cases, the error was a priority/move-order issue where a threat needed neutralization before repositioning (positions 1, 2). The correct moves across all positions shared a common thread: address the immediate obligation FIRST (save the hanging piece, make the forced trade, defend the critical square), and only then pursue the desired plan. 6/10 blunders were bishop moves to 'active' squares, 3/10 were king moves, and 1/10 was a knight repositioning — all appearing purposeful but ignoring what the position actually demanded.

728.label: Advancing a pawn in one's own king's shelter to 'lock' the structure, but actually creating fatal weaknesses or targets.
728.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance on the same flank as the player's own king, intended to fix or stabilize the pawn structure defensively. In 7/10 cases, the move is specifically a g- or h-pawn advance near a kingside-castled king (g4 for White with king on g1/g2, g5 for Black with king on g8, h4 for White with king on h1/h2). In 2/10 cases, it's a c-pawn advance near a queenside-castled king (c4 with White's king on c1, c5 with Black's king on c8). The stated intent across all positions is prophylactic — to prevent the opponent from advancing their own pawns (blocking h6, preventing g5, freezing the structure) — but in every case the advance backfires catastrophically. The average cp_loss of 1322 reflects the devastating consequences. In 9/10 positions, the move creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities: weak squares for piece invasion (f4 in positions 1/9), pawn targets (g4 in positions 3/9, h4 in positions 6/8), wedge-pawn opportunities (h6 in positions 2/4/5), or exposed diagonals for checks. Only 1/10 (position 10) is primarily a tempo-loss rather than a structural weakening, though it still advances near the queenside-castled king.

726.label: A bishop-takes-bishop exchange is played when the correct move was to eliminate or target a dominant/vulnerable knight instead.
726.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing another bishop (Bx bishop), when the position demanded dealing with a critical knight first. In 9/10 cases, the opponent had a powerfully centralized knight (on e4, e5, d4, or d5) that was the true source of positional advantage, and the correct move was to capture or challenge that knight (via pawn captures like dxe5/exd4, rook captures like Rxe5, or bishop captures like Bxe4). In 1/10 cases (Position 10), the player's own side had the chance to exploit a misplaced knight on a6 but instead traded bishops. The consistent error is prioritizing a bishop exchange—often seemingly logical because it simplifies or removes pressure—while completely ignoring that a knight is the dominant piece in the position. In 8/10 positions, the best move specifically involved a pawn or piece capture of the critical knight before any bishop trade. The average cp_loss of 368 reflects how catastrophic it is to leave a dominant knight untouched while trading away active pieces.

733.label: King moves to a square immediately exploitable by a check, check sequence, or checkmate, when a safer king destination was available.
733.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves where the king steps onto a square that is immediately tactically vulnerable. In 9/10 cases, the primary refutation begins with a direct check or checkmate on the very next move (Positions 1: Qxc6+, 2: gxh3 enabling Rc1+/Rf2+, 3: Rf8+, 5: c5+, 6: Bc3#/Rb1#, 8: Qf3+, 9: Qxg6#, 10: Re3+), with Position 4 (Qg5+) also following this pattern. Only Position 7 (Kh8) deviates slightly, being a passivity error rather than walking into an immediate check, though even there White's Kg5 advance exploits the cornered king. In every case, an alternative king move to a different square (often just one square away in a different direction) would have avoided the tactical exploitation. The average cp_loss of 2963 reflects that several of these walk directly into forced checkmate (Positions 3, 5, 6, 9). The positions span endgames (6) and middlegames (4), both sides (White 6, Black 4), confirming this is a universal pattern of choosing the wrong king destination.

737.label: Passive king retreat to a back-rank corner or home square that walks directly into a lethal tactical pattern on a file or diagonal.
737.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king retreating to the back rank (h1, h8, or e8) seeking perceived safety, but instead walking into immediate tactical catastrophe. In 5/10 cases the result is forced checkmate (positions 1, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10), and in the remaining cases the evaluation worsens by 279-467cp. The h-file is the killing mechanism in 6/10 positions (Kh8 or Kh1 allowing rook/queen checks on the open h-file), while the h5-e8 diagonal is exploited in 4/10 positions (Ke8 allowing Qh5+). In every case, the correct move was either to capture an attacking piece (Kxh2 in position 3, Kxh7 in position 4), move the king counterintuitively forward (Kg6 in positions 6, 7, 9; Kh2 in position 5), or play an active non-king move addressing the real threats (Nf7, Rf7, Rf2, d5 in positions 1, 2, 8, 10). The average cp_loss of 6038 reflects that these retreats are almost uniformly catastrophic rather than merely suboptimal.

736.label: A knight (or minor piece) jumps deep into enemy territory attempting a fork or material gain, but the invading piece becomes trapped or leaves other pieces undefended.
736.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight invasion (the exception is a bishop doing the same thing in position 3), and 5/10 specifically go to c2 targeting the a1 rook. In all 10 positions, the piece aggressively enters enemy territory attempting to win material through a fork or direct attack on a rook. The 'trapped_piece' motif appears in 8/10 positions and 'tempo_loss' in 9/10. The consistent punishment pattern is that the invading piece becomes stranded or trapped (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 9, 10) or is simply captured unfavorably (positions 6, 8), while the opponent exploits the tempo to attack other undefended pieces (especially bishops left hanging in positions 1, 9) or to consolidate with gaining moves (f4 in position 8, Ke1 in position 7). Only 2.4 good moves were available on average, suggesting these positions already required careful play, making the speculative raid especially costly.

738.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn advance (or quiet move) when the position demands an immediate tactical blow or urgent defensive action.
738.description: 9/10 positions feature a one-square pawn advance and 1/10 a passive rook retreat — all non-forcing moves with no check, no capture, and no direct threat. In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete action: 6/10 positions had a winning tactic available to the player (dxc4 opening a diagonal, Rxg8 simplifying, Rd2 invading, Qxb7 capturing material, Nxd3+ clearance, Nxe3 deflection), while 4/10 required urgent defensive moves to prevent an opponent's tactic (Nc7+ fork, Qxa3+ mating attack, Nf5/Qg7# mating net, Nxc5 winning material). The average cp_loss of 2269 confirms these are catastrophic errors. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions were tactically narrow and demanded precise calculation rather than general positional play. The blunder consistently gave the opponent one free tempo — enough to either neutralize the player's entire winning plan or execute a devastating counter-tactic.

730.label: Queen moves to an aggressive-looking square while the player's own king is unsafe, abandoning a critical defensive responsibility that the opponent immediately exploits.
730.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen relocating to a seemingly active or threatening square (checks, attacks on pawns, centralization) while the moving side's king remains uncastled or exposed in the center. In 10/10 cases, the queen was previously performing an essential function — blocking a file (positions 2, 4), defending a piece or pawn (positions 6, 7, 8), covering key squares around the vulnerable king (positions 3, 9), or simply needing to stay near the center for coordination (positions 1, 5, 10). The moves go predominantly to flank squares (8/10: Qh4, Qh4, Qh5, Qb4, Qb4, Qb5+, Qc4+, Qc7) with 2/10 landing on exposed central squares (Qe5, Qe6) where they're immediately hit with tempo. The punishment in every case involves the opponent exploiting exactly what the queen abandoned: a hanging piece on the diagonal (position 6), an open file check (positions 2, 8), exposed king diagonals (positions 3, 9), undefended pawns (positions 4, 7), or simply gaining development tempo (positions 1, 5, 10). The average cp_loss of 361 reflects how severely these moves backfire.

734.label: Pawn captures that open a file directly toward the player's own king, handing the opponent's rook a devastating attacking lane.
734.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (pxp) where the capturing pawn vacates its original file, opening it as an attacking corridor that the opponent immediately exploits against the player's king. In 6/10 cases, the move is hxg5 (or hxg4), opening the h-file toward a castled kingside king while the opponent's rook on h1 is already perfectly positioned to dominate it. In 4/10 cases, the move is exd4/exd5/dxe5, opening the e-file toward an uncastled king on e1/e2/e8 where the opponent's rook on e1 (or similar piece) creates pins or checks. In 9/10 positions, the opponent had a rook already stationed on or aimed at the file that was opened. The king safety tag appears in all 10 analyses, confirming this is the unifying factor. The average cp_loss of 256 reflects how catastrophic these file-openings are — in several cases (positions 5, 10), the swing exceeds 400cp, representing full piece losses through the exploitation of the opened file.

739.label: Playing a natural-looking queen centralizing/checking/capturing move instead of the position's concrete tactical demand.
739.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves to seemingly active squares (central squares like e3, d2, d6, e6, e7, or aggressive squares like g4+, g3, f6). In 8/10 cases, the correct move was either a forcing tactical sequence involving a different piece (Positions 1, 5, 10: rook moves like Rxf1+, Rxc3+, Rb8) or a more precise queen move to a specific square serving a concrete defensive/offensive purpose (Positions 6, 8: Qf1 to trade/defend; Position 4: Qd7 to infiltrate with checks). The average cp_loss of ~3000 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in allowing forced mate. In 9/10 cases only 1 good move existed within 50cp of best, showing these were positions demanding calculation over intuition. The played moves consistently chose 'general improvement' (centralizing, checking, looking active) over the specific concrete action the position required.

723.label: Playing a superficially aggressive or active-looking move while missing a much stronger concrete tactical continuation.
723.description: All 10/10 positions feature a player choosing a move that looks aggressive or improving (centralizing a piece, advancing a pawn, or even giving check) while missing a clearly superior forcing tactical solution. In 5/10 cases the missed best move was a tactical shot (Rd8#, Rxf6 sacrifice, Ng3+ windmill, Nxe4 capture, Na5 winning material). In 3/10 cases the missed move was a quiet preparatory move that maintained a winning tactical framework (Kh1, Nd2, Rfe8). The average cp_loss of 2186 is extreme, and the average of only 1.7 good moves means these were narrow critical positions demanding precise calculation rather than general principles. 5/10 moves were knight moves to 'active' squares (Ne3×2, Nd6, Nb4, Nxf7+), 3/10 were pawn advances (d5×2, f2), showing the player consistently chose piece improvement or space-gaining over concrete tactical execution. In 7/10 positions the played move had a clearly logical intent (attacking a piece, threatening a fork, advancing a passer) that was simply less important than the available forcing continuation.

740.label: A superficially logical pawn move (capture or advance) played when the position critically demands immediate piece activity or a different, more precise pawn decision.
740.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves — either pawn captures (gxf3, dxe4, exf6, fxg4, dxc4 = 5/10) or pawn advances (c4, e4, c5, a3, f3 = 5/10) — that appear to gain something tangible (material, space, or structural solidity) but fatally ignore the position's true urgent requirement. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a piece move (Qxb7, Rc6, Bxf3, Qe3, Nd6+, Bxd6, Qe2, Be3), while in 3/10 cases the correct move was a different pawn capture (fxe4 instead of dxe4, gxf5 instead of dxc4). The positions averaged only 1.7 good moves available, indicating critical moments where precision was essential. The pawn moves consistently created or permitted concrete tactical vulnerabilities: opening diagonals to the king (fxg4, gxf3), removing key defensive pawns (exf6, dxe4), self-blocking retreat squares (e4), opening squares for opponent pieces (c5), or simply squandering the one critical tempo needed (a3, f3, c4). The average cp_loss of 389 reflects how these 'natural-looking' pawn moves convert winning or equal positions into losing ones.

735.label: Passive, non-forcing moves (especially knight retreats from strong squares) chosen when the position demands immediate tactical/forcing action.
735.description: All 9 positions share a striking common thread: the played move is entirely non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no direct attacks on pieces), chosen in positions where only 1-2 good moves exist (avg 1.6) and those good moves are concrete/forcing. In 6/9 positions, a knight is moved to a passive or peripheral square (Nd6 retreating from e4, Nd3 retreating from e5 twice, Na5 leaving c6 for the rim, Nfd2 retreating from f3), abandoning critical central influence. The remaining 3/9 are slow pawn pushes (h4, a6, c6) or a quiet rook move (Rfe1) that similarly ignore urgent tactical demands. In contrast, the best moves across these positions were forcing: checks (Qa5+, Qh5+ in 2 positions), captures (Nxe5 in 1 position), attacks on the queen (c5 in 1), or moves that address a concrete tactical vulnerability (Rb1, Kd4, Nh4). The average cp_loss of 253 reflects that these quiet moves allow the opponent to seize the initiative in positions where the tactical window was narrow and time-sensitive.

731.label: Playing a passive pawn push or developing move while a bishop is under direct tactical threat, resulting in its loss.
731.description: In 9/10 positions, a bishop is under immediate attack (by a pawn or knight) and requires urgent action — either retreat, exchange, or counterattack. Instead, the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (typically a one-square pawn push to the 3rd rank) that completely ignores the threat. In 7/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 10), the bishop is directly captured on the next move as refutation. In 2/10 positions (9, 10), the move actually blocks the bishop's retreat square, trapping or dooming it. Position 8 is the slight outlier where a passive pawn move allows the opponent to favorably exchange a powerful bishop. The pawn moves e3 (3x), d3 (3x), f3 (1x), and c6 (1x) account for 8/10 blunders, with quiet knight moves (Nd7, Nc3) comprising the other 2. All 10 moves share the character of appearing 'natural' or 'developing' while catastrophically failing to address the most urgent requirement of the position.

732.label: Quiet piece repositioning that removes a piece from a square where it was performing an essential defensive or tactical function, immediately enabling the opponent's combination.
732.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing 'improving' move (no checks, no captures) that relocates a piece away from a square where it was performing a critical function the player failed to recognize. In 8/10 cases, the piece was directly preventing an opponent's tactical blow: blocking an invasion route (Rg1 abandoning c-file, Rf8/Rc8 abandoning e-file), maintaining a defensive blockade (Ba4 leaving e8 where it blocked Rh8, Bd7 wasting the tempo needed for Rg8+), or sitting on a capture/threat square (Be2 leaving f1 where Bxh3 won material). In 7/10 positions, a forcing alternative (check or capture) was available that would have exploited the moment instead. The moves all share the appearance of 'natural improvement' — centralizing a knight (Nc4), developing a bishop (Bd7, Ba4), activating a rook (Rg1, Rf8, Rc8, Rhe8) — but each one unknowingly surrenders the critical resource that was holding the position together. The average cp_loss of 4082 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic misunderstandings of which piece is doing what job.

743.label: A knight is passively repositioned to a seemingly attractive square when the position demands immediate concrete action (pawn break, capture, or forcing move).
743.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight being moved to a new square in a non-forcing repositioning maneuver, while the position critically demanded immediate concrete action. In 9/10 cases, the best move was a pawn break (d5, f4, exf4, b5), a capture (Nxc4, Nxe5), or a forcing centralization (Ne5, Ned4). The knight moves overwhelmingly target rim or peripheral squares: 3/10 go to h5 (from f6), 3/10 go to b-file squares (b3, b4, b6), and the remaining 4 go to repositioning squares (g3, f3, f8, f6). In 7/10 cases, the knight abandons a critical defensive or offensive function at its original square — guarding against pawn breaks (f6 preventing e5/f5), attacking key pawns (d2 attacking c4), or maintaining central tension. Tempo loss is explicitly identified in 9/10 positions. The average cp_loss of 246 reflects how costly a single wasted tempo is in these sharp middlegame positions where the opponent can seize the initiative or execute a decisive plan.

744.label: Playing fxe5 in a King's Gambit structure with the king on e1, catastrophically removing the f-pawn's shield of the h4-e1 diagonal and allowing Qh4+ to win material.
744.description: 5/10 positions are the identical or near-identical blunder: White plays fxe5 in a King's Gambit setup (after 1.e4 e5 2.f4) with the king still on e1, removing the only pawn blocking the h4-e1 diagonal, immediately allowing Qh4+ followed by Qxe4+ forking king and h1-rook. Positions 1, 2, and 10 are literally the same position (eval +16 → -335), position 6 is nearly identical (+30 → -395), and position 5 is the same pattern in a slightly different King's Gambit variation (-118 → -461). The remaining 5/10 positions share the broader theme of removing a defensive element (piece or pawn) to pursue a greedy or superficially attractive plan: positions 3-4 play Bf4 abandoning pressure/ignoring king safety, position 7 plays a slow pawn move ignoring a hanging rook, position 8 places a rook on a diagonally-attacked square, and position 9 moves the king away from a necessary blockading role. Across all 10, the common thread is prioritizing an offensive/material idea while catastrophically ignoring an immediate defensive obligation, but the feature is overwhelmingly dominated by the specific King's Gambit fxe5 blunder.

741.label: Queen repositioned to a seemingly active square while a concrete forcing move (check, capture, or checkmate) was immediately available.
741.description: 9/10 positions feature queen moves (with 4/10 being specifically Qg3), and 10/10 are quiet, non-forcing repositioning moves. In 7/10 cases, the best available move was a check or capture; in 3/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 9), a forced checkmate was missed entirely. The blundered moves all share the character of placing the queen on a square that appears active (controlling a file, aiming at the enemy king, or maintaining 'pressure') but actually abandons a critical function or misses immediate tactical execution. The average centipawn loss of 3122 is catastrophically high, driven by multiple missed mates. In 8/10 positions, the queen retreats or moves laterally rather than advancing with tempo. The positions consistently had very few good moves available (avg 1.7), indicating razor-sharp positions where only forcing moves preserved the evaluation.

747.label: Playing slow, non-forcing pawn moves (especially on the flanks) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
747.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (c4, f6, h4, a3, h4, a4, h3, a3, g3) and 1/10 a passive bishop retreat (Bd2), all sharing the critical property of being non-forcing and prophylactic/structural when the position demanded immediate tactical engagement. In 10/10 cases, the best move was a forcing piece action: sacrifices (Rxh7, Rxg7+), tactical centralizations (Nd4, Nc5), attacks on pieces (Be3, Rg3), forced mate (Qf6), or urgent king safety (O-O, Nxd4). The missed opportunities averaged only 1.9 good moves available, indicating these were narrow tactical windows. 6/10 moves were specifically edge-file pawn pushes (a3, a3, a4, h3, h4, h4), suggesting a tendency to play 'prophylactic' rook-pawn moves as a default when uncertain. The average cp_loss of 1265 is enormous, with positions 4 and 6 missing forced winning sacrifices/mates. The common thread is prioritizing long-term prophylaxis over present-moment tactical demands.

742.label: A short pawn advance (f3/g3 for White, g6/e6 for Black) to the player's third rank that weakens the king position or removes defensive pawn coverage when active play was demanded.
742.description: 10/10 positions feature a one-square pawn advance to the player's own third rank (f3/g3 for White in 6 positions, g6 for Black in 3 positions, e6 for Black in 1 position). In 9/10 cases, the move specifically advances the f-pawn or g-pawn near the castled king. The common error is that these 'quiet' pawn moves create immediate tactical vulnerabilities: in 3/10 positions (8, 9, 5), the g6 advance removes pawn protection from a piece (knight on f6 or h6), allowing it to be captured. In 3/10 positions (3, 7, 10), g3 weakens critical squares (f3, dark squares) enabling devastating piece infiltration or mating attacks. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 6), f3 is a passive tempo loss when forcing moves (checks, queen activations) were available. The average cp_loss of 2079 is enormous, with positions ranging from 105 to 9451 centipawns lost. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions typically demanded precise active play rather than prophylactic shuffling.

746.label: A routine-looking pawn capture wastes a critical tempo while an urgent tactical demand (king safety, piece threats, or required move-order) goes unaddressed.
746.description: All 10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture that looks structurally or materially logical but fatally ignores a more pressing obligation. In 7/10 positions, the urgent need was king safety — either defending one's own king (positions 1, 5, 7, 8, 9) or avoiding opening lines that benefit the opponent's attack on one's own king (positions 6, 7). In 2/10 positions (4, 10), the capture itself was thematically correct but executed in the wrong move-order — a preparatory move (Rxa1 or e4) was required first to maximize the capture's effectiveness. In 1/10 positions (3), the capture released central tension prematurely when a tempo-gaining alternative (f4) existed. The average centipawn loss was 298, and only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments. In 9/10 cases, the opponent had one clear best punishment that exploited the wasted tempo — typically a forcing attacking sequence (Qc1→Qh6, Ne3 fork, Re7 invasion, Rf3 lift, Qf7+/Ng6+, hxg3 reforming shelter) that the pawn capture failed to prevent or address.

753.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn push on the wing when the position demands immediate tactical or piece-activating moves.
753.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, single-square pawn advance that creates no immediate threat while ignoring a critical demand in the position. 8/10 moves are on the a-file or h-file (the absolute rim), with the remaining two on the b-file and f-file — all peripheral. The tactical motif is labeled 'tempo_loss' in 9/10 positions. In every case, concrete action was available: winning material via tactics (positions 5, 6, 7, 8, 9), activating the king in an endgame (positions 2, 3, 10), or executing a decisive pawn break on the opposite wing (position 1). The average cp_loss of 1127 is extreme, reflecting that these positions were sharp and demanded precision — only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning the margin for error was razor-thin. The pattern represents a player defaulting to a 'safe-looking' autopilot pawn push rather than engaging with the position's true requirements.
753.old_chip: Quiet flank pawn instead of action

745.label: Playing a tempting but non-urgent move (capture, retreat, or check) in a critical position that demanded a single precise forcing continuation.
745.description: 9/9 positions share a defining characteristic: the position was on a knife's edge with very few good moves (avg 2.1), yet the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' move that ignored the most critical demand of the position. In 3/9 cases (Nxa3, Rxa2, fxe5), the move was a greedy material capture that left something catastrophically undefended or destroyed a critical defensive/attacking structure. In 3/9 cases (Nfd7, Na8, Nd7), the move was a passive knight retreat/repositioning that wasted crucial tempo when the position demanded immediate central or tactical action. In 2/9 cases (Rf7, Rg2), a rook was placed on a seemingly active square instead of executing the winning tactical blow. In 1/9 case (Re6+), a pointless check was given that drove the opponent's king to safety and abandoned the mating construction. The correct moves in ALL cases were forcing: eliminating a critical threat (Rxf8), opening the center against an exposed king (e6), delivering immediate checkmate (g5+, Bf3→Rh5#), or executing a winning tactical combination (Nxb2+, Rc1+). The average cp_loss of 2366 reflects that these positions all had extremely narrow correct paths where any deviation was catastrophic.
