752.label: The player moves the king to what appears to be a safe square but chooses a destination that creates new tactical vulnerabilities or misses a stronger alternative.
752.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves played as defensive or prophylactic retreats that select the wrong destination square. In 8/10 cases, the correct move was also a king move (just to a different adjacent square), meaning the player correctly identified the need to move the king but picked the inferior square. In 2/10 cases (positions 3 and 10), the king shouldn't have moved at all — a capture was correct instead. The wrong square typically creates specific geometric vulnerabilities: 5/10 positions saw the king walk into checks, forks, or checkmate (positions 4, 6, 7, 8, 9); 3/10 saw the king entomb itself in a corner losing critical mobility (positions 1, 2, 5); and 2/10 saw a wasted tempo when a non-king move was decisive (positions 3, 10). The average cp_loss of 2186 is extremely high, and only 1.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were razor-thin positions where the precise king square was the difference between survival and catastrophe. 6/10 moves went to corner squares (h1, a1, h8, h1, f8, d1), suggesting a bias toward tucking the king away rather than keeping it active or mobile.

754.label: Queen moves to a square where it immediately becomes a target for tempo-gaining attacks by the opponent's pieces or pawns.
754.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves to squares that appear active or aggressive but are immediately exploitable by the opponent. In 8/10 positions, the primary tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' — the opponent gains one or more free developing moves while chasing the misplaced queen. In 7/10 cases, a bishop or pawn attacks the queen with tempo (Ba3 in positions 1 and 3, Bf5 in position 2, Bg3 in position 6, Be5 in position 8, a3 in position 10, Rf4 in position 5). The average cp_loss is 292 with only 1.1 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the queen must be placed precisely. In 3/10 positions (2, 6, 7), the queen is effectively trapped or won. In the remaining 7/10, the queen survives but is chased repeatedly, allowing the opponent to coordinate their pieces harmoniously. Notably, in 6/10 positions the correct alternative was a queen retreat to a safer square (Qa6 twice, Qd5, Qa6/Qa5, Qxc1+, Qxh3), suggesting the feature fires when players choose 'active-looking' queen squares over genuinely safe ones.

756.label: Pushing a pawn forward aggressively when the position demands development, concrete tactics, or preparatory moves first.
756.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances that look aggressive and space-gaining but are tactically premature. 7/10 involve central pawn pushes (d or e pawns), while 3/10 are kingside pawn storms (f6, g4, g4). In 6/10 positions, the better alternative was a piece development or concrete tactical move (Qa4+, Qc7, Nf6, Be2, Bd6, Rgb8). In 3/10 cases, a preparatory move was needed before the advance could work (g4+ before d3, cxb3 before anything else). The pawn advances consistently either opened lines that benefited the opponent (positions 4, 9, 10), removed defensive pawns from critical posts (positions 1, 4, 5, 6), created exploitable weaknesses (positions 6, 8), or missed winning tactical shots in favor of generic space-gaining (positions 3, 5). 8/10 positions featured at least one uncastled king, and in those cases the premature advance typically opened files or diagonals that exposed the advancing side's own monarch.

748.label: Playing a natural-looking improving or activating move that ignores the single most critical tactical demand of the position.
748.description: All 10 positions share a defining characteristic: they are narrow tactical moments (avg 1.5 good moves available) where the position demands ONE specific urgent action, yet the player chooses an 'improving' move that would be reasonable in a calmer position. 8/10 moves are piece developments or piece activations to seemingly logical squares (Be3, Nc4, Be2, Bb5, Re5, Bf5, Rd6, Rdc7), while 2/10 are pawn pushes with apparent purpose (g3, b5). In 5/10 cases, the urgent requirement was king evacuation or addressing a mating threat (positions 1, 3, 5, 8, 9). In 3/10 cases, a piece was hanging and needed to be captured or saved (positions 2, 7, 10). In 2/10 cases, a time-critical tactic needed immediate execution rather than preparation (positions 4, 6). The average cp_loss of 4069 is catastrophically high because these positions had essentially zero margin for non-specific moves — 4/10 allowed immediate checkmate, and 3/10 lost a full piece or more.

751.label: Quiet piece moves to d2/d7 (or similarly passive squares) in positions demanding immediate tactical action, squandering a critical tempo.
751.description: 7/10 positions feature a piece moving to d2 or d7 on the d-file (Kd2, Qd7×4, Nd7, Rd7, Rd2), while the remaining 3 are equally passive non-forcing moves (g6×2, Ne2). All 10 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), meaning they were critical moments requiring precision. In every case, the player chose a 'natural-looking' quiet repositioning move — placing a piece on a seemingly logical central/d-file square — when a forcing tactical opportunity existed (Bh6 deflection, Rh4 attacking the queen, Ng6 activation, Qh4 counterplay, h4 chasing, etc.). The common punishment is that the opponent gains a full tempo to either execute their own tactic, consolidate a vulnerable piece, or exploit the newly created weakness. 8/10 positions had 'tempo_loss' or 'missed_tactic' as primary tags. The average cp_loss of 256 reflects that these aren't minor inaccuracies but critical failures to recognize tactical urgency.

757.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended or tactically exposed square where it is immediately captured, attacked with tempo, or forced to retreat.
757.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop repositioning move that places the piece on an exposed square, resulting in immediate punishment. In 4/10 cases (Bc6, Bf6, Be4, Bf5), the bishop lands on an undefended square where it can be directly captured or its target moves away with tempo, winning material. In 4/10 cases (Bb4, Ba3, Bd4, Be2), the bishop moves to a square where it is immediately attacked by an enemy piece (knight or queen), forcing a humiliating retreat that wastes two full tempi. In 2/10 cases (Bf8, Bc4), the bishop retreats to a passive square that blocks its own pieces or abandons a critical defensive role. The tempo_loss tag appears in 8/10 positions, and piece_activity/hanging_piece tags appear in all. The average cp_loss of 262 reflects that these are severe errors — the bishop 'improvement' actually creates an immediate tactical target that the opponent exploits for material or decisive positional gain.

755.label: King voluntarily moves to a corner, edge, or back-rank square where it becomes entombed by its own pawns/pieces and is immediately checkmated or fatally attacked.
755.description: All 10 positions feature king moves, and 8/10 involve the king moving to a square where it becomes catastrophically confined. In 6/10 positions (3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10), the king walks directly into a back-rank or corner mate where its own pawns seal off all escape squares — enabling immediate checkmate in 1-3 moves. In 7/10 cases, the destination square is on the absolute edge of the board (a-file, h-file, 1st rank, or 8th rank). The king is often lured by a capture (5/10 positions involve Kx captures), tempting the player with material while the destination square is fatal. The average cp_loss of ~6559 reflects that 7/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate or near-mate sequences. Positions 1 and 4 are mild outliers (4cp and 62cp loss respectively) where the king move to the edge happened to be acceptable or best, suggesting the feature detects the geometric pattern of king-to-trapped-square broadly but fires most strongly on the catastrophic instances.

759.label: A quiet, non-forcing queen repositioning move (typically to a 'natural' c-file square) squanders a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate tactical action.
759.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet queen move (no checks, no captures) to a seemingly natural square when the position urgently demanded concrete tactical play. 7/10 moves specifically placed the queen on the c-file (Qc7 x4, Qc8 x2, Qc2 x1), with the remaining three going to nearby queenside/central squares (Qb3, Qa5, Qd2). In 9/10 positions, the primary tactical motif was identified as 'tempo_loss' — the queen move looked like reasonable positional play (connecting rooks, supporting pieces, aiming at diagonals) but fatally wasted the one tempo needed to execute or maintain a tactical advantage. The best alternatives in all cases were concrete, forcing moves: tactical strikes (Nxf2, e4, Bxh7+), aggressive piece deployment (Qh4, Qg5, Ne4), or immediate exploitation of opponent weaknesses (Re1+, Nd5, Bxd5). The average cp_loss of 273 confirms these are severe blunders. 8/10 positions had the player holding an advantage that was squandered; the remaining 2 turned a slight disadvantage into a losing one. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions requiring precision rather than generic improvement.

760.label: Queen moves (often pawn captures or non-forcing repositions) that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate urgent action.
760.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that squander a decisive tempo in tactically critical positions. 4/10 are direct pawn captures (Qxb3, Qxc2, Qxb3, Qxb7) representing material greed, while 6/10 are non-forcing queen repositions (Qd3, Qf3, Qh8, Qc4, Qa5, Qh6) that look active but miss the position's urgent demand. In 9/10 cases, king safety is the primary concern being neglected — either the player's own king is left vulnerable (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8) or a decisive mating attack against the opponent's exposed king is abandoned (positions 4, 9, 10). The punishments are severe (avg 3892cp loss), with 4/10 resulting in forced mate and 3/10 converting forced mates into merely winning positions. The unifying thread is that the queen ends up on a square where it cannot address the position's most critical tactical need — either too far from defensive duties or choosing a non-forcing continuation when immediate decisive action exists.

749.label: Playing a natural-looking piece repositioning (usually a rook along a file) when the position demands immediate concrete action—either a tactical strike or maintaining a critical defensive guard.
749.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves to seemingly active squares (d6, d3, d5, d7, e5, g3), while the remaining 2 involve minor piece repositioning (Bf2, Ne7). In all 10 cases, the move looks positionally reasonable—centralizing, penetrating to the 7th rank, challenging an enemy piece, or defending a pawn—but catastrophically ignores the position's immediate tactical demands. In 5/10 positions (1, 5, 6, 7, 9), a DIFFERENT piece had an immediately winning tactical shot that the repositioning move forfeits (Bf4+ winning a rook, Bf7 winning a rook, Nxd2 capturing material, Bd5 dominating, Rd7 with Nd6+ follow-up). In 3/10 positions (2, 3, 8), the moved piece was performing an indispensable defensive function—two cases specifically involve a d2-rook moving to d3 and allowing immediate checkmate on f2. In 2/10 positions (4, 10), active counterplay was needed rather than passive repositioning. The average cp_loss of 3941 is enormous, with 4/10 positions resulting in immediate checkmate or forced mate. The average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where 'natural' moves are punished severely.

763.label: Playing a non-urgent wing pawn push in a pawn endgame when king activity or addressing an immediate positional crisis is required.
763.description: 10/10 positions are endgames and every move played is a one-square pawn advance on a non-central file (a, b, c, g, or h). In 8/10 positions, the best alternative was a king move (Kd3, Ke6, Kf2, Kd5, etc.) that would have maintained active king positioning or blocked the opponent's king infiltration. In the remaining 2/10 (positions 5 and 8), the best move was a different pawn advance addressing an urgent threat on the opposite flank. The average cp_loss is 420, with 3/10 positions showing catastrophic swings exceeding 690cp. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where a single tempo decides the outcome. The consistent thread is that every blundered move addresses a secondary concern (queenside structure, kingside space) while ignoring the position's critical demand—typically a king race to a key square (d5, e6, f5) or preventing an imminent pawn breakthrough (g5, h5). The feature identifies the moment a player 'putters' with a flank pawn instead of fighting for the decisive factor.

758.label: Rook moves along a rank in the endgame, seeking activity but abandoning a critical defensive file or landing on a tactically vulnerable square.
758.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves in the endgame, and 9/10 involve the rook sliding laterally along a rank (rather than vertically along a file). The catastrophic blunders (positions 1, 3, 5, 9, 10 with cp_loss >300) all share the pattern of a rook leaving a critical defensive file to slide toward the center or opposite wing: Re1 abandons h-file defense (pos 1), Rf2 abandons h-file allowing Qxh5# (pos 3), Rc2 slides onto a fork-vulnerable diagonal (pos 5), Rf2 slides into the path of White's rook on f8 (pos 9), and Re7 abandons back-rank coverage allowing Rd1# threats (pos 10). The moderate errors (positions 4, 8 with cp_loss 44-171) show the same pattern of choosing lateral rook activity over more urgent tasks (capturing a pawn or defending the king). Only 2/10 positions (positions 2 and 6) had cp_loss of 0, where the lateral rook slide happened to be optimal. Exposed kings appear in 10/10 positions, confirming the endgame context where defensive precision is critical.

762.label: Aggressive pawn advances that remove critical protection from friendly pieces, squares, or diagonals, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
762.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances as the blunder move — every single mistake is a pawn pushing forward. In 8/10 cases, the advanced pawn was performing a specific defensive function that its movement destroyed: blocking a critical diagonal (positions 5, 8 — g4 blocked e6-h3, d4 blocked a7-g1), defending a friendly piece (positions 3, 10 — f4 guarded e5 pawn, e6 guarded f5 knight), or restricting an enemy piece (positions 2, 4 — g5 denied bishop access to h4, e4 restrained the d2 knight). In the remaining cases, the pawn advance ignores an immediate existential threat in favor of offensive ambition (positions 1, 7 — ignoring mate/rook domination) or pushes the pawn into a blockadable square when piece play was required first (position 6). The average cp_loss of 2187 reflects that these self-inflicted wounds range from positional concessions to instant checkmate. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where precise (usually piece-based) moves were required instead of the tempting pawn push.

761.label: Pieces retreat to passive squares that obstruct their own king's escape or defensive coordination, typically when active play was urgently required.
761.description: 10/10 positions feature king safety as the critical tactical concern, and in every case the played move worsens the player's own king safety through self-obstruction. 4/10 moves are knight retreats to the board's edge (Nh2 ×3, Nb8 ×1) that either block the king's escape route or become immediate tactical targets near the king. 3/10 are queen misplacements (Qe3, Qe4, Qf6+) to squares where they become capturable after forced checks or allow the opponent's king to escape punishment. 2/10 are king moves (Kg7, Ka6) that walk into mating nets or self-trap on the rim. 1/10 is a passive pawn push (b4) ignoring urgent back-rank king safety. The average cp_loss is ~4949 with only 1.8 good moves available on average, showing these are critical decision points with narrow paths to survival. 7/10 positions involved open files (h-file or d-file) aimed at the player's king, meaning the self-obstruction was maximally punishable. In all cases, the best moves involved either active counterplay (Ng5, Nb5, Qf7+) or urgent king escape (Kh2, Kb4, Bxg5), contrasting sharply with the passive/retreating nature of the blunders.

767.label: Advancing a pawn (typically central) when the position demands immediate piece action, wasting a critical tempo and often weakening the position structurally.
767.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance (9/10 are center or queenside pawns on the c, d, or e files) in sharp tactical positions where the player needed to act with pieces instead. In 8/10 cases, a concrete tactical shot was available (winning material, trapping a piece, or addressing a direct threat) but was ignored in favor of a slow structural pawn push. The 'tempo_loss' theme is universal across all positions — the pawn advance either fails to address the most urgent positional demand or actively creates new weaknesses. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 10, and 8), the pawn advance specifically removes a pawn from a critical defensive square, opening diagonals or granting the opponent access to key squares (e.g., e3→e4 removing d4 control, c5 opening the c5-g1 diagonal). In 3/10 positions (3, 6, 7), the pawn push ignores an opponent's passed pawn or promotion threat that needed immediate attention. The average cp_loss of 1148 reflects that these are catastrophic errors in positions requiring precision.

766.label: Playing a superficially attractive aggressive move (usually a check) instead of finding the one truly decisive tactical solution nearby.
766.description: In 10/10 positions, there was exactly 1 good move available (avg good moves = 1.0), and the player chose a move that LOOKED similar in aggression/style to the best move but missed the precise geometry. 7/10 moves played were checks or captures with check (Qe5+, Qh4+, Qh8+, Qf5+, Qg3+, Nxh3+, hxg6 creating a threat). In 5/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 6, 7, 9), the CORRECT move was also a check but on a different square—the player picked the wrong checking square. In 2/10 cases (positions 1, 8), the player chose a flashy attacking move over a simple capture of an undefended piece. In 2/10 cases (positions 3, 5), the player chose a non-forcing move when a check was the precise solution. The average cp_loss of 2201 reflects the catastrophic nature of these near-misses: the moves look so similar to the correct idea that the error appears small, but the consequences are devastating.

765.label: Voluntary king moves played as prophylaxis when the position demands immediate tactical action on pieces or pawns.
765.description: 10/10 positions feature voluntary king moves (not escaping check) in complex middlegame/endgame positions with active piece tension. In 9/10 positions, the king move was a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 2094 excluding the one correct instance). The best moves in these positions were overwhelmingly piece actions: 7/10 demanded rook activation or exchange (Rd3, Bxg4, Re1, Rc5, Rxe1+, Rd8, Re8), 1/10 required a queen attack on a hanging piece (Qe2), and 1/10 needed a pawn advance to close a file (g4). The king moves shared the fatal characteristic of wasting a critical tempo while unresolved tactical obligations existed—hanging pieces (positions 2, 10), pieces in tension requiring immediate resolution (positions 3, 5, 9), or exposed king geometry requiring piece coordination rather than king shuffling (positions 1, 4, 6, 7). In 6/10 cases, the king move actively worsened king safety by walking onto exposed files/diagonals (Kf7 into Qd7+, Kd7 into Rxb7+, Ke2 into Qa2+/Qc2+, Kg7 into Bd4+, Kh3 into Ng5+, Kg3 into e4-e3 attacks). Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, indicating these were narrow tactical positions where the single correct resource had to be found—and a passive king move was never it.

750.label: Playing an obvious-looking aggressive, materialistic, or active move when the position demands a specific precise action that addresses a more urgent tactical requirement.
750.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a move that appeared natural or attractive — a capture (6/10: Bxf8, bxa5, Bxh2, Bxg6, and arguably Ng5/Nf5 attacking pieces), a forward king march (2/10: Kf6, Ke6), or an aggressive pawn/piece advance (2/10: g4, f3) — while the position demanded a fundamentally different, often less obvious action. In 7/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, meaning these were critical junctures requiring extreme precision. The correct moves varied widely: piece retreats (Nd2, Bb2), prophylactic pawn moves (h5), forcing checks (a4+, Qxf8#), eliminating threats (Nxf6), rook invasions (Rg2), proper move order (Kf2), or central breaks (e4). In every case, the played move either created a new vulnerability by removing a piece from a critical defensive duty (Nf5 abandoned e8 control, Kf6 abandoned knight protection, Bxg6 left d4 bishop hanging) or wasted critical tempo on a secondary goal while the primary tactical issue remained unaddressed.

769.label: Advancing the g-pawn (g3/g6) when the king sits on the h-file, fatally removing protection from the f2/f7 pawn and allowing capture with check.
769.description: 9/10 positions involve advancing the g-pawn one square (g6 for Black with king on h7, or g3 for White with king on h2). In all 9 cases, the g-pawn previously protected the adjacent f-pawn (f7 or f2), and its advance leaves that f-pawn undefended. The primary refutation in 8/10 positions is an immediate capture on f2/f7 (Qxf2+, Qxf7+, or Rxf7+), almost always with check because the king remains on the h-file where the f-file diagonal/rank now reaches it. The king placement on h2/h7 is consistent across all g-pawn cases (5 positions with Black's king on h7, 4 with White's king on h2). The average cp_loss of ~4067 reflects that several of these moves convert winning or equal positions into forced mates. Position 10 (b3) is a minor outlier involving a similar concept—a pawn advance near an exposed king creating tactical weaknesses—but targets the queenside rather than the kingside.

764.label: King moves forward toward the center in positions where active enemy pieces immediately exploit the advanced square with checks, diagonal attacks, or mating combinations.
764.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king moving forward (toward the center or away from the back rank) to a square that is immediately tactically exploitable. In 8/10 positions, this occurs in the middlegame where queens, rooks, and bishops remain active—making king centralization premature and dangerous. In 9/10 positions, the advanced king square sits on a vulnerable diagonal or file where an enemy piece delivers a punishing check (g4+ in position 3, Bc4+ in position 1, Bf4+ in position 4, Bd5+ in position 9, Bf6+ in position 8, Ba3+ in position 7, Ra7+ in position 6, Qe5+ in position 2, Be3/Bxd4+ in position 2). The best moves were retreats toward the back rank in 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 9), moves to a different forward square avoiding the specific tactical vulnerability in 4/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 6, 8), and non-king moves (queen trade) in 1/10 cases (position 7). The average cp_loss of 2124 reflects the catastrophic nature of exposing the king—with 2/10 resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, showing these were razor-thin decisions where the advancing instinct was almost always the single worst direction.

770.label: Playing a non-forcing rook repositioning move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical action.
770.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that is non-capturing and non-checking, aimed at 'improving' the rook's placement (centralizing, occupying an open file, or challenging an opponent's piece). In every case, the position required an immediate forcing move — typically a capture (Nxd5, Bxe5, Nxg4, Kh4), a check sequence (Qxd6+, Ra4+), or a critical pawn advance (f4, e4). The rook moves look positionally natural: Re1 appears in 4/10 positions, Rf1 in 2/10, and the remainder are rook moves to 'active' squares along open files. However, 10/10 positions were tactically sharp, with an average of only 1.6 good moves available, meaning these were narrow decision points requiring concrete calculation, not general improvement. The average centipawn loss of 1227 reflects how catastrophic these tempo-losing rook moves are — in 3/10 cases they allowed forced mate or threw away a completely won game, and in 7/10 they gave the opponent time to consolidate, escape danger, or execute a devastating tactical response (discovered attacks, sacrifices, or forcing sequences).

772.label: A knight captures a seemingly available pawn, but the resulting recapture or exchange sequence costs more material than the pawn was worth.
772.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight capturing an enemy pawn (Nx-pawn), and in every case the capture triggers a tactical or exchange sequence where the opponent's recapture creates devastating consequences — forks (2/9), opening of diagonals or lines (2/9), unfavorable capture chains (3/9), or dominant centralized pieces that attack multiple targets (2/9). In 8/9 cases it is White making the greedy capture, and 6/9 occur in the opening phase where development and coordination outweigh a single pawn. The average centipawn loss is 310, reflecting that these aren't minor inaccuracies but catastrophic miscalculations. In every position, quiet developing or repositioning moves (bishop retreats, checks exploiting open files, piece redeployment) were clearly superior — averaging 2.1 good alternatives available. The consistent error is prioritizing material gain over positional/structural considerations, failing to calculate the full consequences of the opponent's recapture on the same square.

768.label: Capturing an enemy pawn with a major piece or king in a decisively won endgame, sometimes missing faster forced checkmates.
768.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture in an already-won endgame (evaluations ranging from +600 to forced mate). Every single capture targets an enemy pawn specifically — never a piece. The capturing side uses a major piece (Rook in 5/10, Queen in 4/10) or King (1/10). In 7/10 positions the capture has 0 cp_loss and is correct or near-optimal, but in 3/10 positions (Qxc2, Rxg5, Rxb7) the pawn grab catastrophically misses a forced checkmate (avg ~9200 cp_loss in those cases). The recurring analytical theme across all positions is 'tempo_loss' — even when correct, the captures are typically identified as slightly less precise than alternatives that gain tempo via checks or advance passed pawns first. The positions where the capture is a true blunder share the pattern of moving a piece AWAY from a mating construction to grab an irrelevant pawn (Rxb7 abandons the d/f-file mating corridor, Qxc2 leaves the attacking diagonal, Rxg5 gives Black a tempo to reposition defensively).
768.old_chip: Greedy pawn capture in won endgame

776.label: A knight delivers check that accomplishes nothing constructive, typically losing tempo while the opponent's king improves or the knight abandons a superior post.
776.description: 10/10 positions involve a knight delivering check. In 8/10 cases, the check is a clear mistake (avg ~193cp loss excluding the extreme outlier), losing tempo because the knight must retreat or reaches an inferior square while the opponent's king actually improves its position. 7/10 positions feature the knight abandoning a strong central post (d6, f5, e7, d4) or active square just to deliver a check that gains nothing permanent. In 6/10 positions, the opponent's king moves to a BETTER square after the check (centralizing or activating). The tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' in 8/10 cases. Only 1/10 (position 10) is the best move—where the check initiates a forced mating attack—and 1/10 (position 9) is technically 'best' only because the position is already hopelessly lost. The feature captures the classic amateur instinct that checks are inherently useful, when in reality the knight check merely wastes a move and often actively helps the opponent.

771.label: The queen (or major piece) moves to an apparently aggressive peripheral square that is actually disconnected from the position's critical needs, either hanging outright or abandoning vital defense.
771.description: 9/10 positions feature queen moves (with 1 rook move sharing the same pattern). 7/10 moves place the piece on the 7th or 8th rank (Qh7, Qc7, Qb7, Qh7, Qa7, Qc8, Rc8), while the remaining moves go to edge/corner squares (Qg1, Qb3, Qb2). In every case, the piece moves to a square that superficially looks active—targeting enemy pawns, pressuring the king, or occupying an open rank—but is actually catastrophically disconnected from the position's true demands. The punishment varies: in 2/10 cases the piece literally hangs on its destination square (Positions 7 and 9), in 4/10 cases it abandons critical defensive coordination allowing an attack to crash through (Positions 1, 2, 6, 8), in 2/10 cases it fails to restrain a passed pawn or critical advance (Positions 3, 10), and in 2/10 cases it reaches a square where it's immediately harassed with tempo (Positions 4, 5). The best moves in contrast were consistently either centralized, immediately forcing (checks/captures), or directly addressed the position's concrete demands. Average cp_loss of 1267 reflects that these optimistic-looking moves meet devastating refutations.

778.label: Bishop captures material or repositions while a decisive tactical threat (checkmate, fork, discovered attack) goes unaddressed.
778.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop move that prioritizes material acquisition or repositioning over addressing an immediate lethal tactical threat. In 7/9 cases, the bishop makes a capture (typically grabbing a pawn: Bxc2, Bxe4, Bxd3, Bxh6, Bxh3, Bxa3, or a piece). The remaining 2/9 (Bb1, Bb2) are bishop relocations to seemingly active squares. In 8/9 positions, the critical ignored threat involves king safety — back-rank mates (positions 1, 8), mating attacks on open files (positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 8), or enabling forks against the king (position 10). The average cp_loss of 6602 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors: 5/9 positions result in immediate or near-immediate checkmate after the refutation. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions were already demanding precise defensive attention — exactly the wrong moment for a greedy bishop excursion.

773.label: Quiet piece repositioning moves (predominantly knight moves) played in positions that demanded an immediate forcing response such as a capture or pawn break.
773.description: All 10 positions share a remarkably consistent pattern: the player chose a non-forcing piece relocation when the position had only ~1.3 good moves available, almost always a concrete forcing response. 7/10 moves are knight moves (Nb4, Nd7, Na3, Ng8, Ne8, Nh5, Ne2) with the remaining 3 being other quiet piece/king moves (Be2, Ke2, Bb4+). In contrast, the best moves were overwhelmingly concrete: pawn captures resolving tension (exd5, fxe6, hxg5), central pawn breaks (f5, e4), captures of key pieces (Nxe5), forcing checks (Qxc6+), or immediate piece activation to critical squares (Rad8, Nf3, Ne4). In 10/10 cases the blunder was a non-capturing piece relocation that ignored the position's tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 2105 reflects that these quiet moves are catastrophic precisely because the positions were tactically critical with razor-thin margins (avg 1.3 good moves), and the passive choice either allowed the opponent a devastating tactical response or squandered a narrow window for the player's own forcing continuation.
773.old_chip: Passive piece shuffling in critical moments

775.label: Moving a knight away from a functionally powerful square to a superficially attractive but strategically inferior one, releasing pressure that was restraining the opponent.
775.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves (the sole exception being Re4 in position 2, which follows the same functional principle). In every case, the piece occupied a square where it served a critical function—creating tactical threats that restrained the opponent (positions 1, 4, 6, 7, 8), paralyzing enemy coordination from a deep outpost (positions 3, 8), blockading or restraining passed pawns (position 5), or simply being safe (position 9). The knight was then moved to a destination that appeared attractive: a central square (Nd5, Ne4, Nd4), a square attacking material (Nb4→a2, Nc4→a3, Nb5→Nc7), a 'natural' developing square (Nc6, Nc3), or a check (Nf2+). In 7/10 positions, the opponent's refutation directly exploited the specific resource that the knight's departure removed—capturing a now-undefended piece (positions 1, 4, 9), invading along a diagonal the knight previously covered (positions 3, 6), launching a freed attack (positions 7, 10), or advancing pawns no longer restrained (position 5). The average cp_loss of 320 reflects the severity: these aren't subtle inaccuracies but position-altering blunders where the knight's former function was irreplaceable.

780.label: A non-forcing move (development, repositioning, or pawn push) played when the position demanded an immediate capture or forcing tactical blow as the only way to maintain evaluation.
780.description: In 9/9 positions, the played move was quiet and non-forcing (pawn pushes h4/h5, piece developments Bd2/Bd7/Qe7, repositioning moves Qb2/Qd6/Qd5, and king move Kf2), while the required best move was a capture or forcing tactical shot in 8/9 cases (Ngxe4, Bxb4, axb4, Bxg5, Nxe3, Qxd4+, b5/Bxc3+, Bxf7+). The average number of good moves was only 1.2, indicating extreme tactical precision was demanded. All positions featured unresolved piece tension or hanging material that required immediate resolution — the quiet moves left this tension intact, allowing the opponent to exploit it. The average cp_loss of 439 reflects how catastrophic it is to temporize in these critical moments. In every case, the player chose a move with a plausible positional rationale (gaining space, developing, centralizing) over the concrete tactical necessity.

774.label: Playing a positional or strategic move while a piece is immediately hanging or becomes tactically vulnerable, prioritizing long-term ideas over urgent concrete threats.
774.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a move with clear strategic intent (gaining space, challenging a piece, repositioning) while a piece was either already hanging or became capturable as a direct consequence. In 6/10 positions, the blunder was specifically a pawn push (f6, e5, d5, f4, b4, c6) that ignored an immediate tactical obligation. In 4/10, a piece move (Qe6, Rg8, Nb3, Rxd8) either abandoned a defensive duty or created a new vulnerability. The tactical motif most frequently triggered was 'hanging piece' (7/10 positions explicitly tagged), with forks (2/10) and promotion threats (1/10) as variants. The average cp_loss of 1327 reflects catastrophic material losses—typically a full piece or queen. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions demanding precise tactical attention rather than broad strategic planning. In every case, the best moves addressed the immediate threat first (defending, capturing the attacking piece, or moving the endangered piece to safety), while the blunder treated the position as though it were strategically quiet.

781.label: Voluntary king step diagonally forward toward the center when urgent tactical moves were available, exposing the king to attacks on open lines.
781.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king taking one diagonal step forward from a relatively sheltered square (f8→e7, g8→f7, g1→f2, f1→e2, c1→d2) into a more exposed central position. In every case, the move was voluntary (not forced by check) and intended as a consolidation/prophylactic measure — the player wanted to centralize the king, connect rooks, or escape perceived threats. However, 10/10 positions had specific tactical alternatives available (queen checks, piece captures, knight forks, material wins) that demanded immediate action. The king moves consistently placed the monarch on squares vulnerable to open files (e-file in 4/10, g-file in 3/10), knight checks (3/10), or rook sacrifices (2/10). The average cp_loss of 2102 is extraordinarily high, with 3/10 positions converting to forced mate. Only 1.6 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than slow consolidation.

782.label: Moving a rook to e1/e8/f1/f8 as generic development while ignoring an immediate tactical threat requiring urgent attention.
782.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being placed on the back rank (e1/e8/f1/f8) as a natural-looking 'developing' or 'activating' move, when the position actually demands immediate attention to a concrete tactical crisis. In 9/10 positions, one side's king is dangerously exposed (on f2, e2, or f7), making tempo critically important. The rook moves are all non-forcing and fail to address the urgent issue: in Position 1 it allows a discovered check on the f-file; in Positions 2, 4, 8, and 10 it wastes tempo with a king on f7 exposed to checks/discovered attacks; in Positions 3 and 6 it ignores piece vulnerabilities with a king on e2; in Position 5 it ignores a hanging queen; in Position 7 it ignores a hanging knight capturable with check; in Position 9 it creates a pin vulnerability on the very file being doubled. The average cp_loss of 418 reflects how catastrophic these tempo losses are in sharp positions. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, confirming these are critical moments demanding precision rather than routine development.

789.label: A knight jumps to a seemingly powerful outpost where it is profitably captured by an opponent's bishop, destroying the mover's structure or coordination.
789.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving to an aggressive-looking square that appears to be a strong outpost or attacking post. In 9/10 cases, the primary refutation is the opponent simply capturing the knight with a bishop (Bxf5, Bxd5, Bxf4, Bxc3, Bxb5, Bxd3). The remaining position (Nc5) involves the knight landing on an undefended square exploited tactically. In every case, the player was seduced by the knight's apparent activity on its destination square — attacking multiple targets, occupying a central outpost, or delivering check — but failed to recognize that the opponent's bishop was perfectly positioned to eliminate it. After the bishop captures the knight, the resulting pawn recapture consistently damages the mover's position: opening files for the opponent's rooks (positions 1, 4), destroying central pawn chains (positions 3, 4, 5), removing defensive anchors (positions 6, 7), or simply losing material when the knight was undefended (positions 8, 9). The average cp_loss of 271 reflects how these moves often transform winning or equal positions into losing ones.

783.label: Quiet flank or structural pawn moves played when the position demands immediate tactical action, wasting a critical tempo.
783.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing pawn move (no captures, no checks) played in a position where concrete tactical action was urgently required. 9/10 moves are on the flanks or wing files (g-file: 5, b-file: 2, a-file: 1, f-file: 1), with only c6 being semi-central. In 8/10 positions, the blundering side's king was uncastled or severely exposed, making the tempo loss especially catastrophic. In at least 3/10 cases (positions 2, 6, 7), the player pushed a pawn to the exact square where a knight should have moved instead (g6 vs Ng6, a5 vs Na5). The intended purposes were consistently slow positional plans — fianchettoing a bishop (5/10), preparing piece development (3/10), or strengthening pawn structure (2/10) — none of which addressed the immediate tactical emergency. The punishments varied but always exploited the gifted tempo: forks (2/10), piece trapping (3/10), king attacks via opened lines (3/10), and direct mating attacks (2/10).

785.label: Playing a natural-looking bishop development or repositioning move when the position demands urgent concrete action to address king safety threats.
785.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-capturing, non-checking bishop moves to 'natural' squares (diagonals like g7, b7, e6, e7, a6, c4, e2) during middlegame positions with severe king safety concerns. In every case, the exposed king (10/10 positions flag king exposure) required immediate tactical responses—capturing a threatening piece (positions 2, 7), blocking an invasion route (positions 1, 10), closing the kingside pawn structure (position 4), or resolving central tension (positions 5, 9)—but instead the player chose a cosmetic bishop placement that contributed nothing to the urgent defensive need. The average cp_loss of 2063 is extreme, with 3/10 resulting in forced mate. In 8/10 cases, the bishop move was a pure tempo loss (the piece either needed to retreat immediately or proved irrelevant to the critical sector). The refutations consistently exploit the same vulnerability the bishop move ignored: open file invasions (positions 1, 2, 6), central breakthroughs with d5 (positions 7, 8), kingside pawn storms (position 4), and mating attacks (position 10).

779.label: Pushing the g-pawn (g6/g3) to evict an attacking piece from f5/h5/g4, catastrophically weakening the king's dark-square complex.
779.description: 7/10 positions involve pushing the g-pawn one square (g6 for Black, g3 for White) as a seemingly natural attempt to chase away a powerfully posted attacking piece — most commonly a knight on f5 or h5. In all 7 cases, the opponent's piece does NOT retreat but instead exploits the newly weakened dark squares via tactical shots: Nh6+ with check (Positions 1, 10), Nxf6+ capturing a bishop since the g-pawn can no longer recapture (Positions 2, 4), Bh6 landing on the vacated dark square (Position 3), Qh6 infiltrating (Position 10), or the g-pawn move simply wastes a critical tempo (Positions 6, 7). The remaining 3/10 positions feature queen moves to slightly wrong squares (Qg5 instead of Qg4, Qe6 instead of Qg6, Qd3 instead of capturing), sharing the theme of choosing an apparently logical but insufficiently forcing move that allows the opponent a concrete tactical response. Across all 10 positions, the average cp_loss of 1286 reflects the catastrophic nature of these mistakes, with several positions flipping from winning to losing or missing forced checkmate.

790.label: The queen is moved to a new non-capture square when the position demanded a queen trade or queen capture of a key piece.
790.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a quiet queen repositioning move instead of the correct queen capture. In 8/10 cases, the best move was explicitly a queen trade (Qxc8+, Qxf3, Qxe7, Qxc5, Qxe7, Qxd6+, Qxe2, Qxe7), and in the remaining 2, the best move was either a queen capture of a critical piece (Qxb3 capturing a bishop) or a specific queen placement maintaining defensive duties (Qa6). All 10 played moves were non-capturing queen moves to open squares (Qa4, Qb2, Qg2, Qh6, Qb7, Qb5, Qa5, Qb3, Qb5, Qb7) that looked active or purposeful but abandoned the critical defensive sector. The average cp_loss was 2128 with only 1.4 good moves available on average, indicating these were narrow positions where the simplifying capture was essentially forced. The refutations consistently exploited the queen's absence from defense: hanging pieces captured (3/10), mating attacks launched (3/10), back-rank invasions (2/10), or tempo-gaining attacks on the misplaced queen (2/10).

788.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing wing pawn move (b, f, g, or h file) when the position demands immediate concrete central or tactical action.
788.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn push on a non-central file (f5 appears 3 times, b6 twice, h3 twice, plus g4, b5, g6) played instead of a concrete forcing move. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a tactical or central action (d4, c4, Nh5, e5, g5, Nc6, g4, Bxc6/O-O). The centers were closed or semi-closed in 7/10 positions, creating a false sense of security that invited slow play. In 8/10 cases, the position had only 1-2 good moves available, meaning these were critical decision points with narrow margins. The average cp_loss of 305 confirms catastrophic consequences. The common thread across all positions is that these wing pawn moves either created permanent structural weaknesses (f5 blocking f6 in positions 2, 7, 10; b6 weakening c6 in positions 6, 8; g4/g6 weakening king shelter in positions 1, 4), lost a critical tempo allowing the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative (h3 in positions 5, 9), or both. In every case, the player chose a 'useful-looking' prophylactic or space-gaining move on the flank while ignoring the tactical urgency at the heart of the position.
788.old_chip: Passive flank pawn when action required

786.label: King advances one square from its shelter (typically off the back rank) into a more tactically vulnerable position, when concrete piece play was required instead.
786.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves advancing one square, typically forward from the back rank or current shelter toward a more exposed square. In 7/10 cases, the correct move was a non-king move (captures like Bxc5, Nxf3, Bxa3, Rxg6, or queen moves like Qd1, Bc8), while in 3/10 cases a king move WAS correct but to a different square (Ke1 vs Kf2, Kh1 vs Kg2, Kc8 vs Kb7). The specific king destinations cluster heavily: g2 appears 3 times (from g1), b2 appears twice (from b1), with single instances of d6, f2, h7, g7, and b7. In 9/10 cases the king moved toward the center or off the back rank into an adjacent rank where it became vulnerable to checks, forks, perpetuals, or mating nets. The average cp_loss of 1352 reflects catastrophic consequences—the 'one step forward' consistently transformed defensible positions into lost ones.

777.label: Moving a piece (usually a rook) to the back rank directly in front of an opponent's passed pawn near promotion, when active counterplay was required.
777.description: All 10/10 positions involve placing a piece on the 1st/8th rank on the exact file of an enemy passed pawn that is 1-2 squares from promotion. 8/10 are rook moves (Rc8, Rb8, Rd8, Rd8, Rg8, Rc1, Rc1, Rh8) and 2/10 are king moves (Ke1, Ka1) to the back rank. In every case, an opponent's pawn sits on the 7th/2nd rank threatening immediate promotion, and the player responds by placing a piece directly in the pawn's path on the promotion square or adjacent square. The correct alternatives varied: 4/10 required advancing the player's own passed pawns in a pawn race (positions 1, 2, 5, 6), 3/10 needed active rook checks or piece play (positions 8, 9, 10), 2/10 demanded king flight away from tactical danger (positions 4, 7), and 1/10 required capturing the pawn's support piece (position 3). The average cp_loss of 2952 reflects several positions where forced checkmates were missed in favor of passive defense.

796.label: Advancing a passed pawn toward promotion in a decisively won pure king-and-pawn endgame where the opponent's king cannot intercept.
796.description: All 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with decisive winning advantages (evaluations ranging from +641 to +862 cp). All 10/10 moves are pawn advances (not king moves or captures). At least 9/10 directly advance a passed pawn toward its promotion square (c3, g6, h2, d7, c4, h7, h7, a6, and c4 creating connected passers), while 1/10 (g3) is a prophylactic pawn fix that supports the winning plan. In every case, the opponent's king is geometrically too far to intercept the passed pawn, making promotion unstoppable. Critically, all 10/10 moves have 0 cp loss (one has 4cp), meaning these are optimal or near-optimal moves—the feature detects correct execution of the most fundamental pawn endgame technique: pushing an unstoppable passed pawn when the king race is already decided.

791.label: Voluntarily moving a bishop (or piece) to a passive, buried, or tactically vulnerable square while missing concrete tactical opportunities.
791.description: 8/10 positions involve bishop moves specifically, with the remaining 2 being analogous rook repositioning moves sharing the same error pattern. The bishops are moved to squares that are either self-entombing (Bh1, Bf1, Bh2 — 3/10 positions bury the bishop behind own pawns or in a corner), tactically vulnerable (Be3 — 3/10 positions place the bishop where it immediately hangs to capture sequences with no recapture or fork follow-ups), or strategically misguided by abandoning a critical diagonal (Bh6 — 2/10 positions remove a fianchettoed bishop from its key diagonal). All 10 moves are quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning moves played in positions where concrete tactical action was available (forks, hanging pieces, forcing checks, or passed pawn pushes). The average cp_loss of 336 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic misplacements. 7/10 positions had the player missing a clear tactic (captures, forks, checks), and in every case the 'improved' piece ended up worse than before the move.

792.label: An already-exposed king attempts to relocate but chooses a destination square that walks into a tactical vulnerability (check, fork, or abandoned defense).
792.description: 10/10 positions involve king moves where the king is already exposed or on an awkward square, and the player attempts to improve its placement but selects the wrong destination. In 8/10 cases, only 1 good king destination existed (avg good moves: 1.4), making these razor-thin decisions. In 7/10 positions, the chosen square places the king on an open line (file, rank, or diagonal) where an enemy piece delivers check that wins material — e.g., Kh3 walks into Rf3+ (pos 1), Kc4 walks into Rc7+ (pos 2), Kf8 walks into Qf5+ (pos 4), Kg6 walks into Rxg3+ (pos 6), Kd1 walks into Qxf3+ (pos 8). In 2/10 cases the king abandons defense of a piece (pos 3: leaves rook on a3 undefended; pos 9: enables capture-then-fork). Position 5 is the most extreme — Kf8 walks into immediate back-rank checkmate. The consistent thread is an exposed king with very few safe squares where the player's intuition about which direction offers safety is wrong.

794.label: A non-forcing rook repositioning move is played when the position demands an immediate tactical action (capture, check, or critical defense).
794.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move to a seemingly active square — an open file, an attacking rank, or a centralized post — that is neither a capture nor a check. In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete action that was missed. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 7), the correct move was a rook CAPTURE of a hanging or critical enemy piece (Rxb4 winning a queen, Rxd1 eliminating a penetrating rook, Rxf1+ capturing a queen with check). In 2/10 positions (8, 10), the correct move was the SAME rook going to a different square with a forcing element (Rg5+ with check before Rf5; Rd8 challenging the queen rather than Re8 challenging the rook). In 3/10 positions (4, 6, 9), the best move wasn't a rook move at all — a pawn push (d6), queen sacrifice (Qxf2+), or king retreat (Kd1) was required. In 2/10 positions (3, 5), a different rook needed to go to a specific defensive square (Rb1). The consistent thread is that the player chose a 'looks-good' rook improvement over the tactically critical move, giving opponents time to consolidate or execute devastating counterattacks.

787.label: Playing the most obvious aggressive/forcing continuation in a dominant position rather than the most precise tactical shot, typically wasting a critical tempo.
787.description: 8/10 positions feature tempo_loss as a core tag, and 7/10 involve missed tactics — the connecting thread is that in already-winning positions (9/10 are White with large advantages or forced mates), the player chooses the most OBVIOUS aggressive continuation rather than the most PRECISE one. 5/10 moves are checks or direct king attacks (Rb8+, Re5+, Rh7+) that look forcing but either simplify unnecessarily or use the wrong piece, while the remaining moves (Nh4, f7, Qxh7, Bg2, Be2, Rc6) represent superficially active moves that miss stronger tactical strikes. In 7/10 cases, a more devastating forcing move existed (checkmate in 1, winning exchange via different break, intermediate check before capture). Positions 3 and 5 (0 cp loss) show the same PATTERN of aggressive king-targeting moves but happen to be optimal, suggesting the feature detects the decision point itself — 'which forcing move in a dominant position?' — rather than purely the error.

793.label: A pawn capture that creates an illusory advanced/promotion threat while opening a critical file or diagonal the opponent immediately exploits for a devastating attack.
793.description: All 10 positions feature pawn captures (always pxp) that create what appears to be a dangerous advanced pawn, typically 1-2 squares from promotion. In 8/10 cases (cxb2, cxb2, gxh7, fxg2, hxg6, hxg6, gxh7, dxc7), the resulting pawn lands on the 2nd or 7th rank threatening immediate promotion. However, in 9/10 positions, the capture simultaneously opens a critical line (file, diagonal, or both) that the opponent exploits for a faster, more lethal counterattack. The opened line is specifically fatal in 6/10 (positions 2, 6, 7, 8, 10 open files; position 4 opens a diagonal) leading directly to mating threats or decisive material gain. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 9), the main cost is tempo loss—the advanced pawn proves completely harmless while the opponent uses the wasted move to execute a crushing plan. The analyses consistently describe the advanced pawn as 'irrelevant,' 'harmless,' or 'dead' while the opponent's attack arrives first. Average cp_loss of 3120 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 4/10 resulting in forced mate.
793.old_chip: Greedy pawn capture opens fatal line

806.label: A knight blocking an enemy bishop's diagonal to the queen is moved away, allowing the bishop to capture the queen outright.
806.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight served as the sole piece blocking an enemy bishop's diagonal access to the player's queen, and the knight was moved away, exposing the queen to immediate capture. In 9/10 cases, the bishop sat on g4 or h5 pinning through a knight on f3 or e2 to a queen on d1 or e2; in 1/10 (Position 8), a Black knight on f6 blocked a White bishop on h4 from reaching the Black queen on d8. The knight destinations varied—e5 appeared 6 times, g3 twice, g5 once, and d2 once—but in all cases the knight left the critical diagonal. The refutation was always the same: the bishop captures the now-undefended queen (Bxd1 in 8/10, Bxe2 in 1/10, Bxd8 in 1/10). In every position, at least 3 good alternative moves existed that either kept the knight in place, challenged the pinning bishop (h3), or moved the queen off the diagonal first.

784.label: Playing a secondary move (development, repositioning, or material grab) while an immediate tactical crisis demands specific defensive action.
784.description: In 9/10 positions, the player made a move that completely ignored an immediate tactical vulnerability—typically a hanging piece, an open-file mating threat, or a fork—choosing instead to address a secondary concern like repositioning a bishop, grabbing material elsewhere, or advancing a pawn. Specifically: 4/10 involved passive bishop moves (Bb7, Bd6, Bc1, Bc1) when the position required addressing king safety or saving a different piece; 2/10 involved captures on the wrong part of the board (Bxg7, Nxe7) while a mating threat or hanging piece existed; 2/10 involved king moves toward danger (Kb4, Kc4) that abandoned defense of critical squares or pieces; 1/10 was an irrelevant pawn push (b5); and 1/10 was a capture with check that inadvertently helped the opponent defend (Nxc2+). In all cases, the opponent had one devastating response (usually a check, capture, or mate) that the played move failed to prevent, while the best moves all directly addressed that specific threat. The average cp_loss of 5637 reflects that 7/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate after the blunder.

800.label: Capturing material when the king is critically exposed, allowing the opponent to punish with checks or mating attacks against the unshielded monarch.
800.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures (pawn takes, piece takes, or queen takes) that prioritize winning material over addressing a critically exposed king. In 8/10 positions, the side making the capture has their king exposed or stuck in the center (e1 in positions 1, 3, 4, 10; e8 in position 5; b6 in position 7; b3 in position 8; g1 in position 9). The correct alternative was to castle in 2/10 cases (positions 5 and 10 both needed O-O), close the center in 1/10 (position 4 needed d5), or play a forcing sequence that addressed the king first (position 1 needed Qa6+ before Nxc6). In 8/10 positions, the refutation involved immediate checks or forced mating sequences exploiting the exposed king. The average centipawn loss of ~2993 reflects that these greedy captures frequently allow forced checkmates (positions 1, 9, and 10 all went from survivable to mate-in-N). Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, showing these were critical moments demanding defensive precision rather than material acquisition.

802.label: Bishop delivers a check (usually discovered) but lands on the wrong destination square, missing a superior square that controls critical escape routes or maintains a forcing sequence.
802.description: 10/10 positions involve a bishop move, and 9/10 deliver check (mostly discovered checks where the bishop clears a line for a rook). In every case, a better bishop destination existed: Position 1 needed Bc4+ not Bd5+ (to maintain perpetual), Position 2 needed Bh3+ not Bf3+ (to force a capturable block), Position 5 needed Bf5+ not Bc8+ (to cover g6 escape), Position 6 needed Bf4+ not Bg3+ (to reach e3 controlling f2), Position 7 needed Bg4+ not Bh3+ (to cover d1 escape), Position 8 needed Bg6+ not Be4+ (to support mate on h7). In 8/10 cases the correct move was also a bishop move to a different square, demonstrating that players recognized the tactical motif (discovered check mechanism) but miscalculated which landing square was optimal. The chosen squares typically offered superficially attractive features—material gain (Bd5+ capturing Ra8, Bxa2+ winning a pawn), attacking a piece (Bg4+ hitting the queen, Bf3+ hitting a bishop), or centralization (Be4+)—but critically failed to control the enemy king's escape square, allowing the opponent to sidestep the entire tactical construction.

807.label: Playing O-O as a routine developing move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical strike against the opponent's vulnerable king or pieces.
807.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling (O-O) played as a 'safe' or 'automatic' move when a specific, time-sensitive tactical opportunity existed. In 10/10 cases, the opponent's king was exposed, stuck in the center, or otherwise vulnerable, creating a narrow window for decisive action. The missed opportunities include knight forks winning material (3/10: positions 2, 7, 10), forced checkmate sequences (2/10: positions 4, 5), winning the exchange or rook outright (2/10: positions 3, 9), capturing undefended/hanging pieces (2/10: positions 6, 8), and maintaining a crushing initiative against a crippled opponent (1/10: position 1). The average centipawn loss of 2148 is catastrophic, and only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these are sharp tactical positions with narrow best continuations where castling squanders a fleeting advantage. In every case, the analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as a core theme — castling spends a critical tempo on generic king safety that was not yet threatened, allowing the opponent to consolidate, defend, or neutralize the tactical vulnerability.

804.label: Unsound knight sacrifice on the f2/f7 pawn, attempting a classic tactical pattern (fork or king attack) when the prerequisites for the combination are not met.
804.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight capturing on f7 (6 by White) or f2 (4 by Black) — the classic weak pawn defended primarily by the king. In 9/10 cases this occurs in the opening with both kings still in the center. The players attempt familiar tactical motifs: Fried Liver-style king attacks with Qh5+ follow-ups (Positions 3, 7, 10), queen-and-rook forks (Positions 2, 8, 9), or exchange-winning combinations (Positions 1, 4, 5, 6). However, in every case the sacrifice fails because the opponent can simply capture the knight — with Kxf7/Kxf2 in 5/10 positions, with the queen (Qxf7) in 2/10, or exploit a more valuable hanging piece elsewhere in 3/10. The average cp_loss of 272 confirms these are consistently major blunders. All positions had 1-3 quieter developing or consolidating moves that maintained or improved the evaluation, making these unnecessary gambles in positions that demanded patient play.

801.label: The queen is moved to a passive or ineffective square, abandoning its critical active role in the position.
801.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a queen move that displaces the queen from an active or needed post to a square where it loses its influence over the position's critical factors. 8/10 positions are endgames where queen activity is the primary resource. The queen moves to passive/peripheral squares in 7/10 cases (Qg2, Qg1, Qh2, Qf2, Qc1, Qxa2, Qh5), while 2/10 give pointless checks (Qb7+, Qf7+) that waste tempo, and 1/10 moves the queen far from defensive duties (Qd7). In every case, the best moves maintained queen activity—either centralizing the queen (Qe4, Qe1, Qb8), capturing critical material (Qxd5, Qd6+), or keeping counterplay alive. The positions consistently featured exposed kings (9/10) and dangerous passed pawns (7/10), where the queen's mobility was the sole compensating factor or winning element. The average cp_loss of 2116 reflects how catastrophically queen passivity compounds in simplified positions.

797.label: A piece (usually a rook) moves to an aggressive-looking but unprotected forward square, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
797.description: 7/10 positions feature rook moves to apparently active middle-board squares (Rf4, Rf1, Rg3, Re5, Rd6, Re3, Rb6), with the remaining 3 being pawn/bishop moves that share the same underlying error. In 8/10 cases, the moved piece ends up on a square where it is either undefended, trappable, or targetable by enemy pieces gaining tempo. In 6/10 positions, the aggressive relocation simultaneously leaves OTHER pieces undefended (f4 abandoning e5's support, Rg3 leaving Nf5 hanging, Rd6 leaving Bf5 unprotected, Rb6 abandoning king defense). The tactical motifs are consistently hanging_piece (6/10) or trapped_piece/tempo_loss (4/10). All moves share the characteristic of looking purposeful — pressuring a pawn, controlling a file, targeting a weakness — but the piece lands on a square with insufficient protection, allowing the opponent to exploit the looseness through checks, pawn attacks, or piece captures that win material.

805.label: A knight voluntarily leaves a powerful or functionally essential square for a superficially attractive but inferior destination, surrendering its key role in the position.
805.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight is moved from a square where it performs a critical function (attacking, defending, or controlling key squares) to a destination that looks appealing but is objectively worse. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 8, 9, 10), the knight leaves a dominant outpost (g5, f5, d4, b4, c3) for a clearly inferior square, abandoning its role as the lynchpin of the position. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 5), the knight moves to a square where it is immediately capturable or creates a hanging piece. In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 7), the knight abandons a defensive/active role for a speculative tactical idea that backfires. The destinations share common weaknesses: rim squares (h6, a4), en-prise squares (g4, d5), squares that block escape routes (e5), or passive squares that lose central influence (c6, c6, f6). The average cp_loss of 1170 reflects that these positions often had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.9), meaning the knight's current placement was uniquely important to the position's evaluation.

803.label: An active-looking knight move (capture, centralization, or attack) that ignores a critical defensive requirement, leaving a piece hanging or removing a key defender.
803.description: All 10/10 positions feature knight moves that appear constructive—captures (7/10), centralizations (2/10), or development (1/10)—but catastrophically ignore a more urgent positional or tactical need. In 5/10 cases the knight was performing a silent defensive function (blocking a file, defending a piece) and its departure allowed the opponent to capture an undefended piece (positions 5, 9, 10) or exploit a newly opened line (positions 4, 5). In 4/10 cases the knight move ignored an already-hanging piece elsewhere (positions 1, 3, 4, 6). In 2/10 cases the knight captured with the wrong piece when a pawn recapture was strategically superior (positions 6, 8). The punishment in 8/10 positions was simple material gain—the opponent captures an undefended piece that the knight move exposed. The average cp_loss of 300 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors but concrete material-losing oversights dressed up as 'active' play.

811.label: A queen delivers a check to a back-rank square that the king easily sidesteps, wasting a critical tempo and misplacing the queen.
811.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen giving check to a square on the 1st or 8th rank (a1, a8, b1, b8, d1, d8, f1, f8, h1), and in every case the opponent's king calmly sidesteps to an adjacent safe square (Kd7, Kc2, Ke2, Kh7, Kf2, Kg2, Ka2, Kh2). In 10/10 cases the analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. The queen ends up stranded on a peripheral square, disconnected from the critical action. In 8/10 positions, a quiet preparatory move (Rc1, e4, Nf6, f4, Re2, g6, Nd5, Rd8) was required instead. The average centipawn loss is 2128, with several positions converting winning/equal positions into forced mates against the player (positions 6 and 7 lost 9000+ cp). Only 1.2 good moves existed on average, meaning these were precision-demanding moments where the instinct to check was maximally punishing.

795.label: Non-forcing positional moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action.
795.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) — moves like bishop developments, pawn pushes for space, or piece repositionings that pursue a strategic plan. In 9/10 cases these are mistakes because the position demanded immediate tactical engagement: 4/10 left pieces hanging (Be7 leaves d5 undefended, Nb4 abandons f4 knight, c5 ignores hanging rook on h8, a3 allows Bxd2+ winning queen), 3/10 ignored imminent checkmate threats (Qg4 allows b4#, e4 opens e-file for mating attack, Rg1 enables pxg1=Q+), and 2/10 wasted critical tempo in sharp positions (g6 allows Bg5 pin, Bc8 shortens mate resistance). The average position had only 2.0 good moves available, indicating these were critical moments where only specific forcing responses worked. Position 1 (Bb2, cp_loss 0) is the exception where the quiet move happened to be correct, suggesting the feature detects the move's aesthetic character rather than guaranteeing error.

798.label: Tempting pawn captures (or captures of pawns) that remove a structurally critical defensive pawn, opening lines the opponent exploits against the player's king.
798.description: All 10 positions feature captures that prioritize material gain over structural integrity. 8/10 moves are pawn captures (exf5, fxe3, dxc6, gxh6, fxg4, gxf3, dxe6, dxe5) and the remaining 2/10 are bishop captures of pawns (Bxe5, Bxg3). In every case, the capture removes a pawn that was serving a critical defensive or structural role — shielding the king (positions 2, 6, 8, 9), maintaining a pawn chain that provided counterplay (positions 1, 5), or preserving central tension that restrained the opponent (positions 3, 7). The consistent punishment across 9/10 positions involves the opponent exploiting the newly opened line (file, diagonal, or square) created by the capture — particularly files aimed at the player's own king. The 'king_safety' tag appears in 9/10 analyses and 'pawn_structure' in 9/10. Crucially, in every position the best alternatives were quiet, non-capturing moves (piece retreats, positional advances, defensive regrouping) rather than captures, yet the average cp_loss of 1162 shows these greedy captures were catastrophically punished.

810.label: The king captures an advanced passed pawn on g7/h7 (or nearby), exposing itself to attack when the pawn was either harmless, could be dealt with by pieces, or when a faster tactical opportunity existed.
810.description: 9/10 positions feature the king capturing (or moving toward) an advanced passed pawn on the g- or h-file, typically one square from promotion. In 6/10 cases the move is specifically Kxg7, and in 3/10 it's Kxh7 (plus Kxh2 and Kg5 as analogues). The critical insight shared across all positions is that the advanced pawn was NOT the most urgent concern: in 3/10 cases (positions 5, 6, 9) the pawn was already blocked and could never promote; in 3/10 cases (positions 2, 7, 4) the player had a faster tactical shot (fork, mating attack) that rendered the pawn irrelevant; and in 3/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 10) a preparatory piece move was needed before the king could safely capture. After the king capture, 9/10 positions feature immediate punishment via queen checks, rook infiltration on open files, or knight forks exploiting the exposed monarch on the g/h-file. The average cp_loss of 1276 reflects that these moves often throw away winning positions entirely. Position 8 (g3) is a partial outlier but shares the theme of voluntarily weakening the king's pawn shelter when better options existed.

799.label: A non-forcing pawn move (or king move) played in a critical position demanding immediate tactical action — either a capture, a central break, or a piece maneuver.
799.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn pushes (h6, f4, a3, c5, h4, e5, h4, g5, h6) and 1/10 a king move (Kh5), all of which are non-forcing, preparatory, or prophylactic moves. The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, meaning these were narrow critical moments requiring precise play. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 7) the best move was to capture or address a hanging piece; in 4/10 (4, 6, 8, 9) the best move was to execute an urgent piece maneuver or central break; in 2/10 (5, 10) the best move was development-enabling or center-challenging. The played moves overwhelmingly target the flanks — 7/10 are h-pawn or g-pawn pushes or a-pawn pushes — while the correct moves tend to involve central action or piece activity. The cp_loss averages 333, reflecting how devastating these tempo losses are in positions where concrete threats exist.

816.label: Moving the king to the corner (Kh1/Kh8/Kb8) as a prophylactic measure in positions that demand immediate tactical or concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
816.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move to the corner square (Kh1 in 6/10, Kh8 in 3/10, Kb8 in 1/10) played as a slow 'improving' or prophylactic move when the position urgently required concrete action. In 3/10 cases, a forced checkmate was available (positions 1, 3 had mate-in-4 and mate-in-1 respectively). In 4/10 cases, a specific tactical combination was the only good move (Nxd6, Rxg3, Bxf2+, Nf6+). In 3/10 cases, the king move directly left a piece or pawn undefended that was immediately captured (Bh5 in position 5, f2-pawn in position 9, b2-pawn in position 10). The average centipawn loss was 2202, and on average only 1.7 good moves existed, confirming these are critical decision points where precision was essential. In every case, the analyses describe the player's intent as wanting to 'remove the king from a diagonal,' 'prepare future play,' or 'improve king safety' — all legitimate prophylactic reasoning applied at catastrophically wrong moments.

814.label: Playing a slow, structural pawn move in a position that demands immediate tactical action or urgent defensive piece play.
814.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing, non-capturing pawn advance (c6×5, e3, c3, c4, g5, e6) chosen to address long-term structural concerns—solidifying pawn chains, preparing queenside expansion, reinforcing central squares—while ignoring a critical short-term demand. In 10/10 cases, the position required either exploiting an immediate tactical opportunity (winning material via pins, forks, or attacks on loose pieces in positions 1, 7, 8, 9) or addressing an urgent defensive crisis (imminent king attacks via Qh5+, g4 pawn storms, or piece invasions in positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 10). The best moves in every case involved piece moves—knight strikes (Ng4, Nxc3), bishop maneuvers (Ba6, Bg7, Bg4), queen evacuations (Qc8, Qe8), or piece regrouping (Nf1, Qg2). 9/10 analyses tagged 'tempo_loss' as a motif, and 10/10 tagged 'piece_activity' as a core theme. The average cp_loss of 308 reflects how devastating a single wasted tempo is in these sharp, dynamic positions.

818.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing rook activation move to an open file while an immediate tactical threat or hanging piece demands attention.
818.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing rook move to a seemingly useful open or semi-open file (c-file, d-file, or b-file), where the player defaults to 'develop the rook' instincts while ignoring an urgent tactical problem. In 8/10 cases, the rook specifically comes from the a-file (Rac1, Rac8, Rad8, Rad1, Rab1, Ra2). In 7/10 positions, the immediate issue was a hanging or inadequately defended piece that could be captured (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10). In 10/10 cases, the best moves were forcing or concrete—captures, tactical shots, or moves that resolved central tension—while the blunder was always a quiet 'improving' move. The average centipawn loss was 342, indicating these are severe mistakes. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical-precision moments where generic positional play was catastrophically inappropriate.

808.label: In rook endgames with critical passed pawns, playing a quiet king or rook move that abandons, blocks, or neglects the most urgent passed pawn duty.
808.description: 10/10 positions are rook endgames featuring active passed pawn races. 7/10 moves are king moves (Ke2, Ke7, Kf2, Kf4, Kc2, Ka1, Kb5) and 3/10 are rook moves (Rb2, Ra8, Rc1) — all are quiet, non-forcing moves that look natural but fatally mishandle the passed pawn situation. The specific errors cluster into sub-types: in 2/10 positions the move directly hangs a passed pawn to capture-with-check (Ke7 leaving e5 en prise, Kc2 allowing Rxc4+); in 2/10 the piece physically blocks its own pawn's promotion path (Kf2 blocking the f-pawn, Ka1 blocking the a1 promotion square); in 3/10 the piece goes to a passive square or wrong side of the board while the opponent's pawn races unopposed (Ra8 abandoning the d-file, Kb5 leaving the kingside, Rc1 making the rook passive); and in 2/10 the move wastes tempo when more forcing continuations exist (Kf4 missing Rh1#, Rb2 instead of Rc4). The average cp_loss of 1352 reflects how time-critical these pawn races are — one wasted tempo is often the difference between winning and drawing/losing.

813.label: The queen (or major piece) retreats to a distant, passive square on the edge or back rank, completely disconnecting from the critical defensive zone around its own exposed king.
813.description: 9/10 positions feature queen moves to passive squares on the board's periphery (corners, edges, back rank), with 1/10 being a rook retreat that follows the same logic. The destination squares are overwhelmingly on the 1st/8th rank or a/h files: Qa2, Qd1, Qb1, Qh7, Rf1, Qc2, Qa7, Qf8, Qh8, Qc8. In 8/10 positions, the player's own king was explicitly exposed or weakly shielded, making defensive proximity essential. In 7/10 cases, the opponent punished with a direct mating attack or mating threat that the distant queen could not intercept. The average cp_loss of 3126 (including 3 positions leading to forced mate) reflects the catastrophic nature of abandoning king defense. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precision—yet the players chose the one move that severed the queen's connection to the battle. In every case, a centralized or defensively-connected alternative existed (Qg2, Qe3, Qe5, Qb7, Qc7, etc.) that maintained the piece's relevance to king safety.

815.label: Quiet one-square pawn advance to the 3rd rank in positions demanding immediate tactical or active piece play.
815.description: 8/9 positions feature a single-square pawn advance to the player's 3rd rank (d3, e3, b3, f3, g3, b6, b6, f3), with only one outlier (d4 locking the center). All 9 moves are non-forcing, non-capturing pawn moves played during the middlegame when the position demanded urgent action—either addressing an immediate tactical threat, seizing a critical initiative, or making a forcing piece move. The best alternatives in every case involved active piece play (Qf2, d4, c4, Qg4, Rxa3) or forcing captures. The pawn moves either create concrete tactical weaknesses (4/9: f3 weakening g3, e3 blocking exf3 recapture, b6 undefending a piece) or simply waste a critical tempo allowing the opponent to execute devastating threats (5/9: Qxa2, Re6-Rg6 rook lifts, d4 breaks, Nxe6 captures). The average cp_loss of 296 reflects that these 'quiet' moves are catastrophic misreadings of positional urgency, disguising full-piece or decisive-advantage losses as safe consolidation.

819.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn move (push or capture) when the position demands immediate tactical piece action such as sacrifices, forks, or mating attacks.
819.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn move (either a push or capture) chosen over a drastically superior piece move. In 6/10 positions, forced checkmates were available (positions 3, 6, 7, 9, 10 had mates between 1-16 moves; position 1 had a queen-winning combination). In 7/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif.
