The pawn moves often appear superficially productive — h4/h5 advances look like kingside attacks (positions 2, 8, 9), captures like fxe3/cxb3/axb5 look like free material (positions 1, 3, 10), and structural moves like c6/b3/b5 look like positional improvements (positions 4, 5, 7) — but all squander the critical tempo needed for decisive piece action. The average cp_loss of ~4996 is extraordinarily high, reflecting that these positions sat at tactical tipping points where only piece moves (knight sacrifices, rook lifts, pins, checks) maintained the advantage or avoided catastrophe.

817.label: Trading queens (or making a major capture) reflexively when a hanging or tactically exploitable piece should be captured first.
817.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a 'natural-looking' capture—almost always a queen exchange (8/10 are Qx moves)—when a superior tactical capture existed. In 6/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8), a piece was completely hanging and could be captured for free, but the player was drawn to the major piece trade instead. In 3/10 positions (2, 5, 9), the queen trade allowed the recapturing piece to land with a devastating fork or tactical threat. In 1/10 positions (10), an intermediate check should have been inserted before the queen trade to eliminate the recapturing piece. The missed better move was capturing a knight in 7/10 cases, capturing a queen in 1/10, and inserting an intermediate move in 2/10. The average cp_loss of 445 reflects that these 'obvious' exchanges consistently squander winning advantages or transform equal positions into lost ones. Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, meaning precision was required and the reflexive trade was almost always the single worst plausible option.

822.label: A knight jumps to an attractive central outpost (d4/d5/e5) but abandons a critical defensive duty, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
822.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight leaping to a classical central outpost — d4 (6 positions), e5 (3 positions), or d5 (2 positions) — that appears positionally dominant but creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities by vacating its prior square. In 7/10 cases, the knight was the sole defender of a specific pawn or piece (e5 pawn in positions 9 and 10, c5 bishop in position 1, h3 pawn in position 7, b5 square in position 8, e-pawn break access in positions 2 and 4). In 8/10 cases, the opponent punishes within 1-2 moves by capturing what the knight left undefended. The average cp_loss of 252 reflects that these are severe mistakes despite appearing thematically sound. 6/10 occur in the opening phase where development priorities should override outpost occupation. In all cases, 2-3 good alternatives existed that maintained the knight's defensive responsibilities while pursuing constructive plans (development, pawn breaks, or concrete tactics).

821.label: King retreats to the h1/h8 corner where it becomes fatally vulnerable to h-file attacks, typically involving rook sacrifices or pawn breaks that crack open the file against the trapped king.
821.description: All 10/10 positions feature the king moving to the h-file corner square (Kh1 for White, Kh8 for Black) during the middlegame. In 8/10 cases, the primary refutation directly exploits the h-file against the cornered king: 5/10 involve immediate rook sacrifices on h2/h7 (Rxh2+ or Rxh7+) that blow open the file with check, 2/10 involve pawn breaks (hxg6 or gxf6) opening lines against the trapped king, and 1/10 features a knight mating pattern exploiting an h-file pin. In positions 8 and 9, while less h-file specific, the king move to h8 is a critical tempo loss that fails to address urgent threats. The average centipawn loss is catastrophic (4915cp), with 5/10 positions resulting in immediate or near-immediate checkmate. In 9/10 positions only 1-2 good moves existed, confirming these were razor-thin defensive situations where the 'natural' corner tuck was fatally wrong. The consistent geometric feature is that the bishop on the a7-g1 or a2-g8 diagonal covers the g1/g8 escape square in 6/10 positions, leaving the king truly trapped once the h-file opens.

826.label: Moving the queen (or major piece) to an active-looking central square instead of playing the concrete forcing move the position demands.
826.description: 8/10 positions feature a queen move to a central or active-looking square (c5, e4, d4, h3, d6, f4), with the remaining 2 being analogous piece-improving moves (Be4, Re5). All 10 moves are non-capturing, non-checking 'repositioning' moves that prioritize piece placement over urgent tactical requirements. In 6/10 positions, there was a forcing capture or pawn advance that was clearly best (bxc6, Nxe5, Nxf4, e3, Rxc1+, etc.). In 4/10, the required move was prophylactic or defensive rather than the centralizing move played. The average cp_loss of 1243 reflects that these 'improving' moves squander decisive advantages or allow devastating refutations. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precision rather than general improvement. 7/10 positions saw the opponent immediately exploit the tempo loss with a concrete tactical blow (Nf3+, g5, exf3, Bxb8, etc.).

830.label: Developing a knight to a natural square while ignoring an immediate tactical emergency requiring urgent action.
830.description: All 8/8 positions feature a knight being developed to a standard 'textbook' square (c3, c6, d2, or d7) while a critical tactical issue goes unaddressed. In 5/8 positions, the ignored crisis was king safety — either the player's own king was vulnerable to a sacrifice (Bxh2+, Bxh7+, Rf7+, Qxh7+) or a mating attack. In 3/8 positions, the ignored crisis was a hanging or undefended piece (bishop on g4, bishop on c4, bishop on g7) that could be captured for free. The average cp_loss of 1506 reflects how catastrophic these moves are — in one case allowing forced mate in 4. Every position had 2-3 good alternatives available that addressed the urgent issue, showing the correct defensive or tactical moves were readily accessible. The knight moves are all non-capturing, non-checking 'quiet' developments that would be perfectly reasonable in positions without immediate tactical demands.

825.label: A material-grabbing capture that leaves the player's own piece of equal or greater value immediately en prise.
825.description: In 9/10 positions, the player made a capture winning significant material (a rook or queen) but left their own piece of comparable or greater value completely undefended and immediately capturable. Specifically: Positions 1, 3, 4, 5 left a rook hanging to the opponent's king (Kxf3, Kxf7, Kxd2, Kxb7). Position 2 left a rook hanging to a pawn (exf4). Position 6 removed a knight that was defending a rook (Nxc7 left Rf8 hanging to Bxf8). Positions 9 and 10 left a queen hanging (bxa4 and Bxe7 respectively). Position 7 left a knight hanging to the queen (Qxh5). Position 8 is the mildest variant, capturing with the wrong piece (rook instead of pawn) which allowed the opponent to safely eliminate a dangerous passed pawn. In all cases, the player had 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.5), and the correct alternative typically involved addressing the vulnerability of their own piece BEFORE capturing, or capturing with a different piece/pawn that didn't create the hanging situation.

812.label: Playing a quiet, generally-principled move that ignores the specific tactical demands of a critical position, surrendering initiative or allowing the opponent to solve their problems.
812.description: All 10/10 positions feature a 'natural-looking' or 'default' move chosen over a concrete, position-specific response: captures that look free (exd5, cxd6), centralizations that seem strong (Nd5, Kd3, Ke7), developments that appear active (Bg4, Bd3, Bd2), retreats that seem safe (Bc2), and space-gaining advances that look logical (c5). In 9/10 positions, a forcing or specifically-targeted alternative was available (checks in 3/10, critical pawn breaks in 4/10, piece-safety moves in 3/10). The tag 'piece_activity' appears in 10/10 analyses, 'tempo_loss' in 8/10, and 'missed_tactic' in 9/10, confirming the pattern of squandering dynamic potential for routine play. The average cp_loss of 1209 is catastrophic, and with only 2.1 good moves available on average, these are critical junctures where autopilot thinking is particularly punishing. In every case, the played move addresses a SECONDARY concern (material gain, general development, space, centralization) while the position demanded addressing the PRIMARY tactical issue (delivering a mating attack, preventing piece entrapment, maintaining forcing initiative, or ensuring king safety).

809.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive role (guarding a piece, blocking a line, or maintaining king safety) for a seemingly active or greedy alternative, immediately exposing a tactical vulnerability.
809.description: In 7/10 positions, the blundering move directly relocates the sole defender of a critical asset—a piece, a square, or a blocking function—leaving that asset immediately exploitable. Positions 1 and 7 are near-identical: the queen leaves e3/e2 where it was the sole protector of a knight (c3/f3), which is instantly captured. Position 2 moves a rook off a critical blocking square (f3), unblocking a diagonal that allows back-rank checkmate. Position 6 moves the queen to a square where it APPEARS to defend h2 but physically cannot due to an obstructing pawn, enabling Qxh2#. Position 9 relocates the queen to g4 for an illusory kingside attack, leaving a pawn hanging after forced exchanges. Position 10 moves the king into an open file for a greedy capture, enabling a devastating discovered check. Positions 3-5 and 8 are variants where the move prioritizes a slow/greedy plan (pawn push, wrong capture, premature development, failure to eliminate a threat) over the critical tactical need. The average cp_loss of 3233 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights—4/10 result in immediate checkmate or mate-in-4. In 8/10 cases, the opponent's refutation is a simple one-move tactical shot (capturing a hanging piece or delivering checkmate).

828.label: A knight delivers check while simultaneously forking a major piece (queen or rook), either as the optimal tactic or as a seductive but suboptimal alternative to a faster checkmate.
828.description: 10/10 positions center on the motif of a knight delivering check while forking another valuable piece. 9/10 moves played are literal knight checks (Ne2+, Ne5+, Nd3+, Nc3+, Ne3+, Nd7+, Nf6+, Nb3+, Nd3+), and the 10th (Qd4) is a position where the player accidentally blocked their own knight from executing exactly this pattern (Nd4+ was the winning move). In 6/10 positions the knight fork check IS the best move (0 cp loss), confirming the feature activates on this geometric motif itself. In the 4 error positions (avg cp_loss ~6948), the knight fork wins material (typically the opponent's queen) but misses a faster forced checkmate: Position 1 missed Qg3# for Ne2+ (fork K+Q), Position 3 missed Nb3+ mate-in-3 for Nd3+ (fork K+Q), Position 4 missed Qb1+/Bc3# for Nc3+ (fork K+Q), and Position 9 blocked Nd4+ by placing the queen on d4. The forked target is a queen in 7/10 cases and a rook in 3/10 cases.

831.label: Moving the queen to a seemingly active central square instead of executing a concrete tactical or defensive necessity, wasting a critical tempo.
831.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen repositioned to a central or semi-central square (ranks 3-6, files d-g) that appears active but accomplishes nothing concrete. In 10/10 cases the move is a non-forcing, non-capturing queen relocation (no checks, no captures). In 6/10 positions, a concrete non-queen move was the best play (Rc7 twice, g4, Nxe4, Qa7, c4/Rfe8), meaning the queen should not have moved at all. In 4/10 positions, a defensive or prophylactic move was needed instead (g6, b6/Kb8, Ng5/Nxd2, Nxe4). The common punishment pattern: 7/10 positions allowed the opponent to exploit the tempo loss with an immediate tactical blow (Rxb3+, Nf7+, Qg4+, Ng3+, Qxe6, ...f5 preventing g4, ...Ba6 hitting undefended rook). In 5/10 cases, the queen's departure from its previous square specifically abandoned control of a critical square or line that the opponent immediately exploited. Average cp_loss is 280, confirming these are serious errors, not minor inaccuracies.

829.label: Pawn captures that fatally open files or diagonals directly toward the player's own vulnerable king.
829.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture (lowercase notation: exf4, dxe4, cxd4, etc.) that opens a critical line exploited by the opponent's already-positioned heavy pieces. In 9/10 positions, the opened file or diagonal leads directly to the capturing player's own king, which is already exposed or weakly shielded (king on f8, e1, d2, g8, h8, f6). In 8/10 cases, the opponent has rooks or queens pre-positioned on the newly opened file (e-file, d-file, f-file, h-file, or g-file). The capturing pawn was either part of the king's pawn shield itself (positions 4, 8, 10 where f7, g6, g7 pawns were captured away) or was blocking a critical file that exposed the king upon removal (positions 2, 3, 5, 9 where d-pawn or e-pawn was exchanged, opening the file to an uncastled king). Average cp_loss of 3114 reflects that many of these lead to forced mate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these arise in razor-sharp positions where the greedy/natural capture is the precise losing move.

837.label: A bishop retreats exactly one square along its current diagonal toward the board edge, wasting tempo while missing critical tactical opportunities.
837.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop retreating exactly one square along its current diagonal toward the edge/corner of the board: c4→b3 (4 positions), c5→b6 (2 positions), f4→g3, b4→a3, g4→h3, and f5→g6. In every case, the bishop moves from a more active central/semi-central square to a more passive rim square. The key error is prioritizing 'keeping the bishop on its diagonal' over concrete action. In 7/10 positions, the correct move was a forcing tactical blow (Bxf7+, Bxd6, f5, Bb5, d4, Nxd4) rather than a quiet bishop shuffle. In 3/10 positions (5, 8, 9), the bishop retreated to a square still attacked by an enemy knight, making the retreat doubly pointless. The average cp_loss of 314 reflects that these positions universally demanded urgent action — either exploiting a hanging piece, launching a pawn break, or delivering a forcing sacrifice — and the passive one-square diagonal retreat squandered the moment entirely.
837.old_chip: Bishop retreats one square to rim

836.label: A bishop is repositioned along a diagonal to a square where it is undefended and immediately capturable by an opponent's piece.
836.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a square where it hangs to an enemy piece with no defender. The tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' in all 10 cases. In 4/10 positions the bishop hangs to a knight (positions 3, 4, 7, 8 — knights on f2, d2, e3, d5 respectively capture the relocated bishop), and in 5/10 positions it hangs to a rook along a rank or file (positions 5, 6, 9, 10 — rooks on e3, c7, h8, h2 capture). In 8/10 cases the bishop was previously on an active, centralized square (d5, c7, f5, e4, g2, d5, f3, d6) and was voluntarily moved to a peripheral or less active square where it becomes undefended. The average cp_loss of 1207 reflects that these are catastrophic material losses. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions often demanded precision that the players failed to deliver.

820.label: A rook or queen moves to a natural-looking but non-forcing square, abandoning a critical defensive duty (usually back-rank or king-cover protection) and allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated coverage with forcing moves.
820.description: 10/10 positions involve a major piece (rook or queen) making a quiet, non-forcing move — no check, no capture, no immediate must-answer threat. In 9/10 cases (excluding Position 3, which is not actually a blunder), the moved piece was performing an essential defensive function that became fatally compromised. Specifically, 5/10 positions feature the piece abandoning first-rank or back-rank coverage, directly enabling back-rank mates or check sequences (Positions 5, 6, 9, 10, and partially 1 with perpetual via back-rank access). In 3/10 positions, the piece left a king-shielding role (Position 1: rook left g7 allowing perpetual; Position 4: queen left f5 losing Qxg7+ counterplay; Position 7: queen went far from own king). The punishment in 8/10 cases involves immediate forcing moves (checks) exploiting the abandoned coverage. All moves appear superficially reasonable — centralizing rooks, placing queens on open files, supporting passed pawns — but each ignores that the position demanded either maintaining the defensive post or executing an immediate forcing sequence instead.

832.label: A rook delivers check when two rooks could reach the same square, requiring the player to choose which rook moves.
832.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check with notation disambiguation (Rh, Rb, R7, R2, R6, Re, Ra), meaning the player had two rooks that could potentially reach the check square and had to choose which one to move. In 5/10 positions (4, 5, 8, 3, 10), this choice was a significant mistake — the wrong rook moved, abandoning control of a critical file or rank that was essential for the tactical idea (costing up to forced mate). In the remaining 5/10 positions (1, 2, 6, 7, 9), the choice was correct or both options were equivalent (0 cp loss). The positions consistently feature doubled rooks or rook pairs on adjacent files/ranks (7/10 rook endgames or rook-dominated middlegames), exposed enemy kings, and open files. The critical tactical thread is that when two rooks can deliver the same check, one rook's REMAINING position on its current file/rank is often far more important than the other's.

827.label: A rook moves to directly attack or challenge an enemy minor piece, but the move is counterproductive—creating new vulnerabilities or allowing the target to improve.
827.description: In 8/10 positions, the rook move directly targets an enemy minor piece (usually a knight on c7, g7, b2, f2, or e2), attempting to chase, pin, or capture it. In all 10/10 positions, the rook move is a 'natural-looking' but ultimately passive or misdirected response that neglects the position's true priority. The correct moves were diverse—king relocations (3/10: Kg3, Kg7, Kh7), piece invasions (2/10: Rd2, Be5), pawn moves (2/10: b4, f6, g5), and bishop developments (2/10: Be3, Be6)—showing that the real need was never simply 'deal with that piece using the rook.' In 5/10 cases, the enemy minor piece actually improves after the rook move (escaping to a better square like Nd5, Nf5, or capturing something). In 4/10 cases, the rook move leaves a piece or pawn undefended (a6, c4, bishop on c8, bishop on c1). In 2/10 cases, the rook physically blocks its own bishop's diagonal, destroying coordination. The average cp_loss of 1194 reflects that these apparently logical moves often transform winning/equal positions into lost ones.

823.label: Active-looking piece moves to seemingly useful squares that ignore immediate tactical vulnerabilities, leaving pieces or critical squares undefended.
823.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing repositioning move that appears constructive but ignores the position's immediate tactical demand. In 8/10 cases, the move directly leaves a piece or critical square undefended (Positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10 leave something hanging; Position 9 puts the wrong piece on a square). In 9/10 cases, the opponent's refutation is a forcing blow—capture with check (Positions 1, 2, 5, 10), winning capture of a hanging piece (3, 4), or a fork/domination (6, 7, 8). The blundered moves are overwhelmingly rooks (6/10: Rf3, Rd3, Rc7, Rb3, Re6, Rc6) or knights (3/10: Nf5, Nd7, Nb3) being moved to squares that look active but abandon their current defensive role. In every case, the best alternative addresses the concrete tactical issue first—either defending the vulnerable piece (Positions 2, 4, 10), stepping the king to safety (5, 7), challenging the opponent's active piece (3), or executing an available tactic (8). The average cp_loss of 262 reflects that these moves consistently create or allow material-winning tactics.

833.label: Playing a non-forcing bishop repositioning move to a seemingly active square when the position demands an immediate tactical response (capture, check, or critical defense).
833.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves to 'active-looking' squares (Bf6 x3, Be6, Bc6, Bb6, Be4, Bf3), with the remaining 2 being other quiet 'improvement' moves (Na3, d3). In ALL 10 positions, the player chose a non-forcing piece repositioning move when the position demanded urgent tactical action. The average number of good moves available was only 1.3, indicating these are critical decision points with essentially one correct response. In 5/10 cases, the best move was a capture or check that wins material (positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 10). In 4/10 cases, the moved piece was abandoning a critical defensive duty—guarding a pawn, blocking a file, or shielding the king (positions 1, 3, 8, 9). In 1/10 cases, a piece was placed on a square where it becomes a tactical target (position 6). The average cp_loss of 2227 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' moves are at precisely the wrong moment.

834.label: Non-forcing queen repositioning moves that abandon the queen's essential defensive, coordinating, or attacking function on its current square.
834.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet queen repositioning moves — short, non-forcing relocations to a nearby square that appears reasonable but fatally disrupts the queen's essential role. In 7/10 positions, the queen starts on or near the open d-file and slides one file sideways (Qc2 x2, Qc7 x2, Qe2 x2, Qd2). The remaining moves (Qa5+, Qf3, Qd6) are similarly non-forcing lateral shifts. In every case, the queen was performing a critical invisible function — defending a piece (positions 1, 9), maintaining kingside coordination (positions 4, 5, 10), preserving counterplay threats (positions 2, 3, 6), or needing to be used for concrete tactical action instead (positions 7, 8). The average cp_loss of 1238 reflects how catastrophic these seemingly quiet moves are. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, indicating these were critical decision points demanding precision rather than generic development.

838.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing 'improving' move when the position demands immediate concrete action to address an urgent tactical priority.
838.description: All 10/10 positions feature a player making a non-forcing move that looks reasonable on general principles (centralization, activation, or development) while completely ignoring a single concrete, urgent demand. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 positions, confirming this as the unifying thread. In 5/10 cases, a forcing tactical sequence (checks, captures, or threats) was available that would have been decisive (Ra1+, Rxc3+, Rxg2+, Bd3, Ra2). In 3/10 cases, an existential defensive need (escaping back-rank mate with Ke7, vacating the c-file with Kb4, blocking promotion with Ra2/Rf8) was ignored. In 2/10 cases, the king moved to the wrong adjacent square, prioritizing activity over a specific defensive function (Ke5 instead of Ke4, Kf7 instead of Rg8). The average centipawn loss of 4813 reflects how catastrophic these tempo wastes are—6/10 resulted in losses exceeding 1000cp or allowing forced mate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, confirming these were narrow positions where only concrete, precise action was acceptable.

843.label: Playing a passive consolidation or king-safety move when the position demands immediate tactical exploitation.
843.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing, quiet move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played instead of a concrete tactical opportunity. 7/10 moves are specifically king moves to perceived safety squares (Kb8, Kb2, Kh1, O-O, Kc2, O-O, Kb1), while the remaining 3/10 are passive queen repositioning moves (Qd6, Qf5, Qd2). In every case, a clearly superior forcing alternative existed: material gains (Qxa4 in positions 2&3, Qxa7 in position 4, dxe5 in position 1, Nxd5 in position 10), central breakthroughs (e5 in position 5, c4 in position 7), piece captures (dxe5/Nxe5/Bxe5 in position 6), or forced mates (Qf6+ in position 9). The tempo loss tag appears in 8/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' appears in all 10. The average cp_loss of 2079 reflects that these consolidation moves are catastrophically costly because they surrender the initiative at precisely the moment action is required.

847.label: An unsound bishop sacrifice capturing the f-pawn with check in the opening, lacking sufficient piece coordination for follow-up attack.
847.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing the opponent's f-pawn with check (9/10 Bxf7+ by White, 1/10 Bxf2+ by Black) during the opening phase with a closed center. In every case, the sacrifice is completely unsound: the attacker gives up a full bishop (≈3 pawns) for only one pawn and a check that displaces the enemy king, but has no developed supporting pieces to continue the attack. 10/10 positions are refuted by simple acceptance of the sacrifice (Kxf7 or Kxf2), after which the king safely retreats within 1-2 moves while the attacker has no follow-up threats. 10/10 positions had at least 2-3 strong developing alternatives (castling, d3, Nf3, etc.) maintaining equality or slight advantage. The average centipawn loss was 316, representing approximately a full piece deficit. The pattern appears inspired by legitimate tactical motifs (Fried Liver Attack, Jerome Gambit) but executed prematurely without the necessary preconditions — particularly a knight on g5/g4 or queen aligned on the f-file.

824.label: Capturing tempting pawns or making materialistic moves that place pieces on tactically vulnerable squares, while ignoring superior dynamic alternatives involving initiative, king safety, or piece activity.
824.description: 7/10 positions involve captures (6 are rook captures of pawns/pieces: Rxc6, Rxc3, Rxe4, Rxf2, Rxg3+, Rxe5, plus Kxh6). The remaining 3 non-captures (Nd7, Be3, Nc3) similarly prioritize a 'natural-looking' static improvement over the position's urgent dynamic demands. In 9/10 cases (excluding the 0cp-loss Rxe4), the move prioritizes material gain or positional repositioning while ignoring that the piece lands on a tactically exploitable square or abandons a critical function. The punishments consistently exploit the newly-placed piece's vulnerability: fork (Rxc3→Qd4+), diagonal check winning the piece (Rxe5→Qa1+/Qxe5+), exchange opening critical lines (Be3→Bxe3), king exposure (Kxh6→Qf4+/Qh2+/Qh7#), or disconnection from defensive duties (Rxf2 leaving king exposed). In 8/10 positions, the better alternative involved maintaining dynamic piece activity (Rc1+, a7, Rd1, Rd7) or prophylactic safety (f5, Kh8, Bc5) rather than grabbing material.

839.label: King moves in decisively won pawn endgames where tempo precision in passed pawn races is critical.
839.description: 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with decisive evaluations (~600-750cp). 10/10 moves played are king moves. 10/10 positions feature passed pawn dynamics where the strategic tension is between king centralization and immediate pawn advancement. The evaluations cluster tightly around ±600-750cp, indicating positions that are theoretically won but require precise tempo management. When significant errors occur (positions 9 and 10, losing 638 and 549cp respectively), the pattern is choosing a king move over an immediately decisive pawn push (Ke2 instead of b6; Kc6 instead of Kc4). In the lower-loss cases (positions 2, 5, 7), the king moves to an adjacent but slightly suboptimal square, choosing a route that is one tempo slower in the pawn race. 8/10 positions had 3 good moves available, indicating forgiving positions where multiple king routes win but subtle tempo differences matter at the margins.
839.old_chip: King Moves In Won Pawn Races

841.label: A passive rook (or major piece) repositioning move that ignores an immediate tactical emergency requiring concrete action.
841.description: 9/10 positions feature rook moves (plus one queen move in Position 1) that reposition a major piece to a 'generally useful' square—typically a new file or rank—while completely ignoring an urgent tactical demand. In 4/10 cases (Positions 1, 9, 10, and 2), the moved piece was actually performing a critical defensive function or the move created a new vulnerability (removing a defender from g8, f8, or abandoning control of a mating square). In 3/10 cases (Positions 5, 6, 7), a concrete tactical opportunity existed (winning the exchange, or an enemy piece was hanging) that was missed in favor of slow rook development. In 3/10 cases (Positions 3, 4, 8), a specific positional/tactical threat needed immediate addressing (defending a weak pawn, the king's exposure) that the rook move completely ignored. All 10 moves are quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played in positions demanding immediate concrete action. The average cp_loss of 2180 reflects the catastrophic consequences of wasting a tempo in a crisis.

846.label: A non-forcing wing pawn advance played in a position that demands immediate tactical action, losing critical tempo.
846.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet pawn advance on the a, b, c, g, or h file — never a central pawn — that ignores an immediate tactical emergency. In 4/10 cases, the player overlooked a hanging piece that could be captured or needed protection (positions 2, 4, 5, 9). In 5/10 cases, the player ignored a critical king safety issue — either their own king was under immediate threat or they missed an opportunity to exploit an exposed opponent king (positions 1, 6, 7, 8, 10). In 1/10 cases, the pawn advance directly weakened defensive structure enabling a tactical combination (position 3). The average cp_loss of 1374 reflects the catastrophic nature of these tempo losses, and the average of only 1.5 good moves confirms these were razor-sharp positions with narrow margins. 9/10 positions were in the middlegame where tactical urgency is highest. In every case, the best moves involved either capturing material (Qxe4, Bxb4, Bxc3), giving check (Rg3+), or addressing a concrete defensive need (c3, Kb1, Rf3) — forceful, targeted moves rather than strategic pawn nudges.

849.label: A bishop is repositioned to an apparently active square, but in doing so abandons a critical defensive duty—leaving a piece, pawn, or king unguarded.
849.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop being moved to what appears to be a more 'active' or 'natural' square, but each move critically abandons a defensive responsibility. In 6/9 positions (Positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 9, and 2), the bishop was the sole defender of a specific piece or pawn, and moving it left that target immediately capturable—Rook on a8 (Pos 3), Rook on f2 (Pos 1), b7 pawn (Pos 8), c8 bishop (Pos 2), c2 pawn (Pos 9), or king shelter (Pos 6). In 2/9 positions (4 and 7), the bishop move was a slow 'improvement' that squandered a concrete winning tactic the player should have executed instead. In 1/9 (Position 5), the bishop move fatally opened geometric lines to the king. The average cp_loss of 1291 reflects how devastating these errors are—the 'activated' bishop provides far less value than what was lost by abandoning the defensive post. Notably, the good alternatives (avg 1.7 available) typically involved keeping the bishop where it was or addressing the position's real demands with non-bishop moves.

848.label: Aggressive pawn advance that releases tension or wastes tempo when immediate piece action (attacks, development, or defense) was required.
848.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance attempting to 'break through' the position — attacking an opponent's pawn chain, opening files, or storming the kingside. In 9/10 cases the side playing was White. In every case, the correct move was a piece move: tactical finishing blows (Nc7, Ng5, e5-with-Qd6+ combination) in 4/10 positions, quiet development/consolidation (Nc3, O-O, h4, c3) in 5/10, and precise pawn timing (h6 instead of g6) in 1/10. The pawn advances uniformly squandered advantages by releasing central tension (positions 3, 4, 6, 7, 8), allowing the opponent to seal the position (position 5), creating targets for tempo-gaining counter-attacks like b5-b4 or c3+ (positions 6, 8, 10), or simply missing forced checkmates (position 1). The average cp_loss of 1170 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' pawn pushes are in positions that demanded calculation.

840.label: A piece abandons a critical defensive, blocking, or coordinating duty to make a tempting capture or seek activity, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated function.
840.description: In 8/10 positions, the moved piece was performing a vital function on its original square — blocking a diagonal (Position 1: Qe7 blocked Bd6-f8), maintaining a blockade (Position 7: Kg6 stopped the h-pawn), preserving a recapture option (Positions 5, 8: Queen on d8/d7 enabled Qxf6), sustaining an attacking formation (Position 4: Qg6 was the linchpin of a mating attack), or keeping a rook actively blockading (Position 9: Rook on c8 blockading c7). In 6/10 cases the blunder was a capture (Qxg3, Qxg3, Qxe7, Qxg6, Kxg5, Rxc7) that seemed to win material or simplify, but the captured material was less valuable than the positional function being abandoned. The average cp_loss of 1391 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirm these are positions with one narrow correct path that requires recognizing the piece's current duty over the temptation of the alternative. 7/10 involve a queen being the piece that erroneously moves, reflecting how queens are often simultaneously performing critical positional duties while appearing to have attractive tactical options elsewhere.

852.label: Pushing a central pawn (e5 or d5) as a liberating break when the position demands quiet development or consolidation, allowing the opponent to exploit opened lines tactically.
852.description: 9/10 positions feature a central pawn advance to the 5th rank (8 times ...e5, 2 times ...d5), with the remaining position being a slow flank push (h5) instead of a concrete capture. In all 10 cases, the top recommended moves were quiet developing, consolidating, or prophylactic moves — castling, piece repositioning, or addressing specific threats — rather than aggressive pawn breaks. 7/10 positions had a king safety vulnerability (king still on e8 in 4 cases, exposed king shelter in others) that made opening the center catastrophic. 8/10 positions featured insufficient piece coordination to support the break, where the opponent had more attackers on the break square or could exploit newly opened lines. The average cp_loss of 278 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors but concrete blunders where the break creates immediate tactical refutations — hanging pieces (positions 1, 4, 5, 7, 8), exploitable diagonals/files (positions 2, 3, 6), or missed move-order finesse (position 10).

844.label: King moves to corner or back-rank squares where it becomes confined, trapped, or mated due to lack of escape squares.
844.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves, and 9/10 land on edge or corner squares (a1, a8, h8, g8, f8, b1, a2, f2, kg5 being the exception). The catastrophic cases (4/10 with cp_loss >9000) all involve the king moving to a corner square (a1, a1, a8, f8) where it is immediately checkmated or trapped in a mating net. The moderate blunders (3/10 with cp_loss 230-250) involve the king retreating toward the edge when it should advance or play actively. 8/10 positions feature advanced passed pawns, and the king move is often motivated by trying to blockade a promotion square or flee from tactical pressure. The near-zero-loss positions (3/10) represent cases where retreating to the corner is actually correct (Position 1, blockading h8) or nearly equivalent to alternatives. The feature consistently activates on king moves directed toward board edges in positions with passed pawn tension.

850.label: Captures or pawn thrusts on the f/g files near the enemy king that are unsound due to insufficient attacking support or that release critical tension.
850.description: 7/10 positions feature a capture or pawn advance targeting squares on the f-file or g-file directly adjacent to the enemy king (g2 in positions 1 and 8, f6 in positions 3 and 4, f7 in position 6, g6 in position 7, g7 in position 10). In each case, the move attempts to breach the king's pawn shelter or eliminate defenders near the king, but fails because: the attacker lacks sufficient supporting pieces to follow through (positions 1, 6, 8, 10 — unsound sacrifices), or the capture actually opens escape routes for the enemy king by removing restricting pawns (positions 3, 4 — where the e5 pawn was trapping the king). The remaining 3/10 positions are outliers: position 2 is essentially the best move (3cp loss), position 5 is a defensive blunder in a collapsing position, and position 9 is a premature queenside pawn advance. The dominant pattern (7/10) involves impulsive aggression toward the king that backfires either by sacrificing material without compensation or by dissolving the attacker's own positional advantages.

845.label: Quiet flank pawn moves (b3/b6/g3) that obstruct the player's own bishop's retreat diagonal, creating trapped piece vulnerabilities.
845.description: 6/10 positions show the exact same geometric pattern: a pawn advance to b3, b6, or g3 that physically occupies a square the player's bishop needs for retreat, enabling the opponent to trap or severely restrict that bishop. In positions 2, 3, and 6, ...b6 blocks the c5-bishop's retreat along the a7-g1 diagonal, allowing the opponent's b4 or d4 to exploit it. In positions 5 and 10, g3 blocks the f4-bishop's retreat to g3, allowing piece attacks (Ne4 or f6/g5) to chase and trap it. In position 8, b3 blocks the c4-bishop's retreat to b3, so after ...Bg4xf3 and ...e6, the bishop has nowhere to go. The remaining 4/10 positions share the broader pattern of quiet, non-urgent flank moves (Qb6, Bh7) that waste critical tempo when the position demands action—positions 7 and 9 move the queen to b6 where it becomes a target or abandons active play, position 4 retreats a bishop passively, and position 1 plays b3 ignoring a kingside emergency. All 10 moves share the characteristic of being slow, non-confrontational moves on the wings that create self-inflicted coordination problems.

842.label: Forward-looking pawn advances or piece moves that create apparent threats against the opponent while leaving a critical piece, pawn, or square in one's own position tactically undefended.
842.description: 9/10 positions feature an aggressive, forward-looking move (7/10 are pawn advances: f5, d5, d5, c3, d3, g4, b4; 3/10 are piece moves: Ne4, Qf4, Qg4) that appears to attack the opponent's pieces or gain space but overlooks a critical tactical vulnerability in the player's own camp. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 8, 10), the move directly leaves a piece hanging for simple capture (Bxa8, Qxe4, Qxa4, Bxf2). In 3/10 positions (2, 4, 7), the move opens lines against the player's own king enabling forcing checks or discovered attacks (Qh5+, Nxf2/discovered check, e4-e3+). In 2/10 positions (6, 9), the move breaks coordination or blocks one's own winning tactic. The average cp_loss of 392 and average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical-moment decisions where the player chose an aggressive-looking alternative over the one required defensive or forcing move. All 10 positions share the pattern of one-dimensional thinking: the player focuses exclusively on what their move threatens without verifying what it leaves undefended.

835.label: Playing aggressive checks, captures, or sacrifices against the opponent's king (or ignoring threats to one's own king) without sufficient tactical justification.
835.description: 9/10 positions directly involve king safety as the critical factor. 6/10 moves are checks or captures aimed at the opponent's king that fail (Qxh2+, Qxf7+, Bxf7+, Qh3+, Bxh7+, Bxg8) — these are speculative attacks or sacrifices lacking the necessary follow-through or positional prerequisites. 3/10 moves (Kg8, Rfd1, Ra4) represent the inverse error: failing to address critical threats to one's own king (walking into mate, ignoring infiltrating pieces, abandoning back-rank defense). The 'king_safety' tag appears in all 10 analyses. The average cp_loss of 3224 is catastrophic, and positions averaged only 1.7 good moves, indicating these are critical moments demanding precise attention to king safety that the players misjudged by choosing superficially attractive alternatives.

857.label: A knight captures a tempting central pawn, but the capture creates tactical vulnerabilities that far outweigh the material gained.
857.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight capturing a pawn on a central or near-central square (e4, d4, d5, e5, c4, or f5), motivated by winning seemingly free or advantageous central material. The captures appear natural—targeting undefended or poorly defended pawns—but consistently backfire. In 3/9 positions (3, 8, 5), the wrong knight captures, leaving a sibling piece hanging or removing a critical defensive guardian. In 2/9 positions (7, 5), the knight abandons a vital defensive post (d2 shielding the back rank, f6 guarding g4/kingside). In 2/9 positions (9, 1), the knight leaves a powerful outpost for a mundane pawn grab, missing devastating alternatives like queen invasions. In 2/9 positions (4, 6), the capture deflects or exposes pieces to winning tactical sequences. The average cp_loss of 1417 reflects that these greedy captures typically lose a full piece or more. All occur in the middlegame where tactical complexity is highest and central pawn captures feel most natural.

863.label: Playing a quiet bishop repositioning move while an undefended piece elsewhere on the board is immediately capturable by the opponent.
863.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical pattern: the player makes a non-forcing, positional move (8/10 are bishop moves, 2/10 are pawn moves) while completely ignoring a piece that is hanging or undefended. In every case, the opponent has a simple one-move capture available that wins material for free. The hanging pieces varied — rooks (positions 1, 3, 4, 8), knights (positions 2, 5, 6, 9, 10), and a bishop (position 7) — but the mistake mechanism was identical: a quiet developing/repositioning move played as if no tactical urgency existed. 10/10 positions were tagged 'hanging_piece' as the tactical motif. The average cp_loss was 396, reflecting that these moves typically cost a full piece or exchange. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical-precision moments demanding immediate attention to the tactical threat rather than positional improvements.

859.label: King retreats to a seemingly safe or natural square instead of making a concrete tactical response, but the destination square creates new geometric vulnerabilities.
859.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing king move retreating toward the back rank, starting square, or corner. In 5/10 cases the move is specifically Ke8 (king returning to its starting square from f7). In 7/10 positions (Black's moves), the king retreats from an exposed square (usually f7 or d7/e7) to what appears safer but is geometrically worse. In 6/10 positions, the best move was capturing a hanging or attacking piece (Qxg5, Bxc5, Nxd5, Qxf4, Qxg4×2) rather than moving the king at all. The destination squares consistently create specific new vulnerabilities: 6/10 place the king on the h5-e8 diagonal enabling Qh5+ sequences, 2/10 create back-rank/file alignment issues, 1/10 walks into immediate checkmate, and 1/10 enables a consecutive-check fork sequence. The average cp_loss of 2388 reflects that these retreats are catastrophic—prioritizing abstract safety over concrete threats.

854.label: The player moves or trades away the exact piece (or pawn) that enables their strongest tactical continuation, destroying their own attacking/defensive infrastructure.
854.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder involves moving or exchanging the specific piece that serves as the linchpin of the player's strongest available tactic. In Position 1, the Bh6 enables Rxf6 but is traded away; in Position 2, the Ng3 enables Nf3# but is captured on f1; in Position 3, the Ne4 enables Nc3-fork but is exchanged on d2; in Position 4, the Nd4 blocks a deadly diagonal but is moved to c6; in Position 5, the Nd7 blocks the open d-file but is moved to b6; in Position 6, the Rf5 can capture the queen but the wrong rook captures on c3; in Position 7, the e-pawn enables e5+ winning a rook but is captured away on f5; in Position 8, the Nd5 enables Nxc7 winning material but is traded on f6; in Position 9, the Ng4 enables Nxf2+ mating but retreats to e5; in Position 10, the h-pawn provides critical counterplay but the b-pawn is pushed instead. The moves are overwhelmingly captures (8/10), giving the illusion of material gain or useful simplification, while actually self-destructing the player's tactical infrastructure.

853.label: Moving a piece (usually a knight) to an attractive-looking active square while missing that the position demands either keeping that piece for defense or sending a different piece to that square.
853.description: 8/10 positions feature knight moves, and the remaining 2 (Bb4, Bc4) are cases where a knight should have gone to that exact square instead. In 3/10 positions (4, 7, 8), the player moved the WRONG PIECE to the correct square—Bb4 instead of Nb4, Qf3 instead of Nf3, Bc4 instead of Nc4—missing devastating knight tactics (forks, queen traps). In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 6, 9), the knight abandoned a critical defensive post (guarding d5, covering the back rank, blocking the queen's path) to reach a seemingly aggressive square, immediately allowing tactical punishment. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 10), a non-forcing centralization was chosen over a more forcing alternative that gained concrete material advantage. All 10 moves share the quality of looking 'natural' or 'active'—attacking the opponent's queen (7/10 target or relate to queen pressure), occupying an outpost, or developing—while catastrophically ignoring either a defensive necessity or a more potent forcing move. The average cp_loss of 2148 and average of only 1.4 good moves confirms these are critical positions requiring precision where the 'attractive' move was a trap.

860.label: Developing the c-file bishop (or knight) to a passive d2/d7 square when the position demands urgent or active piece placement.
860.description: 10/10 positions feature a piece being developed to the second rank (d7 for Black in 6 cases, d2 for White in 3 cases, e7 in 1 case, Nd2 in 1 case) as a seemingly routine developing move. In every case, the position contained urgent tactical requirements that demanded either a more active square for the same piece (e.g., Bf5/Be6/Bg4 instead of Bd7 in 4/10 positions; Bb2/Bf4 instead of Bd2 in 3/10 positions) or an entirely different move addressing an immediate threat. The d7/d2 square consistently proved too passive: in 2/10 cases the piece was immediately capturable on the open file, in 3/10 cases it failed to block a critical file or diagonal that the opponent exploited, in 3/10 it missed a concrete tactical resource (perpetual check, queen trap, active counterplay), and in 2/10 it was simply the wrong diagonal leaving a key pawn undefended. The average cp_loss of 1274 reflects the severity of choosing 'autopilot development' in positions requiring calculation.

861.label: Aggressive queen sorties to h4 or h5 creating shallow kingside threats while abandoning critical defensive duties in the opening.
861.description: 8/10 positions feature queen moves specifically to h4 or h5, with the remaining 2 being conceptually identical wing-piece sorties (Qb4 and Ra5). All 10 moves target superficial tactical threats — f2/f7 attacks, g2 grabs, or kingside pressure — that are neutralized in one move by the opponent. In 7/10 cases, the move leaves a piece hanging (usually a knight on e4 in positions 1-3, or exposes g2/h1 in positions 5-6). 8/10 occur in the opening phase with at least one king still in the center. The average centipawn loss is 1291, indicating catastrophic consequences. In 6/10 positions, the queen can be attacked with tempo by a simple pawn push (g3 or g6), and in 5/10 the move directly abandons the defense of a specific piece or square that is immediately exploited. Only 1-3 good moves existed in each position, meaning these are moments demanding precision where players instead chose the most obviously aggressive (but hollow) option.

858.label: Pawn captures that remove a structural shield pawn, opening a file or line directly toward the player's own king.
858.description: 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (hxg, cxb, bxc, exf, dxe). In 8/10 cases, the capturing pawn was serving as a critical structural barrier — either shielding the king on its file (positions 1, 3, 6: h-pawn guarding the h-file), blocking an open file toward the king (position 4: c-pawn sealing the c-file from White's queen), or maintaining central tension that kept the position closed around an uncastled king (positions 7, 8: e-pawn on e5 shielding king on e8). In 5/10 positions, the specific pattern is hxg (h-pawn captures toward g-file), opening the h-file for devastating rook/queen infiltration. The remaining positions show the same principle on other files: cxb5 opens the c-file (pos 4), exf4 opens lines and vacates key squares (pos 7, 8), dxe6 removes restraint (pos 10). Even the 3 positions where the move is best/near-best (positions 2, 5, 9) involve the same geometric pattern — the feature recognizes the structural signature regardless of whether it's forced. The avg cp_loss of 5478 reflects that in most cases, these captures are catastrophic.

866.label: A slow one-square advance of the a-pawn or h-pawn on the wrong flank while the position demands immediate tactical action elsewhere.
866.description: All 10/10 positions feature a one-square advance of a rook pawn (a-pawn in 7/10, h-pawn in 3/10) during the middlegame when urgent tactical or strategic demands exist elsewhere on the board. In 10/10 cases, the correct move was a concrete piece action — a capture (positions 1, 6, 8, 9), a central pawn break (positions 4, 10), a forcing check/fork (position 2), or castling/development (positions 7, 3, 5). The positions overwhelmingly feature opposite-side castling or king safety crises (8/10), where the pawn push occurs on the 'attacking' flank while the player's own position is collapsing on the other side or in the center. The average cp_loss is 326, indicating these are severe blunders. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments demanding precise play. The pattern reflects a systematic failure to assess urgency — choosing a slow, speculative flank advance over addressing immediate tactical threats like hanging pieces (positions 1, 6, 9), forced tactical sequences (positions 2, 3), or critical defensive needs (positions 5, 7, 8).

862.label: A pawn advances to attack or displace a well-placed enemy piece (usually a knight), but the pawn was performing a critical defensive function on its original square, creating an immediate tactical refutation.
862.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance motivated by attacking or displacing a strong enemy piece. In at least 8/10 cases, the target is specifically a well-placed knight (f5, c5, c4, d5, f4, c3). In 9/10 cases, the advancing pawn was performing a critical defensive duty on its original square: guarding an adjacent pawn (g7 guarding h6 in positions 7 and 5's e7 rook geometry), protecting a friendly piece (b5 defending Nc4 in position 8), controlling a key square (c3 controlling b4 in position 2), or blocking a dangerous diagonal (d6 blocking f2-c5 in position 10). The refutations consistently exploit the abandoned defensive function — knight forks exploiting unguarded pawns (positions 4, 7, 9, 10), captures of newly hanging pieces (positions 3, 5, 6, 8), or infiltration on weakened squares (position 2). Position 1 is slightly variant — b3 drives the knight to a superior square rather than strictly removing pawn defense — but shares the core theme of a piece-chasing pawn move that backfires tactically.

868.label: A bishop passively retreats to the player's own back rank (1st or 8th rank), typically losing tempo, blocking friendly pieces, or abandoning a critical defensive role.
868.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to the player's own back rank — Be1/Bf1/Bd1 for White (rank 1) or Bd8/Bf8 for Black (rank 8). In 7/10 cases this was a genuine mistake (avg cp_loss of 2830 among the errors), while 3/10 were actually the best move (0cp loss), indicating the feature detects the geometric pattern regardless of correctness. Among the 7 errors, the common thread is passivity: 2/10 self-blocked the king's escape route (positions 2 and 6, both catastrophic — one allowing immediate checkmate), 2/10 blocked the player's own rook on the d-file (positions 4 and 9), 2/10 created a static tactical target for the opponent's heavy pieces (positions 5 and 8), and 1/10 abandoned a critical defensive square (position 1, losing control of c3). The 3 correct instances (positions 3, 7, 10) involved either a winning position where precision mattered less, a deflection sacrifice forcing a favorable queen trade, or prophylactic blockade of a passed pawn — situations where back-rank placement served a concrete tactical purpose rather than being merely passive.

865.label: A knight moves away from an active or defensively critical square to a passive or peripheral square, losing a crucial tempo and abandoning a key function.
865.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a knight away from a square where it was performing a vital role (defending a pawn, controlling a key square, or poised for an immediate tactic) to a less effective square as part of a slow repositioning plan. In 6/10 cases the knight moved to a rim or back-rank square (h2, a4, d1, h5, a5, Nb4 retreating). In 7/10 positions, the knight's departure left a specific pawn or square immediately undefended (e4 pawn in Position 2, g5 pawn in Position 4, e3 pawn in Position 5, f2 square in Position 10, c7 capture missed in Position 8, a7 capture missed in Position 9, kingside defense in Position 7). The consistent pattern across all positions is that the best move was either keeping the knight on its current square and acting with another piece, or moving the knight to a MORE active square (often one hop closer to the action rather than away from it). The avg cp_loss of 189 reflects that these tempo losses are especially costly because they simultaneously create a concrete tactical vulnerability.

855.label: Reflexive captures (especially king takes) that place the piece on a square vulnerable to immediate knight-based tactical punishment.
855.description: 8/10 positions involve captures (Kx or Nx), with 5/10 specifically being king captures on tempting material. The refutation in 7/10 positions involves a knight delivering a fork or check (Ne3+, Ne5+, Nc6+, Nxc3+, Nxe5+). In 4/10 positions the exact move is Kxf7 where the king grabs a piece/pawn but lands in a knight fork zone. In 8/10 positions only 1-2 good moves existed, and the correct alternative was typically a quieter king retreat (Ke7, Kf8, Kg1, Kc2) that avoided the tactical vulnerability. Positions 3 and 10 show the complementary pattern: a knight captures with check prematurely, surrendering a strong centralized piece before collecting hanging material. The 2 positions with 0-35cp loss (positions 4, 8) represent the feature firing on similar tactical textures where the capture happened to be correct.

856.label: Choosing a flashy piece check/capture to a square where a humble pawn capture (often en passant) would have been far more devastating.
856.description: 7/10 positions show the same distinctive geometric pattern: the player moves a piece (usually delivering check) to the exact same square where a pawn capture would have been superior. In positions 2, 5, 7, and 10, a knight or queen check was played instead of a pawn capture to the same square (Nf3+ vs exf3, Nf6+ vs exf6, Qxf4+ vs exf4+, Ne3+ vs dxe3). In position 4, Qxg5+ was played instead of hxg5#. Position 3 shows the reverse — exd6 was played instead of Nd6+. Position 8 (0 cp loss) correctly chose the piece capture to f6. En passant captures specifically appear as the missed best move in 4/10 positions. 8/10 moves played were checks, suggesting the player is drawn to the forcing nature of checks over quiet pawn moves. The average cp_loss of 2122 reflects that these 'quiet' pawn moves often created unstoppable passed pawns, opened critical files, or even delivered checkmate.

867.label: King marching toward distant targets in pawn endgames where the position is already decisively won or lost.
867.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames with king moves, and 9/10 are pure king-and-pawn endgames (one has a rook). All positions feature evaluations of +483 or greater magnitude, meaning the game is already effectively decided. In every case, the kings are far apart (typically on opposite sides of the board) and the moving king is marching toward a distant target — usually enemy pawns to capture or friendly pawns to escort. 6/10 positions have 0 or near-0 cp loss, indicating the feature fires on the positional pattern itself rather than exclusively on errors. When mistakes do occur (positions 3, 6, 9, 10), they involve choosing a slightly suboptimal path in the king race — typically one tempo slower or arriving on a less flexible intermediate square. The consistent structural features are: open center, both kings exposed with weak pawn shields, and a long-distance king march as the primary strategic action.
867.old_chip: King racing in decided pawn endgames

851.label: Moving a piece to an apparently useful square while ignoring an immediate tactical obligation (hanging piece, mate threat, or critical defensive function).
851.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a 'natural-looking' piece repositioning move that ignored the most concrete tactical element in the position. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 7, 8, 9), a piece was hanging or immediately capturable and the player chose development/centralization instead. In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 6), checkmate in 1-2 moves was threatened and the player made an unrelated improving move. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 8, 10, and partially 3), the piece was moved AWAY from a square where it performed a critical function (blocking a rank, attacking a key piece, paralyzing the opponent). The tag 'missed_tactic' appeared in 10/10 positions, 'tempo_loss' in 8/10, 'king_safety' in 9/10, and 'piece_activity' in 9/10. The average cp_loss was enormous (5798) because ignoring concrete tactical obligations in sharp positions with exposed kings leads to catastrophic consequences. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, confirming these were critical decision points requiring precision over aesthetics.

869.label: Aggressive queen moves to peripheral attacking squares (h-file, a-file, g-file) that miss stronger forcing tactics or abandon critical defensive duties.
869.description: 10/10 positions feature queen moves to aggressive flank squares, with 7/10 specifically targeting the h-file or g-file (Qh3×2, Qh5×3, Qh4, Qg5) and 2/10 targeting the a-file (Qa3, Qa6). In 8/10 cases, a more concrete forcing move existed—typically a sacrifice with check (Rxh7+, Rxf2, Bxf2+, Nf6+), a capturing sequence (Rxf8+, Nxc3), or a precisely-calculated central queen move (Qe4+, Qg4). The common error in 7/10 positions is that the queen move abandons defense of a critical piece or pawn (e4 knight in positions 4 and 7, d4 pawn in positions 7 and 9, d3 pawn in position 3). Only 2/10 positions (5 and 6) show moves with negligible cp_loss, where the aggressive queen placement was actually correct but a more elegant forced mate existed. Average cp_loss of the remaining 8 is ~1004, showing catastrophic consequences.

870.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) to a centralized or active-looking square while abandoning a critical defensive function, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
870.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moves a piece to a square that appears active or centralized but fatally neglects a defensive requirement. 7/10 moves are queen moves to seemingly powerful squares (Qf5, Qf6, Qe6, Qf6, Qb4, Qf3, Qd5), while the remaining 3 involve other pieces (Re4 twice, Bf4) making similar 'improving' moves. In every case, the piece was serving a latent defensive role — guarding a back rank (positions 1, 4), blocking a file (position 9), protecting a pawn (position 7), maintaining counterplay near the king (positions 5, 6, 10), or preserving pawn-advance tempo (positions 2, 8). The refutations are diverse — back-rank mates (2/10), piece infiltrations (3/10), pawn captures (2/10), discovered checks (1/10), unfavorable trades (2/10) — but all exploit the specific defensive vacancy created by the move. The average cp_loss of 2188 reflects that 3/10 positions result in forced mate, showing how catastrophic this pattern can be.

877.label: Developing the f1/f8 bishop passively to e2/e7 when the position demands immediate concrete action (captures, threats, or pawn breaks).
877.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same geometric move: developing the kingside bishop one square diagonally to its 'natural' square (Be2 for White's f1-bishop in 5 cases, Be7 for Black's f8-bishop in 4 cases, Bd2 in 1 case). In every case, the position contained a specific urgent demand — a hanging piece (3/10), a critical pawn break (3/10), a concrete threat to deliver (2/10), or a tactical vulnerability requiring defensive attention (2/10) — yet the player chose the safe, textbook developing move instead. 10/10 positions had both kings still near the center (at least one uncastled), and the average cp_loss of 267 reflects that these 'quiet' moves squandered decisive advantages or created losing positions. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions demanded precise, forcing play rather than general development. The consistent error is treating a critical tactical moment as a routine development phase.

875.label: A passive, non-forcing rook repositioning move is played when the position demands immediate concrete action (check, capture, or pawn advance).
875.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet rook move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) that looks like natural piece improvement but critically wastes tempo. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'piece_activity' in 10/10. In 4/10 cases (Positions 3, 4, 9, 10), the correct move was advancing a passed pawn; in 3/10 (Positions 1, 5, 7), a forcing tactical blow was available (mate, queen win, or material); in 3/10 (Positions 2, 8, 10), a capture or pawn break was needed to seize the initiative. The rook moves share a deceptive quality: they place the rook on 'active-looking' squares — open files, ranks controlling key territory — that would be perfectly good in a slower position but are catastrophically slow here. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments with narrow paths to success, yet the players chose the broad 'improving' move over the sharp concrete one.

878.label: A rook moves to blockade or stop a dangerous passed pawn, becoming passive and sacrificing activity or creating tactical vulnerabilities.
878.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to directly blockade or neutralize a dangerous passed pawn (typically 1-2 squares from promotion). In every case, the rook lands on the file of the passed pawn in a defensive/blocking posture. The passed pawns blockaded were on d6, a6, a7, e2, c2 (twice), g2, c3, b2, and d2. In 7/10 positions, superior alternatives involved either creating active counterplay first (f4, f7, Rcf8), moving the king to safety before committing the rook (Kg5, Kf2, Kg2, Kg3), or using a different piece for the blockading task (Bd5 in position 3). The tactical punishments varied: 4/10 allowed immediate tactical exploitation (trapped rook, mating net, exchange sacrifice, deflection), while 6/10 simply surrendered activity and counterplay, leaving the rook passively tied down while the opponent improved freely.

872.label: Trading an active bishop for a knight on f3/f6 when maintaining pressure or finding a stronger tactical blow was available.
872.description: 8/9 positions feature a bishop capturing a knight (7/9 specifically on the f-file: f6 or f3), prematurely releasing tension that was generating a larger advantage. In 6/9 cases, the bishop was actively pressuring from g5/h4 (targeting f6) or g4 (targeting f3), creating pins or restricting enemy pieces. In 2/9 positions (positions 2 and 4), the exact same error occurs: Bxf6 when Bxh5 was correct—a wrong capture-order mistake where the other enemy piece should have been eliminated first. In 3/9 positions (1, 5, 6), a much stronger tactical continuation existed (Nxd7, Qg3+, Bg3) that exploited the pressure the bishop was generating rather than cashing it in. In 2/9 positions (3, 9), Black's bishop on g4 pinning/pressuring Nf3 was traded prematurely, releasing central tension before exploiting it (exd4 or Nd5 was better). The lone outlier (position 7, Rxh1) shares the deeper theme: making a natural-looking capture immediately instead of an intermediate move (Ne4+) first. Average cp_loss of 257 confirms these are consistently significant mistakes.

874.label: King makes an active marching move in an endgame with exposed kings and passed pawns, often prioritizing material over urgency.
874.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves (no other piece type) in simplified endgame or endgame-like positions where both kings are exposed and actively placed outside their pawn shields. 8/10 are pure endgames and 2/10 are simplified middlegames with endgame character. In all cases, passed pawns or pawn races are the dominant strategic element. The moves that are actual mistakes (6/10 with cp_loss > 25) share the pattern of the king marching toward enemy material or a peripheral target when a more urgent action was available—typically a pawn advance (positions 2, 4, 6), preparatory piece move (positions 7, 8), or centralizing king move (position 9). The 4/10 positions with 0 or near-0 cp_loss show the same geometric pattern (active king march) but happen to be correct because the king advance IS the most urgent action. The feature consistently activates on one-square king marches in open endgame positions with mutual king exposure.

876.label: Aggressive rook moves to deep ranks (7th/8th) that look forceful but waste a critical tempo compared to more precise alternatives.
876.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving aggressively into the opponent's position—to the 7th rank, 8th rank, or equivalent deep infiltration squares. These moves appear natural and attacking (invading open files, giving checks, making captures), but they consistently miss more forcing continuations. In 6/10 cases, the correct move was a queen check or queen threat that was more immediately decisive (positions 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8). In 3/10 cases, the rook itself should have gone to a different rank—typically the 7th instead of 8th or vice versa (positions 3, 5, 10). In 2/10 cases, an intermediate check was needed before the rook move (positions 7, 9). The common thread is that the rook invasion grants the opponent a tempo they wouldn't have had with the correct move, allowing king escapes (5/10), defensive regrouping (3/10), or neutralization of attacking potential (4/10). The average cp_loss of 3905 reflects that 5/10 positions had forced mates that were squandered.

871.label: Player reflexively captures available material instead of finding a much stronger forcing move, typically exploiting the opponent's king vulnerability.
871.description: 9/10 positions feature a capture as the blunder move (5 knight captures, plus Rxg7, Bxf8, Qxc2, exf4), with the remaining position (Rae1) being a materialistic doubling that similarly ignores a tactical priority. In all 10 cases, the player grabbed or pursued tangible material (a piece, pawn, or positional asset) when a dramatically stronger move existed. The missed best moves frequently involved king attacks: 5/10 positions had a check, checkmate, or king-targeting move as the optimal play (Qe6#, Qa5+, Qh4+, Bxf3 capturing a queen, Rxf8 preserving king shield). In 4/10 positions, the correct move was to play an intermediate tempo-gaining move BEFORE capturing (Bg5 before Nxd4, Qh4+ before Nxd4, Qc8/a5 before Nxd5, Bxd4 before Nxd5). The average cp_loss of 3065 with only 1.3 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding precise calculation where the 'obvious' capture is a trap.

880.label: King moves to a square immediately exploitable by a check that wins material or delivers checkmate.
880.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves (the exception being Bd8 in Position 8, a passive retreat with similar logic). In 8/10 positions, the king moves to a square that allows an immediate devastating check: back-rank rook checks (Positions 1, 6), knight checks leading to forks or mate (Positions 4, 5, 7), h-file rook checks (Position 3), and queen diagonal checks (Position 9). The average cp_loss of 3012 reflects that these checks typically lead to checkmate (Positions 4, 5, 6) or win decisive material through forks/discoveries (Positions 1, 3, 7, 9). Position 2 (Kb1, 0 cp_loss) is actually the best move—it fires on the feature because the king retreats to the back rank in a pattern that resembles the blunder but is correct in context. Position 10 (Kb6) shows a milder version where the king advances without creating a check vulnerability but loses a critical tempo. The consistent thread is that players misjudge which squares are safe for the king, moving it to squares that appear to improve safety or activity but are actually in the tactical crosshairs of opponent pieces.

884.label: Playing b3 or b6 to chase/trap an enemy bishop infiltrated on a2 or a7, when the pawn advance is too slow, weakening, or tactically unsound.
884.description: 9/10 positions feature the identical pattern: an enemy bishop has infiltrated deep into the player's queenside on a2 (3 positions, White plays b3) or a7 (6 positions, Black plays b6), and the player advances the b-pawn to challenge, trap, or chase that bishop. In every case this is a significant mistake. The reasons vary but cluster into clear sub-patterns: in 3/10 positions (Positions 5, 10, and partially 3), the b-pawn advance actually OPENS a diagonal allowing the bishop to escape with check (Ba6+ or Ba3+), turning a 'trapped' piece into an active attacker. In 3/10 positions (Positions 1, 4, 6), the b3 advance fatally weakens the king's pawn shelter on the queenside, with Position 6 allowing immediate checkmate via Ba3#. In 3/10 positions (Positions 2, 9, and 8), the move wastes a critical tempo allowing White to seize the initiative with central breaks or tactical shots. Position 8 specifically demonstrates a move-order error where eliminating the defender (Bxc3) was needed before b6. The one outlier (Position 7, Nf3+) shares the broader theme of voluntarily giving up a well-placed piece to capture a less important one. All 10 positions occur in the middlegame, and 8/10 feature opposite-side castling where tempo and king safety are paramount.

883.label: Moving the king away from (or instead of capturing) a hanging enemy piece that was freely available to take.
883.description: All 10 positions feature a king move played instead of capturing a hanging enemy piece. In 7/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 10, and arguably 4), the king itself was adjacent to an undefended enemy piece and should have captured it directly (Kxc8, Kxe2, Kxh7, Kxd1, Kxh7, Kxf7), but instead the king moved to a different square—fleeing from or walking past the free material. In the remaining 3/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 8), a different piece should have captured a hanging piece (Nxd5, Qxg2, Rxg3) but the player moved the king instead, completely ignoring the available capture. All 10 blunders share the common thread of 'capture blindness'—the player perceived enemy pieces near the king as threats rather than targets, triggering a flight instinct instead of a capture instinct. The average cp_loss of 2492 reflects how catastrophic this oversight is: in every case there was exactly 1 good move available, and that move was always a simple capture of undefended material.

879.label: Player instinctively moves the king to a seemingly safer square under pressure, but the move either walks into worse tactical danger or wastes critical tempo when a non-king move was required.
879.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move played under significant pressure where the player defaults to a 'get the king to safety' instinct that proves catastrophic. In 4/10 positions (3, 5, 7, 10), the best move was not a king move at all — the correct response was a piece move (Be3, Re2, Bxa1, Qxb6) that addressed the actual tactical demands. In the remaining 6/10, a king move was correct but to a fundamentally different square than chosen. The average cp_loss of 5685 reflects that 6/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate after the blunder. Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, meaning these are razor-thin positions where reflexive play is deadly. The king destinations chosen (g2×3, c2, f8, d3, b2, f1, f6, b8) all appear superficially reasonable — tucking behind a pawn, fleeing an open file, escaping to a corner — but each walks into a specific tactical vulnerability: queen penetration on the second rank (positions 1, 3), knight discovered checks (2, 8), open-file mating attacks (4, 9), diagonal sacrifices (6), missed hanging pieces (7, 10), or immediate mating nets (5).

881.label: A pawn advance that severs its defensive connection to an adjacent pawn or square, leaving material immediately capturable.
881.description: All 10 positions feature single-square pawn advances that break a critical defensive relationship in the player's own pawn structure. In 8/10 cases, the pushed pawn was directly protecting an adjacent pawn (g2 protecting f2 in positions 2 and 5, g7 protecting h7 in position 3, c5 protecting b5 in position 4, b7 protecting c7 in position 7, d5 protecting e5 in position 8), or its advance removed a key defensive resource (a7's potential a5 tempo in position 9, b2 remaining undefended after a3 in position 1). In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 10), the explicit intent was to chase an enemy queen from an active square, but the tempo 'gained' is illusory because the queen (or another piece) captures the newly-undefended material instead of retreating. The refutations consistently involve capturing the hanging pawn/piece that was previously in the chain (Qxb2, Qxf2+, Qxh7+, Rxb5, Qxf2+, Qxc7, Rxe5+, Qxb7, Qxg2). Average cp_loss of 320 confirms these are severe errors, not minor inaccuracies.

886.label: A piece actively posted on g4 or g5 (creating pressure on f3/f6/f7) is moved away — retreated, exchanged passively, or sacrificed unsoundly — releasing critical attacking tension.
886.description: 9/10 positions feature a minor piece (bishop or knight) actively posted on g4 or g5 that gets moved away from that aggressive outpost. In positions 1, 4, and 7, a bishop on g4 (pinning or pressuring the f3 knight) retreats or captures away from g4. In positions 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, and 10, a piece on g5 (pressuring f6, f7, or e6) is retreated, traded, or sacrificed unsoundly. Position 9 is the slight outlier where a knight retreats from f4 to g6, but follows the same logic of abandoning a forward aggressive post. In all cases, the piece on g4/g5 was the linchpin of the player's attacking pressure — restraining opponent development (7/10), supporting tactical threats against f7/e6 (6/10), or maintaining a pin (3/10). The average cp_loss of 1229 reflects how catastrophic this release of tension is, with the opponent immediately seizing the initiative through counterattacks (b4-b5 storms, central breaks like c4 or cxd4, or direct tactical shots like Qb4+ or Qe6#).

889.label: Playing a quiet rook move to the back rank (typically b8/b1) instead of addressing an immediate tactical crisis requiring a different piece.
889.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking rook move to a back-rank square, with 8/10 specifically going to the b-file (Rb8 or Rb1). In every case, the position demanded urgent tactical action with a different piece: 4/10 required capturing or challenging a dominant enemy bishop, 3/10 required launching an immediate attack on a weak point, and 3/10 required addressing king safety or development emergencies. The average cp_loss of 299 reflects that these positions had extremely narrow windows (avg 1.4 good moves), yet the players chose superficially logical rook 'development' that wasted the critical tempo. The rook moves appear purposeful (activating on a semi-open file, supporting future pawn breaks) but ignore the position's concrete tactical demands. In 9/10 cases, the best move involved a completely different piece type (queen, knight, bishop, or pawn), showing the error is not just choosing the wrong square but the wrong piece entirely.

890.label: In time-critical pawn endgames, the king retreats or moves sideways instead of advancing toward the action or pushing a pawn, losing a decisive tempo in the race.
890.description: All 10/10 positions are pure endgames featuring king moves that retreat toward the back rank or move sideways away from the critical sector. In every case, the best move was either advancing the king toward targets (Ke4, Kc5, Kf5) or immediately pushing a pawn (g4, b4, g5, f4+). The played moves (Kd2, Ke7, Kf4, Ke2, Kc3) all share the geometric property of moving the king backward or laterally relative to the optimal direction. 10/10 positions involve passed pawns and pawn race dynamics where a single tempo is decisive. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in all 10 analyses, confirming this is the unifying thread. The average cp_loss of 174 reflects that these retreats transform winning positions into draws (positions 2, 3) or deepen losing positions significantly. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, highlighting how narrow these endgame positions are — the margin for passive play is zero.

882.label: Unnecessary pawn advances that weaken the position when piece or king improvement was the priority.
