882.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances as the mistake move. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a piece or king move (bishop repositioning, king centralization, knight rerouting, or rook activation) rather than any pawn push. 7/10 positions are endgames where king activity was paramount, yet the player chose a pawn advance instead. The pawn pushes are predominantly on the flanks: 7/10 involve a/b/g/h file pawns (h5, b5, a5, h4, h5, a4, a5). The common structural consequence is that the advance either removes a pawn from a critical defensive role (positions 4, 8, 10 where a-pawn supported b5), weakens an interdependent pawn chain allowing breakthroughs (positions 5, 7), releases tension prematurely giving the opponent favorable exchanges (positions 2, 4, 10), or wastes a crucial tempo when immediate piece action was needed (positions 1, 3, 8). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 10/10 analyses and 'pawn_structure' in 10/10, confirming the universal thread.

888.label: An aggressive knight jump to a central square (d4/d5/e4/e5) that can be immediately captured, leaving another piece undefended in the resulting exchanges.
888.description: All 10 positions feature a knight leaping aggressively to a central outpost (d5 in 6/10, e5 in 2/10, d4 in 2/10, e4 in 1/10) where it appears to create powerful threats but is immediately capturable with devastating consequences. In 7/10 positions, after the opponent simply captures the knight, a different piece (most often a bishop on g5 in positions 1-4, but also Bb4 in position 6, Bb5 in position 7) becomes completely undefended because the exchange sequence removed its protector or displaced the piece coordination. In 8/10 positions, the primary refutation involves simply capturing the knight (Nxd5, Nxe5, Nxe4, or Nxd4). The move-order error is remarkably consistent: in positions 3, 4, 7, and 10, the analysis explicitly identifies that the same knight jump would be correct AFTER a preparatory exchange (typically Bxf6 first, or Bxc6 first), but playing the knight move before eliminating the defensive piece creates the tactical vulnerability. The average cp_loss is 394, indicating these are full-piece-level blunders disguised as strong centralizing moves.

885.label: The queen (or king) moves away from a square where it was the sole defender of a critical piece, pawn, or square, immediately leaving something hanging or a lethal threat unanswered.
885.description: In 10/10 positions, the moved piece (queen in 8/10, king in 2/10) was performing a critical and irreplaceable defensive function before the blunder. In 6/10 positions (1, 4, 7, 8, and arguably 2, 6), the move directly leaves a specific piece en prise to immediate capture (Rf4, Rf8, Ra8, Rf1, a2 pawn, or enables Bxf7+ sacrifice). In 1/10 (position 10), it allows immediate checkmate. In 2/10 (positions 5, 9), it abandons queenside/positional defense enabling a devastating tactical sequence (fork or buildup). In 1/10 (position 3), the queen lands on a tactically vulnerable square allowing tempo gains. The moved piece typically goes to an apparently active-looking square (Qb6 targeting b2/d4 in 4/10, Qg2 appearing to support kingside in 2/10), creating the illusion of purposeful play while neglecting the far more urgent defensive requirement. The average cp_loss of 1284 reflects the catastrophic nature of removing a sole defender.

891.label: Pawn captures that appear natural but fatally open files or diagonals which the opponent immediately exploits for tactical blows.
891.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture (axb, bxc, dxe, fxg, or gxf/gxh notation) where the capturing pawn leaves its original file, creating a newly opened line that the opponent immediately exploits. In 5/10 positions the g-pawn captures sideways, opening the g-file and exposing the king to checks or mating attacks (positions 1, 3, 5, 8, 9). In 4/10 positions the b-pawn captures toward the c-file, opening the b-file or a critical diagonal (positions 4, 6, 7, 10). In 7/10 cases the opened line directly threatens the player's own king via checks (Qh4+, Qg5+, Bxc6+, Bxg3+). The captures all appear logical—removing an advanced enemy pawn, recapturing a piece, or winning material—but the player fails to recognize that the geometric consequence of removing their pawn from its file is more dangerous than the tactical gain. Crucially, in 8/10 positions the best alternative avoids the capture entirely or recaptures differently (Qxf3 instead of gxf3, moving the queen first before bxc6, keeping structural tension with g3 or Ke2).

892.label: Rook moves that look purposeful but abandon a critical defensive function, allowing devastating tactical exploitation.
892.description: 8/9 positions feature rook moves (the exception being a passive pawn move with similar characteristics). In every case, the rook is relocated with a superficially logical intent—defending a pawn (Ra1, Rh7), controlling a file (Rc8, Rd8), attacking material (Rg5), or repositioning for future use (Rb2, Rh1, Ra8)—but the move catastrophically abandons a more urgent duty. In 5/9 positions, the rook move directly enables a forcing tactical refutation (knight fork after Rc8, capture of the rook after Rh1 and Ra8, back-rank exploitation after Rb2, rook invasion after Rg5). In 3/9 positions, the rook move fails to address a critical king safety issue (Rh7 ignores king evacuation, Rd8 abandons king defense, Ra1 ignores the c3 break). The average cp_loss of 1330 is enormous, with 3/9 positions resulting in forced mate or near-mate. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these arise in critical positions demanding precise play where the 'natural' rook move is a trap.

893.label: Moving a Queen or Rook to the g-file third rank (g3 for White, g6 for Black) as a seemingly aggressive attacking move that actually abandons critical duties or creates tactical vulnerabilities.
893.description: All 10/10 positions feature a heavy piece (Queen or Rook) moving to g3 (White, 5/10) or g6 (Black, 5/10) — symmetric third-rank g-file squares. In every case, the move appears to be building a kingside attack (threatening the opponent's king, supporting g-file pressure, or coordinating with other attacking pieces). However, the move is consistently a mistake for overlapping reasons: 6/10 positions involve abandoning a critical defensive duty (back-rank coverage in Position 1, pawn protection in Positions 5 and 7, e-file blocking in Position 9, queen capture opportunity in Position 8, f6-knight pressure in Position 4). 3/10 positions feature the piece landing on a tactically vulnerable square subject to forks or captures (Nf5 fork in Position 2, Nh5 fork in Position 6, Nxg3+ in Position 7). 3/10 are move-order errors where the g-file move needed preparation first (Positions 3, 4, 10). The average cp_loss is extremely high at 1188, with only 1.9 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the 'natural-looking' aggressive g-file deployment is a trap.

864.label: Superficially logical piece placement or pawn moves that follow general principles while missing concrete tactical demands of the position.
864.description: 8/10 positions feature minor piece moves (5 bishop, 3 knight) to squares that appear 'natural' or 'improving' but are concretely wrong. In 4/10 cases the piece is left hanging or tactically vulnerable (Bg4 captured by Nxg4, Nd5 by Nxd5, Bb5+ by Qxb5, Bh6 exposing the h8 rook). In 3/10 cases a decisive tactical shot was missed in favor of a slow 'developing' move (Bh6 missing Qxh7+ forced mate, Nf3 missing f5 pawn break, g4 vs Ra6). In 3/10 cases the move relieves tension or commits to an inferior plan (c5 closing the center, Ba3 with wrong move order, Nh3 to a passive square). The consistent thread is that every move satisfies some general chess principle—develop pieces, give check, centralize knights, stabilize the center, activate bishops—but ignores what the specific position concretely requires. The average cp_loss of 1210 and average of only 2.2 good moves confirms these are critical positions demanding precise calculation, not routine improvement.

894.label: A rook moves to the edge of the board (a/b/g/h files), abandoning a vital defensive duty on a central file or key square, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of what was left unguarded.
894.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to a rim file (a, b, g, or h file), forsaking a critical defensive function. In 6/10 cases the rook specifically left the e-file where it was guarding a pawn (e4 in positions 2, 6), protecting a piece indirectly (d4 knight in position 7, f6 queen in position 9), or defending a structural point (e6 in position 4, e1 control in position 10). In 3/10 cases the rook moved to the a/b file pursuing queenside activity while a central tactic was available (positions 3, 5, 1). In 1/10 cases (position 8) the rook moved to h1 placing itself on a vulnerable diagonal. The average cp_loss is 1178, reflecting that these moves consistently enable devastating tactical refutations — from winning hanging pieces (positions 4, 6, 7) to winning queens (position 9) to enabling forced mate (position 10). The consistent thread is that the rook was the sole or critical defender of something important, and its relocation to the rim for a peripheral objective (attacking the queen, supporting a flank pawn, opening a side file) gave the opponent one free tempo to exploit the abandoned responsibility.
894.old_chip: Rook abandons critical post for rim

873.label: Positions where the critical decision involves trading a rook for a minor piece to transition into a pawn endgame.
873.description: 5/10 positions involve a rook literally capturing a knight to enter a pawn endgame (Rxd7, Rxe7+, Rxf7, Rxd3+ twice). In 4 of these 5 the simplification is correct (cp_loss 0-17) because the resulting pawn endgame is trivially won due to material advantage or unstoppable passed pawns. In 1 case (Position 4, cp_loss 382), the Rook-takes-Knight exchange is catastrophic because the rook's superiority over the knight WAS the winning advantage, and the resulting pawn endgame is drawn. The remaining 5 positions share the broader theme of activity-vs-simplification decisions: Position 5 (Be7) chooses passivity over active piece play, Position 9 (Rec1) removes a rook from its attacking file, Position 10 (Qxf3) grabs material instead of executing an exchange tactic, Position 8 (a4) wastes tempo when aggressive action was required, and Position 7 (O-O-O) commits the king to the wrong side. The 'piece_activity' tag appears in 9/10 positions, and 'pawn_endgame' is the tactical motif in 5/10. The consistent thread is positions where the player must correctly evaluate whether trading down (especially major-for-minor piece) leads to a winning, drawing, or losing simplified position.

896.label: Bishop captures a knight prematurely, allowing the opponent's queen to recapture on a dominant central square instead of the hoped-for pawn recapture.
896.description: In 10/10 positions, a bishop captures (or moves to) a square where the opponent's queen can recapture, gaining a powerful centralized post. Specifically, 7/10 involve Black playing Bxf3 hoping White will recapture gxf3 (damaging the kingside pawn structure), but White's strongest response is Qxf3, placing the queen on a commanding square with threats along multiple diagonals. 2/10 involve White playing Bxf6 or Bxc6 where Black recaptures Qxf6/Qxc6 activating the queen. 1/10 (Be5+) hangs the bishop to Qxe5. In 9/10 cases, the best alternatives involved either preparatory developing moves first (Ne5, Nc6, Nf6) that would make the eventual exchange more favorable, or moves that forced the pawn recapture (like h3 provoking the trade under better circumstances). The average cp_loss of 1153 reflects how devastating the queen activation is, particularly when 8/10 positions featured at least one uncastled king vulnerable to the newly centralized queen.

898.label: Moving a knight to a corner or rim square (often capturing material) while ignoring critical king safety threats that demand immediate attention.
898.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving to a rim or corner square (a1, a8, h8, h7, h2, b8, c2, c7) while the player's own king faces lethal or near-lethal threats. In 6/10 cases the knight captures material (usually a rook in the corner: Nxa1 twice, Nxh8 twice, Nxa8, Nxc7), representing pure material greed. In 4/10 cases the knight retreats passively to the rim (Nb8, Nh7, Nh2, Nc2). In every single case, the position demanded addressing immediate king safety — whether defending against mating attacks (3/10 resulted in forced mate), preserving attacking chances against the opponent's king, or maintaining critical central control. The knight consistently ends up trapped or irrelevant on its destination square: in positions 4 and 10 (Nxh8) the knight is permanently entombed, in positions 2 and 3 (Nxa1) it's buried in the corner, and in positions 7 and 9 (Nh7/Nh2) it's sidelined from the fight. The average cp_loss of 3096 reflects catastrophic consequences, with only 1.0 good moves available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring the one precise response.

887.label: Superficially logical moves (challenging pieces with pawns, capturing attackers, or giving checks) that address a visible concern but create a worse problem than they solve.
887.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: the player faces a visible concern (an annoying piece, a threat, a capture opportunity, or a check available) and responds with the most 'automatic' or 'natural-looking' move — but this reactive move creates or exposes a deeper vulnerability. 6/10 positions involve pawn advances near the king (h6×2, h3×2, g6, hxg6) that either create sacrifice targets (Bxh6 or Bxh3 in 5 cases) or open critical files for the opponent. 2/10 involve d-pawn moves (d5, dxc5) that ignore hanging pieces or open diagonals against the uncastled king. 2/10 involve bishop checks (Bf4+, Bc6+) that appear to gain tempo but actually improve the opponent's king position while stranding the checking piece. The average number of good alternatives was only 1.6, indicating these are critical moments where the 'obvious' move is a trap and only deeper calculation finds the correct path. In every case, the correct move required ignoring the surface-level concern and addressing a more fundamental issue (king safety, piece coordination, or concrete counterattack).

904.label: A pawn push attacks an aggressively-posted enemy knight, expecting it to retreat, but the knight leaps forward into a devastating fork instead.
904.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder is a single-square pawn push (a3, a6, h6, h3, or e6) aimed at an enemy knight sitting on an aggressive outpost (b4, b5, g5, g4, or d5), expecting the knight to retreat passively. Instead, the knight jumps FORWARD to deliver a fork — typically Nc2+ (positions 1, 7), Nc7+ (positions 2, 3, 8, 9), Ngxf7 (position 4), or Nxf2 (position 10) — winning major material (usually a rook via king-rook fork, or in position 10 a queen-rook fork). The remaining 2/10 positions (5 and 6) are close variants: passive piece moves (Nh3, Na6) that fail to address an advancing knight threat, allowing similar tactical devastation. In all 10 cases, the king remains uncastled or exposed (10/10 have at least one king in the center), and the correct defensive moves involve either developing actively, capturing the threatening piece, or moving the king off the fork diagonal — never a slow pawn push.

897.label: A knight captures a rook on a corner or edge square, becoming trapped or abandoning its dominant post, while ignoring more critical tactical priorities.
897.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight capturing a rook (Nxh1, Nxa8, Nxa1, or Nxf8). In 9/10 cases, the capture lands the knight on a corner square (a1, a8, h1) where it becomes completely trapped and out of play. In 8/10 positions, the knight was previously on a powerful active square deep in enemy territory (b3, c2, c7, d7, f2) where it exerted enormous tactical pressure. The captures uniformly prioritize raw material gain (winning the exchange) while ignoring more urgent concerns: king safety was compromised in 6/10, a better capture existed on a more important target in 4/10, and an enemy threat went unaddressed in 5/10. The tagged motif of 'trapped_piece' appears in 7/10 analyses, and all 10/10 are tagged with tempo_loss and piece_activity, confirming that the universal error is trading a knight's dynamic attacking power for a static material gain that leaves it entombed on the board's periphery.

899.label: A knight (or minor piece) leaps aggressively to a seemingly dominant central or attacking square without adequate preparation, but the piece is tactically refutable because it can be captured, triggers a losing exchange sequence, or abandons a critical defensive duty.
899.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves (Ne4, Ng5, Ne5, Nd5, Nb5) while 1/10 is a bishop lunge (Bg4) — all are forward, aggressive minor piece jumps to apparently strong squares. In 3/10 positions (Nd5, Nb5, Bg4), the piece lands on a square where it is simply captured by a pawn with insufficient compensation. In 3/10 positions (Ne4 ×3), the knight centralizes but enables a refuting capture sequence that wins material through exchanges or intermezzos. In 2/10 positions (Ng5 ×2), the knight is a move-order error — it's the correct second move of a Greek Gift combination played without the prerequisite Bxh7+ sacrifice. In 2/10 positions (Ne5 ×2), the knight abandons a critical defensive duty (protecting d4 or maintaining piece coordination), leaving pawns or squares fatally unguarded. The average cp_loss of 1244 reflects the severity, with one position resulting in immediate checkmate. 7/10 occurred in the opening phase, suggesting these are impulsive attacking attempts before development is complete. The king was uncastled in 7/10 positions (either the player's own or the opponent's), creating the illusion of attacking opportunity that tempted the premature lunge.

901.label: A rook abandons a file where it performs a vital restraining or tactical function, usually to double rooks on a different file, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated file's absence.
901.description: In 9/10 positions, a rook is moved laterally from one open file to another (the remaining case is a queen retreat with similar logic). The disambiguation notation (Rdc8, Rcd1, Ref1, etc.) reveals the player had two rooks and chose to move the one serving a critical duty. In 7/10 cases, the stated intent was explicitly to 'double rooks' on the target file. The abandoned file served diverse but always critical functions: preventing a pawn capture (Position 1: d-file restrained fxe4), guarding a key square from a fork (Position 2: c-file controlled c4; Position 9: d-file prevented Nb4), enabling a back-rank combination (Position 3: d-file needed for Rd1+), defending a piece tactically (Position 6: d-file's Rxd7 threat protected Ng5), and restraining a central pawn advance (Position 10: e-file prevented ...d4). In 6/10 positions, the opponent's punishment involved an immediate tactical shot (fork, capture, or combination). The average cp_loss of 328 reflects that these are catastrophic strategic errors disguised as logical positional improvements.
901.old_chip: Rook leaves critical file to double

907.label: Moving the rook to passively guard a pawn instead of choosing active counterplay, piece mobility, or addressing more critical positional needs.
907.description: All 10/10 positions involve rook moves, and in 9/10 the rook relocates specifically to defend a pawn (c4, a4, h4, h7, h3, f4, a3, a4). The remaining position (Re6) moves the rook to attack an irrelevant pawn rather than positioning behind a critical passed pawn. In every case, the best moves involved active play: invading the 7th/8th rank (5/10), giving checks (3/10), advancing pawns or centralizing the king (4/10), or sacrificing the defended pawn for dynamic compensation (3/10). 8/10 positions are rook endgames where piece activity is paramount. The average cp_loss of 1214 reflects how catastrophic passive defense is in positions demanding initiative. In 7/10 cases, the passive rook allowed the opponent's king or pawns to march forward unopposed, while in 1/10 (Position 8), the rook abandoning its post allowed an immediate back-rank mate.

900.label: Knight jumps to an apparently active or aggressive square while abandoning a critical defensive duty or ignoring a more urgent tactical requirement.
900.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving forward to a seemingly strong outpost (central squares like d4, e4, e5, or advanced squares like b5, c5, h5, f6) that looks actively placed but is concretely wrong. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 8, and indirectly 2), the knight abandons a critical defensive function—guarding against a breakthrough (e5-e6+), protecting another piece (Nf6 guarding d7), shielding the king (Nf3 guarding against Qa3+), or maintaining structural integrity (Nc6 supporting Nf6). In 3/10 positions (6, 7, 9), the knight moves to a square where it is immediately capturable or tactically exploitable (hanging to queen, rook, or enabling a fork). In 3/10 positions (2, 5, 10), the move is a move-order error where the knight activation was correct in principle but needed a preparatory move first (king safety, intermediate check, or decisive breakthrough). The average cp_loss of 278 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies—they're significant blunders driven by the seductive appearance of knight activity.

906.label: A knight is moved from a critical defensive post to an apparently active square, fatally exposing the player's own king to immediate mating threats.
906.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight being relocated from a square where it performed a vital defensive function (guarding key squares adjacent to the king, serving as the only interposing piece, or blocking critical files/diagonals) to a more 'active' or aggressive-looking square. In 9/9 cases, the immediate consequence is a catastrophic king safety collapse, with 7/9 resulting in forced checkmate within 1-4 moves. The knight destinations are invariably central or attacking squares (e5, f5, g5, g4, d4, c6, e3) that look superficially strong but ignore the lethal threats already aimed at the player's king. The average cp_loss of ~3968 reflects the severity. In 8/9 positions the player's king was already exposed or weakly shielded before the move, meaning defensive vigilance was paramount. The positions span both sides (5 White, 4 Black) and feature diverse tactical refutations (back-rank mates, smothered mates, queen-knight mating patterns, promotion threats), but the unifying error is identical: prioritizing knight 'activity' over its irreplaceable defensive role.

908.label: A non-forcing pawn capture resolves peripheral tension while squandering a much stronger tactical or attacking continuation against the opponent's king.
908.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture (cxb4, cxd4, cxb5, dxe4, dxc4, exf3, exd5, axb4, fxe4, bxc3) played instead of a vastly superior forcing move. In 10/10 cases, the missed best move involved direct attacking action—rook lifts (Rae1, Rf3, Rf6, Rxd4), queen checks (Qf6, Qg6+, Qxd4+), exchange sacrifices (Rxe2), or decisive pawn pushes (f7, e3+). In 9/10 positions, the opponent's king was vulnerable or exposed, and the pawn capture gifted the defender a critical tempo to consolidate. The average cp_loss of 2111 reflects that 2/10 positions involved missed forced mates (#+3 and #+7). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in all 10 analyses, confirming the universal mechanism: the pawn capture is non-forcing (never delivers check or creates an immediate threat), allowing the opponent to reorganize defenses, trade queens, blockade passed pawns, or neutralize attacking diagonals.

905.label: Capturing apparently free material with an active piece, sacrificing critical piece coordination or exposing a fatal vulnerability.
905.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures of seemingly available material (pawns, minor pieces) where the capturing piece moves away from a critical duty or lands on a vulnerable square. In 8/10 cases, a non-capture or different capture was vastly superior — typically a consolidating, centralizing, or prophylactic move that maintained piece harmony. The captures created specific exploitable weaknesses: 3/10 exposed back-rank or mating threats (positions 4, 8, 9), 3/10 moved a piece away from essential attacking/defensive pressure (positions 1, 5, 6), and 4/10 traded an active piece for a passive one while missing a stronger tactical continuation (positions 2, 3, 7, 10). The average cp_loss of 1255 and average of only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are critical positions where the natural-looking materialistic capture is a trap. Captures were made by Queens (5/10), Rooks (3/10), and Bishops (2/10) — predominantly the most active piece in the position.

910.label: The king reflexively captures an enemy bishop that has infiltrated adjacent to it, squandering a critical tempo that should have been spent on a more urgent tactical priority.
910.description: In 10/10 positions, the king captures an enemy bishop that has infiltrated to an adjacent square (7/10 on g7, 2/10 on g2, 1/10 on c2). In every case, the bishop was essentially trapped or harmless and could be captured later or ignored entirely. The critical error is tempo misallocation: 4/10 positions featured a stronger intermediate forcing move that should have preceded the capture (f2+ check, dxc3 with tempo, Bh3+ check, Nxf6+ check), 3/10 positions required ignoring the bishop entirely to maintain king shelter or launch a decisive attack (Qxg2, Qe7, Rf4), 2/10 positions missed a forced checkmate (Qe1#, Qg5 with mate in 4), and 1/10 was a trivial move-order issue. The average cp_loss was 2067, with 8/10 having only 1-2 good moves available, confirming these are sharp positions demanding precise calculation rather than reflexive captures. The bishop's placement adjacent to the king creates an irresistible psychological lure—it feels dangerous and 'free'—but 10/10 times the capture either exposed the king to checks/attacks on its new square or wasted the tempo needed for something decisive.

903.label: King moves directly toward enemy pawns in pawn endgames, sometimes missing subtle tempo or routing improvements.
903.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring active king marches toward enemy pawn weaknesses, with 9/10 being pure pawn endgames (one has a bishop). The king is already exposed and actively placed in every case, moving toward vulnerable enemy pawns with the intent to capture them. The average cp_loss is only 42, with 5/10 positions showing 0-1cp loss (essentially correct moves), indicating the feature detects the general pattern of king-approaches-pawns rather than exclusively mistakes. When errors occur (positions 3, 7, 5, 8, 1 with losses of 230, 106, 39, 27, 20cp respectively), they share a common theme: the king takes the most obvious direct route but misses a subtlety — either failing to make a preparatory pawn move first (position 1), abandoning support of a passed pawn (position 3), releasing control of a key square (position 7), or failing to 'shoulder' the opponent's king via a better geometric route (position 5). The avg good moves available is only 2.6, confirming these are constrained positions where the king march is the only strategic concept but the precise square choice matters.
903.old_chip: Direct king march in pawn endgame

895.label: Single-step pawn advances in simplified endgame positions with exposed kings, often when more active king/piece play is urgent.
895.description: All 10/10 positions feature single-step pawn advances (no double pushes, no captures, no checks). 8/10 are endgame positions and 10/10 have both kings described as exposed with weak pawn shields. The moves span various files (d, e, h, b, f) with no strong directional bias, but share the common context of simplified material where king activity and tempo are critical. 7/10 positions directly involve passed pawn dynamics (creating, advancing, or blocking passed pawns). In 6/10 cases the error stems from a tempo loss—the pawn push is too slow compared to more urgent alternatives like king activation (Position 5: Kxe3), piece maneuvers (Position 3: Ba3-Bf8), or captures (Position 9: Qxc3). However, 2/10 positions show 0 cp_loss where the pawn advance was actually correct (Positions 6 and 10), suggesting the feature detects the structural pattern of quiet pawn advances in exposed-king endgames rather than exclusively detecting errors.

902.label: Passive piece repositioning moves (mostly rooks) to seemingly active squares when the position demanded a concrete forcing move, usually a capture.
902.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves, and all 10 moves share the pattern of repositioning a piece to what appears to be an active square while completely ignoring the position's urgent tactical demands. In 7/10 positions, the best move was a capture (Rxc8+, Nxf3, Rxf6, Nxc6, Rxg2, Rxf7, or the pawn thrust g6 creating forcing threats), yet the player chose a quiet repositioning move instead. In 5/10 positions (Rf4, Rc3, Qb5, Rd6, Ng6), the piece literally moved to a square where it could be immediately captured or fatally pinned/forked. In the remaining positions, the piece reached a 'safe' but irrelevant square while a critical threat went unaddressed. The average cp_loss of 486 reflects how catastrophically wrong these quiet moves are—the positions were tactically sharp with only 1.5 good moves available on average, demanding precision that a passive developing move cannot provide.

913.label: Passive piece repositioning moves (mostly bishop) played in positions demanding immediate forcing action, wasting critical tempo and abandoning tactical opportunities.
913.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing piece relocation (no checks, no captures, no pawn breaks) when the position urgently demanded concrete tactical action. 8/10 moves were bishop repositioning moves, and all shared the character of 'improving' a piece's square for positional reasons while ignoring immediate tactical necessities. The best moves in these positions were invariably forcing: captures with check (Bxd4+ in position 4), queen checks initiating forced mate (Qe1+ in position 5), critical pawn advances (g4 in position 6, d5 in position 1), rook lifts for queen traps (Ra6 in position 9), or queen trades reaching winning endgames (Qd5 in position 8). The average cp_loss of 2242 is catastrophic, with 2/10 missing forced checkmate. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, confirming these were narrow, critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than positional judgment. In 7/10 cases, the repositioned piece actually abandoned a square where it performed a vital tactical function — blocking a diagonal, preventing a fork, supporting a combination, or defending a vulnerable pawn.

914.label: Pawn-takes-pawn captures that remove a structurally critical defender, immediately enabling a tactical refutation.
914.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing another pawn (pxp), where the moving pawn was performing a vital defensive function — guarding a key square, supporting another pawn, blocking a dangerous diagonal, or shielding the king. In 10/10 cases the capture resolves tension or grabs material in a way that looks natural but catastrophically abandons that defensive role. The consequences vary: 3/10 enable knight forks on the newly unguarded square (positions 1, 9, and indirectly 10), 3/10 expose the king by opening files/diagonals (positions 7, 8, 10), 2/10 release structural tension that was trapping or constraining an enemy piece (positions 3, 4), 1/10 leaves a pawn hanging that was previously supported (position 2), and 1/10 chooses a mundane capture over a devastating tactical combination (position 5). The average cp_loss of 388 reflects that these are severe errors, and the average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are critical moments demanding precise non-capturing alternatives. 6/10 occur in the opening phase, suggesting players are particularly susceptible to reflexive tension-resolution early in the game.

918.label: Advancing a passed pawn (usually with check) in an endgame pawn race, regardless of whether the timing is correct.
918.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring passed pawns or connected passers in a promotion race. Every single move is a pawn advance, and 8/10 deliver check. The positions universally feature exposed kings on both sides (10/10) and weak pawn shields. The feature fires on the aggressive instinct to push a passed pawn forward with tempo (via check) in a racing scenario. Critically, this pattern captures both correctly-timed advances (5/10 have 0 cp loss, where the check gains an essential tempo for promotion) and premature/counterproductive ones (5/10 lose 104-505 cp, where the check improves the opponent's king position or breaks pawn coordination). The blunders share a common mechanism: the pawn check either drives the enemy king to a superior blockading square (positions 2, 10), pushes the pawn onto an attacked square (position 6), or misses a more forcing tactical sequence (positions 5, 8).

922.label: A knight leaves a critical defensive or blocking square to make a materialistic capture, exposing a devastating tactical vulnerability.
922.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a knight FROM a strong, centrally-placed or defensively critical square TO capture an enemy piece on a less important square. In 8/10 cases, the knight was on a powerful central post (e4, d5, e6, d4) and moved to a peripheral square (c3, c4, f4, c6, f6, g6). The knight was performing an essential defensive function: blocking a deadly diagonal (3/10 — positions 2, 5, 8), blocking file penetration (2/10 — positions 6, 7), guarding a critical pawn or square (3/10 — positions 1, 4, 10), or restraining a passed pawn (1/10 — position 9). In all cases, the player prioritized winning material over maintaining their knight's defensive role, resulting in immediate tactical catastrophes including checkmate (2/10), queen loss (1/10), devastating file-opening toward their own king (4/10), or fatal diagonal exposure (3/10). The average cp_loss of 1201 reflects the severity of abandoning these critical posts.
922.old_chip: Knight abandons defensive post to capture

909.label: A piece leaves its critical defensive or positional post to create a superficially active threat against an enemy piece that can be easily sidestepped or ignored.
909.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder involves a piece relocating to create what looks like an aggressive 'threat' (usually targeting an enemy rook or knight) while abandoning a far more important role. In 7/10 cases, the piece specifically targets an enemy piece on an open file that simply sidesteps (Be2→Rd1, Bg2→Rf1, Bc2→Rd1, Rf2→Rd2, Bd7→Rc8, Rc2 invades 2nd rank, Re7 invades 7th rank). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, and 'piece_activity' in 10/10. The average cp_loss is enormous (2972), with 4/10 positions resulting in forced mate because the abandonment was catastrophic (Qd3, Bc2, Rf2 all led to #+5-14). In 8/10 positions the side was Black, and 10/10 were middlegame positions where the critical need was maintaining coordination around an exposed or vulnerable king rather than seeking speculative activity. All best moves shared the theme of patient improvement (piece centralization, pawn breaks, or contesting the opponent's active piece) rather than flashy piece sorties.

923.label: King moves to a suboptimal square (or moves at all) in endgame positions where precise tempo in a pawn race is critical.
923.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves, with 9/10 occurring in endgames involving passed pawns and promotion races. The 'tempo_loss' tactical motif was identified in 8/10 positions, and 'passed_pawn' appeared in 9/10. The serious blunders (positions 2, 4, 6, 8 with cp_loss 169-812) all share the same mechanism: the king either goes to a geometrically inferior square when a specific adjacent square was required (Kg6 instead of Kg7/Kh7 blocking its own pawn; Kxb6 instead of Kb7 landing on a checking diagonal), or the king moves at all when an immediate pawn push or piece move was the only way to maintain the promotion race tempo (Ka5 instead of a2; Kc6 instead of Nb2). The minor inaccuracies (positions 1, 5, 7 with cp_loss 11-62) show the same pattern in softer form—the king chooses a natural-looking but slightly imprecise path. Positions 3, 9, and 10 (cp_loss 0) represent near-equivalent king moves in already-decided positions, suggesting the feature also activates on king route decisions in won/lost endgames even when the choice is inconsequential.
923.old_chip: King tempo loss in pawn races

917.label: The king (usually via castling) moves away from a piece it was the sole defender of, leaving that piece immediately capturable.
917.description: 9/10 positions feature a king move (6/10 are castling, 3/10 are regular king moves) that abandons defense of a piece, and 1/10 features a rook moving away from a critical defensive post (back rank). In 8/10 cases, the king was the sole or critical defender of a specific piece (Ne7 in positions 1 and 7, Be7 in position 6, Ne2 in position 4, Be2 in position 5, Bf8 in position 9, Rd3 in position 8, Rd7 in position 10). The tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' in 7/10 positions explicitly. The moves all appear natural or improving — castling looks like standard development (6/10), and king walks look prophylactic (3/10) — but each fatally severs a defensive connection that the opponent exploits with a simple capture. The refutations are almost always straightforward piece captures (Rxe7, Qxe7, Qxe2, Bxd3, Qxf8, Kxd7) rather than complex combinations, indicating the blunders create immediately exploitable hanging pieces rather than deep tactical vulnerabilities.

920.label: Quiet queen repositioning moves to central squares that ignore concrete tactical vulnerabilities, allowing the opponent to gain tempo or exploit abandoned defensive duties.
920.description: All 10/10 positions feature non-capturing, non-checking queen moves to central or semi-central squares (d2, d3, d4, d6, d7, e3, e8, c7) that appear positionally motivated but create immediate tactical problems. In 6/10 positions, the queen lands on a square where it is immediately attacked with tempo by a pawn advance (e5 forking in position 5, c5 in position 4, f5 in position 10) or a knight jump (Nb5 in position 9, Nc4 in position 2, Nxe3 in position 7), forcing the queen to waste another move. In 3/10 positions (1, 3, 8), moving the queen abandons a critical defensive function—leaving a knight hanging (position 8), enabling a back-rank mate (position 3), or creating a pin along a newly opened file (position 1). Position 6 is the lone outlier where the queen move is merely passive rather than directly punished, missing a winning tactical blow. The average cp_loss of 1226 reflects the severity: these 'natural-looking' queen moves consistently ignore the concrete tactical demands of the position.

911.label: Rook moves to the opponent's back rank or 7th/8th rank that look aggressive but miss stronger concrete alternatives.
911.description: 9/10 positions feature rook moves, and 8/9 of those rook moves target the opponent's back rank (8th/1st rank) or second rank (7th/2nd rank) — the classic 'deep penetration' squares. 6/10 moves involve check or capture, making them appear forcing and powerful. However, the blunders (8/10 positions with cp_loss > 0 or significant missed wins) share a common flaw: the rook's aggressive placement either lands on an undefended square where it's captured (positions 1, 7, 8), abandons a critical defensive duty (position 3), prematurely trades a dominant piece (position 9), gives a pointless check that improves the opponent's king (position 10), or delays an immediate promotion (position 4). The 2 positions with 0 cp_loss (positions 2 and 6) show the correct version: Rb1 attacking the defender of a promotion square, where back-rank rook placement directly enables queening. The g4 pawn push (position 5) is the sole outlier. The average cp_loss of 1242 reflects that these 'natural-looking' penetration moves often catastrophically misfire.

921.label: King moves to a plausible-looking but precisely wrong square in endgame positions with extremely narrow margins for correct play.
921.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring king moves where the player selects a seemingly reasonable destination square but misses the one (or two) correct options. The average number of good moves available was only 1.8, indicating these are positions with razor-thin margins where king placement on a specific square determines the game's outcome. In 7/10 positions, the king moves in the wrong direction relative to where counterplay or defensive needs exist (e.g., toward the kingside when queenside counterplay is needed, or retreating when advancing was critical). In 3/10 positions, the king moves to the right general area but lands on a square that allows the opponent to gain tempo via checks, opposition, or pawn advances with tempo. The cp_loss ranges from 2 to 488, but the pattern is consistent: endgame positions where one specific king square is correct and adjacent squares are significantly worse, and the player chooses the intuitive-but-wrong destination.

926.label: Playing a slow pawn advance to chase an enemy piece instead of finding the urgent concrete tactical solution the position demands.
926.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing pawn advance aimed at harassing or displacing a specific enemy piece that is exerting pressure: h3 to kick a bishop on g4 (positions 1, 3, 6), h6 to kick a bishop on g5 (positions 5, 7), f6 to challenge a bishop on g5 (position 2), g4 to kick a knight on h5 (position 4), g3 to chase a rook on h4 (position 8), c4 to attack a bishop on b3 (position 9), and f4 to push back a queen on e5 (position 10). In every case, a far stronger forcing move existed — typically a capture, exchange, or tactical combination (Nxe4, Ne5, Nxd2+, Bxc3+, Qxd4, etc.). The average cp_loss of 373 is extremely high, and 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating sharp tactical moments where precision was critical. In 8/10 cases, the pawn advance also structurally weakened the player's own king position, and in 6/10 cases the 'chased' piece actually had a superior option to retreating (e.g., capturing on f3 instead of retreating from g4).

928.label: A knight on an active central square (c3/c6/f3/f6) retreats to a passive second-rank square (e2/e7/d2/d7), leaving a key pawn or square undefended.
928.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving from an active third/sixth-rank post to a passive second/seventh-rank square — specifically c3→e2 (4 positions), c6→e7 (3 positions), f6→d7 (2 positions), and f3→d2 (1 position). In every case, the knight was performing a critical defensive function on its original square: guarding a central pawn (e4 in positions 1, 5, 8, 9; d5 in position 10), restraining opponent piece invasions (Ng5 in positions 7, 4), or enabling tactical sequences (Nxd4 in position 6, b5 pin in position 3). 7/10 positions featured closed centers where slow knight repositioning feels natural but proves catastrophic. The intended purpose was always a slow regrouping maneuver (typically aiming for g3/f4/f5/b6), but in every case concrete tactical demands made the retreat immediately punishable — most commonly via capture of the now-undefended pawn (6/10 positions) or a forcing tactical sequence exploiting the abandoned square (4/10 positions).

912.label: Moving a piece (usually bishop or queen) to a natural-looking active square that abandons its critical function or misses an available concrete tactical shot.
912.description: 9/10 positions involve moving a bishop (5/10) or queen (4/10) to a square that appears purposeful—aiming at the opponent's king, controlling a file, or pursuing a thematic strategic plan—but actually fails the concrete demands of the position. In 7/10 cases, a specific tactic was missed (forks in positions 2, 5, 7, 9; mating threats in 3, 8; a key pawn break in 1). In 4/10 positions the moved piece was already optimally placed and the repositioning abandoned a critical duty (the Bf1 needed for recapture in position 1; Bd4 controlled c5 in position 6; Qh4 coordinated with h-file rooks in position 8; Nb5 pressured from its outpost in position 9). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/10 analyses, confirming the moves waste time on secondary plans. The average cp_loss of 1108 is enormous, reflecting that these positions typically had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.8), meaning precision was critical and the natural-looking move was catastrophically wrong.

919.label: Heavy pieces moved to aggressive-looking setup squares (batteries, 7th rank, kingside files) when an immediate forcing move (check, capture, or sacrifice) was available.
919.description: 9/10 positions feature a non-forcing heavy piece move (Queen or Rook) to an attacking-looking square when a direct tactical blow would have been dramatically stronger. 4/10 moves land on the 7th rank (Rfh7, Rg7, Qh7, Rb7), 4/10 move to kingside pressure squares (Qh5 x2, Qg2 x2), and all share the quality of 'aiming' at the enemy king without actually forcing anything. In contrast, the best moves in 8/10 positions involved immediate checks, captures, or sacrifices (Rxa7+, Rxh2+, Rxh6, e6+, Rb8+, Rxg6, Qg5 enabling Nf7+, Qe2 attacking Rf1). The average cp_loss of 6006 reflects that many positions had forced mates available (5/10 positions featured mate-in-N for the playing side). Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, showing these were critical moments demanding precision. The one outlier (Position 1, Reg2, 0cp loss) shares the same geometric profile—rook doubling on the g-file—but happened to be the correct execution in that specific case.

925.label: Non-forcing 'improving' moves played at critical moments when the position demands immediate concrete action—either exploiting a tactic or addressing an urgent threat.
925.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, captures, or direct threats) while the position demanded urgent concrete action. 6/10 are pawn pushes (f5, f5, b5, d5, g5, d4), 2/10 are passive piece retreats (Bd7, Nf2), 1/10 is a prophylactic king move (Kh1), and 1/10 is development to a tactically exposed square (Nh6). In every case, the chosen move pursues a vague 'strategic' improvement—undermining a pawn chain, chasing a piece, prophylaxis, or consolidation—while ignoring the position's most pressing tactical reality. 9/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic', confirming these are wasted tempi at critical junctures. The refutations consistently exploit exactly what was ignored: an undefended piece (positions 1, 2, 5), a forcing tactical sequence (positions 3, 7, 9), a king safety crisis (positions 6, 8), or a piece retreating to a vulnerable square (positions 4, 10). The average cp_loss of 278 with an average of 2.0 good alternatives confirms these were avoidable errors where multiple concrete options existed.

915.label: Capturing or attacking material (usually with a rook) when a quiet preparatory move maintaining piece coordination was required, allowing tactical punishment.
915.description: 7/10 positions involve rook moves (Rxf5, Rxd4, Rxf5, Rxd5, Rb5, Rde1, Rxh8), and 8/10 involve direct captures or moves targeting material. In every case, the correct move was a quiet repositioning or preparatory move: Positions 1 and 2 both required Bf3 (bishop retreat), Position 3 needed Kd3 (king advance), Position 4 needed Rhf6 (rook to attack the strong piece indirectly), Position 5 needed Qb6 (queen retreat), Position 6 needed Rbd1 (doubling on the critical file), Position 7 needed Red4 (simplifying exchange), Position 8 needed Ndxe5 (correct piece selection), Position 9 needed Ne5 (knight reposition BEFORE exchanging), and Position 10 needed Nf6 (knight retreat). The blundering moves all prioritize immediately removing a strong enemy piece or grabbing material, while the correct moves prioritize maintaining one's own piece coordination first. 6/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating these were critical moments requiring restraint rather than action.

931.label: Playing hxg6 or hxg3 to open the h-file while ignoring a more critical tactical demand elsewhere in the position.
931.description: All 10/10 positions feature the exact same mechanical move: an h-pawn capturing onto the g-file (8/10 hxg6, 2/10 hxg3), intended to rip open the h-file for a kingside attack. In every case, this capture is premature or misguided because it ignores a more urgent issue. In 3/10 positions (1, 6, 9), the error is a move-order mistake where a preparatory move (Qh6, Bxg7, Nxh7) should precede the capture to maximize its impact. In 2/10 positions (3, 8), the capture leaves a piece completely hanging (queen on g4, queen on b5). In 3/10 positions (2, 5, 10), it ignores a critical threat on the opposite wing—including one case of allowing immediate checkmate (Qxb2#). In 2/10 positions (4, 7), it misses a stronger tactical continuation (f4 neutralizing a bishop, Nxh2 winning the exchange). The average cp_loss is 2260, reflecting how catastrophic these routine-looking pawn captures can be. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions demanding precision rather than generic attacking moves.

927.label: A bishop captures a piece (usually another bishop) while ignoring a more urgent tactical threat that the opponent immediately exploits with a devastating response.
927.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a bishop capture (Bx__) that prioritizes winning or exchanging material over addressing a critical tactical requirement. 8/10 captures target another bishop, 1/10 captures a knight, and 1/10 captures a rook — all are piece captures, never pawns. The common error mechanism splits into two sub-patterns: in roughly 4/10 positions (2, 4, 6, 8), the bishop being moved was itself a KEY DEFENDER of a critical square or piece, so moving it to capture opens a tactical vulnerability (e.g., removing a bishop guarding c2 allows Nc2+ fork, removing a bishop guarding h7 allows Qxh7+). In the remaining ~6/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10), the bishop capture simply wastes a critical tempo while an urgent opponent threat (back rank mate, pawn promotion, advancing passed pawn, intermediate check) goes unaddressed. The average cp_loss is an enormous 3079, and only 1.1 good moves were available on average, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where the 'natural-looking' bishop exchange or material grab was a critical trap.

924.label: Single-step pawn pushes or king advances that ignore immediate tactical demands like capturing hanging pieces or avoiding forks/mates.
924.description: 9/10 positions feature significant blunders (avg 2256cp loss) where the player chose a quiet, forward-moving pawn push or king step instead of addressing an urgent tactical requirement. In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 5), the player pushed a pawn while a completely undefended enemy piece was available for free capture (hanging queen twice, hanging bishop once). In 3/10 positions (3, 8, 9), the player advanced their king into an exposed square that allowed a devastating tactical response (knight fork, checkmate in 2, or rook checks winning material). In 3/10 positions (2, 6, 7), a pawn advance weakened a critical square that the opponent immediately exploited with a piece invasion or fork. Position 10 is an outlier (1cp loss) where the king step was actually correct, suggesting the feature fires on the structural move type regardless of quality. All 10 moves are non-captures; 6/10 are pawn advances and 4/10 are king moves. None are piece moves (no knight, bishop, rook, or queen moves appear).

933.label: The king voluntarily steps one square out of its castled/sheltered position onto a tactically vulnerable square, either walking into forks/checks or wasting a critical tempo.
933.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king moving exactly one square from a sheltered position (typically castled kingside on g1/h8/g8) toward the center or along a nearby file (g1→f2, g1→g2, h2→g3, h8→h7, g8→g7). In every case, the king move is a quiet, non-forcing 'improvement' that either directly exposes the king to tactical exploitation or squanders a critical tempo in a dynamic position. Specifically, 3/10 positions saw the king walk into a knight fork square (Positions 5, 7, 9 with Nd3+, Ng5+, Ne6+ respectively), 3/10 saw the king step onto a rank/diagonal enabling devastating checks that win material (Positions 2, 3, 10), and 4/10 were pure tempo losses in positions demanding immediate forcing play like central breaks or piece captures (Positions 1, 4, 6, 8). The average cp_loss of 2062 reflects several catastrophic cases where the king walked into forced mate or decisive forks. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, confirming these were sharp positions requiring precision rather than slow maneuvering.

930.label: Active-looking queen moves (checks, captures, centralization) that waste critical tempo or place the queen on a vulnerable square, when a quieter precise alternative was required.
930.description: 8/10 positions involve queen moves that appear forceful or active but are actually counterproductive. 3/10 are aimless queen checks (Qe1+, Qe2+, Qd7+) that allow the opponent to improve piece placement during the forced response. 2/10 place the queen on undefended squares where it hangs (Qf1, Qb6). 1/10 captures material while missing a forced checkmate (Qxc1). 1/10 threatens a capture instead of executing it immediately (Qa4 instead of Qxa2). The non-queen moves (Bh5, Kf3) follow the same logic: choosing an aggressive-looking move over the position's actual demand. In 8/10 positions, only 1 good alternative existed within 50cp, meaning these were critical moments requiring precision. The consistent error is prioritizing apparent forcefulness — checks, captures, centralization — over the position's true tactical or strategic requirement, which was typically a quieter move (Bd4 pin, Rb8 blockade, Qxh3 pawn grab, a5 consolidation, Qe4+ mating sequence, Ba4 regrouping).

943.label: An aggressive knight leap lands on a completely unprotected square where the opponent's queen (or major piece) simply captures it for free.
943.description: All 10 positions feature a knight jumping to an aggressive-looking square with zero defenders, where it is immediately captured. In 9/10 cases the knight is taken by the opponent's queen (Qxg4, Qxg5, or Qxh4), and in 1/10 by a rook (Rxd6). The destination squares are g4 (4/10), g5 (3/10), h4 (2/10), and d6 (1/10)—predominantly kingside rim/near-rim squares that appear aggressive but lack any pawn or piece support. In every case the player's intent was to attack something valuable—a bishop (2/10), a rook (1/10), key pawns like e6/f7 (5/10), or to establish an outpost (2/10)—but they failed to verify the knight's own safety. The tactical motif is identical across all 10: 'hanging_piece' where the piece simply has no defenders. The average cp_loss of 405 confirms these are severe blunders, typically costing a full piece. The refutation is always a simple one-move capture requiring no deep calculation.

940.label: A rook captures a peripheral pawn while ignoring a critical king safety threat or superior tactical opportunity.
940.description: All 10 positions feature a rook capturing a pawn (Rx_), with 8/10 targeting rim pawns on the a-file or h-file. In 6/10 positions, this greedy capture allows or overlooks an immediate checkmate (back-rank mates in positions 1, 2, 4; king mating nets in positions 5, 7, 10). In the remaining 4/10, the pawn grab causes significant tempo loss by diverting the rook to a passive peripheral square while urgent priorities exist (stopping a passed pawn in position 8, maintaining piece activity in positions 3, 6, 9). The average cp_loss of ~5990 reflects that most of these are catastrophic, with 6/10 resulting in forced mate being either allowed or missed. The consistent thread is that all moves prioritize trivial material gain over existential positional demands — the rook wanders to the edge of the board to collect a pawn while the center of gravity of the position lies elsewhere.

934.label: Aggressive moves targeting the h3/h6 area that create seemingly dangerous kingside threats but are easily refuted by simple defensive resources.
934.description: 8/10 positions feature moves landing on or targeting the h-file (specifically h3 or h6 in 7/10 cases), with 9/10 moves ending on the 3rd or 6th rank. All 10 moves are aggressive in nature, attempting to create immediate kingside threats (mating attacks, piece captures, or pawn advances) targeting the opponent's king shelter. The refutations are consistently simple: in 4/10 cases a single pawn move blocks the threat (f3, gxh3, hxg3, f6); in 3/10 cases the moved piece is simply hanging to recapture (Qxh6, Qxg1#); in 3/10 cases a tempo-gaining counterattack ignores the threat entirely (Rxe8+, Nf4, Rg3). The average cp_loss of 2097 is extremely high, with 3/10 positions resulting in immediate forced mate. 7/10 positions had the blundering side playing Black, and all were middlegame positions.

932.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn move when the position demands immediate tactical action — missing forced checkmates, critical defenses, or hanging material.
932.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (h6, h6, h6, g3, h3, f6, a2+, d2, b4), with the remaining 1/10 being a passive piece retreat (Nf8). In 5/10 positions, the move was specifically a kingside pawn 'luft' push (h6×3, g3, h3) intended to create escape squares or prophylactically address king safety. In 6/10 positions, the player had a forced checkmate available (positions 1, 2, 7, 9 missed delivering mate; positions 3, 4 missed the only move preventing mate). The average cp_loss of 7035 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical tactical moments with narrow correct solutions. The unifying thread is a player operating on 'autopilot' — choosing a natural-looking quiet pawn push that addresses slow strategic concerns while completely ignoring the immediate tactical demands of the position. The moves feel reasonable in a vacuum but are catastrophically wrong given the concrete tactical reality.

939.label: King moves that advance directly toward a target in pure pawn endgames, often skipping triangulation or preparatory moves.
939.description: 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with no other pieces on the board, and all moves played are king advances toward a natural target (a capturable pawn or a dominant central square). The feature fires on positions where the critical decision involves precise king maneuvering—opposition, triangulation, or move order. 6/10 positions had 0 centipawn loss (the direct advance was correct), while 4/10 involved actual inaccuracies where the direct approach missed a subtlety: in Position 1, Kc4 instead of the more dominant Kc5; in Position 8 (810cp loss), Kf4 before the prophylactic h5; in Position 10, Kd4 without triangulating via Kd3/Ke2 first; in Position 7, Kd4 giving Black flexibility that Kc4 would deny. The recurring tactical tags are tempo_loss (6/10), opposition (3/10), and king_activity (10/10). Evaluations are typically decisive (avg ~550cp advantage for the moving side), indicating these are conversion-phase decisions where the winning side must choose the precise king route.
939.old_chip: Direct king advances in pawn endgames

944.label: A bishop moves to create a pin (or pseudo-pin) on a knight that is easily and immediately broken, squandering critical tempo and often abandoning a superior diagonal.
944.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to a wing square (b5, b4, g5, g4, or a4) to create a pin or pseudo-pin against a knight — typically Nc6 pinned to Ke8 (6/10 via Bb5), Nf6 pressured via Bg5 (2/10), Nf3 pinned via Bg4 (1/10), or Nc3 pinned via Bb4 (1/10). In every case, the pin is trivially neutralized: 7/10 positions feature a king still in center where simple castling instantly breaks the pin, while others are refuted by pawn kicks (h6, b5), developing interpositions (Bd7), or even winning the stranded bishop (Ba4+ refuted by b5). The average cp_loss of 271 reflects that these moves uniformly squander significant advantages. In 8/10 positions, the bishop abandons a functionally superior square (e.g., c4 targeting f7, e3 guarding the center) for the cosmetically aggressive but strategically hollow pin square. The positions consistently show that stronger alternatives involved concrete central action (d4 breaks, piece captures) or quiet development rather than premature pinning operations.

937.label: Voluntary king moves that place the king on a square immediately exploitable by checks, forks, or mating sequences, when non-king defensive moves were available.
937.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder, and in 9/10 cases the immediate refutation begins with a check or series of checks against the newly-placed king. The king was already in a somewhat precarious position, and the player attempted to 'solve' the king safety problem by moving the king itself, but inadvertently placed it on a square accessible to opponent forcing sequences. In 8/10 positions, the best alternative was a non-king move (piece development, blocking, capturing, or pawn advance) rather than a king retreat. The average cp_loss of 4807 reflects catastrophic consequences: 6/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the king move. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were already critical moments requiring precise defense. The consistent error is prioritizing king flight over addressing threats with pieces, resulting in the king landing on tactically vulnerable squares (open files, diagonals, or knight-hop squares).

936.label: Queen moves that relocate the queen away from a square where it performed an essential function — guarding a key square, maintaining counterplay, or restraining the opponent — often for a tempting but inferior purpose like grabbing material or giving check.
936.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that abandon the queen's most critical role in the position. In 4/10 cases (Qxf3, Qxg4, Qxg7, Qxf2), the queen grabs material (usually a pawn) while abandoning a vital defensive or counter-attacking function. In 2/10 cases (Qh7+, Qa4+), the queen delivers a purposeless check that allows the opponent's king to escape to a safer square while displacing the queen from its optimal post. In 4/10 cases (Qb5, Qf3, Qg2, Qa3), the queen repositions to an apparently reasonable square but loses control of a critical square or diagonal. The consistent mechanism across all positions is that the queen was performing an indispensable function on its original square — controlling b5 to prevent checkmate (position 6), threatening Qxd1+ as counterplay (position 10), covering a2 to prevent back-rank mate (position 9), maintaining pressure on c3 (position 1), defending the e8 rook via g2 threats (position 5) — and the played move severs that function. The average cp_loss of 4052 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 4/10 resulting in immediate checkmate or forced mate sequences.

945.label: King moves in pure pawn endgames where both sides have passed pawns racing to promote, requiring precise directional choice.
945.description: All 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with no other pieces, and all 10/10 involve pawn races where both sides have passed or potential passed pawns advancing toward promotion on opposite wings. The moves are exclusively king moves choosing a direction amid the race. When mistakes occur (6/10 positions have cp_loss > 25), the error is consistently choosing the wrong direction or square: in Position 3, Kd5 moved toward a pawn that couldn't be stopped instead of creating counter-threats; in Position 4, Kb2 chose the wrong square for the resulting queen endgame; in Position 6, Kc5 moved away from blockading instead of toward it; in Position 7, Kf4 landed on a fatal diagonal; in Position 10, Kf5 was one tempo too far from the interception path. The 4/10 positions with 0cp loss show the feature fires on the decision type itself—king directional choices in pawn races—regardless of correctness.

929.label: Superficially attractive moves (centralizations, captures, checks, pawn breaks) that ignore concrete 1-2 move tactical refutations by the opponent.
929.description: All 10/10 positions feature a move with a clear strategic justification — centralizing a piece (Nd4, Bd5, Nd6+), capturing material (Nxd5, cxd5), challenging opponent's pieces (d5, f5, Bf2, f4), or simplifying (Rb6) — yet each one overlooks a straightforward tactical consequence. In 10/10 cases, the refutation involves a simple concrete idea: a fork (Ne6 in position 10), a pin on a diagonal (Bxd5+ in position 5), en passant opening lines (position 1), capturing an undefended piece (Qxb4 in position 9), a winning trade into a superior endgame (Bxf2 in position 3), or exploiting an exposed king (positions 2, 4, 6, 7, 8). The average cp_loss of 1204 and average of only 2.0 good moves confirms these are precise positions demanding calculation rather than general principles. 6/10 positions involved the weaker side playing the blunder, suggesting players under pressure default to 'reasonable-looking' moves. 4/10 involved the stronger side squandering an advantage by playing for positional beauty (Nd4, Nd6+, f4, Rb6) instead of cashing in tactically.

935.label: The player makes a superficially attractive move (capture, piece attack, or aggressive advance) while ignoring a more critical immediate tactical requirement in the position.
935.description: 8/10 positions show a clear pattern where the player is drawn to a tempting secondary goal—capturing material (Nxh2, Nxe6, Qxa3), attacking an enemy piece (a3, Qa6), or advancing aggressively (Kc5, Ra7, Rh1)—while a concrete tactical vulnerability demands immediate attention. In 5/10 cases, the move involves a capture or pawn grab that appears to gain material. In 4/10, the player attacks or chases an opponent's piece. The critical thread is that each position had one specific urgent tactical requirement (defending a fork square, maintaining a key defender, covering a mating square, or exploiting an existing hanging piece) that the played move completely ignores. The average cp_loss of 1367 reflects how catastrophic these oversights are, and the average of only 2.0 good moves confirms these are narrow positions where the critical move is non-obvious. Positions 7 and 8 are trivial endgame inaccuracies (1cp and 20cp) that don't meaningfully fit the pattern, likely noise in the feature activation.

916.label: Moving a piece (usually a rook) to a quiet, repositioning square when the position demands an immediate forcing continuation (check, capture, or direct threat).
916.description: In 9/10 positions where the feature fires on mistakes (excluding Bc6 which was actually the best move at 0cp loss), the player chose a quiet piece relocation over an available forcing alternative. 7/10 moves are rook moves to apparently active squares (Rc2, Rc8, Rf7, Re8, Rd5, Rg8, Re8). The best moves in these positions consistently involved direct forcing actions: checks (Rxd5+ in position 3, Re8+ in position 6), captures creating threats (Nxd4 in position 5, b5 attacking the knight in position 8), forcing queen trades (Qb6 in position 9), or directly threatening enemy pieces (Bc2 attacking a rook in position 1, R2e7 challenging the queen in position 10). The blundered moves instead relocate pieces sideways or backward without creating concrete threats, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute tactical combinations. The average cp_loss of 2168 and average good moves of only 1.7 confirm these are critical moments demanding precision where quiet moves are punished severely.

942.label: Choosing an aggressive-looking pawn advance when the position demanded active piece play or coordination.
942.description: 9/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the blunder (a6, d5, c4, b6, d5, g5, e4, f3, f4), with only 1/10 being a piece move (Nd5). In contrast, the best alternatives were overwhelmingly piece moves: 8/10 positions had queen moves as the top recommendation (Ra2/Qb1/Nc3, a6/Kb8/Qxb2, Qe5/Qxd7/Qf4, e5/Rh3/Qc2, Qe6/h4/g5, h5/Kg2, Qa3/Qd4/Re7, Qc7/Qc6/Qe2, Rxh3+/Qg4/Qh5). The blundered pawn moves consistently look proactive — attacking an enemy pawn, advancing a passer, opening lines — but ignore the concrete demands of the position. In 5/10 cases the pawn advance released favorable tension or eliminated a restraining pawn (positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 9). In 4/10 cases the push created fatal weaknesses in the player's own camp (positions 2, 6, 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 1270 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural-looking' pawn pushes are when piece activity was the priority.

947.label: A rook is lifted to an intermediate rank (3rd/4th for White, 6th/7th for Black) as a vague improving move, missing an urgent tactical opportunity and often leaving the rook exposed as a target.
947.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving forward along an open or semi-open file to an intermediate rank — the 3rd or 4th rank for White (Rc4, Re4, Rf3, Re3), or the 6th/7th rank for Black (Rd6, Re7). These are 'half-lifts' that stop short of full penetration. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded an immediate forcing move (checks, tactical strikes, or critical pawn breaks) rather than gradual piece improvement. In 7/10 positions, the rook becomes a direct tactical target after landing (fork via Nd4, double attack via Bg4, pawn attack via f4, or exchange-winning Bishop attacks). In 8/10 positions, only 1 truly good move existed within 50cp of the best, meaning these were narrow positions requiring precision rather than general improvement. The average cp_loss of 257 reflects how severely these 'natural-looking' rook moves punish the player — they appear active and developmental but actually waste the critical tempo needed for forcing continuations.

946.label: Queen moves to an apparently powerful central square (typically rank 4 or 5) that is actually tactically flawed, losing tempo or enabling opponent resources.
946.description: 10/10 positions feature queen moves to central or semi-central squares that appear dominant but are concretely punished. 8/10 moves land on rank 4 or 5 (e4×2, d4, d5×2, f4, c5, e5), with h5 and b3 as partial outliers still aimed at 'active' squares. The common thread is that the queen reaches a square that looks impressively centralized but is tactically vulnerable: in 3/10 cases the queen gets attacked by pieces gaining critical tempo (positions 1, 3, 6 — pawn attacks or rook lifts/knight jumps force retreat); in 3/10 cases the move offers or enables an unfavorable queen trade that exposes back-rank or endgame weaknesses (positions 2, 4, 9); in 2/10 cases the queen abandons a defensive duty or leaves material hanging (positions 5, 7); and in 1/10 the queen blocks its own tactical resources (position 8). Position 10 (0 cp_loss) represents the rare case where centralization IS correct, suggesting the feature detects the move pattern itself rather than guaranteeing error.

938.label: King moves to a natural-looking but suboptimal square in won/lost pawn endgames, losing tempo or allowing the opponent resources.
938.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves (the one exception is h6, a tempo-wasting pawn push). 8/10 are pure king-and-pawn endgames with decisive evaluations already in place. The consistent pattern is the king choosing a plausible destination square that fails to optimize the specific technique required — whether that's maintaining opposition, outflanking, or racing to the correct wing. 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as a motif. The cp_loss varies enormously: 5/10 positions lose fewer than 15cp (mere technical imprecisions), while 3/10 lose over 150cp (where the directional error is catastrophic, as in Position 8 where Kf5 toward the kingside squanders a won game that required queenside play). The average good moves available is only 2.4, indicating these are critical junctures with narrow paths to optimal play.

941.label: Playing a constructive-looking move (piece activation, material gain, advancement) when the position demands addressing a more urgent concrete priority first.
941.description: 8/10 positions feature moves tagged with 'tempo_loss' — the player makes a seemingly reasonable improving move but critically misjudges the position's urgency. 5/10 moves are knight maneuvers (Ngxe5, Nc5, Ne4, Nc7, Nxe4) that look natural but are either premature or out of sequence. In 6/10 positions, the correct move required addressing a specific tactical threat before improving pieces (e.g., Position 3 needed Nxe5 before Ne4; Position 2 needed h4 before Nc5; Position 4 needed Kxh7 before Kg7). The average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions demanding one precise response, yet the players chose moves that would be reasonable in slightly different circumstances. 9/10 positions show the blunder enabling a concrete tactical punishment (mate, fork, passed pawn creation, piece win) that the 'improving' move either directly allowed or failed to prevent. The moves share a quality of looking purposeful to a human eye — capturing center pawns, repositioning passive pieces, advancing passed pawns — while ignoring the one forcing requirement the position actually demands.

951.label: Capturing with a pawn when a piece should have taken the same (or adjacent) target, forfeiting tempo, tactics, or critical pawn structure.
951.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical move pattern: the player captured with a pawn (exd5, dxe5, bxa6, dxe4, exd4, exf4, exf5) when a piece capture was dramatically superior. In 3/10 cases the best move was Qxd5 (queen takes instead of e-pawn). In 2/10 cases the best move was a queen capture with check (Qxd4+, Qxf4+), gaining a decisive tempo. In 2/10 cases a knight capture was best (Nxe5, Nxf5), enabling forks or outpost dominance. In 2/10 cases bishop or rook captures were best (Bxe5, Rxe4, Rxa6), maintaining piece activity. In 1/10 cases a rook capture prevented self-obstruction (Rxa6 vs bxa6). The consequences of the pawn capture varied but fell into consistent sub-patterns: removing a restraining pawn that held back the opponent (5/10), blocking one's own piece behind the advanced pawn (3/10), or missing a capture-with-check tempo (3/10). Average cp_loss was 333, confirming these are severe errors.

948.label: Player captures material or pursues offensive play while ignoring an immediate checkmate threat against their own king, resulting in mate-in-one or rapid forced mate.
948.description: In 9/9 positions, the player made a move focused on material gain or offensive ambition while their own king faced a lethal mating threat. 6/9 moves were captures (Qxh5, Rxa2, Qxc2, Qxf3, Rxa2) or promotion (a8=Q) — directly grabbing material — while the remaining 3 (Rg2, Qb8, Rd7) were aggressive piece placements pursuing attacking goals. In 7/9 positions, the immediate refutation was checkmate in 1 move (Re1#, Qxg7#, Qg2#, Qxd2#, Rd1#, Qxg7#, and Qc1+ leading to forced mate). The average number of good moves available was just 1.2, meaning in nearly every case there was exactly ONE defensive move that addressed the king's vulnerability. In 8/9 positions, the correct move directly addressed king safety — either trading the attacking piece (Rxe8+, Rxe2), moving the king (Kf8, Kxd6), or guarding the critical mating square (Qb2 covering g2, Rc6+ removing king coverage of c3). The positions consistently feature kings with compromised pawn shields or back-rank weaknesses where a single piece removal from defensive duty proves fatal.

949.label: A rook makes a tempting check or capture that removes it from a critical defensive role, allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned post.
949.description: All 10 positions feature rook moves that are either checks (5/10: Rb7+, Re1+, Rb1+, Rd1+, Rxc2+), captures (6/10: Rxc2, Rxg4, Rxe6, Rxg7, Rxb2), or both (1/10: Rxc2+). In 9/10 cases (excluding Position 7 where cp_loss=0), the rook abandons a critical defensive function — guarding the back rank (Positions 2, 3, 6), blockading passed pawns (Position 9), or maintaining pressure from its current file (Positions 1, 4, 5, 8, 10). The checks are uniformly pointless tempo-wasters where the opponent's king simply sidesteps (5/10), while the captures grab peripheral material while the real battle rages near the player's own king. The average cp_loss of 4737 reflects how catastrophic these moves are — 5/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the refutation. The pattern is strongest in middlegame positions (8/10) where king safety is paramount and the rook's defensive role is most critical.

958.label: The king moves to the exact square its own passed pawn needs to advance to, physically blocking its promotion or advance.
958.description: In 10/10 positions, the king moves directly onto the promotion square (or next advance square) of its own passed pawn. Specifically: Positions 1&2 have Kg8 blocking a g7 pawn, Positions 3&4 have Kf1 blocking an f2 pawn, Position 5 has Kf8 blocking an f7 pawn, Positions 6&10 have Kg1 blocking a g2 pawn, Position 7 has Kc1 blocking a c2 pawn, Position 8 has Ka8 blocking an a7 pawn, and Position 9 has Kb2 blocking a b3 pawn's next advance square. All 10 positions are endgames featuring a far-advanced passed pawn (on the 7th, 3rd, or 2nd rank). The severity varies enormously—from 1cp (Position 1) to ~10,000cp (Positions 2-4)—but the geometric pattern is perfectly consistent. The best alternatives always involve the king moving laterally or away from the pawn's file (e.g., Kg6, Ke7, Kh2, Kb4, Kc6) to clear the promotion path.

950.label: Player makes an active-looking move while completely overlooking an immediate forced checkmate (typically mate-in-1 or mate-in-2) that the opponent can deliver.
950.description: In 10/10 positions, the player's move allows a forced checkmate — in 9/10 cases mate-in-1 or mate-in-2, and in 1/10 a forced mate-in-13. The average number of good moves available was only 1.8, indicating razor-sharp positions where survival depended on addressing a single critical threat. In 10/10 cases, the player instead pursued their own plan: attacking (Ng5, f5), capturing material (dxe4), repositioning pieces to 'active' squares (Rc7, Rg5, Qg4, Qb6, Rd1, Qd7, Rf2).
