In approximately 7/10 positions, the blundering move specifically removed a piece from a critical defensive duty — the queen left g3 unguarding h2 (Qg4), the queen left proximity to e8 (Qb6), the rook abandoned back-rank coverage (Rg5, Rd1, Rf2), or the queen left contact with g7's defense (Qd7). The mating patterns exploited include back-rank mates (3/10), queen-to-weakened-pawn mates on g7/f7/h2/b2 (6/10), and rook-on-open-file mates (1/10). King safety tags appear in 10/10 positions.

952.label: A knight is moved away from a square where it performed an essential blocking or defending function, motivated by apparent tactical gains that prove illusory.
952.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight being relocated from a square where it served a vital structural role. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 7, 8, and partially 6 and 10), the knight was blocking a line (diagonal or file) that protected a queen from capture—once removed, the queen hung immediately. In 2/10 cases (positions 2 and 9), the knight was defending a specific piece or blockading a passed pawn, and its departure left material en prise. In 9/10 cases, the knight move was motivated by an apparently attractive tactical idea: giving check (positions 3, 6), capturing material (positions 4, 5, 10), centralizing aggressively (positions 1, 9), or repositioning 'defensively' (positions 7, 8). The average cp_loss of 1385 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—the functions being abandoned were typically the single thread holding the position together. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments where precise understanding of piece function was essential.

957.label: Slow, non-forcing rook repositioning moves played in positions demanding immediate tactical action (checks, captures, or critical pawn advances).
957.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves (Ra7, Rf2, Rg7, Rfe1, Ra2, Rf8, Rd5, Re7) with the remaining two being similarly passive piece repositioning (Qd7, Kf7). All 10 moves share the critical trait of being quiet, non-forcing repositioning moves—no checks, no captures, no direct threats—played in positions where an immediate tactical blow was available. In 6/10 cases, a forcing move (check or capture of hanging material) was the best option: Nh6+ winning the queen (Position 7), Rd3+ winning a knight (Position 10), Qxa6 capturing a free bishop (Position 2), Nc8 blockading a promotion threat (Position 1), d2! threatening promotion (Position 9), and Nxd3 capturing an undefended queen (Position 5). The average cp_loss of 322 and average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where only precise, concrete play works. In every case, the opponent exploits the gifted tempo to consolidate, defend hanging pieces, or execute their own tactical ideas that were previously impossible.

960.label: Speculative rook-pawn advances on the flank that waste a critical tempo while urgent central or tactical demands go unaddressed.
960.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-step rook-pawn advance (9/10 h-pawn, 1/10 a-pawn) played as a slow, speculative flank operation while the position demanded immediate concrete action elsewhere. In 5/10 cases, the correct move was resolving central pawn tension (capturing with Rxd5, cxd5, dxe4, Nxe4, or pushing e5/c5). In 3/10 cases, the correct move was addressing an immediate tactical threat (defending against Nxf7+, preventing f6 breakthrough, or shielding a queen from x-ray). In 2/10 cases, the correct move was a positional necessity (evacuating a piece from a dangerous file or square). The average cp_loss of 1194 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirm these are critical-decision positions where the one or two correct moves involve concrete central/tactical action, yet the player chose a non-forcing flank pawn push that creates no immediate threat and grants the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan. 8/10 positions were tagged with 'central_tension' or featured unresolved central pawn structures, and 10/10 were tagged 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif.

953.label: A knight on a rim or passive square is repositioned to an active-looking square, but this improvement move ignores a critical tactical vulnerability in the position.
953.description: In 9/9 positions, the blunder is a knight move that attempts to improve the knight's placement rather than addressing an urgent tactical problem. In at least 7/9 positions, the knight starts from a clearly offside square (a2, a5, a6, h2, h4) and jumps toward the center or an attacking square (c4, b4, f5). The destinations appear active—attacking pawns on b2, bishops on e3, or aiming for outposts—but create no immediate forcing threat. Meanwhile, the position demands addressing a concrete issue: a hanging piece (3/9), a king safety vulnerability (3/9), a critical move-order sequence (2/9), or a tempo-sensitive defensive task (1/9). The punishment is typically straightforward—the opponent captures an undefended piece, executes a forcing tactic against the king, or advances a decisive passed pawn—exploiting the fact that the knight move gave a free tempo for the opponent to act on their threat.

956.label: A knight moves to a seemingly attractive or aggressive square while abandoning a critical function or walking into a tactical vulnerability.
956.description: All 10/10 positions feature knight moves to squares that appear active or centralizing but are concretely refuted. In 6/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 7, 10, and partially 1), the knight abandons a critical defensive or controlling post — guarding key squares, blocking pawn breaks, or maintaining piece coordination. In 3/10 positions (5, 8, 9), the knight lands on a square where it becomes immediately capturable or trapped (via pawn fork, rook capture, or pawn advance). In 2/10 positions (1, 2), the knight move ignores a more urgent tactical priority (a hanging piece) in favor of a repositioning maneuver. The destination squares (h4, d6, b6, f4, b6, e4, g4, d5, d5, f5) all share the quality of looking superficially strong — they appear to be outposts, central squares, or attacking positions — but the player fails to calculate the concrete one-move consequences. The average cp_loss of 251 reflects the severity: these aren't subtle inaccuracies but major miscalculations driven by positional intuition overriding tactical awareness.

961.label: Moving the Queen or King to the a-file or h-file edge where it becomes displaced, vulnerable, or irrelevant to the central action.
961.description: All 10/10 positions feature the Queen or King moving to the absolute edge of the board — specifically the a-file (5 positions: Qa5×3, Qa4, Qa6) or the h-file (5 positions: Kh5×2, Kh4×2, Qh5+). In every case, the piece lands on ranks 4-6 of the rim. The consequences vary but cluster into clear sub-patterns: in 4/10 positions the move is a pure tempo loss where a concrete tactical strike was available (positions 1, 2, 3, 9); in 2/10 the piece literally hangs on the rim square (positions 4, 6); in 3/10 the King walks to the edge and becomes fatally exposed or offside (positions 5, 7, 8); and in 1/10 the King chooses the wrong edge square when a central alternative was equal (position 10). The average cp_loss of 1192 is enormous, and only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than peripheral repositioning.

964.label: Trading an actively-placed bishop for a knight on f3/f6/c6 when the bishop's pressure was enabling stronger tactical or positional opportunities.
964.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a knight (9/10 on f3 or f6, 1/10 on c6). In every case, the bishop was actively pressuring the knight from a diagonal (g4→f3 in 5 positions, g5→f6 in 4 positions, b5→c6 in 1 position), and this pressure was creating tension that enabled stronger plans. The exchange resolves this tension prematurely. In 5/10 positions, the player miscalculated the recapture — expecting a structurally-damaging gxf3 but facing a superior Bxf3 or Qxf3 (positions 2, 6, 8, 10) or expecting to weaken the opponent's structure with Bxf6 when the bishop recapture activates the opponent's pieces (positions 1, 4, 7). In 3/10 positions, the error is specifically a move-order mistake where capturing later (after a preparatory move) would have been far stronger (positions 3, 6, 9). The average cp_loss of 257 confirms these are significant errors, and the average of only 1.7 good moves available shows these were critical decision points where the tension needed to be maintained rather than resolved.

969.label: Playing a bishop to a square where the knight would have created a devastating tactical threat.
969.description: In 7/9 positions, the player moved their bishop to the exact same square where their knight should have gone instead: Bg4 instead of Ng4 (positions 1, 2, 3), Bb5 instead of Nb5 (position 4), Bg5 instead of Ng5 (positions 5, 9), and Bb4 instead of Nb4 (position 7). The remaining 2/9 positions (6, 8) still feature a bishop developing to create a superficial pin while missing concrete tactical strikes. In every case, the bishop move creates only a shallow pin or positional pressure that is easily challenged with tempo (h3, a3, h6+g5, or simply castling), while the knight on that same square would have generated forcing tactical threats: forks (Nc7+, Nc2+), attacks on vulnerable squares (Nxf7, Nxh2, Nxf2), or checks that exploited the opponent's uncastled king. All 9 positions occurred in the opening phase with at least one king still in the center.

962.label: Advancing a c-pawn or f-pawn one square forward vacates the origin square, allowing an enemy knight to invade with a devastating fork.
962.description: In 9/10 positions, the played move advances a pawn from c2→c3, c7→c6, f2→f3, or f7→f6, and the primary refutation is an enemy knight immediately invading the vacated square (c2, c7, f2, or f7) to deliver a fork — typically targeting two rooks or a king+rook. In 7/10 cases, the pawn advance was specifically intended to chase an enemy piece (usually a knight on b4/d4/e5/g4), but ironically created a superior invasion square for the opponent's pieces. The vacated squares (c2, c7, f2, f7) are particularly lethal because they sit adjacent to both the king's zone and the rook corners, making knight forks geometrically devastating. Position 1 is a partial outlier where the knight-to-vacated-square is a secondary refutation rather than the primary one (which exploits king exposure instead), but the mechanism still exists. The tactical motif is explicitly 'fork' in 9/10 analyses.

954.label: A knight is moved to a superficially attractive destination (centralizing, checking, capturing, or attacking) while missing a much stronger concrete tactical opportunity in the position.
954.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight move to a square that appears purposeful—centralizing (Nd5, Nd6, Ne4, Nd7), attacking a piece (Nc5, Nh5×2), giving check (Ng6+), capturing material (Nxg5), or retreating from perceived danger (Ng1)—but every move either abandons a critical function or misses a devastating tactic. In 7/10 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of optimal, meaning the position demanded precise calculation rather than general principles. The missed best moves varied: 3/10 required a non-knight piece (Be2, Be4, Rg1), 3/10 required the SAME knight to go to a different square (Ng4 instead of Nh5, Nxe5 instead of Nxg5, Nxf3# instead of Ng6+), and 4/10 required a completely different plan (pawn breaks, different knight captures). The average cp_loss of 1379 is catastrophic, with one position missing checkmate in one. The pattern strongly suggests players defaulting to 'natural-looking' knight moves based on positional intuition when concrete calculation was required.

970.label: A pawn advance aimed at attacking an enemy knight, creating weaknesses or ignoring superior alternatives.
970.description: All 10/10 positions feature the exact same pattern: the player advances a pawn to attack an enemy knight, but the pawn move creates critical weaknesses or squanders more important opportunities. The targeted knights were on f4 (2x), h4 (3x), g4 (1x), f5 (1x), e4 (2x), d4 (1x), and c5 (2x). In 7/10 cases the pawn advance weakened the player's own king shelter (g5, h5, f5, g4 near a castled king). In 4/10 cases the player missed a much stronger tactical continuation (Qh1# mate-in-one, Qh5+ winning attack, Qe3+ infiltration, Rhb8 back-rank invasion). The knight 'chase' consistently proved counterproductive because the knight either relocated to a superior square exploiting new weaknesses, or the opened lines/diagonals created by the pawn advance gave the opponent devastating counterplay. Average centipawn loss was 1231, reflecting that these positions often had only 1-3 good moves available (avg 1.9), making the impulsive pawn push particularly costly.

959.label: Aggressive pawn advances chosen over more forcing moves like captures, checks, or precise piece play that the position demanded.
959.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the played move — this is the most consistent geometric signal. In 9/10 cases these are mistakes (avg 249cp loss), with only position 10 (d6) being correct. The core error pattern: the player chose a superficially aggressive or logical-looking pawn push while missing a stronger alternative. In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 7, 9), a direct tactical shot was available — a capture or check (Kxe5 taking a hanging rook, Qxb2+ with check, Qxg7 winning material, Bxc6 enabling a safe d5). In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 8), piece development or repositioning was needed instead (Nc6, O-O, Nd2). In 2/10 positions (2, 6), a different move order was critical before committing the pawn. The average number of good moves was only 1.6, indicating these are positions demanding precision where the 'natural' pawn push was a trap. The pawn advances typically created immediate tactical vulnerabilities: overextended targets (e5 in positions 5, 7, 9), structural weaknesses (c5 in position 2, b3 in position 8), or simply squandered a concrete opportunity (positions 3, 4).

963.label: Critical move-order decisions in endgame passed pawn races where a single tempo determines the outcome.
963.description: 10/10 positions feature passed pawns as the central strategic element, and 9/10 are endgames. The unifying thread is that each position presents a critical tempo decision: advance the passed pawn immediately, or make a preparatory move first? In the positions where the move was correct (4/10 with 0cp loss: f5+, Kg5, c6, b6+), the player correctly identified the need to advance the pawn or king with maximum urgency. In the positions where the move was a mistake (6/10 with average 295cp loss: e3, Nd5, g6, Nc7, Ke6, Kc4), the player chose a natural-looking alternative—often a king move, piece move, or wrong pawn push—that squandered the critical tempo needed to win the pawn race. The consistent error in the mistakes is prioritizing preparation over immediate execution: Ke6 instead of d6 (position 9), e3 instead of d3 (position 2), g6 creating a blockaded pawn instead of maintaining flexibility (position 6), and knight moves instead of pawn advances (positions 4, 7).

973.label: Advancing the h-pawn (or a-pawn) as a slow flank attack when the position demands immediate concrete central action, development, or tactical exploitation.
973.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-developing rook pawn advance (9/10 are h4 or h5, 1/10 is a5) played instead of urgent concrete moves in the center. In 8/10 cases, at least one side's king was still uncastled or inadequately safe, making tempo critically valuable. In 10/10 positions, the best available moves involved immediate central action (e5, d4, exd5, Nxd5, Bxf7+), development completion (O-O, Nf6), or tactical exploitation of existing piece placement. The average cp_loss of 277 reflects that these positions were at critical junctures where concrete play was non-negotiable. In 6/10 positions the blunder occurred in the opening phase when development was incomplete, and in all 10 cases the tactical motif was identified as 'tempo_loss.' The intended purpose of the pawn push varied—kingside pawn storms (7/10), prophylaxis against opponent's pieces (2/10), queenside space (1/10)—but the fundamental error is identical: choosing a slow preparatory plan when the position's tactical demands required forcing moves.

967.label: A rook captures a bishop or knight that is adequately defended, losing the exchange after recapture.
967.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing a defended minor piece (bishop or knight), after which the defender recaptures and the capturing side loses the exchange (~2 pawns of material). In 5/10 cases the target is a bishop (positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 10) and in 5/10 cases a knight (positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 9). The defenders that recapture vary: queen (2/10), rook (5/10), pawn (1/10), and king (2/10). In every case, the rook was performing crucial functions—back-rank defense (positions 1, 7), maintaining pressure on open files (positions 3, 5, 9), or providing the only source of counterplay (positions 2, 8, 10)—making its loss far more costly than the nominal exchange value. The captured minor pieces often appeared dominant or annoying (centralized knights in positions 4, 7, 9; powerful bishops in positions 1, 3, 6), tempting the player to eliminate them regardless of cost. The average cp_loss of 1170 reflects that losing the exchange in these positions was typically catastrophic rather than merely suboptimal, because the rook's positional value far exceeded its material worth.

966.label: Making 'active' moves (typically rook lifts to open files) that challenge an opponent's strong piece while ignoring an immediate undefended piece or critical defensive obligation.
966.description: In 9/9 positions, the player made a move that appeared active—typically placing a rook or piece on an open file to challenge a powerful enemy piece (usually a queen)—while ignoring a far more urgent tactical vulnerability in their own position. In 7/9 cases, the move was a rook deployment to a back-rank square on an open file (Rb1, Rab8, Re8, Rbd1, Rd8). In 6/9 positions, the refutation involved the opponent's queen simply capturing an undefended piece or pawn (Qxc3+, Qxd5+, Qxa8, Qxh4+, Qxe6, Qxd5+). The blundered moves all share the quality of looking 'normal' or 'developing'—they appear to gain activity or challenge the opponent—but they fundamentally misread the position's priorities. In 8/9 cases, the best alternative involved a defensive or prophylactic move (Na4, Ne7, Rc8, Nd6, Rf3, Ra4, Qe2, Qf7, Kf8) that addressed the actual vulnerability rather than pursuing illusory activity. The average cp_loss of 1374 reflects that these moves typically lose a full piece or more.

968.label: Pawn advances or piece relocations that fatally weaken the player's own king's protective structure when the king is already under pressure.
968.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn advances of pawns directly adjacent to the player's own king (c4 near Kd1, f5 near Kg8, f3 near Kg1, b6 near Kc8, h5 near Kh8, h3 near Kg1, g3 near Kf1, g4 near Kf1), while 2/10 feature bishop moves that abandon defensive posts shielding the king (Be3 leaving c3/d2 unguarded near Kc1, Bc3 leaving the g5-c1 diagonal open near Kc1). In all 10 cases, the player's king was already exposed or under active attack, with the position already disadvantageous (avg starting eval significantly worse for the side playing the move). The moved pawn or piece was performing a specific defensive duty—guarding a critical square, blocking an invasion line, or covering a diagonal—and its removal immediately allowed a forcing tactical sequence. 9/10 positions resulted in the opponent exploiting the newly created weakness within 1-3 moves via checks, invasions, or mating attacks. Only 1.6 good moves existed on average, indicating these were already desperate positions where the narrow survival path required extreme precision rather than 'improving' pawn moves.

972.label: Moving a rook to double on a file or rank instead of executing an available concrete tactical strike.
972.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to join the other rook on the same file or rank (doubling rooks), when the position demanded an immediate forcing move instead. The disambiguated notation confirms this pattern: Rcc6 (doubling on 6th rank), Reg8 (doubling on g-file), Rgf3 (doubling on f-file), Rca1 (doubling on a-file), Rae8 x3 (doubling on e-file), Rdh1 (doubling on h-file), Rdh8 (doubling on h-file), Rdd3 (doubling on 3rd rank). In 9/10 cases, the best move was a concrete tactical strike: a queen invasion (Qe7), a rook sacrifice (Rxh2+), a passed pawn advance (d2), a knight capture (Nxd4), a discovered attack sequence (Qg1+), or simply moving the threatened piece to safety. The doubling moves look generically aggressive but are uniformly too slow, costing an average of 1151 centipawns. In 8/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating sharp positions where precision was required rather than generic improvement.

965.label: King moves in pawn endgames where a critical pawn advance or pawn-securing move should take priority over king repositioning.
965.description: 10/10 positions are endgames, and all moves are king moves in positions featuring passed pawns or critical pawn races. In the 4 positions with significant cp_loss (>100cp: positions 1, 3, 4, 9 averaging 360cp loss), the king moved when a time-sensitive pawn advance was required first — specifically Kg3 instead of a4, Kc7 instead of Ke7 (enabling ...f6), Kh8 instead of ...b6, and Kc6 instead of ...f6. In each of these cases, the pawn move was needed to secure a tempo advantage or deny the opponent a key square before the king repositioned. The remaining 6/10 positions had minimal cp_loss (avg 16cp) where the king move was actually the correct or near-correct choice, but they share the same structural fingerprint: pawn endgames with passed pawns where the king-vs-pawn-move decision is the critical fork point. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, confirming these are razor-thin tempo positions.

974.label: The queen passively retreats to the back rank (8th/1st) when an active or forcing move was urgently required.
974.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen retreating to the player's back rank (8th rank for Black in 9/10 cases, 1st rank for White in 1/10). The destinations are universally passive squares: Qc8 (5/10), Qf8 (2/10), Qd8 (1/10), Qe8 (1/10), Qf1 (1/10). In every case, the position demanded an active or forcing response—either a pawn break (e5, f5, fxg5 in positions 2, 4, 7, 9), a piece challenge (Na5, Nf6 in positions 3, 8), a tactical capture (Bxd4, Bxf3 in positions 6, 10), or centralization (Qd6 in position 1). The average cp_loss of 341 reflects how severely these passive retreats are punished. In 8/10 cases, the retreat abandoned a specific defensive responsibility—guarding a piece (e7 bishop in position 8, f3 knight in position 10), controlling a key square (d6 in position 1), or maintaining a pin (position 2). The positions consistently had only 1-2 good alternatives available (avg 1.4), indicating critical moments where precision was essential.

971.label: King moves in pure pawn endgames with passed pawns approaching promotion, where the critical decision is whether to advance the king or push the pawn.
971.description: All 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with no other pieces on the board. 10/10 moves are king moves, and 10/10 positions feature at least one advanced passed pawn threatening promotion. The evaluations are heavily decisive (avg |eval| ~550cp), indicating won/lost positions where conversion technique matters. Most moves (7/10) have cp_loss ≤ 11, meaning the king move was actually optimal or near-optimal. However, the catastrophic errors (Position 6: 9457cp loss from Kf7 instead of g7 promotion push; Position 10: 148cp from Kd6 before fixing pawn structure; Position 7: extending mate from 15 to 19 by Kd2 instead of c2) all share the same mistake pattern: moving the king when a pawn push was more urgent. The feature detects the decision point in pawn endgames where king activity competes with pawn advancement for priority.

977.label: Unnecessary king moves in the middlegame that waste critical tempo when the position demands immediate active play (pawn breaks, captures, or piece activation).
977.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forced, one-square king move during the middlegame when the position urgently demanded active play. In every case, the best move was a concrete action: a pawn break (f5, h6, e4, g5 in 4/10), a tactical capture or exchange (Bxe4, Nxe5 in 3/10), or a piece activation (Ne5, Rac1 in 3/10). The king moves were motivated by vague prophylactic ideas—improving king safety, clearing back ranks, centralizing for endgames—but the positions were too dynamic for such luxury. In 7/10 cases, the king move specifically created a new tactical vulnerability: pins on the e-file (positions 2, 5, 7), fork squares becoming checks (position 4 with Nf4+, position 9 with Ne5+), or exposing the king as a target for pawn storms (position 3). The average cp_loss of 223 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these were critical-moment positions with narrow paths to maintain the evaluation, making the tempo loss particularly devastating.

981.label: Immediate pawn promotion to queen in won king-and-pawn endgames, occasionally missing a slightly faster win by centralizing the king first.
981.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn on the 7th rank (or 2nd for Black) promoting directly to a queen in a pure king-and-pawn endgame where the promoting side has an overwhelming advantage (+700 or forced mate). The feature fires almost exclusively on correct or near-correct moves: 8/10 positions had 0cp loss, and only 2/10 (positions 1 and 8) showed any inaccuracy at all (4cp each). In those two marginal cases, the engine preferred centralizing the king one square closer to the opposing king before promoting (Kd4 before a8=Q, and Kd4/Kd5 before b8=Q), gaining a subtle tempo in the mating net construction. The promoting pawns landed on various squares (a8, b8, e8, g8, h8, d1, g1), showing no file preference. All positions featured exposed kings on both sides and the opposing king far from the promotion square.

955.label: A pawn or bishop makes an inferior capture (or advance) when a clearly superior target was available to the same or similar piece.
955.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder is a capture (Bxc8, exd3, dxc3, Bxe3, Bxf5, dxc3) or a pawn push that should have been a capture (e4 twice). In 7/10 cases, the SAME piece or pawn had direct access to a superior target: Position 1 (Bxc8 vs Bxa4 — same bishop, queen vs bishop), Position 2 (exd3 vs exf3+ — same pawn, wrong direction), Position 4 (dxc3 vs dxe3 — same pawn, pawn vs bishop), Position 5 (e4 vs exf4 — same pawn, push vs capture of bishop), Position 6 (Bh6 vs Bxe7 — same piece, reposition vs capture), Position 8 (Bxf5 vs Bf7 — same piece, wrong exchange), Position 3 (Bf5 vs Qf5 — wrong piece to same square). The remaining 3 positions involve making a greedy/aggressive capture when a completely different approach was needed. All 10 share the characteristic of the player being 'in the right neighborhood' tactically — using a reasonable piece, making a capture-like gesture — but selecting the inferior specific target. Average cp_loss of ~2993 reflects the enormous cost of these 'close miss' decisions.

976.label: An aggressive-looking wing pawn advance is played instead of a concrete piece move, tactical shot, or necessary defensive action that the position demands.
976.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing pawn advance, with 8/10 being wing pawn pushes (g4/g5: 6 times, h4/h5: 2 times, b5: 2 times). In 9/10 cases, the strongest alternative was a piece move or tactical capture (Ng4, Qh6, Qh4, Kb8, Nxc4+, Bd2, Ba6, Qf7, dxc3 en passant), while only position 5 had a pawn push (f4) as best—but one that directly attacked pieces. The pawn advances look aggressive and thematic but are critically premature or irrelevant: in 6/10 positions they weaken the player's own king shelter (positions 2,3,5,8,9 and partially 1), in 3/10 they miss available tactical combinations (positions 1,6,10), and in 1/10 the move addresses the wrong side of the board entirely (position 4). The average cp_loss of 2098 is enormous, and with only 1.8 good moves available on average, these are narrow positions where the flashy pawn push is a critical misevaluation of what the position requires.

975.label: King moves to a more confined square (typically the back rank or corner) that enables immediate mating attacks or decisive tactical exploitation.
975.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves as the blunder, with the king relocating to a square where its escape routes become fatally restricted. In 6/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8), the king moves directly to the back rank and allows immediate or near-immediate checkmate (Rb8#, Rh1#, Rxe1#, etc.). In 2/10 positions (4, 9), the king moves to the wrong adjacent square—creating a geometric alignment that allows capture-with-check or rook infiltration—when moving one rank differently would have been safe. In 2/10 positions (2, 10), the king makes a passive retreat to a slightly suboptimal square losing tempo. The average cp_loss of 5903 is extreme, driven by 7 positions where the king move allows forced mate. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision. The correct alternatives typically involved either keeping the king one rank further forward (Kf1 instead of Kg1, Kf3 instead of Kf2), moving to a square with more escape routes (Ke8 instead of Kd8), or playing an entirely different non-king move (Rg7, f3, Nf8, Qg2).

987.label: Advancing a passed pawn when piece coordination, king activity, or a tactical blow was required first.
987.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the blunder, and at least 9/10 involve pushing a passed pawn (or near-passed pawn) forward prematurely. The best moves instead demanded piece/king improvement (7/10 positions had king moves or piece repositioning as the best alternative), or an immediate tactical strike (1/10 featured a missed knight fork). The common thread is that the player fixated on the passed pawn's promotion potential—viewing it as the 'primary winning asset'—and pushed it forward one square too early, before the position was prepared to support it. In 6/10 cases the pawn advance allowed the opponent to blockade, capture, or simply ignore the pawn while exploiting the tempo loss. In 2/10 cases (positions 8 and 9) the premature push was catastrophic because the player needed that tempo for king escape from a mating net. The average cp_loss of 2108 reflects several positions where the push led to forced checkmate. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, confirming these are narrow positions requiring precision rather than intuitive 'push the passer' play.

982.label: A quiet pawn advance to the third rank (preparing a fianchetto or structural consolidation) played when the position demands immediate tactical action.
982.description: All 10/10 positions feature a one-square pawn advance to the third rank (from the moving player's perspective: b3, g3, b6, c6, e6, g6) in positions with urgent tactical demands. In 8/10 cases, the explicit intent was to prepare a bishop fianchetto (Bb2, Bg2, Bb7, or Bg7), while the remaining 2 (c6, e6) were slow structural/prophylactic pawn moves of the same character. In every case, the position contained at least one critical unaddressed issue: an undefended piece (4/10), an exposed king requiring immediate exploitation or defense (8/10), a forcing tactical opportunity being missed (9/10), or a piece needing urgent repositioning (7/10). The tempo wasted on these preparatory moves consistently allowed the opponent to either castle to safety (Position 10), execute a devastating fork or capture with check (Positions 1, 2, 8), win hanging material (Positions 3, 5, 7), or launch a breakthrough attack (Positions 6, 9). The average cp_loss of 324 reflects the catastrophic cost of choosing a multi-move positional plan in a single-tempo tactical crisis.

979.label: A pawn advance that removes the pawn's protective duty over a piece or square, leaving something hanging or critically weakened.
979.description: In 9/10 positions, the blunder is a pawn advance that directly removes the pawn's diagonal or lateral defense of a friendly piece or pawn, leaving it immediately capturable. Specifically: Position 2 (d5 removes d6-pawn's protection of Ne5), Position 4 (h5 removes h6-pawn's protection of g6-pawn), Position 5 (b5 removes b6-pawn's protection of Ba5), Position 6 (h5 removes h4-pawn's protection of Bg5), Position 7 (e5 removes e4-pawn's protection of Nd5), Position 8 (c3 removes c2-pawn's ability to recapture on d3), Position 9 (c3 removes c2-pawn's diagonal defense of Bb3), Position 10 (a4 removes a5-pawn's defense of b5-pawn), and Position 1 (h6 removes h7's ability to recapture on g6, forcing the structurally devastating fxg6). Position 3 (h4) is a tempo-wasting pawn push that ignores an overloaded defender situation, making it the one slight outlier. All 10 moves are pawn advances, 7/10 are flank pawns (a/b/h), and in every case the opponent's refutation involves immediately capturing the now-undefended piece or pawn. The average cp_loss of 379 reflects how devastating this pattern is—typically losing a full piece or equivalent.

985.label: King moves to escape pressure but steps onto a square that is MORE tactically vulnerable, walking into checks, open files, or mating nets.
985.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves where the player attempts to relocate their king but chooses a square that increases tactical vulnerability rather than decreasing it. In 10/10 cases, the king moved onto a square directly in the line of fire of enemy pieces — onto open files (Kd1 into d-file, Kc7 into d-file, Kd8 into d-file), into check sequences (Kg2 allowing Qxf2+, Ke2 allowing Qxf2+, Ka2 allowing Qxa3+), into rook penetration range (Kh7 allowing Rxg7+, Kg7 allowing Rxh7+), or forward into attacking piece coordination (Kg4 into f-file checks). In 7/10 positions, the refutation began with an immediate check on the square the king moved to or an adjacent square newly accessible. The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were desperate positions where king direction was critical — and in every case, a different king move (or non-king move) to a LESS exposed square existed. The better alternatives consistently involved retreating the king away from open lines (Kf2 instead of Kd1, Kh2 instead of Kg4, Kf8 instead of Kd8, Kc1 instead of Ka2).

983.label: A rook is developed to the back rank on an open or semi-open file as a 'natural' improving move while the player's own king faces an immediate tactical crisis that demands urgent attention.
983.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moved to the player's own back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black), and all 10/10 involve a critically exposed king. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 7, 8), the rook move to the first rank ignores an immediate tactical threat to the player's king (mating attacks, forks, or checks) that required a specific prophylactic or active countermeasure. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 6, 9, and partially 10), the rook move actually worsens king safety by blocking the king's own escape square on f8, directly enabling forced checkmate or perpetual check patterns. In 1/10 cases (position 5), the rook move is merely slow when a forcing tactical blow existed. The average cp_loss of 4015 is catastrophically high, with 4/10 resulting in forced checkmate (positions 2, 6, 7, 9). Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions demanding precise play where the 'natural' rook move was uniquely punished.

980.label: The queen is moved to a quiet repositioning square when an immediate capture (usually by the queen itself) was available and decisive.
980.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a queen move. In 9/10 cases, the move was a non-capturing queen relocation to a seemingly 'active' square (the exception, Qxa2, captured the wrong target). Meanwhile, in 8/10 positions the best move was an immediate capture — and in 6/10 of those, it was specifically the queen that should have been capturing (Qxf2+, Qxf1, Qxe2, Qxd5, Qxc1+, Qxd4, Qxf5). The average cp_loss of 2217 reflects that these 'repositioning' moves catastrophically miss concrete tactical opportunities. The consistent error is prioritizing queen aesthetics — placing it on a visually appealing square — over immediate material gains or forcing sequences that were available right now. The positions span both sides equally (5 White, 5 Black) and occur overwhelmingly in the middlegame (9/10), suggesting this is a pattern of calculation failure under tactical pressure rather than a phase-specific issue.

978.label: Quiet piece repositioning moves that place the piece on an undefended square directly attacked by an opponent's piece, resulting in immediate material loss or decisive tactical exploitation.
978.description: In 7/10 positions, the moved piece lands on a square directly controlled by an opponent's piece and is immediately captured or attacked with decisive tempo (Nc5 taken by Rxc5, Bd6 by Bxd6, Qd2 by Nxd2+, Bc2 by Bxc2, Qe7 targeted by Nd5, Nf7 taken by Qxf7, Bh6 vacates f8 enabling Qg8+). In 2/10 positions (Na6, Bd7), the piece itself isn't captured but the move ignores an existing piece/square that's already hanging to the opponent. All 10/10 positions feature the player already in a losing position (avg eval heavily against them), and only 2.2 good moves were available on average, indicating positions demanding emergency precision. The moves are exclusively piece moves (4 knight moves, 4 bishop moves, 2 queen moves — no pawns or rooks) that appear to be natural development or repositioning, masking their tactical vulnerability. 8/10 resulted in catastrophic losses (avg 4626cp), with 6/10 converting non-mating disadvantages into forced mates.

986.label: A passive one-square pawn advance (d3/e3/d6/e6/b3) that ignores an immediate tactical crisis where a piece is en prise, allowing the opponent to capture it.
986.description: In 8/10 positions, the player pushes a pawn one square forward as a 'supporting' or 'consolidating' move while a piece (almost always a bishop) is directly attacked and can be captured for free. In 3/10 cases, d3 leaves a bishop on c4 capturable by ...dxc4. In 3/10 cases, e3 leaves a bishop on f4 capturable by ...exf4 or ...gxf4. In 2/10 cases (d6), a piece remains undefended and is captured by the opponent's bishop or pawn. The remaining 2/10 positions (e6 and b3) show the same structural error—a 'quiet' pawn move that ignores an urgent tactical demand—though the punishment mechanism is slightly different (opening the e-file to expose the king, or weakening the back rank). All 10 moves share the characteristic of being small, positional-looking pawn advances that would be perfectly natural in similar but tactically quiet positions, but here they fatally ignore that a piece is hanging or a forced sequence wins material. The average cp_loss of ~2386 reflects that these moves typically lose a full minor piece worth of material or more.

992.label: A rook moves away from a critical defensive square near its own king, enabling an immediate mating attack that the rook was single-handedly preventing.
992.description: All 9/9 positions feature a rook move that abandons a vital defensive post, with 7/9 specifically involving Black's f8-rook leaving (Re8, Rd8, Rfe8, Rf6) and the remaining 2 involving White's rook vacating a key defensive square (Rf3 abandoning g2 defense, Rc1 abandoning e1/e2 control). In 7/9 positions, the immediate refutation is a queen invasion delivering checkmate within 2-5 moves via patterns like Qxh7+ Kf8 Qxf7# or Qh7+ Kf8 Qh8#. The average cp_loss is 7645 with only 1.1 good moves available on average, indicating razor-thin positions where the rook's defensive function was the single thread holding the position together. The moves all appear 'active' or 'developing' (centralizing on d8, e8, or the third rank) but catastrophically ignore that the rook was the sole guardian preventing an immediate tactical catastrophe.

984.label: A non-forcing pawn advance played in a position requiring immediate tactical attention, either creating a new vulnerability or ignoring an existing critical threat.
984.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance as the blunder, spanning every file from a to h across both colors. The critical commonality is that each pawn move is a slow, non-forcing action played in a position where urgent tactical issues demand immediate attention. In 6/10 cases (g5, g4, g4, e3, d4, d5), the pawn advance itself directly creates a tactical vulnerability—weakening a key defender's pawn cover (positions 1, 10), creating an immediately capturable target with tempo or check (positions 2, 3, 5), or severing a tactical interlock between pieces (position 4). In the remaining 4/10 cases (e3, a4, b5, h6), the pawn advance ignores an existing critical threat—a hanging piece (position 6), an imminent sacrifice (position 7), material loss (position 8), or literal checkmate-in-one (position 9). The average cp_loss of 2152 is catastrophic, and in every case, better moves existed that either addressed the tactical emergency or improved piece activity. The blundering player consistently chose a 'positional-looking' pawn advance over the required tactical response.

988.label: A bishop voluntarily retreats or repositions away from a powerful active square, surrendering a key attacking, controlling, or defensive function.
988.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved away from an aggressive or functionally critical square to a seemingly reasonable but actually inferior destination. In 8/10 cases the bishop retreats backward along a diagonal; in 2/10 (Be6, Bf6) it repositions laterally but still to the wrong square. The bishops were performing irreplaceable functions: controlling key squares that prevented enemy piece maneuvers (3/10: Bg5→Be3 abandoning h4 control, Be5 needed to cover d6, Bg3 maintaining mating threats), creating direct attacking pressure near the enemy king (3/10: Bh6→Be3, Bd7→Bh3, Bg3→Bd6), maintaining tactical tension enabling forcing sequences (2/10: Be6→Bh3 missing Bxd7+, Ba2→Be6 removing pressure), or holding critical defensive/structural duties (2/10: Bc5→Be3 abandoning blockade, Bd6→Ba3 leaving d4 hanging). The average cp_loss of 285 reflects that these retreats consistently transform winning/equal positions into losing ones by granting the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate, execute tactics, or seize the initiative.

997.label: A knight captures the f-pawn next to the opponent's uncastled king, but the king simply recaptures and the sacrifice lacks follow-up.
997.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight capturing the f-pawn (f2 for Black, f7 for White) adjacent to the opponent's king that remains on its starting square. In every case, the knight had been aggressively posted on a square attacking f2/f7 (typically g4 for Black's knight, e5 or g5 for White's knight). The critical shared error is that the Kxf2/Kxf7 recapture is always the strongest reply, winning a full piece for a single pawn. In 10/10 positions, the sacrificing side lacked the developed supporting pieces needed to generate real threats against the displaced king — no active queen access, no second attacker lined up, and typically a closed or semi-closed center preventing exploitation of the king's new position. The apparent tactical justification (forking queen and rook on f2, or exposing the king on f7) fails because the king itself eliminates the forking piece, and in every case the king proves perfectly safe on f2/f7 or simply walks back. All 10 positions were in the opening phase with both kings uncastled, and every position had 1-3 good quiet developing moves available instead.

991.label: Moving a bishop or knight to an attractive central/active square while ignoring an urgent tactical prerequisite (a check, capture, exchange, or defensive necessity).
991.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (6 bishops, 4 knights) being moved to a visually appealing square (e5, d5, f4, c4, f5, b4, c6) that appears strategically desirable but is played one tempo too early. In 7/10 cases, the exact same piece move or destination appears in the correct line but only AFTER a preparatory step (e.g., Position 1: Be5 appears as move 38 in the best line but is wrong on move 36 without Qf3+ first; Position 6: Nc4 appears in the best line but only after Bxf4; Position 10: Nc4 is correct only after securing the h5-bishop). In 10/10 positions, the move ignores a more urgent tactical demand—a check to deliver (Positions 1, 5), an exchange to force (Positions 6, 7, 10), a defensive post to maintain (Positions 3, 9), or a concrete threat to address (Positions 2, 4, 8). The average cp_loss of 2180 is extreme, and only 1.7 good moves were available on average, confirming these are critical positions where the 'attractive' move is uniquely punished while only precise tactical responses survive.

993.label: Knight jumps to a classical central outpost (d4/d5/e4/e5) when the position demands something more concrete—defense, development, or a tactical strike.
993.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving to one of the four ideal central squares (e5 in 6 positions, e4 in 2, d4 in 2, d5 in 1), choosing 'textbook centralization' over the position's actual demands. In 8/10 cases, the knight lands on an inadequately supported or outright undefended square, allowing it to be captured, driven back with tempo, or tactically exploited. In 7/10 positions, the move ignores an immediate crisis—either the player's own king safety (positions 1, 3, 7) or a concrete tactical opportunity like a removal-of-guard or overloaded-defender combination (positions 8, 9). In 5/10 cases, the knight literally returns to where it came from or is simply captured, meaning the move amounted to a pure tempo loss. The average cp_loss of 294 reflects how severely these 'attractive' centralizations are punished when the opponent has concrete refutations. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, suggesting these errors tend to occur in sharp positions demanding precision rather than general improvement.

994.label: Castling played as a routine developing move when the position demands immediate concrete action — either exploiting a tactic, avoiding a specific threat, or not walking into the opponent's prepared attack.
994.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling (O-O or O-O-O) played as an automatic 'improving' move when the position screamed for something more concrete. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 6, 10), castling missed a clear winning tactic available that turn (capturing a hanging piece, executing a pin, exploiting a temporary piece placement, or opening the center with a critical break). In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 8, 9), castling placed the king directly into the teeth of the opponent's pre-existing or easily-activated attack along files and diagonals pointing at that wing (queenside pawn storms, Greek Gift sacrifices, c-file breaks). In 2/10 cases (positions 3, 7), castling ignored an immediate concrete issue (a tactical break with tempo, or a hanging piece that needed defending first). The average cp_loss of 249 is extremely high for a non-capture/non-check move, and the average of only 1.7 good moves available shows these were critical moments requiring precision. 9/10 positions were in the opening phase, confirming this as a pattern where players default to the general principle 'castle early for safety' without verifying that castling actually improves the position at that specific moment.

999.label: Moving a knight away from a powerful central/active square to a passive square, missing concrete tactics the knight's position enabled.
999.description: All 10/10 positions involve voluntarily moving a knight FROM a dominant or active square (d4, d5, e4, e5, f5, c5, g5) TO a passive or inferior square (f5, b4, h3, c5, f3, g4, d3, e7, e7, h6). In every case, the knight occupied a classically powerful outpost — 6/10 from the canonical central squares e4/e5/d4/d5, and 4/10 from strong attacking squares f5/c5/g5. The departure consistently enabled the opponent to exploit newly opened lines (positions 1, 2), eliminated tactical coordination needed for forcing sequences (positions 5, 6, 7), or simply surrendered the initiative by wasting tempo (positions 8, 9, 10). 10/10 positions had a concrete tactic available that relied on the knight staying put or moving forward with force. The average cp_loss of 272 reflects the catastrophic nature of these retreats. Tagged as 'tempo_loss' in 9/10 and 'piece_activity' in 10/10 analyses, confirming the consistent theme of sacrificing dynamic potential for imagined safety.

990.label: A natural-looking developing or repositioning move places a piece on a square directly attacked by an enemy long-range piece, ignoring urgent tactical demands.
990.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing move (no captures or checks) played in a position demanding immediate tactical attention. In 7/10 cases, the moved piece lands directly on a square where it is immediately captured or won by an enemy long-range piece (Bf3 captured by rook on c3, Nf3 captured by bishop on b7, Nf6 captured by bishop on e5, Rf7 captured by rook on e7, Ra7 won via skewer on 7th rank, Nc6 captured by bishop with check, Rg2 won via exchange sacrifice). In the remaining 3/10 cases (Qd7, Bd7, Bb7), the move ignores an immediate mating threat rather than hanging the moved piece itself. The average cp_loss of 2968 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirm these are critical positions where one specific tactical need must be addressed. The behavioral signature is consistent: the player makes a move that would be logical in a quiet position—developing a piece, connecting rooks, challenging an enemy piece—but catastrophically misjudges the tactical urgency, essentially playing 'positional chess' in a position screaming for concrete calculation.

989.label: Material-grabbing captures or flashy checks that miss much stronger tactical resources already available in the position.
989.description: 8/10 positions feature a capture or check that wins material or gives a forcing move, yet misses a dramatically stronger tactical continuation. 6/10 moves are knight moves (Nd2+, Nxg2, Nxe6, Nxe3+, Ng6+, Nf8), while the remaining are bishop/rook captures of pawns (Rxh7, Bxa4, Bxh7, Rxg7). In 3/10 positions, an immediate checkmate was available but missed (positions 3, 5, 6). In 4/10 positions, the move grabs a pawn while ignoring a critical vulnerability—either the opponent's mating threat or the player's own exposed king (positions 2, 5, 8, 9). In 5/10 positions, the move displaces a piece from a square where it was enabling something stronger—a mate, fork, or coordinated attack (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6). The average cp_loss of 2967 is enormous, and only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these are sharp positions requiring precise calculation where the 'obvious' tactical move is a trap.

1000.label: The queen voluntarily leaves a powerful central or attacking square for a peripheral, less coordinated position—often lured by a check or side target.
1000.description: In 10/10 positions, the queen was already optimally placed on a dominant square (typically a central file like e4, e5, e6, f5, f6, or an aggressive post like e3/c6) and was moved to a less effective peripheral square. In 4/10 cases the move was a check (Qc7+, Qc1+, Qd1+, Qa8+) that looked forcing but allowed the opponent to neutralize pressure by simply sidestepping or blocking. In 6/10 cases the queen moved to a flank square (h5, h6, g3, e7, e3, c6) targeting secondary objectives while abandoning primary positional dominance. The analyses consistently identify 'tempo_loss' (9/10), 'piece_activity' (10/10), and 'centralization' (6/10 explicit) as key tags. In every case, the best moves involved maintaining the queen's current powerful position while improving other pieces (rook lifts, pawn advances, minor piece activation). The average cp_loss of 2048 reflects that these dominant queen positions often contained forced wins or overwhelming advantages that evaporated the moment the queen relocated.

995.label: Rook moves to a plausible-looking but incorrect square, abandoning a critical defensive post or missing the position's true priority.
995.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that appears natural—targeting an open file, attacking a piece, or doubling rooks—but fatally misses the position's actual requirement. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), the rook abandons a critical defensive duty: leaving f2 undefended, vacating the f8 defensive post, or moving off the d-file where support was needed. In 3/10 cases (positions 8, 9, 10), the rook targets the wrong piece or pawn when a superior capture or attack was available. In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 7), the rook actively self-harms by blocking its own pieces' escape or retreat. The average cp_loss of 1170 reflects how devastating these 'natural-looking' rook placements are—with only 1.8 good moves available on average, these were critical decision points where choosing the wrong rook destination was catastrophic. The moves share a seductive logic: placing rooks on open files (e-file in positions 1 and 4, c-file in positions 3, 5, and 9), but each time the position demanded the rook serve a specific tactical or defensive function elsewhere.

1002.label: Pushing the d-pawn to challenge an enemy e-pawn that attacks your piece, instead of moving the attacked piece to safety.
1002.description: In 8/10 positions, the player has a knight (on f3 or f6) directly attacked by an enemy e-pawn (on e4 or e5), and instead of relocating the knight, pushes the d-pawn (d3 or d6) to counter-attack the threatening e-pawn. The opponent simply captures the knight with the e-pawn (exf3 or exf6), winning a full piece since the d-pawn push does nothing to defend the attacked square. Positions 1, 6, and 10 show White's Nf3 attacked by Black's e4-pawn with White playing d3; positions 3, 4, 5, and 7 show Black's Nf6 attacked by White's e5-pawn with Black playing d6; position 2 shows Black's Ne5 attacked by f4 with d6 failing similarly. The remaining 2/10 positions (d4 leaving Bc4 undefended, e3 ignoring Bf4 attacked by g5) follow the broader principle of pushing a pawn to 'do something useful' while ignoring a piece hanging to a pawn capture. All 10 positions are in the opening phase, and the average cp_loss of 335 reflects losing approximately a full minor piece.

1007.label: Playing a routine rook centralization to the e-file (Re1/Re8) when the position demands an urgent forcing move or critical defensive action.
1007.description: All 10/10 positions feature the exact same type of move: a rook being placed on the e-file (Re1 for White in 4/10 cases, Re8 for Black in 6/10 cases) as a generic centralizing/developing move. In every single case, the position demanded something far more urgent: 6/10 had concrete forcing tactics available (checks, captures of hanging pieces, or sacrificial combinations), while the remaining 4/10 required critical defensive moves addressing immediate king safety crises. The average centipawn loss of 1207 is enormous, reflecting that these 'natural-looking' moves were played at moments of extreme tactical tension. In 7/10 positions, king safety was the dominant theme being ignored. In 8/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, meaning precision was critical. The rook-to-e-file move was always non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), granting the opponent a free tempo to either consolidate defenses or launch a decisive attack.

1006.label: Advancing a passed pawn one move too early, ignoring a more urgent preparatory move (king activity, piece repositioning, or addressing an immediate threat).
1006.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance — specifically a passed pawn push or pawn advance aimed at creating/supporting a promotion threat — played prematurely before a critical preparatory move. In 10/10 cases the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a core tag, and 10/10 involve 'passed_pawn' dynamics. The correct move was typically king activity (positions 4, 5, 6, 8: king moves needed), piece repositioning (positions 3, 9, 10: queen activation, knight jump, or rook-behind-pawn), or a critical capture/exchange (positions 1, 7: capturing a key pawn first). In 7/10 positions the pawn push itself appears in the best move's subsequent line — meaning the push was correct in principle but catastrophically wrong in timing. The average cp_loss of 3778 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but fundamental priority errors where a slow pawn move is played in positions demanding immediate action.

998.label: Playing a seemingly constructive piece move (usually a rook repositioning) while catastrophically ignoring an immediate king safety crisis that demands emergency action.
998.description: 8/10 positions feature explicit king safety crises where the played move ignores or worsens the situation. 7/10 moves are rook moves to seemingly 'active' squares (Rb1, Rg8, Rc1, Rg1, Rc1, Re8, Re8), with the remaining being a knight retreat, a queen relocation, and a king capture. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 8), the move directly self-blocks the king's escape route or walks the king into a mating net. In 5/10 positions (2, 6, 7, 9, 10), the move ignores an immediate tactical threat (forced mate, hanging piece, or promotion) to pursue a different plan. 6/10 positions had forced or near-forced mates as the punishment. The average cp_loss of 3120 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but catastrophic oversights of immediate tactical danger. The average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these were crisis positions with very narrow survival paths, yet players chose 'routine' constructive moves instead of the required emergency responses.

1003.label: A pawn advance that abandons its critical defensive duty—guarding a piece, protecting an adjacent pawn, or controlling a key square—leaving something immediately exploitable.
1003.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance where the moved pawn was the sole (or primary) defender of something critical. In 4/10 positions (2, 8, 9, 10), a b-pawn or d-pawn advance removed the defense of an adjacent piece (knight on c6, bishop on c5), allowing an immediate capture winning material. In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 5), a g-pawn advance removed protection of an adjacent pawn (h3 or h6) or created a structural hook, allowing the opponent to crash through on the newly opened file. In 2/10 positions (6, 7), a d-pawn or f-pawn advance vacated control of a critical square (c4 or e4), enabling an enemy pawn or piece advance that won material. Position 3 is the weakest fit, where g6 was primarily a tempo loss but also created a g6 target for h5. The refutations are strikingly consistent: 8/10 positions were punished by an immediate capture or advance exploiting the abandoned defensive function (Nxc6, Nxc5, Rxh3, Rxh6+, ...c4, ...e4, h5). Average cp_loss of 288 confirms these are serious blunders, not subtle inaccuracies.

1008.label: Playing a routine, passive bishop development move when a concrete forcing tactical shot (check, capture, or fork winning material) was available.
1008.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to a 'natural' square (Be7 x4, Be2 x2, Be3, Bd6, Bb2) while 1/10 is a quiet king move (Kb7) — all are non-forcing, non-threatening moves. In every case, a concrete tactical opportunity existed: 5/10 had available queen checks or forks (Qa5+, Qh5+, Qd4), 3/10 had piece captures winning material (Nxe5, Bxb5, Nc6), and the remainder had critical defensive or prophylactic moves. The average cp_loss is 323, and the average number of good alternatives was only 1.6, indicating these are narrow tactical windows where only one or two moves maintain the advantage. 9/10 positions are in the opening phase with at least one king still in the center, creating the tactical preconditions (exposed kings, undefended pieces on diagonals) that the forcing moves exploit. The bishops are consistently placed on 'textbook' squares (second/third rank: e2, e3, e7, d6, b2) suggesting the player is following general development principles rather than calculating concrete variations.

1009.label: Bishop moves to an undefended square where it is immediately or quickly captured, most often by an enemy knight.
1009.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop move to a square where it lacks adequate protection. In 9/10 cases, the bishop is captured or becomes capturable by a knight (positions 1-7, 9-10), with the remaining case (position 8) being a wrong capture-order error where the bishop leaves a critical restraining diagonal. In 7/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10), the bishop is immediately hanging on its new square and can be taken within one move. The moves consistently look purposeful—developing (Bg4, Bc4), centralizing (Be5, Bd4), attacking (Bb4, Bh4, Bc3), or repositioning (Bh5)—but all overlook that the destination square is directly controlled by an enemy piece, usually a knight. The average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these typically cost a full minor piece. Both sides commit this error (Black 7/10, White 3/10), across all phases (opening 4/10, middlegame 5/10, endgame 1/10), suggesting a universal pattern of prioritizing bishop activity over basic piece safety.

996.label: Non-forcing moves (no checks, captures, or threats) played in positions that demanded immediate concrete action to address tactical vulnerabilities.
996.description: All 10/10 positions share the critical feature that the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) in a position where concrete tactical action was urgently required. In 3/10 cases (c6, Nh7, c5), the player missed an immediately available winning or maintaining capture (cxd6, Nxe4, Rxa3). In 3/10 cases (Rf8, Rc2, Rd2), the player moved a piece to a square where it either abandoned a critical defensive duty or became tactically vulnerable (leaving Be6 hanging, allowing Nb4 fork, exposing e1 to mate). In 2/10 cases (h3, Qc2), prophylactic or developmental moves ignored the exposure of key pieces (f2 pawn, Bb5). In 2/10 cases (Kf3, Nd5), pieces were placed on squares easily exploited by the opponent. The average cp_loss of 1224 and only 2.2 good moves available confirm these were critical junctures. The consistent error is prioritizing abstract positional improvement (piece repositioning, pawn advances, prophylaxis) over the immediate tactical reality screaming for attention.

1005.label: Captures (mostly queen captures) that grab apparently free material but overlook immediate tactical refutations exploiting what the capturing piece left undefended.
1005.description: 10/10 positions feature a capture that grabs material (pawns or pieces) that appears free or advantageous. 8/10 involve the queen making the capture directly. The captures all share a common flaw: they prioritize short-term material gain over piece coordination, defensive obligations, or tactical precision. In 4/10 cases (positions 3, 6, 7, 10), the player captured with the wrong piece when a different piece could capture the same target more effectively. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4), the capture removed a piece from a critical defensive post, enabling devastating counterattacks. In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 9), the capture displaced the queen to an exposed square where it could be exchanged or attacked with tempo. In 1/10 cases (position 8), the target was simply defended and the queen was immediately recaptured. The average cp_loss of 1389 reflects catastrophic consequences — these aren't subtle inaccuracies but game-losing blunders stemming from insufficient calculation after a tempting capture.

1012.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing rook repositioning move in a position that demands immediate tactical action with a different piece.
1012.description: All 9/9 positions feature a rook move that is passive, non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no direct attacks), and purely consolidating or repositioning in nature. In every case, the position demanded immediate sharp play — typically with a completely different piece type. In 3/9 positions (Positions 1, 3, 4), the rook move left another piece tactically hanging. In 3/9 positions (Positions 5, 6, 7), the rook move missed a decisive forcing blow (a capture, check, or forced mate). In 2/9 positions (Positions 8, 9), the rook moved to a square that created a new tactical vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 1530 is catastrophic, and the average of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these were narrow, critical positions where only forcing continuations maintained the evaluation. The best moves were overwhelmingly non-rook moves: checks (Qf5+, Re2+), captures (Bxe2, Nxg4), or active piece redeployments (Bd1, Ne2, Ng6, Nf5). The consistent error is treating a tactically explosive position as one requiring patient consolidation.

1001.label: Playing a passive king move instead of addressing an urgent tactical obligation, typically a piece that is hanging or capturable.
1001.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves as the mistake. In 5/10 positions (2, 6, 7, 8, 9), there was a clearly hanging piece—either the player's own piece left undefended (positions 2, 6, 7) or an opponent's piece that could be captured for massive gain (positions 8, 9)—and the player chose a king move instead. These 5 positions account for the largest cp_losses (295, 680, 331, 1285, 10263), strongly indicating the feature activates most on king moves that ignore material crises. In the remaining 5 positions, the king moved to a tactically inferior square: walking into check diagonals (position 1), allowing tempo-gaining checks (positions 4, 5), retreating to a passive corner instead of centralizing (position 10), or making the only available move in a lost position (position 3). The average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are high-pressure moments where the urgent tactical priority is narrow, yet the player defaults to a king repositioning move—prioritizing perceived king comfort over concrete board obligations.

1015.label: After capturing a knight sacrifice on f7 in the Two Knights Defense, Black passively retreats the king to e8 instead of consolidating with d5 or advancing to g6/h7, fatally opening the h5-e8 diagonal.
1015.description: 10/10 positions arise from Italian Game / Two Knights Defense lines where White sacrificed a knight on f7 (Nxf7 Kxf7), leaving Black's king exposed on f7 but up material. In all 10 cases, Black retreats the king backward (9/10 play Ke8, 1/10 plays Kf8) instead of the correct consolidating moves (d5 or Kg6→h7). The catastrophic version appears in 7/10 positions where Ke8 opens the h5-e8 diagonal for Qh5+, leading to forced checkmate (eval swings of 10,000+ cp). In 3/10 positions, the same Ke8 retreat is less immediately fatal but still costs ~279cp by wasting a crucial tempo that allows White to complete development and generate full compensation for the sacrificed piece. The consistent thread is that the king on f7 actually serves a defensive purpose by blocking the diagonal, and the 'natural' retreat to its starting square is the worst possible choice.

1013.label: A pawn captures an enemy knight while ignoring a more urgent tactical threat, allowing a devastating response.
1013.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing an enemy knight, prioritizing immediate material gain while overlooking a critical tactical vulnerability. In 10/10 cases, the captured piece is specifically a knight. The pawn performing the capture was typically serving a defensive function—blocking a file (positions 1, 6), shielding diagonal access to the king (position 8), restraining an enemy piece from attacking (positions 7, 10), or maintaining tension that should have been resolved differently (positions 4, 5). In 7/10 positions, the punishment involves an immediate king-safety crisis (discovered checks, opened files/diagonals toward the king, or mating attacks). In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 10), the punishment involves capturing an undefended piece that the moved pawn was indirectly protecting or that the opponent's newly-freed piece can now reach. The average cp_loss of 2202 reflects how catastrophic these captures are—including 2 forced mates. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical positions requiring precise calculation rather than automatic captures.

1017.label: Playing a non-queen move while the player's own queen is en prise to immediate capture.
1017.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical core pattern: the player's queen is directly attacked or undefended on an open line (diagonal, file, or by a knight), and instead of addressing this critical threat, the player makes an unrelated move — developing a piece, pushing a pawn, or moving a rook. In 10/10 cases, the best moves involved either moving the queen to safety (positions 2-5, 7-10) or capturing the attacking piece (position 1 Qe7, position 6 Qb3). The moves played are superficially reasonable — bishop development (Be3, Bc3, Bg5, Bh6 = 4/10), rook centralization (Rg3, Rfe1, Rc1 = 3/10), pawn advances (b4, a4 = 2/10), and a pawn capture (cxd4 = 1/10) — but all completely ignore the one-move tactical threat to the queen. In 9/10 positions, the refutation is a simple one-move capture of the queen (Bxg5, Rxc2, Nxd3, bxc3, Bxd2, Bxb6, Bxd3, Bxc4, Nxa7), with position 10 requiring a check before the capture. The average centipawn loss is 617, corresponding approximately to losing a queen for a minor piece.

1010.label: Moving a piece away from a critically exposed king to pursue irrelevant activity elsewhere, ignoring an immediate tactical crisis.
1010.description: 9/9 positions feature a king (usually the player's own) that is acutely vulnerable — exposed on f1/d2/c1/d8 without castling, or with a fatally weak pawn shield. In every case, the player chose a move that either removed a key defender from the king's vicinity (Qa5, Qa4, Qh5, Na4 moving queens/knights to the rim), pushed a pawn that weakened the king's shelter (f4 opening f3, d5 ignoring a fork), or redirected an attacking piece away from the decisive zone (Rge7 leaving the back rank, Rh1 abandoning the e-file). The best moves in 9/9 positions involved addressing the king's immediate danger first — keeping the queen on its defensive post (e8), relocating the king to safety (Kg2, Kg1, Kb1), trading off attacking pieces, or blocking infiltration routes. The refutations in 8/9 positions directly exploited the abandoned defensive zone within 1-3 moves, with 4/9 resulting in immediate checkmate or forced mate. Queen moves to the queenside rim (Qa5, Qa5, Qa4) account for 3/9 positions, all sharing the exact same error of pulling the queen far from a kingside crisis.

1011.label: A pawn performing a critical structural or defensive function is pushed one square too far, abandoning its duty and creating immediate exploitable weaknesses.
1011.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance where the pawn was already optimally placed for a structural role. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 6, 8, 10), the pawn was guarding an adjacent pawn or blocking a critical diagonal toward the king, and its advance immediately exposed a tactical vulnerability (Nxg6, f6 wedge, h6 wedge, Bxh1, Qh5+). In 3/10 positions (5, 7, 9), a strong outpost pawn (c5 or d4) was pushed one square further, converting from a cramping anchor into an unsupported overextended target that could be captured for free. In 2/10 positions (2, 4), the pawn advance wasted the critical tempo needed to address the actual positional demands. The average cp_loss of 1206 reflects how catastrophic these seemingly innocuous space-gaining pushes are — the player perceives forward motion as progress while actually demolishing the structural foundation of their position.

1016.label: A minor piece is quietly moved to a seemingly better square, not realizing it was tactically protecting another piece from capture.
1016.description: In 10/10 positions, a minor piece (bishop in 7/10, knight in 3/10) is repositioned with a quiet, non-capturing move to what appears to be a more active or natural square. In 9/10 cases, the moved piece was performing a critical but non-obvious defensive function—either directly defending another piece, blocking a dangerous line, or maintaining a tactical threat (like a check or counter-capture) that prevented the opponent from capturing something else. Once the guardian is relocated, a piece is immediately left hanging: undefended rooks (positions 2, 6, 9), undefended knights (positions 1, 4), an undefended queen (positions 5, 7), an undefended bishop (position 8), or a knight en prise without its tactical justification (position 3). Position 10 is a slight variant where the repositioned piece itself becomes trapped. The average cp_loss of 411 reflects that these moves typically lose a full piece worth of material. In 9/10 positions, the refutation is simply capturing the newly-undefended piece.

1018.label: A non-forcing knight repositioning move that looks active but fatally ignores an immediate tactical crisis requiring a forcing or defensive response.
1018.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight move that is neither a check nor a capture — a pure repositioning to a seemingly 'active' or 'aggressive' square. In every case, the position demanded urgent action: 4/10 required addressing immediate mating threats against the player's own king, 3/10 needed to execute available forcing sequences (checks, captures of hanging material), 2/10 required maintaining a critical piece configuration that was the foundation of the position's evaluation, and 1/10 needed to keep the knight on a safe square rather than moving it to where it's trapped. The average cp_loss of 3041 is extreme, with 4/10 positions involving mate-in-N collapses. The average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are razor-thin positions where one tempo wasted on knight improvement is catastrophic. The knight destinations vary (central: d5, e5, f3, d3, c3; rim: g4, h3; mixed: f2, c6, d7) but all share the quality of appearing purposeful while actually being irrelevant to the position's critical demand.

1019.label: Moving a piece to an edge-file square (a4/a5/h4/h5) where it becomes offside, when the position demands central action or maintaining defensive duties.
1019.description: 9/10 positions feature a piece moving to the a-file or h-file on ranks 4 or 5 (Nh5, Na4, Ra5, Qh4, Qa4, Nh4, Ba5, Ba5, Qa5), with only 1/10 (Nc5) deviating geometrically but sharing the same thematic error. In every case, the move looks superficially active—targeting a specific piece or pawn on the rim—but actually abandons a critical function. In 5/10 positions, the piece was directly guarding key squares or the king (Nh5 left f6 unguarded, Nh4 left f3/d4/e5 unguarded, Ba5×2 abandoned the c3-c1 diagonal defense). In 4/10 positions, urgent central action was available (e5 break, c4 break, Bf4 development) but the player chose peripheral repositioning instead. The average cp_loss of 1169 reflects that these rim-ward moves consistently allow devastating tactical refutations—forks, back-rank mates, passed pawn advances, or queen invasions through the vacated squares.

1023.label: Pawn captures that prematurely resolve pawn tension in endgames, when maintaining the tension or improving the king first would preserve more options.
1023.description: All 9/9 positions are endgames where the player makes a pawn capture that resolves existing pawn tension between adjacent files. In 7/9 positions, the better alternative was a king move (improving king position before committing to the exchange) or maintaining the tension entirely. The captures consistently create structural concessions: 6/9 positions involve creating or enabling passed pawns for the opponent, while the remaining cases eliminate the player's own dynamic resources (breakthrough potential, blockading pawns, or restraining barriers). The average cp_loss of 249 is skewed by one catastrophic 1211cp blunder (position 9, where axb3 eliminated a winning breakthrough motif), while 4/9 positions show near-zero loss, suggesting the feature identifies the move TYPE rather than severity. The positions span both kingside tension (hxg4, fxg4, fxg5, hxg6, fxe5) and queenside tension (axb5, axb3, dxc3), but all share the same strategic error of committing to an exchange before the position demands it.

1026.label: A rook delivers a tempting check along an open file against an exposed king, but the check wastes tempo, misplaces the rook, or allows the king to reach a superior square.
1026.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check along an open file (primarily the e-file or d-file) against a king that appears exposed in the center. In 9/10 cases this was a significant blunder (avg ~4800cp loss), and in 8/10 positions there was only 1 good move available, meaning precision was critical. The recurring error is the 'patzer sees a check' syndrome applied specifically to rook checks: the check appears forcing and aggressive but actually helps the opponent. In 4/10 positions, the check drove the king to a safer square (Kd8, Kd6, Kf7, Kd1) where it escaped the attacking geometry. In 3/10 positions, the wrong piece delivered the check (a queen check would have forced a weaker interposition or controlled key squares). In 2/10 positions, the wrong rook was used, removing it from a critical file. In 1/10 the rook checked on the wrong square (e8 instead of e6), failing to cover escape routes. The common denominator is that a quiet or differently-ordered move would have maintained a mating attack or decisive advantage, but the instinct to give an immediate rook check squandered the position's potential.

1014.label: Non-forcing preparatory or repositioning moves played in positions where an immediate tactical strike (usually a capture or fork) was available.
1014.description: All 10 positions share the same fundamental error: playing a quiet, non-forcing move when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 10/10 cases, the played move was non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat). In 7/10 positions, the best available move was a capture or tactical strike (Nd4, Nxe5, Nxf7, Nb4, Nxb4, Qxd4, c4 with tempo).
