The moves are typically piece repositioning (Rg8, Rb1×2, Ra1 — 4/10 rook moves), bishop 'development' (Bg5, Ba6, Bg4 — 3/10), prophylactic pawn pushes (a3, h6 — 2/10), or misguided knight development (Na6 — 1/10). In 9/10 cases, 'tempo_loss' was identified as a key motif, and 'missed_tactic' appeared in 9/10. The average cp_loss of 311 confirms these are severe blunders, with the quiet moves allowing opponents to either consolidate advantages, execute tactical refutations, or exploit the hanging/misplaced pieces that result from the wasted tempo.

1024.label: Playing an indirect or preparatory move in an endgame when the position demands immediate, direct execution of the winning or drawing plan.
1024.description: 9/9 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif, and 8/9 are endgame positions. In each case, the player makes a move that appears reasonable or even active (5/9 are rook moves, often along the a-file), but which addresses a secondary concern instead of executing the most urgent plan. The best moves consistently involve immediate direct action: capturing available material (Positions 4, 8), advancing the key passed pawn (Positions 7, 8), placing the rook behind the passed pawn (Position 2), or marching the king (Position 10). Instead, the played moves are one step removed—prophylactic pawn pushes (b3, g6), rook repositioning to passive squares (Ra5, Rc5, Ra7), pointless checks (Ra6+), or piece retreats from ideal squares (Ne1). In 6/9 positions, the opponent exploits the wasted tempo by centralizing their king or advancing a passed pawn unchallenged. The average cp_loss of 121 reflects that these aren't random blunders but systematic failures to identify the position's urgency.

1028.label: Non-forcing moves to peripheral squares (a/b/h files) that squander critical tempo when immediate action is required elsewhere on the board.
1028.description: All 10/10 positions feature moves to edge files (a, b, or h) or rank-1 squares that create no immediate threat. 6/10 are bishop moves to rim squares (Ba5, Ba6, Bb1, Bh5, Bh4, plus Nb2 as a minor piece). 4/10 are quiet pawn pushes on the a or h file (b5, a3, a4, h6). None are checks, captures, or forcing moves. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 analyses. In 7/10 positions, king safety was the critical concern being ignored. In 4/10 endgame positions, pawn races demanded every tempo. The consistent thread is that the player redirects a piece or pawn toward the board's periphery—away from the critical sector—while the opponent has concrete threats (mating attacks, pawn promotion, piece activation) that exploit the wasted move. The average cp_loss of 1030 (inflated by one position allowing forced mate) reflects how punishing these tempo losses are in sharp positions.

1032.label: A knight moves away from a square where it was shielding or defending a rook, leaving that rook immediately capturable or fatally exposed.
1032.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight moves away from a critical defensive post, and in at least 8/10, the knight was specifically functioning as a physical shield or direct defender of a friendly rook—blocking a file or rank from enemy penetration, or serving as the sole piece protecting the rook from capture. The knight moves typically appear active or tempting (6/10 involve captures or attacks on enemy pieces, 4/10 target pawn grabs or centralization), but they all fatally remove a structural defensive function. In positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10, the knight was explicitly blocking a file or rank, preventing an enemy rook from capturing a friendly rook. In position 7, the knight moved to an entirely undefended square. The punishment in 8/10 cases is an immediate or near-immediate capture of the now-exposed rook (or forced mate via the opened line in position 10). The average cp_loss of 1255 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors—they're structural collapses triggered by a single knight move.

1030.label: Non-forcing knight repositioning moves that ignore immediate tactical vulnerabilities requiring urgent attention.
1030.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight move that is non-capturing and non-checking — a purely repositioning maneuver that looks attractive (centralizing, attacking a piece, rerouting) but fatally ignores a more urgent tactical need. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 7, 8), the knight move leaves a major piece hanging or undefended, allowing simple capture. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 6, 10), the knight moves AWAY from a critical defensive duty, enabling the opponent to exploit the vacated control (queen traps, checks on newly unguarded diagonals). In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 9), the knight lands on a square where it is immediately vulnerable to pawn attack or is completely passive, gifting the opponent free tempi to launch decisive operations. The average cp_loss of 314 reflects that these are catastrophic errors, and the average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these were high-tension positions demanding precise, often forcing play — yet the player chose a quiet knight maneuver instead.

1022.label: Playing quiet, non-forcing moves (typically pawn pushes) in tactically critical positions that demand immediate concrete action.
1022.description: 10/10 positions involved playing a slow, non-urgent move when the position required addressing an immediate tactical crisis. 7/10 moves were quiet pawn pushes (e5, a5, d3, h5, h5, e3, cxd4), 2/10 were king moves to vulnerable squares (Kb8, Kd7), and 1/10 was a bishop development (Be6). In every case, the position had extremely few good options (avg 1.6 good moves), signaling that only precise, forcing responses worked. The best moves were typically checks (Qa5+, Qd2+), captures (Qxb2, exd5), urgent piece improvements (Nc5, Nf6), or prophylaxis addressing the specific threat (Kf8, a6). Instead, the played moves addressed secondary positional concerns—undermining pawn chains, preparing future plans, or 'improving' king placement—while the opponent's most dangerous tactical resource went unaddressed for one critical tempo. 8/10 positions featured an uncastled or exposed king, and in 9/10 cases the refutation exploited the exact threat the quiet move failed to address.

1029.label: A piece performing a critical (often hidden) defensive function is moved for a tempting capture or 'active' relocation, immediately creating a catastrophic tactical vulnerability.
1029.description: In 9/9 positions, the blundering move removes a piece from a square where it was performing an essential protective duty—blocking a dangerous diagonal, contesting a key file, or restraining an opponent's forcing sequence. In 6/9 cases the move is a material capture (Bxf4, Bxg4, Rxf6, Qxc3, Rxf2, cxb3), while in 3/9 cases it's a relocation to a seemingly strong square (Nf6, Qg6, Nd5). The defensive function being abandoned varies: in 4/9 positions the piece was blocking a check/fork diagonal (Qg6 vacates f7 allowing Qd5+ fork; Qxc3 vacates f6 allowing Rf7+ mating attack; Bxf4 allows Qc4+ winning the piece; Rxf2 allows c6+ discovered attack). In 3/9 positions the piece was controlling a critical file or restraining an attack (Rxf6 removes rook from h-file destroying mate-in-12; Bxg4 wastes tempo during a mating attack; Nd5 places the piece where it gets attacked with tempo). The average cp_loss of 5301 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 6/9 positions resulting in forced checkmate after the blunder. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are high-tension positions where the defensive duty of the piece is non-obvious.

1036.label: A bishop sacrifices itself on a pawn shielding the enemy king (h7, h2, f7, or f2) with check, attempting a classic attacking pattern without the necessary preconditions being met.
1036.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a pawn with check to expose the enemy king — 7/10 are Bxh7+, 2/10 are Bxh2+ (the mirror image for Black), and 1/10 is Bxf2+ or Bxf7+ targeting the f-pawn instead. In every case, the sacrifice is unsound: the attacker lacks sufficient supporting pieces to convert the exposed king into a mating attack. The analyses reveal recurring deficiency patterns: in 6/10 positions, a key piece is undeveloped or too far from the kingside to support the standard Ng5+/Qh5 continuation. In 3/10 positions, the attacker's own king is vulnerable (still in center), making the queen commitment to the attack risky. In 1/10 (Position 6), the correct idea existed but the move ORDER was wrong — Ng5 needed to come before Bxh7+. Defensive resources consistently available to the opponent include knight retreats to f6/f8 blocking the h-file (5/10), king retreating safely to g8 (4/10), or the king escaping to h6 where it's paradoxically safe (1/10). The average centipawn loss of 306 reflects that these are decisive blunders, typically converting equal or advantageous positions into losing ones.

1027.label: Queen moves to a seemingly active square while leaving a friendly piece undefended and immediately capturable.
1027.description: In 7/10 positions, the queen was performing a critical defensive duty (protecting a knight, bishop, or pawn) and moved to a square that looked purposeful—centralizing, attacking, or regrouping—while severing its defensive connection to a piece that the opponent then captured for free. Specifically: Position 4 (Qd3 leaves Bb4 hanging to Rxb4), Position 5 (Qc1 leaves Be2 hanging to Bxe2), Position 7 (Qb6 leaves Ne4 hanging to Bxe4), Position 10 (Qf3 leaves Bh6 hanging to gxh6), Position 3 (Qe2 leaves h2 hanging to Qxh2+ with mate), Position 2 (Qe3 fails to address the undefended Nd5, allowing Bxd5), and Position 6 (Qf6 removes the queen's ability to recapture on e5, leaving Ne4 capturable by Qxe4). The remaining 3 positions share the broader theme of choosing an attractive-looking move over addressing concrete material threats: Position 1 plays Qg3 'attacking' instead of advancing a passed pawn, Position 9 captures the wrong piece while a bishop hangs on g5, and Position 8 checks prematurely. Average cp_loss of 1367 reflects the catastrophic nature of leaving pieces en prise.

1031.label: Advancing a flank pawn (especially the a-pawn) in an endgame when the position demands immediate tactical action such as checks, captures, or addressing mating threats.
1031.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet pawn advances on rim or flank files during endgames. 6/10 moves are specifically a-pawn advances (five a4 moves plus one a5), while the remainder are b3, b4, c5, g5, and h5—all on non-central files. In 9/10 positions, the move ignores an urgent tactical requirement: 3/10 allow immediate checkmate or mate-in-3 (positions 2, 5, 9), 4/10 surrender critical tempo that allows the opponent to double rooks on the 7th rank, consolidate a king, or capture a hanging piece (positions 1, 4, 7, 8), and 2/10 represent premature passed pawn advances that allow blockade or counterplay (positions 3, 6). Only 1/10 (position 10) is actually the engine's top choice—a pure king-and-pawn endgame where the advance is objectively correct. The average cp_loss of 2934 is extreme, heavily skewed by three positions where forced mate was available. The unifying error is choosing a slow, strategically-motivated pawn push when concrete calculation (checks, captures, threats) was required.

1034.label: Capturing a key square with the wrong piece when a different attacker on the same square yields a far superior tactical outcome.
1034.description: In 9/10 positions, the player captures on the correct target square but with the wrong piece—the best move also captures on that same square (or immediately adjacent) using a different attacker. Specifically: positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, and 9 show the best move capturing the exact same square with a different piece (Rxf2 vs Bxf2+, Nxg2 vs Bxg2+, Bxg7 vs Rxg7+, Bxf7+ vs Rxf7 twice, Nxf7 vs Bxf7+). Position 1 has Rxg6+ vs hxg6 on the same square. Position 3 has Nxc8/Rxe6 vs Bxe6+. Position 10 has Qxg5 vs Rxh6+ (adjacent targets in the same attack). Only position 8 diverges slightly, where the capture itself is wrong rather than just the piece. The average cp_loss is enormous (3938) because piece selection on these critical captures determines whether forcing sequences (checks, forks, mating nets) are maintained or broken.

1035.label: A non-forcing wing pawn advance played in a position that demands an immediate tactical response, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
1035.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing pawn move on a flank file (7/10 are literal rim pawn moves on the a-file or h-file; the remaining 3 are on the b, c, or g files). In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical requirement—either a winning combination to execute (6/10: knight forks, pins, material-winning sequences) or a critical defensive need to address (4/10: exposed king, hanging pieces, devastating attacks). The moves are uniformly prophylactic or preparatory in nature: preventing a future threat (a6 stopping b5), preparing a later advance (a3 before b4), gaining space (h4, g5, a5), or supporting a piece (c6 backing d5, h6 backing g5). The average cp_loss of 306 and average good moves of only 1.8 confirm these are critical moments where the position demanded precision rather than slow maneuvering. In 9/10 positions, the opponent's refutation directly exploited the wasted tempo—executing the very tactic that the best move would have either delivered first or prevented.

1020.label: Aggressively moving a piece to directly attack an enemy piece or king, when the attacking move is tactically flawed — either the piece is capturable, defense is abandoned, or a stronger continuation is missed.
1020.description: 10/10 positions feature moves that aggressively target a specific enemy piece or the king. 7/10 specifically attack heavy pieces (rooks or queens), with Qb8, Qf8, Qe1, Ra8 targeting back-rank pieces, and Nf7 (twice) and Nh7 attempting deep knight infiltrations toward rooks. 4/10 place the attacking piece where it is simply captured by the king (Nf7×2 captured by Kxf7, Qg2+ by Kxg2, Bh2 by Kxh2). 3/10 abandon critical defensive duties (Qb8 leaves g2 unguarded allowing mate, Qe1 abandons mating threats, g5 ignores king safety). 3/10 miss stronger tactical continuations on the same theme (Nh7 misses Nxe6 discovered attack, Nf7 in position 9 misses preparatory Qh5+, Qf8 is suboptimal vs Qe6). 8/10 involve placing pieces on the opponent's back rank or 7th rank. The common thread is tunnel-vision on a visible target — the player spots an enemy piece to attack and lunges at it without verifying the move's soundness.

1021.label: Natural-looking piece placement moves (usually contesting open files) that inadvertently create pins, forks, or hanging pieces the opponent immediately exploits.
1021.description: 8/10 positions involve placing a piece on an open file or seemingly active square as a 'routine improvement' that actually creates a critical tactical vulnerability. Specifically: 5/10 moves are rooks going to open files (Re8, Rd8×2, Rc1, Rb2), 3/10 are queens placed on active-looking squares (Qd1, Qb6, Qf3), and 1/10 is a bishop development (Be6). The tactical consequences created include pins (3/10: Be6 creates e-file pin, Rd8 creates diagonal pin on Nd7, Rc1 enables capture+fork), removal of a key defender (2/10: Rd8 removes f7 guard, Re8 abandons knight on e3), hanging pieces (2/10: Qb6 leaves Bb4 undefended, Qf3 leaves Bf4 undefended against g5), and back-rank issues (1/10: Qd1 exposes e1). The average good moves available was only 2.0, indicating these were critical moments demanding precise tactical moves rather than routine improvements. In every case, the best moves addressed the position's specific tactical demand (relocating a vulnerable piece, forcing simplification, or preventing a concrete threat) rather than making a general 'improving' move.

1037.label: The king (or critical piece) captures an infiltrated enemy piece, moving to a fatally exposed square where it faces immediate checkmate or devastating attack.
1037.description: In 10/10 positions, the player captures a tempting enemy piece that has infiltrated deep into their position. 8/10 moves are king captures, and 2/10 are rook captures that critically compromise king safety. The captured piece is a knight in 9/10 cases (and a bishop in 1/10), always a piece that appeared dangerously active and worth eliminating. The catastrophic result is consistent: 7/10 positions result in immediate checkmate (mate-in-1 to mate-in-8), while the remaining 3/10 suffer devastating positional/material collapse. The average centipawn loss of 5698 reflects this severity. Only 1.6 good moves existed on average, meaning these positions demanded extreme precision — the player chose the one natural-looking but fatal option. In every case, the key error is that the destination square of the capture places the king (or blocks its escape) in a position surrounded by the opponent's coordinated forces — queens on open files/diagonals, bishops on key diagonals, and pawns/pieces sealing escape routes.

1038.label: Giving a queen or rook check on the 1st/8th rank that allows the opponent to escape or interpose, when a quieter or differently-ordered move maintains a forced mate or much larger advantage.
1038.description: All 10/10 positions feature checks delivered specifically to the first or eighth rank (5 to rank 1: Qf1+, Qh1+, Qb1+, Qg1+, Qd1+; and 5 to rank 8: Qh8+, Qd8+, Rh8+, Qf8+, Qh8+). In 7/10 cases, the correct move was a quiet non-checking piece deployment (Bh3#, Rab8, Nxe6#, Nd6, Bd5, Bg6#, Bg3) that either delivered immediate checkmate or maintained an inescapable mating net. In 8/10 positions the blunder converted a forced checkmate into merely a large advantage. The average centipawn loss of 6624 reflects catastrophic damage. The defensive resource consistently exploited after the premature check was either king escape to a safer square (Ka7, Kf7, Kg2, Kd2, Ke2) in 6/10 positions, or piece interposition on the checking line (Qe1, Qg1, Nf8, Re2) in 6/10 positions. The key geometry is that back-rank checks travel along the entire rank, giving the defender maximum options for interposition or lateral escape.

1033.label: A quiet one-square pawn push adjacent to the player's exposed king, wasting a critical tempo when concrete active play is required.
1033.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet (non-capturing, non-checking) pawn push on a file immediately adjacent to the player's own exposed king. In every case, the king has a weak pawn shield or is directly exposed (10/10 positions explicitly tag king vulnerability). The pawn moves are all one-square advances: a4, b6, c3, f3, g3, h3, f6, f6, g3, b3 — each on the file directly neighboring the king (e.g., king on b2/a4, king on c7/b6, king on g2/f3, king on h2/g3, king on c2/b3). The intent appears to be 'consolidation' or 'creating shelter,' but the position demands immediate active play instead. 9/10 positions explicitly identify tempo_loss as the core error. The average cp_loss is enormous (3052cp) because these positions are tactically critical with very narrow best-move paths (average 1.6 good moves available). The refutations universally exploit the wasted tempo to launch attacks against the very king the pawn move was trying to protect — through checks, discovered attacks, invasions on open files, or mating sequences.

1040.label: A non-forcing wing pawn advance played when the position demands an immediate tactical response, typically a capture or forcing move.
1040.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance on the b, c, or g file (3 on b-file, 3 on c-file, 4 on g-file) played instead of an urgent tactical obligation. In every case, the average number of good moves available was exactly 1.0, meaning the position demanded a single precise response. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a capture (Nxe5, Nxd7, cxd4, exd5, Qxd4, Nxc3, Nh5→Nf6, Rd1 blocking promotion). The played pawn moves were all 'preparatory' or 'positional' in nature — attacking an enemy piece (b4 chasing a bishop, c6 challenging a knight/bishop, g5/g4 attacking a bishop), gaining space, or creating long-term threats — but they universally ignored an immediate concrete tactical problem: a hanging piece (5/10), an unaddressed threat requiring a capture (3/10), or an urgent promotion/forcing sequence (2/10). The blunders average 297cp loss, reflecting the catastrophic cost of one tempo in sharp positions.

1039.label: A rook captures on an open file, but the opponent recaptures on that same square with check (usually with a queen), gaining decisive tempo to exploit king safety.
1039.description: In 9/10 positions, the blunder follows an identical geometric pattern: the player uses a rook to capture a piece on an open file (e, d, c, or f file), and the opponent immediately recaptures on that exact square with check — most commonly Qxe1+, Qxd8+, Qxd1+, Qxe8+, or Qxf7+ (8/10 involve queen recaptures with check, 1/10 a rook recapture with check leading to mate). The recapture with check gains a critical tempo that enables devastating follow-ups: back-rank mates (positions 3, 4, 8, 9), pins on blocking pieces (position 2), diagonal attacks on the exposed king (position 7), winning material back plus extra pieces (positions 1, 5, 10). All 10 positions occur in the middlegame with open files. The average cp_loss of 3057 is extreme because the check tempo often converts to forced mate or massive material gain. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points requiring precise calculation of the recapture consequences.
1039.old_chip: Rook trade allows recapture with check

1041.label: A knight captures a pawn (or jumps aggressively) while abandoning a critical defensive role, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of the resulting weakness.
1041.description: All 10 positions feature a knight moving away from a critical defensive post to grab material or seek activity. 9/10 are direct pawn captures (Nxe5 x3, Nxe4 x3, Nxb5 x2, Nxd5 x1), and 1/10 is an aggressive knight jump (Nb4). In every case, the knight was performing a vital defensive function—guarding key squares around the king (5/10 involved uncastled kings on e1/e8), protecting other pieces from capture (3/10 left bishops or other pieces hanging), or maintaining central coordination against attacking plans (2/10). The removal of the knight consistently exposes a specific tactical vulnerability: knight forks in 3/10, back-rank/rook-swing attacks in 3/10, zwischenzug captures of now-undefended pieces in 2/10, and positional collapse enabling pawn-break attacks in 2/10. The average cp_loss of 291 reflects how severely the knight's absence is punished. In 7/10 positions, quiet consolidating moves (castling, prophylactic g3, piece retreats) were available as clear alternatives.

1025.label: Playing a seemingly reasonable repositioning or non-forcing move when the position critically demands one specific concrete action, allowing the opponent to exploit the lapse with a tempo-gaining tactical blow.
1025.description: All 9 positions share a common structure: the position demands ONE urgent concrete action (avg only 1.7 good moves available), but the player instead opts for a 'natural-looking' move—piece repositioning, a pawn capture, or passive defense. In 5/9 positions, a piece is moved from a critical post or to a square that becomes an immediate target (Bf6 targeted by Nd5, Bc5 targeted by exd4, Nd6 abandoning attack on queen, Nf6 retreating from e4 outpost, Nb3 unblocking a lethal diagonal). In 4/9 positions, a non-urgent pawn move is played while a forcing tactical requirement goes unaddressed (h5 ignoring Bxf6, cxd4 allowing e5 with tempo, f3 weakening e3 instead of playing Nd6+, hxg4 leaving rook hanging on a diagonal). In every case, the opponent punishes with a single forcing move that gains decisive tempo—a check, fork, discovered attack, or capture of an undefended piece. The average cp_loss of 313 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but missed-crisis situations where one precise move was required.

1047.label: A queen move to a seemingly active square that abandons its sole defensive duty protecting a piece, pawn, or critical square, leaving something immediately exploitable.
1047.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move that removes the queen from a square where it was performing an essential defensive function — the sole or critical protector of another piece or key square. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8), the queen was the only defender of a minor piece or rook that immediately becomes hanging after the queen departs. In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 9), the queen's departure from the c-file removed X-ray defense of the back rank, enabling immediate back-rank checkmate patterns (Rxc1+ Re1 Rxe1#). In 2/10 cases (positions 7, 10), the queen abandoned defense of a critical kingside pawn (g7 and f7 respectively), enabling either a windmill combination or instant checkmate. The intended moves universally target superficially attractive squares — attacking pawns (Qb6→b7, Qxb7, Qa7→a6), centralizing (Qc6, Qd6), or seeking kingside activity (Qg5, Qh5, Qf6) — but all fail to recognize the queen's indispensable guardian role on its original square. Average cp_loss of 4034 and only 1.2 good moves available confirms these are high-stakes positions demanding precise defensive awareness.

1046.label: A pawn advances forward, removing its diagonal protection of an adjacent pawn or piece that immediately becomes capturable.
1046.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance that removes the moving pawn's diagonal defense of a neighboring pawn, piece, or critical square. In 8/10 cases, the abandoned target is an adjacent pawn (b4 left by b3→b4, c4 left by b3→b4, e5 left by d6→d5, d6 left by c7→c6, b4 left by a3→a4, b5 left by c6→c5 twice, d4 left by e5→e4, d3 left by c2→c3). In 1/10 cases (Position 1), the c3→c4 advance exposes the b4 square to knight invasion rather than leaving a piece hanging. In 1/10 cases (Position 3), f6→f5 leaves e5 undefended while also exposing the king to a queenside assault. The tactical consequence is overwhelmingly 'hanging piece' (9/10 tagged), with the opponent immediately capturing the undefended target. The average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these are not subtle positional mistakes but concrete tactical oversights where the player fails to recognize their pawn's defensive role before pushing it forward.

1052.label: A knight moves to the edge of the board (a4/a5/h4/h5) to attack a bishop, ignoring far more urgent tactical demands in the position.
1052.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight moving to the absolute rim of the board (a-file or h-file), and in at least 8/9 cases the explicit intent is to attack or chase an enemy bishop (Bc4 in 6 positions, Bf5 in 2, Bg3 in 1). This is a well-known positional motif (e.g., ...Na5 vs Bc4 in the Italian Game) being applied at catastrophically wrong moments. The average cp_loss is 354, indicating these are severe blunders rather than minor inaccuracies. In every single case, the position demanded something far more urgent: exploiting king safety (positions 4, 7), executing a winning tactic (positions 1, 6, 10), addressing a critical passed pawn (position 8), maintaining piece coordination and defense of key squares (positions 3, 5, 9). The knight consistently ends up either hanging (positions 3, 10), stranded far from the action (positions 1, 6), or abandoning a critical defensive square like f3 (positions 7, 9). Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were sharp positions requiring precision rather than routine maneuvers.

1045.label: Knight jumps to an optically impressive central square that is tactically unsound, either because the knight can be profitably captured, the move abandons a critical function, or it allows a forcing counter-response.
1045.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight jumping to a central or near-central square (e4 in 4 cases, e5 in 2, d5, d4, f6, f2) that appears powerful but is concretely refutable. In 5/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 7, 10), the knight can be immediately captured with material or positional gain because the square is inadequately defended. In the remaining 5/10 positions, the knight move either abandons a critical blocking/defensive function (positions 3, 9), allows the opponent's piece to reach a more dangerous square with tempo (positions 6, 8), or permits simplification that dissipates a large advantage (position 1). The average cp_loss of 1295 reflects how catastrophic these moves are. The common psychological thread is the player being seduced by the visual appeal of a centralized knight—attacking multiple pieces, occupying an 'outpost'—without verifying whether the knight survives or whether the position demands something entirely different (development in 4/10, a forcing tactical strike in 3/10, defensive simplification in 2/10, maintaining a blockade in 1/10). Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions generally demanded specific non-knight-jump solutions.

1055.label: Playing a slow, prophylactic flank pawn advance (a3/a6/h3/h6/g6) when a concrete tactical opportunity demands immediate action.
1055.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet one-square pawn advance to the 3rd or 6th rank on a flank file (a6 appears 4/10, h3 appears 2/10, plus h6, a3, c3, and g6) played instead of a forcing tactical move. In 9/10 positions, the best move was an active piece move or capture (Qxd2, Nxd4×2, Bg5, Bd6, Bxh6, Kc1, h3-as-prophylactic, Bg6). The average number of good alternatives was only 1.6, meaning these were sharp positions with narrow solutions — yet the players chose the most passive possible option. In 8/10 positions, the missed best move involved either capturing material (hanging pieces, tactical combinations) or activating a piece against an exposed king. The common 'intent' across all positions was prophylaxis — preventing Nb5, Ng5, Bg4, or preparing b5/b4 advances — but the positions were too tactically urgent for such luxury moves. The opponent's exposed or uncastled king featured in 8/10 positions, creating the urgency these pawn moves fatally ignored.

1048.label: King retreats toward the back rank in endgames when active forward king movement or triangulation was required to maintain counterplay.
1048.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves that retreat backward (toward the player's own back rank or away from the center of action). 8/10 are explicitly tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (9/10), predominantly pawn endgames (7/10 are pure king-and-pawn positions). In every case, the correct alternative involved the king advancing forward (Kh4, Kf3, Kf5, Kh3) or making a sideways triangulating move (Kc1/Ke1 to reach d1 with correct move order). The one outlier (Position 5, Ra8) involves a different error type (hanging piece) but still features a piece moving to the back rank passively. Positions 7 and 10 show negligible cp losses (6-7cp), suggesting the feature may fire on the structural pattern of backward king movement regardless of severity.

1044.label: Playing a natural-seeming rook or bishop move that looks purposeful but ignores an immediate concrete tactical obligation, typically leaving a piece undefended.
1044.description: All 10 positions feature a rook move (7/10) or bishop move (3/10) that appears active or purposeful—filing a rook on an open file, giving a check, developing a bishop, or capturing a pawn—but fatally ignores an immediate tactical crisis. In 6/10 positions, the move specifically leaves a knight undefended or trapped (positions 1, 3, 5, 6, 9, and arguably 10). In 3/10 positions, the move removes a critical defender from its post (positions 2, 3, 4 where the rook leaves a key square). In 3/10, the blunder is a check that looks forcing but misses something better or activates the opponent's king (positions 6, 7, 8). The average good moves available was only 1.3, meaning these were narrow tactical moments demanding concrete calculation, yet the players defaulted to 'general principle' moves. The average cp_loss of 1209 reflects the catastrophic cost of autopilot thinking in critical positions.

1042.label: Retreating a piece to the player's own back two ranks where it immediately becomes tactically capturable or abandons a critical defensive function.
1042.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece being moved to the player's own 1st or 2nd rank (ranks 1-2 for White, ranks 7-8 for Black): 6/10 retreat to the back rank (Qb1, Rh1, Bc1, Rh1, Rf1, Qg8) and 4/10 to the second rank (Re2, Rf7, Rb2, Rb7). In 9/10 cases, the retreated piece becomes immediately capturable—either hanging directly (positions 2, 4, 7, 9 where the piece is taken in one move) or won through a simple 1-2 move forcing sequence like a discovered check, deflection, or intermediate check (positions 3, 5, 6, 8). In position 1, the retreat instead abandons a critical defensive square allowing immediate checkmate. The average cp_loss of 3098 reflects that 4/10 positions result in mate or near-mate, while the remaining 6 lose significant material. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these blunders occur in positions already demanding precision, making the passive retreat especially costly.

1051.label: A reflexive capture that trades away a strategically dominant pawn or piece whose static pressure was worth far more than the material gained.
1051.description: 10/10 positions feature a capture that resolves strategic tension in the opponent's favor. In 9/10 cases, the blunder is a pawn capture; 8/10 involve trading away a pawn (or piece) that was part of a space-gaining, cramping formation (e5 pawns in positions 1/2/4/5/8, f5 pawn in position 6, knight on f5 in position 7, d4/f4 pawns in positions 9/10). In every case, the correct approach was to either maintain the tension and improve pieces (positions 2/5/6/8/9), advance the pawn forward rather than capture sideways (positions 4/10), capture in a different direction (position 1), or avoid the capture entirely (positions 3/7). The average cp_loss of 287 and only 1.4 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where the 'obvious' capture is catastrophically wrong. The common consequence is activating the opponent's dormant pieces (6/10), opening files/diagonals against one's own king (5/10), or losing the positional foundation of one's advantage entirely (10/10).

1053.label: Quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning moves played in positions demanding immediate tactical action, squandering a narrow window for concrete play.
1053.description: All 10 positions share the same fundamental error: a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking piece repositioning move is played when the position demands specific tactical action. 10/10 moves are non-forcing piece shuffles — 5/10 are king walks (Kf2, Ke3, Kh6, Kh7, Kh7), 4/10 are bishop retreats/repositions (Bg3, Bb6, Bg3, Bb3), and 1/10 is a knight retreat (Ng6). The average number of good moves was only 1.6, confirming these were narrow positions requiring precise solutions, not generic improvement. In 6/10 cases, the piece moved away from guarding a critical square (e3, d3, f8/e7, d5), directly enabling opponent tactics like knight forks. In 5/10 cases, a king move either exposed it to new tactical patterns (fork on c4, Ng5+ checks, g4-g5 pawn storms) or simply wasted tempo while a piece urgently needed rescuing. The common tactical refutations include knight forks (positions 2, 5, 6), sacrificial attacks on exposed kings (positions 3, 9, 10), and exploitation of undefended pieces given a free tempo (positions 1, 4, 7, 8).

1060.label: A rook pawn advance (a3/a6/h6) attacks an aggressively posted knight that has a devastating forward leap instead of retreating.
1060.description: In 10/10 positions, the player advances a rook pawn (a3, a6, or h6) to 'ask the question' of an enemy knight posted on the 4th or 5th rank (b4, b5, or g5). In every single case, the knight's strongest response is to jump FORWARD into the position rather than retreat — typically delivering a fork or enabling a mating attack. 8/10 positions feature a knight fork as the primary refutation (Nxc7+, Nxc2+, Nf7, Nxd3+, Nc7+), while 2/10 exploit king safety via checks on open diagonals/files. 10/10 positions involve at least one uncastled or centrally-placed king, which is the structural prerequisite enabling the knight's tactical leap. The best alternatives in every position address king safety first (castling, blocking diagonals, creating flight squares) — only AFTER neutralizing the knight's forward threats does the pawn push become safe. All 10 moves occur in the opening (8) or early middlegame (2), when kings are most vulnerable to central forks.

1054.label: A non-urgent pawn advance or promotion played in a position demanding an immediate piece move or tactically precise response.
1054.description: All 9/9 positions feature a pawn advance (or wrong pawn promotion) played when the position urgently required a piece move or tactically precise alternative. In 7/9 cases, the best move was a knight move (Nf6, Na4, Nc6, Nb5, e8=N+) or piece redeployment, yet the player chose a quiet pawn push instead. The average cp_loss of 2396 is enormous, reflecting that these are critical moments (avg good moves: 2.0) where tempo is decisive. The pawn moves share a common intent: the player pursues their own slow plan—gaining space (a4, h4, g4, b5), creating a passed pawn (c6), promoting (h2, e8=Q), or attacking (g5)—while ignoring that the opponent has an immediate tactical refutation exploiting the tempo loss. In 6/9 positions, the refutation directly exploits king safety weaknesses that the pawn move either created or failed to address. The irreversibility of pawn moves makes these especially costly: unlike a misplaced piece, a pushed pawn cannot retreat.

1043.label: Moving a rook away from a uniquely important file or square to create a redundant doubling/stacking formation with the other rook, sacrificing irreplaceable tactical function.
1043.description: 9/10 positions involve rook moves (the exception being Qc1 in Position 4, which follows the same logic of choosing a passive grouping over a forcing continuation). In all cases, the moved rook occupied a critical file, rank, or penetration square where it performed an essential function—controlling the e-file for deflection tactics (Positions 5, 8, 10), maintaining back-rank defense (Position 6), anchoring a mating net (Position 2), or pressuring from a unique vantage point (Positions 3, 7, 9). The player chose to 'double' or 'stack' heavy pieces on a different file or rank, creating a formation that looks powerful but is actually redundant—the target file was already controlled or blocked. 8/10 positions show the rook leaving an open file where it had unique tactical potential (discovered checks, deflection sacrifices, back-rank threats, or 2nd-rank penetration). The average cp_loss of 3085 is extreme, with 4/10 positions converting forced wins into draws or losses. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the rook's original position was irreplaceable.
1043.old_chip: Rook abandons critical file to double

1056.label: Voluntarily walking the king forward to an exposed central square (typically the 2nd/7th rank) instead of developing, castling, or retreating to the back rank, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
1056.description: All 10/10 positions feature a premature, voluntary king move from the center where the king was already insecure. 7/10 moves specifically advance the king FORWARD off the back rank to the 2nd or 7th rank (Kd2 x5, Kf2, Ke7, Kf7), placing it on exposed squares vulnerable to diagonal checks and knight forks. The remaining 3/10 (Kd8 x2, one Kf7) move the king sideways/forward to squares that increase rather than decrease exposure. In 8/10 positions, a non-king move (developing a piece, playing c6, or interposing) was the best alternative, showing these king moves were fundamentally unnecessary. The most devastating sub-pattern is Kd2 vs Kd1 (5 positions), where one single rank of difference determines whether the king sits on exploitable diagonals. The average cp_loss of 1204 reflects that these forward king moves consistently walk into forcing tactical sequences—checks, forks, or mating nets—that wouldn't exist against a back-rank king.

1063.label: Voluntary king relocation to a square that is immediately exploitable by checks, pins, or mates — often when a preparatory forcing move was needed first.
1063.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forced king move where the player voluntarily relocates the king to a seemingly safer or more active square, but the destination square is tactically compromised. In 7/10 cases, the king move allows an immediate check (Qb5+ in pos 1, Rxe2+ in pos 2, Rxe1+ in pos 3, Qxf6+ in pos 4, Qf4+ in pos 6, Qc5+ in pos 9, Qd3+ in pos 10). In 2/10 cases, the king walks into a pin or back-rank mate (pos 5: pin along 6th rank; pos 7: Rd1#). In 6/10 positions, the exact same king move appears in the BEST line but only AFTER a preparatory forcing move (check, threat, or interposition) that makes the relocation safe. The average cp_loss is enormous (2196), reflecting that these 'quiet' king moves catastrophically misread the tactical landscape. 8/10 are White moves, and 7/10 are middlegame positions where active piece play was available instead.

1057.label: Voluntary piece repositioning to seemingly active squares while ignoring an immediate concrete tactical obligation, enabling devastating punishment.
1057.description: All 10 positions share a critical feature: the player makes a non-forcing 'improving' move (developing, repositioning, grabbing space) in a position where only 1-2 moves are acceptable (avg 1.6 good moves). In 8/10 cases, the move abandons a critical defensive function — Ba6 abandons central defense enabling c5+ discovered check, Qb6 releases diagonal pressure enabling Bxb4/Bd6, Qc5 abandons defense of the f6 knight, Be3 vacates the d2 square exposing the king to d-file checks, and Bc5 fails to defend the e5 knight. In 10/10 cases, the move is non-forcing (no checks, no captures) and appears purposeful — targeting a pawn, developing a piece, centralizing — but ignores the one concrete requirement of the position. The punishments are severe (avg 1276cp loss) because these positions are tactically critical moments disguised as positional ones, and the 'active' move creates an immediate exploitable vulnerability that wasn't there before.

1050.label: Voluntary piece-improving moves to plausible squares that ignore the position's specific tactical demands, leaving critical weaknesses unaddressed.
1050.description: All 10 positions share a consistent pattern: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move to a square that looks attractive (outpost, central square, active diagonal) while the position demanded a specific tactical solution. In 10/10 cases, the move played is a voluntary 'improvement' — no check, no capture, no immediate threat — when the position required either exploiting a concrete tactic (3/10: g4 winning the queen, Rd5 winning a knight, advancing passed pawns), defending a specific weakness (4/10: protecting a2, guarding f2, maintaining g2's defensive function, addressing Bg6+ threats), or avoiding placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (2/10: Bf6 into Rxf6, Nc4 enabling f4+Qxh6+). The average cp_loss of 422 reflects that these positions had narrow best-move margins (avg 1.9 good moves), meaning precision was required but the player chose a 'normal-looking' move instead. In 8/10 positions, the attractive move directly created or exposed a tactical vulnerability — a hanging piece, an undefended pawn, or a removed defensive guard — that the opponent could immediately exploit.

1049.label: A knight is moved to an apparently active square (usually capturing on e5), but the move creates or exposes an immediate devastating tactical vulnerability that the knight was preventing.
1049.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight move that looks natural or aggressive but overlooks a critical tactical consequence. In 6/10 positions, the specific pattern is Nxe5 (knight captures a White knight on e5) when the bishop should have captured instead (Bxe5); after dxe5, the advancing pawn creates a lethal fork simultaneously attacking the bishop on d6 and the knight on f6, winning a full piece. In the remaining 4/10 positions, the knight moves away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function: in 2 cases (Ne4 from c3, Nc4 from a3) the knight abandons back-rank coverage allowing immediate checkmate; in 1 case (Nf6 from h5) the knight stops guarding g7 allowing Qxg7#; and in 1 case (Nf3 from h4) the knight stops guarding g6 allowing Kxg6 material gain. All 10 moves share the characteristic of appearing active—capturing a strong centralized piece, centralizing, or attacking—while catastrophically ignoring the defensive responsibilities the knight was fulfilling (either directly guarding a square, or indirectly by being the wrong piece to execute a capture).

1065.label: A non-forcing pawn advance wastes a critical tempo when the position demands an immediate forcing move or a more precise move order.
1065.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the mistake. In 9/10 cases, the primary tactical motif is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss.' The positions divide into two sub-patterns: (1) move-order errors where a different pawn or piece should go first (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 — e.g., g4 before h4, d4 before e4, Qb5+ before a5), and (2) slow pawn pushes that squander an existing initiative when a concrete forcing move (check, capture, or direct threat) was available (positions 4, 7, 9, 10 — e.g., c6 instead of Qe5+, b3 instead of Ra3, g4 instead of Qxc6). In 6/10 positions, the better move involved a piece move rather than a pawn move. The average cp_loss of 1969 is inflated by two positions where forced mates were missed in favor of pawn pushes. 8/10 positions are endgames where single tempi are critical, and the typical good-move count of 2.0 confirms these are narrow positions where precision matters.

1064.label: A reflexive one-square pawn advance near the castled king that weakens the shelter instead of addressing urgent tactical demands.
1064.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance on the file adjacent to (or directly in front of) the castled king: 7/10 are g6/g3 (the knight-pawn), 2/10 are h3 (the rook-pawn near a kingside-castled king), and 1/10 is a3 (near a queenside-castled king on b1). All moves share the same defensive intent—'shoring up' the king's shelter against perceived threats—but in every case the position demanded immediate active play (counterattack, piece development, or tactical resolution of central tension). 9/10 positions had the player's king already under significant pressure from the opponent's pieces, making the tempo loss catastrophic. The weakening manifests in two primary ways: creating exploitable dark-square holes (f6/h6 after g6 in positions 2, 3, 6, 8) or creating pawn targets that invite piece sacrifices (Rxg3+ in position 1, Bxh3 in position 7, bxc2+ in position 5). The average cp_loss of 2120 reflects that these seemingly safe moves often convert manageable disadvantages into forced mates or decisive material loss.

1070.label: Capturing a peripheral pawn with the queen (or key piece), deflecting it far from the king which faces an immediate mating or decisive tactical threat.
1070.description: 9/9 positions feature a piece capturing a wing or edge pawn (a2, b2, a7, b7, a5, g2, c7) on a square far removed from the player's own king. 8/9 involve the queen making the capture; 1/9 is a bishop capture (Bxg2). In every case, the player's king was already exposed or facing latent tactical threats that required the capturing piece to remain nearby for defensive purposes. The average centipawn loss is ~7805, with 7/9 positions resulting in forced checkmate (ranging from mate-in-2 to mate-in-9). In all 9 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, meaning the positions demanded precise defensive awareness rather than materialistic play. The captures target pawns on the a-file (4 times), b-file (3 times), c-file (1 time), and g-file (1 time) — consistently peripheral squares that maximally displace the piece from the king's vicinity.

1071.label: Advancing wing pawns (b4/b5 or g4/g5) aggressively while the player's own king remains uncastled in the center.
1071.description: All 10/10 positions share the same critical feature: the moving side's king is still on its starting square (e1 or e8) when a flank pawn is pushed aggressively. 7/10 positions involve a g-pawn advance (g4 or g5) while 3/10 involve a b-pawn advance (b4 or b5), but the underlying error is identical. In 10/10 cases, the side playing the move has a significant development deficit — typically with multiple minor pieces undeveloped. 8/10 positions feature a closed or semi-closed center that the opponent can blast open as punishment. The refutations consistently involve either opening the center (d4/d5 breaks in 7/10), directly capturing the undefended advanced pawn (2/10), or exploiting newly created weaknesses around the exposed king. The average cp_loss of 218 reflects how severely this pattern is punished — these aren't subtle inaccuracies but position-destroying blunders.

1059.label: A piece is actively moved to a square where it is immediately capturable or tactically exploitable by the opponent.
1059.description: In 5/10 positions, the moved piece is literally captured on its destination square on the very next move (Re3 by fxe3, Qe4 by dxe4, Rb3 by Qxb3, Qa1 by Bxa1, Rd8 via promotion on d8). In 3/10 additional positions, the piece lands on a square where it is immediately attacked with tempo or becomes tactically lost (Qc4 hit by Rd4, Rb4 removed from defense allowing forced mate, Qxc2 allowing Nd4 fork winning material). The remaining 2/10 (g4, Ke6) represent the same fundamental blindness—failing to see that the opponent controls or exploits the consequences of the move. The average centipawn loss of 3882 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights rather than subtle positional errors. 7/10 involve major pieces (queens or rooks) being placed on specific squares, and in 8/10 cases there existed at least 2 good alternatives that kept the piece safe. The consistent thread is an active, seemingly purposeful move that walks directly into a one-move tactical refutation.

1068.label: A knight is repositioned to a natural-looking square when the position demands an immediate forcing move (capture, check, or concrete threat).
1068.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight being moved to a seemingly logical square without giving check or making a capture. In 9/10 cases, the position demanded a concrete forcing move instead — either a tactical capture (3/10: positions 3, 5, 8 where Nxf6+, Nxe5, or Bxe2 won material), a forcing check or pawn break (3/10: positions 4, 9, and 2 where Bc4+/e6, Ne7→Nf5+, or d3+Be3 were required), or an urgent defensive necessity (2/10: positions 7, 10 where the knight abandoned a key post or ignored mating threats). The average centipawn loss of 1208 reflects how catastrophic these slow moves are in sharp positions. In 7/10 positions, the knight move either created a new vulnerability (pin on c3, fork on e2, capture of the knight itself) or gifted the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate or deliver a finishing blow. Only 1/10 (position 6, Nf5) was actually the best move, serving as a control case where the knight move WAS the concrete action needed.

1058.label: Playing a natural-looking piece repositioning or developing move when the position demands one specific forcing or critical action.
1058.description: All 10 positions share a critical feature: extremely narrow margins (avg 1.8 good moves available) where only one or two specific moves maintain the evaluation, yet the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' move that addresses a secondary concern. 6/10 moves are rook repositions to seemingly active files (Rfc1, Rf1, Re1, Rxc5, Rf2+) that look natural but miss the point. 2/10 are identical Nc7 knight activations from a trapped-on-a8 position, both ignoring critical king safety needs. 2/10 are queen moves to tactically vulnerable squares (Qb7, Qf6). In every case, the best move was more forcing or addressed the ONE critical demand: g4 attacking a piece, Nf4 seizing initiative, Bd3 clearing king escape, Rxd7 winning material, Rg1 preserving a critical defender. The played moves all prioritize generic piece improvement (activating a rook, repositioning a knight, developing a queen) over the specific tactical requirement, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the real vulnerability.

1069.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move in a position that demands immediate tactical or concrete action, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their plans.
1069.description: 9/10 positions feature 'tempo_loss' as a primary tag, and in all cases the played move is non-forcing (no check, no meaningful capture, no immediate threat) while a forcing alternative existed. 5/10 moves are quiet king moves (Kg4, Kd4, Kg5, Kf4, Kf1), 3/10 are passive bishop moves (Be7 developing, Bb6 retreating, Bxf6 exchanging), and 2/10 are slow pawn moves (c5, a3). The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these positions had narrow critical paths requiring precision. In 7/10 positions, the best move involved an immediate capture, forcing pawn advance, or piece activation that created concrete threats. The played moves all look 'reasonable' in a vacuum—developing, centralizing, prophylactic—but catastrophically ignore the position's urgency. The average centipawn loss of 250 reflects that one wasted tempo allows the opponent to either escape danger (positions 1, 3, 5, 10), launch a decisive counterattack (positions 4, 7, 8, 9), or consolidate an advantage (position 2).

1061.label: Playing a natural-looking piece development or pawn push when the position critically demands a king move (evacuation, march, or check).
1061.description: In 5/7 positions, the correct move was explicitly moving the player's own king (Kc7, Kd1, Kb6, Kd7/Kd5/Kd6 in positions 3, 5, 6, and 8), yet the player chose a knight move or pawn push instead. In position 9, the key was advancing a pawn WITH CHECK against the opponent's king (e2+ vs d2), and in position 4, the critical requirement was preserving the pawn cage around the opponent's king (keeping h3 in place rather than pushing h2). Position 7 is the weakest fit, involving a passive knight retreat vs. aggressive centralization. The moves played (4/7 were knight moves: Nf6, Ne5, Ne7, Nf1; 3/7 were pawn pushes: h2, d5, d2) all appeared natural or active — developing, centralizing, or advancing passed pawns — but catastrophically ignored that the position's most critical factor was king positioning. The average cp_loss of 4157 reflects that in 5/7 cases the error converted winning/playable positions into forced mates or draws.

1062.label: Moving a knight to a seemingly active square (often attacking the opponent's queen) where it is immediately captured or creates a fatal tactical vulnerability.
1062.description: 8/10 positions feature knight moves to apparently active squares, with 4/10 specifically being Nf6. In 6/10 positions, the knight move directly attacks the opponent's queen (positions 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9), creating the illusion of gaining tempo. However, in every case the knight lands on a tactically doomed square: in positions 7 and 9, the knight on f6 is immediately captured by Rxf6/Bxf6 because gxf6 would catastrophically open the g-file; in position 8, Nf6 creates a fatal pin along the e-file; in position 3, Nf6 allows immediate checkmate on f7; in positions 1 and 2, knight captures (Nxg5/Nxg6) remove critical defenders or leave other pieces unprotected. The 2/10 non-knight positions (Rf7, a5) share the broader pattern of playing a superficially reasonable move while ignoring a critical tactical requirement. Average cp_loss of 2195 reflects the severity—these 'active-looking' moves walk directly into devastating refutations.

1067.label: A non-forcing pawn move wastes a critical tempo in a position where an immediate tactical threat demands urgent attention.
1067.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance played instead of addressing an urgent tactical obligation. In 8/10 cases, king safety was a critical factor (either the player's own exposed king or the opponent's vulnerable king needing immediate exploitation). In every position, the pawn move was slow and structural in nature—aiming to support pieces, grab space, or shore up pawn chains—while the position screamed for forcing moves. The average cp_loss of 352 reflects that these tempi were catastrophically expensive: the opponents had concrete threats ready to execute (Bxf3+ exploiting an opened diagonal, Qxf5+ capturing an unguarded pawn with check, d3 advancing a passed pawn into a piece, Qa4+ exploiting a newly opened diagonal, bxa5 winning a now-trapped piece). Only 2.0 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions requiring precision rather than leisure. The 'tempo_loss' tag applies to all 10 positions, confirming the unifying mechanism: a quiet pawn push hands the initiative to the opponent at the worst possible moment.

1072.label: Moving a rook to double on a rank (especially the 7th/2nd) while abandoning a critical defensive duty or missing a more forcing continuation.
1072.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that doubles rooks on a rank or file — the disambiguating notation (Rcc2, Rbb7, Ree7, etc.) confirms a second rook already occupies the target rank. In 7/10 positions the doubling targets the 7th rank (from White's perspective) or 2nd rank (from Black's), the classically 'strong' formation. However, 9/10 of these are mistakes (avg cp_loss 2054 excluding the 0-loss position). The core failure mechanism splits into two sub-patterns: in 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8), the rook being moved was performing a critical defensive function — guarding the back rank, covering an invasion square, or defending a piece — and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 4/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 9, 10), the doubling is simply non-forcing when a much stronger forcing move (check, passed pawn advance) was available, gifting the opponent a critical tempo to reorganize. Position 3 (Ree2, 0 cp loss) represents the rare case where doubling IS the best move because no defensive function is abandoned and the attack is already overwhelming.

1066.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing pawn advance or bishop relocation when the position demands an immediate concrete response (tactical strike, castling, or defensive necessity).
1066.description: All 9 positions share a critical pattern: the player chose a slow, non-forcing move—either a pawn advance (5/9: b5, c4, b5, g5, e5) or a bishop relocation (4/9: Bg4, Bh6, Ba4, Bf1)—in a position that demanded urgent concrete action. In 6/9 positions, there was a specific tactical opportunity being missed (Qh3-Ng4-Nxe3, castling, removing an attacker, prophylactic h5). The average number of good moves available was only 2.1, confirming these were critical moments requiring precision. The 'tempo_loss' tag appeared in 8/9 positions and 'king_safety' in 6/9, indicating that the quiet moves consistently gifted the opponent time to address their vulnerabilities or launch attacks against exposed kings. The moved pieces/pawns uniformly ended up on squares that were either immediately capturable (Bg4, Bh6, Ba4 in 3/9), structurally weakening (g5, e5, c4 in 3/9), or strategically irrelevant to the position's demands (b5 twice, Bf1). The average centipawn loss of 1289 reflects that these 'reasonable-looking' moves are catastrophic precisely because they waste the one tempo that separates advantage from disaster.

1083.label: Pushing the h-pawn forward as a passive, non-constructive move in a critical position that demands an urgent piece action or king move.
1083.description: 9/9 positions feature a kingside pawn advance (8/9 specifically h-pawn pushes, 1/9 an f-pawn push). In every case, the position demanded a specific urgent action — a piece relocation (Ba4, Bxb2, Bg6 in 3/9), a king move (Kg6, Kg2, Kh7, Ka4 in 4/9), or a critical defensive maneuver — but the player instead pushed the h-pawn forward as if 'doing something' without addressing the actual crisis. 8/9 positions were endgames with exposed kings, and the average cp_loss of 6029 confirms these are catastrophic errors. In 6/9 positions there was only 1 good move available, meaning the positions were razor-sharp defensively and demanded precision. Multiple analyses explicitly tag these as 'tempo_loss' moves. In at least 3/9 cases, the h-pawn advance actually worsened the king's safety by removing pawn shelter (Positions 3, 5, 10). The f5 outlier (Position 7) follows the identical logic: a kingside pawn advance instead of moving the king off the back rank.

1080.label: Playing a generic rook-to-central-file developing move when the position demands an immediate concrete action (tactical strike, resolving tension, or addressing a specific vulnerability).
1080.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to a central file (d-file or e-file) as a 'natural development' move, with 9/10 specifically being Ra-file rook moves (Rad1, Rad8, Rae1) and 1/10 being Rc1. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical or strategic demand that required immediate attention: 4/10 had a clear winning tactic available (Ng5 attacking f7, Bb5 attacking the queen, Nf4 winning a bishop, e5/Bxf3 seizing the center), 3/10 required addressing a specific defensive vulnerability (e-file control, diagonal weakness, exposed piece), and 3/10 needed immediate resolution of central pawn tension before the opponent could exploit it. The average cp_loss of 243 is severe, and 7/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating highly concrete positions where the 'default development' heuristic completely fails. The rook moves are consistently punished because they waste a critical tempo: in 6/10 cases the opponent immediately executes the very tactical operation the player should have preempted, and in 4/10 cases the opponent gains time to neutralize the player's existing advantages.

1076.label: A knight leaves a dominant central outpost to make a superficial tactical attack (fork or piece harassment) that is easily sidestepped, leaving the knight trapped or misplaced.
1076.description: In 9/10 positions, a knight occupies a powerful outpost or dominant central square (d4, e5, d6, b6, f4, d3) and abandons it to jump to a square attacking an enemy heavy piece (usually a rook or queen). In all 10 cases, the attacked piece simply sidesteps to a better square, and the knight ends up worse off. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 5, 6) the knight becomes literally trapped after the target moves away. In 4/10 positions (1, 7, 9, 10) the knight must retreat having wasted critical tempi while the opponent reorganizes. In 2/10 positions (3, 10) the knight's departure leaves behind undefended pawns that are immediately captured. The average cp_loss of 334 reflects how devastating it is to voluntarily abandon strategic dominance for a one-move tactical illusion. The target squares (b2, c2, b3, b5, b7, d3, d6, d7, c6) are consistently unstable squares where the knight lacks support and can be challenged by pawns, rooks, or bishops.

1073.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) away from a square where it was incidentally performing a critical defensive function, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
1073.description: 8/10 positions involve moving a piece to a seemingly reasonable square that abandons a crucial but non-obvious defensive role. 6/8 blunders are queen moves (Qc6, Qg3, Qf3, Qf6, Qg3, Qb2) where the queen shifts a short distance but severs a vital connection — defending a piece (positions 5, 10), controlling a diagonal against checks (positions 2, 8), covering key squares against knight forks (position 3), guarding a pawn (position 4), or maintaining favorable trade conditions (position 6). Position 1 (Rh8) self-blocks a king escape square, and position 10 (Rd1) places a rook where it hangs. 2/10 positions (7 and 9) are actually best moves with near-zero cp loss (pawn endgames where the only winning move is the pawn push), suggesting the feature partially fires on critical-decision positions. The consistent thread across the 8 blunders is that the moved piece was performing an 'invisible' defensive function the player didn't recognize — the defensive role was incidental to the piece's apparent purpose on that square.

1081.label: A knight captures a seemingly undefended central pawn while the king remains vulnerable, allowing the opponent's queen to exploit the opened diagonal with a check or double attack that wins the knight back with interest.
1081.description: All 10 positions feature a knight capturing an undefended central pawn (7/10 Nxe4, 3/10 Nxe5 or Nxc3), where the capturing side's king is uncastled in 9/10 cases. The critical shared mechanism is that the knight capture leaves the knight stranded on its new square without adequate support, while simultaneously opening or failing to block a diagonal that the opponent's queen immediately exploits. In 9/10 positions, the refutation is a queen move—specifically Qa4+ (4/10), Qd5 (2/10), Qa5+ (1/10), Qd4+ (1/10), or Qc2/Qxg5 (2/10)—that either delivers check along the exposed diagonal or creates a double attack on the undefended knight and a second target (usually f7 or the king itself). The average cp_loss of 280 reflects roughly losing a full piece for a pawn. In every case, 2-3 good developing/castling moves were available that maintained the position, making these unnecessary greedy captures when king safety should have been prioritized.

1079.label: Moving a bishop to a back-rank, second-rank, or corner square where it becomes passive or disconnected from the critical action.
1079.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to the peripheral ranks of the board: 4/10 go to the absolute back rank (d1, g8, c8, h8), 3/10 go to corners (a1, g8, h8), and the remaining moves land on the 2nd or 7th rank (c7, e7, f2, d2, g7). In every case, the bishop previously occupied a more central or functionally important square. The analyses unanimously cite tempo_loss (10/10) and piece_activity degradation (10/10) as core issues, while 8/10 positions also involve king_safety consequences. The average centipawn loss is extremely high (1134), indicating these moves are catastrophic rather than minor inaccuracies. The positions span middlegame (6/10) and endgame (4/10), both sides roughly equally (White 6, Black 4), showing this is a universal pattern rather than phase- or color-specific.

1082.label: Developing a minor piece to a square where an enemy pawn advance immediately forks it with another friendly piece already in place.
1082.description: 8/10 positions show the exact same geometric pattern: a minor piece is placed on a square such that it and another friendly piece occupy the same rank, separated by exactly one file, allowing a central pawn advance to fork both diagonally. Specifically, positions 1, 2, and 6 feature Be3 creating a fork target with Nc3 via ...d4; positions 3 and 5 feature Nf6 creating a fork target with Bd6 via e5; and positions 9 and 10 feature Bd6 creating a fork target with Nf6 via e5. The remaining 2/10 positions (7 and 8) show a closely related pattern where a bishop is placed on a square immediately vulnerable to a pawn advance with tempo (Be6 hit by f5, Bd3 hit by c4), costing decisive time in sharp positions. Position 4 is the weakest fit but still involves a piece retreating to a square attacked by a pawn advance. All 10 moves are natural-looking developing moves to seemingly active squares, making the pawn fork vulnerability non-obvious.

1087.label: The losing side sacrifices their only remaining significant piece for a meaningless check or pawn capture, converting a slow loss into immediate forced mate.
1087.description: In 10/10 positions, the blundering side was already significantly losing (avg eval ~10+ pawns disadvantage) and possessed very few pieces — typically just one rook or bishop as their sole defensive resource. The blunder in every case involves giving away this last piece, usually via a capture-with-check (8/10 give check) or a pawn capture that leaves the piece en prise (2/10). The result is universally catastrophic: 9/10 positions convert from 'losing but no forced mate' into forced checkmate (average mate-in-9). The pieces sacrificed are rooks in 8/10 cases and bishops in 2/10. In all cases, the best alternatives involved keeping the piece alive — either retreating, repositioning defensively, or using the king to escape — while the blunder strips away the only resource preventing the opponent's overwhelming material from delivering immediate checkmate against the naked king.

1074.label: The player makes a natural-looking developing, trading, or repositioning move that abandons a critical defensive responsibility, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability.
1074.description: 9/10 positions feature king safety as the central issue that the blunder ignores. 7/10 involve clear tempo loss where the piece must return or the opponent gains a free move to strike. 8/10 feature a missed tactic that was the position's actual demand. The blunders are diverse in piece type (3 bishop moves, 3 queen moves, 1 knight, 2 king moves, 1 pawn) but unified in character: each looks purposeful (Bb5/Ba6/Bd7 attack or trade pieces, Qf1/Qf5/Qc5 reposition for defense or counterplay, Na7 reroutes, O-O/Kg2 seek safety, g4 attacks a piece) yet each fundamentally abandons the position's most urgent defensive requirement. In every case, the best move addressed the critical demand directly — prophylactic king safety (positions 1,4,7), maintaining defensive piece placement (positions 3,5,10), precise tactical strikes (positions 8,9), or forced exchanges to neutralize threats (positions 2,6). The average cp_loss of 2188 reflects how catastrophically these 'reasonable-looking' moves fail when the position demands urgency over improvement.

1075.label: Playing non-forcing 'improving' moves when the position demands an immediate capture, exchange, or forcing response to resolve critical tactical tension.
1075.description: In 9/10 positions (excluding the 0cp-loss outlier Position 3), the player chose a non-forcing move — typically a pawn push (4/10: a2, g6, e6, h2) or quiet piece repositioning (5/10: Ra8, Rac1, Qf7, Qd7, Nd7) — while the position demanded immediate tactical resolution. In 5/10 positions, the best move was a CAPTURE resolving piece tension (Bxd6, Bxd7, Bxf5, Bxe2, Qxd2+). In 3/10 others, the best move was a defensive piece placement addressing an immediate threat (Nf6, Be6, Rh3). 7/10 positions had only 1 good move available, showing how narrow the correct path was and how critical the timing of the forcing move was. The average cp_loss of 1314 reflects catastrophic consequences — the unresolved tension or unaddressed threat explodes on the very next move, with opponents exploiting forks (Position 1), hanging pieces (Positions 2, 4, 9), king exposure (Positions 5, 6, 7), or pawn races (Position 8).

1088.label: The queen moves to a superficially attractive square (check, capture, or centralization) but abandons a vital defensive or coordinative role, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting weakness.
1088.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that displace the queen from where it is critically needed. In 3/10 cases the queen gives a pointless check (Qb3+, Qc8+, Qg3+) that accomplishes nothing while losing tempo. In 2/10 cases the queen captures material on the wrong square (Qxa2 grabs a pawn in the corner; Qxg7 captures a bishop far from the king). In 2/10 the queen moves offside to an edge square (Qb1, Qa6) abandoning kingside defense. In 2/10 the queen goes to a central/active-looking square that actually allows tactical exploitation (Qd4 permits forced queen trade via check; Qf2 abandons c-file control allowing a passed pawn advance). In 1/10 the queen captures with the wrong piece (Qxf6 instead of Bxf6), exposing the back rank. The consistent thread across all positions is that the queen was serving an essential function—defending a key square (d7 in positions 3 and 4), coordinating with rooks (positions 1, 6), maintaining pressure (positions 5, 8, 10), or staying near the king (position 9)—and the played move severs that connection. Average cp_loss is 2200, with 6/10 positions having only 1 good alternative within 50cp of best, confirming these are narrow critical moments where the queen's role is irreplaceable.

1078.label: A seemingly purposeful move (usually a queen move) that catastrophically ignores an immediate one-move tactical refutation in a razor-sharp position.
1078.description: All 10 positions share two defining characteristics: extremely high centipawn losses (average 5154cp) and very few good alternatives (average 2.1 good moves), meaning these are razor-sharp positions demanding extreme precision. 6/10 moves are queen moves to active-looking squares (Qxg2, Qc5, Qg4, Qd7, Qd4, Qf5) that appear to centralize, capture material, or create threats. The remaining 4 moves (h3, Kc7, h5, Kg3) similarly look purposeful—supporting pawns, improving king position, or chasing pieces. In every case, the moved piece lands on a square that is immediately and devastatingly exploitable: 3/10 allow instant checkmate (positions 2, 3, 5), 2/10 walk into knight/queen forks or traps (positions 1, 10), 3/10 lose a critical tempo in an urgent pawn race/promotion situation (positions 4, 8, 9), and 2/10 enable forced exchanges that create unstoppable passed pawns (positions 6, 7). The refutations are typically one move deep—the punishment is immediate rather than requiring a deep combination. 8/10 positions had only 1-3 good moves available, confirming these are positions where one specific defensive or prophylactic move was essential.
1078.old_chip: Active-looking move walks into instant punishment

1089.label: King moves toward an open file or forward rank under doubled-rook pressure, when retreating to the corner or back rank was the only safe option.
1089.description: In 10/10 positions, the king faces extreme pressure from enemy rooks (usually doubled on a rank or file), and must choose its escape direction with only 1-2 viable options. In the 7 positions with significant cp_loss, the king moved TOWARD the center or an open file (Kc1 toward d-file in 2/10, Kd1 toward center in 3/10, Kg3/Kf6 forward into rank-based mating nets in 2/10, Ka6 forward allowing rank check in 1/10), when the correct move was always a retreat toward a corner or back rank (Ka1, Kg1, Kf8, Ka8, Kb1, Kf1). The remaining 3/10 positions show 0 cp_loss where the king retreat IS played (or is the only option in a lost position), confirming the feature activates on positions requiring this critical directional choice. In 9/10 cases, enemy rooks were doubled or coordinated on the 2nd/7th rank or open files. The average cp_loss of ~3007 is inflated by 3 positions resulting in immediate checkmate, demonstrating that the wrong direction is often instantly fatal.

1077.label: Quiet pawn advances or slow piece moves that block a critical retreat square for one's own piece, resulting in that piece becoming trapped or a devastating tactical blow landing.
1077.description: 7/10 positions feature a quiet move (usually a pawn advance) that directly blocks or removes a critical square needed by one's own piece: positions 1 and 4 play ...c6 blocking the Na5's retreat to c6; position 8 plays h4 blocking the Nf5's retreat to h4; position 3 plays e4 abandoning d4 control; position 5 plays ...f6 removing the Bg4's Bxf3 resource; position 2 plays Bb2 placing the bishop where ...c5 entombs it; position 6 plays ...f6 removing f7's defensive coverage of g6. The remaining 3/10 (positions 7, 9, 10) share the broader pattern of playing non-urgent quiet moves (Bb7, c3, a6) while an immediate tactical crisis demands concrete action. All 10 moves are non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats), all appear 'natural' or positionally motivated, and all ignore that a specific piece or square requires immediate attention. The trapped-piece motif appears explicitly in 7/10 positions, making it the dominant mechanism. Average cp_loss of 1248 reflects that these self-inflicted wounds are catastrophic.

1091.label: Playing a quiet rook repositioning move (or king retreat) along the back rank when the player's own king is exposed and the position demands immediate tactical action.
1091.description: 10/10 positions feature moves played exclusively on the back rank (1st or 8th rank), with 8/10 being rook moves (Re1, Rf1, Re8, Rf8) and 2/10 being king retreats to h1. In 9/10 positions, the player's own king is explicitly exposed or vulnerable (on e2, f2, f7, e7, or weakened on g1/h8). In every case, the move played appears to be a natural 'developing' or 'improving' move — centralizing a rook on the e-file or f-file, or tucking the king into the corner — but actually wastes a critical tempo while an urgent tactical crisis goes unaddressed. The average cp_loss of 1209 reflects that these positions are razor-sharp moments where only 1-2 good moves exist (avg 1.6 good moves), and the common punishment involves the opponent exploiting the exposed king via checks, forks, discovered attacks, or perpetual check mechanisms that the passive move failed to prevent.

1090.label: King moves away from the critical sector of the board or toward danger, losing decisive tempo when precise directional choice was required.
1090.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves that go in the wrong direction. In 8/10 cases, the best move was also a king move but to a different square (typically the opposite direction or toward the center), while in 2/10 cases (positions 6 and 8) the king shouldn't have moved at all. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, confirming the unifying theme. Specifically: in positions 1, 3, and 9, the king moves toward the kingside when queenside passed pawns demand attention; in position 2, the king goes queenside when a kingside pawn break must be prevented; in positions 5, 7, and 10, the king advances into squares vulnerable to checks or mating patterns instead of retreating or centralizing; in positions 6 and 8, the king moves at all when an immediate tactical or pawn-break move was critical. The average cp_loss of 1276 is extremely high, and only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where the king's directional choice is the entire game.
