1085.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or repositioning move in a tactically critical position that demands immediate concrete action (capture, forcing move, or urgent defensive task).
1085.description: All 10 positions share a defining characteristic: the player chose a 'quiet' or 'improving' move — developing a piece to a natural square, advancing a pawn for activity, or repositioning — when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 5/10 cases (Bg2, Nf3#2, Qh3, Qf6, Nf3#6), a capture or forced tactical blow was the best move but was passed over in favor of piece improvement. In 4/10 cases (Bf5, Nh6, f5, b4), the best move addressed a critical positional urgency (king safety, maintaining a guardian piece, or developing before advancing). The average number of good moves was only 1.7, confirming these were razor-sharp positions with extremely narrow paths. The average cp_loss of 2090 (inflated by two mate-misses) reflects how catastrophic it is to play 'slow' in critical moments. In 7/10 positions, the quiet move actually CREATED new weaknesses: f3 removed the fxg3 recapture, Nf3 blocked king escape routes (positions 2 and 6), f5 weakened the pawn shield, b4 left a3 undefended, Nh6 removed a critical guardian, and Bf5 placed a piece on an undefended square exploitable by checks.

1084.label: The king (or a piece) moves to a square that appears safe but directly enables an immediate devastating check, mate, or major piece invasion along an open line.
1084.description: 8/10 positions feature king moves (Kd7, Kf1, Ke7, Ke8, Ke1, Kf8, Kh8, Kg8) that walk the king directly into a square where the opponent's rook or queen can immediately exploit an open rank or file. In 7/10 cases, the punishment involves a rook delivering check or mate on the rank/file the king moved to (Rh1#, Rg8#, Rg7+, Ra8+, etc.). The remaining 2 non-king moves (Bxh6 missing Qg6# and Ng4+ hanging to Qxg4) share the same structural error: making a natural-looking move that catastrophically ignores the opponent's immediate tactical response on an open line. The average cp_loss of 4848 reflects that these are nearly always game-ending blunders. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were razor-thin positions requiring exact play, where the player chose a seemingly logical move (fleeing, capturing, checking) that violated the one critical constraint the position demanded.

1092.label: Developing a bishop to a natural-looking square when the position demands an immediate forcing move, wasting a critical tempo.
1092.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to a seemingly reasonable central square (e3, e6, d6, c4, d3) during the opening or early middlegame, when a concrete tactical opportunity was available instead. In 7/10 cases, the bishop move directly creates a tactical vulnerability—most commonly to a central pawn advance (d4 or d5) that attacks the newly-placed bishop (positions 1, 2, 5, 7, 8). In the remaining cases, the tempo spent on passive bishop development allows the opponent to neutralize a winning tactical shot (positions 4, 6, 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 281 reflects how punishing these errors are—these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments of the position's demands. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than generic development. The positions span both sides (White 6/10, Black 4/10) and both opening (6/10) and middlegame (4/10), but share the universal thread of choosing a 'textbook' bishop development over a forcing, often tactical continuation.

1104.label: King retreats to the corner (h1/h8/f8) instead of capturing a hanging enemy bishop on the adjacent square.
1104.description: In 10/10 positions, an enemy bishop sits on a square directly adjacent to the king (h2 for White's king in 4 positions, h7 for Black's king in 5 positions, f7 in 1 position), and the only good move is for the king to CAPTURE that bishop (Kxh2, Kxh7, or Kxf7). Instead, the king retreats one square further into the corner (Kh1, Kh8, or Kf8), declining the free piece. In all 10 cases, only 1 good move existed (the capture), and the average cp_loss was 1329, with one position resulting in forced mate. The bishop left alive becomes the cornerstone of a devastating attack: in 5/10 positions it enables discovered checks or mating nets, in 4/10 it simply retreats to safety meaning the player gave up a free piece for nothing, and in 1/10 it costs a critical tempo allowing the opponent to resolve other tensions first.

1095.label: Moving a minor piece to an aesthetically appealing central/active square while ignoring the position's concrete tactical demands.
1095.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (7 knight moves, 3 bishop moves) being placed on a classically 'strong' square — outposts, central squares, or attacking diagonals — that looks positionally desirable but misses the one urgent tactical requirement. In 10/10 cases, the average number of good moves was only 1.4, meaning these were razor-narrow positions demanding precise concrete play rather than general improvement. In 3/10 positions (Nf3, Nc6, Nc5-pos10), a forcing tactical strike was available (capture with check, fork) that the player missed in favor of a quieter piece relocation. In 4/10 positions (Ng2, Nd4, Nf4, Nc5-pos9), the piece move to the attractive square created an immediate tactical vulnerability (self-blocking, exposing queen, allowing discovered attack, abandoning defense). In 3/10 positions (Bd4, Bc5, Bxd5), the bishop left a critical defensive or functional square for a superficially active one, enabling the opponent's main threat. The target squares (d4, c5, f3, g2, f4, c6, d5) are all classically desirable minor piece posts, suggesting players were thinking in terms of piece placement principles rather than calculating the concrete tactical situation.

1086.label: Choosing a superficially attractive aggressive move (capture, check, or piece placement on an 'outpost') that is easily refuted, when a quieter or more precise move maintained the advantage.
1086.description: 9/10 positions featured a player with an equal or better position who chose an aggressive-looking move that squandered their advantage. 6/10 moves were captures or checks (Nxc7, Qxe6, Bxc4, d2+, Nxc3, Bc7+), and the remainder were aggressive piece placements toward the opponent's position (Nf5, Kf6, Rg8, Qf3). In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 5, 10), the moved piece landed on a square where it was simply captured by an obvious defender—tagged as 'hanging_piece.' The correct moves were consistently more patient or precise: quiet centralization (Kf5, Rd4, Ndb4), prophylactic defense (Rf2, Ke3), or capturing the actual vulnerable target (Qxd7 instead of Bxc4). The average number of good moves was only 1.7, meaning these were demanding positions requiring restraint rather than aggression. The refutations were overwhelmingly simple—basic recaptures, natural defensive moves, or exploiting what the aggressive move left undefended—suggesting the players didn't verify their opponent's most obvious reply.

1093.label: Placing the queen on e2/e7/e8 in positions where a knight can immediately jump to d4 or d5 to exploit the queen's placement with tempo.
1093.description: 9/10 positions involve the queen moving to a square on the e-file (Qe2 for White in 5 positions, Qe7 for Black in 3, Qe8 in 1), while the remaining position (c3) is an outlier. In 7/10 cases, the immediate refutation involves a knight jumping to d4 or d5 that directly attacks the queen with devastating consequences — either forking the queen and another piece (Positions 1, 2, 6, 8), attacking the queen while enabling a follow-up structural or material blow like Nxf6+ (Positions 5, 7), or exploiting a pin that the queen's e-file placement maintains (Position 9). The moves are uniformly described as 'natural developing moves' intended to connect rooks or support the e-pawn, but all ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability created by the queen landing on that specific square. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, indicating these were critical decision points requiring tactical awareness rather than routine development.
1093.old_chip: Queen to e-file allows knight fork

1097.label: Using the Rook to make a tempting material capture when a different piece should capture or a stronger forcing move exists.
1097.description: 9/10 positions feature Rook captures (Rx-), almost always taking a piece on an open file or attacking a target. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 9, 10), the exact same square should have been captured by a minor piece instead (Nxd3 vs Rxd3, Nxd4 vs Rxd4, Bxg5 vs Rxg5, Nxf3 vs Rxf3) — the 'wrong capturing piece' error where the Knight or Bishop capture simultaneously activates a passive piece and preserves the Rook's defensive duties. In 4/10 positions (1, 6, 7, 8), the Rook capture grabs material but misses a far stronger Queen-based forcing move (Qxc5+, Qh3+, Qg5, Qd5+) that exploits superior geometry. Only 2/10 positions (3, 5) featured the Rook capture as actually correct (0-14cp loss). The Rook captures frequently come with check (6/10 include +), making them visually seductive as 'forcing' moves.

1106.label: A knight captures a pawn that is defended by an adjacent pawn, losing the knight for insufficient material (1-2 pawns).
1106.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight captures a pawn that is defended by an adjacent pawn which immediately recaptures, resulting in a net material loss of approximately one pawn's worth (knight ≈ 3 points traded for 1-2 pawns ≈ 1-2 points). The defending pawns are consistently on adjacent files: a-pawn defending b4 (2/10), d-pawn defending e4 (2/10), f-pawn defending g4 (2/10), h-pawn defending g5 (3/10), and c-pawn defending b5 (1/10). 9/10 positions occur in the opening phase with both kings still in the center, suggesting these are impulsive pawn-grabbing decisions before development is complete. The average cp_loss of 314 reflects the consistent loss of roughly a full minor piece for insufficient pawn compensation. In all cases, quiet developing or retreating moves were available that maintained material balance.

1103.label: A piece retreats or repositions to a quiet square when an immediate forcing tactical strike (check, sacrifice, or pawn break) was available.
1103.description: All 10/10 positions share a single unmistakable pattern: the player chose a non-forcing, passive piece move (typically a retreat or quiet repositioning) when the position demanded an immediate concrete tactical blow. 7/10 moves are bishop retreats/repositions to passive squares (Bb1, Ba1, Bb6, Bc1, Bg4, Bg3, Bh6), 2/10 are queen retreats to inactive squares (Qd8 to starting square, Qa7 to corner), and 1/10 is a king retreat (Kf1). In every case, a forcing alternative existed: a knight sacrifice (Nf6+, Nb3+, Ne4), a pawn breakthrough (h4, e4-e3-exf2+), or a piece advance into the opponent's position (Be5). The average cp_loss of 277 reflects that these positions all had narrow windows—only 1.4 good moves available on average—meaning the tactical opportunity was fleeting and the tempo loss was catastrophic. 10/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif, and in 8/10 the opponent's strongest refutation explicitly exploited the free tempo to neutralize the missed threat permanently.

1094.label: A piece is relocated away from a square where it performed an irreplaceable defensive, blocking, or attacking function, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated duty.
1094.description: 10/10 positions feature a piece (or king) being moved away from a square where it was performing an essential function that no other piece could fulfill. In 4/10 cases a knight left a dominant or blocking square (Na6 from b4 near the enemy king, Nh7 from f6 blocking the a1-h8 diagonal, Ne2 from c3 while blocking the queen's line to g4, Nd7 from the dominant e5 outpost). In 4/10 cases a bishop abandoned its duty (Bd1 from e2 leaving a mating corridor, Bxe2 capturing non-forcingly when the queen needed to stay defended, Be4 from f5 allowing a draw by repetition, Bc5 from d6 releasing a passed pawn blockade). The remaining 2 cases involve a king leaving pawn protection (Kf3 from f4 unguarding f5) and a pawn advance ignoring back-rank vulnerability (d3). In every case, the opponent's strongest refutation directly exploits the specific function the piece just abandoned — whether that's capturing a newly undefended pawn/piece (6/10), advancing through a vacated blockade (2/10), or exploiting a newly opened line/square for checkmate (3/10). The moves are uniformly non-forcing (0/10 give check, only 1/10 is a capture) and represent repositioning attempts that misjudge which piece placement is most important.

1101.label: Playing a quiet minor piece development or repositioning move to a natural square while the position demands an urgent tactical response.
1101.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing minor piece move (7 knight moves, 3 bishop moves) to a 'textbook' development square (d2 four times, d7 twice, plus e2, e6, b7) while a critical tactical demand goes unaddressed. In 4/10 positions (3, 6, 7, 10), the move actively removes or displaces a piece from a vital defensive duty (guarding c3, blocking a back rank, covering a passed pawn). In 3/10 positions (2, 5, 8), a hanging or freely capturable piece is ignored in favor of development. In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 9), the move fails to address an opponent's infiltrating piece or imminent mating attack that required a forcing response (queen trade, piece retreat to safety). The average cp_loss of 1157 reflects the catastrophic nature of playing slowly in urgent positions. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, meaning these were critical moments with almost no margin for 'natural' play.

1096.label: Advancing a passed pawn in an endgame promotion race before the king is optimally positioned or before a more forcing move order is available.
1096.description: All 10/10 positions feature non-capturing pawn advances in endgame (9/10) or late middlegame (1/10) positions with exposed kings and active pawn promotion themes. Every position involves passed pawns or pawn races where tempo is critical. Among the 5 positions where the move was a mistake (avg cp_loss 342 for those), the consistent error was advancing the pawn before the king reached its optimal square: Position 1 played g5 instead of Kh6, Position 6 played b4 instead of Kb5, Position 8 played a3 instead of Kb2, Position 7 played e5 instead of the forcing f6+, and Position 9 pushed the wrong pawn (c5 instead of the immediate b4). In all 5 correct instances (0 cp_loss), the pawn advance was either the only winning move in a razor-sharp promotion race (Positions 2, 4) or tied for best with king moves that transpose (Positions 3, 5, 10). The feature detects the specific moment of choosing to push a passer forward in tempo-critical endgame positions where king placement determines whether the advance wins or throws away the advantage.

1099.label: Trading or displacing a piece (usually a rook) that is performing an essential protective function, immediately allowing tactical exploitation of the newly unguarded squares or ranks.
1099.description: 7/9 positions involve rook moves or rook exchanges (Rxe4, Re1, Rxc1, Rxd1, Rxd8, Rxe8, plus the pawn moves that relate to piece protection). In 6/9 cases, the blunder is specifically a rook being traded or moved away from a square where it was guarding something critical: the d2 square (Position 2), the back rank (Positions 4 and 7), the only active piece maintaining pressure (Positions 1 and 6), or a piece needed for a follow-up combination (Position 3). The remaining moves (g6, c4, g4) share the same underlying error of abandoning a critical function—g6 neglects the tactical dxc4 that the position demanded, c4 pushes a pawn away from king protection creating open lines, and g4 frees the opponent's knight from needing to spend a tempo capturing. In 8/9 positions, the refutation involves immediate tactical exploitation (forks, back-rank mates, discovered attacks, or queen captures with check) of squares/lines that the moved piece was previously covering. The average cp_loss of 1228 reflects that these are often catastrophic—the piece was the linchpin of the entire defensive setup.

1105.label: Rook repositioned to a passive peripheral square when the position demands immediate forcing action or critical defense.
1105.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to a non-forcing, passive square rather than executing urgent tactical or defensive duties. 8/10 moves place the rook on an edge file (a-file: Ra2, Ra2, Ra8, Ra7, Ra6, Ra6; h-file: Rh7, Rh8), with the remaining 2 (Rd6, Rf7) still representing passive repositioning rather than decisive action. In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete play — whether king evacuation (Position 1), forcing checks before quiet moves (Position 7), capturing instead of threatening (Position 8), or pushing pawns to restrict opponent's pieces (Position 9). Instead, the player spent a tempo shuffling the rook to a square where it accomplishes nothing urgent. 9/10 positions are tagged 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif, and 10/10 are tagged 'piece_activity' — the rook consistently ends up less useful than it started. The average cp_loss of 1151 reflects how devastating a single wasted tempo can be in sharp middlegame positions.

1108.label: A minor piece already attacking a hanging high-value target moves elsewhere instead of capturing it.
1108.description: In 10/10 positions, the piece that was moved (9/10 a knight, 1/10 a bishop) was already positioned to capture a hanging or vulnerable high-value piece, but instead made a different move—abandoning the winning capture. The missed captures included queens (4/10: positions 3, 7, 8, 10), rooks (4/10: positions 1, 4, 6, 9), and key minor pieces (2/10: positions 2, 5). The blunder moves fell into clear sub-categories: giving a pointless check (4/10: Ne6+, Nd3+, Ng3+, and implicitly Nf3), 'centralizing' to an aesthetically pleasing square (3/10: Nd5, Ne5, Ne3), making the wrong capture (1/10: Nxf6 instead of Nxh2), retreating (1/10: Ng6), or repositioning to a different diagonal (1/10: Bf3). The average cp_loss of 1403 reflects that these moves typically swing the position by an entire major piece worth of material, since the player literally walks away from capturing a queen or rook.

1102.label: A non-forcing pawn move (usually a kingside pawn advance) played when an immediately decisive forcing tactic is available.
1102.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing pawn move played in a critical tactical moment where a concrete forcing continuation was available. 9/10 moves are pure pawn moves (the exception, Bxg6, is a speculative sacrifice involving the kingside pawn structure). 7/10 specifically involve the g-pawn or a move to/on the g-file (g3, g6, g4, fxg3, Bxg6). The missed tactics vary widely — knight forks (positions 4, 1), back-rank mates (position 2), queen captures (position 7), piece-winning combinations (positions 3, 9), and mating attacks (position 6) — but the error is always the same: playing a slow, prophylactic, or positional pawn push when the position demanded immediate tactical precision. The average cp_loss of 3061 and average of only 1.5 good moves confirms these are razor-sharp moments where tempo is everything. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' appears in all 10.

1098.label: Playing non-critical moves (captures, repositions, or passive king moves) in positions where a single urgent tactical issue demands immediate attention.
1098.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a move that would be reasonable in a different context but catastrophically ignores the ONE critical demand of the position. In 5/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 6, 7, 10), the player ignored an immediate concrete threat from the opponent (Rxc2+, Qxb2#, Nxd3+, Rxh4+, Qh3+). In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 8), the player created a new tactical vulnerability that didn't previously exist (allowing Nxg6+ with check, Rxh7+ with check, or Rxe5 capturing a hanging piece). In 2/10 cases (positions 1, 9), the player missed their own overwhelming tactical opportunity (forced mate, holding a dominant outpost). The average cp_loss of 2195 reflects catastrophic consequences, and the average of only 1.8 good moves confirms these are positions with a single dominant concern. 8/10 positions featured immediate tactical threats or hanging pieces that required concrete calculation rather than general planning.
1098.old_chip: Ignoring urgent threats for routine moves

1100.label: Forward-moving pieces or pawns that overextend into tactical vulnerability, granting the opponent decisive tempo.
1100.description: All 10/10 moves are forward/advancing in nature — pawn pushes (e5, g4, g5+, fxg6, c5), piece advances (Ne3, Re5), king advances (Ke4), or forward captures (Nxd5, Kxb5). Not a single retreat appears. In 9/10 cases the best move was more restrained: retreats (Kd2, Nf1), quiet development (Nf3), a different forcing move (Re1+ check), or a defensive capture (Nxh3). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 positions, making it the strongest signal. The common mechanism is that the advancing move either abandons a critical defensive duty (6/10: Ne3 leaves blockade, g4 removes king shield, Ke4 walks into passed pawns, Re5 blocks own pawn, fxg6 ignores forcing check, c5 allows knight relocation with check) or places the moved piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Nxd5 into a pin, e5 creating a hanging pawn). In 8/10 positions White made the error, and the average cp_loss of 244 reflects serious consequences from what appear to be natural-looking aggressive moves.

1107.label: Player captures obvious material or centralizes a piece when a more forcing tactical continuation (mate, fork, capture with check) would yield far greater returns.
1107.description: In 9/10 positions (excluding #5 which was correctly played at 0cp loss), the player chose a visually tempting but suboptimal move over a more concrete, forcing continuation. The most striking sub-pattern involves knights capturing rooks in corner squares (h8, a8, h1) — this occurs in 4/10 positions, and in 3 of those the knight becomes trapped or the capture misses a vastly superior tactic (mate in position 3, queen capture in position 1, bishop-with-check sequence in position 6). Another 4/10 positions show knights being centralized to 'strong' squares (d4, d5, b5) instead of executing immediate tactical shots — hanging piece captures (positions 4, 8) or devastating forks (positions 7, 10). The remaining positions show similar 'attractive but wrong' piece placements (wrong rook in position 2, rook to 7th allowing exchange in position 9). In ALL mistake positions, the correct move was more FORCING: delivering check, capturing with check, forking pieces, or delivering immediate checkmate. The average cp_loss of 1254 reflects how catastrophic these 'obvious over optimal' decisions are.

1114.label: Moving a bishop to a rim square (h6/h3/a3/g5) to exchange the opponent's bishop when concrete tactical or developmental priorities demand attention.
1114.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop moving to an edge square (h6 in 5 positions, h3 in 2, Ba3 in 1, Bg5 in 1) with the explicit intent of trading off the opponent's bishop — typically a fianchettoed bishop on g7 (5/9) or g2 (2/9). In every case, the bishop sortie is strategically motivated but tactically premature: 6/9 positions are in the opening phase where development and king safety should take priority, and in 7/9 positions one side's king remains uncastled. The common punishment pattern is that the bishop either lands on an undefended rim square creating hanging-piece tactics (Positions 1, 2, 4, 8), removes itself from a critical defensive function (Position 8: releases pin on f6 knight; Position 3: abandons attacking diagonal), or simply wastes crucial tempo allowing the opponent to resolve their weaknesses (Positions 9, 10: White castles or wins central pawns). The average cp_loss of 335 reflects that these moves consistently squander significant advantages or convert equal positions into losing ones.

1120.label: The queen captures material but was serving a critical defensive function, leaving the king or a piece fatally exposed.
1120.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen capture (Qx__) that grabs material — pawns (4/10), pieces (3/10), or rooks (3/10) — while the queen was simultaneously performing an essential defensive duty. In 6/10 cases, the queen was directly protecting a piece that becomes hanging with check after the queen moves (positions 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10). In 4/10 cases, the queen was shielding an exposed king from invasion or perpetual check (positions 1, 2, 7, 8). The refutations almost universally begin with a check or forcing move that exploits the newly undefended target: 8/10 refutations start with check. The average centipawn loss is an enormous 3084, with 4/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate. The pattern is remarkably consistent: in every single case, a stronger non-capturing move existed that maintained the queen's defensive coordination (avg 2.0 good moves available), but the player was lured by visible material gain into displacing their most versatile defender.

1111.label: A non-forcing 'improving' move (pawn push, development, king walk) is played while a critical piece or pawn is tactically vulnerable, resulting in immediate material loss.
1111.description: All 10 positions share a defining pattern: the player chose a non-urgent, strategically motivated move while an immediate tactical obligation existed. In 9/10 cases the 'tempo_loss' tag applies—the move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary goal. The tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' in 7/10 positions, meaning the punishment typically involves winning undefended material. 5/10 moves are pawn pushes (c6, a3, a3, f6, cxb3), 3/10 are piece development moves (Rd3, Rhf1, Ne2), and 2/10 are king moves or queen relocations—all sharing the quality of being non-forcing (no checks, no captures addressing the threat). In every case, the best moves directly addressed the tactical crisis first: eliminating a dangerous enemy piece (Nxd3, Ne4), securing a hanging piece (f3, h3, Be1), or simplifying to neutralize threats (Rc8, Qd6). The average cp_loss of 1386 reflects how catastrophic ignoring immediate tactics can be—6/10 positions swung from one side winning to the other side winning or forced mate.

1118.label: Rook captures a pawn prematurely, prioritizing material over more urgent tactical or strategic needs.
1118.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing an enemy pawn (Rx pawn), and in every case this material grab is a significant mistake because something more important was required. In 3/10 positions (6, 8, 10), the player missed a forced mate or promotion-based win while grabbing an irrelevant pawn. In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 4, 7), the capture was a move-order error where a defensive or prophylactic move was needed first to secure a vulnerable pawn before the capture could safely be made. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 9), the capture abandoned a superior strategic plan (king advancement, passed pawn push, or dominant piece placement) in favor of eliminating an enemy pawn that was actually harmless or secondary. The endgame phase dominates (8/10), and the average centipawn loss of 3127 is extreme, reflecting the catastrophic nature of these grabs when they enable back-rank mates, miss forced checkmates, or squander decisive positional advantages. The best moves consistently involved non-material actions: king moves (positions 1, 2, 4, 7, 10), prophylactic pawn pushes (positions 3, 7, 9, 10), or piece repositioning (position 5).

1119.label: A rook is moved to passively blockade or directly confront an advanced passed pawn near promotion, when a more active or forcing alternative exists.
1119.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a rook to the 1st or 8th rank specifically to address a dangerous passed pawn within 1-2 squares of promotion. The rook was placed directly in front of, or onto, the promotion square to physically stop queening. In 7/10 cases, the position featured connected or multiple passed pawns where blockading one left the other free (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10). In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 7), the blockading square was tactically vulnerable—the rook was immediately capturable by an opponent's piece. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 7, 9, 10), a forcing attacking continuation against the opponent's exposed king was available but ignored in favor of the defensive rook move. The average cp_loss of 1090 reflects that these passive reactions to promotion threats consistently miss superior alternatives: capturing the pawn outright (position 8), sacrificing material to eliminate multiple threats simultaneously (position 6), or ignoring the pawn entirely to deliver a decisive attack (positions 7, 9).

1116.label: Playing a slow c3/c6/f3/f6 pawn move to the 3rd rank that blocks a knight's natural development square while ignoring urgent tactical demands.
1116.description: All 10 positions feature a pawn advance to the player's 3rd rank (c3 in 7/10, c6 in 2/10, f3/f6 in 1/10 each) chosen as a 'solidifying' move when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 6/10 positions, the pawn directly blocked a knight from occupying that exact square — and in positions 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10, the knight move to that square was explicitly one of the top recommendations (Nc3 was the best move in position 6, second-best in positions 2 and 4; Nf3 was second-best in position 8; Ne4/Nf3 were top moves in position 10). The average centipawn loss was 261, with 8/10 positions in the opening phase where development tempo is most critical. In every case, the opponent punished the wasted tempo with either a tactical blow (forks in positions 4, 10; queen checks in positions 7, 9) or consolidation that neutralized White's attacking chances (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 6). Only 2.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments where the 'safe' pawn push was uniquely costly.

1113.label: Impulsive queen moves (usually checks) that look forcing but squander a winning/drawing resource by choosing apparent activity over the actually correct continuation.
1113.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move as the blunder, and 7/10 are queen checks. The average centipawn loss is a catastrophic 4140, with only 1.4 good moves available on average, indicating razor-sharp positions requiring precision. The core pattern is a player choosing an aggressive-looking, often forcing queen move instead of the actually correct continuation. In 5/10 cases, the best move was NOT a queen move at all (Rd8, Ra7, f4, g5, or a quiet rook/pawn move), while in the other 5/10 the best move was a queen move to a *different* square (Qd7 not Qg4, Qe2 not Qa1, Qd3+ not Qd5+, Qh5# not Qh4+, Qg8+ not Qb1+). The blunders share the quality of being 'seductive' — they appear active, centralizing, or forcing (especially checks), but they consistently abandon a more powerful resource: 7th/8th rank penetration (positions 1-3), central pressure (position 4), escape-square creation (position 5), precise mating geometry (positions 6, 8), defensive counterplay preservation (positions 7, 9), or stalemate tricks (position 10).

1122.label: A knight on f3/f6 moves to h4/h5 to attack a bishop, landing on an undefended rim square where it can be captured or wastes critical tempo.
1122.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving from the f-file to the h-file (Nf6→h5 for Black in 6 cases, Nf3→h4 for White in 4 cases), invariably intending to attack an opponent's bishop sitting on g3, g5, f4, or f5. In 5/10 positions, the knight lands completely undefended and is simply captured (by queen in positions 2, 3, 8, or by bishop in positions 1, 10), often resulting in catastrophic material loss or pawn structure destruction. In the remaining 5/10 positions, the bishop sidesteps or White/Black simply ignores the threat, leaving the knight stranded on the rim having abandoned critical defensive duties — particularly guarding central squares, supporting pawn structures, or maintaining piece coordination (positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 9). The average centipawn loss is 347, reflecting both outright piece-hanging blunders and severe positional degradation. In 7/10 positions the opponent had fianchettoed or had castled kingside, meaning the knight's departure from f6/f3 often compromised king safety as well.

1121.label: A knight move creates an apparent offensive threat (fork, attack, centralization) while catastrophically ignoring a more urgent tactical necessity in the position.
1121.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight making a non-capturing, non-checking move to an apparently active square that creates some form of offensive threat. In 7/10 cases the knight creates a fork or dual attack on enemy pieces (e.g., Ne3 forking Rd1+Bf5, Nc3 forking Qd1+Re1, Nd6 forking Bb7+Rf8). In every case, the threat is either illusory (the opponent escapes with tempo via check in 3/10 cases) or simply irrelevant because a far more urgent tactical element dominates: king safety threats demanding immediate defense (5/10), unstoppable passed pawns requiring blockade or elimination (3/10), hanging pieces that should be captured immediately (2/10), or a simple superior knight move available (1/10). The average cp_loss of 4041 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—4/10 positions result in forced mate. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments demanding precision, yet the players chose an aggressive-looking knight sortie over the one necessary move.

1110.label: The defending/losing side's king makes a seemingly active or centralizing move in a lost endgame, but moves in the wrong direction relative to the critical threat.
1110.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where the side making the king move is already losing significantly (evaluations range from -400 to -800+ for the moving side). In every case, the defending king makes a move that appears reasonable—often toward the center or along a logical-looking path—but fails to address the specific critical threat. In 6/10 positions the mistake involves moving the king away from advancing passed pawns that need to be blockaded (positions 4-9), while 3/10 involve K+R vs K scenarios where the king moves to a square that allows it to be cut off more efficiently. Notably, 3/10 positions (1, 2, 3) have essentially 0 cp_loss, meaning the position is so lost that no king move makes a difference—the feature fires because the defending king is helplessly wandering in a resignable position. The moves that ARE true blunders (positions 5, 7, 8, 9) share a specific geometric error: the king moves toward apparent 'activity' (centralization, counterplay targets) while abandoning the defensive perimeter around the critical promotion square or mating zone.

1115.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or improving move while a critical king-safety tactical threat demands immediate concrete action.
1115.description: 10/10 positions feature king_safety as the dominant tactical theme, with the played move either directly worsening king exposure or ignoring an urgent tactical threat related to the king's vulnerability. 3/10 positions involve Qe2 placing the queen on the e-file directly in front of an uncastled king on e1, creating a fatal queen-king alignment exploitable by ...Re8. 3/10 involve castling (O-O) directly into an immediate tactical refutation — twice into knight fork/capture threats from a dominant Nd5, and once into a diagonal check (Qb6+) enabled by an advanced f-pawn. The remaining 4 positions feature other 'improving' moves (Kxe7 exposing the king, Qd2 placing the queen on an attacked diagonal, e5 missing a decisive rook check, f4 removing a critical defensive pawn). 6/10 positions are in the opening phase where castling or queen development appears natural. The average cp_loss of 2184 reflects that these are catastrophic blunders disguised as reasonable moves, and the average of only 2.2 good alternatives shows these positions demanded precise concrete play rather than general principles.

1109.label: Playing a routine or greedy pawn move (usually a capture) when the position demands one precise defensive piece move to survive.
1109.description: 9/10 positions feature a pawn move as the blunder (h4, cxb4, axb4, exf3, dxe5, bxa5, c5, hxg4, g4), with only one exception being a knight move (Nh4). Critically, in 9/10 positions the correct move was a PIECE move — Rfe1, Qe4, Bxd5, Bb7, Rh3, Kf2, Qc1, Qd6, Rd2 — meaning the player consistently defaulted to a pawn action when only a precise piece deployment would address the emergency. The average number of good moves was just 1.4, confirming these are narrow defensive positions where the player had essentially one correct resource. 8/10 positions involved king safety crises (exposed kings, mating threats, back-rank weakness), and the pawn moves uniformly failed to address these threats. 6/10 blunders were pawn captures that appeared to gain material or simplify but actually removed critical defensive barriers (c3 pawn shielding d2, d4 pawn blocking the d-file, e4 pawn blocking the e-file, a5 pawn sheltering the king). The remaining pawn pushes (h4, c5, g4) wasted decisive tempi on space-gaining or structural ideas while the position burned.

1112.label: Moving a bishop (or minor piece) for development that removes a critical back-rank blocker, allowing the opponent's queen to capture a rook — usually with check.
1112.description: In 8/10 positions, the player moves a minor piece (9/10 are bishops) as a seemingly natural 'developing' move, failing to recognize that the piece was performing a vital defensive function — typically blocking a rank between the opponent's queen and an undefended rook. The immediate punishment in 7/10 cases is the opponent's queen capturing a rook WITH CHECK (Qxh8+, Qxa1+, or Qxh1+), gaining a devastating extra tempo that prevents any compensation. In 6/10 positions, the piece literally sat on the back rank (f8, f1, c1, or b1) physically blocking queen access to the corner rook; once it moved, the geometric line opened catastrophically. The remaining positions (6, 8) share the spirit — bishop development that is immediately punished tactically — though via different mechanisms (bishop forced back losing tempo, or bishop left hanging). All 10 moves share the characteristic of prioritizing piece activation over concrete tactical awareness.

1127.label: Moving the queen (or rook) when the exposed king urgently needed to relocate to safety first.
1127.description: In 9/10 positions, the best move was a king move to escape an exposed square, but the player instead moved their queen (9/10) or rook (1/10). The kings were consistently exposed — on h3, f3, d6, h8, e6, g7, e4, g7, and f3 — sitting on open files, diagonals, or ranks vulnerable to checks. The correct king moves (Kh4, Kg3/Ke3, Kc6, Kg8, Kf7, Kh6, Kd5, Kh6/Kf7, Ke3) all prioritized evacuating the king from the danger zone before committing other pieces. The played queen moves often looked natural — centralizing (Qe5, Qf6), offering exchanges (Qf7, Qf4, Qe2), or attacking (Qg3) — but fatally left the king stranded. The most common consequence was perpetual check (6/10 positions), while others suffered queen captures with check, deflection tactics, or decisive material loss. Position 7 (11cp loss) was the sole outlier where the queen move was actually near-optimal.

1117.label: The player makes a natural-looking capture of an enemy piece (often one that has invaded their position) but in doing so abandons a critical defensive, attacking, or tactical function their piece was performing.
1117.description: 9/10 positions involve captures of enemy pieces that appear threatening or annoying (intruding bishops on f3, centralized knights on d6, checking pieces on g3, infiltrating rooks on d1). In 6/10 cases, the capturing piece was actively defending another piece or maintaining a crucial attacking configuration (Position 1: queen left f4 abandoning g4 bishop; Position 2: queen left e2 abandoning e7 bishop; Position 4: knight left f3 abandoning d4 pawn; Position 5: queen left g6 dissolving mating attack; Position 6: queen left e7 abandoning e5 knight; Position 10: rook left d8 abandoning d2 pawn). In 3/10 cases, the player missed a much stronger tactical blow available (Position 7: Qxa1+ winning a rook; Position 8: Nf6+ fork winning both rooks; Position 9: exd5 winning the queen). In 1/10 (Position 3), the wrong piece recaptured, exposing the king. All 10 share the thread of being drawn to an 'obvious' or 'reactive' capture that addresses a visible threat while overlooking the hidden cost to their own position's integrity. Average cp_loss was 381, and only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow decision points requiring precise calculation over instinct.

1123.label: Playing a natural-looking positional or developing move while a piece is left completely undefended and immediately capturable.
1123.description: All 10/10 positions share the same core mistake: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move with clear positional intent (developing, centralizing, advancing a pawn, or improving the king) while a critical piece is left hanging or a devastating capture/mate exists. In 4/10 positions (Be6, Qa5, Ne5×2), the move itself removed the defender of a hanging piece — the moved piece was the sole guard of another unit. In 6/10 positions (Nc4, c5, Qd6, Be2, c4, Kb1), a piece was already under threat or undefended and the player simply didn't address it. The consequences were catastrophic (avg cp_loss 2516), with 2/10 resulting in immediate checkmate (Qxg2#), 4/10 losing a queen, and the remainder losing at least a full piece. Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, confirming these were urgent tactical moments demanding immediate attention rather than routine improvement.

1128.label: King moves to a seemingly safer square that actually creates new tactical vulnerabilities, turning survivable positions into lost ones.
1128.description: All 9/9 positions feature a king move motivated by escaping perceived pressure (open file, check threats, attacking pieces) that paradoxically worsens the position by creating a new, more severe tactical vulnerability. In 4/9 positions (Ka8, Kh8, Kf4, Kf1) the king retreats to a corner or edge where it becomes trapped or more exposed to mating/material-winning patterns. In 3/9 positions (Kf8, Ke7, Kg2) the king lands on a specific square that enables a concrete tactic (pin, fork, trapped piece). In 2/9 positions (Kc8, Kf6) the king move wastes a critical tempo when a non-king move was urgently needed. The average cp_loss of 2285 is enormous, with 4/9 positions resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these occur in tense positions where the player panics and reaches for a 'safety' king move rather than calculating concrete alternatives. The best moves in 7/9 positions were non-king moves (piece activity, exchanges, pawn breaks) that addressed the root cause of the pressure rather than fleeing from it.

1132.label: Queen delivers a tempting check that squanders advantage by improving the opponent's king position or missing a stronger non-checking move.
1132.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen delivering check (Qh3+, Qd3+, Qe3+, Qg6+, Qe1+, Qxe6+, Qb5+, Qf5+), and in 9/10 cases this check is a meaningful mistake (avg cp_loss 2058, with one position at 0 cp_loss being a harmless transposition). The consistent error is that the check either drives the opponent's king to a safer square (5/10: positions 1, 5, 6, 9, 10), allows a critical defensive resource that wouldn't exist without the tempo gift (3/10: positions 2, 3, 10 where interpositions or triangulations become available), or places the queen on a vulnerable/inferior square (2/10: position 8 where the queen hangs, position 9 where it abandons a dominant post). In 8/10 positions, the best move was either a quiet developing/improving move (Be5, d5, Rg8, Rh4) or a different forcing move (Rxd8+, Rxf4+, Qb4+, Qe2+) that exploited the position's true tactical potential. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, indicating these are precise positions where the 'obvious' check is a trap.

1126.label: A slow, non-forcing pawn advance (or quiet move) that squanders a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1126.description: 9/10 positions feature one-square pawn advances (with 5/10 specifically being f-pawn pushes: f3, f4, f4, f5, f6), while 1/10 is a quiet rook repositioning. All 10 moves share the defining trait of being non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats) in positions where the evaluation demanded urgent, concrete action. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears explicitly in 8/10 analyses, and the average cp_loss of 370 confirms these are critical moments squandered. In every case, the best moves involved immediate piece activity (Rg4, Rxh6, Bc6), addressing tactical vulnerabilities (Rfb1 saving a hanging piece, Kh8 preventing perpetual), or king activation (Kc6, Kg5). Instead, the blundering side spent their move on a slow positional pawn advance that either created no threats or actually weakened their own structure, gifting the opponent exactly the tempo needed to execute a devastating plan. Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, confirming these were critical junctures requiring precision rather than quiet consolidation.

1130.label: Moving a bishop away from an essential defensive post (blocking a file, defending a piece, or shielding the king) to a seemingly more active square, immediately allowing a tactical punishment.
1130.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a bishop that was performing a vital but non-obvious defensive function — blocking a file (5/10: positions 1, 2, 5, 8, 10), defending a hanging piece (2/10: positions 4, 9), or shielding the king from diagonal/file attacks (3/10: positions 3, 6, 7). In every case, the bishop was relocated to what appeared to be a more 'active' square (centralized or on a longer diagonal), but the move catastrophically exposed a latent tactical vulnerability. The punishments ranged from immediate checkmate (2/10: Qa7# and Qxe2#) to devastating discovered attacks (2/10), hanging pieces captured with tempo (3/10), and crushing sacrificial breakthroughs on newly-opened files (3/10). The average centipawn loss was extreme (2156cp), and in 7/10 positions only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating these were critical moments where the defensive bishop's role was the single thread holding the position together. Notably, 8/10 blunders were made by Black, suggesting defending players are particularly prone to 'activating' bishops that are secretly load-bearing defensive pieces.

1137.label: Playing a routine knight development move (Nf3/Nf6/Nc3) to its most natural square when the position demands an immediate concrete action—a pawn break, queen strike, or prophylactic move.
1137.description: All 10/10 positions occur in the opening with both kings still in the center, and in every case the player develops a knight to its most 'textbook' square (Nf3 in 7/10, Nf6 in 3/10, Nc3 in 1/10) instead of executing an urgent concrete move. In 7/10 positions, a specific tactic was available: winning material via a queen fork (positions 3, 4, 5, 6), capturing a hanging piece (position 7), or exploiting a pawn break that creates a fork (position 9). In the remaining 3/10 (positions 1, 2, 10), the knight development ignored an urgent prophylactic need (preventing Nb5, preventing d5, or resolving central tension), allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with tempo-gaining attacks. The average cp_loss of 204 and average of only 1.5 good moves confirms these are narrow tactical windows where only specific calculation—not general principles—would suffice. In at least one case (position 4), the knight physically blocks the queen's diagonal to g4, permanently eliminating the winning tactical resource.

1133.label: A non-forcing pawn advance on the wing when the position urgently demands concrete tactical action (captures, sacrifices, or piece moves).
1133.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step, non-capturing pawn advance on a flank file (8/10 on the a, b, or h files; 2/10 on the c or f files). In every case, the best move was either a capture (5/10: exf3, Nxf6, Rxe3, Nxh2, bxa5), a piece activation move (3/10: Rde1, Rfe1, Re5), or a more purposeful pawn move addressing a specific threat (2/10: h3, b4-preparing-c3). The blundered pawn pushes share a critical failure: they are non-forcing moves that waste a tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete resolution. In 4/10 cases the pawn advance directly weakened the player's own king safety (f5, h5, h5, h4). In 2/10 cases it left other pawns undefended (b4 leaving c3 hanging, c4 abandoning a3). In 4/10 cases it simply squandered the tempo needed to execute a winning or saving tactic (a4, a5, b4, b5). The average cp_loss of 2086 reflects several positions where forced mate resulted from the tempo waste.

1131.label: In rook endgames with a pawn one square from promotion, the player repositions their rook to the promotion file to capture or blockade rather than pursuing more active counterplay.
1131.description: All 10/10 positions are rook endgames featuring a passed pawn exactly one square from promotion (b7→b8, c7→c8, f7→f8, h7→h8, a7→a8, etc.). In every case, the player moves their rook to the file of the promotion square or the advanced pawn, intending to directly capture the promoted piece or prevent promotion. 10/10 moves are rook moves, and 10/10 positions have both kings exposed with weak pawn shields. In the positions where this is a genuine mistake (6/10 with cp_loss > 30), the error stems from choosing this reactive/passive approach over more dynamic alternatives like delivering checks, creating counter-promotion threats, or exploiting the opponent's exposed king. In the remaining 4/10 positions (cp_loss ≤ 10), the rook-to-promotion-file approach happens to be correct or near-optimal, but the structural pattern is identical: rook + imminent promotion + repositioning to that file.

1135.label: Bishop is moved to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured for free by an opponent's piece.
1135.description: 8/9 positions involve a bishop being moved to a square where it is completely undefended and immediately capturable by an opposing piece (usually another bishop along an open diagonal). In Position 2 (Bf6), the bishop lands on a square controlled by the opponent's Bc3. In Position 9 (Ba6), the bishop is captured by Bxa6. In Position 10 (Bb5), White simply plays Bxb5 taking a free piece. In Position 8 (Ba3), Black's Bf8 captures it via Bxa3. In Position 3 (Bd6), White's Bf4 takes it with Bxd6. In Position 6 (Bc6), White has Qxc6 winning the piece outright. In Position 1 (Be7), the bishop lands undefended enabling Nxd5+/Bxe7 combinations. In Position 4 (Bc3), Black captures with Bxc3 removing a critical defender. Only 1/9 positions (f4) deviates from this bishop-hanging pattern. The common intent across positions is repositioning the bishop to a seemingly 'active' square while failing to verify the square is actually safe from immediate capture. The average cp_loss of 1362 reflects that multiple positions involve losing a full piece for nothing.

1136.label: King moves to a seemingly natural square in a heavily imbalanced endgame, but the chosen square is subtly wrong due to tempo, opposition, or tactical vulnerability.
1136.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves, and 9/10 are endgames with large existing imbalances (evaluations ranging from ±500 to ±1000+). Every position shows both kings exposed with weak or absent pawn shields. The average number of good moves available is only 2.1, indicating these are critical junctures where king square selection is razor-sharp. The errors manifest in several ways: 4/10 positions involve the king moving to a square that loses a critical tempo in a pawn race or opposition battle (Positions 1, 2, 7, 10); 2/10 involve the king walking into tactical vulnerabilities like forks or checks (Positions 3, 7); 2/10 involve the king moving toward the wrong sector of the board, abandoning the critical defensive task (Positions 5, 8). Notably, 3/10 positions (4, 6, 9) show 0-1 cp loss, suggesting the feature fires on the general pattern of king square decisions in imbalanced endgames rather than exclusively on mistakes. The unifying thread is that in these sparse, king-dominated positions, the player selects a king square that appears active or natural but fails to address the position's most critical geometric requirement.
1136.old_chip: Imprecise King Square in Decided Endgames

1138.label: A rook move that worsens the player's own king safety by blocking escape squares, abandoning defensive posts, or creating tactical alignment vulnerabilities.
1138.description: All 10 positions feature a rook move made when the player's king is exposed or vulnerable. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 6, 10), the rook directly occupies the king's critical escape square (f8 or g8), enabling perpetual checks or immediate checkmate. In 2/10 (positions 3, 4), the rook abandons its defensive post on the h-file, leaving the king's flank unguarded against invasion. In 2/10 (positions 7, 8), the rook lands on a square aligned with the king, creating skewer or fork vulnerabilities. In 2/10 (positions 5, 9), the rook makes a passive move while the king urgently needs active defense. The average cp_loss of 2133 is astronomical, with the self-blocking cases (positions 2 and 10) producing near-instant checkmates. All 10 moves look superficially reasonable—centralizing, developing, or defending—but catastrophically ignore how the rook's new position interacts with the king's safety requirements.

1143.label: A knight is retreated from a powerful advanced outpost to a passive 'natural' square, squandering concrete tactical opportunities that the outpost enabled.
1143.description: In 9/9 positions, the player retreated a knight from an aggressively advanced outpost (b5, b4, c5, d4, or e4) backward to a conventional developing square (c3, c6, d3, f3, or f6). In every case, the outpost knight was the tactical linchpin enabling a concrete combination — sacrifices on f7 (Position 1), fork sequences via Nd6+ (Positions 7, 8), passed pawn creation (Position 3), material-winning queen raids (Positions 9, 10), or maintaining critical pressure on weak points (Positions 2, 5, 6). The average cp_loss of 291 reflects that these retreats consistently converted winning or advantageous positions into equal or worse ones. In 9/9 cases only 1 good move existed (avg 1.1), confirming these were sharp critical moments demanding tactical precision. The destination squares (c3 appeared 4 times, c6 appeared 4 times, f3/f6/d3 once each) are all 'textbook' knight squares, suggesting players defaulted to pattern-matching natural development rather than calculating concrete threats.

1125.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active or forward square that is immediately exploitable by the opponent through captures, forks, or attacks with tempo.
1125.description: In 8/10 positions, the player moved a piece (bishop, queen, or king) to a square that appeared active or purposeful but was immediately punishable by a concrete tactical shot on the very next move. In 5/10 cases, the moved piece was directly captured or forked by an enemy knight (Nxe4, Nxc2+, Nxa7+, Nxd4 after exchange, Nxe4). In 3/10 cases, a bishop moved to a square where it was immediately captured or attacked with tempo (Bxh4, f3 attacking Be4, Bxg5 removing a key defender). The best alternatives were typically humble retreats or simple development moves (Bf4/Bd2/Bc1 in position 2, Qd1 in position 10, Qb6 in position 5), suggesting the players chose 'active-looking' moves over safer options. All 10 positions share the characteristic that the punishment was available on the immediate next move — no deep calculation was required to see the refutation, just awareness that the destination square was within the opponent's tactical striking range.

1124.label: Player chooses a superficially attractive move (capture, check, fork, or aggressive repositioning) while overlooking an elementary tactical punishment available within one or two moves.
1124.description: 9/10 positions show the player selecting a move with obvious surface appeal — a material grab (Qxf5, Qxg2, Rxd6), an aggressive attack (Qh5, Qf3), a seemingly clever fork (Ne3), or a natural-looking repositioning (Rc3, Kg7, Kc7) — that is immediately punished by a straightforward tactical response. In 6/10 cases, the move abandons defense of a critical square or piece (Kg7 and Kc7 both leave e6 undefended; Qh5 abandons g2; Qf3 leaves the g5 knight hanging; Rc3 allows a knight fork on e2; Ne3 leaves the e2 rook undefended to counter-attack). In 4/10 cases, the move is an unsound material grab that loses more than it gains (Qxf5 captures into a pawn defense; Qxg2 grabs a pawn losing all tempo; Rxd6 trades an active piece for a passive pawn). The refutations are almost universally simple: 7/10 are punished by a one-move response (recapture, fork, or direct capture of hanging material). Average good moves available was only 1.9, meaning these positions demanded precision, yet the player chose the flashy option over the careful one.

1129.label: Moving a piece (usually a bishop) to an undefended square where it can be immediately captured, typically by the opponent's queen.
1129.description: 7/10 positions are tagged with the 'hanging_piece' tactical motif, and in at least 6/10 cases the move directly places a piece on a square with zero defenders where the opponent captures it (Qxf5, Qxb7, Qxg5, Qxb5+, Qxa5, Kxh7). 6/10 moves are bishop moves (Bf5, Bb7, Bg5, Bb5, Ba6, Ba5), and in 5 of those the bishop lands on an undefended square immediately captured by the opponent's queen. The remaining positions share the broader pattern of prioritizing apparent activity over piece safety: c4 and c5 attack the opponent's queen while leaving material tactically vulnerable, g5 attacks the queen while fatally opening a diagonal, and Qh7+ attempts a mating move to an unprotected square. In most cases the move looks superficially aggressive—developing a bishop to an active diagonal, attacking the opponent's queen, or delivering check—but catastrophically ignores that the moved piece has no protection. The opponent's queen is the capturing piece in 7/10 refutations.

1139.label: Developing a bishop to a standard square while ignoring an immediate tactical demand—a hanging piece, a critical threat, or a concrete vulnerability.
1139.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing bishop development move (Bd3, Be7, or Bd6) to a 'textbook' square during the opening (9/10) or early middlegame (1/10). In every case, the position demanded something more urgent: 3/10 positions had a hanging piece the player either left undefended (positions 2, 8) or failed to capture (position 10); 4/10 featured an uncastled king where the bishop move created or ignored a devastating e-file/diagonal vulnerability (positions 1, 3, 5, 6); and 3/10 had the bishop block its own pieces or enable a tactical sequence exploiting its placement (positions 4, 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 287 reflects that these 'natural' moves uniformly squander significant advantages or convert manageable positions into losing ones. The consistent thread is prioritizing generic development over concrete calculation—the player sees an undeveloped bishop, picks the most natural-looking square, and fails to ask 'what does my opponent do next?'

1141.label: Developing a bishop to g4 or g5 when the f-file knight can be captured or deflected, leaving the bishop hanging.
1141.description: All 10 positions feature a bishop developed to g4 (4/10) or g5 (6/10), and in at least 7/10 cases the immediate tactical punishment follows the identical pattern: the opponent captures or deflects the f3/f6 knight (which is the only piece theoretically associated with defending the g4/g5 square), then wins the now-undefended bishop. In 5/10 positions (positions 3, 6, 9, 10, and partially 4), White plays Bg5 while the Nf3 is pinned by Black's Bg4, allowing Bxf3 followed by Qxg5. In 2/10 positions (1 and 7), Black plays Bg4 and the Nf6 is capturable with Bxf6 or Nxf6+ (with check), deflecting the queen and allowing Qxg4. The remaining 3 positions show variant mechanisms: position 2 exposes f7 to a queen-bishop battery, position 5 allows ...f6 attacking the undefended Bg5 with tempo, and position 8 misses capturing a hanging piece entirely. 9/10 positions are in the opening phase with at least one king still in the center. The average cp_loss of 362 reflects that most of these moves lose approximately a full minor piece.

1142.label: Playing a piece move (interposition, blockade, or retreat) when only a king move to safety saves the position.
1142.description: In 7/9 positions, the single best move was a king retreat or sidestep to a safer square (Kd7, Kb4, Kf7, Kf8, Ke2, Kb8, Kd8), yet the player moved a different piece instead — typically interposing on a line, blocking a file, or retreating a minor piece. The remaining 2 positions (Rb2, Nh7) similarly feature passive piece moves when the position demanded active measures to address king vulnerability. In all 9 positions the king was exposed or under direct attack, and the played move attempted to solve the problem indirectly (blocking a file, challenging the attacker, shielding a diagonal) rather than physically relocating the monarch. The average cp_loss of 2442 reflects how catastrophic this error pattern is — in 3/9 cases it resulted in forced mate. Only 1 good move existed in 8/9 positions, confirming these are razor-sharp situations where only the king move works.
1142.old_chip: Piece move instead of king escape

1140.label: A rook passively repositions (retreat or quiet shuffle) away from a critical active square, squandering a tactical opportunity or abandoning a vital defensive/offensive function.
1140.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook making a non-capturing, non-checking repositioning move — typically a retreat or lateral shuffle — that abandons a square where the rook was performing a critical function. In 7/10 positions the rook moved backward toward its own back rank (R5e2, Rf2, Rf8, Rc8, R6c7, Rg2, Rg4 from g3). In at least 4/10 positions (4, 7, 9, 10), the correct move was a rook CAPTURE or sacrifice from its current active square (Rxc3, Rxf6, staying on f5 to enable Qd3). In 3/10 positions (2, 3, 6), the passive move placed the rook on a tactically vulnerable square (self-blocking the king, getting trapped by a pawn, or landing on a pin diagonal). In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 8), the rook left a square where it was restraining a critical threat (blocking promotion, restraining a passed pawn, defending a key pawn). The average cp_loss of 2148 reflects how catastrophic these seemingly quiet moves are — 8/10 had only 1 good move available, meaning these positions demanded precision rather than generic piece improvement.

1146.label: Advancing a pawn (usually a passed pawn) when an immediate piece move wins tactically or positionally.
1146.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player making a pawn advance when a superior piece move was available. Specifically, 8/10 involve pushing a passed pawn toward promotion (a7, h7, e6, a2, d6, e5, c2, a4), 1/10 is an actual promotion (e8=Q+), and 1/10 is a prophylactic pawn move (a3). In every single case, the correct move was a piece move: queen moves in 5/10 (Qxe8#, Qe8+, Qe5, Qf5, Qe3), bishop moves in 2/10 (Be8, Be5), a king capture in 1/10 (Kxe2), a rook capture in 1/10 (Rxg4+), and a tactical pawn thrust with check in 1/10 (e3/fxe2+). The missed piece moves ranged from checkmate in 1 (positions 1, 2) to winning hanging pieces (positions 8, 9) to critical queen activation (positions 4, 5, 7, 10). Average cp_loss was 2980 with only 1.3 good moves available on average, indicating razor-sharp positions demanding calculation over general principles.

1144.label: An early bishop development to an apparently active square (often creating a pin) that actually introduces a concrete tactical vulnerability the opponent can exploit.
1144.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to the 4th or 5th rank in the opening, appearing aggressive but actually creating tactical problems. In 7/10 cases, the bishop attempts to create a pin (Bg4 pinning Nf3 in positions 5,6,8; Bg5 pinning Nf6 in positions 3,4,10; Bb4 pinning Nc3 in position 7). In 3/10 of these pin attempts (positions 5,6,8), the refutation is a Bxf7+ sacrifice followed by Ne5+ forking king and bishop. In 3/10 positions (3,4,10), Bg5's 'pin' is refuted because the pinned piece simply moves, exposing the bishop as hanging or the center as undefended. Position 2's Bf4 leaves the bishop undefended to a pawn fork, position 1's Bb4 abandons defense of e5, position 7's Bb4 exposes the a4-e8 diagonal for Qa4+, and position 9's Bb5+ is a tempo-wasting check. The average cp_loss is 284, indicating these are serious blunders despite appearing natural. Only 2.3 good moves were available on average, suggesting these are positions where accuracy matters.

1145.label: Advancing a passed pawn in a pure pawn endgame promotion race instead of using king activity or better move order.
1145.description: 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with no pieces remaining. 10/10 moves played are single-step pawn advances of passed or semi-passed pawns. 10/10 positions feature active promotion races where at least one pawn is within 1-3 moves of queening. In the 8/10 positions where the move was actually a mistake (cp_loss > 0), the correct alternative was king activity — specifically capturing enemy pawns (positions 1, 3, 10 with Kxg4 or Kxb4), repositioning the king toward the promotion zone (positions 5, 6, 7 with Ke3/Ke7/Kg7), or executing a different pawn break (positions 8, 9). The 2/10 positions with 0 cp_loss (c7, b5) represent cases where the pawn advance IS the most urgent tempo play, confirming the feature detects 'pawn advances in promotion-race endgames' broadly, with the majority being tempo errors.

1148.label: Queen delivers a check (usually to the back rank) that the opponent's king easily sidesteps, leaving the queen stranded on a passive edge square.
1148.description: 9/10 positions feature a queen giving check, and 9/10 moves land the queen on the 1st or 8th rank (Qb1+, Qd8+, Qd1+, Qh8+, Qf1+, Qc1+, Qa1+, Qe8, Qa8+), with Qd3+ being the sole outlier. In every case except Position 6 (where the check correctly forces a won queen trade), the opponent's king calmly sidesteps to a safe square (Kh2, Kh7, Ka2, Ke7, Kg2, Kg7), and the queen is left marooned on a corner or edge square completely disconnected from the critical battle. The analyses consistently describe these as 'check first, think later' instincts, 'spite checks,' or 'pointless checks.' The correct alternatives were overwhelmingly quiet moves: defensive resources (f4, Rd8), simplifying trades (Qc7, Rd8), king moves (Kc7), or even immediate checkmate (Qxg4#). Average cp_loss of 3046 reflects that 4/10 positions converted into forced mate or near-mate, demonstrating the catastrophic consequences of queen displacement.

1149.label: Retreating the queen (or bishop) to a safe but passive square instead of executing an available forcing tactical move (capture, check, or pawn break).
1149.description: 10/10 positions feature a piece (9/10 queen, 1/10 bishop) being moved backward toward the player's own back rank or corner when a concrete forcing move was available. In every case, the best move was a capture, check, sacrifice, or aggressive pawn break: Position 1 missed Nxb7 (combination), Position 2 missed Rxh6+ (mate in 2), Position 3 missed Rae1 (piece mobilization), Position 4 missed Qa4+ (check), Position 5 missed Bxc5 (capture of dominant piece), Position 6 missed dxe6 (pawn break), Position 7 missed Qf2 (active placement), Position 8 missed Qxd1 (simplifying exchange), Position 9 missed Bxf7+ (sacrifice with check), Position 10 missed e5 (central break). 10/10 played moves are non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no direct threats), and 10/10 move the piece away from the opponent's position. The average cp_loss of 1160 reflects that these positions demanded immediate concrete action, and the passive retreat squandered critical tactical windows that were often narrow (avg 1.0 good moves available).

1159.label: White captures fxe5 in a King's Gambit structure, removing the f4-pawn that shields the h4-e1 diagonal, allowing Qh4+ winning the h1 rook.
1159.description: 10/10 positions feature the identical blunder: White plays fxe5 with the f4-pawn in an early King's Gambit or King's Gambit-like opening structure where the king remains on e1. In every case, the f4-pawn was the sole defender of the h4-e1 diagonal, and its removal by capturing on e5 allows the devastating sequence Qh4+ (check on the now-open diagonal), g3 (forced), Qxe4+ (forking king and h1 rook), followed by Qxh1 winning a full rook. 10/10 positions have White's king on e1 with no pieces developed to guard h4 or interpose on the diagonal. The refutation Qh4+ appears as the top punishment in all 10 positions. 7/10 positions are essentially identical (the 1.e4 e5 2.f4 d5 3.fxe5?? line), while the remaining 3 feature slight variations (2...Nc6 or 2...f5) but the exact same tactical mechanism.

1147.label: Material-grabbing captures that place the capturing piece on a tactically vulnerable square where it is won back (or more) through a forcing counter-blow, usually involving check.
1147.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures where the player grabs material (8/10 capture pawns, 2/10 capture knights) but the capturing piece lands on an undefended or tactically exploitable square. In 7/10 cases, the refutation involves an intermediate or direct check (Bxh7+ discovered attacks in positions 2 and 3, Bb5+ intermezzos in positions 4 and 6, Bh2+ discovered attack in position 10, Rh5+ skewer in position 9, Nd4+ fork in position 7). In the remaining cases, the piece is simply recapturable on its destination square (positions 1, 5, 8). The best alternatives in all 10/10 positions were quiet, non-capturing moves focused on king safety, development, or prophylaxis rather than material gain. The average cp_loss of 312 reflects that these are severe tactical oversights, not minor inaccuracies. The common thread is prioritizing immediate material gain over positional safety, with the opponent exploiting the exposed piece through forcing geometry.

1155.label: Playing h3/h6 to chase or prevent a piece on g4/g5 when the position demands immediate tactical action or the h-pawn is a critical defensive barrier.
1155.description: All 10/10 positions feature the h-pawn advancing one square (h3 for White, h6 for Black) as a reflexive prophylactic move intended to kick or prevent an enemy piece (usually a knight) from g4/g5. In 3/10 positions (2, 6, 8), moving the h-pawn literally removed the last barrier preventing immediate checkmate on h7/h2, with the queen delivering mate along the now-open diagonal or file. In 5/10 positions (3, 4, 5, 9, 10), the move was a critical tempo loss in positions where urgent tactical action was required—such as winning material via e5, capturing hanging pieces, or exploiting an uncastled king. In 2/10 positions (1, 7), the h-pawn advance created a new tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploited (a fork opportunity or a pawn sacrifice target). The average centipawn loss of 3266 is catastrophic, with only 1.5 good moves available on average, indicating these were already demanding positions where a 'routine' pawn push was maximally punished.

1152.label: Knight captures a pawn but its departure from a critical square (or the pawn's removal) opens lines or exposes weaknesses worth far more than the material gained.
1152.description: All 10 positions feature a knight capturing a pawn (Nx pawn). In 9/10 cases (excluding position 9 which was actually the best move at 0cp loss), the knight capture is a mistake because the knight's previous square was performing a critical defensive or coordinating function. In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 10), the knight's departure opens a diagonal that the opponent exploits to win material (typically via bishop or back-rank tactics). In 2/10 positions (5, 1), the knight leaves a square essential for maintaining a mating net or superior coordination, throwing away a decisive advantage for a mere pawn. In 2/10 positions (2, 7), the knight lands on a square where it becomes exposed or trapped, losing more material than the pawn was worth. In 1/10 (position 8), the knight captures the wrong target entirely—a pawn instead of a hanging rook. The average cp_loss of 1142 confirms these are severe errors. The consistent thread is that the player prioritizes the concrete material gain of one pawn while failing to assess what the knight's departure costs positionally or tactically.

1165.label: Developing a bishop to a square directly attacked by an enemy central pawn, hanging the piece for free.
1165.description: 10/10 positions share an identical pattern: a bishop is developed to what would normally be an 'active' square (targeting f7, f2, or the center), but that square is directly controlled by an opponent's central pawn that can immediately capture it. In 7/10 cases, it's Bc4 into a d5 pawn (Scandinavian Defense positions after 1.e4 d5). In 2/10 cases, it's Bf4 into an e5 pawn (Englund Gambit positions after 1.d4 e5). In 1/10 cases, it's Black playing Bc5 into a d4 pawn (after 1.e4 e5 2.d4). All positions are in the opening with both kings still in center, and in every case the player appears to be applying a familiar development pattern (Italian Game Bc4, London System Bf4) to a position where the opponent's pawn structure makes that square fatally unsafe. The average cp_loss is 505, representing approximately a full piece lost for nothing.

1134.label: Major piece captures or checks that look natural but fail because a more precise forcing move (different check route, preparatory move, or different target) was needed first.
1134.description: 8/10 positions involve captures with rooks or queens, while 2/10 are rook checks — all are 'obvious-looking' aggressive moves by major pieces. In 9/10 positions, the correct alternative was either a different check (positions 3, 5, 6, 8, 10), a different capture target/piece (positions 1, 2, 7), or a preparatory move before the capture (position 9). The 'missed_tactic' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, 'tempo_loss' in 7/10, and 'piece_activity' in 8/10. Only 1.3 good moves existed on average, meaning these are razor-sharp positions where the 'natural' aggressive move is nearly always the only bad option. The phase is overwhelmingly endgame (7/10), where rook coordination and move order precision are critical. The player consistently chose the immediate material grab or check over the more calculated alternative that maintained piece coordination or exploited a deeper tactical mechanism.

1156.label: Advancing a pawn (f/g/h) near one's own king that was performing a critical defensive function, creating immediate tactical exploitation.
1156.description: 9/10 positions involve advancing a kingside pawn (f, g, or h file) in front of the player's own king, while 1/10 (Ng4) removes a piece from king defense with identical consequences. In 6/10 cases, the move directly allows checkmate or forced mate (positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 10 yield immediate or near-immediate mate; position 1 creates a mating attack). The average cp_loss of 4981 is catastrophic, with 5/10 positions resulting in checkmate. In every case, the moved pawn was performing an irreplaceable defensive function: g2 prevented Qg2# (positions 8, 10), f2 prevented Qf2# (position 5), h2's knight guard prevented Qh1# (position 4), g7 defended the f6 knight (position 9), and other pawns maintained light-square integrity or king shelter (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 7). The average good moves available was only 1.2, showing these were already razor-thin positions where the king-shield pawn was the last line of defense. 8/10 were played by White, and 9/10 occurred in the middlegame when piece activity was already threatening the king.

1161.label: The queen captures a seemingly free wing pawn (usually on b2/b7) and becomes trapped or fatally displaced by the opponent's coordinating pieces.
1161.description: 10/10 positions feature the queen capturing an apparently undefended wing pawn. 9/10 captures occur on the b-file (6x Qxb2, 3x Qxb7), with 1 on a7 and 1 on g2. In every case, the queen ventures to the edge of the board for a single pawn and is punished — 9/10 positions have 'trapped_piece' as the primary tactical motif, where the queen is boxed in by rooks swinging to the b-file (Rb1/Rb8), bishops cutting diagonals, or knights covering escape squares. The average cp_loss is 371, reflecting near-game-losing consequences. 5/10 occur in the opening and 5/10 in the middlegame, showing the pattern persists regardless of phase. In 8/10 cases, the player had 2-3 good developing or positional moves available that maintained the evaluation, meaning there was no pressure to grab material. The fianchettoed bishop on g7 appears in 6/10 positions (typically the side grabbing b2), suggesting players with passive bishop structures are especially tempted by 'free' queenside pawns.

1158.label: Passively retreating a knight (or other piece) to the h-file rim, abandoning critical central/defensive duties when active play was demanded.
1158.description: 6/10 positions feature a knight retreating specifically to h2 or h7 (Nh2 twice, Nh7 four times), making this the dominant geometric signal. The remaining 4 positions share the broader pattern of passive, non-forcing moves (Kh7, g4, Kf2, Kb7/Re6) that waste tempo and abandon critical functions. In all 10 cases, the position demanded immediate active counterplay or precise tactical execution, but instead the player chose a slow retreat that failed to address the most urgent threat. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, confirming these were critical moments requiring precision. The average cp_loss of 1155 reflects how catastrophic these passive retreats are in sharp positions. In the knight-specific cases, the knight was invariably leaving f3 or f6—squares where it controlled the center and defended key points—to land on a rim square where it contributed nothing and often blocked escape routes or exposed pieces behind it.

1150.label: Pawn captures that remove a threatening enemy pawn but open a critical square or line that the opponent immediately exploits with a decisive tactic.
1150.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing an enemy pawn that appears threatening or advanced, where the 'obvious' recapture actually creates a worse problem than it solves.
