In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 4, 9), the pawn capture directly vacates or creates a square that an enemy knight immediately occupies with a devastating fork (Nxg6+, Nxe6, Nxe3, Nxe4+, Nxd5). In 3/10 positions (5, 6, 10), the capture creates an isolated or undefended pawn that the opponent's rook immediately captures, destroying the player's structural advantage. In 2/10 positions (7, 8), the capture opens a file directly toward the player's own king, enabling piece invasion. Across all positions, the best move involved NOT capturing the pawn — instead developing pieces (positions 1, 7, 8), repositioning the queen away from fork danger (positions 2, 9), improving rook placement (position 3), capturing with a piece instead of a pawn (position 4), or advancing the pawn past the enemy pawn rather than trading (positions 5, 6, 10).

1160.label: A knight (or piece) is moved from a square where it performs a critical but non-obvious defensive function to a seemingly aggressive square, immediately allowing a tactical exploitation of the newly unguarded target.
1160.description: 7/9 positions involve a knight being relocated from a key defensive square to an ostensibly active or aggressive destination. In Position 2 (Nh5), the knight left g3 which guarded e2, enabling an Ne2+ fork. In Position 4 (Nb5), the knight left c3 which blocked the c-file, allowing Qxf1+ and Rc8+. In Position 6 (Ne5), the knight left f3 which defended the e1 rook, enabling Rxb2+ and Qxe1+. In Position 7 (Na4), the knight left c3 which enabled Nxd5 tactical resources. In Position 10 (Nc5), the knight left d7 which covered f6/f8 kingside defense, allowing Bxg6. In Positions 3 and 9 (Ne3), the knight abandoned outposts (c4 and c2) that restrained opponent actions. The 2/9 pawn moves (d5, d3) fit the broader pattern of choosing aggressive-looking moves that ignore critical defensive needs or immediate tactical opportunities. The average cp_loss of 1338 reflects how devastating these errors are—the defensive function was load-bearing, and its removal triggers immediate tactical collapse.

1154.label: Moving a piece or pawn to a square directly capturable by an adjacent enemy pawn, losing material or creating fatal weaknesses.
1154.description: In 7/10 positions, the blunder move places a piece or pawn on a square where an adjacent enemy pawn immediately captures it: Bd6 falls to exd6 (position 1), Bg5 to hxg5 (position 3), Bf5 to exf5 (position 4), Bf3 to gxf3 (position 7), Bf4 to exf4 (position 8), f3 allows exf3 (position 2), and f5 allows exf5 (position 9). Bishops are the most common victim, appearing in 5/10 cases where they are moved directly into a pawn's capture range. The remaining 3 positions (5, 6, 10) involve pawn advances that create adjacent structural weaknesses exploitable by enemy pawns or pieces. The average cp_loss is 360, indicating these are severe blunders. In 8/10 cases, good alternatives existed (avg 2.3 good moves available), suggesting these are avoidable oversights rather than desperate situations. The pattern is overwhelmingly one of failing to notice that the destination square is controlled by a simple pawn.

1166.label: Playing a quiet, repositioning rook move to the first/eighth rank when the position demands immediate forcing action such as a sacrifice, capture, or pawn breakthrough.
1166.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to the back rank (c1, e1, b1, d1, or b8 for Black) in a non-capturing, non-checking manner. In every case, the position demanded urgent tactical action: 4/10 required an immediate pawn break or advancement (e6, f6, c6+, d5), 3/10 required a capture or sacrifice (Rxd5+, Qxa4, Rxe4/Rxf6), and the remainder needed active forcing moves rather than quiet repositioning. The average cp_loss of 2084 is extreme, with 3/10 positions involving missed forced mates. In 7/10 cases only 1-2 good moves existed, confirming these were critical moments requiring precision. The consistent error is defaulting to a 'normal-looking' rook development move — placing it on an open or semi-open file — when the position's tactical demands make such routine play catastrophic. The rook moves often abandoned a critical defensive duty (guarding f1, defending e4, supporting the e-file) or wasted the tempo needed to execute a winning forcing sequence.

1153.label: Playing apparently active moves (mostly knight maneuvers, checks, or pawn advances) that look purposeful but waste critical tempo when the position demands patient improvement or a different tactical resource.
1153.description: 7/10 positions feature knight moves to seemingly active squares (Nb2 attacking a4, Ne3 forking, Nh5+ checking, Nf7 heading toward h7, Ne7+ checking, Nd2 repositioning, Nh6 targeting g5), while 3/10 are pawn advances (d6 pushing the passer, e4 advancing, f4 creating a passed pawn). In all 10 cases, the played move pursues a secondary or illusory goal while the position's primary requirement goes unmet. The correct moves instead involved king activation (5/10 positions had king moves as best: Kg4, Kc4, Kg8, Kg6, or king centralization), maintaining existing piece placement (positions 4, 9 where the piece was already optimally placed), or finding a precise tactical resource (Nxe6+ in position 6). The average cp_loss of 1117 and average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where choosing the 'active-looking' option over the genuinely necessary one proves catastrophic. Tempo loss is tagged in 10/10 analyses, and piece_activity concerns appear in 9/10.

1168.label: A knight delivers check but the move is significantly inferior to a quieter or differently-timed alternative, typically abandoning a strong square, landing on an undefended square, or missing a winning non-check.
1168.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight delivering check that turns out to be a serious blunder. In every case, a non-checking move (or a different piece's check) was dramatically stronger — often by thousands of centipawns. The checks are seductive because they're forcing, but they fail for specific tactical reasons: in 4/10 cases the knight lands on an undefended square where it is simply captured (Positions 2, 3, 8, 10); in 3/10 cases the knight abandons a dominant outpost or critical square needed for a winning tactic (Positions 1, 6, 7); in 3/10 cases the check drives the enemy king to a safer square rather than a worse one (Positions 1, 5, 9). The average cp_loss of 2363 is extreme, with 3/10 positions involving missed forced checkmates. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments requiring precision where the flashy knight check was the worst instinct. The missed best moves ranged from quiet developing moves (12...Bf5), to simple captures (21...Nxc3, 18...Qxf4), to superior checks by other pieces (28...dxe4+, 15...Rxe4+), demonstrating that the 'check reflex' overrode proper calculation in each case.

1163.label: Non-forcing wing pawn advances that squander critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action or piece activity.
1163.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn advances (the exception, position 9, has 0 cp_loss and is effectively a non-blunder). 8/10 are specifically wing pawn pushes on the a, b, f, or g files. In every case, the position demanded urgent concrete action—a tactic (Ng4 in position 1), addressing a direct threat (position 2), maintaining piece pressure (positions 5, 6, 10), or preserving key square control (positions 4, 7). Instead, the player chose a slow, non-forcing pawn expansion that either created new weaknesses (3/10 opened critical lines/diagonals as in positions 3, 4, 7), left material hanging (positions 2, 6), or simply wasted the one tempo needed to maintain dynamic equilibrium (positions 1, 5, 8, 10). Notably, 4/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating these pawn pushes occurred at critical moments where precision was essential. The average cp_loss of 330 reflects how severely tempo is punished when concrete action is required.

1169.label: A quiet one-square king move away from the corner that wastes a critical tempo and/or walks the king onto a tactically vulnerable square.
1169.description: All 10/10 positions feature a voluntary, non-forced king move of exactly one square, typically from a corner or edge (h1→g1 in 5/10, h8→g8 in 2/10, h2→g2, g8→f8, a7→b7 in the others). In 7/10 cases, the king specifically moves TO a square where a new check or tactical blow becomes possible that didn't exist on the original square (Positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8 enable checks like Bxf2+, exf2+, Bf3+, Qe3+, Bxh2+, f7+; Position 7 leaves the queen hanging to Qxb3). In 8/10 positions the move is played during the middlegame when urgent tactical or forcing moves were required. The average cp_loss of 2052 is enormous, with 3/10 positions involving missed forced mates or mate-level swings. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points where precision was mandatory. The positions span both sides (White 6/10, Black 4/10) and vary in evaluation direction, confirming the pattern is about the move type rather than the position type.

1171.label: Developing the a-rook to the b or c file as a non-forcing 'improving' move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1171.description: All 10 positions feature the a-rook (Ra1 or Ra8) being moved one or two squares sideways to the b-file or c-file in a generic activating gesture, while a critical forcing opportunity goes unexploited. 10/10 moves are non-forcing (no check, capture, or direct threat). The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were narrow tactical positions requiring precision, not general improvement. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a concrete forcing action: a capture (Nxd7+, Bxb7, Nxe5, Bxb3), a check (Bg5+), or a pawn breakthrough (e5). In 5/10 cases, the rook actually landed on a square immediately exploitable by the opponent (vulnerable to Nd6, Bd6, or Nxf3+ counterplay). The pattern is consistent across both colors (5 White, 5 Black) and predominantly middlegame positions (8/10) where dynamic factors outweigh static development considerations.

1175.label: Playing a routine bishop fianchetto (Bg7, Bg2, or Bb7) when an immediate tactical opportunity or threat demands attention first.
1175.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to a fianchetto square on a long diagonal (7 Bg7, 3 Bg2, 1 Bb7) as a 'natural' opening developing move while a critical tactical situation is ignored. In 4/10 positions, the player missed a free material capture (hanging piece or undefended pawn leading to winning the exchange). In 3/10 positions, a forcing tactical sequence (knight fork or queen check) was available that would win material. In 2/10 positions, the player's own piece was left en prise (knight on f6 attacked by e5 pawn, bishop on g4 attacked by h3 pawn). In 1/10 positions, the fianchetto enabled the opponent's sacrificial combination. 9/10 positions occurred in the opening phase with kings still in the center. The average cp loss was 314, indicating these are severe blunders disguised as normal development. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning the tactical window was typically narrow and the fianchetto was almost never among them.

1151.label: Active piece moves (especially rook moves and checks) in endgame positions with advanced passed pawns and exposed kings, prioritizing apparent activity over critical positional requirements.
1151.description: 10/10 positions feature exposed kings on both sides with weak pawn shields, and 9/10 involve advanced passed pawns creating promotion threats. 7/10 moves are rook moves, with 4/10 being checks and 2/10 being captures. 7/10 positions are endgames. The feature fires on 'active-looking' piece moves in pawn-race positions — but critically, 5/10 moves are actually optimal (0-11 cp loss), while the other 5 are serious errors (307-9281 cp loss). When these moves ARE mistakes, they share a common flaw: abandoning a critical defensive/strategic duty in favor of superficially aggressive activity. Position 4 (Rg5) abandons back-rank defense; Position 5 (Re5) abandons the open c-file; Position 1 (Nc4) ignores a promotion threat; Position 6 (Qg2+) gives a purposeless check; Position 7 (Rd3) places a rook on a tactically vulnerable square. The correct alternatives in the mistake cases were all quieter, prophylactic moves (Kc3, Ne8, a5, Qh1, Re3).

1167.label: Moving a rook off an open file where it was performing an essential defensive function, leaving a piece unprotected or a key tactical resource unavailable.
1167.description: 8/10 positions involve rook moves, and in 7/10 the rook was actively stationed on an open file (e-file, d-file, c-file, or h-file) where it defended another piece or enabled a tactical combination. When the rook is relocated to a seemingly useful but actually inferior square, the piece it was guarding becomes hanging (positions 1, 2, 3, 9 explicitly show a bishop left undefended after the rook departs), or a critical tactical opportunity disappears (positions 7 and 10 where leaving the e/d-file kills a winning combination). The 2 non-rook moves (Kh1 in position 4, c4 in position 8) still share the deeper pattern of wasting a tempo when a piece/square requires immediate attention. The punishment is remarkably consistent: 7/10 positions feature the opponent simply capturing what was left undefended, with the tactical motif 'hanging_piece' appearing in 5/10 analyses. The average cp_loss of 337 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but immediate tactical oversights — the player fails to recognize that their piece on the open file is performing an invisible but essential guardian role.

1162.label: Playing a plausible but non-forcing move in a critical position that demands one specific, concrete response.
1162.description: 9/10 positions (excluding the 0cp-loss outlier) share a common structure: the position demands a specific, often forcing response (a check, a key capture, or addressing an immediate threat), but the player instead makes a 'reasonable-looking' move that ignores the critical demand. The average number of good moves was only 1.7, meaning these are razor-sharp positions with almost no margin for error. In 6/10 cases, the correct move involved a direct tactical action (capture on g5, check with Bb5+, pawn break dxe4, restricting with Rc5, retreating the bishop to safety), while the played move addressed a secondary concern. The moves span all piece types and both sides, but consistently represent defaulting to generic chess logic (develop a piece, grab a pawn, reposition the queen, push a passed pawn) rather than reading the concrete tactical demands of the specific position. 7/10 positions involved an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, exposed king, undefended pawn) that the played move failed to address.

1157.label: Captures (especially rook exchanges) that force a recapture, deliberately transitioning into a materially simpler position — sometimes correctly into a won endgame, sometimes incorrectly with the wrong piece.
1157.description: 9/10 positions feature a piece capturing a defended piece/pawn where the natural response is a recapture that fundamentally changes the material balance. 5/10 involve rook captures (Rxg5+, Rxe3+, Rxf3, Rxh5+, Rxe2+), and 3/10 involve bishop captures on e4. Critically, 4/10 positions (Rxg5+, Rxe3+, Rxf3, Rxe2+) are CORRECT moves with 0 cp_loss — these are precisely calculated exchange sacrifices where the rook captures a defended piece, the king recaptures, and the resulting pawn endgame is trivially won due to passed pawns or material superiority. The other 6/10 are mistakes: 3 involve capturing on e4 with the bishop instead of the knight (wrong piece selection), losing the superior minor piece; 1 involves Nxd4 removing a key defensive piece from a critical diagonal; 1 involves Rxh5+ where the knight simply recaptures winning the exchange; and 1 involves Rd4 instead of the winning Nd4. The unifying geometric pattern is a piece moving to capture on a defended square where recapture is forced or natural, creating a material transition point.

1184.label: White plays the unsound Halloween Gambit in the Four Knights Game, sacrificing a knight on e5 for insufficient central pawn compensation.
1184.description: 10/10 positions are the identical Four Knights Game position after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Nc3 Nf6, where White plays the Halloween Gambit 4.Nxe5. In every case, White's f3-knight captures Black's e5-pawn, sacrificing a full piece since Black's c6-knight simply recaptures on e5. The evaluation swings approximately 175-179 centipawns in all positions (from roughly +20 to -158), and all positions feature both kings in the center, closed center pawn structure, and no bishops yet developed. The refutation is trivially simple in all cases: 4...Nxe5 wins a full knight, after which White's compensating pawn center (d4+e5) is objectively insufficient. 10/10 positions had exactly 3 good alternative moves available (Bb5, d4, a3), all maintaining equality through standard development.

1170.label: Non-forcing rook repositioning moves (typically to the 7th rank or open files) when immediate forcing moves like checks, captures, or concrete threats were available.
1170.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that is non-capturing and non-checking, chosen for its apparent 'activity' (open file control, rank penetration) over a concrete forcing alternative. In 7/10 cases, the rook moves to the 7th rank or the opponent's 2nd rank (Re7 x4, Rh7, Ra2 x2 for Black penetrating), reflecting the classic 'rook on the seventh' positional instinct. The remaining 3 positions (Rb2, Rg2, Rh5) similarly place the rook on ostensibly active squares along open files or ranks. In every case, the best move was a forcing continuation: back-rank checks (positions 1, 2), immediate captures (positions 3, 7), queen attacks on hanging pieces (position 4), tempo-gaining checks (position 5), defensive king-safety moves under mating threat (position 6), checkmate in one (position 8), forcing perpetual check (position 10), or maintaining maximum pressure on critical files (position 9). The average cp_loss of 1168 reflects catastrophic outcomes, including a missed mate-in-1 and a blunder into forced mate. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than general improvement.

1173.label: The queen moves to a seemingly active or aggressive square while leaving another piece (or itself) undefended and capturable.
1173.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a queen move to an apparently purposeful square — centralizing, attacking, or invading — that fatally neglects a defensive responsibility. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10), the queen was the sole defender of another piece (rook or bishop) and moved away, leaving it hanging for immediate capture. In 2/10 cases (positions 3, 6), the queen moved to an exposed square where it could be attacked with tempo, simultaneously leaving another piece (knight on a4, or allowing a fork on c2) undefended. In 1/10 cases (position 4), the queen moved directly onto a square capturable by an existing piece. In 1/10 cases (position 2), the queen abandoned critical king defense. The 'hanging_piece' motif was explicitly tagged in 8/10 positions. The average cp_loss of 1248 and average of only 1.6 good moves available shows these are critical moments demanding defensive precision, but the player chose 'active' queen moves instead.

1164.label: A piece voluntarily relocates to a passive, peripheral, or vulnerable square, abandoning a critical defensive function or missing a concrete tactical opportunity.
1164.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing repositioning move (no captures, no checks) that takes a piece away from where it was critically needed. In 7/10 cases, the piece abandons a specific defensive function: the knight guarding central squares (Na5, Position 1), the rook defending f7 (Re8, Position 6), the bishop blockading a passed pawn (Bd7, Position 7), the bishop guarding a back-rank square (Ba8, Position 8), and the bishop covering central squares (Bh8, Position 4). In 5/10 cases, the destination is specifically a rim or corner square (Na5, Bh8, Na4, Ba8, Ra3). In 4/10 cases, a concrete tactic was available instead (f4 missing Bxg7+, Ra3 missing cxd6, Nc5 missing Ra8, g5 when Kh8 was needed). The average cp_loss of 1236 is extreme, and the average of only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are critical positions where the 'natural-looking' repositioning move was particularly costly. All moves appear purposeful (attacking something, saving a piece, improving placement) but are counterproductive.

1176.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing rook or king move to defend a pawn or reposition slowly when the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation (check, exchange, or pawn break).
1176.description: All 10 positions share the same fundamental error: choosing a quiet, non-forcing move when exactly one critical forcing continuation existed. 8/10 moves are rook moves and 2/10 are king moves, but all 10 are non-capturing, non-checking, non-threatening moves. In every case, the correct move was forcing: a check (Rf5+, Ra2+, Rf6+), a checkmate (Rg7#), a forcing exchange (Ra4 provoking Rxf4+), or a pawn break (e4, g3). The blundered moves consistently prioritize visible but non-urgent concerns—defending a pawn (Rc8 defends c7, Ra5 defends b5, Ra8 defends a7, Kc2 defends b2), passive repositioning (Re3, Rg6, Rc1), or slow centralization (Kc3)—while the position's true requirement was immediate concrete action. The average good moves available was only 1.2, confirming these are razor-sharp moments with essentially one correct path. The average cp_loss of 2162 reflects that these quiet moves catastrophically squander decisive advantages or convert forced wins into equality.

1177.label: A knight develops to the exact square a friendly bishop needs as its escape route, allowing a pawn advance to trap the bishop.
1177.description: 9/10 positions feature a piece (almost always a knight) developing to a square that blocks a friendly piece's critical retreat path. In 7/10 cases, a knight directly occupies the bishop's escape square (Ne7 blocking Be7 retreat in positions 2, 3, 9; Nd7/Nbd7 blocking Bd7 retreat in positions 5, 6, 10; Ne2 blocking Be2 retreat in position 4). Position 7 shows the same mechanism with Qd2 blocking a bishop's d2 retreat. Position 1 is a slight variant where Ne7 leaves the queenside knight undeveloped, removing support from a vulnerable bishop. Position 8 is the weakest fit, where Ne7 ignores a queen-trapping threat rather than directly blocking a retreat. In all 10 cases, the opponent punishes with a pawn advance (b4, d5, e4, or e5) that attacks the now-trapped piece, winning material. The average cp_loss of 285 confirms these are near-piece-value blunders. All moves appear natural and developmental, making the self-blocking extremely easy to miss.

1172.label: A rook move targeting a pawn or seeking superficial activity while ignoring the position's critical tactical demand (checkmate, defense against mate, or decisive forcing sequence).
1172.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that pursue secondary objectives — typically pawn captures or 'active-looking' placements — while the position demanded something far more urgent. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 4), a checkmate in one was available but the rook moved elsewhere. In 3/10 positions (4, 8, 9), the rook move allowed the opponent to deliver or threaten immediate checkmate. In at least 5/10 cases (5, 6, 7, 8, 9), the rook specifically targeted a pawn (h4, a4, b4, h2, a5) rather than addressing the tactical crisis. The rook frequently moved to the edge of the board (a-file in positions 6, 7, 9; h-file in positions 5, 8) or the 7th rank (positions 1, 3, 10) — squares that look aggressive but abandon the rook's critical defensive or offensive station. The average cp_loss of 3216 is extreme, reflecting that these 'greedy' rook deployments consistently squander winning positions or allow devastating tactical refutations.

1179.label: Moving a piece that guards critical squares to a passive position, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the abandoned function.
1179.description: 10/10 positions feature a piece being moved AWAY from a square where it performed a vital defensive or positional function, replaced by a passive repositioning. 5/10 involve knight retreats from key squares (f6→d7 twice, c3→e2 twice, d5→e7), and 4/10 involve queen retreats from active posts to passive back-rank squares (Qd8, Qe8 twice, Qc2). In every case, the moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical square or function: the f6 knight guarded h5/g7 (positions 2, 10), the c3 knight controlled d5 and the c-file (positions 3, 6), the d5 knight blocked invasion routes (position 4), the queen on d7 defended f7 (positions 7, 9), and the queen on the c-file maintained attacking pressure (position 5). All 10 positions demanded concrete/dynamic action (avg 1.9 good moves available), yet the player chose slow regrouping. The immediate punishment consistently exploits the exact square or function abandoned: Nh5 after Nd7, Bg4 winning the e2 knight, d6 advancing after queen leaves, Bf7 winning the exchange, h6 shattering the kingside.

1183.label: Playing h3/h6 as an automatic bishop-preventing or bishop-challenging move when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1183.description: All 10/10 positions feature the h-pawn advancing one square (h2-h3 for White in 6 positions, h7-h6 for Black in 4 positions) as a prophylactic or bishop-challenging move. In 7/10 cases, an enemy bishop was already on g4/g5 or threatening to go there, and the player reflexively 'put the question to the bishop.' In the remaining 3/10, the h-pawn advance prevented a hypothetical future pin. The critical shared error is that every single position contained a concrete tactical opportunity worth 112-362 centipawns more than the h-pawn move: piece-winning combinations (3/10), central pawn strikes (2/10), moves exploiting an uncastled enemy king (2/10), or urgent piece-activity improvements (3/10). The average cp_loss of 237 with only 1.4 good moves available confirms these were positions demanding precision, not routine play. In 8/10 positions, the wasted tempo directly allowed the opponent to neutralize a specific vulnerability — escaping a tactical trap, castling to safety, or consolidating a cramped position.

1178.label: Captures that win material (usually a pawn) but fatally abandon the capturing piece's critical defensive or coordinating role.
1178.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture that wins material — 9/10 capture a pawn, 1/10 captures a minor piece. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 7, 9), the capturing piece abandons a critical defensive duty: protecting another piece (positions 4, 9 where Rxf7/Rxd4 leave knights hanging), guarding key squares (position 1 where Qxc3 abandons b7 defense), or maintaining coordination with another active piece (positions 2, 7 where knights leave dominant outposts). In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 6), the capture targets the wrong material — either the wrong pawn (position 5), with the wrong piece (position 6), or a pawn that strands the capturing piece (position 3). In 2/10 positions (8, 10), the capture itself is correct but executed prematurely — a stronger intermediate move (check or zwischenzug) should precede it. The average cp_loss is 326, and only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the temptation of visible material overrides deeper coordination concerns.

1180.label: A rook moves to the player's own back rank for file occupation or development, missing an urgent tactical need in the position.
1180.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the player's own first/eighth rank (Re1/Re8/Rf1/Rf8/Rg1/Rc8), targeting what appears to be a useful open or semi-open file. These moves look natural and positionally motivated—occupying files, activating idle rooks, supporting queens—but in every case they miss more urgent tactical demands. In 5/10 positions, the rook move creates a new tactical vulnerability (becoming a fork target on e1/e8 in positions 3 and 7, exposing the back rank in positions 2 and 10, or abandoning a critical defensive file in position 1). In the remaining 5/10, the rook move wastes critical tempo when immediate forcing sequences were available (missed forks in positions 5 and 9, missed captures in position 4, move-order errors in positions 6 and 8). The average cp_loss of 1248 reflects that these seemingly routine moves occur at moments of extreme tactical sensitivity. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise action rather than generic development.

1190.label: A rook captures an enemy piece on the back rank, but the opponent's second rook recaptures with check leading to an unstoppable back-rank checkmate.
1190.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing a piece on the 1st or 8th rank (Rx_1 or Rx_8), after which the opponent's second heavy piece recaptures on that same square with check, initiating a forced back-rank mating sequence. In every case, the blundering side's king is entombed behind its own pawns (10/10 positions show the king boxed in by 2-3 friendly pawns on adjacent squares). The captured piece varies — sometimes it's a rook (positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 10), sometimes a queen (positions 3, 4, 5, 8, 9) — but the mechanism is identical: the capture opens the file for a lethal recapture with check. In 10/10 cases, the opponent had doubled heavy pieces on the same file or a second rook/queen ready to recapture. The resulting mate is always within 2-3 moves. Only 1 good alternative move existed in 9/10 positions (avg 1.1), showing these were razor-thin defensive positions where the material grab was the most natural-looking but fatal choice.

1181.label: A rook moves to an apparently active middle-rank square but either hangs to an enemy piece or fatally abandons a critical defensive duty.
1181.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook moving to an exposed square on ranks 3-6 (Re6, Rg6, Re3, Rg5, Rb6, Rf6, Rd5, Rg6, Rg4), with the remaining position (g3) sharing the same 'ignoring defensive obligations' theme. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 7, 9), the rook lands on a square directly controlled by an enemy minor piece (bishop diagonal or knight), allowing immediate capture. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 10), the rook abandons a critical defensive function—guarding the back rank, protecting f2, or shielding a pawn that prevents check—enabling devastating tactical strikes against the now-exposed king. The moves universally appear aggressive or active (often attacking an enemy queen or occupying a central square), but all 10 positions are middlegame scenarios where the rook's defensive role far outweighed any offensive potential on its destination square. The average cp_loss of 3052 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors.

1182.label: Non-forcing queen relocation to a central square when the position demanded an immediate forcing move or maintaining a critical defensive post.
1182.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet (non-check, non-capture) queen move to a central or semi-central square (c3-f5 zone) that appears active but critically fails to address the position's urgent tactical demands. In at least 4/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 10), the correct move was a forcing move first (check or pawn advance) that the queen move could have followed on the NEXT move — the queen arrives at the right square one tempo too late. In 5/10 positions (1, 5, 7, 8, 9), the queen abandons a critical defensive duty on its current square (guarding mating squares, protecting pieces, or controlling key files). The average cp_loss of 2947 is extreme, with 3/10 positions resulting in immediate checkmate or forced mate. Only 1/10 (position 2) was actually the best move, suggesting the feature fires on 'centralizing queen moves' with high confidence, most of which are errors. The consistent thread is prioritizing aesthetic queen placement over concrete positional requirements.

1185.label: Capturing an enemy bishop while a more urgent tactical priority (often involving a dangerous knight or mating attack) goes unaddressed.
1185.description: All 9/9 positions feature the player capturing an enemy bishop — the target is always a bishop (Bxf5, Bxb5, fxg5 taking Bg5, cxb5 taking Bb5, Bxe7, Bxe6, cxb4 taking Bb4, Nxc1 taking Bc1, Bxb4). In every case, this bishop capture is a 'distraction capture' that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring a far more critical tactical or strategic priority. In 6/9 positions, the ignored threat specifically involves an enemy knight: a knight fork with check (positions 1, 6, 9), a knight capturing an undefended rook (positions 7, 8 indirectly), or a knight improving to a dominant square (position 5). The remaining cases involve missing a forced checkmate (position 2), capturing the wrong target in a move-order error (position 3), or failing to exchange rooks before capturing (position 4). The average cp_loss of 2311 reflects that these captures routinely squander mates, decisive attacks, or full pieces.

1187.label: An aggressive-looking knight (or piece) jump to a central/outpost square where it is simply captured because it has no protection.
1187.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves to seemingly powerful squares (e5, c4, d4, c5, b5, h4, d3), and 1/10 is a bishop move to d4 following the same logic. In all 10 cases, the piece lands on an undefended square where the opponent can simply capture it, usually with a bishop (7/10 are captured by bishops: Bxc4, Bxc5, Bxb5+, Bxh4, Bxd3, Bxd4+, and Bc5 attacking). The average cp_loss is 329, reflecting that these are full-piece or near-piece losses. 7/10 occur in the opening phase when players are most tempted by aggressive centralization. The average number of good alternative moves is only 1.2, meaning these positions demanded precise play rather than speculative jumps. The intent in every case is aggressive centralization, creating forks, delivering checks, or establishing outposts — moves that LOOK strong but fail the basic safety check of whether the piece is protected on its destination square.

1186.label: Playing slow, non-forcing moves in positions that demanded immediate tactical or dynamic action, wasting critical tempo.
1186.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player choosing a quiet, non-threatening move (no check, no capture, no direct tactical threat) when the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation. The best moves available were consistently concrete forcing actions: pawn breaks (d4, e3 in positions 2,4), piece sacrifices/captures (Rxg3 in pos 5, Rxh2 in pos 3), deep penetrations (Rc2 in pos 1), or piece deployments that created immediate threats (Ne4 in pos 6, Bg5 in pos 8, Be5 in pos 10). Instead, the players chose 'improving' moves like king walks (Kf7, Kg7, Ke5 — 3/10), passive pawn pushes (c5, c5, g5 — 3/10), or piece repositioning to non-critical squares (Ra4, Ra6, Rb6, Nb2 — 4/10). The average number of good moves was only 1.6, confirming these were narrow tactical moments where only concrete calculation would find the solution. The average centipawn loss of 1137 reflects the catastrophic cost of missing these critical windows.

1188.label: Pawn moves that open or weaken critical diagonals/lines leading directly to the player's own vulnerable king.
1188.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances that fatally compromise the player's own king safety. In 8/10 cases, the pawn move directly opens a diagonal toward the player's king, allowing the opponent to deliver check, capture with check, or execute a mating sequence along that diagonal (f6 opening the h8 diagonal in positions 1-2, c5 opening the a3-f8 diagonal in position 3, c4 opening the a4-e8 diagonal in position 4, g3 opening the g1-a7 diagonal in position 7, e4 opening the e4-b7 diagonal in position 8, c6 enabling a discovered attack on the b5-e8 diagonal in position 9). In 10/10 positions, the king was already exposed or weakly shielded before the pawn move. The average cp_loss of 2070 is extremely high, with 3/10 resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions were already precarious—but the pawn advance chosen was consistently the one that transformed a difficult position into a lost one by creating the specific geometric vulnerability the opponent's pieces were poised to exploit.

1189.label: Playing a routine knight development or repositioning move when the position demands an immediate concrete forcing action, typically a pawn capture or aggressive pawn advance.
1189.description: 8/10 positions feature knight moves (Nf3, Nf3, Nf6, Ne3, Ndf2, Nf6, Nd3, Nc6), and all 10/10 are quiet, non-forcing moves that prioritize 'improving piece placement' over addressing an urgent tactical demand. The best moves in 7/10 positions were pawn moves — specifically pawn captures (fxe5, fxe5, fxe4) or aggressive pawn advances (h6, h5, g4, Qf6 removing from danger). In positions 1-3, the identical error occurs: fxe5/fxe4 pawn captures win material with tempo but the player instead develops a knight to f3/f6. In positions 4 and 8, the correct h6/h5 pawn thrust attacks an enemy piece directly while the played move (h5/g6) is one square off or structurally weakening. In positions 5, 6, 9, and 10, the knight repositioning ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability (exposed rook, king on check-prone square, hanging piece, or d-file pin). Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, confirming these are razor-sharp moments demanding calculation rather than routine development.

1192.label: King moves to a suboptimal adjacent square in the endgame, wasting a critical tempo in a race or positional contest.
1192.description: All 10/10 positions involve king moves in the endgame where the king selects the wrong destination square among several adjacent options. The tempo loss tag appears in 9/10 positions, confirming the consistent mechanism of error. In 7/10 positions, the king moved to a square one file off from optimal (e.g., Kc3 instead of Kd3, Kg4 instead of Kf4, Kc2 instead of Kd2, Kc5 instead of Kd5), typically choosing a less central or less direct path. In 2/10 positions, the king went one rank too deep or too far back (Kd7 instead of Kd6, Kf8 instead of Kf7). In 1/10 (Position 3), the king moved at all when a critical pawn move was needed first. The average cp_loss of 159 reflects a mix of catastrophic errors (473, 395, 328cp) where the tempo was decisive in a race, and minor inaccuracies (0-29cp) where the position was already won/lost. Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these are narrow positions where precise king routing is essential.

1197.label: A knight is aggressively moved to a square where it is immediately captured because it has no protection.
1197.description: 8/10 positions feature a knight being moved to a seemingly powerful or aggressive square (an outpost, a central square, or a square giving check) where it is completely undefended and can be immediately captured for free by the opponent. The capturing pieces vary — queen captures in 3/10 (positions 1, 4, 8), bishop captures in 3/10 (positions 2, 5, 10), king captures in 1/10 (position 3), and knight captures in 1/10 (position 9). The remaining 2/10 positions involve pawn captures (gxf3, dxc6) that are move-order or tempo-loss errors rather than piece-hanging blunders, making them partial outliers. The consistent thread across the knight moves is that the player was attracted to the destination square's apparent tactical qualities (attacking multiple pieces, occupying an outpost, delivering check) without verifying whether the knight could actually survive there. The average cp_loss of 301 reflects that most positions involve losing approximately one full piece worth of material.

1174.label: A piece (usually a rook) is repositioned along an open line to a square where it or another piece becomes immediately capturable.
1174.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves, and in all 10 cases the moved piece lands on a square that creates an immediate hanging-piece vulnerability. In 4/10 positions (5, 6, 9, 10), the piece moves directly onto a square controlled by an opponent's piece along the same rank or file and is captured outright (Rxa4, Rxa4, Rxd8, Rxa5). In 3/10 positions (3, 7, 8), the piece's departure leaves another piece or pawn undefended (knight on d1, h3-pawn, bishop on c4). In 2/10 positions (2, 4), the rook moves to the wrong square on the same file—one square away from the critical promotion square that needed coverage (Rh2 instead of Rh1, Ra2 instead of Ra1). In 1/10 (position 1), the rook move enables a forced mating pattern by creating a fatal interposition-capture geometry. All 10 moves are quiet repositioning moves (no checks, no captures) that ignore the immediate tactical reality, and 9/10 share the 'tempo_loss' tag indicating the move achieves nothing useful while creating a vulnerability.

1194.label: The queen moves to an apparently active square where it is immediately attacked with tempo or abandons a critical tactical opportunity.
1194.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen repositioning moves to squares that appear active or aggressive but are tactically flawed. In 7/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10), the queen lands on a square where it is immediately challenged with tempo by a minor piece, rook, or check — forcing retreat and losing the initiative (Bg1+ in pos 1, Nf3 in pos 3, Na5 in pos 5, Nxb4 in pos 6, Rhe1 in pos 7, Qb8+ in pos 9, Ne5 in pos 10). In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 8), the queen move specifically abandons a concrete winning capture or tactic (Qxe1+ in pos 4, Qxe4 in pos 3). The best alternatives consistently involved either capturing material (4/10), placing the queen on a square immune to tempo attacks (Qf1/Qb1 patterns in pos 1, 5), or delivering check first to gain tempo (pos 7). Average cp_loss of 1224 reflects that many of these are game-deciding errors where the 'active-looking' square conceals immediate tactical refutation.
1194.old_chip: Queen to tempting but vulnerable square

1198.label: A pawn captures another pawn in a routine-looking exchange when a piece capture or active piece move was far superior.
1198.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player making a pawn-takes-pawn capture (cxd, exd, fxe, fxg patterns) that appears natural or structurally desirable but is actually a significant blunder. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 9, 10), the correct move was to capture the SAME target with a piece instead (Qxd4 not cxd4, Qxd5 not exd5, Nxg4 not fxg4, Bxe5 not fxe5, Qxd5 not cxd5). In the other 5/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 7, 8), the correct move was an entirely different tactical or dynamic piece move (Qh6+, Bxf3, Rxf3, Bg4, e4). The pawn captures consistently create concrete tactical vulnerabilities: 4/10 opened critical diagonals to the king (positions 1, 4, 8, 10), 3/10 enabled devastating knight forks (positions 1, 9, 7), and 3/10 removed defensive pawns from key squares (positions 4, 5, 9). The average cp_loss of 1211 and average of only 1.2 good moves available confirm these are critical moments where the 'autopilot' pawn recapture is catastrophically wrong.

1204.label: A quiet pawn advance on a wing file (a/c/f/h) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate piece activity, pawn breaks, or resolution of central tension.
1204.description: All 10/10 positions feature non-capturing pawn advances on flank files (a-file: 4 positions, c-file: 2, f-file: 2, h-file: 2) — never on the central d or e files. In 8/10 cases, the best move was either a piece move (Re8, Ng5, Rd4, Kc8) or an immediate pawn break/capture (b5, g5, d5, gxf5) rather than a preparatory wing push. In 7/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. Beyond wasting time, 6/10 of these pawn advances permanently destroyed a critical structural resource: the ability to recapture (positions 2, 4 with ...axb5), support a future break (position 6 losing d5 support), maintain a piece's defensive diagonal (position 7 blocking the c2 bishop), or resolve pawn tension favorably (position 10 ignoring g4/f5). The average cp_loss of 1104 (with several positions shifting from equal to lost or winning to drawn) demonstrates these are not minor inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments of positional urgency.
1204.old_chip: Slow flank pawn when action urgent

1191.label: A minor piece (9/10 knight) jumps to an aggressive-looking square instead of simply capturing a key enemy piece — often with the same piece that should have made the capture.
1191.description: In 9/10 positions, the correct move was a straightforward capture of a critical enemy piece (Nxf7, Nxe5, Nxg1, Nxd4, Nxd5), and in 9/10 cases it was the SAME piece that should have captured but instead jumped to an apparently aggressive square (f3+, d4, b6, g5, a5, g4, h6). The 'aggressive' destination creates superficial threats — checks (1/10), attacks on pieces (3/10), central domination (2/10), or kingside attacking squares like g5 (3/10) — but these threats are either easily parried or slower than the opponent's counterplay. The captures that were missed would have eliminated the opponent's most dangerous piece: a powerfully-placed knight (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7), a strong bishop (position 5), or won decisive material outright (positions 1, 3, 8). Average cp_loss of 1245 reflects that these pseudo-active moves frequently allow devastating tactical refutations because the piece's departure simultaneously abandons a critical defensive or offensive function.

1205.label: A non-forcing pawn advance is played in a position demanding immediate tactical or forcing action, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
1205.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same error type: the player advances a pawn (c5, e4, d6, f4, d3, b4) in a position that urgently demands a forcing response—whether a piece move, tactical combination, check, capture, or specific defensive resource. 8/10 positions are explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss,' and 9/10 involve a 'missed_tactic.' The pawn advances appear constructive (gaining space, supporting pieces, solidifying structure) but create zero immediate threats, allowing the opponent to execute a devastating plan. The average good moves available was only 1.3, meaning these were narrow positions with essentially one correct answer—and in every case that answer involved a piece move or forcing play, not a quiet pawn push. The positions span all game phases (4 opening, 3 middlegame, 3 endgame) and both colors equally (5 White, 5 Black), but the mistake is always the same: choosing a slow structural pawn move over an urgent dynamic necessity.

1207.label: A rook passively moves to contest an open file where the opponent is already established, missing a more urgent tactical or strategic priority.
1207.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to an open or semi-open file (d-file: 3, e-file: 4, f-file: 2, c-file: 1) where the opponent already has a piece established. In every case, the move is a 'natural-looking' positional idea to contest file control, but the position actually demands something far more urgent. In 5/10 positions the player missed a concrete tactical strike (Ng4 winning an exchange, Qxh5+ with a winning attack, Bxd5 winning a pawn, b4 counterplay, h3 preventing mate). In 4/10 positions the rook move actually created a new tactical vulnerability (Ba6+ exploiting a diagonal, Bxg7+ deflection, Bg4 winning the exchange, self-blocking an escape square allowing checkmate). In 3/10 positions the move allowed the opponent to simplify favorably on their terms. The average cp_loss of 1292 reflects how costly these 'autopilot' file-contesting moves are when concrete calculation is required. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions demanding precision rather than generic development.

1199.label: Materialistic captures that simplify the position by removing the player's most dynamic pieces, entering an inferior endgame or missing stronger tactical continuations.
1199.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures that prioritize immediate material gain over maintaining dynamic piece activity. In 7/10 positions, a rook makes the capture, and in 6/10 positions specifically, the move initiates a rook-for-rook exchange that enters a structurally lost simplified position where the opponent's advantages (passed pawns, pawn majority, centralized king) become decisive without the rook's counterplay potential. The remaining 4/10 positions involve greedy pawn/piece captures (cxb5, bxa5, Bxh6, Rxf8) that ignore urgent tactical needs — missing a forced mate in 1 case, missing winning a full piece in another, and leaving critical pieces undefended in others. In all 10 cases, the better alternatives involved preserving dynamic tension: keeping rooks on the board (6/10), addressing immediate threats before capturing (2/10), or executing a stronger tactical blow instead of a peripheral grab (2/10). The average cp_loss of 1227 reflects the catastrophic nature of these simplifications.

1201.label: Playing a non-forcing, slow move in a position demanding immediate tactical action—either executing an available forced win or addressing a lethal threat.
1201.description: All 10 positions share a striking commonality: the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, no captures, no immediate threats) in a position where the tactical tension was at a breaking point. In 7/10 positions, the blunder either allowed or missed forced checkmate (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 allowed mate; positions 2, 6 missed delivering mate). The moves break down into pawn advances (4/10: g4, e5, e3, b5), piece retreats to passive squares (3/10: Nd7, Nh8, Na2), and rook relocations to seemingly natural but critically wrong squares (3/10: Rh1, Rc7, Rc2). The average cp_loss of 7440 reflects catastrophic consequences, yet the average of 2.3 good moves available shows these positions were not especially tricky—the correct move was generally findable. In 8/10 cases, the best move involved either a forcing continuation (check, capture, or direct threat) or addressing an immediate forced mating threat. The players consistently misread the position's urgency, treating a razor-sharp tactical moment as a quiet positional one.

1206.label: Advancing a flank pawn (especially the h-pawn) as a slow attacking gesture when the position demands immediate concrete action such as tactics, castling, or simplification.
1206.description: 6/10 positions feature an h-pawn advance (h4 or h5), and all 10/10 involve pawn moves chosen over far more urgent alternatives. The best moves available were remarkably diverse — a tactical sacrifice (Bxf7+), castling (O-O-O), a forced exchange (Rxf6+), king repositioning (Ke5), queen activation (Qb3), and dynamic pawn breaks (f5, d5) — yet in every case the player chose a slow, speculative pawn push instead. 8/10 moves are non-capturing pawn advances; the 3 captures (fxe4, fxe5, cxd5) share the same underlying error of releasing tension or opening lines prematurely rather than maintaining dynamic potential. The positions cluster heavily in the middlegame (7/10) and are overwhelmingly played by White (8/10). The average cp_loss of 291 reflects that these moves consistently squander large advantages or turn balanced positions into losing ones, with only 1.6 good moves available on average — meaning these were critical moments requiring precision.

1196.label: In tactically critical positions with essentially one correct move, the player chooses a superficially attractive alternative—often using the wrong piece to capture/attack or playing a non-forcing move when a forcing sequence wins.
1196.description: All 9 positions share an extremely narrow solution space (avg 1.2 good moves available), meaning the position demanded one specific precise move. In 5/9 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 10), the error was using the WRONG PIECE for the task—capturing with the Queen when the Bishop should capture the same square (positions 3, 4), moving the Queen to a defended square instead of using the Bishop first (position 1), moving the Knight to g2 when the King needed that square (position 5), or moving the wrong bishop entirely (position 10). In 4/9 positions (2, 6, 8, 9), the error was playing a non-forcing 'improving' move when a concrete forcing solution existed—missing mate in 1 (position 2), missing a check sequence leading to forced mate (position 8), missing a winning capture of a hanging piece (position 9), or playing a premature queen sortie instead of concrete central action (position 6). The blunders are overwhelmingly White moves (8/9), predominantly Queen moves (6/9 involve queen moves as the error), and produce catastrophic evaluation swings (avg 3537cp loss), often converting winning positions into lost ones.

1209.label: Advancing a pawn to give check to an exposed king, which paradoxically improves the king's position by granting it access to better squares or weakening the attacker's own structure.
1209.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to deliver check against an already-exposed enemy king. In 7/10 cases, the primary refutation involves the king stepping FORWARD (toward the pawn or into the attacker's position) to a square that was previously denied — Kxc6, Kg4, Kg5, Kh5, Kh4, Kf4, Kf6 — where it paradoxically finds safety or counterattacking potential. In at least 6/10 positions, the pawn advance permanently weakened the checker's own pawn structure by removing a key restraining pawn (e.g., g5 guarding h4, c6 preventing Kxc6, h5 creating kingside holes). 8/10 positions had clearly superior alternatives available — forced mates (Position 8), material-winning captures (Positions 1, 3), perpetual checks with the queen (Position 6), or quiet positional moves (Positions 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 1140 confirms these are severe errors despite appearing aggressive. The irreversibility of pawn moves makes these especially costly: unlike piece checks where the piece can retreat, the pawn permanently alters the structure and can never undo the damage.

1208.label: Voluntary king moves to exposed squares that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities, when the position demands active piece play or concrete defensive measures.
1208.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder — no other piece type is involved. In 5/10 cases the king specifically moves to h6 (or h3 for White, the mirror square), walking toward the edge of the board where it becomes a target for checks, rook lifts, and pawn storms. The remaining moves (Kg8 x2, Kg7, Kb5, Kc2) similarly place the king on squares that create immediate tactical problems: back-rank vulnerabilities (2/10), skewer alignments (1/10), or hanging pieces left undefended (2/10). In 8/10 positions, the king was already on a reasonably safe square and moved to a worse one without necessity — no check forced the move, no piece was captured, and no concrete threat was addressed. The average cp_loss of 1246 reflects that these are catastrophic errors. In every case, the best alternatives were either active piece moves (Qf6, f6, Qxe3), safer king retreats (Kg8 vs Kh6, Kh7 vs Kg8), or defensive improvements (Be1 saving a piece). The positions span middlegames (7/10) and endgames (3/10), suggesting the pattern is phase-independent — it reflects a habitual tendency to make quiet king moves when concrete action is required.

1212.label: King moves to a suboptimal square in a pure pawn endgame, losing a critical tempo in the king race or opposition battle.
1212.description: All 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with no other pieces on the board. Every single move is a king move. The consistent error is a tempo loss: the king moves to a square that appears natural or centralizing but is precisely one square worse than the optimal destination, costing exactly one critical tempo. In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The mistakes manifest as: moving to the wrong adjacent square and losing the opposition (positions 2, 7), retreating the king to the rim when it needs to stay central (positions 4, 9), moving toward the center when a waiting move preserves tempo (positions 1, 3, 5, 8). The cp_loss varies enormously (0 to 9339), reflecting how in pawn endgames a single tempo can be the difference between a slow grind and immediate forced mate. Positions 4 and 7 show catastrophic losses (mate forced) from what appears to be a simple one-square king move, while positions 3, 6, and 10 show minimal losses — all unified by the same structural error of imprecise king placement in a tempo-critical pawn ending.

1193.label: Playing a non-forcing move (advance, retreat, or check) when a direct capture or critical piece placement was immediately available.
1193.description: 7/10 positions involved choosing a less forcing continuation when a direct capture or strong tactical shot existed. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 8), the player specifically bypassed an available capture of material—h5 instead of hxg5 winning a bishop, d4 instead of dxc4 winning a bishop, and Qb5+ instead of Nxd5 winning a pawn with tempo. In 2/10 positions (6, 7), the player made the intended capture but in the wrong move order, missing a critical intermezzo (Rh1+ or e4+) that would have been more forcing first. In 2/10 positions (3, 9), the player retreated a knight to a passive square (Ne3, Nb3) instead of jumping to the dominant active square (Nd6, Rc1). The 3 non-mistake positions (5, 7, 10 with 0-4cp loss) share the same positional structure—tension between captures and repositioning—suggesting the feature detects this decision point regardless of whether the player errs. The consistent consequence across all mistakes is tempo loss: the opponent gains time to consolidate, activate, or execute tactics that the forcing move would have prevented.

1202.label: Premature pawn advances (or committal moves) that push material into squares directly controlled by the opponent's pieces, typically captured by knights or exploited by tempo-gaining counterblows.
1202.description: 7/10 positions feature pawn advances that are immediately punished: in 5/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 8, 10, and partially 1), the advanced pawn lands on a square directly attackable by an enemy knight which simply captures it (Nxc4, Nxc5, Nxe4, Nxd5). In 2/10 cases (positions 1 and 9), the d5 advance enables the opponent's e5 push with devastating tempo against a piece. Position 3 (g5) weakens the king shield enabling Qh5. The remaining 3/10 are piece moves that share the same underlying flaw: making a 'positionally logical' repositioning move while ignoring the opponent's immediate tactical response—Bc7 removes a defensive piece enabling a mating attack, Qe1 wastes the critical tempo needed for king shelter, and Bd3 misses a queen capture. Across all 10 positions, the played move appears strategically motivated (challenging the center, creating passed pawns, repositioning pieces) but fatally ignores the opponent's concrete tactical reply. The average cp_loss of 2080 reflects that several of these (positions 5, 6) escalate to forced mate.

1200.label: A rook (or heavy piece) moves to an apparently useful square but abandons a more critical defensive responsibility, typically allowing an enemy passed pawn to advance decisively or a piece to be lost.
1200.description: In 9/10 positions, a rook moves to attack, blockade, or seemingly improve its position, but the move fatally neglects the most urgent threat. 8/10 positions feature dangerous passed pawns where the rook's repositioning either leaves the promotion square unguarded (positions 3, 10: back-rank mate or pawn queens), allows the pawn to slip past the rook's coverage (positions 1, 5, 8, 9), or places the rook where it blocks a friendly piece or self-traps (positions 2, 3). The consistent error is a priority misjudgment: the player sees a reasonable-looking rook destination but fails to recognize that the rook was serving (or needed to serve) a more vital function on its current file or rank. In 4/10 cases, the correct move involved a different piece handling the task (king blockading in positions 1, 5; bishop retreating in position 2; capturing tension in position 8). In 3/10 cases, the rook needed to stay on its current file to prevent promotion (positions 3, 8, 10). The average cp_loss of 2164 reflects that many of these allow immediate forced mate or decisive material loss.

1203.label: Delivering a queen or rook check against an exposed/wandering king, often prematurely when a quieter move would be stronger.
1203.description: All 10/10 positions involve delivering check with a major piece (queen: 7/10, rook: 3/10) against a king that has lost its pawn shelter or wandered into the open. Every single position explicitly notes the checked king as 'exposed' or having a 'weak pawn shield,' with kings sitting on unusual squares like f2, c2, e2, d1, f3, d2, b7, e6, and d8. While 5/10 positions show 0 cp_loss (the check was correct), the other 5 are significant errors—3 catastrophic blunders (~9200 cp_loss each) converting forced mates into merely winning positions. In the error cases, the check either drives the king to a safer square (positions 1, 9), leads to unwanted piece exchanges that remove attacking potential (positions 4, 7), or abandons defense of another piece (position 5). The correct checks all share the trait of immediately winning material (capturing a queen/rook on the next move). 7/10 positions are endgames where kings are naturally more exposed. The feature captures the classic 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' instinct—positions where checking is the most natural/tempting move regardless of whether it's objectively best.

1195.label: Moving a piece to a plausible-looking square while failing to address the position's single most critical concrete demand.
1195.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move that looks reasonable (centralization, development, pawn defense) but completely ignores the one thing the position urgently requires. In 2/10 cases (Rf5, Rg5), the rook occupies the exact square the king needed for centralization. In 4/10 cases involving knights (Ng3, Ng4, Ne4, Nd3), the knight retreats or repositions to a natural-looking square but either blocks the king's escape, wastes critical tempo, or lands on the wrong retreat square that fails to perform the needed defensive function. In 2/10 cases (Bb7, Bf3), bishops are moved while ignoring hanging material (an undefended rook in one case, a dangerous attacking piece that should be captured in another). In 2/10 rook cases (Ne2, Rd4), the piece abandons a dominant position or creates a tactical liability. The average cp_loss of 1201 is extremely high, and 8/10 positions are endgames where precision is paramount. Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow positions demanding specific solutions — yet the players chose the aesthetically reasonable but concretely wrong option every time.

1210.label: A quiet, one-square pawn advance played as a structural/consolidating move when an immediate tactical blow (piece capture or aggressive pawn thrust) was available.
1210.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing pawn advance as the mistake, with an average cp_loss of 326 and only 1.2 good moves available on average, indicating narrow critical moments. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 7, 8, 9), the correct move was the SAME pawn advanced TWO squares instead of one (d4 instead of d3, e5 instead of e6, d5 instead of d6), where the extra square created forcing threats against enemy pieces. In 3/10 positions (4, 5, 6), the correct move was a direct capture of a hanging piece (Nxg4 winning a queen, Qxf3 winning a knight, Nxf6+ addressing a hanging knight). In 2/10 positions (2, 10), a completely different move type was required (castling or a defensive bishop move). The consistent thread is that players chose a 'natural-looking' positional pawn move—supporting center, preparing development, reinforcing structure—in positions demanding immediate tactical action. 8/10 occurred in the opening phase, suggesting this pattern emerges when players follow general principles rather than calculating concrete threats.

1211.label: Aggressive pawn advances that sacrifice material without compensation, where the opponent simply captures the pawn.
1211.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances (no piece moves, no captures) played as speculative attacks. 9/10 push the pawn to the '6th rank' relative to the moving side (rank 6 for White, rank 3 for Black), representing deep advances into enemy territory. In every case, the refutation involves the opponent simply capturing the advanced pawn — Nxf6, Nxf3, Bxe6, axb3, bxa3, fxe3, cxd6, Qxg3, dxe5, or Qc4+ exploiting the weakened structure. The best alternatives were consistently piece moves (development, centralization, or tactical strikes): 10/10 positions had superior piece-based options. Several cases specifically break up a strong pawn structure — the b4/c4 duo (position 4), connected d4/e4 passers (position 6), and a protected passed a-pawn (position 5). The player consistently overestimates the dynamic value of the pawn thrust while ignoring that the opponent can cleanly capture it.

1213.label: Capturing or exchanging a piece (predominantly with a bishop) when a more forcing tactical or strategic continuation was available.
1213.description: 8/10 positions involve bishop moves (7 captures, 1 placement), with the remaining 2 being analogous captures/exchanges with other pieces. In all 10 positions, the player chose a 'natural-looking' capture or exchange over a significantly stronger continuation. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 5, 7), the player exchanged a piece that was more valuable in its current attacking/defensive role than the material gained. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 6, 10), the move placed or left a piece on a square where it immediately hung or where a crushing tactic existed. In 2/10 cases (positions 8, 9), a rook moved to a square allowing a devastating recapture with check. The average cp_loss of 2082 is extremely high, with 2/10 positions involving missed checkmate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points requiring precise calculation rather than routine exchanges.

1214.label: Advancing a wing pawn (a/b/g/h file) to a square where it is immediately captured by an enemy piece, often when preparation was required first.
1214.description: All 10 positions feature a flank pawn advance (a, b, g, or h file) that lands on an undefended square. In 9/10 positions, the pushed pawn is immediately capturable — by a queen (positions 2, 3, 6), rook (positions 4, 5, 8, 10), or bishop (position 7). In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 5, 6), the capture comes with check or enables an immediate mating attack, making the error catastrophic. Critically, in 5/10 positions (4, 7, 8, 9, 10), the analysis shows the SAME pawn advance was the correct plan but needed one preparatory move first — placing a rook behind it, blocking a diagonal, or improving the king. The average cp_loss of 3048 is astronomical, driven by 4 positions where the push allowed immediate checkmate. 7/10 occurred in endgames where passed pawn advances feel natural but support is still essential. The moves are uniformly non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no threats), giving the opponent full freedom to exploit the hanging pawn.

1216.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move in a critical position where only one specific immediate action maintains the evaluation.
1216.description: 10/10 positions share the pattern of choosing a slow, non-urgent move when the position demanded one precise action. The average number of good moves available was only 1.3, meaning these are razor-sharp positions with essentially ONE correct continuation. 7/10 moves are quiet retreats or shuffles (king moves to h8/h1/h7/corner, bishop to a1, pawn pushes a4/a6/c6), while the remaining involve misprioritizing (capturing the wrong pawn on c5 instead of a5, moving a knight to b6 while a bishop hangs). In every case, the correct move addressed an immediate concrete need: capturing a dangerous piece (gxh6, Bxc1), restraining an opponent's pawn break (b5), advancing a passed pawn (d5/c4), generating instant counterplay (f5), or defending an attacked piece (Qa5). The blundered moves instead chose 'comfort' — tucking the king away, making preparatory pawn pushes, or attacking secondary targets — giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a winning plan.

1217.label: Non-forcing wing pawn advances that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate tactical or defensive action.
1217.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn pushes as the blunder move, with 9/10 being specifically on the a, b, or h files (the wings/flanks). The moves are: a5, h3, b5, h5, a4, b5, a4, h5, f6, a6 — exclusively non-capturing, non-checking pawn advances that fail to address the position's most urgent demand. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 5, 6, 9), a concrete forcing tactical blow was available (Bf3 for mate, Bxf6 winning material, Ne7+ winning the exchange, O-O escaping a mating net). In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10), a critical defensive or positional necessity was ignored — such as addressing king safety, blocking a passed pawn, or relocating the king. The average cp_loss of 1248 reflects the severity: these tempi are wasted at moments of maximum urgency. In 8/10 positions, the refutation directly exploits the free tempo Black/White gains (e.g., ...f3 cracking the kingside, d3+ with deflection, Qe5-Qg5+ exploiting the weakened square). Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions demanded precision rather than generic play.

1221.label: A rook or queen captures a seemingly free pawn, abandoning a critical defensive or strategic duty that costs far more than the pawn gained.
1221.description: All 10/10 positions feature a major piece (rook in 7/10, queen in 3/10) capturing a pawn that appears free or lightly defended. In every case, the capturing piece moves away from a critical responsibility, creating a far larger vulnerability than the pawn is worth. The specific consequences vary: in 4/10 positions (2, 6, 7, 9), the capture leaves the player's own piece hanging or ignores a bigger capture available elsewhere. In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 8), the capture abandons restraint of a dangerous passed pawn that then races to promotion. In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 10), the major piece strays too far from defensive duties, allowing tactical strikes against undefended pawns, forks, or invasions. The average cp_loss of 375 reflects that these are catastrophic errors—typically losing a full piece or equivalent. Notably, 7/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating these are critical moments where the 'obvious' greedy capture was the one clearly wrong choice.

1215.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn advance in a position that demands an immediate concrete piece move with tactical impact.
1215.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn advances (e5+, e5, e4, e5, a5, h6, e4, d4, h4) and 1/10 a misplaced knight move, all played instead of a superior piece move that had immediate tactical consequences. In every single case (10/10), the best move was a piece move: Rbc1, Qc7, Nf4, Bxg7, Bf4, Nd7, Nd4, Nxc7+, Ke8, Be4. The blundered moves all look purposeful—aggressive central expansion, pawn storms, prophylaxis—but are catastrophically slow because the position demanded forcing action. 5/10 involved e-pawn advances specifically (e4 or e5), 3/10 were flank pawn pushes (a5, h6, h4), and 1/10 was a d-pawn push. The average cp_loss of 1322 is enormous, reflecting that these are critical moments where one tempo determines whether an attack succeeds or collapses. 7/10 positions had only 1 good move available, confirming these were sharp tactical moments where precision was essential and slow play was punished immediately.
1215.old_chip: Slow pawn push over piece tactic

1227.label: The bishop captures a pawn (or defended piece) for material gain when it should be preserved, repositioned, or a different piece should capture instead.
1227.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop making a capture (Bx__), and 9/10 specifically capture a pawn (the exception, Bxf6, captures a defended piece). In every case, the bishop grab is a materialistic impulse that ignores a more important positional or tactical consideration. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 5, 9, 3), the captured target is adequately defended and the bishop is simply lost or traded unfavorably in the resulting exchange sequence. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 10), the bishop was a critical piece needed for attack or defense, and removing it from the board dissolved a winning initiative or allowed forced mate. In 2/10 cases (positions 4, 8), the bishop capture was the wrong piece to take with — either a different piece should have captured first (move order) or the capture opened dangerous files against the player's own king. In 1/10 cases (position 7), the capture created a tactical vulnerability for an adjacent piece. The average cp_loss of 1204 reflects the severity of these errors, with many turning winning positions into losing ones.

1219.label: Moving the queen to an aggressive-looking square (often with check) instead of a more concrete, precise alternative that wins material or maintains a critical function.
1219.description: All 10/10 positions involve queen moves to ostensibly active or threatening squares that prioritize aggression over precision. 4/10 are premature queen checks (Qg6+, Qc5+, Qd6+, Qe6+) where the check allows a defensive interposition or wastes a tempo when a non-checking move was decisively stronger. 3/10 involve the queen abandoning a critical defensive or attacking function by relocating (Qc6 leaves e4 hanging, Qf3 abandons the powerful h5 post, Qf3 blocks the knight's needed f3 square). 2/10 involve moving the queen to an 'active' square instead of making a simple capture (Qg6 instead of Qxh5, Qf6 instead of Qe7 blocking a diagonal). 1/10 is a greedy pawn grab (Qxg2) that abandons piece defense. The consistent thread: in every case, the player was drawn to queen activity/aggression when the position demanded a more concrete action — a material capture, a correct move order with another piece, or maintaining the queen's existing critical role.

1228.label: A rook is placed on an open file as a generic positional move while the position demands addressing a concrete tactical or defensive necessity.
1228.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to an open or semi-open file (c-file, d-file, e-file, or b-file) in a non-forcing manner — no checks, captures, or direct threats. In every case, the move looks 'textbook' positional (contesting a file, doubling rooks, activating a passive rook) but critically ignores a more urgent concrete need. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 10), the rook abandons a critical defensive duty — guarding f7, supporting a key piece, or protecting a vulnerable bishop. In 3/10 positions (6, 7, 8), the move wastes tempo when development or piece coordination is desperately needed. In 2/10 positions (9, 10), the wrong rook is committed or rooks are doubled when an attacking/defensive move with a specific piece was required. The average cp_loss of 252 reflects that these autopilot moves consistently allow the opponent to execute a concrete tactical blow (discovered attacks, forks, diagonal checks, captures of undefended pieces) that the 'natural' rook move fails to prevent or address.

1223.label: Retreating a bishop (or piece) to a passive back-rank square while ignoring immediate tactical demands in the position.
1223.description: 9/10 positions feature bishop moves (the exception being Rg8), and in virtually all cases the piece retreats toward the back rank or a passive square (Be1, Bf8×2, Bd8, Bc8, Be3, Be7, Bc3). The core error is consistent: the player chooses a 'consolidating' or 'defensive-looking' repositioning move while the position demands concrete, forcing action. In 5/10 positions (Bf8 pos3, Rg8 pos4, Bd8 pos5, Be7 pos6, Bf8 pos10), the retreating piece critically self-blocks its own king's escape route or obstructs friendly piece communication, enabling immediate tactical exploitation. In 3/10 positions (Bf6 pos2, Bc8 pos9, Bc3 pos7), the retreat leaves another piece hanging or places itself on an undefended square. In 8/10 positions the player had only 1-2 good alternatives, meaning these are narrow positions demanding precision where the instinct to 'consolidate' is fatally wrong. Average cp_loss of 3944 reflects that many of these passive retreats allow immediate checkmate (4/10 positions result in forced mate).

1226.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing 'improving' move in a position where only one precise urgent move (tactical or defensive) maintains the evaluation.
1226.description: All 10/10 positions share a razor-thin margin for error (avg 1.3 good moves available), yet the player chose a slow, non-forcing move instead of the single critical response. In 10/10 cases, the played move involves no check, no capture, and no immediate threat—it's a generic 'improving' move (pawn pushes in 5/10, piece repositioning in 5/10) that would be perfectly reasonable in a quiet position. However, the actual positions demand extreme precision: 4/10 required an urgent defensive move to prevent immediate mate or devastating invasion (positions 3, 5, 7, 1), 4/10 required finding a specific forcing tactical shot (positions 4, 6, 9, 10), and 2/10 required a precise prophylactic move addressing a concrete positional threat (positions 2, 8). The average cp_loss of 3166 reflects that these 'quiet' moves are catastrophic because the positions are critical inflection points where tempo is everything—the opponent has concrete threats that punish any delay.

1220.label: King moves away from the critical sector in pawn endgames, losing decisive tempi to address passed pawns or defensive duties on the opposite side of the board.
1220.description: In 10/10 positions, the mistake is a king move in the endgame that heads in the wrong direction relative to the decisive action. The 'tempo_loss' tag was identified in 10/10 analyses, and 'passed_pawn' appeared in 9/10, establishing these as the defining features. The critical pattern: the opponent has an advanced or advancing passed pawn (or pawn majority) on one side of the board, and the played king move heads toward the OTHER side or advances forward when retreat is needed. In positions 6, 9, and 10, the king moves toward the queenside while a kingside h-pawn races to promote. In positions 5 and 7, the king heads toward the center/kingside while a queenside b-pawn advances.
