In positions 1, 3, and 4, the king advances forward only to be forced into retreat, wasting two full tempi. In position 2, the king steps onto a square allowing a pawn advance with check. The cp_loss ranges wildly (2 to 9164), but the geometric error is identical: the king's compass bearing is wrong relative to where it's most needed.

1230.label: Rook captures a seemingly free pawn, but the resulting displacement costs more in activity, safety, or tempo than the pawn is worth.
1230.description: All 10 positions feature a rook capturing a pawn (Rx-pawn), with 9/10 being mistakes averaging 211cp loss. The captures target wing or peripheral pawns (a3 in 5/10, g6 in 2/10, plus b3, b6, c2, d5). In 3/10 positions, the player should have improved king or piece placement first before taking material (positions 1, 2, 4 — where Bf4, Ke3, and Kf2 were needed). In 4/10 positions, the rook becomes stranded, passive, or trapped after the capture (positions 3, 5, 6, 8). In 2/10 positions, the rook lands on a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable to forks or intermediate moves (positions 7, 10 — Be4+ discovered attack and Bc4+ fork). Only 1/10 (position 9) was actually the correct move with 0cp loss. The consistent thread is that players see an undefended pawn and reflexively capture it with the rook, failing to assess whether the rook's new position is worse than its old one, or whether the tempo spent capturing allows the opponent a critical resource.

1225.label: Rook moves prioritizing material gain or aggressive positioning while ignoring a critical immediate threat (usually king safety or a forced tactic).
1225.description: All 10 positions feature rook moves that look 'natural' or 'active' but catastrophically miss the position's urgent requirement. In 7/10 positions, the critical need was king safety (either defending the player's own exposed king or preventing a mating attack). In 2/10 cases (Rxh7, Rxh2), the rook greedily captures a wing pawn while the position demands defensive action. In 3/10 cases (Rc2, Rb2, Rb3), the rook seeks second/third-rank activity or pawn pressure when the position requires capturing a key piece (Rxd6), moving the king (Kg8), or improving a different piece (Nc5). In 2/10 cases (Rb6, Rg4), the rook lands one square away from the critical square (b7 to cover e7, g3 to give check), missing by a single rank. In 2/10 cases (Rdd1, Rc1), the rook abandons or fails to reach a critical defensive post. The average cp_loss of 2982 confirms these are catastrophic errors. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical positions where precision was essential but the players defaulted to a generic 'make the rook active' heuristic instead of calculating the position's actual demands.

1229.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves (predominantly aimless king moves) played when the position demands concrete tactical action.
1229.description: 7/10 positions feature unnecessary king moves (Kh7, Kg2, Kc6, Kh2, Kg7, Kb3, Kh2) and the remaining 3/10 are quiet pawn pushes (g5, a3, g4). All 10 moves share the critical property of being completely non-forcing — no checks, no captures, no direct threats — played in positions where a specific tactical opportunity existed. The best moves available were consistently concrete: captures (Nxd5, Qxb5, Bxc6 in positions 2, 5, 7), forks (Nf3+ in position 6), active piece deployment (Rf1 in position 1), or development (Bb5 in position 9). With an average of only 1.9 good moves available, these were high-precision moments where the passive move was uniquely punishing. In 8/10 cases, the quiet move either worsened king safety or abandoned a defensive duty, and in 9/10 cases, the resulting position allowed the opponent a concrete tactical refutation exploiting the wasted tempo.

1218.label: Playing slow, non-forcing moves (typically flank pawn pushes) while the position demands an immediate tactical response to a concrete threat or opportunity.
1218.description: 9/10 positions feature a player making a non-forcing, quiet move when an immediate tactical emergency exists. 6/10 moves are pawn pushes on the rim files (h5, h5, h3, a3, a5, hxg6), with c3 adding a 7th pawn advance. The remaining non-pawn moves (Nf6, Rfe1) are similarly quiet and non-addressing. In 5/10 positions, a piece or pawn was left hanging or a capture was available (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 9). In 3/10, king safety was the ignored crisis (positions 4, 7, 8). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, confirming the universal thread: a wasted tempo in positions demanding precise action. Position 10 (Kh4) is an outlier with 0 cp loss, being actually the best move. The average cp_loss of 1124 (inflated by the mate-in-1 miss) reflects how catastrophic these passive moves can be. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical-decision positions where the one correct response was forcing or concrete.

1222.label: Playing a slow, natural-looking developing or improving move when the position demands immediate tactical action to address a hanging piece or exploit a forcing opportunity.
1222.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, no captures) played when the position demanded urgent tactical attention. In 7/10 positions, the best move involved either a capture, a check, or saving an attacked piece. Specifically: 4/10 positions had the player's own piece left hanging by the move (Positions 1, 5, 6, 8 — leaving knight on f3, queen on d8, queen on d2, and knight on h3 undefended), 3/10 positions had an opponent's piece capturable with check or strong forcing move that was missed (Positions 2, 3, 7 — Nxg3+, Nxc4/Qf3, Qxe3+), and 3/10 involved overextension or move-order errors (Positions 4, 9, 10). The blundered moves cluster around piece development (Nd7×2, Ng7, Bb7 = 4/10) and rook lifts to open files (Rg1×2, Rhg1, Rad1 = 4/10). All 10 moves appear 'logical' in a vacuum — developing an undeveloped piece, placing a rook on an open file, infiltrating with the queen — but catastrophically ignore the concrete tactical reality demanding immediate resolution.

1237.label: A rook captures a g or h pawn (usually with check) attempting to rip open the opponent's king shelter, but the resulting attack is insufficient.
1237.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing a pawn on the g-file (7/10: Rxg2, Rxg7, Rxg6) or h-file (3/10: Rxh2, Rxh7) adjacent to the opponent's castled or sheltered king. 9/10 of these captures deliver check, making them feel forcing and 'free.' The universal intent is to strip the king's pawn cover and open a file for a mating attack with queen and remaining pieces. In every case, the sacrifice is unsound: the opponent simply recaptures the rook (Kxg7, Kxh2, etc.) and the attacker lacks sufficient piece coordination to sustain threats. 10/10 positions had better alternatives available—typically quiet improving moves, simple captures of hanging pieces, or correctly-ordered sacrifices that actually work. The average cp_loss of 2217 reflects the catastrophic nature of gifting a full rook for a single pawn without compensation.
1237.old_chip: Unsound Rook Sac on King Pawns

1232.label: Captures that move a piece away from its critical defensive duty, leaving another piece or square fatally unguarded.
1232.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures where the moving piece was performing an essential protective function. In 8/10 cases, the capturing piece was the sole defender of another piece or was blocking a critical line: Position 1 (knight guarded e7 recapture for queen), Position 4 (queen guarded rook on e8), Position 5 (knight blocked e-file protecting back rank), Position 6 (rook on d6 protected rook on d1), Position 7 (d-pawn supported bishop on c4), Position 8 (rook on e5 blocked diagonal to queen on f4), Position 10 (knight on f6 defended bishop on g4). Position 9 is slightly variant—the capture ignores that the player's own queen is already attacked. Position 3 captures the wrong target while a more dangerous threat persists. The refutations are remarkably consistent: 8/10 involve simply taking the now-undefended piece (tagged 'hanging_piece' in 7/10 analyses). The average cp_loss of 2388 reflects how catastrophic these errors are—4/10 result in mate or near-mate.

1234.label: Pieces passively repositioned to the player's 3rd rank, wasting critical tempo while urgent tactical threats demand immediate attention.
1234.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece moving to the 3rd rank from the moving side's perspective (rank 3 for White: Qb3, Qa3, Kg3, Rh3, Ra3, Ra3; rank 6 for Black: Kg6, Kg6, Qa6, Qb6). This geometric consistency is absolute. The moves share a common strategic error: 10/10 are tagged as tempo losses in positions where immediate decisive action was required. In 6/10 cases, a critical tactical threat was ignored (mate in 1, passed pawn promotion, piece capture). In 7/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, showing these were razor-sharp moments demanding precision rather than slow repositioning. The average cp_loss of 1445 reflects that these half-measures in critical positions lead to catastrophic consequences. The 3rd rank appears to be a 'comfort zone' — neither fully committed to defense (back rank) nor aggressive penetration (7th rank) — representing indecisive, non-committal play at precisely the wrong moment.

1236.label: Moving the queen to a seemingly logical but passive square when the position urgently demands a non-queen forcing move (pawn break, piece activation, or tactical shot).
1236.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet queen repositioning move played in a sharp or dynamic position where immediate concrete action was required. In 7/10 cases, the best move was NOT a queen move at all — it was a pawn break (c5, e4, f4 in positions 1, 7, 5), a knight activation (Nd5, Nc5, Ncb4 in positions 3, 8, 6), or a bishop check (Bg4+ in position 10). In the remaining 3 cases, the correct queen move was drastically more active or forcing (Qxc3 capturing a key piece, Qe7 covering a critical infiltration square, Qg3 creating a concrete threat). The average cp_loss of 1200 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical-accuracy positions where the player defaulted to a 'comfort move' — shuffling the queen to a safe-looking square — rather than reading the position's tactical urgency. 8/10 moves were played by Black, suggesting the pattern emerges especially when under pressure.

1224.label: Making a natural-looking capture, exchange, or check before the optimal preparatory move, prematurely resolving positional tension.
1224.description: 8/10 positions involve captures or checks that resolve material or structural tension at the wrong moment. In 7/10 cases, the error is specifically a move-order mistake where a preparatory move should have preceded the forcing action (e.g., Kb6 before axb3, e6 before fxg6, Qb3 before Bxg8, b4 before hxg3). 5/10 involve premature exchanges/simplifications that eliminate the player's primary source of compensation or attacking potential (Rxb2+ trades away an active rook, Qxd6+ removes queens when the opponent's king is exposed, Rxh8 captures the wrong piece). The positions uniformly feature open d-files (10/10), exposed kings on at least one side (10/10), and most are endgames (6/10) where precise timing matters enormously. Position 8 (c6+, 0cp loss) represents the CORRECT version of this pattern—a well-timed forcing move with check—serving as contrast to the 9 incorrect examples. Position 9 (O-O) is the inverse error: playing a quiet move when immediate tactical forcing was required, but still reflects the same timing miscalculation.

1235.label: Moving a piece to an attractive-looking central or active square when the position demands an immediate forcing move (capture, check, or pawn break).
1235.description: All 10 positions feature a non-capturing piece relocation to a square that appears strategically desirable—typically a central outpost or active diagonal. 9/10 moves are minor piece relocations (7 knight moves to squares like d5, c4, b4, d4, d3; 2 bishop moves to e4, f5, c4), and 1/10 is a queen move to a4. In every case, the correct move was more forcing: 4/10 required an immediate capture of hanging material (gxh3, Nxe4, Nxh4, Qxc3+), 3/10 required a decisive pawn break (e5, e6, f4), and 3/10 required concrete positional/defensive moves that addressed the position's tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 1211 reflects that these 'improving' moves consistently squandered enormous advantages—including one missed forced mate. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning the positions demanded precision, not aesthetic piece placement. The seductive quality of the chosen squares (d5, e4, c4, d4—all classic knight outposts or bishop centralization points) appears to be what drew players away from the critical concrete action.

1246.label: Advancing the g-pawn (g4 or g5) to chase an enemy bishop off h5/h4, fatally weakening the king's pawn shelter while missing stronger tactical alternatives.
1246.description: All 10/10 positions feature an identical pattern: a g-pawn advance (g4 for White, g5 for Black) aimed at dislodging an enemy bishop sitting on h5 (6/10) or h4 (4/10). In 9/10 positions, the player's king was castled kingside or nearby, meaning the g-pawn advance directly weakened their own king's pawn shelter. In every case, the bishop simply retreats to a safe square (typically g6 or f7/g3), meaning the advance accomplishes nothing concrete while creating permanent structural damage. Critically, 10/10 positions had superior alternatives available — often sharp tactical shots (Qxe4, Nxe5+, Nfxe4, Nxd4) that would have won material or maintained a significant advantage. The average cp_loss of 1327 reflects that these moves frequently turn winning positions into losing ones. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points requiring calculation rather than pattern-based bishop-chasing reflexes.

1231.label: King moves one square in an open-center endgame, choosing a destination that is tactically vulnerable or strategically suboptimal compared to a nearby alternative.
1231.description: All 10/10 positions feature single-square king moves in endgames with open central files and exposed kings. In 3/10 positions (1, 3, 9), the king walked onto a square within knight fork/check range (c3 forkable from e4, d6 checkable from b5, c6 checkable from e7) when an adjacent square (d3, d7, c7/d8) was safe. In 3/10 positions (5, 8, 10), the king moved toward a passed pawn or tactical target when a pawn advance (h4, g5, h3) was urgently needed first—a move-order error where the king's natural instinct to 'deal with the threat' cost critical tempo. In 2/10 positions (2, 4), the king moved in the wrong direction—toward a passive defensive stance instead of toward active counterplay or forcing piece retreats. Only 2/10 positions (6, 7) were essentially correct moves (cp_loss 0-14), where the king moved toward the correct target at the right time. The average cp_loss of 266 with only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are razor-thin decisions where one adjacent square is correct and all others fail.

1243.label: A rook repositions laterally to an adjacent file in a non-forcing way, abandoning critical pressure or missing an urgent tactical/prophylactic need.
1243.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving sideways (typically one file over) in a non-forcing manner—no checks, no captures, no direct threats. In 7/10 positions, the rook specifically abandons an open or semi-open file where it was exerting critical pressure (c-file in positions 1 and 6, d-file in positions 9 and 10, h-file in positions 3 and 5, a-file in position 4). In 8/10 positions, the position demanded immediate concrete action—either a tactical strike (positions 8, 10), prophylaxis against a specific threat (positions 7, 9), or maintaining piece coordination on a critical file (positions 1, 4, 5). The average cp_loss of 262 reflects that these 'natural-looking' rook improvements are catastrophic because they squander a tempo in positions where urgency is paramount. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the quiet rook shuffle is punished by the opponent seizing the initiative or exploiting the abandoned file/square.

1239.label: Moving a bishop to a seemingly active square while ignoring an immediate tactical demand (threat, combination, or critical tension) in the position.
1239.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop move — 7/10 are development moves from the back rank or repositioning to squares like f4, e3, g5, g4 (appearing active), while 3/10 are captures (Bxb2, Bxe4, Bxg7) that remove the bishop from a critical defensive post. In every case, the position demanded a concrete tactical response: 4/10 required capturing or resolving piece tension (hxg4 or similar pawn captures to eliminate dangerous enemy pieces), 3/10 missed forcing tactical blows (Qxf7+, Nxf2+, or exploiting an uncastled king), and 3/10 moved the bishop away from essential defensive duties while immediate threats existed. The bishop consistently lands on a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable — to tempo-gaining counterattacks like ...g5, ...Ne5, ...Nf3+, or ...Bxe3. The average cp_loss of 321 reflects that these positions were razor-sharp (avg 1.8 good moves available), demanding concrete calculation rather than natural development.

1248.label: Natural-looking rook development moves to open files or active squares that fatally ignore concrete tactical demands in the position.
1248.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that appear positionally sensible—placing rooks on open files, activating them to 'useful' squares, or supporting pawns—but critically miss urgent tactical requirements. In 4/10 cases (positions 5, 6, 9, 10), the rook move wastes a crucial tempo when the position demanded immediate concrete action (advancing a passed pawn, capturing a pinned piece, or blocking a dangerous diagonal). In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 7), the rook abandons a critical defensive square or destroys a key tactical resource by moving away. In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 8), the rook move physically blocks the king's escape square, enabling devastating discovered checks or mating attacks. The average cp_loss of 1177 is enormous, with several positions swinging from winning to losing. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments requiring precision, yet the players defaulted to generic rook activation instead of addressing the position's concrete demands.

1247.label: A bishop captures a knight as a seemingly routine exchange, but the timing is wrong because it ignores a more urgent tactical or strategic priority in the position.
1247.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a knight on a classic knight square (f3, f6, c3, or c6), appearing to be a normal minor piece exchange but costing an average of 1224 centipawns. The specific reason the trade is bad varies: in 4/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 8), the capture leaves a piece hanging or enables a devastating intermediate move because the bishop that moved was restraining an opponent's tactic. In 2/10 positions (3, 5), the traded bishop was the sole guardian of critical dark squares around the player's king, and its removal unleashes an unstoppable attack. In 2/10 positions (6, 7), the capture opens the g-file toward the player's own king or grants the opponent a powerful pawn center. In 2/10 positions (9, 10), the capture is a mundane exchange that completely misses a winning tactic or ignores a forced mating sequence. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where the 'obvious' trade was a trap.

1245.label: An aggressive-looking pawn advance chosen instead of addressing an urgent tactical obligation such as capturing a hanging piece, defending the king, or maintaining a critical pawn structure.
1245.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the blunder move — f4, b3, e4, f4, d6, c6, g4, d4, d5, e4 — every single one a forward pawn push with aggressive intent. In each case, the position demanded a more urgent concrete action: 2/10 ignored a completely hanging piece (positions 1 and 7 where Qxg5 and Bxa1 won free material), 4/10 ignored critical king safety requirements (positions 4, 5, 8, 9 where the king needed an escape square or defensive cover), and 4/10 destroyed the player's own pawn structure or released tension prematurely (positions 2, 3, 6, 10). The average cp_loss of 2120 is catastrophic, and with only 1.5 good moves available on average, these were positions requiring precise play where the player instead chose a superficially active pawn thrust. In 6/10 cases the pawn advance directly opened lines or diagonals that the opponent exploited (positions 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10). The blunders occur overwhelmingly from Black's side (7/10), mostly in the middlegame (7/10), suggesting players under pressure default to aggressive-looking pawn moves rather than finding the critical defensive or tactical resource.

1233.label: Moves that prioritize piece repositioning or superficial forcing moves over the concrete tactical or safety need of the position.
1233.description: 9/10 positions feature severely exposed kings (both sides frequently have weak pawn shields), and 8/10 involve open files or ranks creating immediate tactical vulnerability. The played moves consistently choose an 'active-looking' action—a piece reposition to an aggressive square, a check, or a capture—that appears dynamic but misses the most urgent concrete need. In 4/10 cases (Bd2, Bc2, Bc3, Bh5), a bishop is repositioned to a seemingly useful square while ignoring a critical defensive or tactical obligation (back-rank safety, king evacuation, piece hanging). In 4/10 cases (Qb8+, Nxf3+, Qd2+, Bg6+), a check or forcing move is chosen over a more decisive action (capturing with check, capturing the queen directly). In 2/10 cases (Rxb7, Rg7), a rook threatens or grabs material indirectly when an immediate capture or king-attacking move was available. The average cp_loss of 2110 and only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where the 'obvious active move' is a trap that ignores the concrete tactical reality.

1244.label: Aggressive knight repositioning to visually appealing but tactically undefended squares, allowing immediate capture or exploitation of abandoned defensive duties.
1244.description: 8/10 positions feature knight moves (Nd7, Ne4, Ng4, Nd4, Nf4, Nc3, Nd4, Nh4), with the remaining two (Qd2, e5) sharing the same underlying logic of placing a piece/pawn on a tactically unsound square. In 5/10 positions, the moved piece is immediately captured in the refutation line (Ne4→Nxe4, Nd4→Nxd4, Qd2→Nxd2, Nc3→Nxc3, Nh4→Qxh4), and in 3 of those cases the capture enables a secondary tactic (fork after Nxc3/Ne2+, queen win after Nxe4/Nxg3, trapped piece after Nxd4/Ba6). In 2/10 positions the knight abandons a critical defensive post (Nf4 leaves e4 unguarded; Nd4 from b5 leaves the king exposed to Rh2+/Ne4+). The moves consistently target squares that appear aggressive—central outposts (d4, e4, c3) or attacking positions (f4, h4, g4)—but fail basic tactical verification. Average cp_loss of 336 confirms these are severe errors, not minor inaccuracies.

1251.label: Moving a knight (or minor piece) from a critically powerful square to capture a pawn or reach a seemingly active but inferior square, dissolving the position's tactical potential.
1251.description: 9/10 positions involve knight moves (one bishop move shares the identical pattern). In all 10 cases, the piece occupied a square where it performed a critical function — restraining the opponent's king (positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 9, 10), enabling a superior forcing sequence (positions 3, 5, 7), or attacking a hanging piece (position 4). The moved piece typically captures a pawn (7/10: Nexc2, Nxh7, Bxh7, Nxd6, Nxg6, Nxd4, and implicitly Nb4-position 9 eyes material) or repositions to a square that appears active but accomplishes far less (Ne3 attacking a rook that simply slides away, Nb4 threatening a bishop that can be ignored, Ng3 attacking a knight that just captures it). In every case, a decisive tactical resource existed on the piece's ORIGINAL square — perpetual check enablement (position 2), deflection sacrifices via Bb5+ (positions 5, 7), winning hanging material (position 4), or maintaining a mating net (positions 6, 10). The average cp_loss of 367 reflects that these moves routinely cost the equivalent of a full piece in positional value.

1238.label: Playing a tempting but non-urgent move in a critical position that demands specific immediate action to address the dominant tactical or strategic factor.
1238.description: All 10/10 positions share a narrow decision point (avg 2.1 good moves) where the position demands one specific type of action, but the player instead pursues a secondary concern. In 5/10 positions the blunder is a capture or trade that looks natural but ignores a bigger issue (dxc6 ignores discovered check, Bxf6×2 trades away key pieces, Qxh1 grabs material instead of delivering mate, Bxf4 trades the only dark-square bishop). In 3/10 positions the blunder is a slow pawn push on the wrong flank (h5, a3, e5) while the position screams for central/defensive action. In 2/10 the blunder is a piece move to an exposed square (Kf8, Qb5) that walks into a tactical pattern. Critically, 7/10 positions featured king safety as the primary concern (either exploiting opponent's exposed king or defending one's own), yet the blunder move addresses queenside play, material gain, or trades instead. The correct moves in all 10 positions directly address the #1 positional priority: defending h2, clearing an escape route, striking the center against an uncastled king, trading queens to protect a hanging piece, or delivering checkmate.

1242.label: Speculative pawn advances that remove critical defensive coverage of key squares, allowing enemy piece invasion or combination.
1242.description: All 10/10 positions feature single-step pawn advances that look aggressive or purposeful (gaining space, attacking enemy pawns, creating breakthroughs) but fatally compromise the player's position. In 8/10 cases, the advanced pawn was directly guarding a critical square adjacent to the player's own king, and its removal allowed immediate enemy piece invasion: f4→f5 opened f4 for a bishop (Position 1), d3→d4 opened e4 for a knight-check (Position 2), e4→e5 left f3 hanging (Position 4), e5→e4 exposed h6 to Bxh6 (Position 6), f2→f3 opened g3 for a knight delivering a mating combination (Position 10), and b4→b5 ignored f2 vulnerability to Ng4+Bxf2+ (Position 8). In the remaining cases, the pawn advance wasted a critical tempo when urgent defensive action was needed — g5→g4 allowed a back-rank mate in 2 (Position 9), d4 ignored b-file invasion (Position 7), and c5 abandoned a queenside storm or coordination (Positions 3, 5). The average cp_loss of 2986 reflects several game-ending blunders where the pawn advance directly enabled forced checkmate.

1241.label: Playing material-seeking or plan-pursuing moves in critical positions while overlooking an immediate tactical catastrophe exploiting one's own vulnerability.
1241.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: the player's position contains a critical tactical vulnerability (usually king exposure — present in 9/10 positions), yet the player ignores this to pursue their own agenda. 4/10 moves are queen captures or queen moves targeting material (Qxf7, Qxb5, Qc4, Qxc4), 5/10 are pawn advances pursuing strategic or attacking goals (g3, f4, g4, e5, c6), and 1/10 is a flashy check (Ne2+) that sacrifices a key defender. The punishment is immediate and devastating: 4/10 allow forced checkmate (positions 7, 8, 10, 6), 3/10 lose the queen or equivalent material (positions 2, 3, 9), and 3/10 create decisive positional damage through exposed king exploitation (positions 4, 5, 1). The average cp_loss of 5108 confirms these are catastrophic errors, while the average of only 2.2 good moves available shows these are razor-edge positions demanding defensive precision. The unifying thread is that each move looks 'logical' in isolation — capturing an available pawn, advancing a passed pawn, giving check — but is completely wrong given the immediate tactical reality of the position.

1255.label: A bishop captures a rook to win the exchange, but a superior alternative exists that wins more material, maintains a dominant piece, or addresses a critical tactical threat.
1255.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical move pattern: a bishop captures a rook (winning the exchange, ~2 pawns of material). In every case, this materialistic capture is a significant mistake (avg 320cp loss). The better alternatives vary but follow recognizable sub-patterns: in 4/10 positions (3, 4, 8, 10) the error is a move-order mistake where capturing a different target first would allow winning BOTH targets; in 3/10 positions (1, 5, 7) the bishop being traded was positionally dominant or the position offered a forcing sequence winning more (e.g., a whole queen); in 3/10 positions (2, 6, 9) the capture neglects an urgent tactical threat the opponent exploits immediately after recapture. The average number of good alternative moves was only 1.5, indicating these are narrow critical moments where the 'obvious' exchange-winning capture is a trap. All 10 occurred in the middlegame where piece activity and dynamic factors outweigh simple material counting.

1253.label: King moves forward/centrally when it should stay put or retreat, walking into tactical vulnerabilities or abandoning critical defensive duties.
1253.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that advances toward the center or opponent's territory rather than retreating or staying on its current square. In 10/10 cases the king moves forward (e.g., d2→e3, f7→e6, e2→d3, c8→c7, b3→c4), never backward. In 5/10 positions (1, 5, 8, 9, 10), the advancing king abandons the defense of a piece (c2 pawn, e1 rook, e4 queen, d2 bishop), leaving it hanging. In 7/10 positions (2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9), the king walks onto a square vulnerable to immediate checks, forks, or mating nets. The phase is overwhelmingly middlegame (7/10), where sufficient attacking material remains for the opponent to exploit the exposed king. The average cp_loss of 5039 reflects that these are catastrophic errors, and with only 1.1 good moves available on average, the positions demanded extreme precision — typically a single non-losing alternative existed (often a king retreat or a non-king move entirely).

1256.label: The player captures with a rook when the queen (or another piece) should have taken instead, losing critical tactical potential.
1256.description: All 10 positions feature a rook capture (Rx__) where a more powerful or more tactically appropriate piece should have made the capture. In 7/10 positions (3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10), the correct move was the queen capturing on the exact same square (Qxh4, Qxf5, Qxf6, Qxf5, Qxf2, Qxa5, Qxf3). In position 2, the queen should have captured on a related square (Qxd5 or Qxc7). In positions 1 and 6, an intermediate knight move with check was superior before recapturing. The consistent error is that the rook capture leaves the queen passively placed elsewhere, forfeiting immediate mating threats (positions 5, 8, 10), defensive coverage against perpetual check (position 8), tempo-gaining attacks on pieces (positions 1, 9), or the ability to force favorable simplifications (positions 4, 7). The average cp_loss of 2076 reflects several positions where forced mates were squandered. 8/10 were played by Black, and 9/10 occurred in the middlegame where queen activity is most critical.

1240.label: A minor piece develops to a natural-looking square that obstructs the queen's defensive line, leaving another piece or pawn unprotected and capturable.
1240.description: In 7/10 positions, a knight or bishop develops to a square on the d-file (d2, d3, d6, or d7) that physically interposes between the queen and a piece it was defending, leaving that piece hanging. The clearest sub-group (positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8 — 5/10) involves a piece landing on d2 or d3 that severs the queen on d1's line of defense to a knight or bishop on d3/d4, allowing immediate capture. Position 4 shows the same logic on the c-file (Nc6 blocks queen's access to the c6 defensive square). Positions 5, 8, and 9 all feature Nbd7 blocking the queen on d8 from defending along the d-file. The remaining cases (3 and 10) share the broader pattern of a seemingly routine minor piece development that ignores an urgent tactical vulnerability. All 10 moves are minor piece developments (6 knight moves, 4 bishop moves), and all look like natural, standard developing moves that a player might make on autopilot — the average cp_loss of 370 reflects how catastrophically these 'routine' moves misfire.

1252.label: A quiet queen relocation to a seemingly active square when the position demands an immediate forcing response (capture, check, or precise counter-threat) to an urgent tactical problem, usually involving an enemy knight.
1252.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a non-forcing queen move (no check, no capture) to a central or semi-central square that appears active or purposeful. In 9/10 positions, an enemy knight deeply infiltrated in the player's territory creates immediate tactical threats (forks, attacks on rooks/queens, discovered attack potential). The correct move in 10/10 cases was a forcing response: a pawn or piece capture of the threatening piece (positions 1, 4, 7, 8), a check that forces the enemy piece to move (position 9), or a precisely calculated queen placement creating a specific counter-threat that the played move lacked (positions 2, 3, 5, 6, 10). The average cp_loss of 360 reflects that these positions are tactically critical with very few good options (avg 1.4 good moves). The queen moves universally share the characteristic of APPEARING to address the threat while actually leaving the opponent free to execute their tactical idea on the next move.

1249.label: Knight moves to an apparently attractive square (centralizing, checking, or attacking) while abandoning a critical tactical duty or landing on a fatally vulnerable square.
1249.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight move to a square that looks superficially strong — central outposts, checks, or attacking moves — but catastrophically ignores the position's actual tactical demands. In 6/9 positions, the knight abandons a square where it was performing a vital function (controlling a mating square in positions 4, 6, 7; enabling a winning tactical sequence in positions 1, 3, 5). In 2/9 positions the knight gives a tempting check that either allows its own capture (Nf4+ where Kf5 wins it) or abandons a dominant outpost for no compensation (Ne2+ leaving f4). In 1/9 positions the knight moves to a completely undefended square where it simply hangs to a queen capture leading to forced mate. The average cp_loss of 4401 is extreme, with 5/9 positions involving missed mates or near-mate swings, reflecting how the abandoned knight functions were often the linchpin of the entire position's tactical equilibrium.

1254.label: Advancing a pawn straight ahead when capturing diagonally (resolving tension) was the correct move.
1254.description: In 8/10 positions, the best or near-best move was to CAPTURE with the exact same pawn that was mistakenly advanced forward (Position 3: exd5 not e5; Position 4: cxd4 not c4; Position 5: cxb4 not c4; Position 6: exf4 not e4; Position 7: bxc5 not b5; Position 8: gxh3 not g3; Position 9: dxe4 not d4; Position 10: hxg5 not h5). In the remaining 2/10, the pawn advance similarly bypassed a tension point where captures were among the good alternatives (Position 1: exf5 was third-best; Position 2: the Nd4/cxd4 exchange was best). All 10 moves are pawn advances, and in every case the pawn was at a point of tension with an opposing pawn where a diagonal capture would have resolved the position favorably. Instead, the player pushed the pawn straight ahead, releasing tension on the opponent's terms and creating permanent structural damage.

1261.label: An already-exposed king attempts to escape pressure but walks directly onto a square where it is immediately checkmated or forced into a short mating sequence.
1261.description: All 9/9 positions feature a king move as the blunder, with the king already exposed and under severe pressure in the middlegame. In 9/9 cases, the king was attempting to flee danger or reposition, but instead walked into a square where immediate or near-immediate checkmate existed. In 6/9 positions, the result was checkmate in exactly 1 move; in 8/9, it was mate in 5 or fewer. The average good moves available was only 1.2, meaning these were already crisis positions with extremely narrow survival paths. The kings moved in varied directions — forward toward the center (Ke6, Kf7, Kd6, Kc5, Kf4), backward to the back rank (Kd8×2, Kf8, Kc8) — but all shared the critical error of landing on a square where opponent pieces had pre-existing coverage creating a sealed mating cage. In 7/9 positions, the king's own pieces contributed to blocking escape squares, making the self-entombment complete.

1260.label: Non-forcing moves to the a-file or h-file that squander tempo when immediate concrete central/tactical action is required.
1260.description: All 10/10 positions feature a move landing on either the a-file or h-file — the extreme edges of the board. Specifically, 6/10 involve h-file moves (h6 appears 3 times, plus Bh6, Qh4, and h4) while 4/10 involve a-file moves (Ra2, a4, Qa3, Ba6). In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete action — a tactical shot, a capture, or a forcing central move — but the player chose a speculative, non-forcing wing gesture instead. The analyses confirm that 'tempo_loss' is tagged in 10/10 positions, and 9/10 positions explicitly identify a missed tactic or urgent concrete move that was available. The average cp_loss of 260 reflects how severely these positions punish wasted time. The best moves in these positions were captures (Bxa5, Nxe6, Rxb8), central breaks (e6, d5, c5), or piece deployments to critical squares (Bb5, Bd5) — all concrete and forcing. Instead, the chosen moves achieved nothing immediate and allowed the opponent to seize the initiative.

1258.label: A quiet queen repositioning move that removes the queen from a square where it performed a vital attacking or defensive function, giving the opponent a decisive free tempo.
1258.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet (non-capturing, non-checking) queen relocation from an active or functionally critical square to a passive or disconnected one. In 10/10 cases, the queen was either maintaining attacking pressure against an exposed king (Positions 3, 5, 6, 7, 8), defending a vulnerable king or key squares (Positions 2, 4), or sustaining initiative through forcing threats (Positions 1, 9, 10). The blunder uniformly replaces concrete, forcing continuation with an aimless repositioning move that looks reasonable but abandons the queen's essential role. In 8/10 positions, there existed an immediate tactical forcing move (capture with check, pawn capture creating threats, or perpetual checks) that the quiet queen move neglected. The average cp_loss of 2160 reflects how severely the opponent punishes the free tempo: 4/10 positions resulted in forced mate or near-mate, while the remaining 6 saw 186-578cp swings. Critically, 6/10 positions had only 1 good move available, confirming these were narrow-path moments demanding precision rather than 'improvement' moves.

1259.label: Moving a heavy piece to the g-file back rank (g1/g8) to passively defend the g-pawn when the king is trapped in the h-file corner, creating tactical vulnerabilities or missing active resources.
1259.description: 10/10 positions feature a king trapped on a corner back-rank square (h1/h8 in 9/10, a8 in 1/10), and the blunder places a heavy piece on the adjacent back-rank square as passive defense. 9/10 moves specifically go to g1 or g8 (the g-file back rank square next to the cornered king), with the intent of defending the g-pawn (g2 or g7). The king is on h1 in 6/10 positions (White) and h8 in 3/10 (Black). In every case, the defensive rationale is fatally flawed: 3/10 positions (7, 9, and partially 10) see the rook on g1 block the king's escape route, enabling back-rank mates or devastating sacrifices on g2. 4/10 positions (2, 8, 9, 10) allow Bxg2+ sacrificial combinations that exploit the rook as overloaded or create pins. 4/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5) represent pure passivity where active moves (queen repositioning, counterattacks, or even forced checkmate sequences) were available. The average cp_loss of 3104 reflects that many of these are catastrophic — 4/10 involve missed or allowed forced mates.

1250.label: Non-forcing moves (king walks, pawn pushes) played in positions demanding immediate concrete action, where very few alternatives maintain the evaluation.
1250.description: All 10/10 moves are quiet and non-forcing — no captures, no checks, no direct threats. 5/10 are single king moves (Kg3, Kd3, Kf6, Kf3, Ke4), 4/10 are pawn pushes (f5, g5, g4, and the opening's equivalent Bg4/Rc8 which are similarly 'improving' moves). The positions share an extremely narrow set of good options (avg 1.9 good moves), meaning precision was demanded. In 4/10 cases, the correct move was a forcing action: a promotion push (b2 in position 4), a capture (bxc5 in position 6), a tactical fork (Nb3 in position 9), or a back-rank check (Re8+ in position 10). In the remaining cases, the best move was a more precise quiet move addressing the specific concrete demand. 7/10 positions are endgames where a single tempo often determines the outcome. The feature fires most strongly when mate-in-N or immediate material gain was available but a 'natural' slow move was chosen instead (positions 4 and 6, both with 9000+ cp loss).

1268.label: White plays Nxf7 from g5 attempting a queen/rook fork in the opening, but the knight becomes trapped on h8 after the queen retreats with a counter-threat.
1268.description: 8/10 positions feature the identical tactical error: a knight on g5 captures on f7, attempting to fork Black's queen (on d6) and rook (on h8). 7/10 positions are the exact same Fried Liver/Italian Game position where the refutation is 7...Qc6, which simultaneously escapes the fork AND attacks the undefended bishop on c4. After White takes the rook with Nxh8, the knight is permanently trapped in the corner with no escape squares (g6 and f7 covered), resulting in a net loss of two pieces and a pawn for one rook. Position 1 is a related Nxf7 capture from g5 where the error leaves f2 fatally weak. The 2 non-Nxf7 positions (g4, d4) share the broader theme of aggressive moves that create fresh weaknesses around the player's own exposed king, but the overwhelming signal is the specific premature Nxf7 fork pattern.

1262.label: Developing a bishop to a natural-looking 'active' square (especially pinning moves like Bg4) instead of playing an available concrete forcing move that wins material or delivers a decisive attack.
1262.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing bishop development move to a seemingly active square, with 6/10 specifically being Bg4 (pinning a knight on f3 against the queen). In every case, the position demanded a concrete tactical blow instead: captures winning material (3/10: Bxb2, hxg5, exf4), checks leading to decisive advantage (2/10: Bh3+, Qa4+), or aggressive pawn thrusts with immediate tactical force (3/10: g4, e4, e4). The average cp_loss of 1239 is enormous, and only 1.2 good moves were available on average, confirming these are narrow tactical positions where autopilot development is catastrophic. 7/10 were played by Black, and the positions split evenly between opening (5) and middlegame (5). The unifying error is treating a position requiring concrete calculation as one requiring 'natural development' — the bishop moves all look like sound positional ideas (creating pins, controlling diagonals, completing development) but ignore that a far stronger forcing continuation exists.

1272.label: Moving the b-pawn or g-pawn forward one square opens the long diagonal and hangs a corner rook to an enemy bishop or queen.
1272.description: 10/10 positions show the identical geometric pattern: the player advances their b-pawn (b2→b3 or b7→b6) or g-pawn (g2→g3 or g7→g6) one square forward, removing the sole blocker on a long diagonal (a1-h8 or a8-h1) and leaving a corner rook (a1, a8, h1, or h8) completely undefended against an enemy long-range piece. In 7/10 cases, the attacking piece is a fianchettoed bishop (on g2, g7, b2, or b7) that immediately captures the exposed rook. In 2/10 cases (positions 6 and 8), the attacking piece is a bishop placed elsewhere on the same diagonal (c6 or f6). In 1/10 cases (position 9), a queen on e5 captures the exposed a1 rook. The intent behind the pawn move was always developmental—typically preparing to fianchetto a bishop (8/10) or to challenge an enemy bishop on the diagonal—but the player failed to recognize the pawn's critical defensive role as a diagonal blocker. The average cp_loss of 331 corresponds almost exactly to a full exchange or rook, confirming the material cost is consistently one rook captured for free.

1257.label: King moves to a passive or retreating square in endgame positions where aggressive advancement (to escort passed pawns, capture material, or attack targets) is critical.
1257.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves, and 8/10 occur in endgames with passed pawns as a central theme. In the significant blunders (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10), the king consistently moves to a square that appears safe or centralizing but is actually too passive relative to the position's demands. In 4/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 10), the king literally retreats away from its most critical task: escorting passed pawns (positions 2, 5), staying near a target pawn (position 6), or capturing an undefended piece (position 10). In 3/10 positions (4, 8, 9), the king moves to a plausible square but in the wrong direction—away from captures (Kxf5 in pos 4, Kxd6 in pos 10) or to an inferior adjacent square (Kf5 instead of Kf6 in pos 9). Only 2/10 positions (1, 7) show negligible cp_loss, suggesting the feature fires broadly on endgame king moves but most strongly when the king chooses passivity over aggression. The average cp_loss of 1169 (driven by position 3's forced mate) reflects how catastrophic passive king play is in endgames where tempo is decisive.

1264.label: Playing an offensive major piece move (usually queen) while ignoring an immediate mating threat against your own king.
1264.description: In 8/8 positions, the player's own king faced an immediate lethal threat (mate in 1-6 moves), yet the move played was an aggressive or active piece deployment aimed elsewhere on the board. 6/8 moves were queen moves (Qg5, Qg6, Qb4, Qd5, Qd3, Qf7), with the remaining 2 being rook moves (Re1, Rb6). In every case, the piece moved AWAY from the defensive zone where the mating threat existed: e.g., queen to the kingside while the king faced a queenside back-rank mate, or queen to the center while the king faced an h-file sacrifice. The average cp_loss was a catastrophic 8594, with 7/8 positions allowing forced checkmate after the blunder. Only 1-2 good moves existed on average (1.5), highlighting that these positions demanded precise defensive awareness rather than creative attacking play. In 5/8 positions, the player was winning or equal before the blunder, meaning they threw away the game entirely by prioritizing offense over survival.

1274.label: Pushing the f-pawn one square to challenge the opponent's e-pawn, fatally weakening king diagonals and key squares.
1274.description: All 10 positions feature the f-pawn advancing one square (f7-f6 in 8/10 positions as Black, f2-f3 in 2/10 as White) with the intent of challenging the opponent's strong central e-pawn (e5 or e4). In every case, the f-pawn was performing a critical defensive role: guarding diagonal access to the king and/or controlling key squares (e6 for Black, g3/e3 for White). The punishments exploit newly opened diagonals in 8/10 positions (Bxe6+, Bg6+, Bh6, Bxg3+, Qh5+), and the weakened e6 square via e6! pawn thrusts in 4/10 positions. In 6/10 positions the king was either uncastled or had its shelter directly compromised. The average cp_loss of 272 reflects how catastrophic this structural concession is — the opponent's pieces are typically already aimed at exactly the squares and diagonals the f-pawn was defending.

1270.label: Placing or capturing a piece on a d-file square (d3-d6) where it is immediately captured by an opponent's piece controlling that file.
1270.description: 8/9 positions involve a piece moving to or capturing on a d-file square (d3, d4, d5, or d6) where it becomes immediately vulnerable to recapture, typically by an enemy rook already stationed on the open d-file. In 5/9 cases (positions 2, 3, 6, 8, 9), a minor piece lands on d5 or d3 and is directly captured by a rook on the d-file. In 2/9 cases (positions 2, 5), a knight captures on d4 and hangs to Rxd4. In 1/9 (position 1), a rook captures on d6 and hangs to the queen. In 1/9 (position 4), Rxd3 removes a knight from its guardian role, enabling a discovered attack. The single outlier (Qxg6, position 10) involves a queen trade rather than a d-file piece, though the underlying theme of capturing material that appears free but creates catastrophic tactical consequences still applies. The consistent element is that the d-file is open or semi-open with an enemy major piece already aimed down it, making any unprotected piece placement there immediately punishable.

1273.label: A bishop captures a pawn when the bishop is worth far more than the pawn gained, either losing the piece outright or squandering a significant positional/tactical advantage.
1273.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop capturing a pawn (Bx[pawn square]), and in every case this is a significant mistake because the bishop's value far exceeds the pawn taken. In 4/9 positions (Bxh6, Bxh7+, Bxh6, Bxh3), the bishop is sacrificed on the kingside with insufficient attacking compensation — the necessary supporting pieces (queen, rooks, knights) are not in position to follow up. In 3/9 positions (Bxf6, Bxe5, Bxd4 pos.6), an active bishop trades itself for a mere pawn while simultaneously relieving pressure on the opponent or allowing simplification that extinguishes the player's advantage. In 2/9 positions (Bxd4 pos.9, Bxe4), the bishop lands on a square where it is simply recaptured, resulting in a direct material loss of a piece for a pawn. The average cp_loss of 304 reflects the consistent ~3-pawn value gap between a bishop and the pawn it captures. Better alternatives (bishop retreats, repositioning, or attacking moves) were available in every position.

1263.label: A capture that takes a less-critical piece or uses the wrong capturing piece, while a more urgent tactical priority (a hanging piece, an advanced pawn, or a critical threat) goes unaddressed.
1263.description: All 9/9 positions feature a capture that ignores the most urgent tactical element. In 7/9 cases, the player captures the wrong enemy piece: a bishop on the rim instead of a central threat (Bxa2), a knight on c6 instead of an infiltrated bishop (dxc6 twice), a knight on e4 instead of a hanging bishop on d8 (dxe4), a fianchettoed bishop instead of an active rook (Bxg7), a bishop on d3 instead of a hanging bishop on d6 (exd3), and a bishop on c5 instead of addressing a dangerous bishop on a2 (bxc5). In 2/9 cases (both Nfxd2), the target is correct but the capturing piece is wrong — using the f3-knight instead of the e4-knight leaves the remaining piece hanging. The consistent error is that a more appetizing-looking or superficially logical capture is chosen over the truly critical one, giving the opponent exactly one tempo to save/exploit the piece that actually mattered. The average cp_loss of 409 reflects that these are catastrophic priority errors, not subtle inaccuracies.

1277.label: Giving a forcing but purposeless check with a major piece in the endgame, wasting a critical tempo while often improving the opponent's king position.
1277.description: All 10/10 positions feature a major piece (9/10 rook, 1/10 queen) delivering check to an exposed king in an endgame. In every case, the check fails to create any lasting threat — the opponent's king simply sidesteps to an equal or superior square. 10/10 analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif. The checks are counterproductive because they either drive the opponent's king forward to a better supporting square (positions 2, 4, 7, 8), abandon restraint of a critical passed pawn (positions 5, 10), miss a stronger move order that would give the check tactical bite (positions 1, 3), or simply waste time in positions demanding constructive play (positions 6, 9). In 7/10 positions, only 1 good alternative existed, meaning these were high-precision moments where the seductive but hollow check was the trap. The average cp_loss of 158 reflects how costly a single wasted tempo is in the endgame phase.

1271.label: Advancing a pawn (usually on a flank) when the position demands immediate piece activity, captures, or checks to address a critical tactical priority.
1271.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves (9 advances, 1 capture) played instead of urgent piece-based solutions. In 7/10 cases, the pawn pushed was on the a-file (3) or h-file (4), making rook pawn advances especially over-represented. The best moves in these positions consistently involved piece activity: rook checks or repositioning (positions 1, 2, 5, 7, 9, 10), king captures or movement (positions 8, 9), knight forks (position 5), or queen evacuation (position 4). In 9/10 positions (all endgames), the player faced an opponent's dangerous passed pawn or immediate tactical threat that required direct confrontation, but instead reflexively advanced their own pawn toward promotion. The average cp_loss of 3117 reflects how catastrophic these tempo losses are — 4/10 resulted in forced mate or near-mate evaluations. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precision that the pawn-pushing instinct completely missed.

1265.label: Pushing a pawn to attack a well-placed enemy knight, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability that's worse than leaving the knight alone.
1265.description: 8/10 positions feature a pawn advance specifically aimed at dislodging a powerfully posted enemy knight: g4 chasing Nf5 (positions 1, 6), g4 chasing Nh5 (position 7), g3 chasing Nf4 (position 8), f3 chasing Ne4 (position 2), f6 chasing Ne5 (position 10), c6 chasing Nd5 (position 4), and b6 chasing Nc5 (position 9). In every case, the pawn push creates an exploitable weakness — weakened king shelter, undefended pieces, opened diagonals, or removed pawn guards — that the opponent punishes with immediate tactics. The remaining 2/10 positions involve related knight-mishandling: one retreats a dominant knight from its outpost (Nf6 abandoning e4), and one plays a slow knight development ignoring forced perpetual check (Na3). All 10 share the pattern of choosing a 'natural-looking' way to address a strong knight when sharper tactical solutions were required. The average cp_loss of 1313 reflects how catastrophic these structural concessions are when punished immediately.

1266.label: A well-placed knight moves to the wrong destination when a clearly superior alternative with that same knight existed.
1266.description: In 9/10 positions, the best move was also a knight move—meaning the player identified the correct piece to move but chose the wrong square. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10), the knight could have captured a MORE VALUABLE target (rook on g1/h8/h7, or a strategically critical piece like a bishop) but instead captured a lesser piece or retreated passively. In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 5, 9), the knight made an unsound sacrifice on f2 when a simple retreat (typically Nf6 or Nh6) was correct. In 1/10 cases (position 7), the knight abandoned a dominant central post for a rim square. The consistent thread: an actively-placed knight (on squares like g5, e4, e2, g4, f5, c4) that had one clearly best continuation was instead used for a superficially attractive but inferior purpose—typically choosing the flashy or obvious target over the objectively strongest one.

1269.label: Moving a pawn on the file adjacent to an enemy advanced 'thorn' pawn as a passive reaction, wasting a critical tempo when active play was demanded.
1269.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a pawn one square forward on the file immediately adjacent to an enemy advanced pawn (g3/g6/g5 reacting to h-file or f-file thorn pawns in 8/10 cases; b6 reacting to an advanced c6-pawn in 2/10 cases). The intent was always defensive — to 'address' or 'neutralize' the perceived threat of the enemy advanced pawn by blocking, supporting, or stabilizing the adjacent structure. However, in every case the position demanded immediate active play: tactical shots (Qh5+ in position 9, Qd2+ in position 1), piece activity (Rfb8 in position 3, Qe2 in position 6, Nf4 in position 7), or central breaks (d4 in position 5, cxd5 in position 10). The average cp_loss was 486, with 7/10 positions having only 1-2 good moves available, indicating critical moments requiring precision rather than prophylaxis. In 8/10 cases the blunder weakened the king's pawn shield or created permanent structural holes (a6 square in positions 2 and 8; dark-square weaknesses around the king in positions 3, 5, 6, 7, 10). The enemy thorn pawns were on h6 (positions 3, 5, 7), h3 (positions 4, 9), f6 (positions 6, 10), c6 (positions 2, 8), and f3 (position 1).
1269.old_chip: Passive pawn reacts to thorn pawn

1281.label: Queen checks to a corner square (a1/a8/h1/h8) that waste tempo by driving the opponent's king to safety before a stronger preparatory move is executed.
1281.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen delivering check to one of the four corner squares (a1, a8, h1, or h8). In every case, the check is premature — the opponent's king calmly sidesteps to a square that is actually safer or better-connected than its original position. 10/10 positions had a stronger non-checking move (or a different forcing move) available that either captured/removed a key piece (Positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 10), cut off an escape square first (Position 4), advanced decisive pawns (Positions 7, 8), activated a passive piece (Position 6), or delivered a knight attack creating irrefutable threats (Position 9). In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 6, 10), the queen corner check actually appears in the BEST line too, but only AFTER a preparatory move — making these pure move-order errors. The average cp_loss was enormous (~3935), with 6/10 positions involving losses exceeding 200cp and 4/10 converting forced mates into non-mating positions. Only 1.1 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical-precision moments.

1267.label: Player makes an instinctive 'safe-looking' king move (or premature promotion) instead of the urgent tactical action the position demands, losing critical tempo.
1267.description: 8/10 positions feature literal king moves (5x Kg7, plus Ke5, Ke1, Kh2) while 2/10 feature premature pawn promotions that serve a similar strategic error. In all 10 positions, the player had urgent tactical moves available (captures of hanging/vulnerable pieces, attacks against exposed kings, file contestation) but instead chose a seemingly prophylactic or 'obvious' move. 5/10 positions specifically feature ...Kg7 moving the Black king from g8, where in 4 of those 5 cases the king on g7 became MORE vulnerable by enabling Bxf6+, Qf6, or diagonal/file attacks that weren't possible on g8. 9/10 positions had the correct move being an active piece move (Nxh5, hxg5, Rad8, Ng4, Nxe5, Kd4, Ra7, Kg1, Rf2) rather than a passive repositioning. The average cp_loss of 362 reflects that these tempo losses occur at critical tactical junctures where one move decides the game. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise action rather than general improvements.

1275.label: Bishop moved to a forward, aggressive-looking square where it becomes tactically exploitable — either undefended, capturable with tempo, or abandoning a critical defensive duty.
1275.description: 8/10 positions involve an explicit bishop move (Bxf2+, Bxg2, Bh5, Bh5, Be3, Bg6+, Bg5, Bxf7+), while the remaining 2 (Ne6, f5) share the same conceptual error of an aggressive-looking piece/pawn advance that ignores tactical reality. In 5/10 cases, the bishop lands on a square where it is immediately undefended or insufficiently defended (Bh5 twice, Bg5, Bg6+, Bxf7+), enabling the opponent to win it through captures, removal-of-defender tactics, or sacrificial combinations. In 3/10 cases (Bxf2+, Bg6+, Bxf7+), the move is a speculative sacrifice with check that lacks sufficient follow-up due to underdevelopment or the opponent's simple capture. In 2/10 cases (Bxg2, Be3), the bishop abandons a critical defensive post — blocking a dangerous diagonal or guarding an attacked piece. The average cp_loss of 1235 reflects that these moves are catastrophic, often losing a full piece or enabling mating attacks. All 10 moves share the quality of appearing purposeful and aggressive while actually worsening the position dramatically.

1276.label: Non-forcing moves in time-critical positions where immediate concrete action (pawn advances, forcing checks, or decisive exchanges) was required.
1276.description: All 10/10 positions feature a move that wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate, forcing action. 7/10 are endgame positions where single tempi are decisive. The wasted tempi take several forms: pointless checks where the opponent's king simply steps to a better square (2/10: Qg2+, Rh3+), passive king retreats when aggressive pawn advances were essential (4/10: Kg2, Kb3, Kc8, Kg3), queen/rook retreats from dominant posts (2/10: Qd4 from d7, Qd2), and non-forcing piece moves when the checking version of the same idea was available (1/10: Rc8 instead of Rh8+). In every case, the best move involved concrete forcing action — typically a pawn push (h4, e4, h5, g3 in positions 1/5/6/7), a decisive exchange (Rxf4+ in position 2, Qxf8+ in position 3), or the same idea executed with check (Rh8+ in position 10). The average cp_loss of 2988 reflects that 3/10 positions converted directly to forced checkmate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow positions where the tempo was truly decisive.

1286.label: Moving a knight to g5 or g4 where it hangs to the opponent's queen, attempting a premature f7/f2 attack without the necessary preconditions.
1286.description: 10/10 positions involve a knight jumping to the g-file (g5 or g4) targeting the f7 or f2 pawn, mimicking the Fried Liver Attack pattern. In all 10 cases, the knight lands on a completely undefended square where the opponent's queen can simply capture it for free along an unobstructed diagonal (d8-g5 for Black's queen, or d1-g4 for White's queen). 7/10 are White playing Ng5 in Italian Game positions where Black has played ...Bc5 instead of ...Nf6 — the critical difference being that without a knight on f6, Black's queen has a clear path to g5. 3/10 are Black playing Ng4 where White's queen can reach g4 directly. 9/10 occur in the opening phase with both kings still in the center. The average cp_loss is 412, consistently representing the loss of a full minor piece. In every case, the primary refutation is the trivially simple Qxg5 or Qxg4 capture.

1278.label: King advances to an apparently active square that is immediately exploitable by a forcing move (check, pawn push with tempo, or piece attack) that negates the centralization.
1278.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves (the outlier is b5, a pawn advance with a similar 'overextension' logic). In all cases, the moving side advances their king (or pawn) to what appears to be an active, centralized square, but this square is tactically vulnerable to an immediate tempo-gaining response. In Position 2, Kg5 abandons the f5 blockade allowing Ke5; in Position 4, Ke5 walks onto the a1-h8 diagonal allowing Bg7+; in Position 6, Kg5 exposes the king to Rg6+ winning the bishop; in Position 9, Kd5 allows e4+ with a knight fork; in Position 3, Ke1 allows d2+ forcing the king back; in Position 7, Kc7 allows b6+ or triangulation. The average cp_loss is 134, with the worst cases (Positions 2, 4, 6, 8, 9) all exceeding 160cp. 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these are positions where the king's placement is the critical decision. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 10/10 analyses, confirming the universal thread: the king occupies a square where the opponent gains a free tempo through a forcing response.

1280.label: Pawn advances giving check to an exposed king, usually premature and counterproductive.
1280.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to deliver check against an exposed enemy king. In 8/10 cases this is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss ~2500 for the errors), while only 2/10 are actually the best move. The exposed kings sit on unusual squares (c3, g5, h4, c4, f3, f4, f6, d2, c6, g4, d5) in every case. In 8/10 blundering positions, the pawn check drives the opponent's king to a safer square or permanently weakens the attacker's pawn structure, while superior alternatives involving piece repositioning (especially queen moves) were available. In 5/10 positions, the same pawn check actually appears later in the CORRECT line — after preparatory moves — confirming the error is one of move order rather than concept. The feature captures the classic 'patzer check' impulse: seeing an exposed king and reflexively throwing a pawn at it without verifying the king actually lands on a worse square.

1279.label: Pawn captures that eliminate an opponent's advanced or passed pawn to remove counterplay in a decisively winning endgame.
1279.description: All 10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture removing an opponent's advanced or passed pawn in a position where the capturing side already holds a large advantage (avg eval ~+800 in the capturing side's favor). 9/10 are endgames and 10/10 involve capturing a pawn that has pushed deep into the capturing side's territory (g3, c4, g6, g5, e3, b3, a5, h4, d3). In 8/10 positions the capture is optimal or near-optimal (cp_loss ≤ 14), correctly prioritizing elimination of the opponent's sole counterplay source. However, in 2/10 positions (positions 7 and 10, cp_loss 238 and 9305), the quiet 'cleanup' capture misses a decisive forcing continuation—a discovered attack (Nc5+) and a rook check leading to forced mate (Re7+), respectively. The feature consistently identifies the moment a player chooses to statically remove a threatening pawn rather than calculate whether a more dynamic winning blow exists.

1285.label: In rook endgames, the rook makes a superficially active move (check, centralization, or attack) that fatally abandons its critical duty of blockading or restraining a passed pawn.
1285.description: 10/10 positions are rook endgames featuring dangerous passed pawns as the decisive factor, and all 10 blunders are rook moves that prioritize apparent activity over essential defensive function. In 7/10 positions, the rook was directly blockading or restraining an opponent's passed pawn and the blunder abandons that file or square (Rc7 leaves the a-file in Position 2, Rf7 abandons the c7 blockade in Position 3, Rf6 releases the b-pawn in Position 6, Rf8+ abandons d8 in Position 5, Rc1+ abandons f1 in Position 7, Ra8 chooses a suboptimal file in Position 8). In 3/10 positions, the move gives a pointless or counterproductive check (Rd8+, Rf8+, Rc1+) that actually drives the opponent's king toward a better square or allows a devastating tactical response. In the remaining cases (Re3, Re5, Rh1), the rook centralizes or repositions when a non-rook move (pawn break or king activation) was critically urgent. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions and 'passed_pawn' in 9/10, confirming the consistent mechanism: the rook move wastes a critical tempo during which the passed pawn advances or the opponent's coordination improves irreversibly.

1284.label: A knight (or minor piece) captures a tempting pawn or piece, but the material gain is outweighed by the tactical or positional cost of moving that piece from its current role.
1284.description: 9/10 positions feature knight moves and 9/10 are captures (the exception being Ne3 which attempts a fork). In every case, the player is drawn to grab material that appears free or advantageous. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 10), the knight captures the WRONG target when a much stronger capture on a different square existed (Nxf5 instead of bxc6, Nxg6+ instead of Nxe6+, Nxe5 instead of Nxg5). In 2/10 cases (positions 1, 7), the knight leaves a critical defensive post, exposing a hanging piece or enabling a fork. In 2/10 cases (positions 2, 5), the knight moves into a square where it is simply recaptured for insufficient compensation. In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 8), the knight trades itself for inadequate material (a pawn) when it was more valuable on its current square. In 1/10 cases (position 9, the bishop outlier), the piece grabs a pawn but gets trapped. The average cp_loss of 1196 reflects that these greedy captures frequently squander winning advantages or forced mates.

1290.label: Moving a powerfully centralized knight away from its dominant square — via capture, relocation, or exchange — surrendering its strategic or defensive value.
1290.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight occupying a dominant central square (e4, e5, d4, d5, or c5) that is voluntarily moved away. In 6/10 cases the knight captures a less important piece (Nxd2, Nxc6, Nxf3, Nxc3), trading a powerfully placed piece for a passive one. In 3/10 cases the knight relocates to a peripheral square (Nc6, Na4, Nb5) abandoning its outpost without compensation. In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 7), the knight was performing a critical diagonal-blocking defensive function, and its removal allowed devastating checks or even checkmate (Qxh2#, Bxf2+, Qxg2). In 8/10 positions, a concrete tactical opportunity existed that exploited the knight's current central placement (forks, king attacks, checks), meaning the player traded away the very piece that enabled a winning tactic. The average cp_loss of 1219 (inflated by one mate) reflects how catastrophic it is to voluntarily relinquish a dominant knight.

1283.label: King moves that abandon a blocking function on a rank or file, allowing an enemy rook to traverse the cleared line and capture material (usually the player's own rook).
1283.description: 9/10 positions feature a king that was performing a hidden blocking function on a rank or file, preventing an enemy rook from exploiting that line. In 6/10 positions (2, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10), the king move directly allowed an enemy rook to capture the player's own rook — the king had been the sole obstacle preventing the enemy rook from traversing the rank/file to reach the hanging piece. In positions 1, 5, and 6, the king move similarly abandoned a defensive function, enabling devastating checks or material-winning attacks along the cleared line. Position 3 (cp_loss=1) was actually the engine's top choice and is an outlier. The average cp_loss of the true blunders is very high (~400+), and in 9/10 positions only 1 good move existed, indicating these are razor-thin decision points where the king's hidden defensive role was the entire difference between maintaining the position and catastrophic collapse.

1293.label: G-pawn (or b-pawn) captures an enemy bishop on the h-file (or a-file), opening the critical file directly in front of the castled king and allowing an immediate queen invasion on that square.
1293.description: 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture of an enemy bishop that was provocatively placed adjacent to the king's pawn shield (h3, h6, or a6). In 9/10 cases the g-pawn captures toward the h-file (gxh3 or gxh6), while 1/10 is the analogous queenside pattern (bxa6 with a queenside-castled king). In all 10 positions, the captured bishop appeared 'free' or 'annoying,' tempting the natural instinct to remove it. However, in every single case the opponent's queen immediately recaptures on the same square (Qxh3, Qxh6, or Qxa6+) as the primary refutation, exploiting the newly opened file to create devastating mating threats against the exposed king. The average cp_loss is 335, with 7/10 positions showing the queen invasion as the only truly punishing response (secondary refutations are dramatically weaker). All 10 positions had the king castled on the same side as the opened file, and in all cases alternative moves existed that either ignored the bishop, challenged it with a piece, or kept the pawn shield intact.

1295.label: A bishop sacrifices itself on h3 or h6 to rip open the opponent's castled king's pawn shelter, but the resulting queen attack lacks sufficient supporting pieces to compensate for the material deficit.
1295.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop capturing the h-pawn (h3 for Black, h6 for White) that is protected by the g-pawn, sacrificing a full piece to open the g-file and land the queen on h3/h6 with apparent mating threats. In every case the sacrifice is unsound: the attacker gives up a bishop for a single pawn and a queen incursion that the defender can neutralize. 9/9 positions feature same-side kingside castling, and 9/9 are in the middlegame. The average centipawn loss is 262, confirming these are major blunders. In all cases, 2-3 good positional alternatives existed (piece development, central breaks, or quiet maneuvers) that maintained the existing evaluation. The refutations show consistent themes: defenders consolidate via queen trades (Positions 1, 8), knight blockades sealing the kingside (Positions 4, 5), counter-attacks exploiting the attacker's weakened coordination (Position 3: Bg5 fork), or simple development that denies open lines (Positions 2, 6, 10). The closed or semi-closed center in many positions (5/9) further undermines the sacrifice by preventing the attacker from opening additional lines.

1282.label: The disadvantaged side voluntarily initiates a rook exchange by capturing an opponent's piece, eliminating their last active piece and all remaining counterplay.
1282.description: 6/10 positions clearly show the losing side capturing an opponent's piece with their rook (Rxb6, Rxa3, Rxe6, Rxd3, Rxe4, Rxc1), resulting in a recapture that eliminates the player's only remaining rook and leaves them in a hopeless endgame with no counterplay. In all 6 cases, superior alternatives existed that kept the rook on the board in an active capacity (invading ranks, targeting weaknesses, or maintaining defensive pressure). 2/10 additional positions (both Rd8) feature passive rook placements that similarly squander the rook's potential activity. Position 4 (Rf1) involves a passive rook move that misses a free piece capture, and Position 9 (Ke2+) is a premature check outlier. The evaluations consistently show that the side already losing makes their position measurably worse (avg 167cp loss) by simplifying into positions where their opponent can convert trivially without resistance.

1299.label: Playing a passive rim pawn advance (a- or h-file) when the position demands immediate king action, piece repositioning, or addressing a concrete tactical threat.
1299.description: 10/10 positions feature a flank pawn advance (a-file: 7/10, h-file: 2/10, g-file: 1/10) as the mistake. In 8/10 cases, the pawn push is a clear tempo waste that ignores an urgent positional or tactical requirement: 4/10 positions needed immediate king racing or centralization to blockade/contest a passed pawn (positions 1, 3, 6, 10); 2/10 ignored an immediate tactical crisis requiring piece defense (positions 4, 8); 1/10 self-blocked the king's escape route creating a mating net (position 5); 1/10 missed a critical bishop repositioning to restrain an enemy passed pawn (position 9). Only 2/10 (positions 2 and 7) were actually the engine's best or near-best move in already hopeless positions. The average cp_loss of 2888 is inflated by four positions where the move allowed forced checkmate. 7/10 occurred in endgames where tempo is paramount, and 9/10 involved exposed kings where time-sensitive play was critical.

1296.label: A slow, non-forcing single-square pawn advance in a position that demands immediate concrete action, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
1296.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance that is quiet, non-capturing, and non-checking. 6/10 are on the edge files (a or h), with the remaining 4 on the b, c, or g files. 9/10 analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a core issue. The positions share a critical urgency that the pawn move ignores: in 4/10 cases a tactical shot was available (Be4+ winning a pawn, exf5 winning material, Rxf3 exploiting a hanging pawn, Ba6+ exploiting a diagonal); in 4/10 cases king activity or safety was the paramount concern (king centralization in endgames, king evacuation in middlegames); and in 2/10 cases an immediate forcing move accomplished the same goal without losing tempo (d4 instead of c3, g6-before-h6 move order). The average cp_loss of 244 and average of only 2.2 good moves confirms these are narrow, demanding positions where the wasted tempo proves catastrophic. The moves uniformly represent a player defaulting to 'prophylactic' or 'preparatory' pawn moves when they cannot identify the concrete requirement of the position.

1292.label: Rook moves to aggressively target enemy pawns (often penetrating to the 7th rank) but either lands on a tactically vulnerable square or abandons a more critical duty.
1292.description: All 10 positions feature rook moves to squares that appear active and pawn-targeting. 6/10 moves place the rook on the 7th or 8th rank (Rf7, Rb7, Rb8, Re7, Rd7, Rg6 on the 6th), while the remaining 4 (Ra5, Ra2, Rc2, Rc1) send the rook sideways to attack specific pawns. In 4/10 positions (Rf7, Rg6, Re7, Rd7), the rook lands on a square directly forkable by an enemy knight — the knight simultaneously checks the exposed king and attacks the rook. In 5/10 positions (Rb7, Rb8, Ra5, Ra2, Rc2), the rook abandons a critical duty (restraining a passed pawn, maintaining a mating net, controlling a key file) in favor of pawn-grabbing that proves too slow or irrelevant. The average cp_loss of 1254 is extremely high, and 8/10 positions had only 1 good alternative move, indicating these were critical positions requiring precise play rather than general activity. The correct moves were frequently non-rook moves: king moves (5/10), pawn breaks (1/10), or the same rook to a specifically safe square (3/10).
