1301.label: Black develops a knight to f6 (or e7) as a seemingly natural move while ignoring a pre-existing tactical threat against the vulnerable f7 square, which the knight does not actually defend.
1301.description: In 10/10 positions, Black's king remained on e8 (uncastled) with the f7 pawn under direct or latent attack from a White piece battery — typically a Bishop on c4 combined with a Queen (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 9) or Knight on g5 (positions 4, 7). In all 10 cases, Black played a knight development move (Nf6 in 9/10, Nge7 in 1/10) that appeared natural but completely failed to address the f7 vulnerability. Crucially, a knight on f6 does NOT control the f7 square (it controls d5, d7, e4, e8, g4, g8, h5, h7 — but not f7), yet players seem to instinctively feel that developing toward the kingside provides defensive coverage. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 5, 7), the knight move even appeared to gain tempo by attacking the threatening piece (usually the queen on d5 or h5), but the queen's best response was to capture on f7 rather than retreat. The refutation involved Qxf7# (3/10 positions — immediate checkmate), Nxf7 fork (2/10), Bxf7+ sacrifice (1/10), e5 winning the knight with tempo (2/10), or Ng5/Qb3 intensifying the f7 pressure (2/10). The correct defensive moves across all positions shared the theme of directly addressing f7: blocking the diagonal (e6, d5, d6), defending f7 with the queen (Qe7, Qf6), or preventing the attacking piece's access (h6, f4).

1302.label: An aggressive knight jump (Ng5/Nxe5/Ng4) in the Italian Game opening that leaves the knight undefended and immediately capturable, losing a full piece.
1302.description: 10/10 positions occur in Italian Game (1.e4 e5, Bc4) opening structures with both kings still in the center. In every case, a knight makes a premature aggressive forward leap—6/10 play Ng5 (attempting the Fried Liver f7 attack), 3/10 play Nxe5 (grabbing the e5 pawn expecting a d4 fork), and 1/10 plays Ng4 (attacking f2). The critical shared error is that the knight lands on an undefended square where it can be trivially captured: in the Ng5 cases, Black's queen captures via the open d8-g5 diagonal (no Nf6 blocking it); in the Nxe5 cases, after ...Nxe5 White has no tactical trick to recover the piece (d4 fork fails because Black captures the bishop first or the d-pawn is already advanced); in the Ng4 case, White's queen simply takes. All 10 positions had 3 good quiet developing moves available, and the average cp_loss of 338 corresponds to losing approximately a full minor piece for a pawn or nothing.

1287.label: Directly capturing the most obviously dangerous piece or passed pawn with a rook/bishop, when a more indirect approach would preserve greater advantage.
1287.description: 10/10 positions feature a capture (bishop or rook taking material) aimed at eliminating what appears to be the most threatening target on the board. 7/10 involve rook captures and 3/10 bishop captures. 8/10 positions involve a dangerous passed pawn near promotion (e2, g7, d7, h8/g7, d2, g2, e7) or a tactically critical piece. In the positions with large cp_loss (6/10 with loss >80cp), a preparatory or indirect approach was superior: Position 1 needed deflection before capture, Position 2 needed a different move order (Ne5 before Bxc6), Position 6 captured the wrong target entirely (rook instead of the pawn), Position 7 needed a tempo-gaining move first (Rh8), Position 8 landed on a square vulnerable to recapture with check, and Position 10 grabbed material at the cost of development. In 4/10 positions (cp_loss 0-10), the direct capture was actually correct or forced, suggesting the feature detects the 'capture the obvious threat' decision pattern regardless of whether it's optimal.

1289.label: A knight is repositioned or rerouted when the position demands an immediate forcing move, abandoning critical functions and squandering tempo.
1289.description: All 10/10 positions involve knight moves, making this the defining geometric constant. In 9/10 cases (excluding position 7 which was actually correct at 0 cp_loss), the knight is slowly repositioned—either retreating from an active post or rerouting to a 'better' square—when the position demanded an immediate tactical strike, pawn break, or forcing move. Specifically, 5/10 moves retreat the knight to passive squares (Nf3←g5, Nc3←b5, Nh7←f6 twice, Nh2←f3), while 4/10 jump the knight to seemingly aggressive but tactically flawed squares (Ng5, Nd5, Ne5, Ng6). In 7/10 positions, the best move was NOT a knight move at all but rather a capture (gxh6, Nfxe5/Qxh5), pawn break (d5, exd5), or tempo-gaining piece move (Rd4, c6). The consistent punishment pattern: the opponent exploits the newly unguarded squares (d5 control lost in positions 3 and 9, g7 weakness in position 3, c2 fork in position 5) or gains a critical tempo to reorganize (positions 4 and 10). Average cp_loss of 287 reflects how costly these 'quiet improvement' moves are in positions demanding action.

1298.label: The queen moves away from defending its own vulnerable king, seeking counterplay or centralization, and allows a decisive attack against the exposed monarch.
1298.description: In 9/10 positions, the player's own king was explicitly described as exposed or vulnerable, and the queen was the primary (often sole) piece capable of providing defensive cover. In all 10 positions, the queen move played prioritized offensive goals—counterplay against the opponent's king (Qd2, Qe2), pawn grabbing (Qxf2), centralization (Qd5, Qd4, Qd3), pawn pressure (Qc7, Qb6, Qb5), or illusory activity (Qc4)—over the critical defensive duty of shielding the king. The best moves in 8/10 positions kept the queen on squares directly covering the king's vicinity (Qf7, Qd7, Qe7, Qg4, Qe1, etc.) or delivered immediate checks to gain tempo. The average centipawn loss of 5576 reflects that 7/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate after the queen abandoned its post. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, confirming these were positions demanding precise defensive queen placement where any 'active' alternative was fatal.

1294.label: A piece (usually a knight) moves aggressively forward to a threatening-looking square where it immediately becomes tactically vulnerable—trapped, hanging, or counterproductive.
1294.description: In 7/10 positions, a knight makes the blundering move, while 2/10 involve bishops and 1/10 a rook—but all share the same structural error. The piece leaves a strong or stable position to jump forward to a superficially aggressive square that turns out to be tactically flawed. In 4/10 cases (Nc2, Nc7, Nd6, Na7), the piece abandons a powerful central outpost (d4, d5, b5) for a square where it hangs or gets trapped. In 2/10 cases (Bxa2, Na7), the piece ventures to a corner/edge square where it becomes completely trapped. In 3/10 cases (Ng6, Ng7, Ng5), the piece moves toward the enemy king in what looks like an attack but removes critical defensive coordination or blocks its own king's escape. In 1/10 (Re7+), a rook delivers a flashy check into a square directly controlled by the opponent's queen. The average cp_loss of 2203 reflects how catastrophic these 'aggressive' moves are—8/10 positions were in the middlegame where tactical complications punish overextension most severely.

1291.label: Player moves a piece to an attractive-looking square instead of executing available concrete tactical actions or maintaining an already-optimal placement.
1291.description: In all 10 positions, the player chose to reposition a piece to a seemingly active or improved square while ignoring the concrete demands of the position. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 7, 10, and 6), an immediate capture or forcing move was available that won material or delivered a decisive blow—the player instead moved the piece to a 'pretty' square (Qb7, Qa1, Qc2, Be4, Qe4). In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 9), the player voluntarily abandoned a piece from a dominant or critical post (Rook leaving f7, Knight leaving e5, Knight leaving d5) to reposition it to a less essential square. In 2/10 cases (positions 3, 8), the player moved a piece to an active-looking square that immediately created tactical vulnerabilities (Bc5 walking into Ne6+ fork, Nxf4 allowing exf4 passed pawn). The average cp_loss of 385 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these were critical moments demanding calculation rather than general principles. 9/10 moves were non-capturing repositions; even the exception (Nxf4) was an exchange that prioritized piece trading over the concrete defensive need (f3).

1305.label: Advancing a kingside pawn to chase an attacking queen when the correct move was relocating the exposed king to safety.
1305.description: In 10/10 positions, the player advanced a kingside pawn (g-file in 8/10, f-file in 2/10) with the explicit intent of attacking an enemy queen that was pressuring the exposed king. In every single case, the best move was instead a KING move to a safer square (Kf8, Kg8, Kh6, Kg2, Kh2, Kg1, Kh1, Kg3, Kf2, Ke7). The pawn advances uniformly worsened the position by either: weakening the king's pawn shield and opening lines (5/10), leaving other pieces/pawns undefended when the queen doesn't retreat as expected (4/10), or blocking the king's own escape routes (1/10). The exposed king was on f7 in 5/10 positions (Black in the opening), and on exposed squares like h3, h2, f3, g2 in the remaining 5/10 (mostly White in the middlegame). Average cp_loss was 1293, reflecting catastrophic consequences. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precise play.
1305.old_chip: Pawn chases queen, king needed moving

1288.label: Playing a forward-looking pawn advance or knight jump that wastes a critical tempo, when the position demands addressing a more urgent priority first.
1288.description: 9/10 positions feature a move that appears aggressive or purposeful (advancing a pawn or jumping a knight forward) but critically misorders priorities, losing tempo against the opponent's most urgent threat. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, making it the dominant unifying theme. In 6/10 positions, the best move involved either delivering check (positions 1, 8, 9), directly addressing a passed pawn threat (positions 2, 3), or making a central counter-strike with tempo (position 4). The played moves consistently chose a secondary plan — a flank pawn push (5/10: b4, b5, g5, c5, g6) or a peripheral knight relocation (5/10: Ng6, Ng3+, Nf6+, Nh6+, Na5) — over the position's most critical demand. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these are narrow positions where the 'obvious-looking' active move is precisely wrong. Position 8 (Nh6+, 0 cp loss) represents the rare case where the aggressive knight check IS the correct priority, confirming the feature fires on the move-type pattern rather than the error being guaranteed.

1300.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move to a peripheral square when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1300.description: 9/9 positions share the same fundamental error: the player makes a non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no real threat) while ignoring an urgent tactical demand. 7/9 moves specifically go to the g/h files or b-file edges (Bh7, Kh2, Ng5, Bh6, h4, Nh6, Nh5), with 6/9 landing on h-file squares specifically. The best moves in these positions were overwhelmingly concrete: captures (Rxe6, Qxa1, exd4, Ra8 winning material), sacrifices (Rh5+), or active centralizing moves (Qe4, Nc5, Qd7). The average cp_loss of 1356 is enormous, and the average of only 1.7 good moves available shows these were critical-moment positions where only precise tactical action maintained the evaluation. In every case, the player chose a vague, plan-oriented or 'improving' move—consolidating pawn structure, repositioning a piece, advancing a flank pawn—while the position screamed for immediate execution.

1306.label: Playing a passive bishop or queen repositioning move when the position demands an immediate forcing tactical continuation.
1306.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing piece move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) when the position demanded immediate concrete action. 6/10 moves are bishop relocations (Bh3, Be3, Bd7, Bf6, Bb5, Be3) and 4/10 are queen repositionings (Qc7, Qc7, Qe2, Qd3). In every case, the best move was significantly more forcing: pawn breaks (e6), tactical checks (Qc2+, Qb1+, Qf7#), or aggressive piece centralizations (Ne5). The moves played all look superficially reasonable—developing, centralizing, or 'improving' piece placement—but ignore that the position has reached a critical tactical moment requiring concrete calculation. The avg cp_loss of 3011 reflects that 3/10 positions had forced mates available, and several others had clean tactical wins. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions punished passivity severely.

1308.label: Reflexive pawn captures (especially hxg6/fxg6) that open a rook file directly toward the player's own king, enabling devastating attacks.
1308.description: 8/10 positions feature a pawn capture (hxg6, fxg6, or hxg3) that removes a pawn from the player's own king shelter, ripping open the h-file or f-file directly toward their castled or exposed king. In every case, the opponent immediately exploits the newly opened file with heavy pieces (queen + rook) for a mating attack or decisive material gain. 6/10 are specifically hxg6 by Black opening the h-file, 2/10 are fxg6 opening the f-file, and 1/10 is hxg3 by White opening the h-file. The remaining 2/10 (cxd4, cxd5) are routine central pawn recaptures that release tension when a dynamic alternative existed — sharing the broader theme of reflexive captures that squander the position. In all 8 king-file cases, alternative recaptures existed that kept the critical file closed (e.g., Bxg6, fxg6 instead of hxg6, or Nxg6), and the analyses consistently identify 'keeping the h-file closed' as the unifying principle of the correct alternatives. The average cp_loss of 3939 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate after the file opened.

1304.label: Knights jumping to threatening-looking squares (g4/g5/h4/h5) that prioritize 'building an attack' over immediately decisive or structurally sound moves.
1304.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight leaping to an aggressive square (g4 in 3 cases, g5 in 4 cases, h5 in 1, h4 in 1, b4 in 1) that superficially threatens the opponent's king or targets a piece. In 2/10 positions (1, 8), the knight move missed an immediate checkmate in one (Qxg7# and Qh7#). In 3/10 positions (4, 6, 10), the knight jump was the second move of a known combination (Greek Gift) played in the wrong order — Bxh7+/Bxh2+ needed to come first to decoy the king before the knight lands with effect. In 3/10 positions (7, 9, 10), the knight abandoned a critical defensive function — blocking a diagonal (pos 7), shielding the king (pos 9), or guarding against checks (pos 10). In 2/10 positions (2, 5), the knight landed on an exposed square where it became tactically vulnerable to discovered attacks or dual threats. The average cp_loss of 3094 reflects that these aren't small positional inaccuracies but catastrophic tactical oversights disguised as 'attacking moves.'

1309.label: Moving or capturing with the f-pawn prematurely strips the king of diagonal protection, enabling immediate queen checks or sacrifices that win material.
1309.description: 9/10 positions involve the f-pawn moving (either advancing ...f6 or capturing fxe5), which fatally opens a diagonal leading directly to the king. In 6/10 positions, White plays fxe5 in a King's Gambit structure, removing the f4 pawn that was the sole guardian of the h4-e1 diagonal, allowing the devastating Qh4+ fork sequence that wins the h1 rook. In 3/10 positions, Black plays ...f6 to kick a centralized knight, which removes the f-pawn's control of critical squares (g6 or the e8-h5 diagonal), enabling Qh5+ combinations or Greek gift sacrifices (Bxh7+/Ng6+) that win major material. Only 1/10 (Position 5, b3) deviates from the f-pawn pattern, though it still involves a pawn move that weakens kingside defenses. The punishment across all positions consistently involves a queen check exploiting the newly opened diagonal, with an average cp_loss of 331. In 8/10 positions, the king was still in the center or had minimal pawn cover, making the diagonal exposure immediately lethal.

1310.label: Moving the king to passively support or escort a passed pawn when an active concrete move (piece move, pawn push, or capture) was urgently needed.
1310.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves in endgames with passed pawns, where the player moves their king toward a passed pawn to support its promotion. In every case, the position demanded immediate concrete action instead: in 4/10 cases the correct move was an active rook move (Rb5+, Na4, Rg5, Ra5), in 4/10 cases it was a pawn push (e3, h5, b4), and in 2/10 cases it was a capture (Rxa7, Kxc4). The king moves all share the characteristic of being one tempo too slow — they look natural as 'escorting' or 'supporting' the passer, but the position is a razor-sharp race where that single wasted tempo allows the opponent to equalize or win. 9/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, confirming these are narrow tactical moments where precision matters enormously. The average centipawn loss of 1305 reflects catastrophic consequences from seemingly natural king moves.

1297.label: Playing a non-forcing move when the position demands an immediate decisive queen capture or trade as the only good option.
1297.description: In 9/10 positions, the single best move available was a decisive queen action — specifically a queen capture (Qxf4, Qxe3+, Qxf3, Qxe5+, Qxe4, Qxc3) in 6/10 cases, a queen centralization/relocation in 2/10 (Qe3, Qh4), or a tactic winning the enemy queen in 1/10 (Nf6+ discovered attack). The average number of good moves was only 1.3, meaning these are razor-sharp positions with a single narrow path. Instead of executing the critical queen action, players chose diverse alternatives: pawn pushes (h4, h3, c5, b3 — 4/10), minor piece moves that removed defenders (Nh6, Nxe5 — 2/10), slow development (Be7 — 1/10), or wrong queen moves (Qxc4, Qe7 — 2/10). In 4/10 positions, the played move specifically removed a piece guarding the player's own queen or key piece, causing it to hang. The consistent thread is that a forcing queen capture/trade was the ONLY way to maintain the evaluation, and the player chose a non-forcing alternative.

1314.label: A slow flank pawn advance that completely overlooks an immediate tactical threat to an undefended or attackable piece.
1314.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a quiet, non-capturing pawn advance on a wing file (b, f, g, or h — never a central d or e push) while a piece is hanging or tactically vulnerable to immediate capture. In 8/10 cases the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece' — the player's own piece is directly capturable (bishop on f5 in position 2, bishop on d6 in position 6, rook on c4 in position 7, knight on f3 in position 8, etc.). In 9/10 cases the pawn move has a plausible positional justification — prophylaxis (h3 vs Bg4, g6 vs Nf6+), space gaining (b4, b5), or kingside fortification (g3, f3) — but it fatally ignores a concrete tactical emergency. The average cp_loss of 471 reflects that these are typically full-piece blunders. All moves share the character of being 'one-tempo-too-slow': the position demanded an immediate tactical response (relocating a threatened piece, capturing first, or delivering a check) but the player chose a slow structural move instead.
1314.old_chip: Quiet pawn push ignores hanging piece

1317.label: Bishop captures material greedily while overlooking a more critical tactical consideration — either a stronger continuation, a devastating counter-blow, or the removal of a vital defensive function.
1317.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop making a capture (Bx__) that wins material — often significant material like a queen (2/9), rook (3/9), or well-placed piece (4/9). However, in every case the capture is a mistake because it prioritizes the material grab over something far more important. In 3/9 positions (1, 2, 8), a forced checkmate existed either for the player or against them that was missed. In 3/9 positions (4, 6, 7), the bishop capture left another piece completely hanging, allowing the opponent to recover or exceed the material. In 2/9 positions (7, 9), the correct move order required a preliminary exchange or zwischenzug before the bishop capture. In 1/9 positions (3), the capture destroyed a drawing resource (perpetual check). The average cp_loss of 3374 reflects how catastrophic these materially-tempting captures are. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating narrow positions where the bishop capture was an obvious-looking but critically wrong choice.

1311.label: Knight jumps to an attractive-looking square (central outpost, check, or attack) but abandons a critical defensive function or misses a more precise alternative.
1311.description: All 10/10 positions feature knight moves to aggressively-placed squares that appear strong on the surface. In 6/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 8, 3, 9), the knight was performing a critical defensive function—guarding a key square (e2 in pos 6, d3 in pos 4), protecting a pawn (e6 in pos 8), restricting the enemy king (f6 in pos 1), or being needed for an urgent defensive task—and its departure allowed immediate tactical exploitation. In 2/10 positions (2, 10), the knight check/jump was conceptually right but the wrong specific square or move order was chosen (Nc5+ instead of Nf6+ fork; Nf4+ before the essential Rg8+ preparation). Only 2/10 positions (5, 7) showed 0 cp loss, where the knight move was actually correct. The average cp_loss of 3773 reflects that many of these allowed forced mates. The common thread is prioritizing the knight's cosmetic activity over its concrete role in the position.

1312.label: A non-forcing queen development or repositioning move in the opening that ignores an immediate tactical obligation — whether a hanging piece, a blocked retreat square, or a time-critical forcing sequence.
1312.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move that is non-forcing (no check, no capture, no real threat) played during the opening when the position demands something urgent. In 5/10 positions (all four Qf3 moves plus Qd2), the queen move leaves the player's own piece completely undefended and capturable — specifically a knight on g5 (positions 1-4) or a bishop on b5 (position 5). In 2/10 positions (both Qd7 moves), the queen occupies a square needed by another piece as a retreat, creating a self-blocking crisis when the opponent challenges that piece. In 3/10 positions (Qc7, Qd6, Qc6), the queen move wastes a critical tempo in a position where a forcing move was required to exploit the opponent's vulnerability before they could consolidate. The average cp_loss of 284 reflects that these moves typically lose material (a full piece in positions 1-5) or squander a decisive advantage. The moves are overwhelmingly in the opening (9/10) and split evenly between White (5) and Black (5), suggesting this is a universal pattern of prioritizing queen 'activity' over concrete tactical demands.

1319.label: Voluntary middlegame king move that steps onto a square immediately exploitable by enemy checks, discovered attacks, or mating combinations.
1319.description: All 10/10 positions feature a voluntary king move (no capture, no escape from check) during the middlegame that relocates the king from a relatively sheltered square to a more exposed one where enemy pieces can immediately deliver devastating tactical blows. In 10/10 cases the king moved to a square attacked along an open file, rank, or diagonal by enemy rooks, queens, or bishops already in position. The refutations universally involve immediate checks: 6/10 result in forced checkmate (positions 2,3,5,6,9,10), while 4/10 result in decisive material gain via check-based tactics (positions 1,4,7,8). The best alternatives in all 10 cases were piece moves rather than king moves, averaging only 1.9 good moves available, indicating these positions demanded precise non-king responses. The king consistently moved one square (forward, sideways, or diagonally) from the back rank or a corner toward the center of the board, landing on the second rank (Kg2, Kf2, Kh2, Kc2, Kh7, Kg7, Kf7) where it intersected with pre-existing enemy attacking lines.

1318.label: King moves forward or sideways to an exposed square when retreating to the back rank or corner was the only safe option.
1318.description: 9/10 positions feature king moves that advance or drift toward exposed squares (Ka3, Kh3, Kb6, Kh6, Ka6, Kf3, Kd2) when the correct move was to retreat to the back rank or corner (Kg1, Kb1, Kh1, Kg8, Kc8, Kc6). In 7/10 cases, the specifically correct move was a king retreat to the first/eighth rank (e.g., Kg1 in positions 2, 4, 6, 9; Kb1 in position 1; Kg8 in position 5; Kc8 in position 3). The average cp_loss of ~3958 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate after the king advanced. In all cases, enemy rooks or queens were actively creating threats along files and ranks, and the king walked into their tactical reach rather than finding shelter. Only 1.4 good moves existed on average, confirming these were razor-thin survival positions demanding precise retreat. The one non-king-move outlier (Rh2, position 8) shares the broader pattern of choosing a passive/misguided move over a forcing defensive resource (perpetual check) that would have maintained safety.

1303.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its dominant post when a forcing tactical blow was available from that very position.
1303.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a piece away from a square where it was performing a critical tactical or strategic function, replacing a forcing opportunity with a quiet repositioning move. Most strikingly, 4/10 involve knights abandoning dominant central outposts (c4→e3, f3→d2, f4→g2, c5→a4), and 4/10 involve kings wandering to wrong areas (e8→f7, e3→d3, c4→b5, d3→c2). In 8/10 cases, the correct move was a direct forcing action—a capture, check, or critical threat—that exploited the piece's CURRENT placement (Bh3#, Nxd3+, Rb2+, Nd3, Bxc3, bxc4). The average cp_loss of 2226 and only 1.5 good moves available confirm these are critical-moment failures where the piece's current square was irreplaceable. The moved piece was consistently the exact piece that should have delivered the winning blow or maintained the position's key element.

1321.label: Developing a bishop to pin a knight (typically Bg4/Bg5 pinning Nf3/Nf6 to the queen) in the opening while ignoring a more urgent tactical vulnerability in the position.
1321.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to create a pin on a knight, with 8/10 specifically being Bg4 pinning Nf3 to the queen on d1, plus 2 Bg5 moves pinning Nf6 to d8, and 1 Bb4 pinning Nc3 to the king. All 9 opening-phase positions share the same fundamental error: the player chose a 'natural-looking' developing move that creates a superficial pin instead of addressing a concrete, urgent tactical need. In 3/10 positions the move left a piece hanging (positions 1, 7, 9), in 2/10 it left a piece trapped (positions 2, 9), in 3/10 it left f7 critically undefended enabling sacrifice combinations (positions 5, 6, and partially 4), and in 2/10 it missed a concrete winning tactical blow (positions 8, 10). The pin was easily neutralized in every case — through queen relocation (positions 1, 4, 9), castling (position 8), h3 (positions 2, 8), or simple counterattack (positions 3, 5, 6, 7, 10). Average cp_loss of 291 confirms these are serious blunders, not marginal inaccuracies.

1322.label: Moving the king when the position demanded capturing an undefended enemy piece, typically a queen.
1322.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder. In 8/10 cases, the correct move was a simple capture of a hanging or undefended major piece — specifically, 7/10 required capturing an enemy queen (Qxd8, Qxf8, Qxh1, Qxe6, Qxe6, Qxg4, Qxg3) and 1/10 required capturing a hanging queen with a knight (Nxd4). The remaining 2/10 positions (4 and 5) involved moving the king in the wrong direction into a mating net rather than fleeing correctly. The average number of good moves was only 1.1, meaning these were all critical 'only move' positions. The average centipawn loss was an extraordinary 6390, indicating catastrophic consequences. The consistent behavioral pattern is a player whose king-safety instinct overrides tactical awareness — they reflexively move the king (to escape checks, flee perceived danger, or 'consolidate') while completely overlooking that an enemy piece is simply hanging for capture.

1315.label: Pushing a pawn (or piece) forward for space when a diagonal capture was the correct way to resolve central tension or win material.
1315.description: 9/10 positions share a strikingly specific pattern: the best move was a capture (8 pawn captures like exd5, dxe4, fxe4, exf4, dxe5; plus 1 piece capture Bxe3), but the player instead chose to ADVANCE a pawn forward. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 8, 9, 10), the exact same pawn that should have captured diagonally instead pushed straight ahead (e.g., e-pawn should play exd5 but plays e5 instead). In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 7, 4), a different pawn advanced while the correct capture was available elsewhere. Position 5 (Nc6) is the only partial outlier, though it still follows the broader theme of an aggressive-looking developing move chosen over a more precise action. All 10 positions occur in the opening (9) or early middlegame (1), all feature existing central tension with mutual pawn confrontation, and the average cp_loss of 282 reflects that these advances consistently squander significant advantages or turn equal positions into lost ones.

1324.label: Aggressive-looking queen repositioning moves that abandon critical defensive duties or land on exposed squares where the queen is immediately harassed.
1324.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that appear active or threatening but are strategically misguided. In 6/10 positions the queen specifically moves to the b4/b5 area (Qb4 x4, Qb4+, Qb5+), while the remaining 4 involve other premature queen centralizations (Qe6, Qh2, Qg4, Qe4, Qd7). The dominant punishment mechanism is tempo loss: 8/10 positions are tagged with tempo_loss as the primary tactical motif, where the opponent gains time by attacking the misplaced queen (via moves like a3, c3, Bd2, Nb5). In 5/10 cases, the queen specifically abandons defense of a key piece or pawn (e5 pawn in Position 1, a7 pawn in Position 5, b2/a1 in Position 9, d4 pawn in Position 8, pin vulnerability in Position 10). The phase skews heavily toward the opening (6/10) with 4 middlegame positions, and 7/10 are Black moves. The average cp_loss of 226 reflects that these moves typically squander significant advantages or convert manageable positions into losing ones. In 6/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating these errors often occur in positions demanding precision.

1313.label: Queen moves (captures or checks) that place it on an undefended square where it is immediately captured or fatally attacked by the opponent.
1313.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves, and in 8/10 the queen is directly captured in the refutation line (Qxg2 in pos 1, Qxf4+ in pos 4, Qxf6 in pos 5, Rd7 winning it in pos 6, Qxa7 forced trade in pos 7, Rd6 winning it in pos 8, Qxc4 in pos 9, Qxd5+ in pos 10). In 6/10 cases, the opponent's queen is the piece that captures the blundered queen. The triggering moves are typically 'attractive' — 5/10 are pawn captures (Qxg2, Qxa2, Qxf4+, Qxc4, Qxd5+) and 5/10 deliver or attempt check (Qd8+, Qxf4+, Qf6+, Qa8+, Qxd5+). The common thread is that the queen moves to a square lacking protection, lured by immediate material gain or the allure of giving check, while the player overlooks that the opponent can capture the queen back — often via a diagonal the player didn't scan (positions 1, 5), a recapture with check (positions 4, 10), a fork/double attack (positions 6, 8), or a self-block preventing friendly recapture (position 9). Average cp_loss of 6215 confirms these are queen-loss-scale catastrophes.

1327.label: Passively retreating a bishop to its starting square (c8/c1/f1/g8) instead of executing an immediately available forcing move.
1327.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop retreating to the back rank, with 9/10 going specifically to the piece's original starting square (c8 for Black's queenside bishop, c1 for White's queenside bishop, f1 for White's kingside bishop). In every single case, the position demanded immediate concrete action — a capture (Rxe5, Qxe4, Rxc2, Rxf5), a pawn break (f5, exf5, dxe5), or a check (Rf1+) — yet the player chose a slow repositioning move instead. The average cp_loss of 1198 reflects catastrophic consequences, and only 1.4 good moves were available on average, confirming these are critical-moment positions where only forcing play works. 10/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. In 7/10 cases the bishop had been on a fianchetto or developed square and was being 'rerouted,' often to a diagonal the player could have exploited immediately with the correct sequence (e.g., Position 5 where Bf1 appears as move 32 in the best line — after first capturing). The blunders consistently arise in the middlegame (9/10) when tactical urgency peaks.

1332.label: Pushing the f-pawn to challenge a centralized enemy knight while the king remains uncastled, fatally opening the diagonal to the king.
1332.description: All 10/10 positions feature an f-pawn advance (f2→f3/f4 for White or f7→f6 for Black) played in the opening while the moving side's king remains uncastled in the center. In 10/10 cases, the move's intent was to challenge or dislodge a powerful enemy knight centralized on e4 (for White's f3) or e5 (for Black's f6). The devastating consequence is identical across all positions: the f-pawn's departure opens the critical diagonal to the king (e1-h4 for White, e8-h5 for Black). In 9/10 positions, the primary refutation is an immediate queen check on that diagonal (Qh4+ or Qh5+), followed by a forced g-pawn block, then a knight sacrifice capturing the g-pawn (Nxg3 or Nxg6) that demolishes the king's last remaining shelter. In 8/10 cases this leads to winning the rook or creating an overwhelming attack. Position 7 is the slight variant where the exploitation comes via Nh4-Ng6 invasion rather than immediate queen check, but the same f-pawn weakness enables it. The average centipawn loss is 372, reflecting how catastrophic this pattern is.

1325.label: A queen or rook voluntarily leaves a powerful, functionally critical square for an apparently active but inferior destination, surrendering the position's key strategic asset.
1325.description: All 10/10 positions feature a major piece (7/10 queens, 3/10 rooks) that was performing a vital strategic function on its current square — guarding a piece (Position 9: Qa8 defending Bc6), preventing a pawn break (Position 4: Qb5 stopping ...b5), controlling a promotion square (Position 6: Qg7 covering h8), paralyzing enemy pieces (Position 2: Qc7 preventing ...f5), maintaining infiltration pressure (Positions 3, 7, 8: pieces on d2, h1, b2), or sustaining initiative (Positions 1, 5). In each case, the player relocates this optimally-placed piece to a square that appears active or aggressive but actually abandons the critical function. The punishment consistently exploits exactly what the piece was preventing: the opponent captures a now-undefended piece (Position 9, -641cp), executes the previously-impossible pawn break (Positions 2, 4), captures the previously-guarded passed pawn (Position 6), develops with tempo against the newly vulnerable piece (Position 7), forces a winning simplification (Position 8), or escapes to safety (Position 1). The average cp_loss of 314 reflects that these aren't quiet inaccuracies but position-destroying errors where the piece's original function was the foundation of the entire advantage.

1307.label: A pawn capture or advance that removes a crucial protective link, leaving another piece hanging or opening a fatal line against the player's own position.
1307.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (7/10 are pawn captures specifically), and in 8/10 cases the moved pawn was performing a vital but non-obvious defensive function — either directly guarding another piece, blocking a dangerous diagonal, or maintaining a tactical threat that indirectly protected something else. In 6/10 positions, the immediate consequence is a hanging piece (Positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 10 clearly, Position 9 via opened diagonal). The moves universally appear 'active' — capturing material (fxe4, dxc3, exf6, fxe5), gaining space (e5, c4, e6), or centralizing (Nd4) — but each destroys a defensive interdependency the player failed to recognize. 7/10 occur in the opening phase where pawn structure decisions are most consequential. The average cp_loss of 245 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic structural oversights. Position 8 (exf6 breaking the e5-pawn's indirect protection of Bc4) and Position 6 (e5 removing e6's guard of d5) are the most archetypal examples of the pattern.

1326.label: Quiet bishop repositioning moves that prioritize piece 'improvement' while catastrophically ignoring an immediate tactical crisis in the position.
1326.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves (Bd7, Bb7, Bg4, Be5, Be3, Be5, Bd7, Bf6) and the remaining 2/10 are quiet pawn pushes (f4, b6) — all sharing the character of 'positional improvement' moves that ignore urgent tactical demands. In 6/10 cases, the move directly abandons or undermines a critical defensive function: removing a blockading piece (Position 1: Bd7 leaves e8), removing a file-blocking piece (Position 7: Be3 opens g-file), self-blocking an escape square (Position 9: Bd7 blocks d7), or placing a piece where it fails to actually prevent what it appears to guard (Position 10: Bf6 doesn't stop g7 advance). In 4/10 cases, the move ignores a lethal king-safety crisis to make a developing/advancing move (Positions 2, 5, 6, and 3). The average cp_loss of 5641 is extreme, with 7/10 positions resulting in forced mate or near-mate. Only 1.8 good moves existed on average, meaning these positions demanded precise defensive awareness rather than generic piece improvement.

1323.label: Captures (usually pawn captures) where the opponent's knight immediately occupies the capture square with devastating tactical force.
1323.description: In 9/10 positions, the blunder follows an identical geometric pattern: the player captures on square X (e.g., dxe5, cxd5, fxe5, bxc4, hxg6, Nxc5), and the primary refutation is the opponent's knight jumping to that EXACT same square X (Nxe5, Nxd5, Nxc4, Nxg6+, Nxc5). The knight landing is never merely a recapture—it arrives with tactical venom: gaining tempo against a queen (positions 1, 4, 7), forking king and rook (position 9), attacking an undefended bishop (positions 5, 8, 10), or threatening a critical pawn/square that leads to material gain (positions 3, 6). Only 1/10 (position 2, exd4→Qc8+) deviates from the knight pattern, instead allowing a queen invasion along a newly opened file. The average cp_loss of 258 reflects that these knight landings typically win material outright. In 8/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating the positions demanded precise calculation before capturing.

1328.label: A rook is moved or captures in a seemingly active way on a central file, but the position demanded a concrete tactical blow with a different piece.
1328.description: All 10 positions feature a rook move that appears actively placed—centralizing, advancing on the e-file, or capturing a pawn—but actually wastes a critical tempo when the position demanded immediate tactical action. In 7/10 positions, the rook move was on or toward the e-file (Re5, Re5, Rxe5, Re6, Re7, Re3, Rxe4). In 6/10 positions, the primary tactical motif was tempo_loss, where a specific forcing move with a minor piece (Nxd5, Nxg6, Ng4, Bxd5, d5) would have exploited a concrete vulnerability. In 3/10 positions, the rook was placed on a square where it hung to an opponent's piece (bishop on long diagonal, knight recapture). The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are narrow tactical positions where timing is paramount. In 9/10 cases, the best move involved a knight strike, bishop capture, or pawn break rather than a rook maneuver, yet the player chose the 'natural-looking' rook move instead.

1320.label: A piece performing a critical defensive or coordinating role is moved away (usually for a tempting capture, attack, or check), leaving another piece or square fatally unprotected.
1320.description: In 8/10 positions, the moved piece was the linchpin holding the position together — it was defending another piece, guarding a critical square, or maintaining a positional bind. The player moved this piece for a tempting reason (material capture in 5/10: Qxe2, Bxa3, Bxf1, Nxh7, Rxg5; aggressive repositioning in 3/10: Qg4×2, Ng6; a check in 1/10: Qb2+). In nearly every case (avg 1.2 good moves available), there was essentially only ONE correct move, meaning the position demanded the key piece stay put or be redeployed precisely. The catastrophic consequence was always the same: something critical was left undefended — a bishop hangs (Position 1: Ng6 abandons defense of Bd4), back rank collapses (Position 4: Bxa3 removes back-rank guardian), a queen hangs (Position 10: Nxh7 removes indirect queen defender), a discovered attack becomes possible (Position 2: Qxe2 places queen where fxe2+ discovers), or a key square is vacated allowing infiltration (Positions 5,8: Qg4 abandons defense of e3/f7). Position 3 (0cp loss) appears to be a false positive where the exchange is forced rather than a true blunder.

1316.label: An aggressive-looking major piece move (usually a rook) that prioritizes attacking or activating while leaving one's own piece undefended and capturable.
1316.description: In 7/10 positions, the player made an active rook or queen move while leaving their own piece hanging or inadequately defended. Specifically: in positions 1 and 4, a rook attacked an enemy bishop while the player's own bishop was en prise; in positions 6 and 10, a rook/queen move left the player's queen or bishop undefended for the opponent to capture; in positions 5 and 8, the rook was placed on a square where it itself became tactically vulnerable (fork or direct capture). The remaining 3 positions (2, 7, 9) show a softer version where the 'active' move abandoned a critical defensive function or gave tempo for the opponent to simplify. 8/10 moves were rook moves to attractive-looking squares (open files, 7th rank, attacking enemy pieces). In all 10 positions, the correct move addressed the vulnerability first—typically relocating the threatened piece (6/10 best moves involved saving/exchanging the vulnerable piece before doing anything else). The average cp_loss of 252 reflects that these moves frequently cost a full piece or exchange.

1333.label: Materialistic captures that grab a pawn or piece while ignoring a more urgent tactical, attacking, or defensive priority.
1333.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture that wins visible material (a pawn or piece) but misses something far more important. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 8), the player grabbed material instead of delivering or continuing a forced mating attack. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 6), the capture removed a critically-placed piece from a dominant post or defensive duty, leaving the king exposed to infiltration. In 3/10 cases (positions 7, 9, 10), the pawn grab ignored the player's own king safety or allowed a tactical counter-shot exploiting exposed pieces. In 1/10 (position 2), the capture was a speculative piece sacrifice with no real follow-up. The average cp_loss of 3149 is extreme, and 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating these were razor-sharp positions demanding precision — yet the player consistently reached for the materialistic option. The common thread is that each capture appears tempting ('free material') but either surrenders tempo, abandons piece coordination, or ignores a more forcing continuation.

1335.label: A pawn captures a seemingly free enemy piece (almost always a bishop) while ignoring a more critical tactical threat or fatally weakening the pawn structure.
1335.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture of an enemy piece, with 9/10 specifically capturing a bishop. In every case, the capture appears materialistic and natural—the enemy piece looks free or en prise—but the pawn capture is wrong because it either removes a critical defensive pawn (5/10 positions: gxh3, fxg5, gxh5, gxf5, hxg4 all damage king shelter or central structure), ignores a more urgent tactical threat that should be addressed first (7/10: positions 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 all had a better capture or defensive priority), or removes a sentry pawn guarding against forks/invasions (positions 5, 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 1298 reflects how catastrophic these captures are—the 'free' material is actually bait or a distraction from the real problem in the position. King safety is the primary exploitation theme in 8/10 positions.

1330.label: Bishop moved to a square where it becomes tactically exploitable (hanging, trapped, pinned, or self-blocking) when safer, more active bishop moves were available.
1330.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a square that creates an immediate tactical liability. In 9/10 cases, the best alternative moves were ALSO bishop moves to different squares, confirming the error is specifically about choosing the wrong destination. The vulnerabilities created break down as follows: 3/10 placed the bishop where it hangs directly to an opponent's piece on an open file (Positions 4, 8 to rook/queen on d-file; Position 1 enables exchange loss via self-block). 4/10 stranded the bishop on a rim or corner square (h3, h3, g1, a3) where it became disconnected, trapped, or dominated by the opponent's pieces (Positions 5, 6, 7, 10). 1/10 placed the bishop on an open file creating a devastating pin (Position 9, Be2 on the e-file). 2/10 involved tempo-wasting repositions that ignored urgent tactical needs (Positions 2, 3). The average cp_loss of 355 confirms these are severe errors. The consistent thread is a bishop being actively moved FROM a useful position TO a square that creates a concrete exploitable weakness.

1334.label: A pawn capture that grabs material but misses a more forcing tactical blow that should be executed first (or instead).
1334.description: All 9/9 positions feature a pawn capture (fxe5, cxd4, dxe5, gxf3, bxc5, fxg5, gxh5) that wins or takes a piece/pawn but squanders a significantly stronger continuation. In 5/9 cases the error is specifically a move-order mistake where the pawn capture could be played LATER but playing it FIRST gives the opponent a critical tempo to address a bigger problem (Positions 3, 4, 6, 7, 8 — e.g., capturing a knight before exploiting a hanging rook or delivering check). In 3/9 cases the pawn capture creates a structural weakness that allows immediate tactical punishment — removing a defensive pawn from the chain and exposing pieces to forks or checks (Positions 1, 9, 10). In 1/9 cases the pawn capture simply misses a free queen capture on an open diagonal (Position 2). The average cp_loss of 418 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but major blunders where the 'obvious' material grab blinds the player to the most forcing move in the position. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments.

1329.label: A piece moves to an apparently attractive square but abandons a critical defensive duty, leaving another piece or square fatally undefended.
1329.description: In 10/10 positions, the blundering move involves voluntarily relocating a piece that was providing essential defensive coverage — either guarding another piece, blocking an enemy attack path, or controlling a critical square. In 4/10 cases (Rf4, Rxb4, Re8, Nc4), the moved piece was the sole defender of another piece or square, and its departure immediately left something hanging (d1 rook, a2 bishop, g8 escape square, e4 pawn). In 4/10 cases (c5, Rd6, Kf4, Ke5), the piece abandoned a positional duty — blockading a passed pawn, covering a critical rank, or staying near the relevant theater. In 2/10 cases (g5, Qxd6), the move placed the player's own piece into a tactical vulnerability (trapped queen, fork square). The average cp_loss of 4023 is extremely high, with 4/10 resulting in forced mate, confirming that the defensive function being abandoned was truly critical. The moved pieces were diverse (3 rooks, 3 kings, 1 knight, 1 queen, 2 pawns), but all shared the characteristic of appearing active or purposeful while fatally neglecting defense.

1337.label: A tempting pawn capture (usually on a wing file) that wastes a critical tempo while ignoring an urgent tactical threat elsewhere on the board.
1337.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures that are non-forcing (no check, no unavoidable threat created). 6/10 are specifically h-pawn captures onto the g-file (hxg2, hxg6, hxg7), while the remaining 4 are flank pawn captures on the a/b/c files or a central release (bxc2, cxb7, axb3, exd5). In every case, the player prioritized grabbing material or advancing a passed pawn over addressing a critical tactical obligation: 4/10 ignored hanging pieces or back-rank mates, 3/10 ignored the need to castle or cover a critical defensive square, 2/10 ignored a stronger forcing continuation of their own (c7+ instead of cxb7, Qe3+ before bxc2), and 1/10 released critical central tension prematurely. The average centipawn loss is an extraordinary 4311, and the average number of good moves was only 1.2, confirming these are razor-sharp positions where the 'obvious' capture is a catastrophic trap. 9/10 positions were middlegames, and the pattern consistently involves positions where one side has latent back-rank, fork, or mating threats that require just one tempo to execute.

1341.label: Knight repositions to a peripheral or distant square in the endgame, ignoring the position's most urgent demand (advancing passed pawns or mating threats).
1341.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where a knight is moved to a square that appears active but is strategically disconnected from the critical action. In 7/10 cases, the urgent threat involves unstoppable passed pawns that the knight cannot address from its new square (positions 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 with advancing passers; position 2 with the knight getting trapped on the rim). In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 7), the knight move ignores an immediate king safety crisis or mating net. The landing squares are consistently peripheral or far from the key theater: Nd7 (×2), Nf7 (×3), Nb3, Nc2 (×2), Nh2, Nh6 — with 4/10 landing on actual rim squares and most others landing on squares disconnected from defensive duties. In 8/10 positions, the best alternative involved either giving check with the knight, capturing a critical piece, evacuating the king, or advancing a counter-pawn — all immediate, forcing actions that the played knight move fails to substitute for. The average cp_loss of 2006 (inflated by two mate-in-one blunders) reflects how catastrophic these tempo losses are in urgent endgames.

1339.label: Aggressive-looking piece moves that send a piece into enemy territory or to a corner where it becomes trapped, captured, or fatally misplaced, when quiet positional moves were correct.
1339.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose an aggressive or forcing-looking move — often a check, attack, or deep infiltration — that actually worsened their piece's placement rather than improving it. In 6/10 positions (1, 4, 7, 9, 10, and arguably 6), the moved piece became trapped or severely restricted after the opponent's response. In 2/10 positions (3, 8), the piece was placed on an undefended square and immediately captured. In 1/10 (position 2), the piece moved to a square creating a fork target. In 9/10 cases, the moved piece itself was directly punished for its destination square. The correct moves in all 10 positions were quiet, constructive improvements (b4, g6, Qxa6, c4, dxc3+, Nd8, Qf2, Bxg7, h5, Bxd6) rather than flashy or forcing moves. The average cp_loss of 2198 reflects how catastrophically these overextensions backfire. Checks specifically feature in 3/10 moves (Qa1+, Nc7+, Qh1+) where the 'free' check actually leaves the piece stranded, and queen moves to corners appear in 3/10 positions (Qa1+, Qh1, Qh1+) with subsequent trapping.

1338.label: In rook endgames, the rook targets a specific pawn with a slow, non-forcing move instead of prioritizing checks, piece activity, or addressing passed pawn threats.
1338.description: All 10/10 positions are rook endgames where the player makes a pawn-oriented rook move that loses critical tempo. In 9/10 cases, the rook moves specifically to attack or blockade a pawn (Rb5→b7, Rd5→b5, Ra4→c4, Rg6→g5, Rh2→h-pawn, Rb7→b6, Ra1→b-pawn, Rh7→h5, Ra3→a5), while 1/10 is a pointless check that displaces the rook from an active post. The better alternatives consistently fall into three categories: immediate checks that gain tempo (positions 6, 8, 10 where Rh4+, Ra3+, Rd4+ were best), maximizing rook activity on optimal ranks/files (positions 1, 3, 4, 7, 9), or king activation (positions 2, 5). The average cp_loss of 2977 is extreme, with 4/10 positions resulting in forced mate, demonstrating how devastating a single tempo loss can be in rook endgames with passed pawns. Tags of 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' appear in 10/10 and 9/10 positions respectively, confirming the pattern's consistency.

1336.label: A pawn advance that removes the pawn's critical defensive coverage of an adjacent square or piece, enabling immediate tactical exploitation in an already-losing position.
1336.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances in already-losing positions (avg starting eval ~+900cp for the stronger side). In at least 7/10 cases, the pawn was specifically guarding a critical adjacent square or piece, and advancing it immediately allowed enemy invasion or capture: h5 left g5 undefended (Position 1, Rxg5+), e5 left d6 undefended (Position 2, Rxd6), b4 left a6 unguarded (Position 3, Qa6 invasion), f6 enabled Nxe5+ sacrifice (Position 4), f5 opened e5/f6 for the knight (Position 5), g6 vacated g7 allowing Ng7+ (Position 8), f4 created an isolated target (Position 9). In the remaining 3/10 positions (c3, c4, a4), the pawn advance was an irrelevant tempo-wasting push that ignored immediate threats (mate-in-1 in Position 7, mating attacks in Positions 6 and 10). The average cp_loss of 5418 confirms these are catastrophic errors, with 6/10 converting survivable positions into forced checkmate.

1340.label: Quiet rook moves to seemingly active squares that abandon critical functions and fail to create concrete threats, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan.
1340.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a quiet rook move (no check, no capture, no forcing threat) that repositions the rook to a square that appears active but serves no concrete purpose. In 8/10 positions, the rook abandons a key file, rank, or defensive duty it was previously performing (d-file control in positions 1/4/5, 7th rank defense in position 8, king defense in positions 2/6/7, blockade support in position 3). The best moves across all positions consistently involve either king activation (6/10: positions 2,3,5,6,7,10), pawn breaks (4/10: positions 4,8,9,10), activating a DIFFERENT piece (3/10: positions 4,9,3), or rook moves that DO gain tempo via checks or true 7th-rank invasions (positions 5,10). The critical distinction is that the best rook alternatives always create immediate forcing threats (Rd7 invading the 7th in position 5, Rd8+ with check in position 10), while the blundering moves are 'improving' repositions that give the opponent a free move. In 9/10 cases, the opponent's refutation involves exploiting the newly unguarded square/file/rank that the rook vacated or attacking the rook on its new unprotected square.

1331.label: Playing a tempting forcing move (usually a queen check or capture) that places the piece on a tactically vulnerable square or abandons a critical defensive function in a winning position.
1331.description: 8/10 positions feature queen moves, and 5/10 are specifically queen checks that fail. In 6/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8), the moved piece lands on a square where it is directly captured by the opponent—by a rook (positions 3, 4), knight (position 5), opposing queen (positions 4, 8), or the king captures an unprotected piece the queen abandoned (position 7). All 10 positions feature a player with a winning or decisively winning position (5 had forced mate) who squanders the advantage with a move that appears aggressive but has a concrete tactical flaw. The average good moves available was only 1.9, indicating these are precision positions where the 'obvious' forcing move is wrong. The common psychological trigger is the irresistible allure of checks and captures overriding careful calculation of whether the target square is actually safe.

1348.label: King moves away from the critical sector of the board in an endgame, losing decisive tempo.
1348.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves in endgames where the king travels in the wrong direction—away from the sector where the decisive battle is occurring. In 7/10 cases, the king moved toward the kingside when the queenside held the critical passed pawns or breakthrough potential (positions 1, 2, 5, 8, 10), or toward the queenside when the center/kingside was critical (positions 6, 7). In 3/10 cases the king retreated or moved sideways when advancing was required (positions 3, 4, 9). The best moves in every position directed the king toward the critical theater: toward queenside pawn majorities, toward centralization to contest opponent's king, or forward to support passed pawns. The average cp_loss of 221 reflects how devastating even a single-tempo directional error is in endgames, with the worst case (position 8) swinging 792cp by moving Kg6 instead of Ke5. Tags 'tempo_loss' appeared in all 10 analyses and 'king_activity' in 8/10, confirming the consistent pattern.

1349.label: An unsupported flank pawn advance (g4/b5/h5) while the king remains uncastled and development is incomplete, leaving the pawn en prise or creating immediate structural weaknesses.
1349.description: All 10/10 positions feature a flank pawn advance (g-pawn in 6/10, b-pawn in 2/10, h-pawn in 2/10) that pushes forward without adequate piece support. In 9/10 positions, the moving side's king is still in the center (uncastled), making the structural damage self-inflicted and irreversible. In at least 8/10 positions, the advanced pawn can be immediately captured for free — by a bishop (Bxg4 or Bxb5) in most cases, or by a knight (Nxg4). The phase is overwhelmingly the opening (8/10), when development should be the priority. The average centipawn loss is 251, and on average only 2.1 good moves existed, indicating these are critical moments where the player chose aggression over completing development. The best moves in every case involved castling, developing a minor piece, or making a prophylactic/preparatory move — never a speculative pawn advance. The refutations consistently involve simply capturing the hanging pawn (often with tempo) and exploiting the exposed king that can no longer hide behind intact pawns.

1346.label: A non-forcing pawn advance played in a position that demanded immediate concrete action (piece invasion, tactical strike, or king activation).
1346.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance chosen over a much more forcing alternative. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a piece action (Nxe6, Qxe3+, Rd3, Rxb2, Kc3, Kf7, d5 as a two-square strike vs. the one-square d6). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 7/10. The average cp_loss of 185 with only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are sharp positions where a concrete, forcing move was uniquely strong. The pawn advances share the quality of being positionally motivated (gaining space, creating passed pawns, fixing structures) but strategically catastrophic because they surrender the initiative at a critical moment. In endgame cases (3/10), the pawn push replaced essential king centralization. In middlegame/opening cases (7/10), it replaced a winning tactical sequence or a sharper pawn strike. The refutations consistently show the opponent consolidating during the gifted tempo or exploiting structural weaknesses the advance created.

1343.label: A quiet pawn advance (or piece move) that places material on a square where an enemy knight can immediately capture it, usually with check or winning significant material.
1343.description: In 9/10 positions, the blunder is a pawn advance; in 7/10 positions, the direct refutation involves a knight capturing the moved pawn or a newly-undefended piece (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10). In 5/10 cases (h3→Nxh3+, c6→Nxc6+, d6→Nxd6+, f3→Nxf3+, Nc3→Nxc3+), the knight captures the exact piece/pawn that just moved WITH CHECK, making the punishment immediately forcing. In 2 additional cases (g6→Nxg6 winning exchange, b5→Nxe6 winning exchange), the knight exploits a square left undefended by the pawn advance. The remaining positions (5, 6, 9) share the broader pattern of a passive/prophylactic move when only one forcing response existed—with position 5's f3 fatally weakening king escape routes, position 6's f3 being passive when f4 was required, and position 9's d5 removing pawn support from a piece while missing mate in 2. All 10 positions had only 1-3 good moves available (avg 1.3), indicating critical moments where precision was mandatory but the player chose a slow, seemingly prophylactic move instead.

1353.label: Queen captures a pawn on a square where the opponent's queen immediately recaptures, resulting in a catastrophic queen trade or outright queen loss.
1353.description: In 10/10 positions, the player's queen captures a pawn (Qx__), and the refutation is the opponent's queen recapturing on that exact same square (opponent plays Qx__ on the same square). The resulting queen exchange or queen loss is devastating. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 7, 9), the queen is literally hanging after the capture — the opponent's queen takes it along an open rank, file, or diagonal the player failed to see, sometimes with check. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 10), the queen trade is technically 'voluntary' but strategically catastrophic because the player's entire advantage depended on queen activity (attacking an exposed king, supporting passed pawns, or maintaining dynamic tension). The average cp_loss of 774 reflects that these are often full-queen-equivalent blunders. All 10 moves capture pawns on peripheral or semi-peripheral squares (a3, a6, b4, b7, c3, c5, d3, d4, g5), drawing the queen away from its critical central/attacking role.

1342.label: Rook moves to a suboptimal square in passed pawn endgames, choosing peripheral targets over strategically critical placement.
1342.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves, with 8/10 occurring in endgames and 10/10 involving passed pawns as the central strategic element. In the significant errors (positions 1, 2, 7, 8, 10 with cp_loss > 50), the rook consistently selects a square targeting a secondary objective — attacking a peripheral pawn (Ra2 targeting a5, Rh7 targeting h6), giving a purposeless check (Ra8+), or choosing a passive defensive post (Rg5 guarding g2) — instead of the strategically critical placement that would support passed pawn advancement or cut off the opposing king. The correct moves in these positions consistently place the rook on more central/active squares: Rc2 over Ra2, Rbb2 over Rd2, Rd5 over Ra8+, Rf7 over Rh7, Re5 over Rg5. Even the 0-cp-loss positions (3, 4, 5, 6, 9) share this profile: the rook moves along a rank or file to a plausible-but-not-optimal square in a passed pawn scenario. The feature appears to detect rook lateral placement decisions in time-critical pawn race endgames.
1342.old_chip: Rook to wrong square in pawn race

1355.label: A pawn capture opens a file or rank that was shielding the player's own queen (or major piece) from immediate capture by an enemy piece.
1355.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture (in axb notation format) that removes a pawn from a critical file or rank where it was acting as a screen/blocker between an enemy piece and the player's own undefended major piece. In 9/10 positions, the exposed piece is the player's own queen; in 1/10 it is a rook. In 8/10 cases the opened line is a file (d-file: 3x, c-file: 3x, e-file: 2x, f-file: 1x), while 2/10 involve a rank being cleared (5th rank, 6th rank). The refutation in every case is immediate capture of the newly-exposed piece along the cleared line — typically Qxc7, Rxe7, Qxd2, Rxf6+, Rxc5, Qxe6, Rxd6, or Qxc2. The player's intent was always a seemingly natural pawn exchange (winning material, eliminating a strong piece, or opening lines), but they failed to recognize the pawn's critical defensive function as a physical barrier. In all 10 cases, the best alternatives involved either moving the vulnerable piece off the line first, capturing with a different piece/pawn, or creating an intermediate forcing move before opening the critical line.

1351.label: Moving a bishop or knight to an active-looking but undefended square where it is immediately capturable by the opponent.
1351.description: In 10/10 positions, a minor piece (5 bishops, 5 knights) is moved to a seemingly strong central or active square without adequate protection. In 8/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9), the moved piece itself is immediately captured by the opponent — by knights with check (Nxd6+), bishops along diagonals (Bxe6, Bxe6), rooks on open files (Rxg3, Rxe4, Rxa5), or knight captures opening tactical sequences (Nxe4). In the remaining 2/10 (positions 7, 10), the piece's departure from its previous square leaves another piece or pawn undefended, allowing the opponent to win material elsewhere. The average cp_loss of 1159 reflects that these moves are catastrophic — the player consistently prioritizes piece centralization or activation (placing pieces on d5, e4, e6, e5, etc.) while completely overlooking that the destination square is undefended and directly accessible to an opponent's piece. All 10 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.4), indicating narrow positions demanding concrete calculation over positional instinct.

1354.label: Natural-looking but non-forcing rook repositioning that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate action.
1354.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that appears logically motivated (supporting a passed pawn, doubling on a file, defending a weakness, attacking a piece) but is ultimately too slow for the demands of the position. In 5/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 6, 7, 10), the correct move was with a completely different piece (knight, queen, or pawn), while in the other 5/10 (positions 1, 3, 5, 8, 9), the correct move was a rook move but to a far more aggressive square. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'piece_activity' appears in 10/10. The average cp_loss is extremely high (2087), reflecting that these natural-looking rook moves occur at critical moments where one tempo determines whether an attack succeeds, a mate is forced, or counterplay is generated. The positions span both sides equally (5 White, 5 Black) and mostly middlegames (8/10), with only 1.2 good moves available on average, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where the player defaults to a conventional rook principle instead of finding the forcing continuation.

1344.label: Moving a piece to seemingly stop a near-queening passed pawn, but the defense is geometrically or tactically flawed.
1344.description: 8/10 positions feature a dangerous passed pawn within 1-2 moves of promotion, and in each case the player makes a move that appears to address the promotion threat but actually fails. The defensive failures take several forms: placing a piece on a square that doesn't actually cover the promotion path (Position 2: Nb3 doesn't control b1), placing a piece directly in the path where it gets captured by the promoting pawn (Position 3: Bb1 gets taken by axb1=Q+), placing a rook on the wrong side of the pawn (Position 5: Rc5 in front; Position 6: Rc1 instead of behind with Ra8), moving to a square that can't reach the promotion path in time (Position 4: Rg5 can't prevent h1=Q), or placing a piece where it becomes immediately capturable (Position 10: Nb2 hanging to the rook). The remaining 2/10 positions (8 and 9) share the broader pattern of ignoring an immediate decisive threat to make a superficially constructive but irrelevant move. All 10 positions feature at least one clear better alternative that properly addresses the threat.

1356.label: A knight captures a rook, winning material but often missing a much stronger continuation or removing a critical piece from its post.
1356.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight capturing a rook (Nx on a rook-occupied square). In 7/10 cases this was a mistake (avg cp_loss ~4191 for those), while 3/10 were actually the best move (0 cp_loss). When wrong, the errors fell into distinct categories: 2/10 missed an immediate checkmate (positions 1 and 4, losing ~9600cp each), 2/10 missed capturing a queen instead (positions 7 and 9, where dxe3 or dxe7 won the queen), and 3/10 removed a knight from a dominant post where it served critical attacking or defensive functions (positions 3, 6, and 8). When correct (positions 2, 5, 10), the rook was genuinely undefended with no superior alternative. The target squares span the entire board (d1, e1, e5, e7, f1, f8×3, g6, h1), and the phase split is middlegame(7)/endgame(3), confirming the pattern is purely about the knight-takes-rook action regardless of position type.

1357.label: Capturing the opponent's queen when a stronger forcing move (usually a check leading to mate or a superior tactical sequence) exists.
1357.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player capturing the opponent's queen — 8/10 with a Rook, 2/10 with their own Queen (trading). In 9/10 cases this is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 4677, with 5/10 missing forced checkmate). The 'better' move was typically a check with a different piece: positions 1, 3, 4, 5, and 7 all required an intermediate check before (or instead of) capturing the queen — Qxh6+, Qxg5+, Nb7+, Qh5+, and Nb7+ respectively. In position 2, the rook needed to stay on its defensive file rather than grab the queen. Positions 6 and 9 had superior tactical sequences (Qxd5 with intermediate Bxd2+; Nxc3 fork) that won more material than the queen trade. Position 8 was a voluntary queen exchange that killed attacking potential. Only position 10 (1cp loss) was essentially correct. The pattern shows 9/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating the queen capture creates a powerful cognitive trap that narrows calculation.

1352.label: A rook is moved aggressively (to attack, check, or double) while abandoning a critical defensive responsibility, typically back-rank protection.
1352.description: 10/10 positions feature rook moves played with aggressive intent—doubling on a file, giving check, or infiltrating—that fatally neglect the rook's existing defensive duty. In 7/10 positions, the abandoned responsibility is specifically back-rank or mating-square coverage (Positions 1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10 involve immediate mate threats; Position 2 involves key rank control). 6/10 moves use disambiguated notation (Rff1, Ree1, Ref8, Ree8, Ree2, Rb5) indicating two rooks were available and the player chose to move the wrong one—the one performing the critical defensive role. 3/10 are pointless checks (Rb2+, Rh6+, Rh4+) that look forcing but accomplish nothing while surrendering defensive control. The punishment is devastating: 5/10 positions result in immediate checkmate (Positions 1, 4, 9, 10, and Position 7 which is actually good), and the average cp_loss of 4071 reflects these catastrophic consequences. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, confirming these were razor-sharp positions demanding defensive precision over aggression.

1345.label: Playing a natural-looking piece improvement or repositioning move when the position demands an immediate forcing tactical blow, often leaving pieces undefended.
1345.description: All 10 positions share a critical feature: an immediate forcing move (check, capture, or fork) was required, but instead a 'logical-looking' repositioning or improving move was played. In 6/10 positions, the move directly left a piece hanging — either the moved piece itself was placed on a square where it could be captured (Rc4 by knight, Rg4 by bishop, Re6 by knight/pawn, Rd1 by knight — 4 cases) or moving away removed guard from another piece (Qd1 left Rg1 hanging, Qg4 left Nf5 hanging — 2 cases). In 4/10 positions, the move wasted the critical tempo needed for a tactical shot (h4 instead of Ng3+ fork, f4 instead of Nxd7, Kd3 instead of Rd2 in an endgame race, Rd2 instead of Kb8 prophylaxis). The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were narrow positions demanding precise concrete play. The average cp_loss of 2272 reflects catastrophic consequences. 8/10 occurred in the middlegame where tactical alertness is paramount. The moved pieces (5 rooks, 2 queens, 2 pawns, 1 king) all made moves that appeared purposeful — activating on open files, supporting pawns, repositioning for attack — but ignored the concrete tactical reality of the position.

1362.label: The king greedily captures a piece (usually an infiltrating rook) and walks into a fatally exposed position vulnerable to checks or mating attacks.
1362.description: 10/10 positions feature the king making a capture (Kx...), and 9/10 specifically capture a rook that has infiltrated deep into the position. The king moves to an advanced or open square where it loses all pawn shelter and becomes immediately vulnerable to forcing sequences. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 10), the primary refutation is an immediate check or series of checks exploiting the king's new exposed square. In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 10), this leads directly to forced checkmate within a few moves. In 2/10 positions (6, 10), a superior tactical resource existed (capturing a higher-value piece with a different unit) that was missed due to the instinct to capture the threatening rook. Only 3/10 positions (5, 8, 9) represent cases where the king capture was actually the best or near-best move, with the error being marginal. The average cp_loss of 2946 is driven by positions 3, 4, and 10 where the king capture converts a survivable disadvantage into immediate forced mate.

1359.label: Aggressive forward knight jumps that leave a critical pawn or square undefended, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
1359.description: All 9 positions feature a knight jumping aggressively forward to an apparently strong square (central outpost, attacking an enemy piece, or targeting a weakness) while critically abandoning a defensive responsibility. In 5/9 positions (Positions 2, 5, 6, 8, 10), the knight was the sole defender of a specific pawn — the e5 pawn in 3 cases (from c6), h7 in one case (from f6), and g2 in one case (from f3) — and its departure allowed immediate capture of that pawn or a devastating sacrifice on it. In 3/9 positions (1, 9, and partially 4), the knight lunge gained apparent tempo against a piece (usually a queen) but the target simply retreated to a good square, leaving the knight misplaced and having wasted two full tempi. In 1/9 positions (3), the knight went to a rim square targeting a pawn and was punished by counter-attacks trapping it. The average cp_loss of 254 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but concrete tactical oversights where the attacking intent of the knight move blinds the player to what the knight was previously holding together.

1363.label: A slow, non-forcing pawn advance (typically on the flank) that wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate concrete action.
1363.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn push played instead of addressing an urgent tactical or safety need. 7/10 moves are rim pawn advances (a-file or h-file: a4, a4, a6, a6, a5, h5, h5), with the remaining 3 being other non-forcing pawn moves (b3, e5, f6). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'king_safety' is flagged in 8/10 positions. In every case, the position demanded immediate action — castling (positions 3, 4), resolving pawn tension (position 2), defending a hanging piece or critical square (positions 5, 8, 10), or generating concrete counterplay against aggressive opposing pieces (positions 6, 7, 9). Instead, the player chose a move that looks vaguely useful (gaining space, preparing a future break) but addresses nothing concrete. The average cp_loss of 326 reflects how severely a single wasted tempo is punished in these tactically charged positions.

1350.label: Quiet developing or repositioning moves played in positions demanding the one precise defensive or tactical response.
1350.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, natural-looking moves (piece development, repositioning, or pawn advances) that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability requiring a specific response. The average number of good moves was only 1.4, meaning these positions demanded extreme precision. 4/10 moves placed a piece/pawn directly on a square where it could be immediately captured (Rg7, Bb7, Nf3, Bg7). 3/10 moved a critical defender away from its post, allowing a tactical breakthrough on the abandoned square or diagonal (Nd7 leaving e6 unguarded, Be7 abandoning the f6 blockade, Nc2 missing Nxc4). 3/10 advanced pawns that weakened the king's shelter or wasted tempo (g4, h5, a3). In all cases, the moves appear constructive—completing fianchettoes, repositioning knights, gaining space—but the position required either maintaining an existing defensive arrangement or executing a forcing tactical sequence. The feature consistently identifies moments where a player follows general principles rather than calculating concrete threats.

1365.label: Routine pawn-takes-pawn captures that prioritize small material gain over far stronger tactical or dynamic continuations.
1365.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing an enemy pawn (pxp) that looks natural or free but squanders a much larger opportunity.
