In 8/10 cases, the best move was a non-capture that exploited a concrete tactical motif (queen check winning a piece, rook lift winning a queen, tempo-gaining attacks on exposed pieces, etc.). The average cp_loss of 1179 is enormous, with 5/10 positions losing over 200cp and one resulting in forced mate. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments demanding precision rather than routine captures. In 7/10 positions, the pawn capture either released central tension that was benefiting the player (positions 4, 7, 8, 10) or grabbed a peripheral pawn while ignoring a hanging/vulnerable piece (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 9). The common thread is that the captures look 'free' or 'logical' but each one either exposes a tactical vulnerability (positions 4, 5, 10), surrenders a dynamic asset like an advanced pawn (positions 4, 7, 8), or wastes a tempo when a forcing move would win material outright (positions 2, 3, 6, 9).

1347.label: Choosing a flashy forcing move (usually a check) against an exposed king when a more concrete move — often a capturing check or quiet decisive tactic — was available.
1347.description: All 10 positions feature exposed kings as a central theme, and 9/10 moves represent choosing a superficially aggressive action over a more precise one. 5/10 moves are direct queen/piece checks that waste tempo: in positions 3, 4, and 9, the correct move was a CAPTURING check (Qxf6+, Qxf5+, Qxe4+) that wins material or maintains perpetual, while the played checks gained nothing. Positions 8 and 5 chose checks that allowed the opponent's king to escape to safety (wrong direction). The remaining mistakes (positions 1, 2, 6, 7) follow the same principle of hollow aggression: grabbing material while ignoring the critical threat (Rxb2), attacking irrelevant targets (Nh5, Nb5), or advancing a pawn instead of capturing with it (f3 vs fxg3). Position 10 (0 cp loss) represents the CORRECT version of the pattern — Qb2 addresses the real threat precisely. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 9/10, confirming the consistent thread of wasted forcing moves.

1358.label: Major piece placed on a far rank (7th/8th/back rank) instead of creating an immediate horizontal barrier adjacent to the enemy king.
1358.description: In 6/6 positions, the player placed a major piece (5 rook moves, 1 queen move) on a deep/distant rank — the 8th rank (Rd8, Re8, Qe8), 7th rank (Rg7), or 2nd rank (Re2, Ra2) — in winning endgame positions. In 3/6 cases (positions 2, 5, 6), the optimal move was explicitly a rook move to the 4th or 5th rank creating a horizontal barrier that cuts off the enemy king (Rh5, Rh4, Rb4). The remaining positions also punished the distant placement: position 8's Rg7 missed forcing checks, position 10's Ra2 missed a concrete capture. All positions were clearly winning endgames (avg cp_loss 1551 inflated by one massive blunder) where the player prioritized long-range file control or back-rank threats over immediately confining the enemy king. The characteristic error is choosing vertical/distant piece placement when a rank-based cut-off adjacent to the king would be far more efficient.

1361.label: Playing a non-forcing flank pawn advance (especially h-pawn) when the position demands an immediate tactical strike or piece action.
1361.description: 6/10 positions feature a non-capturing flank pawn advance (h5 in 4 positions, h4, c5, f5) when the correct move was a forcing piece action (capture, check, or retreat). In 8/10 positions, the move played was a pawn move of some kind. The core error in 7/10 blunders is tempo loss — wasting a move on a slow pawn push while the opponent gains time to reorganize. In positions 1, 2, 3, 5, and 7, the player advanced a flank pawn to 'support' something or create vague threats, while the position demanded immediate captures (Rxg7+, hxg6) or piece retreats (Bh4, Bh5). Position 8 (b1=Q+) is a move-order variant of the same tempo-loss theme — promoting before eliminating the defender first. Position 4 (Nc7) abandoned a powerfully centralized piece for a superficial fork. The two 0-cp-loss positions (6, 10) appear to be edge cases where the pawn advance happened to coincide with an already-winning position. The unifying thread is choosing a committal, non-forcing move that gives the opponent a critical free tempo.

1369.label: Playing a strategic or aggressive queen move instead of a simple piece capture that wins material.
1369.description: All 10 positions feature a queen move to an 'active-looking' square (pressuring pawns, giving check, repositioning) while a concrete piece-winning capture was available. In 7/10 positions, the missed tactic specifically involved capturing a knight on f3 (Bxf3 or Nxf3) to exploit an undefended bishop on g5 — this sub-pattern appears in positions 1, 2, 3, 6, and 10 almost identically. In 9/10 cases the missed best move was a non-queen piece capture (bishop takes knight, knight takes knight, etc.). The queen moves themselves appear purposeful — Qb6 attacks b2/d4, Qd7 'develops', Qa5+/Qb4+ give check, Qb3 pressures pawns — but all sacrifice a concrete material-winning tactical shot for vague strategic pressure. 9/10 positions are in the opening phase where both sides have pieces in the center, and the average cp_loss of 377 reflects that full pieces are being left on the table. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, confirming these were narrow tactical moments demanding precision rather than general principles.

1370.label: A passive, non-forcing queen repositioning move that squanders a concrete tactical opportunity demanding immediate action.
1370.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet queen move (non-capturing, non-checking) to a seemingly reasonable square when the position demanded concrete forcing play. The missed best moves include captures with check (Qxe3+ in position 2), pawn grabs (Qxg2 in position 1, Rxa5 in position 3), piece captures (Qxe6 in position 5), knight sacrifices with check (Nf5+ in position 8), centralizing checks (Qe5+ in position 7), exchange sacrifices (Rxd5 in position 4), and simplifying trades (Rxd8 in position 9). 10/10 positions carry the 'missed_tactic' tag, and 8/10 are labeled with 'tempo_loss' as the move gives the opponent time to consolidate or escape. The average centipawn loss is 329, indicating these are catastrophic errors. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow critical moments where only forcing play maintained the advantage. In 9/10 cases the queen retreats or slides sideways to a passive square; even the one exception (Qf5 in position 10) is a non-forcing move to an exposed square that becomes a target.

1374.label: In a Sicilian Dragon/Accelerated Dragon fianchetto setup, Black plays ...e6 or ...e5 which catastrophically weakens the d6 square, enabling a Ndb5-Nd6 knight invasion.
1374.description: 9/9 positions feature Black with a fianchettoed bishop on g7 in an opening structure, and all moves are e-pawn advances (...e6 in 7/9, ...e5 in 2/9). In 7/9 positions, the setup is specifically an Accelerated Dragon where White has knights on c3 and d4 with a bishop on e3, and the punishment is the devastating Ndb5 followed by Nd6, planting an unassailable knight deep in Black's position and often costing castling rights. The remaining positions share the theme of an e-pawn advance being inconsistent with the fianchetto structure — either blocking the g7 bishop's diagonal, creating dark-square weaknesses, or missing concrete tactics that the g7 bishop enables. In all 9 cases, Black had natural developing moves (typically ...Nf6 or ...d6) that would have maintained the position, but chose a structurally committal pawn move that violated the principles of the fianchetto setup.

1371.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing positional move (pawn push, piece regrouping, or passive development) in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1371.description: All 10 positions share a critical feature: the player chose a non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) in a position where only immediate tactical action could maintain the evaluation. 6/10 moves were slow pawn pushes (c4, f4, g5, f4, f3, b5) and 4/10 were passive piece moves (Nd2, Be7, Bf5, Ne7). In every case, the best move was forcing: captures (Qxd6, Nxf4+), invasions (Rc6, Re2, Re3), checks (Qf4+, Bd4+), or the single defensive resource (Rg1, Rh5). The average good moves available was only 1.3, meaning 8/10 positions had at most 1 viable option — all of which were concrete and tactical. The average cp_loss of 1205 reflects the severity of ignoring tactical urgency. The common thread is treating a razor-sharp, time-critical position as though it were a quiet strategic affair where general improvement suffices.

1366.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) to a seemingly forcing square where the opponent simply captures it, dissipating the player's attack or advantage.
1366.description: 9/9 positions share the core pattern of moving a piece to a square where the opponent immediately captures it, with the player apparently attracted by the 'forcing' nature of the move. 6/9 moves are checks (Bd4+, Qd5+, Qh4+, Qe4+, Qe4+, Qxd5+), creating the illusion of gaining tempo, but the best response is simply to capture the checking piece. In 6/9 cases specifically, the opponent's queen captures the blundering queen (Qxd5, Qxh4, Qxe4, Qxe4, Qxd5, Qxc3). The remaining 3 positions involve bishops moved to squares where they're immediately taken (Bxd4, Bxa6, Bxa7). In 7/9 positions, the blundering side had an active attacking position or mating threats that were completely neutralized by the forced exchange. The average cp_loss of 1422 reflects how catastrophically these trades destroy the moving side's position — typically converting winning attacks into lost endgames or hanging material.

1373.label: Developing a knight to its natural square in a position that demands urgent concrete action for king safety.
1373.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight being developed from its starting square to a classical development square (Nc3, Nc6, Nf6, Ne2) — textbook moves in a normal opening. However, in every case the position is tactically critical: 9/10 positions have an exposed or centralized king, and the average cp_loss of ~2956 reflects catastrophic consequences. The correct moves were always concrete and non-developmental: bishop repositions for defense (positions 1, 3), rook lifts to attack exposed pieces (position 2), pawn pushes to block critical squares (positions 5, 7), central pawn strikes to win material (positions 4, 6), rook exchanges to neutralize pressure (position 8), queen trades to defuse attacks (position 10), or pawn moves to avoid forced mate (position 9). In 7/10 cases, only 1 good move existed, showing these were razor-thin defensive positions. The knight moves are universally non-forcing (0/10 deliver check or capture) and fail to address the specific tactical emergency at hand.

1360.label: Moving a piece (usually a knight) to an undefended square that is immediately capturable or tactically exploitable, when the position demanded forcing action.
1360.description: 7/10 positions feature knight moves to passive or vulnerable squares. In 6/10 positions (Nd2, Rf2, Qf3, Na3, Ng6, and Nh5), the moved piece lands on a square directly capturable by an opponent's bishop along an open diagonal — Bxd2+, Bxf2+, Bxf3, Bxa3, Bxg6, and Bxh5 respectively. 6/10 knight moves go to rim or near-rim squares (Na3, Na6, Nb3, Nfh3, Nh5, Ng6). In all 10 positions, the best available moves involved immediate tactical action — checks, captures, or forcing piece exchanges — yet the player chose a slow, non-forcing repositioning move instead. The average cp_loss of 2118 is extreme, with 3/10 positions losing a piece or more outright. The positions demand urgency (exposed kings in 8/10, immediate tactical opportunities in all), but the played moves uniformly ignore threats and place material in danger.

1368.label: A quiet, non-forcing move (usually a pawn push) played in a position where an immediate tactical blow — check, sacrifice, fork, or checkmate — was available.
1368.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a preparatory or 'building' move while a concrete forcing solution existed. 7/10 of the blunder moves were pawn advances (b6, c3, g5, h5, g4, fxe5, a7), while the remaining 3 were non-forcing piece repositioning moves (Rgf2, Nf3, Neg4). In every case, the best move was a sharp tactical blow: sacrifices (Bh7+, Bxe4), double attacks (Qb7), centralizing forks (Qd4), or immediate checkmate (Re2#). The average number of good alternatives was only 1.5, indicating these were critical-path positions demanding precision, yet the player defaulted to 'improving' or 'preparing' rather than calculating. The average cp_loss of 3019 reflects that the missed tactics were often devastating (3/10 missed forced checkmates). The positions span all phases (7 middlegame, 2 opening, 1 endgame) and both colors equally (5 each), suggesting this is a universal pattern of choosing positional autopilot over concrete calculation.

1372.label: Voluntarily initiating a minor piece exchange that removes the player's most strategically important bishop from the board.
1372.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop capture (Bx...) where the player uses their own most active or defensively critical bishop to capture an enemy minor piece, and 1/10 (Nxe3) captures a key defensive bishop at the wrong moment in a capture sequence. In all 10 positions, the piece being traded away was performing a vital role: in 4/10 it was a centralized or fianchettoed bishop controlling a critical long diagonal (positions 3, 7, 9 with bishops on e4/g2, and position 10 with Bg5), in 3/10 it was a bishop shielding the king from a dangerous diagonal or providing dark-square cover (positions 1, 4, 6), and in 3/10 it was a timing/move-order issue where the bishop capture was thematically correct but executed prematurely without necessary preparation (positions 2, 5, 8). The average cp_loss of 271 reflects that these trades consistently squander significant advantages or deepen existing disadvantages. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions demanded precise play rather than simplification.

1367.label: King or queen moves to a square that appears active but falls on a tactically exploitable open line or fork-prone junction, when a nearby safer square was available.
1367.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a high-value piece (king in 7/10, queen in 3/10) to a square that seemed reasonable or active but was specifically vulnerable to a tactical blow along an open line, diagonal, or fork pattern. The correct alternative was almost always an adjacent or nearby square that dodged the specific vulnerability: Ke2 instead of Kd2 (positions 1-2, avoiding the open d-file check), Qd6/Qd7 instead of Qc7/Qe7 (positions 3, 8, avoiding e-file exploitation or Nd5 fork), Kg8/Kd8 instead of Ke6/Kd6/Kg6 (positions 6, 7, 10, retreating instead of advancing into checks). In 9/10 positions the king was uncastled or exposed in/near the center. The average cp_loss of 1110 reflects the catastrophic nature of placing a royal piece on a tactically loaded square. In 8/10 cases there was only 1-2 good moves available, showing these are narrow decisions where the 'slightly wrong' nearby square leads to disaster.

1381.label: King moves to a square on an open diagonal where an enemy bishop or queen immediately delivers a devastating check.
1381.description: In 10/10 positions, the king voluntarily moves to a square that sits on an open diagonal controlled by (or accessible to) an enemy bishop or queen, which then delivers a check along that diagonal as the primary refutation. In 6/10 cases, a bishop delivers the diagonal check (Bf5+, Bd3+, Bd4+, Be4+); in 4/10 cases, a queen delivers it (Qc6+, Qxe4+, Qf6+). In every single case, an alternative king move to an adjacent square that avoids the dangerous diagonal was available and significantly better — Kh2 instead of Kg2 (positions 1, 8), Kc1 instead of Kc2 (positions 2, 3), Kh1 instead of Kf1 (position 5), Kd7 instead of Kf6 (position 9), Kh7 instead of Kg7 (positions 6, 10). The average cp_loss was 3011, with 4/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate after the diagonal check. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, showing these are typically razor-thin defensive situations where the specific diagonal awareness is critical.

1376.label: Developing or repositioning a bishop to a natural-looking square while missing that the position demands an immediate tactical response.
1376.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves (Bg7, Bb3, Bxc2, Bd7, Bg7, Bg4, Bb7, Be7), and the remaining 2 (dxe6, Nc7) share the same underlying error pattern: a quiet, 'natural-looking' piece repositioning that catastrophically ignores urgent tactical realities. In 5/10 positions, the bishop was placed on an undefended square directly in the firing line of an opponent's piece (Bg7 x2 onto Bb2's diagonal, Be7 enabling Nxd5+/Bxe7, Bxc2 creating a queen-infiltration target, Bg4 leaving the king unguarded). In 3/10 positions, the bishop was moved away from a square where it was critically needed (Bd7 abandoning the capture of a hanging knight on e3, Bb3 leaving the a4 square that enabled forced mate, Bg4 abandoning kingside defense). The average cp_loss of 2989 reflects that these are not small inaccuracies but catastrophic blunders — the position demanded concrete action (capturing hanging pieces, delivering checkmate, creating counterplay) but the player chose passive development instead.

1379.label: Moving a knight to the edge of the board (a5 or h5) to harass an opponent's well-placed bishop, abandoning critical defensive duties in the process.
1379.description: 8/10 positions feature a knight moving to the rim specifically to attack an opponent's bishop: 6/10 are Na5 targeting a bishop on c4, and 2/10 are Nh5 targeting a bishop on f4. These are mirror-image maneuvers where a knight leaves a central 6th-rank square (c6 or f6) and jumps to the edge (a5 or h5) with the sole intent of chasing the bishop. In 7/10 positions both kings are still in the center, making the abandoned defensive duties even more critical. The punishment is remarkably consistent: 6/10 positions feature a Bxf7+ sacrifice exploiting the newly undefended f7 square, while 2/10 punish the knight being en prise on its rim square (Qxh5). The remaining 2 positions (Bf8 and Be6) follow the broader pattern of moving a piece to a passive square while abandoning a critical blocking/active function. 9/10 moves are played by Black. The average cp_loss of 323 reflects that these moves consistently transform equal or advantageous positions into losing ones.

1377.label: Pieces retreat to the player's own 1st or 2nd rank when the position demands urgent, forcing action.
1377.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece moving backward to the player's own home territory: for Black, 7/7 moves go to the 7th rank (Nd7, Rf7, Nd7, Ne7, Re7, Bd7, Nc7), and for White, all 3 moves go to the 1st or 2nd rank (Re1, Rd2, Be2). These moves universally appear 'natural' — developing, consolidating, or defending — but in every case the position demanded urgent forcing action instead. In 5/10 positions, the best move was a king safety move (Kf1, Kf8, etc.); in 3/10, it was a capture or material-winning move (Bxa7, Rxc2, b5 attacking the queen); and in 2/10, it was a precise tactical resource. The average cp_loss of 1332 reflects how catastrophically wrong these retreating moves are. Only 1.6 good moves existed on average, showing these are critical positions with narrow paths to survival where backward piece shuffles are fatal.

1375.label: Superficially attractive moves (captures, checks, active placements, plans) that completely neglect the position's single most urgent tactical requirement.
1375.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: there is ONE critical concrete demand (a tactic to execute, a threat to neutralize, or a defensive duty to maintain), yet the player makes a move that looks productive on the surface while completely ignoring this demand. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 acceptable moves (avg 1.7 good moves), meaning the margin for error was razor-thin. In 4/10 positions the ignored need was capturing or eliminating a specific piece/pawn (Positions 1, 5, 6, 10). In 3/10 positions the ignored need was addressing an immediate mating or promotional threat (Positions 3, 4, 9). In 2/10 positions the move abandoned a critical defensive function (Positions 2, 8). In 1/10 the move opened lines toward the player's own king (Position 7). The chosen moves are diverse in type—king moves (2), bishop moves (4), knight moves (2), pawn moves (2), captures (3), checks (2)—but uniformly share the quality of appearing purposeful or aggressive while missing what the position actually requires. The average cp_loss of ~4000 reflects the catastrophic nature of neglecting the single critical factor.

1382.label: Playing a non-urgent or aimless move in a position where only one or two precise moves survive, wasting the critical tempo needed to address an immediate tactical demand.
1382.description: 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the core error, and the average number of good moves available was only 1.5, meaning these are razor-sharp positions with almost no margin for error. The moves themselves are diverse in piece type (5/10 rook moves, 3/10 pawn pushes, 2/10 king moves) but united in their failure to address the single most urgent demand: 3/10 are premature checks that drive the opponent's king toward safety or place the rook on a vulnerable square (Re8+, Rg8+, Rb8+); 3/10 are slow pawn moves when immediate tactical action was required (f3, a6, b3); 2/10 are passive rook moves accomplishing nothing (Rh8, Rh1); and 2/10 are aimless king moves when concrete action was needed (Kg3, Ka6). In every case, the opponent gained a free tempo to execute a devastating tactic that didn't exist one move prior — whether a mating pattern (4/10), a fork/material win (3/10), or an unstoppable passed pawn (2/10). The average cp_loss of 3076 reflects how catastrophically these single wasted tempi were punished.

1386.label: King voluntarily moves to a square that falls on an enemy piece's attacking line, enabling immediate checks or captures-with-check that weren't previously possible.
1386.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move as the blunder. In 9/10 cases, the king walks to a square where an enemy piece can immediately deliver check (or a capture becomes check) that was geometrically impossible on the previous square: Positions 1 and 6 have Kg7 walking into Nf5+ (knight controls g7 from f5); Position 2 has Kd2 placing the king on the c3-bishop's diagonal enabling Bxc3+; Position 3 has Kg2 enabling Re3+ on the open e-file; Position 4 has Kg7 enabling Qg5+; Position 5 has Kf2 enabling Bxe3+ and Qf6+; Position 7 has Kb2 enabling Qc3+ driving the king into a mating net; Position 9 has Ke5 enabling Bxd4+; Position 10 has Ke7 enabling both Rc7+ and Qb4+. Position 8 (Kf7) is the mildest outlier, where the king enables a discovered check with d5+. The average cp_loss of 4860 and 6/10 positions resulting in forced mate confirm these are catastrophic self-inflicted wounds. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, suggesting the positions were already critical, making the voluntary king exposure especially lethal.

1387.label: Capturing the opponent's rook on a shared open file when the rook serves a critical function or a stronger intermediate move should come first.
1387.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capturing the opposing rook on the same open file (Rx_1/Rx_8 patterns), and in every case this exchange is premature or counterproductive. In 5/10 positions (3, 4, 6, 7, 9), the error is specifically a move-order mistake where a tactical blow (Nxh3+, Nxc2+, Bf4+, Bh7+, Nxa2) should have been played BEFORE the rook exchange, because the exchange alters the geometry needed for the combination to work. In the remaining 5/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 8, 10), the traded rook served a critical offensive or defensive function—contesting a file, defending the back rank, or maintaining pressure—and its removal handed the opponent unchallenged dominance or exposed a fatal weakness. 7/10 moves gave check, suggesting the 'free tempo' of a check seduced players into the exchange. The average cp_loss of 3136 reflects that many of these convert winning/equal positions into losses or miss forced checkmate.
1387.old_chip: Premature rook exchange on open file

1385.label: In endgames with enemy passed pawns threatening promotion, the king moves defensively toward the threat instead of creating active counterplay with own pawns or pieces.
1385.description: 10/10 positions are endgames where the played move is a king move, and 10/10 involve critical passed pawn dynamics where an enemy pawn is advanced or threatening promotion. In 9/10 cases, the king moves toward the enemy's passed pawn or promotion square in a futile attempt to stop it defensively, when the correct move was to create counterplay elsewhere — typically advancing one's own passed pawn (positions 3, 4, 6, 10), capturing hanging material (position 2), using a knight for blockade instead of the king (positions 5, 9), gaining tempo with a check (position 7), or racing the king toward a different target (positions 1, 8). The common thread is the king being used as a passive defensive piece against an unstoppable threat when the position demanded active pawn-racing or tactical counterplay. Average cp_loss of ~1997 reflects that several of these tempo losses were catastrophic (positions 3, 9 turned winning chances into forced mates). Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow decision points where the counterplay-generating move was the only viable option.

1384.label: A non-forcing pawn push (or passive repositioning) played when an immediate, concrete tactical threat demands urgent attention.
1384.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (5 f-pawn pushes, 2 c-pawn pushes, 2 a-pawn pushes) with 1 passive rook retreat. In all 10 cases, the position contained an immediate tactical crisis requiring concrete resolution—a hanging piece (3/10), a dangerous pin or alignment (2/10), an attacking threat about to land (3/10), or a critical defensive resource about to be lost (2/10). Instead of addressing the emergency, the player chose a slow, preparatory, or positional-looking move that would be reasonable in a quiet position but is catastrophic given the urgency. The average cp_loss of 1263 and average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are critical-moment failures where the 'normal' move is the losing move. The blundered moves typically intended legitimate positional goals (preparing pawn breaks, gaining space, consolidating) but completely missed that the position had crossed a tactical threshold requiring immediate concrete action.

1364.label: Intuitive captures or king moves that fail to exploit (or walk into) precise intermediate checks against exposed kings near the g-file.
1364.description: 8/10 positions feature a critically exposed king (especially on g6, g7, or h7), and in 7/10 the mistake involves either missing an available intermediate check or enabling one against oneself. Three positions (6, 7, 8) share the identical move Kg7—Black stepping off the back rank into a tactical disaster (Nf5+, Rxa8, Bf8+ discovered check). Positions 2, 3, 4, and 10 all feature the player making a 'natural' move (capture, centralization, or wrong check) while a stronger forcing check existed (Re6+, Rf8+, Rf1+, Nf5+). The avg cp_loss of 3811 is driven by 4 catastrophic blunders (9000+ cp) where the move allowed forced mate. Positions 1 and 9 (0 cp loss) activate the feature due to matching positional characteristics (exposed king, open files, rook activity) despite being correct moves. 9/10 positions have rooks on open files, and 8/10 involve advanced passed pawns near promotion, creating the tactical tension that makes precision critical.

1391.label: Queen moves to a seemingly active square where it immediately becomes a target for enemy pieces or pawn breaks, causing severe material or tempo loss.
1391.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move to a central or semi-central square (b3, b6, a4, a5, c7, d5, d6) that appears to offer activity or pressure but is tactically deficient. In 7/10 positions, the queen lands on a square immediately or imminently attacked by a minor piece (usually a knight): Nb5 in position 1, Nxa5 in position 2, Nd4 in positions 3 and 5 (via Na5), Nxd5 in position 7, Ne4 in position 8. In 3/10, the queen is captured by a bishop along an open diagonal (position 6, Bxc7) or becomes the target of a pawn break (position 10, c5 hitting Qd6). The common intent across all positions was seemingly reasonable—centralizing the queen, pressuring pawns, or connecting rooks—but the player consistently failed to verify whether the destination square was safe from tactical exploitation. The average cp_loss of 334 reflects that 3/10 positions involved outright queen hanging (positions 2, 6, 7) while the remaining 7/10 involved devastating tempo gains against the misplaced queen.

1380.label: Player moves the wrong one of two knights (or makes a passive disambiguated knight move) when the other knight or a tactical alternative was critically needed.
1380.description: 8/9 positions feature disambiguated knight moves (Nfd2, Nce7, Nce7, Nge2, Ndf3, Nbc3, Nbd7, Nbd2), where the notation itself reveals two knights competed for attention. In 3/9 positions (1, 2, 6), the best move was literally the SAME destination square but with the OTHER knight (Nbd2 not Nfd2, Nge7 not Nce7, Nf4 not Nbc3). In the remaining positions, the player made a quiet developing knight move when a forcing tactical option existed—often a capture or sacrifice (Nxd4, Nxf7, Bxf3, Rxe2). The average cp_loss of 321 is very high, reflecting that these 'wrong knight' choices systematically remove critical defenders (positions 1, 9), abandon pressure on key squares (positions 2, 3), hang the moved piece (position 4), or miss winning tactics (positions 5, 6, 8). Only 1.3 good moves existed on average, indicating these are narrow positions demanding precise piece selection.

1389.label: Playing a routine developing move (typically queen or bishop to e7/e2) when an immediate capture, check, or forcing move was critically needed.
1389.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing repositioning move instead of executing an available concrete tactical action. The moves overwhelmingly target 'standard' development squares: 5/10 go specifically to e7, 2/10 to e2, and the remaining 3 go to similarly passive squares (g7, c2, f1). 8/10 are queen moves and 2/10 are bishop moves — all non-capturing and non-checking. In every case, a forcing alternative existed: 4/10 positions had a hanging piece to capture (Bxf5, Qxg5, Rxf7, Bxg4), 3/10 required a simplifying queen trade (Qxd8+, Qxd1+, Qxd8), and the remainder demanded piece activation with tempo. 7/10 occur in the opening phase where 'natural development' thinking is most seductive. The average cp_loss of 252 confirms these are serious errors, and only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise concrete play rather than generic development.

1396.label: Advancing the g-pawn in front of one's own castled king to chase an enemy piece, catastrophically weakening the kingside pawn shelter.
1396.description: All 10/10 positions feature a g-pawn advance (g5, g4, or g3) made by the side whose king is castled kingside, directly weakening their own pawn shield. In 9/10 cases, the primary motivation was to chase an active enemy piece from a strong square near the kingside (bishop on h5/f4 in 5 positions, knight on h4/f4/h5 in 3 positions, queen on f4 in 1 position). The remaining case (Position 5) involved g3 leaving a knight undefended. The average cp_loss of 318 reflects the severity — these moves consistently create permanent dark-square holes, expose the king to attacks along opened files/diagonals, grant the opponent superior outposts (especially f5 for knights), and often leave pawns tactically hanging. In 9/10 positions, same-side kingside castling was present. The refutations consistently involved exploiting the weakened pawn shelter through piece invasions, pawn levers (h4 hook), or direct captures of the advanced/undefended pawns.

1392.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (one square from promotion) without first preparing with piece activity, intermezzo checks, or neutralizing counterplay.
1392.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn being pushed to the 7th rank (from the promoting side's perspective: rank 2 for Black, rank 7 for White), placing it one square from queening. In 9/10 cases this is a significant error (avg cp_loss 2241), and 10/10 are rook endgames with advanced passed pawns on both sides. The better alternatives consistently involve preparatory moves first: 6/10 positions called for an intermezzo check or rook activation (Ra8+, Rd8+, Rc1+, Rb2, Rg2), 3/10 called for king centralization (Kd4, Kc3, Kc5), and 2/10 required eliminating a defending piece before the push. The punishment mechanism varies but revolves around the opponent gaining a critical tempo: in 4/10 cases the opponent's king intercepts the pawn (Ke2, Ka5, Kc7), in 4/10 the opponent wins a counter-promotion race because the premature push triggers their own faster threats, and in 2/10 the push makes the rook passive by trapping it behind the pawn. Position 7 (h7, 0 cp_loss) is the sole exception where the push was correct because two rooks could handle the opponent's counter-threats simultaneously.

1399.label: A non-forcing rim/flank pawn advance (a, g, or h file) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate tactical or central action.
1399.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance on the a-file (3 cases), g-file (2 cases), or h-file (5 cases) — exclusively flank pawns pushed one square in positions that urgently required something else. 10/10 moves are non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), and 10/10 are tagged as tempo_loss in their analysis. The best moves in these positions were consistently immediate tactical strikes (Nc5, c5+, Rxe6+), central pawn breaks (c5, c4, d4), piece centralization (Qe5, Ba7, Ra1), or urgent defensive measures (Re2, Kd2). The average cp_loss of 1112 (inflated by one forced-mate case) and the average of only 1.8 good moves available indicate these positions were sharp and demanded precise, forcing play. The blunders span middlegames (5/10) and endgames (5/10), both White (6/10) and Black (4/10), showing the pattern is universal — it's not phase- or side-specific but rather a consistent human tendency to play 'preparatory' wing moves when no preparation time exists.

1378.label: Moves that pursue material gain or apparent piece activity while fatally removing a piece from its critical defensive post, leaving something undefended.
1378.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder specifically removes a piece from a square where it performs a critical tactical or defensive function (or captures material while leaving another piece undefended). In positions 2, 5, 8, the knight/pawn was moved away from a restraining square (c3, a5, or blocked the c-pawn), directly enabling the opponent's refutation. In positions 6 and 9, a rook captured material but left a bishop (d5) or knight (a6) completely undefended. In position 4, the rook captured a pawn while ignoring an existing checkmate threat. In position 7, the rook moved to an 'active' square where it immediately became a tactical target. Only position 10 is a mild outlier (minor inaccuracy in a lost position). The average cp_loss of 2219 and only 1.4 good moves available confirms these are critical moments requiring precise calculation, where the superficially attractive move catastrophically disrupts the player's own piece coordination. 6/10 moves involved captures or material-grabbing, and in 7/10 the refutation directly exploited the newly undefended piece or square.

1388.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing preparatory move in a position where one specific immediate tactical blow or urgent piece action was required.
1388.description: 10/10 positions feature a player choosing a quiet, 'improving' move (pawn push, piece repositioning, or prophylactic king move) when the position demanded a concrete forcing response. The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, meaning these are critical-moment positions with essentially one right answer. 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic'. In 5/10 positions, the correct move was a forcing check that initiated a winning/drawing combination (Rg6+, Nh6+, Rf8+, Re1#, Rf8+). In 3/10 positions, a piece was hanging and needed to be captured or saved immediately (Nxd4, Be4, Nd4). In 2/10, an urgent defensive move was required to address a concrete threat. The blunders share the character of looking 'reasonable' from a positional or preparatory standpoint — doubling rooks, gaining space, challenging strong pieces with pawns, tucking the king away — but catastrophically ignore that the position has crossed a tactical threshold requiring immediate concrete action. The enormous average cp_loss of 2222 reflects that these are positions where the gap between the one correct forcing move and any quiet alternative is vast.

1398.label: Advancing the g-pawn (g3 or g6) in front of the castled king as a prophylactic measure, but actually weakening the king's pawn shelter and enabling tactical exploitation.
1398.description: All 9/9 positions feature the same geometric move: a one-square g-pawn advance (g2-g3 for White in 4 positions, g7-g6 for Black in 5 positions) directly in front of or adjacent to the castled king. In every case, the move was played with defensive or prophylactic intent — blocking a diagonal (3/9), preventing piece infiltration (3/9), or shoring up perceived dark-square weaknesses (3/9) — but instead catastrophically weakened the king's pawn shelter. The refutations share a tight cluster of patterns: in 3/9 positions the g-pawn advance left an adjacent pawn undefended (h3 or g5 hanging), in 3/9 it enabled a piece sacrifice on the weakened g3/g6 square leading to perpetual or mating attacks, in 2/9 it enabled a pawn break (h5 against g6) tearing open the h-file, and in 1/9 it failed to block the actual attacking route (queen rerouted via h-file for mate). The average cp_loss of 1280 and only 1.1 good moves available on average confirm these were critical moments where passive pawn moves were especially punished.

1390.label: Playing a positional or preparatory move (typically a pawn break) in a critical position where an immediate tactical resource—a capture, fork, or forcing sequence—demands precise execution.
1390.description: 9/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 8/10 with 'missed_tactic', revealing the core pattern: the player defaults to a 'logical-looking' positional move while a concrete tactical opportunity goes unexploited. 5/10 moves are pawn pushes challenging the opponent's pawn structure (c6 four times, f6 once, c5 once), while the remaining moves are quiet piece repositionings (Nbd2, Nc3, Rf5, Kc8) or a misguided check (Be6+). In every case, the best move involved a forcing tactical resource: a capture of undefended material (positions 7, 9), a defensive piece maneuver addressing an immediate threat (positions 1, 2, 4), a fork winning the queen (position 5), or a knight route winning the exchange (position 8). The average number of good moves was only 1.6, confirming these are narrow, critical moments demanding calculation rather than positional instinct. The average cp_loss of 374 reflects how catastrophic it is to 'play chess' when the position demands 'solving a puzzle.'

1397.label: The queen voluntarily moves to a seemingly active square but abandons a critical defensive duty, leaving a piece, pawn, or square unprotected.
1397.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a non-forcing queen move (no check, no capture) to reposition the queen to a square that appears active or useful. In 7/10 cases, this directly leaves a specific piece or pawn undefended (Positions 2, 3, 5, 8, 9: hanging piece; Position 1: queen itself becomes trappable; Position 10: loses ability to capture opponent's exposed queen). In the remaining 3/10 cases, the queen abandons a critical central or defensive post, enabling the opponent to seize the initiative through tempo-gaining attacks (Positions 4, 6, 7). The average cp_loss of 502 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights, not subtle inaccuracies. In 6/10 positions, only 1 good move existed, indicating the queen was performing an irreplaceable function. The refutations are typically simple one-move tactical shots (capturing undefended material) rather than deep combinations, suggesting the player failed to ask 'what was my queen defending?' before relocating it.

1395.label: Rook moves to the player's first/eighth rank (typically activating a dormant rook onto an open file) during attacking middlegame positions, often missing more urgent tactical moves with other pieces.
1395.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the player's back rank (1st rank for White, 8th rank for Black), typically from a corner or edge square onto an open or semi-open file. In 7/10 positions, the move is a significant mistake (avg ~4240 cp loss among errors), while 3/10 are actually correct. The common thread is a 'natural developing' rook activation that looks logical—bringing the last piece into play on an open file—but in the error cases, it misses more forcing moves with other pieces: Position 2 missed Bc5# (mate in 1), Position 3 missed Bc5+ (move-order preparation), Position 4 missed dxe4 (capturing a dominating knight), Position 5 missed Qh3 (defending against Rh5+), Position 6 missed Nf3 (neutralizing a knight fork threat), Position 7 missed Nxg6 (decisive sacrifice), and Position 8 missed Bxh5 (capturing a hanging piece). The positions where Rf1 is correct (1, 9, 10) share the trait that no more urgent non-rook move exists.

1393.label: Players make aggressive or space-gaining moves (usually pawn advances) when their own king urgently needs defensive attention, catastrophically weakening their shelter or leaving tactical vulnerabilities unaddressed.
1393.description: In 9/9 positions, the player's king had an urgent safety concern—either an exposed king needing shelter (positions 2, 4, 5, 7 with weakened castled positions), an uncastled king needing to evacuate (positions 3, 6, 9, 10), or a piece threat targeting the king area (position 8). In all cases, the best moves prioritized king safety: castling (position 6), king relocation (positions 3, 10), maintaining shelter pawns intact (positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 9), or prophylaxis against incoming threats (position 8). Instead, 7/9 moves were pawn advances—with 5/9 specifically pushing pawns directly in front of their own king (g5, g6, f3, g4, f5), stripping critical defensive cover. The remaining moves (a5, e5, Rf3, Nd4) pursued queenside/central ambitions while ignoring the king's plight. The average cp_loss of 1314 reflects how catastrophically these positions punish neglected king safety, with multiple positions converting to forced mate.

1402.label: An already-exposed king advances or centralizes into a square where enemy pieces exploit it with checks, forks, or mating nets, when non-king alternatives offered better resistance.
1402.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves where an already-exposed king advances or centralizes into greater tactical vulnerability. In 9/10 cases, the king moves toward the center or forward (toward enemy forces) rather than retreating. The positions are already difficult (avg starting eval heavily favoring the opponent), but the king move catastrophically worsens things — avg cp_loss of 3756, with 6/10 resulting in forced checkmate. In 8/10 positions, the better alternatives were non-king moves (pawn breaks like f5/g6, captures like Qxb5, piece moves like Ba3/Rg7) that disrupted the opponent's coordination before committing the king. Only 2/10 had the same king move as best but with critical move-order differences. The consistent thread is a player who sees their king is awkwardly placed and instinctively tries to 'improve' it by walking toward activity, but the destination square is precisely where enemy piece geometry (rook checks along files, queen diagonal checks, bishop-supported mating nets) can exploit the king most efficiently.

1383.label: Pawn captures or active-looking moves that inadvertently remove a pawn from a hidden defensive role, leaving a piece or king tactically vulnerable.
1383.description: 8/10 positions involve pawn moves (7/10 specifically pawn captures) where the moved pawn was quietly performing a critical defensive function—shielding the king, maintaining tension that pinned an opponent's pawn to a defensive duty, or indirectly supporting another piece. In positions 1 and 7, the g-pawn captured away from the king/piece it was guarding (gxf4 removed king shield; gxf5 left the g5 knight hanging). In positions 3, 6, and 9, the captured pawn was maintaining tension that kept an opponent's pawn tied to a defensive duty (exd4 freed c3 to capture the bishop; c4 removed c3's ability to recapture on d4, leaving the queen capturable; cxd4 ignored h3's threat to the knight). In positions 8 and 9, the pawn capture was made while ignoring an existing hanging piece (knight on g4 capturable by Qxg4/hxg4). Positions 4, 5, and 10 extend the pattern: active-looking moves (Kg1, Nxf2, Nd7+) that ignore the most urgent defensive requirement. Across all 10 positions, the player chose a 'tempting' or 'natural' capture/advance while being blind to the defensive role being abandoned.

1401.label: Moving a bishop to aggressively attack an enemy piece while ignoring a more critical positional or tactical need, resulting in the attack being easily refuted or losing tempo.
1401.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop move (the lone exception is Nc4, a minor piece to the same type of 'aggressive outpost'). In all cases, the piece moves to a square that appears to create an immediate threat against a higher-value enemy piece — 6/10 directly attack the opponent's queen (positions 3, 6, 9, 10) or rook (positions 1, 5, 7), while the others centralize aggressively. The common failure is that these 'attacks' are illusory: in 4/10 positions the attacked piece escapes with a stronger counter-threat (check in positions 9, 10; back-rank invasion in position 3; deflection in position 6). In 3/10 positions the bishop move ignores a far more urgent need (capturing a hanging piece in position 8, eliminating a passed pawn in position 9, generating counterplay in position 7). In 2/10 positions the bishop abandons a critical defensive duty (blocking Qg6+ in position 2, protecting c6 in position 5). The average cp_loss of 1177 reflects that these superficially active moves often catastrophically misread the position's true demands.

1411.label: Playing a quiet developing move while the player's own queen is directly attacked or en prise, allowing it to be captured.
1411.description: In 9/9 positions, the player's queen was under direct attack by an opponent's piece or pawn, and instead of moving the queen to safety, the player made a routine developing move (bishop, knight, or rook to a natural square). In every single case, the opponent could simply capture the queen — often with check or fork — resulting in catastrophic material loss. The attacked queens sat on central squares (d5, e3, f6, d4, d2, c7, d3, c2, c7) and the attacking pieces were predominantly knights (7/9) or a pawn (1/9). The 'developing' moves were always non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no threats) — purely positional improvements like Bd7, Be2, Nge7, Bd3, Rad1, Rc8, Nc3, Be2, Rad8. The best moves in every position involved simply moving the queen to a safe square, confirming this is a pure oversight pattern rather than a miscalculation.

1406.label: The queen (or key piece) captures peripheral material or moves to an offside square, abandoning a critical defensive or attacking function and allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated responsibility.
1406.description: 9/10 positions involve the queen moving to capture or target material (usually a pawn) on the board's periphery, while 1/10 (Bc1) shows the same pattern with a bishop. In 6/10 cases the move is a direct pawn capture (Qxf4, Qxb2, Qxa7, Qxg3, Qxh2, Qxh7), in 1/10 the queen moves to target a pawn (Qb4→a4), in 1/10 the queen relocates to a seemingly dominant but tactically vulnerable square (Qd4), and in 1/10 the queen gives a purposeless check (Qb7+). The common punishment is that the piece abandons a specific duty: guarding a critical square (Bc1 abandons c5 allowing Nc5+ fork; Qxf4 abandons d5 allowing Nd5+ fork), maintaining attacking pressure (Qxb2, Qxg3, Qxh2 all abandon winning attacks for a pawn), or keeping the opponent's king under constraint (Qxa7 allows perpetual, Qb7+ loses the winning technique, Qxh7 drops c4 with check). The average cp_loss of 1226 reflects that these greedy diversions often convert winning positions into draws or losses. All 10 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag, confirming that the fundamental error is wasting a move on material that doesn't contribute to the position's primary demand.

1400.label: Aggressive captures or flashy moves that prioritize immediate material gain while catastrophically ignoring the position's most urgent tactical requirement.
1400.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: the player chose a materialistic or aggressive-looking move while being blind to the single most critical tactical demand of the position. In 6/10 cases, the move was a direct capture (Qxh2, Qxe7, Nxc4, Rxh7, Qxg7, c5+). In 4/10 cases, it was an aggressive queen move or check (Qf6, Qf3, Qf3, Qe1+). The critical requirement being ignored varied: 4/10 ignored an immediate mating threat from the opponent (positions 5, 8, 9, 10), 3/10 missed a superior forcing tactical sequence that was available (positions 2, 3, 7), and 3/10 left their own pieces hanging or miscoordinated by prioritizing attack over structural integrity (positions 1, 4, 6). The average cp_loss was enormous (3974), and critically, only 1.4 good moves were available on average — meaning these were razor-sharp positions where ONE specific response was required and the player chose the tempting but wrong alternative. 8/10 positions feature a queen making or enabling the error, and in all cases the opponent had a clear, forcing punishment available.

1394.label: Player makes a positional repositioning move while failing to notice an urgent capture or tactical vulnerability requiring immediate concrete action.
1394.description: In 8/10 positions, the best move involved either capturing a hanging/vulnerable enemy piece (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 9) or protecting one's own piece from immediate capture (positions 2, 7, 8). Instead, the player chose a 'quiet' repositioning move — typically a bishop development (Bd2, Be3, Bc4, Bd4 in 4/10) or a king move (Kh5, Kxg2, Kc2, Kh7 in 4/10). The critical commonality is that all 10 moves look 'natural' or 'improving' in isolation (developing, centralizing, fleeing) but completely ignore the concrete tactical demand of the position. In 7/10 cases the blunder directly leaves a piece hanging or creates an immediate tactical vulnerability that wasn't present before (queen hanging in positions 4 and 8, bishop capturable in 3 and 9, pawn hanging in 2, king walking into mate in 1, enabling sacrifice in 7). The average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical moments demanding precise calculation rather than general improvement.

1405.label: Moving a knight away from a powerful or functionally essential square to a seemingly attractive destination (check, capture, or centralization), abandoning its vital role.
1405.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a knight move that relocates the piece from a square where it serves a critical function. In 8/10 cases, the knight departs a strong established outpost (e2, d6, f6, f5, e5, e4, b4) where it was either supporting a mating attack, blocking an open file, paralyzing the opponent's position, or anchoring a defensive structure. In 6/10 cases the move involves a capture or check — superficially forcing moves that create the illusion of progress. The destinations look appealing: Nf4 attacks h3, Nd6+ gives check, Nxg4 wins a pawn, Nxd6 eliminates a passed pawn, Nxc5 wins material, Ne4 centralizes. But in every case, the knight's PREVIOUS square was performing irreplaceable work — blocking the e-file (Position 9), controlling g1 for a mating net (Position 1), maintaining Nc2+ fork threats (Position 5), shielding the king (Positions 3, 6), or supporting a direct king attack (Position 10). The average cp_loss of 1110 reflects that many of these positions had a single brilliant alternative (avg 1.6 good moves) that the knight move completely abandoned.

1413.label: Advancing a strategically valuable pawn (usually with check) that gets immediately captured, eliminating a critical restraining threat or secondary front.
1413.description: 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance that prematurely pushes a strategically valuable pawn forward where it is immediately captured or rendered indefensible. 6/10 moves deliver check (d2+, e6+, h3+, d1=Q+, h4+, h4+), reflecting the 'patzer sees a check' instinct, while 4/10 are non-checking advances (h3, e7, c4, c7) that push into easily captured territory. 9/10 positions involve passed pawns being advanced, and in every case the pawn was more valuable alive — serving as a restraining force pinning the opponent's king (positions 6, 10), creating an indispensable second front stretching defensive resources (positions 1, 7, 10), or maintaining structural tension (positions 4, 8). The better moves in all 10 cases involved NOT advancing the pawn: instead improving piece/king activity (Ke5, Ka2, Bd8, Ke4), maintaining the pawn as a living threat (d2 staying on d3, keeping h5 alive), or addressing other priorities first (Ra8, axb4, b4). 7/10 occur in endgames where every pawn is a precious asset, making the voluntary surrender especially costly (avg 189cp loss).

1410.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) to f1/f8 as a slow pseudo-castling maneuver when the position demands immediate active play or actual castling.
1410.description: All 10 positions share the exact same destination square: f1 for White or f8 for Black (the square the king occupies after kingside castling). In 10/10 positions, the king had not yet castled and remained on e1/e8. In 8/10 cases, the king itself moved to f1/f8 as a one-step 'artificial castling' attempt; in 2/10 cases, a piece (knight or bishop) retreated to f1, passively blocking the castling square. In every case, stronger alternatives existed: actual castling (O-O) was available in at least 6/10 positions, while the remainder demanded immediate tactical strikes (Ng5, Nh4, Nxe5) or active development. The average cp_loss of 1212 reflects how catastrophically wasteful these moves are—they surrender a critical tempo while achieving what castling would have done in one move (for king moves) or obstructing castling entirely (for piece moves). 7/10 positions were in the opening phase where development tempo is most precious.

1409.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move in a position that demands immediate tactical precision, gifting the opponent a decisive tempo.
1409.description: All 10 positions share the pattern of a non-forcing 'improving' move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played in a critically sharp position with very few acceptable alternatives (avg 1.7 good moves). 5/10 are rook moves to seemingly active squares (Rd8, Rb5, Rd1, Rd6, Rb3), 4/10 are king moves to seemingly better squares (Kh3 x3, Ke5), and 1/10 is a prophylactic pawn move (h6). In every case, the correct move was either a forcing tactical sequence (Nxf3, e7, Qh5+, Qd6), a precise neutralization of the opponent's key threat (Nf5, Rbe8, c4), or prophylactic defense against a specific tactical mechanism (Kh7, Rb8). The blunder moves all superficially 'improve' the position—contesting a file, centralizing the king, preparing future plans—but catastrophically ignore concrete tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 3919 reflects that these tempo gifts allowed opponents to execute winning combinations (discovered checks, mating attacks, forks, perpetual-denying moves) that would have been impossible with the correct response.

1414.label: King captures an enemy pawn on its own wing in a decided pawn endgame where the real race is happening on the opposite side of the board.
1414.description: 10/10 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames with decisive evaluations (all ±549 or greater). In all 10, the kings are separated on opposite wings of the board, and the capturing king takes an enemy pawn on the flank where it is already located, while the opponent's king is far away shepherding a passed pawn on the other wing. The captured pawn acts as a 'decoy' — its existence keeps the capturing king distant from the critical promotion race. 7/10 positions have cp_loss ≤ 4, meaning these captures are usually correct or near-optimal; the position is already decided regardless. The clearest error case (Position 9, cp_loss 57) shows the king being lured to g6 when it should race toward the queenside instead. The feature identifies the specific moment a king 'cashes in' a distant pawn in a pawn race that is already determined.

1415.label: A bishop is moved to an undefended square directly controlled by an enemy knight, which simply captures it.
1415.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a square where an enemy knight immediately captures it for free. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 7, 8, and the Bd3 in position 6), the capturing knight is centrally posted on e5, exploiting its control of g4 or d3. In positions 4, 9, and 10, the capturing knight sits on c5, g4, or d5 respectively. In position 2, a bishop moves to e7 where Black's f6-knight takes it. The single outlier is position 5 (f6+), which is a pawn overextension rather than a hanging piece. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 7, 8), the tactical pattern is compounded: after Nxg4 Nxg4, the recapturing knight also hangs to the queen (Qxg4), losing two pieces for one. The blundering moves are overwhelmingly bishop moves (9/10), played by Black in 6/10 cases, and the average cp_loss of 438 reflects approximately one full piece lost.

1403.label: Playing an attractive-looking minor piece move (capture, centralization, or check) that targets a secondary objective while missing the single decisive tactical opportunity in the position.
1403.description: 9/10 positions involve bishop or knight moves (6 bishop, 3 knight), with 7/10 being captures or checks that LOOK forcing but aren't the best. The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these positions had essentially ONE critical path that the player missed. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 7, 10), the player captured a lesser target while a much more valuable one was available (pawn instead of piece, knight instead of queen, weaker fork instead of stronger fork). In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 8, 9), the player made a natural-looking developing/centralizing move instead of addressing the urgent tactical demand. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 6), the player missed a forcing central breakthrough or sacrifice in favor of a plausible positional continuation. The consistent thread is that all 10 moves pass the 'looks reasonable at a glance' test but fail the 'did you check for something even better?' test.

1416.label: Playing a routine-looking developing or positional move while completely ignoring an immediate tactical crisis that demands attention.
1416.description: 9/10 positions feature piece development or repositioning moves (Nc3 x5, Nc6, Bg4, Bf8, Bb4) plus one quiet pawn push (a4), all played as if the position were calm when in fact an immediate tactical threat demands urgent attention. In 5/10 positions (all identical), White plays Nc3 ignoring a bishop directly attacking the queen on d1, losing the queen outright. In the remaining 5 positions, the moves similarly prioritize 'normal' piece placement over concrete threats: a knight moves to a square attacked by a pawn (Position 2), a pawn push removes a critical guard of a key square enabling a fork (Position 3), a bishop development removes a critical defender enabling forced mate (Position 7), a bishop retreat opens a file for devastating checks (Position 9), and a bishop move to an active diagonal allows tempo gain + back-rank exploitation (Position 10). The average centipawn loss is an enormous 1524, reflecting that these aren't subtle positional misjudgments but catastrophic tactical oversights. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning precise responses to the threats were required.

1412.label: Moving a piece (usually a bishop) to an undefended peripheral square where it can be immediately captured or won through simple tactics.
1412.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves, with 1 knight move (Na6) and 1 pawn move (h6). The defining geometric pattern is movement to rim squares: 8/10 moves land on the a-file or h-file (Ba6, Bh6, h6, Ba3, Bh4, Bh3, Bh4, Na6), with the remaining two (Bf4, Bb5) going to exposed squares near the edge. In all 10 positions, the piece arrives on a square where it is either completely undefended (5/10: Ba6, Ba3, Bh4×2, Bf4) or defended by only one piece that can be removed or the piece can simply be captured cleanly (Bh3, Bb5, Bh6). The refutations are overwhelmingly simple: direct captures (Nxa6, Qxa3, Bxh3, Nxb5), remove-the-defender tactics (Bxf3 then Qxh4), or knight sacrifices that win the hanging piece with check (Nxh3+, Nd3+). Only 1/10 positions required complex calculation to punish; the rest involved 1-2 move sequences to win material. The average cp_loss of 372 reflects near-piece-value blunders.

1407.label: Moving a well-placed piece (usually a knight) away from a dominant infiltrated or critical square to a seemingly active but actually inferior destination.
1407.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundering move involves voluntarily relocating a piece that was already optimally placed—either deeply infiltrated in the opponent's camp or serving a critical positional/defensive function—to a square that appears more active but actually degrades the position. Specifically: in positions 1, 5, 8, and 9, a knight is moved away from c2/d2 (deep infiltration squares pressuring the opponent's back rank or blocking critical files). In positions 3 and 7, a bishop abandons a dominant diagonal/outpost (a2 or b7) that was the foundation of all attacking pressure. In position 4, a knight leaves a powerful post (b7 attacking a rook) for the passive rim (a5). In position 6, a knight leaves d8 for f7 without check when e6+ with check was available. In position 10, a knight repositions passively (Nb5) when concrete forcing action was needed. 8/10 moves are knight moves, and 8/10 involve a piece that was on an infiltrated/dominant square before the blunder. The common thread is choosing apparent activity over actual effectiveness.

1418.label: Moving the queen away from a powerful attacking or restraining square to a superficially active but functionally inferior one, surrendering critical pressure.
1418.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves where the queen leaves a square of maximum influence — often threatening mate, pinning the opponent's king to a vulnerable corridor, or preventing a key tactical operation — and relocates to a square that looks reasonable but loses the position's critical tension. In 7/10 cases, the queen was directly pressuring the opponent's king or preventing a specific tactical blow (Positions 1, 2, 6, 9: queen on h2/g1/d2/h3 restraining the king; Position 9: preventing Qxc4+). In 3/10 cases, the queen move is a premature or misdirected check that actually improves the opponent's king position (Positions 5, 10: driving king to safety; Position 4: missing the right check direction). The destination squares consistently appear 'active' — central (e5, e6, f5, d7), checking (b4+, g4+), or aggressive-looking (h5, c6) — but fail to maintain the concrete threats the queen was generating. 9/10 moves are by Black, and the average cp_loss of 1224 reflects how catastrophic it is to release pressure from a dominant queen post.

1417.label: Rook moves that appear forcing (checks or material attacks) but miss a more decisive continuation in positions with exposed kings.
1417.description: All 9 positions feature rook moves that look aggressive—4/9 give check (Rb5+, Ra5+, Re5+, Rd4+) and 5/9 attack a pawn or piece (Ra6, Rg8, Rd8, Rg2, Ra5)—but all are aimless relative to the position's critical requirement. In 8/9 positions (all endgames), one or both kings are exposed, and the correct move exploits this decisively: 2/9 are missed checkmates in one (Rc6#, Rg6#), 2/9 require capturing a critical piece/pawn with check (Rxf3+, Rd7+ into Rxd2), and the remainder demand king restriction or dominant rook placement (Rh5, Re4, Rcc7). The blundered moves instead chase peripheral targets (pawns on a3, a6, d5, g5) or deliver checks that allow the opponent's king to escape to better squares. Average cp_loss of 2347 is extremely high, with 7/9 positions having only 1 good move available, confirming these are critical-precision moments where the 'obvious' active rook move is a trap.

1426.label: Advancing the h-pawn to challenge a bishop on g5/g4 near the castled king, creating a sacrificial target that the opponent exploits with Bxh6/Bxh3 or a bishop advance to f6/f3.
1426.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same geometric pattern: the player advances their h-pawn one square (h7→h6 for Black in 7 cases, h2→h3 for White in 3 cases) to 'put the question' to an enemy bishop actively posted on g5 (7/10) or g4 (3/10), adjacent to the player's castled king. In every case, instead of the bishop meekly retreating, the opponent punishes the pawn advance: 9/10 positions feature Bxh6 or Bxh3 as a top refutation (a sacrifice that tears open the king's pawn cover), and 2/10 also feature the bishop advancing forward to f6/f3 as an even stronger response. The average cp_loss of 258 reflects positions where concrete tactical alternatives existed (Ne4 forks, queenside attacks, central strikes) but the player chose a routine-looking prophylactic move that actively created the weakness the opponent needed. In 8/10 cases the h-pawn advance directly enabled a bishop sacrifice that exposed the king to mating attacks or won material, while in 2/10 it simply gifted a free pawn. All positions shared the king_safety tactical motif.

1408.label: Non-forcing moves (usually pawn pushes) that squander critical tempo in endgame positions where passed pawn dynamics demanded immediate concrete action.
1408.description: 9/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the core error mechanism, and 8/10 feature passed pawns as a dominant positional element. 6/10 blunders are literal pawn advances (e6, a6, g6, f3, h2, h5) that look purposeful but waste the crucial tempo needed for the position's concrete demands. 7/10 positions are endgames where a single tempo often determines whether a pawn promotes or a piece achieves a critical task. The average good moves available is only 1.5, indicating these are razor-sharp moments requiring precise calculation. In every case, the best move involved forcing piece play—checks (Rh7+, b6+, Rb1+), captures (Rxh3), or active rook repositioning (Re6, Ra2, Rb5, c5 break)—while the played move either pushed a pawn without immediate threat or moved a piece self-destructively. The 2/10 hanging-piece blunders (Rg2+, Rg3+) share the same underlying mechanism: they appear forcing but actually lose the critical tempo by gifting material, leaving the opponent free to execute their passed pawn plan.

1425.label: A rook aggressively invades the opponent's 2nd rank (7th rank) looking for activity, but the infiltration is premature and ignores more critical tactical or positional needs.
1425.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the opponent's back ranks — specifically 9/10 to the opponent's 2nd rank (7th rank from the attacker's perspective) and 1/10 to the 1st rank. The move always looks strategically appealing (a rook on the 7th is a classic positional advantage), but in every case it's premature or superficial. In 4/10 positions, the rook invasion came with check (Rd7+, Re2+, Rg2+, Rb2+), making the move even more tempting but no less misguided. The common punishment is that the rook becomes offside or tactically vulnerable: in 3/10 cases the opponent's king actually improves by being checked (positions 5, 7, 8), in 3/10 the rook gets captured or trapped (positions 6, 8, 9), and in 4/10 the rook simply ends up decoratively placed while the opponent exploits the real weaknesses in the center or on other files (positions 1, 2, 3, 10). Average cp_loss of 1123 reflects that these positions typically had one clearly superior concrete move (avg 1.5 good moves available) that was overlooked in favor of the seductive invasion.

1424.label: Voluntary middlegame king moves that abandon critical defensive duties or walk into tactical danger.
1424.description: All 10/10 positions feature a voluntary (non-forced) king move in the middlegame that appears prophylactic or repositional but creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities. In 6/10 positions (1, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 6), the king was defending a specific pawn or square from its original position, and the move abandoned that defense — Kc7 abandoned a7, Kd8 abandoned f7, Ka7 abandoned c7, both Kf8 moves created f7 weaknesses, and Kg7 exposed h7. In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 4, 5), the king walked directly into a mating net, allowing immediate or near-immediate checkmate. The average centipawn loss of 4091 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in checkmate within 1-3 moves. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions demanded precise non-king moves (piece retreats, captures, or prophylactic pawn pushes) rather than king repositioning.

1421.label: Moving the rook to a square that blocks the king's only escape route, enabling immediate or near-immediate checkmate.
1421.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a rook move played in a position where the king is under serious mating threats. In at least 7/10 cases, the rook physically occupies the king's only flight square, creating a fatal self-obstruction: Rh7 blocks h7 (king on h8), Rh2 blocks h2 (king on h1) in two positions, Rb2 blocks b2 (king on a3), Rg8 blocks g8 (king on h8 or f8) in two positions, and Rd8 blocks the d-file escape (king on e8). In 8/10 positions, the correct move was a king move (Kg8, Kg1, Kd7, Kh7, Kf7, Ke7), stepping the king to safety before the mating net closes. The average cp_loss of 7697 reflects that most of these self-blocks enabled checkmate in 1-3 moves. Only 1.1 good moves were available on average, confirming these are razor-thin defensive positions where the king's escape was the singular priority.

1404.label: In critical positions with king safety tensions, choosing a plausible aggressive move that narrowly misses the most forcing continuation, resulting in catastrophic evaluation loss.
1404.description: 10/10 positions feature exposed or weakly-shielded kings as the dominant tactical element. The average cp_loss is 3941 with only 2.0 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical moments requiring precise calculation. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 7, 10), a forced checkmate was available but missed in favor of a thematically similar but non-forcing move. In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 5, 9), the player chose an active-looking piece placement that abandoned a critical defensive or forcing function. In 2/10 (6, 8), aggressive piece development/sacrifice was tactically refuted. The moves consistently LOOK correct—they attack, centralize, capture, or check—but fail at the final step of precise execution: Qe5+ instead of Qg5+, Rd7 instead of Rd8, Rf8 instead of Rh8#, Kd5 instead of maintaining defensive stance. The feature fires on positions where the correct idea is visible but the execution is fatally imprecise.

1419.label: Playing a superficially attractive move (check, fork, capture, or aggressive jump) in a position where only one precise continuation works, wasting the decisive tempo.
1419.description: All 10/10 positions feature critical moments where very few good moves exist (avg 1.4 good moves), and the player chose a 'natural-looking' aggressive or materialistic move instead of the one truly decisive continuation. 6/10 moves are knight maneuvers (Ng5+, Nb4, Nb4, Ne4, Ne4, Nc7+) that look active—creating forks, checks, or centralizations—but miss the point of the position. 3/10 involve pawn captures (hxg5, fxg4, g6 preparing fianchetto) that prioritize material or slow development over forcing moves. 3/10 deliver checks (Ng5+, Qe6+, Nc7+) that accomplish nothing concrete. In every case, the best move required deeper calculation: a rook activation (positions 1, 9), an urgent defensive capture (positions 2, 7), a forcing queen check or sacrifice (positions 5, 6, 10), or addressing a concrete threat rather than launching counterplay (positions 3, 4, 8). The average cp_loss of 4120 reflects that these 'tempting' moves catastrophically squander positions that demanded precision.

1427.label: Greedy bishop captures an undefended a-file pawn (a2 or a7) and gets permanently trapped by a b-pawn advance.
1427.description: 5/10 positions show the exact same geometric pattern: a bishop captures an undefended pawn on a2 or a7, then gets trapped by the opponent advancing b3 or b6 respectively, sealing the only escape diagonal. Positions 1, 10 feature Bxa2 trapped by b3; positions 3, 4, 6 feature Bxa7 trapped by b6. In all five cases, the bishop has no escape squares because the b-pawn blocks the diagonal while the opponent's c-pawn blocks the alternate retreat square (c2 or c7). The remaining 5 positions share the broader theme of greedy material-first moves that backfire: position 2 (dxc6 leaves own bishop hanging), position 7 (dxc3 allows recapture of bishop), position 9 (Rxd2 simplifies away a winning attack), positions 5 and 8 (non-capture moves that create fatal self-inflicted weaknesses). 7/10 positions involve captures motivated by material gain over positional considerations. The average cp_loss of 2078 reflects catastrophic consequences, often losing a full piece for a single pawn.

1431.label: A major piece performing a critical defensive function is moved to a seemingly active square, immediately leaving a key piece, pawn, or square undefended.
1431.description: In 10/10 positions, the blundering player moved a major piece (6/10 rooks, 4/10 queens) to what appeared to be an active or aggressive square—doubling rooks, invading ranks, giving checks, or capturing material—while that piece was currently performing an essential defensive duty. In 4/10 cases (Positions 1, 5, 8, 10), the moved piece was directly defending a critical pawn (a7, e3 rook, d4 pawn, c2 blockade). In 3/10 cases (Positions 3, 7, 9), a queen abandoned coverage of key squares near the king (f7, back rank). In 3/10 cases (Positions 2, 4, 6), a rook made a move that looked aggressive but lost tempo or allowed a favorable exchange/capture with check. The opponent's punishment in all 10 positions was to immediately exploit the specific thing left undefended: capturing an unguarded pawn (Positions 1, 10), taking an unprotected piece (Positions 3, 5), promoting a passed pawn (Position 8), or launching an attack on the now-unguarded king/squares (Positions 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 2057 reflects several catastrophic results (3 positions leading to forced mate), confirming these are not subtle inaccuracies but fundamental failures to recognize a piece's defensive function.

1420.label: A rook (or piece) makes an active-looking move to a square where it either hangs immediately or fatally abandons a critical defensive/supporting duty.
1420.description: 9/10 positions feature rook moves (the exception being Bg4 which leaves the queen hanging). In 4/10 cases (Rxf3, Rh8, Rb2, Rc6), the rook moves directly to a square controlled by an opponent's piece and is immediately captured for free. In 5/10 cases (Rh3, Rd2+, Rg5, Rd1, Rf6), the rook abandons a critical post — leaving a passed pawn undefended, destroying a mating net, or exposing the king — and the opponent exploits the vacated function. In all 10 positions, the blunder LOOKS active or purposeful (capturing material, giving check, attacking a piece, seizing an open file) but is catastrophically flawed. The average cp_loss of 1416 reflects the severity: these aren't subtle positional inaccuracies but gross miscalculations about what the rook's most important job is. Only 2.0 good moves were available on average, indicating these positions required precise rook placement with little room for error.

1423.label: Moving a piece away from its critical defensive role, leaving another piece or key square fatally unprotected.
1423.description: In 7/10 positions, the played move removes a piece that was the sole protector of another piece or critical square, immediately leaving something hanging: Kf2 abandons the queen on d1 (pos 2), Nc3 removes the d5 blockade shielding the d7 rook (pos 4), Ne5 removes the c6 knight defending the b4 bishop (pos 5, 7), Rg7 breaks the rook coordination protecting c6 (pos 8), Kc4 unblocks the diagonal to the f2 knight (pos 1), and Nc3 places a piece on a capture-with-check square exposing the queen (pos 10). The remaining 3/10 involve kings walking directly into mating patterns (Kd6 into Nb7+/Qe4#, Kg8 into Qg7#) or subtle endgame king race errors. The consistent thread across all 10 is that an apparently reasonable move (centralizing, developing, escaping) overlooks an immediate tactical consequence stemming from what the piece was guarding from its original square. Average cp_loss of 3098 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights.

1429.label: King moves to a square that immediately enables a devastating check winning material or forcing mate.
1429.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move where the king relocates to a square that directly allows the opponent to deliver a check that was not previously available (or not previously dangerous). In 10/10 cases, the primary refutation begins with or centrally features a check against the king on its new square: Qxb2+ (pos 1), Rh7+ (pos 2), Rf2+ (pos 3), Qxh4+ (pos 4), Rh5+ (pos 5), Rh1+ (pos 6), Qf8+ (pos 7), Qxf3+ (pos 8), Rxe8+ (pos 9), Qd2+ (pos 10). The check is always catastrophic — leading to forced mate (4/10), winning a full piece or rook (4/10), or winning decisive material through a combination (2/10).
