In 6/10 positions, the correct move was a king move to a DIFFERENT square that avoided the check vulnerability, while in 4/10 the player shouldn't have moved the king at all. The average number of good moves was only 1.3, indicating these are razor-thin positions where one square survives and all others lose. Notably, in 6/10 cases the king moved onto a rank/file occupied by enemy heavy pieces (2nd/7th/8th rank), directly entering the line of fire.

1433.label: Capturing a piece on an open file when the opponent's recapture delivers a lethal check exploiting back-rank weakness.
1433.description: 7/10 positions feature the exact same pattern: the player captures an enemy piece (almost always with a rook) on the d-file or e-file, but a second enemy piece recaptures on that same square with check, exploiting a fatally weak back rank. In positions 1, 3, and 10, White captures Black's infiltrating rook but Black's SECOND rook recaptures with check leading to mate. In positions 2, 5, and 7, Black captures White's rook/queen on e8 but White's second heavy piece recaptures on e8+ leading to forced mate. Position 4 follows the same exchange-with-check template but results in material loss rather than mate. The 3 remaining positions (6, 8, 9) involve rook/queen moves that abandon defensive duties near the king but don't follow the exact recapture-with-check template. Across all 10 positions, the average cp_loss is enormous (6711), and 8/10 had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating razor-thin margins where the 'natural' simplifying capture was the one fatal choice.

1435.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn advance on the a/b/c/h files in positions demanding immediate tactical action.
1435.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet single-step pawn advance on a wing file (b-file: 5 positions, c-file: 2, h-file: 2, a-file: 1) when the position contained an urgent tactical opportunity — a hanging piece to capture (4/10), a forcing sacrifice or combination (3/10), or a critical defensive/counterplay move (3/10). The average cp_loss of 2319 reflects catastrophic consequences, and only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow critical moments. In every case, the played pawn move addressed a non-urgent positional concern (preventing a knight jump, preparing a fianchetto, blocking a pawn, gaining space) while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis: undefended pieces (positions 3, 4, 7), forced mating attacks (positions 1, 5), discovered check combinations (position 2), or exposed king vulnerabilities requiring instant attention (positions 8, 9, 10). The moves are universally non-forcing — no check, no capture, no direct threat — giving the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, escape, or counter-attack.

1430.label: Moving a knight from f6 (or f3 for White) that was shielding a bishop on e7 (or e2) from capture, allowing the opponent to take the undefended bishop and exploit the consequences.
1430.description: 8/10 positions feature a knight on f6 (Black) or f3 (White) that was performing a critical shielding/defensive function for a bishop on e7 or e2. In all 8 cases, an opponent's bishop (typically on g5 for White attacking Be7, or Bg4 for Black attacking Be2) was being blocked by the knight on the f-file. When the knight moved away, the immediate refutation began with capturing the now-undefended bishop (Bxe7 in positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10; Bxe2 in positions 7, 9). The remaining 2/10 positions (6 and 8) still involve knights abandoning critical defensive posts but with different specific tactical consequences. In 7/10 positions, the knight moved FROM f6 specifically. The subsequent exploitation after the bishop capture varied: fork on d5 (positions 1, 3), e-file pin (position 2), pawn structure collapse via Rxg7 (position 5), knight invasion to e4/c6 (positions 4, 10), or deflection/fork sequences (positions 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 276 reflects that these are severe tactical oversights disguised as natural-looking improving moves.

1422.label: Playing slow, non-forcing moves (especially pawn pushes) in critical positions where only one concrete action maintains the advantage or avoids disaster.
1422.description: 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available (avg 1.5), yet the player chose a non-forcing, 'improving' move that lost a critical tempo. 6/10 moves played were pawn pushes (g4, g4, g5, e4, fxe5, b4), while the remaining were quiet piece shuffles (Kc3, Rae1, Kf8, Qe6). In contrast, the best moves typically required concrete piece actions: tactical captures (Nxe5 in positions 5 and 6), checks (Bd4+ in position 8), rook lifts to deliver mate (Rh1 in position 10), or forcing pawn breaks (b5 in position 4). The 'tempo_loss' tactical motif was explicitly identified in 4/10 positions, and 'missed_tactic' appeared in 8/10. The average cp_loss of 2114 reflects catastrophic consequences—including two positions where forced checkmate was available but missed in favor of irrelevant pawn pushes. Position 2 (b4, 0cp loss) appears to be a false positive where the pawn push happened to be correct.

1432.label: Moving a rook to an open file/rank to confront the opponent's queen, while overlooking a much more forcing tactical continuation.
1432.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves to open files or ranks. In 9/10 cases, the rook move directly targets or confronts the opponent's queen along that line (Re1 attacking Qe2/Qe4, Rf1 attacking Qf2, Rh1 attacking Qh2, Rf8 attacking Qf5/Qf7, Re8 challenging Qe7, Rd5 attacking Qg5, Rd2 attacking Qe2). In 9/10 positions, this 'natural aggressive' rook move is a mistake (avg cp_loss ~3900 excluding the one correct move), typically because a far more devastating forcing sequence existed — often involving the player's own queen delivering checks or immediate checkmate (Qg1# in position 5, Qh1# in position 8, Qh3+ forcing sequence in position 2, Qxe6+ in position 4). The rook moves are seductive because they look active and threatening, but 7/10 times the opponent simply captures the rook or ignores it to exploit the newly created vulnerability (back-rank exposure in positions 7 and 10, discovered checks in positions 1 and 6).

1437.label: Queen captures a pawn for material gain while ignoring superior tactical or positional considerations, typically exposing the player's own king or missing a forcing sequence.
1437.description: All 10 positions feature queen captures (Qx__), with 9/10 capturing pawns and 1/10 capturing a bishop. In 8/10 positions, the queen capture is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 1179 for the blunders), while 2/10 happen to be the best move. The consistent thread is a materialistic queen capture that prioritizes winning a pawn over more pressing demands. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 8, 10), the greedy capture displaces the queen from a defensive or dominant square, exposing the player's own king to tactical exploitation via discovered checks, diagonal attacks, or forced queen exchanges. In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 9), the capture misses a significantly stronger forcing continuation (sacrifices or mating attacks). King exposure is the dominant consequence, appearing as the refutation theme in 7/10 positions. The average number of good alternative moves was only 1.6, indicating these were critical decision points where the 'obvious' material grab was uniquely punished.

1440.label: A bishop moves to h6 (White) or h3 (Black) targeting the opponent's g-pawn in a speculative kingside attack that is tactically unsound.
1440.description: All 10/10 positions involve a bishop moving to the h-file's third/sixth rank (Bh6 for White, Bh3 for Black) aiming at the opponent's g-pawn near their castled king, typically in conjunction with a queen already on the g-file (Qg3/Qg6). In every case, the move is premature and creates no forcing threat. 8/10 positions feature the attacking side having significant underdevelopment or unresolved positional issues (hanging pieces, uncastled king, undeveloped knights). The bishop consistently becomes a liability: in 3/10 cases it gets trapped, in 3/10 it's left hanging after its sole defender is deflected or distracted, and in 4/10 it simply wastes tempo while the opponent exploits something else left undefended. The average cp_loss of 288 confirms these are severe blunders. In 7/10 positions, better moves involving development, castling, or addressing structural weaknesses were available within 30cp of optimal.

1439.label: Moving a bishop to the h1 corner where it becomes trapped or irrelevant, wasting a critical tempo.
1439.description: 6/10 positions feature the literal move Bh1, where the player retreats a bishop (typically from an active central square like e4, f3, or g2) to the h1 corner. In all 6 Bh1 cases, the bishop was performing a vital role on its original square — controlling key diagonals, pressuring enemy pawns, or contributing to defense — and the retreat to h1 either trapped it (3/6 positions saw White seal it in with f3), removed it from critical defensive duties (2/6 allowed promotion or mating attacks), or simply surrendered a dominant centralized piece for a passive corner placement (1/6). The remaining 4/10 positions share the broader theme of displacing a piece to an irrelevant square while ignoring urgent tactical demands (Qa2+ as a pointless check, Be5 abandoning c6, O-O-O walking into an attack). In 9/10 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of the best, confirming these were critical moments where the wasteful retreat was maximally punished.

1438.label: Playing an attractive-looking knight jump to a central outpost when the position demands a more immediate forcing or defensive move.
1438.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight jumping to a classically 'strong' square (e5 in 5 cases, e4 in 2, d5 in 2, b4 in 1), creating what appears to be a powerful centralization or outpost. However, in every case, the position demanded something more concrete — a forcing check (positions 5, 10), a defensive move to protect a hanging piece (positions 1, 2, 6), a prophylactic move addressing king safety (position 8), or a preparatory move to avoid being kicked with tempo (positions 3, 7, 9). The tempo spent on the knight move consistently allows the opponent to exploit a specific tactical vulnerability: 8/10 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' in the analysis, and 8/10 involve a 'missed_tactic'. In 6/10 cases the centralized knight is immediately challenged, deflected, or captured with tempo (via Qh3, Bb5+, d5, Bxd5, Qd5+, or Nxg4). The average centipawn loss of 1116 (with one missed mate) reflects how costly it is to choose aesthetic piece placement over concrete demands.

1428.label: Moving a minor piece to a square aligned with the player's own exposed king, enabling capture with check or tactical exploitation of that alignment.
1428.description: In 8/10 positions, a minor piece (knight or bishop) is moved to a square that lies on the same file, rank, or diagonal as the player's own king and an enemy attacking piece, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 7/10 cases, the piece can be captured with check or triggers a sequence involving check along that shared line (Be6 captured by Qxe6+ through f7 to king on g8; Ne2 captured by Bxe2+ along diagonal to king on d1; Bd6 captured with check along diagonal to king on b8; Nge7 enabling captures along the e-file toward king on e8; Nb7 self-blocking the king's escape enabling Bxd6+ mate). The remaining positions involve removing a piece FROM a critical defensive line (Be7 leaving the back rank; Qf6 abandoning c7 defense). 9/10 positions feature severely exposed or uncastled kings. 9/10 are Black moves. The average cp_loss is enormous (3040), with 5/10 resulting in forced mate, reflecting how placing a piece on the king's vulnerable line creates catastrophic tactical collapses. Position 6 (0 cp loss) is the sole exception where Bd6 was actually the best move in an already-winning position.

1436.label: In rook endgames, passively repositioning the rook behind own passed pawn (or to a non-restraining square) when the rook's current active placement was the critical factor holding the position.
1436.description: 7/10 positions feature the rook moving to the 1st or 8th rank, almost always behind the player's own passed pawn (Ra1 x3, Rc1, Rc1+, Ra8, Rb8). In 6/10 of these, the rook was previously placed on the 2nd or 7th rank exerting critical pressure on opponent's pawns (especially f2) or constraining the opponent's king. The best moves in 8/10 positions involved maintaining rook activity—staying on the 2nd/7th rank, giving intermediate checks, or capturing actively—rather than retreating. The pattern represents a misapplication of the 'rook belongs behind passed pawns' principle at moments when the rook's restraining function (preventing king advance, pressuring pawns) is more valuable than supporting the passer. All 10 positions are rook endgames, 8/10 are played by Black, and the average centipawn loss of ~1189 confirms these are catastrophic errors that typically convert winning/equal positions into losing ones.

1443.label: Moving a second rook to double on a file where one rook already sits, wasting a critical tempo when an immediate tactical strike was available.
1443.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player moving their second rook to a file already occupied by their first rook (doubling rooks), when a more forcing concrete action was available. In 6/10 cases, there was an immediate capture or sacrifice available (Rxc2, Rxa3, Bxd3, Bxg2, Rxh7, Nf6+). In 10/10 cases, the rook doubling was a preparatory/building move that gave the opponent exactly one tempo to consolidate, defend a weakness, or launch a counter-resource. The best moves were always more direct: immediate captures (positions 1, 6, 8), piece exchanges to resolve tactical tensions (position 5), sacrifices (position 9), checks (position 4), or queen activations (position 10). The average cp_loss of 280 reflects how devastating this single wasted tempo consistently is. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precision rather than slow buildup.

1434.label: Tempo-wasting pawn advances (or queen moves) aimed at chasing aggressive pieces that have devastating forward tactical continuations instead of retreating.
1434.description: 7/10 positions feature pawn kicks (h6, h3, or a6) directed at aggressively-posted pieces (usually a knight on g5, but also Ng4, Bg4, or Nb5), where the player assumes the attacked piece must retreat. In 5/10 cases specifically, h6 targets a knight on g5 that instead leaps forward (Nh7 fork, Nxf7+ fork, Nxe6 sacrifice) or enables a combination on the vacated square (Bh7+). The remaining 3/10 are queen moves (Qg3, Qh5, Qe6) that similarly waste tempo while ignoring critical tactical vulnerabilities—placing the queen where it can be captured, trapped, or exploited via checks. Across all 10 positions, the common thread is a move whose sole purpose is displacing or threatening an enemy piece, failing to recognize that the piece has no obligation to retreat and that the tempo spent creates or ignores a devastating tactical blow. The average cp_loss of 336 reflects how catastrophically wrong these 'natural-looking' piece-chasing moves go. Only 1.3 good moves existed on average, showing these positions demanded precise calculation rather than routine responses.

1450.label: Queen moves to an apparently active square while abandoning a critical defensive function, allowing immediate tactical punishment.
1450.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move that relocates the queen away from a square where it performed an irreplaceable defensive task. In 7/10 cases the queen moved to the d-file (Qd5, Qd6, Qd3, Qd7×4), and 10/10 moved to central or semi-central squares that appeared active. The defensive duties abandoned include: guarding a knight on f6 (3/10: positions 3, 6, 10), defending a back-rank or key pawn (3/10: positions 2, 7, 8), providing a critical interposition on a diagonal (1/10: position 9), and covering a hanging pawn (1/10: position 4). In 8/10 cases the move was played by Black. The average cp_loss was 4027, with 4/10 resulting in forced checkmate. The moves consistently look purposeful—centralizing, capturing material, or preparing activity—but fatally ignore that the queen was the sole piece preventing an immediate tactical blow.

1452.label: The king captures an enemy piece (knight or bishop) that infiltrated next to it, exposing itself to tactical exploitation when a better recapture or intermezzo existed.
1452.description: In 10/10 positions, an enemy minor piece (knight or bishop) has infiltrated to a square directly adjacent to the king (f1, f8, or g7), and the player reflexively captures it with the king rather than finding a superior alternative. In 9/10 cases, the king moves from the g-file to the f-file (g1→f1 or g8→f8), displacing it from its safe shelter. In every position, at least one clearly better alternative existed: 6/10 positions had a rook or queen recapture that kept the king safe; 4/10 had a devastating intermezzo (check or fork) that should be played before addressing the intruder; and 2/10 featured positions where the intruder could simply be ignored in favor of a stronger attacking move. After the king displacement, opponents exploited via back-rank/file checks (positions 1, 2, 4, 8), knight forks gaining material (positions 4, 7), queen infiltration to exposed squares (positions 3, 5, 6, 9), or tempo gained for regrouping (position 10). The average cp_loss of 248 reflects how consistently devastating these reflexive king captures are.

1453.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (one square from promotion) without adequate preparation, allowing the opponent to blockade, capture, or neutralize it.
1453.description: All 10/10 positions feature the exact same structural error: pushing a passed pawn to the 7th rank (White) or 2nd rank (Black) — the square immediately before promotion — prematurely. For White, the moves were c7, e7, h7, a7, d7; for Black, f2, b2, e2, d2, d2. In every case, the pawn was more powerful as a latent threat on its prior square than as a concrete advance. 10/10 positions occurred in endgames (9 pure endgame, 1 middlegame). The refutations consistently involved either: the opponent's king stepping directly in front to blockade (6/10 positions: Kc2, Kf2, Ke2 responses), a rook seizing the file to capture the promoted piece (3/10: Rf7, Rd5, Rd2), or the king simply walking to capture the promoted queen (1/10: Kd7xQe8). In all 10 cases, the correct approach was to improve piece positioning FIRST — typically advancing the king to escort the pawn (7/10 best moves involved king moves like Kd4, Kb4, Kf5) or repositioning a supporting piece (3/10 involved bishop moves like Bf3, Be8). The average cp_loss of 1271 reflects that these moves frequently convert winning positions into drawn or lost ones.

1442.label: Non-forcing moves played when the position demands urgent action to address an immediate king safety emergency, either weakening the king's defenses or wasting a critical tempo.
1442.description: All 10/10 positions feature a severely exposed king (the player's own in most cases) under immediate or imminent tactical threat. In every case, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move — no checks, no captures, no direct threats — that either actively worsened king safety or squandered the last tempo needed to survive. Specifically: 3/10 moved a pawn that served as a critical shield (f4 removing f3 shield, d3 opening the second rank, g3 vacating g2), enabling immediate mating attacks on the newly opened lines. 3/10 moved the king to perceived safety that was actually worse (O-O into a weakened kingside, Kg8 onto a file that could be ripped open, Kf8 to a dark square immediately exploitable by Bh6+). 2/10 made irrelevant pawn pushes (a5, f4) while facing immediate checkmate threats, completely ignoring the crisis. 2/10 retreated pieces defensively (Bf8 saving a bishop from attack while mate-in-2 existed, Rh1 shoring up h3 while abandoning the g-file that prevented mate). The average centipawn loss of 5,586 reflects that 6/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate after the move. All punishments involved king-targeting tactics — checks, mating nets, or exploiting newly opened lines to the monarch.

1445.label: Playing a non-forcing bishop development/repositioning move when an immediate forcing continuation (check, capture, or sacrifice) was available and dramatically stronger.
1445.description: 9/10 positions feature bishop moves (Bh6, Bc5, Bc5, Ba6, Ba5, Ba6, Bf4, Bd3, Bf4) and the remaining position (h5) shares the same underlying error. In all 10 positions, the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move — typically relocating a bishop to an active-looking square — instead of an immediate forcing continuation. In 6/10 positions, a check or capture was the best move (Rfe1+ in pos 1, Qxc7 in pos 4, Qxf4+ in pos 6, Rxg6+ in pos 8, Bxc3 in pos 9, Qg2+ in pos 10). In the remaining 4, the bishop move created a specific tactical vulnerability (hanging piece in pos 5, dark-square weakness in pos 2, pawn fork in pos 3, Qg4 invasion in pos 7). The bishop moves consistently LOOK purposeful — attacking enemy pieces, developing to active diagonals, threatening positional pressure — but in every case they grant the opponent a critical tempo. The average cp_loss of 2259 reflects that these 'natural-looking' bishop moves occur in sharp positions where one tempo is the difference between winning and drawing/losing.
1445.old_chip: Slow bishop instead of forcing move

1447.label: A slow, non-forcing pawn advance to the 3rd rank (b3/c3/e6 etc.) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate tactical action or concrete piece play.
1447.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance to the 3rd rank from the mover's perspective (b3/c3 for White, b6/c6/e6 for Black). Every move is a quiet, preparatory pawn push—typically intending fianchetto, structural reinforcement, or slow positional plans. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded urgent concrete action: either capturing a piece (positions 5, 7), exploiting a forcing tactical sequence (positions 6, 10), addressing an immediate defensive crisis (positions 3, 8), or simply developing before the opponent creates threats (positions 4, 9). In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 9), the pawn move specifically opens a long diagonal exposing an undefended rook to queen or bishop invasion. In 6/10 positions, the error squanders a significant existing advantage by allowing the opponent time to consolidate or kick active pieces. Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these are sharp positions where this particular type of quiet move is especially inappropriate.
1447.old_chip: Quiet third-rank pawn prep wastes tempo

1451.label: A quiet one-square central pawn advance (d3/e3 or d6/e6) that blocks critical diagonals for the player's own pieces, squandering tactical opportunities.
1451.description: All 10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance on the d or e file to the player's third rank (d3/e3 for White, d6/e6 for Black) played as a 'solidifying' move in the opening. In 7/10 positions, the pawn directly blocks a critical diagonal needed by the player's own pieces: positions 1, 3, and 6 show ...e6 blocking the d7 square so the queen cannot simultaneously answer Qa4+ and defend a hanging Bg4; position 10 shows ...e6 blocking the f5 retreat for Bg4, allowing Ne5 to trap it; position 4 shows d3 blocking the bishop's retreat square; position 8 shows e3 creating a geometry where ...e5 forks two pieces. In the remaining 3/10 (positions 2, 5, 9), the pawn move is purely a tempo loss that allows the opponent to consolidate or neutralize concrete tactical shots (Nd4 fork, Nh4-Qh5+ attack, Nd5 harassing the queen). All 10 positions occurred in the opening with both kings in the center, and the average cp loss was 295, reflecting that these 'safe-looking' moves routinely cost near-piece-value advantages.

1457.label: A queen moves to h5 or h4 in a speculative kingside attack that lacks supporting pieces and loses tempo when easily repelled.
1457.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen moving to either h5 (7 positions) or h4 (3 positions), attempting a kingside attack that proves premature and unsupported. In 10/10 cases the tactical motif is tempo_loss — the queen lands on an exposed square where it can be challenged with simple developing moves (g6 kicking the queen in 6/10 positions, Nf3 gaining tempo in 2/10, Bg5 trapping in 1/10). In 9/10 positions, the player had clearly superior alternatives involving development, central pawn breaks, or concrete tactical wins (e.g., Bxb7 winning pawns, dxc5 exploiting a pin, f5 opening lines, c3 challenging a centralized piece). The average cp_loss is 302, reflecting how severely these moves squander existing advantages. In 4/10 positions the blunder occurred in the opening with pieces still undeveloped, while 6/10 were middlegame positions where a won or better position was thrown away for a phantom attack. Only 1/10 positions (position 5) resulted in an outright trapped queen; the remaining 9/10 simply lost multiple tempi when the queen was driven back.

1446.label: Non-capturing knight moves to seemingly reasonable squares that ignore the position's critical tactical demand, costing massive material or allowing devastating threats.
1446.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight being moved (never a capture) to a square that appears natural or useful but catastrophically fails to address the position's tactical crisis. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 9, 10), the knight abandons a critical defensive or offensive post (guarding a key square, maintaining pressure, or covering a checkmate threat). In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 6, 7), the knight move misses a far more important tactical opportunity available to the same or a different piece—including 2 cases where a queen could be captured outright. 10/10 moves are non-captures, and 8/10 are retreats or lateral repositions rather than aggressive advances. The average cp_loss of 1358 is enormous, and the average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical positions requiring precise action—not generic knight development. 3/10 positions involve disambiguation (Ngh6, Nbc3, Nfd7), suggesting the player specifically chose the wrong knight when two were available.

1441.label: Advancing a pawn (especially a passed pawn) without the necessary preparatory king centralization, piece repositioning, or forcing move to make it effective.
1441.description: 8/10 positions feature pawn advances as the mistake move, with 4/10 specifically advancing the b-pawn (three b5 moves and one b4). 7/10 positions are endgames with exposed kings on both sides, where the correct plan required king activation or piece repositioning BEFORE advancing the pawn. In the major blunders (positions 2, 6, 9 — averaging 506cp loss), the pattern is strikingly consistent: a passed b-pawn is pushed one square forward without the king first reaching a supporting square, allowing the opponent to establish an unbreakable blockade (Kc5 in position 9, Ba7 in position 2) or create counterplay on the opposite flank. Positions 4 and 7 show the same principle applied to central pawns — advancing f5 or d5 released tension and created structural weaknesses rather than maintaining pressure. Even the 2 piece-move outliers (Qg3, Bg5) follow the meta-pattern of choosing a 'natural-looking' non-forcing move when the position demanded captures, checks, or immediate tactical action. The 3 near-optimal moves (positions 1, 3, 5 with 0-1cp loss) confirm the feature detects the move TYPE — forward pawn pushes in exposed-king positions — regardless of whether they happen to be bad.

1454.label: King moves to a square that is immediately exploitable by checks, forks, or discovered attacks, when a safer alternative square (usually a corner or edge) was available.
1454.description: All 10/10 positions involve king moves that select the wrong destination square, walking into an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 7/10 cases, the best move was also a king move but to a different, safer square (typically Kh1 or Kh8 — the corner). The played moves chose more central or exposed squares: Kg7 instead of Kh8 (positions 1, 5), Ke2 instead of Kf1 (position 2), Kd8 instead of Ke7 (position 3), Kf1 instead of Kh1 (positions 4, 8), Kd7 instead of Ke8 (position 9). In 3/10 cases, the correct move wasn't a king move at all (Rxd4, Qxf7, d4). The average cp_loss was an extreme 3092, and on average only 1.1 good moves were available, indicating these are razor-thin decisions where one square difference is catastrophic. The consistent error is the king stepping onto a line (file, diagonal, or fork-target square) that the opponent's pieces can immediately exploit with forcing moves.

1444.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active or natural square while ignoring a concrete tactical vulnerability that the move either creates or fails to prevent.
1444.description: In 8/10 positions, the blundering move develops a piece (usually a bishop or queen) to an 'active-looking' square that either places it on a tactically exploitable square or abandons a critical defensive function. 7/10 positions feature the blundering side's king still in the center, making the tempo wasted on superficial development especially costly. In 6/10 cases specifically, a bishop is moved to an apparently natural diagonal (Bf4, Bg4, Bf5, Be6, Bc5, Bf4) where it becomes an immediate tactical target or removes itself from a needed defensive role. The remaining moves (Nh6, Qa5, Qb6, a4) follow the same logical error: choosing a 'reasonable-looking' move that ignores a concrete, punishable tactical reality. In every case, the best alternatives address the position's actual urgent demand — typically king safety, prevention of a specific tactic, or maintaining defense of a vulnerable point — rather than pursuing illusory piece activity. The average cp_loss of 293 confirms these are catastrophic errors despite appearing superficially reasonable.

1460.label: Rook moves to an active-looking square while abandoning a critical defensive responsibility, allowing the opponent to deliver a decisive tactical blow.
1460.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving away from a vital defensive assignment to pursue an apparently active goal — attacking a piece, centralizing, or contesting a file — that proves irrelevant to the position's actual demands. In 6/10 cases the rook abandons back-rank or key-rank defense, enabling mating attacks or 7th-rank invasions (positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10). In 2/10 cases the rook stops blockading or guarding against a passed pawn's advance (positions 1, 5). In 2/10 cases the rook leaves defense of a critical pawn or blocks the king's escape route (positions 4, 8). The positions are overwhelmingly already difficult (8/10 the side blundering is already losing), suggesting a psychological pattern where the player 'tries to do something' rather than hold a grim but necessary defensive stance. The average cp_loss of 5360 reflects that the defensive duty abandoned was load-bearing — removing it causes immediate structural collapse. The best moves in all 10 positions involved keeping the rook on its defensive post or making quiet non-rook moves (pawn pushes, king moves) that maintained the rook's existing guardianship.

1449.label: Queen moves (predominantly checks) in open positions with exposed kings that look forcing/active but squander advantage by failing to achieve anything concrete.
1449.description: 10/10 positions feature queen moves in open positions where both kings are exposed. 6/10 are direct queen checks, while the remaining include queen captures or aggressive-looking queen repositionings. 7/10 positions identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif — the queen move appears forcing but actually helps the opponent (typically driving their king to safety or allowing a tactical counter). In 8/10 blundering cases, a quieter or differently-timed move was far superior: quiet king moves (Positions 1, 7, 8), a different piece checking first (Position 2), an immediate checkmate (Position 3), a non-checking queen reposition (Position 4), or a check that gains material (Position 9). The average cp_loss of 1321 reflects catastrophic consequences. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these are precision-demanding positions where the 'natural' queen check is a trap. Position 5 fits as a queen capture (Qxc3 grabbing a pawn) that ignores threats — the same prioritization of apparent activity over concrete calculation.

1461.label: Active or defensive pieces are relocated to edge squares (a/h/b/g files), abandoning critical central duties or defensive functions.
1461.description: All 10 positions feature a piece moving to a rim or near-rim square: 8/10 land directly on the a-file or h-file (Nh5, Rh4, Nh4, Rh5, Rh4, Bh6, Ba4, plus Nb5/Nb4 on the b-file), while 2/10 land on g or b files (Qg4, Nb4). In every case, the moved piece was performing a crucial role—defending the king (3/10: Nh4 abandoned f3 defense, Nb5 removed king's last defender, Bh6 removed back-rank shield), maintaining coordination that tactically protected material (2/10: both Rh4 moves left pawns or files undefended), or occupying a dominant central outpost (2/10: Nb4 left d5, Nh5 abandoned central activity). The average cp_loss of 2040 is enormous, with 3/10 positions resulting in forced mate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than speculative rim maneuvers. In 9/10 cases, the refutation directly exploits the square or function the piece abandoned—capturing undefended material, advancing passed pawns through vacated files, or delivering checks through newly opened lines.

1455.label: Unnecessary pawn advances that remove a critical defensive function from the pawn's original square, allowing tactical exploitation of the newly created weakness.
1455.description: All 10/10 positions feature non-capturing, single-square pawn advances that appear active or prophylactic but actually destroy a critical element of the player's own defensive structure. In 7/10 cases, the advanced pawn was directly controlling a key square that the opponent immediately exploits (g5 guarding f4 in position 1, c6 guarding d5/d7 in position 7, b4 guarding c3 in position 10, f2 guarding the a7-g1 diagonal in position 5). In 2/10 cases (positions 6 and 9), the move 'puts the question' to a bishop that responds by advancing forward (Be7) rather than retreating, winning material. In 2/10 cases (positions 2 and 4), the pawn push wastes a critical tempo when a concrete tactical shot or urgent development was required. The average cp_loss of 256 and average of only 1.9 good moves available shows these are critical moments where the best alternatives consistently involved piece activity, development, or tactical shots rather than pawn advances. In all 10 positions, the refutation directly targets the weakness created by the pawn leaving its original square.

1468.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move (usually a king move) while an opponent's piece is hanging and can be captured for free.
1468.description: In 10/10 positions, the player had a simple one-move capture available that would win significant material — a completely undefended enemy piece sitting en prise. Instead, they played a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking move. 6/10 moves were king moves (Kh2, Kh2, Kg5, Kf1, Ke3, Ke7), 2/10 were rook retreats to e2, 1/10 was a pawn advance (d4), and 1/10 was a bishop retreat (Bf2). The missed captures span all piece types: capturing queens (3/10: gxf5, cxd4, Qxc2), capturing rooks (4/10: Nxe1, Qxe6, Bxd6, Qxf3), and capturing bishops (3/10: Rxe7, Bxg5, Rxe7+). All 10 positions had exactly 1 good move available, and the average centipawn loss was 2692, reflecting catastrophic oversights. The played moves consistently reflect positional thinking — improving king position, activating rooks, gaining space — applied at precisely the wrong moment when a tactical opportunity demanded immediate attention.

1464.label: Material-grabbing captures (usually with check) that trade away the very piece needed for a forced checkmate or drawing mechanism.
1464.description: All 10 positions feature captures of high-value enemy pieces (rooks or queens), and 7/10 are captures delivered with check, making them feel maximally forcing and natural. Yet in 9/10 positions (excluding Position 2 at 0 cp loss), a forced checkmate or perpetual check existed that required keeping the attacking pieces on the board rather than exchanging them. In 6/10 positions, the forced mate was in 2-6 moves — trivially short. The blunders consistently trade away the player's own key attacking piece (the rook needed for a mating net in Positions 1, 3, 6; the queen needed for mating checks in Positions 4, 7, 8; the knight needed for perpetual in Position 9). The average cp_loss of 5814 reflects that most of these convert forced checkmates into merely 'winning' positions. The captures target the opponent's strongest-looking piece (opposing rook on the same file, enemy queen), creating an illusion of decisive simplification when in fact the position demanded maintaining maximum attacking force.

1467.label: A bishop on g4/g5 retreats to h5/h4 instead of exchanging for the knight on f3/f6, becoming vulnerable to pawn attacks.
1467.description: All 10 positions feature a bishop that was actively posted on g4 (Black) or g5 (White), pressuring a knight on f3/f6, which retreats to h5 or h4 along the rim rather than capturing the knight. In 8/10 positions, the clearly best move was Bxf3 or Bxf6 (the immediate exchange). The refutation in 8/10 cases involves a pawn advance (g4 against Bh5, or ...g5 against Bh4) that further harasses the bishop with tempo, leading to a trapped or permanently passive piece. In 6/10 positions the tactical motif is explicitly 'trapped_piece,' while 9/10 feature 'tempo_loss' as a core tag. The average cp_loss of 259 reflects that the bishop typically ends up either captured outright or driven to a useless square (often g6/g3) behind its own pawns. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow decision points where the exchange was nearly the only correct continuation. 9/10 positions occurred in the opening phase with at least one king still in the center, making the wasted tempo especially costly.

1469.label: Playing a routine, non-forcing rook move to the e-file (Re1/Re8) when the position demands immediate tactical action.
1469.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook moving to the e-file (Re1 or Re8), with 1/10 being a similar passive rook repositioning (Rb8). In all 10 cases, the player chose a 'natural' developing rook move—placing it on an open or semi-open central file—while ignoring an immediate concrete tactical opportunity. 8/10 positions had a forcing tactic available (Nxf3+ winning a piece, Bxf2 winning a pawn, Bxg6+ with a crushing attack, exf6 resolving tension favorably, Ba4 establishing a deadly pin, e5 pawn fork, Nxe4 winning material). The average cp_loss of 1313 confirms these are catastrophic errors. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 7), moving the rook specifically FROM the f-file created a concrete defensive weakness—unguarding f7, enabling Greek Gift sacrifices, or allowing back-rank mates. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow tactical positions disguised as quiet ones, where the 'safe' developing move was actually the worst choice.

1459.label: Quiet piece repositioning moves that abandon a critical defensive or attacking function when the position demands urgent action.
1459.description: All 10 positions feature a non-forcing piece move (no checks, no captures, no immediate threats) that relocates a piece to a seemingly natural or 'improving' square, but fatally abandons its current critical function. In 7/10 positions, the moved piece was directly guarding a key file (e-file in positions 1, 8; d-file in positions 2, 4; critical rank/square in positions 5, 9, 10). In the remaining 3/10 (positions 3, 6, 7), the move chose passive repositioning over the single forcing/urgent continuation required. The best moves across all positions were overwhelmingly forcing or purposeful: pawn advances for counterplay (7/10 had pawn pushes among top options), forced exchanges (position 6), or tactical strikes (position 10). The average cp_loss of 293 reflects how these slow moves uniformly give opponents the tempo needed to execute winning tactics—pin exploitations (position 8), passed pawn advances (positions 1, 2, 7), skewers (position 3), or forced exchanges into won endgames (positions 6, 9).

1463.label: The queen voluntarily relocates away from a square where it was performing an essential defensive or coordinating function, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned responsibility.
1463.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move that displaces the queen from a post where it was defending a key piece, controlling a critical square, or maintaining pressure that constrained the opponent. In 5/10 cases the queen moves toward the board's edge or corner (Qa5, Qxa2, Qb4, Qb3, Qc5+), while in the remaining cases it retreats or shifts to a less functional central square. In 7/10 positions, the opponent's refutation immediately exploits a now-undefended piece or square (b4 fork on unprotected knight, Nxd5 capturing undefended pawn, Rfc8 winning abandoned knight, Qg2+ exploiting unguarded mating square, Nh5 attacking the misplaced queen with tempo). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 analyses and 'piece_activity' in 9/10, confirming the queen consistently moves to a less active square. In 4/10 positions the queen specifically leaves a piece unprotected (positions 2, 9, 10, and partially 1), in 4/10 it exposes the king (positions 3, 4, 8, 9), and in 3/10 it releases constraining pressure that allowed the opponent to consolidate (positions 1, 5, 6). Average cp_loss of 1294 reflects the catastrophic nature of abandoning the queen's essential duties.

1462.label: Moving a knight to the second/seventh rank (d2/e2/d7) that blocks friendly pieces or abandons critical defensive duties, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
1462.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight moving to the player's second rank (d2 or e2 for White, d7 for Black), with 1/10 being a queen moving to e2 into a knight's capture range. The tactical consequences fall into clear sub-groups: 4/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 9) involve the knight on d7 blocking the queen's escape route or creating a pin/fork target along a diagonal to the king; 5/10 positions (3, 5, 7, 8, 10) involve a knight on d2/e2 abandoning a critical defensive post (guarding c3, f2, d4, f3, or b7), enabling devastating forks or material raids; and 1/10 (position 2) places the queen directly on a square attacked by an enemy knight. The consistent thread is that these 'natural-looking' development moves to routine squares on the second rank create immediate tactical vulnerabilities that were absent before the move. All positions had 1-3 good alternatives available, suggesting these were avoidable errors where players defaulted to routine development without calculating concrete threats.

1465.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action or critical defensive duty.
1465.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-forcing piece moves (8/10 queen moves, 1 rook, 1 bishop) that reposition a piece to a seemingly reasonable square but catastrophically waste the tempo that the position demands for urgent action. In 6/10 cases, the best move was an immediate forcing tactical strike (Ne5 in positions 2/3, Nxd5 in position 4, Qe5+ in position 5, Qf6+ in position 8, Nd5 in position 6). In 3/10 cases, the best move was defending a specific critical square (Rc8 covering c7 in position 1, Qb8/Rc8 covering c7 in position 10, d5 contesting the bishop in position 7). In 1/10 cases, the best move was preparing immediate castling (Qe2 in position 9). The average good moves available was only 1.2, confirming these were narrow positions where only 1-2 moves maintained the evaluation. All 10 blundered moves share the characteristic of being 'building' or 'regrouping' moves — they look like reasonable positional improvements in a vacuum but ignore the position's concrete tactical urgency.

1448.label: Active-looking moves (advances, developments, checks, captures) that waste a critical tempo by failing to address the position's single most urgent demand.
1448.description: 8/10 positions featured a move that appeared purposeful—advancing a pawn, developing a piece, giving a check, or making a capture—but critically failed to address the ONE thing the position demanded. The positions are characterized by extreme narrowness (avg 1.8 good moves available), meaning precision was essential. In 6/10 cases, the played move put a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Ne5 hanging to a rook, Bf7 forkable by Ng5+, Na6+ getting trapped, Nxg6 abandoning f2 defense, Bc5 offering illusory defense, Bf4 exposed without coordination). In 4/10 cases, an irrelevant pawn advance (a4 twice, h4, h5) was chosen over the critical king activation or decisive pawn push. Notably, 2/10 positions (h5, h4) actually had 0cp loss, suggesting the feature detects the PATTERN of choosing a plausible secondary plan over the engine-preferred primary action, regardless of whether it's technically punishable. The positions split evenly between middlegame and endgame, and White made these errors in 8/10 cases.

1466.label: Bishop makes a capture or move that looks active but is inferior to a pawn capture or non-bishop alternative, costing significant evaluation.
1466.description: 9/10 positions involve a bishop move (8 captures, 1 quiet retreat) that appears natural or active but proves significantly worse than the correct alternative. The dominant sub-pattern (4/10: positions 1, 4, 6, 7) is capturing with the bishop when a pawn should have recaptured instead — the pawn capture gains space/tempo while the bishop capture trades away a valuable active piece. Another 3/10 positions (2, 9, 10) feature bishop captures that lose material due to tactical oversights (trapped piece, hanging piece left behind, or immediate recapture). Position 3 removes a critical defensive bishop from a blocking diagonal. Position 5 is a quiet bishop retreat ignoring urgent tactical demands. The outlier (position 8, b5) is the only non-bishop move. Across all positions, the average cp_loss is 342, indicating these are severe mistakes. 7/10 had only 1-2 good moves available, meaning these are critical decision points where the 'obvious' bishop move is a trap.

1471.label: Rook captures that exchange away the player's most active or dynamically important rook, relieving pressure on the opponent.
1471.description: All 10 positions feature a rook capture (Rx) that initiates or completes a rook exchange in the middlegame. In 9/10 cases, this constitutes a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 2056 excluding the 0-loss outlier). The consistent thread is that the captured/exchanged rook was the player's most dynamically valuable piece: 3/10 involved trading a rook dominating the 2nd/7th rank (positions 7, 8, 10), 2/10 traded away the player's last rook exposing fatal weaknesses (positions 1, 9), 2/10 traded an active rook when a free piece/superior capture was available (positions 3, 5), and 2/10 exchanged a rook that was the primary source of attacking pressure (positions 2, 6). In every case, the better alternative involved keeping the rook active — repositioning it (Re3, Rb3, Ra8, Rc8) or capturing a different target first (Qxe2, Raxa3, g3). The positions span both sides (Black 6/10, White 4/10) and feature open files in 9/10 cases, but the unifying error is always prioritizing material exchange over preserving piece activity.

1473.label: A quiet wing pawn push (a/b/g/h file) played for positional reasons while an urgent tactical opportunity or defensive necessity exists in the position.
1473.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing pawn advance on a flank file (5 on the b-file, 2 on the h-file, 2 on the g-file, 1 on the a-file) chosen over an immediate concrete requirement. In 8/10 positions, the blunder ignores critical king safety concerns (exposed kings on e1, unprotected kingside pawns, back-rank vulnerabilities). In 9/10 positions, a specific winning or essential tactic was available (Nxd3+ fork, Rc1+ back-rank mate, Nxc3 winning exchange, Qc5 winning bishop, Bc5 winning material, Bxc3 preventing Qa4+). The average cp_loss of 2215 reflects that many of these are catastrophic—4/10 positions involved missing mate or near-mate. The moves share a common strategic 'intent': challenging opponent's pawn structure (b3 undermining c4, b5/b6 attacking c-pawns, g5/g6 challenging f5/f-pawns, h5 cracking kingside). Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments requiring precision where the player defaults to generic positional thinking.

1456.label: Pieces move to aggressive-looking (often peripheral) squares while fatally abandoning a critical defensive function they were performing.
1456.description: In 10/10 positions, the played move removes a piece from a square or sector where it was performing a critical defensive or coordinating role—guarding another piece, controlling a key square, or maintaining a tactical threat. 7/10 moves land on the a-file or h-file (board edges: Nh4, Ra1, Qg1, Qh4, Qa5, Rh8, Qa3), pulling the piece far from the critical action. The refutations consistently exploit what was abandoned: in 5/10 positions the opponent captures a now-unguarded piece or pawn (Kxf3 in pos 3, Kxc3 in pos 5, Bxd6 in pos 8, Qxa3 in pos 10, Bxf3 in pos 1); in 2/10 the moved piece itself hangs (Qxh4 in pos 2, Qxa3 in pos 10); in 3/10 the opponent exploits the newly uncontrolled square (Qf5+ in pos 9, Re1+ in pos 4, Ne4 in pos 6). The average cp_loss of 2231 reflects catastrophic consequences, and only 2.1 good alternatives existed on average, meaning these were high-stakes moments requiring precision rather than 'active' moves.

1458.label: Positions where an exposed king creates a single-move-critical situation demanding immediate tactical precision.
1458.description: 10/10 positions feature at least one exposed or vulnerable king (weak pawn shield, king in center, king on open file/rank). The average number of good moves is only 1.4, indicating extremely narrow tactical corridors. The moves played vary widely in piece type (rooks, bishops, pawns, knights), but the positions consistently share this king-exposure dynamic. In 7/10 blunder cases, the player chose a 'natural-looking' move (developing Be2, attacking Bxg7, pushing f4, material-seeking Rh1/Nxc4) that ignored the king safety imperative—either failing to move their own king to safety (positions 3, 7, 9 where Kf2/Kd2/Kc1 was needed) or failing to exploit the opponent's exposed king with a decisive blow (positions 4, 5 where checkmate or piece wins were available). In 3/10 positions the player correctly found the critical king-exploiting move (Re1 back-rank infiltration, c2 promotion threat against distant king, e5 pawn advance). The feature fires on the POSITION TYPE rather than a specific geometric move pattern.

1474.label: Developing a knight to a rim square (especially a6 or h6) instead of capturing a hanging piece or delivering a forcing check.
1474.description: All 10 positions feature knight moves as the blunder, with 9/10 placing the knight on a rim square (6x Na6, 2x Nh6, 1x Nh3). In 8/10 positions, the best move available was a queen move — either capturing an undefended piece (positions 3, 4, 8, 10: Qxg4, Qg5, Qxg5, Qxb5) or delivering a forcing check exploiting an uncastled king (positions 1, 2, 5: Qa5+). The average cp_loss is 1260, reflecting that these knight moves squander enormous tactical opportunities. 8/10 occur in the opening phase with both kings still in the center. In 9/10 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed, making these narrow critical moments. The consistent thread is a player on 'developing autopilot' — placing a knight on a passive rim square as if following general opening principles — while completely missing a concrete tactical resource (usually a queen capture or check) that would have won material or seized a decisive advantage.
1474.old_chip: Passive knight to rim ignoring tactics

1477.label: Moving a rook to the back rank on an open file as a 'natural' developing move when the position demands concrete tactical action or addresses a more urgent priority.
1477.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the 1st or 8th rank on an open file (d-file or f-file), appearing to follow the textbook principle of 'occupy open files with rooks.' However, these moves are uniformly catastrophic (avg 2133cp loss). In 6/10 positions, a much stronger forcing tactical sequence existed (winning material, delivering checkmate, or executing a multi-check combination). In 7/10 positions, king safety was a critical unresolved concern — either the player's own king was uncastled/exposed (positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10) or the move created back-rank vulnerabilities (positions 1, 6). In 4/10 positions (2, 5, 7, 9), the rook placed itself on a square where it became an immediate tactical target via deflection, exchange exploitation, or trapping. In 2/10 positions (4, 10), a far superior move achieved the same rook activation PLUS king safety (O-O-O) or won material outright (Qc3+). The pattern reflects players defaulting to generic positional autopilot rather than calculating concrete requirements of the position.

1470.label: Choosing a superficially attractive move (capture, check, centralization) in a position where essentially only one specific move is correct, resulting in catastrophic evaluation loss.
1470.description: All 10 positions share an extremely narrow set of correct options (avg 1.3 good moves available), combined with a very high average cp_loss of 4169. In 5/10 positions, the move played was a material capture (Qxc4, Qxe4, Qxd6, Bxb5, or the pawn-grab motivation behind Kh3). In 6/10, the blunder was a queen move to a seemingly active square. In 4/10 positions, the blunder either missed a forced checkmate (positions 1, 3) or immediately allowed one (positions 5, 10). The consistent thread is that each move LOOKS like reasonable chess — it captures material, delivers check, centralizes a piece, or activates the king — but ignores the position's single critical tactical requirement. The 'tempting alternative' quality is what unifies them: Qb5+ looks strong but misses Nxe5+ mate; Qxc4 wins material but misses Qb8+ mate; Qd4 centralizes but abandons e1 defense; Qf5 looks active but unblocks a mating diagonal; Kf6 looks natural but walks into Nxd5+ fork. In every case, the best move required either deeper calculation or counter-intuitive thinking (a sacrifice, a retreat, an indirect move), while the played move was the most obviously attractive alternative.

1472.label: Playing a superficially logical capture, check, or developing move while missing the single most important tactical demand of the position.
1472.description: 9/9 positions share a common structure: the position has ONE critical tactical requirement (a hanging piece to capture, a mate to deliver or defend against, or a key piece to save), but the player instead makes a 'reasonable-looking' active move that addresses a secondary concern. In 5/9 cases the played move is a capture (Nxd7, fxg3, dxe6, Bxc3, axb3→a3), in 1/9 it's a check (Nd6+), and in the rest it's a developing or repositioning move. The missed critical requirement varies: in 3/9 positions a piece was hanging and freely capturable (fxg3 missed Qxh3, dxe6 missed Qxd4, Bg4 left Bc5 hanging), in 3/9 positions a checkmate was available or needed defense (Ra1 missed Ne7#, Nxd7 allowed Qxh2+/Qh1#, Bxc3 allowed Qa7#), and in remaining positions the critical demand was structural/forcing (axb3 vs a3, Qe4 vs Nd6+). The average cp_loss of 5462 and only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where only one move works, yet the player chose a distraction.

1479.label: A major piece capture (usually with check) that trades away the player's most dominant attacking piece, releasing all pressure and allowing the opponent to consolidate.
1479.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture of an equivalent piece (rook takes rook or queen takes queen), and 9/10 deliver check, making the move feel forcing and natural. However, in every case, the captured piece was a passive defender while the capturing piece was the player's most active, dominant attacker — the very piece generating the winning advantage. In 6/10 positions this was a rook exchange (trading an actively-placed rook for a passive one), and in 4/10 it was a queen trade. The common thread across all positions is premature simplification via an apparently strong forcing move: 7/10 positions had the player missing a tactical combination that required keeping the traded piece on the board (mating attacks, forks, coordination). The average cp_loss of 2172 reflects that 3/10 positions threw away forced checkmate. In 8/10 cases, the best move involved maintaining piece coordination or exploiting the opponent's weakness with the very piece that was traded away.

1475.label: Rook moves to a plausible-looking but critically wrong square, failing to address the most urgent positional demand (usually a passed pawn or promotion threat).
1475.description: All 10 positions feature a rook move that places the rook on a square that appears reasonable but is fundamentally misplaced relative to the position's most urgent demand. 8/10 positions involve dangerous passed pawns near promotion, where the rook needed to be on a specific square to blockade, capture the promoted piece, or get behind the passer. In 5/10 cases, the rook needed to reach the 8th rank (positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 8) but went elsewhere; in 2/10 cases it needed the 1st rank behind a passed pawn (positions 3, 10). The 'piece_activity' tag appears in 10/10 positions and 'tempo_loss' in 9/10, confirming that the core error is always about the rook losing a critical tempo by going to an inferior square. The moves often look like reasonable alternatives — same file but wrong rank (Rd7 instead of Rd8, Rf2 instead of Rf8), or wrong file entirely (Rb6 instead of Rh6, Ra8 instead of keeping centralized). The average cp_loss of 2042 reflects how catastrophic a single misplaced rook move is in these positions where only one or two squares maintain the evaluation.

1480.label: Advancing a passed pawn toward promotion instead of playing a more forcing move (usually a check) that wins material or maintains a mating attack.
1480.description: All 10/10 positions feature a passed pawn being advanced toward the promotion square, with 9/10 moves landing on the 2nd or 7th rank (c2, b2, a2, f2, e2, b2, b7, d7, b6). In 8/10 positions this occurs during endgames where the side to move holds a dominant material advantage (typically queen vs rook). Of the 8 actual mistakes (2 positions had 0cp loss and were correct), 5/8 missed an immediate forcing check (Qd5+, Qd3+, Qb8+, Qa1+, Qd4+) that would have won material or maintained a forced mate, while 3/8 involved premature pawn advances that needed piece support first (Nd7, Nf5, Ke5, or d4 were better). The average cp_loss of 2011 is inflated by positions 1-2 where forced mates were squandered. The consistent theme is that the player sees a pawn one or two squares from queening and reflexively pushes it, neglecting that a tactical intermezzo (especially a check) would have been far more forcing.

1478.label: The king retreats to a corner square instead of capturing an adjacent hanging enemy piece (typically a bishop on h2/h7), or makes a passive backward move when an active forward move was required.
1478.description: 5/10 positions share an extremely specific pattern: an enemy bishop sits on h2 (or h7), directly adjacent to and capturable by the king, but the player sidesteps the king to the corner (Kh1 or Kh8) instead of taking it — these are the 5 highest-activation positions with avg cp_loss of 525. In all 5 cases, the correct move was Kxh2 or Kxh7/Nxh7, winning a free piece. The remaining 5/10 positions show a broader version of the same instinct: the king (or piece) retreats passively toward the back rank or corner (Ke1, Kd2, Kb1) when the position demanded an active forward move — centralizing (Ke5/Ke3), advancing pawns (g4/h4), or maintaining rook activity. 8/10 moves are king moves, and 7/10 place the king on the back rank or in a corner. The common psychological thread is timidity — fearing engagement with an enemy piece or advancing into apparent danger, choosing retreat over action.

1476.label: A rook (or major piece) is quietly repositioned to a seemingly natural square that either hangs to a bishop's diagonal or abandons critical activity.
1476.description: 8/10 positions involve rook moves and all 10 are quiet, non-forcing repositioning moves — no checks, no captures, no direct threats. The strongest sub-pattern is rooks placed on squares controlled by an opponent's bishop along a diagonal: 4/10 positions (Rc8 into Bxc8, Re5 into Bxe5, Re8 into Bxe8, Rc6 into Bxc6) show this exact 'diagonal blindness' where the player thinks in terms of files/ranks but forgets bishop geometry. Another 3/10 (Rc3, Ra7#8, Rc2) involve abandoning an active rook post (7th/8th rank or active file) for a passive square, immediately ceding the opponent decisive tempo or penetration opportunities. The remaining positions (d5, Ra7#2, Qe8) share the theme of choosing a natural-looking quiet move when a forcing or tactically urgent alternative existed. Average cp_loss of 295 confirms these are serious errors, and the average of only 2.0 good moves available indicates these arose in critical positions demanding precision.

1485.label: Passive king-safety moves (usually king retreats to edge/corner) played when the position demands immediate concrete action, squandering critical tempo.
1485.description: 8/10 positions feature direct king moves (Kh1, Kb7, Kc8, Kg1, Kh2, Kh8, O-O counted as king move), while the remaining 2 (b6 and Rg1/Rf7) are similarly passive moves motivated by perceived safety or consolidation. In 10/10 cases, the position demanded immediate concrete action — capturing hanging material (positions 7, 10), activating pieces (positions 2, 4), centralizing the king toward the correct zone (positions 1, 3), or maintaining pressure on an open file (position 9). Instead, the player chose a non-forcing, non-threatening move aimed at 'improving king safety' or 'prophylaxis.' In 10/10 cases the opponent punished this by executing the very plan the player should have preempted — advancing passed pawns (positions 1, 3, 7), invading on abandoned files/ranks (positions 5, 9), or capturing newly undefended pieces (positions 5, 6, 8). The average cp_loss of 405 confirms these are severe errors, not marginal inaccuracies. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions requiring precise play rather than quiet moves.

1483.label: Pushing a passed pawn forward in a simplified endgame position, regardless of whether king activation or other priorities should come first.
1483.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames, and all 10/10 moves are single-step pawn advances of passed pawns (a5, h5, g4, f3, a4, h3, b6, a6, a4, d3). The feature fires specifically on the concept of advancing a passed pawn toward promotion in simplified positions. 7/10 are on rim or near-rim files (a, b, g, or h files), with only 1/10 being a central pawn (d3). Notably, 6/10 moves are actually the engine's top choice (0 cp_loss), indicating this feature captures the *concept* of passed pawn advancement rather than purely mistakes. When these moves ARE errors (4/10 positions), the common failure mode is premature pawn pushing before completing king centralization (positions 1, 5) or ignoring urgent tactical threats in favor of the pawn advance (position 7's catastrophic b6 allowing mate-in-one). The positions universally feature exposed kings, open centers, and material imbalances typical of converted endgames.

1488.label: A rook slides laterally along the back rank, abandoning a contested open file where it was needed for defense or attack.
1488.description: In 10/10 positions, a rook moves sideways along a rank (almost always the back rank) from a critical open file to a less important file. Specifically, 8/10 involve abandoning the d-file or e-file — the central contested open files where both sides had rooks facing each other. In every case, the correct move involved either exchanging rooks on the contested file (Positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 9), actively advancing the rook up that file (Positions 7, 10), or first neutralizing the opponent's tactical potential before relocating (Position 3). The lateral rook moves are universally non-forcing (0/10 are checks or captures), passive repositions that give the opponent immediate control of the abandoned file. The consequences follow a consistent pattern: the opponent either invades on the 7th/2nd rank through the uncontested file (Positions 2, 8, 9), exploits the newly unguarded squares along the abandoned file for piece infiltration with tempo (Positions 3, 10), or wins material that was previously protected by the rook's file presence (Positions 1, 5, 7). Average cp_loss of 1283 reflects how catastrophic abandoning file control is in sharp middlegame positions.

1484.label: A pawn capture that fatally opens a line or removes a shield pawn near one's own king, allowing the opponent's already-positioned pieces to crash through.
1484.description: All 10 positions feature pawn captures (fxg6, hxg6, exd4, etc.) where the capturing pawn was part of — or adjacent to — the player's king shelter. In 8/10 positions, the capture directly opens a file (g-file in positions 1, 4, 7; e-file in positions 3, 6; a-file in position 8) or removes the last shielding pawn (positions 7, 9) against an opponent who already has major pieces aimed at that sector (doubled rooks on the g-file, queens ready to infiltrate via open files, etc.). In 4/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 8), the error specifically involves capturing with the WRONG pawn — choosing hxg6 over fxg6, exd5 over cxd5, axb3 over cxb3 — where the alternative capture direction would have maintained the critical shield. The average centipawn loss is enormous (3095), with 4/10 positions resulting in immediate checkmate or forced mate, demonstrating that these captures are not merely suboptimal but catastrophic. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical decision points with almost no margin for error.

1482.label: Repositioning a minor piece to a quieter square instead of making the forcing capture that the position demands.
1482.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a minor piece (7 knights, 3 bishops) to a passive or less effective square when the position demanded an immediate forcing move. In 9/10 cases, the best move was a concrete capture (Nxf7, gxf5, Nxe5, cxd5, Qxe5, Nxb7, bxc3, Kxc3/Bc7, Qxc3). The retreating moves shared a common geometry: pieces left active central or pressuring squares (e5, f4, d4, c4, d6, f5, g4) for peripheral or blocked squares (h3, h6, g4, b5, c2, d3, d7, f4). In 7/10 positions, the piece moved to a square where it subsequently became a tactical target (forks, pins, tempo-gaining attacks like ...h5 or ...Bf6). The average cp_loss of 257 reflects that these positions typically had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.3), meaning they were narrow critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than general development.

1481.label: Queen relocates to a seemingly useful square but abandons a critical defensive or coordinative function, leaving pieces hanging or key sectors uncontrolled.
1481.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves that relocate the queen away from where it was performing an essential function. In 6/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 7, 8, and partially 2), the queen directly leaves a piece undefended — specifically, in 4 of those cases the abandoned piece sits on d2 (bishop or knight). In 3/10 positions (2, 3, 10), the queen wanders to the flank (a5 or h5) abandoning coordination with active pieces or ceding control of a critical file/sector, giving the opponent time to invade or consolidate. In 2/10 positions (6, 9), the queen retreats passively (to f1 or f8) when an active alternative was required, resulting in overloaded defense or missed attacking opportunities. The common punishment mechanism is immediate tactical exploitation of what the queen left behind: simple piece captures (positions 1, 5, 7, 8), file invasions through uncontrolled squares (positions 3, 10), or neutralization of the player's initiative through simplification (positions 2, 6, 9). Average cp_loss of 446 reflects that these queen relocations typically convert winning or equal positions into lost ones.

1495.label: Moving a misplaced knight from a corner/edge square toward the center while ignoring a more urgent tactical necessity in the position.
1495.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight stranded on a corner or edge square (a8 in 4 positions, h8 in 3 positions, a1 in 2 positions, h1 in 1 position) where the player attempts to bring it back into play with a non-forcing knight jump toward the center. In every case, the knight activation is premature because a more critical tactical issue exists: 6/10 positions involved leaving a piece hanging or undefended (bishop on c4, queen on b3, rook on a8, etc.), 4/10 involved ignoring immediate king safety threats, and 3/10 missed a clearly stronger forcing tactic (check/capture). The move-order error is consistent: 7/10 analyses explicitly label this as a move-order mistake where the knight reactivation would have been correct ONE MOVE LATER after first resolving the urgent issue. The average cp_loss of 1262 reflects how catastrophic it is to spend a tempo on a slow repositioning move when the position demands immediate tactical attention.

1487.label: A knight makes a tempting aggressive move attacking enemy material, but leaves a critical square unguarded or lands undefended, getting punished by an intermediate check.
1487.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight making an aggressive jump to attack an enemy piece or pawn (queens in 5/10, rooks in 4/10, pawns in 3/10), abandoning a square where it served a crucial defensive or positional function. In 8/10 positions, the refutation involves an immediate check (Rxg6+, Rd8+, Bd4+, Qf5+, Qh5+, Bxh2+, Rf6+, R1g7+) that exploits the knight's departure—either winning the knight itself on its new undefended square (6/10) or unleashing a devastating attack through the square the knight previously controlled (4/10). In 9/10 cases, the knight's intended target (the piece it attacked) simply escapes or the opponent ignores the threat entirely because the intermediate forcing move is stronger. The knight consistently moved FROM a strong/useful square (f6 guarding kingside twice, e4 controlling key squares twice, d4 as central outpost twice, g5 as part of a mating net) TO an optically aggressive but tactically vulnerable destination.

1486.label: A heavy piece (usually rook) is placed on an open file/back rank when a different rook, piece, or move order was required.
1486.description: 9/10 positions involve a rook move (1/10 is a queen move to a rook's intended square), and 9/10 target the 1st or 8th rank along an open file. The moves all look like 'natural' piece activation—placing a heavy piece on an open file to pressure a target. However, 4/10 positions are explicit 'wrong rook' errors where the other rook should have gone to that square (positions 2, 5, 7, 9), preserving the original rook's control of a critical file or rank. 1/10 uses the wrong piece type entirely (Queen instead of Rook to c1, position 1). 3/10 are rook moves that should have been preceded by a forcing check with the queen first (positions 3, 4, 6—move order errors). 1/10 places a rook on a file where it immediately blunders to a back-rank tactic (position 8). Position 10 (0cp loss) fires because the geometric pattern matches—rook sliding laterally to attack—even though it's actually the correct move. The average cp_loss of 3873 is inflated by 4 positions where forced checkmates were missed.

1497.label: Player makes a capture using the wrong piece when a different piece on the same square (or a different capture entirely) would have been vastly superior.
1497.description: All 10/10 positions involve the player executing a capture with a suboptimal piece. In 5/10 positions (3, 5, 6, 7, 9), the Queen should have captured on e5 or h5 but a lesser piece (rook, bishop, knight, or pawn) was used instead. In 2/10 positions (1, 8), a Knight capture was required but the Bishop was used on e7/e4. In 2/10 positions (4, 6), a pawn capture was chosen over a piece recapture. In 1/10 (10), the Rook captured a pawn when the Bishop should have captured the opponent's last rook. The consistent thread is that the chosen capturing piece either lands passively on the target square, fails to generate the threats the correct piece would create, leaves other pieces undefended, or misses a concrete tactical sequence only available to the correct capturer. Average cp_loss of 398 confirms these are severe errors with narrow correct paths (avg 1.3 good moves available).

1491.label: King moves in endgames that waste a critical tempo by going in the wrong direction or when a piece move should take priority.
1491.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring a king move as the played move. The positions are overwhelmingly decided (8/10 have evaluations beyond ±600cp), and the king moves represent a reflexive 'activate the king' instinct rather than calculated precision. In the positions with meaningful cp_loss (positions 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10), the king consistently moves toward the wrong sector of the board or at the wrong moment: 3/10 feature the king walking toward the wrong flank (Kf7 instead of Kd5, Ke6 instead of Kg6, Kg6 instead of Re7), 3/10 feature the king moving when a piece move should come first (Kf4 instead of Bd3, Ke4 instead of Bd5+, Kf1 instead of Bf3). The remaining 4/10 positions with 0-4cp loss represent near-equivalent king moves in already-decided positions. The average of 2.5 good moves available confirms these are typically narrow positions where king direction matters, yet the player defaults to a generic king march.

1490.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn move to chase a piece or challenge the center when the position demands immediate concrete piece action.
1490.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet pawn advance (d6, a6, c3, f3, c5, c6, d4) in the middlegame that addresses a secondary concern—typically poking at a well-placed enemy piece or slowly challenging the center—while ignoring a more urgent tactical or developmental need. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a piece move (captures like Nxb3/Kxf7, piece activations like Rfe1/Rd2/Rad8/Nf5, development like Bd7, or retreat like Nh2). The pawn moves share a common flaw: they give the opponent a free tempo to reposition the attacked piece to an even stronger square (Positions 1, 8, 10), consolidate against threats (Positions 2, 5, 7), or find devastating tactical replies (Positions 3, 6, 9). Average cp_loss of 228 reflects how costly a single wasted tempo is in these sharp middlegame positions where only 1.5 good moves existed on average.

1498.label: Passive rook repositioning to peripheral squares in positions demanding immediate tactical action, resulting in the rook becoming a target or leaving critical vulnerabilities unaddressed.
1498.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to a passive, non-forcing square in a position that demands concrete tactical play. 8/10 moves go to rim files (a-file: 5 moves, h-file: 3 moves), with the remaining two going to relatively peripheral squares (c2, f3). The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision. In 4/10 positions, the rook landed on a square immediately vulnerable to a fork (Positions 1, 2, 3, 8). In 2/10, the rook became trapped or targeted by a bishop (Position 6) or hung to a queen along a diagonal (Position 4). In 3/10, the rook became a completely passive spectator while the opponent exploited the tempo loss to attack the player's exposed king or win material (Positions 5, 7, 10). In 1/10 (Position 9), the rook move left another piece undefended. The consistent thread is a slow 'positional' rook maneuver that fundamentally misjudges the tactical urgency of the position.

1496.label: An aggressive forward advance (usually a pawn push) that removes protection from a critical piece or square, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
1496.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a forward-advancing move — 8/10 were pawn pushes (f7, d5, d5, d4, g4, b7, b4) and 2/10 were knight leaps to aggressive squares (Nd4, Ng5, Ne3 counts as 3 knight moves total) — that abandoned a critical defensive duty. The moved unit was actively protecting something vital: in positions 3, 5, and 6, a d-pawn advanced leaving the e4 square/pawn undefended; in position 9, b7 moved the pawn past its bishop's protection square (a6); in position 10, b4 eliminated the ...bxa4 counter-resource and abandoned e5; in position 2, Nd4 removed the f3-knight defending g2; in position 8, Ne3 removed the knight shielding the king from a double knight sacrifice. In 9/10 cases, the refutation involved immediately capturing or occupying the newly undefended piece/square. The average cp_loss of 1213 reflects that these positions often had narrow decision points (avg 1.6 good moves available), where the aggressive-looking advance was catastrophically the wrong choice versus defensive or prophylactic alternatives.

1489.label: Playing aesthetically appealing centralizing or advancing moves instead of concrete forcing continuations that gain tempo.
1489.description: 9/10 positions feature moves that place a piece on an impressive-looking square or advance a pawn aggressively (Nd6 x3, Nd5, Kd5, Bc4, Ng6, b6, c3, Qxg8+), while a more forcing alternative—typically involving check, a tactical strike, or a tempo-gaining sequence—was available. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses. In 5/10 positions the move is specifically a knight being placed on a central outpost (d5, d6, g6). The pattern extends beyond knights: b6 advances a pawn when Kc4 occupies a key square first; Bc4 centralizes a bishop when Kc7 dodges a check with tempo; Kd5 aggressively centralizes the king when defensive positioning was required. Positions 5 and 7 show 0 cp loss, indicating the feature fires on the move *pattern* (non-forcing improvement) regardless of severity. Average good moves available was only 2.1, confirming these are positions requiring concrete precision rather than general improvement.
