1492.label: Playing a natural-looking 'improving' move that squanders the one tempo needed to address the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
1492.description: All 10/10 positions feature a move that looks logical in isolation — advancing a pawn, repositioning a piece to an active square, or delivering a check — but catastrophically wastes the critical tempo the position demanded. In 5/10 cases the move is a pawn advance (a4, a4, f5, f5, h5) that appears to create threats or improve structure but ignores an immediate tactical blow or defensive necessity. In 4/10 cases it's a knight move (Ne6+, Ne4, Nf6, Nb4) to a seemingly active square that either hangs the piece or enables the opponent's tactic. The average cp_loss of 3828 is enormous, and the average number of good moves was only 2.1, confirming these are razor-sharp positions where only precise moves work. In 10/10 positions the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a core theme. The blunders share the property of addressing a secondary concern (queenside expansion, piece activity, king safety improvement) while the position's critical factor — whether a forced mate, a tactical combination, a move-order requirement, or a defensive emergency — goes unaddressed for exactly one tempo too many.

1500.label: A passive one-square rook pawn advance (a or h file) played as prophylaxis in a position demanding immediate concrete action.
1500.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square advance of a rook pawn (h-pawn in 6/10, a-pawn in 4/10) played as a slow, non-forcing 'useful' move — creating luft, preventing hypothetical intrusions, or gaining marginal wing space — in positions where urgent tactical or strategic action was required. 9/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The critical action needed varied: back-rank defense (Position 1), central breakthrough like e5 (Positions 4, 10), piece repositioning (Positions 2, 7), addressing concrete threats like Nb5 or Qe3+ (Positions 3, 6, 9), or exploiting an advantage with Bd6 (Position 5). The average cp_loss of 1160 reflects that these tempo losses are catastrophic precisely because the positions were at critical inflection points where one tempo determined whether the opponent could execute a winning tactical idea. Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, confirming these were narrow positions where only concrete, forcing moves maintained the evaluation.
1500.old_chip: Quiet rook pawn when action needed

1502.label: Playing Kh1/Kh8 as a 'useful waiting move' in positions that demand immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
1502.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical geometric move: the king shuffles one square from g1 to h1 (6 positions, White) or g8 to h8 (4 positions, Black) — tucking into the corner behind the castled rook pawn. In every case, the position demanded urgent concrete action: 4/10 positions had hanging or capturable material that needed to be taken or defended (positions 1, 4, 5, 10), 3/10 required immediate attacking continuation to justify aggressively posted pieces (positions 7, 8, 3), 2/10 needed active resolution of central tension (positions 2, 6), and 1/10 actually worsened king safety by walking into a mating net (position 9). The average cp_loss of 270 and average of only 1.9 good moves available confirm these were critical moments where precision was demanded. In 10/10 cases, the opponent punished the tempo loss by either executing a tactic that should have been prevented, capturing undefended material, consolidating a defensive weakness, or launching an attack that could have been preempted.

1493.label: King retreats to the back rank (or toward it) in endgames when the position demands immediate active counterplay, usually pawn advances.
1493.description: All 10 positions feature king moves in the endgame, with 8/10 being moves directly onto the back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black), and the remaining 2 (Kf7, Kf2) also being retreating king moves toward the back rank. The consistent error is choosing a passive, defensive-looking king retreat when the position urgently demanded active counterplay. In 7/10 positions, the best alternative involved an immediate pawn advance (f4, g6, h4, g4, b4, etc.) rather than a king move. In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as a key theme — the retreating king wastes critical time in positions where passed pawns and racing dynamics make every tempo decisive. The positions share a common psychological profile: the player sees a dangerous threat (usually an opponent's passed pawn) and reflexively moves the king toward it in a blockading posture, but this passive approach fails because the position requires generating counter-threats rather than merely defending. Average cp_loss is 102, with the biggest blunders (positions 5, 10, 4) occurring when the retreat directly enabled a tactical exploitation.
1493.old_chip: Passive king retreats to back rank

1504.label: King moves forward toward the center or enemy territory, walking into checks, mates, or leaving pieces undefended.
1504.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king advancing forward (toward higher ranks for White, lower ranks for Black, or toward the center) rather than retreating or staying safe. In 6/10 positions, the correct move was a different king move to a safer square (retreating or sideways), while in 4/10 positions a non-king move was needed entirely to address an immediate tactical issue (defending a hanging piece or centralizing the queen). The punishment consistently exploits the king's new exposed square: 4/10 resulted in immediate or near-immediate checkmate (positions 3, 6, 7, 9), 4/10 allowed the opponent to win material through checks that deflect the king from defending pieces (positions 2, 4, 5, 10), and 2/10 allowed devastating check sequences that worsened a technical position (positions 1, 8). The average cp_loss of 3009 reflects the catastrophic nature of these forward king walks.

1505.label: King repositions to an adjacent square that falls on a dangerous line of attack, when a nearby alternative square was safe.
1505.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves where the player must choose between multiple king destination squares, and selects one that exposes the king to tactical exploitation. In 8/10 positions, the chosen square falls on an open file, rank, or diagonal where opponent pieces deliver checks, forks, or mating threats (e.g., Kh7 instead of Kg7 allowing Rf8; Kf7 instead of Kd8 allowing Ne5+; Ke7 instead of Kg7 allowing Bd8+/discovered checks; Ka7 instead of Kb7 allowing Qxa5+ and mate). The correct alternative was typically an adjacent square just one step away that avoids the dangerous line entirely. In 7/10 cases, the wrong square lands specifically on an open file or unguarded diagonal, while the correct square either controls a critical invasion point or stays off all attacking lines. The average cp_loss of 3073 reflects several positions where the wrong king square leads to immediate checkmate (positions 3, 4, 5). Positions 7 and 8 show negligible or zero loss, serving as near-miss examples where the distinction between squares was minimal.

1499.label: A piece is relocated to an apparently active or ideal square without concrete purpose, while a forcing continuation (check, capture, or trade) was required by the position.
1499.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a non-forcing piece repositioning move—placing a queen, rook, or knight on a square that looks active, central, or well-placed—while missing a concrete, forcing continuation that the position demanded. The best moves involved checks (5/10: Rxe4+, Re8+, Qxe6+, Rh6+, Qh4 creating check threats), captures/trades (3/10: Rxh2, Qxb6, Qd3 attacking the rook), or direct defense against immediate threats (2/10: Bf6 blocking mate, Rc8 challenging a dominant piece). The played moves were universally non-forcing: 0/10 delivered check, 0/10 were captures, and 0/10 created an immediate concrete threat. Instead, pieces went to squares that appear ideal—rooks to open files (Rb8, Rg1, Re1, Rb2), queens to central squares (Qc5, Qe4, Qc3, Qe3, Qa2), a knight to an active-looking post (Nc3). The average cp_loss of 2071 reflects that these 'soft' moves consistently allowed the opponent one free tempo to execute a devastating plan.

1503.label: Queen delivers check to deflect the king from defending an unprotected piece, enabling its capture on the next move.
1503.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen delivering check, and in 9/10 the immediate intent is to capture an undefended piece (usually a rook) on the following move once the king is deflected. Specifically: Pos 1 (Qd1+ → Qxa4 wins rook), Pos 2 (Qc4+ → Qxa6 wins rook), Pos 5 (Qd5+ → Qxh1 wins queen), Pos 6 (Qf3+ → Qxd1+ wins rook), Pos 8 (Qb3+ forks king and rook on a2), Pos 9 (Qf3+ → Qxa8 wins queen), Pos 10 (Qd3+ → Qxc2 wins rook). 7/10 are the best move (0 cp loss), while 3/10 are catastrophic blunders where the player applied this 'check-then-capture' template incorrectly: Position 3 (missed forced mate for a check winning only the rook), Position 4 (chose the wrong checking square allowing an interposition), Position 7 (played a deflection check missing checkmate in one). 8/10 are endgame positions, typically Queen vs Rook imbalances where the rook is left undefended on an open file.

1494.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that targets a secondary objective (usually a pawn) when an immediately decisive forcing move was available.
1494.description: In 7/10 positions, the played move attacks a specific pawn or square (Re6→e5, Ra4→a3, Ng5→f7, Qe6→f6, Qg2→g3, Rg7→g6, Rad1→d-file) rather than executing the available decisive action. In 4/10 positions, the best move was a check or capture-with-check (Rxa3+, Qh1+, Qh3+, Rf7+). In 3/10, it was an immediate tactical blow (b4 trapping the queen, Qc6 creating a mating net, a5 advancing a passer). The average cp_loss of 2940 reflects how catastrophic this pattern is—4/10 positions involved missing forced checkmate. Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, meaning these were razor-sharp positions demanding the one precise continuation. Position 8 (Rc2) is an outlier that doesn't fit the pattern (0 cp_loss, good move). Positions 5 (Kxg7) and 6 (a4) are partial fits where the 'non-forcing' theme manifests as accepting material that exposes the king or making a premature break without preparation.

1501.label: King retreats to the 1st or 8th rank in the endgame, becoming confined and vulnerable to checks rather than staying active.
1501.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves to the absolute edge of the board (1st or 8th rank), with 9/10 landing exactly on rank 1 or 8 and 1/10 (Kf2) retreating toward the edge. In every case, the retreat sacrifices king activity and creates confinement: 6/10 positions explicitly cite back-rank vulnerability or trapping as the key punishment mechanism, and 10/10 analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as a contributing factor. The better alternatives consistently involved keeping the king more centrally active (Kb6 instead of Kc8, Ka6 instead of Ka8, Kh6 instead of Kg8) or choosing the correct back-rank square that provides pawn shelter (Kg8 instead of Kf8 in positions 3 and 9). 8/10 positions involve passed pawns near promotion where precise king placement is critical, and the back-rank retreat typically allows the opponent's queen or rook to deliver tempo-gaining checks that disrupt the promotion plan. The average cp_loss of 1141 reflects several catastrophic instances where the single-square difference between active and passive king placement swung the evaluation by 800+ centipawns.

1507.label: A rook moves away from a square where it was the sole defender of a piece or pawn, leaving that target immediately hanging or tactically exploitable.
1507.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that prioritizes activation or offense while abandoning a critical defensive role. In 8/10 cases, the rook was the sole protector of a specific piece or pawn (Position 1: d1 rook defended d4 knight; Position 2: f8 rook defended f7 pawn; Position 4: b8 rook defended b7 pawn; Position 6: b3 rook defended c3 pawn; Position 7: g8 rook defended g5 bishop; Position 8: e8 rook defended e6 pawn; Position 9: a8 rook defended a6 bishop; Position 10: rook near kingside defended h6 pawn). In the remaining 2/10, the rook move created a different tactical catastrophe: Position 5 moved the wrong rook to c1, stripping back-rank coverage and trapping the piece; Position 3 gave a premature rook check that drove the opponent's king to safety. The player's intent was consistently to 'improve' the rook—doubling on a file, contesting an open line, challenging an enemy piece, or giving check—but each time the rook was already performing an invisible yet essential defensive function.

1510.label: Developing a different knight to a natural square while an existing piece is en prise to an enemy pawn capture.
1510.description: 9/10 positions show the identical pattern: the player has a piece (usually a knight, once a bishop) directly attacked by an enemy pawn, and instead of saving or exchanging that piece, they develop their OTHER knight to a textbook square (Nc3, Nc6, Nf3, or Nf6). In positions 1-2, the f3-knight is attacked by e4-pawn and the player develops Nc3. In positions 4, 5, and 8, the f6-knight is attacked by the e5-pawn and the player develops Nc6. In position 3, the g4-knight is attacked by the h3-pawn and the player develops Nc6. In position 6, the g5-bishop is attacked by the h6-pawn and the player develops Nc3. In position 7, the c3-knight is attacked by the d4-pawn and the player develops Nf3. In position 10, the c6-knight is attacked by the d5-pawn and the player develops Nf6. Position 9 is a slight variant where the player develops Nc3 instead of exploiting a decisive tactical opportunity. All 10 moves occur in the opening phase, and the average cp_loss is 289, corresponding to roughly losing a full minor piece for a pawn.

1509.label: Pawn captures that resolve tension by opening a file or diagonal that the opponent's already-positioned pieces immediately exploit against the player's king.
1509.description: All 10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture that opens a critical line (file or diagonal) into the capturing player's own king position. In 9/10 positions, king_safety is the primary tactical motif exploited after the capture. The opponent's heavy pieces (rooks, queens) or minor pieces are already aimed at the line that gets opened: 5/10 involve h-pawn captures opening the g-file where the opponent's rooks are already doubled or poised (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 9); 4/10 involve d-pawn or c-pawn captures opening central files/diagonals toward an exposed king (positions 4, 6, 8, 10); 1/10 opens an outpost square for a knight (position 7). In every case, the best move was NOT to capture: alternatives included prophylactic king moves (3/10), pawn advances instead of captures (3/10), piece moves ignoring the tension (3/10), or counterplay elsewhere (1/10). Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, showing these are narrow positions where the 'natural' capture is uniquely wrong.

1516.label: A bishop exchange is played as a natural simplification when a much stronger tactical or strategic move was available in the position.
1516.description: All 10 positions feature a bishop capture (Bx__) that initiates or completes a piece exchange, trading one's own bishop for an opponent's piece. In 10/10 cases, the exchange appears 'natural' or positionally motivated — eliminating a defender, trading bishops, or simplifying — but squanders a concrete tactical opportunity. The missed best moves include queen captures winning material (positions 1, 6, 8), piece-winning combinations (positions 7, 9), pawn breaks (position 3), rook invasions (position 2), forks (position 10), and urgent development/castling (positions 4, 5). In 7/10 positions, the traded bishop was actually a key attacking piece whose removal relieved pressure on the opponent. The average cp_loss of 334 reflects how costly these 'safe-looking' exchanges are. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than routine play.

1517.label: A rook is moved to an apparently active square where it is immediately capturable or lost through a simple tactical sequence.
1517.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to what appears to be an aggressive or active square (open file, central rank, attacking something), but the rook is tactically vulnerable on arrival. In 6/10 positions (Positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9), the rook is directly captured on the square it just moved to with no adequate recapture. In 2/10 positions (2, 10), the rook's apparent defender is illusory — a discovered attack or X-ray means the 'protecting' piece can't actually recapture. In 1/10 (Position 5), moving the rook breaks coordination and leaves another piece hanging. In 1/10 (Position 7), the forced exchange destroys a critical structural asset. The rooks consistently move to middle-board squares (ranks 4-6 in 9/10 cases), suggesting the player sees an 'active' destination but fails to verify whether the square is tactically safe. The average cp_loss of 1326 reflects how catastrophic these errors are — often losing a full rook for nothing.

1511.label: Knights leap to seemingly powerful central/aggressive squares but the move is tactically or strategically flawed, typically abandoning a critical defensive role or landing unprotected.
1511.description: All 10 positions feature knight moves to visually impressive squares (e5×3, d5×2, e4, d4, g5, b6, d7) — classic 'outpost' or 'attacking' destinations. In 7/10 positions, the knight was performing a critical defensive function before moving (guarding the king, protecting key pawns, or controlling vital squares), and its departure created immediate tactical vulnerabilities. In 6/10 cases, the knight could be simply captured with devastating follow-up (fork, hanging piece, or positional collapse). In 3/10 positions (1, 6, 8), the knight's departure specifically exposed the player's king to a mating attack or severe threats. In 2/10 positions (5, 7), the knight move was a slow centralizing idea that missed a far more urgent tactical blow. The average cp_loss of 2255 reflects catastrophic consequences. 8/10 moves were played by White, suggesting over-eagerness to 'attack' with knights rather than maintain defensive responsibilities. Only 2/10 were Black's errors. The consistent thread is that these moves LOOK strong to a human pattern-matcher (knight on d5/e5 = good!) but FUNCTION terribly because they ignore concrete tactical consequences.

1506.label: Passive major piece repositioning (usually rooks to files) that wastes critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical action.
1506.description: 9/10 positions feature major piece moves (7 rook moves, 2 queen moves) that appear 'natural' — contesting an open file, giving a check, or connecting rooks — but catastrophically fail to address the position's urgent tactical demands. The average good moves available was only 1.5, meaning these were all critical moments with essentially one correct response. In 6/10 cases the position explicitly required an immediate tactical strike (Nb5 fork, Nd5 jump, c4 pawn advance, Be4 defense) that the player missed in favor of a slow piece deployment. In 4/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 6, 10) the piece moved directly into a tactical vulnerability — either immediate capture with checkmate (Qxf8#, Qxg1#) or a forcing sequence exploiting the piece's new square (Bh4+/Bxg3+/Rxe1, Nxe5+/Rxe5/Qxe7+). The consistent thread is a player choosing a 'developing' or 'file-contesting' move that looks logical in isolation but completely ignores the concrete tactical reality of the position.

1514.label: A routine pawn-takes-pawn capture that resolves tension while ignoring an urgent tactical demand in the position.
1514.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing a pawn on an adjacent file (axb, hxg, cxd, fxe, fxg, bxc patterns), resolving structural tension in what appears to be a natural or automatic move. However, in every case the position contained a far more critical demand: 6/10 positions required urgent king safety measures (defending against mating attacks or addressing exposed kings), 2/10 required executing a superior tactical sequence first, and 2/10 required preserving a structural restraint or avoiding opening lines for the opponent. The average cp_loss of 3977 is catastrophic, with 4/10 positions resulting in immediate forced mate or near-mate after the capture. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions demanding precision — yet the player defaulted to the most 'obvious' pawn exchange. In 7/10 cases, the capture opened lines or removed protective pawns that directly enabled the opponent's punishment (back-rank mates, bishop checks on cleared diagonals, rook infiltrations on opened files, or escaping forced mating nets).

1512.label: Playing a quiet, non-urgent move while the player's own knight is tactically en prise or requires immediate action to avoid capture.
1512.description: In 10/10 positions, the player has a knight that is under direct tactical threat (attacked by an enemy pawn or piece with no adequate defender), yet plays a slow, positional move instead of addressing the knight's crisis. In 9/10 cases, the opponent can immediately capture the knight for material gain; in 1/10 (position 5), the player misses using their knight for a critical tactic (Nxe6 fork). The quiet moves played are predominantly pawn pushes (6/10: d6, c6, c3, c3, h3, c3), with the remainder being non-urgent developing or repositioning moves (Rhg1, Bc5, Qe7, O-O). The threatened knights sit on central squares (e4 in 3 positions, f3 in 3 positions, d4/d5/f5 in the others) where they are attacked by enemy pawns advancing from adjacent files. The average cp_loss of 340 corresponds closely to the value of a full minor piece, confirming that the consistent punishment is winning the neglected knight outright.

1513.label: Playing a slow piece-improving or repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action (tactical strike, pawn break, or critical defense).
1513.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a non-forcing piece repositioning or 'improving' move when the position demanded urgent concrete action. The tempo_loss tag appears in 8/10 analyses, and missed_tactic in 7/10. Specifically: 8/10 moves are minor piece relocations (4 knight moves: Ng4, Nc4, Nf8, Nf1; 4 bishop moves: Bf3×2, Bb4, Bh6), with the remaining being a pawn push (f4) and castling (O-O-O). In every case, the engine's top recommendation was a forcing move: a pawn break (f5, g4, c3, bxc5), a capture (Bxc5, Nxd5, Nxf3), or a survival priority (Kh8, g6). The average cp_loss of 1174 reflects that these seemingly reasonable 'development' moves are catastrophically ill-timed. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where accuracy was essential. King_safety concerns were present in 8/10 positions, suggesting the urgency often stems from an exposed king that demands immediate tactical resolution rather than slow maneuvering.

1508.label: Playing an active-looking or purposeful move (often a queen move or check) while missing a simple capture of an undefended piece, usually the opponent's queen.
1508.description: In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 8, 9, and partially 10), the correct move was to simply capture an undefended enemy queen or major piece — typically along a clear diagonal that the player's own queen already controlled. In 5 of those cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 8, 9), the opponent's queen was completely hanging and capturable in one move. Instead, the player made a 'reasonable-looking' alternative: 8/10 moves played were queen moves to seemingly active squares, and 2/10 were pointless checks (Qc6+, Qc3+) that allowed the opponent to escape. The remaining positions (5, 6, 7) share the narrower trait of having exactly one critical tactical move available (avg 1.3 good moves) while the player chose a plausible-but-fatal alternative. All 10 positions feature enormous evaluation swings (avg 4206cp) caused by choosing strategic or active-looking moves over concrete tactical necessities.

1519.label: Active bishop repositioning to an unprotected or inadequately defended square where it is immediately won or exploited through tactical means.
1519.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being actively moved to a seemingly purposeful central or active square (d3, c4, d4, f4, e4×4, e6, c5 — predominantly 4th-rank centralization). In 8/10 cases, the bishop lands on a completely unprotected square or one whose defender is illusory (e.g., a pinned pawn in position 3). The direct consequence in 7/10 positions is the bishop being captured outright — via knight fork (positions 1, 5), direct knight capture (positions 6, 9), queen capture through pin (position 3), pawn tempo kick (position 8), or exchange leading to back-rank exploitation (position 7). In position 10, the bishop vacates a critical blockading square rather than landing on a vulnerable one, but the common thread remains: an 'improving' bishop move that creates immediate tactical vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 1338 is extreme, reflecting that losing a bishop typically costs ~300+ cp, with several positions involving cascading disasters (king exposure, back-rank mates). Only 2.1 good moves were available on average, suggesting these occur in positions already requiring precision.

1518.label: Forward knight jumps to seemingly strong squares that abandon defensive duties, leaving pieces undefended or creating exploitable tactical vulnerabilities.
1518.description: All 9 positions feature a knight jumping forward to an active-looking square (e4 in 5/9, e5 in 2/9, plus f4, b5, a5). In 7/9 cases the knight departs from c3 or c6, squares where it was serving critical defensive or coordinating functions. In 8/9 positions at least one king remained uncastled or exposed, meaning the defensive role was especially important. The consistent punishment pattern is that the departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability: in 4/9 positions a piece left behind becomes hanging (Bg5, Bb4, Bg4), in 3/9 the knight itself becomes the target (trapped on a5, forked by f5, captured with check), and in 2/9 the vacated square opens a deadly diagonal for checks or double attacks. The refutations typically involve simple one-move tactical shots (Qa5+, Qa4+, Nxe4, f5, b4) that any intermediate player could find, yet the aggressive-looking nature of the knight move apparently blinded players to these replies. Average cp_loss was 313, indicating these are severe blunders rather than subtle inaccuracies.

1522.label: A rook (or queen) moves to an active-looking square, breaking mutual defense with its partner rook and leaving it hanging for capture.
1522.description: 10/10 positions share an identical tactical pattern: the player moves a piece that was providing the sole defense of another major piece (almost always a rook defending its partner rook), leaving that partner completely undefended and capturable. In 9/10 cases the moved piece is a rook; in 1/10 it's a queen vacating the back rank. The abandoned piece is always a rook. The refutation in every case is a simple capture of the now-hanging rook — often with check (Rxe8+, Qxa8+, Qxa1+, Kxb7, Kxh7, Kxa8, Rxd8). The blundered moves themselves appear active: giving check (Rg3+, Rh7+), capturing material (Rxe5), infiltrating on the second/third rank (Ra2, Ra3, Rf3), or activating on the sixth rank (Rf6 appears twice). But in every case the 'activity' is illusory because the cost — losing the undefended partner piece — exceeds any benefit gained.

1520.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn advance in a critical position that demands an immediate tactical piece move (capture, check, or fork).
1520.description: 8/9 moves played are single pawn advances (h4, a5, b4, f4, h6, a5, g6, exf6), with the one outlier being a quiet queen centralization (Qd3). In contrast, the correct moves were overwhelmingly piece actions: 7/9 required piece moves (Kh3, Bxb1, Bxb4, Ne5, Qc8, Bf4, Ne3+), with only 2/9 being pawn moves (g7+ and g3—both forcing moves that deliver check or attack a piece). Every single position had exactly 1 good move available (avg = 1.0), indicating extreme tactical tension where precision was mandatory. The played pawn moves are predominantly on flank files (a, b, f, g, h), are non-checking and non-capturing (7/9), and address long-term strategic concerns (space, pawn chains, piece restriction) while ignoring immediate tactical emergencies like hanging pieces (positions 3, 2), mating threats (positions 1, 5), knight forks (position 9), discovered attacks (positions 2, 7), or critical tempo for piece activation (positions 8, 4, 6).

1526.label: Playing a non-capturing pawn push or quiet move when the position demands an immediate capture of a hanging or en-prise piece.
1526.description: 10/10 positions featured a hanging piece or obligatory recapture that was the overwhelmingly correct move, yet the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move instead. In every case, the best move(s) were captures: recapturing a piece that just took something (positions 1, 5, 6, 10 — 4/10), taking a free undefended piece (positions 2, 7, 9 — 3/10), or capturing an attacking piece to resolve a direct threat (positions 3, 4, 8 — 3/10). The blunders themselves were almost exclusively pawn pushes (8/10: d3, c4, d5, d6, d3, e5, b4, e4), with one king move (Ke3) and one bishop development (Bh6). The average cp_loss of 510 corresponds closely to a full piece value, confirming that in nearly every case the player lost approximately one minor piece worth of material. The average number of good moves was only 1.6, indicating these were narrow positions with very few acceptable alternatives — all of which were captures.

1521.label: King moves to a tactically vulnerable square instead of finding the one safe square or playing a forcing non-king move.
1521.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves exclusively, making this the defining geometric pattern. In 8/10 cases, the king move is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 2142). The errors fall into two sub-types: in 4/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 9), a forcing tactical move (check or pawn break) should have been played instead of any king move, with the player choosing passive king repositioning over concrete tactical blows like Rg7+, Ra2+, Qb7+, or g5. In 4/10 positions (3, 6, 8, 10), the king needed to move but went to the WRONG adjacent square—one that allows the opponent to gain tempo via check or pawn advance (Kd6 allowing f5 with tempo, Kg6 allowing g5 with tempo, Kf8 walking onto Bd6+ diagonal, Kf2 allowing Rxe2+ with check). Only 2/10 positions (2, 7) feature king moves that are actually correct. The average number of good moves available was just 1.3, indicating these are razor-sharp moments requiring extreme precision in king placement.

1515.label: Player makes an active-looking move (check, pawn grab, or positional maneuver) while overlooking a simple capture of an undefended enemy queen or rook.
1515.description: In 10/10 positions, an opponent's major piece (queen or rook) was undefended and available for immediate capture along an open file, rank, or diagonal. In 8/10 cases, the player missed this simple capture entirely: 3/10 played a flashy check instead (Qh1+, Qh8+, Qh8+ — classic 'checking blindness'), 2/10 grabbed a lesser target like a pawn (Qxb2, Ra2), and 3/10 played positional or centralizing moves (Qc7, Qc6, Re2). Only 2/10 positions (Qxc3 and Qxe7) show the player correctly finding the capture, which the feature also activates on as the pattern is present. The hanging pieces were consistently major pieces — queens in 6/10 cases and rooks in 4/10 — sitting undefended on open lines where the player's piece had a clear geometric path to capture them. The average cp_loss of 2305 reflects the catastrophic nature of missing a free queen or rook.

1527.label: Moving a knight to a natural-looking central square in time-critical positions where urgent threats (especially passed pawns) demand immediate, forcing action instead.
1527.description: All 10 positions feature a knight moving to a classically 'strong' central square (Ne4 in 4/10, Ne3 in 3/10, Nd4/Nc3/Nc6 in 1/10 each) that appears to improve the piece but fatally wastes tempo. 9/10 positions are endgames where passed pawns are racing to promote and every tempo is decisive. The tempo_loss tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and passed_pawn appears in 9/10. In each case, a more forcing alternative existed: checks that gained time (positions 2, 3, 5, 7), captures with check winning material (position 9), king moves addressing the actual threat (positions 1, 6, 7), or immediate pawn advances (position 8). The knight destinations look textbook-correct — central, controlling key squares — but the positions demand tactical urgency over positional aesthetics. In 3/10 cases the knight also landed on a tactically vulnerable square where it was immediately captured or won through deflection checks (positions 8, 9, 10), compounding the tempo loss with material loss.

1523.label: Advancing a pawn (usually a passed pawn) one square forward when piece preparation or repositioning was required first.
1523.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance toward the opponent's side as the mistake. In 8/10 cases, the correct move was a piece move (bishop, king, or knight repositioning) rather than any pawn push. The most common consequence is allowing the opponent to establish a blockade on the pushed pawn (5/10 positions: c2, g2, f7, e3, e3), rendering it a static weakness rather than a dynamic asset. In 2/10 positions the pawn push removed a critical defensive function the pawn was performing (Position 10: e4 blocked lateral rook checks; Position 4: f4 controlled key squares). In 2/10 positions the pawn push was irrelevant activity when urgent piece safety demanded attention (a6 leaving a bishop hanging, a3 ignoring mating threats). The average cp_loss of 2124 is extreme, with 3/10 resulting in forced mate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical decision points where the 'push the pawn' instinct is most dangerous.

1524.label: A bishop is moved to an attacking square (toward opponent's king, to capture material, or to give check) while abandoning a critical defensive or positional function it was performing.
1524.description: All 10/10 positions feature bishop moves that appear aggressive but are fundamentally misguided. In 6/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, and 1), the bishop was actively performing a crucial defensive or positional role — guarding key squares (f4, d4, c3), supporting central pawns (e5), or blocking dangerous lines (6th rank) — and its departure creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities that the opponent exploits. In 3/10 cases (positions 7, 8, 10), the bishop is sent on an aggressive sortie (non-forcing placement on g6, premature exchange attempt on h3, hollow check on b5) when a more precise and forcing alternative existed. In 1/10 cases (position 4), the bishop captures peripheral material (Bxb7) abandoning a dominant central post. The consistent thread is that the bishop move targets the opponent's king area or grabs material, creating a superficially threatening appearance, but concretely fails because it either leaves something critical undefended or wastes tempo on a non-forcing idea. Average cp_loss of 322 reflects the severity of these errors.

1525.label: Advancing a pawn that was serving a critical defensive/structural role, creating an immediate tactical target or opening lines toward the player's own king.
1525.description: All 10/10 positions feature single-step pawn advances that create concrete weaknesses the opponent immediately exploits. 7/10 involve pawns advancing on the f-file or adjacent to the player's castled/exposed king (f5, f6, h6, f3), directly compromising king safety by opening diagonals or creating capture targets. The remaining 3/10 (d5, d4, d4) advance pawns into unsupported positions where they become indefensible targets. In 9/10 cases, the best alternatives were piece moves (Qd7, Rf7, Ra3, c5, fxe6, g6, Kh7, Ne5, Ke2, h5) rather than pawn advances—showing the player chose a structurally committal pawn push when patient piece improvement was required. The refutations consistently exploit the newly created weakness: opened diagonals toward the king (6/10), direct capture of the advanced pawn (4/10), or mating threats along files the pawn vacated (3/10). Average cp_loss of 234 and only 1.7 good moves available confirm these are critical moments where the impulsive pawn push was one of very few losing options.

1533.label: A pawn capture landing on the 2nd/7th rank creates an illusory promotion threat while ignoring a far more urgent tactical crisis (usually a mating attack).
1533.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture that lands on the penultimate rank (7th rank for White, 2nd rank for Black), placing the pawn one square from promotion. In every case, the player's intent was to create an unstoppable queening threat, but the promotion is too slow or easily neutralized: 8/10 positions have king safety as the primary tactical motif being ignored, 9/10 feature 'tempo_loss' as a key tag, and the average centipawn loss is a catastrophic 4788. The opponent's refutation consistently involves ignoring the promotion threat entirely and delivering checks, sacrifices, or mating attacks that arrive faster. In 6/10 positions the promoting side's own king was exposed or in the center, making the tempo waste fatal. The pawn destinations cluster heavily on g-file squares (7/10: fxg7, fxg7, fxg7, hxg2, fxg2, fxg2, gxh7) with b-file captures (2/10: cxb2) and one e-file capture (dxe2).

1531.label: Non-forcing rook redeployments to central files that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1531.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move to a seemingly logical square (central or open file), yet every single one is a tempo-wasting mistake. In 6/10 cases the rook moves to the e-file, in 3/10 to the d-file, and 1/10 to each of the c-file and g-file — all 'natural-looking' centralizations. The core error takes two forms: in 5/10 positions the player missed an immediate tactical blow (dxc6/Nd5, Qg4, Nxd5, h4, f6), while in 5/10 positions the rook abandoned a critical defensive post (d8 leaving d5 undefended twice, f1 removing kingside cover twice, e1 weakening back rank). The average cp_loss of 305 reflects how costly these quiet moves are — opponents punish them with concrete tactics that exploit either the vacated square, the freed tempo for development/consolidation, or the now-unguarded weakness. Only 1.5 good alternatives existed on average, indicating these are positions demanding precise, forcing play rather than general improvement.

1534.label: King moves to a square that allows an immediate tactical punishment—typically a fork, discovered attack, or mating sequence—when a safer king destination existed.
1534.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that lands on a tactically vulnerable square, inviting an immediate punishing blow. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 9, 10), the king walks directly into a knight fork that wins major material (rook or queen). In 2/10 cases (positions 3, 7), the king move abandons defense of a piece, leaving it hanging. In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 6), the king lands on an exposed square allowing queen infiltration with check. In 2/10 cases (positions 4, 8), the king moves to a square enabling a mating attack or decisive pawn capture. Critically, in 9/10 positions the best move was ALSO a king move—just to a different, safer square (e.g., Ke3 instead of Ke4, Kf1 instead of Kd2, Kg6 instead of Ke7, Kd7 instead of Kf6). Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions demanding precise king placement. The average cp_loss of 1270 reflects that choosing the wrong king square in these critical moments leads to catastrophic material loss or mate.

1529.label: A non-forcing pawn advance (usually to the 4th rank) that prioritizes space over an available concrete tactical opportunity or urgent positional need.
1529.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn advances (with 1 knight move to d4), and 9/10 of all moves land on the 4th rank. In every case, the player chose a 'space-gaining' or 'structural' pawn push when the position demanded immediate tactical action. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 7, 8, 10), the best move was a forcing continuation that won material or created decisive threats. In 4/10 positions (3, 4, 5, 6), the advance either ignored an opponent's concrete tactical threat or overextended the pawn structure fatally. The average cp_loss of 1182 (inflated by Position 5's mate) reflects how catastrophic these tempo-wasting advances can be. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision. The refutations consistently exploit that the advance either left the pawn itself undefended (Positions 4, 7, 10), weakened key squares (Positions 2, 5, 6, 9), or simply wasted the one tempo needed to address a concrete threat (Positions 1, 3, 8).

1536.label: A knight jumps to an aggressive-looking central outpost but creates no concrete threat, wasting a critical tempo while the opponent resolves their problems.
1536.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight moving forward to what appears to be a dominant outpost square (e5 in 6/10, c5 in 2/10, e4/g5/b4 in the remainder), with none being captures or checks. In 9/10 cases, the position demanded concrete action — exploiting an exposed king, seizing an open file, executing a tactical blow, or maintaining a critical defensive post — yet the player chose an aesthetically pleasing but strategically vacuous knight centralization instead. In 7/10 positions, the opponent's primary refutation involved simply sidestepping the knight's 'attack' (moving a queen away, castling, or gaining a tempo with a pawn kick), revealing the knight's placement created no binding threat. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 5, 10), the knight actively abandoned a superior square where it performed defensive or structural duties. In 3/10 cases (positions 6, 9, 1), a clearly superior forcing move (fork, pawn breakthrough, rook activation) was available. The average cp_loss of 327 reflects how much these 'natural-looking' moves squander.

1530.label: Quiet, natural-looking moves (recaptures, repositioning, preparatory actions) played when the position demands immediate tactical urgency.
1530.description: 9/10 positions show the player choosing a move that appears reasonable on general principles—a routine recapture (bxc3, cxd3), a piece repositioning (Nh6, Rdf8, Bg7, Rf1, Ke8), a quiet pawn push (b6), or a simplifying exchange (Bxd6)—but critically wastes tempo when immediate action is required. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and the average number of good moves available is only 2.0, indicating narrow positions where precision mattered enormously. In 7/10 cases, the best move involved immediate aggressive or urgent action (Ng5 attacking, Ng7 forcing queen retreat, h5 advancing, Bxg7 winning material, f4 creating escape, Kg6 racing toward the critical sector, Bxd3 recapturing with the right piece). The played moves all share the quality of being 'autopilot' decisions—moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the primary demand of the position. Position 10 (Kc7, 0cp loss) is the exception, representing a correct quiet move in a position where urgency was not required.

1540.label: The queen captures a peripheral pawn (usually a- or h-file), displacing itself from the critical action and allowing the opponent to exploit tempo, king safety, or tactical opportunities.
1540.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen capturing an undefended pawn on the edge of the board — 8/10 on the a-file (a2, a6, a7) and 2/10 on the h-file (h2, h7). In every case, the queen moves TO a peripheral square to collect material worth only one pawn, while the position demands either development (5/10 are opening positions), king defense (7/10 involve exposed kings), or executing a stronger tactic (6/10 had a clearly superior tactical continuation missed). The refutations universally exploit the queen's absence: in 4/10 the queen becomes trapped or attacked with tempo (Nc6 patterns), in 5/10 the opponent launches a direct king attack that the offside queen cannot help defend against, and in 2/10 a superior tactical blow (fork/hanging piece) was available instead. The average centipawn loss of 1237 reflects catastrophic consequences — including one position where it allows forced mate.

1543.label: A pawn capture that removes a critical shielding pawn, opening a line (diagonal or file) directly toward the player's own king for the opponent to exploit.
1543.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture (lowercase piece notation: fxe5, fxg3, exd4, cxb4, cxd5, cxd4, hxg4) that opens a line directly toward the capturing side's own king. In 8/10 positions, the punishment is an immediate check or queen invasion along the newly opened line (Qh5+, Qxg3+, Qxd4+, Bxb4+, Qxg3+). In 7/10 cases, the king is still in the center (uncastled), making the opened diagonal especially lethal. In 2/10 cases (positions 9 and 10), even a castled king is fatally exposed because the pawn captured was part of the remaining kingside shelter. The average centipawn loss is 1290, reflecting that these captures are typically catastrophic—often allowing checkmate, queen wins, or rook captures. In every case, the best alternative involved either developing a piece first, gaining tempo, or addressing the structural vulnerability before making the capture. The captures all appear 'natural' or 'greedy' at surface level (winning material, removing an intruder, simplifying) but fatally ignore that the captured-from pawn was the keystone of the king's defensive structure.

1546.label: Playing a natural king-centralizing move one tempo too early, before executing an urgent concrete action (pawn break, piece maneuver, or capture) that must come first.
1546.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move toward the center or off the back rank that looks like sound endgame technique but fatally wastes a critical tempo. In every case, there was an urgent concrete action that needed to precede the king move: pawn breaks (c5 in positions 3,4; e4 in position 1; h5 in position 10; a3 in position 6; gxf3+ in position 5; exd4+ in position 8), piece activity (Na4 in position 2; Rb4 in position 9), or piece redeployment (Ne2 in position 7). The king move itself was often part of the BEST continuation — but one move later (e.g., positions 1,3,4,5,8 show the king move appearing in the best line after the concrete action). 9/10 positions had only 1 good move available, showing these are razor-sharp timing positions disguised as quiet endgames. The average cp_loss of 230 reflects how a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to either seize an outpost, create a passed pawn, invade with a rook, or resolve pawn tension on favorable terms.

1545.label: Playing a rook-pawn advance (h3/a3/h6/a6) to challenge an actively-placed enemy piece that is happy to capture rather than retreat, wasting a critical tempo and often wrecking the pawn structure.
1545.description: All 10 positions feature a one-square rook-pawn advance intended to 'put the question' to an opponent's actively-placed piece — most commonly a bishop pinning a knight. In 8/10 positions, White plays h3 against a Bg4 that pins Nf3, expecting the bishop to retreat; instead, the bishop (or a cooperating knight) captures on f3, forcing gxf3 and devastating the kingside pawn structure. In 1/10, Black plays h6 to challenge Bg5 but creates a target exploited by Nxf6+ and Bxh6. In 1/10, White plays a3 to challenge Bb4 but invites Bxc3+ with check. In 1/10, Black plays a6 to challenge Bb5 but enables a favorable exchange that eliminates a key tactical resource (Nd4 fork). In 9/10 positions, the opponent's strongest refutation involves capturing the piece the pawn was 'defending' against rather than retreating, proving the pawn move addressed a threat that didn't exist. The average cp_loss of 228 reflects that these positions consistently demanded concrete tactical action (average 1.4 good moves available) rather than prophylactic pawn pushes.

1542.label: Advancing or promoting a passed pawn onto a square directly controlled by an opponent's minor piece, when preparation or patience was required.
1542.description: 10/10 positions involve pushing a passed pawn to the 7th rank or promoting it, with the target square directly attacked by an opponent's piece. In 8/10 cases, the controlling piece is a bishop on a long diagonal (e.g., Bc4 controlling f1, Bb4 controlling e1, Bf7 controlling a2, Be5 controlling g7/a1). In 2/10, a knight controls the key square (Na4→b2, Nc6→b8). The refutation in every case is a simple capture of the advanced/promoted piece. The best moves in 9/10 positions involved first neutralizing the controlling piece (via deflection, intermediate check-capture, or rerouting) or maintaining the pawn as a latent threat while improving other pieces. The average cp_loss of 276 reflects that these premature promotions often turn winning positions into draws or dramatically reduce advantages. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where pawn-pushing instinct overrides tactical awareness.

1532.label: Playing an active-looking or natural-looking move that ignores the single most critical need in the position, allowing immediate exploitation of the abandoned responsibility.
1532.description: All 10 positions share a remarkably consistent pattern: the player makes a move that appears purposeful—developing (Nc3), centralizing (Qd4, Qc2), attacking (Qa5, Qh6, Qh7, Qg4), repositioning (Rg8, Kb7), or gaining space (g4)—but fundamentally ignores the ONE urgent task the position demands. In 8/10 positions, that urgent task involved defending a vulnerable king (either shoring up pawn cover, maintaining back-rank defense, or addressing an immediate check threat). In 9/10 positions, the refutation directly exploited the specific responsibility the moved piece abandoned. The positions averaged only 2.1 good moves available, meaning these were narrow, forcing positions where only precise moves addressing the critical need could hold. In 7/10 cases, the best move involved either directly eliminating a threat (Bxe3, Rd7, c5), delivering check first (Qh4+, Qg4+), or moving the king to safety before the crisis hit (Kh7, Kc8). The blundered moves universally chose secondary goals over primary needs.

1535.label: Bishop is relocated to a seemingly better diagonal in an endgame, often when more urgent actions (forcing moves, king activity, pawn advances) should take priority.
1535.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing bishop move that relocates the piece to a new diagonal. 9/10 occur in endgame positions with exposed kings and active pawn play. The moves target squares that appear 'better' for the bishop (e.g., centralizing on d5/e5, activating on long diagonals like b3/c3/g4). However, 8/10 are mistakes (ranging from 30cp to 9289cp loss) because the position demanded something more urgent: forcing checks that lead to mate (positions 3, 4, 5), king centralization (positions 2, 7), pawn advances for tempo (position 9), or avoiding the bishop being trapped (position 8). Only 2/10 (positions 1 and 10) are correct, where the bishop genuinely needed repositioning and no more urgent priority existed. The average cp_loss of 2874 is heavily skewed by three catastrophic blunders (9000+ cp) where forced mates were missed in favor of passive bishop improvement.

1539.label: A non-forcing pawn advance wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate tactical piece action or a specific forcing move.
1539.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn pushes as the played move. In 9/10 cases these are blunders (avg cp_loss 3195 excluding the 0-loss outlier), turning winning or equal positions into lost ones or throwing away forced mates. In 7/10 positions, the best move was a piece move (Queen, Rook, Bishop, or King), while in 2/10 it was a different, more forcing pawn push (g2 for promotion or g5+ with check). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 8/10. The positions consistently feature exposed kings (both sides) and sharp tactical tension where one tempo determines whether a mating net, fork, pin, or promotion threat is decisive. The player chose a 'strengthening' or 'progressing' pawn move—appearing natural for long-term plans—while the position screamed for immediate concrete action. Position 4 (g4, 0 cp loss) is the lone exception where the aggressive pawn push happened to be the best tactical shot, suggesting the feature activates on 'kingside/flank pawn advances in sharp positions' regardless of correctness.

1544.label: A rook retreats to the player's own second rank as passive defense, but this fails to address the critical tactical vulnerability (usually king safety) and often makes things catastrophically worse.
1544.description: 10/10 positions feature rook moves, and 9/10 specifically move a rook to the player's own second rank (f2, b2, e2, g2 for White; d7, f7, g7 for Black). The one exception (R6g3) still shares the defensive intent. In every case, the move attempts to shore up defenses passively—blocking a file, protecting a pawn, or guarding the king—when the position demanded an active solution. The best moves available were overwhelmingly active: king evacuations (positions 1, 3, 4), forcing checks (positions 5, 6), active sacrifices (position 8), or pawn advances for counterplay (position 9). In 6/10 positions the passive rook move led to forced checkmate (positions 1, 5, 7, 8, 10 with immediate mates; position 2 already lost). The average cp_loss of ~4800 reflects how catastrophic passive defense is when the position requires decisive action. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, showing these are critical moments where only active play survives.

1537.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn advance or passive piece move in a critical position that demands an immediate capture or forcing tactical response.
1537.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking, non-threatening move played when the position required immediate tactical action. 7/10 moves are flank pawn advances (a4, h5, h3, h5, b3, g5, g4) and 3/10 are passive bishop moves (Bh6, Bf4, Bf8). In contrast, the best moves were captures or forcing moves in 8/10 cases (Bxd5, Nh3+, Nxd3+, hxg3, Bxg5/hxg5, fxg4, Rxc3, Qxf4). The average number of good moves was only 1.2, indicating these were critical positions with essentially one correct response. The average cp_loss was 2134, reflecting catastrophic consequences. The common thread is choosing a 'quiet' continuation—often a seemingly logical pawn advance for space or prophylaxis—in a position that is tactically on fire and demands immediate engagement through captures or forcing sequences.

1538.label: Rook moves to an aggressive-looking square but abandons a critical defensive duty or lands on a tactically vulnerable square, allowing the opponent to exploit the exposed king or win the rook.
1538.description: All 10 positions feature rook moves to 'active' squares—attacking pawns, invading ranks, or giving checks. In 9/10 positions, the player's king is exposed or vulnerable. The core error in 8/10 cases is that the rook abandons a critical defensive axis (a key file or proximity to the king) in favor of offensive activity that proves irrelevant. In 3/10 positions (2, 6, 7), the rook lands on a square where it is immediately forkable by the opponent's queen checking the king. In 5/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 8, 9), the rook moves away from king defense, enabling mating attacks or forcing sequences. In 1/10 (position 3), a rook check improves the opponent's king. Position 10 shows 0cp loss but fits the geometric template. The average cp_loss of 3804 reflects how catastrophic these 'active' rook moves are—6/10 positions convert to forced checkmate. Consistently, the best alternatives involve the rook staying on a defensive file (f-file, b-file) or the king moving first before the rook repositions.

1528.label: Playing a seemingly useful major piece move to an active square when the position demanded an urgent king safety measure, typically a king move.
1528.description: 9/10 positions featured critically exposed kings where king safety was the overriding concern. 8/10 moves were rook moves to apparently active squares (open files, 2nd/7th ranks, central positions). In 5/10 positions, the correct move was specifically a king move (Ka8, Kg2, Kd7, Kb7, Kh6) — quiet prophylactic relocations that addressed the root vulnerability. In 2/10 positions (4 and 7), the error was using the rook instead of the queen on the same square (Rd2 vs Qd2, Qf2 vs Rf2), where the queen's broader defensive coverage was essential. Position 10 was slightly different (missed cxd4 capturing a queen) but still involved an unnecessary queen redeployment. The average cp_loss of 3086 reflects that these 'natural-looking' moves often allowed forced checkmates (5/10 positions led to mate). Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, confirming these were razor-sharp positions demanding the single precise response.

1548.label: Voluntarily capturing the opponent's rook on a contested open file, surrendering file control to the opponent's remaining heavy pieces which then invade decisively.
1548.description: All 10/10 positions feature rooks from both sides occupying the same open file, and the mistake is always the player initiating the rook exchange by capturing the opponent's rook (Rx__). In 10/10 cases, the opponent recaptures with another rook (or the exchange otherwise leaves them with uncontested file dominance), and the resulting invasion proves devastating. The best alternatives consistently involve NOT exchanging: 8/10 positions recommend improving a different piece (developing a knight, repositioning a bishop, moving the king) or redeploying the rook to a better square while maintaining the file contest. The punishment is remarkably uniform: after recapture, the opponent's rook penetrates to the 6th or 7th rank (seen in positions 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10), often attacking multiple weak pawns or creating mating threats against an exposed king (positions 3, 4, 7, 8, 9). The average cp_loss of 1146 reflects that several of these lead to forced mate or near-immediate decisive advantage. The positions span various file (c, d, e, f, g) but the geometric and strategic error is identical in every case.
1548.old_chip: Premature rook exchange on contested file

1550.label: Moving a knight (or minor piece) to a passive rim/corner square while an urgent tactical crisis demands immediate defensive action.
1550.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight moving to a rim or corner square (Na3 x3, Na6 x2, Na7, Nb8, Nh1, Nh6), while 1/10 is a bishop retreating to the edge (Bb6). In all 10 positions, there is an immediate tactical crisis — typically a king safety emergency (8/10 involve direct mating threats or devastating attacks). The average cp_loss of 3857 reflects that 5/10 positions resulted in forced mate after the move. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow positions demanding precise defensive responses. In every case, the played move is a slow repositioning/developmental move that addresses zero immediate threats, while the piece lands on a square completely disconnected from the critical sector of the board. The knight on the rim has no influence over the squares where the tactical battle is raging — typically the kingside or center — leaving the opponent free to execute their attack unopposed.

1549.label: A non-forcing rook move to an open file while an immediate tactical threat (usually a hanging piece) goes unaddressed.
1549.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being placed on an open or semi-open file as a 'natural developing move' while a critical tactical emergency demands immediate attention. In 9/10 cases, a piece is directly hanging or under imminent capture threat: knights hanging to pawn captures (positions 1, 5, 9, 10), pieces capturable by opponent's queen (positions 5, 6), a rook en prise to a pawn (position 8), an undefended bishop (position 2), and a rook attacked by an enemy bishop (position 3). Position 4 and 7 involve immediate mating threats being ignored. The average cp_loss of 2354 is catastrophic, and only 1.5 good moves existed on average, confirming these are critical moments requiring specific tactical responses. In 7/10 cases the rook moved from its starting corner square (prefix Ra- or similar), emphasizing the 'development' intent. All 10 moves are completely non-forcing — no checks, no captures, no threats created.

1554.label: Retreating a bishop (or queen) to a passive square, abandoning a critical defensive or controlling function that the opponent immediately exploits tactically.
1554.description: 8/10 positions involve bishop moves and 2/10 involve queen moves, but all 10 share the defining characteristic of retreating a piece backward along a diagonal to a more passive square when the position demanded concrete or active play. In 10/10 cases the retreating piece was previously performing a critical function—guarding a key square, maintaining pressure, or covering a diagonal—that is abandoned by the move. In 9/10 positions the piece moves toward the player's own back rank or corner (Bc1, Bd8, Bb2, Bc2×2, Qb1, Bc7, Qd7, Bb7), and in 10/10 cases the opponent gains at least one free tempo to execute a tactical blow. The tactical punishments vary (forks in 1/10, mating attacks in 2/10, positional crushing in 4/10, material wins in 3/10), but the mechanism is consistent: the retreat vacates control of a critical square (e6, c4, f8, g2, kingside squares) that the opponent immediately occupies or exploits. The average cp_loss of 1156 reflects that these passive repositioning moves are particularly catastrophic because they combine tempo loss with removal of a key defender.

1552.label: A bishop is developed or repositioned to an active-looking square while a more critical tactical or defensive need goes unaddressed.
1552.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop move to an apparently aggressive square (attacking a piece, pinning, developing to an active diagonal), while 1/10 is a supporting pawn push (f4) with similar intent. In all 10 positions, the move prioritizes optical piece activity over addressing a concrete, immediate need. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 10), the critical neglected need is king safety — the player's king is exposed or uncastled and the bishop move does nothing to remedy this. In 3/10 positions (5, 6, 8), the bishop move leaves another piece hanging or a pawn undefended, allowing a simple capture. In 3/10 positions (4, 7, 9), the bishop arrives on a square where it can immediately be challenged or deflected, resulting in net tempo loss and positional collapse. The average cp_loss of 1247 and the low average of 2.2 good moves available confirm these are critical moments where the position demanded concrete solutions, not cosmetic improvements.

1551.label: A well-placed knight abandons a dominant square to capture a pawn, only to be immediately recaptured, losing the knight or critical positional value.
1551.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight makes a capture (9/10 are Nx captures, 1 is a knight move to create a fork). In 8/10 positions, the knight starts on a powerful centralized square (d5 in 5/10, d4 in 1/10, g4 in 2/10). The critical shared error is that the knight lands on a square where it is immediately recaptured or rendered useless — in 8/10 cases the queen specifically recaptures the knight (Qxf6, Qxc7 three times, Qxf5, Qxh6+, Qxc2, Rxe3). In 4/10 positions (2, 8, 10, plus partially 4), the player saw an 'illusory fork' on c7 or c2 thinking they were attacking king+rook, but the queen defended the target square. In 2/10 positions (7, 9), the knight abandonment squandered a forced checkmate. The average cp_loss of 2267 reflects catastrophic consequences, as the knight was typically the single most important piece in the position.

1564.label: The king greedily captures a pawn or piece, moving to an exposed square where it is immediately punished by checks exploiting its new vulnerability.
1564.description: All 8/8 positions feature the king making a capture (Kx__), always taking a tempting pawn (usually a passed pawn or advanced enemy pawn). In 7/8 cases, the refutation begins with an immediate check—rook checks on open files (Rd8+, Rad1+), bishop diagonal checks (Bd4+), pawn advance checks (f4+, d4+), or queen checks (Qc3+)—exploiting the king's newly exposed square. In every position, safer king retreats or non-king moves were available (Kd1, Kd2, Ke2, Kg7, Ke8, Be3, Nxb6) that avoided the exposure, but the player chose material gain instead. The captures moved kings to central/open squares (d3, b2, g5, e3, d6, d4, e6) where they lacked pawn shields and sat on open lines. The average cp_loss of 2439 reflects how catastrophic these captures are—5/8 led to forced mate or near-mate, while the remaining positions lost major material (queens, rooks, bishops) through the resulting tactical exploitation.

1561.label: An aggressive-looking f/g/h pawn advance that weakens the player's own structure while ignoring the position's concrete tactical demands.
1561.description: All 10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance (9/10 on the f, g, or h files; 1/10 on the c-file) that appears active but is strategically or tactically misguided. In every case, the best moves involved piece activity — captures (2/10), piece repositioning (5/10), or king centralization (3/10) — rather than pawn thrusts. The pawn advances uniformly create permanent structural damage: opening diagonals against the player's own king (positions 3, 5, 9), creating isolated/weak pawns (positions 3, 10), blocking key squares for the player's own king (position 8), or simply wasting a critical tempo (positions 6, 7). In 4/10 cases, the player pushed a pawn to chase a piece that could be captured outright or was already tactically hanging. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 analyses, confirming the universal thread: these pawn moves spend time on non-critical objectives while the position demanded immediate concrete action.

1560.label: A passive minor piece development to a standard square (d7/e7/e2/d6) when the position demands an urgent tactical or defensive response.
1560.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing minor piece development move (9/10 are bishop moves to stereotypical squares: Bd7 x3, Be7 x4, Be2 x2, Bd6 x1; plus one Nbd2) played in a position that demands immediate concrete action. In every case, the player treats a tactically critical moment as a routine development phase. The urgent needs varied: 4/10 required contesting a file or square to prevent an invasion (Re8, Rf6, Rc1, Rb8), 3/10 needed to neutralize a specific fork or checking threat (Qb6/c4/Qa5, d5/Nf6/Qd7, a3), 2/10 demanded prophylactic pawn moves to prevent kingside attacks (g3), and 1/10 required maintaining dynamic pressure with the queen. The average cp_loss of 309 reflects that these 'natural-looking' moves consistently hand the opponent a critical tempo to execute devastating tactical plans that were one move away from realization.

1557.label: King moves in endgame pawn races where the efficiency of the king's path is critical to the promotion timing.
1557.description: 10/10 positions are endgames featuring king moves during active pawn races with passed pawns on both sides. 8/10 are pure king-and-pawn endgames, and the remaining 2 involve rook endgames with passed pawns. In all cases, both sides have passed pawns racing to promote, and the king's move determines whether the tempo balance is maintained. The serious errors (positions 3, 5, 7 with 400-9200 cp_loss) all involve the king taking an indirect/inefficient path that loses exactly one critical tempo — e.g., Kg6 instead of Kg7 (positions 3 and 7), or Kb7 retreating away from the action (position 5). However, 4/10 positions show 0 or near-0 cp_loss, where the king move was actually optimal or equivalent, suggesting the feature activates on the SITUATION (king navigating a pawn race) regardless of whether the move chosen is correct or erroneous.

1553.label: Playing slow wing pawn moves or greedy edge captures when exactly one forcing move is required to avoid catastrophe.
1553.description: 8/9 positions feature moves on the a, b, g, or h files (the board edges), with 4/9 being h-file pawn pushes (h3, h3, h6, hxg2) and 3/9 being captures on the a/b files (Rxa7, Rxa6, Kxb2). The average good moves available was only 1.2, meaning nearly every position had exactly ONE correct continuation. In every case, the position demanded immediate tactical action — either seizing a concrete opportunity (capturing a hanging piece in positions 4, 5, 8; exploiting a check in position 7) or addressing a lethal threat (positions 2, 6, 9, 10). Instead, the player chose a non-forcing peripheral action: a prophylactic pawn push (h3/h6/a3), a wing pawn grab (Rxa7/Rxa6/Kxb2), or a slow positional move (Qd2). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3520 reflects that these single-tempo wastes consistently transformed playable positions into forced mates or decisive material losses.
1553.old_chip: Peripheral tempo waste in critical positions

1563.label: The king advances aggressively in the endgame but lands on an exposed open line where it becomes vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks that neutralize or reverse the position's evaluation.
1563.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that advances toward the action (supporting a passed pawn, centralizing, or approaching the opponent's position) rather than retreating or staying put. In 8/10 cases, the direct refutation involves a check against the misplaced king (Rc1+, f4+, e5+, Re5+, Qb7+, Rc3+, or a promoted queen giving check on a diagonal). In 7/10 positions, the best move was actually a rook move or a king move in a different direction that avoided the open line. The average cp_loss of 1244 reflects catastrophic consequences, and with only 1.9 good moves available on average, these are narrow decision points where the 'natural' advancing king move is specifically the wrong choice. The kings consistently land on open files (c-file in positions 1, 10; d-file in position 3; b-file in position 6), open ranks, or dangerous diagonals (position 8) where enemy pieces exploit them with tempo.

1562.label: Playing a quiet preparatory or repositioning move when an immediate forcing tactical blow (check, sacrifice, or concrete threat) was available.
1562.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no unavoidable threat) played in lieu of an available forcing continuation. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 analyses. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 5, 8), the best move was an immediate check or sacrifice with check. In 3/10 positions (6, 9, 10), the player chose the wrong piece for a correct square—a weaker piece (rook or bishop) where a stronger piece (queen) was needed to generate immediate threats (Ra4 vs Qa4, Rh2 vs Qh2, Be8 vs Qe8). The average cp_loss of 3050 is enormous, with 5/10 positions involving missed forced mates. In 8/10 positions, the opponent's refutation was simply to use the gifted tempo to shore up defenses (block a file, advance a defensive pawn, retreat the king, or neutralize an attacking wedge). Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical-moment positions demanding precision rather than general play.

1547.label: Rook moves focused on passed pawn support or blockade that miss immediate tactical opportunities (mates, forks, promotions).
1547.description: 8/10 positions feature prominent passed pawns as the central strategic theme, and in 7/10 cases the rook move specifically targets a passed pawn (supporting own passer from behind, blockading opponent's passer, or moving to its file). However, the position demanded an immediate tactical solution instead. In positions 6 and 10, back-rank/mating-net mates were available but the rook moved to support/block a passed pawn. In position 5, a quiet pawn capture enabled forced mate but the player gave a premature rook check. In positions 2 and 8, the rook repositioned for passed pawn play while immediate promotion tricks or king-safety crises demanded attention. In position 9, the rook went behind a passer instead of an immediate knight fork. Positions 3 and 4 (0 and 19 cp loss respectively) appear to be noise in the feature activation. The average cp_loss of 4816 is driven by 5 positions with 9000+ cp loss where forced mates were missed, confirming these are critical moments where strategic thinking about pawns overrode tactical calculation.

1566.label: A rook moves to a seemingly defensive or active square while the king is critically exposed, but the rook move itself worsens the king's safety by blocking escape squares or removing critical defenders.
1566.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a 'natural' rook move (usually to f1, a3, f8, or c8) that appears to save material, defend a pawn, or seek activity — yet the real priority was king safety. In 6/10 positions, the specific move was Rf1 while the king sat on e1. In 4/10 of those (positions 1,2,3,6), the rook on f1 directly blocked the king's only escape square, enabling immediate checkmate patterns. In 2/10 positions (7,8), Ra3 removed the rook's defense of the b1 knight, allowing captures with check that exposed the king fatally. In 2/10 (4,9), Rf1 was a passive defensive move that squandered a tempo when an attacking move (Rg1 or Qxg4) would have exploited hanging material. In 1/10 (position 10), Rc8 removed the f8 rook from its critical defensive role on the kingside. The average cp_loss of 5640 and average of only 1.3 good moves available confirm these are extremely narrow, desperate positions where king safety was the paramount concern and the rook move was always wrong.

1541.label: Making an apparently active or aggressive move that displaces a piece/pawn from a critical defensive or structural function, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated role.
1541.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player moves a piece or pawn that was performing a critical (often non-obvious) function—blocking a diagonal, guarding a key square, anchoring an attack, or maintaining structural integrity—tempted by a seemingly attractive alternative goal. In 5/10 positions, the moved piece was explicitly blocking or guarding a specific tactical vulnerability (positions 4, 5, 6, 8, 9: a pawn blocking a diagonal to the queen, a knight controlling escape squares, a knight preventing back-rank mate, a pawn shielding the king, a bishop covering a check diagonal). In 3/10 positions, the error was specifically an en passant capture that traded away a structurally vital pawn (positions 2, 3, 4). In 3/10, a knight was moved away from a dominant/critical outpost (positions 5, 6, 7). The temptation varied—material gain (1), aggressive-looking passed pawn creation (2, 3), opening attacking lines (4), giving check (5), repositioning (6, 7), space gain (8), attacking an enemy piece (9), or advancing toward promotion (10)—but in every case the secondary objective was far less important than the function being abandoned. The average cp_loss of 3005 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors but catastrophic tactical oversights, and the average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these were demanding positions requiring precise recognition of what mattered most.

1568.label: A bishop captures (or aggressively advances toward) a kingside pawn in a speculative sacrifice intended to rip open the opponent's king shelter, but the attack is objectively insufficient.
1568.description: 8/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a kingside pawn (Bxh3 in 5 positions, Bxh6, Bxg6, and Bxg3 in the others), while the remaining 2 involve a bishop aggressively repositioning toward the kingside (Bf4, Be5). In all cases, the player's intent was to generate a kingside attack — typically by opening the g-file or h-file after gxh3...Qxh3 — but the sacrifice is objectively unsound. 7/10 positions explicitly involve the opponent having clear defensive resources that neutralize the attack (Nh2+Qf3, Bf1, Bg4, N1h2, etc.). The average cp_loss of 295 reflects that these moves transform manageable or even advantageous positions into losing ones. 9/10 positions offered at least one patient positional alternative (piece development, rook activation, quiet improvement) that maintained the evaluation. The core failure is overestimating attacking potential while underestimating the defender's consolidating resources.

1558.label: Moving a piece (usually queen or king) to a square that creates a geometric alignment with another friendly piece, enabling immediate tactical exploitation via forks, pins, skewers, or discovered attacks.
1558.description: In 6/10 positions, the moved piece (queen or king) lands on a square that places it in direct geometric alignment with another friendly piece, creating a fork or pin vulnerability exploitable in 1-2 moves. Specifically, positions 1, 2, and 3 all feature a queen moving to a square where it becomes forkable alongside the king by a knight (Nd2+, Ne7+, Ne3+ respectively). Position 9 shows the queen stepping behind a knight on the same diagonal as an enemy bishop, creating a catastrophic pin. Position 6 shows the king stepping onto a diagonal enabling a discovered check. Position 4 creates an e-file skewer. The remaining 4/10 positions extend the pattern more loosely: the piece moves to a seemingly safe square but either abandons a critical defensive duty (positions 7, 8 — Kf7 abandoning pawn/piece defense) or misses a concrete forcing continuation in favor of passive repositioning (positions 5, 10). All 10 moves share key properties: they are non-forcing (no checks, captures, or threats), they appear defensive/logical, very few good alternatives existed (avg 1.6), and the punishment is immediate and severe (avg 1250cp loss).

1555.label: Rook moves to a natural-looking active square that is tactically vulnerable to forks, skewers, or captures after intermediate moves.
1555.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves to seemingly active or purposeful squares (open files, active ranks, checks, blockading) that overlook concrete tactical vulnerabilities at the destination. In 5/10 positions (Rb4, Rd2, Rb5, Rc1+, Re7), the rook lands on a square directly exploitable by knight forks or skewers — the opponent wins material immediately through geometric piece coordination.
