In 3/10 positions (Rg8, Rh1, Rc7), the rook move is premature or misordered, allowing intermediate checks or consolidating moves that exploit the rook's new placement. In 4/10 positions (1, 4, 9, 10), the correct alternative was a king move rather than a rook move, suggesting the pattern involves prioritizing rook 'activity' over more urgent positional needs. The average cp_loss of 289 is high, and only 2.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the natural-looking rook move is specifically the wrong choice among limited options.

1559.label: Seemingly active or material-gaining moves that fatally neglect the position's most urgent defensive requirement, allowing an immediate tactical refutation.
1559.description: All 10 positions share a critical pattern: the player makes a move that appears active, productive, or materially gaining (captures in 6/10, piece 'improvements' in 4/10) while ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical demand. In 8/10 cases, king safety is the neglected factor—either the player's own king becomes fatally exposed (positions 1, 2, 4, 7, 9) or a piece abandons a critical defensive post guarding against a king attack (positions 5, 6, 9). In 5/10 positions, the moved piece directly leaves material hanging (Bf4 leaves e4 undefended, Na3 fails to guard c4, Rb1 abandons a3, Rxd5 places rook in queen's sightline, Nxe5 leaves knight en prise). The average cp_loss of 3151 reflects catastrophic consequences—4/10 positions result in immediate mate or near-mate. The average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are critical junctures where precision is mandatory, yet players chose 'natural-looking' moves over the one or two options that addressed the real problem.

1572.label: Castling as a routine developing move while a piece (or critical square) is left tactically unresolved, allowing the opponent to win material or execute a devastating tactic.
1572.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling played while an urgent tactical issue demands immediate attention. In 7/10 cases, a specific piece is directly hanging or effectively undefended (Position 2: Bf4, Position 3: Nc4, Position 5: Bc4, Position 6: Bd4, Position 7: Qc5, Position 9: Nc6 to dxc6, Position 10: Nd5 to Bxd5). In the remaining 3/10, castling specifically enables a tactic that wasn't previously available: Position 1 (O-O-O puts king on c1 enabling Bxg5+ check), Position 4 (O-O enables Nxd4/Nxf3+ with check to g1), and Position 8 (O-O places rook on f8 creating Nxe6 fork target). The best moves in every position share a common structure: first resolve the tactical tension (capture, trade, retreat, or reposition the vulnerable piece), THEN castle. Average cp_loss is 428, confirming these are severe blunders. 6/10 are White castling, 4/10 Black; 6/10 occur in the opening, 4/10 in the middlegame—showing this pattern spans both sides and phases.

1565.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn advance (or quiet developing move) to attack or challenge an enemy piece, when an immediate capture or forcing tactical blow was available.
1565.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (e6, f6, c4, c5, d6, e4, f3, f4, d5) and 1/10 a quiet piece development (Bd3), all sharing the critical flaw of being non-forcing when the position demanded immediate tactical action. In 6/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10), the correct move was a direct capture (Qxe4+, Qxb5, Qxg5, Qxc4, or winning a piece via forced sequence). In 8/10 positions, the played move specifically attacks or challenges an enemy piece with a pawn, when a more forcing capture of that piece (or another) was available — notably positions 9 and 10 where the player pushed a pawn to attack the very piece they could have simply captured outright. The average number of good moves was only 1.4, indicating these are narrow tactical positions where only one correct move exists, yet the players consistently chose the 'natural-looking' positional/spatial move over the decisive tactical one. All 10 positions show the played move giving the opponent a critical tempo to regroup or execute a counter-resource that wasn't available after the correct forcing continuation.

1556.label: Rook moves toward a tempting target (pawn capture, check, centralization, attack) but abandons its critical defensive post, typically exposing the king.
1556.description: 10/10 positions feature rook moves that appear purposeful—targeting pawns, giving checks, centralizing, or joining attacks—but are strategically flawed because they abandon the rook's more important defensive function. In 8/10 positions, king safety was the primary factor compromised (positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 2), where the rook was providing essential protection along a file or rank near the king. In 6/10 positions, the rook specifically moved AWAY from the file or rank where it was shielding the king (g-file in positions 5 and 6, f-file in position 8, 4th rank in position 9, back rank in position 10, kingside in position 4). In 4/10 cases, the rook targeted a specific pawn (Rc2→c4, Rd5→d6, Ra5→d5, Rxc5), making the 'lure' material gain. Position 3 (Re3, cp_loss=0) is an outlier where the rook correctly confronted an active enemy piece—suggesting the feature detects the geometric pattern of rook repositioning rather than the mistake itself. The average cp_loss of 2869 (driven by 3 positions with forced mates) confirms these are catastrophic errors when they occur.

1569.label: Moving a rook to an open/semi-open file as a routine 'improving' move when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1569.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being placed on an open or semi-open file (c-file 5 times, d-file 4 times, b-file once) from a passive home square, with the notation specifying which rook moved (Rf- 8/10, Rh- 2/10), confirming both rooks were available. In every case, the move is non-forcing—no check, no capture, no direct threat—and represents a stereotypical 'positional improvement' that ignores urgent tactical demands. The best moves in 7/10 positions were concrete actions: pawn breaks (e5, d4, c5), piece challenges (Bd6, a6, Be5), or forcing tactics (Bf3+, Ng4). The average cp_loss of 284 reflects catastrophic consequences: the opponent either consolidates (positions 4, 7, 9), executes a tactical strike (positions 6, 8, 10 with forks), exploits self-blocking (position 1), punishes wrong-rook selection leaving key squares undefended (positions 2, 10), or seizes the initiative with counterplay (positions 3, 5). Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision, not routine development.

1570.label: Retreating a knight or bishop from an active position to a passive square on the 1st or 8th rank, losing critical tempo and abandoning key square control.
1570.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight retreating, and 1/10 a bishop, with 9/10 destination squares on the literal 1st or 8th rank (e8, a8, c1, d1, b8, c1, b1, f1) and 1/10 on the 2nd rank (d2). In every case, the piece leaves an active centralized post: from d6→e8 (positions 1,5), b6→a8 (position 2), b3→c1 (position 3), f3→d2 (position 4), c3→d1 (position 6), c6→b8 (position 7), b2→c1 (position 8), c3→b1 (position 9), e3→f1 (position 10). The consistent punishment is that the opponent exploits the resulting tempo and/or abandoned square control: 3/10 positions resulted in immediate forced mate, 7/10 had 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif, and the average cp_loss of 2126 reflects multiple catastrophic miscalculations. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, confirming these were critical moments where precise piece maintenance was required rather than repositioning.
1570.old_chip: Minor piece retreats to back rank

1571.label: A bishop (or piece) is repositioned to a seemingly reasonable square, but in doing so abandons a vital defensive or restraining function that the opponent immediately exploits.
1571.description: 9/10 positions feature bishop moves (the outlier c3 shares the same passive-repositioning logic). In every case, the moved piece was performing a critical function — restraining an opponent's piece (Position 1: Bg4 restrained Nf3 from reaching d4), defending a key pawn (Positions 8-9: bishop defended d5), controlling a tactical square (Position 3: Bg2 controlled e4), or maintaining attacking pressure (Positions 4, 7: active placement demanded concrete action). The player chose to reposition the bishop for apparently reasonable goals: attacking an opponent's piece (Positions 8-9), retreating to 'safety' (Positions 1, 6, 7), grabbing material (Position 3), or centralizing (Position 5). However, 10/10 moves gave the opponent a critical tempo to exploit the abandoned function — whether winning material via newly available tactics (7/10 positions) or achieving full consolidation that neutralized the opponent's initiative (3/10 positions). The average cp_loss of 224 reflects that these are not minor inaccuracies but significant blunders where the bishop's prior role was far more valuable than its destination.

1581.label: A knight is moved to an apparently aggressive or centralizing square where it can be immediately captured with no adequate recapture.
1581.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight move to a square that appears active or threatening but is immediately capturable. In 9/10 cases the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece.' The knight lands on a square controlled by the opponent's pieces: in 4/10 cases an enemy knight captures it (positions 3, 5, 9, 10), in 3/10 cases multiple enemy pieces attack the landing square creating an arithmetic imbalance (positions 1, 7, 8), in 2/10 cases a bishop captures with no viable recapture (positions 4, 8), and in 1/10 cases a queen captures with check (position 2). The intended purpose of the knight move is consistently aggressive — centralizing, attacking king-adjacent squares, or threatening enemy pieces — but the player fails to verify that the destination square is adequately defended. The average cp_loss of 368 reflects that most of these moves lose approximately a full piece worth of material.

1578.label: The player makes a non-forcing king move while a major piece is hanging or a critical tactical threat goes unaddressed.
1578.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing king move that ignores an immediate material crisis. In 7/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10), a major piece (queen or rook) was directly hanging or about to be captured for free, and the correct move involved either capturing, exchanging, or making a forcing move to address the threat. In 2/10 cases (positions 4, 6), the king walked directly into a mating net. In 1/10 cases (position 5), the king moved away from the only square that allowed a critical recapture. The best moves were diverse — queen sacrifices (positions 1, 3), rook exchanges with check (positions 8, 10), forcing deflections (position 2), capturing a dangerous pawn (position 7) — but all shared the quality of being ACTIVE and FORCING. The blundered king moves were universally passive and purposeless relative to the tactical emergency, typically motivated by vague notions of king safety or centralization while a concrete hanging-piece or mating problem demanded immediate attention.
1578.old_chip: Passive king move ignores hanging piece

1576.label: Playing a tempting-looking active rook move (invasion, check, or capture) when the position demands a different priority — a better tactic, proper move order, or addressing a defensive need first.
1576.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that appear aggressive but are premature or misdirected. 7/10 involve rooks invading the 2nd or 7th rank (Re2, Rd2, Rb2, Rb7, Rxb7+, Rxg2, Rxc6), while 3/10 are rook checks (Rg1+, Rf1+, Rxb7+). The correct moves were strikingly different: in 4/10 positions the best move was a non-rook tactical shot (Be3, Nf6, Nxd7, Qe3+), in 3/10 a prophylactic/defensive move was required first (Nf1, Bc4/Kf8, Bxd2), and in 3/10 the rook move needed a precise intermediate move beforehand (Rf2+ before Rxg2) or patient consolidation (Ka6/g5). The average cp_loss of 333 reflects that these 'active' rook moves consistently squander significant advantages or turn equality into losses. 9/10 positions were middlegame, where tactical complexity makes hasty rook activity particularly punishable. Only 1-3 good alternatives existed on average (1.8), meaning these were critical moments requiring precision rather than instinctive aggression.

1575.label: Moving a rook to a seemingly active but ultimately misplaced square, abandoning critical defensive coordination and creating tactical vulnerabilities.
1575.description: 9/10 positions involve rook moves (the exception, Bg6, ignores a tactical threat to a rook). In all cases, the piece moves to a square that appears active — attacking pawns (Rb4, Rb3), occupying open files (Rad8, Rg8, Rg5), penetrating to the 7th rank (Ra7), or centralizing (Re3, Rb6) — but actually neglects the most critical defensive requirement of the position. 7/10 are Black moves in already difficult or losing positions where maximum resistance demands precise defensive coordination. The punishments exploit the resulting vulnerabilities: in 4/10 positions the moved piece becomes tactically hanging via check-and-capture sequences (Rb4, Rb3, Re3 skewer, Bg6); in 3/10 the king is fatally exposed to back-rank or corridor mates (Ra7 position 2, Rad8, Rg8); and in 3/10 the piece simply loses coordination allowing the opponent's advantage to grow unchecked (Rb6, Ra7 position 9, Rg5). The average cp_loss of 3091 reflects that several of these represent catastrophic evaluation collapses (positions 2, 7, 8 all exceed 9000cp loss), turning survivable positions into forced mates.

1579.label: A rook (or major piece) moves aggressively to an undefended square that is already covered by an opponent's piece, and is immediately captured for free.
1579.description: 10/10 positions feature a major piece (9 rooks, 1 queen) moving to a square where it is immediately captured by the opponent with no compensation. The tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' in 9/10 cases. The moves all look superficially aggressive — checks (2/10: Rg7+), back-rank/8th-rank penetrations (2/10: Rd8, Rc8), 7th-rank invasions (3/10: Rd7, Qb7, Rg7+), 2nd-rank invasions (2/10: Rd2, Rf2), or centralizations (2/10: Rd5, Rd6) — but the destination square is already defended by an opponent's piece that simply captures. In 6/10 positions, the player missed a simple capture of their own (opponent's piece was hanging), choosing an 'active' move instead of a winning trade. 7/10 moves land on the d-file specifically. The average cp_loss of 3530 reflects that these are catastrophic one-move blunders, not subtle positional errors.

1580.label: A non-forcing flank pawn advance wastes a critical tempo when the position urgently demands piece activity or a concrete tactical operation.
1580.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance on a wing file (a, b, f, g, or h) when the best moves all involve piece play — rook activations (Rf1, Rb4, Rg4, Rg5, Ra6), knight repositioning (Nf1, Nxf6+), or king safety moves (Ka8). In 9/10 positions the move is on the outermost files (a/b/g/h), with one on the f-file. The tactical motif is tagged as 'tempo_loss' in 8/10 cases. The average cp_loss is 274 with only 1.7 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical moments where only piece moves maintain the position. In 6/10 cases the best move involved immediately contesting or seizing an open file with a rook, while the pawn push addressed a different flank entirely. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 8, 10, 2), the pawn advance directly weakened the player's own king position or blocked their own pieces. The common thread is a 'positional autopilot' pawn push substituted for the precise, forcing piece move the position demanded.

1574.label: Playing a quiet repositioning move (usually the queen) when the position demanded an immediate forcing tactical blow.
1574.description: 10/10 positions feature the player choosing a non-forcing, non-capturing preparatory move in a position where a concrete tactical opportunity existed. 6/10 moves are queen repositions to natural-looking squares (Qe2 x3, Qd2, Qf6, Qf2), while the remaining involve piece moves (Nd2, Nh3, Be7, Rd7) that similarly prioritize 'improving' over 'executing.' The best moves in 9/10 positions were forcing: checks (Qg4+, Re8+), captures (Qxd6, Nxc5), concrete threats (Nb5 threatening Nc7+ fork, Rf3 direct invasion, g5 attacking with tempo), or moves maintaining a critical tactical resource (Ne2 keeping the h-file clear). The average cp_loss of 278 and average of only 1.4 good moves available confirms these are narrow tactical windows that punish delay. In every case, the opponent used the gifted tempo to consolidate—neutralizing king exposure (positions 1, 2, 4, 9), launching counterplay (positions 5, 7, 10), or capturing a piece that was previously untouchable (position 3).

1583.label: Voluntarily withdrawing a bishop that was aggressively planted adjacent to the opponent's king (h7/h2/f2) to a less threatening square, abandoning the attack.
1583.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a bishop that was aggressively stationed directly adjacent to the opponent's king — on h7 (4 positions: 1, 3, 4, 6), h2 (4 positions: 5, 7, 8, 10), or f2 (2 positions: 2, 9) — to a retreated or centralized square further from the king (e4, h4, d3, f5, d6, f4, e5). In every case, the bishop's proximity to the king was creating immense positional/tactical pressure, either directly threatening mating ideas, indirectly protecting other pieces by tying down defenders, or restricting the opponent's king mobility. The retreat consistently gave the opponent time to consolidate, activate pieces, or exploit tactical vulnerabilities that the attacking bishop had been masking. In 7/10 positions, the best move involved maintaining or improving the attacking bishop's influence near the king; in 8/10 positions, the retreat enabled a specific tactical refutation (hanging piece, rook lift, checking sequence, or pawn break) that wasn't possible while the bishop was restricting the opponent.

1582.label: A rook is moved to the player's own back rank (1st/8th) as a seemingly natural activating or repositioning move, but this non-forcing rook placement ignores urgent tactical or king-safety priorities.
1582.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the player's back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black). These moves look like reasonable 'development' or 'activation' — placing the rook on an open or semi-open file — but they are uniformly too slow or misdirected. In 7/10 positions, the critical need was king safety (either evacuating one's own king or exploiting the opponent's exposed king with forcing moves). In 6/10 positions, the best move was something entirely different from a rook move (king moves in positions 5/9, a queen check in position 10, g6 prophylaxis in position 2, f6 pawn break in position 4, Qxe4 capture in position 7). In 3/10 positions the rook specifically became a tactical target or liability on its new back-rank square (position 2: skewer target on e8; position 4: fork target on g8; position 5: Rh1+ wins it). The average centipawn loss of 1127 (excluding the 0-loss position 8) reflects how severely these slow moves are punished in sharp positions demanding immediacy.

1567.label: Aggressively deploying a minor piece (usually bishop to h6) toward a weakened enemy king without first playing a more forcing check, capture, or perpetual.
1567.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop moves and 2/10 feature knight moves, all directed aggressively toward a weakened enemy king position. 4/10 positions specifically play Bh6 aimed at restricting a king on h8 with a compromised pawn shield. 9/10 positions feature an enemy king with a weak or absent pawn shield. In the 8 positions where the move was a mistake (avg cp_loss 1222), the correct continuation was almost always a more forcing move: perpetual checks (positions 2, 4), preparatory checks before committing the piece (positions 1, 2, 4), concrete captures of threatening pieces (position 9), or tactical blows exploiting the position (positions 3, 5, 8, 10). 2/10 positions (6, 7) show the move was actually correct — these are cases where the attacking piece deployment truly created an unstoppable mating net. The critical distinction: in error positions, the player's queen was already aggressively placed (typically on g6/h5/h6) and a perpetual check or forcing sequence was available but ignored in favor of committing another piece.

1587.label: A pawn advance to attack a well-posted enemy knight creates catastrophic weaknesses around the player's own king.
1587.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to directly attack a strong enemy knight: f3 attacks knights on e4/g4 (4/10), f6 attacks knights on e5/g5 (5/10), c6 attacks a knight on b5 (1/10), and c3 attacks a knight on d4 (1/10). In 9/10 cases the moving side's king was uncastled or centrally exposed, and the pawn advance fatally weakened critical diagonals or squares adjacent to that king. The refutations consistently exploit the newly created weakness: 7/10 positions feature Qh5+ or Qh4+ checks along the diagonal opened by the f-pawn, often followed by piece sacrifices on g3/g6 to demolish the pawn shield. In 8/10 positions the player had better alternatives involving piece development or king safety (castling, moving the queen off a dangerous file, or developing bishops). The average cp_loss of 310 confirms these are severe blunders, not marginal inaccuracies.

1573.label: A rook repositions (often toward the king) when the king urgently needed to move to safety, frequently self-blocking escape squares or abandoning critical defensive duties.
1573.description: In 8/10 positions the blunder was a rook move, and in 7/10 the engine's best move was a king move (Kg8, Kf8, Kg1, Ke7, Ke3, etc.). The player consistently chose to reposition a rook — usually with a defensive or challenging intent against an enemy queen — rather than evacuating their vulnerable king. In 4/10 positions (2, 6, 8, 9), the rook literally self-blocked the king's escape square, enabling immediate checkmate (Qxg7#, Qxf1#, Qf8#, and a forced mating sequence). In 3/10 positions (1, 3, 5), the rook abandoned a critical defensive post or made a passive repositioning instead of making a forcing capture with check. The remaining 2/10 were pawn moves that similarly neglected king safety. The average cp_loss was 3015, with 4 positions resulting in immediate mate. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were razor-thin survival positions where king evacuation was the singular defensive resource.
1573.old_chip: Rook moves instead of king evacuation

1590.label: A bishop on g4/g5, challenged by the h-pawn, captures on h3/h6 in a premature sacrifice to open the g-file against the opponent's castled king.
1590.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop that was actively placed on g4 (Black) or g5 (White), pressuring the opponent's knight on f3/f6, being challenged by the h-pawn (h3 or h6). Instead of the correct response—trading for the knight (Bxf3/Bxf6 was best or near-best in 9/10 positions) or retreating (Bh5/Bh4/Be6/Bd7 appeared as alternatives in all positions)—the player sacrifices the bishop by capturing the h-pawn, hoping gxh3/gxh6 opens the g-file for a kingside attack. In 10/10 cases, simple recapture refutes the sacrifice as the attacker lacks supporting pieces to sustain threats. In 7/10 positions, the sacrificing side's own king was still in the center (uncastled), making the attack doubly unjustified. The average material cost was 252cp, consistently representing a full piece sacrificed for one pawn with insufficient compensation.

1585.label: Non-forcing pawn advances that challenge the opponent's pawn structure while ignoring more urgent tactical, prophylactic, or king safety priorities.
1585.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance that directly confronts an opponent's pawn (f3 attacks e4/g4, g6 attacks f5, d5/d6 attacks e5/c4, f6 attacks e5, c4 attacks d5, h5 attacks g6). In every case, the player chose this slow, non-forcing structural challenge over something more urgent: 6/10 positions required addressing king safety (positions 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 9), 3/10 had concrete tactical shots missed (positions 4, 6, 10 — Nf6+ fork, Rb7+ forced mate, queen repositioning before the break), and 3/10 involved releasing central tension that exposed the player's own king or trapped their pieces (positions 3, 5, 9). The pawn breaks are all thematically logical in a vacuum — they're standard structural ideas against pawn chains — but catastrophically mistimed. The average cp_loss of 2143 reflects that several turned winning positions into losses or allowed forced mates. In 7/10 cases the pawn advance either weakened squares near the player's own king or opened lines toward it.

1584.label: Non-forcing pawn advances prioritizing positional goals over urgent concrete tactical opportunities in critical positions.
1584.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn moves (c4, b4, e5, c6, f3, e5, c4, f6, b3) and 1/10 a passive knight relocation (Nf4), all sharing the critical property of being non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no immediate threats). In 9/10 positions, the best available move was a forcing tactical blow—a check (Bxe6+, Rc1+, Ba6+), a capture (Bxd5), castling to safety (O-O in 3 positions), or a concrete central break (e4, d5). Instead, the player chose a slow pawn push aimed at 'attacking' enemy pieces or gaining space. In 6/10 positions, the pawn push specifically chased an enemy piece that relocated to a superior square (positions 5, 7, 8, 9 drove bishops to better diagonals; positions 2, 10 freed opponent's coordination). King safety was the dominant missed theme: 9/10 positions featured an exposed king (either the opponent's exploitable king or the player's own uncastled king needing urgent attention). The average cp_loss of 300 reflects the catastrophic cost of playing slowly in tactically critical positions.

1593.label: Giving a check that accomplishes nothing concrete while missing a stronger non-forcing move, allowing the opponent to improve their position when responding to the check.
1593.description: 10/10 positions feature a check (+) that fails to achieve any constructive goal. In 4/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 7, 8), the player gave check instead of capturing a hanging piece (an undefended rook worth 5+ pawns of material). In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10), the check allowed the opponent to beneficially interpose or reposition — examples include allowing a queen to reach an ideal defensive square (positions 1, 10), enabling a pawn to advance creating a passed pawn (position 2), letting a rook escape from a vulnerable square to a safe one (positions 7, 8), or permitting an interposition that creates an unbreakable drawing fortress (position 9). 7/10 moves are queen checks and 3/10 are rook checks, all in middlegame positions (9/10) with open files. The average centipawn loss is 1240, with the worst case being a missed mate-in-5 turned into merely a large advantage (position 7, 9579 cp loss).

1589.label: Moving a knight away from a critical central defensive role to a peripheral square, leaving a key central pawn (usually d4) undefended and immediately capturable.
1589.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight decentralizing from a square where it defended or supported a critical central pawn. In 6/10 cases the specific move is Na4, typically chasing an enemy queen on b6 that can simply capture the now-undefended d4 pawn instead of retreating. In 8/10 positions, the immediate refutation involves capturing the d4 pawn (Qxd4 in 6/10, ...e5 attacking d4 in 2/10). The Ne2 moves (2/10) similarly relocate the c3-knight away from central support, and the Nc4/Nec4 moves (2/10) abandon a powerful e5 outpost. In 9/10 cases the knight moves FROM c3 or e5 (major central squares) TO a4, e2, c4, or h5 (peripheral or passive squares). The average cp_loss is 305, reflecting that these decentralizations catastrophically undermine the structural foundation of the position. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision.

1592.label: Advancing a passed pawn (or creating pawn threats) while ignoring an immediate checkmate or devastating tactical threat against the player's own king.
1592.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet pawn advances as the blunder move — no captures, no checks, purely strategic pushes. In 8/10 cases, the pawn being pushed is a passed pawn or creates passed-pawn threats (e6, b6, c5, b3, c4, d6, d7, b5). Critically, 8/10 positions allow immediate checkmate in 1-3 moves after the push (positions 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 allow mate-in-1; position 1 allows mate-in-2; position 2 allows mate-in-3). The remaining 2/10 still feature severe tactical oversights (hanging piece in position 4, critical counterplay enabling in position 5). The king-safety crisis is present in 9/10 positions — typically back-rank mates (positions 1, 3, 6, 7) or smothered/suffocation mates (positions 8, 10) or queen-battery mates on open files (positions 2, 9). The average cp_loss of 9035 and only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where the sole priority was defensive, yet the player chose an offensive pawn push every time.

1588.label: Moves that spend a tempo on a visible but secondary concern while ignoring the position's true critical priority.
1588.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: the player identifies something seemingly logical to address (a threatened pawn, an annoying piece, a file to contest) but this target is secondary to the position's actual critical requirement. 10/10 moves were tagged as 'tempo_loss' in the analysis. In 5/10 positions (Rb8, Rf1×2, Bc1, b3), the player defensively addressed a pawn weakness (b6, f2, e3) that wasn't the real problem. In 3/10 positions (Bxa6, b6, Bxf2+), the player attacked a target that was either irrelevant or insufficient. In 2/10 positions (Kg8, Rd8), the player moved a piece away from where it was critically needed. The average number of good moves was only 1.9, indicating these are positions where the margin for error is extremely thin and the true priority is narrowly defined. The refutations consistently exploit the tempo waste: the opponent either captures the actual critical target (Ncxe6 in position 10, Nxe3 forks in position 5), forces a favorable transformation (Qxg3 trade in position 4, Rxf2 deflection in position 6), or exploits the piece's absence (Be2 challenging f3 in position 9, Rxg7+ in position 3).

1595.label: A minor piece retreats from an active central/semi-central post to a passive corner-adjacent square (h2/h7/a7), abandoning critical defensive duties.
1595.description: All 10 positions feature a minor piece moving to one of the 'graveyard' squares on the rim's second/seventh rank: Nh2 (4/10), Nh7 (3/10), Na7 (2/10), and Bh2 (1/10). In 9/10 cases it's a knight; 9/10 occur in the middlegame. The piece invariably leaves a critical post where it was performing essential functions — defending a central pawn (d4 in positions 2, 3, 8), controlling key squares (c6→a5 in position 10, c6→b4/d4 in position 1), or maintaining central presence (f6 guarding d5/e4 in positions 4, 6, 9). The average centipawn loss is 286, reflecting that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but severe errors. In every case, 2-3 good alternatives existed that maintained the piece's active role. The refutations consistently exploit the abandoned function: queen invasions (positions 1, 2), central pawn breaks (positions 3, 8), pawn advances into vacated territory (positions 5, 10), or simple capture of the now-undefended piece (position 6).

1596.label: A passive flank pawn advance (overwhelmingly h-pawn) played when the position demands immediate concrete action such as piece trades, king escape, or forcing moves.
1596.description: 9/9 positions feature a single-step flank pawn advance (6/9 are h-pawn moves specifically, with the remaining being a5, f5, and b4) played in positions requiring urgent tactical responses. In 7/9 cases, the correct move involved active piece play: queen exchanges (Positions 1, 4, 5), king repositioning (Positions 2, 7, 8), or completing development/castling (Positions 3, 9). The average cp_loss of 2164 is extraordinarily high, with 3/9 positions converting survivable disadvantages into forced checkmate. In 8/9 positions, the player was already worse or under significant pressure, making the tempo loss catastrophic. The positions consistently punish the pawn push by exploiting the exact weakness the player should have been addressing: back-rank invasions (Positions 1, 8), mating nets around an exposed king (Positions 7, 10), hanging pieces (Position 3), or opening dangerous lines (Position 9). Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these are typically critical moments where precision—not prophylaxis—was required.

1594.label: An aggressive-looking knight move (capture or attack) is played instead of a stronger tactical or strategic opportunity that exists elsewhere in the position.
1594.description: All 10/10 positions feature knight moves to apparently active squares — 5/10 are captures of central pieces (Nxd4, Nxd5, Nxd5, Nxe5, Nxe5) and 5/10 are jumps to attacking squares (Ng5, Ng4, Nf4, Ng5, Nc5). In every case, the player is drawn to an aggressive-looking knight action while missing a superior continuation. In 4/10 positions (1, 5, 7, 9), the player misses a clearly hanging piece or tactical fork available with a different move. In 3/10 positions (2, 8, 10), the knight abandons a square where it was performing a critical coordinating or defensive function, leaving key pieces/pawns undefended. In 2/10 positions (3, 6), the knight move has poor timing — the same capture would be fine after preparation but is premature and allows a punishing central advance. The average cp_loss of 281 reflects that these are high-impact errors in positions with narrow best-move margins (avg 1.9 good moves available), suggesting the aggressive knight move acts as a cognitive trap that prevents the player from scanning for the actual best continuation.

1591.label: A piece is moved away from a square where it was performing an essential (often hidden) defensive function, allowing an immediate tactical exploitation.
1591.description: 8/10 positions clearly show a piece being relocated from a square where it was serving a critical defensive purpose — blocking a passed pawn, guarding a key square against forks/mates, or protecting another piece. The moves typically look constructive on the surface (developing a bishop to b7 or d5, repositioning a rook to b8, centralizing a queen to e4, grabbing a pawn with Bxg5) but fatally abandon a defensive obligation. In 5/10 cases the moved piece is a bishop (Bb7, Bc7, Bg6, Bxg5, Bd5), suggesting a particular tendency to relocate bishops for 'activity' while overlooking their defensive role. The punishments are severe: 6/10 positions result in forks, hanging pieces, or immediate checkmate patterns. The average cp_loss is enormous (2139), with 3/10 positions allowing forced mate. Only 2.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were already tense positions requiring defensive precision rather than improving moves.

1586.label: Developing a bishop to a square where it's immediately exploitable by a pawn advance, capture, or trapping move — most often a central d-pawn fork with a friendly knight.
1586.description: 7/10 positions involve a bishop being moved to a tactically vulnerable square where it's immediately punished: Be6 appears 3 times (positions 1, 2, 10) where the bishop lands alongside a knight on c6, enabling a d5 pawn fork of both pieces; Be3 (position 8) mirrors this exactly with Nc3 forked by ...d4; Bd3 (position 3) places the bishop directly capturable by an e4 pawn; Bc5 (position 7) drops it to an undefended square within knight-capture range; Ba8 (position 9) traps the bishop with ...c6. The remaining 3/10 positions (b5, a4, Qc7) share the broader pattern of a slow positional/prophylactic move that ignores a concrete one-move tactical refutation, but don't involve bishop placement specifically. The tight core pattern (5/10) is specifically a bishop placed on the e-file (e6 or e3) alongside a friendly knight on the c-file, punished by a d-pawn advance forking both pieces. Average cp_loss of 364 reflects near-piece-value blunders, and only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating critical moments requiring precision.

1597.label: Advancing a wing pawn in the endgame when king or piece activity should take priority.
1597.description: All 10 positions feature single-step pawn advances in endgame positions, with 9/10 on wing files (b-file: 6 times, g-file: 3 times, a-file: 1 time) and only 1 central push (e5). In the positions with significant cp loss (positions 2, 5, 7, 9, 10 averaging ~342cp loss), the correct move consistently involved king activity or piece repositioning BEFORE any pawn advance: Position 2 needed Kd2/Ke3 to rush the king back; Position 5 needed Rb6 for rook activity; Position 7 needed Nc3 for knight coordination; Position 9 needed Re6 for rook repositioning; Position 10 needed Kh2 for king safety. In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 6), the pawn push was actually optimal or nearly so (0-9cp loss), suggesting the feature detects the general pattern of wing pawn advances in endgames, which is frequently but not always incorrect. The average good moves available was only 2.4, indicating these are critical positions requiring precise play rather than generic moves.

1601.label: Aggressive pawn advances that attack opponent's pieces but create tactical or structural vulnerabilities worse than the tempo gained.
1601.description: All 9/9 positions feature a single pawn advance that directly attacks an opponent's piece (queen in 5/9, bishop/rook/knight in 3/9, king via check in 1/9), intending to gain tempo by forcing that piece to move. However, in every case the pawn push backfires catastrophically. The attacked piece either relocates to a superior square (4/9: positions 5, 7, 9, 10 where the queen/king moves to a more dangerous post like Qa4 or Qg3+ or Kd3), enables an immediate tactical refutation exploiting the new weakness (6/9: positions 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10 featuring combinations like Qxh5, Nxf5+Rxg7+, Bxg5+ fork, Rxd8+ desperado, Qg3+ deflection, Qa4 pin), or both. The pawn structure damage is a consistent secondary theme — 7/9 positions feature king safety compromise or structural weakening as the mechanism through which the refutation works. The average cp_loss of 252 reflects that these moves frequently convert winning or defensible positions into equal or lost ones.

1600.label: A piece captures a tempting pawn when the capture either loses the piece, exposes it to tactics, or misses a far superior alternative.
1600.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece (knight, bishop, rook, or queen) capturing a pawn that appears to be a free or weakly-defended target. In 6/10 cases, the capturing piece itself is immediately lost or trapped after the recapture (positions 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 10 — where Bxb5 trades a bishop for a pawn, Rxd4/Qxd4+/Rxg3+ are recaptured by adjacent pawns, Bxb6 gets trapped, and Bxd6 is exploited tactically). In 2/10 cases (positions 4, 8), the capturing piece triggers a forced sequence that loses material or removes a critical defender enabling mate. In 2/10 cases (positions 1, 5), the pawn grab ignores a vastly superior move. The piece types are varied — N(4), B(4), R(2), Q(1) — and target squares span the board (d6, b5, d4, d5, b5, d4, g3, e6, b6, d6), but the psychological lure is identical: a pawn that looks 'free' but is actually poisoned or irrelevant compared to stronger alternatives. The average cp_loss of 1202 reflects that these are not minor inaccuracies but catastrophic decisions driven by material greed.

1598.label: A pawn push played one tempo too early, before the necessary preparatory piece move that would make the advance effective.
1598.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances that are either the right strategic idea executed with incorrect move order, or pawn pushes that ignore more urgent positional needs. In 4/10 positions (2, 3, 7, 10), the exact same pawn advance appears in the best move's continuation but only AFTER a preparatory piece move (Re6+, Bb3, Nd5, c5/Be4 respectively). In 3/10 positions (1, 4, 6), the pawn was serving a critical structural/defensive role and its advance removed a guard from a key piece — the e5 pawn supporting a d4 knight, the b7 pawn covering a c6 knight, or the g5 pawn shielding the c6 pawn. In 3/10 positions (5, 8, 9), the pawn advance chased or attacked a piece while ignoring a more urgent existing threat (exposed queen, imminent kingside breakthrough, hanging c2 pawn). The average cp_loss of 310 reflects that these positions were sharp and demanded precise sequencing — 7/10 had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating critical moments where the wrong pawn push was catastrophic.

1602.label: Knight moves that grab material or attempt forks but land on tactically vulnerable squares or abandon critical duties, allowing devastating counter-tactics.
1602.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight making an aggressive move aimed at immediate material gain — either capturing a pawn (7/10: Nxa7×2, Nxd2, Nxc2, Nxh2, Nxf3, Nxc7+) or lunging to attack/fork pieces (3/10: Nf7, Nb7, Nc7). In every case, the correct move was quieter and addressed a more fundamental positional need: king safety (5/10), passed pawn control (2/10), piece development (3/10), or maintaining a strong knight outpost (1/10). The punishment falls into three categories: the knight lands on an immediately capturable square with no compensation (3/10: Nb7, Nc7, Nxc7+ where the gain is insufficient), the knight's departure exposes a critical weakness behind it like a hanging piece or open diagonal (4/10: Nf7 leaves queen hanging, Nxd2 opens diagonal to b7 bishop, Nxc2 exposes king to queen fork, Nxf3 abandons d5 defense), or the knight gets stranded on the periphery while counter-tactics develop against the exposed position (3/10: Nxa7×2, Nxh2). The average cp_loss of 297 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirm these are critical positions where the flashy knight tactic was one of the worst options.

1609.label: A minor piece captures a central pawn or piece when a higher-priority move exists — a better capture, a stronger attack, or a critical defensive duty.
1609.description: All 9/9 positions feature a minor piece (7/9 knight, 2/9 bishop) capturing material on a central square (e5 in 5 positions, plus e4, c4, d5, f6). In every case, the capture appears attractive — winning a pawn or gaining centralization — but ignores a more important priority. In 3/9 positions (1, 2, 8), the best move was capturing a MORE valuable piece instead (a dominant knight on d5 or a hanging bishop on h5). In 3/9 positions (3, 5, 9), the best move was a forcing attacking continuation (Bg4+, Ba6, or e4) that exploited the opponent's exposed king rather than grabbing material. In 2/9 positions (6, 7), the error was capturing with the WRONG piece — the other minor piece enabled critical tactical follow-ups (Nc7 fork) or maintained vital defensive coverage (dark squares). In 1/9 positions (10), the knight abandoned its defensive role guarding another piece. The average cp_loss of 336 reflects that these are positions demanding precise calculation over intuitive material grabs, with only 1.4 good moves available on average.

1599.label: A rook is moved to a seemingly active or preparatory square when the position demands immediate tactical action, prophylaxis, or concrete threats.
1599.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook being repositioned to what appears to be an active or constructive square (lifts to the 3rd/6th rank, shifts along files, etc.) in the middlegame. However, in every case the rook move is too slow for the position's concrete demands. In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 9), the rook move directly hangs material — placing the rook on a tactically vulnerable square or leaving another piece undefended. In 3/10 positions (2, 4, 10), the move misses an immediately winning tactical strike that was available. In 4/10 positions (3, 6, 7, 8), the move ignores critical king safety concerns or allows the opponent a devastating counter-attack. The moves share a common intent: the player chose a 'building' or 'improving' rook move — a lift, a repositioning, a transfer — rather than addressing the position's most urgent need. The average cp_loss of 389 reflects how severely these slow rook moves are punished in sharp middlegame positions. Only 2.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision rather than general improvement.

1608.label: A passive, positional-looking pawn advance played when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action to address or prevent a lethal threat.
1608.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet pawn push (no captures, no checks) on a central or semi-central file (c, d, e, or f) when a critical tactical threat exists that demands urgent attention. The average centipawn loss is an enormous 4008, reflecting that these are catastrophic blunders disguised as routine moves. In 7/10 cases, the pawn move either directly enables the opponent's tactic (e5 vacating e6 guard of d7 allowing Nd7#; f3 opening the king diagonal for Qxh2+; d3 creating the d2 escape square used in a mating net) or fails to address the one critical defensive need (d6 instead of d5 to block a diagonal; c6 ignoring a devastating pin). Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical-precision moments where a slow structural move was especially fatal. 8/10 positions are middlegame where piece play should dominate over pawn pushes. The moves all share the character of looking 'normal' in isolation—shoring up structure, gaining space, preparing development—but catastrophically misread the position's tactical urgency.

1611.label: Reflexively recapturing with a rook when a stronger intermediate move (zwischenzug) or different capturing piece should be used first.
1611.description: All 10 positions involve a rook capture/recapture on a central or back-rank file (d1, d8, c1, c8, e1) where an enemy piece is 'obviously' meant to be taken. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9), the error is failing to insert a critical zwischenzug (intermediate forcing move, usually a check with a knight or pawn promotion) before the recapture—the enemy piece was doomed anyway, so tempo could be gained first. In 3/10 positions (5, 7, 10), the error is using the wrong piece or wrong rook for the capture, either exposing a hanging piece, removing a defensive rook from its post, or failing to save a vulnerable piece by using it as the capturing unit. Only 1/10 (position 4) was actually correct with 0cp loss. The average cp_loss of 1260 reflects the catastrophic nature of these 'obvious' captures—multiple positions involved missing forced mates or losing full pieces. In 8/10 cases, there was only 1 good move available, confirming these are narrow tactical moments where autopilot fails.

1613.label: A quiet rook development to an open file (e or g) when an immediate forcing move (capture or pawn thrust) was critically required.
1613.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-capturing, non-checking rook move to the back rank (e1/e8 or g1/g8), placing the rook on a seemingly natural open or semi-open file. In every case, the position demanded an immediate forcing move instead: 6/10 required a capture (Bxf3, Bxc6+, Bxd5, dxe4, Nxe4, exd6) and 4/10 required a pawn thrust (f4, d5, e4, e4). The rook moves are seductive because they often support the very idea that should have been executed immediately — e.g., Re8 'preparing' e4, or Rg1 'preparing' to attack the queen — but playing the preparation first gives the opponent a crucial tempo to escape, reposition a vulnerable piece, or launch a counterattack. 10/10 positions had exactly 1 good move available, confirming these were narrow tactical moments demanding precision. The average cp_loss of 253 reflects how consistently devastating the tempo waste was.

1605.label: Queen or Rook captures a pawn (or minor piece) prioritizing material over urgent tactical demands like king safety, checks, or initiative.
1605.description: 10/10 positions feature a major piece (Queen in 7/10, Rook in 3/10) making a capture, with 9/10 targeting pawns specifically. The common error pattern (present in 7/10 positions with significant cp_loss) is choosing a materialistic capture when the position demands a forcing move—typically a check or an initiative-maintaining maneuver. In 6/10 positions, the correct move involved giving check or maintaining piece coordination against the opponent's exposed king, while the actual move grabbed material and allowed a devastating counter-blow. King safety issues are present in 9/10 positions (either the player's own king becomes vulnerable or the opponent's exposed king should have been attacked). Positions 4, 5, and 9 show the same move type but where the capture happens to be correct, suggesting the feature detects the move pattern itself (material-grabbing captures by major pieces in tactically tense positions) rather than exclusively the error.

1614.label: A knight jumps to an apparently strong central outpost where it is immediately exchangeable, and the forced pawn recapture (usually with the d-pawn) damages the player's own structure or leaves material hanging.
1614.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight jumping forward to a seemingly powerful central or semi-central square (c5, e4, e5, or b4) that looks like a strong outpost but is immediately capturable. In 9/10 cases, the refutation involves exchanging the knight and forcing a d-pawn recapture (dxc5, dxe4, or dxe5) that destroys the player's pawn center — either creating isolated/doubled pawns, leaving the recaptured pawn undefended, or catastrophically opening files against the player's own king. 8/10 positions featured closed centers where the d-pawn was a structural keystone; the knight exchange forced that pawn forward, shattering the chain. In every case, 2-3 quiet alternatives (typically involving castling, development, or prophylactic pawn moves) maintained the position's integrity. The average loss of 221cp reflects how devastating the structural collapse is — the knight appears aggressive but simply donates pawn structure or material once the trivial exchange sequence unfolds.

1607.label: Moving the king (or weakening its shelter) to a seemingly active square that is immediately exploitable by checks, forks, or invasions.
1607.description: 7/10 positions feature direct king moves (Kg3, Kf4, Kf7, Kg6, Kf3, Kc6, Kc2) that advance or reposition the king to an apparently active or centralizing square, while 3/10 feature pawn moves (a6, f6, e6) that either weaken the king's shelter or waste tempo when urgent counterplay was needed. In 9/10 cases, the strongest refutation involves an immediate check, fork, skewer, or invasion through squares the move just weakened. The correct alternatives in 8/10 positions prioritized piece activity (Rb2, Re3, Rg5, Rb8, Nd3, Re2+, d3) over king relocation, while the remaining 2/10 required moving the king to a genuinely SAFE square (Kf8, Ke3) rather than a seemingly 'active' one. The average cp_loss of 1954 is extremely high, driven by 2/10 positions resulting in forced mate, demonstrating how catastrophic this pattern can be. All positions featured exposed kings with weak pawn shields (10/10), and the consistent error was choosing long-term positional improvement over addressing short-term tactical dangers.

1604.label: A natural-looking, non-forcing piece redeployment that either abandons a critical function or places the piece on a tactically exploitable square in a position demanding precision.
1604.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet (non-check, non-capture) piece repositioning move that looks like normal piece improvement but catastrophically ignores the tactical demands of the position. In 9/10 cases the moved piece is a major piece (queen or rook); only 1/10 involves a bishop. The average number of good moves available was just 1.4, meaning these are narrow positions requiring precise play, yet the player chose a 'consolidating' or 'natural-looking' move instead. In 6/10 positions (Rc1, Qh4, Qd5, R8h3, Rf2, Rb6), the piece was moved AWAY from a square where it was performing a critical offensive or defensive function—protecting a hanging piece, maintaining pressure on a key file/rank, or guarding a mating square. In 4/10 positions (Qf8, Rc7, Be8, R8d7), the piece was moved TO a square where it immediately becomes a tactical target via discovered attacks, forks, or capture sequences. The consistent thread is that positions with very high tactical tension (avg cp_loss 1316) were treated as if they permitted quiet reorganization, when in fact they demanded either forcing continuations or meticulous maintenance of piece placement.

1616.label: Moving the a-rook to the e-file as a generic developing move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1616.description: All 9/9 positions feature the identical structural move: the a-rook crossing to the e-file (Rae1 for White, Rae8 for Black) as a seemingly natural centralization. In every case, this 'improving' move is a critical-moment blunder (avg 325cp loss) because the position demands immediate forcing play instead. In 4/9 positions (1, 3, 4, 7), there was a concrete capture or tactic winning material (Qxf5+fork, Nxb4, e5, Bc2). In 3/9 positions (2, 8, 10), the rook move created or failed to prevent a piece vulnerability — trapping the f1-rook, exposing f8-rook to Bd6, or enabling a Nd6 fork on queen+rook now stacked on the e-file. In 2/9 positions (5, 9), the move ignored a critical threat requiring an immediate forcing response. The average number of good moves was only 1.8, confirming these are critical junctures where generic development is punished. Notably, 6/9 positions had only 1 good move available, meaning the position was at a razor-sharp tipping point that demanded calculation over routine.

1618.label: Queen (or piece) captures a peripheral pawn on the wing, becoming fatally displaced from the critical area of the board.
1618.description: 9/10 positions feature a queen capturing a pawn, and 10/10 are pawn captures on peripheral squares. 8/10 captures occur specifically on the a-file or h-file (the absolute edge of the board: a3×2, a5, a7, h3×2, h5, h7), with the remaining two on b5 and d4. In every case, the capturing piece moves far from the critical battleground — typically the opponent's king or a central tension point. The refutations universally exploit the queen's absence: 7/10 involve direct attacks on the player's own king that the displaced queen cannot help defend, 6/10 feature central pawn advances (d5, e6, f4) that gain tempo against the stranded queen, and 3/10 result in the displaced piece being trapped or permanently misplaced. The average centipawn loss of 3010 reflects that several positions convert forced mates or overwhelming advantages into merely large advantages.

1612.label: Moving a piece to the player's own back rank (1st/8th) when the position demands maintaining active posts or addressing urgent threats.
1612.description: 9/10 positions involve a piece being moved to the player's own back rank (1st rank for White, 8th rank for Black): Rd1, Re1, Bc1, Rc1, Nd1 for White; Rg8, Rd8, Rfe8, Ne8 for Black. The sole outlier is Rh5, which is still a passive repositioning that ignores critical threats. In 8/10 cases, the piece on the back rank either abandoned a critical defensive duty (Position 1: rook left f1 exposing back-rank mate; Position 8: knight left g7 exposing the h8 rook), invited an unfavorable exchange that enabled forks or deflections (Positions 6, 7), or wasted tempo allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow (Position 3: Bc1 allowed Qxb5 capturing the hanging queen). The average cp_loss of 1260 reflects how catastrophically these seemingly natural repositioning moves fail. Only 2.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these were positions demanding precision rather than routine piece shuffling.

1622.label: Playing ...Qe7 to pressure the e5 pawn when it fatally blocks the f8-bishop's development and prevents kingside castling.
1622.description: 9/10 positions feature Black playing ...Qe7 in response to White's e5 pawn attacking a knight on f6, and 10/10 occur in the opening with both kings in the center. In all 9 Black cases, the queen on e7 blocks the f8-bishop from developing to e7 or d6, making kingside castling impossible. The primary refutation in 8/10 positions involves White castling (O-O) and seizing the e-file with Re1, exploiting the queen-king alignment. In every case, better alternatives existed: actively relocating the attacked knight (Ne4, Nd5, Ng8, Ng4) or counterstriking with ...d5 — moves that address the e5 threat without self-blocking. The average cp_loss of 201 reflects how a seemingly natural 'developing' move creates a catastrophic developmental bottleneck. The one White example (Qe2) shares the same theme: a passive queen-to-e-file move when concrete tactics were demanded, wasting a critical tempo.

1615.label: Queen moves (usually checks) in Queen vs. advanced passed pawn endgames that choose the wrong square, failing to optimally control the promotion square or address the pawn threat.
1615.description: 10/10 positions are endgames featuring a queen battling against dangerous passed pawns 1-2 squares from promotion. 8/10 moves are queen checks, while the remaining 2 are non-checking queen moves. The critical error in 8/10 positions is selecting the wrong queen destination square — one that looks active but fails to geometrically control the promotion square or allows the opposing king to reach its ideal pawn-supporting position. In 3/10 positions (1, 3, 7), the identical mistake occurs: Qd7+ is played instead of Qd5+, where only the diagonal check from d5 covers the g8 promotion square. In Position 4, Qd6+ drives the king TO its ideal c8 square. In Position 6, Qf7 attacks the pawn directly but misses Qh5+ which forces mate. Positions 5 and 9 show 0cp loss (correct moves), but share the same structural context. The average cp_loss of 1147 reflects catastrophic consequences when the wrong square is chosen in these razor-thin positions where only 1.7 good moves exist on average.

1621.label: Trading an active, well-placed bishop for an opponent's passive or misplaced piece (usually a knight), solving the opponent's positional problems.
1621.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capture (Bx__) that trades away the player's active or strategically important bishop for a target that is passive, misplaced, or positionally irrelevant. In 9/10 cases the captured piece is a knight (the exception is Position 6 where the target is also technically a knight on b8). In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify the traded bishop as the player's 'most active piece,' 'best-placed piece,' or 'key attacking piece.' The consistent punishment is that the recapture either activates the opponent's position (e.g., Bxa6 activating Black's bishop to the a6-f1 diagonal in Position 3, Rxb8 activating Black's rook in Position 6) or removes constraints that were holding the opponent's position together (e.g., Bxd2+ letting White castle easily in Position 4, Bxh6 letting Black castle safely in Position 7). The average cp_loss of 223 reflects a severe positional concession rather than a tactical blunder. 9/10 positions are tagged with 'piece_activity' and 9/10 with 'positional_mistake' or 'positional' themes.

1620.label: Quiet bishop development to a long diagonal (fianchetto square) when the position demands immediate tactical action or critical defensive measures.
1620.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop being developed to a long diagonal square — specifically 9/10 are pure fianchetto moves (Bb7, Bg7, Bg2, Bb2) and 1/10 is a quiet bishop development to e2. In every single case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand: either a forcing winning sequence was available (positions 1, 4, 8 where concrete tactics won material), a critical defensive need existed (positions 2, 5, 6, 9, 10 where the king was vulnerable to immediate exploitation), or a prophylactic move was essential to prevent a tempo-gaining attack (positions 3, 7). The average centipawn loss of 1250 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors. 7/10 positions involved an uncastled or exposed king, and in 8/10 cases the fianchetto move specifically failed to address an immediate geometric vulnerability (undefended pawns on b7, exposed queens, fork opportunities, sacrifice possibilities). All moves share the characteristic of being 'natural-looking' development that would be correct in a calmer position but is fatally slow given the concrete tactical reality.

1623.label: Developing a knight to a natural square (c3/f3/c6/f6) when the position urgently demands a concrete tactical action such as capturing a hanging piece, executing a forcing break, or addressing an immediate threat.
1623.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight being developed to one of the four classical 'textbook' squares (Nc3, Nf3, Nc6, or Nf6) — moves that would be perfectly reasonable in a calm position but are catastrophically wrong given the specific tactical demands of the moment. In 6/10 positions (positions 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10), the correct move involved capturing or addressing a hanging/undefended piece that the knight move completely ignored. In 2/10 positions (2, 9), a critical pawn break (e5 or e4) was needed to seize the initiative. In the remaining positions, urgent queen maneuvers or exchanges were required. The average cp_loss of 324 is enormous, and the average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these were critical decision points with narrow tactical windows. In 10/10 cases, the knight development gave the opponent a free tempo to either capture undefended material, consolidate a precarious position, or launch a devastating counterattack that the concrete best move would have prevented.

1603.label: Moving a piece (especially a bishop) to a square where it is undefended and immediately captured by an opponent's piece, often disguised as a forcing check or aggressive placement.
1603.description: 4/10 positions clearly feature a piece moving to a square where it is immediately captured for free (positions 2, 4, 6, 10), and these constitute the three highest cp_loss instances (9204, 9176, 9502). In positions 6 and 10, the piece gives check (Qf5+, Bb8+), creating the illusion of a forcing move while landing on a square controlled by an opponent's piece (bishop on b1-f5 diagonal, rook on e8-b8 file). Position 2 (Bf1) puts the bishop where the knight on e3 captures it, and position 4 (Bc7) places the bishop on a diagonal controlled by Black's Ba5. The remaining 6 positions show related but milder errors: passive piece retreats to back-rank squares (Ke1, Kd1 in positions 3 and 5), a bishop blocking its own rook (Bf3 in position 8), and captures that ignore urgent tactical threats (dxe4 in position 9). 7/10 moves are made by White, and 6/10 occur in endgames. The average of 2.5 good moves available confirms alternatives existed in every case.

1625.label: In endgames requiring urgent king activation or pawn advancement, the player makes a quiet bishop repositioning move that loses decisive tempo.
1625.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where the player made a quiet, non-forcing bishop move to a seemingly active or useful square, when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a king move (Kg7, Kf4, Kd1, Kf2, Kg8, c4+, h5 etc.) or pawn push rather than bishop repositioning. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, confirming the core issue: the bishop moves look purposeful (centralizing, targeting pawns, controlling diagonals) but waste the one tempo needed to address the position's most urgent demand. In 6/10 positions, the opponent exploits the wasted tempo by advancing a passed pawn, activating their king, or constructing a mating net. The average cp_loss of 3902 reflects that many of these tempo losses are immediately catastrophic (4/10 result in forced mate). Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, showing these are critical decision points where the correct non-bishop action was narrow.

1617.label: Capturing a pawn on or toward the g-file that releases critical attacking tension, when a more forcing piece move (usually a check or direct attack) was required.
1617.description: 8/10 positions involve pawn captures, and 7/10 specifically feature captures on the g-file (hxg6, hxg5, hxg3, or fxg6). In nearly every case, the player had a dominant attacking position with forcing continuations available — 5/10 positions had forced checkmates that were missed. The common error is choosing a superficially aggressive pawn capture that opens lines near the enemy king, but actually dissipates a carefully built attacking configuration. In positions 3, 6, and 9, forced mates (in 2-6 moves) were available via piece checks but the player instead captured a g-file pawn. In positions 2 and 8, simple superior alternatives (Rxa1 winning a piece; Qh6 preparing the attack properly) were missed in favor of hxg6. The average cp_loss of 3008 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — releasing pawn tension when the position demanded maximum force. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, confirming these are critical-precision moments where the 'natural' pawn grab is the wrong instinct.

1606.label: Pawn pushes or piece relocations that worsen the player's own king safety when the king is already exposed, instead of taking urgent active measures.
1606.description: 9/10 positions feature the player's own king already exposed or vulnerable. In 6/10 cases, the mistake is a pawn push (f4, g6, h4, g4, c5, f3) that either destroys pawn shelter, blocks king escape routes, or wastes critical tempo. In the remaining 4/10, a piece is relocated away from a critical defensive role (R3g2 removes f3's defender, Rge4 vacates the attacking g-file, Nf3 fails to capture the dangerous attacker, Bg4 moves to a controlled square). The best alternatives consistently demand active measures: king movement to safer squares (5/10), captures of threatening pieces (3/10), or maintaining critical defenders in place (2/10). The common refutation pattern exploits the newly-created weakness—checks that force unfavorable trades (3/10), seizure of vacated files or squares (3/10), pins against misplaced pieces (2/10), or tempo gains in pawn races (2/10). The average cp_loss of 2903 reflects that many of these self-weakening moves convert defensible positions into forced mates.

1627.label: The queen (or key defensive piece) leaves a critical protective post near the king to chase pawns or seek activity on the a/b/c files, allowing immediate exploitation of the undefended king zone.
1627.description: In 10/10 positions, the moved piece (queen in 9/10, bishop in 1/10) was performing an essential defensive function — guarding key squares adjacent to the king, protecting critical pawns in the king's shield, or maintaining coordination with other defenders. The destination square was on the queenside periphery in 9/10 cases (a3, a4, a5, b7, c7, or Ba5), typically targeting opponent pawns or seeking 'counterplay' far from the main battlefield. In every case, the opponent immediately exploited the abandoned zone: 5/10 resulted in forced checkmate or mate-in-7 or fewer, while the remaining 5/10 saw evaluation swings of 255-741cp. The defensive functions abandoned included: guarding mating squares like f2/g2 (positions 1, 9, 10), protecting critical central pawns like e6 (position 2), maintaining piece coordination on open files (positions 3, 5), and preventing rook invasions to the 7th rank (position 8). In 7/10 positions, the queen was specifically the last piece preventing a lethal infiltration.

1619.label: Rook moves to penetrating or active-looking squares in endgames, often prioritizing rook placement over more concrete forcing continuations.
1619.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move, and 9/10 occur in the endgame phase. In 8/10 cases, the rook moves to a deep penetrating rank (7th or 8th rank from the opponent's perspective) or to an active-looking square on an open file. Positions consistently feature passed pawns (10/10), exposed kings (9/10), and open files/ranks. When the moves are mistakes (5/10 have cp_loss > 0, averaging 250cp among those), the common error is choosing a 'natural' rook placement or pawn capture over a more concrete alternative: pawn advancement (Positions 4, 6), exchange sacrifice (Position 3), move-order precision (Position 7), or a forcing check/deflection (Position 10). However, 5/10 positions show 0cp loss, indicating the feature fires on the general pattern of endgame rook repositioning regardless of whether it's correct — the mistake variant specifically involves rook activity appearing strong but being less forcing than available alternatives.

1632.label: Playing a prophylactic h-pawn (or a-pawn) one-square advance when the position demands immediate tactical action, squandering a narrow window for the only winning/surviving move.
1632.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-square rim pawn advance (9/10 h-pawn, 1/10 a-pawn) played as a prophylactic 'luft' move in positions with extremely narrow best-move windows (avg 1.3 good moves available). In every case, the position demanded one specific forcing move: capturing a hanging piece (positions 4, 5, 7), advancing a passed pawn (positions 2, 7), exploiting an exposed king with checks (positions 1, 3, 6), or defending a critical pawn under attack (positions 8, 9). The avg cp_loss of 2038 reflects that 2/10 allowed forced mate, while the remainder converted winning positions to equality or worse. The consistent refutation mechanism is that the opponent uses the gifted tempo to reorganize: seizing open files (positions 2, 10), activating queens via centralization or checks (positions 1, 5), neutralizing passed pawns (position 2), or launching mating attacks through the now-undefended pawn structure (positions 8, 9). 8/10 were middlegame positions where calculation, not prophylaxis, was required.

1626.label: A knight is passively repositioned to g3/g6 (seeking outposts like f5/h5) while a concrete tactical opportunity—typically a capture, fork, or sacrifice—goes unexploited.
1626.description: 8/10 positions feature a knight moving specifically to g3 or g6 (the mirror equivalent for Black), and 10/10 involve a slow knight repositioning that misses an immediate concrete tactic. The missed tactics vary widely: 3/10 miss direct captures of hanging/insufficiently-defended pieces (Bxe8, Bxd7, Bxh6), 3/10 miss forks or discovered attacks (Rxf7/discovered check, Nxe5 fork, Nb3 fork), 2/10 miss central pawn captures (Nxe4), and 2/10 fatally remove the knight from a critical defensive post (allowing d3+ discovery, blocking own knight's retreat). The knight consistently moves FROM e2/f1/e7 (seemingly passive squares) TO g3/g6 (seemingly active squares with access to f5/h5 outposts), but in every case the 'passive' starting square was either tactically essential or the tempo spent repositioning allows the opponent to neutralize a decisive advantage. The average cp_loss of 265 and average of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these are critical moments demanding calculation, not positional maneuvering.

1624.label: A pawn captures an adjacent-file pawn, resolving critical pawn tension prematurely instead of maintaining it or improving pieces first.
1624.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing another pawn on an adjacent file, resolving a tension that was a defining structural feature of the position. 7/10 are actual mistakes (avg 277cp loss among errors), while 3/10 are correct moves where the capturing side already held an overwhelming advantage (evals of -719, +599, -600). Among the 7 mistakes, the common error is resolving tension without first activating pieces or king: Position 4 needed Rc1 before axb6, Position 7 needed Kf2 before gxf5+, Position 9 needed e5 advance instead of exd5, Position 10 missed ...e5 breakthrough before fxg5. The 3 correct captures all created concrete advantages (passed pawns or structural damage that exploited opponent's displaced king). Endgame positions dominate (7/10), where pawn structure decisions are irreversible and king activity often determines whether tension should be maintained or released.

1630.label: Queen captures seemingly free material but misses a stronger intermediate move, better recapture piece, or critical defensive duty.
1630.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen capturing material (pieces or pawns) in situations where a more precise move was required first. In 3/10 positions (4, 5, 9), the error was recapturing with the queen instead of a minor piece that would maintain better coordination. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 8), the material wasn't going anywhere and a stronger intermediate move should have preceded the capture (move-order error). In 4/10 positions (3, 6, 7, 10), the queen capture displaced it from critical defensive or offensive duties, allowing the opponent to exploit the queen's absence. The average cp_loss of 1210 reflects severe consequences. Notably, 8/10 positions had only 1 good alternative move available, indicating these were narrow decision points where the 'obvious' materialistic capture was a trap. The captures targeted various pieces (bishops in 5/10, knights in 3/10, rooks/pawns in 2/10), but the common thread is always: the queen takes something that looks attractive while a deeper tactical or strategic priority goes unaddressed.

1634.label: Playing h3/h6 to challenge an enemy bishop on g4/g5 when the position demands addressing a more urgent tactical or structural concern first.
1634.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same move pattern: pushing h3 (White, 4 positions) or h6 (Black, 6 positions) to 'put the question' to an enemy bishop sitting on g4 or g5 that is pressuring a knight on f3/f6. In every case, there exists a more urgent tactical obligation that makes this routine pawn kick catastrophic. In 7/10 positions, the primary refutation involves capturing the knight on f3/f6 (via Nxf3+ or Bxf6) immediately after the h-pawn push, exploiting the tempo loss to shatter the pawn structure or win material. In 4/4 White h3 positions, the specific punishment is Nxf3+ (with check!) followed by Bxh3, turning the pushed pawn into a tactical target while ripping open the g-file. In the h6 positions, refutations vary more: 3/6 feature Bxf6 followed by exploiting the opened position, while others exploit hanging pieces (position 9), discovered attacks on the e-file (position 5), or knight invasions (position 4). The average cp_loss of 320 reflects that these are severe blunders, not minor inaccuracies. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions already demanded precise play, making the tempo-wasting h-pawn push especially costly.

1638.label: Castling (either side) directly into a position where the opponent already has pieces and/or pawns aimed at the castling wing, enabling an immediate tactical or strategic punishment.
1638.description: All 10/10 positions feature a castling move (O-O or O-O-O) that places the king on the exact wing where the opponent has already assembled attacking forces. In 3/10 positions (4, 6, 10), kingside castling walks into a textbook Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+ or Bxh2+) where the opponent's bishop already sits on the b1-h7 or b8-h2 diagonal with a knight ready to leap to g5. In 4/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 8), queenside castling places the king in front of an opponent's pre-existing pawn storm structure (b4+a4-a5, or Qa5+b5-b4) that needs only 1-2 moves to rip open files. In 2/10 positions (2, 7), kingside castling walks into an advanced h-pawn/g-pawn storm that immediately cracks the king's shelter. In 1/10 positions (9), queenside castling leaves a pawn hanging to a bishop that was already controlling the diagonal. The average centipawn loss is 286, and the average number of good alternatives is 2.2, meaning better moves were usually available. 8/10 occurred in the opening phase, suggesting premature or 'autopilot' castling decisions.

1629.label: Quiet b-pawn advances (b3 or b6) that remove critical pawn protection from a knight or waste tempo when forcing moves are required.
1629.description: 8/10 positions feature b-pawn advances (b3 or b6), with the remaining 2/10 being other quiet wing pawn moves (g3, f6, g7+). In 4/10 positions (Positions 1, 7, 8, 10), the b-pawn advance directly removes pawn protection from a knight — specifically, b3 leaves the c3-knight undefended in three positions, and b6 leaves the a6-knight hanging in one — enabling immediate exploitation via pins (Bb4) or direct capture (Bxa6, Qxc3). In 4/10 positions (Positions 2, 3, 5, and partially 10), the b6 advance is a slow, non-developing pawn move that wastes critical tempo in positions demanding active piece play, castling, or tactical exploitation. In 2/10 positions (4 and 6), non-b-pawn wing moves (g3, f6) similarly waste tempo when forced checkmate was available. All 10 moves are non-capturing pawn advances on wing files played in positions where the engine strongly preferred forcing moves (castling, piece development, tactical strikes). The average cp_loss of 2141 reflects the catastrophic mismatch between these passive gestures and the positions' urgent tactical requirements.

1637.label: Moving a fianchettoed bishop away from its critical defensive post near the castled king, typically for a pawn grab or misguided centralization, fatally weakening the king's shelter.
1637.description: All 10/10 positions feature a fianchettoed bishop (g7, g2, or b7) being moved away from its defensive diagonal where it protected the castled king. In 7/10 cases the bishop was on g7 or g2 defending a kingside-castled king; in 1/10 it was on b7 defending a queenside-castled king. The motivation was material gain in 6/10 positions (capturing pawns on g2, b7, b2, e5, c3) and misguided centralization/activity in 4/10 (Be5, Bf6, Bh3). The punishment consistently exploited the newly created weaknesses: kingside pawn storms after g7-bishop removal (positions 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10), tactical combinations exploiting unguarded squares (positions 1, 2, 4, 5), and dark-square collapses (positions 6, 7, 8, 9, 10). Average cp_loss was 303, reflecting the catastrophic nature of removing a king's primary defensive piece.

1628.label: A rook or queen displaces itself laterally (often to the a/b-file) to attack or defend a pawn, abandoning critical duties and creating tactical vulnerabilities.
