1628.description: All 10/10 positions feature a major piece (8 rooks, 2 queens) relocating to a secondary target, typically a pawn. 7/10 moves go specifically to the a-file or b-file (Ra4, Rcb5, Qa4, Rb1, Rb7, Ra1, Qb4), while the remaining 3 (Rd6, Rd5, Re5) involve similar lateral displacement to target minor material. In 8/10 cases the piece explicitly targets or defends a pawn (b4 pawn in positions 1/2/6, a2 in position 8, c7 in position 7, c5 in position 5, queenside pawns in positions 3/10). The consistent consequence is that the displaced piece either becomes tactically vulnerable itself (positions 1, 3, 9 — hanging piece/discovered attack), abandons king safety duties (positions 2, 5, 7, 10), loses critical tempo (positions 4, 8), or surrenders an open file (position 6). The average cp_loss of 2080 reflects how catastrophic these lateral displacements are — 4/10 positions had forced mates available that were missed. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments demanding precision.

1635.label: Moving a bishop away from a square where it performs a vital defensive function (blocking a file, defending a pawn, or maintaining a key diagonal) to a seemingly more active or aggressive square that is actually tactically exploitable.
1635.description: 8/9 positions involve bishop moves where the bishop vacates a square that was performing an essential defensive or structural role. In 4/9 positions (Bh4, Bd7, Bxc7, and partially Bg7), the bishop was physically blocking a file or defending a specific pawn, and its removal immediately allowed a devastating tactical blow along that line (back-rank mate, Rxb7, Rxh1+, Kxg7). In 3/9 positions (Bg5 #2, Bf7, Bf6), the bishop moved away from a square that enabled a stronger tactical continuation (the battery on a1-h8, the Rxf6 combination, or the zwischenzug-proof coordination). In 1/9 positions (Bg5 #5), the bishop developed to a square where it achieved nothing because the target simply moved. The sole outlier (a6) shares the thematic DNA: making an 'active' offensive gesture while ignoring a defensive emergency. In all cases, the moved piece appeared to gain something concrete (tempo, material, activity, development) but actually surrendered something far more valuable by leaving its original post.

1641.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the 7th rank (one square from promotion) while ignoring faster mating threats or critical tactical dangers.
1641.description: 10/10 positions feature a pawn being moved or captured onto the 7th rank (from the moving side's perspective), creating an immediate promotion threat. In 9/10 positions, this constitutes a serious blunder (avg cp_loss ~3952 excluding the non-blunder) because the player prioritizes the visually seductive one-square-from-queening threat over urgent defensive necessities. 7/10 positions resulted in the opponent having immediate mate or mate-in-few (positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 with forced mates; position 4 with perpetual check). In 8/10 cases, the opponent's attacking threats involved direct king safety exploitation—back rank mates, queen infiltration checks, or mating nets already in place. Only position 6 (g2, 1cp loss) was actually a reasonable move, serving as a control case where the pawn advance happened to be one of the best options because no immediate tactical threat existed. The pattern is remarkably consistent: the player sees a pawn on the 6th rank and reflexively pushes it to the 7th, blinded by promotion fever to the point of allowing instant catastrophe.

1636.label: Queen moves (often checks or passive repositioning) in overwhelmingly won queen endgames where king activation or pawn advances would convert more efficiently.
1636.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where one side has an overwhelming advantage with a queen against minimal material (pawns, occasionally a lone minor piece). Every single move is a queen move, and 4/10 are queen checks (Qf5+, Qc5+, Qd5+, Qc7+). Despite the positions being completely won (evaluations ranging from forced mate to +600-1100cp), the chosen queen moves are either non-productive checks that allow the opponent's king to escape to safer squares, or passive repositioning when the winning technique demands king centralization, pawn advancement, or piece coordination. Notably, 6/10 positions show 0cp loss, indicating the feature fires on the behavioral pattern itself rather than strictly on blunders. The worst case (Position 6, Qd5+ losing 185cp) exemplifies the 'patzer sees a check' syndrome where the check drove the defending king to safety behind its pawns. The average good moves available was only 2.1, confirming these are positions with narrow optimal paths typically requiring non-queen winning techniques.

1631.label: Capturing material or making superficially attractive moves that place the moving piece on a tactically vulnerable square, ignoring safer development/coordination alternatives.
1631.description: 8/10 positions involve capturing material (usually a pawn) or attacking a piece, while 2/10 involve king moves to exposed squares. In all 10 cases, the piece lands on a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable—trapped, pinned, skewered, or driven away with tempo. 6/10 are direct pawn captures (Qxb2, Bxh5, Bxc2, Qxe4×2, Nxg6), 2/10 are piece moves attacking material (Bg2 targeting a rook, Qa1+ giving check), and 2/10 are king moves to exposed squares (Kh2, Ke7). In 7/10 positions, the player's king was uncastled or exposed, making development/coordination the urgent priority. The best alternatives in 9/10 positions involved quiet development, piece coordination, or king safety moves rather than material gain. All 10 moves resulted in the piece being immediately punished via tempo-gaining attacks (Rb1, Rg1, Re1, Rh8+, Rc7+, Kd2, etc.) that exploit the piece's new vulnerability.

1639.label: Moves that place or leave pieces (especially rooks) on squares vulnerable to devastating knight forks, typically with check against the king.
1639.description: 8/10 positions feature the player's move directly enabling an opponent's knight fork that wins material, typically by forking the king with check and a rook or major piece. In positions 2, 3, 4, 8, and 9, the player places a rook on a square where a knight can simultaneously check the king and attack it (Ne2+, Ne7+, Ne5+, Ne6+, Ne7+). In position 1, the capture leaves a knight alive to deliver a crushing Nd6+ fork. Position 7's rook move abandons defense of a knight while landing on a fork-vulnerable square. Position 5 places a rook directly on a knight-controlled square (Nxd8). Even the pawn push outliers (positions 6 and 10) involve knight-related tactics—g4 leaves a knight hanging, and g5 enables Nxf2 forking queen and rook. 9/10 positions involve the opponent's knight delivering the punishment, and 7/10 specifically involve a rook being placed or left on a forkable square relative to the king.

1642.label: Moving a piece to an aggressive-looking square while ignoring critical defensive duties or urgent tactical threats in the position.
1642.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a piece (queens 5x, bishops 4x, knight 1x) to a seemingly active or aggressive square that created no real threats while abandoning a critical defensive responsibility or ignoring an urgent tactical demand. In 7/10 positions, the moved piece was directly performing a defensive function before being relocated (Qg2→g4 abandoned back-rank coverage, Qe8→h5 abandoned back-rank defense, Bc1→a3 abandoned e3 pawn defense, Bc1→g5 abandoned king defense in both cases, etc.). In 8/10 positions, the piece moved toward the kingside or to a forward attacking square (h4, g5, g4, h5, h4, h5, g5, f8). The average cp_loss of 1221 reflects how catastrophic these moves are—they look purposeful but address the wrong problem entirely. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions typically demanded precise defensive awareness that the player lacked.

1643.label: The queen moves to a square that is directly attackable, capturable, or exploitable by an enemy minor piece (knight or bishop), losing material or decisive positional value.
1643.description: All 10 positions feature queen moves that place the queen on a tactically unsafe square. In 7/10 positions, the queen lands on a square where it is immediately captured or won by an enemy minor piece: knight captures on g3 (positions 3 and 8), bishop captures on c2 (position 4), bishop forks queen and another piece on e4 (position 10), discovered attack by knight clearing a diagonal to the queen on b7 (position 6), and intermediate knight check enabling queen capture on c6 (position 7). In position 1, the queen overextends to b2 where a knight attack traps it. Position 2 shows the queen moving to b7 where it abandons defense of a piece that then hangs. Position 5 has a passive queen retreat that surrenders a critical square. Position 9 is a negligible 1cp loss. The average cp_loss of 334 reflects that these are overwhelmingly catastrophic queen placements. In 8/10 cases, the queen's destination square was within the direct attacking range of an enemy knight or bishop, and the player failed to recognize this vulnerability.

1644.label: A bishop makes a natural-looking capture (removing an intruder, recapturing, or stopping a threat) while a more forcing or urgent move goes unplayed.
1644.description: All 10/10 positions involve a bishop capture (Bx__) that appears logical — removing a threatening piece, making a standard recapture, or neutralizing an obvious danger — but misses a significantly stronger alternative. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10), the missed move was a more forcing tactical blow: a check, a promotion, a queen capture, or a piece activation that created unstoppable threats. In 3/10 cases (positions 6, 7, 10), the error was specifically a move-order mistake where the bishop capture needed to be delayed or executed differently (wrong piece recapturing). In 2/10 cases (positions 8, 9), king safety required immediate attention before any captures. The average cp_loss of 1206 reflects the catastrophic cost of these 'safe' choices — including one position converting to forced mate in 6. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, meaning precision was critical and the reflex capture was almost always the wrong choice.
1644.old_chip: Reflexive bishop capture over forcing move

1633.label: Playing a natural-looking 'improving' move when the position demands an immediate forcing action (capture, check, or precise preparatory exchange).
1633.description: All 8 positions share a common structure: the player had a concrete, often forcing best move available (a capture in 4/8 positions, a check in 1/8, a precise preparatory exchange in 2/8, or a specific restrained move avoiding a tactical vulnerability in 1/8), but instead chose a non-forcing 'improving' move that appeared reasonable in isolation—piece development (Nf2), queen activation (Qb6, Qf5), king centralization (Ke6, Kb2), prophylactic pawn moves (a3, f4), or rook activation (Rf5). In 7/8 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. In 6/8, a concrete tactic was missed. The positions average only 1.9 good moves, indicating critical moments with narrow paths to maintain the advantage. The mistakes uniformly reflect prioritizing general chess principles (centralization, development, prophylaxis) over the specific urgent tactical demand of the position.

1646.label: Developing a knight to e7/e2 (the second rank) as a seemingly natural move that self-blocks critical retreat paths or leaves key squares undefended.
1646.description: 9/10 positions feature a knight being developed to the player's second rank (e7 for Black in 6 positions, e2 for White in 3 positions, d7 in 1 position), with 1/10 being a queen move to e7 that blocks the knight from reaching that square. In 7/10 positions, the piece on the second rank directly blocks another piece's escape or movement path (blocking queen retreats in positions 1, 3, 4, 7; blocking king escape in position 8; blocking knight development in position 6; removing a defender in position 10). In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 8, 9), the knight specifically goes to e7 instead of the more active f6, which would have controlled critical squares (g5, h5, e4) that the refutation exploits. All 10 positions occur in the opening (9/10) or early middlegame with the moving side's king still in the center (10/10). The average cp_loss of 238 reflects how severely these 'natural-looking' developing moves are punished by immediate tactical strikes.

1652.label: A non-forcing pawn advance on a wing file (a/b/c/f/g) played in a position that demands immediate concrete or tactical action, squandering a critical tempo.
1652.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-central pawn push (files a, b, c, f, or g) that is slow and non-forcing, played in a position where one specific concrete move (a capture, check, piece activation, or direct attack on a weakness) was urgently required. 9/10 positions had 'tempo_loss' tagged as a key motif. The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were razor-sharp moments where only precise concrete play maintained the advantage. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a piece move or capture (gxh5, Kh2, Bc4+, Qd8, Nxe3+, Rc8/Ra3) rather than a pawn push, yet the player chose a quiet pawn advance instead. 6/10 positions were endgames and 4/10 middlegames, but all shared the characteristic that the opponent could immediately exploit the gifted tempo with a forcing continuation (pawn break, piece invasion, or tactical shot). The pawn moves themselves often created structural weaknesses (opening squares for the opponent's king, enabling pawn breaks, or removing defenders) as a secondary cost beyond the tempo loss.

1640.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or positional move while an immediate tactical emergency demands a specific forcing response.
1640.description: All 10 positions share a critical structural feature: the position contains an urgent tactical obligation (a hanging piece, a mating threat, a forced sequence) that requires immediate attention, but the player instead plays a quiet, non-forcing 'improvement' move. 5/10 positions specifically involve bishop development to g4 or g5 — squares that look active and often attack the opponent's queen — but are completely irrelevant to the actual crisis. The remaining 5 moves (c6, Kc8, h5, c3, Qe3) are similarly quiet positional moves (pawn advances, king repositioning, queen centralization) that ignore immediate tactical needs. The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, confirming these are positions demanding precise, specific responses where 'general improvement' moves catastrophically fail. 8/10 positions had the blundering side's king in or near the center, adding urgency. The cp_loss averaged 1258, reflecting that these 'natural' moves typically allow devastating tactical refutations — forks (2/10), hanging pieces (3/10), king attacks (3/10), or promotion failures (1/10).

1656.label: Playing a prophylactic king move to a corner/edge square when the position demands an immediate capture to address a tactical crisis.
1656.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing king move played when there was exactly ONE good move available — and that good move was always a capture addressing an immediate tactical obligation. In 9/10 positions, the tactical motif was a hanging piece (the player's own or an opponent's piece that must be taken). In every case, the best move was a capture: Qxc5, Qxf5, Qxe5, Bxd5, Qxe4, Qxb6, Bxf6, Qxe3, Qxg5, Qxc7. The king moves uniformly go toward corners or edge squares (Kh1×2, Kh8×2, Kb1×2, Ka1, Kh6, Kg6, Ke8), suggesting a habitual 'tuck the king to safety' instinct. The average cp_loss of 496 reflects that these king moves typically allow the opponent to capture a queen or major piece for free on the next move. The pattern is remarkably consistent: perceived prophylaxis overrides recognition of immediate tactical emergencies.

1645.label: Aggressive bishop moves along diagonals (often giving check or attacking a piece) that look powerful but miss stronger alternatives or allow defensive resources.
1645.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving along a long diagonal to create an immediate threat — 5/10 are direct checks (Bc4+, Ba3+, Bf5+, Bxg5+, Bc5+), and the remaining 5 attack key pieces (Bh6 pins the queen, Bf4 attacks the queen, Ba6 attacks a rook, Bc6 attacks a rook, Ba3 targets a bishop). In 8/10 positions this was a mistake (avg cp_loss ~3738 for the errors), while 2/10 (Ba6, Ba3) were actually the best moves. The common thread for the mistakes: 6/8 blunders allowed the opponent a defensive interposition or blocking move (c5 blocking Ba3+, Bf2 blocking Bc5+, Ne4 blocking Bf5+, Ndf6 blocking Bxg5+, Kf8 sidestepping Bc4+, c5 blocking Ba3+). In 4/8 error positions, a non-bishop move was clearly superior (Ne5+ in positions 6 and 5, Qh5+ in position 2, Qf3+ in position 8). The feature detects the impulse to activate bishops along open diagonals with apparently forcing moves, regardless of whether the geometry actually traps the opponent.

1648.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move in a critical position where only one precise move exists, directly leaving a major piece undefended or exposed to immediate capture.
1648.description: 8/10 positions show the player making a move that directly results in one of their own pieces being captured or a mating threat being executed because a critical piece/square is left undefended. In Position 2 (Kf3), the rook on h5 is left hanging to Kxh5. In Position 4 (Kd7), the queen on d8 is exposed to Bxd8. In Position 5 (Rf2), the queen on g2 hangs to Bxg2. In Position 6 (Bd4), the bishop itself is placed on an undefended square for Rxd4. In Position 7 (Qe1+), the queen lands on a square captured by Bxe1. In Position 8 (Rxc2), the back rank is stripped of defense allowing Qd1#. In Position 9 (Bd3), the queen on h6 is left hanging to gxh6. In Position 10 (Rcc7), the rook on b7 is left vulnerable to Bxb7. All 10 positions had an average of only 1.2 good moves available, meaning the positions were razor-sharp and demanded the single precise response. The average cp_loss of 3358 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights in critical moments.

1650.label: Advancing a pawn aggressively when the position demanded patient piece coordination or defensive consolidation.
1650.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same fundamental error: the player chose an aggressive one-square pawn advance when the correct approach required piece moves (king repositioning, rook activation, or defensive consolidation). In 9/10 positions, the top recommended moves were piece moves — particularly king safety moves (positions 1, 4, 7, 10) or rook repositioning (positions 3, 5, 7, 9). The pawn advances consistently failed because they either surrendered a pawn's superior static value as a restraining/controlling force (positions 1, 5, 8 — strong passed pawns pushed prematurely into liquidation), abandoned critical square control enabling opponent tactics (positions 2, 9 — opening diagonals/allowing passed pawns), or simply wasted a critical tempo when immediate threats demanded attention (positions 4, 6 — ignoring kingside attacks or back-rank mates). The average centipawn loss of 1152 reflects how catastrophically these tempo-wasting pawn advances compound when the opponent exploits the granted time.

1653.label: Queen moves to a seemingly active square without creating concrete threats, when a more forcing or tactically precise move was required.
1653.description: All 10/10 positions feature queen moves to squares that appear aggressive or centrally dominant but lack concrete tactical justification. In 8/10 positions, the blunder was tagged with 'tempo_loss' because the queen lands on a square where it can be immediately challenged or driven away (e.g., Qg5 hit by f4, Qd5 hit by f3, Qd3 targeted by ...Bf5). In 7/10 positions, a more forcing alternative existed — often a check, pawn break, or specific tactical sequence (Qc2+ winning the queen in Position 7, Qb1+ winning a rook in Position 8, Qc5 setting up Qxc3+ in Position 10). The average good moves available was only 1.4, meaning these were critical positions demanding precision rather than general improvement. In 3/10 cases (Positions 4, 5, 7), the queen abandoned a critical geometric relationship (defensive coverage or attacking diagonal). The common thread is prioritizing the queen's cosmetic appearance on the board over solving the position's concrete tactical demands.

1658.label: Knight captures a 'weak' pawn on f2, f7, or c7 expecting a fork or king exposure, but the opponent simply recaptures the knight with no real compensation.
1658.description: All 10 positions feature a knight making a speculative capture on a classically 'weak' square — 7/10 are Nxf2, 2/10 are Nxf7, and 1/10 is Nxc7+. In every case, the knight captures a pawn hoping to exploit fork geometry (typically threatening queen and rook simultaneously) or king exposure, but the opponent has a trivial recapture (Kxf2 in 7 positions, Kxf7 in 1, Rxf2 in 1, Qxc7 in 1) that simply wins the knight back, leaving the sacrificer down a full piece for a single pawn. All 10 positions occur in the opening phase with closed or semi-closed centers, meaning no open lines exist to generate attacking compensation against the displaced king. In 10/10 cases, multiple quiet developing moves (avg 2.8 good alternatives) existed that would have maintained a playable position. The average cp_loss of 289 corresponds almost exactly to the value of a minor piece minus a pawn, confirming the consistent material deficit pattern.

1654.label: King captures a Rook or Queen in the endgame, transitioning into a (typically losing) pure pawn endgame where the capture is forced or nearly forced.
1654.description: All 10/10 positions feature the King capturing a major piece (7/10 Rooks, 3/10 Queens) in the endgame phase, entering a pawn endgame or near-pawn endgame. The captures are overwhelmingly forced: the average number of good moves is only 1.2, and 7/10 positions have a cp_loss of 10 or less, meaning the capture IS the best move. The 'mistake' element is subtle—in the few cases with meaningful cp_loss (positions 2, 4, 9), the error is either that the king ends up on a suboptimal square after capturing (position 4: king pulled to c6 away from advancing kingside pawns), or that a more sophisticated alternative existed (position 9: Ka8 exploiting the opponent's piece placement was stronger than simplifying). In 9/10 positions, the side making the capture is losing or already lost, suggesting the opponent deliberately placed the piece en prise knowing the resulting pawn endgame favors them. The tactical motif tagged across all positions is 'pawn_endgame' or 'passed_pawn.'
1654.old_chip: King Takes Major Into Pawn Endgame

1659.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) to a square that falls within a knight's attack radius, enabling a devastating fork of two valuable pieces.
1659.description: All 10/10 positions feature the identical tactical motif: the played move places a piece onto a square that completes a knight fork geometry. In 8/10 cases, it is specifically a king move that walks onto a square attackable by an enemy knight from a square that simultaneously attacks another high-value piece (rook or queen). In position 6, a queen walks into the fork geometry with a rook (Qa5 allows Nc4 hitting both), and in position 9, a rook is placed on a fork-vulnerable square (Rb2 allows Nd3+ hitting king and rook). In 9/10 positions, the fork delivers check, making the material loss unavoidable. The best moves in every case share the common thread of choosing an adjacent square that is NOT within the knight's attack range from the critical forking square — often differing by just one square (e.g., Kf1 instead of Kf2, Kh2 instead of Kh1, Ke1 instead of Ke2). The average cp_loss of 1300 reflects the catastrophic nature of allowing a fork that typically wins a full exchange or queen.

1651.label: A major piece (usually a rook) captures a pawn or low-value target that is defended, needed elsewhere, or tactically unsound to take.
1651.description: 10/10 positions involve captures of low-value targets (9/10 pawns, 1/10 a knight). 7/10 moves are specifically rook captures (Rxf3, Rxg6+, Rxd6, Rxd5, Rxf7, Rxh6+, Rxf1+), with the remaining being Bxd5, Nxf2, and Qxd6. The captured targets all appear tempting — they look free, weakly defended, or tactically exploitable — but in every case the capture is catastrophically unsound. The reasons vary: in 3/10 positions the pawn is adequately defended and the piece is simply lost for a pawn (positions 1, 7, 8); in 3/10 the capturing piece abandons a critical defensive or attacking role (positions 4, 5, 6); in 2/10 the capture allows a devastating intermediate tactic like a check or fork (positions 2, 9); and in 2/10 the piece lands on an undefended square where it is captured back (positions 3, 10). The average centipawn loss is enormous (2272), reflecting that these pawn-grabs often convert winning positions into losing ones or throw away forced mates.

1655.label: Advancing an edge-file passed pawn in an endgame promotion race when a more urgent action (king move, capture, or tactical strike) was required.
1655.description: 10/10 positions are endgames featuring active promotion races where the player pushes a pawn on the a, b, or h file instead of addressing a more critical immediate priority. 8/10 moves are specifically rim pawn advances (a-file or h-file), while 2/10 are b-file pushes. In every case, the move played has a 'tempo_loss' tag in the analysis — the pawn advance looks natural in a race context but wastes the critical tempo needed for king repositioning (5/10: positions 3, 4, 5, 7, 8), gaining tempo via check or capture (2/10: positions 1, 3), making a tactical strike (1/10: position 7), choosing the correct promotion square (1/10: position 9), or activating a piece (1/10: position 10). The average centipawn loss is 4719, driven by several positions where the tempo waste converts a survivable deficit into forced mate. 6/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these are razor-sharp moments where the 'obvious' pawn push is a trap.

1649.label: King moves in materially imbalanced endgames where both kings are exposed and active, often the only or best option but occasionally walking into fatal danger.
1649.description: 10/10 positions feature king moves in simplified endgames with both kings exposed and actively participating (no castled safety). 9/10 positions have large material or evaluation imbalances (typically +300cp to +800cp or more) before the move is played. In 6/10 positions, the king move played was actually the best or near-best option (cp_loss ≤ 28), reflecting positions where the losing side has very few alternatives. However, 3/10 positions (Kf6, Kxh6, Kh5) represent catastrophic blunders where the king stepped into immediate checkmate or forced mate, accounting for the extreme average cp_loss of 2895. The feature consistently fires in positions with open centers (7/10 have open d/e files), minimal pawn shelter for both kings, and few pieces remaining. The average number of good moves available was only 2.1, confirming these are heavily constrained endgame positions where king move selection is critical.

1657.label: A knight is relocated from a key defensive square (usually e7) to a seemingly active square (usually g6), removing the sole defender of a critical pawn, diagonal, or square and allowing an immediate tactical exploitation.
1657.description: In 9/10 positions, Black moved a knight away from a square where it was the sole guardian of a tactical vulnerability, and in the remaining position White made the equivalent error. Specifically, 7/10 moves were Ne7-g6, 1 was Nd7-f6, 1 was Ne7-c6, and 1 was Nd2-f1 — all sharing the pattern of a knight leaving a critical defensive post for a 'more active' destination. In 8/10 positions, the knight was specifically guarding against exploitation of the a4-e8 diagonal or protecting a key pawn (c6 in positions 1, 2, 10; f7 in position 3). The king was uncastled in 9/10 positions, making the defensive duty even more essential. The destination square (g6 in 7/10) appeared active — targeting e5 or f4 pawns — but provided no concrete threats, while the vacated square allowed devastating tactical shots (Qd4+Bxc6+ zwischenzug, Qxc6+ fork, Qa4+ winning a piece, Ng5+Bxf7+, f5 with tempo, or Qxf3+ into knight forks). The average cp_loss of 320 reflects that these moves typically convert equal or slightly worse positions into losing ones.

1647.label: Playing a superficially logical move that addresses a visible but non-critical concern while missing the position's actual tactical requirement.
1647.description: 8/10 positions show a player making a 'natural-looking' move motivated by an obvious positional goal (eliminating a passed pawn, contesting a file, chasing a piece, occupying an outpost) that turns out to be tactically flawed because it either creates a new vulnerability or ignores a more urgent need. In 5/10 positions (Rxc7, Rxg7, Rc8, Rxb2, Rxa7), the move involves a rook addressing a passed pawn that was already neutralized or blockaded, when king activation or a different piece was called for. In 3/10 positions (g3, h6, Rd1), the player makes a defensive or prophylactic move that leaves a critical tactical weakness exposed. In 2/10 (Nf5, dxe6), an aggressive-looking move is chosen over a more forcing alternative. The average cp_loss of 1208 with only 2.2 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where the player's instinctive prioritization fails catastrophically. The best moves were typically quieter (king moves in 4/10) or more forcing (checks/captures of different targets).

1662.label: Knight leaves a critical defensive or positional post to execute a tempting fork (usually against rooks), but the departure allows a devastating counter-attack that far outweighs the forked material.
1662.description: 10/10 positions feature knight moves that create forks or attack multiple pieces simultaneously. In 9/10 cases, these forks are blunders (avg cp_loss 2333) because the knight was performing a vital function before moving. The most common target square is f2 (5/10 positions), with others going to c2, e3, d7, and f7—all squares that fork rooks or other heavy pieces. In 8/10 cases, the refutation involves a king-safety exploitation (Bxf7+, Qxg6, Qxf2+, Nf6+/Qxh7#, Rxg7+, Rxe8+) where the knight's departure from its post strips away a critical defensive resource. The knight's original square was typically a dominant outpost (e4 in 3 positions, e5 in 2, f5 in 1, g4 in 1, f4 in 1) from which it controlled key squares around the player's king or the opponent's attacking lanes. Only 1/10 (Position 7) represents a correct fork where the knight wasn't performing a defensive function and the position was already winning. The consistent trigger is prioritizing material gain over positional/defensive duties in sharp middlegame positions, typically with opposite-side castling (6/10) or exposed kings.

1661.label: Non-forcing bishop repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding concrete tactical action.
1661.description: All 10/10 positions feature quiet (non-capturing, non-checking) bishop moves to seemingly improved squares — central posts, safer diagonals, or more 'active' positions. In 9/10 cases, the analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as a key tag, and 9/10 feature 'missed_tactic.' The bishops move to squares that look aesthetically strong but are either immediately challengeable by a pawn advance (Be4 hit by ...f5 in positions 4 and 10; Be5 hit by f4 in position 7; Bd5 hit by c4 in position 9) or simply waste the move needed to execute a concrete winning combination (Qa4+ in position 3, Qa3 in position 2, Nf4 in position 6, Nxe4 in position 5). In 7/10 positions, the opponent's king was exposed or uncastled, demanding forcing play rather than quiet improvement. The average cp_loss of 290 reflects how punishing it is to make a 'positional' bishop move when the position demands concrete action.

1660.label: The queen (or major piece) greedily captures an apparently free or attractive piece, but the target square is defended by an overlooked piece, resulting in immediate loss of the queen.
1660.description: In 9/10 positions, the queen captures a piece (Qxg7, Qxh7, Qxa2, Qxf7, Qxf7, Qxf5, Qxf5, Qxb2, Qxf2; the exception Rxg4 still results in queen loss). In 7/10 positions, the queen is immediately lost or captured after landing on the target square because a hidden defender recaptures — typically a bishop along a diagonal (positions 3, 5), a knight attacking the capture square (positions 4, 9), a rook on the same file (position 2), or a pawn recapture opening a lethal file (position 6). In position 7, capturing with the rook exposes the queen to a knight fork. The key shared error is that the player sees material to grab and fails to notice a defending piece that controls the capture square or creates a winning tactical response. The average cp_loss of 1187 reflects that most of these are queen-losing blunders. Only 2/10 positions (1 and 10) don't involve catastrophic material loss, and those are the two with 0-32cp loss. The typical game phase is middlegame (7/10) where piece coordination creates these hidden defensive resources.

1663.label: Quiet flank pawn advances (predominantly b6) played when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1663.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-forcing single-square pawn pushes on the rim or flank. 6/10 are specifically ...b6, while the remaining 4 are a4, a5, d3, or h3 — all sharing the character of slow preparatory moves. In every case, the position demanded urgent concrete action: either exploiting a tactical shot (positions 1, 9), defending against an imminent kingside attack (positions 2, 5, 8), executing a critical central break (position 4), or pushing a passed pawn immediately (position 10). In 3/10 positions (3, 7, 9), the b6 move specifically removed the b7-pawn's guard of the c6 square or the long diagonal, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability (Nc6 fork or Bxa8 discovery). The average centipawn loss is 292, and the average number of good moves available was only 1.9, indicating these were high-precision moments where the slow pawn move was catastrophically inappropriate. 7/10 moves were played by Black, and 8/10 occurred in the middlegame, typically in positions with active piece tension requiring resolution.

1670.label: A piece (usually a knight) retreats to the player's first rank in a position demanding urgent action, wasting critical tempo.
1670.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece retreating to the player's back rank (1st or 8th rank) when the position demanded immediate active play. 7/10 are knight retreats (Nd8, Nc8, Nf8, Ne8, Ne1), 2/10 are queen retreats to d8, and 1/10 is a bishop retreat to e1. In every case, the retreat abandons control of critical squares or defensive duties: in positions 1, 2, and 8, the knight left a key square unguarded (enabling central breaks or forks); in positions 6 and 7, the retreat squandered a large existing advantage by giving the opponent time to consolidate; in positions 4 and 10, it left material undefended. The average cp_loss of 223 reflects positions where urgency was paramount—the average number of good moves was only 1.6, meaning these were critical moments with narrow paths to survival. The retreating intent was typically a slow regrouping maneuver (rerouting a knight via the back rank to a 'better' square), but the tempo cost proved catastrophic.

1667.label: The king marches forward in the endgame seeking activity but walks directly into checks, forks, or mating patterns.
1667.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that advances forward (toward the center or the opponent's side) during the endgame, motivated by the general principle that kings should be active in endgames. However, in every case the advance exposes the king to concrete tactical vulnerabilities. In 4/10 positions the king walks into an immediate check or checkmate (Positions 1, 5, 7, 9), including two instant checkmates (Positions 1 and 9 with cp_losses of 9454 and 9340). In 3/10 positions the king steps onto a vulnerable diagonal or square allowing a tempo-gaining check by bishop or queen (Positions 6, 7, 4). In 2/10 positions the king advance wastes a critical tempo when piece moves were urgently needed (Positions 2, 8). The average cp_loss of 2108 is extremely high, reflecting that these 'natural-looking' king activations frequently walk into catastrophic tactical shots. Better alternatives existed in every case — typically active piece moves (Rb5, Ne5+, Bf6, Be7) or retreating king moves (Kc3) that prioritized concrete safety over abstract activity.

1675.label: Pushing a pawn to attack an enemy piece instead of executing an available concrete tactical blow.
1675.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical pattern: the player advances a pawn to attack an enemy piece (a bishop in 8/10 cases, a knight in 1/10, and a queen in 1/10) when a direct tactical shot—a capture, fork, or forcing sequence—was immediately available. The missed tactics include: capturing a hanging piece (Nxe3, Nxb4, Qxd6), delivering a knight fork via check (Nf3+/Ncd4+), a knight invasion creating a double attack (Nd6), a forcing bishop development (Bg5), and resolving critical pawn tension (fxe5). In every case, the pawn push gives the attacked piece time to escape to a safe or even improved square, while the opponent gains counterplay or consolidates. The average cp_loss of 282 reflects how these 'lazy tempo' pawn pushes squander significant advantages. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical moments demanding precise calculation rather than routine positional moves.

1672.label: Playing an unnecessary king move (Kh2, Kh7, O-O-O, or Ke7/Kd7) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1672.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move (including castling) played instead of a concrete forcing move that was available. In 6/10 positions, the move was a king tuck to the h-file (Kh2 or Kh7), while 3/10 were queenside castling and 1/10 was Ke7 or Kd7. In every case, at least one concrete tactical action was available: material-winning captures (positions 1, 3, 8), critical defensive moves preventing forks or attacks (positions 2, 10), or forcing moves maintaining initiative (positions 5, 6, 7, 9). Crucially, in 8/10 positions the king move actually WORSENED king safety—placing the king on squares vulnerable to checks (Qf4+ in position 3, Nxa7+ in position 9, Qh3+ in position 10), discovered attacks (position 7), or outright checkmate (position 4). The average cp_loss of 1285 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic tempo losses at critical moments. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise action rather than quiet maneuvering.

1668.label: Knight moves away from an effective central or defensive square to a worse square, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
1668.description: All 9/9 positions feature a knight moving from a strong, actively-placed square to an inferior one. In 8/9 cases, the knight departs a clearly superior post: f3→h4 (abandoning g5 control), e3→f1 (abandoning g2 guard), e4→d2 (leaving centralization), d5→c7 (leaving dominant outpost), d5→b6 (leaving central/defensive post), c5→d7 (leaving active defense), f5→d6 (leaving safe square for open file). The destinations are consistently worse: rim squares (h4, b6), squares where the knight hangs to pieces already aiming at them (d2 to bishop, c7 to queen+knight, d6 to rook battery), squares that self-block (d7 blocking king escape), or squares that abandon critical defensive coverage (f1 allowing mate in 2). The average cp_loss of 1309 reflects catastrophic consequences. In 6/9 positions the side playing the move was already worse, suggesting desperation-driven repositioning. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding precision rather than experimentation.

1669.label: A minor piece captures a defended central pawn, but the recapture sequence leaves the capturing side down material or with catastrophically degraded piece activity.
1669.description: All 9/9 positions feature a minor piece (7 bishop captures, 2 knight captures) greedily capturing a defended pawn on a central or near-central square (d4, d5, e4, e5, c5, f6). In every case, the opponent recaptures cleanly, and the result is devastating: in 5/9 positions the capturing side loses a full minor piece for just a pawn after the recapture sequence; in 3/9 the recapture activates the opponent's pieces or creates forks (Nxf6+, Nxc6+); and in 1/9 the wrong capture order hands the opponent a dominant position. The capturing piece was consistently well-placed or active BEFORE the capture (dominant dark-square bishops, powerfully-posted knights on c7, fianchettoed bishops), making the trade-for-pawn particularly costly. The average cp_loss of 373 reflects that these are severe blunders transforming balanced or advantageous positions into lost ones.

1666.label: Pawn captures that resolve structural tension prematurely, opening lines or weakening the pawn shield when maintaining tension or improving pieces was superior.
1666.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture that resolves an existing pawn tension (e.g., gxf5, exd5, gxh5). In 7/10 cases, the capture specifically weakens the player's own king shelter — 5/10 involve the g-pawn capturing (gxf5 or gxh5), destroying the castled king's shield, while 3/10 involve e-pawn captures that open the center when the player's king is still on e1. In 8/10 positions, the capture opens a file or diagonal that the opponent immediately exploits (e-file against uncastled king in positions 3/4/9, h-file for rook attacks in positions 6/7, g-file in position 5). The best alternatives in 9/10 positions involved maintaining the pawn tension while improving pieces (Nf4, Bb5, Nxe5, Bg5, Rf8, Bxe4). Position 8 (gxf4 with cp_loss=0) was actually correct, suggesting the feature fires on the structural pattern of the capture itself rather than perfectly isolating mistakes. The average cp_loss of 204 across erroneous positions reflects how severely these tension releases damage the position, typically transforming winning/equal positions into losing/much worse ones.

1665.label: Moving a minor piece to a seemingly active square while ignoring a more critical forcing continuation or defensive necessity.
1665.description: 9/10 positions feature a minor piece (7 bishops, 2 knights) being moved to what appears to be a natural, active square—developing, attacking something, or improving placement—while a much more urgent tactical demand exists. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 4, 8), a forcing tactical shot was available that would win material or deliver checkmate. In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 7, 9), the piece was performing a critical defensive function on its original square, and moving it exposed the king to attack. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 10), the destination square created a new concrete vulnerability (capture with check, diagonal exposure, deflection). The average cp_loss of 1196 is heavily inflated by the missed mate in position 3, but even excluding that outlier, the average loss is ~262cp—a full positional reversal. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these arise at critical decision points where concrete calculation, not general principles, determines the outcome.

1679.label: Uncastled king moves one square forward (e1→e2, e8→e7, d8→d7) into a fatally exposed central square vulnerable to immediate diagonal attacks.
1679.description: All 10/10 positions feature an uncastled king moving exactly one square forward from its starting rank — Ke2 in 6/10 (White), Ke7 in 3/10 (Black), and Kd7 in 1/10 (Black). In every case, the king was already under pressure on its starting square and the player attempted to 'castle by hand' or escape threats by stepping forward. The devastating consequence is consistent: 9/10 positions are punished by an immediate diagonal check (Ba6+, Bc4+, Bg4+, Qg4+, Qb4+, Bd8#) that exploits the king's new square sitting on an open diagonal. In 5/10 cases, this diagonal check wins the queen outright via a forced interposition-then-capture sequence (Qd3 Bxd3+ pattern). In 4/10 cases, it leads to forced checkmate. The average cp_loss of 4839 reflects catastrophic consequences. Only 1.1 good moves existed on average, meaning these were desperate positions where the only salvation was typically a queen trade or simplification (Qd2, Qe8, Qxc2), not a king move.

1664.label: A rook moves laterally or to an adjacent square, abandoning the one file or rank where it fulfilled a vital tactical or defensive function.
1664.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook moving away from a file or square where it was tactically essential — either enabling a forcing combination, defending a critical weakness, or blocking an enemy invasion. In 6/10 cases the rook moves laterally along a rank to an adjacent file (f2→e2, e4→d4, f4→g4, b3→c3, d8→c8, c2→e2). In 3/10 the rook moves vertically but to the wrong depth (e2→e3 instead of e8, b7→b6 instead of c7, f6→f4). The moves all appear 'reasonable' — centralizing, attacking a piece, or repositioning — but each one surrenders the position's single most important resource. 4/10 positions allowed back-rank or mating threats after the rook departed (positions 1, 5, 6, 10). 3/10 squandered decisive tactical shots that required the rook on its original square (positions 2, 3, 8). 2/10 placed the rook on a tactically vulnerable square where it became trapped or won (positions 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 3086 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirms these are razor-sharp positions where one specific rook placement was critical.

1676.label: Capturing a pawn or piece on a central square (d4/d5/e4/e5/e6) when the opponent's recapture is devastatingly strong, sacrificing initiative, development, or piece safety for illusory material.
1676.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture on a central square (d4, d5, e4, e5, e6, or c3) where the player grabs material but underestimates the opponent's recapture strength. In 8/10 cases, the best alternative moves involved improving piece activity, completing development, or exploiting king safety rather than capturing. The recaptures punish via: opening a devastating diagonal (positions 1, 2, 5, 10), creating a pin on a central file (positions 4, 7), activating a previously dormant piece (positions 2, 8, 9), or winning back more material through a superior exchange sequence (positions 3, 6, 8). In 7/10 positions, one side's king was still in the center, making the premature opening of central lines especially dangerous. The average cp_loss of 317 reflects how dramatically these 'free' captures reverse positional dynamics.

1673.label: A passive one-square king move played in a position where an urgent tactical response with another piece was required.
1673.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing king move (no check, no capture, one square). In 6/10 positions, the best move was NOT a king move at all but rather a forcing tactical response (rook defense in P1, queen threat in P4, bishop forcing move in P5, rook sacrifice in P6, queen exchange in P7, queen sacrifice in P10). In 3/10 positions, the best move was a king move to a DIFFERENT square that avoided specific tactical vulnerabilities (P3, P8, P9). Only 1/10 (P2) was the actual best move (in an already hopeless position). The catastrophic cp_loss averaging 3862 reflects that 7/10 positions had only 1 good move available, meaning these were narrow critical moments where the passive king move was maximally punished. The king moves typically look 'natural' — centralizing (Kd2, Ke2, Kf3), escaping (Kf1, Kg7, Ke7), or prophylactic (Kh2, Kg2) — but all fail to address the board's most critical tactical feature.

1684.label: Playing a quiet king repositioning move when the position demands immediate tactical action with other pieces or pawns.
1684.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing king move (no check, no capture) played instead of a critically needed active move. In 9/10 cases with meaningful cp_loss, the best move was an active piece move or pawn advance: passed pawn pushes (positions 1, 9), rook invasions (positions 2, 7), pawn advances creating threats (position 3), forcing checks (positions 4, 8), a bishop redeployment enabling forced mate (position 6), and a checkmate-in-one pawn push (position 10). The king moves share a common intent of 'improving' the king position — centralizing (Ke4, Ke6, Kg6, Kd3), fleeing perceived danger (Kf8, Kh2, Kf2, Kb3), or retreating to safety (Kf3 twice) — but all waste a critical tempo in positions where urgency was paramount. The average cp_loss of 2152 and average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are narrow tactical moments where precision was required, yet the player defaulted to a slow king move.

1674.label: A piece occupies f3/f6 and either blocks another knight's only retreat to that square or abandons a superior outpost to reach it.
1674.description: All 10 positions feature a piece moving to f3 (for White, 6/10) or f6 (for Black, 4/10). In at least 6/10 positions, the move directly blocks a knight's retreat path to that square, creating a trapped piece: Position 1 (Bf6 blocks Ng4→f6), Position 2 (Qf3 complicates Ng5→f3), Position 3 (Qf3 blocks Ng5→f3), Position 5 (Qf3 blocks Nh4→f3), Position 9 (Ndf3 blocks Nh4→f3), and Position 8 (Qf3 occupies the square the knight needs after ...e5). In 3/10 positions (6, 7, 10), a knight voluntarily retreats TO f3/f6 from a superior outpost (g5→f3, h5→f6, e4→f6), abandoning central dominance and exposing other pieces to tactical exploitation. The trapped-piece variant is punished by pawn advances (g5 in positions 5/9, h6 in positions 2/3) attacking the stranded knight, while the outpost-abandonment variant is punished by captures of now-undefended pieces or pawns (Bxe5/Nc6 fork, Qxe4, b4 trapping). Average cp_loss is 252, indicating these are consistently severe mistakes.

1683.label: Playing a developing, repositioning, or capturing minor piece move that ignores an immediate king safety emergency requiring urgent defensive action.
1683.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece move (7 bishop moves, 3 knight moves) played in a middlegame where the player's king faces an immediate mating threat or catastrophic tactical vulnerability. In 7/10 positions, the correct move involved a completely different piece type (queen retreat, rook defense, or king escape) rather than any minor piece maneuver. In 3/10 positions (Bxf6, Nxf6, Bxf3), the error was capturing with the wrong piece—the minor piece that moved was needed on its original square for defensive coverage. The average cp_loss of 5724 reflects that 6/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate (including two mate-in-1s). The moves share a common psychological profile: they look like reasonable developing moves, natural recaptures, or aggressive counterplay attempts in a normal position, but the position is actually in tactical crisis. The correct moves were typically non-obvious defensive resources (Rd1, Qf2, Bh5, Bd6, Qc6) that required recognizing the king's danger as the overriding priority.
1683.old_chip: Minor piece fiddles while king burns

1677.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete or tactical action.
1677.description: 8/10 positions share the explicit tag 'tempo_loss' in their analysis, and 8/10 feature 'piece_activity' as a core theme. The blunders are all non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves (piece retreats, developments, or king walks) played in positions where one specific forcing continuation was required. In 7/10 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of optimal, indicating these are sharp positions with narrow margins where wasting even a single tempo is catastrophic. The correct moves across all positions share a common character: they are active, forcing, or immediately confrontational (Bg4 attacking a trapped piece, a6 advancing a pawn race, d4 breaking the center, Qxe2 trading queens, Rc1 attacking the queen). The 2/10 positions with negligible cp_loss (positions 2 and 5) are already hopelessly lost positions where no forcing move exists—the feature still fires because the quiet repositioning move pattern is present, even though it happens to be correct when no urgent alternative exists.

1671.label: Playing slow strategic or repositioning moves in positions that demand an immediate tactical response to capture, defend, or address a hanging piece.
1671.description: 9/10 positions featured an immediate tactical opportunity or threat that was completely ignored in favor of a move with long-term strategic intent. In 6/10 cases, the best move involved capturing a vulnerable or hanging piece (Bxd8, Bxd6, Bxh3-deflection, Nxe3, Bxa4, Bxd8-queen). In 3/10 cases, the player needed to save or address an immediately threatened piece (positions 1, 5, 9). The moves actually played were overwhelmingly pawn pushes (6/10: d3, a3, dxc6, dxe5, d5, e5) or knight repositioning moves (3/10: Nf2, Ne7, Na5) — all moves that would make sense in quiet positions but catastrophically misread the tactical urgency. The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were critical-decision positions with razor-thin margins. In 7/10 positions, the refutation involved exploiting a piece left hanging or undefended by the played move. The consistent thread is treating a tactically charged position as though it were a calm maneuvering phase.

1681.label: Moving a rook laterally to a new file as a slow positional improvement when the position demands an immediate concrete action (tactical strike, piece defense, or king evacuation).
1681.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing rook move to a different file — repositioning along the back ranks to 'improve' placement on a seemingly attractive file. In 10/10 cases, this rook shuffle ignores the single most urgent tactical demand in the position. The positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.4 good moves), meaning the critical moment demanded one specific concrete action: in 3/10 cases the correct move was a pawn capture or piece capture (Rxd4, Rxa4), in 3/10 it was king evacuation (Kb5, Kh2, king flight), in 2/10 it was a knight retreat saving an attacked piece (Nh5, Ne7), and in 2/10 it was an active central pawn break (e5, Qd6 defending). The rook moves frequently abandoned a file where the rook was performing a critical defensive function — in positions 1, 7, and 8, the rook left a file that protected a key piece or pawn, directly enabling the opponent's refutation. The average centipawn loss of 305 reflects that these moves transform playable positions into losing ones.

1680.label: A pawn or knight move that occupies the critical retreat square of a friendly bishop, allowing it to be trapped.
1680.description: 6/10 positions show a crystal-clear pattern: the player moves a pawn or knight to the exact square their bishop needs as a retreat path, allowing the opponent to win the bishop (via pawn advance or central strike). In positions 1, 4, and 8, the move b3 blocks the light-squared bishop's retreat to b3 (bishops on c4 or a4). In position 2, Nbd7 blocks the Be6's retreat to d7. In position 3, Ne2 blocks the Bd3's retreat to e2. In position 10, the pawn e6 blocks the Bf5's retreat diagonal through e6. In all six cases, the opponent immediately exploits this with a pawn advance (typically ...b5, ...e4, or e4) that attacks the bishop, which now has no escape. The remaining 4/10 positions share the broader theme of passive moves that create tactical vulnerabilities (position 5: b5 ignores Bxf7+; position 6: b5 weakens c6; position 7: Nd7 misses Qxe4+; position 9: Nb3 decentralizes), but the trapped-bishop-via-blocked-retreat is the dominant specific mechanism.

1682.label: Queen moves to a seemingly active square but leaves a piece, pawn, or key defensive square unprotected, enabling immediate tactical punishment.
1682.description: All 10 positions feature queen moves that abandon a critical responsibility in pursuit of apparent activity. In 6/10 positions (2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8), the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece' — the queen move leaves a specific piece or pawn undefended that the opponent immediately captures. In 2/10 positions (6, 9), the queen abandons control of a critical square (g7 for mate, e6 for a devastating check). In 2/10 positions (1, 6), a forced mate existed but the queen made a preparatory/repositioning move instead. In 1/10 positions (10), the queen moves to a square where it can be attacked with tempo, freeing the opponent's trapped piece. The consistent thread is that the queen was performing an essential function on or near its original square — defending a piece, controlling a key square, or enabling a forcing sequence — and the player moved it away for an illusory improvement. The average cp_loss of 2249 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 8/10 positions having only 1-2 good moves available.

1685.label: Playing a non-forcing, non-urgent move while a piece (usually one's own) is undefended and immediately capturable.
1685.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct material threat) while an urgent tactical situation demanded immediate action regarding an undefended piece. In 6/10 cases (Nc6, Kh6, Qa5, Rh3, Qa6, h3), the move left the player's OWN piece completely hanging for the opponent to capture. In 2/10 cases (Na3, h3-position-10), the player failed to capture an opponent's undefended piece. In 2/10 cases (f6, Qb3), the move ignored a critical weakness that the opponent could immediately exploit for material. The moves themselves look 'reasonable' in isolation—natural development (Nc6, Na3), prophylactic pawn pushes (f6, h3), queen repositioning (Qa5, Qa6, Qb3), piece activity (Rh3, Bh4), king safety (Kh6)—but all catastrophically ignore that material is en prise. The average cp_loss of 1389 reflects that these are massive material-losing oversights, not subtle positional errors.

1689.label: Player makes a passive or misguided king move in the middlegame when the position urgently demands active piece play, counterattack, or addressing immediate tactical threats.
1689.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves during the middlegame that waste critical tempo or create new vulnerabilities. In 7/10 positions, the king move was intended as a prophylactic safety measure (tucking into a corner or retreating), but the position actually demanded immediate active piece play: counterattacks (Position 1 needed ...a4), pawn breaks (Position 10 needed ...f4), piece saves (Position 9 needed to move the hanging rook), or queen trades (Position 8 needed ...Qg5). In 3/10 positions (2, 4, 6), the king captured a piece/pawn and walked into direct tactical danger (forks, mating nets). The average cp_loss of 1300 is catastrophically high, reflecting that these positions had narrow windows for correct play (avg 2.0 good moves), and the king move squandered the opportunity. 8/10 moves were by Black, and most moved the king toward the back rank or corner (Kh8×3, Kg8×2, Kf8×2), suggesting a pattern of reflexive king-tucking when under pressure.

1687.label: Major piece relocates to an active-looking square instead of performing its critical defensive or simplifying duty.
1687.description: All 9 positions feature a major piece (rook in 7/9, queen in 2/9) moving to a seemingly powerful square—a central square, the 7th/8th rank, or an open file—when the correct move was either a simplifying trade (4/9: Rxc1, Rxc1, Rxc6, Qxe2) or a defensive retreat to protect the king (4/9: Rb1, Qd8/Qe7, Ra8, Rb2). In 7/9 positions the side was already losing, making defense or simplification the only viable strategy. The blunders share the common consequence of leaving the king fatally exposed (7/9 tagged king_safety) or a piece undefended (1/9 hanging piece). The average cp_loss of 5110 reflects that these 'active' moves typically cross the threshold from survivable to immediately losing or forced mate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions requiring precise defensive judgment where the temptation to seek counterplay was strongest.

1678.label: Moving a piece to a superficially attractive square instead of executing the position's critical concrete action (usually a pawn push, a capture, or maintaining the piece on its optimal square).
1678.description: 9/10 positions share the pattern of a piece being relocated to an apparently active or aggressive square that misses the position's actual demand. In 7/10 cases the blunder is a rook move to a 'natural-looking' square (7th rank, open file, checking square, attacking something). In 7/10 positions, the actual best move involved either a critical pawn advance (h7, e7, e6 in positions 5/7/8), a material capture (Rxg3 in position 3), or keeping the piece on its current optimal square while using the king or checks (positions 1, 4, 6). The recurring punishment is that the relocated piece either abandons a critical protective function (positions 2, 5), lands on a square where it's immediately challenged or trapped (positions 5, 9, 10), targets the wrong objective entirely (positions 1, 6), or gives the opponent crucial tempo to advance passed pawns or execute tactics (positions 3, 7, 8, 10). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 7/10 analyses and 'piece_activity' in 9/10, confirming that these moves prioritize APPARENT activity over the position's TRUE requirements.
1678.old_chip: Flashy Piece Moves Miss Concrete Best

1688.label: A pawn advance removes the only piece blocking a diagonal, exposing a high-value piece (usually the queen) to immediate capture.
1688.description: In 6/10 positions, the blunder is a pawn advance that vacates a square serving as the sole blocker on a diagonal, directly exposing the player's own queen or bishop to capture. Positions 1, 4, and 5 all feature an e-pawn clearing the a8-h1 diagonal for a fianchettoed bishop to capture a queen on f3. Position 3 sees ...e6 opening the g5-d8 diagonal for a bishop to take the queen. Position 8 has e6 opening the c7-f4 diagonal, and Position 9 has d4 opening the g5-c1 diagonal for a queen to capture an undefended minor piece. The remaining 4/10 positions share the broader theme of pawn advances that neglect the pawn's critical defensive duties: Position 2 pushes c3 ignoring diagonal vulnerability, Position 6 advances c4 abandoning defense of d6, Position 7 plays d4 instead of capturing a hanging piece, and Position 10 sacrifices f3 weakening king shelter. All 10 moves are central or semi-central pawn advances (e-file: 6, d-file: 2, c-file: 1, f-file: 1) where the player prioritized aggression or structure over the pawn's blocking/defensive function.

1691.label: Player captures an enemy pawn in tension when the correct move was to push the pawn forward past the point of contact, creating superior tactical or strategic threats.
1691.description: In 8/10 positions, the player captured an enemy pawn (exd4, exd5, fxg5, fxe5, dxc3, fxe4, dxe4, fxe5) when the objectively best move was to ADVANCE the same pawn one square forward past the tension (e4, e5, e5, f5, f5+, d3, f4, d4 respectively). Position 5 shows a related error of capturing the wrong target pawn (cxd5 instead of cxb5), and position 10 is a marginal 55cp case. The advances created devastating tactical effects: pawn forks of two pieces (positions 1, 2, 9), tempo-gaining checks against exposed kings (position 6), unstoppable passed pawns deep in enemy territory (positions 4, 7), sealed files protecting the player's own king (position 8), and spatial wedges restricting enemy pieces (position 3). All 10 moves are pawn-takes-pawn captures that resolve central/flank tension in a routine way, averaging 281cp loss. The avg of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these were narrow critical moments where only the advance worked.

1686.label: Advancing or capturing with a pawn when the position urgently demands a piece move (king centralization, rook activation, or piece capture).
1686.description: 10/10 positions feature pawn moves (8 non-capture advances, 2 pawn captures). 9/10 positions involve active passed pawns or pawn promotion races as a dominant positional theme. In 8/10 cases the pawn move was a mistake (avg cp_loss 1160), while 2/10 were actually optimal (positions 5 and 6, both 0 cp loss). For the 8 mistakes, the consistent error pattern is choosing a pawn advance when piece activity was more urgent: in positions 1, 2, and 8 king centralization was needed to blockade an enemy passed pawn; in positions 3, 9, and 10 rook activation or repositioning was critical; in position 4 capturing a piece instead of a pawn was available; in position 7 a different pawn breakthrough (b6) was far stronger than the static c5 push. The 2 correct pawn advances (positions 5 and 6) occurred in positions where the pawn advance WAS the most forcing piece-like action available — connected passers rolling forward unstoppably. The feature appears to detect 'pawn advances in positions with passed-pawn dynamics' and fires regardless of correctness, though the vast majority represent tempo-losing choices.

1692.label: Aggressive central or forward pawn advance that opens lines against the player's own unsafe king instead of developing pieces or addressing king safety.
1692.description: All 10 positions feature a one-step pawn advance (d5 in 4/10, f4/f5 in 3/10, e5 in 1/10, d4 in 1/10, c7 in 1/10) played as an aggressive space-grabbing thrust. In 8/10 positions, the side making the move has an uncastled or exposed king. In 9/10 positions, the pawn advance directly opens a line, diagonal, or square that the opponent immediately exploits (e.g., e8-h5 diagonal after f5, the e1-h4 diagonal after f4, fork squares after d5). In 9/10 cases, the correct move was a piece move (development, repositioning, or tactical capture) rather than a pawn advance — the positions demanded piece coordination, not space. The average cp_loss of 1191 is catastrophically high, with 2 positions resulting in immediate checkmate. The refutations consistently involve checks, forks, or pins along the newly opened lines (Qh5+, Qh4+, Nc2+, Nc7+, Qf2#). Only 1.7 good moves existed on average, showing these were delicate positions requiring precise piece play, not speculative pawn thrusts.

1698.label: Bishop captures a pawn (or moves to a vulnerable square) prioritizing material over urgent positional or defensive requirements, resulting in catastrophic tactical punishment.
1698.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a pawn, and 10/10 are bishop moves that prioritize material gain or repositioning over critical positional demands. The captures target periphery pawns (g2, g5, g7, g3, h6, h3, e4, e6) rather than addressing the most urgent factor in the position. In 5/10 cases, the bishop abandons a critical defensive role or vacates a key diagonal (positions 2, 4, 8 removing defensive guardians; positions 1, 5 ignoring exposed king urgency). In 4/10 cases, the bishop gets trapped or fatally displaced after the capture (positions 4, 10, and partially 2, 5). In 7/10 positions, the opponent's refutation exploits king safety—either the player's own exposed king or a mating net that the bishop's departure enabled. The average cp_loss of 4062 and an average of only 1.2 good moves available indicate these are critical moments where the sole correct move addresses the position's real demand (defense, blockade, or capturing a more important target), but the player chose the superficially attractive bishop capture instead.

1702.label: The player makes an active or greedy move while leaving one of their own pieces undefended and immediately capturable.
1702.description: In 9/10 positions, the played move completely ignores a concrete threat to one of the player's own pieces, allowing the opponent to simply capture it. The hanging pieces are diverse (knight in positions 1, 5, 8, 9; bishop in positions 4, 7, 10; rook in position 3; rook as back-rank target in position 6), but the mechanism is identical: the player pursues their own agenda—king activation (5/10: Kg7, Kd4, Kc7, Kd2, Kc7), pawn grabbing (3/10: Rxe2, Qxf2, Rxg3), a pawn push (b5), or aggressive development (Bg4)—while a piece sits en prise. In every case, the top recommended moves all involve first saving or relocating the threatened piece before doing anything else. The refutations are uniformly simple: just capture the undefended piece (Qxd5, Rxh6+, Rxc2, Kxd3, Rxg4+, Qxa8+, Kxc3, Kxd6, Rxh6). Position 2 (Kg7 with only 5cp loss) is the outlier, involving a microscopic tempo difference rather than a full piece loss, but even there the theme is allowing a capture without check that the best move would have prevented.

1696.label: Quiet queen repositioning to a seemingly natural square when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical response.
1696.description: All 9/9 positions feature a non-forcing queen relocation move — no checks, no captures, no direct threats — to a 'natural-looking' square (d7, d8, d2, c8, or a6). In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand that the queen move ignores. The consequences vary: in 2/9 positions (Positions 5 and 9), the queen physically blocks a friendly bishop's retreat square (Qd7 blocks Bd7, Qc8 blocks Bc8), allowing the bishop to be trapped or sacrificially captured. In 3/9 positions (1, 6, 8), the queen abandons a critical defensive function — guarding a piece, a key pawn, or preventing a discovered/back-rank tactic. In 2/9 positions (2, 4), the player misses a dramatically superior forcing move (capturing a hanging queen, or a back-rank checking sequence). In 2/9 positions (3, 10), the queen lands on a square where it becomes tactically exploitable or fails to prevent an incoming attack. The average cp_loss of 1347 reflects that these 'quiet' moves often collapse winning or equal positions entirely. The unifying thread is that all moves prioritize abstract positional goals (connecting rooks, centralizing, supporting pawns) over the concrete tactical reality screaming for attention.

1700.label: The king retreats toward the back rank or corner seeking false safety, when it should centralize or yield the tempo to an active piece move.
1700.description: All 10 positions feature king moves, with 9/10 retreating toward the back rank or corner (Ke8, Kg1, Kg8, Kd7, Kf8, Kd8). The remaining move (Kg3) similarly abandons a critical defensive post. In 7/10 positions, the best move was NOT a king move at all but rather an active piece move (Qf3, Nf6, Qf6, Nc5, f3/Nxb7, f5, Re7). In the other 3/10, the best king move was FORWARD toward the center (Kd6, Ke6, Ke6) — the exact opposite direction of the blunder. The retreats uniformly create worse problems than they solve: 4/10 enabled back-rank tactics (Rh1#, Re8+, Rxd8#, Rxe8+), 4/10 walked into mating nets created by advanced pawns and coordinated pieces, 2/10 abandoned critical defensive duties (guarding g3, blocking a diagonal). Average cp_loss was 5064, with 5/10 positions resulting in forced mate. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, indicating these arise in razor-sharp positions where the instinct to seek king safety is maximally punished.

1690.label: Playing a reasonable-looking non-forcing move (capture, push, or quiet piece maneuver) when a more forcing tactical continuation (check, discovered attack, or critical capture) was available.
1690.description: In 9/10 positions (excluding Position 5 which was correctly played at 0cp loss), the player chose a slower, less-forcing move when a significantly stronger forcing alternative existed. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 8/10. Specifically: 4/10 positions involved pawn pushes (b3, e5, c3, a5) when a capture or check was correct; 3/10 involved captures on the wrong square or with the wrong piece (hxg5, bxc5, cxd5) when a more forcing capture/check existed; 2/10 involved quiet knight moves (Nf2, Nc4) when checks or better placements were available. In every case, the best move was more forcing: a check (positions 2, 6, 8), a critical structural capture (positions 4, 7, 10), saving a piece before executing a plan (position 7), or activating the queen with immediate threats (position 1). The player consistently addressed a real positional/material concern (taking a hanging piece, pushing a passed pawn, attacking something) but missed that doing so surrendered the initiative or a critical tempo that the opponent could exploit.

1697.label: Routine queenside knight development to c3/c6 when the position demands a concrete tactical or structural response.
1697.description: In 9/10 positions, the blunder is specifically developing the b-knight to its 'natural' square (Nc3 for White, Nc6 for Black), with 1/10 being a similar routine Nf6. All 10 moves are opening-phase (9/10) or early middlegame knight developments that look textbook but ignore urgent concrete needs. In 5/10 positions (2, 6, 7, 9, 10), placing the knight on c3/c6 critically blocks the c-pawn, causing structural damage (trapped bishops, doubled pawns, inability to support the d-pawn with ...c6). In 4/10 positions (3, 5, 8, 10), a concrete tactical opportunity was missed in favor of the routine development (capturing a hanging piece, exploiting overextended enemy pieces, or striking at a vulnerable center pawn). In 3/10 positions (1, 5, 6/7), the knight on c6 immediately becomes a target for a d-pawn advance that wins tempo or material. The average cp_loss of 256 with only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical moments disguised as routine development.

1693.label: Capturing with a minor piece before playing a necessary preparatory move, releasing tension and squandering the position's tactical potential.
1693.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture by a minor piece (7/10 knight captures, 3/10 bishop captures) that is executed too early in the sequence. In at least 6/10 cases, the exact same capture appears in the BEST line but only after a critical preparatory move (e.g., Position 10: Bxf3 first then Nxd4; Position 5: Ne4 first then Bxc3+; Position 7: Nh4 first then Bxf3; Position 8: dxe6 first then piece captures; Position 3: Bd2 first then Bxc6+). In the remaining cases, the capture itself is simply wrong because a superior alternative exists that maintains the active piece rather than trading it (Positions 1, 2, 6). The analyses explicitly tag 'move_order' in 5/10 positions and 'premature_exchange' in 3/10. All 10/10 involve trading away a piece that was generating pressure or capturing a target that appears attractive but hasn't been properly set up. The average centipawn loss of 330 reflects how these seemingly natural captures catastrophically alter the position's character.

1699.label: Player makes a routine pawn capture (usually eliminating a threatening pawn) instead of finding a critical forcing move like a check, piece capture, or mating sequence.
1699.description: All 10 positions feature pawn captures (notation xNN) chosen over far superior forcing moves. 7/10 involve capturing an advanced pawn on the g-file (fxg6 appears 6 times, hxg6 once), with the remaining 3 being gxf4, axb4, and bxc3. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a forcing move involving a piece (check, piece capture, or sacrifice): positions 4, 7, and 8 missed forced checkmates; positions 2 and 9 missed capturing hanging pieces; positions 1, 3, 5, and 6 missed critical counter-attacking checks or piece repositioning. The average cp_loss of 2963 is astronomical, driven by 3 missed forced mates. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were almost all 'only move' situations requiring precise calculation. 9/10 were middlegame positions where the pawn capture addressed a seemingly urgent concern (removing a threatening advanced pawn near the king, eliminating a passed pawn, or protecting a piece) but squandered a decisive tactical opportunity.

1705.label: The queen captures a seemingly free pawn on the opponent's side of the board, displacing itself from defensive or coordinating duties and allowing tactical punishment.
1705.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen making a capture (Qx__) of material — 9/10 capture a pawn and 1/10 captures a knight. In 7/10 cases, the target is specifically a b2 or c2 pawn on White's second rank, with the remaining captures on d4, e2, and g6. In 9/10 positions, it is Black's queen that grabs the material. The king is uncastled or has a weak pawn shield in 9/10 positions, meaning defensive coordination was critical at the moment of the grab. The refutations exploit the queen's absence through king attacks (6/10), queen trapping (3/10), or winning undefended material elsewhere (1/10). The average centipawn loss of 2040 reflects catastrophic consequences — 2/10 resulted in forced checkmate. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise defense rather than materialistic captures.

1703.label: A rook captures peripheral material (usually a pawn) but in doing so abandons a critical defensive or controlling function, allowing the opponent to exploit the rook's absence with immediate tactical or mating threats.
1703.description: 10/10 positions feature a rook capture (Rx__) that grabs material — 9/10 capture a pawn and 1/10 captures a minor piece. In every case, the rook was previously occupying or had access to a square/file/rank performing a vital function: blocking a passed pawn (1/10), defending the back rank (4/10), shielding the king from checks along files or diagonals (4/10), or maintaining a mating net (1/10). After the greedy capture, the rook becomes stranded far from the critical zone of the board. The refutations consistently exploit the rook's absence: 4/10 result in immediate or near-immediate checkmate, 3/10 allow devastating king attacks via checks on newly unguarded lines, 2/10 allow unstoppable passed pawn advances, and 1/10 simply loses the rook itself to a piece on an open diagonal. 8/10 positions are endgames where piece activity and coordination are paramount over raw material. The average cp_loss of 3869 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 5/10 positions swinging to forced mate. In all cases, multiple better alternatives existed (average 2.7 good moves) that prioritized maintaining piece coordination, king safety, or defensive structure over the tempting material grab.

1701.label: Active-looking bishop or knight moves that ignore the player's own king vulnerability, allowing punishment via checks, pins, or forks along open lines to the exposed king.
