1701.description: All 10/10 positions feature the moving side's king being exposed, uncastled, or lacking adequate pawn shelter. All 10/10 blunders are minor piece moves (7 bishop, 3 knight) that appear active or aggressive but critically ignore the king's tactical vulnerability. In 9/10 cases, the refutation involves a direct check or pin exploiting an open line to the exposed king (Qa4+ in 3/10, rook checks in 3/10, queen checks on other diagonals in 3/10). The moved piece frequently ends up undefended (6/10 positions), making it capturable after the intermediate check forces the defender to address king safety first. Three positions specifically feature ...Bb4 with king on e8 punished by Qa4+, representing the most concentrated sub-pattern. In 8/10 positions, the king remains on its starting square (e1 or e8), making the diagonal and file vulnerabilities entirely predictable.

1704.label: Advancing a pawn when the position urgently demands a piece move (king evacuation, rook repositioning, or capture) to address an immediate tactical or structural emergency.
1704.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance as the blunder, while the correct move was a piece move in every case: king centralization/evacuation (5/10: Kd4, Kh2, Ke2, Kf1, Ke6), rook repositioning (4/10: Rf8, Rf1, Ra1, Rc8), or a pawn capture that eliminates an enemy threat (2/10: gxf5, Bxb3). The pawn pushes uniformly waste a critical tempo in positions where time is of the essence — 7/10 occur in endgames where single tempi are decisive, and the average cp_loss of 2224 reflects catastrophic consequences. In 6/10 positions the pawn push was completely irrelevant to the critical battle (h5×2, g5, e6, a6, c6 — all on the wrong side or wrong priority), while in 4/10 the pawn advance actively created a target or weakness (g3×2, d3, e3). The positions share exposed kings (8/10), passed pawn tensions (8/10), and open files requiring piece activity (7/10), yet the player consistently chose the 'active-looking' pawn push over the essential defensive/positional piece move.

1694.label: Major piece (usually queen) moves to a new square that creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—either the piece itself becomes capturable/forkable/trapped, or its departure leaves another piece undefended.
1694.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder is a queen move; the remaining 2/10 are rook moves that share the same structural error. In every case, the player repositions a major piece to a square that appears reasonable (defensive consolidation, attacking probe, material grab) but creates a concrete tactical exploitation. In 4/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 10), the piece moves to a square where it becomes directly vulnerable—trapped by rook invasions, forkable by minor pieces, or geometrically aligned with another piece for a double attack. In 3/10 positions (2, 3, 9), the queen's departure from its current square removes a critical defense of another piece, which is immediately captured. In 3/10 positions (6, 7, 8), the move abandons the piece's optimal active post, surrendering decisive initiative or counterplay resources. The average cp_loss of 1256 reflects how catastrophic these positional self-inflicted wounds are—the player sees no immediate threat to the piece on its new square but misses the second-order tactical consequence that follows.

1709.label: King captures a seemingly free pawn in the endgame but moves in the wrong strategic direction, enabling the opponent's counterplay or passed pawn advance.
1709.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where the player makes a king move, with 9/10 being king captures of pawns (Kxd5, Kxa5, Kxh4, Kxa3, Kxc6, Kxc6, Kxg3, Kxc4, Kxh3) and 1/10 being a king move toward material (Kc4). The consistent error is that the king prioritizes winning material over its critical positional duty — in 7/10 positions the king moves AWAY from the sector where the decisive battle occurs (a passed pawn race or promotion threat), while in 3/10 the king walks into tactical vulnerability (mating nets, exchange sacrifices, or piece checks). The analyses reveal that in 8/10 cases, the best moves involved either advancing the king in a DIFFERENT direction, pushing a pawn first, or relocating a piece before the king capture. The average cp_loss of 1965 is inflated by catastrophic cases (positions 3 and 4 where the king walked into forced mate), but even the smaller losses (positions 5, 9) reflect subtle move-order errors where the king capture was available but needed to be deferred by one move. Tags across all positions consistently include 'tempo_loss' (9/10) and 'passed_pawn' (8/10), confirming the pattern centers on wasting king tempo on material while an enemy passed pawn advances unchallenged.

1707.label: Routine-looking pawn captures that fatally open a diagonal or file the opponent immediately exploits tactically.
1707.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn captures (xd5, xb5, xe4, xg5, xf6, xc5) where the moving pawn was serving as a critical line-blocker. In 8/10 cases, the capture specifically opens a diagonal that an opponent's bishop or queen immediately exploits — often with check, a fork, or an attack on an undefended piece (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 show direct diagonal exploitation by a bishop). In position 6, the capture opens a file allowing a devastating rook pin. In positions 9-10, the capture removes structural tension that was restraining the opponent's pieces or protecting an aggressive placement. The average cp_loss of 406 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights — the player sees a 'natural' pawn exchange or material gain and fails to recognize the structural defensive role the pawn was playing. In 7/10 positions, the opponent's refutation involves a piece landing on the newly opened line with tempo (check, queen attack, or threat to undefended material). The exposed kings (present in 9/10 positions) make the opened lines particularly lethal.

1695.label: Playing a natural-looking positional or routine move in a critical position where only one precise concrete tactical resource exists.
1695.description: All 10 positions share an extremely narrow set of good options (average 1.3 good moves available), meaning each demanded a single specific concrete solution. In 10/10 cases, the player chose a 'routine' or 'natural-looking' chess move — doubling rooks (Rcd8), defending passively (Re7, Rc2), centralizing the queen (Qe2, Qf5, Qh4), retreating the king (Kf8, Ka6), or making an 'obvious' capture (Rxh7, Rxe6) — while missing the ONE critical tactical resource: a time-sensitive capture (dxc4, axb3 in positions 5-6), a counterintuitive exchange sacrifice (Rxe2+ in position 8), a deflection tactic (Bc7 in position 2), an indirect attack (Rf6 in position 7), or a precise piece placement (Qg7, Kg6, Qh5 in positions 3, 4, 10). The played moves all 'look like chess moves' based on general principles (improve piece position, capture material, escape danger) but ignore the position's concrete tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 370 confirms these are catastrophic, and in 8/10 positions White has a clear single best punishment that exploits the error immediately.

1713.label: A bishop retreats along its diagonal to a seemingly active square where it becomes vulnerable to being trapped or exploited by an advancing enemy pawn or knight maneuver.
1713.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop retreating backward along a diagonal to a square that appears safe or active but is tactically flawed. In 7/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 10, and partially 6), the bishop lands on a square where an enemy pawn advance (c4, c5, g4, e4, or h5-h4) directly traps it or wins it for minimal material. In 2/10 cases (positions 8 and 9), the bishop retreat to h5 removes the piece from guarding a critical central square (e6), allowing a devastating knight fork. In 1/10 cases (position 3), the retreat loses a critical tempo in a won position. The squares chosen are consistently on the board's periphery or near-rim (b3×3, h5×4, g3×2, b6×1), where the bishop has limited escape routes once challenged. The retreats consistently reject the correct alternative of either exchanging the bishop actively (Bxf3, Bxc3, Nxc6 first) or repositioning to a more central/safe square (Bf1, Be2, Bd3, Bc8, Bd7).

1711.label: King advances away from its back rank into exposed territory, walking into checking sequences or mating nets instead of retreating to safety.
1711.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that advances the king FORWARD (away from its own back rank or corner) into more exposed territory. In 9/10 positions, the correct alternative was either retreating the king backward (Ke2, Ke7, Kc2, Kh8, Kg8, Kh1, Kb8) or playing a non-king move entirely (hxg6, Rxh2, Rxe8). The punishment in 7/10 positions is forced checkmate (ranging from #-1 to #-11), while the remaining 3 positions suffer 100-400cp losses. The average cp_loss of 5806 reflects that these forward king walks are almost always catastrophic. Specifically, 4/10 moves are Kh6 (king advancing from g7), 2/10 are moves to the third rank (Ka3, Kb3, Kh3), and others advance to central squares (Kd6, Ke5, Kg4). In every case, the advanced king lands on a square where the opponent's pieces — especially queens coordinating with rooks, bishops, or pawns — can initiate checking sequences that trap the king in open territory with no pawn shelter or defensive piece support.

1706.label: Repositioning one rook of a dominant pair on the 7th/2nd rank, allowing exchanges or breaking the mating geometry.
1706.description: In 8/10 positions, the player had two rooks powerfully doubled on the 7th rank (or 2nd rank for Black), creating overwhelming mating threats or positional domination against a trapped king. The mistake was sliding one rook laterally to a different file (or off the rank entirely) for material concerns like capturing a pawn or attacking a piece. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 5, 6, and partly 2), the move converted a forced checkmate into merely a winning position. In 7/10 positions, the specific error was that the rook's new square either allowed an exchange that dissolved the two-rook battery (positions 1, 2), broke mating geometry by releasing key escape squares for the opponent's king (positions 3, 4, 5), or removed critical defensive coverage (position 6). Position 8 (0 cp loss) demonstrates the boundary case where the rook maintained 7th-rank presence correctly. Positions 7 and 10 show the broader variant where rook repositioning breaks dynamic coordination in favor of material or passive placement.

1712.label: Directly capturing an opponent's advanced passed pawn (typically one square from promotion) in simplified endgame positions, usually with the king.
1712.description: 10/10 positions involve capturing a pawn, and in 9/10 cases the captured pawn is an advanced passed pawn (often on the 7th rank, one square from promotion). 8/10 captures are made by the king itself. 9/10 positions are endgames with heavily simplified material. The average cp_loss is only 26, with 7/10 positions showing 0 cp_loss — meaning the feature detects this specific move pattern regardless of whether it's optimal. The captured pawns were located on a7, g6, e2, a2, d2, h5, g7 (twice), h3, and e7 — all dangerous passed pawns requiring immediate attention. When the move IS suboptimal (positions 7 and 10, with 70 and 186 cp_loss respectively), the error stems from the king capturing directly rather than using indirect methods (approaching without capturing in position 7, or using the knight to address the threat in position 10).

1716.label: A pawn advance or capture that leaves one's own piece undefended, allowing the opponent to win material.
1716.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn move (advance or capture) that results in a piece being left en prise. In 7/10 cases the pawn move directly removes a defender from the piece (e.g., d5 leaving a knight on f6 unprotected from exf6, cxd4 removing the c-pawn that shielded b5/a6, dxe4 removing the d-pawn that justified the bishop on b4). In 3/10 cases the pawn move wastes a critical tempo when a piece is already under attack and needs immediate rescue (a4 ignoring Rxc3, a3 ignoring Rxc4, d5 ignoring Nxe3). The tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece' in 8/10 positions. The average cp_loss is 353, indicating these are severe blunders. The moves look strategically motivated—gaining space, advancing passed pawns, or resolving tension—but fatally ignore the immediate piece-safety consequences. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, showing these were critical moments demanding tactical precision over positional aspirations.

1719.label: Playing a routine non-forcing move (pawn push or passive development) in a narrow position where one specific forcing move wins material.
1719.description: All 10 positions share a striking pattern: the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move when exactly one concrete tactical blow was available. 7/10 moves were pawn pushes (d6, a6, a6, d6, h3, h5, c5) and 3/10 were passive piece moves (Nbd2, Nf3, Kb8). The best moves in these positions were overwhelmingly forcing — winning captures (Nxe4, Bxe3, Nxe5 in 3/10), queen checks winning hanging pieces (Qa5+ in 2/10), material-winning pawn forks (b4 in 1/10), or critical pawn advances (f4, Nc3/cxd5 in 2/10). The positions were extremely narrow with an average of only 1.3 good moves available, meaning the tactical shot was essentially mandatory. The average cp_loss of 310 reflects that these weren't minor inaccuracies but catastrophic failures to recognize concrete opportunities. 6/10 positions were in the opening phase where tempo is most critical. The played moves typically had a plausible strategic rationale (preventing Bg4, preparing b5, chasing a knight, tucking the king away) but fatally prioritized prophylaxis or long-term plans over immediate material gain.

1718.label: King captures an enemy piece (usually a rook) in a hopelessly lost endgame, entering a simplified but still losing position where the king's landing square concedes a critical tempo.
1718.description: 10/10 positions are endgames where the side to move is already deeply lost (average eval ~670cp against them). 10/10 moves are king captures (Kx__). At least 9/10 involve the king capturing a rook, with the remaining case being a pawn capture. In 10/10 cases, the capture is the best or near-best move available (avg only 1.5 good moves), and the alternatives are typically catastrophically worse (leading to forced mate). The average cp_loss is only 58, confirming these are mostly forced or optimal moves. The subtle error in each case is that the king's landing square after the capture gives the opponent a tempo for pawn advancement or allows the opponent's king to seize superior opposition/activity. In position 8 (Kxg3, 255cp loss), the move-order mistake was most pronounced—capturing immediately allowed Black's king to seize opposition on g5, whereas delaying the capture would have forced Black to alter the pawn structure first. The feature identifies the specific moment where a losing player eliminates the opponent's last major piece as damage limitation, transitioning from a piece-dominated endgame into a pure (or near-pure) pawn endgame that remains technically lost.

1710.label: Playing a natural-looking piece improvement or repositioning move when the position demands an immediate forcing continuation (capture, precise check, or concrete tactical threat).
1710.description: In all 10/10 positions, the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' piece move (repositioning, development, file-contesting, or wrong check) while the position had a narrow critical forcing move that was drastically superior. The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were 'now or never' tactical moments. In 8/10 cases the correct move was a capture or sacrifice (Qxf3, Qxe5, Re2+, Rd2+, Qf4+, Bxf6, axb7+, Rc4, Kd7 for safety, Qxf7+), while the moves played were non-forcing piece improvements: knight repositionings (Nb4, Nc5), rook developments (Rb8, Rg3, Re1), bishop moves (Bc2, Be7), a king move (Kf1), or checks from the wrong square (Qe1+, Qg5+). In 7/10 positions, the blunder allowed the opponent to seize the initiative with a forcing counter-blow (Rc6#, Rxe1, Rxh8+, Qh1+, Bxe5, Rc7+, g6). The enormous average cp_loss of 3186 reflects that these positions were tactically critical — the 'slow' move catastrophically squandered a winning advantage or walked into an immediate refutation.

1720.label: A bishop is moved exactly one square diagonally in a passive repositioning when a concrete tactic or critical function demanded the bishop stay put or a different piece act.
1720.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving exactly one diagonal square (g4→h3, g4→f5, c4→b5, b5→c4, c4→b3, h5→g6, g5→h4, g4→h5, f5→e6, g4→h5) — a short, non-capturing repositioning that appears natural but catastrophically wastes tempo. In 8/10 cases, the bishop was already performing a critical function on its original square (guarding a key square like e6, enabling a combination like Bxe6/Nxc6, or coordinating with another piece). In 9/10 cases, there was a concrete tactical opportunity available (queen capture, knight fork, bishop sacrifice, pawn thrust) that demanded immediate action rather than quiet maneuvering. The average cp_loss of 1222 reflects how devastating these seemingly innocuous shuffles are — they uniformly surrender initiative at critical moments. In 7/10 positions the bishop moved toward the board's edge (h-file or back rank), becoming more peripheral rather than more active.

1723.label: Impulsive rook checks (or activations) that skip a critical preparatory move, allowing the opponent to escape or neutralize the attack.
1723.description: 8/10 positions feature rook checks, and 10/10 feature rook moves to seemingly active squares (back ranks, open files). The consistent error is executing the rook move prematurely without necessary preparation. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9), the correct sequence required a DIFFERENT move first (queen check, knight deflection, pawn capture, or using the other rook) before the rook check would become lethal. In 2/10 cases (positions 1, 7), the error was specifically checking with the wrong rook, destroying mating geometry. In positions 3, 4, and 6, the premature check allowed the king to escape to a safe square that would have been blocked had preparation come first. The non-check positions (2, 5) share the same structural error: moving a rook to an 'active' square while abandoning its crucial current post. Average cp_loss of ~3072 confirms these are severe errors, with 3/10 missing forced checkmates entirely.

1708.label: A rook moves to contest an open file but leaves its own a-pawn (or other wing pawn) undefended, allowing immediate material gain.
1708.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a rook to a seemingly active file (b-file, c-file, d-file, or e-file) to 'contest' enemy pieces or pressure central targets. In at least 7/10 cases, the rook specifically left the a-file, directly abandoning defense of the a-pawn (a2, a3, a6, or a7), which the opponent immediately captured. Positions 3, 5, 7, and 10 show White's rook leaving a1 with the a2/a3 pawn falling to Qxa2, Rxa2, or Bxa3. Positions 2 and 4 show Black's rook leaving a8 with a6 or a7 captured by Qxa6 or Rxa7. Position 8 also involves the a-rook leaving, enabling a passed pawn advance rather than direct capture. In the remaining cases (1, 6, 9), the rook abandons counter-pressure or positional duties for false file activity, enabling passed pawn advances, tactical exploitation, or freeing the opponent's pieces from defensive obligations. The average cp_loss of 225 reflects how immediately punishing these oversights are.

1722.label: Voluntarily moving an already well-placed piece (often an infiltrated or outposted piece) to a tactically vulnerable or positionally inferior square.
1722.description: 10/10 positions feature a piece that was already excellently positioned — on an infiltration square, dominant outpost, or critical file — being voluntarily relocated to a worse square. In 3/10 cases (Be4, Bb3, Bd3), the piece was specifically an infiltrated bishop on c2 that moved to a square where it could be captured or lost its sting. In 3/10 more cases (Bc7, Bc5, Nxg5), a piece abandoned a dominant central outpost (e5, d6, e6) for a peripheral or tactically exploitable square. In 2/10 cases (Ra2, Rg6), a rook left the critical zone of attack to a square where it participated less in the winning plan. 'Tempo_loss' was identified as the motif in 7/10 positions and tagged in 9/10, while 'piece_activity' was tagged in all 10. The average cp_loss of 238 reflects how dramatically these repositioning errors change the assessment, as the piece's prior placement was often the foundation of the position's advantage.

1721.label: A rook moves to the 1st or 8th rank passively, abandoning an active function or walking into a tactical vulnerability.
1721.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to rank 1 or rank 8 (the back ranks). In 7/10 cases, the rook abandons a critical active role: blockading a passed pawn (position 3), pressuring the 2nd/7th rank (positions 2, 9), controlling a key file (positions 4, 7), or threatening promotion (position 1). In 4/10 cases (positions 5, 6, 8, 10), the rook lands on a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to a tactical blow—checkmate (Rh3#), knight fork (Nxf6+, Nd3+), or a rook-check-wins-rook pattern (Rf3+). The moves often look purposeful—'doubling rooks' (positions 4, 7, 9), 'centralizing on an open file' (positions 5, 8), or 'activating to the f-file' (position 10)—but in reality accomplish nothing concrete while the position demanded immediate action. The average cp_loss of 2051 reflects that several of these passive retreats walked into forced mate.

1727.label: Unsound bishop sacrifices (typically Bxf7+ or Bxf2+) in the opening that win only a pawn with check but lack sufficient piece support for a real attack.
1727.description: 9/9 positions feature bishop moves in the opening that give up the bishop for insufficient compensation. The dominant sub-pattern is the speculative Bxf7+/Bxf2+ sacrifice: 5/9 positions involve the bishop capturing on f7 or f2 with check, winning only a pawn while the opponent's king safely retreats. In all 5 of these cases, the sacrificing side had undeveloped pieces (queenside knight and bishop still on starting squares) making follow-up attacks impossible. The remaining 4 positions share the same underlying error—giving up a bishop's full value prematurely: Bxc6+ traded a fianchettoed bishop for a pawn (1/9), Bxd5 traded the only active defensive bishop for a knight in a worse position (1/9), Bc6 misplaced a bishop allowing it to be trapped (1/9), and Bc7 committed a bishop before the correct preparatory capture (1/9). In all 9 cases, the player had 1-3 good alternative moves focused on development or material recovery, and the average cp_loss was 291—approximately the value of the sacrificed piece minus the captured pawn.

1714.label: Playing a non-forcing central pawn advance when an immediate piece-based tactical action is urgently required.
1714.description: 8/10 positions feature a central pawn advance (c5, d4, c4, e4, d5, d4, e5, d6+), while the remaining 2 are slow piece moves (Rce2, Rf6). In the 8 clear mistakes (positions 1-8, avg cp_loss ~366 excluding the mate), the correct move was overwhelmingly a PIECE action: a capture of a hanging piece (positions 1, 2, 6), a knight fork/double attack (position 5), a rook penetration to the 7th rank (position 4), a rook lift initiating attack (position 8), a defensive king/piece relocation (position 7), or an aggressive pawn challenge of an enemy piece (position 3). In all 8 mistake cases, the player chose a 'positional' or 'preparatory' pawn advance that appeared logical on the surface but ignored a concrete, forcing tactical opportunity. The avg good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are narrow critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than general positional play. Position 9 (d6+ with discovered check, cp_loss 0) represents the rare case where a pawn advance IS the forcing tactical move, serving as a boundary case where the pawn push creates immediate threats rather than being slow.

1728.label: Black gives a rook check from a doubled-rook position but moves the rook that was performing a critical guarding or blocking function.
1728.description: 10/10 positions feature Black delivering a rook check while possessing two active rooks, typically dominating the second rank. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9), the specific error is choosing the WRONG rook to give check—the moved rook was controlling a critical escape square for the enemy king (g-file preventing Kg1, b-file preventing Kb1, or guarding the checking rook from capture). In 2/10 positions (4, 8), a rook check is played when a simpler pawn check accomplished the same goal in fewer moves. 2/10 positions (6, 10) are actually the best move with 0cp loss, representing correctly-executed versions of the same pattern. The consistent geometric feature is a rook sliding along a rank to deliver check (to f2, c2, e2, e4, h2, b2, f4), almost always toward or along the second rank. The average cp_loss of ~1985 is driven by positions 1 and 2 where forced mates were squandered.

1717.label: Moving a piece away from a critical blocking/shielding role on a line, immediately exposing a higher-value piece (usually the Queen) to capture or devastating attack.
1717.description: In 7/9 positions, the blundering piece was physically interposed on a critical line (file, rank, or diagonal) between an enemy attacker and a friendly high-value target. The move relocated this shield piece elsewhere, instantly exposing the target to capture. Specifically: Position 1 (cxd5 removed the c4 pawn blocking the a6-f1 diagonal, exposing the Queen on e2), Position 3 (Bf4 removed the bishop blocking the d-file between Rd1 and Qd8), Position 5 (Be6 removed the bishop blocking the f-file between Rf8 and Qf3), Position 8 (Nd5 removed the knight interposing on the g5-e7 diagonal between Bg5 and Qe7), and Position 9 (Bf4 removed the bishop blocking the h-file between Qh7 and Qh5). Position 2 (Bxa7) removed the sole defensive piece shielding the king from a mating attack. Position 4 (d4) broke the pawn chain supporting the e5 pawn, leaving it and others hanging. Position 6 (Be5) abandoned the d-file blocking role while simultaneously walking into a queen capture with check. Position 7 (Bxf5) moved the extra bishop from a safe square to one capturable by the opposing queen. In 8/9 cases the result was immediate loss of a Queen or equivalent catastrophe. The moves were typically motivated by material gain (capturing a pawn), piece 'improvement,' or centralization—failing to recognize the moved piece's invisible defensive function.

1733.label: A piece retreats passively to the player's first rank, wasting a critical tempo and allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical strike.
1733.description: 10/10 positions feature a piece moving backward to the player's back rank (1st or 8th rank): Queens retreat to g8, d8, d1 (5/10); Bishops retreat to d1, c1, d8 (3/10); Rooks move to e1, f8, c1 (2/10). In every case, the position demanded urgent action — defending against mating threats (5/10 allowed immediate or near-immediate checkmate), maintaining coverage of critical squares (3/10 abandoned defense of key pawns like e5 or f7), or generating counterplay. Instead, the player made a backward, 'safe-looking' move that squandered tempo. The average cp_loss of 3089 reflects that 4/10 positions resulted in forced checkmate. In 8/10 cases, king safety was the dominant motif exploited by the refutation. Only 2/10 positions had fewer than 2 good alternatives, meaning better moves were typically available and findable.

1732.label: A premature queen check (Qa4+/Qa5+/Qh4+/Qh5+) in the opening or early middlegame that is easily blocked while the opponent gains development tempo.
1732.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen delivering check from a wing square (a4, a5, h4, or h5) while the enemy king sits in the center during the opening or early middlegame. In every case, the check is trivially blocked — 6/10 by a developing piece move (typically ...Bd7 blocking Qa4+/Qa5+, or Bd2/Nc3 blocking ...Qa5+) and 4/10 by a simple pawn move (g6 blocking Qh5+, or g3 blocking ...Qh4+) that simultaneously attacks the queen and gains tempo. In 10/10 positions, the player had clearly superior alternatives: concrete tactical strikes (winning hanging pieces, capturing pawns, delivering meaningful checks with preparation), quiet developing moves, or positional consolidation. The average centipawn loss was 379, with 8/10 positions showing the opponent blocking the check while developing a piece or gaining space, forcing the queen to retreat having accomplished nothing. Both kings were in the center in 9/10 positions, creating the visual illusion that a check should be effective.

1736.label: A knight jumps to an aggressive-looking square that is directly captured by an unobstructed enemy bishop along its diagonal.
1736.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight leaps to a seemingly powerful square (central outpost, attacking post, or check/fork square) but lands completely undefended on a square directly controlled by an enemy bishop. In every single case, the refutation is simply Bx[square], capturing the knight for free with no possible recapture. The bishops capturing are varied: 3/10 involve a bishop on c8 or f7 taking on f5/d5, 2/10 involve Bf1 taking on d3, 2/10 involve Bc1 taking on e3, and the remaining involve long-diagonal bishops (b7→e4, g3→d6, b6→d4). In 3/10 cases the knight move delivers check, yet the bishop capture simultaneously blocks the check and wins the piece. The average cp_loss is 468, representing approximately a full piece lost in each case. The moves are split evenly between White (5) and Black (5), occurring in both middlegame (7/10) and opening (3/10) positions.

1724.label: Queen moves to a plausible-looking but incorrect square (often giving check) when only one precise queen destination was available.
1724.description: 8/9 positions involve queen moves where the player chose an attractive-looking destination square that turned out to be catastrophically wrong. 5/9 are checks (Qa8+, Qd2+, Qc2+, Qc1+, and the missed Qc4+ in position 9) that appear forcing but are counterproductive—the queen is captured on the new square (Qd2+ by Qxd2, Qc1+ by Qxc1), easily blocked (Qc2+ by f5), or stranded (Qa8+ leaving the queen passive). The remaining queen moves (Qf3, Qh5 twice) go to squares that look active/attacking but fail to address the position's critical need—whether defending a key pawn, capturing a hanging piece, or maintaining access to a crucial defensive square. The average good-moves count of 1.2 confirms these were positions demanding extreme precision with essentially ONE correct queen destination. The 1 non-queen example (Re1) shares the same logic: an 'active' centralizing move when only the king escape Ke8 addressed the actual mating threat.

1715.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a position with extreme tactical urgency where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
1715.description: 10/10 positions share the tag 'tempo_loss' and feature positions where the average number of good moves is just 1.4, meaning extreme precision is required. In 9/10 positions (excluding position 7 where cp_loss=0), the player chose a non-urgent action—typically a slow pawn push (a3, a4, a4 in 3/10), a passive piece repositioning (Rb8, Rb7, Kb3 in 3/10), or a materially-tempting but positionally ruinous capture (Rxd7+, Qe5, Qxc5 in 3/10)—when the position demanded one specific forcing move. In 6/10 cases the best move was a capture or check (Rxa1, Bb4+, Rxf3, dxe3, h5-defensive-necessity, Rf2-active). The average cp_loss of 1191 reflects catastrophic consequences. The positions share the characteristic that both sides have competing urgent threats, and the tempo wasted hands the initiative completely to the opponent: in positions 4, 5, and 9, the player pushed the a-pawn while a winning/saving tactic existed; in positions 1 and 6, the player moved a rook passively when an exchange or active counterattack was essential; in positions 2, 3, and 10, the player made an attractive-looking move that abandoned a critical defensive or positional function.
1715.old_chip: Critical tempo waste in urgent positions

1730.label: Pawn captures resolving structural tension in simplified endgame positions, particularly king-and-pawn endings.
1730.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture that resolves pawn tension in a simplified endgame (9/10 endgame, 1/10 late middlegame). 10/10 moves are pxp captures on an adjacent file. The positions overwhelmingly involve pure pawn endgames or near-pure endgames (9/10 are king-and-pawn or king+minor piece+pawns). In all cases, the capture resolves a critical structural tension point where two pawns are mutually attacking each other. Notably, 4/10 positions show 0 cp_loss (the capture was actually best), while 2/10 show catastrophic errors (426 and 293 cp loss), with the remaining 4 being marginal inaccuracies (9-36 cp). The feature fires on the structural decision moment itself rather than purely on mistakes. When the captures ARE errors (positions 4, 6, 7, 8), the common thread is that maintaining tension, using a different move order, or making a non-capturing pawn advance was superior because the capture gave the opponent a passed pawn or surrendered a blockade.

1726.label: A rook (or major piece) is moved to a seemingly active square on an open file or rank, ignoring an urgent tactical opportunity or creating a new vulnerability.
1726.description: 8/9 positions involve rook moves (Rh7, Rd6, Rc7, Rc7, Rc8, Rd2, Rad8, Re8) and 1/9 a queen move (Qg2), all placing major pieces on 'natural-looking' squares along open files or ranks. In every case, the move appears positionally motivated—contesting a file, occupying the 7th rank, developing a rook—but critically misses an urgent tactical demand. In 4/9 positions, the piece lands on a square where it becomes directly vulnerable (trapped by Bg8, captured by knight on b5, skewered via Rd8+, targeted by discovered attack). In 4/9 positions, the move wastes a critical tempo when an immediate tactical shot was available (Nxd3+, Nh5 attacking queen, O-O-O, f6 prophylaxis). In 1/9, the queen abandons a defensive post enabling a mating attack. The average cp_loss of 1369 and average of only 1.8 good moves confirms these are critical-precision moments where 'autopilot' piece development is punished severely. The moves share the quality of being exactly what a player would choose if thinking purely about piece activity principles rather than calculating concrete variations.

1738.label: A natural-looking d/e pawn advance in the opening that ignores an immediate free capture or critical tactical obligation.
1738.description: All 10 positions feature a central pawn advance (d or e pawn) during the opening with both kings still in center. In 7/10 positions, the best move was a simple capture of hanging material (Qxg5, cxd5, Nxd1, dxe4, dxc6, Kxf7, exd5) that was ignored in favor of pushing a center pawn. In 2/10 positions (8, 10), the pawn push itself created a new hanging target or exposed the king to a devastating check sequence. In 1/10 (position 3), the pawn push missed a tactical fork sequence (Qe7/Nxd4). The average cp_loss of 284 reflects that these are major blunders — typically worth a full piece or more in missed opportunity. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow critical moments demanding concrete calculation rather than general principles. The consistent thread is a player prioritizing abstract center-building over immediate tactical reality.

1731.label: A knight voluntarily leaves a powerful outpost or functionally critical square for a superficially attractive but inferior destination, allowing tactical punishment.
1731.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving away from a square where it performed a crucial function — either maintaining a dominant outpost, defending a key weakness, or enabling a winning tactic. In 7/10 cases, the knight departed from a strong central square (e5, e4, d5, c5, c4, or f3). The destination squares often appeared aggressive (threatening pieces, centralizing, or attacking pawns) but were tactically inferior: 4/10 moved to squares where the knight became immediately vulnerable (undefended, forkable, or trappable), while 6/10 simply abandoned a function that was irreplaceable. The departing square's critical role varied: in 4/10 positions the knight was preventing a specific tactic (Qxg7, Bxf2+, Qe3+, e-file check); in 3/10 it had a winning tactic available from its current square (Nxc7+ fork, Nd6+ fork, Nf3+ threat); and in 3/10 it occupied a dominant positional outpost that controlled the game. The average centipawn loss of 1232 reflects how catastrophic these voluntary relocations were.

1739.label: Capturing a centralized enemy piece (usually a knight) with the wrong piece, allowing a pawn recapture that forks or attacks multiple remaining pieces.
1739.description: In 9/9 positions, the player captured a well-placed enemy piece on a central square (e4, e5, or d5), and the opponent's pawn recapture created a devastating fork or dominant advanced pawn attacking multiple pieces. In 7/9 cases, the blunder was specifically a knight capture (Nxe5 or Nxd5) where capturing with the bishop instead would have eliminated the fork target — the bishop trades itself off the critical diagonal, so the advancing pawn only attacks one piece, not two. In positions 1, 3, 8, 9, and 10, the pattern is identical: Nc6xe5 leaves the Bd6 and Nf6 both vulnerable to dxe5. In position 2, Nf6xd5 leaves Be6 and Nc6 vulnerable to cxd5. In positions 5-7, capturing on e4 (with bishop or wrong knight) allows fxe4 or dxe4 to create a powerful central pawn attacking additional pieces. The correct alternative in 7/9 positions was to capture with a different piece (usually bishop for knight), and in 2/9 it was to avoid the exchange entirely.

1734.label: Pawn-takes-pawn captures that prioritize material gain or superficial forcing moves over addressing the critical strategic or tactical demand of the position.
1734.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing a pawn (pxp) as the blunder, and in every case, the better moves involved piece play (capturing dangerous enemy pieces, repositioning pieces, or addressing urgent threats). 4/10 of the captures come with check (positions 2, 7, 8, 10), making them appear especially 'forcing' but actually helping the opponent by improving their piece placement or eliminating the capturer's own strategic asset. In 8/10 positions, the pawn capture released critical tension that was restraining the opponent or maintaining the player's own attacking potential (e.g., the f4-pawn in position 10, the b6 cramping pawn in position 4, the e6 passed pawn in position 8). In 6/10 cases, the correct move was capturing or eliminating a powerful enemy piece (rook on d8, bishop on d4, knight on d6, bishop on f6) rather than grabbing a pawn. The average cp_loss of 299 reflects how costly these 'autopilot' captures are when the position demands precise piece coordination.

1737.label: A committal pawn advance played when patient piece improvement or tactical piece play was the correct approach.
1737.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn advances (g6, f4, b6, a5, d4, f4, d5, h5, d4, b6) that attempt to create immediate threats or structural changes, but are premature because the player's pieces aren't properly coordinated to follow through. In 9/10 positions, the best available moves were piece moves (queen repositioning, development, rook activation, or concrete tactical strikes like Nxe5). The refutations consistently exploit structural weaknesses created by the advance: in 4/10 cases the opponent pushes a pawn through the abandoned square (e.g., ...e4 after f4 removed the f3 guardian), in 3/10 cases the advanced pawn becomes a static liability that can be neutralized (e.g., ...a6 trapping the b6 pawn), and in 3/10 cases the advance opens lines that favor the opponent. The average cp_loss of 226 reflects how these superficially aggressive moves backfire catastrophically when properly punished. The positions span all phases and both flanks, but the error type is remarkably consistent: choosing an irreversible pawn commitment over flexible piece play.
1737.old_chip: Premature pawn break before pieces ready

1735.label: Pawn captures that resolve mutual pawn tension in endgames, often removing a structural blockade and facilitating passed pawns.
1735.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames featuring pawn-takes-pawn captures that resolve direct pawn tension (where two pawns attack each other on adjacent files). 9/10 involve kingside or central pawns (f/g files predominantly: gxf4 appears 4 times, fxe5 twice, fxg4 twice, gxh5 and gxf5 once each). The captures occur on the 4th or 5th rank where pawns typically clash. Critically, 7/10 of these moves were actually the best or near-best available option (cp_loss under 50), meaning the feature detects the structural moment of tension resolution rather than purely the mistake itself. In 8/10 positions, the resulting position involves passed pawn dynamics — the capture either creates a passed pawn for the opponent, removes a blockading pawn, or captures with the 'wrong' pawn leaving structural targets. 8/10 are pure or near-pure pawn endgames. The avg good moves available (1.6) confirms these positions offer very limited alternatives, typically forced or nearly-forced structural decisions.

1729.label: A rook is repositioned to a seemingly natural square (open file, back rank, 7th rank) for general improvement, missing a critical forcing move the position demands.
1729.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-capturing rook moves to 'natural' squares — retreats to the back rank (Rd8 twice, Re1), moves to the 2nd rank (Rc2, R4d2), or advances to the 7th/8th rank (Re7, Rf8, Rf3). In 5/10 cases, the best move was not a rook move at all (f4 pawn break, h4 pawn push, Qf4 queen defense, Bg7+ bishop check, Bf5 bishop block), while in 3/10 the best rook move was a CAPTURE (Rxb2 taking a queen, Rxd5 taking a bishop, Re6 a rook sacrifice). Only 2/10 required a different quiet rook move (Rf2, Ref1 for defense). The average cp_loss is enormous (3982), with 6/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate or near-mate after the error. Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise calculation rather than positional maneuvering. The player consistently defaults to 'good rook placement' based on general principles rather than addressing the position's concrete tactical requirements.

1741.label: A rook is moved to the 7th rank (from the moving side's perspective) seeking generic activity, while ignoring a more urgent tactical or defensive requirement.
1741.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook moving to the 7th rank from the player's perspective (Rg7, Rc7, Rd7, Rf7, Re7 for White; Re2, Rb2, Rc2 for Black), with 1/10 (Re6) being a closely related aggressive rook incursion to the 6th rank. In every case, the rook move looks strategically attractive—invading the opponent's position, attacking pawns on the 7th, pressuring the opposing king—but fatally ignores a concrete tactical demand. In 6/10 positions, the rook abandons a critical defensive duty (back-rank coverage in positions 6, 7, 10; blocking a check path in position 3; guarding a key pawn in positions 4, 9). In 4/10 positions, a forcing tactical shot (mate-in-3, capture with check, winning fork prevention) was available instead. The average cp_loss of ~4939 is enormous, with 5/10 positions involving missed or allowed forced checkmates. Only 1.9 good moves were available on average, indicating these are positions requiring precision rather than general principles.

1747.label: The king captures a seemingly free or threatening piece/pawn, stepping from a sheltered square onto an exposed one where it becomes vulnerable to immediate tactical punishment via checks, skewers, or mating attacks.
1747.description: 10/10 positions feature a king capture (Kx...) where the king leaves a relatively safe square to take material that appears dangerous or free. In every case, the captured piece/pawn was effectively bait—whether a knight (positions 2, 4, 9), bishop (5, 8), or pawn (1, 3, 6, 7, 10)—and the king's new square is immediately exploitable by forcing moves. 10/10 positions result in the opponent delivering check within one move of the capture. The punishments include diagonal checks (7/10: Bd4+, Bf8+, Qe7+, Qd7+, Qh3+, etc.), discovered attacks (2/10), and skewers (1/10). 5/10 positions resulted in mate or near-mate (avg cp_loss 3045). In 9/10 positions, superior alternatives existed that either ignored the capturable piece, used a different piece to take it, or addressed the threat indirectly while keeping the king sheltered. Only 1/10 was an endgame; 9/10 occurred in the middlegame where piece density made exposure more dangerous.

1742.label: A rook moves to a seemingly active square on an open file or rank, but the placement creates a concrete tactical vulnerability that the opponent can exploit.
1742.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to a square that appears useful for centralization, file control, or doubling, but actually creates or exposes a tactical weakness. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 8, 10, and partially 4), the rook itself becomes a direct target on its new square—attacked with tempo by a minor piece, pawn advance, or queen. In 3/10 positions (2, 6, 9), the rook's new placement creates an indirect tactical vulnerability: it either blocks a critical retreat square for another piece (Position 9: Rd7 blocks the knight's d7 retreat), leaves another piece undefended by moving away (Position 4: Ra6 abandons the a5 pawn), or creates a geometric pattern enabling a fork (Position 6: Re6 means Rxe4 allows Nxd6+ fork). In 2/10 positions (5, 7), the rook move is simply passive relative to a crushing tactical opportunity that was available instead. The better alternatives in nearly all cases were quiet prophylactic moves—retreating bishops (Positions 2, 6), moving kings (Position 7), advancing pawns (Position 1), or capturing with minor pieces (Positions 3, 5, 10)—rather than 'activating' the rook. The average cp_loss of 365 confirms these are serious errors, and the fact that only 2.1 good moves were available on average shows these were often critical moments requiring precision rather than general improvement.

1725.label: Playing natural-looking, non-forcing moves in sharp positions where one specific forcing continuation (check, sacrifice, or precise move order) was required.
1725.description: 10/10 positions featured narrow tactical situations with an average of only 1.6 good moves available, yet the player chose a 'routine' or 'autopilot' move instead of the critical forcing resource. In 5/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 8, 10), the best move involved a check or capture with check (Bxh7+, Qh5+, Bxe6+, Nxd3+, Be6 blocking check) that the player completely missed. In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 4, 5), a knight was moved to a 'standard' or 'natural' square (Nf1, Nf3, Nd3, Nf3) or a piece captured an obvious target (Bxd6), reflecting general-principle thinking rather than concrete calculation. 8/10 positions featured exposed or uncastled kings creating tactical urgency. The played moves consistently look reasonable at the level of general principles — developing pieces, capturing annoying pawns, centralizing kings — but ignore that the position demands one specific, often counter-intuitive forcing sequence. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2155 reflects how these seemingly sensible moves collide with the razor-sharp tactical demands of the actual position.

1740.label: Making a natural-looking developing, castling, or space-gaining move while completely overlooking that a piece or pawn is immediately capturable.
1740.description: All 10 positions share the pattern of a player executing a 'textbook' move — developing a piece, castling, or advancing a pawn for space — while ignoring the most immediate tactical reality: material is or will be en prise. In 4/10 positions (Bc4 x3, Bf4), a bishop is developed directly onto a square controlled by an opponent's center pawn, resulting in instant capture. In 2/10 positions (O-O x2), castling removes the king as the sole defender of a piece (Bd7 in one case, Nd2 in the other), leaving it hanging. In 2/10 positions (c5, c4), a flank pawn move ignores that the player's own central pawn is undefended. In 1/10 (d5), a space-gaining push bypasses a free capture of a hanging pawn. In 1/10 (g4), an attacking pawn push ignores king safety, enabling forced mate. All occur in the opening (8/10) or early middlegame (2/10) with kings predominantly in the center (9/10 have at least one uncastled king). The average cp_loss is 1385 with only 1.7 good moves available on average, indicating these are positions requiring concrete calculation rather than autopilot play.

1752.label: A bishop develops passively to the player's second rank (d7/e7/e2) when the position demands immediate concrete action — a tactical capture, forcing move, or urgent king safety measure.
1752.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to the player's own second rank: Bd7 (4 positions), Be7 (3 positions), or Be2 (3 positions). In every case, the move is a quiet, 'natural-looking' developing move that prioritizes routine development over an urgent tactical or strategic demand. In 7/10 positions, a concrete tactic was missed (forks in positions 1 and 8, hanging pieces in position 2, pawn captures in positions 3, 5, 7, and 10). In 6/10 positions, the king remained in the center with open files creating immediate danger. The average centipawn loss of 234 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but critical-moment failures where only 1-3 good moves existed. The consistent error is that these second-rank bishop moves address superficial concerns (breaking pins, connecting rooks, preparing castling) while ignoring the position's actual demands: winning material, resolving central tension favorably, or escaping open-file danger immediately.

1754.label: Moving a rook to an active-looking square when the position urgently demanded a king move for safety.
1754.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a rook instead of the king, and in 9/10 positions the best move was explicitly a king move (Ke6, Ke7, Kf7, Kf2, Kh8, Kg8, Kf5, etc.). The remaining position (Position 5) was already a forced mate where king moves were the best alternatives. In 8/10 positions the king was described as 'exposed' or lacking pawn shelter, creating urgent evacuation needs. The rook moves appeared natural—defending key squares (Rf7 defending f7), activating along open files (Rd6, Rd7, Rc7), or seeking counterplay (Rg7, Re7)—but in every case the priority was king relocation rather than piece activity. The average centipawn loss of 2974 reflects that 5/10 positions converted from survivable disadvantages into forced checkmate after the rook move. The rooks typically landed on squares where they became targets (open file attacks in 4/10), blocked the king's own escape routes (2/10), or vacated critical defensive squares (3/10).

1746.label: A materialistic pawn capture that either removes a critical defensive barrier or wastes a vital tempo while a far more urgent tactical need exists.
1746.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture (xNotation) in the middlegame that prioritizes small material gain over a critical tactical or defensive need. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9), the capturing pawn was itself serving a vital defensive function—blocking a file, shielding the king, or protecting a piece—and by moving it to capture, the player opened a devastating line for the opponent (back-rank mates in positions 1 and 10, king exposure via diagonals in 8 and 9, hanging pieces in 4 and 5, exposed rook in 2). In 4/10 positions (3, 6, 7, 10), the pawn capture simply wasted a critical tempo when a far more forcing or defensive move was required—missing a hanging queen (position 3), a forced mate (position 7), or allowing back-rank infiltration (position 10). The average centipawn loss of 4041 reflects the catastrophic nature of these captures, and the average of only 1.9 good alternatives shows these were high-stakes moments demanding precision rather than greed.

1750.label: A quiet one-square flank pawn advance played in a position demanding immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
1750.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance on a flank file (g-file: 5/10, f-file: 2/10, b-file: 2/10, h-file: 1/10) played during the middlegame when the position urgently demands piece activity, addressing tactical threats, or evacuating the king. In every case, the best moves involve concrete piece actions — rook lifts, queen repositioning, castling, or forcing captures — yet the player chose a slow, non-forcing pawn nudge instead. The average cp_loss of 1136 (inflated by one checkmate) reflects how catastrophic tempo loss is in these critical moments. In 7/10 positions, the pawn advance also directly weakened the player's own structure or removed a critical defensive function, compounding the tempo problem with a positional concession. The positions share a common urgency: 6/10 had exposed or uncastled kings, 8/10 featured active enemy pieces creating immediate tactical threats, and the average number of good moves was only 2.5, indicating narrow positions with little margin for passive play.

1743.label: Playing a routine, non-forcing developing move when the position demands an urgent concrete tactical action.
1743.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-forcing moves (9/10 minor piece development, 1/10 a pawn push) played in positions with extreme tactical sharpness where only 1-2 good moves existed. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 7), the developing move removed a piece from a critical blocking/defensive role on a rank or file, directly exposing hanging material or back-rank weaknesses. In 3/10 cases (positions 9, 10, and partially 2), the player missed an available capture of undefended material (Qxa1+, Bxf1, Qxa8). In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 8), the move wasted the last available tempo before forced mate by developing instead of addressing the immediate mating threat. All 10 blunders share the characteristic that the best move was a concrete, forcing action (a capture, a pawn block, a queen trade, or moving the king), while the played move prioritized abstract piece improvement over the position's urgent tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 2162 reflects that these are catastrophic errors occurring at critical decision points.

1749.label: A rook or queen is repositioned to a seemingly logical square, abandoning the file or diagonal where it was directly attacking an undefended or vulnerable target that should be captured immediately.
1749.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet major piece repositioning move (8 rook moves, 2 queen moves) that abandons a concrete tactical opportunity. In 8/10 cases, the correct move was a direct capture of undefended material (Rxd3, Qxc5+, fxe5/Rxe5, Rxc5, Rf7, Rxf1+, Rxe6, Rxb6, Rxg2), while in 2/10 cases it was an aggressive invasion (Rc2/Re2, Rxf1+ deflection). The blunder moves all share a geometric signature: the major piece leaves the file or rank where it has a concrete attacking function and moves to a different file that appears reasonable (centralizing, defending a pawn, pressuring a different target) but is tactically hollow. In 6/10 positions, the missed opportunity was capturing a completely undefended piece or pawn (positions 1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 476 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — typically converting a winning or equal position into a losing one. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these are narrow critical moments where the obvious capture/invasion is the ONLY correct action.

1748.label: A pawn capture that removes a defensive barrier pawn, opening a file or diagonal that the opponent's pre-positioned pieces immediately exploit against the player's king.
1748.description: All 10 positions feature a pawn capture that removes a pawn serving as a critical barrier/shield, opening a line directly toward the capturing player's own king. 7/10 positions involve removing an h-pawn or f-pawn from the king's flank (positions 1-3, 5-8), directly opening the h-file or a king-facing diagonal for the opponent's already-active heavy pieces. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 7, 8), the opponent had rooks already stationed on or aimed at the h-file, making the opened line immediately lethal. Positions 5-6 (fxe5) remove the f-pawn to open the h4-e1 diagonal for Qh4+. Position 9 (axb5) opens the a-file toward White's own queenside-castled king in an opposite-side castling attack. Position 4 (cxb4) removes a structural barrier allowing passed pawn creation. Position 10 (dxe4) opens a diagonal enabling a piece-winning tactic. In all 10 cases, the best alternatives involved either keeping the barrier intact (advancing the pawn instead of capturing: 3/10), developing/repositioning pieces first (6/10), or attacking on a different flank entirely (1/10). The average cp_loss of 285 reflects that these captures consistently transform defensible positions into ones with unstoppable attacks.

1745.label: A non-forcing piece repositioning or exchange that ignores the position's most critical tactical demand, squandering advantage or creating vulnerability.
1745.description: All 10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, no threats) when the position demanded concrete action. 6/10 are bishop repositioning moves (Ba4, Ba5, Be6, Ba4, Bf6, Bg5) to seemingly logical squares, while 4/10 are rook exchanges/moves (Rxb1, Rxf1, Rxd1, Ree8). In every case, the moved piece was either performing a critical latent function where it stood (4/10 — restraining an enemy piece or controlling a key square), or the exchange was made without first addressing an urgent tactical priority (3/10 — hanging pieces or promotion threats requiring move-order precision), or the piece moved to a square creating a new tactical vulnerability (3/10 — becoming a target or leaving something undefended). The average cp_loss of 415 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but position-destroying errors. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, suggesting these arise in sharp positions where one precise response exists but the player defaulted to a 'natural-looking' quiet move instead.

1751.label: Passive pawn advances in endgames that waste critical tempo when urgent king activation or piece play is required.
1751.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where the mistake is a pawn push instead of active play. In 6/10 positions (b5 vs Kb5, g6 vs Kg6, h3 vs Kh3, c6 vs Kc6, f3 vs Kf3, f3 vs Kf3), the pawn literally occupies the exact square where the king should move, blocking its own king's optimal path. In the remaining 4/10 (h4, g4, g3, c5), the pawn push creates a fixed weakness or wastes the decisive tempo when immediate action was needed. The best moves in all cases prioritize king centralization (8/10 have a king move as the top or second-best choice) or urgent piece activity. The average cp_loss is extremely high (2839), reflecting how devastating tempo loss is in endgames where every move counts. Punishments are typically easy to find (multiple refutations in 7/10 positions), as the pawn moves create concrete targets or simply hand the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan.

1758.label: Jumping a minor piece to a visually aggressive forward square that is easily challenged by pawns or abandons a more critical function.
1758.description: 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (8 knights, 2 bishops) leaping to an advanced square (typically 4th-7th rank) that appears threatening but lacks concrete justification. In 7/10 cases, the piece lands on a square immediately vulnerable to a simple pawn advance (g4 hitting Nf5, h3 hitting Ng4, e5 hitting Bc5/Nf6, g6 hitting Nf5), granting the opponent free tempo while expanding their position. In 3/10 cases (Ne5 from f3, Nf7 from d6, Ng5 from e6), the piece actively abandons a dominant or defensive outpost for a speculative attack, removing a piece from where it was doing critical work. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions. The average cp_loss of 226 reflects how severely these moves are punished—the opponent either chases the piece back while improving their position or exploits the vacancy left behind. In all cases, better alternatives existed involving concrete threats, consolidation, development, or positional play rather than superficial aggression.

1761.label: Giving a rook check without a concrete follow-up, wasting a critical tempo while often improving the opponent's king position.
1761.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check to an exposed king, and in 9/10 cases this occurs in the endgame. The tactical motif identified in every single analysis is 'tempo_loss,' with 7/10 positions explicitly tagged as 'pointless_check' or 'aimless_check.' In 8/10 positions, the opponent's king actually improves its placement after the check — moving to a more centralized, active, or safer square (e.g., Kf4 in Position 7, Ke7 in Position 10, Kc3 in Position 3, Kg7 in Position 5). The average centipawn loss is 174, with only 1.7 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical moments where precision matters. In 9/10 positions, the correct move was a quiet constructive move — advancing a passed pawn (Positions 1, 3, 5, 8), improving the king (Positions 6, 7, 8), repositioning a piece (Positions 4, 9), or capturing material (Position 10) — rather than giving check. The rook check frequently also displaces the rook itself from an ideal square: leaving the 7th rank (Position 10), abandoning the e5 outpost (Position 6), or moving away from where it pressured key pawns (Positions 5, 9).

1759.label: A bishop is moved away from a square where it was performing an essential defensive or blocking function, leaving a rook (or back rank) fatally exposed on the vacated file or rank.
1759.description: In 9/9 positions, a bishop is relocated from a square where it served a crucial but non-obvious protective role. In 5/9 cases (positions 5, 8, 10, 4, 9), the bishop was physically blocking an open file — shielding a friendly rook from an enemy rook's attack — and moving it immediately allowed the opponent to capture the now-undefended rook or deliver a back-rank mate along that file. In 2/9 cases (positions 1, 3), the bishop was moved to a square where it became vulnerable to a skewer or decoy along a rank, allowing a forcing sequence that won the piece or delivered checkmate. In 2/9 cases (positions 2, 6), the bishop move was a slow repositioning that squandered critical tempo when the position demanded immediate dynamic action. The average cp_loss of 2414 reflects that these are catastrophic errors — the bishop often appeared to move to a 'better' square (capturing a pawn in 2/9, centralizing in 3/9, developing in 2/9), but its hidden defensive function was far more important than its apparent activity gain.

1744.label: Moves that damage the player's own piece coordination or pawn structure by removing a critical defensive resource while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical demand.
1744.description: 9/10 positions feature a move that actively worsens the player's own position by removing or blocking a critical resource: cxd4 removes pawn support allowing a discovery, f5 ignores an overloaded defender, Na3 (twice) either vacates a critical blocking square or places a piece as a capture-with-check target, d5 (twice) closes the center eliminating counterplay or missing a winning tactic, b4 creates a target while ignoring development, f4 removes the f-pawn's support of e5, Nge7 blocks the bishop's only retreat square, and Rhg1 blocks the king's escape square. 8/10 positions have king safety as the primary concern being ignored. 6/10 moves are pawn pushes or captures, suggesting a tendency toward structural changes that feel 'improving' but actually undermine coordination. The average cp_loss of 1169 and average of only 2.0 good moves available indicate positions demanding precise attention where the critical need was ignored in favor of a secondary plan.

1757.label: A pawn advance or capture that removes the pawn from a critical guarding or coordination role, leaving a piece hanging, trapped, or a position collapsing.
1757.description: All 9 positions feature pawn moves that abandon a defensive function the pawn was performing. In 4/9 positions (h4, cxb3, g5+, b4), the pawn was directly protecting a piece — the rook on g4, bishop on d3, bishop on f5, or knight on c3 — and moving it left that piece immediately capturable. In 3/9 positions (e2, g2, h2), a passed pawn was pushed prematurely toward promotion when its greater value was as a static threat restraining enemy pieces; the push either enabled the opponent to capture a supporting piece or rendered the promotion meaningless through immediate recapture. In 1/9 (c7), the pawn advance blocked its own rook's escape route, trapping it. In 1/9 (c5), the pawn advance was played without first addressing a tactical vulnerability it enabled (Qxd5+). The average cp_loss of 1625 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — every single case involves losing at least a piece worth of material or equivalent positional value.

1753.label: A rook is repositioned from a strong or penetrating square to a seemingly active but actually inferior square, sacrificing its key tactical or strategic function.
1753.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves where the piece is relocated from (or fails to reach) its optimal square. In 6/10 positions (R2e5, Rac2, R7d5, R3d5, R2a5, Rf4), the rook explicitly leaves a powerful post—most commonly the 2nd/7th rank or a square providing essential defensive coverage. In 3/10 positions (Rb2, Ra2, Re8), the rook moves to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable (hanging or capturable). In 1/10 (Rc7), the rook reaches the 7th rank but misses a far more forcing alternative (Rc8+). The consistent thread is that the player makes a 'positional-looking' rook maneuver—doubling, infiltrating, centralizing, or reorganizing—that ignores the concrete tactical reality: the rook was already doing critical work on its current square, or a forcing alternative existed. The new square invariably gives the opponent a tempo to exploit via captures, checks, mating threats, or consolidation. 8/10 positions involved doubled rooks or two active rooks, suggesting the error stems from the false sense that with two rooks, one can be 'improved' without cost.

1766.label: A quiet, non-forcing queen repositioning move is played when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical action, typically with a different piece.
1766.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet queen move (no check, no capture) to a central or 'improving' square, while a forcing tactical blow was available. In 8/10 positions, the best move was with a completely different piece (pawn break exf3, bishop sacrifice Bxe6+, pawn breakthrough g6, tempo-gaining h4, knight fork Ng5+, developing Bd7, aggressive Bg5, rook attack Ra8), while in 2/10 the best move was the queen to a more aggressive square (Qf4, Qd4). The average cp_loss of 266 reflects that these positions contained fleeting tactical opportunities that demanded immediate exploitation. 9/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the core motif—the quiet queen move grants the opponent a critical free tempo to escape danger, consolidate, or launch counterplay. 9/10 had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these were sharp positions with narrow paths to maintain the advantage. The queen destinations (e6, d3, d4, b2, e4, f3, d4, e2, c7, e2) all appear to be reasonable positional squares, making this a pattern of choosing plausible-looking positional improvement over necessary tactical precision.

1755.label: Playing non-forcing piece improvement moves in positions where one or both kings are exposed, missing more concrete or forcing continuations.
1755.description: 9/10 positions explicitly feature at least one king with a weak pawn shield or fully exposed (active in the open without pawn cover). The moves consistently involve quiet piece repositioning — king advances (5/10: Ke5, Kd5, Kg4, Kg3, implied king walks), knight centralizations (4/10: Nd4+, Nc3, Nxe4, Nd3), and one bishop retreat (Bb3) — in positions where the exposed kings create tactical urgency. When these moves are actual blunders (positions 3, 4, 8, 10 with avg ~6900 cp loss), the error is consistently ignoring forcing moves that exploit king exposure (checks, captures with tempo, passed pawn advances). When the moves are correct (positions 2, 5, 9 with 0 cp loss), the positions are technically won endgames where quiet improvement happens to be optimal. The feature fires on the combination of exposed-king positions + piece-improving moves regardless of whether the move is objectively correct, suggesting it detects the positional pattern of 'active/exposed kings with non-forcing continuation' rather than strictly detecting errors.

1756.label: Playing passive prophylactic or peripheral moves when the position demands an immediate concrete central strike or forcing continuation.
1756.description: 7/10 positions feature the player making a slow, non-forcing move (typically a flank pawn push or preparatory move) when the position urgently required a specific concrete action — usually a central pawn break or forcing sequence. In positions 1 and 3, the player chose a6 (prophylactic queenside pawn move) when e4 was a powerful central thrust with tempo. In position 5, h6 was played prophylactically instead of the dynamic c5 central counterattack. In position 10, d6 was a slow preparatory move when c5 immediately blocked a critical diagonal. In position 4, a4 wasted the one tempo needed for h4 in a pawn endgame. In position 9, h4 was a slow pawn advance when only perpetual check (Qe6+) saved the game. The captures (positions 2 and 7) share the same underlying issue: addressing a secondary concern (eliminating a piece, grabbing material) instead of the truly urgent priority. Position 8 is an outlier with 0 cp_loss. The average good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are narrow positions where the one correct continuation was time-sensitive and the tempo loss proved decisive.

1765.label: A quiet rook repositioning to a seemingly defensive square fatally abandons a critical protective function, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
1765.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook making a non-capturing, non-checking move to what appears to be a useful defensive square, but in doing so the rook vacates a square where it was performing an irreplaceable defensive task. In 6/10 cases the rook was guarding against king-safety threats (back-rank mates, checkmates on specific squares, or shielding from checks along ranks/files). In 4/10 cases the rook blocked a critical escape route or created a new tactical vulnerability (pin, fork) on its destination square. The punishment is severe (avg 2034cp loss) because the abandoned function is immediately and concretely exploitable: 3/10 positions result in forced checkmate, 4/10 allow winning tactical combinations, and 3/10 create decisive positional collapses. Notably, 7/10 positions had very few good alternatives (1-3 moves), suggesting these are critical moments where the rook's current placement was load-bearing and nearly any repositioning is fatal.

1764.label: Non-forcing moves (usually pawn pushes) played in positions demanding immediate tactical action, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss.
1764.description: All 10 positions share a strikingly consistent pattern: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move — typically a pawn push — in a position where urgent tactical demands exist. 6/10 moves are pure pawn advances (c5, a4, a3, g6, h5, c4) that gain no immediate contact with the opponent's pieces, while the remaining 4 (Qf7, Kd8, Rf4, Na6) are similarly non-forcing piece relocations that ignore the critical tactical requirement. In every case, the position demanded either: winning material through an available tactic (3/10: Be3 trapping a queen, Bxd4 winning a knight, Qe2/Re1 recovering a piece), preventing an immediate lethal threat (2/10: stopping checkmate, addressing kingside breakthrough), or fixing a critical structural/coordination problem (3/10: capturing c4 to connect rooks, playing b5 before the king move, centralizing the knight). The average cp_loss of 1342 — with positions swinging from winning to losing or from equal to hopeless — confirms these as catastrophic priority failures. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow tactical moments requiring precision, yet the players chose the one category of move that was categorically wrong: doing nothing urgent.

1770.label: Trading the sole remaining minor piece for a dangerous passed pawn in the endgame, allowing the opponent to recapture with the king.
1770.description: 10/10 positions are endgames where the player uses their only remaining minor piece (bishop or knight) to capture an advanced or passed pawn, after which the opponent recaptures with the king. The targets are consistently dangerous pawns: promotion-threatening pawns on a2, a3, a7, b3, d5, d7, f5, g6, h3, h6. In every case the refutation is the obvious king recapture (Kxa3, Kxf5, Kxh6, Kxh3, Kxg6, Kxa2, Kxa7, Kxb3, Kxd5, Kxd7). In 6/10 positions this was a meaningful mistake (cp_loss ≥36), while 4/10 positions show the capture as the best or near-best move (cp_loss ≤1). When wrong, the better alternatives consistently involved keeping the piece alive for blockading, counterplay, or fortress defense (e.g., Ke5 to blockade, Ke6 to create counterplay, or repositioning the bishop to a defensive diagonal). The feature identifies this specific endgame decision point regardless of whether the trade is correct.

1767.label: A slow, non-forcing pawn advance played in a position that demanded immediate piece activity or tactical action.
1767.description: All 10/10 positions feature the same fundamental error: the player chose a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking pawn advance when the position urgently required piece moves or tactical shots. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a piece move (Qc2, Kf2, Bd6, Qe4+, Rd1+, Qc7, Rd8, Kg6) while the player pushed a pawn instead. The pawn moves are predominantly flank advances (8/10 on the a, b, g, or h files: a4, a5, a3, g6, b4, h4, b6, plus c3), with only e5 and c6 being more central. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 analyses, confirming these moves squander critical time. The average cp_loss of 1195 is catastrophic — far beyond normal inaccuracies — because these positions typically had only ~2 good moves available, meaning they were critical decision points where the player defaulted to a slow structural idea. In 6/10 cases, the pawn push also damaged the player's own pawn structure (breaking connected pawns, creating weaknesses, or fixing targets), compounding the tempo loss with a permanent structural concession.

1760.label: Aggressive-looking bishop or knight moves that prioritize superficial activity or attacking intent over concrete tactical reality, allowing the opponent a forcing refutation.
1760.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (bishop or knight) making a move that appears strong—occupying an outpost, capturing a pawn, delivering a check, or launching an attack—but is concretely refuted. 6/10 are bishop moves (Be6, Bf4, Bxc6+, Bxg6, Bxh6, Bxh3) and 4/10 are knight moves (Nd5, Ng5, Ne5, Ne5). In 4/10 cases, the piece captures a pawn for inadequate compensation (Bxc6+, Bxg6, Bxh6, Bxh3). In 4/10 cases, a knight jumps to an impressive-looking square where it can be captured or its departure creates a tactical vulnerability (Nd5 allows Bxd2+, Ng5 hangs to Nxg5, both Ne5 moves abandon d4/f3 defense). In 7/10 positions, the moving side's king is still in the center, meaning development or king safety should take priority over aggression. The average cp_loss of 307 reflects that these aren't subtle positional inaccuracies—they're moves where concrete calculation would reveal an immediate tactical flaw, but the player chose based on general impressions of piece activity.

1768.label: Giving an impulsive Queen check that destroys a winning combination requiring a different piece to check or a different move order.
1768.description: All 10/10 positions feature a Queen delivering check, and 9/10 of these are severe mistakes (avg ~6400cp loss for the 9 blunders). In 5/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 6, 10), the correct move was a BISHOP check on the same or nearby square that would have enabled a discovered attack/check mechanism — the Queen check destroys this because it removes the Queen from the square where it needs to remain as the 'uncovered' piece. In 2/10 positions (3, 7), the Queen should have checked on a DIFFERENT square to set up the combination correctly. In 2/10 positions (4, 9), a non-checking move (preparatory or pawn advance) was needed instead. 7/10 positions had forced checkmates available that were squandered. The average number of good moves was only 1.4, indicating these are razor-sharp positions with essentially one correct continuation. Position 8 (0cp loss) is the sole exception where the Queen check was actually correct, suggesting the feature detects the general pattern of 'Queen check in a sharp attacking position' regardless of correctness.

1772.label: Voluntarily relocating a powerfully-placed knight away from its dominant square, missing the tactical opportunities that the knight's current position uniquely enables.
1772.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a knight FROM a dominant, actively-placed square (e5 in positions 2/3/5, d4/d5 in positions 9/10, e4 in position 7, g4 in position 1, e2 in position 8, f2 in position 4, g5 in position 6) TO a more passive or routine square (f3 appeared 3 times, f6 twice, plus g4/c4/d3/f4/b6). In 8/10 cases, the knight's current strong position was the prerequisite for a specific winning tactic: fork sequences (positions 1, 2), sacrificial king attacks (positions 3, 5, 9), defensive duties (position 4), restraining functions (positions 7, 10). The average cp_loss of 314 reflects that these moves typically squandered decisive advantages. In 9/10 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of the best, confirming these were critical moments requiring the player to exploit (not abandon) their knight's dominance.
