The retreats universally went to 'natural' or 'safe' squares, suggesting players defaulted to general principles rather than calculating the concrete tactical potential of the knight's current powerful placement.

1762.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move in a tactically demanding position where an immediate capture, check, or forcing threat was required.
1762.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, captures, or direct threats) played in a sharp middlegame position where only 1-2 good moves existed. In 9/10 cases, the best move was either a direct capture (Qxc4, Nxc3, Qxf4 in 3 positions), a check (Qh5+ in 1 position), or a move creating an immediate concrete threat (Qe7, Qh4, Nd2 maintaining tactical resources in 3 positions). The played moves are all 'reasonable-looking' improvements—rook repositioning (6/10: Rg6, Rg7, Rf3, Re5, Rf2, and implicitly Rg6 in position 1), pawn consolidation (2/10: b6, c3), knight retreat (1/10: Nd2), or quiet development (1/10: Be6)—that either remove a piece from a critical defensive/offensive function (4/10) or leave existing pieces undefended (3/10). In every case, the opponent exploited the gifted tempo to either capture loose material (4/10), execute a previously-prevented tactic (3/10), or fully consolidate a previously unstable position (3/10).

1773.label: A non-forcing queen repositioning move is played instead of executing an immediately available winning capture or combination.
1773.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking queen move to a seemingly active or improving square, while a decisive tactical blow (usually winning a full piece or queen) was available. In 7/10 cases, the winning move was NOT a queen move at all—it was a capture by a different piece (bishop, rook, or knight), suggesting the player was fixated on queen activity rather than calculating with all pieces. In 8/10 positions, the missed tactic involved capturing or winning the opponent's queen outright. The average cp_loss of 1400 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirm these are narrow tactical windows where one forcing move was drastically superior. In every case, the queen relocation removed a critical tactical element—either abandoning coordination with another piece, giving the opponent a tempo to escape a hanging piece, or vacating a square that enabled a winning combination.

1771.label: King moves that waste critical tempo when urgent pawn actions (pushes or captures) are needed to address passed pawn threats or create counterplay.
1771.description: All 10 positions feature a one-square king move, and in 7/10 cases, a pawn move or pawn capture was clearly superior (positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 9, 10 needed pawn pushes; position 2 needed Ke6 or h5). The average cp_loss of 2743 is driven by three catastrophic cases (positions 1, 3, 10 with losses of 8848, 9190, 9057cp) where the king move allowed an opponent's passed pawn to promote or exposed a critical piece to capture. 8/10 positions are endgames where pawn races are decisive, and the king move squanders a tempo that should have gone to pawn advancement (a4, b5, c5, exd5, etc.). In 3/10 positions (4, 5, 7), the cp_loss was negligible (0-2), suggesting the feature fires on all king-repositioning moves in these position types, with activation strength correlating to how badly the tempo is wasted. The consistent thread is prioritizing king 'activity' or 'safety' over concrete pawn action in time-critical positions.

1769.label: Playing a strategically-motivated or routine move that completely ignores an immediate tactical emergency requiring precise forced response.
1769.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a move that appeared reasonable from a strategic or developmental standpoint — developing a piece (Be7, Bd5, Bg2), centralizing (Qd4, Ke2), pushing a pawn (f3, d4, f6), or making a capture (dxe5, bxc6) — while a single critical tactical threat demanded an immediate forced response. In 7/10 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.6), indicating these were razor-sharp moments where only precise play survived. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 8, 9), the player's own major piece (usually the queen) was hanging or could be won by a simple tactical sequence. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 10), the player's king faced an immediate mating threat requiring a specific defensive resource. In 3/10 cases (positions 2, 3, 7), a forcing continuation was available that the player missed in favor of a slow positional improvement. The average centipawn loss of 2192 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights — the moves are not subtle inaccuracies but complete tactical blindness.

1776.label: Queen moves to a square where the opponent can profitably capture it via queen trade, squandering the player's advantage which depended on keeping queens on the board.
1776.description: In 9/10 positions, the primary refutation is the opponent simply capturing the queen via exchange (Qxc4, Qxd4, Qxg5, Qxe3, Qxc3, Qxf6, Qxc4, Qxd6, Qxe5), transforming the position from one where the moving player's queen was their most active and important piece into a simplified endgame or position where their advantage evaporates. In all 10 positions, the queen was the engine of the player's advantage—whether attacking an exposed king (positions 1, 3, 4, 9), pressuring weak pawns (position 5), escorting passed pawns (positions 6, 7), or compensating for inferior minor pieces (position 10). The moved queen lands on a square directly capturable by the opponent's queen, often on an open file facing it (positions 2, 8) or a central square the opponent's queen controls (positions 5, 7). Position 9 is a slight variant where the queen abandons a critical defensive square rather than offering a trade, but the underlying error is identical: relocating the queen to a tactically vulnerable square that allows the opponent to neutralize it. The average cp_loss of 1226 reflects how catastrophic these simplifications are when the queen is the key piece.

1774.label: A rook is moved to an undefended square where the opponent's queen can capture it immediately or after a simple intermediate check.
1774.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move to an unprotected square that falls to the opponent's queen. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 5, 6), the queen captures the rook directly on its destination square (Qxf8, Qxb1+, Qxg8+, Qxe1). In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 7, 8), the queen first delivers an intermediate check to gain tempo, then captures the undefended rook on the following move (e.g., Qa8+ then Qxb7, or Qc8+ then Qxb7, or Qh7+ then Qxg8+). In 1/10 cases (position 9), the rook lands on an undefended square exploitable through Bc7+ discovered attacks or direct Qxe1. Only 1/10 (position 10) involves a slightly different mechanism where the rook abandons its defensive post on f1, enabling a mating attack through the now-unguarded g2 pawn rather than direct capture. The average cp_loss is extremely high (5632), reflecting that losing a rook to the queen in already-difficult positions is typically game-ending. The positions span all rook destination squares (g8, f8, b7, b1, e1) but share the geometric reality that the queen controls or can reach the destination with one tempo move.

1779.label: A piece abandons its blockade of an advanced passed pawn (or captures it counterproductively), when maintaining the blockade while improving elsewhere was correct.
1779.description: All 10/10 positions feature an advanced passed pawn (typically on the 6th or 7th rank) that is being blockaded or restrained by the moving piece. In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 8), the piece physically abandons the blockade square, allowing the pawn to advance or promote. In 5/10 positions (4, 5, 6, 9, 10), the piece captures the passed pawn but transitions into a worse position—either a lost pawn endgame (positions 4, 5), allows recapture with check/tempo (positions 6, 9), or simplifies unhelpfully (position 10). In 1/10 (position 7), the queen leaves its blockade square allowing a discovered check with pawn advance. The correct moves in 9/10 positions involved maintaining the blockade while improving piece placement elsewhere (typically king activation or creating counter-threats). The average cp_loss of 1150 reflects the catastrophic consequences of releasing an advanced passed pawn.

1778.label: A rook moves to an aggressive-looking central or forward square (capturing a pawn or centralizing) but ends up exposed, misplaced, or abandoning critical duties.
1778.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook making a forward or lateral move that appears active — either capturing a pawn (4/10: Rxe6, Rxe6+, Rxb2, Rxb4) or centralizing to an ambitious square (6/10: Rc3, Rc6, Rc4, Re5, Re4, Rd4). In every case, the rook lands on a middle-rank square (ranks 2-6) where it becomes tactically vulnerable or strategically misplaced. The punishments vary but share a common mechanism: 7/10 positions see the rook attacked by a minor piece or pawn on its new square (Ne5 attacking Re6, Bxb4 capturing Rb4, ...d5 hitting Re4, Be5 hitting Rd4), while 6/10 positions show the rook's departure creating a fatal defensive void (Re5 abandoning back-rank defense, Rc3 abandoning kingside, Rc4 losing a tempo for h6 breakthrough, Rxb2 leaving knights undefended). The average cp_loss of 1197 reflects that these seemingly purposeful rook moves consistently trigger devastating tactical refutations that the player failed to foresee.

1763.label: Playing tempting active moves (captures, checks, penetrations) that remove a piece from a critical but non-obvious defensive function, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
1763.description: 7/9 positions clearly show a piece being moved away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function—typically blocking a dangerous diagonal or defending a key square/piece. In positions 1, 2, and 3, the moved piece (rook or queen) was blocking a critical diagonal; once removed, the opponent exploited the open line with devastating effect (Bxe6+, Bxf4+, Bxb2). In positions 9 and 10, rooks abandoned defense of specific squares (b2 and g2 respectively), allowing immediate piece capture or checkmate. In positions 7 and 8, powerfully placed pieces (knights) were voluntarily moved to squares where they were immediately captured or neutralized, liquidating the position. Position 6 (Qg3) represents a self-obstruction variant where the queen blocked the king's own escape routes. Position 5 (Re5) is the weakest fit, representing a tempo-loss subvariant rather than pure function-abandonment. The average cp_loss of 2639 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—the hidden function was always more valuable than what the active move achieved.

1775.label: Rook moves to seemingly active squares that ignore the position's critical tactical demands, leaving the rook or another piece fatally vulnerable.
1775.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a middlegame rook move that appears purposeful—centralizing, attacking, defending, or activating—but fails to address the most urgent tactical issue. In 4/10 cases (Rf4, Rg4, Rf3, Rc7), the rook lands on a square where it is immediately exploitable by pawn advances, diagonal attacks, or knight forks. In 4/10 cases (Rd2, Rxe3, Rb2, Rd1), the rook move ignores a hanging or tactically loose piece elsewhere, allowing the opponent to win material. In 2/10 cases (Rg6, Rd4), the rook move is simply too slow, missing a concrete tactical blow that would have been far superior. Critically, in 8/10 positions the best move was NOT a rook move at all—the correct plan involved a different piece entirely (bishop, knight, or pawn). The average cp_loss of 267 and average of only 1.3 good moves available indicate these are narrow positions where the player's instinct to 'improve the rook' led them astray from the position's true requirements.

1781.label: Quiet king moves that worsen the king's safety by walking into tactical vulnerabilities or wasting critical tempo when forcing moves were available.
1781.description: All 10/10 positions involve a quiet (non-capturing, non-checking) king move that catastrophically worsens the position. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 8, 9, and partially 1), the king move allows immediate or near-immediate checkmate (mate-in-1 to mate-in-3). In 5/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 6, 7, 10), the king moves to a square that creates new tactical vulnerabilities—exposing it to diagonal checks, file-based attacks, or pins that didn't exist on the previous square. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 4, 10), the player should have been making an active non-king move entirely (tactical captures, piece exchanges, or piece improvements). A striking sub-pattern appears in positions 3 and 7, where the king needed to go to h8 specifically but went to h7 or g7 instead—the wrong adjacent square. The average cp_loss of 3940 and the fact that only 1.6 good moves existed on average confirms these are positions where king placement is razor-critical and the player misjudges which direction constitutes safety.

1780.label: Rook moves to a seemingly active square (open file, check, or attacking rank) that abandons a critical defensive duty or misapplies a tactical idea that another piece or square would execute correctly.
1780.description: All 9/9 positions involve rook moves to squares that appear superficially active—open files, checks, or attacking positions—but are fundamentally flawed. In 4/9 positions (Rd1, Rh8, Re1 in position 5, Rg2), the rook abandons a critical defensive function: guarding a piece, protecting a passed pawn, or maintaining file coordination. In 3/9 positions (Re1+ twice, Rg2), the wrong piece or wrong rook is chosen for a tactical idea that would work with the correct piece (queen check instead of rook check, or f3-rook instead of c2-rook). In 2/9 positions (Re6, Rb8), the rook move is premature—played without necessary preparatory moves that would make the rook deployment devastating rather than toothless. The average cp_loss of 299 reflects how these moves systematically squander advantages by prioritizing apparent piece activity over maintaining critical positional/tactical infrastructure.

1783.label: Passive rook moves to open files (almost always the e-file) that waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical action.
1783.description: 10/10 positions feature non-forcing rook moves to back-rank squares, with 9/10 specifically being rook-to-e-file moves (Re1/Re8) and the remaining one (Rb1) sharing the same generic 'activate the rook on an open file' logic. In every case, the position demanded concrete tactical play — either an attacking combination (7/10 positions had a specific tactic available: Bg4, f4, Bd4/Bxf2+, Rxe8+, Nxd5 sequences, etc.) or an urgent defensive necessity (3/10 needed moves like h3 or Kg7 to prevent imminent threats). The average cp_loss of 273 reflects that these moves consistently squander large advantages or create decisive vulnerabilities. In 3/10 cases, the rook move actually created a new tactical vulnerability (removing the rook from f8 to expose f7 or the back rank, or placing the rook where it hangs to a bishop). The average number of good moves was only 1.8, indicating these positions had narrow windows requiring precise play, not generic development.

1784.label: A critically-positioned minor piece abandons its vital defensive role to capture an inconsequential pawn, catastrophically exposing the position.
1784.description: In 10/10 positions, a minor piece (8/10 bishops, 2/10 knights) that was serving as the linchpin of the position's defensive structure captured a pawn, removing itself from its essential post. The captured pawns were overwhelmingly kingside pawns (8/10 on g7, g6, g2, h2, f2, or f3). In every case, the analyses explicitly identify the moved piece as the 'key defensive piece' (Pos 1), 'sole defender' (Pos 2), 'crucial defensive post' (Pos 3), 'critical piece blocking the d-file' (Pos 10), 'primary defensive piece shielding the King' (Pos 9), or 'linchpin coordinating' the winning plan (Pos 6, 7). The average cp_loss of 2145 reflects how catastrophic these trades are—4/10 resulted in forced mate or near-mate. In 8/10 positions, the refutation directly exploited the square or file the piece had been guarding (back-rank invasions, king attacks, piece captures on now-undefended squares).

1785.label: Quiet one-square king moves that lose critical tempo or walk into tactical danger when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1785.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing king move (one square, no capture, no check) played in a position that demanded urgent tactical or strategic action. In 6/10 cases, the king move was a pure tempo loss—the player shuffled the king to a 'safer' or 'more comfortable' square while missing a critical attacking continuation (Rd5, h5, Qd6+, Qxf6, Rc7) or defensive obligation (Rd2). In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 8, 10), the king actually walked INTO tactical danger—onto vulnerable diagonals (b1-h7), into mating nets (Nd6+/Qc4+/Qb5#), into corners enabling Bf6+ patterns, or onto squares where Rc2+ became decisive. The average cp_loss was 2974, with 4/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were precisely the moments where a 'quiet' king move was least affordable. The king destinations cluster toward edges and corners: h7 (3x), g2 (2x), h8, h2, a2, b7, f2—suggesting a reflexive 'tuck the king away' instinct overriding concrete calculation.

1791.label: Premature O-O-O that places the king on a queenside square where the opponent has immediate tactical or pawn-storm resources to exploit.
1791.description: All 10/10 positions feature O-O-O (queenside castling) as the blunder, with an average centipawn loss of 250. In 9/10 positions the game is still in the opening phase, and in most cases the center is closed (8/10 explicitly noted). The critical shared pattern is that the castling is premature — the king lands on the queenside where the opponent already possesses (or can immediately create) concrete attacking resources. In 5/10 positions (Positions 2, 5, 6, 7, 10), the refutation involves an immediate tactical blow (knight fork, hanging piece, queen win) made possible specifically by the king's arrival on c1/c8. In 4/10 positions (Positions 1, 3, 4, 9), the refutation involves rapid pawn breaks (b4, a5, d4) that tear open lines against the freshly castled king. Position 8 is unique: the castling squandered a queen-trapping opportunity rather than castling into an attack. In all cases, 1-3 superior alternatives existed that either resolved tactical tensions first, played prophylactic moves denying the opponent's attacking resources, or simply developed pieces without committing the king prematurely.

1789.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing piece-improvement move in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1789.description: All 10/10 positions feature the player choosing a quiet, non-forcing move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) aimed at general piece improvement or development, while the position urgently demanded concrete tactical action. In 4/10 cases, the move was a piece repositioning to a 'better' square (Bd2, Bb3×2, Nc5). In 4/10 cases, it was a rook placed on an open or semi-open file for 'activity' (Rd8, Rcd1, Ra6, Rad8). The remaining moves were a queen 'development' (Qd7) and a king walk (Kg6). The urgent tactical demands ignored included: immediate checkmate delivery (2/10: Qh8#, Qxg2#), hanging pieces to capture (2/10: Rxa5, Nxe4), defending against immediate checkmate threats (2/10: Bb3 positions allowing Qxh1# and Qxg2#), pieces left undefended by the repositioning (3/10: Rcd1 abandoning c3-knight, Nc5 self-hanging, Ra6 placing rook on bishop's diagonal), and critical defensive needs (1/10: Rad8 ignoring kingside crisis). The average cp_loss of 3248 reflects the catastrophic nature of ignoring concrete demands. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical positions requiring precise calculation rather than general development.

1794.label: Moving a bishop to an undefended square where the opponent's queen can simply capture it for free.
1794.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a square that is directly capturable by the opponent's queen along a clear line (diagonal or rank), with no piece defending the bishop's destination square. In every case the refutation is the trivially obvious Qx capture winning a full piece. The intent behind the moves typically falls into two categories: 8/10 positions involve the bishop seemingly 'developing' or 'activating' to attack an enemy piece or control a diagonal, while 2/10 involve the bishop moving with apparent tactical purpose (a check in position 10, targeting a queen in positions 2/4/6/9). In all cases the player overlooks that the queen's reach along the relevant line makes the bishop immediately capturable. The average cp_loss of 429 (~full piece) confirms the material nature of the error. 6/10 are White bishop moves and 4/10 are Black bishop moves, showing no side preference. 9/10 occur in the middlegame where queens are actively placed on open lines.

1786.label: King moves to peripheral or exposed squares instead of centralizing or playing a more critical move.
1786.description: All 10 positions feature king moves, and 9/10 involve the king moving toward the edge of the board or away from the critical area of play. 5/10 moves specifically go to the h-file (Kh3, Kh4, Kh5, Kh5, Kh4), while others drift to the a-file (Ka6), c-file away from action (Kc6, Kc3), or g-file wing (Kg5). 8/10 positions are endgames where king centralization is paramount. In 7/10 positions, the correct move was a king move toward the center (Kf4, Ke5, Kf6, Ke5, Kc6, Kg7, Ke5), while in 2/10 the correct move wasn't a king move at all but a piece/queen move (Be7, Qe8+). The average cp_loss of 1210 is extremely high, reflecting how catastrophic king misplacement is in endgames. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were high-precision moments where the correct direction was critical.

1796.label: Queen moves to a new square while abandoning its sole defensive duty protecting a piece, pawn, or square from immediate capture or checkmate.
1796.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a queen move that relocates the queen away from a square or line where it was performing an irreplaceable defensive function. In 7/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8), the queen was the sole defender of a specific piece or square, and moving it allowed immediate capture of that target — often with devastating follow-up (including checkmate in 2/10 positions). In 8/10 positions, the opponent's refutation was a direct capture on the now-undefended square (Qxd5, Qxd4, Qxg6+, Bxd5, Qxg7#, Qxd4, Qxg2#, Bxg7). The queen typically moved to an 'active-looking' square (attacking something or appearing to generate threats) but the defensive role it abandoned was worth far more than any offensive potential gained. In 5/10 positions the queen left the d-file or back rank where it was guarding a centralized piece (d4/d5 knight or pawn), while in 3/10 the queen left a rank or file defending a critical kingside square (g2, g6, g7) against mating patterns.

1795.label: Quiet rook repositioning to a seemingly logical square while ignoring the position's urgent tactical demand.
1795.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-forcing rook move to a square that appears reasonable by general principles (open file, central placement, back rank) but catastrophically ignores the position's critical tactical priority. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 7), the king was uncastled on e1 and needed immediate attention—two of these allowed instant Qe2# checkmate. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 9, 10), the rook went to the wrong file when an adjacent file was clearly correct (Rc8 instead of keeping blockade; Rd8 instead of Rc8; Rd1 instead of Rf1). In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 8), the rook retreated passively when an attacking rook move or non-rook move was required. The average cp_loss of 2158 is extremely high, and only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these are sharp positions demanding concrete solutions rather than generic development. The moves share a common psychological profile: the player defaults to 'improving' a rook by placing it on an open or semi-open file without calculating the opponent's immediate tactical response.

1799.label: The f-pawn captures on the e-file (fxe5/fxe4) prematurely, removing the last defender of a critical diagonal to the uncastled king and allowing an immediate queen invasion with check.
1799.description: 8/10 positions feature an f-pawn capturing toward the e-file (7 fxe5 by White, 1 fxe4 by Black), all in the opening phase with the king still in the center. In 7/8 of these f-pawn captures, the immediate refutation is Qh4+ (or Qh5+), exploiting the now-completely-open diagonal to the uncastled king. The resulting tactical sequence typically involves queen check → forced g3/g6 → Qxe4+ forking king and rook → winning the h1/h8 rook. All 10 positions share the broader theme of king safety failures where the f-pawn's defensive role is catastrophically underestimated. The 2 outlier positions (Kd6 and Nd2) still involve exposing the king to diagonal/f-file attacks, but through different mechanisms — Kd6 walks into queen checks, and Nd2 leaves f2 tactically vulnerable to a knight sacrifice. 9/10 positions are in the opening with both kings uncastled, and the average cp_loss of 316 reflects the devastating nature of these diagonal-opening errors.

1798.label: A routine pawn capture on one part of the board while a critical tactical emergency (checkmate threat, hanging piece, or mating attack) demands immediate attention elsewhere.
1798.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture (axb, gxf, bxc, cxd, dxe, hxg pattern) played while a far more urgent tactical demand exists elsewhere on the board. In 6/10 cases, the ignored threat is an immediate or near-immediate checkmate (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 allow mate-in-1 to mate-in-8). In 3/10 cases, the pawn capture leaves a piece hanging or fails to address a hanging piece (positions 2, 7, 10). In 1/10 cases, the capture squanders a winning attack by allowing the opponent to eliminate the key attacking piece (position 8). The average cp_loss of 3931 is extraordinarily high, reflecting that these 'quiet' pawn captures frequently allow catastrophic tactical consequences. The positions span all phases and both colors equally (5 White, 5 Black), and in 7/10 cases only 1-2 good moves existed, showing these were critical moments demanding precise responses rather than routine captures.

1777.label: Captures or active-looking moves that prioritize material gain or attack while fatally weakening one's own position, particularly pawn structure and king safety.
1777.description: 7/10 positions involve captures where the player takes material that appears attractive but creates an immediate, exploitable weakness. 5/10 specifically involve pawn captures/advances that remove a critical pawn from king defense (gxh5 opening the g-file for mate, exf5 opening the e-file against an uncastled king, fxg3 removing f-pawn defense of e3, gxf5 stripping the g-pawn shield, g5 exposing h7 to a bishop sacrifice). 2/10 involve bishop captures on d6 that place the piece en prise to the queen. The remaining 3 positions (Nd4, c4, Nb3) involve placing pieces on immediately vulnerable squares or ignoring tactical threats for strategic-looking moves. The unifying thread is that every move appears logical on the surface—capturing material, centralizing, attacking—but the player failed to calculate the immediate 1-2 move tactical refutation that exploits the new weakness. Average good moves available was only 1.9, indicating these were razor-thin positions demanding precise defensive choices rather than greedy ones.

1792.label: A pawn advance that vacates a critical square, immediately allowing an enemy knight to land there with a devastating fork.
1792.description: In 8/10 positions, the blundering move is a pawn advance that directly vacates the exact square an enemy knight needs to deliver a fork winning major material. The vacated squares and resulting forks are: f3→Nf3+ (positions 1, 9), c6→Nc6+ (positions 2, 5), f2→Nf2+ (position 3), c7→Nc7+ (position 4), e6→Ne6 (position 6), f6→Nf6+ (position 8). In 7/8 of these, the fork comes with check. Position 10 is a variant where f4 ignores an existing Nxe2+ fork threat while also hanging the pawn, and position 7 is slightly different (b3 attacks a knight but ignores its stronger intermediate capture leading to a pin). The motif is 'fork' in 9/10 positions. The pawns were serving as sentinels blocking knight invasion squares, and their advance—typically motivated by attacking a piece or gaining space—catastrophically removes that protection.

1790.label: A bishop captures a knight on f3 or f6 while overlooking a critical queen-level tactical issue — either leaving one's own queen hanging or squandering a queen-winning combination.
1790.description: All 9/9 positions feature a bishop capturing a knight on either f3 (5 positions, Black playing Bg4xNf3) or f6 (4 positions, White playing Bg5xNf6). In every case, the bishop had been pressuring the knight for some time, making the capture feel like a 'natural' culmination of the pin/pressure. However, in 6/9 positions, the capture directly leaves the player's own queen en prise or capturable by an intermediate move (Positions 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9 — queens left hanging to Bxf6, exf3, Bxf3, Nxd5, Bxf3, and cxd5 respectively). In the remaining 3/9 positions (5, 6, 10), the capture squanders a superior tactical mechanism involving the queen — either exposing the opponent's queen to a devastating x-ray/removal, or destroying an overloaded-defender combination that would have won the opponent's queen. The average cp_loss of 354 reflects that these are severe errors. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, indicating these are sharp positions demanding precision, yet the correct move was almost always a queen move (retreating or attacking) rather than the knight capture.

1787.label: A non-forcing piece relocation that either removes a critical defender, places a piece on a vulnerable square, or wastes tempo when the position demanded concrete tactical action.
1787.description: All 10 positions share a common error: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move in a position that demanded concrete tactical precision. In 10/10 cases the move played involves no check, no capture, and no immediate threat — it's purely a 'piece improvement' that ignores urgent tactical realities. In 5/10 positions (Nc6, Nb6, Nh4, Rf6, Ra4), the move directly removes a critical defender or places the piece where it immediately hangs — the knight on f3 was defending d3 (pos 10), the knight on e5 was protecting c5 (pos 4), the rook on f8 was guarding the back rank (pos 3), and the rook goes to a4 in the bishop's firing line (pos 8). In 4/10 positions (Rh3, Rh6, Rf2, e4), the piece moves to a passive/irrelevant square while active forcing moves were available. In 8/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, meaning the position was tactically critical yet the player chose a 'looks reasonable' placement move. The average cp_loss of 394 confirms these are severe errors. The moves are overwhelmingly pieces (9/10) rather than pawns, with rooks (5/10) and knights (3/10) most common — pieces that frequently get repositioned but whose relocation can create immediate tactical consequences.

1797.label: Quiet piece repositioning to e2 or e7 (back-rank squares) when the position demands immediate concrete/tactical action.
1797.description: 7/10 positions feature a piece moving specifically to e2 (White) or e7 (Black), with the remaining 3 going to adjacent back-rank squares (Bd2, Bd7, Rae8). All 10 moves are quiet, non-forcing piece repositions to the player's second rank or back rank. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand: 6/10 had immediate mating threats or king safety crises, 2/10 had pieces that could be trapped, and 2/10 had hanging central pawns or critical captures available. The average cp_loss of 3206 is extreme, and with only 1.3 good moves available on average, these were razor-sharp positions requiring concrete action. The e2/e7 square specifically seems to attract 'looks safe and developing' moves — connecting rooks, providing passive defense, or repositioning for a future plan — but in each case the tempo spent on this quiet move allows the opponent to execute a devastating tactic (checkmate, queen trapping, discovered attacks, or winning material).

1802.label: Pawn promotes to a Queen when an intermediate move, underpromotion, or entirely different tactical idea was superior.
1802.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn promoting to a Queen. In 8/10 cases this was a mistake (avg cp_loss ~4870 across all, but ~6088 for the 8 errors specifically). The errors cluster into clear sub-types: 3/10 positions missed a critical intermediate check before promoting (Positions 2, 5, 9), where checking first would deflect a defender or displace a piece, making the subsequent promotion far stronger. 2/10 positions allowed immediate back-rank checkmate by promoting instead of addressing the first rank (Positions 1, 9). 2/10 positions missed a stronger non-promotion tactical idea entirely—a mating king-hunt (Position 6) or a winning pin (Position 7). 1/10 should have underpromoted to a rook instead (Position 4). Only 2/10 positions (Positions 8 and 10) represent correct queen promotions with 0 cp loss, serving as baseline examples of when queening IS correct. The consistent error is that players are magnetically drawn to the material reward of creating a queen, overriding their calculation of immediate tactical threats.

1803.label: A minor piece captures a kingside shelter pawn (h3, h6, or g6) as a speculative sacrifice, but the resulting attack is easily neutralized after the simple pawn recapture.
1803.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece (bishop or knight) capturing a pawn on the castled king's outermost shelter squares — h3 (4/10), h6 (4/10), or g6 (2/10) — sacrificing a full piece for one pawn with the hope of generating a mating attack against the exposed king. 9/10 positions feature same-side kingside castling, and all occur in the middlegame. In every case, the simple pawn recapture (gxh6, gxh3, fxg6) is the strongest refutation, after which the defender deploys a defensive resource — typically a knight blockade (Nh7, Ng7, Ng6 in positions 1-2), a bishop repositioning (Bf3 in position 8), or queen coverage of critical squares (Qf6 in position 9, Qe7 in position 10) — that completely neutralizes the attack while maintaining the full-piece material advantage. The average cp_loss of 286 confirms these are consistently severe errors. In 8/10 positions, at least 3 good quiet alternatives were available, typically involving patient piece improvement or positional maneuvering rather than premature tactical violence.

1804.label: A passive one-square central pawn advance (d or e file) played in a position demanding immediate tactical action, ignoring concrete threats or opportunities.
1804.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn push on the d-file or e-file (e6 x3, e3 x3, d6 x2, d3 x1, d5 x1) — never a capture, never two squares, always a quiet 'developing preparation' move. In every case, the position had very few good alternatives (avg 1.5 good moves), signaling a critical tactical moment. 9/10 positions occurred in the opening phase with at least one king in the center. The consistent error is that these natural-looking pawn moves ignore an urgent tactical demand: in 4/10 positions the player missed a forcing winning move (Qxe5+, Qd4, Qb3, Qa5+); in 3/10 positions a piece was left hanging or vulnerable to a fork (bishop on g4, b4, or a5); in 3/10 positions the move enabled an opponent's tactical combination (Nd5 clearance, Ne4 attack, g5 trapping). The avg cp_loss of 277 reflects that these seemingly innocuous pawn moves are catastrophic in tactically charged positions.

1801.label: A knight captures an active enemy piece (usually centralized) while missing a far stronger tactical opportunity or creating a critical vulnerability.
1801.description: All 10 positions feature knight moves (9/10 are captures, 1/10 a retreat) that target an opponent's active or centralized piece — typically another knight on d4, e4, e5, f3, or f4. In every case, the capture appears natural and motivated by eliminating a threatening piece, but catastrophically misses a more urgent tactical priority. In 5/10 positions, the player missed a stronger attacking continuation (Qf8+, Ng5, Rxb8, g4-deflection, Nxd4-trap). In 4/10 positions, the move is a move-order error where preparation was needed first (Re8 before Nxe5, f6 before Nxe5, Rxb8 before Nxe5, g4 before Nxf3). In 3/10 positions, moving the knight away left another piece fatally undefended (Nc3 hanging in position 10, back rank exposed in position 1, Qh2# allowed in position 9). The average cp_loss of 2280 reflects how catastrophic these 'obvious' captures are — with only 1.2 good moves available on average, these were critical moments requiring calculation rather than pattern-matching to the natural capture.

1788.label: Playing a plausible piece-improvement or repositioning move in a tactically critical position where only one or two concrete solutions maintain the evaluation.
1788.description: All 10 positions share the pattern of a player choosing a move that LOOKS like a natural improvement — centralizing a piece, advancing a pawn, or capturing material — while catastrophically ignoring the position's single concrete demand. In 8/10 positions, a specific tactical shot existed (check, sacrifice, forcing sequence) that the player missed in favor of their 'improving' move. 7/10 moves are minor piece relocations (5 knight moves, 2 bishop moves) to squares that appear strong but are actually tactically flawed. The average number of good moves available was only 1.8, confirming these are razor-sharp positions with minimal margin. In 5/10 cases the blunder specifically moved a piece AWAY from the square where it performed a critical function (Ng3 from h5, Ne5 from f3, Nf3 from e5, Nf5 failing to use f3, Nb8 blocking escape). In 3/10 cases the move resulted in immediate forced checkmate. The played moves consistently prioritize abstract piece placement over concrete tactical necessity.

1810.label: A rook moves away from a square or file where it was the sole defender of a critical piece or mating square, leaving it immediately exploitable.
1810.description: All 9/9 positions feature a rook move that abandons a critical defensive responsibility. In 7/9 cases, the rook was the sole protector of another piece that immediately hangs after the move (Rf7 leaving Rb8 undefended in Position 1; Re1 leaving Rf7 hanging in Position 2; Ra1 leaving Bd3 unprotected in Position 3; Ra3 abandoning Ne6 in Position 4; Rf7 leaving Rd8 exposed in Position 5; Rc8 leaving Rd7 capturable in Position 6; Rd8 leaving Re5 hanging in Position 7; Rb1 leaving Nc3 undefended in Position 9). In 2/9 cases, the rook was defending a critical mating square—particularly g7 (Position 8's Rf5 abandoning g7 defense) and the back rank (Position 5). The average cp_loss of 4494 reflects that these errors are often immediately catastrophic, with 4/9 positions resulting in forced mate. In every case, the player had an offensive intent (activating the rook, attacking a target, contesting a file) but failed to recognize the rook's irreplaceable defensive role.

1800.label: Quiet rook repositioning moves that waste critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action like pawn advances, captures, or forcing checks.
1800.description: 10/10 positions feature rook moves to seemingly natural or active squares (open files, central squares, the seventh rank) that are non-forcing and repositional in nature. In 9/10 cases these moves are mistakes (avg 160cp loss), with the core error being tempo loss: 9/10 positions are tagged with tempo_loss, and 8/10 involve missing concrete pawn action (advances toward promotion, prophylactic pushes, or pawn captures). The best moves in 7/10 positions were NOT rook moves at all—they were pawn pushes (h6, c4, b3, h5, cxb4) or king moves (Kf2)—while in the remaining 3, the correct rook move was a FORCING one (Rg2+ with check, Rg8 directly targeting a weak pawn, Rg7+ forcing a winning exchange). The played rook moves instead relocate to squares that look positionally desirable but don't address the position's concrete demands: Rc8 goes to a 'nice file' when Rg8 attacks g5 directly; Rd2 'centralizes' when h6 defends crucial pawns; Rb1 'attacks b3' when c4 breaks through; Rf6 'activates' when b3 promotes. The positions are predominantly endgames (7/10) with passed pawns (8/10), where one tempo often determines whether pawns promote or get blockaded.

1807.label: A non-urgent single-square rim pawn advance (a3/a6/g6/h6) that wastes a critical tempo while ignoring an immediate tactical demand in the position.
1807.description: All 10 positions feature a single-square advance of a flank pawn (a-file or g/h-file) — specifically a3 (4/10), a6 (2/10), g6 (2/10), h6 (1/10), and g5 (1/10). In every case, the position demanded immediate forcing action: 3/10 had hanging or undefended pieces that needed saving or capturing, 3/10 had devastating tactical shots available (fork, skewer, Greek gift), 2/10 required urgent king activation or blocking in endgames, and 2/10 needed exploitation of the opponent's exposed king. The average cp_loss of 297 reflects that these 'do-nothing' pawn moves allow the opponent to execute their threat unopposed. Critically, 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating high-urgency moments where only precise play maintained the evaluation — yet the player chose the least committal possible move. The moves share a prophylactic or consolidating intent (securing pawn chains, preventing future incursions) but address concerns that are completely irrelevant given the position's tactical demands.
1807.old_chip: Quiet flank pawn when action needed

1809.label: Making a pawn capture (or piece exchange) while the player's own queen is undefended and can be taken by the opponent on the next move.
1809.description: In 10/10 positions, the player makes a capture — 9/10 are pawn captures (axb5, fxg6, exd4, cxd4, fxe6, fxg3, fxe6, fxg7, cxd4) and 1/10 is a knight capture (Nxd7+) — while their own queen is en prise on a file, rank, or diagonal where an opponent's piece has a clear path to capture it. In every case, the refutation is simply taking the hanging queen: Rxa7 (rank), Rxd4 (file), Bxb3 (diagonal), Bxc6 (long diagonal), Bxc7 (diagonal), Bxd1 (diagonal), Nxe2+ (zwischenzug), Rxc7 (file), dxc2 (pawn), Rxf3 (file). The best moves in all 10 positions share the pattern of addressing the queen's safety FIRST — either moving the queen, capturing the attacking piece, or interposing — before making any other capture. The average cp_loss of 494 is consistent with losing a queen (~900cp value) minus the material gained from the erroneous capture.

1793.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful piece repositioning move when the position critically demands a concrete forcing action (pawn break, capture, check, or essential defense).
1793.description: All 10/10 positions share a single defining pattern: the position demanded exactly ONE concrete forcing move (a capture, check, pawn break, or defensive necessity), but the player instead chose a quiet piece repositioning move that appeared logical or active. Specifically, 4/10 positions required a central pawn break (d5 in positions 1, 2, 4, 9), 4/10 required a forcing capture or check (Bg3+, Nxd4, Nxh2, Bxf4 in positions 3, 4, 5, 8), 1/10 required a pawn counter-strike (f5 in position 7), and 1/10 required critical defense (Qd7 in position 10). The average number of good moves was only 1.4, confirming these were extremely critical moments. The played moves all LOOKED purposeful — attacking a piece (Bh3 attacking g2, Nh5 attacking Bf4, Nb4 attacking Bc2, Bb5 attempting a pin), developing (Be7, Bd7), centralizing (Kd6, Qd3), or retreating (Ke8) — but every single one was a non-forcing repositioning move that ignored the one concrete action the position required. 9/10 were Black moves, suggesting this pattern particularly afflicts the defending side who confuses 'active-looking' piece moves with genuinely forcing play.

1808.label: Advancing the g-pawn (or f-pawn) in front of an exposed king, removing a critical defensive barrier and allowing the opponent to exploit the opened lines with checks or perpetual check.
1808.description: 9/10 positions involve advancing the g-pawn (7 are g3, 1 is g4, 1 is g2), with the remaining position featuring f6 and f5 advances following the same logic. In 8/10 cases, the king was already exposed on h2 or h3 (the kingside flank), and the pawn advance removed a critical shield that was blocking enemy checks along a rank or file. The punishment in 9/10 positions involved immediate checks along the second rank (Qf2+, Qd2+, Rc2+) or the third rank (Qf3+), exploiting the newly opened line. 5/10 positions resulted in perpetual check (drawing from won positions), while 4/10 resulted in forced checkmate. In 8/10 positions, the correct alternative was a king move (Kg1, Kh1, Kh6, etc.) rather than the pawn advance, indicating the player mistakenly tried to create luft or drive away an enemy piece when relocating the king was the actual defensive priority.
1808.old_chip: Kingside pawn push strips king shield

1806.label: Aggressive-looking rook moves that prioritize apparent activity (checks, captures, attacks) while leaving a critical piece undefended or missing a stronger continuation.
1806.description: All 10/10 positions feature rook moves that appear active or forcing on the surface but create concrete tactical vulnerabilities. In 5/10 positions (1, 4, 6, 7, 9), the rook move abandons defense of another piece, leaving it hanging (bishop on d3 in positions 7 and 9, queen on h4 in position 4, the rook itself in positions 1 and 6 via unguarded diagonals). In 2/10 positions (2, 5), the rook gives check but misses an immediate checkmate on the same file — Rc4+ missing Rc8# and Ra4+ missing Rd1#. In 2/10 positions (8, 10), the rook captures or challenges an exchange that dissipates a decisive advantage (abandoning blockade duty or allowing an equalizing trade). Position 3 features the rook enabling an unfavorable queen exchange that preserves the opponent's passed pawn. The average cp_loss of 2198 reflects that several positions involved missing forced checkmate.

1782.label: Non-forcing moves (especially pawn pushes) played in positions demanding immediate concrete tactical action, typically missing a free capture or allowing a devastating combination.
1782.description: 6/10 positions involve pawn advances (h4, h3, e2, h4, h6, and Bxd6 captures a pawn), with 4/10 specifically being h-pawn pushes. In 5/10 positions, the best move was a simple capture of hanging or loose material (hxg4, hxg3, Qxg8, Rb1/Rc1 winning material, Ba6 winning the b2 bishop). In 9/10 positions (excluding the 0-cp-loss e2 which appears to be an outlier), the played move gives the opponent a critical extra tempo that enables a tactical refutation—whether a recapture with check (Rxd6+), a deflection (Qxg6+), a discovered check (cxb2+), or a simple free capture (Qxh3). The moves all LOOK purposeful: h4 appears to attack a pawn chain, h6 appears to kick a knight, Rf8 appears to defend f7, Nc2 appears to attack a bishop, Rg8 appears to challenge a rook—but each fundamentally ignores the position's most pressing tactical demand. The average cp_loss of 1136 reflects catastrophic consequences, and the average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are sharp positions with narrow paths to survival.

1816.label: A rook greedily captures peripheral material (usually a pawn), displacing itself from a critical defensive task and allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow.
1816.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook capture (Rx) of material — 9/10 capture a pawn and 1/10 captures a knight. In every case, the rook abandons a critical defensive station or active position to grab material that appears free but is actually a tactical trap. The punishment most commonly involves an unstoppable passed pawn promotion (6/10 positions: 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9), while in 3/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 7) it enables a mating attack, and in 1/10 (position 10) it allows a discovered check combination. The captures overwhelmingly target edge-file or peripheral pawns (a-file: 4/10, b-file: 2/10, h-file: 3/10), with only 1/10 capturing centrally. The average cp_loss of ~4915 reflects that 7/10 positions resulted in mate or near-mate evaluations, indicating these are not minor inaccuracies but catastrophic oversights where the player prioritized material gain over positional/tactical urgency.

1805.label: Advancing a pawn in the king's protective shield (especially the g-pawn) when the opponent already has active pieces targeting that sector, instead of making forcing/active moves.
1805.description: 7/9 positions involve the player advancing a pawn that forms part of their own king's pawn shield — in 6/9 cases specifically the g-pawn (g3 for White or g6 for Black), and in 1 case the b-pawn near a queenside-castled king. In all these cases, the opponent already had pieces (typically rooks on open/semi-open files, or knights on outposts) aimed directly at the weakened sector. The refutations consistently exploit the newly created weakness: Rxg4+ sacrifices (positions 8, 1), Nxg6 knight sacrifices (position 2), Nxf6+ winning hanging pieces because the g-pawn can no longer recapture (position 9), h5-h4 hook attacks (position 7), and queen invasions through weakened squares (position 5). In every case, superior alternatives existed involving active piece play — piece repositioning (Nc4, Nh4, Nd7), forcing captures (Bxe5, dxc4), or king safety moves (O-O, Kh1) — rather than passive pawn moves that worsen the king's shelter. The 2 outlier positions (c3 and Nc6) still share the meta-pattern of playing a slow/passive move that ignores urgent king safety demands.

1812.label: Playing slow, non-forcing pawn pushes or piece moves in positions demanding immediate tactical action, either missing a winning combination or ignoring a lethal threat.
1812.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing, non-capturing, non-checking move played in a position of extreme tactical urgency. 8/10 are one-square pawn pushes (g5, b3, f4, f6, d3, c3, e5, f5) and 2/10 are quiet bishop moves (Be7, Bc6). In every case, the position demanded either an immediate tactical strike (Qf8+ deflection in pos 2, Nxd7 queen capture in pos 9, Qb3+ fork in pos 8, Nh4 attack in pos 5) or an urgent defensive measure (Rh1 sacrifice in pos 1, Kf7 king evacuation in pos 6 and 7). The average cp_loss of 3087 and average of only 1.6 good moves confirm these are razor-sharp moments where only forcing play maintains the evaluation. 6/10 positions had the player's king under immediate threat or in a tactically fragile state, yet the move chosen addressed structural concerns rather than the crisis at hand.

1818.label: The queen (or major piece) captures a peripheral pawn, displacing itself from critical defensive or attacking duties and getting punished by tempo-gaining counterplay.
1818.description: In 10/10 positions, the played move sends the queen (9/10) or rook (1/10) to capture or target material on a distant square — typically b2, c2, c7, b7, a4, or d3 — while abandoning essential responsibilities elsewhere on the board. In 8/10 cases the move is an explicit pawn capture (Qxb2, Qxc2, Qxc7, Qxa4, Qxd3, Qxb7); the remaining 2/10 are queen invasions to d7 that overextend for similar reasons. The refutations in 10/10 positions exploit the displaced piece via tempo-gaining attacks (Rb1, Rac1, Rfb1 chasing the queen), king safety exploitation (Qxe5 with mate threats, Rfb1 with back-rank pressure), or piece trapping (rooks contesting open files against the stranded queen). In 9/10 cases king safety is a critical factor — either the player's own king becomes vulnerable without the queen's defensive coverage, or the opponent's attacking pieces gain free tempi. The average cp_loss of 308 reflects that these are not subtle positional inaccuracies but severe tactical misjudgments where stronger alternatives (attacking moves, development, prophylaxis) existed in every case.

1811.label: The player moves their king (or a key shielding piece) to a square that is immediately or quickly fatal due to open lines controlled by the opponent's pieces.
1811.description: In 8/10 positions the blunder is a direct king move, and in the remaining 2/10 a bishop moves to f8, either exposing the king on an open file or blocking its own escape. The defining feature is that the destination square is fatally covered by the opponent's heavy pieces along open files or ranks. 6/10 positions result in checkmate within 1 move (positions 1, 2, 7, 8) or within 3-5 moves (positions 4, 9), while the other 4 result in catastrophic king exposure enabling forced material wins. Back-rank mate is the single most common motif (explicitly present in 4/10), but the broader pattern encompasses any open-line mate: h-file mates (positions 2, 4), d-file mates (position 8), and diagonal-assisted mates (positions 1, 9). The average cp_loss of 5923 reflects that most of these are checkmate blunders. Critically, in every case only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.1), meaning the positions were already razor-sharp — but the player chose the one move that made the king maximally vulnerable rather than the narrow survival path.

1829.label: A knight delivers a tempting check that accomplishes nothing concrete, leaving the knight misplaced or trapped while the opponent's king safely sidesteps.
1829.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight delivering check that proves counterproductive. In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 8, 9, and partially 10), the knight becomes trapped or stranded on its destination square after the king sidesteps. In 5/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 5, 6, 7), the knight abandons a powerful outpost (f4, c6, f5, c4, c8) for a meaningless check. In 4/10 cases (positions 6, 8, 10, and partially 4), the check actually improves the opponent's king position (e.g., driving it from d3 to the safer c2, or from c1 to the tucked b1). The average cp_loss of 349 reflects these moves converting winning or equal positions into lost ones. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, suggesting these were difficult positions where the flashy knight check provided a psychologically tempting but fatally flawed shortcut past genuine calculation.

1820.label: Non-forcing flank pawn advances (a, b, f, or h files) played when the position demands urgent piece activity or defensive action to address king safety.
1820.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance on one of the four wing files (a-file: 3/10, b-file: 3/10, h-file: 3/10, f-file: 1/10) in positions where immediate tactical or defensive action was required. In 8/10 positions, the player's or opponent's king was critically exposed and the position demanded forcing moves (checks, captures, or piece redeployments). In 7/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating extreme tactical urgency. The average cp_loss of 2833 is catastrophic, with 3/10 positions resulting in immediate forced checkmate. In every case, the best alternatives involved piece activity — rook repositioning, knight maneuvers, or centralizing the queen — rather than static pawn moves. The pawn advances create no threats, address no immediate problems, and surrender the critical tempo that opponents exploit via checks, back-rank invasions, or mating attacks against exposed kings.

1815.label: Non-forcing moves that squander dynamic advantages by prioritizing secondary strategic goals over the most concrete tactical demand of the position.
1815.description: All 10 positions share a consistent pattern: the player chose a move that addresses a secondary concern (king safety, piece repositioning, pawn advance, centralization) while ignoring the single most urgent tactical requirement. 9/10 positions were tagged 'tempo_loss' and 10/10 tagged 'piece_activity' — the played moves uniformly waste critical tempo in positions where concrete action was demanded. In 4/10 cases (Ba6×2, Bc2, Bh6), a piece was moved to a square where it could be immediately captured or where it left a critical piece undefended. In 3/10 cases (Kg8, Kg1, g4), a 'safety-first' repositioning move was played when the position demanded immediate exploitation of the opponent's vulnerability. In 2/10 cases (f5, Qd4), a preparatory/centralizing move was played when a forcing tactical blow was available right now. In 1 case (Qxc3), the wrong capture target was chosen. The average cp_loss of 444 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments of priority, and the average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these were critical moments requiring precision.

1817.label: Quiet queen repositioning moves that abandon a critical tactical function, enabling the opponent to exploit newly undefended resources.
1817.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing queen move (no check, no capture) to a square that appears natural or purposeful but critically disconnects the queen from its most important role in the position. In 7/10 positions, only 1 good move was available, indicating razor-sharp moments requiring precision rather than repositioning. The queen's prior placement (or an alternative square) maintained a tactical thread—either offensive counterplay (positions 1, 4, 7, 8) or defensive control of a key square (positions 6, 9)—that the player failed to recognize. After the passive relocation, 6/10 positions were punished by the queen becoming immediately tactically exploitable (trapped via Rf5+Bh5, attacked via Bg5, forked via Qd5+/Nxb6+, or invaded against via Re3). The average centipawn loss of 301 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but fundamental misreadings of the position's tactical demands. The moves share a common psychological profile: treating a concrete, tactical position as a slow maneuvering game.

1830.label: Advancing the g-pawn (g6 or g3) to kick an enemy Queen off the h-file, but the move creates a fatal weakness or overlooks a more urgent tactical reality.
1830.description: In 10/10 positions, the player advances their g-pawn one square (g7-g6 for Black in 6 positions, g2-g3 for White in 4 positions) specifically to chase an enemy Queen sitting on h5 (all 6 Black cases) or h4 (all 4 White cases). This is the quintessential 'natural-looking defensive move' that backfires catastrophically. The failures split into two sub-patterns: in 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 10), the g-pawn advance fatally weakens the king's pawn shelter — opening the h-file, exposing h7/h2, removing control of f3/f6, or making the g-pawn itself a tactical target for sacrificial captures (Bxg6, Nxg6, Rxf7). In 4/10 positions (4, 5, 7, 9), the queen being chased has a devastating 'escape' that captures an undefended piece or pawn (Qxe4, Qxd4, Qxh7, Qxe5) — the player focused on driving the queen away without noticing it had a productive square to go to. The average cp_loss of 1371 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 3/10 resulting in immediate mate or mate-in-one.

1823.label: A powerfully centralized knight (typically on d4/d5) is traded or moved away for an inferior short-term gain, surrendering its positional dominance.
1823.description: In 9/10 positions, a knight makes a capture that removes it from a dominant central square, and in 7/10 cases specifically the knight sits on d4 or d5 before the blunder (Positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10). The remaining cases involve knights on other strong squares (d3, e4, g6) being misused. In every case, the player is seduced by an immediate tactical reward — a check (5/10), winning material (4/10), or simplification — without recognizing that the knight's positional value on its outpost exceeded the value of the capture. The best moves in 8/10 positions involved maintaining the knight on its dominant square while pursuing alternative plans. The average cp_loss of 1181 reflects that these knight trades routinely dissolve mating attacks (Position 4: mate-in-11 becomes +458), surrender decisive advantages (Position 9: +130 to -207), or throw away winning positions (Position 6: -251 to +92).

1831.label: The Queen greedily captures a Rook that is defended, resulting in an immediate recapture that nets a catastrophic Queen-for-Rook trade.
1831.description: In 10/10 positions, the player's Queen captures an enemy Rook (Qx_), but the Rook is defended by another piece — a second Rook, a Queen, a Knight, a King, or a pawn — which immediately recaptures the Queen. The net result in every case is trading a Queen (~9 points) for a Rook (~5 points), a devastating material loss of roughly 4 pawns. In 4/10 cases the capture came with check (Qxg3+, Qxf8+, Qxf8+, Qxg8+), making the move feel forcing and 'free,' which likely contributed to the miscalculation. In 7/10 positions the recapture was trivially obvious (one clear defender), while in 3/10 multiple pieces could recapture. The average cp_loss of 1239 reflects that these trades are almost always immediately decisive. Only position 10 (Qxg8+) led to forced mate rather than merely a material deficit, as the recapture opened a file for a mating attack.

1821.label: Moving a critically-placed attacking piece to capture material (usually a pawn), only to have it simply recaptured, eliminating the piece's superior positional value.
1821.description: In 10/10 positions, the blundering side moved their strongest or most strategically important piece to make a capture (or forcing move), and the opponent's straightforward recapture eliminated that critical piece from the board. In 7/10 cases, the piece captured was a pawn (h7 three times, f7, g7, b7, g2). In 9/10 positions, the refutation was a simple recapture (Qxh7, Qxf7, Qxe7, Qxg7, Qxg2, Qxb7, etc.). The captured piece was consistently the player's BEST piece: a dominant outpost knight (positions 3, 4, 7 with knights on f6/e5/g5), a bishop on a controlling diagonal (positions 5, 6 with bishops on f6/h6), or the queen itself being traded off (positions 1, 6, 8, 10). The average cp_loss of 1338 reflects the catastrophic nature of voluntarily removing one's own key piece. In 8/10 positions, the blunderer was already winning or equal, making the greedy capture entirely unnecessary.

1826.label: Non-forcing rook repositioning moves that prioritize development over immediate tactical opportunities or critical defensive duties.
1826.description: 10/10 positions feature rook moves to seemingly logical squares (open files, attacking enemy pieces, centralizing) that are actually slow tempo-losers in critical positions. In 5/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 8, 9, and partially 4), the rook move missed an immediate capture of an undefended or vulnerable piece (Rxd5, Qxe5 enabling, Rxd3, Qf3+ combination). In 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 10), the rook move abandoned a critical defensive function—either vacating back-rank coverage (positions 2, 4), removing protection from a key pawn or square (positions 1, 6), or breaking a dominant formation like doubled 7th-rank rooks (position 10). The average cp_loss of 4012 is extreme because 6/10 positions involved forced mates being missed or allowed. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were tactically sharp positions demanding precision rather than 'improving moves.'

1814.label: Moves that capture or attack material when the position demands addressing a more critical tactical or strategic need (perpetual check, checkmate, defensive coordination, maintaining pressure).
1814.description: 8/10 positions feature moves that directly capture material or attack enemy pieces (Qxh7, Qxd8+, Qxb2, Qxd1+, Ra1 targeting Na2, h5 attacking Ng6, Nb5 targeting pawns, Ng5 targeting h7), while the remaining 2/10 (Nf6, Qc7) are superficially active-looking moves that ignore critical positional demands. In 9/10 cases these are mistakes (avg cp_loss 2145), with 7/10 having 'missed_tactic' identified in analysis. The positions demand something non-materialistic: perpetual check (Position 2), defensive coordination (Positions 3, 4, 7), maintaining attacking pressure by keeping the queen on (Position 6), delivering immediate checkmate (Position 9), or defending against checkmate (Position 10). Only 1/10 (Position 1, Ng5) is actually correct, suggesting the feature detects the 'materialistic impulse' pattern regardless of correctness. 6/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating these are narrow tactical moments where the greedy choice fails.

1828.label: Playing a passive king repositioning move (or non-forcing quiet move) when the position demands an immediate tactical response to a concrete hanging piece, fork, or forcing sequence.
1828.description: 7/10 positions feature literal king moves (Kg3, O-O, Kd2, Kh2, Kg3, Kd4, Kf2), while the remaining 3 are similarly quiet, non-forcing moves (Rde8, e6, f3) that share the same error type. In all 10 positions, an immediate tactical demand existed—a hanging piece (6/10), an available fork (3/10), or a time-critical forcing sequence (5/10)—yet the player chose a slow, positionally-motivated move instead. The best moves across all positions were concrete tactical responses: saving a hanging bishop (positions 2, 6), blocking a fork square (positions 1, 4), executing an immediate pawn break (position 5), or developing to cover a critical diagonal (position 10). The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were razor-sharp positions where only precise tactical responses maintained the evaluation. 8/10 moves were played by White, and the blunders span all phases (opening through endgame), suggesting the pattern transcends game stage—it's fundamentally about prioritizing king comfort or preparation over urgent tactical necessity.

1819.label: Playing a natural-looking piece placement or prophylactic move when the position demanded an immediate concrete forcing action (pawn break, active capture, or tempo-gaining check).
1819.description: In 9/10 positions, the player chose a piece move that appeared purposeful—blockading a passed pawn (Ba8, Bb8), pinning (Bg5), attacking a piece (Ne7, Rf7), capturing material (Bxd8, Rxf4), or passive defense (Re6, Nf2)—but missed the position's critical concrete requirement. In 4/10 positions the correct move was a pawn advance or pawn break (g5 in position 3, d3 in position 6, g4 in position 8, fxe4 in position 5). In 3/10 the correct move was an active piece maneuver with immediate tactical purpose (Rxh5, Rf4, Ra6+). The blunders overwhelmingly occurred in endgames (8/10) where passed pawns were a dominant theme (7/10), and tempo was the decisive resource. The average cp_loss of 242 reflects that these positions typically had only 1-2 good moves (average 1.9), meaning the positions demanded precision but the players defaulted to 'natural' or 'logical-looking' moves instead of calculating the forcing lines.
1819.old_chip: Passive piece move over forcing play

1833.label: A rook moves to the 2nd/7th rank pursuing general activity instead of executing a more forcing or concrete continuation.
1833.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the 7th rank from the mover's perspective (2nd rank for Black's Ra2/Rb2/Rd2/Rxa2/Re2, 7th rank for White's Rc7/Rd7/Rh7). In every case, the rook move appears 'active' — targeting pawns, invading the opponent's position — but is actually a non-forcing, slow move that squanders the position's concrete demands. In 7/10 positions, a more forcing alternative existed (captures on e2, checks with Rg7+/Rg8+, pawn pushes like e6 or c5). In 5/10 positions, the rook abandoned a critical defensive or coordination duty on its original square (back-rank defense in positions 2 and 3, mutual rook protection in positions 7 and 9, tactical potential in position 1). The average cp loss of 1228 reflects the catastrophic nature of choosing a 'principled' but slow rook placement over concrete calculation. The pattern represents players defaulting to the heuristic 'rooks belong on the 7th rank' without verifying whether the specific position requires something more urgent.

1825.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) to a seemingly aggressive forward square that is actually tactically unsound, disconnected, or exposed to tempo attacks.
1825.description: 8/10 positions involve queen moves, and 6/10 specifically feature the queen moving to a square on the f-file (Qf2 three times, Qf8, Qxf7, Qf5). In all 10 cases, the piece is repositioned to what appears to be an active, attacking square but actually becomes vulnerable to tempo attacks, disconnected from critical coordination, or simply exposed. The correct moves were overwhelmingly concrete tactical operations: captures of hanging pieces (fxg4 in Position 3), tempo-gaining attacks (Ng4 in Position 4, Ne5 in Position 7, Nf6 in Position 9, Nd4 in Position 10), forcing infiltrations (Rb1 in Position 1, Qa8 in Position 6), or central pawn breaks (e5 in Position 2). The blundered moves instead chose 'looks aggressive' piece placements that ignored the position's tactical demands. 10/10 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.3), indicating critical moments requiring precision rather than general improvement moves.

1835.label: Giving a reflexive queen check that wastes tempo, displaces the queen from an optimal position, or allows the opponent's king to improve or find defensive resources.
1835.description: 10/10 positions feature a Queen delivering check, and 9/10 of these checks are mistakes (the one exception, Position 8, lost 0cp). The core pattern is choosing a flashy queen check over a quieter but vastly superior alternative. In 7/10 positions, the check drives the opponent's king to a safer or more centralized square (Kxc8 creating a fortress, Kf2 centralizing, Kh2 finding shelter, Kh3 escaping mating nets). In 6/10 cases, the queen moves to a peripheral square (a1, a2, b2, b4, c1) abandoning a powerful central post. In 3/10 positions, the check allows a critical defensive interposition or queen trade that dissolves the attacker's advantage. The average cp_loss of 4801 is extreme, with 5/10 positions involving the loss of a forced checkmate. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow tactical moments demanding precision rather than reflexive forcing moves. The analyses repeatedly cite 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif (appearing in 8/10 positions).

1836.label: An aggressive knight move (capture or centralization) ignores that another piece is left en prise to a simple pawn capture.
1836.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight making an ambitious move — either capturing a pawn (7/10: Nxd4, Nxg5) or jumping to a strong outpost (3/10: Ne5, Nd5, Nb5, Ng4) — while leaving another friendly piece hanging to a trivial one-move pawn capture. In 5/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 7, 8), the knight moves away from a bishop already attacked by a pawn (Bg5 attacked by ...h6 in positions 4, 7, 8; Bg3 by ...h4 in position 1; Bc4 by ...b5 in position 3), and the knight was either the direct defender or its departure removes tactical coordination. In 4/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 10), the Nc6 captures the d4 pawn while leaving either a bishop on d6 or knight on f6 exposed to exf6 or cxd6. In position 9, Ng4 leaves the Nb4 hanging to axb4. The refutation in every case is the simple pawn capture of the abandoned piece. 8/10 occurred in the opening phase with at least one king uncastled, and the average cp_loss of 315 reflects that the punishment is typically winning a full minor piece for a pawn.
1836.old_chip: Knight ignores piece hanging to pawn

1813.label: Playing natural-looking developing or repositioning moves when the position demands an immediate forcing continuation (check, capture, or sacrifice).
1813.description: 8/10 positions show the player choosing a quiet, 'improving' move (typically a minor piece development or repositioning) when a concrete forcing move was available and necessary. In 6/10 positions, the move played was specifically a minor piece development (Bd8, Nc3, Bd7, Ng5, Nc6, Bf5) to a seemingly natural square. In at least 5/10 positions, the best available move was a check or capture with check (Qh4+, Qf1+, Nxf3+, Qxe4+, b4 attacking a piece). The 2 positions with near-zero cp_loss (positions 1 and 5) are notably the ones where the player DID play the forcing move (a capture and a capture-with-check respectively), confirming the feature fires on critical tactical moments. The average number of good moves was only 2.0, with 5/10 positions having exactly 1 good move, indicating narrow critical moments. 9/10 moves were by Black, suggesting the pattern may relate to the defending side's tendency to play 'normal' moves when under pressure instead of finding the one saving/winning tactical shot.

1832.label: Moving a piece to a peripheral or back-rank square in a slow, non-forcing way when the position demands immediate tactical action or maintaining a critical post.
1832.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing repositioning move that places a piece on an edge square (a-file, b-file, or back rank) when the position demanded urgent, forcing play. 9/10 moves land on the first two files (a or b) or the back rank (Ra1×2, Rh1, Qb7, Rc8, Rb8, Bb7, Qb3, Qd7, Qa7). In every case, the player had concrete tactical alternatives available — checks, captures, or forcing moves — that maintained their advantage (avg cp_loss: 1351). 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision. The consistent thread is abandoning a critical file or defensive post: pieces leave the e-file (positions 1, 3, 5), abandon the c-file where mating attacks existed (position 6), withdraw from defensive posts protecting the king (positions 4, 9, 10), or sidestep forcing knight tactics (positions 2, 8). 8/10 are middlegame positions where tempo is most valuable, and all 10 represent the choice of a 'general improvement' move over concrete calculation.

1827.label: A piece (usually a rook) is moved to an apparently active square that is directly controlled by an enemy piece, most commonly a knight, resulting in immediate material loss.
1827.description: The strongest signal in this feature is rooks being placed on squares directly attacked by enemy knights: 5/10 positions (Rb8 attacked by Nd7, Rc7+ attacked by Nd5, Rh5 attacked by Nf6, Rh6 attacked by Nf5, Rd4 attacked by Nc6) show this exact pattern where the rook is immediately capturable for free. Expanding slightly, 7/10 positions involve rook moves that look superficially active (penetrating to the 7th rank, centralizing, occupying open files) but overlook a basic one-move tactical refutation. The remaining 3/10 positions (e3, Bd1, Kh2) share the broader theme of making a 'purposeful-looking' move that ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability, resulting in material loss or a devastating combination. The average cp_loss of 2199 is extremely high, and the average of only 2.0 good moves available suggests these are positions where the critical path was narrow, yet the chosen move was an elementary piece-safety oversight rather than a deep calculation error. In all 10 positions, the player prioritized an active concept (rook to 7th rank, piece centralization, pawn advance) over basic board vision regarding which squares the opponent controls.

1839.label: Playing a quiet one-square rook pawn advance (a3/a6/h3/h6) as false prophylaxis when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1839.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-step rook pawn advance (h3 in 3, a3 in 3, a6 in 2, h6 in 2) played with prophylactic intent — trying to prevent an opponent's advance or piece incursion on the rim. In every case, the position demanded immediate tactical or dynamic action instead: 7/10 had a specific tactic available (Nxf2, Qf5, Qxc6+, Qxh5, cxd4, d4, Bb4), while 3/10 required urgent piece improvement or active pawn breaks. The average cp_loss was 266 with only 1.5 good moves available on average, confirming these were critical decision points requiring precision. In 4/10 positions, the prophylactic move actually enabled the very plan it tried to prevent (h3 not stopping ...h4, a6 creating a hook for a5-b5). In 6/10 positions involving dynamic pawn races (opposite-side castling or pawn storms), the tempo loss was particularly devastating because the opponent used the free move to consolidate or accelerate their own attack.

1838.label: Defensive king moves in theoretically lost King+Pawn vs King endgames where the lone king attempts to stop an unstoppable passed pawn.
1838.description: All 10/10 positions are pure King+Pawn vs lone King endgames where the side making the move is the losing/defending side trying to intercept or blockade a single passed pawn near promotion. In every case, the defending king moves toward the pawn or its promotion path (Kf6 toward g7, Ke6 in front of f6, Kf4 in front of e4, Kh5 toward g5, etc.). 7/10 positions show 0 cp_loss because the position is already theoretically lost regardless of move choice — all king moves are equally futile. The 3/10 positions with massive cp_loss (9440-9458) represent cases where the king moved too close to the promotion square, walking into an immediate mating net after promotion (positions 2, 5) or allowing promotion with check (position 4). The evaluations cluster tightly around ±530-600cp in the non-blunder cases, confirming these are positions of identical strategic character: hopelessly lost defensive struggles.

1834.label: A materialistic capture (usually with a knight) that grabs material without giving check, when a more forcing alternative—often a sacrifice with check on the same or nearby square—was available.
1834.description: 10/10 positions involve a capture that wins material but surrenders the initiative. 8/10 are knight captures specifically (Nxh7, Nh2, Nxh2, Nxg7, Nxh7, Nxd2, Nxg2, Nxg5), while 2/10 are pawn captures (hxg6, gxh5) following the same logic. In 4/10 positions (4, 7, 9, 10), the correct move was to capture on the SAME square with a DIFFERENT piece that delivers check (Rxg6+, Rxh5+, Bxg2+, Rxg5+). In 4/10 positions (1, 2, 5, 6), a knight was removed from a dominant outpost (g5, g4, f5) to grab material, dissolving a powerful attacking formation. In 2/10 positions (3, 8), the capture ignored a more urgent threat (back-rank vulnerability, h-file rook infiltration). 9/10 captures land on kingside squares (g/h files). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, 'missed_tactic' in 9/10, and 'king_safety' in 10/10.
