The average cp_loss is massive (3230), reflecting how giving up a single tempo in a sharp attacking position collapses the entire advantage.

1824.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move in a position with very few acceptable options, fatally ignoring the single concrete requirement of the position.
1824.description: All 10 positions share an extremely narrow margin for error (average 1.6 good moves available) combined with a catastrophic average loss of 4715 centipawns. In 8/10 positions, the player was already in a difficult or losing position where only 1-2 moves avoided disaster. The blunder moves all appear purposeful on the surface — blockading (Be7, Qa1), retreating defensively (Qd8, Bd3), grabbing material (Qxc2), infiltrating (Qc7), attacking (Qf6, Qf4), giving checks (Qd1+), or challenging pawns (f6) — yet each fatally ignores the position's single most urgent concrete demand. In 4/10 cases the correct move was a simplifying queen exchange (positions 7, 9, 10, and partially 4). In 3/10 cases the correct move required counterplay or piece activation rather than passive defense (positions 1, 3, 8). In 2/10 cases the correct move was a waiting/maintaining move (positions 2, 6). The refutations are diverse (back-rank mates, knight forks, pawn advances winning pieces, king infiltrations, queen invasions), confirming that the shared pattern is not the tactical motif that punishes but rather the TYPE of error: choosing a plausible alternative in a position demanding surgical precision.

1837.label: Advancing a pawn (usually on the flank) in an endgame when king centralization or maintaining tension was the priority.
1837.description: 9/10 positions are endgames with exposed kings and pawn tension, where the player commits a pawn advance instead of improving king activity. 8/10 moves are pawn pushes (h5×3, h4×2, a5, g6, f3, c4), and the remaining move (Kf3) is a king lunge toward a flank pawn rather than centralization. 7/10 of the pawn advances target wing files (a, g, or h). In at least 7/10 cases, the top engine recommendation was a king move (Kf7, Kf3, Kc6, Kf5, Kh7, Kd5, Kc2) that maintained flexibility. The common punishment mechanism is that the premature advance either resolves tension favorably for the opponent (3/10 allow captures with check or tempo gain), creates a fixed target (4/10), removes a critical structural barrier (2/10 - c4 removing blockade, h4 opening lines), or allows the opponent to simply ignore it and centralize (2/10 - g6 and h5 where Ke5 bypasses). Average cp_loss of 1013 reflects several catastrophic cases where the commitment was fatal.

1840.label: Voluntarily capturing/exchanging a well-placed piece (almost always a bishop) when maintaining it or finding a stronger alternative would preserve a significant advantage.
1840.description: 8/10 positions feature bishop captures (Bx moves), and 10/10 are voluntary exchanges where the player trades away their most active or positionally important piece. In 7/10 cases, the captured piece was the player's strongest positional asset: a dominant centralized bishop (positions 2, 5, 9), a key defensive piece (positions 1, 7), or a fianchettoed bishop controlling a critical diagonal (positions 5, 8). In 6/10 positions, the analyses explicitly describe the error as 'trading your best-placed piece' or 'surrendering' a dominant piece without compensation. The missed alternatives consistently involve either maintaining the strong piece while improving other pieces (positions 2, 4, 9), finding devastating tactical blows like forks or queen-winning combinations (positions 6, 8), or properly preparing the exchange with an intermediate move first (positions 2, 7, 10). The average cp_loss of 262 reflects how much positional pressure evaporates when the linchpin piece is voluntarily removed.

1841.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing flank pawn move in a position demanding immediate tactical action, surrendering a critical tempo.
1841.description: 8/10 positions feature a slow, non-forcing move (predominantly quiet a-file or b-file pawn pushes) played when the position urgently demanded concrete tactical action. Specifically, 6/10 moves are literal rim/flank pawn advances (a6 appears 3 times, b5 once, b4 once, h3 once), while 2 more are non-threatening piece relocations (Qe6 retreating, Ba4 premature). The tactical motif tagged in 8/10 positions is 'tempo_loss.' In each case, the opponent used the gifted tempo to either consolidate a defense that was previously impossible (positions 3, 6, 10), launch a counterattack (positions 1, 4, 5), or exploit a newly created weakness (positions 2, 7). The average cp_loss of 317 reflects catastrophic consequences. Position 9 (axb4, 0 cp loss) is an outlier that was actually the best move. Position 8 (Re5) is a related but distinct error—placing a piece on an undefended square rather than maintaining its dominant position.

1848.label: The king moves forward or toward the center into an exposed square on open lines, when retreating to a safer back-rank or corner square was required.
1848.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move that advances the monarch forward or centrally into an exposed position, when the correct move was to retreat or stay back. In 9/10 cases, the best move was a king retreat (Kc3, Kh4, Kf8, Ke7, Kh7, Kd6, Kh1, Kg8, Kd1) or in 1/10 a defensive piece move (Be2). The blundered king moves consistently land on squares intersecting open files (d-file in positions 1,3,4,7; f-file in positions 2,5,8) or exposed diagonals, where the opponent's queen and/or rook can deliver devastating check sequences. The average cp_loss of 3938 is extreme, with 5/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate. In every case, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.0), indicating razor-thin defensive margins where the natural-looking centralizing king move was always the fatal choice.

1822.label: Playing natural-looking centralizing or activating moves in open positions with exposed kings, instead of executing the most forcing tactical continuation.
1822.description: 8/10 positions feature mutually exposed kings with weak pawn shields in open or semi-open positions. The moves played are overwhelmingly 'active-looking' — rooks to the 7th rank or central files (5/10), queens to central squares like d3/d4/c4 (3/10), and kings centralizing to d4/d5 (2/10). In the 7 positions where these are genuine mistakes (avg cp_loss ~337 excluding the 9221 outlier), the best move was always a more FORCING continuation: a tactical shot (Bc6+ skewer in P1), an immediate check leading to mate (Rb1+ in P5), a pawn capture resolving tension (hxg5 in P7), or a defensive priority move (Kc8 in P8, Be2 in P10). The 3 non-mistakes (P4, P6, P9) fired because they share the same geometric profile — piece/king to central squares in exposed-king positions — but happened to also be the forcing move. The consistent error is prioritizing general positional principles (centralize, activate, occupy open files) over concrete tactical requirements that the specific position demands.

1845.label: Bishop repositions from a critically active square to one vulnerable to a tempo-gaining pawn advance, abandoning its key tactical or positional duty.
1845.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop non-capture repositioning move that simultaneously abandons a critical function and lands on a square immediately punishable by a pawn advance. In 6/10 positions (1,2,5,8,9,10), the bishop moves to the h-file (Bh5 or Bh4), where a g-pawn advance (g4 or g5) attacks it with tempo—specifically, Bg4→Bh5 allowing g4 appears in 3/10 positions, and Bg5→Bh4 allowing ...g5 appears in 3/10 positions. In 3/10 positions (3,4,6), the bishop vacates a blockading square (controlling d6, blocking the d-file), enabling a devastating pawn advance or piece invasion. In 1/10 (position 7), the bishop moves to c4 where b3 attacks it. In 9/10 cases, a concrete tactical blow was available instead (captures, forks, or forcing sequences exploiting the very pressure the bishop was exerting). The average cp_loss of 1206 reflects that these moves consistently transform winning or equal positions into losing ones.

1844.label: A rook moves to an apparently active square but is non-forcing, missing an immediately decisive tactical continuation.
1844.description: All 10/10 positions involve rook moves to squares that appear active or aggressive (open files, attacking ranks, doubling positions) but fail to deliver the critical blow. In 7/10 positions, a forcing move (check or capture) was available that would have maintained a forced mate or vastly superior outcome. In 5/10 cases, the correct move was the SAME rook going one square further with check (R8h3+ not R8h4, Rg8+ not Rg4) or a different forcing piece move entirely (Nc5+, Ke6, e5). The average cp_loss of 5694 is enormous, with 6/10 positions involving missed forced checkmates. The rook consistently lands on a 'preparatory' square—positioning for a future threat—when the position demanded immediate execution. In 4/10 cases the rook's landing square was directly punished (captured on g7, attacked by Ke4, back rank abandoned), while in the others it simply gave the opponent one critical tempo to escape or reorganize.

1847.label: An aggressive central or kingside pawn advance that ignores a more pressing tactical or positional obligation in the position.
1847.description: All 10/10 positions feature an aggressive pawn advance (d4, e4, f5, g4, d5, e5) that prioritizes gaining space or attacking enemy pieces over addressing a critical immediate obligation. In 10/10 cases, the correct move involved either a piece move, a capture, castling, or prophylaxis rather than a pawn push. The ignored obligations include: unresolved piece safety (3/10 had hanging or threatened pieces — positions 3, 7, 10), king safety requiring castling (3/10 — positions 4, 7, 9), exploiting or resolving a pin/tension (2/10 — positions 2, 5), prophylactic necessity (1/10 — position 1), and the need for development over aggression (1/10 — position 6). The average cp_loss of 281 and only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where the allure of a space-gaining pawn push masks a narrow correct path. The refutations typically involve simple captures of now-undefended material, checks along newly opened lines, or the opponent safely neutralizing the position that the pawn push was supposed to prevent.

1851.label: A bishop captures material on an edge or corner square, abandoning its defensive post or becoming stranded far from the critical action.
1851.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing material (pawns or pieces) on rim/corner squares (a2, a8, b2, b7, c7, g2, h7, h8). The captures target the absolute edge of the board — 9/10 land on the a/b or g/h files, with 6/10 on corner-adjacent squares (a2, a8, h7, h8, g2). In every case, the bishop's journey to the periphery creates a devastating positional cost: in 6/10 positions, the bishop abandons a critical defensive function (guarding key squares like e1, f6, c3, or the kingside), enabling opponent checks, invasions, or even mate. In 4/10 positions, the bishop becomes trapped or stranded on the rim (particularly a2 and h7), losing multiple tempi to recover. The average cp_loss of 1238 reflects catastrophic consequences — including one instant checkmate (Bxc7 allowing Qe1#). All positions occurred in the middlegame where piece coordination and king safety outweigh a single pawn's value.

1850.label: Moving a second rook to join the first on the same rank or file, creating superficially impressive but tactically hollow doubled rooks while abandoning a critical defensive duty.
1850.description: All 10/10 positions show exactly the same structural move: the player already has one rook on a key rank or file and commits the second rook to join it, attempting to 'double rooks.' In 8/10 cases, this is doubling on the 2nd/7th rank (Rcc2 ×4, Rcc7, Rdd2, Rdd7, Rff7), while 2/10 double on the h-file (Rdh1, Rfh3). In every case, the analyses explicitly state that the moved rook was performing a hidden defensive function on its original square—guarding the back rank (positions 4, 10), defending a piece or pawn (positions 3, 5, 7, 9), controlling a critical file (position 2), or providing flexible counterplay options (positions 1, 6, 8). The doubled rooks consistently create no new concrete threats that the single rook didn't already produce, because the key targets are already adequately defended. The average cp_loss of 2000 (including two forced mates) demonstrates how catastrophic this pattern is. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points demanding precision rather than 'natural-looking' moves.

1849.label: Developing a bishop to attack the opponent's queen when a much stronger concrete tactical move exists, resulting in tempo loss as the queen simply sidesteps.
1849.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to the 4th or 5th rank on a wing file (Bg5 x4, Bg4 x5, Bb5 x1) with the apparent intent of targeting the opponent's queen. In 9/10 cases, the queen easily sidesteps the bishop's 'attack' to an equal or superior square, rendering the bishop move a pure tempo loss. The missed best moves were overwhelmingly knight-based: 7/10 positions had a knight move as the strongest alternative (Nxd4, Nd5, Nxe4, Nd4, Ne5, Nxe5), typically a capture or a leap to a dominant central outpost with multiple tactical threats. The remaining 3 missed a concrete capture (Bxb2, hxg5) or pawn advance (d4). The average cp_loss of 328 reflects that these superficially active bishop moves consistently squander large advantages or convert winning positions into equal ones. All positions shared the characteristic that the bishop's target (the queen) had an obvious safe retreat, making the 'attacking' move strategically pointless.

1846.label: Moving a rook (or king near a rook) to a seemingly active square where an opponent's forcing check immediately wins it.
1846.description: 9/10 positions feature a rook being moved to a square that appears purposeful — contesting a file, attacking a piece, or centralizing — but where it becomes tactically indefensible because the opponent can deliver check (via discovered attack, knight fork, or check sequence) and then capture the rook on the next move. In 5/10 cases the mechanism is a discovered attack (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 10) where a piece moves with check while uncovering an attack on the rook along a rank or file. In 2/10 cases (positions 4, 7) it's a knight fork delivering check while simultaneously attacking the newly-placed rook. In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 9) it's a sacrifice or check sequence that leaves the rook hanging. Position 8 is the loosest fit (missed mate-in-one for a rook move), but even there the rook goes to a square where it's subsequently captured. The consistent thread across all 10: the player makes a natural-looking rook move that ignores the opponent's ability to deliver a forcing intermediate check that leaves the rook undefended and lost.

1843.label: Playing an aggressive or improving move that ignores a critical tactical obligation, typically leaving one's own piece undefended or missing a free capture.
1843.description: In 8/10 positions, the played move directly created or ignored a hanging piece situation: Position 1 (Qb3+ left Bd3 undefended), Position 2 (Ba5 abandoned defense of e7), Position 3 (c3 ignored queen hanging on d1), Position 4 (f6 left queen fatally exposed on e-file), Position 5 (Bb2 left king vulnerable and bishop itself became a target), Position 6 (a5 ignored a free capture of Black's undefended bishop), Position 8 (Qa5 left Be7 hanging), and Position 10 (Ng5 left f4 pawn hanging with check). All 10 moves share the characteristic of looking purposeful—giving check, repositioning pieces, advancing pawns, attacking enemy pieces—while catastrophically failing to address the most urgent tactical reality in the position. The average centipawn loss of 312 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but concrete tactical oversights. 7/10 positions had 'missed_tactic' tagged, and 6/10 specifically featured 'hanging_piece' as the tactical motif. The best moves in these positions were typically defensive or precise tactical responses (blocking a diagonal, moving the king to safety, capturing free material) rather than the flashy improving moves chosen.

1842.label: Playing a natural-looking developing move to e2 or e7 with the wrong piece, ignoring an urgent tactical demand that required a different piece on that square or a completely different response.
1842.description: 7/10 positions involve a piece being placed on the e2 square (White) or e7 square (Black) — the 'default' development squares in the opening. Strikingly, in 5/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 9), the correct move was to place a DIFFERENT piece on the exact same square: the player chose Be2 when Qe2 was needed (pos 1), Be7 when Qe7 was needed (pos 2, 8, 9), or Qe2 when Be2 was needed (pos 4). Position 3 is the inverse (Qe7 played, Be7 second-best). Position 5 sends a knight to e2 that blocks the bishop's natural path there. The remaining 3/10 positions (Bd7, b5, b4) share the broader pattern of generic-looking developing or space-gaining moves that ignore concrete tactical urgency. All 10 positions featured immediate hanging material or tactical shots (forks, undefended rooks) that the 'autopilot' move failed to address. 9/10 were opening positions with kings still in the center.

1852.label: King moves that worsen the monarch's safety, often walking into mating nets, checks, or abandoning critical defensive duties when a non-king resource was required.
1852.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves as the blunder, with the king relocating to a square where it becomes more tactically vulnerable. In 3/10 positions (1, 2, 8), the king walks directly into a forced checkmate (cp_loss 8896-9235). In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 8, 9), the best move was NOT a king move at all but rather a piece sacrifice or capture (Re3 exchange sac, Rxh3 eliminating attacker, Qxf6 desperate queen sacrifice, Bxd6 capturing the dangerous piece), meaning the player reflexively moved the king when creative non-king solutions were required. In 3/10 positions (1, 6, 10), the best move was a king move to a DIFFERENT square, showing the player chose the wrong destination. The average cp_loss of 2767 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirm these are critical moments where the king's position was already precarious and demanded precise calculation rather than instinctive relocation.

1855.label: Moving a rook to challenge an opponent's piece on an open file when the position demands an urgent tactical action instead.
1855.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to occupy or contest an open file — a natural-looking positional move that follows the general principle of 'rooks belong on open files.' In 9/10 cases, the rook specifically moves to directly confront an opposing rook on the same file or rank (Ra1 vs rook on a2, Re7 vs rook on f7, Rg2 vs rook on g6/g3, Rc2 vs rook on c3, Rd7 vs rook on d8, Rc8 vs rook on c1, Rfd1 vs rook on d2, Rd6 vs rook on d3). However, in every case, the position demands something far more urgent: 3/10 positions had hanging pieces to capture (positions 8, 9, 10), 3/10 had critical defensive squares being abandoned (positions 2, 3, 7), 2/10 allowed losing exchanges or forks (positions 4, 5), and 2/10 ignored existential king safety threats (positions 1, 6). The average cp_loss of 2203 is enormous, with 3/10 resulting in immediate mate or near-mate. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were sharp positions requiring precise calculation rather than routine development.

1854.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move when an immediate tactical opportunity (capture, check, or concrete threat) demands action.
1854.description: 10/10 positions featured a clearly available forcing move (capture, check, or concrete threat) that the player missed in favor of a quiet, non-forcing move. The missed tactics include: hanging piece captures (positions 1, 8), knight forks winning the queen (positions 2, 5), concrete pawn breaks exploiting uncastled kings or piece vulnerabilities (positions 3, 6), passed pawn advances creating counterplay (position 7), a forcing mating combination (position 10), and positional untangling to avoid tactical exposure (position 9). Only 1/10 moves played was a check (Re5+ in position 4), but even that was a premature forcing move that functioned as a tempo loss. The average number of good moves available was just 1.7, confirming these were sharp, critical moments with narrow correct paths. The average cp_loss of 1149 reflects the catastrophic cost of defaulting to 'natural-looking' quiet play when concrete calculation was required.

1856.label: Capturing peripheral material (usually a bishop) with a powerfully-placed knight instead of exploiting its dominant position for a stronger tactical continuation.
1856.description: 7/10 positions feature knight moves, and 6/10 specifically involve a knight capturing a relatively passive piece (usually a bishop on the rim: a6, b7, b7, g7, h7, f2) when the knight had a far stronger tactical use from its current or a nearby square. In Position 1, the c7-knight captures on a6 instead of supporting Rd5+ for forced mate. In Positions 5 and 7, the c5-knight captures the b7-bishop instead of playing Nd7 (a devastating fork). In Position 9, Nxh7 prematurely executes a capture when Qh5 maintained crushing threats. In Position 10, the centralized e4-knight trades itself for a defensive bishop instead of enabling Qf4's crushing attack. The remaining positions extend the pattern to non-knight material grabs (exd1=Q wrong promotion order, fxg7 exchanging a powerful pawn). The average cp_loss of ~2978 reflects that these 'obvious' captures consistently miss forced mates, forks, or winning attacks. 9/10 positions had only 1 good move available, showing how critical these moments were.

1859.label: Playing a slow, non-urgent wing pawn advance while an immediate tactical emergency (usually a hanging piece) demands attention.
1859.description: All 9/9 positions feature a non-capturing pawn advance on a wing file (a, b, c, or h) played when the position contains a screaming tactical emergency. In 7/9 positions, the player's own piece is directly en prise to a simple one-move capture (bishops on g5, c5, d4, d3; knights on f6; queens on f6 and d7). In 2/9 positions (both h4), the player missed a decisive winning combination that was immediately available (Greek Gift Bxh7+ or Qh6 threatening mate). The pawn moves themselves are all positionally reasonable ideas in a vacuum—a6 to kick a bishop (3 positions), a3 to support b4, h4 to open a file, b5 for queenside space, c3 to bolster the center—but each is catastrophically mistimed because a one-move tactical threat makes them unplayable. The average cp_loss is 513, reflecting that most positions involve losing a full piece or queen.

1858.label: Queen repositions to a seemingly active square (usually queenside b/c-file) while abandoning a critical defensive duty, enabling immediate tactical punishment.
1858.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen move that relocates to what appears to be an active or attacking square while silently abandoning a crucial defensive function. In 8/10 cases the queen moves to the b-file or c-file (Qb3×2, Qb6×2, Qc2×2, Qc4, Qc6), targeting pawns like b7 or aiming for central/queenside activity. The remaining 2 moves (Qd5, Qf4+) similarly relocate the queen to seemingly strong squares that miss the actual positional requirement. The common thread is that the queen was previously covering something essential—a piece (e7 bishop in position 8, f4 pawn in position 7, e2 bishop in position 1), an invasion square (c8 in position 3, e1 in position 2), or holding the ability to force simplification (queen trade in position 10). The average cp_loss of 294 reflects how immediately and severely these moves are punished. In 7/10 positions the queen's destination square is also tactically vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks (Nd4 hitting Qc2/Qb3, c6 hitting Qc4, Ba5 hitting Qb6), compounding the error with additional tempo loss.

1860.label: Voluntarily relocating a knight from a critical square where it restricts the enemy king or anchors a winning attack, to an apparently active but functionally inferior square.
1860.description: In 10/10 positions, the player moved a knight that was already optimally placed — typically adjacent to or restricting the enemy king — to a different square that appeared active but dismantled the position's tactical foundation. In 8/10 cases, the knight was directly restricting the enemy king's escape squares or supporting a mating net (e.g., Nf7 covering g5/h6/e5, Ne6 covering c7/d8/f8/g7, Nf2 threatening the king on g3, Nb7 paralyzing the king on b8/c7). The destination squares often looked centralized or aggressive (e4, e5, g5, c5) but failed to maintain the critical restrictive function. In 7/10 positions, the blunder converted a forced or near-forced mate into merely a winning or even losing position. The average cp_loss of 4909 reflects the catastrophic nature of releasing a trapped king. Only 1/10 positions (Ne4, Position 4) was a trivial error; the remaining 9 were devastating.

1853.label: The king (or piece) retreats to the player's own back rank (1st/8th) in positions where king activity or forward positioning is critical.
1853.description: 8/10 moves are king moves directly to the 1st or 8th rank (Kd8, Kg8, Kg1, Ke8, Kd1, Ke1, Kf1, and Kg2 to the 2nd rank). 1/10 is a queen retreat to the 8th rank (Qc8). The outlier is f3, a passive pawn move. 9/10 positions feature evaluations of approximately ±500cp or more, indicating heavily one-sided positions where the outcome is essentially decided. 7/10 positions are endgames (mostly king-and-pawn) where king advancement is the primary strategic imperative. The cp_loss varies enormously: 5/10 positions have near-zero loss (the back-rank retreat is one of several equivalent moves in a decided position), while the remaining positions show catastrophic losses (102-9570cp) where the retreat enables checks, leaves pieces hanging, or wastes critical tempo. The feature appears to detect the geometric act of king-to-back-rank movement in lopsided positions regardless of whether the move is actually a mistake.

1862.label: Knight aggressively enters enemy territory (usually capturing) but lands on a square where it is immediately captured or won, resulting in material loss.
1862.description: 10/10 positions feature a knight making an aggressive forward move into the opponent's position. 7/10 involve the knight capturing a pawn or piece (Nxf2, Nxh4, Nfxd4, Ncxe5, Nxe5 ×3), while 3/10 are non-capturing aggressive lunges (Ne6, Nc4, Ng5). In all cases, the knight lands on a square where it is insufficiently defended. In 8/10 positions, the primary refutation is simply capturing the knight directly (Nxe6, Rxf2, Bxc4, Rxh4, Nexd4, Nxe5 ×3). In 2/10 cases (Ng5, Ncxe5), the refutation is ...f6, a pawn advance that attacks the knight while simultaneously hitting a second piece. The average cp_loss of 287 reflects that these moves typically lose approximately a full minor piece worth of material. 7/10 occur in the opening phase, suggesting the pattern involves premature aggression before proper development or piece coordination is established.

1857.label: Playing a pawn advance or piece development instead of the required king relocation when the king is dangerously exposed.
1857.description: In 10/10 positions, the player's king was exposed or vulnerable (explicitly noted in position features). In 8/10 positions, the single best move was a king retreat to safety (Kh6, Kf7, Kd1, Kg2, Kd8, Kd4, etc.), yet the player chose a 'constructive' pawn advance (7/10: b4, f5, f4, g4, e4, c6, d6) or piece development (3/10: Be7, Be2, Bg7) instead. In 6/10 positions, the pawn/piece move directly enabled a capture or recapture WITH CHECK against the exposed king (Rc3+, Qxf5+, Rxe7+, Qxe2#, gxf4+, Qxg4#, dxc6+). The average cp_loss of 5638 reflects that 7/10 positions resulted in immediate forced mate or near-mate. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical moments demanding the single correct defensive response.

1867.label: Advancing a kingside pawn (f4/g4/g5) that was serving as critical king shelter, fatally exposing the king to tactical exploitation.
1867.description: 9/10 positions feature a kingside pawn advance (f4 or g4/g5) where the moved pawn was part of the king's defensive infrastructure. In 8/10 cases the king sits on g1, g2, or h1, relying on the f2 and/or g2 pawns as a shield. The advance removes the pawn from its defensive post, opening critical lines (second rank, diagonals, or files) toward the king. In 5/10 positions the refutation involves an immediate check or invasion on the newly exposed rank/diagonal (Rc2+, Qe3+, Be4, Rb1+). In 4/10 positions the advance creates weak squares that enemy pieces exploit (e3 fork, rook penetration). The one outlier (b4) still fits the broader pattern of a premature pawn push before pieces are properly activated. All best alternatives in these positions prioritize piece repositioning, king activation, or prophylaxis over pawn commitments—the average number of good moves available was only 2.3, yet players chose the weakening advance instead.

1870.label: Playing a prophylactic h-pawn advance (h3/h6) for king safety when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1870.description: 10/10 positions feature an h-pawn advance (h3 for White in 5 cases, h6 for Black in 4 cases, h5 in 1 case) intended as a prophylactic 'luft' move for the castled king. In every single case, the position contained an urgent tactical demand that the h-pawn move completely ignored: 4/10 involved hanging or attacked pieces requiring immediate relocation, 3/10 involved winning material or exploiting a concrete tactical opportunity, 2/10 involved preventing a devastating opponent piece jump (Nf4, Bc3 fork), and 1/10 allowed immediate checkmate. The average cp_loss of 1255 is catastrophic, and the average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these were sharp positions requiring precise calculation, not quiet positions suitable for prophylaxis. In 10/10 cases the 'tempo_loss' tactical motif was identified as primary, and all analyses cite the same root cause: wasting a critical tempo on a non-urgent pawn move while an immediate tactical problem went unaddressed.

1866.label: Moving a pawn or queen to f6 (or f3 as White) in the opening while the king remains uncastled, fatally weakening the light-square diagonal to the king.
1866.description: All 10 positions feature a move to the f6 square (Black) or f3 square (White) during the opening phase with the king still in the center. 7/10 are f-pawn advances (6x ...f6, 1x f3) that critically weaken the diagonal leading to the uncastled king (e8-h5 for Black, e1-a6 for White). In 6/10 positions, the direct punishment involves Qh5+ exploiting the newly opened diagonal after ...f6, often combined with devastating piece sacrifices on g6. The remaining 3/10 are queen moves to f6/f3 that either leave the d5 pawn undefended (2 cases of Qf6 allowing Qxd5) or block the knight's natural development to f3 (1 case of Qf3). In every single case (10/10), both kings remain uncastled or the moving side's king is uncastled. The average cp_loss of 296 reflects the catastrophic nature of these weakening moves. 8/10 positions had 2-3 good alternatives available, typically natural developing moves (Nf6, Nd7, Bd6) that would have maintained equality.

1865.label: Advancing or promoting a passed pawn immediately without first preparing the tactical prerequisites (removing defenders, correct move order, or maintaining pawn coordination).
1865.description: All 10/10 positions involve either a direct pawn promotion (6/10: dxe8=R+, g8=Q+ ×2, d8=Q, b8=Q, g1=Q) or a pawn advance to the penultimate rank threatening promotion (4/10: h7, a3, c2, h2+). The mistakes (8/10 with cp_loss > 0, avg ~1500cp for those) share a common tactical failure: the player rushes the promotion without first neutralizing the defender that controls the promotion square or captures the promoted piece. In positions 4, 6, and 9, a knight directly captures the newly promoted queen. In positions 1 and 2, the correct move order involves an intermediate rook move before promoting. In position 5, the promotion happens on the wrong square (d8 instead of capturing on c8). In positions 7 and 8, advancing the pawn one square closer to promotion allows immediate capture by a piece the player should have deflected first. Only 2/10 positions (3 and 10) show 0cp loss where the promotion/advance was actually correct, suggesting the feature identifies the decision point of 'promote now vs. prepare first' rather than exclusively bad moves.

1863.label: The move places a friendly piece or pawn on a diagonal, blocking one's own piece from capturing an undefended enemy piece (or delivering checkmate) along that diagonal.
1863.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical geometric error: the player moves a piece or pawn onto a square that lies directly between their own attacking piece and an undefended enemy target along a diagonal. In Position 1, Qe3 blocks c1-g5 (Bxg5 wins queen). In Position 2, Nf6 blocks d8-g5 (Qxg5 wins knight). In Position 3, d5 blocks e6-b3 (Bxb3 wins queen). In Position 4, Qb2 blocks g7-a1 (Bxa1 wins rook). In Position 5, Be2 blocks d1-h5 (Qxh5 wins rook). In Position 6, Nc6 blocks g2-a8 (Bxa8 wins rook). In Position 7, e4 blocks d5-g2 (Qxg2#). In Position 8, Kb2 blocks e5-a1 (Bxa1 wins rook). In Position 9, d6 blocks f8-c5 (Bxc5 wins queen). In Position 10, Nf3 blocks d1-h5 (Qxh5 wins rook). The missed target was a hanging piece in 9/10 cases and checkmate in 1/10. The piece types that get blocked vary: bishops (6/10), queens (4/10). The blocking pieces also vary: pawns (4/10), knights (3/10), queens (2/10), king (1/10). The average cp_loss of 1277 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights of trivially available material.

1861.label: A piece (usually the queen) is moved to an apparently active square, abandoning a critical tactical or defensive function it was performing, allowing immediate exploitation.
1861.description: 10/10 positions feature quiet, non-capturing, non-checking repositioning moves to squares that appear more active or centralized. 7/10 are queen moves specifically (Qc3, Qe6, Qg6, Qg6, Qf3, Qb5, Qf6). In every case, the piece was fulfilling a critical function on its original square: defending a piece (5: queen defended rook on e7), guarding a mating square (7: queen on g2 guarded h2), threatening a concrete target (1: rook threatened b2; 4: queen threatened b2/a1), enabling a specific tactical resource (2: queen needed to reach e3 for forced trade), or providing recapture ability (6: bishop on b2 needed to recapture on c1). After the repositioning, 8/10 positions suffer immediate tactical punishment—the relocated piece becomes a target (positions 3, 8, 10), a defended piece is left hanging (positions 1, 5), or the king is fatally exposed (positions 2, 7). Only 1.9 good moves existed on average, indicating these were positions demanding precision rather than general improvement.

1872.label: A knight makes an aggressive forward jump to an attacking square, abandoning its critical defensive role and leaving pawns or pieces unprotected.
1872.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight making a forward, aggressive-looking jump to a seemingly powerful square. In 7/10 cases, the knight departs from the f-file (f3 for White or f6 for Black), which is typically the key defensive post supporting central pawns. In 6/10 positions, the specific consequence is that an e5 pawn is left undefended or a critical central/defensive function is abandoned. The 4 Ng5 moves by White all aim at the f7 square in a premature Fried Liver-style attack, while the Black knight jumps (Nxe4, Nfg4, Ng4, Nxe5, Ne4) grab or target material that turns out to be poisoned or leaves the knight itself tactically vulnerable. The refutations consistently involve simply capturing what was left undefended (8/10 positions) or exploiting the now-uncoordinated knight's vulnerability on its new square. Average cp_loss of 336 reflects catastrophic consequences, and only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these occur at critical moments demanding precision rather than speculation.

1871.label: Moving the queen to a seemingly active square instead of making the critical capture or exchange that the position demands.
1871.description: In 9/10 positions, the blunder was a queen move to a non-capture square (the one exception being Rg8, still a non-capture repositioning). In 8/10 positions, the best move was a concrete capture — specifically a queen exchange in 6/10 cases (Qxa8, Qxd6, Qxd6, Qxd5, Qxd1, Qxd6) or winning/capturing a piece in 2/10 (Rxf5+, Bxd6). The average cp_loss was an enormous 2247, and on average only 1.5 good moves existed, meaning these were critical moments demanding precision. The played moves relocated the queen to squares that appeared active (Qb3 eyeing diagonals, Qg5 targeting pawns, Qa4 aiming at the king, Qf6 guarding squares) but in every case abandoned either a defensive duty (2/10: leaving pieces undefended for back-rank mates), missed a free capture (3/10: hanging pieces on open files/ranks), or refused a simplifying exchange that was the only way to maintain the evaluation (5/10: queen trades). The queen destinations were consistently peripheral or disconnected squares (b3, g5, c3, b6, c2, f3, b4, a4, f6) rather than the concrete capture squares required.

1868.label: Playing a non-forcing piece repositioning move to a natural-looking square when an immediate tactical blow (capture, fork, or forcing sequence) was available.
1868.description: All 10 positions share a clear pattern: the player moved a piece to a conventionally 'good' or 'natural' square — often a knight to f6, f3, d7, or c5 (6/10 are knight moves to textbook squares) — while missing a concrete tactical opportunity that demanded immediate execution. In 5/10 cases the missed tactic was a capture of hanging/undefended material (positions 3, 6, 8, 9, 10). In 3/10 cases it was a knight fork with check (positions 1, 4, 7). In all 10 cases the played move was non-capturing and non-checking, giving the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate. The average cp_loss of 321 reflects catastrophic consequences: these positions all had narrow windows (avg 1.5 good moves) where only one or two moves maintained the advantage. The played moves look reasonable — they 'improve' piece placement — but ignore the position's tactical urgency.

1878.label: A non-forcing rook repositioning move (doubling, defending, centralizing) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demanded immediate concrete action.
1878.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that appears natural and constructive — doubling on a file, defending a rank, or centralizing — but fatally squanders tempo when a forcing continuation was available. In 4/10 cases the move doubled rooks on a file (R1e2, R1d2, R1e5, Rbc1), in 3/10 cases the rook moved to the 7th rank in a passive/defensive capacity (Rd7, Ra7, Rf7), and in 3/10 cases the rook repositioned to a seemingly logical square (Re3, Rb5, Re2). The best moves available were overwhelmingly concrete: forcing checks (positions 1, 2, 5, 7), pawn captures creating connected passers (position 4), material captures (position 6), exchanges on favorable terms (position 8), or counterplay-generating piece activity (positions 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 252 reflects catastrophic tempo waste — 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating critical moments demanding precision rather than preparation. In 8/10 positions the refutation directly exploited the wasted tempo through immediate tactical threats the opponent now had time to execute.

1875.label: Knight forks to c2 or c7 that appear to win material (usually the exchange) but are actually inferior because the knight gets trapped, recaptured, or a stronger tactic is missed.
1875.description: 9/10 positions involve knight moves, and 8/10 specifically feature knight forks targeting the c2 or c7 squares (4 positions each), typically delivering check while attacking a rook in the corner. The signature pattern is a knight jumping to c2+ (forking Ke1/Kd1 and Ra1) or Nxc7+ (forking Ke8/Kd8 and Ra8), apparently winning the exchange. However, these forks consistently fail for three related reasons: in 5/10 positions the knight becomes trapped or immediately recaptured after the king sidesteps (Kd1 captures on c2, or the knight on a8 has no escape squares); in 2/10 positions a far superior tactic exists (capturing an enemy queen with Nxd4 or Nxf4); and in 2/10 positions it's a move-order error where the fork should come only after preparatory moves. Position 7 (Ne7+, cp_loss=0) is the sole example where the knight check is actually correct, and Position 8 (g6) is a geometric outlier. The average cp_loss of 242 reflects these moves' seductive but ultimately self-destructive nature.

1884.label: A rook pawn (a or h) advances one square to chase an enemy knight from an adjacent square, wasting a critical tempo when the position demands concrete action.
1884.description: All 10/10 positions share an identical geometric pattern: a rook pawn (a-pawn or h-pawn) advances one square to attack an enemy knight posted on the adjacent file (b4/b5 or g4/g5). In every case, the move is a low-priority prophylactic nudge that ignores urgent tactical demands. In 7/10 positions, the knight being chased has a superior forward option rather than retreating (Nxe5 in positions 1&2, Nbxd5 in positions 5&10, Nd6# in position 9, exd6+ discovered attack in position 7, Nf3 improving the knight in position 6). In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 10), the knight safely retreats while the tempo loss allows the opponent to seize initiative through other tactical means. The average cp_loss of 1294 reflects the catastrophic nature of these tempo-wasting moves, with losses ranging from 170cp to forced mate. 8/10 positions featured critical hanging pieces or tactical shots that the player missed in favor of the routine pawn push, and 10/10 positions had concrete developing or tactical moves available that maintained the advantage.

1874.label: Capturing material (usually a pawn) while neglecting critical promotion-related threats or defensive duties in positions dominated by advanced passed pawns.
1874.description: All 10/10 positions feature captures that grab material at the expense of a more critical need. 9/10 positions prominently feature advanced passed pawns (6th-7th rank) creating imminent promotion threats. In 7/10 cases, rooks capture pawns; the remaining involve a bishop, queen, or knight capture. The consistent error is prioritizing material gain over the position's dominant strategic requirement: 4/10 moves abandon back-rank defense enabling opponent promotion (Positions 2, 3, 9, and partially 1), 3/10 trade away pieces essential for blockading or stopping promoters (Positions 7, 8, 10), and 3/10 capture a secondary target while missing a far stronger tactical resource (Positions 1, 5, 6). The average cp_loss of ~1990 reflects how catastrophic these greedy captures are. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, confirming these positions demanded precise play over material appetite.

1876.label: Queen relocates to an aggressive or active-looking square while ignoring the position's concrete tactical requirements.
1876.description: All 10/10 positions involve queen moves to squares that appear powerful, central, or aggressive, but which fail to address the position's critical tactical need. In 3/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 5), the queen abandons defense of a piece or key diagonal, leaving material hanging or destroying a latent tactic. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 8, 9), the queen goes where a different piece should operate — blocking a rook (Qf1 vs Rf1), capturing with the wrong piece (Qxe5 vs Bxe5), or occupying a square the knight needed (Qd5 vs Nd5). In 2/10 cases (positions 3, 7), the queen move fatally abandons control of a critical mating square (g7 in both). In 1/10 (position 10), the queen checks from the wrong square (a6 vs a8), missing a precise combination. In 1/10 (position 6), the queen ignores an immediate threat to another piece. The average cp_loss of 2141 is extremely high, with 4/10 positions having only 1 good alternative, confirming these are positions where concrete calculation was required but replaced by general queen-activity thinking.

1864.label: Playing a forcing move (usually a check) with a piece landing on a suboptimal square when the same piece on a nearby square would have been dramatically more effective.
1864.description: 8/10 positions feature moves that give check, and in 7/10 cases the best move was ALSO a check — revealing that the error isn't in choosing to be forcing, but in selecting the wrong destination square. In positions 2, 4, 7, and 10, the same piece needed to land just one or two squares away on the same file/rank to attack a critical target (usually winning an enemy rook). In positions 3 and 8, the rook needed to stay on the same file but reach a deeper rank to invade decisively. In position 9, the player chose a discovered check winning material over a direct check leading to forced mate. The 2/10 non-checking moves (Bc2, Bd3) follow the same geometric principle: a piece retreating/repositioning to a passive square when it belonged on an active one. Across all 10 positions, the seduction is a visually attractive forcing move — often combining check with material gain (capturing a pawn in positions 8, 9, 10) — that obscures the much stronger alternative destination for the same piece.

1885.label: Multiple pieces can recapture on the same square, but the player chooses the wrong one, leaving a critical vulnerability.
1885.description: All 10/10 positions involve a square where multiple friendly pieces can capture, and the player selects the inferior capturing piece. In 6/10 cases, a knight capture was best but the player used a bishop, queen, or king instead (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8). In 2/10 cases, the king capture was best but the player used a knight (positions 6, 7). In 2/10 cases, the queen capture was best but the player used a knight or king (positions 9, 10). The consequences fall into clear sub-categories: in 5/10 positions, the wrong capture left another piece hanging (positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 10); in 4/10 positions, it exposed the king to immediate tactical exploitation via checks or forks (positions 2, 6, 7, 9); in 1/10, it removed a crucial defender from a key square enabling invasion (position 8). The average cp_loss of 323 reflects that these decisions are almost always catastrophic, and 9/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating extreme criticality of the recapture choice.

1869.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves (often to the rim) played in positions demanding immediate captures or forcing tactical action.
1869.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a slow, non-forcing move while a critical tactical opportunity (usually a capture or forcing sequence) was available and essentially required. In 6/10 positions (1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10), the best move was an immediate capture or forcing tactic that wins material, yet the player played a quiet repositioning move instead. The geometric pattern is striking: 6/10 moves go to the a-file or rim squares (a3, Na3, Nb3, Na6, a6, Na3), with 4/10 being specifically knight-to-rim moves. The average good moves available was only 1.6, meaning these were 'must-find' moments with essentially one correct action, and the player chose something entirely off-topic. The cp_loss averaged 1350—catastrophic—confirming these are critical junctures. In positions 1, 3, and 10, a simple pawn capture (axb3, Ncxe4, dxe4) would win material outright. In position 2, Re1 forces a queen win. In position 5, the player allowed immediate checkmate. The consistent thread is prioritizing 'improving' piece placement or 'preventing' something vague over seizing concrete tactical opportunities that the position demands.

1880.label: Aggressive knight jumps to central/attacking squares (4th-5th rank) that look impressive but are tactically premature or inferior to more precise alternatives.
1880.description: All 9 positions feature knight moves to aggressive central squares (c4, e5, d4, d5, c5, f5 — all on the 4th or 5th rank). In 8/9 cases these are mistakes averaging 262cp loss, while 1/9 (Nxd5+) is actually the best move. The knight moves are universally 'seductive' — they involve checks (4/9), captures (2/9), or attacks on high-value pieces like queens (3/9), making them appear forcing and strong. The common error is that 5/9 positions had a stronger non-knight move available (d4, Qa3, g4, Qa4, Be5/Kh7), 3/9 involved move-order errors where preparation was needed before the knight jump (Kh7 before Nf5, Bd7 before Nxd4, Be5 before Ne5+), and 2/9 allowed the opponent to favorably capture the knight, relieving defensive problems (Bxf5, Bxc5, Nxe5). Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, confirming these are narrow positions where the flashy knight move is a specific trap.

1883.label: A pawn on a flank file captures toward the center, opening the edge file directly toward the player's own castled king for the opponent's attack.
1883.description: 10/10 positions feature a pawn capture on a flank file (h, a, g, or b pawn) taking toward the center. In 8/10 cases, the specific mechanism is that after the capture and opponent's recapture, the outermost file (h-file or a-file) adjacent to the player's own castled king is ripped open, giving the opponent's rooks and queen a direct invasion route. 7/10 involve the h-pawn capturing on the g-file (hxg), directly opening the h-file toward a kingside-castled king. 2/10 involve the a-pawn capturing on the b-file (axb5), opening the a-file toward a queenside-castled king. 7/10 positions feature opposite-side castling where the opened file is especially lethal. In every case, the player resolves flank pawn tension for materialistic or tension-relieving reasons without recognizing that the structural consequence — the opened edge file — benefits the opponent far more than the pawn capture benefits the player. The average cp_loss of 268 reflects how devastating these file-openings are when the opponent has rooks and queens already aimed in that direction.

1873.label: Natural-looking quiet moves (usually king moves) in positions with exposed kings where only one precise concrete continuation is acceptable.
1873.description: 8/10 positions feature at least one critically exposed king in the center or on unusual squares. 6/10 moves played are king moves, and 9/10 are quiet moves (no checks, only 1 capture). The average number of good moves available is just 1.6, meaning these are extreme 'only-move' positions. In 8/10 cases the played move loses significant material or allows mate by ignoring a concrete tactical necessity — the player chose a 'natural' or 'slow' continuation (king repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, positional capture) instead of the single precise action the position demanded. Even the 2 positions with 0cp loss (positions 6 and 9) share the same structural signature: exposed kings, open boards, and razor-thin margins. The feature captures the moment where a player defaults to positional thinking in a position that requires exact calculation due to mutual king exposure.
1873.old_chip: Quiet moves in razor-sharp king positions

1881.label: When two knights can reach the same square, the player moves the wrong one — typically displacing the better-placed knight from its dominant position.
1881.description: All 10/10 positions feature disambiguated knight moves (algebraic notation specifies WHICH knight moves because both could reach the target square), and in every case the player chose the wrong knight. In 6/10 positions (1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10), the correct move was actually moving the OTHER knight to that same destination square. In the remaining 4/10 (2, 5, 7, 9), the best move was something else entirely, but the player still erred by selecting the knight that was better-placed on its current square. The core mistake in 8/10 positions involves removing a knight from a dominant outpost (e5, e3, e4, d6, c4, d4) where it controlled critical squares, exerted pressure, or maintained defensive duties. In 4/10 positions (4, 8, 10, and partially 6), the analyses explicitly describe this as a 'wrong recapture' or 'wrong knight' error. The average cp_loss of 1277 reflects how catastrophic these decisions are — the wrong knight selection frequently leaves the other knight hanging (positions 8, 10), abandons key defensive posts (positions 1, 3, 5), or surrenders attacking coordination (positions 2, 6).

1877.label: Bishop captures that grab material on one square while leaving a more valuable own piece (queen or rook) undefended elsewhere.
1877.description: 8/10 moves are bishop captures or bishop moves, and 9/10 are captures or forcing moves that prioritize winning material on the target square while neglecting a bigger liability in the position. In at least 6/10 positions (1, 4, 7, 9, 10, and arguably 3), the move directly leaves the player's own more valuable piece hanging — typically a queen (positions 1, 9) or rook (positions 3, 4). In 3/10 positions (4, 6, 8), the error is specifically capturing with the wrong piece or in the wrong order, allowing an intermediate tactic. The consistent thread is a materialistic, non-forcing capture (usually Bx-something) that fails to account for what becomes undefended as a consequence. Position 2 is an outlier with 0 cp_loss (the move was actually correct), but the remaining 9 average 488cp loss. Only 1.5 good moves existed on average, showing these are razor-sharp positions where the greedy capture is the one critical trap.
1877.old_chip: Greedy bishop captures leave pieces hanging

1879.label: Advancing an unmoved pawn two squares forward when it either enables en passant, abandons a critical defensive duty, or wastes a decisive tempo.
1879.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn making its initial two-square advance (from the 2nd/7th rank to the 4th/5th rank). The specific punishments fall into three sub-categories: 4/10 positions (2, 3, 5, 9) enable a devastating en passant capture that creates an unstoppable passed pawn or wins material outright. 3/10 positions (1, 7, 8) remove the pawn's protection of an adjacent square or piece — g5 leaves f6 unguarded, g4 leaves Nf3 hanging, h5 leaves g6 capturable. 3/10 positions (4, 6, 10) are critical tempo losses where the player wastes time on a speculative flank advance while a decisive central action (d3, a4, exd4) was available. The average cp_loss of 296 reflects how catastrophic these moves are. The positions span endgames (6/10) and middlegames (4/10) roughly equally, and both sides commit this error (Black 6/10, White 4/10). The common geometry is unmistakable: a flank pawn jumping two squares from its starting rank.

1886.label: The queen moves away from a critical defensive responsibility to pursue an offensive goal, immediately allowing a tactical punishment.
1886.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a queen move that relocates the queen away from a square, piece, or king it was protecting to chase an offensive target (material, centralization, or counter-threats). In 8/10 positions, the queen specifically abandons king safety coverage—either leaving its own king exposed to checks/mates (positions 3, 5, 6, 9, 10) or abandoning the defense of the opponent's attacking target near its king (positions 1, 2, 8). In 7/10 cases, the queen move leaves a specific piece or square undefended that is immediately exploited (Nf3 in position 2, f2 in positions 5 and 6, g2 in position 9, Rd8 in position 7, the c2/king complex in position 10). The best moves in all positions share the theme of the queen staying near its defensive duties—either retreating toward the king, guarding a key square like f3/f2/g2, or simplifying via trades. The queen's destination square in the blunder typically looks active (attacking enemy pieces, centralizing, or threatening material) but is strategically disconnected from the position's true requirements.

1890.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (one square from promotion) in an endgame.
1890.description: All 10/10 positions involve pushing a passed pawn to the 7th rank (from the promoting side's perspective) — the 7th rank for White (h7, a7, a7, c7, a7) and the 2nd rank for Black (f2, a2, a2, h2, d2). Every position is an endgame (10/10) where the pawn is already far advanced and the push creates an unstoppable or near-unstoppable promotion threat on the next move. 9/10 positions have 0 cp loss, meaning this is nearly always the correct move; only 1/10 (c7, 51cp loss) was a minor inaccuracy where a preparatory king move first would have arranged promotion with check. The feature fires on the specific geometric pattern of a pawn reaching the penultimate square before queening, regardless of which file (a, c, d, f, h files all represented) or which side is promoting.

1891.label: Moving the rook onto the same file as the opponent's rook, enabling an exchange that transitions into a hopelessly lost pawn or piece endgame.
1891.description: 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to the same file as the opponent's rook, directly enabling a rook exchange that devastates the player's position. In every case, the resulting rookless endgame is decisively worse (avg 250cp loss) because the player's rook was providing irreplaceable defensive resources — checking distance, lateral defense, counterplay against weaknesses — that vanish once traded. 9/10 positions explicitly identify 'pawn_endgame' as the tactical motif, where the opponent's superior king position, pawn majority, or structural advantages become unstoppable without rooks on the board. The best alternatives in all 10 positions share a common theme: keeping the rook on a different file where no exchange is possible, maintaining piece tension and dynamic defensive chances. The blunders span both sides (White 6/10, Black 4/10) and both middlegame and endgame phases, but the mechanism is identical throughout: the player 'contests a file' or 'challenges the opponent's rook' using standard positional logic while catastrophically misjudging the resulting simplified position.

1882.label: Captures or piece-saving moves that prioritize material while the player's own king is fatally exposed, allowing the opponent to exploit with check or mate.
1882.description: 10/10 positions feature a critically exposed or vulnerable king belonging to the side making the blunder. In 7/10 cases, the move is a capture (6 queen captures of enemy pieces on e3, f7, e4, d3, g5, f4, plus one rook escape). In the remaining 3 rook moves (Rb1, Rg1, Ra3), the intent is saving material or attacking an enemy piece. The devastating punishment in 8/10 positions involves a response with check—most commonly a recapture with check (positions 3, 6, 7, 8, 9 all feature the opponent recapturing the queen's prize with Qx__+ check), exploiting that the capturing piece moved onto a line connecting the enemy's piece to the blunderer's exposed king. In positions 1 and 2, ignoring the king's vulnerability allows immediate checkmate. The average cp_loss of 2831 reflects that these moves convert survivable (if bad) positions into instant catastrophes. Only 2.2 good moves were available on average, confirming these arise in already-critical positions where king safety must take absolute priority over material concerns.

1893.label: A two-square pawn advance that allows a devastating en passant capture, creating a passed pawn or winning material.
1893.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing two squares from its starting rank, allowing the opponent to execute a crushing en passant capture. In 8/10 cases, the en passant capture creates a dangerous advanced passed pawn (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10). In 2/10 cases, the en passant pawn directly attacks and wins a piece (position 5: bishop on g7; position 10: bishop on e2). The moves span all central and wing files (b4, c4, c5, d4, f4, f5) and affect both sides equally (5 White, 5 Black). In every case, the player had multiple good alternatives (avg 2.1 good moves) that involved piece activity or quiet positional play rather than pawn advances. The average loss of 319 centipawns confirms these are catastrophic oversights of the en passant rule's tactical implications rather than subtle positional errors.

1894.label: A rook delivers check that wastes tempo, displaces itself from a critical task, or actually helps the opponent's king improve its position.
1894.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook delivering check that is tactically or strategically counterproductive. In 10/10 cases the move is a rook check (+), and in every case the check fails to accomplish anything constructive. The specific harms vary: in 5/10 positions the check actively improves the opponent's king position (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 10 — king centralizes or reaches an active square); in 4/10 the rook abandons a critical defensive or offensive duty (positions 5, 8, 9, 10 — blockading passed pawns, holding key files, or addressing hanging pieces); in 3/10 the check leads to the rook being captured or sacrificed for insufficient compensation (positions 5, 7, 8). The average cp_loss of 1140 reflects the severity — these aren't subtle inaccuracies but major blunders where good alternatives existed (avg 1.9 good moves available). The positions span middlegame (5/10) and endgame (5/10), both sides (White 7/10, Black 3/10), and various pawn structures, confirming the pattern is purely about the reflexive rook check regardless of context.

1889.label: Playing a quiet, natural bishop development move to a standard square when the position urgently demands a concrete tactical action (capture, fork, or pawn break).
1889.description: All 10/10 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing bishop move to a 'natural' developing square (e7, e3, e2, d6, or e6) in positions where only 1.1 good moves existed on average — indicating critical tactical moments requiring precise calculation. In every case, the correct move was a concrete tactical action: 4/10 required a capture (Bxe2, Bxb5, fxe5, Bxf3), 3/10 required a knight fork or fork-enabling move (Nxe5, Nxe4, Nxe5), 2/10 required a central pawn break (d4, d5), and 1/10 required a queen reroute for attack (Qc8). The bishop moves are universally 'principled' in appearance — breaking pins (positions 2,3,4,8), preparing castling (1,4,8,9), or challenging opponent's pieces (5,6,10) — but they ignore the narrow tactical demands of the position. In several cases, the bishop move actively creates vulnerabilities: 3/10 positions saw the bishop move leave another piece hanging (h5 bishop in positions 2,3; h4 pawn in position 10), and 2/10 saw the bishop self-block a critical defensive line (blocking queen's recapture path in position 2, blocking queen's diagonal in position 4).

1895.label: Playing a non-forcing pawn advance (or passive retreat) when a concrete capture, check, or forcing move was immediately available and necessary.
1895.description: 9/10 positions featured pawn pushes (d4×3, d5×3, b5, e6, b3) and 1/10 featured a passive knight retreat (Nh7) — all non-forcing, 'positional' moves played in positions demanding immediate tactical action. In 10/10 cases the best move was a forcing move: 5/10 required a simple capture (Qxc3, axb6, axb5, Nxc5, Nxd4), 2/10 required a check (Ne2+, Qh5+), and 3/10 required a piece move creating an immediate tactical threat (Bf4, Nf4, Bf3). The average number of good moves available was only 1.2, meaning nearly every position had exactly one correct forcing continuation. 7/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The consistent error is that the player chose a move that appeared to improve their structural/spatial situation but gave the opponent a free tempo to neutralize the concrete tactical opportunity that existed.

1887.label: Non-forcing pawn advances (or equivalent slow moves) that waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical action.
1887.description: 8/10 positions feature single-step, non-capturing pawn advances, and the remaining 2 are similarly slow, non-forcing piece relocations. In every case, the position demanded immediate tactical attention — capturing a hanging piece (position 4), addressing a mating threat (positions 6, 7), maintaining a critical defensive resource (positions 2, 3), or preserving structural integrity (positions 1, 9, 10). Instead, the player chose a move that *appeared* constructive — gaining space (c5, d4, f4), kicking a piece (h6, h4), attacking a strong piece (c6), advancing a passed pawn (b5, a4), or activating a piece (Rcf8, Bc7) — but fundamentally ignored the most urgent requirement of the position. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 10/10 position analyses, confirming that the unifying error is wasting the move on something non-urgent. The average cp_loss of 2162 is extremely high, reflecting that 4/10 positions featured forced mates or near-mates that the slow move enabled.

1905.label: A bishop retreats from g4/g5 to the h-file edge (h5 or h4) where it becomes trapped by a g-pawn advance.
1905.description: In 10/10 positions, a bishop that was actively posted on the g-file (g4 for Black, g5 for White) — typically pressuring a knight on f3/f6 — retreats to the h-file rim (h5 or h4) instead of exchanging or retreating to a safer interior square. In every single case, the opponent punishes this with a g-pawn advance (g4 against Bh5, or ...g5 against Bh4) that traps the bishop with no escape. The trapping mechanism is especially lethal because the player's own g-pawn (g3 for White or g6 for Black) blocks the bishop's only retreat diagonal in 8/10 cases. All 10 positions had at least one clearly superior alternative: either exchanging the bishop for the knight (Bxf3 or Bxf6) or retreating to a safe interior square (Be3, Bf4, Bd2, Bd7, Be6, Bc8). The average centipawn loss was 270, reflecting that the punishment typically wins a full piece for one or two pawns.

1896.label: A major piece captures a tempting enemy piece but fatally abandons its critical defensive duty, enabling an immediate tactical punishment.
1896.description: All 10/10 positions feature a major piece (Queen in 7/10, Rook in 3/10) capturing an enemy piece that appears strong, active, or free — but the capturing piece was secretly performing an essential defensive function. In 5/10 positions the abandoned duty was back-rank defense (positions 1, 3, 4, 6, 8), leading to immediate mating attacks. In 3/10 positions the piece left other pieces undefended, enabling forks or discovered attacks (positions 2, 5, 9). In 2/10 the queen moved to a square where it became tactically vulnerable via discovered attack or Greek Gift sacrifice (positions 7, 10). The targets captured were consistently attractive — powerful centralized knights (4/10), active bishops deep in the player's territory (4/10), infiltrating rooks (1/10), or a queen (1/10) — making the capture psychologically irresistible. The average centipawn loss of 4829 reflects the catastrophic nature: 6/10 resulted in forced checkmate or near-checkmate. All positions had 1-3 reasonable alternatives that preserved the critical defensive function.

1897.label: King moves in endgames that waste critical tempo or abandon blockading/defensive posts against passed pawns.
1897.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves as the blunder, and 9/10 occur in endgames dominated by passed pawn dynamics. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in all 10 analyses, and 'passed_pawn' in 9/10. The specific manifestations cluster into three sub-types: (1) King directly abandons a blockade of a passed pawn (4/10: positions 2, 6, 7, 10 where the king leaves h6, f7, f7, and g3 respectively, immediately allowing the blocked pawn to advance); (2) King moves to the wrong side of the board or in the wrong direction, losing a decisive tempo in a pawn race (3/10: positions 1, 5, 8); (3) King moves when a more urgent non-king action was required—a pawn breakthrough or piece sacrifice (3/10: positions 3, 4, 9). The catastrophic losses (positions 2, 6, 7 averaging ~9300cp loss) all involve abandoning blockades, while moderate losses involve move-order or directional errors. Only 2.0 good moves were available on average, indicating these are razor-sharp positions where the king's precise placement is paramount.

1901.label: Bishop captures a rook (or major piece) to win the exchange, but this greedy material grab ignores a critical tactical prerequisite or devastating counter-tactic.
1901.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing a higher-value piece (9/10 rooks, 1/10 queen), motivated by the appeal of winning material immediately. In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 3, 7, 8), the error is a move-order mistake where a preparatory move (Nxc6, Qxe2+, Qxd3, f5) should precede the bishop capture to make it safe or more profitable. In 4/10 cases (positions 2, 4, 6, 9), the capture leaves the player's position fatally exposed to an immediate counter-tactic — checkmate (positions 2, 6), a winning fork/discovered attack (positions 4, 8), or a hanging piece (position 9). In 2/10 cases (positions 5, 10), the bishop itself was more valuable as an active piece than the exchange gained, and its removal collapses the position. The average cp_loss is extremely high (2367), with 4/10 resulting in forced mate. Only 1.3 good moves were available on average, confirming these are sharp positions requiring precise calculation rather than materialistic reflexes.

1900.label: A reflexive central pawn exchange is played when the position demands addressing an urgent tactical threat, leaving pieces hanging or missing forcing sequences.
1900.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn-takes-pawn capture on a central square (c4-e5 range) that resolves pawn tension in a structurally natural way but catastrophically ignores the position's immediate tactical demands. In 5/10 positions (2, 5, 6, 8, 9), the capture left the player's own piece hanging or undefended, allowing a simple win of material. In 2/10 positions (1, 7), a forcing winning tactical sequence (checks, captures on f2) was available but the player chose a quiet pawn grab instead. In 3/10 positions (3, 4, 10), the capture enabled the opponent's specific tactical shot — a knight fork, a queen check on an opened diagonal, or a powerful centralization. The average cp_loss of 304 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic oversights. The positions span openings (3/10) and middlegames (7/10), both colors equally (5 White, 5 Black), confirming this is a universal pattern of 'autopilot' central exchanges played when the position screams for concrete tactical attention.

1892.label: King moves to the first/eighth rank in endgames instead of addressing urgent tactical or structural demands.
1892.description: 8/10 positions feature king moves, and of those, 7/8 are king moves specifically TO the back rank (f8, d8, g8, d1, f1). 9/10 positions are endgames. The 6 actual blunders (positions 1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10) all share the same pattern: the player chose a quiet, retreating king move when a more urgent forcing action was available—a tactical shot (Bc5+ in pos 1), piece activation (Bg5 in pos 3, Ne5/Nh6 in pos 4, Ne5/Nb8 in pos 8), correct king direction (Ke2/Kf1 in pos 9), or critical pawn restraint (f4 in pos 10). The 4 positions with 0 cp_loss (2, 5, 6, 7) show the feature also fires when this type of move happens to work—typically because the advantage is so overwhelming that tempo doesn't matter. The average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions where the 'natural' endgame king move is often the wrong instinct.
1892.old_chip: Passive king retreats to back rank

1899.label: The same piece that should make an available capture instead plays a passive move to a nearby square, ignoring a hanging or dominant enemy piece.
1899.description: In 9/10 positions, the correct move was an immediate capture of a vulnerable enemy piece (hanging, under-defended, or positionally dominant), and in 9/10 cases the piece that SHOULD have made the capture is the very piece that moved — but to the wrong square. Position 1: b-pawn goes b3 instead of bxc3. Position 2: Rook goes Rd7 instead of Rxd6 (same file, wrong direction). Position 3: a-pawn goes a3 instead of axb3. Position 4: Queen goes Qc7 instead of Qxc6+. Position 5: Queen goes Qd3 instead of Qxe3. Position 6: Rook goes Rf3 instead of Rxg3 (same rank, one square short). Position 7: Queen goes Qe3 instead of Qxe4 (adjacent square). Position 8: Rook goes Rd7 instead of Rxd5 (same file, wrong direction). Position 10: Knight goes Ne7 instead of Nxe5 (same piece, wrong destination). Only position 9 deviates slightly (passive rook move instead of queen check). The average cp_loss is 1514, reflecting that these missed captures typically involve winning a full piece or more. 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available, showing these are critical-precision moments.

1902.label: Retreating or repositioning a well-placed minor piece to a quieter square when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1902.description: All 10 positions feature a minor piece (7/10 bishops, 3/10 knights) being moved from an active or aggressive post to a less effective square in a single quiet, non-forcing move. In 10/10 cases the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as the core error. In 8/10 positions, the piece was explicitly retreating backward or sideways (Bh4←g5, Nc3←b5, Be6←h3, Bg3←h4, Bf5←e6, Nf3←g5, Bd2←c3, Bb5←a4). The remaining 2 (Nf5, Bd7) appear forward but move pieces away from critical defensive duties. In 9/10 positions only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating these were critical moments requiring precise tactical or prophylactic play rather than quiet repositioning. The average centipawn loss of 297 reflects the catastrophic cost of wasting a tempo when the position is tactically charged. The best moves in these positions were overwhelmingly concrete actions: tactical strikes (Bxg2, Re6, e5 pawn breaks), maintaining attacking pieces on dominant squares (keeping Ng5, Nb5), or precise prophylaxis (Re8, Bc6).

1904.label: Aggressive queen moves (captures, checks, or attacking sorties) to exposed squares that leave critical pieces or pawns undefended while the position demanded quiet development or consolidation.
1904.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen making an aggressive-looking move — either capturing a seemingly free pawn (4/10: Qxd5, Qxd5, Qxc6, Qxd4), delivering a check (2/10: Qh4+, Qa5+), or launching an attacking sortie (4/10: Qh5×3, Qa5) — when the position required a quiet developing or consolidating move instead. In 8/10 positions, the correct move was a modest piece retreat or development (knight retreat to d4/f3, bishop retreat to c1/b3/d2, or a simple pawn capture). The queen moves fail because they leave critical pieces hanging (5/10: Nb5, Bf4, Ng5, d4-pawn, queen itself), allow tempo-gaining attacks on the exposed queen (8/10), or walk into traps (2/10: Nxh4, Bb2 trapping). 6/10 positions occurred in the opening phase where development should have been prioritized. The average of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these were critical moments demanding precision over aggression.

1903.label: Playing a slow piece-improvement move when the position urgently demanded an immediate forcing continuation (check, capture, or concrete threat).
1903.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing piece repositioning move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played in a position where a specific forcing tactical sequence was available and critical. 5/10 moves are knight maneuvers to seemingly active central squares (Nf4, Ng3, Nd3, Nd6, Ne7), 4/10 are queen repositionings to apparently strong squares (Qf3, Qc3, Qf1, Qd5), and 1/10 is a 'strengthening' pawn push (f6). In every case, the best move involved immediate concrete action: a rook invasion to the 7th rank (positions 3, 4), a back-rank check (position 10), a pawn capture enabling a queen sacrifice (position 5), or active counterplay moves creating threats (positions 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9). The average cp_loss of 1239 is extremely high, and only 1.9 good moves were available on average, confirming these are critical moments demanding precision where the 'natural-looking' positional move was catastrophically wrong. 8/10 positions had tactical refutations exploiting the lost tempo, often involving the opponent gaining a forcing sequence (check or invasion) that wouldn't have been possible had the player chosen the immediate action.

1906.label: Castling kingside as a routine developing move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical response.
1906.description: All 10/10 positions feature kingside castling (O-O) played as a 'safe' developing move when urgent tactical demands exist. In 9/10 positions the game is still in the opening phase with both kings near the center, making castling feel natural and principled. However, in every case a specific concrete issue trumps general development: 4/10 positions had the player's own pieces tactically vulnerable (exposed bishop on a4, hanging knight on e5, unresolved Ne4/Bb4 tension, queen exposed to Na5 fork); 3/10 had opponent pieces hanging that could be captured immediately (free knight on a3, winning Ne4 with Qc2, literal checkmate in one); 2/10 featured time-sensitive crushing continuations against a cramped opponent (a4 queen trap, a6 pawn breakthrough); and 1/10 allowed the opponent a winning pawn fork (e5 hitting bishop and knight). The average centipawn loss is extremely high (1265), with one position missing forced checkmate. The behavioral signature is unmistakable: choosing king safety from general principles over position-specific tactical calculation.

1909.label: Playing an unnecessary prophylactic king tuck (usually Kb1) when the position demands immediate concrete action—attacking, defending a threat, or exploiting a tactical opportunity.
1909.description: 7/10 positions feature the exact move Kb1, while all 10 share the pattern of a quiet, non-forcing prophylactic or developmental move played at a moment requiring immediate concrete action. In 8/10 positions, White had castled queenside and the king was already adequately safe on c1. The best moves available were aggressive central breaks (d4 in positions 2, 7, 10), attacking thrusts (g4 in position 5, Qh3 in position 4), prophylaxis against a specific threat (a3 in position 1), or development addressing a tactical weakness (Nf3 in position 6).
