The average cp_loss of 262 reflects how catastrophically these tempo losses compound: in opposite-side castling positions (4/10), the wasted tempo allowed opponents to consolidate or launch counterattacks; in positions with development leads (3/10), it let the opponent catch up; and in positions with concrete tactical opportunities (3/10), it allowed the opponent to defuse the threat entirely. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical-precision moments where the standard 'tuck the king' autopilot move was uniquely punished.

1908.label: Pawn captures (usually with check) that prematurely resolve kingside/central pawn tension in endgames, allowing the opponent's king to activate by recapturing.
1908.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn-takes-pawn captures in the endgame on files e through h, where the opponent's king is exposed and typically 1-2 squares from the capture square. 8/10 moves deliver check. The captures resolve critical pawn tension that was restraining the opponent's position. In the 7/10 positions where the move was a mistake (avg cp_loss ~360 for those), the error was releasing tension prematurely—allowing the opponent's king to recapture and centralize (positions 2, 5, 6, 8), reach a perfect blockading square (position 7), or enabling the opponent to eliminate structural weaknesses (positions 9, 10). The 3/10 positions where the capture was correct (positions 1, 3, 4 with 0 cp_loss) share the same geometry but the timing was right—either creating an unstoppable passed pawn or setting a practical trap. In all cases, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.3), indicating these are razor-thin positions where move order determines the outcome.

1898.label: Moving a piece to a square controlled or defended by an opponent's piece, resulting in immediate capture or permanent entrapment.
1898.description: 8/10 positions show a piece being moved to a square where it is immediately captured or inescapably trapped by an opponent's piece that already controls that square. In positions 1 (Bd8 into Nxd8), 6 (Bc2 into Bxc2), 7 (Qb6 into Qxb6), 8 (Qxc2 recaptured by Bxc2), and 9 (Qxe5+ recaptured by Nxe5), the piece lands on a square directly attacked by an opponent's piece and is captured on the next move. In positions 4 (Ba1 entombed) and 10 (Na8+ trapped by Kb7), the piece reaches a square from which it cannot escape. Position 3 (Rc2) places the rook where it becomes a tactical target via Bxc2. The remaining 2 positions show the softer version: position 2 (Bc4 instead of Bxf1) moves a piece away from its attacking duty to an ineffective square, and position 5 (Bf8) commits the bishop to a passive blockade square where it becomes functionally dead. The average cp_loss of 5815 reflects that these are catastrophic one-move errors, and 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available, indicating extreme tactical narrowness that the players failed to recognize.

1913.label: Capturing a pawn when more critical priorities (king safety, maintaining key pieces, or winning tactics) demand attention.
1913.description: All 10/10 positions involve capturing a pawn — using various pieces (pawns, knights, bishops, queens, rooks, even the king) — when the position demanded something fundamentally different. In 6/10 cases, the player's own king was exposed or vulnerable, and the pawn grab allowed the opponent to exploit that weakness with checks or mating attacks (positions 3, 4, 5, 8, 10, and indirectly 1). In 2/10 cases, the player missed a stronger forcing continuation like checkmate in 1 (position 7) or a queen-winning fork (position 6). In 2/10 cases, the capture traded away or displaced a critical attacking piece for merely a pawn's worth of material (positions 2 and 9). The average cp_loss of 1180 is extreme, and only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are positions where precision was required and the tempting pawn was a trap. The consistent thread is that a pawn appeared loose or capturable, but taking it violated a more important positional or tactical principle.

1912.label: A knight aggressively jumps to a central outpost (4th/5th rank) where it can be immediately and profitably captured, leading to material or structural loss.
1912.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight moving to an aggressive central square (e4, f4, e5, d4, d5, c4, f5) on the 4th or 5th rank that appears to be a strong outpost but is tactically vulnerable to immediate capture. In 8/10 positions, the knight is directly captured by a bishop or knight on the very next move, and the forced recapture (usually with a pawn) creates exploitable structural weaknesses or leaves additional material hanging. In 3/10 positions (3, 10, and partially 6), the knight move leaves two pieces capturable in sequence, allowing the opponent to harvest material through precise capture order. In 7/10 positions, quiet prophylactic alternatives (king safety moves, piece development, bishop repositioning) were clearly superior. The average cp_loss of 246 reflects that these moves consistently transform manageable positions into losing ones because the 'outpost' is illusory—the knight lacks genuine support and its capture triggers cascading tactical problems (opened diagonals, hanging pawns, forks, trapped pieces).

1911.label: Pawn advances to the 4th/5th rank in endgames that prematurely fix the structure, allowing the opponent to lock the position or exploit the commitment.
1911.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing to the 4th rank (White: b4×4, c4×1) or 5th rank (Black: g5×3, a5×1, f5×1) — crossing the board's midline into contact with the opponent's pawns. In every case, this confrontational pawn push commits the structure too early, and 10/10 positions are pure endgames where such structural commitments are irreversible and decisive. The correct approach was typically king activation first (positions 2, 4, 9, 10 all needed king moves), prophylactic/flexible pawn moves that avoid contact (positions 1, 3, 5, 8 needed quieter pawn moves like ...a6, ...c2, ...g5→best was ...g5 only when it PREVENTS opponent contact, or ...b5), or piece improvement (position 6). In 7/10 positions, the pawn advance specifically allowed the opponent to lock the pawn structure with a symmetrical reply (f5 answering g5, g5 answering f5, a4 answering a5, Ke3 blocking after g5), converting winning advantages into draws. The average cp_loss of 341 reflects how devastating these structural commitments are in endgames.

1915.label: Playing a non-forcing queen repositioning move when a concrete tactical blow (check, capture, or sacrifice) was immediately available.
1915.description: 9/10 positions feature queen moves (the exception being Rh5, a rook repositioning), and all 10 moves share the critical property of being non-forcing—no checks, no captures, no immediate threats. In every case, the player chose to reposition their piece to a seemingly 'better' or more 'active' square instead of executing an available concrete tactical continuation. The missed best moves were overwhelmingly forcing: 5/10 involved checks (Qxg2+, Nf3+, Bg8+, Qf4+, Qxh3+), 5/10 involved captures (Qxg2+, Qxh3+, Qxb2, Rxg5, Qxe3), and several were combination sacrifices. The average cp_loss of 306 reflects that these positions had narrow best-move paths (avg 1.3 good moves available), meaning the forcing continuation was typically the only way to maintain the advantage. All 10 moves gave the opponent time to consolidate—typically resolving king safety issues (castling, king retreat) or reorganizing piece coordination that was about to be tactically exploited.

1910.label: A rook (or queen) moves to capture material or give a flashy check on a peripheral square, abandoning its critical file/rank where it enabled a forcing tactical sequence (usually forced mate or winning much more material).
1910.description: 8/9 positions feature a rook move (the exception being Qxh1 in position 3). In all 9 cases, the piece leaves a critical attacking line to grab material on a distant or peripheral square. 5/9 positions specifically involve a discovered check where the player chose the WRONG destination square for the piece unmasking the check—in positions 1, 2, 6, 7, and 9, the correct discovered check keeps the rook on its critical file (f-file or g-file) to enable winning heavier material or delivering mate on the next move, while the blunder sends the rook to a square that merely captures a pawn or lesser piece. The remaining 3/9 (positions 3, 5, 8) involve removing an attacking piece from its dominant post to capture material elsewhere, destroying the mating net. Position 4 is the mildest variant—simply moving to the wrong file and losing tactical pressure. The average cp_loss of ~4391 is enormous, with 4/9 positions involving missed forced mates. In 7/9 cases, the rook goes to capture something on the a, b, or c file (Ra7, Rg8 excepted) when it should stay on the f or g file near the enemy king.

1907.label: Playing a non-forcing minor piece repositioning or suboptimal capture when an immediately decisive forcing continuation was available.
1907.description: In 9/9 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (8/9 are minor piece moves — 6 bishop, 2 knight) when the position demanded immediate tactical action. In 5/9 cases (positions 2, 3, 4, 8, 10), the best move was capturing a hanging or inadequately defended piece outright. In 3/9 cases (positions 5, 9, and partly 4), the best move began a forcing check sequence leading to material gain. The blunder moves are all 'one tempo too slow' — they look natural or positionally reasonable (developing a piece, capturing a suboptimal target, making a prophylactic move) but fatally waste the critical tempo needed to exploit a concrete tactical shot before the opponent escapes. Average cp_loss of 338 and average good moves available of only 1.3 confirm these are narrow critical moments where only the forcing move works. The played moves are never checks and rarely threaten immediate decisive action.

1888.label: A non-forcing advance to the 3rd or 6th rank (usually g3/h3) when an immediate forcing check or tactical shot was required.
1888.description: All 10/10 positions feature moves landing on rank 3 (7 positions: g3, Qg3, h3, Kg3, h3, Kb3, Kg3) or rank 6 (3 positions: g6, Qh6, Qa6). In 8/10 positions, the move lands on the g-file or h-file. The critical 'why bad' pattern: in 8/10 mistake positions, the correct move was an immediate CHECK (Qh7+, Qg5+, Re1+, Re4, Qe8+, Re1+, Rd1+, Qe3+), but the player chose a slow advancing move instead. King safety themes appear in all 10 positions. The moves look aggressive—advancing toward the opponent, creating vague threats, or 'improving' the position—but they fatally surrender the initiative. Three positions feature Kg3 walking the king into mating nets or forced queen trades. Two h3 pushes represent move-order blunders where the same pawn push was part of the winning sequence but needed to come AFTER the check. The average cp_loss of 3973 reflects multiple positions where forced mates were missed in favor of these creeping advances.

1924.label: A rook that was the sole defender of the back rank moves to an active square, allowing an immediate back-rank mating sequence.
1924.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook that was guarding the 1st or 8th rank moving away to an ostensibly active or material-gaining square, instantly enabling a back-rank checkmate or mating sequence. In 10/10 cases the tactical motif is back_rank mate. The king in every position is sealed in by its own pawns (typically f/g/h pawns on the 2nd or 7th rank), making the rook the sole piece preventing infiltration. The rook moves to aggressive squares — capturing pawns (Rxe5, Rxc5, Rxd4), invading ranks (Re2, Ree7, Rd3, Rd6), or lifting to attack (Re3, Rf4, Rff4) — but in each case the opponent immediately exploits the vacated back rank with a check (Rc8+, Rd8+, Rb8+, Rd1+, Ra1+, Qa1+, Qb1+) leading to forced mate in 1-3 moves. 7/10 positions had the refutation deliver checkmate in exactly 2 moves, and 10/10 primary refutations involved back-rank invasion. The best alternative moves in all positions shared the common thread of either keeping the rook on the back rank, creating luft (h5/h6/g6), or moving the king off the vulnerable square.

1919.label: Premature pawn promotion (or greedy pawn move) into a square directly controlled by an enemy knight, which immediately captures or exploits the result.
1919.description: 5/10 positions involve promoting a passed pawn into a square directly guarded by an enemy knight, which immediately captures the new queen (positions 2, 3, 5, 6, 7). In every single promotion case, the capturing piece is specifically a knight positioned one jump away from the promotion square (Nc2→a1, Nc6→b8, Nc2→a1, Nf2→d1, Nb6→c8). The best moves in all 5 promotion cases involve first displacing, capturing, or diverting the knight before promoting. An additional 2/10 positions (1 and 9) feature pawn moves punished by immediate knight captures or forks (Nxd4 after c4 removed its guard; Nxd6+ fork after bxa3 left pieces aligned). The remaining 3 positions involve other greedy/impulsive moves (back rank ignore, suboptimal rook placement, weakening pawn push) that share the broader theme of executing an apparently attractive move while ignoring a piece's tactical control of the critical square.

1917.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing king or queen repositioning move in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical or strategic action, wasting a critical tempo.
1917.description: All 10/10 positions share a devastating pattern: the player makes a passive king move (6/10: Ke3, Kc1, Kg1, Kg3, Kb6, Kc5) or a purposeless queen repositioning (4/10: Qb4, Qf6, Qe3, Qh3) in a position where urgent concrete action is required. In every case, the best move involves forcing play—a pawn break (positions 5, 7), a tactical sacrifice or combination (positions 6, 1), saving a hanging piece (position 8), or activating a piece with purpose (positions 9, 10). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 10/10 analyses. The average cp_loss of 2157 reflects that these positions have razor-thin margins where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic. In 7/10 cases, the moved piece actually lands on a worse square (vulnerable to checks, forks, or geometric exploitation). Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, meaning these are high-urgency positions with narrow paths to survival where 'waiting' is never an option.

1918.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn move (typically on the flank) when the position urgently demands a concrete tactical action such as a capture, piece activation, or forced trade.
1918.description: 9/10 positions feature a quiet pawn push (b6, h5, b3, h4, b3, f4, a5, g5, c6), with 1/10 being a quiet knight redeployment (Nd4). All 10 moves are non-capturing, non-checking, and create no immediate threat. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 analyses. In 5/10 positions, a hanging or capturable piece was available (positions 1, 3, 6, 7, 10 — missed Nxe4, Bxa8, fxe4, Qxh5-target, Nxe5). In 3/10, critical king moves or queen trades were needed for safety (positions 2, 4, 9). In 2/10, urgent piece activation was required (positions 5, 8). The average number of good moves was only 1.4, meaning these were almost always 'one correct move' positions where the quiet pawn push was categorically wrong. 7/10 moves were on the a/b/g/h flanks, emphasizing that the player's attention was drawn to the wrong sector of the board.

1914.label: Moving a knight to a visually appealing or classically strong square while ignoring concrete tactical demands—either abandoning a critical function, missing a forcing sequence, or landing on a square that is immediately vulnerable.
1914.description: All 10/10 positions feature a knight move to a square that appears positionally desirable (central outposts like d4, e4, d5, f6, f3; active-looking squares like c4, b6, d3) but is concretely wrong. In 6/10 cases (Positions 1-3, 6, 9, 10), the knight was performing a vital function on its original square or had access to a much stronger tactical continuation that was abandoned. In 4/10 cases (Positions 4, 5, 7, 8), the 'attractive' destination square turns out to be immediately tactically vulnerable—challenged by pawn breaks (c5 in Pos 1), attacked with tempo (Nb4 in Pos 8), capturable in a way that creates further problems (Nxf6 in Pos 9), or simply leaves another piece hanging (gxf5 in Pos 7). The average cp_loss of 279 reflects that these moves uniformly transform positions from manageable into losing ones. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where the 'natural-looking' knight move was a trap. The common thread is prioritizing classical piece placement aesthetics over the position's concrete tactical requirements.

1922.label: Playing a passive flank pawn move (a/b/h file) in a position that demands immediate active piece play or tactical execution.
1922.description: 9/10 positions feature pawn pushes on the a, b, or h files (the rim columns), while the remaining position (Re7) is similarly a passive repositioning move. In every case, the best available move involved urgent active play: piece sacrifices (Rf6+ in position 1), piece activation (Be3, Bg5, Qd3 in positions 2, 7, 8), king centralization (Kd4 in position 3), captures of hanging material (dxc4 in position 4, axb3 in position 6), a different pawn check (f4+ in position 5), critical defensive moves (Rf1 in position 9, Kh6 in position 10). The average cp_loss of 1255 reflects how catastrophic these tempo losses are in time-critical positions. 10/10 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.6 good moves), confirming these were narrow decision points where the one active move was essential. The blundered moves share the appearance of 'useful' prophylaxis—securing pawns, creating luft, claiming space on the wing—but in reality accomplish nothing against the position's critical demands.

1916.label: Captures (usually pawn takes) that remove a piece or pawn blocking a file/diagonal, directly exposing the player's own more valuable piece to immediate capture on the opened line.
1916.description: 7/10 positions involve captures, and of those, 6/10 clearly remove a pawn or piece that was blocking a critical file or diagonal, directly exposing the player's own queen or rook to capture on that opened line. In positions 2 and 8, hxg6 opens the h-file exposing the h8 rook to Qxh8(+). In positions 5 and 10, dxc6/dxc3 removes a d-pawn that was shielding the player's own queen from the opponent's queen on the same file, allowing Qxd4/Qxd5. In position 6, Bxc3 removes the b2 bishop that was blocking the b-file, allowing Rxb1+. In position 7, bxc6 opens the b-file exposing the b8 rook to Rxb8. The remaining positions fit a related pattern: position 3 (Rxb2) displaces a rook from coordination leaving e8 hanging, while positions 1, 4, and 9 involve non-captures that abandon defensive coordination. The dominant motif (6/10 positions) is a capture that acts as self-inflicted destruction by opening a line directly to one's own major piece.

1926.label: Playing a non-forcing rook move to an open file when the position demands an immediate concrete action (capture, fork, check, or king safety).
1926.description: All 9/9 positions feature a rook being passively placed on an open or semi-open file (d, e, b, or c-file) on the back rank, without delivering a check or capture, when the position urgently demanded a forcing move. In 4/9 cases, material was hanging and could be captured immediately (Positions 4: free c5-pawn via Bxc5, 5: Rxh7 winning a rook, 6: bishop en prise on g5, 7: undefended knight on f5). In 2/9 cases, a tactical strike was available (Position 3: Nc6 fork, Position 1: Ba3 enabling a superior move order). In 1/9 cases, king safety was the overwhelming priority (Position 9: Kf2 escaping the exposed e2 square). In 1/9 cases, the rook itself became a tactical target on the file (Position 2: Rad8 allowing exchange-winning combination, Position 8: Re1 creating an overloaded-defender scenario). The average cp_loss of 267 reflects that these 'natural-looking' positional moves consistently squander concrete advantages or create decisive weaknesses. Only 1.6 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points where generic principles failed.

1921.label: Choosing a superficially attractive or aggressive-looking move instead of addressing the position's most critical tactical requirement.
1921.description: 8/10 positions were tagged with 'tempo_loss' in the analysis, and in all 10, the played move ignored a concrete urgent tactical priority in favor of something that merely *looked* productive. In 4/10 cases (Nxc7+, Nb4, Qf5, Rc5), a piece was moved to an 'active' square where it was immediately captured or trapped. In 3/10 cases (Ra8, Kg4, f5), the player made a slow improving move while immediate forcing continuations (checks, captures, queen trades) were available. In 2/10 cases (Qd2, e4), the move created a new tactical vulnerability by removing a key defensive function or weakening the structure. In 1/10 (exf5), the player chose the wrong capture direction, selecting the obvious-looking one over the far superior en passant. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow positions demanding precise identification of the single most important priority. The average cp_loss of 296 reflects the severe cost of giving the opponent one free tempo to exploit the unaddressed issue.

1928.label: A quiet minor piece development move to a standard square while a piece is hanging (own or opponent's), resulting in massive material loss.
1928.description: All 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing minor piece development move (knight or bishop) to a 'natural' square while an immediate tactical crisis demands attention. In 8/10 cases, a piece is directly hanging and capturable — either the player's own undefended piece (positions 2, 4, 6, 8) or the opponent's undefended queen/piece that could be captured for free (positions 3, 5, 7). The remaining cases involve a checkmate threat (position 1) and self-blocking that enables a piece capture (positions 9, 10). The average cp_loss of 1473 reflects that these 'autopilot' moves turn winning or equal positions into lost ones. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions demanded precise tactical attention rather than casual development. The moves all share the quality of looking like reasonable chess moves in isolation — developing dormant pieces — but are catastrophic because they treat a tactically critical position as if it were a quiet one.

1923.label: Capturing apparently free material with a piece or pawn that was serving a critical defensive function (blocking a line or guarding a key square near the player's own king), allowing an immediate devastating attack.
1923.description: All 9/9 positions feature a capture of seemingly free or winning material where the capturing unit was performing an essential but unrecognized defensive duty. In 6/9 cases, a pawn captures a piece (gxh6, dxe4, gxf6, exd2, exf6, gxh3), opening a file or diagonal directly toward the player's own king. In 2/9 cases, a queen captures material (Qxe4, Qxh5) but abandons its guard of a critical square (f1 and g2 respectively). In 1/9 cases, a bishop captures (Bxf6) leaving its diagonal unguarded. The consequences are catastrophic: 7/9 positions result in forced checkmate (often in 1-5 moves), and the average cp_loss is 6631. In every case, the opponent had deliberately placed or sacrificed material specifically to lure the capture. All 9/9 positions occur in the middlegame, and 9/9 involve king safety as the primary exploitation theme. The refutations consistently exploit the newly opened line or unguarded square: open g-files (3 positions), back-rank mates (4 positions), or unguarded mating squares (2 positions).

1927.label: A quiet flank pawn move to the 3rd rank (b3/b6/g3/g6) passively defends a pawn under queen pressure, wasting a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate active play.
1927.description: 10/10 positions feature a flank pawn advance to the 3rd rank from the player's perspective (7x b3, 2x b6, 1x g3, 1x g6). In 9/10 cases, the move is motivated by defending a specific pawn (usually b2, b7, or g7) from queen pressure or preventing the opponent's queen from accessing a square. 10/10 positions had urgent tactical or strategic demands being ignored: castling the king to safety (3/10), defending a hanging central pawn (2/10), exploiting a winning tactical sequence like a fork (2/10), maintaining critical central tension (2/10), or activating pieces (1/10). The average centipawn loss is 310, making these catastrophic blunders. In 7/10 positions, the player's king was still in the center or exposed, making tempo even more precious. Only 1-3 good alternatives existed per position (avg 2.2), indicating these were critical moments where precision was demanded.

1931.label: A knight is moved to an apparently active square (often with check or attacking intent) where it can be immediately and advantageously captured by the opponent.
1931.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a knight move to a square where it is immediately capturable, and the primary refutation in every case is simply taking the knight. In 4/10 positions the knight delivers check (Ne5+, Ne5+, Nf4+, Nd6+) but can still be cleanly captured. In the remaining 6/10, the knight moves to a 'central' or 'active' square (Nf3, Nc3, Nc3, Ne4, Nc6, Nd6) where an opponent's piece already covers. The captures refute these moves because they either: win material outright (positions 7, 9), relieve critical positional pressure by exchanging a passive piece for an active attacker (positions 3, 6, 8, 10), force simplification that neutralizes the opponent's dynamic advantages (positions 4, 5), or destroy the mover's own pawn structure via recapture (position 1). In all cases, a much better quiet or positional move existed (avg 1.1 good moves), typically involving patient buildup rather than a flashy knight jump.

1933.label: King retreats toward the player's own back rank, wasting a critical tempo when an active move or forward king march was required.
1933.description: All 10/10 positions feature a king move retreating toward the player's home ranks (ranks 1-2 for White, ranks 7-8 for Black). The White moves (Ke2×3, Kf1×1) all retreat from rank 3 or 2 toward ranks 1-2, while the Black moves (Kf8, Kf7, Ke7, Ke8×3) all retreat toward ranks 7-8. In 9/10 positions, the primary tag is 'tempo_loss,' and the average number of good moves available is only 1.6, indicating these are critical moments demanding a specific active response. In 6/10 cases, the correct move was not a king move at all (a pawn break, rook check, bishop activation, or pawn advance), while in 4/10 cases the king should have moved FORWARD toward the opponent's side of the board (toward g5, kingside activity). The consistent error is choosing a seemingly safe, centralizing, or defensive king retreat when the position demanded immediate aggressive action elsewhere — the retreat surrenders the initiative and allows the opponent to execute a winning plan (pawn structure lockdown, piece infiltration, passed pawn advance, or elimination of counterplay).

1941.label: Playing a generic rook centralization to the e-file instead of executing an immediately available concrete tactic.
1941.description: 10/10 positions feature a rook being moved to the e-file (e1 for White, e8 for Black), with 8/10 specifically being the f-rook after kingside castling (Rfe1/Rfe8). In 9/10 cases, this was a significant blunder (avg 232cp loss) because a concrete forcing move was available — a knight fork (Position 1), a passed pawn advance (Positions 2, 4), a tactical combination (Position 3), a hanging piece capture (Position 5), an attacking strike against an uncastled king (Positions 7, 10), a prophylactic move preventing a breakthrough (Position 8), or a queen maneuver winning material (Position 9). Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these were narrow tactical windows. The rook-to-e-file move creates no immediate threat in any position, giving opponents a free tempo to castle to safety (3/10), move a targeted piece (3/10), execute a counterattacking pawn advance (2/10), or challenge the rook itself (2/10). Position 6 is the sole outlier where the move was essentially harmless due to an already overwhelming advantage.

1925.label: Moving a piece away from its essential blocking, defending, or restraining role, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of the vacated function.
1925.description: At least 6/9 positions show a piece that was performing a critical role — blocking a file, defending a pawn, or restraining an enemy passed pawn — being moved away, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the now-unguarded line or square. In Position 4, the queen left f2 (blocking Rxf8#); in Position 5, the rook left the g-file (allowing g1=Q+); in Position 6, the bishop left d5 (unblocking Qxd1+); in Position 2, the queen left g3 (hanging e3); in Position 1, the rook left h6 (abandoning f6's defense). Positions 3, 8, and 9 fit a broader version where the piece gives up its functional role through capture or trade, enabling the opponent's pieces to activate or simplify favorably. Position 7 (Bd3) is the weakest fit, being more about a passive retreat missing a forcing tactic. The avg cp_loss of 1374 reflects that many of these abandonments allow catastrophic tactical blows (back-rank mates, promotions, decisive material wins).

1932.label: Moving the one piece that was preventing an immediate tactical catastrophe, allowing checkmate or decisive material loss.
1932.description: All 10 positions share a critical pattern: the player moves a piece that was the sole (or key) defender of a vital square or the only preventer of a lethal tactic. 9/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.2), indicating razor-thin defensive margins where one piece held the position together. In 6/10 cases the blunder enabled immediate checkmate or forced mating sequences (positions 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, and nearly position 7). The moved pieces are predominantly queens (5/10) and rooks (4/10), always redirected to squares that appear constructive but are completely disconnected from the critical defensive obligation. The pattern manifests as: Position 3 (Rh1 abandoned d2 defense → Rxd2+ Qxd2#), Position 8 (Qg2 abandoned king cover → Ra3+...#), Position 9 (Rdb1 abandoned d2 control → Nd2+ Nf3+ Qg1#), Position 7 (Qc1 abandoned e2 → Nxe2 fork), Position 5 (Qg7 abandoned f5 rook → Bxf5 wins exchange). In every case, the opponent's refutation directly captures or invades the square the moved piece was guarding.

1937.label: A knight voluntarily leaves a deeply embedded, paralyzing outpost for a superficially attractive central square, giving the opponent critical tempo to consolidate.
1937.description: In 10/10 positions, a knight is moved to a 'textbook' central square (d4, d5, e4, e5, c5, or c6), but in at least 8/10 cases, the knight was already on a FAR more powerful square deeply embedded in the opponent's position (d3 in positions 1, 7; e3 in positions 3, 4; c2 in position 8; c3 in positions 5, 9). These embedded knights were actively paralyzing the opponent—attacking rooks (positions 4, 7, 8), preventing castling (positions 3, 4), restricting piece development (positions 1, 3, 8), or guarding critical squares (position 5). The destination squares all look attractive in isolation but are immediately challengeable by pawns (c4 hitting d5 in positions 3, 9; f4 hitting e5 in position 7) or allow the opponent's trapped/passive pieces to suddenly activate (bishop develops with tempo in positions 8, 10; king safely consolidates in positions 1, 3). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, and 'piece_activity' in 10/10, confirming that the universal punishment is the opponent gaining a free move to untangle. Average cp_loss is 298, reflecting how devastating it is to voluntarily release positional pressure.

1939.label: Playing a slow rook-pawn advance (a3/a6/h3/h6) to chase an enemy bishop when a concrete forcing move wins material or delivers a decisive blow.
1939.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook pawn advance (a6 in 6 cases, a3 in 3, h6 in 1, h3 in 1) specifically intended to 'put the question' to an enemy bishop pressuring a knight (Bb5 targeting Nc6 in 7/10, Bb4 targeting Nc3 in 2/10, Bg5/Bg4 targeting Nf6/Nf3 in 2/10). In every case, a much stronger forcing move existed: 4/10 had a devastating queen check available (Qa5+, Qb6+, or Qg6+), 3/10 had an immediate piece capture/exchange (Nxe4, Nxb3), 2/10 required a knight relocation (Ne7) before the pawn kick, and 1/10 demanded a central pawn advance (d5). The average centipawn loss was 286, and only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning these were critical decision points. In 7/10 positions at least one king was still in the center, making tempo especially precious. The pattern is remarkably consistent: the player addresses bishop pressure with the slowest possible remedy instead of exploiting tactical vulnerabilities created by that very pressure.

1920.label: Choosing locally attractive moves (captures, checks, attacks on pawns) while the position demands addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability or maintaining a critical defensive structure.
1920.description: All 9 positions share a common thread: the player chose a move that appears immediately productive but ignores the position's most urgent requirement. 4/9 moves are material-grabbing captures (Nxd7, exd4, cxb4, Na2+→exchange), 3/9 are piece moves targeting enemy pawns or king (Bh3, Rg1, Rg6), and 2/9 are positional moves ignoring concrete threats (Kb1, c5). In every case, the position demanded something specific and non-obvious—maintaining a blockading piece on a critical square (e5 pawn blocking Nd5 in position 6, bishop on g4 defending f3 in position 2, rook on h6 defending f6 in position 7), addressing immediate king safety (back-rank in position 9, king attack via Rxg2 in position 8), or executing a precise forcing sequence (Ra1+ in position 10). The average good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are razor-sharp positions requiring precision. 7/9 moves were made by Black. The average cp_loss of 2425 reflects that 3 positions involved missing forced mates entirely.

1938.label: A slow, non-forcing bishop repositioning move played in a position that demands immediate tactical action (captures, checks, or critical defensive resources).
1938.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a seemingly reasonable square (Be7, Bd3, Bd4, Bd2, Bd1, Ba8, Bc3, Be2, Bf3) in a quiet, non-forcing manner, while the remaining position (Kd2) shares the same underlying error of slow piece improvement. In every case, the position demanded urgent tactical action: 3/10 required capturing an undefended or hanging piece (positions 4, 8, 10 — Nxd5, Nxd2, cxd4), 3/10 required forcing defensive moves against mating or queen-loss threats (positions 2, 3, 5), and 4/10 required active tactical shots or simplification (positions 1, 6, 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 1243 is catastrophic, and only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating razor-sharp positions where the 'improving' bishop move was uniquely punished. 10/10 moves are non-captures and non-checks — pure quiet repositioning in positions screaming for forcing play.

1942.label: A passive one-square pawn advance (overwhelmingly b3) played as prophylaxis in a position demanding immediate tactical action or piece activation.
1942.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square, non-capturing pawn advance played in a middlegame position that demands concrete tactical engagement. The move b3 specifically accounts for 6/10 instances, with the remaining being f3, g3, e3, b6, and c6 — all quiet one-square pawn pushes. In every case, the position contained either an immediate tactical shot (Rxd6, Bh5, Nxf7, Qxf7+), a critical development need (Nd2, Nc3, O-O), or urgent piece activation (Rae8, Rf8, Qf3). The average centipawn loss of 1164 reflects the severity of these tempo losses. In 8/10 positions, the player was White with an initiative or advantage that evaporated. In 9/10 cases, the move addressed a secondary concern (defending b2, preventing Nc4, solidifying structure) while ignoring the primary tactical demand. The punishment typically involved the opponent either seizing the initiative with active piece play (7/10), executing a tactical combination that the pawn move failed to prevent (8/10), or engineering simplifications that neutralized the squandered advantage (4/10).

1935.label: The king advances to an apparently active square in the endgame but gets driven back, exposed, or sidelined from the critical theater of play.
1935.description: All 10/10 positions are endgames where the player advances the king to a seemingly aggressive square that turns out to be misplaced. In 10/10 cases the move is tagged as a tempo loss — the king either gets immediately driven back by the opponent (e.g., checked by an advancing pawn in positions 5, 8), lands on a square with no productive follow-up (positions 1, 3, 7), or marches toward the wrong sector while the decisive action occurs elsewhere (positions 2, 6, 10). The better alternatives consistently involved either retreating the king to a safer/more central square (positions 5, 8, 10 — Kh2, b4-pawn-break, Ke3), centralizing toward the critical pawn battle (position 2 — Kf5 instead of Kh5), or making a timely pawn break before committing the king (positions 4, 8 — f5/h4 or b4 first). 8/10 positions move the king toward the rim (a/b/g/h files) when the correct plan demanded central presence. The average cp loss is 95, with positions 2 (283cp), 8 (235cp), and 10 (195cp) being the most severe, while 3 (8cp), 4 (13cp), and 7 (18cp) are negligible inaccuracies — suggesting this pattern spans from catastrophic to trivial depending on whether the opponent can exploit the misplacement with check or immediate counterplay.

1936.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active or aggressive square while abandoning a critical defensive responsibility, enabling an immediate tactical refutation.
1936.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a move that appeared to increase piece activity (centralizing a queen, giving a check, repositioning to an attacking square) but actually removed a piece from a vital defensive post. In 8/10 positions, the moved piece was directly guarding a specific pawn or square whose abandonment was immediately exploited (f7 unguarded in positions 3 and 8, e6 unguarded in position 10, d4 unguarded in position 6, rook driven to bad square after checks in positions 4 and 5). Queens were the most common offenders (5/10: Qh4, Qg5×2, Qe5, Qc6), followed by rooks giving pointless checks (2/10: Rh6+, Re5+) and bishops relocating from dominant squares (2/10: Bb4, Bc5). In every case, the best available moves were defensive, prophylactic, or developmental — 9/10 positions had at least one quiet consolidating move as the top recommendation. The average cp_loss of 397 reflects that these aren't small inaccuracies but catastrophic misjudgments where the refutation is typically a forcing tactical sequence (Qxf7+, Rxe6+pin, Nxd4 fork, queen capture) exploiting the newly created vulnerability.

1929.label: Moves that pursue a plausible secondary plan while ignoring the position's single most critical tactical or structural requirement.
1929.description: All 10 positions share a common structure: the position demanded one specific urgent action (addressing a hanging piece, exchanging to simplify, eliminating a key defender, or avoiding a fatal weakening), but the player chose a reasonable-looking alternative that catastrophically ignored this priority. In 10/10 cases, very few good moves existed (avg 1.7), indicating critical decision points with extremely narrow correct paths. In 5/10 positions (Rce2, exd4, b6, Rc6, d2), the error was specifically a wrong move-order — the player needed to do something FIRST (capture a piece, exchange rooks, kick a knight) before executing their intended plan. In 3/10 positions (Ra7, Qa1, Ra7+), the player moved a piece to a square that disconnected it from the critical sector of the board or placed it where it hangs. In 2/10 positions (g3, Rg5), the player addressed a secondary concern while a more urgent tactical reality went unaddressed. The average cp_loss of 2136 reflects that these positions had essentially one correct answer, and any deviation was catastrophic.

1945.label: Advancing a pawn adjacent to an exposed king (typically to chase an attacker) when the king should relocate or a piece should defend instead.
1945.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advance immediately adjacent to the player's own king that destroys critical shelter. The moves are f3 (4/10), g3 (2/10), g5 (2/10), g6 (1/10), and c6 (1/10) — every single one advances a pawn that was shielding the king. In 7/10 cases, the correct move was a king relocation (Kh3, Kg1, Kf1, Ke7, Kg7, Kh2). Strikingly, in 4/10 cases (positions 5, 7, 8, 10), the best move was placing a PIECE (usually the queen) on the exact square the pawn moved to — Qg3 not g3, Qg5 not g5, Qg6 not g6. The intent was consistently defensive-looking: chasing an attacking queen from f4/e4, blocking a diagonal, or seemingly creating luft. But the consequence was always catastrophic: opening ranks for checks (f3 opens the 2nd rank in positions 1,2,4,9), blocking king escape squares (g3 enables Qf2# in positions 7,8), or clearing ranks/diagonals for mating attacks (g5/g6 in positions 5,6,10). Average cp_loss of 6590 reflects that 7/10 resulted in forced checkmate.

1940.label: Aggressive-looking moves that place a piece on a square with no protection, allowing the opponent to simply capture it or exploit the tactical vulnerability.
1940.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder directly places a piece on a square where it has zero defenders, enabling the opponent to win material through simple capture or a secondary tactical blow. Specifically, 6/10 moves are bishop deployments to undefended squares (Bg5, Bf5, Bb6, Bg4, Bg5, Bxh4), while 2/10 are knight moves to unprotected squares (Nxc7, Nh4). In positions 2, 4, and 7, the bishop is placed where the opponent's queen immediately captures it. In position 3, the undefended bishop creates a double-attack vulnerability (Nf6 hits both queen and bishop). In position 10, the undefended knight on h4 is captured after an exchange sacrifice. The remaining 2/10 (h2+ and Rd3) share the broader pattern of creating undefended pieces—Rd3 leaves the queen on e1 without protection, and h2+ offers the pawn for free capture. All 10 moves share aggressive intent (attacking, developing with tempo, checking, or capturing) but fatally neglect piece safety. The 'hanging_piece' motif is explicitly tagged in 6/10 positions, and 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10.

1934.label: A major piece (usually a rook) moves to an active-looking or material-grabbing square, fatally abandoning its defensive duty on a critical file or rank, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of king safety.
1934.description: 8/10 positions feature rook moves and 2/10 feature queen moves, all sharing the same structural error: the piece redirects from a critical defensive post to an aggressive/greedy square. In 6/10 positions, the punishment directly exploits king safety (back-rank mates in positions 1, 5, 6; open-file attacks in positions 7, 9, 10). In 7/10 cases, the piece specifically abandons an open file it was controlling (g-file in positions 1 and 5, b-file in position 7, e-file in position 2). Material greed motivates the error in 5/10 positions (Rxd5, Rxc3, Re7, Rf5, Rf6 all target enemy material). The refutations consistently exploit the defensive gap via forcing moves — checks, captures, or intermediate moves that the aggressive relocation failed to account for. Only 1/10 positions (position 4) shows 0 cp_loss, making it an outlier. The average cp_loss of ~2966 reflects how catastrophic this type of error is — 4/10 positions result in immediate checkmate.

1944.label: Aggressive pawn pushes that remove a pawn from a square where it was performing a critical protective function, exposing tactical vulnerabilities.
1944.description: All 10/10 positions feature pawn moves (advances or captures) that prioritize gaining space or attacking over maintaining a critical defensive responsibility. In 8/10 cases, the advancing pawn was directly protecting something vital: another pawn (positions 1, 6, 8), a piece (position 2), key squares around the king (positions 3, 5, 9), or shielding the king from attack along a file/diagonal (positions 9, 10). The refutations consistently exploit what the pawn was previously defending — capturing a now-hanging piece (positions 2, 8), invading weakened squares (position 3), winning undefended pawns (positions 5, 6), sacrificing into the opened file (position 9), or launching a mating attack through the abandoned defensive zone (position 10). In 7/10 cases, the player had alternatives that addressed more urgent problems (contesting files, resolving piece threats, securing the king) rather than pursuing space. The average cp_loss of 1213 reflects the catastrophic nature of removing load-bearing pawns.

1930.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive or offensive function, often for an illusory gain like a check or repositioning, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
1930.description: All 10/10 positions feature a piece that was performing a critical function (blockading a passed pawn, supporting a key advance, maintaining active pressure, or occupying a vital square) being voluntarily moved away from that post. 4/10 positions involve giving checks that appear active but are counterproductive (Nc5+, Re8+, Nd6+, Bf2+), driving the opponent's king to a better square or placing the checking piece on a vulnerable square. 4/10 involve passive retreats or repositioning (Bd7, Rg1, Nf1, Qf7) when the piece was already performing its most important function in situ. 2/10 involve moving a piece into direct tactical danger (Ne8 into bishop's attack, Rxg7 allowing Kxg7 trade). In 8/10 cases, the opponent's primary refutation directly exploits either the square the piece abandoned (e.g., White seizing d5 after Qf7, White's king reaching blockade squares after Nc5+) or the piece's new vulnerability (e.g., Bxe8, Bxd6, Kxg7, Ra8+ exploiting Bd7). The average cp_loss of 1371 reflects how devastating it is to remove a piece from its critical role, and the low average of 2.0 good moves confirms these were positions where piece placement was razor-critical.

1948.label: A queen or rook captures a peripheral pawn, displacing itself from the critical sector where king safety or a decisive attack demands its presence.
1948.description: All 10/10 positions involve a major piece (queen in 6/10, rook in 4/10) capturing an undefended or loosely-defended pawn on a peripheral square. 10/10 captures target pawns on edge files (a-file: 4, b-file: 3, h-file: 2, c-file: 1). In every case, the capturing piece moves AWAY from the critical sector — typically the side of the board where the player's own king is under pressure or where a decisive attack on the opponent's exposed king was available. 9/10 positions feature at least one exposed king (the player's own in 6 cases, the opponent's as an untapped target in 5 cases). The average centipawn loss is 2084, with 3/10 positions converting forced mates or near-mates into merely large advantages. In 8/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating that precise play — not pawn collection — was demanded. The refutations consistently exploit the displaced piece's inability to return in time: king attacks (7/10), forks exploiting undefended pieces left behind (2/10), and passed pawn promotions (1/10).

1943.label: Reflexive pawn-takes-pawn captures that prioritize material or tension resolution over more important tactical or structural considerations.
1943.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn capturing another pawn (pxp) as a seemingly natural or materialistic move. In 8/10 cases, the correct move was a piece move (Bxe5, Qa4+, Bf6, Ra8, Na4, Nf6, Kg2, g4) rather than any pawn capture, while in 2/10 (positions 7 and 8), the correct move was capturing a DIFFERENT pawn (cxb5 instead of cxd5, dxc5 instead of dxe5). The captures resolve tension prematurely or in the wrong direction: 5/10 positions involved missing a concrete tactic that was more important than the pawn grab, 4/10 involved removing a structurally critical pawn that served as a defensive barrier or positional anchor, and 3/10 specifically exposed the king by removing shelter pawns (gxh5, gxh3, bxa4). The average cp_loss of 370 reflects catastrophic consequences, and only 1.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical-precision moments where the 'obvious' capture was a trap.

1947.label: A non-urgent wing pawn advance wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate piece activation or tactical precision.
1947.description: All 10/10 positions feature a single-square pawn advance on a wing file (a, b, f, g, or h) played instead of an urgent piece-activity move or tactical shot. In 7/10 cases, the best move was a piece move involving immediate rook activation (Rc4, Rb6, Ra6, Rc1, Re1, Rad1) or knight repositioning (Nc5). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions, and 'piece_activity' in 7/10, confirming the consistent pattern: the player chose a slow, structurally committal pawn push when the position demanded immediate dynamic action. The pawn advances are never captures and never central (d/e file) — they distribute across a-file (3), b-file (3), g-file (3), f-file (1), and h-file (1). In every case, the advance either creates a new weakness (undefended pawn, abandoned square, structural damage) or simply fails to address the most urgent positional demand, giving the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, centralize, or execute a tactical idea.
1947.old_chip: Slow flank pawn when action needed

1952.label: A non-forcing rook/knight pawn advance (h3, h6, a3, g6) wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate tactical action.
1952.description: 10/10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance on the a, g, or h files (h3 in 5 positions, h6 in 2, a3 in 2, g6 in 1) played as a prophylactic 'luft' or waiting move when the position contained an urgent tactical demand. In 5/10 positions, the player missed capturing a hanging or insufficiently defended piece (positions 2, 3, 4, 8, 10). In 2/10 positions, a forced mating sequence was available (positions 5, 7). In the remaining 3/10, a critical piece relocation or forcing move was required to address an immediate tactical crisis (positions 1, 6, 9). The average cp_loss of 2205 reflects the catastrophic nature of these tempo losses. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning these positions had razor-thin margins where the one correct forcing move was drastically superior to everything else. All 10 positions were middlegame positions where the tension was at its peak and demanded resolution rather than deferral.

1954.label: A pawn advance giving check to an exposed king that actually helps the opponent by driving the king to safety, removing a critical pawn, or missing a stronger continuation.
1954.description: All 10/10 positions feature a pawn advancing one square to deliver a diagonal check against an exposed enemy king wandering in the open (typically in the center or on a wing). In every case, the check appears aggressive but is catastrophically counterproductive. In 7/10 positions, the check drives the king from a fatally exposed square to a safer one (e.g., g5→f5, h4→h5, f5→g6, c5→b6, a4→a5). In 2/10 positions (7 and 8), the king captures an undefended piece while responding to the check. In 3/10 positions, a forced checkmate was available but missed in favor of the pawn check (positions 4, 6, 9). In position 10, the pawn check removed a critical defensive shield pawn, allowing a forced mating attack. The average centipawn loss is ~4957, with 4/10 positions losing forced mates entirely. Only 1.4 good moves were available on average, meaning these were high-precision moments squandered by reflexive checking.

1950.label: Rook moves to a peripheral or distant square, abandoning the file/rank where it was performing an essential defensive or strategic function.
1950.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook move that relocates the rook away from the critical sector of the board. In 9/10 positions (all endgames), the rook abandons either: a key file controlling a passed pawn (positions 2, 4, 6, 7, 8), a back-rank/mating-net defensive duty (positions 1, 10), a dominant rank restricting the opponent's pieces (positions 3, 5), or a checking corridor (position 9). In 7/10 cases, the rook moves toward the a-file or board edge (Ra1, Ra8, Ra6, Rb3, Rb8), typically chasing an unimportant pawn target. The average cp_loss of 1144 reflects catastrophic consequences — in 3/10 cases the move allows immediate or near-immediate mate (positions 1, 9, 10), while in 5/10 cases it allows an unstoppable passed pawn promotion. Only 2.4 good moves were available on average, indicating these were positions demanding precise rook placement with razor-thin margins for error.

1957.label: The queen captures a rook on a distant back-rank square, removing itself from the critical zone where a mating attack or king defense was needed.
1957.description: All 10/10 positions feature a queen capturing a rook on a back-rank square (a1 in 5 cases, h1 in 2, a8 in 1, b8 in 1, f8 in 1, e1 in 1), luring the queen to the edge/corner of the board far from the decisive action. In 8/10 positions, a forced checkmate was available (or immediately allowed) that required the queen to remain centralized or near the exposed king. In 9/10 positions, one side's king was critically exposed, making queen proximity essential. The average cp_loss of 7438 reflects that these are catastrophic errors — typically converting forced mates into merely winning positions. Only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these were narrow tactical moments where the material grab was uniquely punished. The common thread is unmistakable: the queen is drawn to a juicy but distant rook, breaking the coordination needed for immediate checkmate or vital king defense.
1957.old_chip: Queen grabs rook, abandons king zone

1949.label: A knight is repositioned to a seemingly active square while unknowingly abandoning essential defensive, supportive, or tactical functions from its current position.
1949.description: All 10/10 positions involve knight moves that look like natural piece improvements but catastrophically abandon critical duties. In 4/10 cases, the knight specifically leaves d2 (three times to b3, once to e4), surrendering access to key tactical routes or defensive coverage. In 7/10 positions, the knight was on a central or back-rank square (d2, e1, e2, d7, e7) performing hidden supportive work — defending pawns, maintaining access to tactical outposts, or controlling key squares — and was moved to what appears 'more active' (b3, e5, c3, d3, g6, f6, e4). The punishment typically involves an immediate tactical strike exploiting what the knight was previously guarding: hanging pieces (positions 1, 2, 10), kingside attacks enabled by removed defense (positions 4, 6, 9), central breaks exploiting the repositioning tempo (positions 8, 5), or loss of piece coordination (positions 3, 7). The average cp_loss of 285 reflects that these are severe errors — the knight's 'passive' placement was actually the linchpin holding the position together.

1956.label: A rook is placed on an open file as a routine positional move, ignoring a more urgent tactical or defensive requirement in the position.
1956.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to an open or semi-open file with the explicit intent of 'contesting' or 'seizing' file control — a textbook strategic principle applied at the wrong moment. In every case, the position demanded something more concrete: 4/10 positions required the rook to stay on its original square to maintain a critical defensive function (Positions 1, 2, 6, 7 — guarding kingside pawns, supporting pawn advances, or preventing pawn storms). 3/10 positions had an existing tactical vulnerability (hanging piece or fork) that the rook move failed to address (Positions 3, 4, 9). 2/10 positions saw the rook voluntarily enter an exchange that deflected a defender from a critical pawn (Positions 5, 8). 1/10 positions featured a concrete attacking opportunity (Ng4 with mating threats) that the slow rook move squandered. The average cp_loss of 346 reflects the severity: these aren't subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic tempo wastes. The opponent's punishment consistently exploits exactly what the rook move neglected — launching a pawn storm against the abandoned wing, capturing a newly-hanging piece, or forcing a deflection exchange.

1959.label: Capturing a piece or pawn on d4 that appears to be a target but the capture loses material to a recapture, fork, or tactical deflection.
1959.description: All 10/10 positions feature a capture on the d4 square that loses significant material. In 7/10 cases, Black's knight captures a seemingly vulnerable d4 pawn, while the remaining cases involve a bishop capture on d4 (1/10), a queen recapture on d4 (1/10), and rook captures on d4 (2/10). The punishment mechanism varies: in 4/10 positions (1, 4, 5, 6), a simple recapture by a knight on f3 wins the capturing piece outright since it was worth more than the pawn. In 2/10 positions (2, 7), the recapture Nxd4 grants White a dominant centralized knight that gives a crushing positional advantage. In 4/10 positions (3, 8, 9, 10), the capture on d4 creates a tactical vulnerability — knight forks (Ne2+ in position 8), bishop sacrifices on h7 (positions 9, 10), or deflection checks (Bh2+ in position 3) that win back more material than was captured. The positions span openings (5/10) and middlegames (5/10), predominantly featuring French Defense or similar closed-center structures where the d4 pawn serves as a structural pillar rather than a genuine weakness.

1958.label: A rook (or piece) aggressively penetrates to a deep rank or enemy territory, but this abandons a more important tactical or defensive function, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated role.
1958.description: 9/10 positions feature rook moves (the exception being Nd2, which follows identical logic of abandoning a key post for aggression). In 8/10 cases, the rook moves specifically to a deep rank—7th rank (Re7, Rc7), 8th rank (Rh8, Rc8, Ra8), 6th rank (Rc6), or deep into the opponent's position (Rc2 twice). These moves follow well-known positional principles (rook on the 7th, rook behind passed pawn, rook invasion) but are concretely premature. In 5/10 positions, the piece abandons a critical defensive function (guarding a pawn, covering the king, maintaining discovered check geometry). In 3/10, the move allows a favorable capture or exchange by the opponent. In 3/10, the error is specifically a move-order mistake where an intermediate check or preparatory move was required first. All 10 positions share the theme of prioritizing superficially attractive piece placement over concrete tactical needs, with the aggressive move giving the opponent exactly the tempo or tactical resource needed to equalize or gain advantage.

1951.label: An aggressive central/semi-central pawn advance that breaks mutual pawn support, creating structural weaknesses or opening lines for the opponent when patient piece play was required.
1951.description: All 10 positions feature a single-step pawn advance (no captures) on the c, e, or f file that pushes past a supported pawn duo or chain. In 10/10 cases, the player chose an aggressive space-gaining pawn push when quieter alternatives existed. In 7/10 positions, the best move was a piece maneuver (Nc5, Qf3, Na4, Nf6, Kg7, Nc5, Qc2) rather than any pawn advance. The pawn push consistently broke the mutual support between paired pawns—e5 advancing to e4 (positions 1, 6, 7, 8), c5 advancing to c4 (positions 5, 10), c4 advancing to c5 (positions 3, 9), e4 advancing to e5 (position 4). In 4/10 cases (positions 1, 6, 7, 10), the advance directly opened a long diagonal for the opponent's bishop, enabling devastating tactical shots. In 3/10 cases (positions 3, 5, 9), it released critical pawn tension that was holding the position together. In 3/10 cases (positions 4, 5, 8), it created isolated/targetable pawns. The average cp_loss of 255 confirms these are serious mistakes, yet 7/10 positions had 3 good alternatives available, meaning the player was not in a forced position.

1965.label: The player repositions the queen to a seemingly active square instead of taking the clearly superior queen exchange.
1965.description: In 10/10 positions, the objectively best move was a queen trade or queen capture (Qxb5+, Qxe7, Qxg3+, Qxf2+, Qxd5, Qxd5, Qxf4, Qxe7, Qxd3 respectively), yet the player instead moved the queen to a different square that appeared active or aggressive (Qe6, Qc2, Qa3, Qg5, Qg5, Qd3, Qf4, Qg6, Qc4+, Qg4). The average number of good moves available was only 1.3, meaning the queen trade was almost always the singular correct path. The repositioning moves universally resulted in the queen landing on a square where it became tactically vulnerable — to tempo-gaining pawn advances (5/10), knight attacks (3/10), or diagonal exploitation (4/10). The queen trades were strong for diverse reasons: winning material via follow-up forks (positions 2, 3, 9, 10), achieving favorable simplification when the player's king was exposed (positions 6, 7), or eliminating the opponent's attacking potential while retaining structural/material advantages (positions 4, 5, 8). The average cp_loss of 293 reflects that these weren't marginal decisions — the queen trade was often dramatically superior.

1968.label: Sacrificing a piece on f7 or f2 without sufficient supporting pieces to generate a real attack against the displaced king.
1968.description: All 10/10 positions involve a piece sacrifice capturing the f-pawn (f7 or f2) — the classically weak square defended only by the king. 7/10 are Nxf7 by White, 2/10 are Nxf2 by Black, and 1/10 is Bxf2+ by Black. All 10 occur in the opening with both kings still in the center. In every case, the sacrificing side has most pieces undeveloped on the back rank (typically only the attacking knight/bishop has left home), meaning after the simple recapture (Kxf7 or Kxf2), there is no coordinated follow-up attack. The best moves in all positions were developing moves (Bc4, Nc3, O-O, Nc6, etc.) rather than immediate tactical strikes. The average cp_loss of 251 confirms these are full-piece sacrifices yielding no compensation. In 10/10 cases, the opponent's strongest refutation is simply capturing the piece, after which the 'exposed' king easily returns to safety or proves invulnerable due to the attacker's lack of developed forces.

1963.label: A bishop is aggressively played to the h-file (h6 or h3) targeting the opponent's fianchettoed kingside, but the move is tactically or positionally premature, leaving pieces undefended or missing stronger alternatives.
1963.description: 10/10 positions feature a bishop moving to the h-file (h6 in 8 cases, capturing on h3 in 2 cases) with the explicit intent of attacking or dismantling a fianchettoed kingside structure — all 10 positions have a fianchettoed bishop on g7 as the target. The move is consistently a mistake because the bishop abandons critical responsibilities. In 4/10 positions (2, 4, 6, 9), the bishop leaving its post (typically e3) removes protection from a central piece or pawn (usually the d4 knight or d4 pawn), enabling immediate tactical exploitation like Nxd4 forks or pawn captures. In 3/10 positions (3, 5, 8), the attacking player's king remains uncastled on e1, and the Nxe4/fxe4/Qh4+ sequence exploits the opened diagonal to win the stranded bishop. In 2/10 positions (1, 7), the bishop is sacrificed on h3 for a speculative kingside attack that lacks sufficient piece support, with defenders easily neutralizing the threat (Nh2 blocking, or simply consolidating up material). In 1/10 positions (10), a devastating concrete tactical opportunity (dxc6) is missed in favor of the slow anti-fianchetto plan. The average cp_loss of 329 reflects that these are consistently severe errors, and 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, meaning the player chose the attractive-looking aggressive plan at a critical decision point.

1961.label: A quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push, piece repositioning, or queen centralization) played in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical action.
1961.description: All 10/10 positions share the same fundamental error: the player chose a 'normal-looking' quiet move — one that would be reasonable in a less critical position — while ignoring an urgent tactical demand. In 5/10 cases the move was a slow pawn push (c6 three times, c5, e5), in 3/10 it was a queen relocation to a seemingly active square (Qd5, Qe5, Qb3), and in 2/10 it was a bishop development/repositioning (Bc5, Bg5). Crucially, 0/10 moves involve checks, captures, or direct threats. The positions demanded concrete action: 4/10 had immediately winning tactics available (Rxf3, Ng4, Qh8#, Qxc3/e3), 4/10 required urgent prophylaxis against a specific threat (preventing dxe5, g4, f6, or f3 trapping a piece), and 2/10 needed to maintain pressure from a dominant piece position rather than relocating. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 8/10, confirming that the universal error is squandering a critical tempo on a non-urgent move when the position's tactical clock is ticking.

1946.label: Playing a positional minor piece repositioning move when the position demands an immediate tactical action, capture, or use of a different piece.
1946.description: 8/10 positions feature a quiet piece-improving move (usually bishop or knight repositioning) played at a moment when concrete tactical action was required. 4/10 specifically play Bc3 as a positional/developmental move. 7/10 are minor piece moves (bishops or knights). The common error is choosing a 'natural-looking' improving move when the position demanded either: (a) a free capture of hanging material (positions 3, 9, 10 — missing Qxf5, dxe4, gxf4), (b) a different piece performing the same function or going to the same square (positions 2, 4 — Be5+ instead of Qe5+, Bc3 instead of Kc3), or (c) a more forcing/urgent move to address an immediate tactical demand (positions 1, 5, 6, 7). The analyses consistently tag 'tempo_loss' (9/10), 'missed_tactic' (8/10), and 'piece_activity' (9/10). The average cp_loss of 275 with only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where precision is demanded but the player defaults to a general-principles move instead.

1967.label: Advancing a passed pawn (usually with check) in a simplified endgame, often prematurely or helping the opponent's king.
1967.description: All 10/10 positions involve pawn advances in simplified endgames, and 8/10 of these advances give check. The positions are overwhelmingly pawn-centric endgames (pure king-and-pawn or king-rook-pawn). In every case, a passed pawn is pushed forward, usually with the tempo-gaining appeal of delivering check. However, 5/10 positions show 0 cp_loss (the move is actually optimal), while the other 5 show significant losses (avg ~405 cp among mistakes). When these are mistakes, the common thread is that the pawn push with check either drives the opponent's king to an improved square (positions 3, 6, 10), allows a fatal blockade by inviting the king in front of the pawn (positions 2, 7), or prematurely fixes pawn structure eliminating dynamic options (position 10). The feature appears to detect the general pattern of forcing pawn advances in endgames regardless of correctness, with the 'check = good' instinct being the temptation that produces errors.

1955.label: Ambitious forward moves (pawn advances or aggressive piece placements) played while the player's own king has an unaddressed concrete vulnerability or a more forcing continuation exists.
1955.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a non-forcing, forward-looking aggressive move — pawn advances (7/10: f3, e5, c4, f5, exf7, f4, e5) or aggressive bishop developments (3/10: all Bb4) — when the position demanded either defensive precision or a more forcing tactical blow. In 8/10 cases, the player's own king had a concrete vulnerability (exposed king on e8 facing Qa4+ in 3/10, back-rank/corner weakness in 3/10, king stuck in center in 2/10), and the best move involved addressing that vulnerability first. In 2/10 cases (positions 4 and 9), the player had a winning forcing continuation available (Nxd2+ fork, fxe4 opening the file for Rxf1+) but chose a slow, non-forcing advance instead. The common thread across all 10: the player selected a move that 'looked aggressive' — attacking enemy pieces, pushing pawns forward, developing with apparent tempo — while ignoring that their own position contained an immediate tactical or structural vulnerability that the opponent could exploit on the very next move.

1960.label: Playing a timid, non-confrontational supporting pawn move (d3 or e6) when the position demands immediate tactical exploitation or aggressive central action.
1960.description: All 10/10 positions feature a player choosing a small, consolidating pawn advance—specifically d3 for White (5/10) or e6/e5 for Black (5/10)—at a critical moment when concrete tactical opportunities exist. In 10/10 cases, the move creates no threats, attacks no enemy pieces, and gives the opponent a free tempo to solve their problems. The missed opportunities include capturing undefended material (positions 2, 3, 7), launching piece attacks against an uncastled king (positions 1, 8), seizing the center aggressively (positions 5, 6, 9), and executing forcing tactical sequences (positions 4, 10). The average centipawn loss of 282 reflects that these positions uniformly demanded immediate action rather than slow consolidation. Notably, 7/10 positions had only 1-2 good alternatives, indicating narrow tactical windows that the passive pawn move squandered entirely. In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly cite 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif—the wasted move allows opponents to develop, consolidate overextended structures, or eliminate tactical vulnerabilities that existed for only one move.

1971.label: Developing a knight or bishop to an edge square (a3/a6/h3/h6) while ignoring urgent tactical demands in the position.
1971.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece being placed on one of four specific rim squares: a3 (3 positions), a6 (2 positions), h3 (2 positions), or h6 (3 positions). 8/10 moves are knight moves and 2/10 are bishop moves, but all share the geometry of placing a minor piece on the 3rd or 6th rank of the a-file or h-file — the classic 'rim' squares. In every case, the move ignores an urgent positional or tactical demand: 6/10 positions had immediate king safety crises requiring defensive attention, 3/10 had hanging or under-defended pieces/pawns that needed protection, and 2/10 had forced mating threats that required specific prophylaxis. The piece placed on the rim consistently becomes either a target (captured in refutation lines in 4/10 positions), completely irrelevant to the critical battle (6/10 positions), or forces immediate retreat (2/10 positions). The average centipawn loss of 1967 reflects that these moves tend to occur in already-critical positions where tempo is precious, making the waste particularly catastrophic.

1953.label: A materialistic capture with a minor piece or pawn when the correct move was a superior queen action (check, capture, or centralization).
1953.description: In 9/10 positions, the best move involved the queen — whether delivering check (positions 1, 4, 7), capturing a more valuable target (positions 2, 6), or centralizing to a dominant square (positions 3, 5, 9, 10). Instead, the actual moves played were exclusively non-queen actions: 5/10 were bishop captures (Bxc4, Bxb4, Bxf3, Bxe5, Bxf4), 2/10 were pawn captures (exf3, exd5), 2/10 were knight moves (Nxg6, Nh3+), and 1/10 was a pawn advance (h4). In every case, the player was drawn to a tempting but inferior material grab or forcing-looking move with a lesser piece, while the queen sat underutilized. The average cp_loss of 1322 reflects how catastrophic it is to ignore the queen's potential — in position 7, it meant missing mate in 2; in position 6, it meant missing a free bishop. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, indicating these were critical decision points where only the queen move preserved the position's full potential.

1969.label: Quiet, non-forcing bishop moves that reposition the bishop to a new square when the position demands immediate concrete action or the destination square is tactically unsafe.
1969.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop being moved to a new square without giving check or making a capture — purely quiet repositioning moves. In 6/10 cases (positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 10), the bishop was slowly rerouted to a 'better' diagonal while urgent tactics or forcing moves were available, allowing the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative. In 4/10 cases (positions 4, 6, 7, 9), the bishop was placed on an undefended square where it could be immediately captured or forked. The common thread is that all moves are non-forcing bishop maneuvers that ignore the position's concrete tactical requirements — the player 'improves' a piece when the position screams for captures, pawn breaks, or piece sacrifices. The average cp_loss of 352 reflects how severely these slow moves are punished. In 7/10 positions, the best move involved an immediate tactical strike (Nxc3, Nxc4, Nxc7, Nxe4, c6, Na4, f4) rather than piece repositioning.

1973.label: Moving a rook to the 1st or 8th rank for passive defense when the position demands active play or addressing a more urgent tactical concern.
1973.description: All 10/10 positions feature a rook moving to the back rank (1st or 8th rank), choosing a passive or defensive posture over active alternatives. The destinations (h1, g1, g8, f8, h1, a8, a1, c1, d8, b1) are uniformly on rank 1 or rank 8. In 10/10 cases, the move prioritizes defending a specific pawn or creating an illusory threat along an edge file rather than maintaining piece activity, creating counterplay, or addressing a more critical tactical issue. The analyses reveal that 7/10 positions had the move tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 10/10 with 'piece_activity' as the core problem. In 4/10 cases, the passive rook move left a piece hanging elsewhere (positions 3, 7, 10 with hanging pieces, position 5 with a missed decisive capture). In the remaining 6/10, the rook move abandoned active play — giving up open-file control, seventh-rank pressure, or queenside counterplay — allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with centralization, passed-pawn advances, or invasions on the vacated files.
1973.old_chip: Passive rook retreats to back rank

1970.label: Premature piece captures that allow the opponent's queen to recapture on a dominant central or active square.
1970.description: In all 10/10 positions, the played move is a piece capture (8/10 bishop captures, 1 knight capture, 1 rook capture) that removes an enemy piece but critically allows the opponent's QUEEN to recapture on the same square, landing on a powerful centralized or active post. The refutations are strikingly uniform: Position 1 (Qxc3), Position 2 (Qxf3), Position 3 (Qxf6), Position 4 (Qxd5), Position 5 (Qxc3), Position 6 (Qxc4), Position 7 (Qxe4), Position 8 (Qxc4), Position 9 (Qxe5), Position 10 (Qxd5) — every single punishment involves the opponent's queen recapturing on the exchange square and gaining a dominant position. In all cases, superior alternatives existed: intermediate moves first (checks, threats, or preparatory moves like g4, Rc8, Rb3, Rc1) that would have either won the piece for free, displaced the enemy queen before the capture, or maintained pressure without enabling the activating recapture. The average cp_loss of 342 reflects how much positional and tactical value is surrendered by gifting the opponent's queen a commanding square.

1972.label: Advancing a pawn near the castled king from its starting square to the third rank as a passive "defensive" gesture, when an active move was required.
1972.description: All 10/10 positions involve pushing a pawn one square from its original second rank to the third rank (f2→f3, g7→g6, f7→f6, b2→b3, c2→c3) in the immediate vicinity of the player's king. In every case, the pawn had not previously moved and was part of (or adjacent to) the king's protective shelter. 10/10 moves appeared to serve a defensive or prophylactic purpose—chasing a piece, blocking a line, or 'solidifying'—but in reality weakened the king's position by creating holes, opening critical diagonals, or abandoning defensive duties. In 9/10 positions, the correct move was an active response: directly challenging an attacking piece (h6 attacking a knight in positions 2, 3; g3 in positions 1, 6), a tactical shot (Nxb2, Nc3+), or a precise retreat/redeployment (Bf1, Qf8, f5 attacking the queen). The average cp_loss of 1169 reflects that these seemingly natural consolidating pawn pushes frequently allow devastating tactical punishments—back-rank mates, diagonal invasions, or hanging pieces.

1981.label: A bishop develops away from its starting square, leaving a wing pawn (b or g file) it was solely defending completely unprotected.
1981.description: All 10 positions feature a bishop moving away from a square where it was the sole defender of a rook-pawn (b-file or g-file), allowing the opponent to immediately capture that pawn with devastating consequences. The pattern splits into four symmetric sub-cases: 3/10 positions show Bf1→d3 abandoning the g2 pawn, 3/10 show Bf8→d6/c5 abandoning the g7 pawn, 2/10 show Bc1→e3 abandoning the b2 pawn, and 2/10 show Bc8→f5/e6 abandoning the b7 pawn. In every case, the bishop move appears natural — developing with tempo, attacking an enemy piece, or challenging a strong opponent piece — yet overlooks its latent defensive duty. 9/10 positions are in the opening phase with kings still in the center, making the resulting material loss especially devastating since there are no compensating structural or king-safety benefits. The refutation always involves an enemy queen or bishop immediately capturing the abandoned pawn, often with additional tactical consequences like winning a rook (Bxg7+Bxh8, Qxb2+Qxa1, Bxg2+Bxh1) or gaining a tempo against an exposed piece.

1977.label: Moving a well-placed knight to a seemingly superior central/aggressive square while abandoning its critical defensive or tactical function.
