1977.description: All 10/10 positions involve a knight being moved to an aesthetically attractive square (typically centralizing: d5, e5, e4, d4, e3, d3, b5, h4) while abandoning a critical role it was performing on its original square. In 4/10 positions (1, 5, 8, and partially 4), the knight was performing an essential defensive duty — guarding key squares around an exposed king or protecting a piece — and its departure allowed immediate tactical punishment (checks, forks, or mating attacks). In 3/10 positions (2, 5, 10), the knight was on the exact square needed to execute a winning tactic (Na5+ fork, keeping d1-rook protected, e5 pawn break) and was moved away before the tactic was played. In 3/10 positions (3, 7, and 6), the knight moved to an undefended square where it immediately became a tactical target via forks or captures. In 9/10 positions, the knight moved to a central or aggressive-looking square that an engine would consider an 'outpost,' yet the position demanded the knight's current placement. The average centipawn loss of 2178 reflects how catastrophic these redeployments are — the knights were almost always the linchpin of the position's tactical integrity.

1975.label: A piece captures material on a square defended by the opponent's queen (or long-range piece) along a clear line, resulting in the capturing piece being lost for insufficient compensation.
1975.description: 9/10 positions feature a piece (knight or rook) capturing a pawn or minor piece, only to be immediately recaptured by the opponent's queen along a clear diagonal or line. The capturing pieces are knights (6/10: Nxf3+, Nxg4, Nxc5, Nxc2, Nxf2, Nxa6) or rooks (4/10: Rxf2, Ra3+, Rxd3, Rxd4). In nearly every case, the opponent's queen is positioned far from the capture square but has an unobstructed path to recapture — e.g., Qb7xf3 along the diagonal (Position 1), Qf5xc2 along the f5-c2 diagonal (Position 6), Qb5xd3 along the b5-d3 diagonal (Position 7), Qe7xa3 along the e7-a3 diagonal (Position 4). Only Position 9 differs slightly, where a bishop recaptures along a diagonal (Bc5xf2). The average cp_loss of 350 reflects that these are major material blunders — typically losing a piece for a pawn. All 10 positions had at least 1 good alternative, and 7/10 had multiple safe options available, confirming these are unforced errors driven by tactical oversight rather than desperation.

1983.label: Queen relocates to a seemingly active square but abandons its critical role defending a friendly piece, which immediately becomes a free capture.
1983.description: In 10/10 positions, the player made a queen move to a square that appeared aggressive or active (centralizing, targeting pawns, or repositioning for attack), but the queen was performing an essential defensive function on its original square. In 9/10 cases, the direct consequence was a piece becoming hanging and being captured for free (Positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10) or a restraining function being lost that unleashed a devastating attack (Position 3). In 9/10 positions, the tactical motif was 'hanging_piece.' The average cp_loss was 346, and on average only 1.1 good moves existed, showing these were critical moments requiring precise awareness of defensive obligations. The queen's destination square always had a plausible aggressive purpose—targeting pawns (Qe2→f3/g2), centralizing (Qd5, Qe4), or creating apparent threats (Qh3, Qh4, Qf6)—but the player failed to recognize that the queen's previous placement was performing irreplaceable guard duty.

1966.label: Impulsive material-grabbing moves (especially knight captures) that ignore superior tactical or positional continuations.
1966.description: All 10 positions feature moves that prioritize an immediate, tangible gain—capturing material, delivering a check, or making a forcing pawn break—while missing a far more powerful continuation. 6/10 moves are knight captures (Nxd4, Nxg6, Nxe4, Nxf5, Na7+, and Ne8 attacking material), and 3/10 are pawn captures/advances (c5, f5, bxc5). In 9/10 cases, the analysis tags 'missed_tactic' as the core issue. The better moves were strikingly diverse: sometimes a quiet piece repositioning (Bf1, Rg3), sometimes a stronger tactic (Rxh6+ for mate, Ng4+ for a fork, Bb5+ for a forcing sequence), and sometimes a purely positional consolidation (c6, fxe3, Kg3). What unifies the blunders is that each move LOOKS productive—it captures something, gives check, or breaks open the position—but fails to account for the consequences: the capturing piece ends up undefended (5/10), the move opens lines against the player's own position (3/10), or it simplifies away a decisive attacking advantage (2/10). The average cp_loss of 2094 with only 1.8 good alternatives shows these are critical moments demanding precision, where the 'obvious' move is a trap.

1976.label: Playing a check or capture near the enemy king where the king simply recaptures the piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss with no follow-up.
1976.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundering move places a piece (usually the queen) on a square where the opponent's KING directly recaptures it. 6/10 positions specifically feature the queen being captured by the king (positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10). All 10 moves are either checks or captures (8/10 are captures with check), suggesting the player is seduced by the forcing nature of the move without verifying that follow-up threats exist after the king takes. In positions 1 and 6, the queen moves TO a square adjacent to the king believing it's defended (but isn't). In positions 2, 3, 7, and 10, the queen captures a piece/pawn next to the king and the king recaptures. In positions 4, 8, and 9, a rook is captured by the king after a premature exchange. Position 5 is the one outlier where a knight (not king) recaptures. The average cp_loss of 2240 reflects how devastating these trades are—the player typically surrenders their strongest attacking piece for far less material value.

1978.label: King moves in endgames that inefficiently address knight-related tactical situations, either missing simple captures or walking into knight forks/checks.
1978.description: All 10/10 positions feature king moves in endgame (9/10) or middlegame (1/10) positions where knights are the central tactical element. In 10/10 cases, the king move loses tempo relative to a more direct solution. The pattern splits into two main sub-types: in 3/10 positions (1, 2, 4), the king moves to threaten or approach an enemy piece when a simple capture by another piece (pawn or knight) was immediately available. In 5/10 positions (3, 5, 9, 10, plus 6 indirectly), the king lands on a square geometrically vulnerable to knight checks or forks, allowing the opponent's knight to gain tempo with check. In the remaining positions (7, 8), the king approaches a knight that simply escapes to a superior square with tempo. Knights are tactically relevant in all 10 positions — either the player's own knight should have executed a capture, or the opponent's knight delivers the punishment via fork/check/escape. The average cp_loss of 315 and average of only 1.3 good moves available confirms these are critical moments with narrow correct paths that all involve using pieces (not the king) to resolve knight interactions.

1962.label: Playing positional, developing, or repositioning moves when an immediately available capture or exchange was concretely required and dramatically stronger.
1962.description: In 9/10 positions (excluding position 1 which is negligible at 4cp), the best move was a forcing capture or exchange (Rxd8, Rxa7, dxe5, dxe4, Qf2#, Qxe7, Nxe5, Rxa1, Rc8), yet the player chose a quiet 'improving' move instead — bishop development (Bc8, Bb7), rook repositioning (Rf3, Re7), pawn advances (d4, h3), or knight lunges (Ng5). In 2/10 positions (Nxe5, Nxe4), the player did capture but with the wrong piece (knight instead of pawn), missing that the pawn capture created a devastating fork. 8/10 played moves were entirely non-forcing, allowing the opponent to seize initiative. The average cp_loss of 2127 and only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where concrete calculation was required but the player defaulted to general principles (develop, centralize, attack) instead of examining what was tactically available on the board right now.

1984.label: A pawn forming part of the king's protective shield captures an enemy piece/pawn, removing itself from its defensive post and fatally exposing the king to attack along the newly opened file or diagonal.
1984.description: In 9/10 positions, the moved pawn was directly adjacent to the king and serving as a critical component of the king's pawn shield (b2 shielding kings on b1/c1, c2 shielding king on b1, b7 shielding king on c8, c7 shielding king on d8, f2 shielding king on g1/g2, g2 shielding king on h1). In all 10 cases, the capture is a pawn taking away from its defensive file — moving laterally outward and leaving behind an open file or diagonal aimed directly at the king. 9/10 resulted in forced checkmate or near-checkmate (avg cp_loss 6612). The typical refutation pattern involves an immediate check or invasion along the newly opened line (Rb8+, Qxg3+, Qxa6+, Bxf3+, Ra1+, Qxe3+, Qxb3+). 7/10 were played by White, and 9/10 occurred in the middlegame. Only 1.5 good moves were available on average, showing these positions demanded extreme precision — yet the player chose the one natural-looking capture that was catastrophically wrong.

1964.label: Positions where an advanced passed pawn creates a critical decision about whether and how to promote or advance it.
1964.description: 8/10 positions involve a pawn on the 7th/2nd rank or an actual promotion move (d8=Q, g1=Q, g8=B+, a8=Q are direct promotions; f7 and b2 advance to the penultimate rank; a5 and b4 are aggressive pawn advances). 6/10 positions feature an actual pawn promotion as the move played. 4/10 moves had 0 cp_loss (positions 2, 6, 7, 8), meaning the promotion/advance was correct, while 6/10 were mistakes — including premature promotion (a8=Q, position 10), wrong pawn choice (f7 instead of e7, position 5), and hanging the pawn (a5, position 1). The 2 outlier positions (Ne6+ and Nxf3+) involve aggressive forcing checks that are similarly 'committal forward moves' in tactically complex positions, though they lack the promotion theme. The common situational element is a position where the most aggressive forward option (push/promote) competes against a more precise alternative.

1980.label: Moving a powerfully centralized knight (or key piece) to deliver a check or fork, only to have it simply captured on its new square, trading away the position's strongest piece for nothing.
1980.description: 8/10 positions involve a knight moving from a dominant central outpost (d4, d5, e5, f5, or d3) to deliver a check or create a fork, where it is immediately captured by a piece the player overlooked or undervalued. 7/10 moves specifically deliver check (Ne2+, Nf4+, Ne2+, Nd3+, Ne7+, Nc7+, Nxc6+). In every case, the piece was already on its optimal square—the cornerstone of the player's entire position—and the 'forcing' move trades it away for inadequate compensation. The remaining 2/10 positions (Bxd4, Bf6) follow the same deeper principle: a critically-placed piece is moved to a seemingly attractive square, destroying the position's foundation. The refutation in all cases is simple capture (Nxe2, Nxe5, Bxf4, Nxe2, Bxd3, Bxe7, Nxc7, Nxc6), typically requiring no deep calculation—just noticing that the destination square is defended.

1993.label: Queen captures the b2/b7 pawn in the opening, becoming trapped or fatally displaced while the opponent gains decisive tempo with developing attacks.
1993.description: All 10/10 positions feature the queen capturing the b-pawn (Qxb2 for Black in 7 cases, Qxb7 for White in 3 cases) during the opening phase. In every single case, the capturing side has significant development deficits — undeveloped minor pieces, uncastled king — and the queen ventures to the second/seventh rank where it lacks safe retreat squares. The punishment follows a remarkably consistent template: 9/10 positions feature Rb1/Rb8 attacking the displaced queen, and 8/10 involve knight fork threats (Nc7+, Nb5, Nd5) that exploit the uncastled king and undefended rook on a8/a1. The tactical motif is 'trapped_piece' in 9/10 cases, with the queen being corralled on the a-file or second rank. Both kings remain in the center in 8/10 positions, and the average centipawn loss of 291 reflects the catastrophic nature of these pawn grabs. The best alternatives in every position were simple developing moves (Bg7, Nf6, O-O, Nge2) maintaining equality.

1987.label: Moving the queen to an aggressive-looking square (usually g/h file) instead of executing a concrete tactical or positional move with another piece.
1987.description: All 9/9 positions feature a queen relocation to a seemingly aggressive square when the position demanded a concrete move with a different piece. In 7/9 cases, the queen lands on the g-file or h-file (g3, g4, g5, g5, g6, h5, h6), with the remaining two (Qe7, Qb3) also being superficially threatening queen moves. Crucially, in 9/9 positions the actual best move was a non-queen piece action: rook moves (Rd1, Rxg7+), bishop captures (Bxg7, Bxb4, Bxg2), knight jumps (Nh4, Nf3), or pawn advances (a4, d5). The average cp_loss of 1448 is enormous, and the average number of good moves was only 1.3, indicating these are sharp positions requiring precision rather than general attacking gestures. The queen moves typically abandoned critical defensive duties (defending key pawns in 3/9 positions), left pieces hanging (1/9), lost tempo to opponent piece activation (4/9), or missed immediate winning combinations (5/9). The unifying error is prioritizing a vague attacking queen reposition over executing the concrete action the position demands.

1989.label: Castling as an autopilot developing move when the position demands precise tactical calculation or a forcing move-order.
1989.description: All 10/10 positions feature castling moves (2 kingside O-O, 8 queenside O-O-O/O-O-O+). In 9/10 cases, the castling is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 1193), with only Position 8 being correct (0 cp_loss). In every erroneous case, there was exactly 1 good move available, and that move was a concrete tactical operation: a capture (Positions 1, 3, 4, 5, 10), a piece check/forcing move before castling (Positions 6, 7), or a pawn thrust exploiting structural weakness (Position 9). The positions share open/semi-open centers (8/10), exposed kings on both sides (9/10), and critical unresolved tactical tensions. In 3/10 cases (Positions 3, 6, 7), the correct sequence was to play a forcing move FIRST and then castle afterward—a pure move-order error. In 4/10 cases (Positions 2, 4, 9, 10), castling placed the king on a square vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation (diagonal checks, forks, or file-based attacks). The one correct castling (Position 8) uniquely combined all three goals—check, rook activation, AND king safety—confirming that the feature detects castling specifically in positions where it conflicts with tactical urgency.

1982.label: King moves to interact with a passed pawn (blockade, support, or capture) but walks into an immediate tactical vulnerability or abandons a critical defensive duty.
1982.description: 8/10 positions feature king moves, predominantly to central squares (d1, d2, d5, d6, d8, c3), almost always in endgame positions involving passed pawns. The remaining 2/10 are pawn advances (c3, e4) that similarly prioritize passed pawn objectives over immediate threats. In 7/10 positions, the move directly involves the king trying to blockade an enemy passer (Kd1 blocking d2, Kd8 blocking d7, Kc3 blocking c4), support one's own passer (Kd5 supporting d6), capture a pawn (Kxa3), or approach a passed pawn (Kd6 toward d5, Kc3 toward b3). The consistent punishment involves an immediate tactical shot that the king move either walks into or enables: checks/forks on the new square (3/10), capture of now-undefended pieces (3/10), or unstoppable pawn promotions due to the king abandoning a critical defensive square (3/10). The avg cp_loss of 3097 reflects catastrophic consequences, with 4/10 resulting in forced checkmate.

1990.label: Playing a quiet, non-threatening wing pawn push when the position demands immediate active play (king activation, tactical strike, or urgent counterplay).
1990.description: All 10 positions feature a one-square pawn advance on a non-central file (9/10 on the a, g, or h files; 1/10 on the c-file) that wastes a critical tempo. In 6/10 positions (endgames), the correct move was immediate king activation (Kg4, Kd6, Kc4, Kc1) or a forcing pawn break (h4, e4+). In 4/10 positions (middlegames), the correct move was either a concrete tactical blow (Bh6, Bf4) or urgent active counterplay (h4, e6). The average cp_loss of 298 is extremely high, and the average number of good moves available was only 1.7, indicating these were critical moments requiring precision. Every single analysis labels the core error as 'tempo_loss' — the player chose a structurally motivated or prophylactic pawn move that created zero threats, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, activate pieces, advance passed pawns, or consolidate a defensive weakness that the correct move would have exploited.

1979.label: Playing an impressive-looking queen/piece move (centralizing, checking, or capturing) instead of the immediately decisive tactical blow that wins the game.
1979.description: All 10 positions featured a dramatically superior forcing continuation (5/10 had forced checkmate available, the other 5 had game-deciding tactical shots), yet the player chose a move that merely 'looked good' — typically a queen move to a central or aggressive-looking square. 8/10 moves were queen moves, with 5/10 going to d-file squares (d1, d2, d5, d6, d7) and 3/10 to e-file squares (e5, e6, e7). Three moves were pointless checks (Qd5+, Qb7+, Qd2+) that gave the opponent a free tempo to consolidate or trade. Two were quiet bishop repositioning moves (Be7, Be6) when a rook delivered immediate checkmate. One was a pawn grab (Qxb2) that abandoned king defense. The correct moves were highly varied — rook sacrifices/mates in positions 2/5/6, a capture of a hanging piece in position 4, a knight move in position 9, a bishop retreat in position 10 — showing the player consistently defaulted to 'queen centralization/aggression' regardless of what the position actually demanded. The average cp_loss of 4926 reflects the catastrophic cost of choosing appearance over calculation.

1986.label: Making a natural-looking but catastrophically wrong move in positions where only one (or very few) precise responses address the critical tactical demand.
1986.description: 9/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.5), making these critical decision points with an extremely narrow correct path. In every case, the player chose a move that looks superficially reasonable—developing a piece (Nh6 ×2), repositioning (Nb3, Qe8, Be7), grabbing material (Bxf2), or walking the king toward 'safety' (Kf7, Kf6, Kf3, Ke7)—but catastrophically ignores the single tactical element that defines the position. 5/10 moves are king moves that walk directly into checks, forks, or mating nets. 2/10 are knight moves to rim squares that ignore free captures of hanging pieces. 2/10 are piece moves that abandon defense of a hanging piece (Nb3 leaving h2, Qe8 leaving Nd7). 1/10 is a pawn-grab that ignores a much stronger tactical continuation. The average cp_loss of 1277 reflects the severity—these positions punish 'routine' play with immediate tactical devastation.

1985.label: A bishop move (development or capture) that places the bishop on a square where it is immediately captured or exploited, with the recapture generating additional tactical damage.
1985.description: 9/10 positions feature a bishop move that lands on a tactically vulnerable square where the opponent immediately captures or attacks it with devastating consequences. 4/10 positions show the specific pattern of ...Bg7 developing into an enemy bishop on h6, allowing Bxg7 which traps and wins the h8 rook. 5/10 positions show the bishop greedily capturing a pawn (Bxb5, Bxd4, Bxb4, Bxg5) where the recapture creates additional tactical threats: forks (Nxb5/Nc7+), back-rank exploitation (Qe1/Ba5), simple piece win (axb4), or tempo-gaining development (hxg5/Bh6). The outlier (position 6, Nd7) shares the broader theme of a 'natural-looking' developing move that ignores an urgent tactical threat requiring immediate attention. In all cases, the player appears to be playing on routine or autopilot—either completing a standard fianchetto setup or grabbing a tempting pawn—without checking the opponent's immediate reply to the bishop's new location.

1988.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (often a king move) in a tactically critical position that demands immediate concrete action, wasting a vital tempo.
1988.description: 10/10 positions feature a non-forcing move (no check, capture, or direct threat) played in a sharp position where the engine found very few good alternatives (avg 1.6 good moves). 6/10 moves are king moves (Ke7 x3, Ke8, Kd2, O-O-O) that actively walk the king into tactical danger—forks, diagonal attacks, or check sequences. The remaining 4/10 are quiet developing or pawn moves (Ba6 x2, Bf4, c4) that squander the critical tempo needed for forcing play. In every case, the best moves were concrete: forcing checks (Qb5+, Nh1+), tactical captures (Nxe2), direct threats (h6), or precise defensive moves (Rd8, Kg8). The blundered moves all appear 'natural'—developing a piece, consolidating the king, strengthening the pawn chain—but in positions averaging 1309cp loss, the tactical urgency demanded calculation over intuition.

1995.label: Advancing the e-pawn from e7 when a bishop on g5 has a direct diagonal line to the queen on d8, allowing immediate queen capture.
1995.description: 7/10 positions share an identical or near-identical pattern: after 1.d4 d5 2.Bg5, Black advances the e-pawn (6/10 play ...e6, 1/10 plays ...e5), vacating the critical e7 square that was the sole barrier shielding the queen on d8 from the bishop on g5 along the g5-f6-e7-d8 diagonal. The refutation in all 7 cases is the simple Bxd8, winning the queen outright. The remaining 3 positions (Bb7, f5, Bb2) share the broader theme of making a natural-looking developing or space-gaining move that ignores an existing piece's critical defensive function, exposing a high-value target to tactical exploitation. All 10 moves were intended as standard positional or developmental improvements but fatally overlooked that a piece/pawn was performing an irreplaceable shielding role along a diagonal.

1991.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing flank pawn move when the position demands an immediate tactical strike or urgent piece activity.
1991.description: 10/10 positions feature a quiet pawn move played instead of a critical piece move. 8/10 moves are on the a, b, or h files (the flanks), with the remaining 2 being f-pawn moves. In 6/10 cases, a direct tactical shot was available (back-rank mate, knight fork winning the exchange, piece capture of a key defender, material-winning combination). In 4/10 cases, the position demanded active piece repositioning (king activation, rook reposition) rather than any pawn advance. The average cp_loss of 2118 is extreme, inflated by 2 positions where forced checkmates were missed in favor of pawn pushes. Critically, 8/10 positions had only 1 good move available (avg 1.6), meaning these were narrow tactical moments disguised as quiet positions. The players consistently chose long-term strategic ideas (creating passed pawns, gaining space) over immediate concrete demands, revealing a pattern of 'autopilot' positional play at moments requiring calculation.

2001.label: Playing a quiet developing or repositioning move while an enemy piece hangs undefended, missing a simple free capture.
2001.description: In 10/10 positions, the best move was a straightforward capture of a completely undefended enemy piece (hanging queen, rook, bishop, knight, or critical pawn). Instead, the player chose a quiet, non-capturing move — typically a piece repositioning, development, or 'natural-looking' positional improvement — that completely ignored the free material. 10/10 positions had only 1 good move available (the capture), averaging just 1.1 good moves per position. The tactical motif was explicitly 'hanging_piece' in 8/10 cases. The pieces captured in the best lines included: undefended rooks (4 positions), undefended queens (2 positions), undefended knights (2 positions), undefended bishops (1 position), and a critical passed pawn (1 position). The average centipawn loss was 1670, reflecting catastrophic blunders where trivially available material was left on the board.

1974.label: Playing materially or positionally motivated moves that ignore the position's single most urgent tactical demand, in critical positions with very few correct options.
1974.description: All 10 positions share a defining characteristic: extremely narrow tactical situations (avg 1.5 good moves available) where the player chose a 'natural-looking' move driven by a secondary goal while ignoring the position's most critical tactical element. 5/10 moves are captures that grab material (Nxd4 x2, dxe5 x2, gxf5), while the other 5/10 are piece/pawn moves attempting to 'improve' the position (Bb5, Nh7, Bf4, f4, d5). In every case, the best move addressed an urgent tactical demand: king safety (positions 6,7,8,9), a forcing tactical continuation (positions 3,4,5,10), or maintaining structural integrity (positions 1,2). The refutations consistently exploit what the blunder left unaddressed: checkmate threats (2/10), forks (1/10), trapped pieces (1/10), hanging pieces (3/10), or devastating positional collapses (3/10). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2099 reflects that these positions sat on a knife's edge where only 1-2 moves maintained the evaluation, and the chosen moves show complete blindness to the single most important feature of the position.

1994.label: Moving the queen (or rook) to a seemingly active square while a simple capture of an undefended piece is available.
1994.description: In 9/10 positions, the best move was a straightforward capture of a completely undefended piece (hanging bishops in 5 positions, hanging knights in 2, hanging rooks in 2), yet the player instead made a queen move to a different square that appeared active or aggressive. The missed captures were: Qxg7 (pos 2), Qxd5 (pos 3, 10), Qxc4 (pos 4, 5, 6), Qxd2 (pos 7), Qxc1+ (pos 8), and Rxb6 (pos 9). Position 1 is the slight outlier where the best move was a centralizing check (Qd5+) rather than a pure material capture. The average cp_loss was 497, reflecting the enormous cost of missing free material. Only 1.2 good moves were available on average, meaning the winning capture was essentially the only strong option. The blundering moves fall into three sub-categories: pointless checks (2/10), inferior pawn grabs (2/10), and positional-looking queen repositions (6/10).

1992.label: Quiet minor piece development to standard back-rank squares (d2, d7, or e7) when the position demands immediate concrete action.
1992.description: All 10/10 positions feature a minor piece being moved to one of three 'textbook' development squares: d2 for White (4 positions) or d7/e7 for Black (6 positions). Every single move is non-forcing — no captures, no checks, no threats — choosing routine piece placement over urgent tactical opportunities. In 8/10 positions, there was a specific concrete tactic or pawn break available (Nb4 attacking a piece, Ng4 winning a bishop, dxc4 exploiting an overloaded queen, d4-d5 central breakthrough, f6 challenging a knight, Bxf4 eliminating a threat, Nd4 centralizing with tempo). In 4-5/10 cases, the move specifically self-blocks a friendly piece or pawn (Nbd2 blocking the d-pawn in Position 4, Nbd2 blocking the c1-bishop in Position 5, Ne7 blocking the f8-bishop in Position 8). The average cp_loss of 245 reflects that these 'do-nothing' moves squander critical moments where one tempo makes the difference between advantage and equality (or worse).

1999.label: A rook that was anchoring a mating attack or dominating a critical file/rank is moved to a less effective square, dissolving the attacking coordination.
1999.description: In 10/10 positions, the blunder is a rook move that removes the rook from a dominant attacking position — typically on the g-file (positions 1,3,4,5,8,10), the 7th rank (positions 1,6,9,10), or both — where it was the structural foundation of a mating net or decisive pressure against an exposed king. In 8/10 positions, a forced checkmate existed that required keeping the rook on its current post while using another piece (knight in 5 cases, queen in 3 cases) to deliver the finishing blow. The rook moves instead to grab material (Rxe6, Rxg2 in positions 5,7), target a pawn (Rh2 in positions 4,8), create generic 'pressure' on a different file (Rd7, Rd2 in positions 1,3), or shift to an adjacent square without purpose (Rh7, Rg6 in positions 6,10). The average cp_loss of 5915 reflects that 7/10 positions involved squandering a forced mate. Only 1.8 good moves were available on average, indicating these are sharp positions where the rook's current placement was irreplaceable.

1997.label: Moving a knight or bishop to a seemingly strong or aggressive square that is actually tactically indefensible or abandons a critical function.
1997.description: All 10/10 positions involve minor piece moves (5 knight moves, 5 bishop moves) to squares that appear attractive—centralized, aggressive, or capturing material—but prove tactically flawed. In 5/10 cases (Nc2, Bd6, Ne4, Nxd5, Nfd5), the piece lands on a square where it becomes an immediate tactical target (trapped on an open file, captured with tempo, or left hanging when defenders are diverted). In the other 5/10 cases (Nf5, Bg5, Bxc7, Bxb7, Bb4), the piece abandons a superior post or trades itself for inadequate compensation, forfeiting positional value that was holding the position together. The common thread is a 'greedy activity' impulse: the player sees an outpost, a pawn to capture, or a piece to challenge, and lunges forward without calculating the tactical consequences. In every case, quieter consolidating moves (retreats, prophylaxis, or patient repositioning) were available and significantly stronger—the average good alternatives numbered 2.3 per position. The refutations consistently exploit the newly-created weakness: exposed pieces on open lines (positions 1, 2, 9), deflection/fork combinations (positions 3, 7), removal of defensive guardians (positions 5, 10), or simple material imbalance from trading strong pieces for pawns (positions 6, 8).

2007.label: A non-forcing wing pawn advance played when the position demands immediate tactical or concrete action elsewhere.
2007.description: All 10/10 positions feature a flank pawn push (h-file: 6/10, g-file: 2/10, a-file: 1/10, f-file: 1/10) that is non-forcing — no check, no capture, no immediate threat requiring a response. In every case, the position contained an urgent tactical priority that the pawn move completely ignores: 6/10 had a specific forcing tactical sequence available (captures winning material or delivering mate), 3/10 had hanging or vulnerable pieces requiring immediate attention, and 1/10 had a passed pawn crisis demanding blockade. The best moves in all 10 positions were concrete actions — captures (Nxc6, Bxf4, Nxf7, Bxd4, Qxe3+), piece development (Ne2, Rh1), or king moves (Kb8, Kf7). The average centipawn loss of 1271 reflects how catastrophically these tempo-wasting moves fail when the position is tactically critical. 8/10 positions had only 1-2 good moves available, confirming these were sharp moments requiring precision rather than general plans.
